documents.subtitle: Run a host loop around a model — call, run a tool, append the result, check the budget — and watch the step cap, a host stop rule and a growing context decide how it ends, a retry become a repair, and small per-step errors compound over a long run.
documents.body: Run a host loop around a model — call, run a tool, append the result, check the budget — and watch the step cap, a host stop rule and a growing context decide how it ends, a retry become a repair, and small per-step errors compound over a long run. Describe an agent as a host loop that repeatedly calls a model, executes its tool calls, and appends the results, not as a different kind of model Explain how a terminal action, a step cap and a host stop rule each end the loop, and what happens when only the cap is left Explain why each model call's input grows with the loop, so cost rises faster than the number of steps Compute the chance that an agent completes every step of a run from its per-step success and the run length, and explain how an approval gate that sometimes catches errors changes it and what it costs in extra steps Tell a retry that repeats the same call from a repair that changes the call after reading the error, and say which of them a stop rule on identical failures can end

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: A program that calls a model in a loop, executes the tool calls it proposes, feeds back the results, and decides when to stop. The model inside can be the same one used for plain chat.
documents.title: Agent

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: The repeated cycle: build the context, call the model, stop if it answered, otherwise run its tool call and append the result, then check the budget.
documents.title: Agent loop

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: What the loop feeds back after an action — a tool result or an error. The model knows only what reaches it as observations.
documents.title: Observation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: An output that ends the loop, here a plain-text answer instead of a tool call. A model that never produces one never ends the loop by itself.
documents.title: Terminal action

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: The host's maximum number of model calls. It guarantees the loop ends, but a loop that hits it stops without an answer.
documents.title: Step cap

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: A host-side condition that ends the loop early, such as the same call failing twice in a row. It lives in host code, not in the model.
documents.title: Stop rule

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: How many steps the loop may take. A longer horizon lets harder tasks finish and also lets errors, cost and side effects accumulate.
documents.title: Horizon

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: Each call reads the whole transcript so far, so input per call grows as the loop runs and the total tokens read grow faster than the number of calls.
documents.title: Context growth

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: Writing out intended steps before or between actions. A written plan is generated text; nothing forces later calls to follow it.
documents.title: Planning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: A mistake early in the loop that later steps build on. With many steps, even a small per-step error rate makes a fully correct run unlikely: the chance is the per-step success probability raised to the number of steps.
documents.title: Compounding error

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: A point in the loop where a person reviews the work so far before the agent goes on. It can catch an error before later steps build on it, at a cost in time and attention, and a reviewer can miss errors.
documents.title: Approval gate

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: What an agent can use beyond the current call: the transcript in its context window, which is exact but finite, or an external store such as a file or database that it writes to and reads from through tools.
documents.title: Agent memory

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Agents
documents.body: Several agent loops working on one task, often a lead agent that hands pieces to sub-agents and combines their results. It can run work in parallel and exceed one context window, but it costs more tokens and adds hand-offs where steps can go wrong.
documents.title: Multi-agent system

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Agents · question 1
documents.body: On Retry forever with no stop rule, you raise Step cap from 4 to 10. What changes? The agent learns from each failure and eventually finds the wind speed More failing calls are made, each reading a longer context The loop still ends after four calls, because the model decides when to stop The tool does not exist, so no number of retries helps. Without a terminal action or a host stop rule, only the cap ends the loop, and the scripted policy never writes an answer. Every call re-reads the growing transcript, so ten calls cost much more than two and a half times four.
documents.title: On Retry forever with no stop rule, you raise Step cap from 4 to 10. What changes?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Agents · question 2
documents.body: In the Agent loop diagram, which steps does the host perform rather than the model? Choosing which tool to call, writing the arguments, and writing the final answer Running the tool, appending the result, and checking the cap and stop rule All of them, because the model runs the tool itself when it writes the call The model only emits text: a tool call or an answer. The host runs the tool, appends the observation, counts calls and decides whether the loop continues. That is why an agent is a loop around an unchanged model, and why every limit on the loop lives in host code.
documents.title: In the Agent loop diagram, which steps does the host perform rather than the model?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Agents · question 3
documents.body: On Look up hours you set Step cap to 1. The tool runs but there is no answer. Why does the loop end this way? The model judged the task impossible and decided to give up after one call The tool call failed on the first try, so the loop could not continue The host refuses a second model call, so the tool result is never read The first call asked for get_dock_hours and the host ran it, successfully. The cap then forbids another model call, so nobody reads the result and nobody writes the answer. A step cap guarantees the loop ends, not that it ends with an answer, and only a terminal action produces one.
documents.title: On Look up hours you set Step cap to 1. The tool runs but there is no answer. Why does the loop end this way?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Agents · question 4
documents.body: On Retry forever, raising Step cap from 4 to 10 raises Tokens read by more than a factor of 2.5. Why? Each call re-reads the whole transcript, so inputs grow with each step Later calls use a larger model, which reads more tokens on every call The failing tool returns a longer error message each time it is called The error text is the same every time. What grows is the transcript: each call's input is the system prompt, the user message and every earlier call and result. Each turn adds a fixed amount, so the input per call rises linearly and the total rises roughly with the square of the number of calls.
documents.title: On Retry forever, raising Step cap from 4 to 10 raises Tokens read by more than a factor of 2.5. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Agents · question 5
documents.body: With the stop rule set to stop after 2 identical failures, you run Recover from error. What happens? The rule ends the run after the first timeout, to be on the safe side The rule fires on the retry, because the same call is being repeated The retry succeeds, the count resets, and the model answers on call 3 The rule counts consecutive identical failures. The first call times out, the identical retry succeeds, and the count resets, so the loop recovers and answers. The same rule ends Retry forever after two calls. A rule is a bet about which repeats are useless, and it cannot catch a loop whose calls keep changing.
documents.title: With the stop rule set to stop after 2 identical failures, you run Recover from error. What happens?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Agents · question 6
documents.body: Why can this lab not tell you how often a real agent gets stuck in a loop? Its model is a fixed rule that repeats the same call, unlike a sampled model Its loop code is a drawing, so the step cap and the stop rule are never applied Real agents never retry a failed call, so the Retry forever task cannot occur The loop, the cap, the stop rule and the token counts are computed, but the policy is scripted: answer after a good result, otherwise repeat the call. A sampled model could answer early, try another tool or give up in words, so how often real agents loop is an empirical question this lab does not measure.
documents.title: Why can this lab not tell you how often a real agent gets stuck in a loop?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Agents · question 7
documents.body: In Reliability you keep Steps in the run at 20 and raise Per-step success from 95% to 99%. What happens to Completes end to end? It rises by about the same four points, because the gain is added once to the whole run It more than doubles, because the four-point gain applies at every one of the steps It barely moves, because only the first few steps of a long run can ruin the result The chance of finishing is the per-step probability raised to the number of steps, so a small gain per step is multiplied across all of them. At 20 steps it goes from about 36% to about 82%. A gain added once would be about four points, and a step late in the run fails as often as an early one.
documents.title: In Reliability you keep Steps in the run at 20 and raise Per-step success from 95% to 99%. What happens to Completes end to end?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Agents · question 8
documents.body: With Reviewer catches at 100% and Per-step success at 95%, a gate after step 10 beats a gate after step 1 on a 20-step run. Why? It covers ten steps instead of one, so more of the run's errors get a second try It ends the run at step 10 and checks the answer, so the later steps can no longer fail It makes every step after the gate more reliable, because a person has looked at the work The gate sends a wrong prefix back to be redone once, so it protects exactly the steps before it. A gate after step 1 covers one step and one after step 10 covers ten, so it rescues many more runs. The price shows in Expected steps run: a later gate redoes more work. It neither stops the run nor changes the later steps, which still compound.
documents.title: With Reviewer catches at 100% and Per-step success at 95%, a gate after step 10 beats a gate after step 1 on a 20-step run. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Agents · question 9
documents.body: Reliability says a 20-step run at 95% per step completes about 36% of the time. Why is that not a forecast for a real agent? The 95% is an assumed value, and real steps differ in difficulty and fail together The curve comes from a simulation that is too short to give a trustworthy figure Real agents recheck every step, so their failures cancel out instead of compounding Every figure follows from assumptions you set: the same success chance at every step, independent steps, and errors the agent cannot see. In a real run some steps are easy and some hard, one mistake can make the next more likely, and the true per-step rate has to be measured. The card shows why length hurts, not how reliable a given agent is.
documents.title: Reliability says a 20-step run at 95% per step completes about 36% of the time. Why is that not a forecast for a real agent?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Agents · question 10
documents.body: Set Stop rule to stop after 2 identical failures. Why does it end Retry forever but leave Fix an argument alone? Retry forever sends one call twice, but Fix an argument changes its call after the error Fix an argument has fewer failures in total, so it never comes close to the step cap The rule only watches get_wind calls, so any task that uses another tool is exempt from it The rule compares the text of consecutive failing calls. Retry forever sends the same get_wind call twice, so the rule fires. In Fix an argument the policy reads the error and changes "Weekday" to "weekday", so call 2 differs from call 1 and succeeds, and the count never reaches two. A rule on identical failures cannot end a loop whose calls keep changing but keep failing.
documents.title: Set Stop rule to stop after 2 identical failures. Why does it end Retry forever but leave Fix an argument alone?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Agents
documents.body: You have probably typed a question into a chatbot and watched it write back a single reply, all in one go. Some AI systems go further: they look things up, read what comes back, try again when something goes wrong, and only then give you an answer. A system that works this way is called an agent, and this lab opens one up so you can watch every step it takes. The surprising part is that an agent is not a new or smarter kind of AI, and the model inside it can be exactly the one a chatbot uses. What turns it into an agent is a second program wrapped around the model, and this program runs the same few steps over and over in a loop. Each time round, the loop asks the model what to do next, carries out what the model asked for, writes down what happened, and checks whether to stop. Agents are used for jobs where one request turns into many steps, such as researching a question or working on computer code. One AI company, Anthropic, has described a research agent that splits a big question into pieces and hands them to helper agents. Without a loop, the model gets a small, fixed number of turns. It can ask for one lookup, read what comes back and reply, and then the conversation is over, whatever happened. The loop removes that limit, so the model can keep looking things up and trying again for as long as the job needs. That freedom brings new trouble: the loop needs a way to stop, it gets more expensive the longer it runs, and mistakes can pile up. That is why this lesson spends as much time on how the loop ends and what it costs as on how it works. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain these five ideas in your own words: why an agent is a loop wrapped around an ordinary model, and not a different or special kind of model; the three ways the loop can end, and what happens when a limit on the number of steps is the only one left; why each step reads more text than the step before it, so the total cost grows faster than the number of steps; how to work out the chance that a long run gets every step right, and how a check partway through can raise it at the cost of redone work; the difference between repeating a failed request and fixing it after reading the error, and which of the two a rule against repeated failures can stop. The lab is set in a harbor, where an assistant answers questions about when the docks close, when the ferry leaves and how windy it is. The Agent loop card draws the loop as a diagram and lets you replay a run one event at a time, while Trace lists every message in order. Budgets sets the limits that end a run, and Context growth shows how much text each step has to read before it can write anything. The last card, Reliability, works like a calculator: you choose how often each step goes right and how long the run is. It then shows how often the whole run comes out right, with and without a person checking the work partway through. Its numbers come from a formula, not from running an agent. The model in this lab is not a real AI: its choices follow a short script written in advance. Everything around it is computed for real, including the loop, the tools, the limits and every count of text read.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Agents
documents.body: The model writes, the host acts The model inside a chatbot does one thing, which is to read text and write more text after it. It cannot click a button, open a website or check a timetable on its own. Anything that has to happen in the world is done by the program that runs the model, which this lab calls the host. The host offers the model a few tools, small programs the host is willing to run, such as one that looks up when a dock closes. To use a tool, the model writes a request in a strict text format that names the tool and fills in the details it needs. That request is called a tool call, and here is the exact one that the lab's first task writes: The details inside it, here the dock and the day, are called arguments, which is why one of the lab's tasks is named *Fix an argument*. The model only writes this text, while the host is the one that reads it, runs the tool and receives the result. The agent loop An agent is a model together with a host that asks it the same kind of question over and over, in a loop. The model can be the same one used for chat, because what makes an agent is the host code around the model, not anything new inside it. Each time round the loop, the host goes through the same five steps, in this order: It gathers everything written so far into one block of text, and the model will read that block from start to finish. It hands that text to the model, which writes back exactly one thing: either a final answer or a tool call. If the model wrote an answer, the loop ends there and the host passes that answer on to the user. If the model wrote a tool call, the host adds that call to the bottom of the text, runs the tool, and adds the result below it. The host checks its limits and, as long as they allow another turn, goes back to step 1 and starts again. This cycle is called the agent loop, and the growing record of every message, in the order the host wrote it, is called the transcript. On every call the model reads the whole transcript, so the diagram's first box is labeled Context: the text the model reads this time. Here is the loop at work on the first task, *Look up hours*, where the user asks, “When does the north dock close on Sunday?” Model call 1 reads the transcript, which so far holds the host's instructions and that question, and writes the tool call shown above. The host runs the tool, which reports that the dock closes at 16:00, or 4 p.m., and adds that result to the transcript. Model call 2 reads everything again, including that result, and writes, “The north dock closes at 16:00 on Sundays,” which ends the loop after two calls. Observations: the model's only news The result the host adds after running a tool is called an observation, and it can be a useful answer, such as a closing time, or an error. One error in this lab reads “timeout after 5 s”, which means the tool took too long and the host stopped waiting for it after five seconds. Either way, the observation is the only way the model finds out what happened, because the model never sees the tool run. The model also remembers nothing from one call to the next. If the host did not write the observation into the transcript, the next call would have no sign that the tool had ever run. Three ways to stop A loop needs a way out, and this one has three, all of which you can trigger in the lab: A terminal action is the model writing a final answer instead of a tool call, where “terminal” means “last”, like the terminal at the end of a bus line. A step cap is the most model calls the host will make in one run, and once they are used up, the host refuses to call the model again. A stop rule is a check in the host's code that ends the loop early when a run looks stuck. In this lab, the stop rule fires when the same tool call fails twice in a row, which is a sign that repeating it will not help. Only the first of these ends with an answer, while the other two are the host stepping in, which stops the run but leaves the question unanswered. This matters most when the model keeps writing tool calls and never writes an answer at all. The model can only end the loop by answering, so if no stop rule is switched on, the step cap is the only limit left. The loop then keeps going until every allowed call is used, each one reading more text than the last, and then it stops with no answer. An analogy: the advisor and the runner Picture a harbor office with two workers, an advisor and a runner, who split the work between them. The advisor sits in a back room with no phone and can only write, while the runner sits at the front desk with the phone and the customers. Each turn, the runner hands the advisor a notebook that holds everything so far, and the advisor reads it from the very first page. Then the advisor writes one line at the bottom, either an answer for the customer or a request such as “phone the dock office and ask about Sunday.” If the line is an answer, the runner passes it to the customer and the job is done. If it is a request, the runner makes the call, writes down what they heard, and checks the office rules before handing the notebook back. One rule limits how many turns a job may take, and another tells the runner to stop if the same request fails twice in a row. In this picture, the advisor is the model, the runner is the host and the notebook is the transcript. Each line the runner writes down is an observation, and the office rules are the step cap and the stop rule. The analogy stops matching in two places, and the first is that a person handed the same notebook again would skip the pages they had already read. A model re-reads every word on every call, and each re-read has a cost, which the next part of this section measures. The second is that a real advisor understands the notebook, while a model is a program that turns text into more text. The “advisor” in this lab is something simpler still, as the last part of this section explains. Every call re-reads everything To measure reading, the lab counts tokens, the small chunks a model reads text in, such as a word, part of a word, a number or a punctuation mark. Reading more tokens takes more work, and in real services re-reading has a price, so the number of tokens read is this lab's measure of cost. The lab counts tokens with a toy rule. Every unbroken string of letters (such as a word), every unbroken string of digits (such as 16) and every single symbol counts as one token. By that rule, the question “When does the north dock close on Sunday?” is 9 tokens, which is eight words plus the question mark. A time such as 16:00 counts as 3 tokens, because the hours, the colon and the minutes each count once. Each call's input starts with a fixed base, which is the host's opening instructions, called the system prompt, plus the user's question. The system prompt tells the model that it is the harbor assistant and lists the tools it may call, asking it to call them one at a time. After that base comes every earlier call and result, so the input gets bigger each time the loop goes round. The task *Retry forever* shows this most clearly, because every one of its turns adds exactly the same text. Its base is 58 tokens, and each failed turn adds 31 more, made up of the tool call and the error message that comes back. So the first four calls read these amounts, with each one paying again for everything before it: Call 1 reads only the base, which is 58 tokens, because nothing has happened yet. Call 2 reads the base plus one earlier turn, so it reads 58 + 31 = 89 tokens. Call 3 reads the base plus two earlier turns, which comes to 120 tokens in all. Call 4 reads the base plus three earlier turns, which comes to 151 tokens in all. Added together, those four calls read 418 tokens, which is the number Tokens read shows at a cap of 4. If you drew each call's earlier turns as a row of blocks, the rows would be zero, one, two and three blocks long, making a triangle. A triangle with 4 rows holds 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 blocks, while one with 8 rows holds 0 + 1 + 2 + … + 7 = 28 blocks, more than four times as many. Doubling the rows more than quadruples the blocks, which is the same pattern you see when you square a number. That is why the total reading grows much faster than the number of calls itself. Allowing ten calls instead of four gives two and a half times as many calls, but the total reading jumps to 1,975 tokens, almost five times as much. The triangle itself grows even faster. With ten calls it holds 45 blocks instead of 6, which is seven and a half times as many. So why does the total grow only about five times? Every call also reads the same 58-token base, and that part grows only as fast as the number of calls. Mixing the two slows the total down a little: The base comes to 10 × 58 = 580 tokens. The earlier turns come to 45 × 31 = 1,395 tokens. Together they make 580 + 1,395 = 1,975 tokens in all. So the total grows much faster than the number of calls, but not quite as fast as the triangle alone. This effect is called context growth, and the card with that name draws it as a row of bars, one for each call the cap allows. Each bar is one call's input, split into two parts. A faded part stands for the system prompt and user message, and a solid, full-color part stands for earlier calls and tool results. The key under the chart names each one. As you move along the row, the solid part grows from bar to bar while the faded part stays the same. Calls that the cap allowed but the run never used show up as short, flat markers, which the key labels “allowed but unused”. The chart also follows Replay step on the Agent loop card. If you move it back, the bars for calls the replay has not reached yet are dimmed as a whole. They come back to full color as you move forward again. Retry or repair When a tool call fails, there are two very different ways to try again, and the difference decides whether a stop rule can help. Picture a friend logging in to a game who types their password, sees “wrong password”, and types exactly the same thing again. That is a retry, the same request sent again in the hope of a different result. This time the screen says “wrong password: Caps Lock is on”, so they switch Caps Lock off and type the password in small letters, and it works. That is a repair: they read the error message and changed what they sent to match it. A retry is the right move when a failure was bad luck, as in *Recover from error*, where the ferry tool times out once and the same call then works. A retry is useless when the failure is built into the request itself, so repeating it can never succeed. In *Retry forever*, the model keeps asking for a wind tool that the host never offered, and no number of repeats will change that. A repair needs an error message that says what went wrong, and *Fix an argument* shows one. Its first call asks about the south dock with the day written as “Weekday”, with a capital W, but the tool only accepts “weekday” or “sunday” in small letters. So the host sends back an error that names the day input and lists the values it allows. The error writes the day input as /day, where the slash is how it points at one part of the request. The second call reads that note and sends “weekday” instead, and this time the tool returns the closing time. The two also look different to a stop rule, because the rule in this lab counts identical failures, meaning the very same call failing twice in a row. It can end a loop of retries, because a retry sends the same call again, but it can never end a loop of repairs. Each repair changes the call, so if a repair kept changing the call and kept failing, the rule would never fire and only the step cap would stop it. Small mistakes multiply Even when every tool works, a long run can still fail, because each step is another chance for something to go wrong. The Reliability card gives every step the same chance of coming out right, a number it calls Per-step success. Picture a quiz with 20 questions where you get each answer right 95% of the time, so it feels as if a perfect score is almost certain. Most of the time you will not get one, though, because a perfect score needs every single answer to be right at the same time. To see why, picture a large number of runs starting at once, and notice that 95% of them get step 1 right. Of those, 95% also get step 2 right, and 95% of 95% is 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.9025, or about 90%. Each new step multiplies the chance by 0.95 again, so the chance of a fully right run keeps shrinking as the run gets longer: With 2 steps, about 90% of runs come out right from start to finish. With 10 steps, about 60% of runs come out right from start to finish. With 20 steps, the chance is 20 copies of 0.95 multiplied together, which is about 36%. So the 20-question quiz gives you only about a 36% chance of a perfect score, even though each answer felt safe. An agent that is right 95% of the time per step does no better, finishing a 20-step run with no mistakes only about 36% of the time. The card shows that as 35.8% under Completes end to end, the chance that a run gets every one of its steps right. This effect is called compounding error. A fully right run needs every step to go right, so each step, early or late, is one more chance to slip, and the chances multiply. A small chance of error at each step therefore becomes a large chance that the whole run goes wrong. In a real agent it is often worse, because a slip early on gets built on by the steps after it. The multiplying also works in your favor. Raising the chance per step from 95 out of 100 to 99 out of 100 looks like a small change. But now 0.99 is the number multiplied 20 times, and 20 copies of 0.99 multiplied together come to about 0.818. So a 20-step run comes out fully right 81.8% of the time, more than double what it was. A check partway through: the approval gate One way to fight compounding error is to have a person look over the work partway through, before more steps get built on top of it. Picture a group project with a long report, where your teacher offers to read the first half before your group writes the rest. If the teacher spots a mistake, your group rewrites the first half, which costs time but gives the second half a better chance of resting on correct work. The rewrite can contain new mistakes of its own, though, because nobody checks it a second time. And if the teacher misses a mistake, it stays, and everything you write next is built on top of it. In an agent, a point where a person reviews the work so far before the agent goes on is called an approval gate. The Reliability card lets you place one after any step, with Approval gate after step, and set how often the reviewer catches a wrong run, with Reviewer catches. In the card's version, a run that gets caught redoes the steps before the gate once, and the redo is not checked again. Here is how a gate after step 10 works out at 95% per step on a 20-step run, with a reviewer who catches every wrong run: About 60% of runs get the first 10 steps all right, so they pass the gate without being sent back. The other 40% reach the gate with a mistake, and the reviewer catches all of them, so they redo the first 10 steps. About 60% of those redos come out right, which rescues 60% of 40%, or about 24% of all runs. Adding the two groups together, about 84% of runs leave the gate with a correct first half. The last 10 steps still have to go right, which happens about 60% of the time. 60% of 84% is about 50%, so the whole run comes out right in about half of all runs. The card shows that figure as 50.2% under With the gate, compared with 35.8% for the same run with no gate at all. The price is extra work, because the runs that get sent back do some of their steps twice. About 4 in every 10 runs redo 10 steps, which is 40 extra steps for every 10 runs. Shared out evenly, that is 4 extra steps per run on average. That is why Expected steps run reads 24.0 with the gate, instead of 20.0 without it. A gate placed later protects more steps but sends back more work when it catches something, while a reviewer who never catches anything adds no protection at all. What stands in for the model here The Agent loop card carries a badge that says scripted policy, which tells you something important about this lab. A policy is the rule that picks the model's next message, and “scripted” means the rule was written out ahead of time instead of coming from a real model. This one says that if the last tool result worked, the model answers, and otherwise it sends the same tool call again. One task, *Fix an argument*, uses a different rule, which reads the error note from the last tool result and corrects the input that the note names. Neither rule is a real model, but everything else on the page is really computed: the loop, the tools, the step cap, the stop rule and every token count. The Reliability card has a different badge, closed-form formula, which means its numbers come straight from formulas like the ones worked through above, and not from running an agent.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Agents
documents.body: The Tools and function calling lab showed one round trip: the model writes a tool call, the host runs it, and the result comes back. Many real jobs need a whole chain of these round trips, where each one depends on what the one before it returned. Think of a job that goes like this: look something up, find that the tool timed out, try again, then use that answer to look up a second thing. A single round trip cannot cover that, so the host needs a loop that hands each result back and asks the model again until the job is done. But a loop creates four problems that a single call never had, and each of them shows up on one of the lab's cards: Errors can repeat, because a call that fails can be sent again and fail again, forever, unless something in the host notices. Trace shows each failed tool result as an outlined row. Costs grow every turn, because each call re-reads a transcript that keeps getting longer, so later turns cost more than early ones. Context growth shows this as bars that get taller. Mistakes pile up, because a run of many steps has many chances to go wrong, and later steps build on earlier mistakes. Reliability shows this as the chance in Completes end to end shrinking. Something has to say stop, because the model may never write an answer, so the host needs limits of its own. Budgets holds those limits and shows the Stop reason. How many steps the loop is allowed to take is called its horizon, and you set it on the Budgets card, whose small heading reads “Horizon and stop rules”. A longer horizon lets harder jobs finish, but it also gives errors, costs and unwanted changes in the world more room to pile up.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Agents
documents.body: Walk a successful loop Leave Task on *Look up hours*, and notice that Replay step starts at the end of the run, where the whole story is already shown. Drag it back to the start, where it reads 1/4 · Model call 1, and then move it forward one event at a time: At 1/4, the Context box, the Model call box and the “final answer?” diamond light up, and the line under the diagram says call 1 reads 56 tokens. At 2/4, Host runs the tool and Host check light up, because the host runs the call, adds the result and checks the step cap. At 3/4, call 2 reads 118 tokens, more than twice as many as call 1, because the transcript now holds the first call and its result. At 4/4, the run leaves through Stop · answer, which the diagram labels terminal action, since call 2 wrote a final answer instead of a tool call. The two dashed boxes, Host runs the tool and Host check, are host code, while the Model call box is marked “writes text only”. You can also click any row in Trace to jump Replay step straight to that event, which makes comparing two calls quicker. Cap the horizon Try this: before you touch anything, guess what will happen if the host allows only one model call, and then set Step cap to 1. The host still runs the tool that call 1 asked for, so the result, 16:00, lands in the transcript. But Host check says stop, because a second call is not allowed, so the run leaves through Stop · step cap instead of Stop · answer. Stop reason reads step cap. The tool result, 16:00, sits in the transcript where no call will ever read it, so no answer is written. Recover from an error Set Step cap back to 4 and Task to *Recover from error*, where the user asks when the afternoon ferry leaves. In Trace, call 1 asks for get_ferry_time, and the host replies with a timeout, which the row outlines as a failure. Call 2 sends exactly the same call, which makes it a retry, and this time it gets back 15:40, or 3:40 p.m. Call 3 answers, so the run ends with a terminal action, and Tool runs reads 2 (1 failed). Loop without a stop rule Set Task to *Retry forever*, where the user asks for the wind speed at the harbor right now, and slide Step cap to 10. The policy asks for get_wind, a tool that was never on the host's list, so the host replies “unknown tool get_wind” every time. All ten calls fail, and the run ends by step cap without ever producing an answer. Now look at Context growth, where each bar is taller than the last, rising from 58 tokens for call 1 to 337 tokens for call 10. That last call reads almost six times as much as the first, even though both of them send the same request. The heading adds every bar together to give 1,975 tokens read in total, the same number Tokens read shows in Budgets (Budgets writes it without the comma, as 1975). Set the cap back to 4 and the total drops to 418, so the last six calls cost far more than the first four did. Add a stop rule Keep *Retry forever* and set Stop rule to *stop after 2 identical failures*, then watch how quickly the run ends. The host now stops after two calls and 147 tokens read, whatever the step cap says, because the same call failed twice in a row. The diagram exits through Stop · host rule, and Stop reason reads host stop rule. Then switch Task to *Recover from error* with the rule still on, and the run still answers on call 3. One failure followed by a success is not two failures in a row, so the rule leaves this run alone. The rule is a bet, though, because it cannot tell a hopeless repeat from a useful one. It allows one repeat, which is enough for a one-off timeout, but it would also stop a tool that happened to time out twice by bad luck. Repair an argument Keep the stop rule on and set Task to *Fix an argument*, where the user asks when the south dock closes on a weekday. Follow the run in Trace, where each row shows one message in the order the host wrote it: Call 1 sends "day": "Weekday" with a capital W, which is not one of the values the tool accepts. The host rejects it with an error that names /day, lists the allowed values "weekday" and "sunday", and quotes the "Weekday" it got. Call 2 reads that note and sends "weekday" instead, and the host returns a closing time of 21:00, or 9 p.m. Call 3 writes the answer, “The south dock closes at 21:00 on weekdays,” which ends the run with a terminal action. The whole run takes 3 model calls and reads 391 tokens, and Tool runs reads 2 (1 failed). Only one call failed in this run, so the stop rule had nothing to stop. Look at the two calls anyway. Compare call 1 and call 2 in Trace, and you will see that they differ only in whether the day starts with a capital letter. So even if call 2 had failed too, the rule would not count it as the same failure repeated. A loop of repairs that keep changing the call and keep failing would slip past this rule, and only the step cap would end it. Compound the error Find the Reliability card, leave Per-step success at 95% and Steps in the run at 20, and read Completes end to end. It shows 35.8%, and next to it Longest run that finishes half the time reads 13 steps. That means that at 95% per step, only runs of 13 steps or fewer come out fully right more often than not. Now raise Per-step success to 99%: Completes end to end jumps to 81.8%, and the longest run that finishes half the time stretches to 68 steps. The solid line in the chart tells the same story, because it shows the chance of a fully right run falling as the run gets longer. At 99% that line falls much more slowly, which is why far longer runs stay above the halfway mark. Set Per-step success back to 95% and try the approval gate, watching the dashed line that the chart adds for the run with a gate: Set Approval gate after step to 10, with Reviewer catches at 100% of wrong runs, and With the gate reads 50.2%. Expected steps run rises from 20.0 to 24.0 at the same time, because some runs now redo their first half. Lower Reviewer catches to 0%, and With the gate falls back to 35.8%, because a reviewer who never catches anything never sends anything back. Put Reviewer catches back to 100% and move the gate to step 1, and With the gate reaches only 37.6%, because it protects one step out of twenty. Move the gate to step 20, the end of the run, and With the gate reaches 58.8%, the highest so far. The catch is that Expected steps run climbs to 32.8, because a run that gets caught now redoes every one of its steps.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Agents
documents.body: The model never ends the loop except by writing an answer, and every other way out, the step cap and the stop rule, lives in the host's code. A step cap makes sure the loop ends, but it does not make sure you get an answer, so a run stopped by a limit leaves the question unanswered. Every call re-reads the whole transcript, so on *Retry forever*, where each turn adds the same 31 tokens, each call reads more than the last. The total therefore grows much faster than the number of calls, and raising the cap from 4 to 10 makes it almost five times bigger. The stop rule leaves *Recover from error* alone, because one failure followed by a success is not two identical failures in a row. A retry repeats the call, while a repair changes it after reading the error. A stop rule on identical failures can end a loop of retries, but it cannot end a loop whose calls keep changing. Small losses at each step multiply, so going from 95% to 99% per step more than doubles the chance of finishing all 20 steps. A gate protects only the steps before it and costs redone work, so its value depends on where you put it and how often the reviewer catches mistakes.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Agents
documents.body: In this lab This lab is a simplified model of an agent, and here are the places where its simplifications show: The model is a fixed rule, the scripted policy, while a real model picks its words with some chance involved. So a real model could answer early, choose a different tool, or write a reply saying it cannot find the answer, which would end the loop as a terminal action. The repair in *Fix an argument* is a matching rule that compares the wrong value with the allowed values in the error note, ignoring capital letters. It does not understand the note, and a real model could misread the same note and repair the call wrongly. The tools return fixed values, and the ferry tool fails on its first try on purpose so that you can watch a retry work. Token counts use the toy rule, not the real method a model uses to split text into tokens, which is called a tokenizer. Nothing is saved between calls to make re-reading cheaper, a trick called prompt caching that Going deeper describes. Nothing runs side by side either, so every call waits for the one before it. The Reliability card is a formula, not a run of an agent, and Per-step success is a number you choose, not a measurement of a real agent. The formula behind that card also rests on assumptions that real runs often break, and these are the main ones: Every step has the same chance of going right, and one step going wrong does not make the next one more or less likely. The agent cannot see its own wrong steps, so it never notices a mistake or fixes one by itself. There is one reviewer, and a run that gets sent back is redone once, with the redo not checked a second time. In real systems Errors compound: if each step is right 95% of the time, a 20-step job is fully right only about 36% of the time. Real steps are not all alike, because some are much harder than others, and one mistake can make the next more likely. That is why a real agent's per-step rate has to be measured on its own tasks instead of guessed. Reviewers miss errors: an approval gate helps only as far as the reviewer catches wrong work, and a reviewer can miss a mistake or be skipped when time is short. Plans are only text: some agents write out the steps they intend to take before or between actions, which is called planning. A plan is text the model wrote, so nothing forces later calls to follow it, and a longer plan has more steps to get right. Observations can mislead: a tool can send back text that is out of date, incomplete or even hostile, meaning written on purpose to trick the model. The next call reads that text as part of the transcript, the same way it reads everything else. Changes in the world add up: each step can do something real, such as sending a message or deleting a file. A long loop with the power to change things needs permissions and confirmations from a person, not only a step cap. Long transcripts cause trouble: they cost more to re-read, and they can bury early details that the model needs later on. They can also grow past the context window, which is the most text a model can take in on a single call. A common mix-up: people often think that a longer loop means a smarter agent, as if the extra steps made the model cleverer. The model inside is the same on call 10 as on call 1, so more steps only give it more chances to finish. They also give it more chances to repeat a mistake, spend more and change things you did not want changed. On *Retry forever*, raising the cap from 4 to 10 bought six more failures and almost five times the reading, but still no wind speed.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Agents
documents.body: Most agent frameworks, the ready-made toolkits people use to build agents, still run a loop like this one and add extras around it. Typical extras are memory, written plans, more than one model, and helper agents that each take on part of a job. A 2022 research method called ReAct helped make this style popular by mixing the model's written reasoning, its actions and the observations into one transcript. Real agents are limited by more than a step cap, because they also get limits on time, on money spent and on which tools are offered. Many are also set up to ask a person before an action that cannot be undone, such as deleting something for good. Some services can store the unchanged start of a transcript so that re-reading it costs less, which is called prompt caching. Even with prompt caching, though, the transcript itself still grows on every turn, along with all the other problems a long transcript brings. Memory What an agent can use beyond the current call is called its agent memory, and it comes in two quite different kinds. Its working memory is the transcript the loop re-reads on every call, which is exact but limited by the context window, and which keeps growing. An external store sits outside the transcript, and it can be a file or a database, which is an organized collection of saved records. The agent saves notes in an external store and reads them back by calling tools. That way a fact can survive even after the host cuts old parts out of a long transcript or starts a fresh one. That comes with costs, because the agent has to choose what to save and what to fetch, and a fetch can miss what it was looking for. A wrong note is also a problem, because it gets trusted the next time it is read, as if it were correct. Anthropic's multi-agent research system saves its plan to external memory, because its transcript would be cut off once it passed 200,000 tokens (Anthropic Engineering, June 2025). This lab does not simulate memory at all, so its agent has nothing to work with except the transcript. Several agents A multi-agent system has several agent loops working on one job, often with one lead agent in charge of the others. In one common pattern, the lead agent splits the job, hands pieces to helper agents that each keep their own transcript, and combines what they send back. That can help when the work splits into parts that can run side by side, or when it is too big for one context window. It also costs more: Anthropic reported that its agents used about 4 times the tokens of a normal chat, and its multi-agent system about 15 times. It added that most coding jobs split into fewer side-by-side pieces than research does. It also said that agents are not yet great at coordinating with each other and handing out work in real time. Every hand-off between agents is one more step that can go wrong, so compounding error applies across a team of agents too. This lab has only one agent, and it simulates none of this. Sources: Anthropic Engineering, “How we built our multi-agent research system” (June 13, 2025), anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system. The Failure modes, safety, and security lab shows how text that arrives as an observation can carry hidden instructions meant to steer the model. Training a model further, as the Post-training lab describes, can make it better at choosing tools and at stopping on its own. Even so, it does not remove the need for limits in the host. Only a hard limit, such as a step cap, a time limit or a spending limit, is sure to end the loop.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Agents
documents.body: This module is about agents: programs that call a model in a loop rather than once. It answers a control question: who chooses each action, and who decides when to stop? The model writes only text: a tool call or an answer. The host, the code around the model, runs the tool and appends the result as an observation to the transcript, the running record that every model call re-reads. Then the host decides whether to call the model again. Each turn is the round trip from *Tools and function calling*. An agent is not a different kind of model: the one inside can be the model used for chat. Where it shows up Most agent frameworks run a loop like this one. ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) popularized interleaving the model's reasoning text with its actions and observations in one transcript. Production hosts also limit time, spend and tool access, and require approval for some actions. Multi-agent systems run several of these loops, often with a lead agent that hands pieces of a task to sub-agents, each with its own context. Anthropic reported that its multi-agent system used about 15 times the tokens of a chat. Why it matters The loop lets a model act on results, retrying after a timeout or fixing an argument an error names, which a single call cannot. It also puts every limit in host code, because the model ends the loop only by writing an answer, a terminal action. Running many steps brings failures a single call does not have: Without a step cap (a maximum number of model calls) or another hard limit such as time or spend, nothing guarantees the loop ends. A cap guarantees an end, not an answer. Without a stop rule (host code that ends the loop early), a repeated call that fails the same way every time spends the whole cap. Every call re-reads the whole transcript, so tokens read grow faster than the number of calls. Small per-step errors compound: if every step is independently right 95% of the time, a 20-step run is fully right about 36% of the time. An approval gate, a person reviewing the work mid-run, catches some wrong runs at the cost of redone steps. What you will be able to explain What an agent is: a host loop that calls a model, executes its tool calls and appends the results, not a different kind of model. How a terminal action, a step cap and a host stop rule each end the loop, and what happens when only the cap is left. Why each call's input grows with the loop, so cost rises faster than the number of steps. How to compute the chance that a run completes every step from per-step success and run length, how an approval gate that sometimes catches errors changes it, and what the gate costs in extra steps. How a retry that repeats a call differs from a repair that changes it after reading the error, and which one a stop rule on identical failures can end. What the lab shows The loop, cap, stop rule, tool runs and token counts are computed. The model is a fixed rule, badged scripted policy: answer after a successful tool result, otherwise repeat the call. On *Fix an argument* it instead corrects the argument the error text names. Tool results are fixed, and token counts use a toy rule. Agent loop and Trace: Task picks *Look up hours*, *Recover from error*, *Retry forever* or *Fix an argument*, and Replay step walks the run event by event. Budgets and Context growth: Step cap (1 to 10 model calls) and Stop rule (*none* or *stop after 2 identical failures*) decide how the run ends. One bar per call shows its input. Reliability: a closed-form formula, not a run of an agent. Per-step success, Steps in the run, Approval gate after step and Reviewer catches set Completes end to end, With the gate and Expected steps run. Per-step success is an input, not a measurement. The key experiment runs *Retry forever* at Step cap 10, then turns on the stop rule: the run ends after two calls instead of ten. Under the same rule *Fix an argument* still answers, because its second call differs from the first.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Agents
documents.body: An agent is a program that calls a model in a loop. The model can be the same one used for chat. What makes the system an agent is the host code around it. The agent loop fits in a few lines: Each turn is the function-calling round trip from the previous lab. The tool result becomes an observation: the only way the model learns what happened. Three ways to stop A terminal action: the model writes an answer instead of a tool call. A step cap: the host refuses to make another model call. A stop rule: host code ends the loop early, here when the same call fails twice in a row. Only the first ends with an answer. The other two end with the task unfinished. What stands in for the model The model on this page is a scripted policy: if the last tool result succeeded, answer; otherwise issue the same call again. One task, *Fix an argument*, differs: its policy reads the error text from the previous tool result and corrects the argument the error names. Both are fixed rules, not models. The loop, the tools, the cap, the stop rule and every token count are computed.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Agents
documents.body: The model never stops the loop except by writing an answer. Every other stop is host code. A cap guarantees the loop ends. It does not guarantee an answer. Every call re-reads the whole transcript. On *Retry forever* each turn adds the same 31 tokens, so the input grows linearly and the total grows quadratically: 418 tokens at cap 4, 1,975 at cap 10. The stop rule does not fire on *Recover from error*. One failure followed by a success is not two identical failures, so a well-chosen rule leaves useful retries alone. documents.subtitle: Standard · Agents
documents.body: In this lab The policy is a fixed rule. A sampled model could answer early, choose another tool, or give up in words. Two tools return fixed values; get_ferry_time fails once by design. The repair is a string rule that matches the wrong value against the allowed values in the error text. It does not understand the message, and a model could misread it. The Reliability card is a formula, not a run of an agent. It assumes identical, independent steps, wrong steps the agent cannot see, one reviewer, and a redo that is not checked again. Token counts use a toy rule — runs of letters, runs of digits and single symbols — not a real tokenizer. Nothing is cached, parallel or asynchronous. In the real mechanism Errors compound. If each step is right 95% of the time, a 20-step run is fully right about 36% of the time, since 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.36. Real steps are not identical or independent, and the true per-step rate has to be measured. Reviewers miss errors. An approval gate helps only as far as the reviewer catches a wrong run, and a reviewer can miss an error or be skipped when time is short. Plans are text. A model can write a plan and then not follow it. A plan is not a promise, and a longer plan has more steps to get right, so the Reliability card applies to its steps too. Observations can mislead. A tool can return stale, partial or hostile text, and the next call treats it as context. Side effects accumulate. Each step can change something in the world. A long loop with write access needs permissions and confirmations, not only a cap. Long transcripts degrade. They cost more, can overflow the context window, and bury early details the model needs.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Agents
documents.body: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) popularized interleaving reasoning, actions and observations in one transcript. Most agent frameworks still run a loop like the one above, adding memory, task planning, several models, or sub-agents. Production agents bound more than steps: wall-clock time, spend, which tools are exposed, and which actions need a human to approve. Prompt caching can reduce the price of re-reading an unchanged prefix, but the transcript still grows. Memory An agent's working memory is its context: the transcript the loop re-reads on every call. It is exact but finite, and it grows. An external store, such as a file or database, sits outside the transcript. The agent writes to it and reads from it through tools, so a fact survives a trimmed or restarted context. The costs: the agent must decide what to save and what to fetch, a fetch can miss, and a wrong note is trusted next time. Anthropic's multi-agent research system saves its plan to external memory because the context would be truncated past 200,000 tokens (Anthropic Engineering, June 2025). This lab does not simulate memory: its agent has only the transcript. Multi-agent patterns In an orchestrator–worker pattern, a lead agent splits a task, hands pieces to sub-agents that each have their own context, and combines what they return. It can help when work parallelizes or exceeds one context window. It also costs more. Anthropic reported that its agents used about 4 times the tokens of a chat, and its multi-agent system about 15 times. It added that most coding tasks have fewer parallel pieces than research, and that agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating in real time. From the mechanism, every hand-off is another step that can go wrong, so the compounding on the Reliability card applies across agents too. This lab has one agent and simulates none of it. Sources: Anthropic Engineering, “How we built our multi-agent research system” (June 13, 2025), anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system. Failure modes, safety, and security shows how text arriving as an observation can carry instructions. Post-training can make a model better at choosing tools and stopping; it does not remove the need for host-side limits.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Agent loop · Agents
documents.body: The loop is host code The host builds a context, calls the model, and checks the output. A plain-text answer is a terminal action and ends the loop. A tool call is executed by the host, its result is appended, and the host checks the step cap and any stop rule before calling the model again. Task: Look up hours, Recover from error, Retry forever, or Fix an argument. A loop diagram: Context → Model call → final answer? → Stop · answer, or → Host runs the tool → Host check → next call or Stop. Solid boxes are the model's side, dashed boxes are host code; the active step is filled. Replay step, which walks every event of the run, and a sentence describing the current event. while calls < cap: output = policy(transcript); if final, stop; else result = host.run(output), append both; if the stop rule is on and the same call failed twice in a row, stop. The policy is a fixed rule standing in for the model: answer if the last tool result succeeded, otherwise issue the task's call again. On Fix an argument it instead reads the error text and corrects the argument the error names. Task and Replay step. Comparison worth running: Look up hours against Retry forever at the same Step cap — one exits at Stop · answer, the other at Stop · step cap. The model box never decides to stop the loop by itself except by writing an answer. With Step cap 1 on Look up hours, the host still runs the tool the first call requested; the answer never comes. In this lab: the policy is scripted and deterministic, and its repair is a string rule that matches the wrong value against the allowed values in the error text. A sampled model could answer early, pick a different tool, give up in words, or misread the error. In general: agent frameworks differ in detail, but each wraps a model in host code that executes actions and decides when to stop.
documents.title: The loop is host code

documents.subtitle: Trace · Agents
documents.body: The transcript, event by event Every model call and every tool result, in order, exactly as appended to the context. Model calls show their text and the tokens read and written. Tool results show the host's JSON, with failures outlined. The user's question in the kicker. One row per event: Model call n with its output and token counts, Host · tool result indented beneath it, and a final Stop row with the reason. The current replay event outlined; later events faded. Clicking a row jumps Replay step to it. Rows are the run's events. Nothing is authored per row: the host produces them by running the loop. Tokens read by call n are the toy token count of the system prompt, the user message, and every earlier call and result. Click any row to replay to it. Comparison worth running: Recover from error — call 1 gets a timeout, call 2 gets 15:40, call 3 answers. Second comparison: Fix an argument — call 1 is rejected for "Weekday", call 2 sends "weekday" and gets 21:00. The two calls differ; in Recover from error they were identical. get_wind was never in the tool list. The policy asks for it anyway, and the host rejects it every time. The model learns about the timeout only because the host wrote it into the transcript. In Fix an argument the error names the argument and lists the allowed values. That text is all the second call has to go on. In this lab: two real tools with fixed answers; get_ferry_time fails on its first attempt by design, and get_dock_hours checks its two enum arguments the way the previous lab does. In general: observations can be incomplete, wrong or hostile, and a long trace makes it harder for the model to use early details.
documents.title: The transcript, event by event

documents.subtitle: Budgets · Agents
documents.body: Three ways a loop ends A run ends by a final answer, by the step cap, or by a host stop rule. The cap bounds the number of model calls; the stop rule ends a run early when the same call fails twice in a row. The metrics total what the run consumed. Step cap from 1 to 10 model calls, and Stop rule: none, or stop after 2 identical failures. Metrics: Model calls, Tool runs (and how many failed), Stop reason, Tokens read and Tokens written. Tokens read = Σ over calls of that call's input. Tokens written = Σ of each output's toy token count. The stop rule compares each failing call's text with the previous failing call's text. Step cap and Stop rule. Comparison worth running: Retry forever at cap 4 then 10 — tokens read go from 418 to 1,975 for 2.5 times as many calls. The stop rule does not trip on Recover from error: one failure followed by a success is not two identical failures. It does not trip on Fix an argument either, because the second call is not identical to the first. A stop by cap or rule leaves the user without an answer. It limits damage; it does not solve the task. In this lab: cost is shown in toy tokens, not money, and every call has the same price per token. In general: production agents cap steps, wall-clock time, spend and tool permissions, and ask a person before irreversible actions.
documents.title: Three ways a loop ends

documents.subtitle: Context growth · Agents
documents.body: Input grows every turn Each bar is one model call's input: the fixed system prompt and user message, plus every earlier call and tool result. Because the loop appends to the transcript every turn, each call reads more than the last, and the running total grows faster than the number of calls. One bar per allowed call: the light part is system prompt plus user message, the dark part is earlier turns. Dashed stubs are calls the cap allowed but the run did not use. The input size above each bar, the call number below it, and the total tokens read in the heading. input(n) = base + Σ over k < n of (output(k) + result(k)). On Retry forever each turn adds the same 31 tokens, so input rises linearly and the total rises quadratically. Token counts come from a toy rule: runs of letters, runs of digits, and single symbols each count as one. This card has no controls. Task, Step cap and Stop rule change the bars; Replay step fades calls not yet reached. Comparison worth running: Retry forever at cap 10 — call 10 reads 337 tokens, almost six times call 1. The first call of every task reads the same base, give or take the user message. A host stop rule removes the tall bars on the right, which is where most of the tokens are. In this lab: real tokenizers split text differently, and nothing here is cached. In general: prompt caching can cut the price of re-reading an unchanged prefix, but the context still grows, and long transcripts can exceed the context window or bury early details.
documents.title: Input grows every turn

documents.subtitle: Reliability · Agents
documents.body: Per-step success, compounded The chance that a run finishes with every step right is the per-step success probability multiplied by itself once per step. The card draws that as a curve over run length and as a table, and adds an approval gate: a reviewer who inspects the work after a chosen step and sends a wrong prefix back to be redone once. Four controls: Per-step success (50 to 100%), Steps in the run (1 to 30), Approval gate after step (0 means no gate) and Reviewer catches (0 to 100% of wrong runs). Metrics: Completes end to end, With the gate, Longest run that finishes half the time, and Expected steps run. A line chart of completion probability against run length: a solid line without a gate, a dashed line with it, and a marker at the current length. A table gives the same values for selected lengths. No gate: P = p^n, where p is Per-step success and n is Steps in the run. With a gate after step k and catch rate d: s = p^k and P = (s + (1 − s)·d·s)·p^(n − k). A gate set beyond the run's last step sits after the last step. Expected steps run = n + k·d·(1 − s): the run itself plus the k steps redone when the reviewer sends a wrong prefix back. Longest run that finishes half the time is the largest n with p^n at least 0.5. The tests check these formulas against a seeded run-by-run simulation, so the numbers are exact formulas that a sample agrees with. Per-step success, Steps in the run, Approval gate after step and Reviewer catches. Comparison worth running: 95% against 99% at 20 steps — 35.8% against 81.8%. Second comparison: a gate after step 10 at 95% per step with Reviewer catches at 100% against 0% — 50.2% against 35.8%. The gate costs 4.0 expected steps at 100% and nothing at 0%. At 95% per step only runs of 13 steps or fewer finish more often than not. At 99% the limit is 68 steps. A gate after step 1 is a retry of step 1, and it barely helps: it protects one step of twenty (37.6% against 35.8%). A gate at the end gives the highest chance but the most redone work: 58.8% for 32.8 expected steps at 95% per step and 20 steps. In this lab: closed-form formulas with fixed assumptions — identical, independent steps; errors the agent cannot see; one check; a redo that is not rechecked. Nothing here runs an agent, and Per-step success is a number you set, not a measurement. In general: real steps differ in difficulty, their errors are linked, and some are never noticed. A reviewer can miss errors or be skipped under time pressure, and a retry can fail too. The per-step rate of a real agent has to be measured on its own tasks.
documents.title: Per-step success, compounded

documents.subtitle: Compare how dense layers, convolutions, recurrent nets, attention, state-space models and mixtures of experts wire their weights, so a transformer looks like one wiring, not the definition of a neural net.
documents.body: Compare how dense layers, convolutions, recurrent nets, attention, state-space models and mixtures of experts wire their weights, so a transformer looks like one wiring, not the definition of a neural net. Match convolution, recurrence, and attention to the reuse pattern each one assumes Treat a transformer as one architecture among several that map sequences to predictions Separate the weights a model stores from the weights each input actually uses
documents.title: The architecture zoo

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Click cells on the 8×8 pad, or move Selected cell and press Flip selected cell. The outlined 3×3 window is all the selected filter output can see; flip a pixel inside it and watch that output's number change.

documents.body: Set Filter to horizontal edge, then to center blob. The same ink and the same 9 weights, reused at all 64 positions, give a different response map.

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Move RNN step from t=0 to t=7 and compare the ∂h7/∂x bars: at Recurrent weight 0.90 column 1 reaches the final state with about 0.009, column 8 with about 0.6.
documents.title: Walk the RNN

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · The architecture zoo
documents.body: In Who sees whom, switch Wiring among Dense MLP, Per-position MLP, Convolution, Recurrent, Attention and State-space, and with Convolution raise Conv layers from 1 to 7 to watch the band widen.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: The wiring that decides which computations share weights and which activations can see which others. It is chosen before training and shapes what is easy to learn.
documents.title: Architecture

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: The assumptions an architecture builds in, such as locality in a convolution or order in a recurrent net. Bias here means a prior, not a social prejudice.
documents.title: Inductive bias

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: A layer where every output has its own weight to every input, as in a multilayer perceptron. Applied to a whole flattened sequence it shares nothing across positions, so its weights grow with the square of the input size.
documents.title: Dense layer

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Reusing the same weights at every position or time step. It is why a convolution needs 9 weights where a dense 64-to-64 layer needs 4,096, and why a pattern learned in one place works in another.
documents.title: Weight sharing

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: A small filter slid over every position, taking a weighted sum of each neighbourhood. Deep-learning libraries compute it as cross-correlation, without flipping the kernel.
documents.title: Convolution

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: The set of inputs one output can depend on. A kernel-3 convolution sees 3×3 after one layer and grows by one pixel in each direction per extra layer.
documents.title: Receptive field

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: A block that reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a fixed-size hidden state forward. Steps must run in order, and long dependencies must survive that state.
documents.title: Recurrent network

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Gradients that shrink as they flow back through many steps, because each step multiplies them by a factor below one. Early inputs then barely affect learning; factors above one explode instead.
documents.title: Vanishing gradient

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Long short-term memory (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997): a recurrent cell with gates and an additive cell state, which lets gradients survive far more steps than a plain tanh recurrence.
documents.title: LSTM

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: A stack of blocks, each an attention layer that mixes positions and a per-position MLP (Vaswani et al., 2017). With a causal mask each position reads all earlier ones in one hop, up to the context length.
documents.title: Transformer

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: A constraint that lets each position read itself and earlier positions but never later ones. It is what lets a language model train on next-token prediction and then generate left to right. Here Attention, Recurrent and State-space are causal; the Convolution is centred and sees the future.
documents.title: Causal

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: The stored keys and values of every earlier position, kept so each new token reuses them instead of recomputing them. It grows with the context length n: 2·n·d numbers per layer here, 1,024 at n = 8 and 524,288 at n = 4,096.
documents.title: KV cache

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: A sequence layer with a linear recurrent state update, so it can train with a parallel scan and generate with a fixed-size state. Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) makes the update depend on the input.
documents.title: State-space model

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The architecture zoo
documents.body: A layer with many expert MLPs and a router that sends each token to only the top k of them. Total parameters grow with the number of experts, while compute per token grows only with k.
documents.title: Mixture of experts

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The architecture zoo · question 1
documents.body: On Drawn digit you ink the same small stroke in a different place, with the same Filter selected. What happens to the response map on Live filter? The strong responses disappear, because the kernel was tuned to the first location of the stroke The same pattern of responses appears at the new location, because one kernel is reused everywhere The map is recomputed with different weights for that region, because each position has its own filter The responses stay where the stroke used to be, because the filter remembers the earlier ink A convolution applies one 3×3 kernel at all 64 positions, so each response depends only on the ink inside its window, not on where the window is. Shifting the ink shifts the response map by the same amount. That sharing is why 9 weights replace a dense 64-to-64 map of 4,096, at the price of assuming the same local pattern matters everywhere.
documents.title: On Drawn digit you ink the same small stroke in a different place, with the same Filter selected. What happens to the response map on Live filter?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The architecture zoo · question 2
documents.body: The Unrolled RNN reuses one recurrent weight at every step. At Recurrent weight 0.90, how do the ∂h7/∂x bars for column 1 and column 8 compare? They are equal, because the same weight is reused at every step, so every input influences the final state equally Column 1 is larger, because the earliest input has had the most steps to build up its influence Column 1 is far smaller, because its influence is multiplied by a factor below one at each step on the way to h7 Column 8 is zero, because the last input has no recurrent steps left to carry its effect The gradient of the final state with respect to an input is a product with one factor per step, w·(1 − h²). With w = 0.9 each factor is below one, so the product shrinks with distance: column 1 reaches h7 with about 0.009 and column 8 with about 0.6. Reusing the weight shares parameters, not influence. Above 1, the same product grows instead of fading.
documents.title: The Unrolled RNN reuses one recurrent weight at every step. At Recurrent weight 0.90, how do the ∂h7/∂x bars for column 1 and column 8 compare?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The architecture zoo · question 3
documents.body: In Who sees whom, which wiring lets output position 8 use input position 1 in a single hop, while never seeing a later position? Causal self-attention, which scores every earlier position directly and masks the later ones A recurrent network, which carries input 1 forward through its hidden state A one-layer convolution with kernel 3, which reaches farther as it slides along the sequence Causal attention scores every earlier position directly, so input 1 reaches output 8 in one hop and the mask hides later positions. A recurrent net also reaches input 1, but through 8 steps that run in order, and a one-layer kernel-3 convolution sees only its immediate neighbours.
documents.title: In Who sees whom, which wiring lets output position 8 use input position 1 in a single hop, while never seeing a later position?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The architecture zoo · question 4
documents.body: In Who sees whom, Per-position MLP fills only the diagonal. In a transformer block, which part moves information between positions? The per-position MLP, because it runs at every position and so connects all of them together The residual connection, which copies each position's vector into every other position as well The shared weights, because every position uses them and so ends up holding the same information Attention, which lets positions read other allowed positions; the MLP rewrites each one alone A transformer block pairs attention, which mixes across positions, with a per-position MLP, which transforms each position independently and so shows only a diagonal. Sharing weights does not mix values between positions, and a residual connection adds a position's own input back to its own output. So a transformer is one particular wiring, attention plus a per-position MLP, not a synonym for neural network.
documents.title: In Who sees whom, Per-position MLP fills only the diagonal. In a transformer block, which part moves information between positions?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The architecture zoo · question 5
documents.body: In Sparse experts, with Experts per token at 2, you raise Experts from 8 to 16. What happens to the two weight counts?
