Both double, because every extra expert also adds work for each token that gets routed to it Total expert weights double while Active per token stays put, as each token still uses two experts Active per token doubles while Total expert weights stays put, because tokens are spread over more experts Each expert is its own MLP, so storing twice as many experts doubles the stored weights. A token is still routed to only the top k experts, so the weights it actually uses depend on k, not on how many experts exist. That is the point of a mixture of experts: capacity grows with the number of experts while compute per token does not.
documents.title: In Sparse experts, with Experts per token at 2, you raise Experts from 8 to 16. What happens to the two weight counts?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The architecture zoo · question 6
documents.body: In Sparse experts some experts get no tokens, and the load row shows 0 for them. What can you conclude from this lab? Only that this untrained, seeded router leaves some stored experts unused; trained routers add a load-balancing loss That those experts have learned nothing useful and could be deleted without changing what the model does That the other experts have specialized on particular strokes of the digit while these have not yet That the router has learned to skip the tokens it judges unimportant The router here is an untrained linear layer with fixed seeded weights, so which experts receive tokens is arbitrary rather than learned. It shows the mechanism: weights can be stored and never used. In real mixtures a trained router learns which tokens suit which experts, and a load-balancing loss keeps any expert from sitting idle or being overloaded. The lab says nothing about what an expert specializes in.
documents.title: In Sparse experts some experts get no tokens, and the load row shows 0 for them. What can you conclude from this lab?

documents.subtitle: Plain · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Before anyone trains an AI model, somebody has to decide how its parts are connected. They decide which pieces of the input each part is allowed to look at, and which stored numbers get reused from place to place. This module is about those decisions, and the lab lets you compare six different sets of them side by side. All six are versions of the same basic machine, a neural network, which is the kind of program behind chatbots and image recognition. A neural network turns input numbers into output numbers by multiplying them by stored numbers called weights and adding up the results, round after round. Training is the long process of nudging those weights until the outputs come out right. The way the parts are connected is called the network's architecture, and it is fixed before training starts, so training never changes it. Each architecture makes its own guesses about the input, such as "nearby pixels belong together" or "the order of the words matters". Built-in guesses like these are called the inductive bias, where "bias" means a starting assumption, not a prejudice. The six wirings in this lab are: a dense layer, where every output has its own weight for every input and nothing is reused; a convolution, which slides one small window of weights across the whole input; a recurrent network, which reads one step at a time and carries a running summary forward; attention, where each position, such as each word, looks directly at every position it may see, which for a model that writes text is itself and every earlier one; a state-space model, a close cousin of the recurrent network that is built to train faster; a mixture of experts, which stores many small networks but runs only a few of them on each piece of input. Where you have met it A language model, the kind of program behind a chatbot, writes its reply one small piece at a time. Each new piece may look back at what came before it but never ahead, and that one-way rule is called causal. Most chatbots today are built on a wiring called attention. While such a model writes, it has to keep notes about every earlier piece, and those notes grow as the reply gets longer. You will meet them later in this lesson as the KV cache, and you will also meet wirings whose notes stay the same size however long the text gets. You have probably heard the word transformer. It names one particular wiring: attention, which moves information between positions, plus a small network that works on each position by itself. People often say "transformer" as if it meant any AI model, but it is one design among several, and many real systems combine designs. The other wirings have real, named versions too: the LSTM, a recurrent design from 1997, built so that early inputs keep affecting learning over far more steps than in a plain recurrent chain; Mamba, a state-space model from 2023; Mixtral 8x7B, a mixture of experts that sends each token, a small piece of text, to 2 of its 8 experts; convolutions, the core of networks that recognise images. When a model that writes text from left to right uses convolutions, they are built so that they never see later positions. Why it matters The wiring decides what is cheap for a model to learn before it has seen a single example. Get it wrong, and a model may need far more weights, far more memory, or far more examples to learn the same thing. It may even be unable to connect two parts of its input at all, because no path joins them. No wiring is cheap at everything, so choosing one means choosing which cost you are willing to pay. Some wirings need huge numbers of weights, some let early inputs fade away, and some need more memory as the text gets longer. One wiring, the mixture of experts, even lets a model store many more weights without each token needing more arithmetic. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain the three ideas below. In them, a sequence means an ordered list, such as the words of a sentence or the columns of a drawing. A hop is one layer or step that information passes through on its way from an input to an output. what kind of reuse a convolution, a recurrent network and attention each build in, and how many hops each needs to link two positions that are far apart; why a transformer is one wiring among several that can read a sequence and turn it into predictions, and which of its two parts moves information between positions; the difference between the weights a model stores and the weights that one piece of input actually uses, and why adding more experts grows only the first number. What the lab lets you do Nothing in this lab is trained, so every number you see is worked out directly from a formula. The filters and the recurrent weights are picked by hand. The mixture of experts has a router, the part that decides which experts each piece of input goes to, and it uses fixed, random-looking numbers instead of trained ones. At the top is Drawn digit, an 8×8 grid of squares, called pixels, with a blocky 3 already inked in. You can click squares to add or remove ink, and three of the cards below read your drawing. Live filter slides a small 3×3 window of hand-picked weights across your drawing and shows the result at every square. Unrolled RNN reads the columns of your drawing from left to right, and shows how much the first column still matters by the end. RNN is short for recurrent neural network. Who sees whom shows six wirings: the ones listed earlier except the mixture of experts, plus the Per-position MLP found inside a transformer. That is a small network that works on each position by itself. MLP is short for multilayer perceptron, an old name for a small stack of dense layers, and the card's name for the dense layer is Dense MLP. For each one it shows which inputs each output can use and how many hops it takes, with a table of costs underneath. Sparse experts sends each column of your drawing to a few experts and counts the weights stored against the weights actually used. The two comparisons that teach the most are Recurrent against Attention in Who sees whom, and raising Experts while Experts per token stays the same.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Weights and layers Most parts of a network do the same basic job: it multiplies each of its input numbers by its own weight, then adds the results together into one output number. A whole row of these jobs running side by side is called a layer. A network stacks many layers, so that each one works on the outputs of the one before. Training adjusts the weights a tiny bit at a time until the outputs come out right. What training cannot do is change which inputs each output is allowed to use, because that was settled when the network was designed. What an architecture decides An architecture answers two questions before training begins: which inputs is each output allowed to use, and which weights get reused in more than one place? Think of it like planning the pipes in a building before any water flows, with the inputs as tanks and the outputs as taps. The pipes decide which taps can draw from which tanks, and how many bends the water passes through on the way. Training is like turning the valves, because it changes how much flows through each pipe but never adds a pipe or takes one away. If a tap has no pipe to a tank, no amount of valve-turning will ever connect them. The picture stops matching when it comes to reuse, because in a network a single weight can sit on many pipes at once. Adjusting that weight changes all of those pipes together, which real valves cannot do. This kind of reuse turns out to be one of the biggest differences between wirings. Each wiring also builds in a guess about the input before it sees any data. A convolution guesses that nearby pixels belong together and that the same small pattern matters everywhere, while a recurrent network guesses that order matters. These guesses are the architecture's inductive bias, and they make some patterns cheap to learn and others expensive. Reusing weights The most straightforward wiring, called a dense layer, gives every output its own separate weight for every input, so nothing in it is shared. On the 8×8 drawing, with 64 pixels coming in and 64 outputs going out, a dense layer needs one weight for every pixel and output pair. That is 64 times 64, which is the 4,096 that the lab shows beside Dense layer, 64 → 64. The other choice is to reuse the same few weights at every position, which is called weight sharing. It has two big payoffs: it needs far fewer weights, and a pattern learned in one place works everywhere else without being learned again. Picture a lifeguard who has learned what trouble in the water looks like. They do not need separate lessons for each end of the beach, because they carry the same trained eye from one patch of water to the next. A layer with shared weights works like that lifeguard, while a dense layer is more like hiring a different guard for every patch and training each one from scratch. A common mix-up: sharing weights does not mean every input gets an equal say in the answer. The weights are the same everywhere, but how much an input affects an output still depends on where that input sits and how many steps lie between them. You will see this clearly in the recurrent network, which uses one weight at every step and yet ends up barely affected by its first input. Convolution: one small window, slid everywhere Picture a square of card with a 3×3 grid of numbers written on it. You lay it over the drawing, where each inked pixel counts as 1 and each blank one as 0. Then you multiply each pixel underneath by the number written above it, add up the nine results and write the total down. Next you slide the card one square along and do it again, until you have a total for all 64 positions. That small grid of numbers is called a kernel, or a filter, and sliding it across the input is a convolution. The lab's Filter control picks one of three hand-made kernels, called vertical edge, horizontal edge and center blob. All 64 outputs come from the same 9 weights, which is why the Live filter card says "9 weights reused at 64 positions". Each kernel looks for a different shape: horizontal edge has −1 along its top row, 0 along its middle row and +1 along its bottom row. So it subtracts any ink above the centre square and adds any ink below it; vertical edge does the same thing sideways, subtracting ink on the left and adding ink on the right; center blob gives +4 to ink in the middle square and −1 to ink in the four squares directly above, below, left and right of it. The four corner squares count 0. So it scores highest for a lone dot with no ink beside it. For a worked example, set Filter to horizontal edge and move the Selected cell slider to r2 c4, which means row 2, column 4. You can also click that square in the grid of totals on Live filter, but not on the drawing itself, because clicking the drawing adds or removes ink. The window around that cell covers rows 1 to 3. Row 1 holds the top bar of the 3, so three inked pixels sit under the kernel's row of −1 weights. The formula row in Live filter shows Σ pixel × weight = 1·(−1) + 1·(−1) + 1·(−1), and the total is −3. The Σ sign means "add all of these up", and each 1·(−1) is one inked pixel times one weight. Blank pixels count as 0, so they add nothing and the lab leaves them out of the list. Now move to r8 c4, the square underneath the bottom bar. Its window holds the same shape of ink in the same spots, so the same 9 weights give it the same total of −3. Nobody had to teach the filter about the bottom bar separately, and that is weight sharing paying off. The outlined 3×3 box on Drawn digit shows the only pixels that the selected output can see. That set of inputs is called the output's receptive field, and the Receptive field readout sums it up as "3×3 per layer". A pixel outside the box has no effect at all, while a pixel inside it can change the output, unless it sits under a 0 weight in the kernel. One layer only sees a pixel's nearest neighbours, but layers can be stacked. Each output of a second layer sees a 3×3 patch of first-layer outputs, and each of those saw its own 3×3 patch of pixels. Picture a pixel two squares to the left of the selected one. The first-layer output just left of the selected square can see that pixel, and the second-layer output can see that first-layer output, so the pixel now counts. The same happens on every side, which turns the 3×3 view into a 5×5 one. Every extra layer widens the view by one pixel in each direction, which means pixels that are far apart only meet after enough layers. Recurrent network: one step at a time Picture a row of eight desks and a note that gets passed from desk to desk. Each student reads one new piece of information, rewrites the note to include it, and hands the note on. The note never gets any bigger, so each rewrite has to squeeze the old news and the new news into the same small space. Every student follows exactly the same rewriting rule, and that one shared rule is what makes this a single network rather than eight. Here the picture stops matching, though. A real student could choose to copy part of the note unchanged. A plain recurrent network instead rewrites and squeezes the whole note at every desk, and that is where old news starts to fade. A recurrent network works the same way: it reads a sequence one step at a time while carrying a fixed-size note, called the hidden state. It applies the same update, with the same weights, at every step, so its reuse is reuse over time. The Unrolled RNN card runs a tiny one on your drawing, where RNN is short for recurrent neural network. It reads the eight columns from left to right, and the input for each column is the fraction of its 8 pixels that are inked, shown as Column mean. On the default 3, column 1 is blank, so its input is 0, while column 7 has 4 of its 8 pixels inked, so its input is 0.5. Its hidden state is one single number: h0 is the state once column 1 has been read, h1 once column 2 has been read, and so on up to h7. The lab starts counting at 0, so every label is one less than its column number. For example, t=0, x0 and h0 all belong to column 1, and h7 belongs to column 8. At each step the net multiplies the number it is carrying by the Recurrent weight, written w, and then adds the new column's input. Finally it squashes the total so it always stays between −1 and 1. The squash leaves small totals almost unchanged but flattens big ones. A total of 0.25 becomes about 0.245, 1 becomes about 0.76, and 3 becomes about 0.995, so the result never quite reaches 1. Here are the first two steps. The net starts with nothing, and column 1 is blank, so h0 is 0. For column 2, it multiplies 0 by 0.9, adds column 2's input of 0.25 and squashes 0.25 to about 0.245, which is h1. Carrying on this way to the end, with the default w of 0.90, the last state, h7, comes out at about 0.634. Because each step needs the note from the step before, the steps cannot all run at the same time, and they have to happen in order. A recurrent network also only ever sees the past, because when it reaches column 3 it has read columns 1 to 3 and nothing to their right. Why early steps fade How much does column 1 still matter by the time the net reaches h7? The lab answers with a number written ∂h7/∂x0, where x0 is column 1's input and the curly ∂ means "a tiny change in". Read the whole thing as a ratio: if you nudged column 1's input up by a tiny amount, how far would h7 move, compared with the size of the nudge? A number like this is called a gradient, and training uses gradients to decide how much to adjust each weight. Training works backwards from the answer. When h7 is wrong, a correction is sent back along the same chain of steps, and it gets multiplied by the same factors you are about to see. If the chain shrinks column 1's effect to almost nothing, almost none of the correction gets back to the step that read column 1. So column 1 gets almost no credit or blame, and the network learns almost nothing about how it should have used column 1. To get from column 1 to h7, the effect has to pass through every later step, and each step multiplies it by its own factor. The lab prints each factor on the arrow between two boxes, and it works out as w·(1 − h²), where h is the state at that step. Take the factor beside h1 as an example, where h1 is about 0.245, as the Hidden h1 readout shows when RNN step is at t=1. Squaring 0.245 gives about 0.06, and taking that away from 1 leaves 0.94. Multiplying 0.94 by w, which is 0.9, gives about 0.85, the factor printed on that arrow. The (1 − h²) part comes from the squashing, and it measures how freely a nudge can pass through that squash. When h sits near 0 there is plenty of room, so (1 − h²) is close to 1 and a nudge passes through almost whole. When h gets close to 1 or −1, the squash is already pressing against its limit, so (1 − h²) drops toward 0 and a nudge barely gets through. The formula row for column 1 starts with (1 − h0²), which equals 1 here because h0 is 0. This first part has no w, because column 1's input goes straight into the first squash without being multiplied by w, so only the squash's (1 − h²) applies. After that, the effect is multiplied by seven factors in a row, all of them below 1. Here is each factor, with how much of the effect is left after it: hop 1 multiplies by 0.85, which leaves about 0.85; hop 2 multiplies by 0.73, which leaves about 0.62; hop 3 multiplies by 0.61, which leaves about 0.37; hop 4 multiplies by 0.45, which leaves about 0.17; hop 5 multiplies by 0.37, which leaves about 0.06; hop 6 multiplies by 0.28, which leaves about 0.017; hop 7 multiplies by 0.54, which leaves about 0.009. So column 1 reaches h7 with a gradient of about 0.009, while column 8, which needs no hops at all, reaches it with 0.598. Column 8 has no arrows to cross, but its input still passes through the squash once, and 1 − 0.634² is about 0.598. The last column has more than 60 times as much say over the final state as the first. This shrinking is called a vanishing gradient, and in a long sentence it means the early words barely shape what the network learns. The factors can be bigger than 1, too, and then the effect grows instead of fading. If the drawing is blank, h stays at 0, so with w set to 1.5 every factor is exactly 1.5. Seven factors of 1.5 multiply to about 17, so column 1's effect is blown up rather than faded. That opposite problem is called an exploding gradient. Real recurrent networks fight fading with gates, small learned switches that let some information ride forward almost untouched instead of being squashed at every step. The best-known gated design is the LSTM, short for long short-term memory, and it keeps gradients alive across far more steps than the plain chain in this lab. Attention: one direct look back Go back to the row of desks, where news from desk 1 reaches desk 8 only by passing through every desk in between. Now change the rule, so that every student leaves their notes on their own desk and each student can turn around and read the notes on every earlier desk directly. That is attention. In a network, each position compares what it is looking for with a short label offered by every position it is allowed to see. In a model that writes text, that means itself and every earlier position. Each position then takes in a blend of content from the positions that match best. Because every earlier position is one hop away, distance stops costing extra steps, and position 1 is reached as directly as the position right before it. Picture the made-up sentence "Maya dropped her phone because she was running." In a trained model, the position for "she" might be looking for a person, and the label offered by "Maya" might say that it is a name. So "she" would take most of its blend from Maya's content, and only a little from "phone" or "dropped". How much each earlier position counts in that blend is not a stored weight. It is worked out fresh from the match scores every time, so the blend changes from one sentence to the next. The stored weights only turn each position into its label, what it is looking for, and its content, and those same weights are used at every position. That is the difference from a convolution, which always mixes the same few neighbours using the same fixed numbers. It is also how attention can link every position to every earlier one in a single hop with only 16,384 weights in the lab's table. A dense layer joining all 8 positions in one hop, the table's Dense MLP row, needs 262,144. Attention's weight count does not grow with the length of the text either. And because it scores every earlier position directly, it builds in no guess that nearby positions matter most. In a language model, each position may look back but never ahead, and that one-way rule is called causal. Picture a practice quiz where you have to guess the next word of a sentence, but the answer is printed right after the blank. You would score perfectly and learn nothing, so a fair quiz hides everything after the blank. A causal model is trained under the same rule, and that is what lets it write text from left to right afterwards, one piece at a time. The price of looking back in one hop is memory, because every earlier position's label and content have to be kept for later positions to read. They are stored as two lists of numbers for each position, called a key, which is the label, and a value, which is the content. The store of all of them is the KV cache, K for key and V for value, and it grows with every new position. A transformer is built from blocks that pair attention with a small network that works on each position by itself, which the lab calls Per-position MLP. MLP is short for multilayer perceptron, an old name for a small stack of dense layers. It is dense inside one position, where every output has its own weight for every input, but the same MLP is reused at every position. Inside each block, attention moves information between positions, while the per-position MLP reworks the numbers at one position without looking at any other. A transformer stacks many of these blocks, one on top of another. State-space model: a recurrent network built for speed A state-space model reads in order and carries a fixed-size state, like a recurrent network, so in Who sees whom its picture looks exactly like Recurrent. The difference is inside the update, because a state-space model's update only multiplies and adds, leaving out the squashing step. That small change unlocks a shortcut for training, because a multiply-and-add followed by another multiply-and-add can always be folded into a single multiply-and-add. For example, "double it, then add 3" followed by "double it, then add 1" is the same as "multiply by 4, then add 7". Start with 5 and you get 13 and then 27 the first way, or 27 straight away the second way. So the computer can merge the steps in pairs, then merge the pairs, and keep going. Eight steps become four, then two, then one. All the merges in one round can happen at the same time, which suits a GPU, a chip that can run many multiplications at once. So the computer waits for three rounds instead of eight steps in a row. The Who sees whom table shows this in its Sequential steps column as "8 as a loop, 3 as a scan". Here a scan means this pair-by-pair merging. A recurrent network cannot use the trick, because a squash followed by another squash does not fold into one simple step. When it writes text, a state-space model keeps a state of the same size no matter how long the text gets, which is 1,024 numbers in the lab's table. Mamba, a state-space model from 2023, goes a step further and lets the update change depending on the input. Mixture of experts: many stored, few used Picture a tutoring centre with 8 tutors on its staff and a receptionist at the door. Each student who walks in is sent to the 2 tutors who seem the best fit, while the other 6 stay free. The centre has to keep all 8 tutors on the books, but any one student only takes up 2 tutors' time. A mixture of experts works the same way. In a transformer block, it replaces the one per-position MLP with many MLPs, called experts, plus a small scoring layer called a router. A token is one piece of input, such as a word or part of a word. For each token, the router scores every expert and sends the token to the top few. The token's result is then a blend of the answers from the experts it was sent to. In Sparse experts, each column of your drawing plays the part of a token, written as the list of its 8 pixels. Experts, labelled E on its slider, sets how many experts exist, anywhere from 2 to 16. Experts per token, labelled k, sets how many experts each token is sent to, from 1 to 4. Each expert in the lab is a small MLP with 32,768 weights. With the default 8 experts, the layer stores 262,144 weights in total, which the lab shows as Total expert weights. Each token runs through only 2 of the 8 experts, so it uses 65,536 weights, shown as Active per token. That is 25% of the expert weights, matching the line at the top of the card. Real models use the same trick at a far larger size: Mixtral 8x7B also sends each token to 2 of its 8 experts. It stores 46.7 billion parameters, the stored numbers that include its weights, but uses only about 12.9 billion of them for each token. That is a little over a quarter, not exactly 2 out of 8. Only the expert MLPs are split up, while shared parts such as attention run for every token. The name suggests 8 times 7 billion, but those shared parts are stored once, not 8 times, which is why the total is less than 56 billion. The tutoring picture stops matching in an important way. Human tutors have subjects, like maths or history, but nothing in this lab says what an expert is good at. This lab's router is not trained either, because its choices come from fixed, random-looking numbers, so it shows how routing works rather than what a real router would learn.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · The architecture zoo
documents.body: The previous module, Why GPUs, showed that a big, even block of multiplications suits a GPU, a chip that can run many multiplications at the same time. This lab shows that the multiplications are only half the design. The same multiply-and-add can be wired to look nearby, to read in order, or to look everywhere at once, and each choice changes what the network can learn cheaply. The problem of size A network that never shares weights has to learn every pattern separately at every position, which takes huge numbers of weights and examples. In a real model, each position, such as a word, is first turned into a list of numbers that describes it, and the lab's table assumes 64 numbers per position. In the Who sees whom table, the Dense MLP row is a dense layer that reads all 8 positions at once, and it needs 262,144 weights. That is 512 numbers in and 512 numbers out, and 512 times 512 is 262,144. Its size also depends on the length of the input, so the input length is locked in, and doubling it would make the layer four times as big. Every other wiring in the table reuses its weights at each position. Their weight counts stay the same whether the text has 8 positions or 8,000, so the same layer works for a short input or a long one. The problem of distance In a sentence, a word often depends on another word far back, such as a name mentioned near the start. Each wiring reaches far back in its own way, and each way has a cost: a convolution reaches only its neighbours, so linking position 1 to position 8 takes 7 stacked layers; a recurrent network reaches back through a chain of 8 steps that must run in order, and the effect fades along the way; attention reaches every earlier position in one hop, but it has to keep a KV cache that grows as the text gets longer. The problem of growth Storing more weights gives a model more room to learn, but if every weight runs for every token, each token needs more arithmetic as the model grows. A mixture of experts breaks that link, because it can store more experts while each token still runs through the same small number of them. Keeping "transformer" in proportion The transformer is one wiring in this zoo, so its strengths came with costs. Seeing the wirings side by side shows what it gave up and what it gained. By choosing attention, it gained one-hop reach to every earlier position, and steps that do not have to wait for each other. In return it took on a KV cache that keeps growing with the text, where a recurrent network or a state-space model would carry a note of fixed size. That trade is exactly what the table in Who sees whom lays out.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · The architecture zoo
documents.body: The lab follows five steps from top to bottom, and each one compares two settings, so make a guess before you move a control and then check it. Draw the digit Click squares on Drawn digit to add or remove ink, or move the Selected cell slider, which names a square by its row and column, such as r3 c5. Pressing Flip selected cell then switches the selected square on or off. The outlined 3×3 window around the selected square is everything that one filter output can see. Flip a pixel inside the window that sits under a nonzero kernel weight, and watch that output's number change in Live filter. A pixel under a 0 weight changes nothing, and that includes the selected square itself under vertical edge, because both edge kernels have 0 in the middle. Then flip a pixel outside the window and see that the output stays put. Pick a filter Try this: with the default 3 on the pad, switch Filter from vertical edge to horizontal edge, and then to center blob. The drawing did not change, yet the grid of totals in Live filter did, because the 9 weights changed. Under vertical edge the right-hand stroke of the 3 lights up, while under horizontal edge the three bars light up instead. The bands just below the top bar and the bottom bar both read −3 in the middle, because the same weights score the same shape of ink. The bottom bar also gets a +3 band above it. The top bar has none, because the pad ends above row 1 and there is no row there to show it. You can click any square in the grid of totals to select it and read its formula. Walk the RNN Move RNN step from t=0 to t=7, which selects column 1 through column 8, and read the bars labelled ∂h7/∂x0 up to ∂h7/∂x7. The formula row multiplies out the selected column's chain of factors, and Hops to h7 counts how many arrows lie between that column and the end. Try this: at the default Recurrent weight of 0.90, compare column 1 with column 8. Column 1 reaches h7 with about 0.009, while column 8 reaches it with about 0.6. Then slide Recurrent weight up to 2.00, and you might expect the bigger weight to keep the early columns alive. Instead, the states get pushed close to 1, so the (1 − h²) part shrinks toward 0 and column 1's gradient gets smaller still. The lab writes such tiny numbers in a short form, so 5.1e−5 means 5.1 divided by 100,000, or 0.000051. For the exploding case, click each of the 16 inked squares to clear the pad, then set Recurrent weight to 1.50. Every factor becomes exactly 1.5, and column 1's gradient grows to 17.086. When you are done, the Reset interactive button brings back the 3, which the experts card in step 5 also reads. Compare wirings Unlike the cards above it, Who sees whom does not read your drawing but imagines a sequence of 8 positions. It draws a grid where each row is an output position and each column is an input position. A number in a square says how many layers or steps lie between that input and that output, and a dot means the output cannot use that input at all. Switch Wiring through Dense MLP, Per-position MLP, Convolution, Recurrent, Attention and State-space, and watch the grid change shape. With Convolution selected, raise Conv layers from 1 to 7 and watch the band of reachable squares widen by one position on each side for every layer you add. Try this: switch Wiring between Recurrent and Attention and look at row 8, column 1. Both wirings let output 8 use input 1, but Recurrent gets there in 8 steps and Attention in 1. The table underneath counts the cost of each wiring for one layer. In it, n is the number of positions, and d = 64 is the length of the list of numbers that describes each position. The kernel width is k = 3, and N = 16 is how many numbers the state-space model keeps for each of the 64 numbers that describe a position. Weights / layer is how many weights the layer stores. Sequential steps is how many steps must run one after another. Longest path is the most hops any input needs to reach any output. Kept to extend is how many numbers must stay in memory to add one more position, shown for 8 positions and for 4,096. The Convolution row shows 12,288 weights, not 9, because here each position carries 64 numbers in and 64 out, so the kernel needs 3 × 64 × 64 weights. The Live filter card reads just one number per pixel, which is why it needs only 9. Route to experts In Sparse experts, the table has one row for each column of your drawing, labelled col 1 to col 8. It has one column for each expert, labelled E1, E2 and so on. A percentage in a square means the token is sent to that expert, and it shows how much that expert's answer counts in the blend. The percentages in each row add up to 100%. For example, with the defaults, col 7 gives about 81% of its blend to E1 and the rest to E7. Set Experts per token to 1, then raise Experts from 8 to 16, and watch Total expert weights double while Active per token stays the same. Each token still runs through one expert's 32,768 weights, however many experts are stored. The third readout, Router weights, counts the router's own weights, 64 for each expert, which is tiny next to the experts themselves.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Sharing on the filter card The filter uses the same 9 numbers at all 64 places, while a dense layer from 64 pixels to 64 outputs would need 4,096. Under horizontal edge, r2 c4 and r8 c4 both read −3, because they sit under bars with the same shape and are scored by the same weights. Only pixels inside the outlined window can change the selected output, which is locality built in before any training. Fading on the RNN card Every factor on the arrows is w·(1 − h²), and the bars for the early columns shrink because those columns have more factors to pass through. Column 1's gradient of about 0.009 against column 8's of about 0.6 shows a vanishing gradient in action, even though every step uses the same weight. Flipping a pixel in column 1 barely moves h7, which is what a vanishing gradient means for learning: early inputs get very little credit. A larger w does not always help, because squashed states near 1 or −1 make (1 − h²) almost 0, and the chain goes quiet. Hops to h7 says 7 for column 1, while Who sees whom says 8 steps for the same trip. The difference is that the grid also counts the step that first reads input 1. Reach and memory on the wiring card Recurrent and Attention are both causal, so each position uses only itself and earlier positions, never later ones. They can see the same squares, but Attention reaches every one in 1 hop while Recurrent needs up to 8. Attention pays for that one hop with its KV cache, and the table's formula for it is 2·n·d. That means 2 lists, keys and values, for each of the n positions, with d numbers in each list. At 8 positions that is 2 × 8 × 64, or 1,024 numbers. At 4,096 positions it is 524,288 numbers, which is 512 times as many, because the text is 512 times longer. Recurrent keeps only 64 numbers. That is because the table imagines a recurrent net whose note holds one number for each of the 64 that describe a position. The note on the RNN card holds just one. State-space keeps 1,024, which is 64 times 16. Neither number grows, however long the text gets. Recurrent and State-space draw exactly the same grid, so their difference shows up only in the table, where State-space can be run as a scan. Per-position MLP fills only the diagonal, from top left to bottom right, so each output sees only its own input, and the table says it "never mixes". In a transformer block, mixing between positions is attention's job. Convolution is the only wiring here, apart from Dense MLP, that can see later positions, because its window is centred on each position. The card's heading line says "can see later positions" when it is selected. Stored against used on the experts card Going from 8 to 16 experts doubles Total expert weights, from 262,144 to 524,288, while Active per token stays at 65,536 when Experts per token is 2. Only Experts per token changes the work each token does: moving it from 2 to 1 halves Active per token to 32,768. Columns with identical pixels always go to identical experts, because the router's choice depends only on the token itself. On the default 3, col 3 and col 4 hold the same pixels, so their rows match exactly. The bottom row, labelled load, counts how many tokens each expert gets. With the defaults, E2, E4, E5 and E6 get none: they are stored but never used. A common mix-up: an expert with a load of 0 is not useless, and the experts that do get tokens have not specialised in anything. This router is untrained, so which experts get tokens is an accident of its fixed numbers. Real routers are trained, with an extra penalty during training, called a load-balancing loss, that pushes them to spread tokens more evenly. Here a loss is a score that training tries to make smaller.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · The architecture zoo
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies Nothing is trained: the three filters are written by hand, the recurrent net's weights are set by hand, and the expert router uses fixed, random-looking numbers instead of trained ones. The numbers come from formulas: the grid and table in Who sees whom come from counting rules, not from trained models. The recurrent net is tiny: its hidden state is one number, while a real one carries a long list of numbers. It also has none of the gates that an LSTM uses. The convolution sees the future: its window is centred, so it covers positions on both sides. Convolutions used for text shift the window so it covers only the current and earlier positions. The experts never answer: only the routing and the weight counts are worked out, so the lab cannot tell you what any expert would do with a token. The counts, for the experts and Router weights alike, also assume tokens of 64 numbers, even though the tokens routed here are lists of 8 pixels. The images are toys: the input is an 8×8 grid of on-or-off pixels that you draw, with no photos, no colour and no real dataset. Where the real mechanisms fall short Weight counts and hop counts do not decide which wiring learns best. That depends on the data, the size of the model and how it is trained. Plain recurrent chains really do fade, but gated designs such as the LSTM and a similar one called the GRU carry gradients far longer than the chain in this lab. Real models add extra parts that change what each wiring can learn in practice. Shortcuts let information skip around a layer, other steps keep the numbers in a steady range, and many models run several attention patterns side by side. Real convolution networks learn their kernels from data instead of having them written by hand. Even so, faraway pixels still meet only after enough layers have been stacked, or through tricks. One trick is pooling, which shrinks the image by summarising each small patch. Another is dilated kernels, which skip squares so one window covers a wider area. Attention's KV cache keeps growing with the text, reaching 524,288 numbers per layer at 4,096 positions in this lab's table. That is why later modules look at ways to cut it down. A mixture of experts saves arithmetic, not storage, because every expert must still be stored even when most of them sit idle for a given token. A common mix-up: people say "transformer" as if it meant any AI model. It is one wiring: attention to move information between positions, plus a per-position MLP to rework each position on its own. Convolutions, recurrent networks, state-space models and mixtures of experts are other choices, and many real systems combine them.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Attention and The transformer block open up the one-hop mixing drawn here, using a real trained model, and show how attention and the per-position MLP stack together. Modern attention at scale looks at the costs this table only hints at, including the KV cache and two designs that cut its cost, called grouped-query attention and sliding-window attention. Inference & KV cache measures how the 2·n·d column grows while a model generates text. Each expert in Sparse experts takes in 64 numbers, widens them to 256 in the middle, then narrows them back to 64. That is two sets of 64 × 256 weights, or 32,768 in all. The squash used in the Unrolled RNN is a curve called tanh, which is why you may see a plain recurrent chain called a "tanh chain". Convolutions can reach farther with dilated kernels, which skip over squares so that one window covers a wider area. Some named designs and the year each was first described: the LSTM in 1997, and both the transformer and sparsely gated experts in 2017. The Switch Transformer, another mixture of experts, and the state-space model S4 came in 2021, and Mamba followed in 2023.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · The architecture zoo
documents.body: This module compares six ways to wire a neural network layer: a dense layer, a convolution, a recurrent network, attention, a state-space model and a mixture of experts. Each is an architecture, a wiring fixed before training. The question it answers is what each wiring assumes about its input, such as locality or order, and what that costs in weights, sequential steps and memory. Built-in assumptions like these are an inductive bias, where bias means a prior, not a prejudice. Where it shows up Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) mix positions with attention. Causal attention reads only the current and earlier positions, and during generation it keeps a KV cache of their keys and values. LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) and GRU are recurrent networks whose gates let gradients survive many more steps than a plain recurrence. State-space models, sequence layers with a linear recurrent state update, include S4 (Gu et al., 2021) and Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023). Mixtures of experts include Mixtral 8x7B, which routes each token to 2 of 8 experts. Convolutions are the core of image convnets, which slide small learned kernels over colour images with many channels. When a model that generates text left to right uses convolutions, they are causal and see no later positions. Why it matters Each wiring pays its cost in a different place. A hop is one layer or step on the shortest path from an input to an output. Dense layer: every input reaches every output in one hop, but the weights grow with the square of the input size, and a pattern learned at one position does not transfer to another. Convolution: few weights, but distant inputs meet only after many layers. Recurrent network: steps must run in order, and the gradient can vanish across them, so early inputs barely affect learning. Attention: every earlier position is one hop away, but the KV cache grows with the context, while recurrent and state-space layers keep a fixed state. Mixture of experts: stored weights can grow while the weights each token uses stay fixed, though every expert must still sit in memory. What you will be able to explain Match convolution, recurrence and attention to the reuse pattern each one assumes, and to how many hops each needs between two positions. Treat a transformer as one architecture among several that map sequences to predictions, and say which of its parts mixes positions. Separate the weights a model stores from the weights each input actually uses, and say why adding experts grows only the first. What the lab shows Nothing here is trained; every readout is computed in closed form. Live filter, Unrolled RNN and Sparse experts read one 8×8 binary digit that you ink on Drawn digit, by clicking cells or with Selected cell and Flip selected cell. Live filter slides a hand-written 3×3 kernel, chosen with Filter, over the pad. Unrolled RNN runs a one-unit recurrent net with hand-set weights over the column means; Recurrent weight and the ink set its exact ∂h7/∂x gradient bars, and RNN step picks which one the formula multiplies out. Who sees whom draws, over a sequence of eight positions, which inputs each output sees and in how many hops. Wiring picks Dense MLP, Per-position MLP, Convolution, Recurrent, Attention or State-space; with Convolution, Conv layers stacks 1 to 7 layers of a centred kernel, which sees later positions. A cost table from formulas counts weights, sequential steps and memory. Sparse experts routes each pad column, as a token, to its top experts through an untrained router with seeded weights. Experts and Experts per token set the routing; Total expert weights, Active per token and Router weights count parameters. Four comparisons carry the outcomes: Switching Filter on Live filter, against Unrolled RNN: the same 9 weights reused at all 64 positions, against one recurrent weight reused at every step. Recurrent against Attention in Who sees whom: how many hops separate the same pair of positions. Attention against Per-position MLP: which part of a transformer block mixes positions. Raising Experts while Experts per token stays fixed: stored weights against the weights each token uses.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · The architecture zoo
documents.body: An architecture fixes two things before training: which weights are shared, and which activations can see which inputs. Those choices are the architecture's inductive bias. A dense layer gives every output its own weight to every input. Nothing is shared. A convolution reuses one small kernel at every position, and each output sees only its neighbourhood. A recurrent network reuses one update at every step and carries a fixed-size state forward, in order. Attention lets each position score every allowed position directly; a transformer block pairs it with a per-position MLP. A state-space model uses a linear recurrent update, so it trains with a parallel scan and generates with a fixed state. A mixture of experts stores many MLPs and runs only the top k of them for each token.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · The architecture zoo
documents.body: The previous lab showed that a big, regular matrix multiply suits a GPU. This lab shows that the multiply is not the whole design. The same weights can be wired to look locally, sequentially, or all at once, and each wiring makes some patterns cheap to learn and others expensive. It also keeps "transformer" in proportion. It is one wiring, attention plus a per-position MLP, not the definition of a neural net.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Locality and sharing Select a cell on Drawn digit and read its value in Live filter. The formula lists every nonzero pixel × weight product in its 3×3 window. Switch Filter between vertical edge, horizontal edge, and center blob: the ink is unchanged, the 9 shared weights are not. Recurrence Move RNN step and read the ∂h7/∂x bars. At Recurrent weight 0.90, column 1 reaches h7 with 0.009 and column 8 with 0.598. Wiring and experts In Who sees whom, compare Wiring options, and raise Conv layers. In Sparse experts, change Experts and Experts per token.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · The architecture zoo
documents.body: The kernel has 9 weights; a dense map from 64 pixels to 64 outputs needs 4,096. Each conv layer widens the receptive field by one position on each side, so joining positions 1 and 8 takes 7 layers of kernel 3. The RNN gradient is a product of per-step factors w·(1 − h²). Below one it vanishes; on a blank pad with w = 1.5 it grows to 1.5⁷ ≈ 17. Recurrent and Attention are both causal, so a position reads only itself and earlier ones. They see the same cells, but in 8 hops versus 1. Attention pays with a KV cache of 2·n·d numbers; recurrence and the SSM keep a fixed state. Going from 8 to 16 experts doubles Total expert weights and leaves Active per token unchanged.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · The architecture zoo
documents.body: In this lab. The kernels are hand-written, the RNN has one hidden unit with hand-set weights, and the expert router is untrained with seeded weights. The matrix and table come from formulas, not trained models. The convolution is centred, so it sees the future; text models use causal convolutions. In the real mechanism. Parameter counts and path lengths do not decide which architecture learns best; data, scale, and optimisation do. Gated RNNs (LSTM, GRU) carry gradients far longer than a plain tanh chain. Residual connections, normalisation, and many heads change what each wiring can learn in practice.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Attention and The transformer block open up the one-hop, all-to-all mixing drawn here, with a real trained model. Modern attention at scale covers the costs this table hints at: the KV cache, grouped-query attention, and sliding-window attention. Inference & KV cache measures how the 2·n·d column grows during generation. Named work: LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), the transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), sparsely gated experts (Shazeer et al., 2017), Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2021), S4 (Gu et al., 2021), and Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023). Mixtral 8x7B routes each token to 2 of 8 experts: 46.7B parameters stored, about 12.9B used per token.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Drawn digit · The architecture zoo
documents.body: An 8×8 image and one receptive field Sixty-four binary pixels that every other card reads: the filter slides over them, the RNN reads their columns left to right, and the expert router treats each column as a token. The outlined 3×3 window is the receptive field of the selected filter output. An 8×8 button grid; inked cells are filled. The default ink is a blocky 3. A blue outline on the 3×3 window around the selected cell, and a dot on the selected cell itself. Selected cell, a slider that names row and column, and Flip selected cell, the keyboard path for inking. State stores `pixels` as 64 characters of 0 or 1 and `cell` as an index 0–63. Clicking a cell or pressing Flip selected cell writes the opposite bit. The window is rows r−1 to r+1 and columns c−1 to c+1 of the selected cell, cut at the edges, because the filter pads with zeros. Click any cell, or move Selected cell and press Flip selected cell. Clicking a cell in the filter response also selects it here. Comparison worth running: select a cell, flip a pixel inside its window, then one outside it. Only the first changes that output. An output of one convolution layer can see 9 pixels and nothing else. Locality is built in before any training. In this lab: 8×8 binary ink that you author. No image file, dataset, or trained classifier is involved. In general: real convnets read colour images with many channels, and stacked layers grow the receptive field until deep units see most of the image.
documents.title: An 8×8 image and one receptive field

documents.subtitle: Live filter · The architecture zoo
documents.body: One kernel, reused at every position A 3×3 kernel is dotted with every 3×3 window of the pad. The same 9 weights produce all 64 outputs, which is weight sharing, and each output depends only on its own window, which is locality. Filter: vertical edge, horizontal edge, or center blob. The 3×3 kernel with signed weights, and an 8×8 grid of signed responses. Positive cells are tinted blue, negative cells orange, and the sign is always printed. A formula row that lists the nonzero pixel × weight products for the selected output, and metrics comparing 9 shared weights with a dense 64 → 64 layer. response[r][c] = Σ over the 3×3 window of pixel × kernel weight, with zeros outside the pad. As in deep-learning libraries, the kernel is not flipped (cross-correlation). Vertical edge is the Prewitt kernel [−1 0 +1] on each row; horizontal edge is its transpose; center blob is a Laplacian, +4 at the centre and −1 at the four neighbours. Tint strength is |response| divided by the largest |response| on the grid. Filter. Clicking a response cell selects it and outlines its window on the pad. Comparison worth running: vertical edge against horizontal edge on the default 3. The bars light up under horizontal edge, the right-hand stroke under vertical edge. The top bar and the bottom bar get the same-shaped response from the same weights. A pattern detector learned in one place works everywhere. A dense layer mapping 64 pixels to 64 outputs would need 4,096 weights and would have to learn the edge separately at every position. In this lab: three hand-written kernels. Nothing is learned; the heatmap is a closed-form dot product. In general: a real convnet learns dozens to hundreds of kernels per layer and stacks many layers. Locality still means distant pixels only meet after enough layers, or through pooling, dilation, or attention.
documents.title: One kernel, reused at every position

documents.subtitle: Unrolled RNN · The architecture zoo
documents.body: A chain of states, and a gradient that must cross every link A one-number recurrent net reads the eight column means in order: h_t = tanh(w·h_(t−1) + x_t). The gradient of the final state h7 with respect to an early input is a product of one factor per later step, so it shrinks or grows geometrically with distance. Recurrent weight w and RNN step t. Eight boxes h0 to h7 with the hidden value and the input x below it, tinted by |h|. The small ×factor above each arrow is w·(1 − h²) for that step; the links from the selected step to h7 are drawn in orange. Bars of the gradient ∂h7/∂x_t for every column, a formula row that multiplies out the selected one, and metrics Hidden, ∂h7/∂x for the selected column, Hops to h7, and Column mean. Inputs x_t are the fraction of inked pixels in column t + 1. h starts at 0; there is one weight on the input (fixed at 1) and one recurrent weight w. ∂h_t/∂h_(t−1) = w·(1 − h_t²). ∂h7/∂x_t = (1 − h_t²) × the product of that factor for every later step. A unit test checks it against a finite difference. Recurrent weight from 0 to 2 and RNN step from 0 to 7. Clicking a box or a bar also sets the step. Comparison worth running: at w = 0.90 read column 1 (about 0.009) against column 8 (about 0.6). Then clear the pad and set w = 1.5: with h stuck at 0 each factor is 1.5, and column 1's gradient explodes to 1.5⁷ ≈ 17. Saturation matters as much as w: when |h| nears 1, 1 − h² nears 0 and the chain goes quiet even for large w. Flipping a pixel in column 1 barely moves h7, which is what vanishing gradients mean for learning: early inputs get little credit. In this lab: a single hidden unit with hand-set weights, no training, no LSTM gates. In general: real RNNs have vector states and Jacobian matrices, so the product's size is governed by their singular values. LSTM and GRU gates add an additive path that keeps gradients alive much longer, and gradient clipping tames explosions.
documents.title: A chain of states, and a gradient that must cross every link

documents.subtitle: Who sees whom · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Connectivity: which inputs each output can use Each wiring is drawn as an 8×8 matrix over a sequence of eight positions: row t is an output, column s an input, and the number is how many layers or steps lie on the shortest path from s to t. The table beside it counts weights, sequential steps, and memory for each wiring. Wiring: Dense MLP, Per-position MLP, Convolution, Recurrent, Attention, State-space. Conv layers appears for Convolution. The matrix: filled cells marked 1 are reached in one hop, lighter numbered cells through a chain, dotted cells cannot be seen. A table at width d = 64, kernel k = 3, state size N = 16, with the current wiring highlighted. Dense MLP: every cell 1. Per-position MLP: the diagonal only. Convolution: |t − s| ≤ layers, needing max(1, |t − s|) layers. Attention: s ≤ t, all 1. Recurrent and State-space: s ≤ t, t − s + 1 steps. Weights per layer: (n·d)², 2·d·4d, k·d², 2·d² (input and recurrent matrices), 4·d² (query, key, value, output), and 3·d·N (diagonal A, B, C of an S4D-style layer). Biases are ignored. Kept to extend is what must be stored to add one more position: the window, nothing, (k − 1)·d per conv layer, the hidden state d, the KV cache 2·n·d, or the SSM state d·N, shown at n = 8 and n = 4,096. Wiring, and Conv layers from 1 to 7 when Convolution is selected. Comparison worth running: Recurrent against Attention. The same cells are visible, but attention reaches input 1 in 1 hop and recurrence in 8. Recurrent and State-space draw the same matrix. The difference is in the table: a linear state update can be trained with a parallel scan, and both keep a fixed-size state. Attention's one-hop reach costs a KV cache that grows from 1,024 to 524,288 numbers per layer between n = 8 and n = 4,096. A transformer block is Attention followed by a Per-position MLP: one mixes across positions, the other within each position. In this lab: connectivity and parameter formulas, not trained models. The convolution is centred (it sees the future); causal convolutions used for text shift the window left. In general: path length and memory are only part of the story. Real models add residual connections, multiple heads, gating, and position encodings, and which wiring learns best depends on data and scale.
documents.title: Connectivity: which inputs each output can use

documents.subtitle: Sparse experts · The architecture zoo
documents.body: Mixture of experts: stored weights versus active weights A mixture-of-experts layer replaces one MLP with E expert MLPs and a router. Each token runs through only its top k experts, weighted by a softmax over those k router scores. Memory grows with E; compute per token grows with k. Experts E from 2 to 16 and Experts per token k from 1 to 4. A routing table: one row per token (each pad column as an 8-number vector), one column per expert, with the gate percentage where a token is routed. The load row counts tokens per expert; zero is marked. Metrics Total expert weights, Active per token, and Router weights. Router scores = x·W + b with W (8 × 16) and b drawn from a fixed seeded generator; the first E columns are used. The top k scores are kept and softmaxed into gates, as in Mixtral. Each expert is a d → 4d → d MLP at d = 64: 2 × 64 × 256 = 32,768 weights. Total = E × 32,768, active = k × 32,768, router = 64 × E. Experts and Experts per token. Comparison worth running: raise Experts from 8 to 16 at k = 2. Total expert weights double to 524,288 while Active per token stays at 65,536. Identical pad columns always pick identical experts: routing is a deterministic function of the token. An untrained router leaves some experts idle. Stored, never used, which is why training adds a load-balancing loss. In this lab: an untrained router with seeded weights and no expert outputs; only the routing and the parameter arithmetic are computed. In general: the idea goes back to Shazeer et al. (2017) and Switch Transformer (k = 1, Fedus et al., 2021). Mixtral 8x7B has 46.7B parameters in total but uses about 12.9B per token, because attention and embeddings are shared. All experts must still sit in memory, and routing adds communication.
documents.title: Mixture of experts: stored weights versus active weights

documents.subtitle: Explore how each token compares its query with other tokens' keys, then mixes their values to bring relevant context into its representation.
documents.body: Explore how each token compares its query with other tokens' keys, then mixes their values to bring relevant context into its representation. Distinguish queries, keys, and values Read an attention pattern without over-interpreting it Tell a head that follows content from one that reads a fixed distance Explain what the causal mask changes and how encoder and decoder-only models differ Say why scores are divided by the square root of the head dimension
documents.title: Attention

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Attention
documents.body: Click a word chip in the arc diagram to make it the query, then read its strongest route and its On spaces share in the readout strip.
documents.title: Choose a query

documents.subtitle: Step 2 · Attention
documents.body: Click a heatmap cell, then compare the Q and K chips and find the inspected key's outlined characters in the score strip.
documents.title: Compare keys

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Attention
documents.body: Step through Score and Softmax: watch scaled scores become weights in the strip, and check that the Softmax row matches the model's own value. Then set Score scaling to No scaling and compare Largest weight and Saturated rows with and without the division.
documents.title: Scale and normalize

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · Attention
documents.body: Step to Mix and read the Mixed value chip. Set Value vectors (V) to Zero all and watch the weights stay put while the Mixed value falls to zero, then try Zero word on a key with a large weight.
documents.title: Mix values

documents.subtitle: Step 5 · Attention
documents.body: In the Attention matrix card set Mask to Bidirectional, then read on later characters in the readout strip and watch the earlier cells shrink. Compare Layer 1 head 3 with Layer 2 head 4, then set Mask back to Causal.
documents.title: Lift the mask

documents.subtitle: Step 6 · Attention
documents.body: Press Pronoun sentence and move the Attention head slider through both layers with it as the query: no head's strongest route is animal. Then press Repeated name, set Layer 2 and head 3, and press Name moved earlier to see whether the route follows the content. Finish with Repeats every 8 and Repeats every 9 in the Characters view and compare which heads' stripes move.
documents.title: Test a route

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: The projected vector describing what the current position is looking for. It is compared against keys and never carries the retrieved payload itself.
documents.title: Query

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: The projected vector advertising what a position can offer. Query-key alignment sets the score, so keys decide who gets read, not what is read.
documents.title: Key

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: The projected vector actually mixed into the output. A high attention weight moves this content; the score alone says nothing about what it contains.
documents.title: Value

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: The normalized share controlling how much one value contributes to one query's output. Every query's weights sum to one, so routes compete.
documents.title: Attention weight

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: One independent query, key, and value projection set. Heads specialize during training, but rarely into cleanly describable roles.
documents.title: Attention head

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: The query-key dot product divided by the square root of the head dimension. Without the division the scores grow with width, softmax saturates toward a one-hot row, and its gradients shrink; the lab can switch the division off at inference to show the saturation, which is not the same as training without it.
documents.title: Scaled dot product

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: Adding minus infinity to the scores of later positions before softmax, so their weights are exactly zero and the matrix is triangular. It lets every position train in parallel on next-token prediction without seeing its own answer; the lab can lift it for one head, but this model was trained with it.
documents.title: Causal mask

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: Several heads run in parallel on the same input, their outputs concatenated and passed through the output projection. Splitting one wide head into several narrow ones costs about the same arithmetic.
documents.title: Multi-head attention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: The learned matrix applied to the concatenated head outputs before they are added back to the residual stream. It decides how retrieved content is written.
documents.title: Output projection

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: The width of one head's query, key, and value vectors, usually the model width divided by the head count (256 over 4 gives 64 here). It is the d in the scaling factor.
documents.title: Head dimension

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: The matrix of weights for one head and layer. It is evidence about routing, not an explanation of behavior: a route can come from position alone, and patterns can sometimes be altered without changing output.
documents.title: Attention pattern

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: A head that attends from a repeated token to the token that followed its earlier occurrence, so it can copy what came next. In the usual two-layer circuit it is fed by a previous-token head in an earlier layer, and in larger models its appearance coincides with better in-context learning.
documents.title: Induction head

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: A head whose weight sits almost entirely on the position just before the query, copying that character's information one step forward. In a two-layer model it can hand a layer-2 induction head the identity of each position's predecessor.
documents.title: Previous-token head

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: A position, often the first token, that absorbs large attention weight when a head has nothing useful to retrieve. Evicting it from a cache degrades output.
documents.title: Attention sink

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: Sharing one key and value pair across several query heads to shrink the KV cache, trading a small amount of quality for a large memory saving.
documents.title: Grouped-query attention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: A transformer stack with bidirectional attention: no causal mask, so the weight matrix is a full square and every position reads both earlier and later ones. It builds a representation of a whole input, for classification or search, but cannot be trained on next-token prediction because each position could see its own answer.
documents.title: Encoder

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: A stack with causal attention, so each position reads only itself and earlier positions (a triangular matrix), trained to predict the next token at every position. This lab's model and most current chat models are of this kind, and they generate by feeding each new token back in.
documents.title: Decoder-only (causal) language model

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: A bidirectional model trained by hiding some tokens and predicting them from the visible tokens on both sides, as BERT does. A causal language model learns to continue text left to right; a masked one learns to fill gaps, which suits understanding better than free-form generation.
documents.title: Masked language model

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Attention
documents.body: A signal about each token's slot, because attention alone cannot tell order. Absolute schemes add a learned or sinusoidal vector to the input; relative schemes such as ALiBi bias the scores by distance; rotary embeddings rotate queries and keys. This lab's model uses learned absolute vectors.
documents.title: Positional encoding

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Attention · question 1
documents.body: You edit the K chip of the inspected word and leave every V vector alone. What can change in the Mixed value for the current query? That position's own value vector, because the key and the value are two views of the same projection Only the weights, and so how much of each value is mixed in, because keys decide who gets read Nothing, because a key only changes the score readout and the mix is built from values alone Query-key alignment sets the scores, softmax turns them into weights, and the mix is a weighted sum of the unchanged value vectors. Editing a key therefore moves the mix by changing who is read and how much, never what each value contains. Keys and values are separate learned projections of the same input.
documents.title: You edit the K chip of the inspected word and leave every V vector alone. What can change in the Mixed value for the current query?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Attention · question 2
documents.body: You set Value vectors (V) to Zero all and look at the strip and the Mixed value. What do you see? The weights stay exactly as before and the Mixed value is zero, since Q and K set the weights and V is the payload Every weight falls to zero as well, because a zero value leaves nothing for the attention to route to anyone at all The weights spread out evenly, because identical values make every key equally useful to the query mix The weights are computed from queries and keys before any value is read, so zeroing V cannot move them. The mix is the weighted sum of the values, so with every value zero it is the zero vector whatever the weights are. A heavy weight on a key whose value carries nothing moves nothing, which is why a weight alone never says what was retrieved.
documents.title: You set Value vectors (V) to Zero all and look at the strip and the Mixed value. What do you see?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Attention · question 3
documents.body: With Pronoun sentence loaded, Layer 1 and head 3 selected, the query it sends nearly all its weight to the word it. What is the sound reading? The head has decided the pronoun refers to itself, because the heaviest arc marks what a word means to the model A stripe one place below the diagonal in the Characters view shows the head reads the previous character, inside it The head is broken, because a working head would send its weight to a different word than the query does A weight is routing evidence, not a reason. This head puts its weight on the character just before the query, and for the word it that character is the i, so the word view credits the word it. The same sentence gives no head a strongest route from it to animal, so a pronoun is not being resolved by a visible arc.
documents.title: With Pronoun sentence loaded, Layer 1 and head 3 selected, the query it sends nearly all its weight to the word it. What is the sound reading?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Attention · question 4
documents.body: On Repeated name, Layer 2 and head 3, the second Mark sends most of its weight to Jones. What does that pattern establish? That the model knows who Mark is, because the heaviest arc lands on the surname that belongs to him in the text it read That the output depends on this head, because a heavy weight means the model used that head's value for its answer That this route is worth testing, but showing the head matters takes an intervention such as switching it off The pattern is a hypothesis about routing: the head sends weight to the word after the earlier Mark. It does not show what the value carried, whether later layers kept it, or whether the output used it. Switching the head off and measuring the loss is the kind of intervention that can show it mattered, and even that has limits.
documents.title: On Repeated name, Layer 2 and head 3, the second Mark sends most of its weight to Jones. What does that pattern establish?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Attention · question 5
documents.body: A head's stripes sit 7, 15 and 23 characters back on Repeats every 8. You press Repeats every 9. How do you tell a copying head from a fixed-distance one? A copying head's stripes move to 8, 17 and 26 back, since it seeks the character after the earlier match; a fixed-distance head's stay put Compare how dark the stripes are at one period, because a copying head always puts more weight on the right character than a distance habit does Check that the head lands on the correct next character at period 8, because only a head that copies can do that, whatever its offset is A head that copies attends to the successor of the earlier occurrence, so its stripes follow the period. A head with a fixed offset keeps its stripes at that distance and only looks right when the period happens to match it. Landing on the correct next character at one period cannot separate the two, which is why the method is to change the period.
documents.title: A head's stripes sit 7, 15 and 23 characters back on Repeats every 8. You press Repeats every 9. How do you tell a copying head from a fixed-distance one?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Attention · question 6
documents.body: Layer 1 head 3 reads the previous character whatever the text says. What makes a rule that depends on distance possible at all? The causal mask only allows keys at fixed offsets from each query, so distance is built into it The value vectors store how far back each character sits and the mix reads that number out Position information is added to the token vectors, so queries and keys can depend on the slot The dot product sees only vectors, so a head can use distance only if the vectors carry the slot. This model adds a learned vector for each of its 64 positions to the token vector, which lets query and key encode where they are; with those vectors zeroed the stripes of its four Layer 1 heads collapse. The causal mask only blocks later positions, and values carry content.
documents.title: Layer 1 head 3 reads the previous character whatever the text says. What makes a rule that depends on distance possible at all?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Attention · question 7
documents.body: You set Mask to Bidirectional. What happens to the weights a query had already given to earlier characters? They stay exactly as they were, because lifting the mask only adds new cells to the grid and leaves the old ones alone They all shrink by the same factor, because the row still sums to 100% and some weight moves to later characters They grow, because the head can now use more context to confirm which of the earlier characters really matter here Softmax divides by the sum over every readable key. Lifting the mask adds keys to that sum, so the denominator grows and every earlier weight is multiplied by the same factor, one minus the weight now on later characters. Ratios among the earlier keys do not change; only their share of the row does.
documents.title: You set Mask to Bidirectional. What happens to the weights a query had already given to earlier characters?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Attention · question 8
documents.body: You set Mask to Bidirectional and a Layer 2 head puts much of its weight on later characters. What does that show? How a BERT-style encoder would read the sentence, because lifting the mask turns this whole model into one of those That the model peeks at later text when it generates, because generation reads the whole sentence at once anyway What this head scores for pairs it never trained on: what a bidirectional layer could read, not a trained one The model was trained with the causal mask, so nothing ever asked this head to score a later key. Lifting the mask at inference shows its raw scores for those pairs, and Layer 2's queries and keys still come from a causal Layer 1. A trained encoder learns different scores because it is trained with every position visible.
documents.title: You set Mask to Bidirectional and a Layer 2 head puts much of its weight on later characters. What does that show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Attention · question 9
documents.body: Why is a decoder-only model trained on next-token prediction with the causal mask on? Each position could otherwise attend to the token it must predict, so the loss could fall by copying the answer Later tokens do not exist yet during training, so there would be nothing for any query to attend to in its own row Without the mask each row of weights would no longer sum to one, so softmax would be undefined for those whole rows Training sees the whole text at once, so the later tokens do exist. Without the mask the position before an answer could read the answer itself, and next-token prediction would be solved by copying it. An encoder avoids this by training on a different task, filling hidden tokens from both sides, which is what a masked language model does.
documents.title: Why is a decoder-only model trained on next-token prediction with the causal mask on?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Attention · question 10
documents.body: You switch Score scaling to No scaling on a trained head. What happens to its rows?
