Nothing changes, because softmax gives the same weights whatever the overall size of all the scores is The scores are 8 times larger, so softmax pushes many rows onto one character and Saturated rows rises The scores shrink, so softmax flattens each row toward equal weights and the Largest weight metric falls Softmax is not scale-free: multiplying every score by 8 makes the largest score dominate far more. Removing the division leaves the raw dot product, which is the square root of the head dimension times larger. This shows saturation in a model trained with the division; it does not show training without it, where the original authors suspect small gradients would be the problem.
documents.title: You switch Score scaling to No scaling on a trained head. What happens to its rows?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Attention
documents.body: Read this sentence from the lab: “The animal did not cross the street because it was tired.” You knew right away that it means the animal and not the street, because you linked one word to another word several places earlier in the sentence. A language model, the kind of program behind a chatbot, has to make links like this for every word it reads. To guess what comes next, a word often needs information from somewhere else in the text, such as the name that a pronoun stands for. It might instead need the opening bracket that a closing bracket belongs to, or the pattern that a few earlier examples set up. The part of the model that fetches that information is called attention, and this module shows you how it works, one small step at a time. In a single breath: every word sends out a search request. It compares that request with what each earlier word has to offer, which gives each one a match score. The word then takes in a blend of information from the words that match best. None of these links is wired in ahead of time, because the model works them out fresh for every sentence it reads. That means the same word can draw on different neighbours in different sentences. Where you have met it Most of today’s chat models are the same kind of model as the tiny one in this lab. They read text in one direction, from left to right, and they learned by guessing the next piece of text over and over again. Suppose a chatbot keeps track of who “she” is in your message, or carries on a list in the same format that you started. In both cases, attention is the part of the model that lets each word reach back to earlier words for the information it needs. Why it matters In a model like this one, attention is the only step that lets one word take information from another. Without it, every word would be stuck with what it knew about itself and its place in the line. The model’s guesses about the next word would then be far worse, because what helps a guess usually sits somewhere else in the text. Attention also changed the way models are trained, and that matters nearly as much. It lets a model practise guessing what comes next at every spot in a long text at the same time. Older models had to work through the text one spot after another. That is a big reason it became practical to train very large models at all. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these ideas in your own words: the search slip, label and packet that every word makes, and why the slip and label decide where information comes from while the packet carries it; how to read a picture of attention carefully, since a thick line shows where information could flow, not why the model answered as it did; how to tell a part of the model that follows the text’s content from one that always looks a fixed number of characters back, spaces included; what the one-way rule changes, since it stops a word from reading later words, and how models that read in both directions differ from this one; why each match score gets divided by 8 before it becomes a share, why 8 is the right number here, and what goes wrong when that step is skipped. What the lab lets you do The lab runs a real, very small model that was trained on the plays of Shakespeare. With the model’s own settings, the numbers you see are measured straight from that model, rather than taken from a cartoon of how attention might work. You can pick a word and watch lines fan out to the words it draws from. You can also see a grid of links for every word at once. You can also step through the arithmetic behind any single link, one stage at a time. Three switches let you break the machinery on purpose and watch what changes as a result. One stops the match scores from being shrunk, one empties out the information being passed along, and one lets a word read ahead to later words. When you flip a switch or type in your own numbers, the lab works out new results from the model’s numbers. You are then looking at an experiment, not at the model as it was trained. A few things are fixed or made up rather than measured, starting with the example sentences, which were chosen for this lesson. About 3 in every 10 of the model’s practice texts were made up on purpose, from a short string repeated over and over. If the model fails to load, the lab shows stand-in numbers that mean nothing, and it tells you so. One warning before you start: in this small model, the line from it to animal is always thin. No part of the model makes it the strongest link or gives it even 10 percent of the attention of it, even though you made that connection instantly. Working out why is part of the lesson, and it is a good reminder that these pictures need careful reading.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Attention
documents.body: Words as lists of numbers Inside the model, every character of your sentence is stored as a long list of numbers that describes it. A list of numbers like this is called a vector, a bit like a player’s stats in a sports game, where each number rates one skill. The model’s vectors differ in one important way: nobody decided what each number stands for. The model settled on its numbers itself during training, a long practice period in which it guessed the next character over and over. After each round of guesses, it nudged all its numbers a little, so that its next guesses would come out better. This model reads characters, meaning letters, spaces and punctuation marks, rather than whole words, so every character gets its own vector. For most of this lesson we will talk about words, since the lab’s main views group characters that way, and return to characters when they matter. Three things on every desk Picture a classroom where every word of the sentence sits at its own desk, in order from left to right. Each desk holds three different items, and each item has an official name that the lab and the glossary use: A search slip describes what this word is looking for in the rest of the sentence, and its official name is the query. A label pinned to the front of the desk advertises what this word can offer to others, and its official name is the key. A packet in the drawer holds the information that actually gets handed over, and its official name is the value. Every word, every time, compares its search slip with the label on every desk it is allowed to see, including its own desk. Labels that match the slip well receive a high score, while poor matches receive a low one. Those scores are then turned into shares that add up to 100 percent. Finally, the word receives a blend of everyone’s packets, in which each packet counts exactly as much as its share. All three items are vectors, and the model calculates all three from the same starting vector, using three separate sets of learned numbers. Each set works like a separate recipe, so a word’s label can differ from its packet. Training shaped the label for being matched and the packet for being useful once it arrives. Keep this split of jobs in mind for the rest of the lesson, because the lab keeps returning to it. The query and the key decide who gets read, while the value decides what gets read. The lab has a switch that tests this split directly, which you will try in How to play with it. The five stages The lab walks through one word’s search in five stages, named on the buttons in the first card: Query, Keys, Score, Softmax and Mix. Each stage below gives the idea first and then a small example that you can check by hand. In the Query stage, you choose the word whose search you want to follow by clicking its chip in the Model attention routing diagram card. A chip is one of the small boxes that hold each word, and the word you click becomes the query. The Q chip in the Query key value inspector card then displays the first four numbers of that word’s query. In the Keys stage, every word that the query is allowed to see presents its key, the label on the front of its desk. The K chip displays the first four numbers of the key belonging to whichever word you are inspecting, which the lab calls the inspected key. You choose which word to inspect by clicking a cell in the Attention matrix grid, as How to play with it shows. In the Score stage, the query is compared with every key using a calculation called the dot product, which takes two steps. First you multiply the two lists position by position, and then you add up all of the answers. Here is a short example with four numbers in each list, matching the four numbers that each chip displays. Suppose the query is (2, −1, 0, 3) and the key is (1, 2, 5, 1): first position: 2 × 1 = 2 second position: −1 × 2 = −2 third position: 0 × 5 = 0 fourth position: 3 × 1 = 3 Adding the four answers gives a score of 3, since the −2 from the second position cancels the 2 from the first and leaves the 3 from the fourth. Whenever the two numbers in a position have the same sign, they increase the score, and whenever their signs are opposite, they decrease it. A high score therefore means that the two lists tend to agree across many positions, which is what a good match looks like in numbers. The inspector shows its working as a stack of labelled lines, like the lines of a worked answer in a maths test. The real lists in this model are 64 numbers long, so the Score line adds up 64 products rather than four. It shows the total next to q · k, which is how the lab writes the dot product of a query and a key. The Score stage does one more thing, and it does it to the query’s whole row of scores, meaning its score with every character it can see. Every score is divided by 8, because each list in this model is 64 numbers long and 8 is the square root of 64. The Scale line shows this step as score ÷ √64, and it gets its own section below, because it matters more than it looks. In the Softmax stage, the scaled scores are turned into shares that are all positive and add up to 100 percent. The tool that does this is called softmax, and the lab writes its formula as exp(s) ÷ Σ exp(s). In that formula, s is one score, and exp(s) means a special number, about 2.718, raised to the power s. The Greek letter Σ, called sigma, means “add this up for every character the query can see”. Put into words, softmax turns every score into a positive number and then divides each one by the total of them all. Try it with three scores, 2, 1 and 0, and turn each one into a positive number first: The score 2 becomes 2.718 × 2.718, which is about 7.39. The score 1 becomes 2.718 itself, which rounds to 2.72. The score 0 becomes exactly 1, because any number raised to the power 0 equals 1. Those three numbers add up to about 11.11, and dividing by that total gives each score its share. The top score gets 7.39 ÷ 11.11, which is about 66.5 percent of the row. The middle score gets about 24.5 percent and the bottom score about 9 percent, so together the three shares make 100 percent. Negative scores work too, and real scores are often negative, so it helps to know that a power below zero means dividing instead of multiplying. The score −1 becomes 1 ÷ 2.718, which is about 0.37, and the score −2 becomes 1 ÷ 7.39, which is about 0.14. The more negative the score, the closer the result gets to zero, but it never reaches zero. Scores with decimals land in between, so a score of 1.5 becomes about 4.48. Two features of softmax matter for everything that follows in this lesson. Every share is positive, because 2.718 raised to any power is above zero, so even a low-scoring character gets a sliver of the row. Softmax also cares a great deal about the gaps between scores, because each step of 1 multiplies rather than adds. A gap of 1 makes one share about 2.7 times the other, and a gap of 2 makes it about 2.7 × 2.7, or 7.4, times the other. A gap of 8 means multiplying by 2.7 eight times over, which comes to about 3,000. These shares are called attention weights, and each one tells you how much of one word’s value ends up in the query’s blend. In the Mix stage, the query collects every value it is allowed to see and blends them together, with each value counting exactly as much as its attention weight. A blend like this is called a weighted average, and you have probably met one already in a class grade. Say a test counts for 75 percent of your grade and a quiz counts for the other 25 percent. You score 80 on the test and 100 on the quiz. Three quarters of 80 is 60 and one quarter of 100 is 25, so your grade for the class works out to 85. Attention does the same calculation with whole lists of numbers instead of single marks, multiplying every number in a value by that value’s weight. Suppose the query gives 75 percent of its weight to a value holding (4, 0) and 25 percent to a value holding (0, 8). Three quarters of the first value is (3, 0) and one quarter of the second is (0, 2). Adding them position by position gives (3 + 0, 0 + 2), so the blend is (3, 2). The lab shows the first four numbers of the real blend, out of 64, in the Mixed value chip. The Mix length readout turns the whole blend into one number that says how big its numbers are overall. To get it, square every number in the blend, add up the squares, and take the square root. For the blend (3, 2), that is √(9 + 4), which is about 3.6. The readout is 0 only when every number in the blend is 0, because any other number has a square above 0. Heads and layers Everything so far describes one attention head: one complete set of the three recipes, with its own learned numbers. This model has four heads working side by side, and each one makes its own slips, labels and packets from the same text. Running several heads side by side like this, so that one sentence can be routed in four different ways at once, is called multi-head attention. Each head’s lists are 64 numbers long in this model, and that length is called the head dimension. The model also has two layers, one after the other, so attention happens twice on the way through. Layer 1 works on the character vectors as they come in and passes updated vectors on to Layer 2, whose four heads then do their own fetching. That makes eight heads in all, and you choose one with the Layer buttons and the Attention head slider at the top of the Query key value inspector card. The grid of attention weights for one head in one layer, showing how every word shares out its attention, is called an attention pattern. The Attention matrix card draws it, with one row for each query word and one column for each key word. Why divide by 8? The divide-by-8 step looks like tidy bookkeeping, but it decides how the shares come out. To see why, picture a game where you flip a coin 64 times, adding 1 to your total for every heads and taking away 1 for every tails. Most of the flips cancel each other out, so your total almost never ends up anywhere near 64. In about three games out of four it lands within 8 of zero, on one side or the other, and it rarely lands more than 16 away. Now change the number of flips. With 16 flips the total usually lands within about 4 of zero, while with 256 flips it usually lands within about 16. How far from zero the total usually lands is called its spread, and four times as many flips only doubles the spread. That is the square-root pattern: √16 = 4, √64 = 8 and √256 = 16. A dot product behaves the same way when the numbers in both lists are about the size of 1 and their signs look random. Each of the 64 positions then adds a product of about size 1, sometimes positive and sometimes negative, like one coin flip. So the score usually lands within about 8 of zero, while lists of 256 numbers would give scores that usually land within about 16. Dividing by the square root of the head dimension brings the typical score back to a size of about 1, however long the lists are. That pattern holds for lists of random-looking numbers, but a trained head can still learn bigger scores on purpose, as you will see in Layer 1. The size of the scores matters because softmax turns gaps between scores into huge differences in share. Go back to the three scores 2, 1 and 0, which gave shares of about 66.5, 24.5 and 9 percent. Now make them 8 times bigger, so they become 16, 8 and 0. The top score now takes more than 99.9 percent of the row, which leaves almost nothing for the other two. When one character takes 99 percent or more of a row, the lab calls that row saturated. A saturated row has stopped blending, because it hands over one value and ignores almost everything else. A dot product divided by the square root of the head dimension is called a scaled dot product. The lab’s Score scaling switch lets you turn the division off and watch rows saturate for yourself. The one-way rule In this model, a word may read itself and the words before it, but it may never read the words after it, and this rule is called the causal mask. It is called a mask because it covers up later words, and causal because each word may only use what came before it, as a cause comes before its effect. The mask works by changing the scores before softmax runs: the score for every later character is set to minus infinity, written −∞, which is lower than any number. That makes it the one exception to “every share is positive”, because 2.718 raised to −∞ shrinks all the way to zero. The later character’s share therefore comes out as exactly zero. The lab draws those blocked spots with diagonal stripes, called hatching, and the Scale line says masked if you inspect one. Because each row can only reach back, the grid in the Attention matrix card is a triangle rather than a square. The diagonal runs from the top-left to the bottom-right corner, where each word or character meets itself, and the corner above it, where later words would sit, stays empty. The diagonal also lets you read distances. In the Characters view, a stripe of dark cells just below the diagonal, one cell to the left of it in every row, means each character looks 1 back. A stripe 7 cells to the left of the diagonal means each character looks 7 back. To see why the rule exists, remember that this model learned by guessing each next character in a 64-character piece of text, called a window, seen all at once. Picture a practice quiz where the answer to each question is printed right underneath it. You could score 100 percent by copying the line below each question, and you would learn nothing at all. Without the one-way rule, the model would be in the same position, because the spot before each answer could read the answer directly. For example, when the model reads “the cat”, the spot holding c has to guess that a comes next. Without the rule, the c could read the a one seat to its right and copy it. The mask hides every answer from the position that has to guess it. That is what makes all-at-once practice fair. Without the mask, the only fair way to practise would be to run the model 64 separate times. Each time, it would see only the text up to the spot it has to guess. With the mask, the model takes in the whole window in one run, and every spot still has to guess its next character without seeing it. One run then gives 64 fair guesses to learn from. Attention lets those 64 guesses be worked out side by side, and the mask keeps them honest. The rule is a design choice, not a law of nature, and keeping it or dropping it divides language models into families: An encoder drops the rule, so every word may look both backward and forward, and its grid is a full square. Reading in both directions like this is called bidirectional attention, and encoders use it to understand a whole text at once. That suits jobs such as sorting emails into spam and not spam, or finding the pages that best match a search. A decoder-only (causal) language model keeps the rule and learns to guess the next piece of text at every position. This lab’s model is one, and so are most of today’s chat models, which write by guessing one piece, adding it to the end, and running again. The name comes from an older design with two halves: an encoder that read the input and a decoder that wrote the output. A decoder-only model keeps only the writing half. An encoder cannot practise by guessing the next word, because every position could see its own answer, so it needs a different practice task. A masked language model is an encoder that practises by covering some words in the middle of a text with a blank. It then guesses them from the words on both sides. A well-known model called BERT works this way, and this kind of practice suits understanding text better than writing it. Be careful with that name, because “masked” here means words hidden behind a blank, which is a different thing from the causal mask. A masked language model has no causal mask at all. The lab’s Mask control can lift the one-way rule for one head so you can see what that head would read. Doing so does not turn this model into an encoder, as Where it breaks explains. Where position comes from The desk story has a gap: nothing on a label says which desk it sits at, so shuffling the desks would leave every match with the same score. Attention on its own therefore could not tell “the dog bit the man” from “the man bit the dog”. The one-way rule leaks a little information about order, because a word near the start can see only a few words while a word near the end can see many. The transformer block lab measures how much. Models close the gap by giving every desk its seat number in some form, so that position becomes part of the calculation. Any way of doing this is called a positional encoding, and four kinds are common: Learned seat numbers (used by GPT-2, an older text-writing model, and by this lab’s model): the model learns one list of numbers for each seat. It adds that list to the vector of whatever character sits there. There is no list for a seat past the last one, so the model has a fixed longest input, which is 64 characters here. Wave-pattern seat numbers (used by the Transformer, the 2017 design that first built a model around attention): each seat gets a fixed pattern made from waves, with nothing to learn. Models that use this kind tend to work poorly on texts longer than the ones they trained on. A distance penalty (ALiBi): instead of seat numbers, the match score between two words is lowered more the farther apart they are, so nearby words tend to win. A twist (RoPE, used by Llama models and many other recent ones): each slip and label is turned by an amount set by its seat, like turning a clock hand. The match still depends on what the slip and label say. The seat part of the match, though, depends only on how far apart the two words sit, not on where in the text they are. Modern attention at scale shows how it works. This lab’s model uses the first kind, and you can see the result in its heads. A head can prefer to look a fixed distance back only if its slips and labels carry the seat number. Some heads in Layer 1 here do exactly that, looking 1, 2 or 3 characters back on every text this lesson tries. Those heads put between 66 and 100 percent of their weight at that fixed distance. If the learned seat numbers are wiped to zero, that share falls to under 6 percent. What is actually running With the model’s own settings, none of this is a simulation: the lab runs a real, very small trained model and reads every vector and route straight out of it. The three switches and the editable chips work out new results from those same vectors. The model has two layers of four heads and about 1.4 million learned numbers, called parameters, which were all set during training. The badge at the top of the first card starts with ONNX model once the model is running, since ONNX is the file format it is stored in. While the model loads, the badge says Loading teaching model…, and if loading fails, it says Model unavailable · inspectable fallback. In both cases the lab shows stand-in values from a fixed wave pattern with no learned meaning, and a note in the Attention matrix card tells you so. The model practised on Shakespeare for 8,000 rounds of training, called steps, and each step gave it a batch of windows to guess its way through. The first 90 percent of the text was used for practice, and over all those steps the model went through it about 23 times. The last 10 percent was kept aside, so the model could be tested on lines it had never seen. About 30 percent of the practice windows were not ordinary Shakespeare text. In every batch of 64 windows, 19 were made-up repeats: a short string, sometimes random symbols and sometimes a snippet of the play text, repeated over and over. They were put in on purpose, so the model would meet lots of repetition and have a reason to learn copying. Each string repeated every 4 to 31 characters. Repeats of 11, 13, 17 and 19 characters were left out on purpose, so they could be used later to test the model on something new. The model knows 66 different symbols, such as letters, punctuation marks and the space. The Words view is one of two settings on the Matrix view control. It adds up the shares of each word’s characters, and it counts the space in front of a word as part of that word. For example, the Words cell for animal adds together the shares on the space before it and on a, n, i, m, a and l. A word’s row is the row of its last character, so the row for it is really the row for its t. Under the one-way rule, that t is the first spot that has seen the whole word. Every character that row can see, spaces included, belongs to exactly one word, so a row’s word totals still add up to exactly 100 percent. The Characters view shows the grid the model really works with, with one row and one column for every character.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Attention
documents.body: Start with the information a word holds before attention runs, which is less than you might expect. Take the t at the end of it. Before attention runs, its vector says only something like “I am a t, and I sit at this seat in the line”. Nothing in it says that an animal appeared earlier, that someone is tired, or even that the letter before it was an i. Guessing what comes next from that alone would be like guessing the next word of a story from a single letter. Picture opening a group chat where the newest message says “she said yes!!” and nothing else. To make sense of it, you scroll back up through the conversation to find out who “she” is and what the original question was. Each word in a model faces the same problem, and attention is how it looks back through the earlier text for what it needs. Some of the fetching is very simple: Layer 1 heads 3 and 4, which you will meet later, look exactly one character back. So after Layer 1, the t can carry information about the i before it, and later heads can build on that. Looking things up by content The important feature is that this looking back is organised by content rather than by fixed wiring. A word has no permanent connection to “three words back” or to “the first word of the sentence”. Instead, its query is compared with every key it can see, and the resulting scores decide where its information comes from. As a result, the same head can pull information from the previous word in one sentence and from a word thirty places back in another. Some heads do learn a fixed-distance habit, as you will see, but they learn it from the seat numbers, not from wiring. After training, the model’s parameters never change again, yet the routes are calculated fresh for every sentence, because they depend on which queries match which keys in that text. That is the whole trick: a fixed set of learned numbers, used to build new connections every time. Doing it all at once Attention also solved a second problem, which was about speed rather than understanding. Older language models, called recurrent models, read text strictly in order and squeezed everything they had read into a single memory of fixed size. That is a bit like remembering a whole book by rewriting one index card after every page. On a single card the details get crowded out, and you cannot start page 50 until you have finished page 49. During training, attention works out the scores for every position at the same time, so none of that work has to wait its turn. The one-way rule keeps that fair, since each spot still has to guess its next character without seeing it. The powerful chips used to train models are built to do huge numbers of small calculations side by side. Attention finally let language models use those chips fully, and that is a large part of why training on huge amounts of text became practical.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Attention
documents.body: The lab opens on the pronoun sentence, “The animal did not cross the street because it was tired”. It starts on Layer 2 head 2, with it as the query and animal as the inspected key. The experiments below build on each other, so try them in order the first time you work through the lab. Follow one word Click any word chip in the Model attention routing diagram card to make that word the query. Curved lines called arcs fan out from it to the other words, and a thicker arc represents a bigger attention weight. Later words get only a very faint, thin line, because the one-way rule gives them no weight at all. The query has no arc to itself, so its weight on itself shows only in the bar under its chip, while the bars under the other chips show their weights. The readout strip underneath names the query, the inspected key, the strongest route and its weight. It also shows how much of the row lands on spaces, a number that needs careful reading, as What to notice explains. With it as the query in Layer 2 head 2, the strongest route goes to because rather than to animal, which is worth remembering. Try this: Keep it as the query and move the Attention head slider through all four heads with Layer set to *Layer 1*. Then do the same with *Layer 2*, and notice that the sentence never changes while the routes do. In Layer 1, head 1 sends most of the weight of it to because. Heads 2, 3 and 4 pile it onto it itself, for reasons you will see below. In Layer 2, the four heads’ strongest routes go to it, because, cross and it. Each head has its own learned numbers for making queries and keys, so each one routes the sentence its own way, though two heads can learn almost the same habit. Check the arithmetic for one pair Click a cell in the grid of the Attention matrix card, where darker cells represent bigger attention weights. Each cell’s row is the query word and its column is the key word, so a single cell describes one pair of words. Clicking sets both words at once and jumps the stages to Score, so the Query key value inspector card shows the arithmetic for that pair. Now step from Score to Softmax and look at the strip in the inspector, which draws the whole row twice. The top band shows each score as a bar that rises above its zero line when the score is positive and drops below it when the score is negative. The bottom band shows each share as a bar, and shares are never negative. The inspected word’s characters are outlined, and later characters are hatched out by the mask, since the query cannot read them. The band titles write the head dimension as d, so √d means √64, which is 8. The Softmax line works out the share for one pair of characters itself. It uses the model’s full query and keys, all 64 numbers of each, not only the four on screen. It then prints the model’s own figure beside it. Next to that, it shows the largest gap between the lab’s sums and the model’s own figures anywhere in the row, written in a short form such as 2.4e-7. That form means 0.00000024, so every share in the row agrees to within about one part in a million. That shows you are looking at the real arithmetic. Two readouts look alike but measure different things, so it is worth telling them apart. Selected score is the scaled score for one pair of characters: the last character of the query word and the last character of the inspected word. Selected weight is the share for the whole word, all its characters plus the space in front, which is the number the grid cell shows. A single character can get a tiny share while its word’s total is large, because the weight is spread across the word’s characters. If you prefer reading numbers to reading shades, open View weights as text under the grid for a list of the current row. Edit a key The Q and K chips are editable, which lets you test how a change to a single key spreads through the whole row. Type a different number into one of the four boxes in the K chip. Then watch the arcs, the bars under the word chips, or the list under View weights as text. Every share in the row moves, not only the one for the word you edited. That happens because every share is worked out by dividing by the same total, and that total changes when one key’s score does. The strip is a poor place to watch this, because it draws every share bar as a fraction of the tallest one. The other bars there keep their heights unless the bar you changed is, or becomes, the tallest. Raising one number in K changes the score by the matching number in Q times the amount you added. So where that Q number is positive, raising the K number raises the score. Where it is negative, raising the K number lowers the score, whatever sign the K number started with. For example, if the matching Q number is 0.5 and you add 2 to the K number, the score rises by 0.5 × 2, which is 1. Selected score shows the change after the division by 8, so it rises by 0.125. Only the first four of the 64 numbers can be edited, while the other 60 stay as the model made them. Press Match the model vectors to switch back to the model’s own numbers. The lab remembers what you typed, though, so if you type in a box again, your earlier changes come back with it. Switch off the scaling Set Score scaling to *No scaling*, so the scores reaching softmax are 8 times bigger than before. In many rows the largest score now takes nearly everything, and two readouts show it as you switch back and forth. Largest weight is the biggest share any single character gets in the current row. Saturated rows counts the rows in this head’s whole grid where one character gets 99 percent or more. For Layer 2 head 2 on the pronoun sentence, no row is saturated with the division, but 26 of 55 rows are saturated without it. The count is out of 55 because the sentence has 56 characters and the first one is left out. That first character can only see itself, so it always gives itself 100 percent and would tell you nothing. So in this head, the division by 8 is what keeps the shares spread across several characters, instead of letting one big score drown out the rest. The division does not ban saturation, though, since all it does is stop scores from growing just because the lists are long. A trained head can still learn scores big enough to saturate when that is useful. Set the control back to *÷ √64*, then move to Layer 1 head 3 or head 4, and Saturated rows still counts most of the 55 rows. Those heads pile onto the previous character on purpose, which is how they put 99.9 percent of it on the i before its t. The trouble the division prevents is saturation that nobody asked for, caused only by long lists. Leave the control on *÷ √64*, so the next experiments use the model’s own setting. Empty the packets Set Value vectors (V) to *Zero all*, which replaces every value with a list of zeros. Look at the strip and the arcs, and you will notice that every attention weight stays exactly where it was. The Mixed value chip, though, drops to all zeros, and Mix length falls to 0. This is the cleanest test of the split of jobs from earlier, between choosing a route and carrying the content. The query and the keys chose the routes and the values travelled along them, so emptying the values changes what arrives but not where it comes from. Next, click a dark cell in the grid, so the inspected word has a large share. Then switch the control between *Model* and *Zero word*, which empties only the inspected word’s values, including the value for the space in front of it. The Mixed value numbers and Mix length change while the shares stay put, because the blend loses exactly that word’s contribution and nothing else. When you are finished, set the control back to *Model*, which restores the model’s own values. Lift the one-way rule In the Attention matrix card, set Mask to *Bidirectional*, so every character may read the whole sentence. Shares now appear above the diagonal, and the triangle fills into a square because later characters can be read too. The readout strip adds two new numbers: the share on later characters and the share on the next character. Every share below the diagonal shrinks by the same factor. The earlier characters’ scores have not changed, so softmax keeps their sizes compared with each other and divides them all by a bigger total that now includes the later characters. For example, suppose 40 percent of a row moves to later characters, leaving 60 percent for the earlier ones. Every earlier share is then multiplied by 0.6, so a share that was 50 percent becomes 30 percent. How much moves depends a great deal on which head you are looking at. For it on the pronoun sentence, Layer 1 head 3 moves only 0.1 percent of its weight to later characters, and head 4 moves only 0.2 percent. Layer 2 head 4, by contrast, moves 90.2 percent of its weight there. Layer 2 heads 2 and 3 put about a third of the weight of it on the very next character, 33.8 and 30.6 percent. That next character is exactly the answer the model practises guessing, so reading it would turn guessing into copying. This is the practice-quiz problem from earlier, and it is why the model trained with the mask on. Set Mask back to *Causal* before you go on, so the grid shows the model as it was trained. A route that is not what it looks like Press the Pronoun sentence button in the Examples row of the first card, which reloads the example and resets the mask, scaling and values to the model’s own settings. With it as the query, move the Attention head slider through all four heads with Layer on *Layer 1*, then again on *Layer 2*. Look for a thick arc to animal, which you might expect to find, since that is what it means in this sentence. There isn’t one: no head’s strongest route goes to animal, and none gives it even 10 percent. Look at Layer 1 heads 3 and 4 instead, which put 99.9 percent of it on the word it itself. That self-route has no arc, so you see it as a full bar under the it chip. To see why it happens, switch Matrix view to *Characters* and find the stripe just below the diagonal. A stripe in that position means that every character looks at the character immediately before it. The lab reads it at its last letter, the t, and the character immediately before that letter is the i inside it. That is why the Words view credits the word it with nearly all the weight. A thick arc or a full bar shows where information could come from, and it is not a sign that the model has worked out what it refers to. So why does no head reach for animal? One likely reason is that the lab reads it at its t, and the only guess that spot has to make is the next character. Here that is a space, and the spelling of it already makes a space a good guess without any help from animal. No head in this model shows a sign of linking it to animal, and these pictures cannot tell you how a large chatbot handles pronouns. A route that follows the content Now press Repeated name, which loads “Mark Jones met Anna Blake and then Mark” with the second Mark as the query. Set Layer to *Layer 2* and move the Attention head slider to head 3. That head sends 92.7 percent of the second Mark’s weight to Jones, the word that came right after the first Mark in the sentence. That is a sensible place to look, because at the second Mark the model has to guess what comes next. The last time Mark appeared, a space and then Jones came right after it. Switch Matrix view to *Characters* to see exactly where the weight lands. Almost all of it sits on one character: the space right after the first Mark, which the Words view counts as part of Jones. That is also why On spaces reads close to 100 percent. Under the one-way rule, that space has seen only “Mark ” so far, so its packet cannot hold the name Jones at all. The head points at the spot that came right after Mark last time, which is the spot it would copy from to guess the next character this time. Press Name moved earlier, which loads “Anna Blake met Mark Jones and then Mark”. The share on Jones stays high, at 97.2 percent, although the space right after the earlier Mark is now 19 characters back instead of 34. A head that always looked a set distance back would have lost its target when the name moved. This route follows the content instead: wherever the earlier Mark sits, the head’s weight lands right after it. For one more check, press Repeated name again, then click at the end of the Sentence box at the top of the first card. Type a space and then Smith, and click the new Smith chip to make it the query, keeping Layer 2 head 3. There is no earlier Smith for the head to match, and no word receives even 20 percent of its attention. Other names can come out differently, because the head matches characters, not whole names. Clark ends in the same k as Mark, so the head lands mostly on the space after the second Mark, which the Words view counts as part of Clark. A name such as Davis makes the head park much of its weight on the first character of the sentence, which the Words view credits to the first Mark. That looks like what Going deeper calls an attention sink, a parking spot for spare weight, not a link to Mark. Even the Jones route is only a lead worth testing, not proof that the model used it, and Where it breaks explains why.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Attention
documents.body: Every row adds up to 100 percent, so routes compete: making one connection stronger has to weaken the others in that row, as you saw when you edited one key. The grid is a triangle, not a square, because each character can look at itself and at earlier characters but never ahead. Attention lets the model practise on every position in one run, and this rule is what keeps that practice fair. Setting Mask to *Bidirectional* fills the empty corner. The On spaces readout needs careful reading. With it as the query, Layer 1 head 2 puts 99.1 percent on spaces. That happens only because the head always looks two characters back, and two characters back from the t in it is the space in front of the word. For because, the same head puts 1.3 percent on spaces, while Layer 2 head 4 puts 61.7 percent on spaces for it. So a big On spaces number does not mean a head is interested in spaces. It can be a side effect of where a word ends and how far back the head looks. Layer 1’s heads look a fixed distance back: head 2 looks 2 characters back, and heads 3 and 4 look 1 character back. Head 1 puts about two thirds of its weight 3 characters back. Layer 2’s routes look different on the same text, because Layer 2’s heads have their own learned numbers and read vectors that Layer 1 has already changed. The division by 8 is not a small detail, even though, with the model’s own setting, the Score and Scale lines differ only by that same factor. Without it, many rows in a head such as Layer 2 head 2 pile almost everything onto one character. With it, a row piles up like that only where a head has learned big scores on purpose, as Layer 1 heads 3 and 4 have. Emptying the packets changes nothing in the strip and everything in the blend, because keys decide who is read and values decide what is read.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Attention
documents.body: Where the desk picture stops matching The desk story explains routing well, but routing is all it explains. Real slips and labels have no words written on them, because they are lists of learned numbers whose meaning nobody chose. A strong match between a slip and a label tells you nothing about what is in the packet that gets handed over. Real desks would also come with seat numbers, while attention gets them only because the model adds them on purpose. A thick arc is not an explanation The biggest caution in this lesson is about how you read these pictures. A thick arc means that one position’s packet was given a large weight in one word’s blend, in one head of one layer. It does not tell you what that packet contained, whether the following step kept it, or whether a later layer cancelled it. It also does not tell you whether the final answer depended on it at all. The Jones route showed this already, since the packet it points at could not even hold the name. A route is a place where information could flow, not evidence that it mattered. Showing that a part of the model matters takes an experiment that changes the model on purpose and then measures the effect. One such experiment is switching a head off and checking whether the model’s predictions get worse, and tests like that are the subject of Interpretability II: circuits. Copying, or a habit? Picture a game where someone reads out a long string of letters that repeats, and two friends race to call out each next letter. The first friend looks back along the string for the last place the current letter appeared and calls out the letter that came after it. The second friend has a habit instead, and always calls out the letter from 7 places back. If the string repeats every 8 letters, both friends are right every time once the pattern has gone round once. Say the letters are ABCDEFGH repeated and you have just heard the second C, so the first friend finds the earlier C and calls out the D that followed it. Counting 7 back from the second C goes B, A, H, G, F, E, D, so the habit friend also calls out D, which is exactly what comes next. Now change the string so it repeats every 9 letters, as ABCDEFGHI. Counting 7 back from the second C now lands on E, which is wrong, while the first friend still finds the earlier C and calls out D. Only the first friend keeps winning. Heads in the model can behave like either friend, and the lab lets you run the same test on them. A head with a fixed-distance habit looks like a copier whenever the repeat length happens to match its distance. The reliable way to tell them apart is to change the repeat length and then watch whether the stripes follow. The game stops matching the model in two places. A head does not call out anything itself, because it only puts weight on a position, and the rest of the model turns that into a guess. Also, nobody can call the letters the first time through the string, since there is no earlier copy to look back at yet. Press Repeats every 8, which loads eight random letters repeated four times and switches to the Characters view. In Layer 2, heads 2 and 3 show stripes 7, 15 and 23 characters back. They put 94 and 88 percent of their weight on earlier copies of the character that comes next. The next character itself is still hidden by the one-way rule, so the heads find where that same letter appeared before. By the last copy of the string, the pattern has already appeared three times, which is why there are three stripes. Now press Repeats every 9 and watch the same two heads. Their stripes move to 8, 17 and 26 characters back. Head 2 now puts 95 percent on earlier copies of the next character, and head 3 puts 89 percent. Less than 1 percent is left at the old distances, so these heads are the first friend: they look for what followed last time, wherever it is. The other six heads do not copy, and none of them puts more than 11 percent on earlier copies of the next character at either repeat length. Layer 1’s four heads keep the same stripes both times: head 1 looks 3 characters back, head 2 looks 2 back, and heads 3 and 4 look 1 back. Those are fixed-distance habits, like the second friend’s, and only the learned seat numbers make them possible. A head that copies like this is called an induction head. A head that looks at the character right before the current one, like Layer 1 heads 3 and 4, is called a previous-token head. Here a token means one piece of text, which in this model is a single character. In the usual explanation of a two-layer model, the two kinds of head work as a pair. Take “Mark Jones met Anna Blake and then Mark” again, where a previous-token head in Layer 1 looks one character back from every spot. So the space after the first Mark picks up a note that says, roughly, “the character before me was k”. When the second Mark reaches its last letter, k, the induction head’s slip asks for a spot whose previous character was k. The space after the first Mark carries exactly that label, so the head reads it, and that space is where Jones begins. This lab has not proven that wiring, as the next part explains. What this model shows, and what it does not The model was given a test built so that a fixed-distance habit would fail it. A random string is repeated once, at a repeat length the model never practised on: 11, 13, 17 or 19 characters. The test then measures how much weight each head puts on the character right after the earlier match. To read the results, you need one more idea, which is how the model’s error gets measured. When the model guesses, it does not pick one character. Instead, it gives each of its 66 symbols a chance, such as 60 percent for e and 10 percent for a. The error is a score called loss, which is higher when the model is more surprised by the character that actually comes next. Being surprised here means the model had given the correct character only a small chance. Lower loss is better, and it is measured in a unit called a nat. To turn nats into something you can picture, raise 2.718 to the power of the loss. The answer is roughly how many equally likely characters the model is choosing among. A blind guess that gives all 66 symbols an equal chance scores about 4.19 nats, because 2.718 raised to 4.19 is about 66. Here is what the test shows about the two copying heads and the rest of the model: On random strings, Layer 2 heads 2 and 3 put 83 and 81 percent of their weight on the character after the earlier match. Those figures come from the worst of the four repeat lengths, so the other lengths score at least as well. A head with a fixed 7-back habit would score near zero here, because none of these repeat lengths puts that character 7 back. On pieces of held-out Shakespeare, each repeated once in the same way and never seen in practice, the same two heads put 40 and 51 percent on that character. Every other head stays under 6 percent on random strings, whatever the repeat length. On random strings, the loss on the first copy is about 4.3, a little worse than a blind guess. That is most likely because the model still bets on characters that are common in Shakespeare, which a random string does not favour. On the second copy the loss falls to between 0.13 and 0.25, so the model is nearly certain of each next character. On Shakespeare text, the loss on the first copy is about 1.6 or 1.7. On the second copy it falls to between 0.39 and 0.53. Layer 1 heads 3 and 4 put 99 percent or more of their weight on the previous character. That is the information a copying head in Layer 2 would need from the layer below. Here is what the test does not show, and these gaps matter as much as the results: It does not show the wiring: nobody traced which Layer 1 head feeds which Layer 2 head. Switching a head off is a blunt test, because it removes everything the head adds to the model rather than one connection. Switching off Layer 2 head 3 makes the loss on the second copy more than ten times higher. If the copying heads relied on a previous-token head, switching that head off should hurt clearly more than switching off a head that does something else. Instead, switching off Layer 1 head 2, which is not a previous-token head, raises the loss about as much as switching off Layer 1 head 4, which is one. So this test cannot tell which head feeds which. It says nothing about big models: this model has about 1.4 million parameters, reads characters, and learned from one author’s plays plus the made-up repeats. So it cannot tell you how big chatbots pick up a pattern from a few examples you type into your message, which researchers call in-context learning. It does not explain the other heads: Layer 1 head 1 and Layer 2 heads 1 and 4 are shown in the lab but not explained. It is not a full explanation, because an attention pattern on its own is evidence about routing and nothing more. Other limits of this lab The model trained for 8,000 steps, which added up to about 23 passes over its practice text. That practice text was the 1.0 million characters in the first 90 percent of the plays. On the held-out last tenth of Shakespeare, its loss is 1.54 nats per character, compared with 4.19 for a blind guess. Since 2.718 raised to 1.54 is about 4.7, that is roughly as unsure as picking among 5 equally likely characters instead of 66. That is far better than guessing, though still a long way from certain. About 30 percent of its practice windows were made-up repeated strings, so this model was shown repetition on purpose. The three switches are experiments run on a model that has already finished training, which limits what they can show: Mask lifts the rule for one head of a model that was trained with the rule on, so that head never practised scoring later characters. In Layer 2, its slips and labels are still built from a Layer 1 that kept the rule, and the rest of the model does not change. Score scaling turns off the division for one head of a model that learned with it on. So it shows that head’s rows piling onto one character, which the lab calls saturation, not what training without the division would have produced. Value vectors (V) changes the lab’s blend for one head, but it does not change the model’s answer, because the emptied blend never runs through the rest of the model. Input stops at 64 characters, which is the window length the model trained on. The Words view adds up characters, while big chat models read pieces of words called tokens, so the lab’s word totals are not real tokens. The editable chips show only the first four numbers of lists that are 64 numbers long. Once you edit them, the shares come from your numbers rather than the model’s. In real systems Full attention compares every position with every other position, so the work grows with the square of the text’s length. Double the length of a text and there are about four times as many pairs to score. Make it ten times longer and there are about a hundred times as many, which adds up fast. That one fact drives most of the engineering behind models that read very long texts. A common mix-up: Attention in a model is not the same as human focus or attention span. A thick arc or dark cell is also not proof that one word caused the model’s answer. Even a link that follows the content, like Mark to Jones, is one weight in a weighted average worked out with dot products, not a reason or a decision.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Attention
documents.body: Many heads, one output Real models run several attention heads side by side, which is what the Attention head slider lets you step through here. Their blends are joined end to end and passed through one more learned mixing step, called the output projection. That step decides how the fetched information gets written back into the model. The result is added into a running record that each position carries through the model, called the residual stream, which The transformer block follows. Splitting the work into heads costs little: this model’s full vectors are 256 numbers long, split into four heads of 64 numbers each. Four heads of 64 cost about the same arithmetic as one head of 256, and in return you get four separate ways to route information. Positions in bigger models Most current models use the twist (RoPE) rather than this lab’s learned seat numbers. Stretching such a model to handle longer inputs works by adjusting how far each seat turns the slips and labels, and Modern attention at scale covers both ideas. Saving work while writing When a model writes text one piece at a time, the keys and values of earlier pieces never change, since under the one-way rule they never read the new ones. They can therefore be saved and reused, instead of being recalculated for every new piece of text. That saved store is the subject of Inference & KV cache, where K stands for keys and V stands for values. Grouped-query attention makes that store smaller by letting several query heads share one set of keys and values. It gives up a small amount of quality in return for a large saving in memory. Other methods, such as FlashAttention, work out exactly the same softmax in small blocks, so the full grid of scores never has to be stored at once. Induction heads in research The copying heads you met are called induction heads, and Olsson and colleagues studied them in 2022. Their paper is titled *In-context Learning and Induction Heads*, and it describes such a head by two behaviours. First, the head looks back for the spot right after an earlier copy of the current token. Second, it copies, which makes the token found there more likely to come next. In a two-layer model, they found an induction head paired with a previous-token head, the same two kinds you saw here. In larger models, they saw a sudden change early in training, when induction heads formed while the models got better at in-context learning. They describe their evidence as preliminary and indirect. It suggests that these heads drive most of that learning, but it is early work and does not prove the link directly. Attention sinks Some heads park most of their attention on the very first token whenever they have nothing useful to fetch from anywhere else. A position that soaks up weight like this is called an attention sink. You may have seen something like it if you typed a name such as Davis earlier. This matters in practice, because deleting that position from the saved store of keys and values makes the model’s output worse. Where the division came from Dividing by the square root of the head dimension comes from the original Transformer paper, by Vaswani and colleagues in 2017. The authors suspected that large scores push softmax into a corner where one share is nearly everything. In that corner, small changes to the scores barely move the shares, so training gets almost no signal about which way to adjust them. For example, if the top share is already 99.9 percent, nudging its score up or down a little barely changes any share. Training can then hardly tell whether a nudge helped or hurt, so learning would become very slow, which is the problem the division was meant to prevent. The lab’s Score scaling switch shows the corner, but not the slow learning, which would only appear during training, and the lab never trains the model. Bidirectional here, and a real encoder The Bidirectional setting in this lab is an experiment on a decoder-only model, not an encoder. A real encoder, such as a masked language model, is trained from the start with every position visible. As a result, it learns different queries and keys from any that this model ever made.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Attention
documents.body: This module is about self-attention, the transformer step that moves information between positions. It answers a routing question: which parts of the context should a position draw on, when the answer changes with the text? Next-token prediction treated the model as a map from a context to a next-token distribution; this module opens the step that does the routing. Each position asks with a query (what it looks for), every readable position answers with a key (what it offers), and the position receives a mix of their values (what each passes on), weighted toward the best matches. One independent set of these learned projections is an attention head. The module also covers position information, the causal mask that stops a position reading later ones, and dividing scores by √d_k, the square root of the head dimension. Where it shows up Model families. A decoder-only (causal) language model, like this lab's, keeps the causal mask and predicts the next token. An encoder drops the mask and reads both directions; BERT is one, trained to fill hidden tokens. Position schemes. GPT-2 and this lab's model add a learned vector per slot, the original Transformer a fixed sinusoidal one, and Llama and many recent models rotate queries and keys (RoPE). Serving. Generation caches past keys and values, grouped-query attention shrinks that cache, and kernels such as FlashAttention compute the softmax in on-chip tiles. Scoring every pair makes cost grow with the square of sequence length. Interpretability. Induction heads (Olsson and colleagues, 2022) attend from a repeated token to what followed its earlier occurrence. Why it matters Attention computes its routes from each input's content and positions, so the same learned weights serve any input. Each design choice around it prevents a specific failure: Without a position signal, attention sees only vectors and, apart from a little order the causal mask leaks, cannot tell *the dog bit the man* from *the man bit the dog*. Without the causal mask, next-token training could be solved by copying the answer. Without the division by √d_k, softmax pushes each query's weights toward a single key, and the original Transformer authors suspected this leaves extremely small gradients in training. What you will be able to explain Tell queries, keys and values apart: queries and keys decide which positions are read, and values decide what is read. Read an attention pattern as evidence about routing, not proof that the output used the route. Tell a head that follows content from one that reads a fixed distance, by moving the content. Say what the causal mask changes, and how encoder and decoder-only models differ. Say why scores are divided by the square root of the head dimension. What the lab shows The lab runs a real two-layer, four-head character transformer with 1.37 million parameters, trained on Tiny Shakespeare plus synthetic repeated strings. With the model's own settings, every attention weight and Q, K and V vector comes from it; the runtime status badge says when deterministic stand-in values show instead. Type a Sentence or press an Examples button, then click a word in the arc diagram to make it the query. The Attention matrix card shows the model's own Characters grid, or the Words view the lab sums from it. The inspector sets Layer and Attention head. The stage buttons under the arc diagram step the inspector through Query, Keys, Score, Softmax and Mix; its Softmax row recomputes one character pair's weight in closed form beside the model's value. Mask set to *Bidirectional*, Score scaling set to *No scaling*, and Value vectors (V) are inference-time experiments on one head, not trained conditions. After you edit a Q or K chip, the arcs, that query's word row, the Softmax row and the mix come from your numbers, not the model, until you press Match the model vectors. The key experiment uses the fixed Repeated name, Name moved earlier, Repeats every 8 and Repeats every 9 inputs to test whether a route follows content or keeps a fixed distance.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Attention
documents.body: Self-attention lets one position read from other positions. Each token's vector is projected three ways by learned matrices, into a query, a key, and a value. The query of one position is compared against the keys of all permitted positions to decide how much of each value to take. For a causal head the calculation is softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k + M) V, where d_k is the head dimension and the mask M is 0 for earlier or equal positions and −∞ for later ones. The lab exposes it as five stages: Query, Keys, Score, Softmax, and Mix. How the five stages fit together Project (Query, Keys). One vector per position becomes three vectors, each of the head's dimension. Queries and keys are compared with each other; values carry the payload. Score. Take the dot product of the query with each key. The Score readout shows q · k for the pair you selected. A high score means the two vectors point in similar directions in the space this head learned. Scale and normalize. Divide by √d_k, shown in the Scale readout, then apply softmax across the visible key positions. The strip in the inspector draws the whole row twice: the scores above, weights below, with masked positions hatched. Score scaling switches the division off so you can see what it does. Mix. Multiply each value vector by its weight and sum. The Mixed value chip shows the first dimensions of that 64-dimensional result, which the output projection then writes back into the residual stream. Value vectors (V) zeroes the payload so you can see which stage owns it. Why the scores are compared, not stored Nothing about this routing is fixed. The same head applies the same projection matrices to whatever text arrives, and the pattern that emerges is a function of content and position. The *weights* of the network are fixed after training, while the *routes* are computed fresh for every input. Where position comes from The dot product q · k sees only vectors. Nothing in it says which slot a vector came from, so with no extra signal, reordering the words only reorders the outputs, and attention cannot tell *the dog bit the man* from *the man bit the dog*. (The causal mask leaks a little order; The transformer block measures it.) Order has to be injected, and the schemes differ in where: Learned absolute (GPT-2, and this lab's model): a trained vector for each slot is added to the token vector at the input. A slot beyond the table has no vector, so context is capped at the table size, 64 here. Sinusoidal absolute (the original Transformer): a fixed sine and cosine pattern of the slot is added at the input. Nothing is trained, but such models extrapolate poorly past their trained length. Relative, ALiBi: no position vector. A penalty proportional to the distance between query and key is subtracted from each score, with a fixed slope per head, so nearer keys score higher. Rotary, RoPE (Llama and many recent models): each query and key pair is rotated by an angle proportional to its position, so the score depends only on the distance between the two. Modern attention at scale has a card for it. This lab's model is the first kind. A head can prefer a fixed distance back only if its queries and keys carry the slot, and here they do: Layer 1 has heads that read 1, 2 or 3 characters back on every text this lesson tries. Zero the 64 learned vectors and those stripes fall from between 66 and 100 percent of the weight to under 6 percent. The order test itself, with and without position information, runs in The transformer block. What this lab is running The interactive drives a real two-layer, four-head character transformer with model width 256, head dimension 64 and 1.37 million parameters, exported to ONNX. It reads the actual Q, K and V tensors and per-head attention weights from that model. The runtime status badge names the execution provider, or says when the lab is showing its deterministic stand-in values. It trained for 8,000 steps on 64-character windows of Tiny Shakespeare: 45 windows of each batch of 64 from the first 90 percent of the text, and 19 synthetic windows holding a random string repeated at a period from 4 to 31 characters, except 11, 13, 17 and 19. The last 10 percent of the text was held out for measurement. Because the model is character-level, the Words view sums character weights over each word, where a word owns the space in front of it. With that convention a row read at a word's last character covers only earlier characters, so word rows sum to exactly 100 percent with nothing discarded. The Characters view shows the model's own grid.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Attention
documents.body: Attention is the mechanism that makes context work. Before it, a position holds mostly local information: this token, at this place. Attention gives it a content-addressed way to retrieve what it needs, such as the subject a pronoun refers to, the matching bracket, or the format established three examples ago. It is also the piece that made scale practical. Recurrent models pushed all history through one fixed-size state, computed strictly in order. Attention compares all positions in parallel during training, which is what allowed sequence models to use modern accelerators fully.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Attention
documents.body: Choose a query token in the arc diagram, then move the Attention head slider across all four heads at each Layer. The same sentence produces visibly different routing, because each head learned its own projection matrices. Select a matrix cell to inspect one query–key pair, then step through Score and Softmax. The Softmax row recomputes the weight from the displayed Q and K and prints the model's own value beside it; they agree to within about 1e-6. Compare Selected score with Selected weight: the first is one character pair, the second sums a whole word. Edit a number in the K vector chip and watch every weight in that row change, not just the pair you edited. Press Match the model vectors to return to the model's own values. Divide, or don't Set Score scaling to *No scaling*. The raw scores are 8 times larger than the scaled ones, so softmax concentrates. Compare Largest weight and Saturated rows, which counts the rows of this head's grid that put 99 percent or more on one character. For Layer 2 head 2 on the pronoun sentence, no row does with the division and 26 of 55 rows do without it. Zero the values Set Value vectors (V) to *Zero all*. The strip, the arcs and every weight stay exactly as they were, while the Mixed value falls to zero: Q and K chose the route, and V is what travels along it. *Zero word* removes only the inspected word's values, and the mix loses exactly that word's share. Pick a cell with a large weight to see it. Lift the mask In the Attention matrix card, set Mask to *Bidirectional*. Each row now reads every character, weight appears above the diagonal, and every weight below it shrinks by the same factor, because the row still sums to 100 percent. For it, Layer 1 heads 3 and 4 move 0.1 and 0.2 percent of their weight forward; Layer 2 head 4 moves 90.2 percent. Layer 2 heads 2 and 3 put 33.8 and 30.6 percent of it on the very next character. In next-token training that character is the answer. Reading it directly would solve the task by copying, which is what the causal mask prevents. Test a route before you believe it Press Pronoun sentence with it as the query and move the Attention head slider through both layers. No head's strongest route is animal, and none gives it even 10 percent. Layer 1 heads 3 and 4 send 99.9 percent to it itself. The Characters view shows why: a stripe one place below the diagonal, because they read the previous character, the i inside it. Now press Repeated name, set Layer 2 and head 3, and read the second Mark: 92.7 percent goes to Jones, the word after the earlier Mark. Press Name moved earlier. The route stays on Jones at 97.2 percent although the earlier name is now 19 characters back instead of 34. A route that follows the content when you move it is worth testing. It is still not proof that the output used it. For a name with no earlier match, type Smith at the end and select it: no word gets even 20 percent. Other surnames land elsewhere: with Davis, about two thirds goes to the first character, which the Words view counts as part of the first Mark.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Attention
documents.body: Every row sums to 100 percent, which makes attention a competition. Strengthening one route necessarily weakens the others in that row, as you see when you edit a single key. The matrix is triangular. This model is causal, so a query can attend to itself and to earlier positions only. That constraint is what allows every position to be trained in parallel on next-token prediction without leaking the answer. Set Mask to *Bidirectional* and the upper triangle fills. The On spaces readout needs interpretation. For it, Layer 1 head 2 puts 99.1 percent on spaces, but only because it reads two characters back and it has two letters. For because the same head puts 1.3 percent there. Layer 2 head 4 puts 61.7 percent on spaces for it. Layer 1 heads 2, 3 and 4 read a fixed distance back (2, 1 and 1 characters), and head 1 puts about two thirds of its weight 3 back. Layer 2 routes differ from Layer 1's on the same text, because layer 2 is attending to vectors that layer 1 already modified. Scaling by √d_k is not cosmetic. The Score and Scale readouts differ by the constant factor 8, but that factor decides whether softmax produces graded weights or a near one-hot row. Zeroing V changes nothing in the strip and everything in the Mixed value. Keys decide who is read; values decide what is read.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Attention
documents.body: An attention weight is not an explanation. It describes how much of one value vector was included at one head in one layer. It says nothing about what that value *contains*, whether the output projection kept it, whether a later layer cancelled it, or whether the final answer depended on it. Establishing that requires intervention, the subject of the circuits lab. How to tell copying from a positional habit A head that reads a fixed distance back looks like copying whenever the repeat length happens to match that distance. The method that separates them is to change the repeat length and see whether the stripes follow. Press Repeats every 8 and view Characters. Layer 2 heads 2 and 3 have stripes 7, 15 and 23 characters back, where the next character of the pattern sits: 94 and 88 percent of their weight lands on it. Press Repeats every 9. The stripes move to 8, 17 and 26, and the share on the true next character is 95 and 89 percent. Less than 1 percent is left at 7, 15 and 23. That is what copying looks like. The six other heads do not copy: none puts more than 11 percent on the true next character at either period. Layer 1 heads 1 to 4 keep their strongest stripe 3, 2, 1 and 1 characters back at both periods. Those are fixed-distance habits, and they depend on the learned position vectors. What this model demonstrates, and what it does not The model passes a check built to fail a position habit. The check repeats a random string once, at a period the model never trained on (11, 13, 17 or 19), and measures each head's attention from the second copy to the character after the earlier match, an offset one less than the period. Demonstrated: Layer 2 heads 2 and 3 put 0.83 and 0.81 of their weight there on random strings, the worst case over the four periods, and 0.40 and 0.51 on snippets of held-out Shakespeare. Every other head stays under 0.06 on random strings at each of the four periods. A fixed 7-back look-up would score near zero. The loss on the repeated half falls from about 4.3 to between 0.13 and 0.25 nats on random strings, and from 1.6–1.7 to 0.39–0.53 on corpus text. Layer 1 heads 3 and 4 put 0.99 or more of their weight on the previous character, the information a layer-2 induction head needs from the layer below. Not demonstrated: The wiring. No path patching was run. Switching a head off removes everything it writes. Switching off Layer 2 head 3 raises the repeated-half loss more than tenfold, but switching off Layer 1 head 2, which is not a previous-token head, costs about as much as Layer 1 head 4. Ablation alone does not isolate the circuit. Anything beyond this model. It has 1.4 million parameters, reads characters, and learned from one author's plays plus synthetic repeats; it says nothing about in-context learning in a large language model. What the other heads do. Layer 1 head 1 and Layer 2 heads 1 and 4 are displayed, not explained. An attention pattern is evidence about routing, not an explanation by itself. Other limits of this lab The model trained for 8,000 steps, about 23 passes over the 1.0 million characters of its training split. Its loss on the held-out last 10 percent is 1.54 nats per character (2.23 bits), against 4.19 nats for a uniform guess over its 66 symbols. About 30 percent of each batch, 19 of 64 windows, was synthetic repeated strings, by design, so this model saw repetition on purpose. The mask, scaling and value controls are inference-time experiments. Mask lifts the mask for one head of a model trained with it on, so the later-position scores were never trained. Score scaling multiplies this head's scores by 8, which shows saturation, not training without the division. Value vectors (V) changes the lab's mix for one head, not the model's output. Input caps at 64 characters, the trained block size. The chips expose only 4 of 64 dimensions, and after an edit the displayed weights come from your vectors, not the model. In real systems. Full self-attention compares every pair of positions, so the score matrix costs time and memory proportional to the square of sequence length. That single fact drives most long-context engineering.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Attention
documents.body: Multi-head attention runs several of these operations in parallel with separate projections. Their outputs are concatenated and passed through one learned output projection, then added back to the residual stream. Splitting a width of 256 into 4 heads of 64 costs about the same arithmetic as one 256-wide head, while providing four independent routing channels. Most current models use RoPE rather than this lab's learned absolute vectors, and context extension methods work by rescaling its angles. Both are covered in Modern attention at scale. Keys and values for past positions do not change during generation, so they can be cached, the subject of Inference & KV cache. Grouped-query attention shrinks that cache by sharing one key/value head across several query heads. Kernels such as FlashAttention compute exactly this softmax in on-chip tiles without storing the full score matrix.
