documents.subtitle: Plain · Backpropagation
documents.body: An AI model is a long chain of small calculations, and the numbers that steer those calculations are called weights. You can picture each weight as a dial on a huge control panel, because turning it changes what the model gives back. Training is the slow process of turning those dials, a little at a time, until the model's answers land closer to the right ones. Big models are built in layers, which are rows of small calculations stacked one after another, so each layer's output feeds the next layer. Each layer has its own dials, and the last card of this lab stacks up to twelve layers. Every time the model gets a practice example wrong, training faces the same question: which dials should turn, in which direction, and by how much? This module is about the method that answers that question, which is called backpropagation. It starts from the error at the very end of the chain and works backward, one step at a time, toward the dials. When it is done, every dial has a number that says which way to turn it and how strongly it affects the error. That number is what the previous lab, Loss & gradient descent, called a tilt. That lab needed a tilt for each of its two dials and used them without saying where they came from. This lesson calls the same number a slope, and this lab finishes the story by showing exactly how it is worked out. Where it shows up Almost every slope used to train a model in this course is found this way. That includes the one-dial model in this lab and the language models in later labs, which are the kind of program behind a chatbot. While a model like these is being trained, backpropagation runs over and over in the background, after every round of practice examples, to tell training how to nudge the dials. The rare exceptions are steps that make a hard choice, such as picking one word, and the end of this lesson comes back to them. Why it matters A large model has billions of dials, so the cost of finding their slopes matters a great deal. Without backpropagation, finding each dial's slope would take a separate run of the whole model for every single dial, so one round of training would need billions of runs. Backpropagation finds every dial's slope in one backward sweep, which costs only about twice as much as one ordinary run of the model from input to guess. It also explains a problem that shaped the design of modern models. In a model with many layers, the slope that reaches the earliest layers can shrink to almost nothing or grow out of control. Several standard design choices exist mainly to stop that from happening. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these ideas in your own words: how numbers flow forward through a small model to make a guess and an error score, and how slopes then flow backward from the error to the dial; how a rule called the chain rule finds the dial's slope by multiplying each step's own small slope along the path, and how to check that answer by measuring; why a model built from many layers can pass almost no slope back to its first layer, or far too much; how four choices change the slope that reaches the first layer: - how many layers are stacked; - which squashing step each layer applies to its numbers; - how big the random numbers are that the dials start at; - whether shortcuts let numbers skip past a layer. What the lab lets you do Every number in this lab is worked out from your settings rather than drawn by hand, and nothing in it is a trained model. The lab is spread across four cards: Interactive backpropagation computation graph shows the one-dial model as a small map of circles and arrows. You step through it and watch numbers fill in from left to right, and then you watch slopes fill in from right to left. Loss versus weight tangent chart draws the error score, called the loss, for every possible setting of the dial. A straight line that touches the curve, called a tangent, shows the slope at the current setting. Backpropagation controls and chain rule holds the sliders, the slope written out as a multiplication, and a button that turns the dial by one step. Gradient flow through depth builds a stack of up to twelve layers with random starting dials. It runs 32 made-up practice examples through the stack once, before any training, and shows how much slope reaches each layer. Along the way you will break the slope on purpose, so that you can see for yourself how a big error can still produce a tiny slope.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Backpropagation
documents.body: A model with one dial Start with the smallest model that still has every important part. It takes one input number, x, and it has one dial, the weight w. It multiplies the two, squashes the result into a number between 0 and 1, and compares that guess with the right answer. Picture it as a short assembly line with three stations, where a number moves along the line and each station does one small calculation and passes its result on. The multiply station works out z = x · w. At the lab's starting settings x is 0.8 and w is 0.6, so z comes out as 0.48. The sigmoid station squashes z into a number between 0 and 1, so large positive numbers come out close to 1 and large negative ones come out close to 0. If z is exactly 0, the sigmoid gives 0.5, right in the middle. Its output is the model's guess, written ŷ and read "y-hat", which is 0.618 at the start. The loss station compares the guess with the right answer, which is called the target and written y. The target starts at 0.9, and the station finds the gap between the two and squares it, which gives about 0.0797. That last number is the loss, a score for how wrong the guess is, where zero means a perfect guess. Squaring the gap makes every miss count as a positive number, whichever side of the target it falls on. It also makes big misses count far more than small ones, because doubling a gap from 0.2 to 0.4 makes the loss four times bigger. The whole map of stations and the arrows between them is called a computation graph, and running numbers through it from left to right is called the forward pass. The lab's tape writes down each forward step in a row, with the formula, the numbers and the result: The σ is the Greek letter sigma, which stands for sigmoid here. In the middle row the tape writes the sigmoid out in full, 1 / (1 + e^(−z)) with z filled in, where e is a fixed number close to 2.718. You never need to work it out by hand, because the lab does that part for you. The question training asks The loss tells you how wrong the guess is, but it does not tell you what to do about it. Training needs one more fact about the dial: if w moved up by a tiny amount, would the loss go up or down, and how fast? That fact is the slope of the loss at the current weight. Picture standing on a hillside, where the slope is how steeply the ground rises or falls under your feet. A measurement of how fast one number changes when another number moves is called a derivative. The slope of the loss for one particular dial is called that dial's gradient. The lab writes this slope as ∂L/∂w, which you can read as "how many times as much L changes as w does, for a tiny nudge to w". The curly ∂ marks a partial derivative, which is a slope measured while everything else stays fixed, so x and y hold still while you nudge w. Each station's own number The trick that makes backpropagation work is that no station needs the whole formula. Each station only has to answer a small question about itself: if my input moves up by a tiny amount, how many times that amount does my output move? The answer is that station's local derivative. Take the multiply station first, and keep x at 0.8 while you nudge w up by 0.01. Then z rises by 0.008, which is 0.8 times the size of your nudge, so the multiply station's local derivative toward w is 0.8, the value of x. The same reasoning works in the other direction, because nudging x moves z by w times the nudge. That makes the local derivative toward x equal to 0.6, the value of w. Each input's local derivative is the *other* input's value from the forward pass, and that detail will matter later. The sigmoid station's local derivative has a short formula, ŷ(1 − ŷ), which appears on the tape once the backward pass reaches it. With a guess of 0.618 it works out as 0.618 × 0.382, which comes to 0.236, so a nudge of 0.01 to z moves the guess by only about 0.0024. This formula is largest when the guess sits exactly in the middle, where 0.5 × 0.5 gives 0.25. It shrinks toward zero as the guess gets close to 0 or 1, and at a guess of 0.99 it is only about 0.01. A sigmoid stuck near one end like this is called saturated, and as you will see, it passes almost nothing backward. The loss station's local derivative is 2(ŷ − y), which is twice the gap between the guess and the target. At the start that is 2 × (0.618 − 0.90), which the lab prints as −0.565. The minus sign carries real meaning, because it says that pushing the guess up would make the loss go *down*, since the guess is below the target. The chain rule: multiply along the path Now you can link the three answers together. A nudge to w moves z by 0.8 times as much, and a nudge to z moves the guess by 0.236 times as much. A nudge to the guess then moves the loss by −0.565 times as much, so a nudge that starts at w gets multiplied by each number in turn: Multiplying local derivatives along a path like this is called the chain rule, and it is the whole engine of backpropagation. The answer, −0.1066, says that nudging the weight up by 0.01 would lower the loss by about 0.001, and because the slope is negative, the weight should go up. Going backward Backpropagation does this multiplication in a particular order, starting at the loss and working back toward the dial. The chain begins with 1 at the loss, because a nudge to the loss changes the loss by exactly that much, and the lab shows this as ∂L/∂L 1. Each station then takes the number arriving from the loss side, multiplies it by its own local derivative, and passes the result to the station before it. The number arriving at a station from the loss side is called the upstream gradient. This right-to-left sweep is called the backward pass, and the lab shows it as a running total under each circle. Each row below shows the number that has arrived at one circle, so the factor in each row comes from the station just to its right. The sigmoid circle receives 1 times the loss station's −0.565, and the multiply circle receives that result times the sigmoid's 0.236: Back on the assembly line, the forward pass carries a number down the line to make a guess. The backward pass carries a report about the error back up the line, and each station scales the report by its own number before passing it on. No station ever uses the whole formula, yet the dial at the far end receives its exact slope. Working out how much each dial contributed to the final error is called credit assignment. Backpropagation answers it with an exact local measure: how much the loss would change for a tiny nudge to each dial right now. Every number in the chain comes from the stations' own formulas, so nothing is guessed. That measure is about sensitivity, not blame. As you will see in the lab, a dial can push the guess far off target and still get a tiny slope. The slope only says how much a small nudge would help from where things stand. Why the forward numbers must be kept Look again at the multiply station, whose local derivative toward w is the value of x and whose local derivative toward x is the value of w. Both values were used during the forward pass, so they have to stay stored until the backward pass comes back to that station. It is a bit like a long sum in a maths test, where a later line reuses a number from an earlier line. If you erased each line as soon as you finished it, you would have to redo the earlier work to get that number back. A memory-saving trick near the end of this lesson makes exactly that trade on purpose. The stored forward values are often called activations, so this storage is called activation memory. The branch toward the input The multiply station also sends a slope back toward x, which comes to −0.1333 × 0.600 = −0.0800. Here x is the training example, which training never changes, so nothing uses that number. In a deeper model, though, the thing feeding a layer is the output of the layer before it, and that output depends on the earlier layer's own dials. This branch is exactly how the backward pass reaches earlier layers. The target gets no slope at all, because it is data rather than a dial, so during the backward pass the lab labels it no gradient: data. Many layers: the product gets long Recall that a real network stacks many layers. Each layer is a row of small stations, called units, that sit side by side. In the lab, each unit takes in 16 numbers from the layer before it, multiplies each one by its own weight, adds them up, and squashes the total. The Activation control chooses which squashing step produces every unit's activation: sigmoid is the squashing step you have already met, and its local derivative is never more than 0.25. tanh squashes numbers into the range from −1 to 1, and its local derivative can reach 1 in the middle. ReLU keeps positive numbers as they are and turns negative numbers into 0, so its local derivative is either exactly 1 or exactly 0. With random starting weights, about half the units get a negative total, so ReLU passes nothing back through those units. On the way back, every layer multiplies the arriving slope by its squashing step's local derivative and by its own weights. With twelve layers that makes a long product, and long products can behave in extreme ways. Picture a made-up game where every round you keep only a quarter of your points. If you start with a million points, then after eleven rounds you are left with about a quarter of one point. Now picture the opposite, a chain message where every person forwards it to three new friends, so that in the eleventh round alone, 177,147 new people receive it. The same thing happens to slopes, because a slope passing back through many layers gets multiplied once at every layer. When most of the numbers in the chain are below 1, the product shrinks toward zero, so the earliest layers get almost no slope and barely learn. That is called the vanishing gradient. When most of them are above 1, the product blows up and hands the earliest layers huge slopes, which is called the exploding gradient. Reading tiny and huge numbers The Gradient flow through depth card prints numbers that are far too small or too large to write out comfortably, so it uses a short form. The number 2.6e-8 means 2.6 with the decimal point moved 8 places to the left, which is 0.000000026. In the same way, 3.5e5 means 3.5 with the point moved 5 places to the right, which is 350,000. The readouts under the bars use this form even for ordinary sizes. So 0.21 appears as 2.13e-1, 1.3 as 1.32e+0, and 350,000 as 3.48e+5, where the + only means the point moves to the right. Each layer in the card has 16 × 16 = 256 weights, so it has 256 slopes, one for each weight. The card sums them up as a single size called the norm: square every slope, add the squares together, and take the square root. A bigger norm means that layer's dials would get a bigger push in a training step, while a norm near zero means they would barely move. What the card measures Take sigmoid units with Glorot starting weights, a setting explained below, and stack twelve layers. On the way back, each layer multiplies the slope by about 0.24 on average. That comes from the sigmoid's slope, which is at most 0.25, multiplied by the effect of the layer's weights, which with this setting stays close to 1. Eleven of those steps separate the last layer from Layer 1, and 0.24 multiplied by itself eleven times is roughly one ten-millionth. The card shows exactly this, since Layer 12 norm reads about 0.21 while Layer 1 norm reads 2.6e-8. Layer 1 ÷ last reads 1.2e-7, which is 0.00000012, so the first layer gets roughly one ten-millionth of the slope that the last layer gets. The readouts print one extra digit, such as 2.58e-8, but the story is the same. Three controls change this product, and the first is Activation. Switching to tanh raises the ceiling on each layer's local derivative from 0.25 to 1. At twelve layers with Glorot weights, Layer 1 then reads about 0.21, almost the same as the last layer's 0.23, so the slope barely shrinks on the way back. The second control is Initial weight scale, which matters because every weight starts out as a random number before training. How spread out those random numbers are is a choice called weight initialization. The control offers four settings, small (std 0.1), Glorot, He and large (std 1.0), where "std" is short for standard deviation. That is a measure of how far from zero the random numbers typically land, so with 0.1 a typical starting weight sits around 0.1 above or below zero. Glorot and He are two recipes for that spread, each named after the first author of the paper that proposed it. For this lab's layers of 16 units, they work out to about 0.25 and 0.35. With ReLU units at twelve layers, the starting spread decides how big every layer's slope is, and Layer 1 norm reads like this: Small starting weights shrink the signal at every layer, while large ones inflate it at every layer. Over twelve layers, that one choice decides whether every slope is a whisper or a roar. Why does Glorot leave every slope at only about 0.02 here? Glorot keeps the weights' own effect close to 1, but ReLU switches off about half the units, so each layer still weakens the signal a little. He uses a wider spread, about 0.35 instead of 0.25, to make up for those switched-off units. That is why He was designed for ReLU, and it keeps each layer's effect close to 1. You might expect large weights to give Layer 1 a far bigger slope than the last layer, yet its 3.5e5 is only about a third of the last layer's 1.05e6. The reason goes back to the multiply station, where the slope on w was the slope arriving at z times x, the number fed in. Every weight in the stack works the same way. With ReLU and large weights, the arriving slopes grow on the way back toward the input. Meanwhile, the numbers fed into each layer grow on the way forward toward the output. Those two effects roughly cancel, so every layer's slope ends up about the same size: all huge, or all tiny when the weights are small. Sigmoid has no such balance. Its outputs always sit between 0 and 1, so the numbers fed into each layer stay about the same size. Meanwhile the slope shrinks on the way back, and nothing makes up for it. The third control is Skip connections. A skip connection, which people also call a residual connection, is a shortcut that adds a layer's input straight onto its output. The numbers can then hop over the layer as well as pass through it. On the way back the shortcut becomes an express lane, because the slope arriving at a layer passes straight back to the layer before. That happens on top of whatever comes through the layer's own weights and squashing step. With sigmoid, Glorot and twelve layers, turning Skip connections on lifts Layer 1's norm from 2.6e-8 to 0.24. The fix has a price, which shows in Loss at the start, the untrained stack's error score on its practice examples: it climbs from 0.90 to 7.30. That score uses a different rule from the small graph, called cross-entropy. Each of the 32 made-up examples has a yes-or-no answer, and the stack ends with a sigmoid, so its guess is the chance that the answer is yes. Guessing a 50 percent chance every time scores about 0.69, and there is no upper limit, because a guess that is confident and wrong costs a great deal. Every shortcut adds more numbers on top, so values grow larger at each layer on the way forward, and this lab has no step that shrinks them back down. By the last layer the stack's guesses are pushed to near-certain answers, and about half of them are confidently wrong.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Backpropagation
documents.body: Every dial needs its own slope Picture a made-up group project with four people that comes back with a low mark. To do better next time, the group needs to know how much the mark would change if each person changed their part a little. With four people you could talk it through, but imagine asking the same question about a billion people at once, after every single practice test. That is the credit assignment problem that training faces with every round of examples. The most direct way to solve it is to nudge one dial, rerun the model, and measure what happens to the loss. The lab's Numeric check does exactly that for its single dial, but in a big model it would mean a separate run for every dial. Backpropagation avoids this by working backward from the one loss at the end. Every number it works out on the way back is shared by all the dials behind it, so each shared part is worked out only once. In the small graph, the slope at the multiply station, −0.1333, is used for both w and x. In a big model, the slope arriving at a layer is reused for every dial in that layer and in every layer before it. That is why one backward sweep gives every dial its slope at once. You could carry nudges forward from one dial toward the loss instead, but that answers the question for only one dial per run. The backward method that programs use is called reverse-mode autodiff, which is short for reverse-mode automatic differentiation, where differentiation means finding derivatives. The weak point: long products The multiplying that makes backpropagation cheap is also its weak point. Because slopes are multiplied along the chain, a long line of layers that each pass back a fraction leaves almost nothing for the earliest layers. That vanishing-gradient problem shaped how modern models are built. The shortcuts you will meet in The transformer block lab are largely a fix for it. Careful starting weights help too, and so does a kind of layer that rescales the numbers passing through it, called normalization. The Gradient flow card lets you measure the first two of these fixes, but it has no normalization layer.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Backpropagation
documents.body: Walk the small graph one edge at a time The Interactive backpropagation computation graph card has six circles: input x, weight w, multiply z, sigmoid ŷ, target y and loss L. A circle shows ? until its value has been worked out. Below the graph sits the Backpropagation trace, six steps you can move through with the Advance one edge button or by clicking any arrow on the graph. The trace opens on step 1, Multiply, with z already filled in, so your first press of Advance one edge moves on to Activate. Multiply multiplies the input by the weight and fills in z, which is 0.480 at the start. Activate sends z through the sigmoid and fills in the guess ŷ, which is 0.618. Measure loss compares the guess with the target and fills in the loss L, which is 0.0797. Loss → output starts the backward pass by multiplying in the loss station's factor, −0.565. Output → product multiplies in the sigmoid's factor, 0.236, which brings the running total to −0.1333. Product → weight multiplies in x, which is 0.800, and gives the weight its slope of −0.1066. During the first three steps the heading reads "Forward pass" with values →, and from the fourth step on it reads "Backward pass" with ← gradients. Each backward step adds a pink × tag under an arrow, showing the factor that arrow multiplies in. A pink pill also appears under each circle with its running total, and the next row of the tape fills in. Check the tape as you go: each pill should equal the pill to its right times the factor on the arrow between them. At the last step the tape reads −0.1333 × 0.800 = −0.1066, and a small line under it gives the slope toward x as well. Break the slope on purpose Before you touch anything, make a prediction: if the loss gets ten times bigger, should the slope on the weight get bigger too? Try this: Set Input x to 1.5, Weight w to 3, and Target y to 0.1, then walk the trace again. Now z is 4.5, so the sigmoid pins its guess near 1, at 0.989. That is a long way from the target of 0.1, and the loss jumps to 0.790, which is about ten times its starting value. Yet the slope on the weight is only 0.029. Ignoring the sign, that is less than a third of the 0.1066 you started with. It is also positive now, because the guess sits above the target, so the weight should go down. The loss station's factor is large, about 1.778, because the miss is big, and x is 1.5. The sigmoid's factor, though, has collapsed to 0.011, because a saturated sigmoid barely responds to a nudge, and that one tiny factor shrinks the whole product: That is the vanishing gradient in miniature, with one layer instead of twelve. You can also move Target y on its own and read the Chain rule row, which updates straight away. First put Input x back to 0.8 and Weight w back to 0.6. Setting the target to 0 then flips the slope to about +0.233, so the weight should now go down. Setting the target to 0.6, close to the guess, shrinks the slope to about 0.0067, because a guess that is nearly right needs only a small correction. Spend the slope A slope only becomes useful when you act on it, and that is the job of the last two controls. The Learning rate slider, written η and read "eta", sets how big a step to take. The button Apply w ← w − η∂L/∂w takes one step, setting the new weight to the old weight minus the learning rate times the slope. Put Target y back to 0.9, so all three sliders are at their starting values again. Then, with a learning rate of 0.70, one press works out like this: Subtracting a negative slope moves the weight up, which is exactly what the slope said to do. The loss falls from 0.0797 to 0.0720, and on the Loss versus weight tangent chart the ball slides a little way downhill. Moving the Learning rate slider on its own changes nothing until you press the button. The chart draws the loss for every weight from −3 to 3, with a ball at the current weight. A dashed straight line, called a tangent, touches the curve at the ball, and its steepness is the slope that the backward pass worked out. A green dashed line marks the weight where the guess would equal the target and the loss would be zero, labelled ŷ = y at w 2.75 at the start. Check the slope by measuring Under the chart, compare Analytic slope with Numeric check. The first comes from the chain-rule formula, while the second comes from nudging the weight and measuring, so the two are found in completely different ways. Picture a student who solves an equation with algebra and then checks the answer a second way, by plugging numbers back in. The Numeric check works in a similar spirit, because it nudges the weight a tiny bit up and a tiny bit down and measures the loss both times. It then divides the change in loss by the distance between the two weights it tried. You can try a rougher version yourself with a much bigger nudge. Drag Weight w to 0.62 and read the Loss readout, which shows about 0.07755, then drag it to 0.58, where it shows about 0.08182. The loss changes by about −0.00427, and dividing by 0.04, the distance between the two weights, gives the slope: Even this rough measurement lands on the chain rule's −0.1066. The lab uses a far tinier nudge of 0.00001, so the two readouts agree in every printed digit wherever you drag Weight w. Stack the layers Now open Gradient flow through depth, which builds a stack of layers, each a row of 16 units. It runs the stack once on 32 made-up practice examples before any training, and then it shows how much slope reaches each layer. The bars run from Layer 1 · in, nearest the input, down to the last layer, which is marked · out. A full bar is split into 20 equal stretches, running from 1e-13 at the empty end to 1e7 at the full end. Each extra stretch stands for ten times more slope. Each factor of ten is called an order of magnitude, so a bar that is three stretches shorter shows a slope three orders of magnitude, or a thousand times, smaller. A bar half as long is therefore not half the slope, so trust the printed number beside it. Under the bars, Layer 1 norm, the last layer's norm and Layer 1 ÷ last give the exact values. Loss at the start gives the untrained stack's average cross-entropy score on its 32 examples. The card opens at six layers, where Layer 1 reads 1.4e-4 and Layer 6 reads 2.3e-2. Run these comparisons in order, and before each change, predict which way Layer 1 norm will move: Set Activation to sigmoid, Initial weight scale to Glorot, and Skip connections to off. Then lower Network depth to 1 and raise it back up to 12, one step at a time. Watch Layer 1's norm start at about 0.15 with one layer and fall at every single step, down to 2.6e-8 at twelve. The last layer's own number wobbles up and down, and at twelve layers it still reads about 0.21. Switch Activation to tanh, and notice that Layer 1 now reads about the same as the last layer. Switch to ReLU, keep twelve layers, and step Initial weight scale from small (std 0.1) through Glorot and He to large (std 1.0). Every bar moves together, from tiny to enormous. Switch back to sigmoid with Glorot and turn Skip connections on. Then compare Layer 1 ÷ last and Loss at the start with the sigmoid readings you saw at the end of step 2. For more detail, open Table of the same numbers, which adds two columns. Mean slope f′(z) is the average local derivative of each layer's squashing step. Here f′(z), read "f-prime of z", is the lab's short way of writing a squashing step's local derivative. Output RMS, short for root mean square, is a typical size for a layer's output numbers. To find it, square the numbers, take the average, then take the square root, much like the norm.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Backpropagation
documents.body: No station uses the whole formula, since each one multiplies whatever arrives from its right by its own local derivative. The running product is what carries the information back to the dial. The multiply station reports the other input's value, so the slope on w is scaled by x and the slope toward x is scaled by w. That is why forward values have to stay in memory until the backward pass reaches them. The sigmoid's local derivative peaks at 0.25 when the guess is 0.5 and falls toward zero at both ends. A sigmoid can never pass back more than a quarter of the slope it receives. A large loss does not guarantee a large slope, because one flat, saturated station in the middle of the chain can block almost all of it. The branch toward x gets a real slope even though it has no dial to turn. In a deeper model, that same branch is how slope reaches the earlier layers. The target is data rather than a dial, so no slope flows toward it, and the graph marks it no gradient: data. Analytic slope and Numeric check agree in every printed digit. Comparing a formula's slope with a measured one like this is called gradient checking, and in real code it catches mistakes in derivatives that someone wrote by hand. The Chain rule row reports that match as Numeric agreement, a relative error, which means the gap between the two slopes as a share of their size. At the start it reads about 9.2e-10 percent, which is less than a billionth of a percent. Vanishing is about the gap between the first and last layers, while the starting weights set the size of every layer at once. With ReLU at twelve layers, Layer 1 and the last layer stay within a factor of ten of each other at every starting setting. At twelve layers, sigmoid vanishes at every starting setting, and even its best setting leaves Layer 1 with less than one part in 250 of the last layer's slope. The table's Mean slope f′(z) column shows why sigmoid struggles. With sigmoid it stays below 0.25 at every layer, so each step back starts by cutting the slope to under a quarter. At twelve layers, tanh with large (std 1.0) shows the opposite problem. Layer 1's slope ends up more than ten times bigger than the last layer's, so the slope grows as it travels back toward the input. A shortcut fixes the gap, not the growth. With sigmoid, Glorot, twelve layers and skips on, the Output RMS column climbs from about 0.55 at Layer 1 to more than 6 at Layer 12. That swelling pushes the final guesses to near-certain answers, about half of them wrong, which lifts Loss at the start from 0.90 to 7.30.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Backpropagation
documents.body: What this lab simplifies The small graph is honestly calculated, but it is tiny, with one dial, one example and one squashing step. It also scores the guess with a squared gap rather than cross-entropy, the kind of loss that language models actually use and that the Gradient flow through depth card uses. No station feeds two others, so the lab never has to combine slopes arriving from different paths. The chart works only because the model has one dial. A real model has millions of dials, so nobody can draw its loss curve. The tangent here stands for one slope out of the millions that the same backward pass would produce at once. The Gradient flow through depth card is one random draw of the starting weights and the practice examples, using a stack 16 units wide on 32 made-up points. It is measured before any training step, it has no normalization layers, and it reports one norm for each layer's weights. A different random draw changes its numbers but not the orderings this lesson describes. The course's own checks re-run the card with seven different random draws to make sure of that. That card shows how big the slopes start, not whether the network would actually learn. Learning also depends on the method that applies the slopes, on the learning rate and on how the error is scored, and the slopes keep changing as training goes on. Where the real method runs into trouble The assembly-line picture and the group-project story both suggest fault and intent, but there is none. The backward pass is arithmetic about how one number responds to a nudge in another. A big slope does not mean a dial is "wrong", only that the loss is sensitive to it right now. Real graphs branch, which this lab never shows. A station whose output feeds several others collects slopes from each of them and adds them together before multiplying by its own local derivative. Picture one path sending back 0.3 and another sending back −0.1, which gives the station a total of 0.2. One weight can also be reused in many places, so its slope is a sum of contributions from every place it appears. The backward pass also has a hidden cost, because the forward values must be kept in activation memory until the backward pass reaches them. That storage grows with the number of layers, the number of examples in each round and the length of the text. For long documents and deep models, that storage, not the arithmetic, is often what limits training. Skip connections on their own make numbers grow, as the card shows. Real deep networks, such as the transformers you will meet in later labs, pair shortcuts with normalization layers. This lab leaves those out, so the card shows what shortcuts do alone, growth included. A common mix-up: Backpropagation is not how brains learn. It needs a single error signal sent backward through the exact same connections used going forward, and biological brains do not appear to work that way. It is an efficient method for finding the slopes of a calculation, and nothing more.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Backpropagation
documents.body: Programs do the bookkeeping The software toolkits that people use to build models, called frameworks, do all of this automatically. Every operation quietly records what it needs to report its own local derivative, building a tape as the forward pass runs, much like the tape in this lab. Asking for slopes then replays that tape in reverse, which is reverse-mode autodiff in action. Nobody has to write derivatives by hand, which is why trying out a new model design is cheap. Saving memory The memory problem has a standard trick called gradient checkpointing. Instead of storing every forward value, the program saves them only at a few chosen points and recomputes the rest during the backward pass. That costs roughly 30 percent more computing in exchange for a large saving in memory. Slopes too small to store Computers store numbers using bits, where a bit is a single digit that is either 0 or 1, and a 16-bit number uses 16 of them. To save memory, training sometimes stores numbers in a 16-bit format called fp16 instead of the usual 32 bits. A very small slope can then round down to exactly zero and be lost. The fix is to multiply the loss by a large number before the backward pass, which scales every slope up, and then divide that number back out afterward. A different 16-bit format, called bf16, covers the same range of sizes as the 32-bit format, so it usually needs no scaling. Taming the size of slopes Glorot and He are short formulas from research papers published in 2010 and 2015. Glorot divides 2 by the number of inputs plus the number of outputs, while He divides 2 by the number of inputs alone, and each then takes the square root. This lab's layers have 16 inputs and 16 outputs, so Glorot gives the square root of 2 ÷ 32, which is exactly 0.25. He was designed for units like ReLU, and the same steps give it about 0.35 here. When a slope grows too large anyway, a trick called gradient clipping shrinks it back whenever its norm passes a set limit. Normalization layers, which rescale the numbers inside the model as they pass through, help keep both the forward values and the slopes in a workable range. Clearing slopes between steps In most frameworks, new slopes are added to the old ones by default rather than replacing them, so programs clear them to zero before each new step. That same adding-up lets a small computer gather slopes from several rounds of examples before taking one step, as if it had trained on one bigger round. Where backpropagation stops Some steps cannot pass a slope backward at all. Picking one word from a list of possible next words is a hard choice, so there is no smooth answer to the question "what if it moved slightly?" Training through a step like that needs different ways of estimating slopes, which is part of why the reinforcement stage in the Post-training lab does not look like ordinary training. The Reinforcement learning foundations lab runs the simplest of these methods on a four-armed bandit. That is a toy game where you keep choosing one of four slot-machine arms and see whether it pays.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Backpropagation
documents.body: This module is about backpropagation, the algorithm that computes the gradient of a scalar loss with respect to every parameter. *Loss & gradient descent* showed how to use a slope: step each weight against it. This module answers where those slopes come from when the loss sits at the end of a chain of operations: how much would the loss change for a small nudge to each weight? The answer is the chain rule. Each operation knows only its local derivative, how its output responds to its own inputs, and the backward pass multiplies those factors along the computation graph, the record of operations from inputs and parameters to the loss. The module follows that product through a one-weight graph, then through a stack of up to 12 layers. Where it shows up Every gradient-trained model. Deep learning frameworks run backpropagation as reverse-mode automatic differentiation, so model code defines only the forward computation and gets every gradient from one backward call. Deep architectures. Transformers and deep convolutional networks pair skip connections, which add a layer's input to its output, with normalization layers, which rescale activations to a steady size. Separately, initialization schemes such as Glorot (Glorot and Bengio, 2010) and He (He et al., 2015) choose the spread of the random starting weights, which sets how much each layer scales the gradient. Training memory. Forward values stay in memory until the backward pass has used them, and this activation memory often limits training before compute does. Why it matters Every training step needs a slope for every parameter. Reverse mode gets all of them from one backward pass that typically costs about two forward passes, however many parameters the model has. Working forward instead would take one pass per parameter; *What it is* shows why. Depth adds a second problem. The gradient that reaches the first layer has passed through every layer above it, so it can arrive too small to move those weights or large enough to blow up the update. In the lab, depth, the activation, the initial weight scale, and skip connections set how small or large that gradient starts, before any training step. What you will be able to explain How forward values fill a computation graph from the inputs to the loss, how backward derivatives fill it from the loss back to the weight, and why the backward pass needs the stored forward values. How the chain rule turns the local derivatives of a small graph into ∂L/∂w, and how a finite-difference check confirms it. How gradient size changes from layer to layer with depth, activation, initial weight scale, and skip connections, so you can predict when the first layers' gradients vanish or explode. What the lab shows Nothing here is a trained model: every number is computed from your settings. The first three cards share one graph, z = x · w, then ŷ = σ(z), then L = (ŷ − y)², with one weight and one example, evaluated with exact formulas. Interactive backpropagation computation graph. Backpropagation trace and Advance one edge step forward through Multiply, Activate, and Measure loss, then back to Product → weight. A tape records each multiplication. Loss versus weight tangent chart. The exact loss curve and its tangent, with Analytic slope from the chain rule beside Numeric check from a finite difference. Backpropagation controls and chain rule. Sliders for Input x, Weight w, Target y, and Learning rate, the Chain rule product, and Apply w ← w − η∂L/∂w for one gradient-descent step. Gradient flow through depth. A multilayer perceptron, a stack of fully connected layers, 1 to 12 deep with 16 units each. It is backpropagated once at one random draw of starting weights, on 32 synthetic points, with no training step and no normalization layers. Bars show each layer's measured gradient norm, the size of its weight gradient. The key experiment: set Activation to sigmoid, Initial weight scale to Glorot, and Skip connections off, then raise Network depth from 1 to 12. Layer 1 norm falls by nearly seven orders of magnitude, while the last layer's norm swings up and down along the way and ends near 0.2, about where it started. Turning Skip connections on lifts Layer 1's norm back up, and Loss at the start shows the cost.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Backpropagation
documents.body: Gradient descent needs ∂L/∂w for every parameter. Backpropagation computes all of them in one backward sweep over the computation graph, by multiplying local derivatives along each path from the loss back to the parameter. This lab runs the smallest graph that still has every feature: z = x · w, then ŷ = σ(z), then L = (ŷ − y)². The forward pass fills in values left to right. The backward pass fills in derivatives right to left. The three local derivatives Each node only knows how its own output responds to its own inputs: Loss node: ∂L/∂ŷ = 2(ŷ − y) Sigmoid node: ∂ŷ/∂z = ŷ(1 − ŷ) Multiply node: ∂z/∂w = x and ∂z/∂x = w The chain rule assembles them: ∂L/∂w = 2(ŷ − y) · ŷ(1 − ŷ) · x. The Chain rule panel shows exactly this product with the current numbers substituted in. On the graph, each edge shows the local factor it multiplies in, each node shows the gradient accumulated so far, and the tape below writes out every multiplication. Notice the pattern in the multiply node. The derivative with respect to w is x, and the derivative with respect to x is w — each input's gradient depends on the *other* input's forward value. That is why the forward values must be kept around until the backward pass reaches them. Why backward rather than forward You could compute derivatives forward instead, propagating "how does everything change if w changes?" from the input onward. That works, but it answers the question for one parameter per pass. Reverse mode answers it for *all* parameters in one pass, because it propagates "how does the loss change if this intermediate changes?" backward from a single output. With one scalar loss and billions of parameters, a reverse pass costs a small constant multiple of a forward pass, typically about twice, while forward mode would need one pass per parameter. Many layers: the product gets long The one-weight graph has three factors. A deep network has more factors for every layer, so the Gradient flow through depth card measures how a long product behaves. It backpropagates a perceptron of 16-unit layers, 1 to 12 deep, at its random starting weights and prints the gradient norm for each layer's weights. With sigmoid units and Glorot starting weights, Layer 1's norm falls from 1.5e-1 at depth 1 to 2.6e-8 at depth 12, while Layer 12's stays near 0.2. Each layer on the way back multiplies the gradient by about 0.24: a sigmoid slope of at most 0.25 times a weight gain near one. That is the vanishing gradient. Three controls change the product: Activation. tanh with Glorot or He weights keeps Layer 1 within a factor of three of the last layer at every seed from 1 to 7. Sigmoid does not: its first-to-last ratio is below 0.004 at all four starting scales. Initial weight scale. With ReLU at depth 12, Layer 1's norm is 2.4e-7 for small weights, 2.0e-2 for Glorot, 1.3 for He, and 3.5e5 for large. The scale sets how big every layer's gradient is, so a bad one means no learning or a blow-up. He initialization (He et al., 2015) was derived for rectifiers and Glorot (Glorot and Bengio, 2010) is the scale the tanh runs hold level. Skip connections. A skip connection adds a layer's input to its output, so the backward pass gets an identity route: ∂L/∂h_(l−1) = ∂L/∂h_l + W_lᵀδ_l. At depth 12 with sigmoid and Glorot, Layer 1's norm rises from 2.6e-8 to 0.24. The price shows in Loss at the start, which rises from 0.90 to 7.30, because the additions make activations grow with depth.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Backpropagation
documents.body: This is the credit assignment mechanism. When a prediction is wrong, backpropagation decides how much each parameter contributed to that error, and the answer is precise rather than heuristic. It also explains two failure modes that shape every architecture decision later in the course. Because gradients are products of local derivatives, a long chain of factors below 1 shrinks toward zero and a long chain above 1 grows without bound. Residual connections, layer normalization, and careful initialization all exist to keep that product well behaved.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Backpropagation
documents.body: Advance the Backpropagation trace through Multiply and Activate and watch values fill in from x and w toward the prediction. Continue to Measure loss and compare the loss node with its position on the loss-versus-weight chart. Then step backward through Loss → output, Output → product, and Product → weight. Read each × tag on an edge as one factor entering the product, and check on the tape that each gradient is the previous one times that factor. At the defaults the tape ends at ∂L/∂w = −0.1333 × 0.800 = −0.1066. Click an edge to jump to it. Set Target y far from the current prediction and watch ∂L/∂ŷ grow. Then set Input x to 1.5, Weight w to 3, and Target y to 0.1: the sigmoid saturates, ŷ(1 − ŷ) drops to 0.011, and ∂L/∂w falls to 0.029, even though the loss is 0.790, ten times its default value. Next, pick a Learning rate and press Apply w ← w − η∂L/∂w, then check that the new point sits lower on the chart. At the defaults and η 0.70, one press moves w from 0.600 to 0.675 and the loss from 0.0797 to 0.0720. Compare Analytic slope with Numeric check as you go: the Numeric agreement readout is a gradient check. Then open Gradient flow through depth. Set Activation to sigmoid, Initial weight scale to Glorot, and Skip connections to off, and raise Network depth from 1 to 12: the Layer 1 norm collapses, while the last layer's norm swings with depth and ends near 0.2 as Layer 12 norm. Switch Activation to tanh and compare. At depth 12 with ReLU, step Initial weight scale from small to large and read Layer 1 norm. Then switch to sigmoid, turn Skip connections on, and compare Layer 1 ÷ last and Loss at the start.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Backpropagation
documents.body: The running product is what travels; the local derivative is what each node contributes. Nothing has global knowledge of the graph. ŷ(1 − ŷ) peaks at 0.25 when ŷ = 0.5 and falls toward zero at both ends. Sigmoid can never pass more than a quarter of the gradient through, which is a per-layer decay factor. The branch toward x has a valid derivative but no parameter to update, so no weight change follows it. In a deep model that same branch is how gradient reaches earlier layers. Target y is fixed data. During the backward pass the graph marks it no gradient: data. Analytic and numeric slopes agree to about eleven significant digits at the defaults. Disagreement in real code almost always means a bug in a hand-written derivative, not a flaw in calculus. A big loss does not guarantee a big gradient. Saturation decouples the two. Vanishing is a ratio between layers; initial scale is a size across all of them. With ReLU at depth 12 the first-to-last ratio stays within a factor of ten at every scale, while the norms themselves run from 2.4e-7 to 3.5e5. Skip connections fix the ratio, not the size: the starting loss they leave behind (7.30 against 0.90) is the activations growing, which normalization layers exist to hold down.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Backpropagation
documents.body: In this lab. The graph is genuinely computed — forward values, every local derivative, the chain-rule product, the finite-difference check, and the weight update are all live. What the first three cards leave out is scale and structure: one parameter, one example, no minibatch, no layers, and a squared-error loss instead of the cross-entropy used for language models. The learning-rate slider affects nothing until you press apply. The Gradient flow card is one random draw (seed 7) of a 16-wide network on 32 synthetic points, measured before any training step and with no normalization layers. Other seeds change its numbers, not the orderings quoted here; the tests cover seeds 1 to 7. It shows how large a gradient starts, not whether the network would train: that also depends on the optimizer, the learning rate, and the loss. In real systems. Nodes have many outputs, so gradients arriving from several paths must be *summed* at each node rather than replaced. Weights are reused across positions and time steps, which means one parameter accumulates contributions from many places in the graph. And the backward pass is not free: it needs the forward activations, so memory grows with depth, batch size, and sequence length. Long-context training is frequently memory-bound rather than compute-bound for exactly this reason. Real deep networks rarely use skip connections alone. Transformers and deep convolutional networks pair them with normalization layers, which this lab leaves out, so the card shows what skips do on their own, including the growth they cause. Backpropagation is also not a model of biological learning. It requires a global error signal and symmetric weight access that brains do not appear to have. It is an efficient algorithm for differentiating a program, and nothing more.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Backpropagation
documents.body: Frameworks implement this as reverse-mode automatic differentiation. Every operation records enough of its inputs to compute its own local derivative, forming a tape; calling backward walks the tape in reverse. You never write a derivative by hand, which is why new architectures are cheap to try. The memory cost has a standard remedy: gradient checkpointing stores activations only at chosen boundaries and recomputes the rest during the backward pass, trading roughly 30 percent more compute for a large memory reduction. Mixed-precision training adds a related wrinkle: small gradients in 16-bit floating point (fp16) can underflow to zero, so a loss-scaling factor multiplies the loss before backward and divides it out afterward. The bf16 format keeps fp32's exponent range and usually needs no scaling. Two more practical notes. Gradients must be zeroed between steps in most frameworks, because accumulation is the default and is what makes large effective batch sizes possible on small hardware. And when a graph passes through a non-differentiable operation such as sampling a token, ordinary backpropagation stops there; policy-gradient estimators or straight-through approximations are needed instead, which is part of why the post-training lab's reinforcement stage differs from ordinary supervised training. Reinforcement learning foundations runs the simplest such estimator on a four-armed bandit.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Interactive backpropagation computation graph · Backpropagation
documents.body: Values move right, gradients move left A one-weight computation graph you walk one edge at a time: input and weight multiply, a sigmoid squashes the product, and squared error against a target gives the loss. The first three steps fill in values; the last three multiply one local derivative per edge onto the gradient, and the tape below writes every step down. Six nodes, `input x`, `weight w`, `multiply z`, `sigmoid ŷ`, `target y`, and `loss L`, each showing its forward value. A value not yet computed shows `?` inside a dashed ring. Once the backward pass reaches a node, a pink pill under it shows that node's gradient: `∂L/∂L 1`, then `∂L/∂ŷ`, `∂L/∂z`, and finally `∂L/∂w` and `∂L/∂x` together. Blue labels above each edge are the forward values it carries. Once the backward pass crosses an edge, a pink `× factor` below it shows the local derivative that edge multiplies in, and a dashed pink stroke with a reversed arrow marks the gradient's path. The tape: six rows, three forward (blue edge) and three backward (pink edge), each with its formula, the numbers substituted in, and the result. Rows ahead of the current step are dimmed with `?`. At the defaults (x 0.80, w 0.60, y 0.90) the tape reads z 0.480, ŷ 0.618, L 0.0797, then ∂L/∂ŷ −0.565, ∂L/∂z −0.1333, and ∂L/∂w −0.1066, with ∂L/∂x −0.0800. Forward: `z = x · w`, `ŷ = σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^−z)`, `L = (ŷ − y)²`. There is no ½ in the loss, so its derivative is `2(ŷ − y)`. Backward, one factor per edge: `∂L/∂ŷ = 2(ŷ − y)`, then `∂L/∂z = ∂L/∂ŷ · ŷ(1 − ŷ)`, then `∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂z · x` and `∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂z · w`. Each pill equals the pill to its right times the factor on the edge between them. The multiply node sends a gradient to both of its inputs in the same step, and each uses the other input's forward value: `∂z/∂w = x` and `∂z/∂x = w`. That is why forward values must be kept until the backward pass reaches them. All numbers come from the SDK's `backpropSnapshot`. A unit test checks them against finite differences for both w and x across the slider ranges. `Backpropagation trace`, `Advance one edge`, or a click on an edge chooses the step. During the backward pass, clicking the `target y` edge changes nothing and announces that the target gets no gradient. `Input x`, `Weight w`, `Target y`, and `Learning rate` live on `Backpropagation controls and chain rule`. Changing any of the first three restarts the trace at Multiply. Comparison worth running: at the defaults, walk all six steps and note each `× factor`. Then set `Input x` 1.50, `Weight w` 3.00, and `Target y` 0.10 and walk again: the sigmoid factor falls to 0.011 and `∂L/∂w` to 0.029, even though the loss, 0.790, is ten times larger. A large error does not guarantee a large gradient. When ŷ is near 0 or 1, `ŷ(1 − ŷ)` collapses and takes the whole product with it. That is sigmoid saturation, and it is one layer of the vanishing-gradient problem. The Gradient flow through depth card stacks twelve of them. `∂L/∂x` is computed even though x is data and never updated. In a deeper network the same branch is how the gradient reaches earlier layers. Nobody in the graph knows the whole formula. Each node only multiplies what arrives from its right by its own local derivative. In this lab: one scalar weight, one example, squared error, and hand-written local derivatives. No node feeds two others, so no gradients have to be summed. In this lab: the graph is a picture of a three-operation chain. A real network's graph has millions of such edges, and frameworks store its activations so the backward pass never recomputes the forward one. In general: when a value feeds several later operations, the gradients arriving from each path are added. Weights shared across positions or time steps collect a sum of contributions this way. In general: vanishing and exploding gradients are this same product becoming tiny or huge as more local factors are multiplied in. Residual connections, normalization, and careful initialization exist to keep it well behaved, and the Gradient flow through depth card measures what two of them do.
documents.title: Values move right, gradients move left

documents.subtitle: Loss versus weight tangent chart · Backpropagation
documents.body: The backward pass is a claim about this slope The loss of this one-weight network for every weight from −3 to 3, with the current weight, a tangent whose slope is the backward pass's `∂L/∂w`, and a finite-difference check beside it. If the two slopes ever disagreed, the chain rule on the graph would be the thing that was wrong. The horizontal axis is `weight w` from −3 to 3. The vertical axis is `loss L` from 0 to the tallest point of the current curve, labelled at 0, half, and full; the scale refits when `Input x` or `Target y` changes. The loss curve sampled at 121 weights, a ball at the current weight with a dashed guide to the axis, and a dashed tangent through the ball. A green dashed line where ŷ = y, the weight at which the loss reaches zero, when it lies in view. At the defaults it sits at w 2.75. Metrics `Loss`, `Analytic slope` from the chain rule, and `Numeric check` from a central difference. Each plotted point reruns the forward pass at that weight: `z = x · w`, `ŷ = σ(z)`, `L = (ŷ − y)²`. The curve belongs to the current x and y. `Analytic slope` is `2(ŷ − y) · ŷ(1 − ŷ) · x`, the same product as the tape. `Numeric check` is `(L(w + ε) − L(w − ε)) / 2ε` with ε = 10⁻⁵. The zero-loss weight is `w* = logit(y) / x = ln(y / (1 − y)) / x`. When y is 0 or 1 it is infinitely far away, so no line is drawn. The tangent is `L + (∂L/∂w)(w′ − w)` for w′ within 0.72 of the current weight, drawn through the same scales as the curve. This card has no controls of its own. `Weight w` moves the ball, `Input x` and `Target y` reshape the curve, and `Apply w ← w − η∂L/∂w` takes one step. Comparison worth running: drag `Weight w` across the range and watch `Analytic slope` and `Numeric check` agree in every printed digit. Then press the update button and watch the ball move downhill along the tangent. Where the sigmoid saturates, with x · w far from zero, the curve flattens and both slopes approach zero. That is not a minimum: at `Input x` 1.50 and `Weight w` −3.00 the loss is 0.790 and the slope only −0.029. It is a vanishing gradient. The ball only reaches the green line if you take enough steps or drag it there. Each step's size is η times the slope, so steps shrink as the curve flattens. In this lab: the curve is the exact loss of this network, sampled densely, with nothing fitted or interpolated beyond straight segments between samples. In this lab: the vertical scale refits to the tallest point, so the tangent's drawn angle is a faithful sign and rough steepness rather than a calibrated angle. In general: you cannot plot loss against a real model's parameters. This tangent stands in for one component of a gradient vector with millions of entries, all produced by the same backward pass.
documents.title: The backward pass is a claim about this slope

documents.subtitle: Backpropagation controls and chain rule · Backpropagation
documents.body: Change a number, then spend the gradient The four sliders that define the graph, the chain-rule product evaluated on those numbers, and one gradient-descent update that moves the weight. This is where the derivative stops being a picture and becomes a step. `Input x` from 0.10 to 1.50, `Weight w` from −3.00 to 3.00, `Target y` from 0.00 to 1.00, and `Learning rate` from 0.05 to 2.00. A `Chain rule` row printing the three factors `∂L/∂ŷ × ∂ŷ/∂z × ∂z/∂w`, their product `∂L/∂w`, and the relative error against the numeric check. A button `Apply w ← w − η∂L/∂w` that performs one update and announces the old weight, the new weight, and the new loss. The factors are `2(ŷ − y)`, `ŷ(1 − ŷ)`, and `x`. Their product is the same number the graph's `∂L/∂w` pill, the tape, and the tangent use. The update is `w ← w − η · ∂L/∂w`, clamped to the slider's range of −3 to 3. There is no momentum and no clipping. Moving `Input x`, `Weight w`, or `Target y` restarts the trace at Multiply, so the graph never shows a gradient computed from stale values. `Learning rate` only scales the next press. The relative error is `|analytic − numeric| / max(|analytic|, |numeric|)`. At the defaults it reads 9.2e-10 percent: the two agree to about eleven significant digits. `Input x` appears twice: inside the forward product z = x · w, and again as the last chain-rule factor `∂z/∂w = x`. `Weight w` is the parameter. Drag it, or press the update button and let the gradient move it. `Target y` is the label. Moving it changes `∂L/∂ŷ` at once and reshapes the loss curve. Comparison worth running: at the defaults, one press at η 0.70 moves w from 0.600 to 0.675 and the loss from 0.0797 to 0.0720. Now set `Input x` 1.50, `Weight w` 3.00, and `Target y` 0.10: the loss is 0.790, yet the gradient is only 0.029 and the step barely moves. A negative `∂L/∂w` means the update increases the weight. The minus sign in the update is the whole of gradient descent. If you set `Target y` equal to the current prediction, `Loss`, `Analytic slope`, and the next update all become zero. The relative error grows when the gradient itself is near zero, because the finite difference then measures mostly rounding error. That is a limit of the check, not of the chain rule. In this lab: one parameter, one example, an exact gradient, and a learning rate you choose by hand. In general: automatic differentiation builds this product for every parameter from a tape of local derivatives recorded during the forward pass, which is why frameworks only ask you to write the forward pass.
documents.title: Change a number, then spend the gradient

documents.subtitle: Gradient flow through depth · Backpropagation
documents.body: How much gradient survives a deep stack A multilayer perceptron with 1 to 12 hidden layers of 16 units and one sigmoid output is backpropagated once, at its random starting weights, on a fixed batch of 32 examples. Each bar is the exact norm of the loss's gradient with respect to one layer's weights, so you can watch the product of local derivatives shrink, hold steady, or blow up as you stack layers. `Network depth` (1 to 12), `Activation` (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU), `Initial weight scale` (small with standard deviation 0.1, Glorot, He, large with standard deviation 1.0), and `Skip connections` (off, on). One bar per hidden layer, Layer 1 nearest the input and the last layer nearest the output, with its gradient norm printed beside it. Bar length is the number of decades above 1e-13, up to 1e7, so equal steps mean equal ratios, not equal differences. Four metrics: the norm at Layer 1, the norm at the last layer, their ratio, and Loss at the start. A badge in the heading repeats the ratio. A collapsible table of the same numbers, with two more columns: the mean slope f′(z) of each layer's units over the batch, and the root-mean-square of the layer's output. Forward: `h₁ = f(W₁x)`, then `h_l = f(W_l h_(l−1))`. With skip connections on, every layer after the first computes `h_l = h_(l−1) + f(W_l h_(l−1))`. The output is `σ(v·h_L)` and the loss is the mean binary cross-entropy over 32 fixed points in 16 dimensions. Backward: `∂L/∂logit = p − y`. Each layer multiplies the arriving gradient by `f′(z)` and then by `W_lᵀ`. With skips on the identity path adds the arriving gradient back, `∂L/∂h_(l−1) = ∂L/∂h_l + W_lᵀδ_l`. The gradient on `W_l` is `δ_l` times `h_(l−1)`, averaged over the batch. Weights are normal with standard deviation `√(2 / (fan-in + fan-out))` for Glorot, `√(2 / fan-in)` for He, and a fixed 0.1 or 1.0 for small and large. Biases are zero and left out of the norms. One seed draws the batch and the weights. A unit test checks every layer's gradient, and the output weights', against finite differences for each activation with and without skips. `Network depth`, `Activation`, `Initial weight scale`, and `Skip connections`. Nothing here moves the other cards. Comparison worth running: sigmoid, Glorot, skips off, depth 1 to 12. Layer 1's norm falls from 1.5e-1 to 2.6e-8 while the last layer's stays near 0.2. Then turn skips on, and then switch Activation to tanh. At the defaults (depth 6, sigmoid, Glorot) Layer 1's norm is 1.4e-4 and Layer 6's is 2.3e-2. At depth 12 each layer on the way back multiplies the gradient by about 0.24 on average: a sigmoid slope of at most 0.25, which the table's mean slope column shows, times a weight gain near one. Sigmoid vanishes at every starting scale: the first-to-last ratio is below 0.004 at all four, at every seed from 1 to 7. Glorot gives 1.2e-7 at depth 12 and He 2.3e-6. tanh with Glorot or He weights holds Layer 1 within a factor of three of the last layer. With large weights tanh saturates yet the gradient grows toward the input, more than ten times larger at Layer 1 at every seed. With ReLU the starting scale sets every layer's size: Layer 1's norm is 2.4e-7, 2.0e-2, 1.3, and 3.5e5 for small, Glorot, He, and large at seed 7, in that order at every seed. Skips on, sigmoid, Glorot, depth 12: Layer 1's norm rises from 2.6e-8 to 0.24 and the ratio from 1.2e-7 to 0.077, while Loss at the start rises from 0.90 to 7.30 because the additions make activations grow. In this lab: one random draw of the weights and batch, a 16-wide network on 32 synthetic points, no normalization layers, no training step, and weight-matrix norms only. Other seeds change the numbers but not the ordering in any comparison the lesson makes; tests cover seeds 1 to 7. In this lab: the loss scale, optimizer, and mini-batch noise are absent. A real run's gradient also depends on them, and it changes as training proceeds. In general: transformers and deep convolutional networks pair skip connections with normalization layers, which this card omits, so it shows what skips do alone, including the growth they cause. Gradient clipping, adaptive optimizers such as Adam, and mixed precision change what a gradient's size means in practice.
