documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: One measured or constructed attribute used as an input coordinate. Choosing it is a design decision; the model cannot recover a feature you never wrote down.
documents.title: Feature

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: The numbers that stand in for a raw example after encoding. Distance, clusters, and later weights all act on this representation, not on the original table text.
documents.title: Representation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: A categorical value turned into a vector with a single 1 in the matching slot and 0s elsewhere. Categories become orthogonal, so the encoding invents equal distance between every pair of labels.
documents.title: One-hot encoding

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: Rescaling a numeric feature so its range or variance is comparable to others. Without it, a column measured in thousands dominates a column measured in fractions.
documents.title: Normalization

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: The geometry whose axes are the chosen features. Neighbors in that space are neighbors only under that encoding. A 2-D plot of a longer vector is a projection.
documents.title: Feature space

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: The straight-line (Euclidean) gap between two vectors: square each coordinate difference, add them, and take the square root. Two different one-hot colors, (1, 0, 0) and (0, 1, 0), are √2 apart. Every neighbor ranking on this page is by distance, so it changes whenever the encoding does.
documents.title: Distance

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: A column whose values are labels rather than amounts. Treating a label as an integer invents an order the original column did not have.
documents.title: Categorical variable

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: Coordinates fitted so that items the later loss treats as similar end up nearby. The sketch on this page is authored to show that geometry; it is not trained.
documents.title: Embedding

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: The target y a supervised model is asked to match. It is not a feature unless you leak it into the input vector.
documents.title: Label

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: A picture turned into numbers by reading its pixels in a fixed order, so a 3×3 picture is a point in nine dimensions. Distance between two pictures is then ordinary distance between two vectors. With each pixel 0 or 1, one flipped pixel adds exactly 1 to the squared distance.
documents.title: Pixel vector

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: A vocabulary is a fixed list of known words, and a token ID is a word's position in it. IDs are labels, not amounts: subtracting them invents an order, and a word outside the list collapses into one unknown ID. The eight-word list in this lab is not a real tokenizer; real ones split text into pieces (Tokens & embeddings).
documents.title: Vocabulary and token ID

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: A cell with no recorded value. A model needs a number, so the row must go or something must fill the gap: reading it as 0, dropping the row, and filling with the mean of the others each move the summary and the neighbours differently.
documents.title: Missing value

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: The same record listed more than once. It double-counts in a summary and, if one copy lands in training and one in a test, lets the test row be answered by looking up its twin, so the score reads too high.
documents.title: Duplicate row

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: Labels that are wrong on some rows, such as a flipped price tag. A model fits a wrong label as faithfully as a right one, so a share, a nearest-neighbour answer, or a fitted boundary can move because of one bad tag.
documents.title: Label noise

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Data, features, and representation · question 1
documents.body: You set How to pack the door to one cubby each. What does Alder 12's packing slip hold? Three numbers: its rooms, the integer code stamped on its door color, and its park bit Six numbers: the five features plus a slot that carries its high-price tag Five numbers: its rooms, a 0 or 1 for each of red, blue, and green, and its park bit Two numbers: its rooms and a single 1 in the slot for its door color One cubby each gives every color its own 0/1 slot, so the slip is rooms, red, blue, green, park: five numbers, with Alder 12 reading 2, 1, 0, 0, 1. The three-number slip is the integer packing. The price tag is the label, so it stays off the slip unless you leak it.
documents.title: You set How to pack the door to one cubby each. What does Alder 12's packing slip hold?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Data, features, and representation · question 2
documents.body: With integer stamps, you stamp blue as 5. What happens to Elm 7, Alder 12's nearest house under the default stamps? It stays nearest, because distance depends only on rooms and park It drops from first place, since the new stamp puts blue far from red It stays nearest, because the stamp changes only how the door is painted It moves closer, because a larger stamp means a more similar color The slip carries the stamp as a coordinate, so changing blue from 2 to 5 changes the distance from every blue door to every other house. Elm 7 loses first place and two houses tie as nearest. The apartments never moved; the packing did. One cubby each would restore Elm 7, since it never reads the stamps.
documents.title: With integer stamps, you stamp blue as 5. What happens to Elm 7, Alder 12's nearest house under the default stamps?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Data, features, and representation · question 3
documents.body: Same-length rulers divides rooms by 4 and color stamps by 5. What does that do to the lineup? It adds a new measurement of each house, so distances become more accurate It makes color the widest axis, because stamps are the largest numbers It leaves every distance unchanged, because dividing keeps the ordering of houses It rescales the coordinates, which makes the 0 or 1 park slot the widest axis Rescaling is not a new measurement. With the default stamps, rooms then span 0.75 and the color stamps span 0.4 while the 0/1 park slot still spans a full 1, so park dominates most distances and the neighbor order can change. Normalization changes the map, which is why a scaler has to be a deliberate choice.
documents.title: Same-length rulers divides rooms by 4 and color stamps by 5. What does that do to the lineup?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Data, features, and representation · question 4
documents.body: On The gate you switch Stamp the gate reads from rooms to door color and keep Gate height t. What changes? Nothing changes, because the rule family is the same threshold on a single number The price tags change, because the gate predicts them from whichever stamp it reads Different houses reach the high yard, since the rule now reads another feature The rooms of every house change, because the gate moves the buildings it sorts The gate is the rule ŷ = 1[stamp ≥ t]. Changing the stamp it reads changes which houses clear t, so the same rule family draws a different cut through the street. The price tags are the labels and never move; the buildings do not move either.
documents.title: On The gate you switch Stamp the gate reads from rooms to door color and keep Gate height t. What changes?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Data, features, and representation · question 5
documents.body: On Two maps, the later-map neighbor of Alder 12 differs from its one-hot color neighbor. What does the later map show? A trained embedding fitted to the six price tags by minimizing a loss The first two slip numbers plotted as a plane, as in the lineup callout Hand-placed coordinates showing what a fitted geometry could look like The later map is authored: similar park-and-price listings were placed close together by hand to show the idea of an embedding. Nothing here was trained. Tokens & embeddings fits coordinates against a loss instead of assigning them. The first-two-numbers plane is the projection from the lineup callout, which is a different picture.
documents.title: On Two maps, the later-map neighbor of Alder 12 differs from its one-hot color neighbor. What does the later map show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Data, features, and representation · question 6
documents.body: On Pixels and words, Sentence is set to the one with a bird, and the word bird comes out as ID 0. What does that show about a fixed vocabulary? Every word outside the list becomes the same unknown ID, so different unseen words look identical The model learned that bird is unimportant, so it gave the word the smallest number IDs are given by how common a word is, so a rare word gets a small number A word outside the list is dropped before IDs are assigned, so the sentence gets shorter A vocabulary maps each known word to its position and sends everything else to one shared unknown ID, here 0. Nothing was learned and no frequency was counted: the list is fixed, and the sentence keeps all six positions, with bird occupying one as ID 0. Two different unseen words would therefore be indistinguishable.
documents.title: On Pixels and words, Sentence is set to the one with a bird, and the word bird comes out as ID 0. What does that show about a fixed vocabulary?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Data, features, and representation · question 7
documents.body: In the fixed vocabulary cat is ID 2, dog is ID 6, and mat is ID 5. If a model subtracted IDs as though they were amounts, what would it conclude? That cat is nearer to dog than to mat, because the IDs count how often words appear That all three words are equally far apart, because every ID is a whole number That cat is nearer to mat than to dog, an order the numbering invented That nothing differs from one-hot, because both encodings invent the same distances The gap from cat to mat is 3 and from cat to dog is 4, so subtraction ranks mat nearer even though cat and dog are both animals. The numbering made that order up, which is the integer-stamp trap again with words. One-hot would put every pair of different words exactly √2 apart.
documents.title: In the fixed vocabulary cat is ID 2, dog is ID 6, and mat is ID 5. If a model subtracted IDs as though they were amounts, what would it conclude?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Data, features, and representation · question 8
documents.body: Missing value is on with Handle missing set to read as 0, and the new listing's neighbour answer changed from high to low. You switch to fill with the mean. What happens? The answer stays low, because any filled value still throws away the true room count The answer returns to high, because the filled 1.8 rooms keeps Dock 2 among the three nearest The answer cannot change, because handling only affects the summary and not the neighbours The answer returns to high only if the row is dropped, because a filled value always lands far away Reading the blank as 0 sends Dock 2 from distance 1.00 to 3.00, so it drops out of the three nearest and the vote flips. Filling with the mean of the other rows (1.8 rooms) puts it at 1.20, still the nearest listing, so the answer is high again. Dropping the row also flips the answer. How a gap is handled is part of the encoding.
documents.title: Missing value is on with Handle missing set to read as 0, and the new listing's neighbour answer changed from high to low. You switch to fill with the mean. What happens?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Data, features, and representation · question 9
documents.body: Duplicate row is on, and the leave-one-out nearest-neighbour accuracy rises from 50 percent to 71.4 percent. What does that rise measure? Better generalization, because the table now has more examples to learn from Nothing about the detector: each copy is matched with its twin at distance 0 A better encoding, because duplicated rows pull the neighbours closer together A fix for the mislabelled row, because two copies outvote one wrong tag In leave-one-out, each row is predicted from its nearest other row. A copy's nearest other row is its twin at distance 0, with the same tag, so both copies are counted right for free. The score rose from 3 of 6 to 5 of 7 without any new information. The same leak happens when one copy lands in train and one in test.
documents.title: Duplicate row is on, and the leave-one-out nearest-neighbour accuracy rises from 50 percent to 71.4 percent. What does that rise measure?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: A computer cannot look at a house, a photo or a sentence and take it in the way you do. Everything it works with has to be a number, so before any AI can learn from examples, a person has to decide how each example becomes a list of numbers. This module is about that step, which sounds like paperwork but quietly shapes everything that comes after it. The lab uses a tiny made-up street of six houses for sale. Each one has some number of rooms, a red, blue or green door, and either a park nearby or not. Every house also wears a price tag marked high or low, and you will turn the houses into numbers in several different ways to see how much that choice matters. Where you have met it Every AI method in the later labs of this app starts from lists of numbers like these. Real pictures are made of thousands of tiny squares called pixels, and each pixel carries numbers for its brightness and color. Text gets the same treatment, because an AI system that reads text, such as a chatbot, first splits the words into pieces and swaps each piece for an ID. Why it matters The numbers you pick decide which examples count as close to each other, and many AI methods work by finding examples that are close. If you number the same houses a different way, a different house can become the nearest match, even though no house changed at all. A model is the part of an AI system that learns a pattern from examples and then uses that pattern to make guesses about new ones. A model cannot use anything you left off the list, and a single blank cell, copied row or wrong price tag can change an answer without any warning. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these ideas in your own words: How to turn one row of a table, such as one house, into a list of numbers by hand. Why two different ways of numbering the same rows can disagree about which rows are near each other. Why the same yes-or-no rule sorts the houses differently when it reads a different number. You will also say what an embedding is: a map of positions fitted so that a model does its job well. This lab draws one by hand, and the Tokens & embeddings lab shows one being learned. How a tiny 3×3 picture and a short sentence can each be turned into a list of numbers. You will also say how a blank cell, a copied row or a wrong price tag can change a summary of the table or a nearest-match answer. What the lab lets you do The lab has seven cards, which you can work through from top to bottom: The street shows the six houses before they become numbers, so you can pick one to study. Packing slip lets you choose how a door color turns into numbers, and shows the list of numbers that stands in for the house you picked. Who stands nearest lines up the other five houses by how far their numbers are from the numbers of your house. The gate sorts the houses with one rule, “is this number big enough?”, and lets you choose which number it reads. Two maps compares a map where every door color is equally far apart with a hand-drawn map of the kind a model might learn later. Pixels and words lets you draw a 3×3 picture and pick a sentence, then shows both of them as numbers. Messy rows spoils the table with a blank cell, a copied row and a wrong tag, so you can see what each problem changes. Nothing in the lab learns from examples, and none of its numbers come from real house sales. Every number is worked out on the spot from the six made-up houses, the picture and sentence you choose, and your settings.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: A packing slip that stands in for the house Picture a moving company that cannot ship a house, so it ships a slip of paper describing the house instead. Whoever receives the slip never sees the house, only what is written on the paper. A computer is in the same spot, because it only ever receives the numbers you write down. In the lab, each house starts as a row in a table, and Alder 12’s row says it has 2 rooms, a red door and a park nearby. Each thing you choose to write down about a house, such as its number of rooms, is called a feature. The slip gives each feature its own slot, and the number in that slot is the house’s value for that feature. A list of numbers kept in a fixed order is called a vector, so the slip is a feature vector. The whole slip, standing in for the real house, is called the house’s representation. Measuring distance, grouping houses and every later model all work on this representation, never on the street itself. Here is Alder 12 packed by hand with the lab’s starting settings. Its room count is already a number, so it goes in as 2, and its red door is written as 1, a number the lab calls the door’s stamp. “Near a park” becomes 1 for yes, where 0 would mean no, so Alder 12’s slip is (2, 1, 1). The price tag is left off that slip on purpose, because it is the label, the answer a model would later be asked to predict. If you copied it onto the slip, a model could read the answer straight off the list, which is called leaking the label. It would score perfectly on these six houses while learning nothing it could use on a new house, whose price nobody knows yet. The packing-slip picture stops matching in two places. A real packing slip only lists what is already in the box, while here you also invent some of the numbers, such as which stamp a red door gets. A person holding a real slip could also go and look at the house, but the computer never can, so anything left off the slip does not exist for it. With no park slot, for example, no later step could tell a park house from one without a park. Numbers for things that are not amounts The room count is an amount, so 4 rooms really is twice as many as 2 rooms. Door color works differently, because red, blue and green are names rather than amounts. A column whose values are names like this is called a categorical variable, and it needs a decision before it can become a number. The lab gives you three ways to pack the door, chosen with How to pack the door: integer stamps gives each color one whole number, which you set from 1 to 5 on the red, blue and green stamp pads. Before you change anything, red is stamped 1, blue is stamped 2 and green is stamped 3. one cubby each gives every color its own slot, which holds a 1 if the door is that color and a 0 if it is not. This is called one-hot encoding, because exactly one of the color slots is “hot”, or set to 1. same-length rulers divides rooms by 4, the most rooms any house has, and the color stamp by 5, the biggest stamp on the pads. After that, no slot can hold a number bigger than 1. Putting features onto shorter rulers of a similar size like this is called normalization, although, as you will see below, it does not make every range exactly equal. Integer stamps sneak in an order that paint does not have, because numbers come in a line while colors do not. With red 1, blue 2 and green 3, blue sits between the other two colors, which puts red closer to blue than to green. Nothing about paint puts blue in the middle, so that order comes entirely from the numbering. Picture a soccer coach who pairs up players for drills by how close their jersey numbers are. Player 7 always ends up with player 8, while player 7 and player 23 never train together, even if they play the same position. Jersey numbers are names, so treating them as amounts invents a closeness that was never there. One-hot encoding avoids that invented order by giving each color a slot of its own. Red becomes (1, 0, 0), blue becomes (0, 1, 0) and green becomes (0, 0, 1), which stretches Alder 12’s slip to five numbers: (2, 1, 0, 0, 1). Those five slots stand for rooms, red, blue, green and park, and the stamp pads stop mattering, because no slot reads them anymore. Normalization fixes a different problem, which is that a feature measured in bigger numbers can drown out the others. Picture a friend comparing two phones by adding up how different they are, where the prices differ by 50 dollars and the battery lives differ by 5 hours. If you add those two gaps as plain numbers, the 50 swamps the 5, only because prices come in bigger numbers, not because price matters ten times more. With same-length rulers, Alder 12’s 2 rooms become 2 ÷ 4 = 0.50, and its red stamp becomes 1 ÷ 5 = 0.20. The park slot stays at 1, so the slip reads (0.50, 0.20, 1.00), and since normalization only rescales numbers you already chose, it adds no new facts about the house. How far apart two slips are To find which house is nearest to another, the lab measures the distance between their slips, which is the same straight-line distance you might work out on a map. If you walk 3 blocks east and then 4 blocks north, you end up √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 blocks from where you started, in a straight line. To get there, you square each walk, add the squares, and take the square root. The recipe for two slips works the same way, except that a slip can hold more than two numbers. Subtract the numbers slot by slot to get the gaps, square each gap, add up the squares, and take the square root of the total. Each extra slot only adds one more square to the sum, so the recipe works for three numbers, five numbers or nine. Take Alder 12 at (2, 1, 1) and Elm 7, which has 2 rooms, a blue door and a park, so its slip is (2, 2, 1). The gaps are 0, 1 and 0, the squares add up to 1, and √1 = 1.00. Cedar 9 has 3 rooms, a green door and a park, which gives (3, 3, 1). Its gaps from Alder 12 are 1, 2 and 0, so the squares add up to 1 + 4 = 5, and √5 is about 2.24. With these stamps, then, Elm 7 is the house nearest to Alder 12, and Cedar 9 is more than twice as far away. You can think of each slip as a point, and each slot as one direction you can move in. Three slots work like the three measurements that pin down a spot in a room: how far along, how far across and how high up. Five slots give five directions, which you cannot draw, although the same recipe still measures the distance between two points. The space whose directions are the chosen features is called the feature space, and “near” in it only means near under the packing you picked. Why the nearest house can flip Now stamp blue as 5 instead of 2, and although no house has changed, Elm 7’s slip becomes (2, 5, 1). Its gaps from Alder 12 are 0, 4 and 0, so the squares add up to 16, and √16 = 4.00. Cedar 9 has no blue door, so it stays about 2.24 away, while Elm 7 drops from first place to fourth. Dock 2 has 4 rooms, a red door and no park, which gives (4, 1, 0). Its gaps from Alder 12 are 2, 0 and 1, so the squares add up to 4 + 1 = 5, the same total as Cedar 9. Cedar 9 and Dock 2 were already exactly the same distance from Alder 12 under the starting stamps. Restamping blue cannot move either of them, because neither has a blue door. Now that Elm 7 has moved back, they tie for nearest, so the lineup marks both as tied nearest instead of quietly picking one. Switch to one cubby each and the stamps no longer count, because no slot on a one-hot slip reads them. Alder 12 is (2, 1, 0, 0, 1) and Elm 7 is (2, 0, 1, 0, 1), so only two color slots differ, by 1 each. The squares add up to 2, which makes the distance √2, about 1.41, whatever the stamps say. In fact, any two houses with different door colors are exactly √2 apart in their color slots. Same-length rulers shift things again. With the starting stamps, Elm 7 becomes (0.50, 0.40, 1.00). Its only gap from Alder 12’s (0.50, 0.20, 1.00) is 0.20 in the color slot, so the distance is 0.20. Cedar 9 becomes (0.75, 0.60, 1.00), with gaps of 0.25 and 0.40, so its squares add up to about 0.22 and it ends up about 0.47 away. Before the rulers, two room counts could differ by as much as 3 while the park slot could differ by only 1, so park had the quietest voice. After dividing, the biggest possible gap between two room counts shrinks to 0.75, and the biggest gap between two starting stamps shrinks to 0.40. The park slot still jumps a full 1 between yes and no, so it now has the loudest voice in most distances. Normalization moved the loudest voice from rooms to park rather than making every voice equal. So with integer stamps, Alder 12 and Elm 7 are 1.00 apart, or 4.00 apart once blue is stamped 5. With one cubby each, the same two houses are about 1.41 apart, whatever the stamps say. Distance is a sum over slots, so any slot you restamp or rescale can change who stands nearest, and it is the packing that chose those numbers, not the houses. A flat picture can mislead The lineup also reports First-two nearest, which is the house that would win if you used only the first two numbers on each slip. That is like judging distance from a shadow on the floor, which keeps length and width but loses height. Two objects can look close together in their shadows while sitting far apart in real life. A flat picture made from only part of a longer list works the same way, and it is called a projection. With blue stamped 5, the first two numbers put Dock 2 only 2.00 from Alder 12, closer than Cedar 9, so First-two nearest reads Dock 2. Once the park slot is counted, Dock 2 moves out to about 2.24 and ties with Cedar 9. Whenever the first two numbers would name a house that is not nearest on the whole slip, a callout under the bars says so. In this example the callout stays hidden, because Dock 2 is still one of the two tied nearest houses. The flat picture only made the tie look like a win. To see the callout, keep blue at 5, switch to same-length rulers and select Elm 7 on The street. Its first two numbers put Birch 4 only 0.25 away. Birch 4 has no park while Elm 7 does, though, so on the whole slip Birch 4 is about 1.03 away. Cedar 9, at about 0.47, is the real nearest house, and the callout warns you that the flat picture got it wrong. A map fitted for a job: embeddings So far, you have chosen every number by hand, but in later labs, training sets the positions instead. Training means letting a model practice on examples and adjusting its numbers after each round so that its guesses get better. While it trains, the model is scored by a loss, a single number for how badly it is doing its job, where lower is better. Training nudges the model’s numbers again and again to push that score down. Picture each house as a dot on a map. Instead of you choosing where each dot goes, training starts the dots anywhere and keeps nudging them. Say the job is guessing price. Two houses that always sell for the same kind of price get nudged toward each other, because that makes the guesses better and the loss lower. The finished set of dot positions is called an embedding, and it puts items that the job treats as alike close together. The positions are a tool built for one job rather than a discovery about the world. Two items can sit close together in an embedding and still differ in ways the job never cared about. The Two maps card puts two maps side by side so you can compare them. On the left, one-hot cubbies say every other door color is equally far away, √2, and they ignore rooms, park and price completely. On the right, a later map places houses with a similar park and price close together. That map was placed by hand to show what an embedding could look like, and nothing was trained to make it. You might wonder whether grouping by price is the label leak from earlier. It is not, as long as price is used in the right place. Training is allowed to look at the price tags, because they are what its guesses are scored against, so price shapes a map like this only through the loss. What it must never do is copy a house’s tag onto the slip it reads when it guesses. A brand-new house would be placed from its features alone, because nobody knows its price yet. With Alder 12 selected, the later map names Cedar 9 as nearest, at an Embed dist of 0.35, because both houses are near a park and both are tagged high. The one-hot color map names Dock 2 instead, because Dock 2 is the only other house with a red door. Neither map is wrong, because each one answers a different question about which houses are alike. Pictures as numbers A picture can be packed into a slip in the same way as a house, by turning each tiny part of it into a number. The lab’s picture is a 3×3 grid of tiny squares called pixels, where each pixel is 1 for ink and 0 for blank. Reading the grid row by row, the way you read a page, gives nine numbers in a fixed order, which is called a pixel vector. The starting drawing is a plus sign, whose top row reads 0, 1, 0 and whose middle row reads 1, 1, 1. Its bottom row matches the top one, so its pixel vector is (0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0). Each of the nine pixels is its own direction, so the picture is a point in a space with nine directions, or nine dimensions. Distance works exactly the way it did on the street, using the same recipe of gaps, squares, a sum and a square root. The lab compares your drawing with three fixed templates: the plus, a ring and a bar. The ring inks the eight outside squares and leaves the middle blank, while the bar is a straight up-and-down line. Because every pixel is 0 or 1, each pixel that differs adds exactly 1 to the sum of squares, so the sum is a count of the pixels that differ. The plus and the bar differ only at the left and right ends of the middle row. Those two differing pixels make a sum of 2, so the two pictures sit √2 apart, about 1.41. The plus and the ring differ in five pixels, so they are √5 apart, about 2.24. Words as numbers A sentence can become numbers by looking up each word in a fixed list. That list is called a vocabulary, and a word’s position in it is its token ID. A token is one piece of text, and in this lab every token happens to be a whole word. The lab’s vocabulary has eight slots, and seven of them hold words: the = 1, cat = 2, sat = 3, on = 4, mat = 5, dog = 6 and ran = 7. Slot 0 is saved for any word that is not on the list, and the lab shows it as <unk>, short for unknown. So “the cat sat on the mat” becomes (1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 5), with “the” getting ID 1 both times. Now try “the bird sat on the mat”, where bird is not on the list, so it becomes ID 0 and the sentence becomes (1, 0, 3, 4, 1, 5). Any other unknown word would also become 0, which means two completely different unseen words would look identical. IDs are names rather than amounts, so treating them as amounts walks straight into the jersey-number trap again. Cat is ID 2 and mat is ID 5, so subtracting puts them 3 apart, while dog is ID 6, which puts it 4 away from cat. Read as amounts, those IDs make cat look nearer to a mat than to another animal, an order the numbering made up. One-hot encoding would avoid this by putting any two different words exactly √2 apart, the same as two different door colors. This tiny list is not a real tokenizer, which is the tool real AI systems use to split text into tokens. Real tokenizers break text into word pieces from a far bigger vocabulary, and the Tokens & embeddings lab is where that happens. Messy rows Real tables are rarely as clean as this street, so the Messy rows card spoils a copy of the table in three ways. It then shows what each problem does to a summary of the table and to one answer. That answer is about a new house that is not on the street: 3 rooms, a red door and no park, packed as (3, 1, 0). The lab finds the three listings nearest to it and lets them vote with their price tags, so the majority wins. On the clean table, the two nearest listings are Dock 2 at 1.00 away and Alder 12 at about 1.41, and both are tagged high. The third is Elm 7, about 1.73 away and tagged low, so two of the three votes are high and the 3-nearest answer is high. One more house matters in a moment. Birch 4 has 1 room, a blue door and no park, which packs as (1, 2, 0), and it is tagged low. Its gaps from the new house are 2, 1 and 0, so it sits √5, about 2.24, away, exactly the same distance as Cedar 9, which is tagged high. This card always packs with the starting stamps, red 1, blue 2 and green 3, whatever you set on Packing slip. Its numbers stay the same while you experiment with the other cards. A missing value A missing value is a cell with nothing recorded in it, like a box someone forgot to fill in on a form. Switching on Missing value blanks Dock 2’s room count, and since the distance recipe needs a number, you have to decide what to do with the gap. Picture a class survey asking how many pets each student has, where one student leaves the box blank. If you count the blank as 0, the class average drops, as if that student had no pets. If you leave the form out, the class shrinks by one, and if you fill the box with the class average, you keep the student but guess their answer. The lab’s Handle missing control offers the same three choices, and each one moves the answer in its own way: read as 0 gives Dock 2 zero rooms, which moves it from 1.00 to 3.00 away from the new house, so it drops out of the three nearest. Third place is now a tie at about 2.24 between Birch 4, tagged low, and Cedar 9, tagged high. The lab breaks a tie by taking the house listed first in the table, which is Birch 4, so the answer flips to low. drop the row leaves Dock 2 out of the summary and the vote, although the table still shows it, marked as dropped. The three nearest become Alder 12 (high), Elm 7 (low) and Birch 4 (low), after the same tie-break, so low wins two votes to one. fill with the mean fills Dock 2’s blank with 1.8 rooms, the average of the other five houses. That puts it 1.20 away, still the nearest listing, so the answer stays high. The summary moves too, because on the clean table Mean rooms is 2.17, and reading the blank as 0 drags it down to 1.50. How you handle a gap is part of the packing, in the same way a door stamp is. A duplicate row A duplicate row is the same record listed more than once, so anything that counts rows ends up counting it twice. Switching on Duplicate row lists Alder 12 twice, which makes the table 7 rows long and adds an extra high tag. The High-price share rises from 50% to 57.1%, even though no new information about any house was added. A duplicate also fools a common way of checking how well nearest-match guessing works. Leave-one-out accuracy hides one row, guesses its tag from its single nearest other row, checks the guess, and then repeats this for every row. On the clean table it gets 3 of 6 right, and Alder 12 is one of the misses, because its nearest other row is Elm 7, which is tagged low. With the duplicate, each copy of Alder 12 finds its twin at distance 0 with the same tag, so both copies are counted right. The three rows that were right stay right, and both copies of Alder 12 now count as right, so the score jumps to 3 + 2 = 5 of 7, about 71%. That rise happens even though the table holds no new information, only an extra copy. Picture a teacher who checks how well you studied by using the exact questions from a practice sheet you already went over. You would score well, but the score would measure your memory of that sheet, not how you would handle a new question. A wrong label When some rows carry the wrong label, the data has what is called label noise. A model learns from a wrong label just as carefully as from a right one, because nothing on the slip says which tags are wrong. Switching on Mislabelled row flips Dock 2’s tag from high to low. The High-price share drops from 50% to 33.3%, which means from half of the houses to a third of them. Dock 2 is also the listing nearest to the new house, so its flipped tag changes its vote. Now only Alder 12 votes high, so the answer flips to low because of one bad tag.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: Every method in the later labs, from a line that splits examples into two groups to a nearest-match search to a learned embedding, works only on the slip. That creates a specific problem, which is that the arithmetic cannot tell a measured number from an invented one. When it subtracts a red stamp from a blue one, it treats the gap as real, even though you made it up a minute ago. So the packing step quietly decides three things before any learning happens, and each one comes from the slots on the slip. It decides which examples count as similar, because distance is built from the slots. It decides what a rule is able to see, because a rule can only read numbers that are on the slip. And it decides what exists at all, because a feature you never wrote down cannot be recovered later. This is why, when two packings of the same houses disagree about who is nearest, the disagreement is a choice you made rather than something you discovered. The lab makes this visible by letting you change the packing while the street stays still. The gate shows the same idea for a rule instead of a distance. A rule family is one kind of rule with a setting you can adjust, like a gate whose height you can raise or lower. Here the family is “call the house high if this one number is at least t”, and t is the setting. Feed that same family the room count and then the door stamp, and it sorts the street in two different ways. What a model can do therefore depends on the features it is given, not only on the model itself. Messy rows is here because real tables always need cleaning before they are packed. Deciding what a blank cell means, spotting copies and catching wrong tags are all part of turning data into numbers. Each of those choices can change an answer as much as a door stamp can. This page does not split the houses into a group to learn from and a separate group to test on, which is called a train and test split. Every score here is measured on the same six houses that are being sorted, and the supervised learning loop lab is where that split first appears.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: Work through the cards in order, since each step builds on the one before it, and the headings below match the step names listed in the lab. Walk the street On The street, click Alder 12 to select it, and notice that clicking only moves the ring around a house, not any of its numbers. The windows show its rooms, the door paint is its color, and the tree means a park is nearby. The high or low pill hanging off the building is the price tag, which stays off the slip. Stamp a door color On Packing slip, leave How to pack the door on integer stamps and read Alder 12’s slip: rooms 2, color 1 and park 1. Then press 5 on the blue door pad, and Alder 12’s own slip stays the same, because its door is red. Every house with a blue door, though, now carries a 5 in its color slot. Watch the lineup On Who stands nearest, Elm 7 has dropped to fourth at d 4.00, where d means distance, while Cedar 9 and Dock 2 read tied nearest at d 2.24. The bars under the lineup show, slot by slot, how far Alder 12 is from its nearest house. Try this: switch How to pack the door to one cubby each, then to same-length rulers, and read Nearest on the slip after each change. With blue still stamped 5, one cubby each brings back Elm 7 at 1.41, while same-length rulers picks Cedar 9 alone at 0.47. That is three packings and three different readouts, a tie, then Elm 7, then Cedar 9, while not one house has moved. Move the gate Before you open The gate, set How to pack the door back to integer stamps and press 2 on the blue pad, so your numbers match the ones below. The card writes its rule at the top as ŷ = 1[one stamp ≥ t], which packs an ordinary idea into very few symbols. You can read ŷ, said “y-hat”, as the gate’s guess. The 1 in front of the square brackets means “1 if the statement inside is true, and 0 if it is false”. So the guess is 1, meaning high, when the stamp is at least t, and 0, meaning low, when it is not. Here is the rule worked through with Stamp the gate reads on rooms and Gate height t at 2.5. Cedar 9 has 3 rooms, and 3 is at least 2.5, so Cedar 9 walks into Predicted high. Alder 12 has 2 rooms, which is below 2.5, so it lands in Predicted low even though its tag says high. A struck-through pill marks that miss, and Tags the gate matches reads 5 of 6. Now switch Stamp the gate reads to door color and leave Gate height t at 2.5. Only the green doors, stamped 3, clear the gate, so Cedar 9 and Fir 1 walk into the high yard. Fir 1 is tagged low, so it is a miss in the high yard. Alder 12 and Dock 2 are tagged high but have red doors stamped 1, so they land in the low yard as two more misses. That makes three misses, so the score drops to 3 of 6, with the same rule and the same houses. Then slide Gate height t across its range, from 0 to 5, and watch which houses cross the fence. If you forget to switch back from same-length rulers, every number on the slips is 1 or less, so a gate at 2.5 sends every house to Predicted low. That is a useful reminder that the gate reads whatever packing you chose. Under one cubby each there is no single color number, so a gate set to door color reads only the red slot. That slot is 1 for a red door and 0 for blue or green. Compare the two maps On Two maps, keep Alder 12 selected and compare the readouts: Nearest on the later map reads Cedar 9, while One-hot color nearest reads Dock 2. Click other houses on either map and see how often the two maps disagree about who is alike. Draw a picture as numbers On Pixels and words, press the pixels at row 2, columns 1 and 3, to switch off the plus sign’s left and right arms. The Picture as nine numbers, row by row chip changes to (0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0). In the template table, the bar becomes nearest at 0.00, while the plus you started with is now 1.41 away. Write a sentence as IDs Set Sentence to “the bird sat on the mat” and find the row where In the list? says no and ID says 0. Then compare ID gap cat–dog, which reads 4, with ID gap cat–mat, which reads 3. Spoil the table On Messy rows, set Missing value to Dock 2 rooms blank with Handle missing on read as 0, and watch the 3-nearest answer change to low. Move Handle missing to drop the row and then to fill with the mean, and compare the answers. Then set Missing value back to off so the next problem shows on its own, set Duplicate row to Alder 12 twice, and read Leave-one-out accuracy. Finally, switch that off too, set Mislabelled row to Dock 2 tag flipped, and watch the High-price share and the answer.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: Integer stamps invent an order, so putting blue between red and green is a spacing you wrote down, not a fact about paint. One-hot gives each color its own cubby, so the stamp pads stop reaching the slip, and any two different door colors sit √2 apart. Normalization only rescales what you already chose, shrinking rooms and stamps to 1 or less, which makes the 0-or-1 park slot the widest and lets it decide most distances. Two houses can tie: with blue stamped 5, Cedar 9 and Dock 2 both sit √5 from Alder 12, and the lineup says tied nearest rather than quietly choosing one. The first two numbers can name a different neighbor than the whole slip does, because a flat picture of a longer list is only a projection. The same cut-off rule, the gate, sends different houses through when it reads rooms than when it reads door color. A better gate score on these six houses is not a better description of the world. With integer stamps, stamp red as 5 and a door-color gate at 2.5 matches 5 of 6, only because of the number you typed. Under one cubby each, a gate reading door color sees only the red slot, so blue and green both read 0 and the gate cannot tell them apart. The distance between Alder 12 and Elm 7 changes with every packing you try, while neither house changes at all. Switch off the plus sign’s left and right arms and the drawing becomes the bar, which is then 0.00 away, while the plus is √2, about 1.41, away. A word that is not on the list becomes ID 0, whatever the word is. IDs also invent an order, because by subtraction cat sits nearer to mat than to dog. A blank room count read as 0 sends Dock 2 from 1.00 to 3.00 away and flips the answer, while filling it with the mean of 1.8 rooms does not. A duplicate raises leave-one-out accuracy from 3 of 6 to 5 of 7 without adding any information. A single flipped tag drops the high-price share from 50% to 33.3% and flips the neighbors’ vote.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies The street is six listings made up for this lab rather than real sales, and the lineup always measures the whole slip. The first-two callout is the only flat projection the lab shows. The later map on Two maps was placed by hand, and no loss was lowered to put the houses there. Same-length rulers divide by fixed numbers, 4 for rooms and 5 for stamps, rather than numbers worked out from a set of training rows. The gate’s matches are counted on the same six tags it is sorting, not on new houses it has never seen, so they are not a fair test of anything. The picture has only nine pixels, each of which is 0 or 1, and there are only three templates. The vocabulary has eight fixed words, so it is not a real tokenizer, and nothing in Pixels and words is learned. The three problems on Messy rows were chosen so that each one shows up on a single row, and there is only one fixed new house. Real tables are much bigger, and one bad cell rarely flips an answer the way it does here. Where the real mechanism fails In real projects, the usual failures are a label that leaks onto the slip, cells with missing values, duplicates and wrong labels. A sneakier one involves the numbers used for rescaling, such as the largest value or the average of a column. Those must be worked out from the training rows only and then kept fixed. Picture a bigger street where the training houses have at most 4 rooms, while one house kept back for testing has 9. If you find the biggest room count using the test rows too, you divide every training house by 9 instead of 4. The training numbers then quietly carry a hint about a house the model is supposed to be seeing for the first time, which is another form of leakage. Sometimes a duplicate ends up with one copy in the training rows and the other in the test rows. That inflates the test score in the same way the duplicate inflates the leave-one-out score here, because the test row gets answered by looking up its twin. A model also cannot recover a feature you never wrote down, however clever the later steps are. Real pictures have thousands of pixels, each with numbers for brightness and color. Real text is split into word pieces from a vocabulary of tens of thousands before it becomes IDs, and those IDs are then mapped to learned lists of numbers. A representation can be convenient and still be wrong as a fact about the world. A trained embedding can put similar items near each other and still be useless for the task you actually cared about. Two houses sitting close on a fitted map only tells you that grouping them helped training do its one job well. It does not prove the houses are alike in every way. A common mix-up: people treat a categorical column as if it were already a set of amounts, because a spreadsheet showed it as 1, 2 and 3. Those whole numbers are a packing you chose, not a measurement, so the order and the gaps between them mean nothing about the real things. People also treat an embedding as a discovery about the world, when it is a set of positions fitted for one job.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: The straight-line distance used all through this lab is known to mathematicians as Euclidean distance. The math you need lab explains why a list of numbers can be treated as a point with a distance to other points in the first place. The gate also shows why some mistakes cannot be fixed by moving t, however carefully you set it. Alder 12 and Elm 7 both have 2 rooms but different tags, so any single cut on rooms puts both of them in the same yard. That is why a rooms gate can never match more than 5 of 6 tags, wherever you set t. Only door color tells those two houses apart, so a model that is never given door color can never separate them. Classical machine learning draws a boundary in the kind of feature space you built here, rather than cutting on one number at a time. Tokens & embeddings then learns positions for words instead of having you assign stamps by hand. The supervised learning loop is where a train and test split first appears, and How we know a model works then shows how to read a test score.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: This module is about how a raw example, whether a table row, a 3×3 picture, or a short sentence, becomes a vector of numbers: its representation, in which each coordinate is a feature. The question it answers: when two examples land near each other, is that a fact about the data or about the encoding you chose? In *The math you need* you read a dot product as a weighted sum of features; this module asks where those features come from. The lab's main case is six apartment listings, whose door color is a categorical variable: a category rather than an amount, with no number until you assign one. Each listing's high or low price tag is the label y and stays off the vector. Where it shows up Tables: categorical columns become integer codes or one-hot vectors, with one 0/1 slot per category, and numeric columns may be rescaled. Images: pixels read in a fixed order form a vector. Real images have thousands of pixels with brightness and color channels. Text: real text is split into subword pieces, and each piece becomes an integer ID from a vocabulary. Embeddings: later models fit coordinates so that items a loss treats as similar end up nearby, as *Tokens & embeddings* does for tokens. Data quality: missing values, duplicate rows, and wrong labels are among the usual failures in real tables. Why it matters Distance and threshold rules read only the numbers, so they treat whatever the encoding invents as real. Integer codes give colors an order and a spacing; one-hot encoding makes every pair of different colors equally far apart; normalization, rescaling a numeric column, adds no measurement but changes which axis dominates. Data errors act through the same numbers: a blank cell, a repeated row, or one flipped tag can move a summary, inflate an accuracy score, or flip a nearest-neighbour vote. The same blank cell gives different answers when it is read as 0, dropped, or filled. What you will be able to explain How to encode a table row as a feature vector by hand. Why two encodings of the same rows can disagree about which examples are near each other. Why a threshold gate reading a different feature cuts the street differently, and what an embedding is: a geometry fitted for a loss, placed by hand here as a stand-in and learned in *Tokens & embeddings*. How a 3×3 picture and a short sentence become numbers, and how a missing value, a duplicate row, or a mislabelled row changes a table summary or a nearest-neighbour answer. What the lab shows Nothing is trained or measured: every readout is a closed-form calculation on fixed, authored data and on the codes, drawing, and settings you choose. The street holds six fixed listings; click one to select it. On Packing slip, How to pack the door chooses integer stamps, one cubby each, or same-length rulers, and the red, blue, and green stamp pads set each color's code from 1 to 5. Who stands nearest ranks the other houses by Euclidean (straight-line) distance on the whole slip, and a callout that appears when the first two slip numbers alone would pick another house is the lab's only projection. The gate predicts high when one feature reaches a threshold, ŷ = 1[stamp ≥ t]: Stamp the gate reads picks rooms, door color, or park, and Gate height t sets t. Tags the gate matches counts agreement with the same six tags, not a holdout. Two maps compares one-hot color distance with a later map placed by hand, not fitted to a loss. Pixels and words reads a 3×3 drawing as nine 0/1 numbers and ranks three fixed templates by distance, and Sentence turns a preset sentence into IDs from a fixed eight-word vocabulary that is not a real tokenizer. Messy rows spoils a copy of the table with Missing value, Duplicate row, and Mislabelled row, each authored to show on one row, while Handle missing sets how the blank is treated. It recomputes the summary, the 3-nearest answer for one fixed new listing, and Leave-one-out accuracy, which predicts each row from its nearest other row. Its distances use the default integer stamps (red 1, blue 2, green 3), whatever How to pack the door and the pads say. The key experiment: select Alder 12 and stamp blue as 5. Elm 7, its nearest house at 1.00 under the default stamps, moves to 4.00 and loses first place. Under one cubby each, which ignores the stamps, it is nearest again at 1.41.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Data, features, and representation
documents.body: A feature is one constructed coordinate. A representation is the numeric slip that replaces a raw listing. Categorical variables become integer stamps or one-hot cubbies; numeric columns may be rescaled. Feature space is the geometry of those chosen axes. A label is the target y; it is not a feature unless you leak it. An embedding is a later kind of representation: coordinates fitted so items a loss treats as similar end up nearby. The later map on this page is authored to show that geometry. It is not trained. Why distances flip Take two listings that differ only in door color: Alder 12 (2 rooms, red door, park) and Elm 7 (2 rooms, blue door, park). Distance is the square root of the summed squared gaps, slot by slot. On the default integer stamps (red 1, blue 2) the slips are (2, 1, 1) and (2, 2, 1). The gaps are (0, 1, 0), so the distance is √1 = 1.00 and Elm 7 is Alder 12's nearest house. Cedar 9 (3 rooms, green 3, park) has gaps (1, 2, 0), so it is √5 = 2.24 away. Stamp blue as 5 and the apartments do not change, but Elm 7's slip becomes (2, 5, 1). The gaps are (0, 4, 0) and the distance is √16 = 4.00. Cedar 9's slip never read the blue stamp, so it stays at 2.24, and Cedar 9 is now nearer than Elm 7. The neighbor order flipped. Under one-hot cubbies the slips are (2, 1, 0, 0, 1) and (2, 0, 1, 0, 1). Two color slots differ by 1 each, so the distance is √2 = 1.41 whatever the stamps are. Every pair of different doors is √2 apart: equal spacing instead of an invented order. Same-length rulers (rooms ÷ 4, stamps ÷ 5) shrink Elm 7's gap to 0.20 and Cedar 9's to 0.47, and make the 0/1 park slot the widest axis. A distance is a sum over slots, so any slot you re-stamp or rescale can change who stands nearest. Nothing in the apartments chose 1.00, 4.00, or 1.41. The encoding did. Pictures and words as numbers A 3×3 picture whose pixels are 0 or 1, read row by row, is a vector of nine numbers: the plus is (0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0). Distance works on it exactly as on the street. The plus and the bar (0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0) differ in two pixels, so they are √2 = 1.41 apart, and one flipped pixel always changes the squared distance by 1. A sentence becomes integer IDs by looking each word up in a fixed list. In the lab's eight-word vocabulary, the cat sat on the mat is (1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 5), and bird, which is not on the list, becomes ID 0. IDs are labels, not amounts: by subtraction cat (2) is 3 from mat (5) and 4 from dog (6), an order the numbering invented. This list is not a real tokenizer. Messy rows Real tables are spoiled. Switch on Missing value, Duplicate row, or Mislabelled row and read a table summary and a three-nearest-neighbour answer for a new listing: 3 rooms, red door, no park. On the clean table its nearest listings are Dock 2, Alder 12, and Elm 7, so the answer is high. A blank cell must be handled. Read as 0, Dock 2 moves from 1.00 to 3.00 away and the answer flips to low; dropping the row flips it too; filling with the mean of the other rows (1.8 rooms) keeps it high. A duplicate (Alder 12 listed twice) raises leave-one-out accuracy from 3 of 6 to 5 of 7 for free, because each copy is checked against its twin. A flipped tag on Dock 2 moves the high-price share from 50% to 33.3% and flips the vote.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: Text that belongs to the website rather than the document: navigation, cookie notices, copyright lines. It is highly repetitive, so a model spends real capacity on it.
documents.title: Boilerplate

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: Removing byte-identical documents, usually by hashing each one and keeping the first of every hash. Cheap, and it stops a copied page from being seen once per copy every epoch.
documents.title: Exact deduplication

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: A document that differs only trivially from another, such as one spelling variant or one changed sentence. Detected by comparing shingles (short overlapping pieces) rather than exact strings.
documents.title: Near-duplicate

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: A signature of k minimum hash values over a document's shingles. Two signatures agree in each position with probability equal to the documents' Jaccard similarity, so near-duplicates can be found without comparing every pair of sets.
documents.title: MinHash

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: Distinct three-character sequences divided by total sequences. A blunt but real measure of how much new signal a corpus carries per character.
documents.title: Trigram diversity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: Three disjoint slices: one to fit on, one to tune decisions against, one to touch once. Splitting by document, not by sentence, is what keeps them disjoint.
documents.title: Train/validation/test split

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: Cross-entropy on text that never entered training. It reports whether a dataset change helped the model predict text like the held-out sample, and only while that sample stays out of training.
documents.title: Held-out loss

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: Evaluation text appearing in training data, usually through copies in a crawl. It makes a model look better on that evaluation without making it better anywhere else.
documents.title: Leakage

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: Removing training documents that overlap an evaluation set, typically any document sharing a long word n-gram with a test item. The threshold trades missed leaks against deleting innocent text.
documents.title: Decontamination

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: Not a single property. In practice it means low duplication, on-target style, correct formatting, and no evaluation contamination.
documents.title: Data quality

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: The share of the training budget each source receives. Filtering decides what is admissible; the mixture decides how often each admissible source is seen, including deliberate repeats of small, valuable sources.
documents.title: Data mixture

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: A model reproducing a stretch of its training text verbatim when given a prefix of it. It grows with the model's capacity, with how often the text was duplicated, and with how much context the prompt supplies; the probe here varies the last.
documents.title: Memorization

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: Text that identifies a person, such as a name, phone number, or email address. A model can memorize it from a single document, so deduplication does not remove the risk.
documents.title: Personal data

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Building a dataset
documents.body: The records and rules around a dataset: where each document came from, under what licence, with what consent or opt-out, and what personal data it holds. These are legal and policy questions that no cleaning filter can answer by reading the text.
documents.title: Data governance

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Building a dataset · question 1
documents.body: Cleaning removes a third of your corpus and the held-out loss improves. What is the most defensible reading? Smaller datasets always train better models, so any cut of this size would have helped as much Fewer training tokens means fewer tokens are scored, so the average loss falls without any real gain in the model The held-out text must have leaked into training, since less data cannot lower the loss Repeated text kept pulling the weights toward itself without new signal, so removing it freed capacity Repeated boilerplate is still gradient signal: a line seen four times pulls the weights four times as hard, so the model spends its limited parameters fitting it. Both models are scored on the same held-out text, so the comparison is fair, and size only helps when the added text carries new signal. That is why held-out loss is the arbiter rather than the token count.
documents.title: Cleaning removes a third of your corpus and the held-out loss improves. What is the most defensible reading?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Building a dataset · question 2
documents.body: One scraped line writes harbour where an earlier line writes harbor and is otherwise identical. Which filter catches it, and why do the other filters miss it? Exact deduplication, because the two lines mean the same thing and the hash compares meaning Near-duplicate removal: exact matching misses it because the bytes differ, but the trigrams overlap Boilerplate stripping, because a repeated sentence is the same kind of junk as a copyright line or a subscribe banner Minimum line length, because a one-letter spelling change turns the line into a fragment Exact deduplication hashes bytes, so one changed letter gives a different hash. The near-duplicate test compares sets of character trigrams and flags a pair when their overlap passes a threshold, which catches spelling variants like this one. Boilerplate and length filters look at what a line says or how long it is, not at whether another line already said it.
documents.title: One scraped line writes harbour where an earlier line writes harbor and is otherwise identical. Which filter catches it, and why do the other filters miss it?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Building a dataset · question 3
documents.body: You switch on Leak a held-out sentence into the scrape, and Cleaned held-out loss improves. What does that improvement mean? The model has seen that sentence, so the score now rewards recall of copied text, not generalisation The pipeline recovered more useful training text, so the cleaned model now generalises better, and the loss shows it The held-out passage became more representative of the scrape, so the same model is scored more fairly Once evaluation text also sits in the training data, part of the score measures recall of a memorised string, so the loss falls without the model getting better at unseen text. The tell in the lab is that loss on the held-out sentences that were not copied does not improve. Decontamination removes the overlap and the score returns to its honest value.
documents.title: You switch on Leak a held-out sentence into the scrape, and Cleaned held-out loss improves. What does that improvement mean?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Building a dataset · question 4
documents.body: In this lab the best-scoring filter setting beats the default by less than a hundredth of a nat, and the winner changes with the shuffle seed. How should you read that gap? As proof that boilerplate is valuable training text that real pipelines should keep in the corpus As an error, since removing less text can never score better than removing more As unresolved, because it is smaller than the spread a different shuffle order would produce As the true ranking, since the seed is fixed and the loss is an exact cross-entropy The lab fixes one shuffle seed, so each score is a single draw without an error bar. Across seeds the raw-versus-cleaned gap stays clearly positive, but the difference between the two best filter settings changes sign, so it is smaller than the noise a different shuffle adds. A gap is only evidence when it is larger than that spread.
documents.title: In this lab the best-scoring filter setting beats the default by less than a hundredth of a nat, and the winner changes with the shuffle seed. How should you read that gap?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Building a dataset · question 5
documents.body: In Regurgitation probe you drag Context length from 1 to 8 on the same training text. What happens to the share of the sample copied verbatim? It stays near zero, because a count-based model only averages the text it saw and never repeats it It rises from near zero to almost everything, because long contexts leave one possible continuation It falls, because a longer context gives the model many more ways to recombine the text it saw It rises only for the raw scrape, because cleaning removes most of the text that a model could copy With one character of context, many different characters follow each context, so sampling mixes the text and copies nothing. As the context grows, nearly every context occurs once, so the table has a single continuation and sampling follows the training text word for word. Cleaning changes how much of the output is footer text, but the cleaned set is also copied almost completely.
documents.title: In Regurgitation probe you drag Context length from 1 to 8 on the same training text. What happens to the share of the sample copied verbatim?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Building a dataset · question 6
documents.body: A scraped page names one person and their phone number, once, in a single document. Why does deduplication not make a model trained on it safe? A repeated page is the only kind a model can memorize, so a page that occurs once is safe from that The phone number is a short string, and short strings are always removed by a length filter A model can memorize text it saw once, so removing copies does not remove the risk of recitation Deduplication also deletes the original, so the remaining model has seen the text too many times Duplication raises the chance that text is memorized, and removing it lowers the rate: one study found deduplicated training cut emitted memorized text about tenfold. But an extraction study recovered names, phone numbers and email addresses from GPT-2 that each appeared in just one document. Personal data needs its own detection and policy, and a licence or consent check is a separate question again.
documents.title: A scraped page names one person and their phone number, once, in a single document. Why does deduplication not make a model trained on it safe?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Building a dataset
documents.body: Copy all the text from almost any web page and you get more than the article you wanted. You also get the menu, a box asking you to subscribe to a newsletter, a row of share buttons and a copyright line at the bottom. A program that collects web pages automatically picks up all of that too, and it often collects the same page, or a copy of it, more than once. Models like the ones behind chatbots learn from huge piles of text gathered in this way. A model here is a program that learns one job: guessing what comes next in a piece of text, one small piece at a time. Learning that job is called training, and it works by adjusting a fixed set of numbers inside the model. The collection of text that a model trains on is called its dataset, and this module is about building one. That means collecting raw text, cleaning out the junk, and then checking honestly whether the cleaning actually helped. That last step is the one people most often skip, even though it is the only step that tells you whether your work paid off. It is tempting to assume that deleting junk must help, or that more text must always be better. This lab tests both ideas with a real model that it trains in front of you, instead of leaving them as guesses. Where you have met it The language models behind today’s chatbots are trained on text that somebody collected and cleaned, so choices like the ones in this lab help shape their habits. The problems in this lab also show up in real datasets, on a far bigger scale. Researchers found one 61-word sentence repeated more than 60,000 times in C4, a large collection of web text used to train models. They also found that models trained on collections like it sometimes write out passages from their training text word for word. Another team got an older model called GPT-2 to write out real names, phone numbers and email addresses, though each had appeared in only one of its training documents. Why it matters Because a model has only a fixed set of numbers to adjust, it has a limited amount of room, a bit like a notebook with a fixed number of pages. Every extra copy of a copyright line pushes those numbers toward guessing copyright lines, which leaves them a little worse at guessing the text you actually care about. You also need an honest way to tell whether a change helped, because a test can be fooled. If you test a model on text it already trained on, its score improves while the model gets no better at anything new. It is like a student who saw the quiz questions in advance and gets a higher mark without learning more. Removing copies does make a model repeat its training text less often, but cleaning has limits. A filter can spot a phone number on a page, but it cannot tell from the text alone whether you are allowed to keep it. Nor can it tell whether you may reuse the page’s words, or whether the website asked not to be collected. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these in your own words: the kinds of junk that cleaning removes from collected text, including copies of test text, and which filter catches each one; why the text you test a model on has to stay out of everything the model trains on, and what goes wrong when some of it leaks in; why you judge a change to a dataset by the model’s score on new text, not by how much text you kept or threw away; when a model starts repeating its training text word for word, and why personal information, permission to reuse text, and consent need checks that removing copies cannot give. What the lab lets you do The lab gives you 20 lines that look like they were copied from a small weather website. They are a fixed, made-up page that you cannot change, and each line is tagged with whether the cleaning kept it or removed it, and why. You switch filters on and off and watch lines change their tags, while a chart shows how much text survives each filter. Every time you change a filter, the lab trains the same tiny model twice, once on the whole collected page and once on the lines you kept. It then scores both models on three sentences that neither one was trained on, so you can see for yourself whether your cleaning helped. Those scores come from real training, not from made-up numbers. Each one comes from a single fixed run, though, so a tiny gap between two scores can be luck. One button sneaks a test sentence into the training text, so you can watch a score improve for the wrong reason. A last card swaps in a simpler kind of model, which is only a table of counts and is not trained at all. You choose how many earlier characters it looks at. As you raise that number, you can watch for the point where it starts copying its training text word for word.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Building a dataset
documents.body: A pile of collected text Text copied automatically from web pages is called a scrape, or a crawl when the program follows links from page to page across the web. The lab’s scrape is 20 lines long, and each line stands in for a document, meaning one item in a dataset, such as one web page. The card Source documents and cleaning verdicts lists every line with a small tag, called its verdict, that says what happened to it. A verdict is one of kept, boilerplate, too short, exact repeat, near-duplicate or held-out overlap, and each line gets exactly one. The Show control switches the list between All lines, which shows everything with its verdict, and Kept only, which shows what would go into training. Four kinds of junk, and one unfair copy Mixed in with real sentences about fog, wind and boats are four kinds of junk, and all four turn up in real crawls: Boilerplate is text that belongs to the website rather than to any article on it, like copyright 2019 all rights reserved. or click here to subscribe to our newsletter. Nine of the 20 lines are boilerplate, and the copyright line alone appears four times. An exact repeat is a line that matches an earlier line character for character. The sentence about morning fog over the harbor appears twice, and removing copies like this is called exact deduplication, since a duplicate is a copy. A near-duplicate says the same thing with a tiny difference: one line writes harbour, the British spelling, where an earlier line writes harbor, and nothing else changes. Two fragments, ok. and yes., are scraps with almost nothing in them for a model to learn from. There is one more problem, which you can add yourself with a button described later. A test copy is a line that repeats one of the three sentences the lab keeps aside to test the model. The section How the lab keeps score explains those sentences. A test copy is not junk to a human reader, but it would make the test unfair. How each filter decides The card Cleaning stages holds four switches, Strip boilerplate, Drop exact duplicates, Drop near-duplicates and Decontaminate, plus a slider called Minimum line length. Each filter removes lines by a rule you could say out loud, so you can check every decision it makes. The filters run one after another in a fixed order, like stations on a production line, and a chain of filters like this is called a cleaning pipeline. That is why the card’s small heading reads Pipeline. Each line gets the verdict of the first filter that catches it: Strip boilerplate removes any line containing one of five phrases: copyright, all rights reserved, click here, subscribe or share this page. Minimum line length removes lines shorter than the number of characters you set, and it starts at off. Drop exact duplicates keeps the first copy of a line and removes any later line that matches it exactly. Drop near-duplicates removes a line that overlaps an already kept line by 0.7 or more, on a measure explained below. Decontaminate removes a line that shares a run of 8 words in a row with the three test sentences, which the lab keeps out of training. This is the filter that catches a test copy. A computer stores text as a row of small code numbers called bytes. That is why the note under Drop exact duplicates calls these copies byte-identical, meaning the same codes in the same order. Add or change one letter and the bytes change, which is why this filter misses the harbour line completely. Real pipelines find exact copies by turning each document into a short code number, called a hash, where the same text always gives the same code. They then keep only the first document with each hash. Measuring how much two lines overlap To compare two lines, the near-duplicate filter chops each one into every run of three characters in a row, called a trigram. The word harbor gives har, arb, rbo and bor, while harbour gives har, arb, rbo, bou and our. Next, the filter counts the trigrams the two have in common and divides by the number of different trigrams found in either one. Here 3 are shared out of 6 different ones in total, so the overlap is 3 divided by 6, which is 0.5. This measure is called the Jaccard similarity, and the lab shortens it to J. For the two full fog lines, one extra letter barely matters, because the rest of the line is identical. Only the few trigrams around the u differ, so the lines share 54 of their 59 different trigrams. That puts their overlap at about 0.915, well over the 0.7 cut-off. So when Drop near-duplicates is on, the harbour line gets the verdict near-duplicate · J 0.92. A shortcut for billions of pages Comparing every pair of lines like this works for 20 lines. Real datasets hold billions of documents, though, and one web page can have thousands of trigrams, so comparing full sets of trigrams would take far too long. A note at the bottom of Cleaning stages shows a shortcut that real pipelines use, called MinHash. It gives each trigram a code number, then scrambles those codes in 64 different ways, like reshuffling a deck of numbered cards 64 times. From each scramble it keeps only the smallest code, so every line ends up with a list of 64 numbers, called its signature. To see why matching signatures tell you about overlap, take harbor and harbour again. Between them they have 6 different trigrams, and 3 are shared. One scramble gives each of the 6 a new random code, and any one of the 6 is equally likely to end up with the smallest code. If the smallest code lands on har, arb or rbo, both words contain it, so their smallest codes match. If it lands on bor, bou or our, only one word has it, so their smallest codes differ. That is 3 chances in 6, or 0.5, which is exactly their overlap. So the share of the 64 places where two signatures match is an estimate of the overlap. For the two fog lines, 5 of the 64 places differ, so 59 of the 64 places match. (This 59 is a coincidence, not the same 59 as the trigram count above.) That gives an estimate of 0.922, close to the exact answer of 0.915. A signature is always 64 numbers, however long the page is, so comparing two signatures is much quicker than comparing two full sets of trigrams. Real pipelines also add a grouping trick, described in Where it breaks, so that they do not have to compare every pair at all.
