A picture to keep in mind Picture getting ready for a weather quiz by studying a stack of pages that someone printed from a website. On the quiz you will be given new sentences about the weather and asked to guess, letter by letter, how each one continues. Many of the pages end with the same copyright line, one page was printed twice, and another was reprinted with harbour spelled the British way. Two scraps of paper say only ok. and yes., and a sensible student would ignore them, skip the footers and read the repeated page once. The model cannot skip anything, because it practises on every pair of neighbouring characters in the pile, and each copy of a line pushes its numbers all over again. Four copies of the copyright line push four times as hard as one copy, so repetition works like a vote rather than harmless clutter. The quiz also means something only if its sentences are not in the pile. If one of them were printed in the stack, a good mark would partly show what you had memorized rather than how well you predict new text. The picture stops matching in two places. A student understands what fog is, while this model only adjusts numbers that score which character tends to follow which. A student can also choose what to study, while the model trains on whatever is in its dataset, as many times as it appears. How the lab keeps score The card Validation loss for both datasets is where the lab checks whether cleaning paid off. It trains the same small model twice, once on the whole collected page and once on the lines you kept, and nothing else differs between the two runs. The whole page is 20 lines, or 21 once you leak a test sentence into it. Only the four switches, the leak button and Minimum line length start new training. Show leaves the chart alone, and so does the Context length slider on the probe card, described below. The model is the simplest kind of language model, called a bigram model, which predicts each character from only the one character before it. It works with 30 symbols: the 26 letters, a space, a full stop and two spare symbols that this text never uses. For each symbol it keeps 30 numbers that score how likely each symbol is to come next, which makes 30 times 30, or 900 numbers in all. Training means going through the text and nudging those numbers so that the real next character gets a slightly higher score each time. Each character and the one after it form a training pair. For example, fog has 3 characters but only 2 pairs, fo and og, because the last character has nothing after it. In the same way, the raw scrape’s 899 characters give 898 pairs, and the default cleaned set gives Those are the numbers in the chart’s labels, raw (898 pairs) and cleaned (515 pairs), and the cleaned one also appears as Training pairs on the card Dataset statistics. Both models go through their whole text 25 times, and each full pass through the text is called an epoch. Both are then tested on the same three sentences, 194 characters in all, which are in neither training set. Text kept out of training like this is called held-out text, and it is the only fair test of how a model handles text it was not trained on. What the score means For every character of the held-out text, the model gives each of the 30 symbols a chance of coming next. After any character, those chances always add up to 100 percent, so giving more chance to one symbol always means giving less to the others. If the model gave the real next character a high chance, it collects a small penalty, and if it gave it a low chance, it collects a large one. A penalty score like this is called a loss, and the average penalty over the held-out text is the held-out loss, where lower is better. The loss is measured in a unit called nats, and the chart’s side axis reads held-out loss (nats/token). A token is one piece of text, which in this lab is a single character. You do not need the maths behind nats, because a few reference points tell you what the numbers mean. A model with no idea at all, which gives every symbol the same chance, would score about 3.4 nats. A score of 2.3 nats is about as unsure, on average, as choosing among 10 equally likely characters. So a model that scores 2.3 has, in effect, narrowed 30 possible next characters down to about 10. Three numbers under the chart sum up the comparison: Raw held-out is the raw model’s score, and Cleaned held-out is the cleaned model’s score. Difference is the cleaned score minus the raw one, so a minus sign means cleaning lowered the loss and the cleaned model predicts new text better. That difference is the only claim the lab makes about whether cleaning helped. The chart itself draws both scores as training goes on, with a dashed line for the raw model and a solid line for the cleaned one. Below it, the card Survival funnel shows how many lines and characters are left after each filter, in the order the filters run. The regurgitation probe The last card, Regurgitation probe, asks a different question: when does a model start giving back its training text word for word? To regurgitate means to bring back up something you swallowed, and a probe is a test that pokes at something to see how it reacts. This card uses a different kind of model, which is nothing more than a table of counts and is not trained at all. You set how many characters it looks back at with the Context length slider, and the characters it looks at are called its context. For every run of that many characters in its training text, the table records which character came next. Here is a made-up example. Say the context length is 3, and in the training text the is followed by a space 4 times and by r once. The table’s row for the then reads space 4, r 1. So after the, the model writes a space 4 times out of 5 and r 1 time out of 5. The table has one row like this for every different run of 3 characters it has seen, and each of those runs is one of its contexts. If a row lists only one next character, the model has no choice but to write it. At a Context length of 1, it predicts from one character, like the bigram on the chart, which is why the slider then reads 1 character · the bigram. The card builds two of these tables, shown as Trained on the raw scrape and Trained on the cleaned set. Each one starts from the opening characters of its own training text and writes 300 characters. The card then measures how much of that writing is copied verbatim, which means word for word, or here, character for character. A character counts as copied when it sits inside a run of at least 16 characters that appears exactly in the training text. That is what the 16 in the readout Copied verbatim (16+ chars) refers to. The bigram model on the chart cannot copy like this, and the probe shows what changes when a model can look further back.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Building a dataset
documents.body: Every copy pulls on the same numbers The model on the chart has only 900 numbers, and the same numbers serve every line it trains on. The number that scores r after y is the same number whether that y comes from copyright or from sky. To see what that means, follow the letter y through the raw scrape, where it is followed by r four times, always inside copyright. It is also followed by a space four times, in words like sky and by. So training pushes the raw model to give r about as much chance after y as it gives a space. The cleaned set has no copyright lines, so r never follows y there. The three held-out sentences use y in stays and in every, and neither one is followed by r. Remember that the chances after y always add up to 100 percent. So every bit of chance the raw model saves for r is taken away from the s or the space that really comes next in the test. That raises its penalty. The raw model’s habit of expecting r after y therefore costs it on the test and earns it nothing. Now repeat that for every letter pair in the footers, and you have the whole idea behind data quality. The term sounds like a slogan, but it is not one single property. In practice it means little duplication, text in the style you want, correct formatting and no test text mixed in. The first three of those come down to where the model’s limited room gets spent, while the fourth is about keeping the score honest, which the next part covers. How much a model can fit is called its capacity, and with 900 numbers this model has very little. A line that appears four times pulls those numbers four times as hard as a line that appears once. So the model’s habits lean toward whatever was copied most, not toward whatever matters most. A test only counts if it is new Cleaning is only half the job, because you also need a fair way to tell whether a change helped. That brings in the second problem this lab is built to show, called leakage, which is when test text slips into the training data. Training on a test sentence nudges the model’s numbers toward that sentence’s exact letter pairs. So on the test, the model is partly marking its own homework. The score rewards it for having trained on that exact sentence rather than for predicting new text well. That is why the three held-out sentences are kept out of both training sets on purpose, and it is the only reason the chart’s comparison means anything. Careful teams go further and cut their data into three separate slices before training starts. The model learns from the training slice, you check your choices against the validation slice, and you save the test slice for one final check at the end. Together these are called a train/validation/test split, and the held-out score is often called a validation loss, which is where the chart’s card gets its name. Real crawls make it hard to keep test text out, because a test sentence can be quoted on some web page that the next crawl collects. The button Leak a held-out sentence into the scrape copies a test sentence into the page in that way, so you can watch what a leak does.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Building a dataset
documents.body: Read before you filter Set Show to All lines and read all 20 verdicts before you touch a switch. Try to spot the four kinds of junk yourself first: the footers, the repeated fog line, the harbour line and the two fragments. At the defaults, Strip boilerplate and Drop exact duplicates are on and everything else is off. That is why the harbour line, ok. and yes. are all still marked kept. Walk through the switches Now step through the settings below in order, and write down Cleaned held-out at each one. Treat it as a small experiment where you change one thing at a time and compare. Turn every switch off and leave Minimum line length at off, so all 20 lines and 899 Characters stay in. Cleaned held-out reads 2.365, the two lines on the chart sit on top of each other, and Difference reads +0.000, because both models trained on the same text. This is your starting point, which scientists call the control: the setting you compare every other one against. Turn on Strip boilerplate alone, which leaves 11 lines and 580 characters. The score falls to 2.306, which is better. Add Drop exact duplicates, which brings you back to the defaults with 10 lines and 516 characters. The score is now 2.300, and Difference reads −0.065. Add Drop near-duplicates, which leaves 9 lines and 451 characters. The score rises to 2.312, which is worse. Add Minimum line length at 20 chars as well, and the score moves to 2.316. That is a change of only 0.004, which is too small to trust on its own, as Where it breaks explains. The −0.065 is small but real, and here it is in the “equally likely characters” terms from earlier. The raw model was about as unsure as choosing among 10.6 characters, and the cleaned one about as unsure as choosing among 10. The Characters readout counts letters, spaces and full stops the way the model receives them. Before counting, the lab turns anything outside the model’s 30 symbols into a space and squeezes repeated spaces into one. So copyright 2019 all becomes copyright all, and the digits do not count. Try this: switch Strip boilerplate off and leave Drop exact duplicates on, with everything else off. You get 13 lines and 623 characters, and Cleaned held-out reads 2.292, a little lower than the defaults, even though footer lines are back in the dataset. The verdicts show why: the footer lines are exact copies of one another, so Drop exact duplicates already removes every copy after the first. The 13 kept lines are the 10 from the defaults plus one copyright line, one subscribe line and one share line, which together add 107 characters. Once each footer appears only once, it stops acting like a loud vote. Its letter pairs, such as th in this and on in on social media, are ordinary English pairs that the weather sentences use too. So at one copy each, the footers cost the model almost nothing. In this one run they even come out slightly ahead, though a later section shows why a gap this small cannot be trusted. Leak a sentence, then clean it out Go back to the defaults, with Strip boilerplate and Drop exact duplicates on and everything else off, and then press Leak a held-out sentence into the scrape. The button copies “the fog returns in the morning and the pattern repeats.” into the page, and that sentence is one of the three test sentences. This is how a quoted test item can end up in a real crawl, and four things change as soon as it lands: Cleaned held-out improves from 2.300 to 2.245, which looks like progress until you read the rest of the card. Raw held-out improves too, from 2.365 to 2.324, because the raw model trains on the whole page, copied sentence included. The leak flatters both scores. The contamination check under the chart, which looks for test text mixed into the training text, now finds a 10-word run shared with the test text. That run is the whole copied sentence, and the check marks it as flagged. A new line appears under the check, giving the cleaned model’s score on the two test sentences that the leak did not copy. It reads 2.422. Now turn on Decontaminate, which removes training lines that overlap the test text, a step called decontamination. The copied line gets the verdict held-out overlap and leaves the cleaned training set, and Cleaned held-out goes back to 2.300. The line about the two untouched sentences now reads 2.397, which is the cleaned model’s honest score on them. Difference reads −0.024 rather than −0.065, because only the cleaned side was decontaminated, and the raw model still trains on the copied sentence. Probe for recitation Before you start, press the leak button again so it reads off, and turn Decontaminate off, so you are back at the defaults. Then scroll down to the Regurgitation probe card, where the Context length slider starts at 3, and move it down to 1 first. Now step the slider up one notch at a time to 8, and at each step compare Copied verbatim (16+ chars) for the two models: At 1 character of context, both models read 0 percent, and the samples are gibberish. The raw model’s sample starts l. cit cl wn yried, which uses real letter pairs but no real words. At 3, the raw model copies 52 percent of its sample and the cleaned one 39 percent. The raw sample now starts yright all with warms the fog settles, which is scraps of real lines stitched together. At 4, the raw model copies 98 percent and the cleaned one 93 percent. At 8, both read 100 percent, and the raw sample reads like a passage lifted straight from the scrape: all rights reserved. by noon the clouds break apart. Keep an eye on Footer text in the sample as well, which counts how much of each sample comes from the footer phrases. At 8 characters of context, footer text makes up 21 percent of the raw model’s sample and none of the cleaned model’s. Below the two columns, a table runs the same test at eight context lengths at once: 1 to 6, 8 and It lets you compare them without moving the slider, and when the slider sits on one of those eight values, that row is shaded.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Building a dataset
documents.body: The filters overlap Watch the badge on Drop exact duplicates, which reads −1 lines while Strip boilerplate is on, because the only copy left for it to catch is the repeated fog sentence. Switch boilerplate off and the same badge reads −7, because now it also catches three extra copyright lines, two extra subscribe lines and one extra share line. The two filters were partly removing the same lines, so you cannot judge how useful either one is by looking at it alone. Lines and characters tell different stories The Survival funnel has one row per stage, named Scraped, Strip boilerplate, Length floor, Exact dedup, Near-dup and Decontaminate. Length floor is the Minimum line length slider, and dedup is short for deduplication. At the defaults, those rows read 20, 11, 11, 10, 10, 10 lines. Boilerplate takes 9 of the 20 lines, which is almost half of them. Yet it takes only 319 of the 899 characters, about a third, because footer lines are short. So the same filter can look huge when you count documents and modest when you count characters. When someone reports how much a filter removed, it matters which of the two they counted. A stage that is switched on but removes nothing still shows a full row that reads removes nothing here. That is not a mistake. Either an earlier stage already took the lines it would have caught, or nothing on this page matches its rule, as with Decontaminate when no sentence has leaked. Less text helped, but only up to a point At the defaults, cleaning removed about 40 percent of the characters and the score still improved. More text helps only when it brings something new, and the fourth copy of a footer brings nothing that the first copy did not. Removing more does not keep helping, though. In the walk above, adding Drop near-duplicates made the score slightly worse in this run, and adding Minimum line length moved it by too little to read. Neither one clearly helped, even though both delete lines that you would call junk if you read them. When a change is too small to read Now compare what a Minimum line length of 20 does in two different setups. With Drop near-duplicates on, it moves the score from 2.312 to 2.316, which is slightly worse. With near-duplicates off, the same setting moves the score from 2.300 to 2.296, which is slightly better. In this one run, the same setting seems to help in one case and hurt in the other. These gaps are only 0.004 nats, though, which Where it breaks shows is too small to trust on its own. So take this as a warning, not a result: this lab cannot tell you whether a length floor of 20 helps. The badge on Drop exact duplicates showed the firmer version of the same lesson. A filter is always measured on whatever text the other filters left, so you cannot judge it by itself. At 12, Minimum line length removes only ok. and yes., the two fragments, and nothing else. The shortest real sentence is 56 characters long, so the slider starts deleting real sentences at 57. Diversity is counted per character Distinct trigrams counts how many different three-character runs the text contains. It drops from 366 in the raw scrape to 285 after cleaning. You might guess that is because the cleaned text is shorter, but it is not. With only Drop exact duplicates on, the text loses about a third of its length and still has all 366, because every copy repeats runs the first one already had. The drop comes from the footer lines. They hold runs like cop and sub, from copyright and subscribe, that no real sentence uses, so removing those lines removes those runs for good. Repetition is the share of all trigrams in the text that are repeats of ones already counted. For example, ha ha ha has 6 trigrams once you count the spaces: ha␣, a␣h, ␣ha, ha␣, a␣h and ␣ha, where ␣ stands for a space. Only 3 of them are different, so half are repeats and its repetition is 50 percent. Cleaning lowers Repetition from a Raw repetition of 60 percent to 45 percent. So the cleaned text has fewer different sequences in total, yet repeats itself less. The share of trigrams that are new rather than repeats is called trigram diversity, so it is the flip side of Repetition: 45 percent repetition means 55 percent diversity. It measures how varied the text is per character, not how much text there is. The split bar At the defaults, the train/validation/test split bar on Dataset statistics reads train 7, val 2 and test 1. It is cut by whole lines, so no sentence lands in two slices. The three held-out sentences on the chart are separate again, and the bar is only a picture of a split, since no model trains or scores on it. A leak looks like progress Picture a class where one question from Friday’s quiz gets posted in the group chat the night before. Everyone gets that question right and the class average jumps, but the average now tells the teacher less about what the class can do, not more. The lab shows the model version of this, with one twist that makes the point even sharper. With the leak on, the headline score got better, but the cleaned model got worse on the two test sentences that were not copied. It scored 2.397 on them without the leak and 2.422 with it. That is not wobble, because the same happens when training is rerun in eight different shuffled orders. The lab does not show exactly why. The bigram cannot recite the copied sentence, but it has now practised every letter pair in it, so its shared numbers lean a little toward those pairs. That lean seems to have cost the other two sentences slightly. Either way, the better headline number came from one copied answer, not from a better model. Ordinary overlaps are short; copies are long Without the leak, the longest run of words that the cleaned training text shares with the test sentences is two words long: “the morning”. Ordinary phrases overlap by a word or two, while a copied sentence shares 10 words in a row. That gap is why a check for 8 words in a row catches the copy and nothing else. A run of words in a row is called an n-gram, where n stands for the number of words. Here the pieces are whole words, while the trigrams earlier were three characters, so this check looks for shared 8-grams. Without the leak, turn Decontaminate on and its badge reads −0 lines, because no ordinary line shares 8 words with the test text. Recitation switches on quickly When a model gives back a stretch of its training text after being handed the start of that stretch, it is called memorization. In the probe, it switches on over a narrow range of context lengths. Nothing is copied at 1 or 2 characters of context, and by 5 almost every character is. Picture a friend who knows every line of one film by heart. Say one word, like “the”, and they cannot tell which scene you mean, because dozens of lines contain it. Say eight words in a row, and only one line in the whole film starts that way, so they can carry on word for word. The probe works the same way, although it is only counting and understands nothing about the text. It also counts characters, not words, so 8 characters is only a word or two. In text this small, even that is enough to pin down one line. Set the slider to 8 and read the note under each sample, which counts how many contexts have only one possible next character. For the raw model, 541 of its 555 contexts are like that, so it has no choice but to carry on with the text it was built from. Set the slider back to 1 and the same note for the cleaned model reads 4 of 26. With one character of context, most contexts have several possible next characters, so the samples wander instead of copying. Repeated footers get recited more Repeated lines carry more counts, so they get picked more often. At a context length of 8, footer text makes up 21 percent of the raw model’s sample, and the raw scrape holds four copies of the copyright line. To see that the copies are what matter, switch Strip boilerplate off and leave Drop exact duplicates on, so each footer survives exactly once. At a context length of 8, footer text now makes up only 6 percent of the cleaned model’s sample. Cleaning does not stop the cleaned model from copying its own sentences, though, because it copies 100 percent at 8 as well. Removing copies changes which text gets recited and how often, not whether a model with enough context recites at all.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Building a dataset
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Both models really train, and both held-out scores are real, so the lab is not faking its results. Its limits come from its small size and from the things you cannot adjust. Twenty lines is nowhere near a real dataset, and the gaps between the good settings are only a few thousandths of a nat. That is smaller than the wobble you would get from training on the same text in a different order. The order in which the model visits its training pairs is shuffled by a recipe that starts from a fixed number, called a seed. The same seed always gives the same shuffle, like dealing a deck of cards in the same order every time. The lab has no slider or switch to change it. So every score you see comes from a single run, with no error bar, a measure of how much a result would wobble if you ran it again. Behind the scenes, the people who built the lab trained both models again with every seed from 1 to Across those runs, the gap between the raw and cleaned scores always stays between 0.065 and 0.085, so you can trust that cleaning helped. The gap between 2.292 and 2.300 points one way at some seeds and the other way at others, so you cannot say which of those two settings is really better. Picture two sprinters who finish a hundredth of a second apart, then swap places when they race again. That tiny gap tells you nothing about who is faster. A gap counts as evidence only when it is bigger than the usual wobble, and the gap between the two best settings here is not. The lab’s filters and readouts are also cruder than they look, in several ways: The 20 lines are a fixed teaching page, not a real crawl, and you cannot paste in a page of your own. The boilerplate filter is a list of five English phrases, so it would miss a footer worded any other way. The near-duplicate test compares single short lines, while real near-duplicate checks compare whole documents that can be thousands of words long. Its 0.7 cut-off is also fixed, with no control to change it. That test compares every pair of lines directly, which works only because there are 20 of them. The MinHash number is computed for real, but the filter itself does not use it. Trigram diversity counts letter sequences, so it calls a page varied for using many of them, not for covering many topics. The split bar on Dataset statistics never trains or scores a model, so the only held-out score on the page is the three-sentence passage on the chart. The model on the chart predicts from one character, so it cannot recite long passages. All the chart can show is the model’s limited room being spent on the wrong patterns. The Regurgitation probe uses a table of counts built from only 516 to 899 characters. In so little text, almost every long context is always followed by the same character, so reciting is certain. A real model is far larger, picks up general patterns where this table cannot, and memorizes only part of what it was trained on. The probe also starts each sample from the opening characters of its training text. That mirrors how an attempt to pull text out of a real model starts from a known beginning. In this tiny table, starting from another point inside the training text would copy about as much, because almost every long context has only one continuation. A prompt that is not taken from the training text at all gives a model less to copy, so it usually copies less. The probe’s own seed is fixed as well, so each context length always prints the same text. A common mix-up: it is tempting to think that deleting data is what helped, but it is not. Removing about 40 percent of this scrape improved the score, but Drop near-duplicates removes even more and makes the score worse. Smaller is not automatically better, and neither is less repeated: the harbour line is a near-repeat, yet removing it did not help here. What tells you whether a change helped is the held-out score, not the character count and not which filter sounds more responsible. Where real pipelines struggle Real pipelines face problems that this lab is too small to show, and each one is a place where the real mechanism can fail. Finding copies at web scale: checking for exact copies with hashes still works across the whole web, but it misses near-copies. Nobody can compare every pair among billions of documents, so near-copy search uses MinHash, or a similar method called SimHash, along with a sorting trick called locality-sensitive hashing. That trick only compares documents whose signatures land in the same group, which saves most of the work. Even so, near-copy search is one of the most expensive steps in the whole pipeline. Judging quality: real boilerplate removal uses a program trained to pick the main text out of a page, not a short list of phrases. Quality filtering usually means a classifier, a program that sorts documents into groups. A classifier scores each document by how much it looks like a reference collection, so whatever that collection leans toward, the filter leans toward too. If the reference is mostly one style of writing, other styles get pushed toward the bottom. Separate steps handle which language a page is in, personal data, licences and toxic text. Each of these is a policy decision as much as a technical one. Keeping test text out: teams search for long runs of words shared with benchmarks, the standard public tests used to compare models, and GPT-3’s report used runs 13 words long. Leaks still happen, because benchmark questions get quoted in posts that the next crawl collects, and reworded copies slip past a search for exact runs. In practice, a held-out set stays held out only until someone publishes it. Counting in tokens: near-copy and contamination checks run on text that has been tidied up first, for example by making it all lowercase. Real models split text into tokens in different ways: some use single characters like this lab, while others use whole words or pieces of words, such as harb plus our. So the same page can count as 900 tokens with one method and 200 with another. A funnel reported in tokens only makes sense for the method that counted them. Memorizing a single copy: removing copies lowers how often a model recites its training text, but a large model can still memorize text that appears only once. The next section shows why that matters for names, phone numbers and email addresses.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Building a dataset
documents.body: Choosing what gets seen twice Filtering decides what is allowed into a dataset, while the data mixture decides what share of the training each source gets. Giving a small, high-quality source a few extra passes is normal practice, so after deduplication removes the accidental copies, teams put some repetition back on purpose. The rule is not “duplicates are bad” but “you should be the one choosing which text gets seen twice”. Picture making a road-trip playlist: first you delete the songs that got added three times by accident, and then you choose to play your two favourites twice. The second step is still repetition, but it is repetition you chose, and that is the difference between an accidental duplicate and a mixture. What a held-out score settles Held-out loss answers one question well: did this change help the model predict text like the held-out sample? It cannot tell you whether that sample looks like the text you actually care about. A filter that strips out blocks of computer code might look fine when you score on ordinary sentences and still ruin the model’s results on a coding test. That is why real pipelines score against several held-out sets and expect them to disagree. Why the split has three parts You check the validation slice again and again while you tune your choices, so it slowly stops being truly held out. Picture trying 50 different filter settings and keeping whichever scores best on the validation slice. Part of the winner’s lead is luck that happens to suit those few sentences, like the sprinters’ wobble. The more settings you try, the more your pick is tuned to the validation slice itself, so its score starts to flatter you. That is why the test slice stays untouched until one final check. Cutting the train/validation/test split by whole document rather than by sentence is what makes the whole thing work. Two sentences from the same page share so much wording that splitting a page between training and testing would leak one into the other. Memorization and regurgitation Memorization is a model giving back a stretch of its training text when it is handed the start of that stretch. Carlini and colleagues measured it across several families of models and found it grows steadily with three things: the model’s capacity, meaning how big it is; how many times an example was duplicated in its training data; how much context the prompt supplies, the prompt being the text you hand the model to start it off. Each time one of these doubles, the amount memorized rises by roughly the same step. The probe’s slider is closest to the third one, though raising it also makes the table bigger, so it changes the model’s size as well. Of the three, duplication is the one that the people building a dataset can control. Lee and colleagues found that over 1 percent of what models wrote without any prompt was copied word for word from their training data. These were models trained on standard datasets, and in C4 the team found one 61-word sentence repeated over 60,000 times. Training on their deduplicated data produced models that gave out memorized text ten times less often, which is a big improvement but not the whole answer. In another study, Carlini and colleagues got GPT-2 to write out hundreds of word-for-word passages from its training text, including names, phone numbers and email addresses. Each of those passages appeared in only one document, and the team also found that larger models were more vulnerable. Data governance: personal data, licences, consent Three questions about a dataset cannot be answered by reading its text: may this person’s details be used, may this text be reused, and did its owners agree? So no filter in this lab can answer them. Keeping records and rules about questions like these, such as where each document came from and what may be done with it, is called data governance. Personal data is text that identifies a person, such as a name, phone number or email address. Spotting it is a detection problem that a filter can help with, while deciding whether it may be used is a legal one. The GPT-2 result above shows why even one appearance matters. Licences are the rules that say who may reuse a piece of text, and how. An audit checked more than 1,800 text datasets on the websites that host them. It found licence information missing in over 70 percent of cases. In a separate count, it found licences labelled wrongly in over 50 percent, so the two figures measure different things and do not add up to one whole. Consent is about whether the owners of a text agreed to its use. Websites state their wishes in their terms of service and in a file called robots.txt, which tells automatic collectors what they may and may not take. A 2024 audit of 14,000 web domains, which are website names, found these restrictions rose sharply in a single year. If they were respected, over 5 percent of all the text in C4 would now be fully blocked by robots.txt files. The audit also found that 45 percent of C4 is restricted by the sites’ terms of service. Rules are arriving, too, and one of them is a European Union law called the EU AI Act. It covers models built for many different tasks, called general-purpose AI models, and it asks their makers to keep a policy for following EU copyright law. Some rights holders, meaning the people who own the copyright in a piece of writing, have stated that their work may not be used this way. This is called reserving their rights. The makers’ policy has to cover these cases, and the law also asks them to publish a detailed enough summary of what they trained on. Both of these duties need a record kept alongside the data, not a better filter. Toy versus real Scale: the lab’s scrape is 20 lines and 899 characters, and its most repeated line, the copyright footer, appears four times. Lee and colleagues found one 61-word sentence repeated over 60,000 times in C4. Overlap checks: the lab flags an 8-word run shared with the test text, while GPT-3’s report flagged any test example that shared a 13-word run with its training data. Lee and colleagues also found that over 4 percent of the validation sets of standard datasets overlapped with their training data. Reciting: the probe copies everything at 8 characters of context because its text is tiny. In the models Lee and colleagues trained, over 1 percent of what they wrote without a prompt was copied word for word. Carlini and colleagues also found that memorization grows as models get bigger, so a real model’s size affects how much it recites. What real pipelines add: language detection, trained quality classifiers, detection of personal data, records of licences and opt-outs, and a log of why each document was dropped. Where these findings come from Every study named in this lesson is on arXiv, a free online library of research papers, and you can find each one by searching for its number. The two studies by Carlini and colleagues are 2202.07646, on what makes memorization grow, and 2012.07805, on pulling training text out of GPT-2. Lee and colleagues’ study of deduplication is 2107.06499, and the GPT-3 report by Brown and colleagues is 2005.14165. The two audits by Longpre and colleagues are 2310.16787, on licences, and 2407.14933, on consent. The EU AI Act is officially called Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Building a dataset
documents.body: This module is about the text a model trains on: building it from a web scrape by removing site boilerplate, copies, and evaluation text, then checking whether the result is better. The question it answers is how to tell a better dataset from one that is merely smaller. *Anatomy of a training run* followed one character model from batch to checkpoint. Here that loop stays fixed and only the training text changes, so held-out loss, cross-entropy on text that never entered training, is the verdict on every change. The last part asks when a model recites its training text, and which questions about a dataset no filter can answer. Where it shows up The first three are pipeline stages that run on real crawls at far larger scale, and the lab has small versions of them. Mixture and governance are decisions and records kept around the data, not filters, and have no control here. Deduplication. Exact hashing first, then MinHash signatures, short fingerprints whose agreement estimates how much two documents overlap, to find near-copies at web scale. Filtering. Trained boilerplate extractors, quality filtering that usually uses a classifier, and further stages for language, personal data, licensing, and toxicity. Decontamination. Training documents that share a long word n-gram with a benchmark item are removed before training. Mixture and governance. A data mixture sets each source's share of the training budget, and the EU AI Act asks providers of general-purpose AI models to publish a summary of their training content. Why it matters Raw scraped text is full of site furniture and copies, and a model with a fixed parameter budget spends part of it fitting them. Yet a filter that deletes junk can still cost accuracy, so a dataset's size says nothing on its own about its quality. Without held-out text kept out of training, no dataset change has a verdict you can trust. Duplication also shapes what a model recites, since memorization grows with the number of times an example was duplicated. Deduplication is not enough, though. Text seen once can still be extracted, and whether a dataset is allowed to hold a person's details, a licensed work, or an opted-out site's pages is not visible in the text, so no filter can settle it. What you will be able to explain The failure modes a cleaning pipeline removes: boilerplate, exact repeats, near-duplicates, low-signal fragments, and text that overlaps an evaluation set, and which filter catches each. Why held-out text must stay separate from every training set, and what leakage, evaluation text inside training data, does to a held-out score. How to judge a dataset change by its validation loss rather than its size, and when a gap is too small to resolve. When a model recites its training text verbatim, and why personal data, licences, and consent need checks that deduplication does not give. What the lab shows The scrape is fixed: 20 hard-coded lines, each given one verdict, which Show filters to All lines or Kept only. Cleaning stages holds four switches, Strip boilerplate, Drop exact duplicates, Drop near-duplicates, and Decontaminate, plus a Minimum line length slider. Each change updates the verdicts, the Survival funnel, and Dataset statistics. The comparison is measured. The same character bigram, which predicts each character from the one before it, is trained for 25 epochs on the raw scrape and again on the kept lines, and both are scored on three held-out sentences. Raw held-out and Cleaned held-out are real cross-entropy, and Difference is their gap, all from one fixed shuffle seed, so none carries an error bar. The key experiment: find which filters lower Cleaned held-out, then press Leak a held-out sentence into the scrape and watch the score improve for the wrong reason until Decontaminate removes the copy. The Regurgitation probe swaps in two tables of counts instead of trained networks, one built from the raw scrape and one from the kept lines, and Context length sets how many characters each conditions on. Each model writes one fixed-seed, 300-character sample that starts from its training text's opening characters, and Copied verbatim reports how much of that sample sits in runs of 16 or more characters copied from the training text. Some parts are simplified. Boilerplate detection is five hard-coded phrases, the near-duplicate stage compares character-trigram sets exactly while the MinHash note only estimates that similarity, and the train/validation/test split bar is a display that neither trains nor scores a model.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Building a dataset
documents.body: A cleaning pipeline is a sequence of filters, each deleting documents by a stated rule. This lab holds 20 lines from a small scrape. Every line gets exactly one verdict — kept, boilerplate, exact repeat, near-duplicate, or too short — and Show switches between All lines and Kept only so you can read the verdicts before trusting them. The scrape carries four distinct kinds of junk, all of which occur in real crawls: Boilerplate: copyright, subscribe, and share lines that belong to the site rather than to any document. Nine of the 20 lines are this. An exact repeat of a real sentence, which exact deduplication catches. A spelling variant — one line writes harbour where an earlier line writes harbor. Same content, different bytes, so only a near-duplicate test finds it. Two fragments, ok. and yes., carrying almost no signal for their length. Then the lab does the part that arguments about data usually skip. It trains the same character bigram model twice — once on all 20 lines joined, once on the kept lines — for 25 epochs each, and scores both on 194 characters of text in neither training set. Those scores are Raw held-out and Cleaned held-out, and Difference is the only claim it makes. The Survival funnel counts what each stage removed, in lines and in encoded characters. A last card, Regurgitation probe, changes the model. It builds a table of counts from the raw scrape and from the cleaned set, lets each write 300 characters, and measures how much of the output is a verbatim copy. The bigram that the rest of the track trains cannot do that, and the probe shows what changes when the model sees more than one character of context.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Building a dataset
documents.body: Repetition is not neutral. Every training pair produces a gradient, so a line appearing four times pulls the weights four times as hard. The model has 900 parameters to spend, and capacity spent predicting all rights reserved is capacity not spent on anything else. That is the mechanism behind data quality, a phrase that means nothing on its own. Held-out text is here for a second reason: leakage. If evaluation text also sits in the training data, the score measures recall of a memorized string rather than generalization, and it improves without the model improving. The passage scored here is outside both training sets on purpose, which is why the comparison carries information at all — until you press Leak a held-out sentence into the scrape.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Building a dataset
documents.body: Set Show to All lines and read all 20 verdicts before touching a filter. Then walk the settings and record Cleaned held-out at each stop: All filters off: 20 lines, 899 Characters, 2.365 nats per token. The curves lie on top of each other and Difference reads +0.000. That is the control condition. Strip boilerplate only: 11 lines, 580 characters, 2.306. Boilerplate plus Drop exact duplicates, the defaults: 10 lines, 516 characters, 2.300, and Difference reads −0.065. Add Drop near-duplicates: 9 lines, 451 characters, 2.312. Worse. Add Minimum line length at 20 chars: 2.316. Worse again. Now turn Strip boilerplate off and leave only Drop exact duplicates: 13 lines, 623 characters, 2.292 — the best score available in this lab. That last result is not a trick. The repeated boilerplate lines are byte-identical, so exact deduplication already removes all but one copy of each. The extra 107 characters are those three surviving footer lines; at one copy each, their ordinary English letter pairs cost the model nothing measurable here. Finally, return to the defaults and press Leak a held-out sentence into the scrape. It copies "the fog returns in the morning and the pattern repeats." into the page. Cleaned held-out improves from 2.300 to 2.245, and the contamination check flags a 10-word run shared with the held-out text. Turn on Decontaminate and the score returns to 2.300. Last, open Regurgitation probe and drag Context length from 1 to 8. At 1 character, Copied verbatim reads 0 percent for both models and the samples are gibberish. At 3 the raw model copies 52 percent of its sample and the cleaned one 39 percent. At 4 it is 98 and 93 percent, and at 8 both read 100 percent. The raw sample at 8 is also 21 percent footer text, the copyright and subscribe lines; the cleaned sample has none.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Building a dataset
documents.body: Watch the badge on Drop exact duplicates. With Strip boilerplate on it reads −1 lines; with boilerplate off it reads −7. The filters overlap heavily, so neither one's value can be judged in isolation. The Survival funnel reads 20, 11, 11, 10, 10, 10 lines and 899 to 516 characters at the defaults. Boilerplate removes 9 of 20 lines but only 319 characters: counting documents and counting tokens tell different stories. Cleaning removes about 40 percent of the characters and the held-out score improves: size helps only when the added text carries new signal. But the direction is not automatic. Drop near-duplicates and Minimum line length each cost a little accuracy here, even though both remove text a human would call junk. The filters are not independent. Minimum line length at 20 makes the score slightly worse when Drop near-duplicates is on (2.312 to 2.316) and slightly better when it is off (2.300 to 2.296). A filter's effect depends on which others are already running. Distinct trigrams falls from 366 raw to 285 cleaned while Repetition falls from a Raw repetition of 60 percent to 45 percent. Fewer distinct sequences and less repetition at once: trigram diversity measures signal per character, not signal in total. The train/validation/test split bar reads 7 / 2 / 1 lines at the defaults, drawn by line so no sentence lands in two slices. The scored held-out passage is separate again. Leakage looks like progress. With the leak on, the cleaned model's loss on the two held-out sentences that were not copied gets worse, 2.397 to 2.422, while the headline score improves. The same happens at every seed from 1 to 8. Without the leak, the longest word run shared with the held-out text is two words, "the morning". Ordinary phrases are short and a copied sentence is long, which is why an 8-word decontamination check catches the leak and nothing else. Memorization switches on over a narrow range of context. Nothing is copied at 1 or 2 characters of context, and at 5 almost every character is. Of the contexts the raw model has seen at length 8, 541 of 555 have only one possible next character, so it has no choice but to continue the text it saw. The duplicated footer is what the raw model recites first. Repeated lines carry more counts, so they are sampled more often: 21 percent of the raw sample at length 8, against none of the cleaned one. But cleaning does not stop the cleaned model copying its own sentences.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Building a dataset
documents.body: In this lab. Both models are trained for real and both scores are real cross-entropy on text neither model saw. The limits are size and what is not adjustable. Twenty lines is not a corpus, and the gaps between the good settings are a few thousandths of a nat — smaller than the spread a different shuffle order would produce. The shuffle seed is fixed and has no control, so every number arrives without an error bar. Across seeds 1 to 8 the raw-to-cleaned gap ranges from 0.065 to 0.085, so treat it as real; the gap between 2.292 and 2.300 changes sign between seeds, so treat it as unresolved. The filters are cruder than they look: boilerplate detection is five hard-coded substrings, and the near-duplicate test is exact character-trigram Jaccard at 0.7 applied to single lines rather than documents. The MinHash note computes a real 64-hash estimate of the harbour pair (0.922 against an exact 0.915), but the stage itself compares sets directly, which only works because there are twenty lines. The validation chart's model is a bigram over 30 characters, so it cannot show verbatim regurgitation of long passages. It can only show capacity being spent in the wrong place. The Regurgitation probe uses a different model for that: a table of counts over 516 to 899 characters, where almost every long context is unique, so reciting is guaranteed. A real model generalizes where this table cannot, and memorizes only part of what it saw. In real systems. Exact hashing still runs at web scale, but it misses near-copies, and comparing every pair of billions of documents is impossible. So near-duplicate search uses MinHash or SimHash signatures with locality-sensitive hashing, which only compares documents whose signatures collide, and it is one of the most expensive stages in the pipeline. Boilerplate removal is a trained extractor, not a substring list. Quality filtering usually means a classifier scored against a reference corpus, which imports that reference's biases. Separate stages handle language identification, personal data, licensing, and toxicity, each a policy decision as much as an engineering one. Leakage is harder there too. Benchmark contamination is checked by n-gram overlap against every evaluation set (GPT-3's report used 13-grams) and still happens, because benchmark items get quoted in posts that the next crawl collects, and paraphrases slip past exact n-gram matching. A held-out set is held out until someone publishes it. Tokenization interacts with all of this. Near-duplicate and contamination checks run on normalized text, and the same page can yield very different token counts under different tokenizers, so a funnel reported in tokens is specific to the tokenizer that counted it.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Building a dataset
documents.body: Mixture weights are the other half of the job. Filtering decides what is admissible; the data mixture decides what fraction of the training budget each source receives. Upsampling a small high-quality source a few times is standard practice, so controlled duplication gets reintroduced deliberately after deduplication removed the accidental kind. The rule is not "duplicates are bad" but "you should be the one choosing which text gets seen twice". What a held-out score settles. Held-out loss answers one question well: did this dataset change help the model predict text like the held-out sample? It cannot tell you whether that sample is the text you care about. A step that strips code blocks looks fine on prose and disastrous on a coding benchmark, which is why production pipelines score against several held-out sets and expect them to disagree. Why the split has three parts. Validation is touched repeatedly while you tune, so it slowly stops being held out — every decision fits it a little. The test slice is what you keep for a single measurement at the end. Drawing the train/validation/test split by document rather than by sentence is what makes any of it work, because two sentences from one page share enough phrasing to leak across a sentence-level split. Memorization and regurgitation Memorization is a model reproducing a stretch of its training text when given a prefix of it. Carlini and colleagues measured it across model families and found it grows log-linearly with model capacity, with the number of times an example was duplicated, and with the number of tokens of context used to prompt the model (arXiv 2202.07646). The probe isolates the third. Duplication is the part a pipeline controls. Lee and colleagues found that over 1 percent of the unprompted output of language models trained on standard datasets was copied verbatim from the training data, and that one 61-word sentence was repeated over 60,000 times in C4. Their deduplication produced models that emitted memorized text ten times less frequently (arXiv 2107.06499). Deduplication is not enough. Carlini and colleagues extracted hundreds of verbatim sequences from GPT-2, including names, phone numbers, and email addresses, even though each sequence appeared in just one document, and they found larger models more vulnerable (arXiv 2012.07805). Data governance: personal data, licences, consent Three questions about a dataset cannot be answered by reading its text, so no filter in this lab can answer them. Personal data. Whether a document names a person is a detection problem, and whether it may be used is a legal one. The extraction result above is why a single occurrence still matters. Licences. An audit of more than 1,800 text datasets found licence information omitted in over 70 percent of cases on the hosting sites it examined, and miscategorized in over 50 percent (Longpre et al., arXiv 2310.16787). Consent. Websites state their preferences in terms of service and robots.txt. A 2024 audit of 14,000 web domains found that restrictions rose enough in one year that, if respected, over 5 percent of all tokens in C4 are fully restricted, and 45 percent by terms of service (Longpre et al., arXiv 2407.14933). Rules are arriving. Article 53(1) of the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, asks providers of general-purpose AI models to keep a policy for complying with Union copyright law, including rights reservations, and to publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training. Each of these needs a record kept with the data, not a better filter. Toy versus real Scale. The lab's scrape is 20 lines and 899 characters, and its most repeated line is the copyright footer, four times. Lee et al. found one 61-word sentence repeated over 60,000 times in C4. Overlap checks. The lab flags an 8-word run shared with the held-out text. GPT-3's report flagged any test example sharing a 13-gram with its pretraining data (Brown et al., arXiv 2005.14165). Lee et al. found train-test overlap affecting over 4 percent of the validation sets of standard datasets. Recitation. The probe copies everything at 8 characters of context because the text is tiny. In the models Lee et al. trained, over 1 percent of unprompted output was copied verbatim, and Carlini et al. found memorization grows with model capacity. What real pipelines add. Language identification, trained quality classifiers, personal-data detection, licence and opt-out records, and a log of why each document was dropped.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Source documents and cleaning verdicts · Building a dataset
documents.body: Every scraped line, and why it stayed or left Twenty hard-coded lines that look like a scraped page — real harbor sentences mixed with copyright footers, subscribe prompts, an exact repeat, a spelling variant, and two fragments — each tagged with the cleaning stage that removed it, or `kept`. A switch can copy one held-out sentence into the page. A kicker counting the scraped lines (20, or 21 with the leak on) and how many the current pipeline removed, plus a `Show` control: `All lines` or `Kept only`. A pressable row, `Leak a held-out sentence into the scrape`, reading `off` or `leaked`. An ordered list. Each row is the line text, a verdict chip (`kept`, `boilerplate`, `too short`, `exact repeat`, `near-duplicate`, or `held-out overlap`), and the line's character count. A near-duplicate chip also prints the trigram Jaccard `J` with the line it matched; a leaked line that survives says `leaked`. Removed lines are struck through and dimmed, so a verdict never depends on the chip colour alone. Verdicts are assigned in pipeline order, first match wins: boilerplate phrases (`all rights reserved`, `click here`, `subscribe`, `share this page`, `copyright`), then `Minimum line length`, then an exact match with a line already kept, then trigram Jaccard of at least 0.7 with a kept line, then any 8-word run shared with the held-out text. Duplicate checks compare only against lines that survived the earlier stages, so a stage's count depends on which stages ran before it. The leak switch inserts “the fog returns in the morning and the pattern repeats.”, one of the three held-out sentences, after the rain line. `Show` filters the list and changes nothing else. `Show` toggles between every line and the kept ones. The leak switch adds or removes the copied sentence. The four switches and `Minimum line length` on `Cleaning stages` rewrite every verdict live. Comparison worth running: with `Show` on `All lines`, toggle `Drop near-duplicates`. The harbour line flips to `near-duplicate · J 0.92`. `copyright 2019 all rights reserved.` appears four times, but with `Strip boilerplate` on every copy is tagged boilerplate first, so `Drop exact duplicates` only catches the repeated fog sentence and reads −1. Turn boilerplate off and it reads −7. The harbour spelling differs from the kept harbor line by one byte, so exact dedup keeps it. Only the near-duplicate stage removes it. `ok.` and `yes.` survive every default stage because they are not boilerplate and `Minimum line length` starts at off. In this lab: the twenty lines are a fixed teaching page, not a crawl. You cannot paste a URL, and the boilerplate list is five English phrases. In this lab: near-duplicate detection computes exact trigram Jaccard for every pair, which is only possible because there are twenty lines. The MinHash readout on `Cleaning stages` shows the estimate a real pipeline would use instead. In general: production cleaning also covers language ID, quality classifiers, toxicity filters, licence and PII stripping, and fuzzy dedup across billions of documents. A line-level switch list is the shape of that pipeline, not its scale.
documents.title: Every scraped line, and why it stayed or left

documents.subtitle: Validation loss for both datasets · Building a dataset
documents.body: What the cleaning actually bought Two real training runs — one on the raw scrape, one on whatever the current pipeline kept — scored at every checkpoint on the same three held-out sentences, plus a contamination check that searches the cleaned set for text copied from those sentences. A chart whose x axis is training progress from 0 to 1 and whose y axis is held-out loss in nats per token, pinned from 1.50 to 3.50. Two series named with their training-pair counts: dashed `raw (N pairs)` and solid `cleaned (N pairs)`. Three metrics: `Raw held-out`, `Cleaned held-out`, and `Difference`, signed with a minus when cleaning wins. A contamination check: the longest run of words the cleaned training set shares with the held-out text, the run itself, and a flag at 8 words or more. With the leak on it also prints the cleaned model's loss on the two held-out sentences the leak did not copy. Each run is minibatch SGD on a character bigram, 25 epochs, batch 16, learning rate 0.6, seed 4, seven checkpoints. The only difference is the training text. Every plotted point is `tinyCrossEntropy` of that checkpoint's weights on the three held-out sentences, not the batch loss of the run. If cleaning removes every line, the cleaned run is trained on the raw text instead of an empty string, so the two curves coincide rather than leaving a missing number. The shared run is found by comparing every word position in the cleaned text with every position in the held-out text. Full stops are ignored. This card has no controls of its own. Every switch, the leak row, and `Minimum line length` retrain both runs. Comparison worth running: with the defaults read `Cleaned held-out` (2.300), turn on the leak (2.245), then read the untouched-sentence line (2.422, up from 2.397). Turn on `Decontaminate` and it returns to 2.300. A lower cleaned curve is not automatic. Dropping useful sentences can raise held-out loss, which is why the Difference metric is signed. The leak makes the held-out score better and the model worse on everything it did not copy. That is leakage: a better number without a better model. Without the leak the longest shared run is two words, `the morning`. Ordinary shared phrases are short; a copied sentence is long, which is why n-gram decontamination works. In this lab: both losses are genuinely computed, but the held-out set is three sentences and each run is one seed. Across seeds 1–8 the raw-to-cleaned gap ranges from 0.065 to 0.085, while gaps between the good settings stay under 0.01 and are unresolved. In this lab: the split bar on `Dataset statistics` is a display. It does not create the held-out text this chart uses. In general: a real cleaning win is measured on held-out distributions you care about, across seeds, against the cost of the tokens you threw away. Contamination checks run against every benchmark, and still miss paraphrases.
documents.title: What the cleaning actually bought

documents.subtitle: Survival funnel · Building a dataset
documents.body: How much of the scrape survives each stage The same verdicts as the line list, counted stage by stage in pipeline order: how many lines and characters are left after each filter, and how much each one removed. One row per stage: Scraped, Strip boilerplate, Length floor, Exact dedup, Near-dup, Decontaminate. A centred bar's width is the number of lines left after that stage. Where a stage removed lines, a hatched ghost bar behind it shows the width before the stage. On the right, lines and characters left, and underneath the stage's own removal (`−9 lines · −319 chars`), `removes nothing here`, or `stage off`. Rows are computed from the verdict list: each stage removes exactly the lines tagged with its verdict, so the removals always add up to the difference between the first and last rows. Characters are counted after `encodeTinyText`, the model's 30-symbol encoding, so the digits in `copyright 2019` do not count and the numbers match the `Characters` metric. The funnel follows every switch, the leak row, and `Minimum line length`. Comparison worth running: at the defaults, the funnel reads 20, 11, 11, 10, 10, 10 lines and 899 to 516 characters. Turn off `Strip boilerplate` and exact dedup takes 7 lines instead of 1. Boilerplate removes 9 of 20 lines but only 319 of 899 characters: the lines it removes are short. Counting documents and counting tokens tell different stories. A stage that is on but removes nothing still appears as a full-width row. That is not a bug: the earlier stages already took its targets. In this lab: twenty lines, five stages, and one order. The funnel cannot reorder stages. In general: published pipelines report funnels like this one in tokens, and the steepest drops usually come from language, quality, and deduplication filters, often removing most of a raw web crawl.
documents.title: How much of the scrape survives each stage

documents.subtitle: Cleaning stages · Building a dataset
documents.body: Toggle a filter and watch the verdicts move Four pipeline switches plus a length floor. Each switch is live: it rewrites every verdict, both training runs, the funnel, and every statistic on the page. A note compares exact Jaccard with a MinHash estimate for the spelling-variant pair. Four pressable rows: `Strip boilerplate`, `Drop exact duplicates`, `Drop near-duplicates`, and `Decontaminate`, each with a one-line rule and a count reading `−N lines` when on or `off` when off. `Minimum line length` from 0 (`off`) to 60 characters. A note giving the harbour/harbor pair's exact trigram Jaccard (0.915) and a 64-hash MinHash estimate of it (0.922). `Strip boilerplate` drops a line containing any of five phrases. `Drop exact duplicates` keeps the first surviving copy of a byte-identical line. `Drop near-duplicates` tags a line when its character-trigram Jaccard with an already-kept line is at least 0.7. Jaccard is shared trigrams divided by the union of both trigram sets. `Decontaminate` tags a line that shares any 8-word run with the held-out text. It runs last. MinHash hashes every trigram with 64 different hash functions and keeps each function's minimum. Two lines agree at a position with probability equal to their Jaccard, so the share of agreeing positions estimates it with error shrinking like one over the square root of the signature length. Each switch toggles that filter; the pressed state is `aria-pressed`. `Minimum line length` at 12 drops `ok.` and `yes.`. The shortest real sentence is 56 characters, so the floor starts eating real text at 57. Comparison worth running: leave boilerplate and exact-repeat on, then turn near-duplicates on and off while watching `Lines kept` and `Cleaned held-out` together. The `−N lines` count is what that stage tagged, not what it would have tagged if earlier stages had not already removed lines. Order matters. Boilerplate runs first, so most copyright lines never become exact-repeat candidates. `Decontaminate` reads −0 without the leak: no ordinary line shares 8 words with the held-out text. Turning every switch off and setting length to 0 makes the cleaned corpus identical to the raw one, the control the comparison chart needs. In this lab: four binary filters and a length floor are the entire cleaner. There is no language detector, no quality classifier, and no way to write your own rule. The MinHash note is computed but the near-duplicate stage itself uses exact Jaccard. In general: a production pipeline is this idea at corpus scale — cheap exact checks first, MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing for near-duplicates, n-gram decontamination against every benchmark, with every dropped document logged so someone can audit why it left.
documents.title: Toggle a filter and watch the verdicts move

documents.subtitle: Dataset statistics · Building a dataset
documents.body: Size, diversity, and a split that is only a picture How much text survived, how repetitive it is, and a three-way split bar drawn by line. The bar is a teaching picture of a split; the validation loss chart does not use it. A first metric row: `Lines kept` as kept / scraped, `Characters` after encoding into the 30-symbol vocabulary, and `Training pairs` from the cleaned run. A second row: `Distinct trigrams` in the cleaned text, `Repetition` as one minus distinct/total trigrams, and `Raw repetition` of the unfiltered page. A split bar labelled `train N`, `val N`, and `test N`, sized by a 70% / 15% / remainder split of the kept lines, with validation getting at least one line. A trigram here is three consecutive characters. Distinct is the number of unique ones; total is `max(1, length − 2)`; repetition is `1 − distinct / total`. `Characters` uses `encodeTinyText`, so case folds, unknown characters such as digits become spaces, and runs of spaces collapse. It will not match the sum of the raw line lengths. The split is `round(0.7n)` train, `max(1, round(0.15n))` validation, and the remainder test. It is not applied to either trainer. The card has no controls; it reports the current pipeline. Comparison worth running: read `Repetition` with defaults (45%), turn every switch off (60%), then turn only `Strip boilerplate` on (51%). `Repetition` uses the loss tone when the cleaned text is more repetitive than the raw page, which can happen if you drop the diverse sentences and keep the furniture. At the defaults `Distinct trigrams` falls from 366 to 285 while repetition falls from 60% to 45%: fewer distinct sequences and less repetition at once. If you keep one line, the bar still draws a validation slice of 1 because of the `max(1, …)` floor — do not treat that as a usable split. In this lab: the split bar never trains or scores a model. The only held-out number on the page is the three-sentence passage on the chart. In this lab: trigram diversity is a character-level toy. It calls a page diverse for using many letter sequences, not for covering many topics. In general: a real split is by document, not by line, and the test set is locked before you tune cleaning. Scoring on a passage written to resemble the training domain, as this page does, is closer to a development set than to a blind test.
documents.title: Size, diversity, and a split that is only a picture

documents.subtitle: Regurgitation probe · Building a dataset
documents.body: More context, and a model recites what it was trained on Two count-based character models, one built from the raw scrape and one from whatever the current pipeline kept. Each starts from the opening characters of its own training text, writes 300 characters, and is scored on how much of that output is a verbatim copy. The `Context length` slider is the only thing that changes how much each model can copy. A `Context length` slider from 1 to 12 characters, and a badge that repeats it. At 1 character the model is the same bigram the rest of the track trains. Two columns, `Trained on the raw scrape` and `Trained on the cleaned set`. Each prints the first 170 characters of its sample and three metrics: `Copied verbatim (16+ chars)`, `Longest copied run`, and `Footer text in the sample`. A line under each sample saying how many of that model's contexts have only one possible next character, in which case it has no choice but to continue the text it saw. A table with the same sweep at context lengths 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 12: the share copied verbatim for each model, and the share of the raw model's sample that is footer text. The row for the current slider value is shaded. The model is a table of counts, not a trained network. For a context length `k`, every run of `k` characters in the training text records which character came next. Sampling draws the next character in proportion to those counts, seeded with 7, after being given the first `k` characters of the training text. Text is encoded as the trainer sees it: lowercase, 30 symbols, runs of spaces collapsed. That makes the raw scrape 899 characters and the cleaned default set 516. A sample character counts as copied when it lies inside a 16-character window that appears verbatim in the training text. `Longest copied run` is the longest verbatim stretch of any length. `Footer text` counts the characters that belong to one of the five boilerplate phrases the cleaning stage looks for. `Context length` is the only control. The raw and cleaned columns also follow every switch on `Cleaning stages`, the leak row, and `Minimum line length`, because the cleaned set is rebuilt from them. Comparison worth running: at a context of 1, both samples are gibberish and 0% is copied. At 3, the raw model copies 52% and the cleaned one 39%. At 4, 98% and 93%. At 8, both copy 100%. Copying switches on over a narrow range. Nothing is copied at 1 or 2 characters of context, and by 5 almost every character is. The training text is only 516 to 899 characters long, so there is almost never a second continuation to choose between. The raw model writes the footer. At a context of 8, 21% of its sample is `copyright`, `subscribe`, and `share this page` text, and the cleaned model's is 0%. Repeated lines carry more counts, so they are sampled more often. The longest copied run is a stretch of one training line or several joined, so it can pass 160 characters in the raw sample at a context of 8, longer than any single scraped line. Both columns copy almost everything at a long context. Deduplication changes which text is recited and how often, not whether a model with enough context recites at all. In this lab: the model is a table of counts over a 516 to 899 character text, so every context longer than a few characters is unique and memorization is guaranteed. A real model with billions of parameters generalizes where this table cannot, and memorizes only part of what it saw. In this lab: the sample starts from the first characters of the training text, as an extraction attempt starts from a prefix. A random prompt would copy less. The seed is fixed, so one context length always prints the same text. In general: published work finds memorization growing log-linearly with model capacity, with how often a text was duplicated, and with the number of tokens of context used to prompt the model (Carlini et al., 2022). Deduplicating training data cut emitted memorized text about tenfold in one study (Lee et al., 2021), but sequences that appear in a single document have still been extracted, including names, phone numbers, and email addresses (Carlini et al., 2021).

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Stored keys and values for every token already processed, in each layer that attends over the whole context. It is charged per token per stream, which makes it the memory term that scales with load.
documents.title: KV cache

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Limited by how fast bytes can be read rather than by arithmetic. Decoding reads every weight to produce one token per stream, so it sits here at any batch size this lab offers on its stated hardware.
documents.title: Memory bandwidth bound

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Scheduling one decode step at a time: finished requests leave and waiting ones join at every step, so the batch stays full. Every stream in the batch shares one read of the weights.
documents.title: Continuous batching

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Total tokens per second across all users, against tokens per second for one user, whose inverse is the time per output token. Batching improves the first and worsens the second.
documents.title: Throughput and latency

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Queueing plus prefill, the pass over the whole prompt before generation starts. Prefill is compute bound and grows with prompt length.
documents.title: Time to first token

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Storing the KV cache in small fixed-size blocks allocated as a stream grows, as vLLM's PagedAttention does with 16 tokens by default. A stream holds only what it has filled instead of a full-context reservation, so the waste per stream is under one block.
documents.title: Paged attention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: A small draft model proposes γ tokens and the large model checks them in one pass, accepting a prefix by rejection sampling. The output distribution is unchanged; with acceptance rate α each pass yields (1 − α^(γ+1)) / (1 − α) tokens, and the wall-time gain divides that by 1 + γc, where c is the draft's cost against the target's.
documents.title: Speculative decoding

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Mixing full-attention layers, whose cache grows with context, with recurrent or linear-attention layers that keep a fixed-size state per stream. Qwen3.5 2B has 6 full-attention layers among its 24, so only those are charged per token.
documents.title: Hybrid attention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Storing cached keys and values in fewer bits, such as llama.cpp's q8_0 at 8.5 bits per value or q4_0 at 4.5. It shrinks the per-token cost and the bytes read each step, at some cost in accuracy. A recurrent state is a separate store and stays float32 in llama.cpp.
documents.title: KV-cache quantization

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: The hourly price of the hardware over the output tokens it generates in an hour, scaled to a million. It falls as batching raises total throughput and rises with idle time. The price is an input, not a property of the model.
documents.title: Cost per million tokens

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Watching latency, throughput, queueing, cache occupancy, and error rates in service, and replaying a fixed evaluation to catch drift: a shift in traffic or behaviour that makes yesterday's measurements stop describing today's use.
documents.title: Monitoring and drift

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Serving a pinned model file, engine, and configuration by exact version, sending a small share of traffic to a new one first, and keeping the old one ready so that a rollback is a switch rather than a rebuild.
documents.title: Versioned rollout

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Checks and limits around the model rather than inside it: input and output filters, tool permissions, rate and length limits, and refusal policies. They are ordinary software and need their own tests.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Running the model on the user's own hardware, as this app does with llama.cpp on a loopback port. Prompts stay on the machine and nothing is billed per token, at the price of smaller models and the speed of the local memory system.
