documents.title: On-device inference

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 1
documents.body: You drag Concurrent users from 8 up toward 64 at a fixed context length. Which part of the Memory budget changes? Both the weights and the cache grow, because each new user needs its own copy of the model Only the KV cache grows; the weights are a fixed cost paid once, however many users connect Only the activations grow, because the runtime allocates more scratch space for each new user Neither changes, because the budget is set by the model and the weight format alone Weights are loaded once and shared by every stream, so they never move with load. The KV cache is charged for every token of every active conversation, so context length times concurrency decides whether a configuration survives real traffic. That is how a model that loads with room to spare can still run out of memory under load.
documents.title: You drag Concurrent users from 8 up toward 64 at a fixed context length. Which part of the Memory budget changes?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 2
documents.body: The lab says 36 streams fit at 4,096 tokens on the 8B shape. Why might a real server using paged attention hold more? Paged attention quantizes the cache to four bits, which divides the memory cost of every token by four or more Real servers skip the activation term, so the flat 1 GiB the lab charges is what limits how many streams fit Paged attention shares one copy of the weights across all streams, so each extra stream adds no memory at all The lab reserves each stream's full context up front; paged attention allocates blocks only as a stream fills them The lab charges every stream for its whole context at once, which is the worst case. Paged attention allocates the cache in small blocks as a stream grows, so streams that have not filled their context hold less and more of them fit. The weights are already shared in the lab, and quantizing the cache is a separate technique.
documents.title: The lab says 36 streams fit at 4,096 tokens on the 8B shape. Why might a real server using paged attention hold more?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 3
documents.body: You raise Concurrent users from 1 to 8 with Continuous batching on. Which readouts move, and in which directions? Total rises and Per user falls: all streams share one read of the weights, while each step also reads more cache Both rise, because a bigger batch keeps the hardware busier and so every user's tokens arrive faster than before Total stays the same and Per user falls, because the available bandwidth is simply split evenly between the users Both fall, because each extra user adds another full copy of the weights that every decode step has to read A decode step reads every weight once and each stream's cache once, then emits one token per stream, so extra streams ride on the same weight read and total throughput rises. The step also grows because it reads more cache, so each user's own tokens per second fall. The even split in the third option is what the One at a time scheduler does.
documents.title: You raise Concurrent users from 1 to 8 with Continuous batching on. Which readouts move, and in which directions?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 4
documents.body: At 64 streams the badge still says memory bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Why? The lab ignores compute altogether, so the badge has no other limit that it could ever report Batching moves the arithmetic off the accelerator, which leaves bandwidth as the only limit left Each token costs only about two FLOPs per parameter, while every weight byte must be read at every step More users add more weights to read, so memory traffic always grows faster than the arithmetic Decoding does about two FLOPs per parameter per token but has to read every weight byte for each step, so the arithmetic finishes long before the bytes arrive. The lab does compute a ceiling for it, far above the throughput the streams reach, and batching helps precisely because more tokens share one weight read.
documents.title: At 64 streams the badge still says memory bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 5
documents.body: Which set of artifacts does an export have to produce before llama.cpp can serve the model? The training checkpoint exactly as it was saved, because the engine converts any format when the first request arrives Only the quantized weights, because the engine rebuilds the tokenizer and metadata from the weights themselves One GGUF file with the merged, quantized tensors, their metadata, and the tokenizer, plus a header a loader can verify A separate KV cache file for each user, because the cache has to be loaded before the first token appears The checklist merges any adapter so inference costs what the base cost, quantizes to the chosen block type, and writes one GGUF file holding tensors, quantization metadata, and tokenizer behind a header the loader checks. This lab names those steps and prices the toy table at the block type; it does not write a file. The KV cache is built at run time, never exported.
documents.title: Which set of artifacts does an export have to produce before llama.cpp can serve the model?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 6
documents.body: The 2B · this app preset charges a KV cache for only 6 of its 24 layers. What do the other 18 layers cost per stream? Nothing, because linear-attention layers keep no information between tokens and so need no stored state at all A fixed recurrent state, shown as Fixed state per stream, that does not grow with the context length The same cache per token as the other six, which the lab leaves out of the bar to keep the chart readable A cache that grows with context but is stored at 4 bits, which is why the total looks so small here Gated DeltaNet layers keep a fixed-size state per stream, about 19 MiB for all 18 layers in float32, so they add a constant per stream and nothing per token. Only the six full-attention layers hold a cache that grows with context: 12 KiB a token, against 48 KiB if all 24 layers cached.
documents.title: The 2B · this app preset charges a KV cache for only 6 of its 24 layers. What do the other 18 layers cost per stream?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 7
documents.body: Moving one stream from the RTX 4090 to the H100 SXM raises its decode speed by about the ratio of their memory bandwidths, not of their compute. Why? The H100's larger capacity lets each stream read its weights from several places at once, so capacity rather than bandwidth sets speed Decode does about two FLOPs per parameter but reads every weight byte, so it waits on memory, far below the compute ceiling Compute decides decode speed, but the lab rounds both cards' compute figures to the same value before dividing A dearer card runs at higher clocks, and its memory bandwidth simply tracks that clock and the hourly price One decode step reads every weight byte for about two FLOPs per parameter, so the time is the bytes over the bandwidth. The H100's bandwidth is 3.3 times the 4090's and its dense FP16 compute is 6.0 times, yet one stream speeds up by 3.3. Capacity sets how many streams fit, not how fast one runs.
documents.title: Moving one stream from the RTX 4090 to the H100 SXM raises its decode speed by about the ratio of their memory bandwidths, not of their compute. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 8
documents.body: You switch on Speculative decoding with acceptance 0.8 and draft length 4. Per-user speed rises, but by less than the 3.36 tokens a pass. Why? Each pass also pays for the draft model's steps, so the gain is the tokens per pass over one plus the draft length times the draft cost The target model has to verify every accepted token a second time, so each accepted token costs two passes Speculative decoding only speeds up the first token of a reply, so the gain is one token per request The acceptance rate caps the gain at the rate itself, however long the draft is made A pass yields (1 − α^(γ+1)) / (1 − α) = 3.36 tokens, but it also runs γ draft steps at a cost c of a target step, so the speed-up is 3.36 divided by 1 + γc: 2.4 at c = 0.1. Verification does not repeat work, and the gain applies to every token, not just the first.
documents.title: You switch on Speculative decoding with acceptance 0.8 and draft length 4. Per-user speed rises, but by less than the 3.36 tokens a pass. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 9
documents.body: Paged attention and a q8_0 KV cache both raise Streams that fit on the same hardware. What does each one change? Paged attention charges only the filled pages of each stream, and q8_0 shrinks the bytes per cached value Both shrink the weights, because the cache is stored inside the model file the engine loads Paged attention stores the cache at fewer bits and q8_0 splits it into pages, so they are two names for one saving Paged attention only speeds up prefill and q8_0 only changes accuracy, so neither adds any capacity Paged attention changes how many tokens each stream is charged for: the filled pages, not the whole reserved context. A q8_0 cache changes the bytes per value, 8.5 bits instead of 16. The two multiply, and neither touches the weights.
documents.title: Paged attention and a q8_0 KV cache both raise Streams that fit on the same hardware. What does each one change?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 10
documents.body: On the RTX 4090 the Cost per million tokens falls as you raise Concurrent users from 1 toward its Streams that fit. Why? The hourly price stays the same while every extra stream shares one read of the weights, so more tokens come out of each hour The provider charges less per hour as more streams connect, so each hour of rental costs less once the machine is busy Each extra stream makes the cache cheaper to store, so the memory part of the bill shrinks as load grows The cost is computed from the model's parameter count alone, so users only change how it is displayed Cost per million tokens is the price of an hour over the tokens produced in it. A batched step reads the weights once for all streams, so total tokens per second rises with users while the price does not. It stops improving once memory runs out, where Streams that fit caps the batch.
documents.title: On the RTX 4090 the Cost per million tokens falls as you raise Concurrent users from 1 toward its Streams that fit. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 11
documents.body: A new model file passes your tests and you roll it out. Which practice makes a bad release cheap to undo? Overwrite the old file in place, so there is only ever one version to maintain Trust the benchmark score alone, since a model's behaviour cannot drift once it has been exported Switch off monitoring during the rollout, so alerts do not hide the real problem Keep the previous pinned file ready and send a small share of traffic to the new one while watching the metrics A pinned artifact with a hash and a small first slice of traffic turns a rollback into a switch. Overwriting in place destroys the thing you would roll back to, a benchmark says nothing about live traffic that shifts later, and monitoring is how a bad release is noticed in the first place.
documents.title: A new model file passes your tests and you roll it out. Which practice makes a bad release cheap to undo?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Deployment & serving · question 12
documents.body: In this app, where does a prompt go when you chat with the local guide, and what changes with a cloud provider? To a llama-server on 127.0.0.1 on this machine; with a cloud provider the text leaves for that provider's servers To Hugging Face, which hosts the model file, and a cloud provider only adds a second copy Into the GGUF file, so later runs can reuse earlier prompts, and a cloud provider reads that file too Nowhere in either case, because the app is local-first and never sends a prompt off the machine, whichever provider you pick The local guide runs llama.cpp bound to a loopback address on a random port, started and stopped by the app, so prompts stay on the machine. Choosing a cloud provider sends the text to that provider, under its own terms. Hugging Face only supplies the model file once, at download.
documents.title: In this app, where does a prompt go when you chat with the local guide, and what changes with a cloud provider?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Training a model is only half of the work. Someone then has to run it on a real machine, so that people can type questions and get answers back. Putting a trained model to work like this is called deployment, and the everyday job of answering people’s requests with it is called serving. This module covers the three questions behind serving a model: does it fit in the machine’s memory, how fast does it write, and what does each answer cost? You will work out all three with plain arithmetic, and you will see why the answers keep pulling against each other. A model writes its reply one piece of text at a time. Each piece is called a token, and a token is often a short word or part of a longer one. Almost every number in this lab is counted in tokens: how long a conversation is, how many come out each second, and what a million of them cost. This lesson keeps returning to one picture, where the machine is a reader at a desk with an enormous book of numbers that stands for the model. To write each new token of a reply, the reader has to flip through the whole book once, from the first page to the last. Each conversation also leaves its own growing pile of notes on the desk. The desk is only so big, and that turns out to matter a great deal. Where you have met it If you have used a chatbot, a model like this was serving you, and you may have noticed a short pause before the reply began. After that pause the words arrived a few at a time, and both the pause and the pace are things this lab predicts. This app serves a model too: in Settings, it can download a small model called Qwen3.5 2B and run it on your computer as its local guide. The lab includes that exact model, so you can see why it fits so comfortably on an ordinary machine. If you pick a cloud provider in the app instead, your words travel to that company’s computers and are answered there. The lab also includes real machines that people rent by the hour, such as the RTX 4090, a graphics card made for home computers. Another is the H100 SXM, a much bigger chip made for data centres, the buildings full of computers that run online services. On the price pages the lab quotes, an hour costs $0.74 on the first and $3.49 on the second. Why it matters A model that loads with plenty of room to spare can still run out of memory once many people use it at the same time. That catches people out, because the part of memory that grows is not the model itself but the notes kept for each conversation. Without a budget, the busiest moment of the day is exactly when the machine runs out of room. Speed and money pull against each other too, because one machine can answer many people at once and spread its hourly rent over far more tokens. The catch is that each person then waits a little longer for every token. Choosing where to sit on that trade is a big part of serving a model well. Running a model for real is also a job that never quite ends. The questions people ask change over time, and new versions have to replace old ones safely. Someone also has to decide where people’s words are allowed to go once they have typed them. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these ideas in your own words: why the model’s own numbers take memory once, while the notes kept for each conversation, called the KV cache, take memory again for every person and every token; why serving many people together raises the total number of tokens written each second, while each person’s own tokens arrive more slowly; what a trained model has to be turned into, step by step, before a program can serve it to people; how swapping the machine, or switching on one of three tricks, changes how many conversations fit, their speed and their cost. The tricks are handing out memory in small pages (paged attention), writing the notes in shorthand (KV-cache quantization), and letting a small helper guess ahead (speculative decoding); what running a model for real adds beyond speed: watching for changes, swapping in new versions safely, putting rules around the model, and knowing where people’s prompts go. What the lab lets you do Nothing in this lab is timed on a real machine, because every number is arithmetic from assumptions the lab states for you to check. The lab is laid out as five cards, each with its own job: Serving controls picks the model, how its numbers are stored, how many people use it at once, how long each conversation may grow and how the machine takes turns. Memory budget draws a bar showing where the memory goes, then tells you how many conversations can fit at once. Throughput and latency charts how many tokens come out each second, both in total and for each person, as you add users. Hardware, levers, and cost swaps in real machines, switches the three tricks on and off, and works out what a million tokens cost. Export the model you trained walks through the steps that turn a trained model into a file that a server can run. One surprise to watch for is that a smaller, cheaper machine can beat a much faster one on cost. That stays true even while the faster machine serves every person several times more quickly. By the end of the lesson, you should be able to explain exactly why that happens.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Deployment & serving
documents.body: This page does arithmetic, not measurement: you state your assumptions, do the division, and find out which resource runs out first. The note under the throughput chart lists every assumption the first three cards use, so you can disagree with any of them. The models in the lab use the real shapes of published models, so 1.5B and 3B follow two Qwen2.5 models and 8B follows Llama-3.1-8B. The fourth, 2B · this app, is the very model this app downloads to run on your computer. For the first three, the size of each storage format comes from real file sizes reported by llama.cpp, the program this app uses to run its own model. A few words you need first Everything a model learned during training is stored as a huge set of numbers called weights, which are also called parameters. The model names in the lab tell you roughly how many there are, so 8B has about 8 billion weights and 1.5B about 1.5 billion. The 8B model has exactly 8.03 billion, and the lab uses that precise count in all of its sums. A model is built as a stack of stages called layers, and every token passes through all of them in order. The 8B model has 32 of them, and they matter here because a model keeps a separate set of notes in every layer. Memory is measured in bytes, where a bit is a single 0 or 1 and 8 bits make one byte, enough room for one letter of plain text. Larger amounts use units that each step up by 1,024, which suits computers because 1,024 is ten 2s multiplied together, 2 × 2 × 2 and so on, ten times: a KiB, or kibibyte, is 1,024 bytes, about as much as a paragraph of plain text; a MiB, or mebibyte, is 1,024 KiB, which is a little over a million bytes; a GiB, or gibibyte, is 1,024 MiB, which is a little over a billion bytes. A GB, or gigabyte, is exactly a billion bytes, so the same amount of memory looks a little bigger when it is written in GB than in GiB. Times are mostly given in milliseconds, written ms, where 1 ms is a thousandth of a second. Speeds are given in tokens per second, which the lab writes as tok/s. Weights: memory you pay for once Before a model can write anything, all of its weights have to be loaded into the machine’s memory. How much room they take depends on how many bits each weight is stored in, which is what the Weight format control picks. F16 stores each weight in 16 bits, which is 2 bytes, while the other formats, such as Q4_K_M, are rounded versions from the *Quantization* lab. Those squeeze each weight into fewer bits at some cost in quality. For example, a weight like 0.73128 might be stored as the nearest of a small set of allowed values, such as 0.75. Rounded formats handle the weights in small groups called blocks. Each block stores a few extra bits that record how its weights were rounded, and the recipe a format follows for its blocks is called its block type. Those shared extra bits are spread over every weight in the block, so the bits per weight need not be a whole number. The note on Serving controls gives Q4_K_M as 4.90 bits per weight for 8B, as an average over the whole file. To get the size of the weights, multiply the number of weights by the bits per weight, then divide by 8 to turn bits into bytes. For 8B at Q4_K_M, that is 8.03 billion × 4.90 ÷ 8, which comes to about 4.9 billion bytes. Because each GiB is a little more than a billion bytes, the lab shows that as 4.58 GiB. At F16, the same model needs 2 bytes for every weight, which comes to about 16 billion bytes, or 14.96 GiB. That is more than three times the room for exactly the same model, with nothing changed but how its numbers are written down. The weights are loaded once and then shared, so whether one person or thirty people are using the model, there is only one copy in memory. That is why the weights part of the Memory budget bar never moves when you add users or make conversations longer. The KV cache: memory you pay for every conversation To write each new token, a model looks back over every token that came before it. This looking-back step is called attention, and the *Attention* lab showed it in detail. For each earlier token, the model uses two lists of numbers that it worked out when it first read that token. One list is a key, a label describing what that token offers. The other is a value, the information that token hands over, in proportion to how much attention it gets. Take the sentence “The dog chased the ball because it was bored.” To make sense of “it”, the model compares what it is looking for with the keys of the earlier words. “Dog” matches best, so the model borrows mostly from the value of “dog”, and only a little from the other words. Working out those lists again for every earlier token, each time a new token is written, would repeat a huge amount of work. So the model saves every token’s keys and values the moment it makes them, in every layer, and reads them back later. That store of saved keys and values is the KV cache, where KV stands for keys and values. The cache grows by one token’s worth every time a token is read or written. Each conversation also needs a cache of its own, because its words are different from everyone else’s. That makes the cache the part of memory that grows as more people use the model, and as their conversations get longer. The lab calls one conversation being served a stream, which is why the Concurrent users slider reads in streams, such as 8 streams. How big one token’s notes are The Memory budget card shows the cost of one token’s notes as Per token, per stream, and the card’s formula multiplies a few numbers that the model’s design fixes: Inside each layer, the looking-back is split into several lookups that run side by side. Each lookup reads from a set of saved keys and values, and several lookups may share one set. These saved sets are called KV heads. Each saved key or value is a list of numbers, and the length of that list is the head dim, short for head dimension. The first 2 is there because every token saves one key and one value. The last 2 is the bytes each number takes in fp16, the 16-bit format that the lab uses for the cache. Now work it out one step at a time for 8B, which has 32 layers, 8 KV heads in each layer and a head dim of 128. One key and one value in one head make 2 × 128 = 256 numbers. Eight heads make that 2,048, and 32 layers make it 65,536 numbers for each token. At 2 bytes per number, that is 131,072 bytes, which is exactly 128 KiB. That is room for about 131,000 letters of plain text, saved for every single token of every single conversation. The 3B model has 36 layers but only 2 KV heads, so the same sum gives 36 KiB per token, and the 1.5B model pays 28 KiB. That means the 8B model pays 3.6 times as much as the 3B model for each token. The KV heads cause all of that gap and a little more. Keeping 8 saved sets per layer instead of 2 costs 4 times as much, and the 3B model’s 4 extra layers pull that back down to 3.6. A model can keep so few saved sets because several lookups share each one, a design called grouped-query attention. The 3B model keeps only 2 sets in each layer for all of its lookups to share, while the 8B model keeps 8. A whole conversation’s notes One token’s notes are small, but a conversation holds thousands of tokens, and the Context length slider sets how many, from 512 up to 32,768. The lab starts at 4,096 tokens, and Per stream at this context multiplies that length by the cost of one token’s notes. For 8B at 4,096 tokens, 128 KiB × 4,096 comes to 512 MiB, which is half a GiB for a single conversation. With 8 users, the cache is 8 × 0.5 = 4.00 GiB, which is already close to the 4.58 GiB that the weights take. The lab charges each conversation for its full context from the very start, even if it has used only a few tokens so far. That is the worst case, as if every conversation might run to its limit, and the part on paged attention shows how real servers do better. The memory budget: will it fit? The machine the first three cards use, called Lab default, has 24 GiB of memory, and three things have to fit inside it. Those are the weights, every stream’s cache, and a flat 1 GiB for activations + runtime. That last part is working space for calculations in progress and for the serving program itself. Streams that fit is how many full conversations the leftover memory can hold, once the weights and working space have taken their share. To find it, take the 24 GiB, subtract the weights and the 1 GiB of working space, and divide what is left by one conversation’s cache. At the start, 24 − 4.58 − 1 leaves 18.42 GiB, and dividing 18.42 by 0.5 gives 36.84. The lab rounds that down to 36, because a 37th conversation would only partly fit, and half a conversation is no use to anyone. Headroom is the memory still spare at the current load. With 8 users, the weights, cache and working space add up to 9.58 GiB, which leaves 14.42 GiB spare. The badge at the top of the card shows the same total as 9.58 GiB of 24.00 GiB. In the bar itself, thin lines split the cache into one slice per stream, so you can count the conversations. A heavy line marks the 24 GiB limit, and anything that spills past it gets a dashed outline you can spot at a glance. The book and the desk Here is a picture that holds the memory budget together, and it will also explain where the speed limits come from. Think of the weights as a giant reference book of numbers. The machine’s memory is a desk, and that book must lie open on it the whole time the model is in use. Each conversation keeps its own pile of notes on the desk, which is its KV cache, and every token adds a little to its pile. A small corner of the desk stays clear as working space, and the size of the whole desk decides how many piles fit beside the book. To write one token for a conversation, a reader flips through every page of the book and reads that conversation’s pile of notes. How fast the pages turn decides how quickly one person is served, and that page-turning speed is the idea behind the next part. The picture stops matching in three places, so keep them in mind as you use it. First, the book is not words that anyone reads with understanding, because it is numbers fed into calculations. Second, a real model keeps a separate pile of notes for every layer. So picture the book as having one chapter per layer, each chapter with its own notes. Third, reading a prompt works differently, as the part on the first token explains. Writing speed: why the chip waits on memory A model handles a request in two stages. It reads your whole prompt first, which is called prefill, and then writes its answer, which is called decode. During decode, every new token needs a full trip through all the layers, which means reading every weight out of memory once. The next token cannot start until the last one exists, because each token looks back at all the ones before it. How fast memory can hand numbers to the chip that does the calculations is called memory bandwidth. It is measured in GB/s, or billions of bytes per second. The Lab default machine reads 400 GB/s, which sounds enormous until you remember that the weights alone are almost 5 billion bytes. Here is one decode step for a single user, which reads the weights, about 4.92 billion bytes, plus that user’s half-GiB cache, about 0.54 billion bytes. That makes about 5.46 billion bytes to read for every single token the user gets. At 400 billion bytes a second, reading those 5.46 billion bytes takes about 0.0136 seconds, which is about 14 ms. One token every 14 ms works out to 73.3 tokens per second, which is the number the lab shows for one user. Now compare that with the arithmetic, where each weight is used in about two calculations for every token, one multiplication and one addition. A single calculation like this on decimal numbers is called a FLOP, so each token of the 8B model costs about 16 billion FLOPs. The Lab default chip can do 120 trillion FLOPs a second, written 120 TFLOP/s, so the arithmetic alone could produce about 7,472 tokens a second. That is roughly 100 times what memory allows, so the chip’s calculators spend most of each step sitting idle, waiting for numbers to arrive. When the time it takes to read memory sets the speed, rather than the time it takes to calculate, a task is called memory bandwidth bound. The Throughput and latency card has a badge that says bandwidth bound for this reason. In the book picture, writing is slow because of the page-turning, not because of the sums. Batching: one flip through the book for many conversations If turning the pages is the slow part, the natural fix is to share each flip among many conversations at once. While the reader turns through the book once, they write the next token for every open conversation. Grouping streams into one step like this is called batching. In a real server, finished conversations leave the group at every step while waiting ones join it. Swapping conversations in and out at every step keeps the group full, which is why this is called continuous batching. The lab’s Continuous batching setting of the Scheduler control keeps it simpler, because a fixed number of streams share every step and nobody arrives or leaves. Every stream in the group shares one read of the weights. There is a catch, though, because each step still has to read every conversation’s own notes, and each one’s cache is different. So the more conversations share a step, the longer that step takes to finish. Here is the step for 8 users, which reads the weights once, 4.58 GiB, plus eight caches of half a GiB each, for 4.00 GiB more. Those 8.58 GiB are about 9.2 billion bytes, and reading them at 400 billion bytes a second takes about 23 ms. That one step produces one token for each of the 8 users. So each user gets one token every 23 ms, which is 43.4 tokens per second. Together, the 8 users get 8 × 43.4 = 347 tokens a second. Compared with one user alone, the machine now writes almost five times as many tokens in total, while each person’s tokens arrive more slowly. Those two numbers have names, starting with throughput, the total tokens per second across everyone, which the card shows as Total. Latency is how long one person waits, and here it is the gap between one person’s tokens, shown as Time per output token. Per user shows each person’s own tokens per second, which is one second divided by that gap. Batching raises throughput and worsens latency. This trade is what the card’s name, Throughput and latency, refers to, and its two charts show it side by side. The top chart, total tokens per second, climbs as you add users, while the bottom chart, each user’s own speed, sinks. Each extra user adds the same amount to every step, the time to read one more pile of notes. Early on, that is small next to the shared weights, so adding a second user costs each person only a little speed, from 73.3 down to 66.8 tokens a second. As the piles of notes become most of each read, the machine spends most of each step reading notes, so each extra user adds less and less to Total. The 2nd user adds about 60 tokens a second to Total, but the 9th adds only about 22. By the 36th user, each newcomer adds only about 3, and their tokens come mostly out of everyone else’s speed. One at a time The other Scheduler setting, One at a time, has the reader serve a single conversation per flip through the book. Each step still produces only one token, so the total stays at 73.3 tokens a second however many people are waiting. With 8 users, those 73.3 tokens are shared out at 9.2 each, and every user waits 109 ms between tokens while the others take their turns. Batching gives each of those same 8 users 43.4 tokens a second, so here it is better for everyone, even though nobody gets the machine alone. The first token: reading the prompt Prefill is different from decode, because the whole prompt is already there, so the machine can push every prompt token through each layer together. That means it reads the weights once for the whole prompt instead of once per token, which changes which limit matters. With thousands of tokens sharing one read, the reading is quick and the arithmetic becomes the wall, because each prompt token still needs 16 billion FLOPs. For a 4,096-token prompt, the 8B model needs about 2 × 8.03 billion × 4,096 FLOPs, which is about 66 trillion. At 120 trillion a second, that takes 0.548 seconds, or 548 ms, which is about half a second. That wait is the time to first token, which is how long you wait before the first token of the answer appears. In a real service it also includes any time spent waiting in a queue, but the lab ignores queues entirely. The lab also assumes a prompt that fills the whole context, so its Time to first token is the wait for the longest prompt allowed. Here the book picture needs one addition. For a prompt, the reader turns through the book once and handles every prompt token on each page, so page-turning costs little. The time spent on the sums, which the picture leaves out, becomes the limit instead. The model this app runs: hybrid attention The app’s own model, 2B · this app, is Qwen3.5 2B, and it saves its notes in a different way from the other three. It has 24 layers, but only every fourth one keeps a growing cache. Those 6 layers are called full-attention layers, because they look back over every earlier token. Run the same formula for those 6 layers, which have 2 KV heads and a head dim of 256: 2 × 6 × 2 × 256 × 2 bytes. That gives 12,288 bytes, or 12 KiB per token. If all 24 layers kept a cache, it would cost 48 KiB per token, four times as much. The other 18 layers are a different kind, called Gated DeltaNet layers. Instead of a pile of notes that grows, each one keeps a single running summary for each conversation. It rewrites that summary as every new token arrives, and a summary that is carried forward and updated like this is called a recurrent state. The summary never grows however long the conversation gets, and for all 18 layers together it takes 19.27 MiB per conversation. The lab shows that as Fixed state per stream, and a model that mixes growing-cache layers with fixed-summary layers like this is using hybrid attention. In the book picture, 6 of the 24 chapters keep a growing pile of notes, while the other 18 keep one index card per conversation. That card gets rubbed out and rewritten again and again, but it never gets any longer. Here is the payoff. At 4,096 tokens, one conversation on this model needs 12 KiB × 4,096 = 48 MiB of cache. It also carries its 19.27 MiB summary, so the total is about 67 MiB per conversation. That is roughly an eighth of the 512 MiB the 8B model needs at the same length. So 331 conversations fit in the same 24 GiB, where the 8B model fits only 36. The 2B model’s weights are small too. The file this app downloads is 1.19 GiB, which works out to 5.445 bits per weight. The machine, and what a million tokens cost So far the machine has been Lab default, but any real machine can be described by the same few numbers. The Hardware, levers, and cost card lets you change each one of them, starting from a preset: Memory is the size of the desk, measured in GiB, and it decides how many conversations can fit beside the book. Memory bandwidth is how fast the pages turn, measured in GB/s, and it decides how fast one conversation is served. Compute is how fast the sums get done, in TFLOP/s, which decides how fast prompts are read and only limits decode when the sums fall behind. Price is the rent for the machine in dollars an hour, which you can edit to match any provider’s price list. Bandwidth and memory do different jobs, and they are worth keeping apart. Bandwidth sets how fast one stream goes, while memory sets how many streams can share each read. Cost per million tokens turns the rent into a price for the tokens written, by dividing the price for an hour by the tokens written in that hour. The answer is then scaled up to a million tokens, so that it is a number you can compare across machines. Here is a worked example on Lab default, whose $1.00 an hour is a placeholder rather than a real quote. With 8 users, the machine writes 347.3 tokens a second, and since an hour has 3,600 seconds, that is about 1.25 million tokens an hour. If 1.25 million tokens cost $1.00, then a million tokens cost $1.00 ÷ 1.25 = $0.80, which is what the lab shows. To give that a size, suppose every reply were 500 tokens long, so that a million tokens would make 2,000 replies. At $0.80 per million tokens, each of those replies would cost four hundredths of a cent. With one user, the machine writes only 73.3 tokens a second, about 264,000 an hour, so a million tokens costs $3.79 instead. The rent stays the same however many people share the machine, while the tokens it writes go up with every user. That is why batching makes each token cheaper, right up until memory is full and no more users can fit. The Busy share of each hour slider covers the time a machine sits idle. A machine that writes for only half of each hour still pays the full rent for half the tokens, so each token costs twice as much. The cost counts only the tokens written, not the prompt tokens read. Three levers that change the budget The card also has three tricks that real servers use, which the lab calls levers, and each one changes a different part of the budget. Paged attention fixes the worst-case reservation by handing out cache space in small pages of 16 tokens, as each conversation grows. Instead of a full 4,096-token space set aside for every conversation up front, each one holds only what it has used, wasting less than one page. In the book picture, this is like handing out single sheets of paper as they are needed, instead of a thick, empty notebook for every new arrival. The Average fill of the reserved context slider sets how full the average conversation is, and it starts at 50%. At that setting, each conversation holds 2,048 tokens instead of 4,096, so its notes take half the room and half the time to read. KV-cache quantization writes the notes in shorthand. The KV cache type control stores each saved number in fp16 at 16 bits, q8_0 at 8.5 bits or q4_0 at 4.5 bits. Fewer bits mean a smaller cache to store and fewer bytes to read each step, at some cost in accuracy. The 2B model’s running summary is a separate kind of memory, so the shorthand does not shorten it. The app’s engine, the program that actually runs the model, keeps that summary in a 32-bit format. Speculative decoding adds a helper, a small and fast draft model that guesses the next few tokens for the big model to check. The big model checks all of the guesses in one step instead of writing them one at a time, keeping them up to the first one it turns down. After the kept guesses it always adds one token of its own, so every check moves the reply forward by at least one token. Checking can happen all at once, even though writing cannot, because the guessed tokens already exist. The big model can push them through its layers together, the same way it reads a prompt. At each spot, it works out the odds it gives every possible next token, and uses those odds to decide whether to keep the guess there. In the book picture, an assistant with a thin pocket version of the book scribbles four words ahead. The reader then checks all four in a single flip through the big book, rather than flipping once for every word. A model picks each next token partly by chance, like rolling dice that are weighted toward some words. A guess the big model finds likely is usually kept, and one it finds unlikely is usually thrown out. The checking is arranged so that those odds stay exactly the same as if the big model had written every token itself. So speculation changes the speed, not what the model is likely to write. Three sliders control the helper, and each starts at a set value: Acceptance rate sets how often a guess is kept, and starts at 0.80, meaning 8 guesses in 10. Draft length sets how many tokens the helper guesses each time, and starts at 4. Draft cost sets what one guess costs as a share of a big step, and starts at 0.10, a tenth. At those values, the lab works out 3.36 tokens per check and a speed-up of 2.4 times. Going deeper counts out where both of those numbers come from. A lever only helps where the slow part is. Speculation speeds up decode while reading memory is the limit, because one check reads the book once for several tokens. If the sums are already the limit, the trick backfires. Each check works through five tokens per conversation, the four guesses plus the big model’s own, which means five times the sums. Getting a model ready to serve: the export path Packing a trained model into the right kind of file, so that a server can run it, is the job of the export path. The Export the model you trained card walks through it with the 900-weight table from earlier labs in this app. That table belongs to the tiny model that guesses the next character of a text from 30 possible characters. The same five steps apply to a real 8-billion-weight model, and only the byte counts change from one to the other: Merge the adapter: a model can be taught a new job after training by adding a small extra set of weights, called an adapter, as in the *LoRA & adapters* lab. Merging adds the adapter’s numbers into the main table, so only one table is left. Serving that one table costs exactly what the original model cost. Quantize to Q4_K_M, or to whichever format you picked. This rounds the weights in blocks, using the block type of your format, the rounding recipe from the *Quantization* lab. For Q4_K_M, the block type is Q4_K, which uses 4.5 bits per weight. Write the GGUF file: a GGUF file holds the rounded weights, notes on how they were rounded, and the tokenizer, the tool that splits text into tokens. Everything travels together in one file, behind a header, a short section at the start of the file that says what is inside. A loading program can check the header before it trusts the rest. Verify before running: the server checks the header and the file’s hash, a short fingerprint worked out from every byte in the file. If even one byte has changed, the fingerprint no longer matches, so a damaged or swapped file is caught before it runs. Serve it: the server starts with the context length you budgeted and a cap on how many conversations it accepts at once, no higher than Streams that fit. The cap in the last step does important work. Without it, a rush of users would push the cache past the memory limit and crash the server. With the cap, the extra users wait in a queue for a free slot, which is slower for them but keeps everyone else running. Two more parts of the job never show up as numbers in the lab. They are keeping a model working over time and deciding where people’s prompts go. The end of Going deeper covers both of them, under the heading “Operating it”.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Deployment & serving
documents.body: The *Inference & KV cache* lab showed the machinery, meaning why a model saves its notes and why writing an answer is slower than reading a prompt. This lab turns that machinery into a budget you can blow, and then into a bill you have to pay. In real life the question arrives all at once: this model, this many people, this much context and this machine. Does it fit, how fast is it for each person, and what does a million tokens cost? Each part is a simple division, but the parts are tangled together, because one setting moves several answers at the same time. Adding users lowers the cost per token, but it also slows each person down and fills up the desk. Longer conversations fill the desk faster still, and they stretch the wait for the first token at the same time. A bigger weight format keeps more detail in each weight, but it takes more room and slows every single step. The lab puts all of these on one page, so that you can watch each knock-on effect as it happens. Picture a made-up school club that sets up the 8B model on one 24 GiB machine to serve as a homework helper for the whole school. The members test it themselves, one or two at a time. The memory bar sits at about 6 GiB, so there seems to be room for a crowd. On launch day, 40 classmates log on at once, each with a conversation that may reach 4,096 tokens. Forty caches of half a GiB each come to 20 GiB. With the weights and working space added, the total is 25.58 GiB, which is more than the machine has, so the server runs out of memory. Nothing about the model changed between the test and the launch. Only the number of conversations changed, and that was the one cost the club never measured. A cap of 36 conversations would have kept the helper running, with the last 4 classmates waiting in a short queue for a free slot. This lab also finishes a story that the *Quantization* lab started, when it rounded weights and weighed the very file this app downloads. Here, the export checklist works out the file size of the 900-weight table, using the block type of your chosen format. The 2B · this app preset is that same downloaded file, now being served.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Deployment & serving
documents.body: The lab starts at 8B, Q4_K_M, 8 users, 4,096 tokens and Continuous batching. At those settings, the Memory budget card shows weights of 4.58 GiB and a cache of 4.00 GiB, and 36 streams fit. The steps below follow the lab’s own six steps in order, so you can check each one off as you go. Add users Try this: drag Concurrent users from 1 up to 64 and watch the Throughput and latency card as the numbers change. With one user, Total and Per user both read 73.3 tok/s, because that one person has the whole machine to themselves. At 8 users, Total reads 347 tok/s while Per user reads 43.4, and Time per output token reads 23 ms. Now keep going, and past 36 users both charts turn shaded, because the saved notes no longer fit in 24 GiB. The shading is labelled over 24.00 GiB beyond 36, which marks the point where memory runs out. At 64 users, the Memory budget badge reads 37.58 GiB, which is more than one and a half times what the machine has. The warning below the bar says you are over budget by 13.58 GiB, and that only 36 streams fit at this context. Through the whole drag, watch which part of the bar moves, because only the cache grows while the weights stay put at 4.58 GiB. The badge on the throughput card keeps saying bandwidth bound, since even 64 users reach only 652 tok/s, far below the 7,472 the arithmetic could handle. Then set the users back to 8 and switch Scheduler to One at a time, and watch Total fall to 73.3 and Per user to 9.2. Time per output token rises to 109 ms, so every one of the 8 users is worse off than with batching. Switch back to Continuous batching before the next step. Extend the context Set Concurrent users to 1, then drag Context length up to 32,768, and watch the cache segment of the bar creep up close to the weights. One conversation’s notes now take 4.00 GiB, which is the same as eight conversations took at 4,096 tokens. Streams that fit drops from 36 to 4, because each conversation now reserves eight times the room. Time to first token grows from 548 ms to 4,385 ms, more than four seconds, because the lab’s prompt now fills a context eight times as long. Here is a neat check on the speed rule: Per user now reads 43.4 tok/s, exactly what each of 8 users got at 4,096 tokens. Each step reads the same number of bytes in both cases, the weights plus 4.00 GiB of notes, so each step takes the same time. Now set Context length back to 4,096, then switch Weight format to F16, and the weights jump to 14.96 GiB. One user drops to 24.1 tok/s, even though nothing changed but how the weights are stored. Every step now reads about three times as many bytes, so every step takes about three times as long. Streams that fit also falls from 36 to 16, because the bigger book leaves less of the desk for notes. Balance the budget Switch Weight format back to Q4_K_M and pick 2B · this app under Model, and Per token, per stream drops to 12.0 KiB. A new readout, Fixed state per stream, appears and reads 19.27 MiB, which is the running summary each conversation carries. Each conversation needs 48 MiB of notes plus that summary, so 331 fit where the 8B model fits 36. The note under the controls explains why, since only the cache-holding layers are charged per token: 12.0 KiB a token here, against 48.0 KiB if all 24 cached. Now set yourself a puzzle: find a Model, Weight format, Context length and Concurrent users that fit with room to spare, using Streams that fit as your cap. For example, say you need 8 users working on long documents of 16,384 tokens each, all with the 8B model. At Q4_K_M, Streams that fit reads 9, so the 8 users fit with one slot to spare, and Headroom reads 2.42 GiB. Switch to F16 and Streams that fit drops to 4, so the same plan is now over budget by 7.96 GiB. The more precise format would cost you half of your users, which is the kind of trade this step asks you to weigh. Change the hardware Go back to 8B at Q4_K_M and 4,096 tokens, set Concurrent users to 1, and open Hardware, levers, and cost. Under Hardware, pick RTX 4090 and then H100 SXM, and compare the Per user readout on each of them. One stream gets 185 tok/s on the RTX 4090 and 614 on the H100 SXM, which is 3.3 times faster. That matches how much faster the H100 turns its pages, which is its bandwidth, and not the 6.0 times by which its sums are faster. Decode spends its time waiting on memory, so all that extra arithmetic barely helps a single stream. The Streams that fit readout on this card tells the other half of the story, with 36 on the 4090 and 148 on the H100. Read it here, not on the Memory budget card, which always uses Lab default and stays at 36 whatever machine you pick. The H100 preset has 80 GiB of memory to the 4090’s 24, so its desk holds about four times as many piles of notes. Now set Concurrent users to 8 and read Cost per million tokens, which comes to $0.23 on the 4090 against $0.33 on the H100. At this load, the H100 writes 3.3 times as many tokens an hour, but its rent is 4.7 times as high. So each of its tokens costs about 4.7 ÷ 3.3, or 1.4 times as much, and the cheaper card wins on cost. Then edit Price while the H100 is picked. The same chip is $3.49 an hour on one provider’s page and $4.29 on another’s, so try $4.29. At $4.29, the cost per million tokens rises from $0.33 to $0.41, and no preset stays pressed, because the machine is now your own description. Finally, try M4 Max laptop and CPU box at 1 user, where the laptop gets 100 tok/s from its 546 GB/s. The CPU box gets 16.4 tok/s from its 89.6 GB/s. The presets set both prices to $0 because you already own the machines, so Cost per million tokens reads $0.000. That leaves out what the machine cost to buy and the electricity it uses, which you could enter yourself as an hourly Price. Pull the levers Pick Lab default again with 8 users, then switch on Paged attention and leave Average fill of the reserved context at 50%. On this card, Streams that fit goes from 36 to 73 and Per user from 43.4 to 56.6 tok/s, because each conversation now holds and reads half as many notes. The levers work only on this card, so the Memory budget card above still reads 36. Switch paging off and set KV cache type to q8_0, and now 69 streams fit while each user gets 55.6 tok/s. The cache costs about half as much per token, though not quite half, for a reason that Going deeper explains. Set the cache back to fp16 and switch on Speculative decoding, and Per user jumps from 43.4 to 104 tok/s, which is 2.4 times faster. Cost per million tokens falls from $0.80 to $0.33, while Streams that fit stays at 36. That is because the lab ignores the helper model’s own memory. In a real server, the helper’s weights and notes would take some desk space too. The bar list below the readouts keeps all of this in view. It has a row for No levers, one row for each lever alone, and one for Your selection. Each bar’s length shows total tokens per second, and its label shows the cost per million tokens for that row. Two more experiments show where speculation stops helping, and the first is to drag Acceptance rate down to 0, so that every guess is wrong. Per user falls to 31.0 tok/s, slower than with no levers at all, because you are now paying for guesses that never get used. Put Acceptance rate back to 0.80, then pick CPU box, whose arithmetic is slow at an assumed 1 TFLOP/s. At 8 users, the sums are already the limit on this machine rather than memory, so watch Total as you turn Speculative decoding off and on. Speculation cuts Total from 62.3 to 38.8 tok/s here. Checking five tokens per conversation means five times the sums, and the sums were already the slow part. Export it Go back to 8B and look at the Export the model you trained card, which follows your Weight format. At Q4_K_M, the heading reads 900 weights → Q4_K_M, and the second step rounds the table into Q4_K blocks at 4.5 bits per weight. The badge shows the toy file at 507 B, where B here means bytes, not billion. That is because 900 × 4.5 ÷ 8 is 506.25, which rounds up to whole bytes. Now compare that 4.5 with the note under Serving controls, which gives 4.90 bits per weight for a real Q4_K_M file. A real file keeps some of its weight tables in a bigger type, which costs extra bits. The toy has only one table, so there is nothing to keep bigger. Switch to F16 and the badge grows to 1.8 KiB. The 900 weights at 2 bytes each make 1,800 bytes, and 1,800 ÷ 1,024 is about 1.76 KiB, which the badge rounds to 1.8. The last step, Serve it, shows the cap, such as ≤ 8 streams, which is the smaller of your user count and Streams that fit.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Deployment & serving
documents.body: The weights never move when you add users or lengthen conversations. Only the KV cache grows, which is how a model that loads with room to spare still runs out of memory under load. Batching splits one read of the weights among everyone, so Total goes up while Per user goes down, which is the trade between throughput and latency. With One at a time, 8 users share 73.3 tok/s and each waits 109 ms between tokens, so batching beats it for every one of them. On the first three cards the badge says bandwidth bound at every user count, since even 64 users reach only 652 tok/s against a ceiling of 7,472. The 8B model saves 128 KiB per token and the 3B model only 36 KiB. That is because the smaller model keeps only 2 saved sets per layer to the 8B model’s 8. Hybrid attention shrinks the notes another way, since the 2B model’s cache is a quarter of what 24 caching layers would cost and its summary never grows. Bandwidth sets one person’s speed, while memory sets how many people share each read. The H100 is 3.3 times faster per stream and holds 148 conversations to the 4090’s 36. Cost per million tokens is the hourly rent divided by the tokens written in that hour. On the 4090 it falls from $1.11 at 1 user to $0.14 at 36. A lever helps only where the slow part is. Speculation is 2.4 times faster while memory is the limit, but it cuts the CPU box from 62.3 to 38.8 tok/s. A price is an input, not a fact about the model. The same H100 SXM is $3.49 an hour on one provider’s page and $4.29 on another’s.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Deployment & serving
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies Every number here is division from stated assumptions, with nothing timed on a real machine, and the arithmetic assumes 100% of peak bandwidth and compute. Real hardware never reaches its peak, so every speed in the lab is a best case rather than a forecast. The working space is a flat 1 GiB that never grows, whatever the load. Every conversation also reserves its full context from the start, unless you turn paging on. That reservation is the worst case rather than the usual one, so real conversations usually hold less. The lab also leaves out the arithmetic of the looking-back step itself, called attention, and counts only the arithmetic on the weights. Time to first token assumes a prompt that fills the whole context, and no queue at all. It prices the longest prompt allowed but ignores any waiting in line. The first three models all use one file-size rate per format, taken from real files of one 8-billion-weight model. The toy export uses only its block type’s bits per weight, such as 4.5 for Q4_K, while a real file mixes in some bigger types. The hardware figures were read on 30 September 2026 and will go out of date, while prices change faster still. Apple publishes no arithmetic figure for its laptop chip and the CPU box’s figure is a round number, so the lab labels both of those as assumptions. The makers quote the 4090 at 24 GB and the H100 at 80 GB, and the lab enters those numbers as GiB, which flatters both cards slightly. The lab also prices only memory and speed. It never measures how much quality is lost when the weights or the cache are stored in fewer bits. That loss is the third side of the trade, and the *Quantization* lab measures it. The levers are simplified too, because paging uses one average fill instead of a real spread of short and long conversations. Speculation uses one acceptance rate for all text and a draft whose cost is a fixed share of a big step, and the draft model’s memory is ignored. Finally, the cost counts only the tokens written and leaves out the time spent reading prompts, so real costs per token run higher. Where the real thing differs Real serving programs reach only a fraction of the peak bandwidth the lab assumes, so real speeds come out lower than the lab’s numbers. Test with real traffic before you trust any number from a page like this one, however carefully it was worked out. Real servers also do better than the lab in places, and paged attention is what makes the average-fill idea real. The paper that introduced it measured earlier serving systems and found only 20.4% to 38.2% of their cache memory holding actual token notes. The rest of that memory sat reserved but unused, which is exactly the waste that handing out small pages avoids. Sometimes every conversation starts with the same long set of instructions, called a system prompt. Prefix sharing stores that prompt only once, so it is nearly free after the first request. Chunked prefill breaks one long prompt into pieces, so that reading it does not stall everyone else’s writing, and the lab models neither trick. Real traffic also comes in bursts rather than as a steady number of users. The number that matters is usually the wait for the slowest few requests. That slowest wait is called a tail latency, and an average can hide it completely. Picture a made-up group chat where nearly every message arrives at once, but one in fifty takes ten seconds to appear. The average wait looks fine, yet that slow message is the one everybody notices, which is why real services watch their slowest requests as well as their average. A common mix-up: “the model is 4.6 GiB, so it needs 4.6 GiB.” That is only the part that never changes. The cache grows with every user and every token, and the cache is what runs out under load. The same weights also read as 4.9 GB, because a GB is a slightly smaller unit than a GiB, so check which unit a number uses before comparing.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Speculative decoding, counted out To see where 3.36 tokens per check comes from, picture 100 checks with Acceptance rate at 0.80 and Draft length at 4. The first guess survives in about 80 of those checks, since each guess is kept 80% of the time. The second guess counts only if the first was kept too, so it survives in about 80% of those 80 checks, which is 64. The third guess survives in about 51 checks and the fourth in about 41, because each one needs every guess before it to be kept as well. On top of the kept guesses, the big model adds one token of its own in every check. That token is either a correction or an extra one after four good guesses. That adds 100 more, so the total is 100 + 80 + 64 + 51 + 41 = 336 tokens over 100 checks, or 3.36 per check. The note under the bar list shows this number for whatever settings you choose. The guesses are not free, though, because each of the 4 draft steps costs a tenth of a big step. So one check costs 1 + 0.4 = 1.4 big steps. Dividing 3.36 tokens by 1.4 steps gives 2.4 tokens per big step, so speculation is 2.4 times faster than writing one token per step. Drag the sliders on Lab default with 8 users and the trade shows up. A better guesser helps, so an Acceptance rate of 0.95 lifts each user to 140 tok/s. A pricier guesser hurts instead, so at a Draft cost of 0.50, each user gets 48.7 tok/s, barely faster than with no helper at all. In real use, the acceptance rate depends on the text and on how closely the helper matches the big model. The 2.4 also holds only while reading memory is the limit, since the extra sums for checking five tokens per conversation are then hidden behind the wait for memory. The paper behind this method treats those sums as free, but the lab counts them, and that is exactly what slows the CPU box down. Why q8_0 is not exactly half The shorthand formats store the cache in blocks of 32 numbers. A q8_0 block spends 8 bits on each of them, plus a 16-bit scale shared by the whole block. That makes 34 bytes for 32 values, or 8.5 bits per value rather than 8. A q4_0 block uses 4 bits per number plus the same scale, which makes 18 bytes for 32 values, or 4.5 bits each. Against the 16 bits of fp16, the notes therefore take 0.53 or 0.28 as much room as before. That small extra is why q8_0 fits 69 conversations at the starting settings, not the 73 that an exact half would fit, the same as paging at 50%. The KV cache type never touches the 2B model’s running summary, which the app’s engine keeps in a 32-bit format called float32 whatever you choose. More on the export path A real export locks in more than the weights, because it also freezes the tokenizer and the chat template, the fixed pattern that marks out each message. It freezes the licence too, which says how the model may be used, so that every piece of a release is pinned down. This app carries out the last two steps for real, with its own engine and model. Before running either one, it verifies each one’s SHA-256 hash, a standard kind of fingerprint. It then starts llama.cpp’s server program, llama-server, on a loopback address, 127.0.0.1. A loopback address can be reached only by programs on the same computer, so nothing outside your machine can talk to it. Operating it A served model is not finished once it fits and runs fast enough, because four more jobs keep it working from day to day. They are monitoring for drift, rolling out new versions safely, guardrails, and deciding where prompts go. Monitoring and drift Monitoring means watching the same numbers this lab computes while the model is in use, along with how often requests fail or get refused. Those numbers are time to first token, time per output token, tokens per second, the length of the queue, and how full the cache is against Streams that fit. Drift is the quiet failure, when the requests or the answers change underneath you while no alarm goes off. Either way, yesterday’s test results stop describing today’s use, and nothing tells you so unless you look. Picture a made-up homework helper set up in September, when a Context length of 4,096 tokens was plenty for students’ questions. By exam season, students are pasting in whole essays, so the helper’s owners raise the context to 16,384 tokens to make room. The machine and the model have not changed, yet Streams that fit on the 8B model falls from 36 to 9, a quarter as many students at once. The fix has two parts, one for each kind of drift. Drift in what people send, like the exam-season essays, shows up in the monitored numbers: longer prompts, a fuller cache and a longer queue. Drift in the answers is caught by rerunning a fixed set of test questions on a schedule and comparing the results, the kind of replay the *Evaluation* lab covers. Versioned rollouts and rollback A versioned rollout names each release by its exact pieces, which are the model file, the engine that serves it, and the settings. This app pins one engine version and one model version, and it checks the fingerprint of both before it runs them. To roll out a new version, a service sends it a small share of the traffic first. It then compares the monitored numbers and the fixed tests against the old version. It widens the share only if the new version holds up, while the old one stays ready the whole time. Going back to the old one, called a rollback, is then a quick switch rather than a slow rebuild from scratch. This app runs one pinned pair, so changing either part means shipping a new version of the app. A larger service would run several versions side by side. Guardrails Guardrails are checks and limits built around the model rather than inside it. They include a cap on conversations at Streams that fit, a limit on prompt length, and checks on what goes in and what comes out. Some models can also use outside programs, called tools, such as a calculator or a web search. A guardrail can list what each of those tools is allowed to do. Guardrails are ordinary computer code, so they have bugs of their own and need their own tests. The *Failure modes, safety, and security* lab covers what they miss. Privacy and on-device inference Running the model on the user’s own machine is called on-device inference, and this app’s local guide is an example of it. The app starts and stops the engine itself on a loopback address, using a channel number, called a port, that it picks at random. The model file it runs is kept in the app’s data folder. Your prompts stay on your machine and nothing is billed per token, which are the two big gains of running the model on your own computer. On a Mac, the app runs every layer on the computer’s graphics chip, and on other computers it runs on the main processor. Those two ways of running are why the lab includes the M4 Max laptop and CPU box presets, and the app uses a 4,096-token context either way. The price is a small model and your own machine’s memory speed, so the 2B model’s ceiling at 1 user is 404 tok/s on the M4 Max laptop. On the CPU box it is 66 tok/s, and both figures are arithmetic rather than measurement. If you choose a cloud provider instead, your text leaves your machine, and that provider’s own terms apply to it.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Serving a trained model means running it for real requests, often many at once, on hardware with a fixed amount of memory and bandwidth. This module budgets that work: the memory a configuration needs, how fast it produces tokens, and what a million of them cost. It then follows the export that makes a model servable, and what keeps a served model working once it is live. The question is concrete. For this model, this many concurrent users, this context length, and this hardware: does it fit, how fast is it, and what does a million tokens cost? Two terms dominate the memory side: the weights and the KV cache, the keys and values stored for every token a stream (one conversation in progress) has already processed. Where it shows up This app. Its local guide runs llama.cpp's llama-server on a loopback port from a pinned Qwen3.5 2B file. The app checks the SHA-256 of engine and model first, and the guide's prompts stay on the machine. Rented hardware. The same H100 SXM is $3.49 an hour on one provider's page and $4.29 on another's, so a price is an input to the budget, not a constant. Serving engines. vLLM stores the cache in blocks of 16 tokens by default, allocated as a stream grows (paged attention); the PagedAttention paper behind it (Kwon et al., 2023) found earlier systems storing token states in only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV cache memory. llama.cpp can store the cache as q8_0 or q4_0 instead of f16. Operations. A live model needs monitoring for drift, versioned rollouts, and guardrails. In this app, choosing a cloud provider instead of the local guide sends your prompts off the machine, under that provider's terms. Why it matters Without this budget, a deployment can pass a one-user test and still fail. The weights do not grow with load, but the KV cache grows with every user and every token of context, so a model that loads with room to spare can run out of memory under traffic. Without a concurrency cap, overload then crashes the server instead of queueing. The same arithmetic predicts the bill and shows which lever is worth switching on. Cost per million tokens falls as more streams share each read of the weights, until memory caps the batch. Each lever helps only while its bottleneck binds. In speculative decoding, a small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model checks them in one pass, so one read of the weights can yield several tokens. That pays while decode, the token-by-token generation phase, waits on memory reads. Once decode is compute bound instead, limited by arithmetic, the extra work of drafting and checking can lower throughput. What you will be able to explain How the fixed cost of the weights differs from the per-stream cost of the KV cache, and how the two together set how many streams fit. Why batching raises total throughput while each user's tokens arrive more slowly. What an export has to produce before a model can be served, from merged weights to a verified GGUF file, llama.cpp's single-file model format. How hardware, paged attention, KV-cache quantization, and speculative decoding change streams that fit, speed, and cost per million tokens. What operating a served model adds beyond speed: monitoring and drift, versioned rollouts, guardrails, and where prompts go. What the lab shows Every readout is closed-form arithmetic on stated inputs: nothing is timed and no model runs. The model shapes are published ones. Quantized bits per weight come from real files (F16 is 16 by definition): the 1.5B, 3B, and 8B presets reuse the rates of llama.cpp's Llama-3-8B files, and 2B · this app, the Qwen3.5 2B file this app runs, uses its own. The first three cards assume an accelerator with 24 GiB, 400 GB/s, and 120 TFLOP/s that is not a product. The other Hardware presets come from vendor documents and price pages read on 30 September 2026. The M4 Max laptop and CPU box compute figures and the CPU box memory are labelled assumptions, the laptop and CPU box are priced at 0 because you own them, and the Lab default price of $1.00 an hour is a placeholder. Serving controls sets Model, Weight format, Concurrent users, Context length, and Scheduler. Memory budget stacks weights, KV cache (plus recurrent state on 2B · this app), and activations + runtime against 24 GiB and reports Streams that fit; Throughput and latency plots Total and Per user tokens per second. The key experiment: at 8B, Q4_K_M, and Continuous batching, drag Concurrent users from 1 toward 64. Total rises, Per user falls, and the chart shades every count past Streams that fit. Hardware, levers, and cost reruns that load on another Hardware preset, or with Paged attention, KV cache type, and Speculative decoding, and reports Cost per million tokens from an editable Price. Export the model you trained names the five export steps for the 900-weight table from earlier labs and computes the toy table's weight bytes at the chosen block type's bits per weight. It does not write or verify a file.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Deployment & serving
documents.body: This lab is a roofline: first-order arithmetic that predicts which resource runs out first. Nothing is timed. The stated assumptions are a hardware profile (24 GiB, 400 GB/s, and 120 TFLOP/s on the first three cards; the hardware card makes them editable), a flat 1 GiB for activations and runtime, two FLOPs per parameter per token, and an fp16 KV cache. The first three cards leave speculative decoding and prefix sharing off. The presets use real shapes: Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-3.1-8B, plus the model this app downloads, Qwen3.5 2B. The first three take their weight formats from llama.cpp's own file sizes for Llama-3-8B: Q4_K_M is 4.58 GiB, 4.90 bits per weight. The 2B preset uses its own file: 1,280,835,840 bytes over 1,881,825,088 parameters, 5.445 bits per weight. Memory: a fixed cost and a per-stream cost The leading 2 counts keys and values; the trailing 2 is fp16. The 8B shape (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dims) costs 128 KiB per token; the 3B shape, with 2 KV heads, costs 36 KiB. A hybrid model: the one this app runs Qwen3.5 2B uses hybrid attention. Of its 24 layers, only every fourth is full attention: 6 layers with 2 KV heads of 256 dimensions. The formula charges those six, so the cache costs 12 KiB a token, not the 48 KiB that 24 caching layers would. The other 18 are Gated DeltaNet layers that keep a fixed state per stream: 19.27 MiB in float32, whatever the context length. The layer layout is from the pinned file's GGUF header and the model card, and the state size is from the llama.cpp b10991 source, all read on 30 September 2026. Speed: two ceilings Decode reads every weight and every stream's cache once per step, then emits one token per stream, so it is memory bandwidth bound: Prefill processes the whole prompt at once, so time to first token is compute bound.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Deployment & serving
documents.body: The Inference & KV cache lab explained the mechanism; this one turns it into a budget you can fail, and then into a bill. It also closes the export path the Quantization lab started, and the 2B preset is the file that lab weighed.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Start at 8B, Q4_K_M, 8 users, 4,096 tokens, Continuous batching. Weights take 4.58 GiB, the cache 4.00 GiB, and 36 streams fit. Drag Concurrent users. One user gets 73.3 tokens/s. Eight users get 347 in total and 43.4 each, 23 ms per output token. At 64 the arithmetic asks for 37.58 GiB, and the throughput chart shades everything past 36. Back at one user, drag Context length to 32,768: the cache reaches 4.00 GiB, Streams that fit drops to 4, and Time to first token grows from 548 ms to 4385 ms. Set Context length back to 4,096, then switch Weight format to F16: weights jump to 14.96 GiB and one user drops to 24.1 tokens/s. Pick 2B · this app. A 4,096-token stream costs 48 MiB of cache plus 19.27 MiB of fixed state, so 331 streams fit where the 8B model fits 36. Open Hardware, levers, and cost on 8B at 1 user. One stream decodes at 185 tokens/s on RTX 4090 and 614 on H100 SXM: 3.3 times faster, the bandwidth ratio and not the 6.0 times compute ratio. But 36 streams fit on one and 148 on the other. At 8 users the cost is $0.23 against $0.33 per million tokens, at the prices on the card. Back on Lab default with 8 users, switch on Paged attention at 50% fill: streams that fit goes from 36 to 73 and per-user speed from 43.4 to 56.6. Set the KV cache type to q8_0: 69 streams, 55.6 tokens/s each. Switch on Speculative decoding: 104 tokens/s each, 2.4 times faster, and the cost falls from $0.80 to $0.33 at the placeholder price.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Deployment & serving
documents.body: Weights never moves with users or context; the KV cache is the only term that does. That is why a model that loads with room to spare runs out of memory under load. Continuous batching trades per-user speed for total throughput. With One at a time, 8 users share 73.3 tokens/s, 9.2 each, and each waits 109 ms between tokens. The first three cards say bandwidth bound everywhere. The 8B compute ceiling is 120 TFLOP/s ÷ (2 × 8.03 B) = 7,472 tokens/s, and 64 streams at 4,096 tokens reach only 652. Grouped-query attention is the biggest architectural lever: the 8B shape pays 3.6 times the 3B shape's cache per token. Hybrid attention is another: the 2B model's cache is a quarter of what 24 caching layers would cost. Bandwidth sets how fast one stream decodes; capacity sets how many streams share each read of the weights. The H100 is 3.3 times the 4090 in bandwidth and in single-stream speed, and holds 148 streams to its 36. Cost per million tokens falls as users rise, until memory caps the batch: on the 4090 it goes from $1.11 at 1 user to $0.14 at 36. A lever helps only while its bottleneck binds. Speculation gives 2.40 times while decode is bandwidth bound. On the CPU box, whose compute is an assumption, 8 streams are already compute bound and speculation cuts total speed from 62.3 to 38.8 tokens/s. A price is an input: the same H100 SXM is $3.49 an hour on one provider's page and $4.29 on another's.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Deployment & serving
documents.body: In this lab. Every number is arithmetic from the assumptions. The activation term is flat, every stream reserves its full context at once unless you turn paging on, attention FLOPs are ignored, and time to first token prices a prompt that fills the context with no queueing. One file-size rate per format is applied to the three Qwen2.5 and Llama presets, and the toy export uses block rates rather than a file mix.
