documents.subtitle: Plain · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: You may have seen a picture that an AI tool made from a few typed words, or heard of tools that make music and video clips in a similar way. This module opens up the machinery behind tools like these, using the smallest pictures that still mean something to a person. Those pictures are handwritten digits from 0 to 9, each one drawn in a tiny square. A program that makes new things, such as sentences or pictures, is called a generative model. Most other labs in this course look at generative models that write text one small piece at a time, guessing the next piece over and over. This lab is about a different family, the ones that make a whole picture at once instead of piece by piece. The lab shows two ways of doing that, and they work almost like opposites: A VAE learns to squeeze each picture down to a code of only two numbers, and to redraw a picture from any two numbers in one go. Two numbers work like the two coordinates of a point on a graph, so every picture gets its own spot on a flat map. Diffusion ruins pictures on purpose by adding static, like the fuzz on an old TV with no signal, a little at a time. It then learns to undo that damage, so it can start from pure static and clean it up, step by step, until a digit appears. Both are real, small models trained on 60,000 handwritten digits, and every digit they make in the lab is worked out on the spot while you watch. Where you have met it The ideas in this lab are the machinery behind image, audio and video generation. In fact, many modern image generators use both ideas at once, starting with a squeezer much like the VAE that shrinks the picture. All the slow diffusion work happens in that smaller space, and the result is expanded back into a full picture at the very end. That combination is most of why making high-quality images with AI became affordable. Why it matters To make a picture, a program must choose a brightness for every pixel, the tiny squares a picture is made of, and here there are 784 of them. Those pixels all have to agree with each other, since a stroke that starts on one side of a digit must carry on and join up with the rest. If you choose every pixel at random, you get static, because nothing makes neighbouring pixels line up. Yet a generative model needs some randomness, or it would draw the same picture every time. Both models in this lab answer the same puzzle, which is how to turn random input into pixels that fit together. Without the VAE’s learned map of codes, two random numbers would mean nothing, and without diffusion’s learned clean-up, random static would stay static. The two answers come with very different costs, and real systems are designed around them. The VAE is quick, because its drawing step runs only once per picture, but its pictures tend to come out blurry. Diffusion’s digits in this lab are readable far more often, but it pays for that by running its whole clean-up calculation again for each of its 100 steps. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these ideas in your own words: how building a picture through many small clean-up steps differs from rebuilding it from a short code in a single step; why the first way is slow, while the second way tends to give blurry pictures; how to read a map where every point is the code for a picture, and why points close together give similar digits; why the crowded middle of that map gives blurry blends of two or more digits; why a perfect clean-up tool would only ever copy its examples, while a real, imperfect network can make new pictures. What the lab lets you do A switch called Model, at the top of the lab, swaps between two views. In the Diffusion view, the Forward process card shows one digit at six points along a 100-step slide into static. The Reverse diffusion card lets you drag through all 100 clean-up steps, one at a time, and watch a digit appear out of static. You can also swap the trained network for a perfect version built from exact math, and compare what each one makes from the very same static. In the VAE view, the Latent map card lets you drag a point across a map of two-number codes and watch the digit change as you go. The Encode a drawing card lets you draw your own digit, or load a ready-made one, and shows what comes back after the squeeze into two numbers. Adding the static in the Forward process card is plain arithmetic, with no network involved. A few numbers the lesson quotes were measured beforehand rather than live, such as how well a separate digit-reading network scored the pictures. Where it breaks lists those.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: A picture is a grid of numbers Every picture in this lab is a small square, 28 pixels across and 28 pixels down, which makes 784 pixels in all. The computer stores each pixel as a single number for its brightness. In the diffusion half of the lab, −1 means black and 1 means white, with greys in between, so a digit is a white stroke on a black background. The digits come from a collection called MNIST, and both models learned from all 60,000 of its training digits. Another 10,000 test digits were kept aside, so the models never saw them during training. Both models are built from neural networks, and a neural network is a large calculation with many adjustable numbers inside it. Training means nudging those numbers, over and over, until the network’s answers come out right. The VAE: squeeze a picture into two numbers, then redraw it Think of the character creator in a video game, where a few sliders set things like height and build. Every position of the sliders gives you a complete character, and moving a slider a little changes the character a little. The VAE builds something like a character creator for handwritten digits, with only two sliders. It does this with two networks that train together as a team. The first, called the encoder, looks at a 784-pixel picture and squeezes it down to only two numbers. The second, called the decoder, takes any two numbers and expands them back into a 784-pixel picture in a single pass. During training, each digit goes through the encoder and then the decoder, and the pair is scored on how closely the copy matches the original. Only two numbers fit through the middle, so those two numbers have to hold whatever matters most about each digit. The pair of numbers is called the picture’s latent, a word that means hidden, since it is a compressed code you never see in the picture itself. The lab calls the two numbers z₁ and z₂, and you can treat them like map coordinates, with z₁ saying how far across and z₂ how far up. So every code is a point on a flat map, which is the Latent map card in the lab. VAE is short for variational autoencoder, and an autoencoder is a model that learns to turn a picture into a code and then turn that code back into a copy. The word “variational” comes from the math used to train it, which you won’t need here. The character creator stops matching the VAE in three ways. In a game, designers decide what each slider does, such as setting the height, but nobody told the VAE what its two numbers should mean, so training settled that. A character creator also goes only one way, from sliders to a character, while the VAE learns the return trip too, from a finished picture back to its two numbers. And in a game every slider setting gives a proper character, while some points on the VAE’s map give only a blurry mix of digits. Keeping the codes packed together If the encoder were free to put codes anywhere, it might push the 0s far off to one side and the 7s far off to the other. That would leave wide empty gaps, and a made-up code for a brand-new digit could land in one of them. No training digit’s code ever landed in such a gap, so the decoder was never taught a digit there. So the VAE adds a second rule to its training score: the codes should stay packed in a round cloud centred on the point (0, 0). That target cloud is called the prior, a word that means “before looking at any picture”, and the lab draws it on the map as two dashed circles. The penalty for not fitting the cloud is called the KL divergence. It compares each picture’s code with the target cloud and charges for two things. One is a code whose spot sits far from the centre. The other is about the size of a small wobble around each code, which you will meet in the next section. If the rule worked perfectly, you could pick any random point from the cloud, hand it to the decoder and get a believable digit back. This lab applies the rule lightly, multiplying the KL penalty by 0.35, about a third of its full strength, before adding it to the training score. As a result, real digits’ codes spread wider than the target cloud. Random picks, though, come from the cloud itself, so most of them land near the centre, where the regions of several digits overlap. Only about half of those picks become a clear digit, as Where it breaks shows. A best-guess spot with a small wobble The encoder actually gives a little more than two plain numbers, because for each of the two it gives a best-guess spot, called the mean and written μ (mu). It also gives a small spread around that spot, written σ (sigma), so you can read its answer as “the code is about here, give or take σ”. During training, the decoder does not receive the exact spot but a point picked at random from the small patch around μ. That way the decoder has to draw well for the whole patch, and not only for one exact point. The lab writes the pick like this, with ε (epsilon) standing for a random number, usually between about −2 and 2, that is rolled before the calculation starts: z = μ + σ·ε Here is a worked example with a ready-made drawing of a 3 that the lab offers, which you can load with the 3 button in Encode a drawing. For this drawing, μ for z₁ is 1.46 and σ is about 0.03. If the random roll gives ε = 0.5, then z₁ = 1.46 + 0.03 × 0.5, which comes to 1.475. The wobble moves the point only a tiny distance, because σ is so small. Rolling ε first has its own name, reparameterization, and it solves a practical problem. Training keeps asking questions like this one: if μ were a little bigger, would the score get better or worse? If z were only “some random point near μ”, no rule would link a change in μ to a change in z, so that question would have no answer. Writing z = μ + σ·ε fixes this. The roll ε is set aside first, like a dice roll written down before the game, and then nudging μ up by 0.1 moves z up by exactly 0.1. Everything after the roll is ordinary arithmetic, so training can see how μ and σ affect the score. The KL penalty from the previous section looks at this wobble too. It compares each picture’s small patch with the whole target cloud, whose spread is 1. A patch far narrower than 1 counts as a poor fit, so it costs points too. Diffusion: ruin pictures on purpose, then learn to undo it Picture someone learning to restore old photos by practising on photos that were ruined on purpose. You take a clean photo and sprinkle a little static over it, then a little more, until nothing is left but static. At every stage, the trainee studies the damaged photo and tries to point out exactly which specks are static. After enough practice, they can take a photo covered in static and remove some of it, so that more of the picture underneath shows through. Diffusion works the same way, in two halves, and the first half, adding static, takes no skill at all. The second half, working out which part of a picture is static, is the part that has to be learned. The photo restorer stops matching in one important way, because a restorer always has a real photo hidden under the static. When diffusion makes a new picture, it starts from static with nothing under it at all, so the digit that appears is built up by the clean-up itself. Adding static: the forward process The first half, called the forward process, adds static to a clean digit over 100 steps, numbered from t = 0 to t = 99. Here t stands for the step, and the lab labels the clean digit x₀, meaning the picture before any static at all. How much static goes in at each step follows a fixed plan called the noise schedule. Nobody trains this plan and no network is involved, so this half is pure arithmetic. At every step, each pixel of the noisy picture is a mix of the clean pixel and a random static value: noisy pixel = signal share × clean pixel + noise share × static The static is a separate random number for each pixel, mostly between −2 and 2, and the lab writes it as ε, the same Greek letter as before. As the steps go by, the signal share falls from about 1 toward 0, while the noise share rises from about 0 toward 1. Under each tile of the strip, the lab prints the signal share as √ᾱ, which you can read as “the square root of alpha-bar”. Here is the mix worked out at step t = 59, where the tile reads 0.60 for the signal share. The noise share there, 0.80, is not printed under the tile, but it follows from a rule explained just below: A white pixel of the digit has the value 1, so if its static is −0.5, it becomes 0.60 × 1 + 0.80 × (−0.5), which is 0.60 − 0.40 = 0.20. A black background pixel has the value −1, so if its static is 0.5, it becomes 0.60 × (−1) + 0.80 × 0.5, which is −0.60 + 0.40 = −0.20. Both pixels end up as greys close to zero, which makes them much harder to tell apart, and that is how the digit fades into the static. You may also notice that 0.60 and 0.80 behave like the sides of a 3-4-5 triangle, because their squares, 0.36 and 0.64, add up to exactly 1. The schedule keeps that true at every step. That rule stops the pixel values from swinging steadily wider, or shrinking toward zero, as the static takes over, and it lets you work out either share from the other. The plan has to end with almost nothing of the picture left, because making a new picture will start from fresh static. The network only knows what to do with the kind of input it practised on, so the last forward step has to look like plain static too. Here the last step keeps just 3% of the digit, which is the 0.03 under the last tile, or 0.031 to three decimal places. Guessing the static: the denoiser The second half needs learning, so a network called the denoiser is trained to guess the static that was added to a noisy picture. It is given the noisy picture and its step number, and one network handles all 100 steps, since the step number tells it how much static to expect. Training runs as a loop: take a digit, pick a random step, add static using the mix above, and ask the denoiser to guess that static. Then score the guess by how far off it is, and nudge the network’s adjustable numbers so that it does a little better next time. The lab’s denoiser has 1,181,217 adjustable numbers, and it was trained for 45 passes over all 60,000 MNIST digits, so it saw every training digit 45 times. Its error is the average, over all 784 pixels, of the squared gap between its guess and the real static. By the end of training that error was 0.036, against 1.0 for a lazy guess of “no static anywhere”. Guessing the static is useful because, once you know what static was added, you can take it away and work out the clean picture. The lab shows that worked-out picture with the caption predicted x̂₀, where the little hat on top means “a guess at”. Beside it, predicted ε̂ shows the guessed static itself, with mid-grey standing for zero. Cleaning up: the reverse process Making a new picture is called the reverse process, and it starts by handing 784 numbers of fresh static to the denoiser, which guesses the static in it. An update then makes three small moves, and the result is a slightly cleaner picture. The denoiser is called again on that, for 100 calls in all. Each move has a reason: It removes only one step’s worth of the guessed static, not all of it, because each call is meant to undo just one forward step. Why not remove it all at once? Why it’s here answers that, under “One jump from static to a digit is too big”. It scales the picture up very slightly, because each forward step shrank the picture a little as the signal share fell, so the way back has to grow it again. It sprinkles in a little fresh static. Each forward step added static at random, so many slightly different pictures could have come just before the current one. The step back picks one of them at random. That keeps the right amount of static for the next call, and it helps stop the run from drifting toward a smooth, blurry average of many possible digits. The very last call skips the fresh static, because its output is meant to be the finished picture. The Reverse diffusion card prints the update for the next call with its real numbers filled in. The recipe is called DDPM, the name of the standard step-by-step method that this lab uses. The calls work backward through the steps: call 1 cleans the picture at step 99, call 2 the one at step 98, and so on. When you first open the lab, the Denoiser calls slider sits at 62, so the line shows call 63. That call works at step 99 − 62 = 37 and turns the picture at step 37 into the picture at step 36: x_36 = (x_37 − 0.0359 · ε̂) × 1.0102 + 0.1415 · z In that line, x_37 is the current picture and ε̂ is the guessed static. The letter z stands for the fresh static, and x_36 is the slightly cleaner picture that comes out. Follow one pixel with a value of 0.50, where the guessed static is 2.0 and the fresh static is −0.3: Remove part of the guess: 0.50 − 0.0359 × 2.0 = 0.4282. Scale up slightly: 0.4282 × 1.0102 is about 0.4326. Sprinkle in fresh static: 0.4326 + 0.1415 × (−0.3) is about 0.39. That pixel moved from 0.50 to about 0.39. Most calls change the picture only a little like this, because the trip from static to a digit has been split into 100 small steps. The numbers in the line change from call to call, because each step of the schedule added a different amount of static. A perfect denoiser to compare against The lab offers a second denoiser, the Ideal denoiser, which is not a network at all but exact math. It works with 64 reference digits that the VAE’s decoder drew, laid out in a grid 8 across and 8 down. At every call, it compares the noisy picture with each reference, faded to match the current step, and gives each reference a share of weight by how well it matches. The shares always add up to 100%. Its guess at the clean picture is a blend of the references, with each one counting as much as its share. If it gave 75% of the weight to one reference and 25% to another, its guess would be three parts of the first mixed with one part of the second. While the weight is spread over many references the guess looks blurry, but once one reference holds almost all of it, the guess becomes that reference exactly. For those 64 digits, no denoiser could guess the static better, which is why the lab calls it ideal. That perfection has a surprising cost, though: the ideal denoiser can only ever give back one of its 64 references. Here is why, in three steps: Its guess at the clean picture is always a blend of the 64 references and nothing else, because those 64 are the only clean pictures it knows. As the static thins out, one reference always ends up matching far better than the rest, so the blend narrows down to that single picture. The finished result is therefore an exact copy of that one reference. Picture two friends getting ready for an art quiz with the same 64 sample drawings. One memorizes all 64 perfectly, so whatever the quiz asks, they reproduce the closest sample line for line. The other cannot hold every line in memory and picks up the general look instead, so their drawings resemble the samples without matching any of them. The ideal denoiser is like the first friend, and the trained network is more like the second. The analogy bends in two places, though. The trained network did not study the 64 references at all, but a much bigger set, all 60,000 MNIST training digits. And the ideal denoiser memorizes nothing, because it is handed the 64 references ready-made. Which one it ends on is settled gradually by the static, not chosen at the start. Two opposite designs, side by side Set next to each other, the two designs differ at almost every point: Where a new picture starts: the VAE starts from two numbers, which make a point on its map, while diffusion starts from 784 numbers of static. What gets learned: the VAE learns a map of codes and a way to draw any point on it, while diffusion learns to guess the static in a noisy picture. How many network runs each picture takes: the VAE’s decoder runs once, while diffusion’s denoiser runs 100 times, one call after another. The usual flaw: VAE pictures tend to come out blurry, while diffusion is slow. The big practical difference is patience, so picture a relay race with 100 runners, where each runner has to wait for the baton before setting off. Even with very fast runners, you cannot finish sooner by starting them all at once. Diffusion’s calls work the same way, since call 50 needs the picture that call 49 produced, so they cannot run side by side.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: One jump from static to a digit is too big You might wonder why diffusion bothers with 100 calls instead of training one network to turn static straight into a digit. From pure static, every digit is about equally likely, so the safest single guess is a blurry blend of many digits at once. To see why a blend is “safest”, picture a game where a friend flashes a digit at you for a split second and you have to redraw it. You lose points on every pixel by how far its brightness is from the right one, and a big miss costs far more than a small one. If you can’t tell whether it was a 3 or a 5, a faint mix of both is only a little wrong almost everywhere. A crisp wrong guess is badly wrong on many pixels, so on average the faint mix loses fewer points. A network trained to make the whole jump in one go is scored in a similar way, so it learns to draw that blurry mix. You can see this in the lab: with the Ideal denoiser, the predicted x̂₀ picture during the first few calls is a soft blend of many references. Diffusion avoids getting stuck with that blur by splitting the trip into 100 small steps. Each call moves the picture only a short way toward the current guess, adds a pinch of fresh static, and then asks again. As the static thins out, the guess gets sharper, and the picture gradually settles on a single digit. Each step is also a much smaller job than the whole trip, because the denoiser only has to deal with the static at one level. Pixels are a poor place to mix pictures The VAE solves a different problem, which is giving you a space where you can move smoothly from one picture to another, something pixels alone are bad at. Averaging a 0 and a 2 pixel by pixel gives you a faint 0 and a faint 2 lying on top of each other, which looks like neither digit. On the VAE’s map, every point is a code that the decoder turns into one picture. A small move on the map gives a small change in the picture, so you can walk from one digit to another and watch the shape change along the way. The map can blur too, in two kinds of places. In a gap between two digits’ regions, few or no training digits’ codes landed, so the decoder was never taught a digit there. It still draws something, because its output changes smoothly from point to point, and what it draws is a blurry mix of the digits on either side. In the crowded middle of the map, the codes of several different digits sit close together, so a point there could belong to any of them. The decoder hedges between them there, for the same reason as in the flash-a-digit game. Even so, the VAE’s walk is far better than averaging pixels, which gives a double image the whole way. Along most of the walk the decoder draws one digit-like shape that changes a little at a time. The blur shows up only in the stretches where one digit’s region hands over to the next. Finding those stretches is part of reading the map. In most models the latent stays hidden deep inside the machinery, but here it becomes somewhere you can explore. Not every generative model guesses the next piece The text models in other labs build their answer one piece at a time, from left to right, and once a word is written it stays. Diffusion works on the whole picture at every step instead, so even a late call can still adjust a stroke in the top-left corner. A text model of that kind cannot go back and change a word it has already written.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: The lab switches views as you move through the lesson’s steps, but you can flip the Model switch between Diffusion and VAE whenever you like. Watch static being added Start in the Diffusion view, where the Forward process strip shows the clean digit x₀, followed by the same digit at six steps from t = 0 to t = 99. The small number under each tile is the signal share √ᾱ, and the last picture, at step 99, reads 0.03 and looks like pure static to the eye. That clean digit is not taken from MNIST. The VAE’s decoder draws it at the point chosen on the Latent map, which is why the caption under the strip names a point z. If you move that point in the VAE view, the digit here changes too. Below the strip, the Noise schedule chart shows the signal share as a solid line falling toward 0 and the noise share as a dashed line rising toward 1. The Noise-prediction error by step chart shows how far off the network’s static guesses are at every step for this digit. Its dotted line is the score you would get by always guessing zero static. Watch a digit come out of static The Reverse diffusion card shows three large pictures side by side: the picture after the number of calls you have chosen, then predicted x̂₀, then predicted ε̂. Below them, the Background pixels readout gives the share of the 784 pixels that are nearly black, meaning −0.9 or darker. Pure static has only about 1 pixel in 6 that dark, while a finished digit is mostly black background, so this number climbs as a digit appears. The number in brackets beside it is the same share for the clean digit x₀, for comparison. The Noise seed slider, which runs from 1 to 24 and starts at 7, picks the random static. A seed is a number that fixes a random draw, a bit like the seed number some games use to build the same random world every time. The same seed always gives the same starting static, and a different seed gives different static. Try this: In Reverse diffusion, keep Denoiser on Trained network and Start from on Pure noise, then drag Denoiser calls slowly from 0 to 100. Each notch is one call to the denoiser, so watch the Background pixels number climb as the black background comes back. Then switch Denoiser to Ideal denoiser, keep the same seed, and compare the two final pictures. Under the slider, a filmstrip shows the picture after 0, 10, 20 and so on up to 100 calls, and clicking a frame jumps straight there. When you reach 100 calls, the update line turns into a summary that names the nearest of the 64 references and gives the distance to it. Compare with the perfect denoiser With Denoiser on Ideal denoiser, the 64 references appear in a grid below the readouts. Each reference has an outline that grows stronger as it gains weight, the heaviest one is highlighted, and a note underneath gives its number and its share. Drag Denoiser calls upward from 0 and watch the weight gather onto one reference. Then move Noise seed, and the ideal denoiser settles on a different reference: seeds 1 to 24 end on 20 different ones. The card shows one denoiser at a time, so switch Denoiser back to Trained network and you will see that the network’s digit changes with the seed too. The seed is the only way you can change which digit you get. Finally, switch Start from from Pure noise to Noised x₀, which starts from the clean digit pushed all the way through the forward process to step 99. It uses the very same static as Pure noise for that seed, with only 3% of the digit added on top. Compare the final picture with the one you got from pure noise. Walk around the latent map Switch Model to VAE, and the Latent map card shows a mosaic of 256 small digits in a 16 × 16 grid. Each tile is what the decoder draws for the code at that tile’s centre. The map runs from −4 to 4 in both directions, with z₁ going across and z₂ going up. The two dashed circles mark the target cloud, at distances of 1 and 2 from the centre. The lab labels them 1σ and 2σ, and this σ is the target cloud’s spread, which is 1. It is not the encoder’s tiny wobble from earlier, even though the two share the same letter. Drag the point, which starts at (−2.00, −0.80) among the 5s on the left, and watch the big digit beside the map change smoothly. You can also move it in one direction at a time with the Latent z₁ and Latent z₂ sliders, in steps of 0.05. Two readouts sit under the sliders. ‖z‖ is how far your point is from the centre, measured in units of the target cloud’s spread. That spread is 1, so the number is just the distance. You can check it with Pythagoras: at the starting point it is √((−2)² + (−0.8)²) = √(4 + 0.64), which is about 2.15. log p(z) says how often random picks from the target cloud land near your point. It uses a squeezed scale measured in nats, where each drop of about 2.3 means random picks land there about 10 times less often. The closer it is to zero, the more often random picks land near that spot. It reads about −1.84 at the centre and −4.16 at the starting point, a drop of about 2.3. So the starting point gets about one tenth as many random picks as the centre. It drops faster the further out you go. Now try a planned route, starting on the 0s along the bottom and going up the right side through the 2s to the 1s at the top right. From there, go along the top to the 7s at the top left. Walking from one code to another, usually in a straight line, and watching the picture change along the way is called latent interpolation. For a straight-line try, pick any two digits on the map and drag the point straight from one to the other. Smooth change tells you the map is well organized, while a blurry stretch marks a spot where one digit’s region hands over to another. Finish by dragging through the crowded middle and watching the digit blur. Squeeze your own drawing In Encode a drawing, click the 7 button and then the 3 button, or draw your own digit with a mouse or pen. Each stroke is sent to the encoder when you lift the mouse button or pen, and Clear wipes the pad. The card shows two copies: decoder(μ), drawn from the encoder’s best-guess spot, and decoder(μ + σ·ε), drawn from a point wobbled at random. The encoded spot also appears on the Latent map as a diamond, with an oval around it that shows twice its wobble. The numbers beside the copies describe this one drawing: Posterior mean μ is the encoder’s best-guess spot, where “posterior” means “after looking at the drawing”, the partner word to prior. Posterior σ (prior σ = 1) is the size of the wobble, shown next to the target cloud’s spread of 1. Reconstruction BCE, decoder(μ) scores how far the copy is from your drawing, added up over all 784 pixels, in nats. Here nats are simply the unit the score is counted in, the same one the KL and training-loss rows use, so the scores can be added together. BCE is short for binary cross-entropy, and lower is better. The pen leaves soft grey edges, so even a perfect copy would score a little above 0. The row starting KL is the packing penalty for this drawing, the KL divergence from earlier. Training loss, BCE + 0.35 × KL is the training score for this one drawing, worked out from the decoder(μ) copy. Training itself scored the wobbled copy, but the two are almost the same here, as the note under the numbers shows. For the 3 preset, the BCE is 121.1 nats and the KL is 7.12. Multiplying the KL by 0.35 gives about 2.49, so the training loss comes to about 123.6 nats. Almost all of that score comes from the copy’s mistakes, and very little comes from the packing rule.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: Making static is arithmetic, but removing it takes a network Adding static is one line of arithmetic for each tile, with nothing to learn. Only the reverse direction, going from static back toward a digit, needs a trained network. Seed 7 gives one new digit and one copy With seed 7 from pure noise, the trained network turns static into a digit. Its Background pixels number goes from 0.17 to 0.82, which means about 1 pixel in 6 is near black at the start and about 4 in 5 at the end. The Ideal denoiser, given exactly the same static, lands exactly on reference #64. The network’s picture is nearest to reference #28, at 0.26, and is none of them. That 0.26 is a mean squared distance: square the gap between the two pictures at every pixel, then average those squares, so that 0 would mean a perfect copy. A distance of 0.26 is what you would get if every pixel were off by about 0.5, on the scale from −1 for black to 1 for white. Across every seed on the slider, the network’s picture never comes closer than 0.07 to any reference. Those 64 references are not what the network learned from, though, so missing them is only part of the story. The stronger evidence, in Where it breaks, compares the network’s pictures with its own 60,000 training digits, and they sit about as far from those as brand-new real digits do. The ideal denoiser makes up its mind The ideal denoiser spreads its weight over many references at first, so its guess at the clean picture is a blurry blend. At seed 7 one reference holds half the weight after 15 calls and 99% after 32, and from then on its guess is that picture. The remaining calls clear away the leftover static around it. Guessing static is hardest when there is little of it The network guesses the static worst at step 0 (error 0.60) and almost perfectly at step 99 (under 0.001). That can seem backwards, since you might expect a lightly damaged picture to be the simplest one to fix. Picture a friend who tries to weigh a single letter by stepping on a bathroom scale with it and then without it, and taking the difference. The letter is so light that the scale’s tiny errors swamp it, yet the same trick works well for a heavy suitcase. At step 0 the static is the letter, because the noise share there is only about 0.025. To get the static out of a noisy pixel, you take away the clean part and then divide by the noise share. You divide because the static was multiplied by that share on the way in. Dividing by 0.025 is the same as multiplying by 40, so any mistake in the clean part grows 40 times. Being off by 0.01 on a pixel’s clean value, for example, means being off by 0.4 in the guessed static, because 0.01 ÷ 0.025 = 0.4. At step 99 the static is the suitcase, since the picture there is almost entirely static, so guessing the static comes close to reading off the picture itself. Even at its worst, the network beats the dotted line, which sits at 1.03 for always guessing zero static. The flip side is that at step 99 the digit is the letter. Only 3% of it is left, so even a tiny slip in the static guess becomes about 32 times bigger in the guess at the clean picture. That is how predicted x̂₀ can still be a blurry blend after the first call, even though the static guess is nearly perfect. It is also another way to see why one jump from static to a digit does not work. Neighbours on the map look alike Neighbouring points on the map give neighbouring digits, so a small move never makes the picture jump suddenly. A map like this, with no sudden jumps anywhere, is called continuous, and that is what makes a two-number code something you can steer around. Each digit owns a region, and the regions meet in a crowded middle, where the decoder blurs. Near the centre, the codes of several different digits sit close together, so a point there could belong to any of them. The decoder hedges by drawing a faint mix, as in the flash-a-digit game. Eight of the ten digits show up among the 12 tiles closest to the centre. The lab’s makers checked those tiles with a separate network trained only to read digits, which gives each picture a confidence score from 0 to 1. Its average score for those middle tiles was only 0.70, against 0.96 for tiles more than 3 from the centre. Two numbers is a tight squeeze The 7 comes back looking like a 3, because the encoder files it among the 3s. Its best-guess spot is (1.55, 0.02), very close to where the 3 preset lands. Its BCE of 211.6 nats is also far worse than the 3’s 121.1, because the copy misses so much of the drawing. The 3 comes back as a blurry 3, and the 0 and 1 presets come back as themselves. That makes the 7, with its heavy bar across the top, the odd one out. Two numbers are a tight squeeze, so a wrong digit is possible, not only a blurry one. The wobble hardly shows For the 3 and 7 presets, σ is only about 0.03 to 0.05, while the target cloud’s spread is 1. That is why decoder(μ) and decoder(μ + σ·ε) look almost identical, since the wobble is tiny next to the distance between different digits on the map. The encoder pins each drawing to a very small patch, and the KL term charges it a penalty for doing so. That penalty is most of the KL row. For the 3, about 6 of its 7.12 nats come from that tiny σ, and only about 1 from its distance to the centre. That is why the 7, slightly further out but with a somewhat bigger σ, has the lower KL, at 6.26. Two starting points that are nearly the same Noised x₀ and Pure noise lead to almost the same final picture. For a given seed, Noised x₀ uses the very same static as Pure noise and adds only 3% of the digit on top. That 3% is all that is left of the digit by the last step of the forward process. The two starting points are therefore nearly identical before the clean-up even begins. A different seed changes the static itself, and that does change the digit.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: This lab is honest about its models, which are both small, and neither one is a production system, meaning the large kind that real products run on. What this lab simplifies or leaves out The trained denoiser is small and cannot be steered: you cannot ask it for a 4, because it takes no label, so the seed picks the digit. It has 1,181,217 adjustable numbers and only ever saw 28 × 28 handwritten digits. Most of its pictures are clear, but not all: the digit-reading network looked at 256 of its pictures made from pure static. It read them with 0.95 average confidence, against 0.99 for real digits. It scored more than 0.9 for 86% of them, and the rest are malformed or ambiguous. Its pictures are new, not copies: on average they sit 4.45 away from the nearest training digit, against 4.11 for real test digits. Bigger means more different, so the network’s pictures sit a little further from its training digits than brand-new real digits do. Only 2% of them sit within 1.5 of a training digit, against 4% of real digits. Those distances use their own scale, which is measured a different way from the lab’s 0.26, so compare them only with each other. The ideal denoiser is not a network: it is exact math over 64 digits that the VAE drew. It shows what a perfect denoiser would do on that set, and it can only ever give back one of those 64. From pure static, seeds 1 to 24 land on 20 different ones. The noise plan does not quite reach zero. Its last step keeps 3% of the digit, so starting from a noised digit or from pure static gives almost the same picture. There is no steering and no shortcut: the lab has no text prompt or way to push the model toward a digit, and every picture takes all 100 calls. The map’s middle is crowded: two numbers cannot keep ten digits apart, so the regions of several digits overlap near the centre. Real digits spread wider than the target cloud: the packing rule is weighted at only 0.35, so the codes of real digits spread out further than the cloud. In fact, 15% of real digits land far out, more than 3 from the centre, where only about 1 random pick in 100 goes. Random picks often make poor digits. Random picks come from the narrower cloud, so they mostly land in the crowded middle and rarely reach the clear outer regions. In a test, only 48% of 10,000 picks came out as a clearly readable digit, against 86% for the diffusion network. The VAE uses two numbers on purpose: two numbers let the lab draw the codes as a flat map, but they force the digits to overlap heavily and blur. Real image systems keep far more than two numbers per picture. Your drawings are not MNIST digits: the MNIST digits were resized and centred in a standard way before training, and drawings and presets skip that step. A digit drawn very small, very thick or off to one side encodes worse than a dataset digit would. The error chart comes from one picture: the 0.60 at step 0 is for this one digit and one draw of static. Averaged over the 10,000 test digits, the network’s error at step 0 is 0.13. The default digit is a harder case, because the decoder drew it with a soft grey background. The presets, with flat black backgrounds, score 0.07 to 0.10 at step 0. Some numbers are quoted, not measured live. The digit-reader’s scores and where the test digits land were measured beforehand and copied in, because the lab carries no MNIST images and no digit-reading network. Where the real mechanisms fall short VAE output is blurry, and that is true of real systems too, not only of this small lab. Think back to the flash-a-digit game from Why it’s here, where a faint mix of a 3 and a 5 lost fewer points than a crisp wrong guess. The VAE’s training score works the same way, because it checks the copy pixel by pixel and charges more for bigger misses. When several answers are plausible, their average scores better than committing to one of them, so the decoder learns to hedge. This lab’s training score is also a loosened version of the textbook one. Weighting the packing rule below 1 buys sharper copies at the cost of a less tidy map, so it is a trade-off rather than a free win. Diffusion is slow, because every step is a full run of the network and each step needs the one before it. Faster methods take bigger steps, but every step they take still costs a full network run. When a text description steers a diffusion model, a setting called guidance strength decides how hard the model is pushed toward the description. Too high a setting gives a scorched, over-contrasted look. Measuring how good a generative model is turns out to be awkward for both families. One way to grade a model is to show it real pictures it never trained on and ask how likely it thinks each one is. A good model should rate real pictures as likely. A text model can give that answer exactly, piece by piece. A VAE can only give a number that the true answer is at least as big as, and a diffusion model gives a similar limit or a costly estimate. The common scores for image quality compare broad patterns across many pictures, so they can miss problems that a person spots at a glance. A common mix-up: “A perfect denoiser would invent brand-new digits.” The ideal denoiser shows the opposite: the perfect answer, for a fixed set of training images, is to reproduce one of them. Real models make new images partly *because* they are imperfect, and big models have still been caught copying training images that appeared many times.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: Why a real network can make new pictures The ideal denoiser shows that the exact best answer to the training task, on a fixed set of pictures, is to memorize them. Trained networks make new pictures because they never reach that perfect answer. Their design and their limited number of adjustable numbers make them smooth over the gaps between training pictures. As a result, their output can land between the examples instead of on top of one. The lab shows the two outcomes side by side. With the same static, the ideal denoiser lands exactly on one of its 64 references, while the network draws something that is none of them. The network never saw those 64, though, so the stronger test is against its own training digits. Measured beforehand, its pictures sit a little further from their nearest training digit than real test digits do, 4.45 against 4.11, so it is not copying those either. An ideal denoiser built on all 60,000 training digits would copy one of them instead. Using both ideas together In practice the two ideas are used together, in a design called latent diffusion. A VAE-like autoencoder first shrinks the picture about 8 times in each direction, so the grid ends up with 64 times fewer positions, since 8 × 8 = 64. All the slow diffusion work then happens in that small space, and the decoder expands the result back to full-size pixels once, at the very end. The small space is still a grid with a few numbers at each position, unlike this lab’s VAE, which keeps only two numbers for the whole picture. Running every denoiser call on a much smaller grid costs far less, and that is most of why high-quality image generation became affordable. Steering with words Text prompts join through attention, the part of a network that lets each piece look at other pieces, which the Attention lab covers. That way the denoiser guesses the static *given a description*. A trick called classifier-free guidance then makes the description count for more. At each step the model makes two guesses, one with the description and one without. The final guess is then pushed past the one with the description, even further in the direction that the description pulled it. A setting usually called guidance strength controls how far that push goes. Here it is with small numbers. Say that for one pixel the static guess without the description is 0.2, and with it is 0.5, so the description pulled the guess up by 0.3. With a guidance strength of 3, the model moves 3 times that pull: 0.2 + 3 × 0.3 = 1.1, which goes well past 0.5. Too low a strength and the model ignores your description, while too high gives the scorched, over-contrasted look from Where it breaks. Getting there in fewer steps The underlying math has been reworked too, and a newer approach called flow matching trains the network to follow a nearly straight path from static to picture. That straighter path needs fewer steps, and several recent image models, such as Stable Diffusion 3 and Flux, use it. Other tricks squeeze a many-step process down to 1 to 4 steps, closing much of the speed gap with a VAE. Each of those steps is still a full run of the network, though. The lab’s denoiser design The lab’s note calls its denoiser a convolutional U-Net, which is the name of its design. It looks at the picture through small windows that slide across it, and it works at several sizes, from fine detail up to the overall shape of the digit. Diffusion for text Diffusion has also been tried on text, refining every position of a passage at the same time instead of one piece after another. So far its quality has trailed the usual one-piece-at-a-time models, and it remains an area of active work.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: This module asks how a trained network can make a whole new image from a compact code or from noise. A variational autoencoder (VAE) compresses each image to a short code, its latent, and decodes a code to an image in one forward pass. A diffusion model trains a denoiser to predict the noise added to an image, then generates by removing noise from a fresh draw over many sequential steps. The encoder and decoder are stacked dense layers like those built in Stacking neurons, and the denoiser is a convolutional U-Net, made of hidden layers that share their weights across image positions. That module's contrast between memorizing and learning the pattern returns here: an exact denoiser that copies, beside a trained one that draws new digits. Where it shows up Image, audio and video generation. Diffusion is a widely used mechanism behind all three. Latent diffusion. Many image generators, Stable Diffusion among them, run diffusion inside an autoencoder's compressed latent and then decode the result once. Prompted generation. The prompt enters the denoiser through cross-attention, and the scale of classifier-free guidance sets how strongly the sample follows it. Newer formulations. Flow matching, which trains the network to predict a velocity carrying noise to data, underlies several recent image models. Distillation cuts a sampler's many steps to a few. Text. Diffusion language models update every position of a passage together rather than one token at a time, but have trailed autoregressive models in quality. Why it matters Both families generate from a random draw, a latent code or a noise image, rather than by looking an image up, and they pay different costs. A VAE decodes in one pass but blurs, because a pixel-wise loss scores a blend of plausible digits above any single guess. Diffusion makes one network call per step, each waiting for the last. Three pieces each prevent a specific failure: A schedule that ends in noise. Generation starts from a fresh noise draw, so the forward process has to end at almost pure noise. Otherwise the denoiser starts from inputs unlike its training data, and the samples stay noisy. Reparameterization. Backpropagation cannot pass through a random draw, so the reconstruction loss would never reach the encoder. Drawing the noise as a separate input lets it through. A network short of the optimum. Sampling with the minimum-error denoiser for a finite training set can only return one of its images, so new samples need a network that does not reach that optimum. What you will be able to explain Contrast iterative denoising (one denoiser call per step, each needing the previous output) with latent reconstruction (one decoder pass from a compact code). Interpret a continuous latent space: why nearby codes decode to similar digits, and why the decoder blurs where digit regions meet. What the lab shows The VAE's encoder and decoder and the diffusion denoiser were trained on MNIST handwritten digits, ship as ONNX model files and run in the app; each card's status chip says what is running. Model switches between Diffusion and VAE, and the diffusion half noises the VAE decoder's output at the current latent point. Forward process noises that digit in closed form, with no network; only its Noise-prediction error by step chart is measured, on this one digit and noise draw. In Reverse diffusion, Denoiser picks the Trained network or the Ideal denoiser, exact arithmetic over 64 VAE-drawn references rather than a model. Start from and Noise seed set the starting point and the randomness, and Denoiser calls scrubs the run from noise to sample. Latent map shows the real decoder on a 16 × 16 grid of latent points: drag the point, or use Latent z₁ and Latent z₂. Encode a drawing sends a drawing or a hand-drawn preset through the real encoder and decoder. For that one image it prints the reconstruction's binary cross-entropy (BCE) and the KL divergence (KL) of the encoder's Gaussian from the prior. Dataset-wide figures in the lesson and card notes, such as classifier readings of generated samples, are fixed offline measurements. The key experiment keeps one Noise seed and switches Denoiser: the ideal denoiser lands exactly on one reference, and the trained network draws a digit that is none of them.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: Every other lab in this course predicts the next token. This one covers the other main family of generative models: those that produce a whole image at once, either from a compact code or from noise. Both halves of the lab run real models trained on MNIST digits. The VAE: compress, then decode A variational autoencoder trains two networks together. The encoder maps an image to a distribution over a low-dimensional latent space: a mean μ and a log-variance for each dimension. The decoder maps a latent point back to an image in one forward pass. The shipped VAE has a two-dimensional latent, so every image becomes a point you can see on a map. Its training loss, per image, is: a reconstruction term, binary cross-entropy summed over 784 pixels; plus 0.35 × a KL divergence that pulls each encoder Gaussian toward the standard normal prior. Sampling is not differentiable, so training uses the reparameterization z = μ + σ ⊙ ε with ε drawn separately. The randomness becomes an input and gradients flow through μ and σ. Diffusion: destroy, then learn to undo The forward process is fixed and needs no learning. With a noise schedule of variances β_t, the noised image at any step has a closed form: q(x_t | x₀) = N(√ᾱ_t · x₀, (1 − ᾱ_t) I), where ᾱ_t is the running product of 1 − β_t. The schedule has to end at almost pure noise, because generation starts from a fresh noise draw. This lab's cosine schedule leaves √ᾱ = 0.031 of the digit at the last step. The denoiser is trained for one job: given x_t and t, predict the noise ε that was added. Generation, the reverse process, starts from noise and applies the DDPM update once per step: x_(t−1) = (x_t − β_t / √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε̂) / √α_t + √β_t · z Each step is one network call, and each call needs the previous one's output. The shipped denoiser is a small convolutional U-Net with 1,181,217 parameters, trained for 45 epochs on all 60,000 MNIST training digits.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: Diffusion and VAEs are a useful contrast: not every generative model works autoregressively. This lab's VAE also turns the latent space into something you can navigate rather than a hidden implementation detail. The two approaches are complementary, a point Going deeper returns to.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: Diffusion In Forward process, read the strip from x₀ to t = 99 and the Noise schedule chart. The signal coefficient √ᾱ falls to 0.031, so the last tile is static. In Reverse diffusion, keep Denoiser on Trained network and Start from on Pure noise, then drag Denoiser calls from 0 to 100. Watch x, the predicted x̂₀ and the predicted ε̂ change call by call, and Background pixels climb. Keep the seed and switch Denoiser to Ideal denoiser. At 100 calls, compare the two samples and the nearest reference printed below the slider. Then change Noise seed and watch both change. VAE Switch Model to VAE and drag the point across the Latent map, or use Latent z₁ and Latent z₂. Watch the digit morph, then drag through the crowded middle and watch it blur. In Encode a drawing, load 7 and then 3, or draw a digit. Compare decoder(μ) with your input and read the BCE and KL rows.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: Adding noise is one line of arithmetic. Only the reverse direction needs a trained network. With seed 7 from Pure noise, the trained network turns static into a digit: Background pixels climb from 0.17 to 0.82. The ideal denoiser, given the same noise, lands exactly on reference #64. The network's sample is nearest to reference #28, at a squared distance of 0.26, and is none of them. The ideal denoiser holds its weight spread over many references at first. At seed 7 one reference has half the weight after 15 calls and 99% after 32, and from then on x̂₀ is that reference. The network's noise-prediction error is 0.60 at t = 0, its worst, and under 0.001 at t = 99. Predicting ε is hardest when there is little of it. On the latent map, nearby points decode to similar digits. Each digit owns a region, the regions meet in a crowded middle, and the decoder blurs there. The 7 preset encodes to μ = (1.55, 0.02), among the 3s, and decodes as a 3. Its BCE is 211.6 nats and its KL 6.26. The 3 preset comes back as a blurry 3 (BCE 121.1). The 7 shows a different failure: a wrong digit, not only a blurry one.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: In this lab The denoiser is small and unconditional. It has 1,181,217 parameters, saw only 28 × 28 MNIST digits, and takes no label, so the seed picks the digit and you cannot ask for one. Offline, an independent classifier read 256 of its pure-noise samples with a mean confidence of 0.95, over 0.9 for 86% of them, against 0.99 for real test digits. The rest are malformed or ambiguous. The samples are new, not copies. Their average distance to the nearest training digit is 4.45, against 4.11 for real test digits, and 2% of them sit within 1.5 of one, against 4% of real test digits. The ideal denoiser is arithmetic, not a model. It is the exact posterior mean over 64 reference digits drawn by the VAE decoder, and it can only ever return one of them. From pure noise, seeds 1 to 24 end on 20 different references. The schedule is not exactly pure noise. √ᾱ is 0.031 at the last step, so Noised x₀ and Pure noise give almost the same sample. The sampler is plain 100-step DDPM, with no guidance. The VAE is two-dimensional on purpose. Its codes spread wider than the prior (standard deviations 1.41 and 1.55), and 15% of test digits land beyond radius 3, where the prior puts 1.1%. A draw from the prior mostly hits the crowded middle: 48% of 10,000 prior draws are read with confidence above 0.9, against 86% of the network's samples. Presets and drawings are not MNIST digits; they skip MNIST's size normalization and centring. In real systems VAE samples are characteristically blurry: a pixel-wise reconstruction loss rewards hedging, so averaging several plausible outputs scores better than committing to one. With a KL weight below 1, as here, the objective is a β-VAE loss rather than the exact negative ELBO. Diffusion sampling needs many sequential network calls. Guidance at high strength causes oversaturation. Diffusion models can reproduce individual training images, especially duplicated ones (Carlini et al., 2023). Likelihoods are awkward for both families. A VAE gives a lower bound (the ELBO), and a diffusion model gives a bound or an expensive estimate, unlike the exact per-token likelihood of an autoregressive model. Common image metrics compare feature distributions and miss failures a human notices at once.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: Why a real network can generate new images The ideal denoiser shows that the exact optimum of the training objective, on a finite set, memorizes. Trained networks generalize because they do not reach it: their architecture and limited capacity smooth between training images. That gap between optimum and practice is where new samples come from, and the lab shows it: same noise, same seed, one copy and one new digit. Combining the two ideas Latent diffusion trains an autoencoder that shrinks each image side by a factor of 8, runs diffusion in that spatial latent, and decodes once at the end. The cost reduction made high-resolution generation practical. Text prompts enter through cross-attention, so the denoiser predicts noise *given* a description. Classifier-free guidance extrapolates from the unconditional prediction toward the conditional one. Guidance scale is the most consequential setting: too low ignores the prompt, too high oversaturates. Newer formulations Flow matching and rectified flow train a network to predict a velocity field that carries noise to data along nearly straight paths. Several recent image models, such as Stable Diffusion 3 and Flux, use it. Separately, distillation compresses a many-step sampler into 1 to 4 steps. Diffusion has also been applied to text, refining all positions in parallel instead of one token at a time as in the inference lab. Quality has trailed autoregressive models, and it remains active work.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Forward process · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: Noise added in closed form One clean digit x₀ shown at six noise levels of the shipped 100-step cosine schedule, computed exactly from q(x_t | x₀) with one seeded noise image. Beside it: the schedule's signal and noise coefficients, and the shipped network's error at predicting that noise at every level. A strip: x₀, then the same digit at t = 0, 19, 39, 59, 79 and 99, each labelled with √ᾱ_t. The outlined tile is the level nearest the reverse process's current step. `Noise schedule`: √ᾱ_t as a solid line and √(1−ᾱ_t) as a dashed line against step t, with a marker at the reverse process's current level. The legend prints the values at t = 99: 0.031 and 1.000. `Noise-prediction error by step`: the trained network's mean squared error at predicting ε (solid) against always predicting zero (dotted), measured on this x₀ with one seeded ε. The status chip reads `ONNX · WASM` (or `WEBGPU`) once the error curve has come back from the model worker. Every image is x_t = √ᾱ_t · x₀ + √(1−ᾱ_t) · ε, with pixels mapped from [0, 1] to [−1, 1] by 2x − 1, which is how `train_mnist_models.py` scales them. ᾱ_t is read from `mnist-diffusion-schedule.json`. Recovering β_t = 1 − ᾱ_t / ᾱ_(t−1) gives a cosine schedule (Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021): tiny steps at first, β = 0.0006 at t = 0, and large ones at the end, β = 0.55 at t = 99. The strip's labels run from √ᾱ = 1.00 at t = 0 to 0.03 at t = 99. The error curve runs the shipped denoiser once on a batch of 100 images, one per t, each built from the same x₀ and ε, and scores ε̂ against ε by mean squared error over 784 pixels. The dotted baseline is the mean of ε², close to 1. x₀ is the VAE decoder's output at the latent point set in the VAE view, so the two halves of the lab share one digit. If the decoder fails, a hand-drawn 0 stands in and the caption says so. `Noise seed` in the Reverse diffusion card changes ε here too; moving the point in the VAE view changes x₀. Worth running: read the error curve at both ends. On the default digit and seed the network scores 0.60 at t = 0, its worst but still well below guessing zero (1.03), and under 0.001 at t = 99. Adding noise needs no learning at all: every tile is one line of arithmetic. Only the reverse direction needs a network. The schedule ends at almost pure noise. At t = 99 the image keeps only 0.031 of the digit's amplitude, so the last tile looks like static, and that is what lets sampling start from noise alone. Predicting ε is hardest when there is little of it. At low t the noise is a faint perturbation of an unknown digit, so the network does worst there; at high t the noise dominates x_t and is read off almost exactly. In this lab: x₀ is a VAE decoder output rather than an MNIST image, and the error curve comes from one image and one noise draw, not the training average over digits, steps and draws. Measured offline on 10,000 test digits, the network's error is 0.13 at t = 0, 0.028 at t = 49 and under 0.001 at t = 99. The t = 0 value is higher here because the decoder's output has a soft grey background; on the hand-drawn presets, whose background is flat, it is 0.07 to 0.10. In this lab: the schedule runs 100 steps, not the 1,000 usual in DDPM, and stops at 98% of the cosine curve, so ᾱ at the last step is 0.00097 rather than exactly 0. A faint trace of the digit is left. In general: production schedules (linear over 1,000 steps, cosine, or flow-matching paths) are designed so the last step is indistinguishable from pure Gaussian noise, and some force it to exactly zero signal, which needs care at the very first sampling step. In general: the training loss averages this error over random steps, images and draws, so a single number hides how uneven it is across noise levels.
documents.title: Noise added in closed form

documents.subtitle: Reverse diffusion · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: One denoiser call per step The DDPM update applied 100 times from a seeded start, calling a denoiser once per step. Choose the shipped ONNX network or the exact posterior-mean denoiser for 64 VAE-drawn reference digits, then scrub through the stored trajectory from pure noise to a sample. Three large images for the current position: x after k calls, and the next call's predicted clean image x̂₀ and predicted noise ε̂ (mid-grey is zero; black and white are ∓2.5). A `Denoiser calls` slider from 0 to 100 and a filmstrip of x after 0, 10, …, 100 calls. Each thumbnail is a button that jumps there. The next update with its numbers filled in, then four readouts: calls made, the noise level t of the current x, √ᾱ and √(1−ᾱ) at that level, and the share of background pixels in x next to the clean digit's. With the Ideal denoiser, the 64 reference digits with outlines whose opacity is each reference's posterior weight at the next call; the heaviest is filled. With the Trained network, a note on how it was trained. Each call k works at t = 99 − k and applies x_(t−1) = (x_t − β_t / √(1−ᾱ_t) · ε̂) / √α_t + √β_t · z, with seeded z and no fresh noise on the last call. This is DDPM's ancestral sampler (Algorithm 2 with σ_t² = β_t); the training script ships no sampler of its own, and repeats this one to judge samples before publishing. The predicted clean image is x̂₀ = (x_t − √(1−ᾱ_t) · ε̂) / √ᾱ_t, the forward formula solved for x₀. `Trained network` makes 100 sequential calls to `mnist-diffusion-denoiser.onnx` in the model worker, each with the current x_t and the integer t. `Ideal denoiser` computes weights w_i = softmax(−‖x_t − √ᾱ_t r_i‖² / (2(1−ᾱ_t))) over references r_i, sets x̂₀ = Σ w_i r_i and derives ε̂ from it. This is the exact minimum-error denoiser for that finite set: what a perfectly trained network would converge to on it. `Pure noise` starts from ε; `Noised x₀` starts from √ᾱ₉₉ · x₀ + √(1−ᾱ₉₉) · ε, which at t = 99 is 0.03 · x₀ + 1.00 · ε. One seed fixes ε and every z, so both denoisers see identical randomness. Background pixels is the share of the 784 pixels at or below −0.9: about 0.17 for the seed-7 starting noise and about 0.82 for the network's sample. Pixel RMS would not do here, because noise and a digit both sit near 1. `Denoiser` switches between `Ideal denoiser` and `Trained network`; `Start from` between `Noised x₀` and `Pure noise`; `Noise seed` redraws ε and z (1 to 24). `Denoiser calls` and the filmstrip move through the finished trajectory without recomputing it. Worth running: with `Trained network`, `Pure noise` and seed 7, drag to 100 calls: static becomes a digit and the Background pixels readout climbs from 0.17 to 0.82. Switch to `Ideal denoiser`: it lands exactly on reference #64, while the network's sample is nearest to reference #28 at a squared distance of 0.26. Every step is one full network call, and step k needs the output of step k − 1. That sequential chain is the cost diffusion pays that a VAE's single decoder pass does not. With the ideal denoiser, x̂₀ is a weighted average of references: blurry while the weight is spread, one exact reference once a single one takes it. At seed 7 the top reference passes half the weight after 15 calls and 99% after 32. The same seed gives two different images: the ideal denoiser returns one of the 64 references (distance 0), the network a new digit that is none of them (its nearest reference is never closer than 0.07 across seeds 1 to 24). The ideal denoiser's choice depends on the seed: from pure noise, seeds 1 to 24 end on 20 different references. Changing the seed changes the digit the network draws too, which is the only control you have over it. In this lab: the ideal denoiser is exact arithmetic over 64 references, not a trained model. It can only ever return one of them, so its samples are memorized by construction. In this lab: the shipped network is small (1,181,217 parameters, 45 epochs, 28 × 28 MNIST only) and unconditional, so you cannot ask it for a digit. Offline, an independent classifier read 256 of its pure-noise samples with a mean confidence of 0.95 and over 0.9 for 86% of them, against 0.99 for real test digits; the rest are malformed or ambiguous. In this lab: the schedule is not exactly pure noise (√ᾱ = 0.031 at t = 99), so `Noised x₀` and `Pure noise` give almost the same sample. There is no guidance, no text prompt and no faster sampler: every sample takes all 100 calls. In general: good diffusion models generalize because a real network does not reach this empirical optimum; its architecture smooths between training images. Duplicated training images can still be reproduced (Carlini et al., 2023). In general: faster samplers such as DDIM and DPM-Solver take 10 to 50 larger steps, and distilled models take 1 to 4, but each step is still a network call.
documents.title: One denoiser call per step

documents.subtitle: Latent map · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: Two numbers in, one digit out The shipped VAE decoder evaluated on a 16 × 16 grid of latent points from −4 to 4, with a draggable point whose digit is decoded at full size. Dashed rings mark the N(0, I) prior at 1σ and 2σ, so you can see which parts of the prior the decoder draws well. A mosaic of 256 decoder outputs; each tile is decoded at its own centre, z₁ running left to right and z₂ bottom to top, with ticks at −4, −2, 0 and 2. Dashed circles at radius 1 and 2 around the origin, the pink point for z, and a blue diamond with a 2σ ellipse for the latest encoded drawing. The digit decoded at z, drawn large, with `Latent z₁` and `Latent z₂` sliders and two readouts: ‖z‖ in prior standard deviations, and log p(z) under N(0, I) in nats. The decoder is an MLP, 2 → 96 → 256 → 784 with SiLU activations and a sigmoid output, so each pixel is a value in [0, 1]. The mosaic is one batched call with 256 latents; the large digit is one call with one. log p(z) = −½‖z‖² − ln 2π for the two-dimensional standard normal prior; at the default z = (−2.00, −0.80) it is −4.16 nats. The VAE was trained with binary cross-entropy summed over pixels plus 0.35 × KL, for 40 epochs on all 60,000 MNIST training digits (see `mnist-models.metadata.json`). Drag on the map, or focus it and use the arrow keys (0.1 per press, 0.5 with Shift). `Latent z₁` and `Latent z₂` do the same one axis at a time, in steps of 0.05. Worth running: start on the 0s along the bottom, go up the right side through the 2s to the 1s at the top right, then along the top to the 7s at the upper left. The digit morphs smoothly and blurs where two regions meet; the default point sits among the 5s on the left. Nearby points decode to similar digits: the map is continuous, which is what makes a two-number code navigable. Each digit owns a region, and the regions meet in the middle. Several classes crowd there: eight of the ten digits appear among the 12 tiles within radius 1. An independent classifier reads those tiles with a mean confidence of 0.70, and the tiles beyond radius 3 at 0.96. Because the KL weight is 0.35, the codes spread wider than the prior: the 10,000 MNIST test digits have standard deviations of 1.41 and 1.55 on the two axes, and 15% land beyond radius 3, where N(0, I) puts 1.1%. So a draw from the prior mostly lands in the crowded middle. Offline, 48% of 10,000 prior draws decode to a digit the classifier reads with confidence above 0.9, against 86% of the diffusion network's pure-noise samples. In this lab: the latent space is deliberately two-dimensional so it can be drawn. That forces heavy overlap between classes and blurry digits. In this lab: the offline measurements (where test digits land, what the classifier reads) are quoted from `mnist-models.metadata.json`, not recomputed, because the lab ships no MNIST images and no classifier. In general: a sample from the prior only decodes well if the encoder used that region. A KL weight below 1, as here, lets the codes drift from the prior; practical VAEs use tens to thousands of latent dimensions.
documents.title: Two numbers in, one digit out

documents.subtitle: Encode a drawing · Diffusion & VAEs
documents.body: Compress, sample, reconstruct A 28 × 28 drawing or preset goes through the shipped encoder to a posterior mean and variance, then back through the decoder, once from the mean and once from a sampled latent. The card prints both terms of the training objective for this one image. A drawing pad with preset buttons `0`, `1`, `3` and `7` and a `Clear` button; the pressed preset is highlighted. Two reconstructions: `decoder(μ)` and `decoder(μ + σ·ε)`, the second using a seeded ε. Five rows: the posterior mean μ, the posterior σ, the reconstruction BCE, the KL to the prior, and the training loss BCE + 0.35 × KL, all for this one image. The encoded mean appears on the Latent map as a blue diamond with a 2σ ellipse. Strokes are rasterized with a soft round brush of radius 1.5 pixels into white-on-black values in [0, 1], the MNIST convention. Presets are hand-authored strokes, not dataset images. The encoder, 784 → 256 → 96 with SiLU, outputs μ and log σ² for each of the two dimensions; σ = exp(½ log σ²). The sampled latent is z = μ + σ ⊙ ε, the reparameterization used in training. BCE = −Σ[x ln x̂ + (1−x) ln(1−x̂)] over 784 pixels, with PyTorch's clamp of each log at −100. KL = −½ Σ(1 + log σ² − μ² − σ²). The loss weights KL by 0.35, as `train_mnist_models.py` does. The BCE row scores decoder(μ); the note below it scores the sampled reconstruction, which is what training actually used. Draw with a mouse, pen or touch; each stroke re-encodes when you lift. The preset buttons are the keyboard route. Worth running: load `7` and then `3`. The 7 encodes to μ = (1.55, 0.02) and decodes as a 3, with BCE 211.6 nats and KL 6.26. The 3 encodes to μ = (1.46, −0.32), decodes as a blurry 3, and scores BCE 121.1 and KL 7.12. σ is about 0.03 to 0.05 while the prior's is 1, so the encoder is confident about where each drawing goes; the KL term is what charges it for that. Reconstructions are blurry and sometimes the wrong digit. Two numbers cannot hold stroke detail, and a pixel-wise reconstruction loss rewards hedging between plausible digits. The 7 preset, with its heavy top bar, lands among the 3s. decoder(μ) and decoder(μ + σ·ε) look nearly identical here, because σ is small next to the spacing between digits on the map. In this lab: drawings are not preprocessed the way MNIST was (size-normalized into a 20 × 20 box and centred by mass), so unusual placement or thickness encodes worse than a dataset digit would. In this lab: the numbers describe one image, not the dataset average that training minimized. Training's last epoch averaged 133.3 nats of BCE and 8.03 of KL; on the 10,000 test digits, 75% of reconstructions are read by the classifier as the original digit. In general: with a KL weight of 0.35 this objective is a β-VAE loss rather than the exact negative ELBO, which needs weight 1. Lower weights buy sharper reconstructions at the cost of a less prior-shaped latent space. In general: image generators that use a VAE, such as latent diffusion, keep a spatial latent (for example 4 channels at 1/8 the resolution), not two numbers.
