documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Training a small model to match a larger one's output distribution, usually as T² times the KL divergence between their temperature-softened distributions, often mixed with ordinary cross-entropy on the labels. The teacher is used at training time only.
documents.title: Distillation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: The teacher's full probability distribution over every token, including the ones it rejected. The relative sizes of those rejected probabilities are the extra signal.
documents.title: Soft labels

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: A divisor on both models' logits before softmax in the distillation loss. It raises the weight the loss puts on small probabilities; it does not move the optimum for a student that can match the teacher exactly.
documents.title: Temperature

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: The information in which wrong answers the teacher considered plausible. A one-hot label discards all of it; a teacher that learned little beyond label frequencies has little of it to give.
documents.title: Dark knowledge

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: How much of the teacher a smaller model can represent at all. Below some size, no amount of distillation closes the gap.
documents.title: Student capacity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Removing the weights closest to zero, on the assumption that they contribute least. Cheap, effective, and only an approximation of importance.
documents.title: Magnitude pruning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Zeroing individual weights anywhere. The matrix keeps its shape, so it saves storage only with a sparse format and little time on dense hardware.
documents.title: Unstructured pruning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: A fixed N:M pattern such as 2:4, keeping two of every four consecutive weights. Recent GPUs' sparse tensor cores skip the zeros, for up to twice the matmul throughput at exactly 50% sparsity.
documents.title: Semi-structured sparsity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Removing whole units: heads, neurons, channels, layers, or here whole context rows. The matrices get smaller, which saves real computation and costs more quality per weight removed.
documents.title: Structured pruning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: The share of weights that are exactly zero. A number worth reporting alongside quality, together with the pattern, since the pattern decides whether any time is saved.
documents.title: Sparsity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Any estimate of how much a parameter matters: its magnitude, its magnitude times the input it multiplies, or the measured rise in loss when it is removed, the ablation from the interpretability labs. Better scores cost more passes over the data.
documents.title: Importance score

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: A storage layout that keeps only the surviving values plus a record of where they were, here one mask bit per position. It is what turns unstructured zeros into saved bytes; real formats use indices or block metadata instead.
documents.title: Sparse format

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Distilling to a smaller model, pruning it, then quantizing what is left, with size and quality measured after each stage. Quantizing goes last because it assumes the weights are final, and each stage inherits the error of the one before.
documents.title: Compression pipeline

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: An importance score that multiplies a weight's magnitude by the size of the input it meets over calibration text, as Wanda does for each output. It needs one pass over the data, and helps when some inputs are far larger than others.
documents.title: Activation-weighted score

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Distillation & pruning · question 1
documents.body: At rank 6 and T = 1 you switch Training target from Teacher distribution to One-hot labels, and KL to teacher rises. Why can the one-hot student not close the gap? One-hot labels are harder to fit, so the training loss stays far above the soft student's loss at every step A one-hot update carries one sampled character, so the student never sees how the teacher ranks the others The one-hot student is given a smaller rank, so it has less capacity to match the teacher's whole distribution The one-hot student is scored against a different teacher, so its KL cannot be compared with the soft one's A soft update carries the teacher's whole next-character distribution, including how it ranks the characters it rejected. A one-hot update carries one sampled character, so the student averages noisier signals. The two training losses nearly overlap while KL differs about twofold: fitting the labels and matching the teacher are different questions.
documents.title: At rank 6 and T = 1 you switch Training target from Teacher distribution to One-hot labels, and KL to teacher rises. Why can the one-hot student not close the gap?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Distillation & pruning · question 2
documents.body: Soft labels carry what one-hot labels discard, yet this lab's teacher has only a thin tail of dark knowledge. Why? Soft labels only help when the student has more capacity than the teacher, and every student here is smaller The lab fixes the temperature at 1, which switches the soft labels off and leaves one-hot training The teacher is a bigram that learned almost exactly the corpus's frequencies, so its rejected probabilities add little The student's rank is too high to benefit, because a large student matches the labels without help Dark knowledge is the information in which wrong answers the teacher found plausible. A teacher that learned little beyond the corpus's own character frequencies has only a thin smoothing tail to give, so its soft labels differ little from the labels. A large pretrained teacher carries far more. The lab shows the mechanism, not the size of the effect.
documents.title: Soft labels carry what one-hot labels discard, yet this lab's teacher has only a thin tail of dark knowledge. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Distillation & pruning · question 3
documents.body: You raise Distillation temperature from 1 to 4 at rank 6. What happens in Soft targets on “h” and in KL to teacher? Teacher mass on characters that never follow “h” shrinks, and KL falls, because a high temperature sharpens the distribution Nothing changes in either, because temperature does not move the optimum for a student that can match the teacher KL falls to zero and the student matches the teacher exactly, because soft targets at high temperature are easier to fit Teacher mass on those characters grows, and KL ends higher, because the student spends capacity on the tail Temperature divides the logits, so a higher value flattens the teacher's distribution and lifts small probabilities, which is where its ranking of wrong answers lives. A student that could match the teacher would not care, but a rank-6 student cannot, so at high temperature it spends capacity on the tail and ends further from the teacher at T = 1.
documents.title: You raise Distillation temperature from 1 to 4 at rank 6. What happens in Soft targets on “h” and in KL to teacher?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Distillation & pruning · question 4
documents.body: At the same share removed, Structured rows costs far more perplexity than Unstructured. Why is structured pruning used anyway? Removing whole rows removes real computation, while a sparse matrix is usually just as slow to multiply Structured pruning gives better quality on the training set once the rows are gone, which hides the perplexity cost Unstructured pruning cannot reach high sparsity, so structured pruning is the only way to remove more weights Structured pruning needs no importance score, so it avoids the cost of deciding which weights to remove Zeroed weights still occupy their place in a dense matrix multiply, so unstructured sparsity buys storage and little speed without specialised hardware or a sparse format. Structured pruning changes the shape of the computation, which is the saving people actually want, and the extra quality cost per weight is the price.
documents.title: At the same share removed, Structured rows costs far more perplexity than Unstructured. Why is structured pruning used anyway?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Distillation & pruning · question 5
documents.body: At a 50% pruned share, where does 2:4 semi-structured land between Unstructured and Structured rows, and what does it buy? Better than both, because the regular pattern lets the optimizer recover the weights that were removed from each group Between them: a fixed pattern costs more than free choice but less than deleting rows, and sparse tensor cores skip its zeros Worse than Structured rows, because a fixed pattern forces the most important weights to be removed first in each group The same as Unstructured, because both remove the same half of the weights and only the mask is drawn differently here Forcing two zeros in every group of four constrains which weights can go, so perplexity sits above free-choice pruning but below deleting whole rows. In exchange the pattern is regular enough that sparse tensor cores on recent GPUs can skip the zeros for up to about twice the matmul throughput. The lab measures quality, not time.
documents.title: At a 50% pruned share, where does 2:4 semi-structured land between Unstructured and Structured rows, and what does it buy?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Distillation & pruning · question 6
documents.body: At 50% pruned and 4 bits, which stage of Compose the three steps gives up the least perplexity for the bytes it saves? Prune: removing the smallest values is free, so it saves bytes without moving perplexity at all in any run Distil: the student copies the teacher, so shrinking to it costs no perplexity Quantize: it saves nearly as many bytes as pruning and adds the least perplexity of the three stages All three give up the same perplexity per byte, because the pipeline reports one running total Reading down the rows: distilling saves 2,160 B for +1.73 perplexity, pruning saves 675 B for +0.23, and quantizing saves 606 B for +0.06. Pruning is not free, a student is not a copy, and every stage adds its own error to the one before. Which stage wins depends on the settings: at 2 bits the quantize stage turns expensive.
documents.title: At 50% pruned and 4 bits, which stage of Compose the three steps gives up the least perplexity for the bytes it saves?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Distillation & pruning · question 7
documents.body: At a 70% pruned share, how do the three importance scores compare after the prune stage? Activation-weighted leaves the lowest perplexity, because weighing each weight by its input always beats magnitude alone Magnitude leaves the lowest, because the simplest score is least likely to overfit the calibration text All three tie, because each removes the same number of values and so the same amount of information Measured ablation leaves the lowest, and activation-weighted ends worse than plain magnitude on this toy Ablation asks the loss directly what each value is worth, so it keeps the right ones. Activation-weighting here only measures how often a context occurs, which ignores how much the softmax cares about a given logit, so it falls behind magnitude. On large models the published result runs the other way, because their input activations have enormous outlier channels that magnitude cannot see.
documents.title: At a 70% pruned share, how do the three importance scores compare after the prune stage?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Distillation & pruning · question 8
documents.body: Measured ablation prunes best here, yet it is not how large models are pruned. Why not? It needs one pass over the calibration text for every weight, 360 here and billions in a real model, so cheaper proxies stand in It needs the teacher model at inference time, so it cannot be used once the student has shipped to the people using it It only works for unstructured pruning, and large models are pruned in structured shapes that skip whole rows On a large model its scores come out the same as magnitude, so the extra work of computing them buys nothing at all The Passes to score readout is the bill: 0 for magnitude, 1 for activation-weighted, and one per factor entry for ablation. At billions of weights that is out of reach, which is why Wanda multiplies magnitude by an input-activation norm and SparseGPT solves a layer-wise reconstruction with second-order information instead. Ablation also measures each weight alone, so it misses interactions between weights.
documents.title: Measured ablation prunes best here, yet it is not how large models are pruned. Why not?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: A language model, the kind of program behind a chatbot, is built from numbers that it learned during training. Every one of those numbers has to be stored somewhere, and many of them are used in a calculation each time the model guesses the next piece of text. So once you have a large model that works well, a practical question follows: can you get a much smaller model that works nearly as well? This module shows two ways to do that, and both of them start from the same trained model. The first way is distillation, which trains a small model to copy the guesses of a big one, the way a student learns from a teacher. The second way is pruning, which keeps the big model but deletes the numbers that seem to matter least. At the end, you chain both of them with the rounding trick from the Quantization lab and measure what each step costs. Where you have met it The model this lab shrinks may already be familiar, because it is the tiny language model from the earlier labs that reads one character and guesses the next one. Here it plays the part of the teacher, and every smaller model in the lab is measured against it. If you did the interpretability labs, you have also met ablation, which means switching a part off to see what it was doing. Here it becomes one of the ways to choose which numbers to delete. Outside this lab, real distillation recipes train a small model on a bigger model’s guesses, usually mixed with ordinary training on the right answers. Pruning even has hardware built around it. Some newer graphics chips, which can do huge numbers of multiplications at once, have parts made to skip zeros laid out in one particular pattern. Why it matters A model’s size decides how much memory it needs and how much multiplying each guess takes. A model that is too big may not fit on the machine you have, or it may answer too slowly to be useful. The next lab, Deployment & serving, turns a model’s size into memory and speed. This module gives you two ways to bring that size down without training a new model from scratch. Without distillation, you would have to train a small model on the right answers alone, and this lab measures what that costs. In the lab’s starting setup, a small model trained that way ends up about twice as far from the teacher as a model of the same size that copied it. Its score on the right answers looks almost the same, so you only see the difference when you measure against the teacher. Pruning, for its part, lets you trim a model that is only a little too big instead of replacing it. Shrinking also has to be checked at every step. Each step passes its errors on to the next, so only a reading after every step tells you which one cost the most quality. The last card in the lab gives you exactly that reading. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these ideas in your own words: what a teacher’s full set of guesses, called soft labels, carries that a single right answer, called a one-hot label, throws away; what the Distillation temperature slider changes about the lesson the student gets, and what it leaves alone; how three patterns of pruning differ in what they really save, whether that is storage space, speed on certain special chips, or less multiplying on any computer; how to read a model’s size and quality after each step of distil, prune and quantize; how three ways of choosing what to delete compare, both in what they keep and in how much work they take to work out. What the lab lets you see and try The lab is a set of cards, and each one lets you change something and watch what happens: Student controls sets how big the students are, the temperature, and how long they train. Its Training target switch picks which student the readouts show: the one copying the teacher or the one learning from right answers. Distillation trains two students of the same size side by side, one copying the teacher and one learning from right answers, and shows how close each one ends up. Soft targets shows the teacher’s guesses after one character, next to how often each character really follows it in the text. Pruning controls and Pruning delete a share of the teacher’s numbers in three different patterns and show how much worse the teacher gets. Compose the three steps shrinks, prunes and rounds one student in a row, and it weighs and tests the model after each step. Everything in the lab is really computed: the students train in front of you, and every score comes from running a model over real text. What is small is the scale, since the teacher holds only 900 numbers and reads one character at a time. Nothing is timed, so the lab can show you size and quality, but never speed. The sizes on the last card are not measured either. They are worked out by counting bits, not by saving a real file.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: The teacher, a model small enough to see whole The teacher reads one character and guesses the next, choosing from 30 characters: the 26 letters, the space, the period, and two special markers. The Instruction tuning & templates lab uses those markers to lay out a chat, so they never appear in ordinary text like the text here. Everything the teacher learned sits in one table of 900 numbers, with 30 rows and 30 columns. Each row belongs to the character the model has been given, and each column belongs to a character that might come next. A model that looks at one character to guess the next is called a bigram model. The number where a row and a column meet is a score for how likely that pair is, and these learned numbers are called weights. The teacher learned its weights from a few short weather notes about a harbor, such as “the morning fog settles over the harbor and the air feels cool.” It went through that text 80 times, and each full pass through the training text is called an epoch. To make a guess, the model turns one row of scores into percentages that add up to 100%, so after “h”, for example, the teacher gives “e” a 76.6% chance. In the harbor notes, “e” really does follow “h” 76.0% of the time, as in the word “the”, so that guess is close to the real count. The lab grades every model with perplexity, which measures how unsure a model is, on average, when it guesses the next character of the text. A perplexity of 6.6 means the model is about as unsure as someone choosing between six or seven equally likely characters, so lower is better. The teacher scores 6.600, and every smaller model in the lab is compared with that. Perplexity is worked out from another score called the loss, which training tries to push down. The loss works like a penalty. Each time the real next character turns up, the model loses more points the lower the chance it gave that character. The loss is the average penalty over the whole text. So the loss and perplexity always rise and fall together. The teacher’s loss appears on the Student controls card as Teacher loss, where it reads 1.887. Two ways to get a smaller model Distillation trains a new, smaller model, called the student, to copy the teacher’s guesses. Pruning keeps the teacher’s own table but deletes some of its weights, and whatever survives becomes the smaller model. Because both start from the same trained teacher, the lab can show you exactly what each one costs. The teacher is needed only while the student trains, and after that the student runs on its own. How the student is built A student still has to give a score for every one of the 900 pairs of characters. It needs a way to produce them all without storing a full table. Instead, it describes each character with two short lists of numbers, one for the character when it is the one given and one for it as a possible next character. To score a pair, the student multiplies the matching entries of the two lists and adds up the results. Here is a small example with lists of two numbers. Say “h” as the given character has the list 2, 1, and “e” as a possible next character has the list 3, −1. Multiply first with first and second with second, then add: 2 × 3 + 1 × (−1) = 5, which is the score for “e” after “h”. The length of these lists is called the rank, and the Student size slider sets it from 1 to 12. At rank 6, each character gets two lists of 6 numbers. Across all 30 characters that makes 30 × 2 × 6 = 360 weights, and the slider shows this as “rank 6 · 360 weights”. Since 360 out of the teacher’s 900 is 40%, the badge on the Distillation card shows the same student as 40% of the teacher. Short lists cannot hold every detail, so a small student has to squeeze what it learns about each character into a few numbers. How much of the teacher a student of a given size can hold at all is called its student capacity. Below some size, no amount of careful teaching closes the gap, because the student has no room left for the details. It trains for as many passes through the text as Student epochs says, from 1 to 40, starting at 18. What the teacher knows that the answer key does not Picture a multiple-choice question on a quiz, where the answer key says only “C”. A good teacher marking the same question might add, “B was nearly as good, and E is ridiculous.” That ranking of the wrong answers is extra information, and the answer key throws it away. Ordinary training uses the answer key, so at each spot in the text the right answer is the character that really came next. It is written as a list of 30 numbers, with a 1 in that character’s slot and a 0 in every other slot. Only one slot is switched on, so this is called a one-hot label, and One-hot labels is one setting of the Training target switch. One-hot labels are also called hard labels, because they allow no shades in between. Distillation uses the teacher’s full set of percentages instead, including the small shares it gives to characters it rates as unlikely. These full sets of percentages are called soft labels, and the Teacher distribution setting shows the student trained on them. The information hidden in how a teacher ranks the wrong answers has an old nickname, dark knowledge. Picture two friends getting ready for the same test. One studies from an answer key, so she learns which option was right each time, and she has to piece together the rest from many questions. The other studies with a tutor who says how close each wrong option came, so he learns more from every question he practises. The student trained on soft labels is like the second friend, while the one-hot student is like the first. During training, the soft-label student is nudged after each small batch of examples, so that its percentages move closer to the teacher’s. The one-hot student is nudged toward the right answers instead, and it never looks at the teacher at all. To check how close a student came, the lab compares its percentages with the teacher’s at every spot in the text and averages the gap. If the teacher says 77% for “e” after “h” and the student says 60%, that spot adds to the gap, while a spot where they agree adds nothing. The average is shown as KL to teacher, where 0 would mean a perfect copy and a bigger number means the student is further away. KL is short for Kullback–Leibler, the two mathematicians who described this way of measuring the gap between two sets of percentages. The gap is measured in a unit called nats, which is why the callout under the controls says “nats per position”. All you need to know about nats is that smaller means closer. Here is where the quiz picture stops matching. On a quiz only one answer is right, but in text several characters can rightly come next, such as after a space. The one-hot student does learn how often each one comes next in the end, but only by averaging many single answers. The teacher, by contrast, hands over the whole spread at every step. This teacher also learned little beyond how often each character follows another, which is why its 76.6% for “e” after “h” sits so close to the text’s 76.0%. Its small guesses for characters that never follow, sometimes called the tail, carry little extra. So most of its help here comes from showing that whole spread, not from ranking wrong answers. A big teacher trained on far more text has much more dark knowledge to pass on. What temperature does Turning a row of scores into percentages can be done sharply or gently, and temperature sets how gently. Back in the quiz picture, think of the teacher handing out 100 points across the answers. At temperature 1 it hands out the points as it really rates the answers, often with a big share for its favourite. A higher temperature moves points away from the favourite and toward the long shots, so the small guesses grow. Say the teacher gives three answers 80, 15 and 5 points at temperature 1. At temperature 2 the same scores give about 59, 26 and 15, so the long shot’s share triples. Inside the lab, temperature divides every score before the percentages are worked out, which shrinks the gaps between big and small scores. Distillation softens both the teacher’s and the student’s guesses this way while the student trains, and the Distillation temperature slider sets how much, from 0.5 to 6. At its starting point it reads “T = 1 (no tempering)”, where T stands for temperature. To see the effect in real numbers, look at “h”: at temperature 1, the teacher puts 4.8% of its guesses on characters that never follow “h” in the text. At temperature 2 that share grows to 39.3%, and at temperature 4 it reaches 64.6%, which is more than half of everything the teacher guesses after “h”. So temperature changes which parts of the teacher’s guesses the training pays most attention to. It does not change what a perfect copy would be, because a student able to match the teacher exactly at one temperature would match it at every temperature. These students are too small to do that, so temperature decides where their unavoidable mistakes land. At a high temperature, training pushes a small student to get the long shots right. It pays for that by matching the big guesses, like “e” after “h”, less well. Since it is graded at temperature 1, where the big guesses matter most, it ends further away. Once training is over, the student is used and graded at temperature 1, because that is how it will run. That is why KL to teacher and the student’s bars in Soft targets always use temperature 1, whatever the slider says. Three ways to prune Pruning needs a rule for which weights to delete, where “delete” means setting a weight to exactly zero. The plainest rule removes the weights closest to zero, on the guess that numbers so small add the least. The size of a number with its minus sign ignored is called its magnitude, so this rule is called magnitude pruning. For example, −0.02 and 0.02 both have a tiny magnitude, while −3 has a large one. The share of a model’s weights that are exactly zero is called its sparsity. On the Pruning controls card, Pruned share sets how much to delete, from 0% to 90%, and Pruning mode picks the pattern the zeros must follow. Picture the teacher’s table as a spreadsheet with 30 rows and 30 columns, which is exactly what the grid on the Pruning card draws: Unstructured, which is unstructured pruning, blanks the smallest cells wherever they happen to be, so the gaps end up scattered across the sheet. 2:4 semi-structured, which is semi-structured sparsity, walks down each column in groups of four cells and blanks the two smallest in every group. A column of 30 cells makes seven groups of four plus one leftover pair, where one cell goes, so exactly half the cells still go. Structured rows, which is structured pruning, blanks whole rows, choosing the rows whose numbers are smallest overall, and the Rows removed readout counts them. In 2:4 mode the pattern fixes the share, so the slider reads “fixed at 50% by 2:4”. Each row of the table holds everything the teacher learned about what follows one character. If every score in a row is 0, no character beats any other, so all 30 get the same share, about 3.3% each. That is as if the teacher had never seen that character. What each pattern really saves In a real model, every guess involves multiplying through big grids of weights like this one. A zero still sits in its place in the grid, so the computer multiplies by it like any other number unless it has a special way to skip it. That is why the three patterns save such different things, even when they remove the same share of weights: Scattered zeros mostly save storage, and only when the model is stored in a layout that keeps the surviving values plus a note of where each one belongs. That layout is called a sparse format, and even with one, scattered zeros save little time. The 2:4 pattern is regular enough that some newer NVIDIA graphics chips, called GPUs, can skip its zeros, using special parts called sparse tensor cores. On those chips, that makes the multiplying up to about twice as fast. Removing whole rows makes the grid itself smaller, so there is less to multiply on any computer. In a real model, a row stands for a part such as a neuron, a single unit of calculation, which can be taken out completely. That is the saving people usually want, but at the same share it costs the most quality. Running the three steps together The Compose the three steps card chains distillation, pruning and quantization into one compression pipeline. It works like packing for a trip in three steps. First you swap to a smaller suitcase, which is distilling into the student, and then you take out the items you need least, which is pruning. Finally you vacuum-seal what is left, which is quantizing. After each step, the card weighs the bag and checks how well you can still make the trip. To weigh the bag, the card counts bits, and a bit is the smallest piece of computer storage, a single 0 or 1. Eight bits make one byte, which the lab writes as B, and before any rounding, each stored value takes 32 bits, which is 4 bytes. So the teacher’s 900 weights take 3,600 bytes, and the rank-6 student’s 360 weights take 1,440 bytes. The student is stored as its two sets of short lists, which is why its size depends on its rank. Here the packing picture needs a warning. Taking an item out of a suitcase frees its space, but a zero in a stored model still fills a full 32-bit slot. Pruning saves room only with a sparse format, which stores just the kept values plus a note of where each one goes. Here that note is a mask: one bit per position, 1 for a kept value and 0 for a removed one. Say you keep 4 of 8 values. You store those 4 values plus the 8 bits 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0, so the computer knows where each kept value belongs. Here is how the numbers work out when half the student’s values are pruned. The 180 values it keeps cost 720 bytes, and the mask adds one bit for each of the 360 positions, which comes to 45 bytes. Together they make the 765 bytes shown on the Pruned row, about half of what the student took before pruning. Quantizing then rounds each kept value so that it fits in fewer bits, which is the trick from the Quantization lab. At 4 bits, a value can only be one of 16 levels, because 4 bits can be set 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 ways. Every group of 32 values also stores two extra 16-bit numbers that say how to turn those levels back into real values. Final bit width sets the bits per kept value from 2 to 8. At 4 bits, the 180 kept values take 720 bits, which is 90 bytes. They fill 6 groups, and each group’s two extra numbers add 4 bytes, so 24 bytes in all. The mask still adds 45 bytes, and 90 + 24 + 45 makes the 159 bytes of the pruned student after quantizing. The packing picture also stops matching at the last step. A vacuum-sealed jacket comes out as the same jacket, but a rounded value is not quite the number it was before. Every step in this pipeline loses a little quality, and the card measures how much. Choosing what to cut The prune step on this card needs a way to decide which values matter least. Any rule like that is called an importance score, and the Importance score control offers three of them: Magnitude uses the size of each value, read straight off the numbers, so it needs no extra work at all. Activation-weighted multiplies each value’s size by how big its input usually is while the model runs. That input is called an activation, so this is an activation-weighted score, and it needs one pass through the text to measure the inputs. In this lab, the input tracks how often a character shows up in the text. So values linked to common characters, like “e” and the space, score higher than values linked to rare ones. Measured ablation removes each value on its own, runs the model over the text, and records how much worse the loss gets. This is the ablation test from the interpretability labs, applied to one value at a time. It needs one run through the text for every value, so 360 runs at rank 6. The text a score studies to decide what to cut is called the calibration text, and here it is the harbor notes. The Passes to score readout shows how many runs through the text the chosen score needs, which is 0, 1 or 360. Picture a coach who has to cut half the players from a big squad. She could cut the players with the weakest stats, which is quick. She could instead weigh each player’s stats by how many minutes they usually play, which means going through the season’s records once. A third choice is to play a full practice match without each player in turn and see how much the team’s score drops. That tells her the most, but it costs one whole match per player.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Distillation solves a specific problem with learning from right answers, which you can see by looking at what follows a space in the harbor notes. Sometimes it is “t”, sometimes “a”, and sometimes “s” or “w”, but a one-hot label shows only one of these at a time. So a student sees “a” at one step and “t” at the next, and it has to average many of these noisy nudges to work out the real shares. A soft label carries the whole spread at every step, so the student gets the full picture each time instead of piecing it together. That is why a student that copies the teacher can get closer with the same size and the same amount of training. Pruning solves a different problem, and it suits a model that is nearly the right size already. It keeps the trained weights and trims a share of them without building a new model. The share and the pattern you choose then decide whether you save storage, time, or both. These steps also stack, because distillation cuts the number of weights, pruning removes a share of what remains, and quantization shrinks the bits each survivor takes. Together, they can make a model far smaller than any one step could on its own.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Copy the teacher Try this: leave Student size at rank 6 and Distillation temperature at 1, then flip Training target between Teacher distribution and One-hot labels while you watch KL to teacher. The copying student ends 0.1348 away from the teacher, while the one that saw only right answers ends 0.2577 away, almost twice as far. Now look at the chart on the Distillation card, which tracks each student’s loss on the right answers as it trains. The solid line for soft labels and the dashed line for hard labels nearly overlap, even though one student ends up almost twice as close to the teacher. The copying student ends at a Student loss of 2.119, and the other student ends at 2.175. The dotted line is the finished teacher, which no student here is expected to reach. Tune the temperature Keep Teacher distribution selected and move Distillation temperature from 0.5 up to 6, reading KL to teacher at each stop: At 0.5, which sharpens the teacher’s guesses instead of softening them, it reads 0.4037. At 1, the starting point, it reads 0.1348. At 1.5 it reads 0.1340, the closest the student gets at any of these stops. At 2 it reads 0.1407, which is a little further away again. At 4 it reads 0.2193, which is still closer than the one-hot student. At 6 it reads 0.2737, which is now further away than the one-hot student’s 0.2577. Then go to Soft targets and pick “h” with Context character. Each of the ten likeliest next characters gets three bars, and a “rest” row collects everything else. The top bar, “one-hot labels, averaged”, shows how often that character really follows “h” in the text. The middle bar shows the teacher at the current temperature, and the bottom bar shows the student. The student is always shown at temperature 1, so compare it with the teacher bar only when the slider is at 1. At other settings the teacher bar is softened, and the two are not meant to match. Below the bars, the readout Teacher mass on unseen next characters, T = 1 stays at 4.8%. Mass here means share of the guesses, so this is the share the teacher puts on characters that never follow “h”. The one beside it, labelled “Same, at T =” with the current temperature, follows the slider, reaching 39.3% at temperature 2 and 64.6% at 4. Now set the temperature back to 1, switch Training target to One-hot labels, and pick “␣”, the space. The hard-label student gives “a” a 46.2% chance after a space, even though the text says 14.1%. Switch back to Teacher distribution, and the soft-label student gives “a” 14.6%, close to the real count. Prune by magnitude On Pruning controls, keep Pruning mode on Unstructured and drag Pruned share down to 0%, since it starts at 30%. Then raise it step by step, watching the perplexity badge at the top of the Pruning card. With nothing removed, the badge reads 6.60, and at 30% it has barely moved, to 6.61. At 50% it still reads only 6.65, so half of the teacher’s weights are gone at almost no cost. After that, the curve bends upward, reaching 6.84 at 70% and 8.07 at 90%. Back on the Pruning controls card, the teacher and the pruned table each write 68 characters starting from “the ”. Each one picks a next character from its guesses, adds it to the text, and then guesses again from it. The label above the pruned sample counts how many characters differ, so you can see the damage in actual text as well as in the score. Compare the three shapes Set Pruned share to 50% and switch Pruning mode between its three settings. The perplexity badge reads 6.65 for Unstructured and 7.15 for 2:4 semi-structured, while Structured rows reaches 8.22. Watch the grid change as you switch: blanks scattered everywhere, then exactly two in every four down each column, and then whole empty rows, with Rows removed at 15 / 30. Compose the stages Put the Student controls card back to its starting values, which are rank 6, temperature 1, 18 epochs and Teacher distribution. Then go to Compose the three steps, set Share pruned from the student to 50%, Final bit width to 4 and Importance score to Magnitude, and read the four rows: Teacher shows 3,600 B at perplexity 6.600, the starting point for everything else. Distilled student drops to 1,440 B, while perplexity rises to 8.326. Pruned drops further to 765 B, with perplexity at 8.560. Quantized ends at 159 B, with perplexity at 8.619. The badge says the final model is 22.6 times smaller than the teacher. In exchange, its perplexity rose from 6.600 to 8.619, which makes it 30.6% worse. Change the importance score Raise Share pruned from the student to 70% and switch Importance score between its three settings. The second bar list shows the perplexity right after the prune step for all three scores, along with the passes each one needs: Magnitude leaves a perplexity of 9.682 and needs 0 passes, since it reads the values directly. Activation-weighted leaves 9.999 and needs 1 pass to measure the inputs. Measured ablation leaves 9.480 and needs 360 passes, one for every value.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Copying wins at every size, at temperature 1: at rank 2 the copying student lands at 0.4200, against 0.4668 for the one-hot student. At rank 12 it lands at 0.0722, against 0.1295. Each soft-label update shows the whole spread of guesses, while each one-hot update shows one sampled answer. A low loss does not mean a close copy: the two loss curves nearly overlap, even though one student is twice as close to the teacher. Fitting the right answers and matching the teacher are different questions, and only KL to teacher shows the second one. Size sets a ceiling: student capacity decides how much a student can match at all, and rank 12 gets nearly six times closer to the teacher than rank 2. Temperature has a sweet spot, which here sits near 1 to 1.5. From 4 upward, the rank-6 student spends its limited room on the tail of small guesses, and at 6 it ends further away than the one-hot student. Right answers alone can mislead a small student: after a space, the one-hot student’s 46.2% on “a” is more than three times the text’s 14.1%. The soft-label student’s 14.6% is close to the real count. The first cuts are nearly free: at 30%, unstructured pruning costs almost nothing, since perplexity moves from 6.60 to only 6.61. Both modes first remove the four rows the text never uses, for “j”, “x” and the two markers, whose weights are already zero. After that, unstructured removes 150 more of the smallest weights, wherever they sit. Structured has to blank 5 whole rows the text does use, big weights included, so at 30% it already reaches 6.95. A pruned table can still write the same text, because the weights it lost may be ones that this particular piece of writing never needed. 2:4 sits between the two curves: a forced pattern costs more than free choice at the same share, but less than deleting whole rows. The three steps are not priced alike: distilling saves 2,160 bytes for 1.73 more perplexity. Pruning saves 675 bytes for 0.23 more, and quantizing saves 606 bytes for only 0.06 more. Drop Final bit width to 2, though, and the quantize step costs 1.34. The best score is the slow one: Measured ablation leaves the lowest perplexity at 70%, because it asks the loss directly what each value is worth. The price is one test per value, which is 360 here. The quick shortcut loses on this toy: Activation-weighted does worse than plain Magnitude. Here, the size of a value’s input only tracks how often its character shows up. That tells you how many guesses a value touches, but not how much each of those guesses changes when the value is removed. On this toy, that leads it to keep the wrong values.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Every loss, KL and perplexity in the lab is really computed, but on a toy. It has 900 weights and one character of context. A real model has many stacked layers, steps of calculation done one after another, and this toy has none of them. The teacher learned almost exactly the text’s own counts, so its dark knowledge is a thin tail. The lab shows how distillation works, not how much it helps when the teacher is big. KL to teacher skips the four characters that never appear in the harbor text at all, which are “j”, “x” and the two markers. Neither model was trained on those rows. Each student is a slimmed-down copy of the teacher’s own shape, not a model with a different design. Each student trains either purely on the teacher or purely on right answers, with no mix, and every result comes from one random starting point, called a seed. Pruning happens once, with no retraining afterward to win back quality. Nothing is timed either, so the speed claims come from how the chips work, not from a stopwatch. The compose card does no retraining between steps and removes the same share from both sets of lists. It also uses the harbor text twice: as the calibration text that picks what to cut, and as the text that tests the result. So for the scores that study that text, the perplexity after pruning looks better than it would on new text. A row of the teacher’s table stands in for a neuron or a group of neurons that a real model would remove. Here the row is only set to zero and stays in the table, so nothing actually gets smaller. The compose card’s sizes are bit counts worked out on paper, not the size of a real file on a disk. Where the real methods fall short A common mix-up: deleting half the weights does not make a model twice as fast. Picture a friend helping to mark a stack of quizzes in which half the answer boxes are blank, using a marking sheet that makes him check every box anyway. The blanks save him no time, and only taking those questions off the quiz would. Scattered zeros work the same way, since the computer still multiplies by every one of them. So unstructured sparsity mostly saves storage, and only with a sparse format. A strict 2:4 pattern can make the multiplying up to about twice as fast, but only on GPUs built to spot that pattern. Deleting whole rows shrinks the grid, which saves work on any computer. Magnitude is the crudest importance score. The authors of a pruning method called Wanda report that, on large models, also weighing how big each weight’s input is does much better than size alone. On large models a few inputs are far bigger than the rest, and weighing by input catches weights that size alone would cut. You can read more about Wanda in Going deeper, and this toy reverses that result for the reason given in What to notice. A student also copies its teacher’s mistakes along with its skills, and matching the next-character guesses does not, on its own, pass on behaviour that takes many steps. That is why a variant called sequence-level distillation exists, aimed at exactly that gap. Measured ablation has limits of its own, since it tests one value at a time and misses values that matter only in combination. Think of two players who can each cover for the other. Benching either one alone barely changes the score, so the test rates both as unimportant, even though cutting both would hurt badly. Ablation also needs one test per value, which is out of reach when a model has billions of them.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Real distillation usually mixes the softened copying lesson with ordinary right-answer training, while this lab keeps the two apart. Both the lab and real recipes multiply the copying lesson by the temperature squared, so each training step stays about the same size whatever temperature you pick. Real teachers learn far more than how often one character follows another, so the way they rank wrong answers carries much more. A higher temperature lifts those small guesses, which is where that ranking lives. There are two explanations for why soft labels help. The first says each position carries a whole set of percentages instead of one sampled answer, so there is more to learn from. The second says the teacher’s percentages are smoother than the raw right answers, so they make gentler targets to aim at. This lab mostly shows the first, since its teacher barely differs from the text’s own counts. Composing the steps The usual order is to prune or distil first, retrain to win back quality, and quantize last, because quantizing assumes the weights are final. Each step also inherits the errors of the one before it, and its own cost depends a lot on the settings. In the lab, the 4-bit quantize step adds only 0.06 to the pruned student’s perplexity. At 2 bits the same step adds 1.34 to that pruned student. Set Share pruned from the student to 0% so nothing is pruned, and at 2 bits it costs 1.76. The Quantization lab prices that last step in detail, and Deployment & serving turns the result into memory and speed. Importance scores beyond magnitude A method called Wanda multiplies each weight’s size by the size of the input it meets, and it compares weights only against others that feed the same output. Its authors report that it does much better than size alone on a family of large language models called LLaMA. Another method, SparseGPT, works layer by layer, choosing what to remove and adjusting what stays so that each layer’s output changes as little as possible. Both methods prune large models in one go without retraining, and they exist to close the gap between magnitude, which is cheap but crude, and measured ablation. Ablation is the most direct test, but it needs one run per weight.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: This module measures two ways to get a smaller model from a trained one: train a small student to imitate the large teacher (distillation), or delete some of the teacher's weights (pruning). It then chains distillation, pruning, and quantization, and prices each stage in bytes saved and perplexity added. The questions are what a student gains from the teacher's whole distribution rather than the labels, what each pattern of zeros actually saves, and which stage of the chain costs the most quality per byte. It builds on Quantization, whose rounding becomes the last stage, and on Interpretability II: circuits, whose ablation becomes one way to score which weights to prune. Where it shows up Distillation recipes. Production recipes usually mix the soft-label loss with ordinary cross-entropy on the labels. Sequence-level distillation exists because matching next-token distributions does not by itself transfer multi-step behaviour. Sparse hardware. NVIDIA's sparse tensor cores, Ampere and later, skip the zeros of an exact 2:4 pattern (two zeros in every four consecutive weights) for up to about twice the matmul throughput. Pruning large models. Wanda and SparseGPT both prune large models one-shot, without retraining, using more than a weight's magnitude: Wanda its input activations, SparseGPT second-order information. Compression pipelines. The usual order prunes or distils, fine-tunes to recover, and quantizes last, because quantization assumes the weights are final. Why it matters A smaller model is worth having only if the saving is real and the quality cost is known. A student trained on one-hot labels sees one sampled answer per position. At the lab's default size and temperature (rank 6, T = 1) it ends about twice as far from the teacher as a same-size soft-label student, with nearly the same cross-entropy on the labels. Zeroed weights still sit inside a dense matrix multiply, so scattered zeros save storage only in a sparse format, a layout that records where the surviving values are, and save little time. Each stage of a pipeline also inherits the error of the one before, so only a reading after every stage shows which step spent the quality. What you will be able to explain What soft labels carry that one-hot labels discard: the teacher's ranking of the wrong answers. What distillation temperature controls: which errors the loss weighs, not where the optimum lies for a student that can match the teacher. How unstructured, 2:4 semi-structured, and structured pruning differ in what each actually saves: storage, matmul throughput, or the size of the matrices. How to read perplexity and stored size after each stage of distil, prune, and quantize, and how to compare importance scores by the quality they keep and the passes they cost to compute. What the lab shows Every loss, KL divergence, and perplexity is computed from trained weights on one small corpus, each from a single seed. The teacher is the 900-weight bigram table from the tiny language-model labs. A soft-label student and a one-hot student of the same size retrain whenever Student size, Distillation temperature, or Student epochs changes; Training target only picks which of the two the metrics and later cards use. Student controls sets Training target (Teacher distribution or One-hot labels), Student size, Distillation temperature, and Student epochs, and reports KL to teacher. The Distillation card draws both students' loss curves and KL, and Soft targets shows the next-character distributions after one Context character. Pruning controls sets Pruned share and Pruning mode on the teacher, and the Pruning card plots perplexity against the share removed and draws the mask of kept weights. Compose the three steps adds Importance score, Share pruned from the student, and Final bit width, and lists stored size and perplexity for each stage, from Teacher to Quantized. Nothing is timed, and stored sizes are idealized bit counts, not a file format. The key experiment: at rank 6 and T = 1, flip Training target. The loss curves nearly overlap, yet KL to teacher roughly doubles with One-hot labels. Then switch Importance score at a 70% share and weigh perplexity after pruning against Passes to score.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Two ways to end up with a smaller model, both measured on the same trained weights. Distillation trains a small model against a large one's output distribution. Pruning deletes weights from the large model and keeps what is left. The teacher is the 900-weight logit table from the tiny language-model labs, trained for 80 epochs to loss 1.887 and perplexity 6.600. Each student is a rank-limited factorization U · V, so Student size at rank r holds 2 × r × 30 weights: 360 at rank 6. The distillation objective Soft labels are the teacher's full next-character distribution. Their gradient with respect to the student's logits is T · (p_student,T − p_teacher,T); the T² factor keeps step sizes comparable across temperatures. Teacher distribution trains on L_soft alone; One-hot labels trains on ordinary cross-entropy. Production recipes usually mix the two. Temperature and dark knowledge Temperature divides both models' logits inside the loss. It does not move the optimum — a student that can match the teacher's logits up to a constant matches it at every T — but it changes which errors the loss weighs. High T lifts small probabilities, where the ranking of wrong answers, the dark knowledge, lives. Three shapes of pruning Magnitude pruning removes the weights nearest zero. Pruning mode picks the pattern: Unstructured (unstructured pruning, zeros anywhere), 2:4 semi-structured (semi-structured sparsity, two of every four weights down each column), and Structured rows (structured pruning, whole context rows by L2 norm). Running the three steps together The Compose the three steps card runs a compression pipeline on one student. It stores the student as its two factors, prunes them with an importance score you choose, then quantizes what survives, and reports stored size and perplexity after each stage. The size counts bits: 32 per value, plus one mask bit per position once anything is pruned, which is a sparse format.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: The next lab budgets memory and speed from a parameter count; these are the two levers that change it without training from scratch. Many small open models learned from a larger model's outputs, and pruning suits a model that is nearly the right size already.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: At rank 6 and T = 1, flip Training target. Soft labels reach loss 2.119 and KL to teacher 0.1348; one-hot labels reach 2.175 and 0.2577. KL is measured at every corpus position, so each context counts as often as the data uses it. Sweep Distillation temperature: KL reads 0.4037 at T = 0.5, 0.1348 at 1, 0.1340 at 1.5, 0.1407 at 2, 0.2193 at 4, and 0.2737 at 6. Then open Soft targets on “h”: the teacher puts 4.8% on characters that never follow “h” at T = 1, 39.3% at T = 2, 64.6% at T = 4. Raise Pruned share on Unstructured: 6.60 unpruned, 6.61 at 30%, 6.65 at 50%, 6.84 at 70%, 8.07 at 90%. At 50%, 2:4 semi-structured gives 7.15 and Structured rows 8.22. In Compose the three steps, at rank 6 with a 50% share and 4 bits, the Teacher is 3,600 B at perplexity 6.600; the Distilled student 1,440 B at 8.326; Pruned 765 B at 8.560; and Quantized 159 B at 8.619. That is 22.6 times smaller for +30.6% perplexity. Raise Share pruned from the student to 70% and switch Importance score. After pruning, Magnitude reads 9.682, Activation-weighted 9.999, and Measured ablation 9.480, for 0, 1, and 360 passes to score.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Soft labels win at every rank: 0.4200 against 0.4668 KL at rank 2, 0.0722 against 0.1295 at rank 12. Each soft update carries the whole distribution; a one-hot update carries one sampled character, so the hard student averages noisier signals. The loss curves nearly overlap while KL differs twofold. Fitting the labels and matching the teacher are different questions. Student capacity decides how much a student can match at all: rank 12 gets nearly six times closer than rank 2. Temperature has a shallow optimum near 1 to 1.5 here. At T = 4 and above, the rank-6 student spends its capacity on the tail. On “␣” with One-hot labels, the hard student gives “a” 46.2% where the labels say 14.1%; the soft student gives 14.6%. 2:4 sits between the curves: a forced pattern costs more than free choice, less than deleting rows. The stages are not equally priced. In the 4-bit run distilling saves 2,160 B for +1.73 perplexity, pruning 675 B for +0.23, and quantizing 606 B for +0.06. At 2 bits quantizing costs +1.34. The best score here is the expensive one. Measured ablation zeroes each value in turn and asks the loss; it needs one pass per value, 360 here, and ranks first at 70%. The cheap proxy loses. Activation-weighted scores do worse than magnitude on this toy: in a one-hot bigram an input's activation is only how often its context occurs, which ignores how much the softmax cares about each logit.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: In this lab. Every loss, KL, and perplexity is computed. The scale is a toy: 900 weights, one character of context, no layers. This teacher learned almost exactly the corpus's bigram frequencies — 76.6% for “e” after “h” against 76.0% in the labels — so its dark knowledge is a thin smoothing tail. KL skips the four context rows the corpus never visits. The student is a low-rank copy of the teacher's own shape, not a different architecture. Pruning is one-shot with no recovery fine-tune, and nothing is timed: the speed claims below come from how kernels work, not from measurement. Each result is one seed. The compose card has no fine-tune between stages, removes the same share from both factors, and uses one corpus for the scores and the perplexity, which flatters any score calibrated on it. Its sizes are bit counts, not a file format. In real systems. Zeroed weights still sit inside a dense matrix multiply, so unstructured sparsity saves storage only with a sparse format, and little time. NVIDIA's sparse tensor cores (Ampere and later) skip the zeros of an exact 2:4 pattern for up to about twice the matmul throughput. Structured pruning shrinks the matrices themselves. Magnitude is the crudest importance score. Wanda scores each weight by its magnitude times the norm of its input activation, compared per output, and its authors report that it significantly outperforms magnitude pruning on LLaMA models. SparseGPT instead solves a layer-wise reconstruction with second-order information. Both prune large models one-shot, without retraining (arXiv 2306.11695 and 2301.00774, abstracts checked 30 September 2026). The toy reverses the first result, for the reason in What to notice. Students inherit their teacher's mistakes, and matching next-token distributions does not transfer multi-step behaviour on its own, which is why sequence-level distillation exists.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Two accounts explain soft targets. The information account: each position carries a whole distribution instead of one sampled answer. The regularization account: the teacher's distribution is smoother than the labels. This lab mostly shows the first, since this teacher barely differs from its labels. Composing the steps Compression steps compose, and order matters. The usual pipeline prunes or distills, fine-tunes to recover, then quantizes last, because quantization assumes the weights are final. Each stage inherits the error of the one before: here the 4-bit quantize stage adds only +0.06 on top of a pruned student, but the same stage on the full student at 2 bits costs +1.76. The Quantization lab prices that last step; Deployment & serving turns the result into memory and tokens per second. Importance scores beyond magnitude An activation-weighted score needs data: one pass over calibration text to measure the inputs. A measured ablation is the causal version, the ablation of the interpretability labs applied to weights. It is exact for one weight at a time, misses interactions between weights, and costs a pass per weight, which is out of reach when a model has billions of them. That is the gap proxies such as Wanda are built to close.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Student controls · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Size, target, temperature, and how long the student trains The knobs that define the student: how wide its factorization is, whether it imitates the teacher's distribution or the one-hot labels, how much both distributions are softened in the loss, and how many passes it gets. Both students retrain on every change, so the comparison is always live. `Training target`: `Teacher distribution` (soft) or `One-hot labels` (hard). `Student size` from rank 1 to 12, printed as `rank r · 60r weights`. `Distillation temperature` from 0.5 to 6, and `Student epochs` from 1 to 40. Metrics `Student loss` (hard-label corpus cross-entropy of the selected student), `Teacher loss`, and `KL to teacher`, plus a callout comparing the two students' KL. Soft labels minimize T² · KL(softmax(teacher/T) ‖ softmax(student/T)) at every corpus position. Its gradient with respect to the student's logits is T · (student_T − teacher_T), which keeps step sizes comparable across temperatures. Hard labels minimize ordinary cross-entropy against the next character. The teacher is never read during that update. `KL to teacher` is KL(teacher ‖ student) at T = 1, averaged over the corpus's own positions, so each context counts as often as the data uses it. All four controls retrain both students; `Distillation temperature` only affects the soft one. Comparison worth running: at rank 6, sweep T through 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 4, and 6. KL reads 0.4037, 0.1348, 0.1340, 0.1407, 0.2193, and 0.2737 against the hard student's 0.2577. Soft labels win at every rank here: 0.4200 against 0.4668 at rank 2, 0.1348 against 0.2577 at rank 6, 0.0722 against 0.1295 at rank 12 (all at T = 1). Temperature has a shallow optimum near 1 to 1.5. Very high T spends the student's limited rank on matching tiny probabilities. In this lab: the loss is either pure soft or pure hard, with no mixing weight, and every run uses seed 3. In general: production distillation usually blends the tempered KL with a hard-label term, and uses a teacher far more confident than a bigram.
documents.title: Size, target, temperature, and how long the student trains

documents.subtitle: Distillation · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Two students of the same size, two targets Training curves for the soft-label and hard-label students, both measured with the same hard-label cross-entropy, and a bar pair for how far each ended up from the teacher's distribution. A kicker `Teacher 900 weights · student N` and a badge with the student's share of the teacher's parameters. A chart of minibatch hard-label loss against optimizer step: solid soft, dashed hard, dotted teacher. Bars for KL(teacher ‖ student) over the corpus's own contexts, lower is closer; the selected target is emphasized. The teacher is a 30 × 30 character bigram trained 80 epochs on Harbor weather notes at seed 1: loss 1.887, perplexity 6.600. Each student's logits are U · V with inner dimension `rank`, so it has 2 · rank · 30 weights. Both use batch 16, learning rate 0.5, and seed 3. The KL average skips the four context rows the corpus never visits (j, x, <, >): neither model was trained there. No controls of its own; everything on Student controls redraws it. Comparison worth running: flip Training target and read the emphasis move. Both bars are real runs whichever is selected. The two loss curves nearly overlap even when the KL bars differ by a factor of two. Hard-label loss is not the same question as closeness to the teacher. The dotted line is a finished 80-epoch model with no rank limit; the students are not expected to reach it. In this lab: a 900-weight bigram teacher and low-rank students on one short corpus. In general: a student inherits the teacher's errors along with its skills, and matching next-token distributions does not by itself transfer multi-step behaviour.

documents.subtitle: Soft targets · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: What one context's soft label looks like For one context character, three next-character distributions side by side: the one-hot labels averaged over the corpus (the frequencies a hard-label student chases), the teacher at the current temperature (the soft target), and the selected student at T = 1. `Context character`: ␣, h, t, e, o, or s, and a kicker counting how many different characters follow it in the corpus. For the teacher's ten most likely next characters plus a `rest` row: grey bar for label frequency, accent bar for the teacher at T, blue bar for the student, and the three percentages. Metrics for the teacher's probability mass on next characters that never follow this context in the corpus, at T = 1 and at the current T. Label frequency counts corpus bigrams starting with the context. Teacher and student bars are row softmaxes of their logit tables. The unseen mass sums the teacher's probability over characters with zero label frequency, excluding the two reserved symbols. `Context character` here; `Distillation temperature` and `Training target` on Student controls. Comparison worth running: after “h”, the teacher puts 4.8% on unseen characters at T = 1, 39.3% at T = 2, and 64.6% at T = 4. Then pick ␣ with One-hot labels: the hard student gives “a” 46.2% where the labels say 14.1%. At T = 1 the teacher is close to the label frequencies (76.6% against 76.0% for “e” after “h”). A bigram teacher knows little beyond the counts, so its dark knowledge is a thin tail. Temperature reshapes the target the soft student sees; the student bars stay at T = 1 because that is how it will be used. In this lab: six context characters and a top-ten view of a 30-way distribution. In general: a large teacher's soft labels carry similarity structure (which wrong tokens are plausible) that label counts cannot, which is where distillation earns most of its value.
documents.title: What one context's soft label looks like

documents.subtitle: Pruning controls · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: How much to delete, and in what shape The two decisions magnitude pruning needs: the share of weights to zero, and the pattern of the zeros. The two samples use the same prompt and seed, so any difference is the missing weights. `Pruned share` from 0% to 90%, reading `fixed at 50% by 2:4` in 2:4 mode. `Pruning mode`: `Unstructured`, `2:4 semi-structured`, or `Structured rows`. Samples from the teacher and the pruned table: prompt “the ”, temperature 0.7, 68 characters, seed 4, with a count of differing characters. Unstructured zeroes the round(share × 900) smallest-magnitude weights anywhere. 2:4 keeps the two largest of every four consecutive weights down each column (along the context dimension); the leftover pair of rows keeps one of two. Exactly 450 zeros. Structured zeroes the round(share × 30) context rows with the smallest L2 norm. `Pruned share` and `Pruning mode`. Comparison worth running: at 50%, Unstructured gives perplexity 6.65, 2:4 gives 7.15, and Structured rows give 8.22. Identical samples at a non-zero share are possible: the removed weights may be ones this draw never needed. The note under the samples is the serving distinction: scattered zeros do not skip work, a 2:4 pattern can on supporting hardware, and removed rows shrink the matrix. In this lab: nothing is timed, so the speed claims are stated from how dense and sparse kernels work, not measured. In general: pruning is usually followed by fine-tuning to recover quality; here the zeros are one-shot.
documents.title: How much to delete, and in what shape

documents.subtitle: Pruning · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Quality against the share deleted, and the shape of the mask Perplexity of the teacher with a rising share of weights set to zero, for unstructured and whole-row pruning, with the fixed 2:4 point at 50%, and a 30 × 30 map of which weights the current setting kept. A chart of share removed (0–90%) against perplexity: solid unstructured, dashed structured, a diamond for 2:4, and a marker at the current share. A mask grid: rows are context characters, columns next characters. Filled cells are kept and shaded by magnitude; empty outlined cells are zero. Metrics `Unpruned`, `Pruned`, and `Rows removed`. Each point re-prunes the frozen teacher and re-measures exp of corpus cross-entropy. Nothing is retrained. The mask is the current setting's zero pattern, from the same pruning call that produced `Pruned`. No controls of its own; `Pruned share` and `Pruning mode` move the marker, the mask, and the metrics. Comparison worth running: at 30%, unstructured costs almost nothing (6.61) because it removes the four never-used rows and the smallest logits first; structured already costs 6.95. The 2:4 diamond sits between the two curves: a constrained pattern costs more than free choice at the same share and less than deleting rows. Unstructured is nearly flat to 50% and then bends: 6.65 at 50%, 6.84 at 70%, 8.07 at 90%. In this lab: a row of a bigram table stands in for a head or neuron, and magnitude is the only importance score on this card; the next card adds two more. In general: unstructured sparsity saves little time on dense hardware, 2:4 gives up to about 2× on the matmul with supporting tensor cores, and structured pruning shrinks the model itself.
documents.title: Quality against the share deleted, and the shape of the mask

documents.subtitle: Compose the three steps · Distillation & pruning
documents.body: Distil, prune, quantize: size and perplexity after each stage The student from the cards above is stored as its two factors, pruned by an importance score, then quantized, and its stored size and corpus perplexity are re-measured after each stage. A second bar list holds the pruned share fixed and compares three importance scores: magnitude, activation-weighted, and measured ablation. `Importance score` (`Magnitude`, `Activation-weighted`, `Measured ablation`), `Share pruned from the student` (0 to 90%), and `Final bit width` (2 to 8). The student itself comes from Student controls. A bar list with one row per stage, `Teacher`, `Distilled student`, `Pruned`, and `Quantized`: bar length is stored bytes, and the detail line gives the stored values, bits each, and perplexity with its change on the teacher's 6.600. The badge is the teacher's size over the final size. A second bar list with the three scores' perplexity after the prune stage at the current share, drawn as the rise over the unpruned student, with the passes each score needs to compute. Metrics `Final perplexity`, `Final size`, `Passes to score`, and `Values kept`. Distil: the student's table is exactly rank-limited, so a one-sided Jacobi factorization splits it into U (30 × r) and W (r × 30) with U·W equal to the table to float precision. The student stores those 60r values. Prune scores every factor entry and zeroes the lowest-scored round(share × 30r) of each factor. Magnitude is |w|, the rule of the Pruning card. Activation-weighted is |w| times the norm of the input over the corpus: the square root of the context's count for U, and the square root of the count-weighted squares of U's component for W, a Wanda-style score. Measured ablation is the rise in corpus cross-entropy when that one entry is set to zero, computed exactly from the corpus's bigram counts. Sizes use a 32-bit baseline. Teacher: 900 × 32 bits = 3,600 B. Student: 360 × 32 = 1,440 B at rank 6. Pruned: kept values × 32 bits plus one mask bit per position when anything was removed. Quantized: the kept values in storage order through the SDK's group quantizer, blocks of 32 with two 16-bit numbers each, so kept × bits + blocks × 32 + the mask. Pruned positions stay zero. Passes to score: 0 for magnitude, 1 for activation-weighted, and one per factor entry (60 × rank) for ablation. Every perplexity is the exponent of the corpus cross-entropy on the harbor text, which is also the calibration text for the last two scores. `Importance score`, `Share pruned from the student`, and `Final bit width` redraw both bar lists. The student comes from the Student controls card: its rank, target, temperature, and epochs. Comparison worth running at rank 6, T = 1, 18 epochs, 50% and 4 bits: Teacher 3,600 B at 6.600, Distilled student 1,440 B at 8.326, Pruned 765 B at 8.560, Quantized 159 B at 8.619. That is 22.6 times smaller for +30.6% perplexity. Then raise the share to 70% and compare the scores after pruning: Magnitude 9.682, Activation-weighted 9.999, and Measured ablation 9.480, for 0, 1, and 360 passes. The stages buy different things: distilling saves 2,160 B for +1.73 perplexity, pruning 675 B for +0.23, and quantizing 606 B for +0.06 at 4 bits. At 2 bits the quantize stage costs +1.34. Activation-weighted does not beat magnitude here, the opposite of what Wanda's authors report on LLaMA models. In a one-hot bigram an input's activation is only how often its context occurs: there are no outlier channels for magnitude to miss, and the score ignores how much the softmax cares about each logit. Pruning only saves bytes here because of the mask, a sparse format: 180 zeros out of 360 values cost 360 mask bits, and a dense matrix multiply would still touch every position. In this lab: there is no fine-tuning after pruning or quantizing, both factors lose the same share, the scores and the perplexity share one corpus and one seed, and the sizes are idealized bit counts rather than a file format. In general: real pipelines recover quality by fine-tuning between stages, prune in shapes the hardware can skip, calibrate on text held apart from the evaluation, and measure speed on the target hardware as well as size.

documents.subtitle: Turn a query and twelve passages into vectors, rank them by cosine or dot product, and watch an approximate index trade recall for fewer comparisons.
documents.body: Turn a query and twelve passages into vectors, rank them by cosine or dot product, and watch an approximate index trade recall for fewer comparisons. Compute cosine similarity and dot product between a query vector and passage vectors, and explain when the two rank differently Explain why dense retrieval can match a paraphrase that keyword search misses, and why the nearest passage is not proof of truth or of an answer Read recall@k to say what an approximate index gives up in exchange for scoring fewer vectors

documents.body: In Ranked neighbours click Dock hours. Find its dot on Angle to the query, then read the q × d row and cos θ in Worked similarity.

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · Embeddings for search and retrieval
