documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: The examples a model was fitted to. Much of it was collected without asking the people who wrote or appear in it, which is a consent problem rather than a math problem.
documents.title: Training data

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Permission to collect, train on, or generate from someone's work or likeness. A public URL is not automatically consent, and a license on the weights cannot supply it.
documents.title: Consent

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: A capability that can help and harm. The same extractor that fills in an intake form can compile a dossier; the mechanism does not choose.
documents.title: Dual use

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Costs paid by people who did not choose the deployment, such as energy, scraped work, or a displaced task. They do not show up in a loss curve or a price.
documents.title: Externalities

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Human work in labeling, red-teaming, and content moderation, often low-paid and invisible behind the product. Alignment data is labor.
documents.title: Labor

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Being able to say who decided to deploy, on whom, and with what recourse when it goes wrong. A model card is not accountability by itself.
documents.title: Accountability

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Reporting a metric separately for each group of people or inputs. An overall score can hide a group for whom the model fails far more often.
documents.title: Disaggregated evaluation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Two group-fairness criteria defined on a classifier's error rates (Hardt, Price, and Srebro, 2016). Equal opportunity asks for equal true-positive rates across groups: the same share of truly positive cases flagged. Equalized odds, the stronger one, also asks for equal false-positive rates. Meeting either says nothing about whether the labels were right or the deployment is justified.
documents.title: Equal opportunity and equalized odds

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: A difference between the data a model was evaluated on and the data it meets in use. A holdout drawn from last year's population cannot promise performance on next year's.
documents.title: Distribution shift

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: A record of where content came from and how it was made or changed, such as a machine-readable mark saying an image was generated. A mark helps only while it survives editing and someone checks it, so it supports judgment and does not replace it.
documents.title: Provenance

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: The arithmetic to train a model, about 6 × parameters × training tokens for a dense transformer. It is paid once per run, plus experiments and failed runs.
documents.title: Training compute

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: The arithmetic to serve a model, about 2 × parameters for each token processed or generated. It is paid on every request, so at scale it can exceed training.
documents.title: Inference compute

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ethics and impact
documents.body: A rule that scales its duties with the harm a use could cause instead of treating every system alike. The EU AI Act sorts systems into unacceptable, high, transparency, and minimal risk levels, mostly by what they are used for. It sets duties and processes; it does not decide whether a given deployment is justified.
documents.title: Risk-based regulation

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Ethics and impact · question 1
documents.body: In each of the four deployments the ledger tags at most one of the five claims as on a leaderboard. What follows? A higher score cannot settle consent, labor, energy, or accountability, so those claims stay open The other claims count for nothing until someone builds a benchmark that can measure them The claims can be weighed against one another and reduced to a single ranking of the deployments Benchmarks add nothing to a deployment decision, so running them before launch is a wasted effort overall A benchmark answers the benchmark. Training text taken without consent, contractors' labeling work, serving energy, and who is accountable for a wrong output are real costs borne by people other than the buyer, and no harness number moves them. That does not make benchmarks useless: the one measurable claim is still worth knowing, and the lab never tallies the rest into a score.
documents.title: In each of the four deployments the ledger tags at most one of the five claims as on a leaderboard. What follows?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Ethics and impact · question 2
documents.body: A triage model scores 93% on a holdout where 10% of patients are in group B. The clinic that will use it is half group B. What does the lab's arithmetic show? Nothing changes, because the model and its accuracy are the same wherever it is deployed Accuracy dips a few points, but missed urgent cases roughly double, mostly in group B Accuracy rises, because the extra group B patients give the model more to learn from Accuracy collapses toward chance, because a clinic that is half group B is a different task Accuracy is a weighted average of the two groups, so moving from 10% to 50% group B takes it only from 93.1% to 89.7%. But the model misses 45% of group B's urgent cases against 10% of group A's, so missed urgent cases per 1,000 go from 27 to 55, and 82% of them are in group B. The benchmark answered the benchmark; it did not answer this clinic.
documents.title: A triage model scores 93% on a holdout where 10% of patients are in group B. The clinic that will use it is half group B. What does the lab's arithmetic show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Ethics and impact · question 3
documents.body: In Training versus serving you move Parameters from 1B to 405B and leave the token counts alone. What happens to Days to break even? It falls, because a bigger model answers more tokens per second and repays its training sooner It rises, because a larger model costs far more to train than it costs to serve It stays the same, because training and serving compute both scale with parameters It drops to zero for the largest models, because serving then outweighs training at once Training costs about 6·N·D operations and serving about 2·N per token, so their ratio is 3·D divided by the tokens served per day, and N cancels. Both bars grow with parameters, but they grow together, so the day on which serving overtakes training depends on training tokens and daily volume, not on model size.
documents.title: In Training versus serving you move Parameters from 1B to 405B and leave the token counts alone. What happens to Days to break even?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Ethics and impact · question 4
documents.body: Which of these is a limit of the lab's training-versus-serving arithmetic, and not a feature of it? It ignores how many training tokens were used, which would change the break-even day It ignores model size, which would shift the break-even day as parameters grow It measures energy at a real data center, so the figure cannot be repeated on other kinds of hardware It assumes a dense model at one utilization and leaves out cooling, the grid, and failed runs The break-even day uses training tokens as an input and model size cancels exactly, so neither is a gap. The estimate is computed, not measured: FLOP counts for a dense model at one utilization figure, converted to energy at an assumed power draw. Real energy use also depends on cooling, the grid, and the experiments and failed runs that published figures often leave out.
documents.title: Which of these is a limit of the lab's training-versus-serving arithmetic, and not a feature of it?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Ethics and impact · question 5
documents.body: In Who the benchmark represents, the triage model flags 90% of urgent cases in group A and 55% in group B, and 5% and 7% of non-urgent cases. Which fairness statement is right? It breaks equal opportunity, which asks for equal true-positive rates, and so fails equalized odds too It meets equal opportunity, because the two groups' overall accuracies are within nine points of each other here It breaks equal opportunity only because of false alarms, since that criterion is about the non-urgent cases It meets equalized odds, because the false-positive rates are close and that is all the criterion requires of it Equal opportunity (Hardt, Price, and Srebro, 2016) asks that among truly urgent cases each group is flagged at the same rate: 90% against 55%, a gap of 35 points. Equalized odds asks for equal true-positive and equal false-positive rates, so the same gap breaks it; the false-positive rates, 5% and 7%, are only 2 points apart. Accuracy blends both error types, which is why it moves so little while the gap stays put.
documents.title: In Who the benchmark represents, the triage model flags 90% of urgent cases in group A and 55% in group B, and 5% and 7% of non-urgent cases. Which fairness statement is right?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Ethics and impact · question 6
documents.body: The lesson's governance section describes the EU AI Act's risk-based approach. What does it settle about the Clinic intake deployment? It sets duties by use, and triage is on its high-risk list, but whether this deployment is justified stays open It bans AI in clinics, because health is the most sensitive area and so sits at the top of the Act's risk levels It exempts a system with high enough holdout accuracy, because a high score is treated as proof that it is safe It treats a model the same wherever it runs, because its duties attach to the architecture and not to the use The Act sorts systems into risk levels mostly by what they are used for. Annex III lists emergency healthcare patient triage among high-risk uses, which brings extra duties, but whether a given system falls under it depends on its intended use. Nothing in it answers the lab's question: who bears the costs and who was left out of the benchmark. The schedule has been amended since the Act was adopted, so check the current text.
documents.title: The lesson's governance section describes the EU AI Act's risk-based approach. What does it settle about the Clinic intake deployment?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ethics and impact
documents.body: When a news story says a new AI model got the top score on a test, it is tempting to hear something bigger. It sounds as if the model is good, so people should start using it. This module is about the gap between those two ideas, and about the people who end up standing in that gap. Putting an AI system to work in a real place, for real people, is called a deployment. A school might deploy a tutor, and a clinic might deploy a tool that helps it sort patients. Every deployment brings benefits and costs, and they rarely land on the same people. A test score can measure a few of them, but most never show up in any score at all. Where you have met it AI models are compared using fixed tests called benchmarks, and their scores are often ranked in public tables called leaderboards. Whenever you read that one chatbot beat another on some test, you are reading a benchmark result. You have also met the costs this module is about, even if nobody pointed them out. Chatbots and image generators learn from huge collections of writing and pictures, and much of that material was gathered without asking the people who made it. Every answer a chatbot gives takes computing power, and that cost comes back each time someone asks a question. An image generator can also make a realistic picture of a real person who never agreed to it. Lawmakers have started to respond to problems like these. The European Union's AI Act, for example, keeps a list of high-risk uses of AI, which have to follow extra rules. Two uses on that list are AI that sorts emergency patients and AI that judges how well students are learning. Why it matters If you treat a top score as the end of the argument, you miss everything the score never looked at. A test that leaves out some of the people who will use a system can give a fine-looking score, even while those people are failed far more often. Nothing in that single number warns you that it is happening. The people who carry the costs are often not the people who chose the system or paid for it. Students whose old essays were used and workers who labeled data by hand never get a line on a leaderboard. Neither do readers who meet a confident mistake, or patients a test left out, so without a deliberate way to look for them, those costs stay out of sight. None of this means tests are useless, because a benchmark tells you something real about the one question it asks. This module helps you see how far that answer reaches and where it stops. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these in your own words: At least two costs that never appear on a leaderboard, such as writing used without permission or the hidden work of data labelers, and who pays for each one. Why a test score cannot settle whether a use of AI is right, by looking at who the test included and who it left out. How the computing it takes to train a model once compares with the computing it takes to answer people every day, and why the daily cost can catch up. Which fairness rule the lab's patient-sorting model breaks, and how a law that sorts AI uses by risk handles a case like this without deciding whether it should go ahead. What the lab lets you do Nothing in this lab runs a real AI model or measures a real system. Everything you see was either written for teaching, worked out from made-up numbers, or calculated with a short formula. The lab is built from four cards, and each one shows a different side of the problem: Deployment lets you pick one of four made-up places where an AI system might be used: School tutor, Newsroom draft, Clinic intake or Image generator. Each comes with five arguments for and against it, and its Score always reads none. Tension explorer shows those arguments one at a time, along with who pays for each one and whether any test score could measure it. Who the benchmark represents tests an invented patient-sorting model on two groups of patients, and lets you change the mix to see what one overall score hides. Training versus serving compares the computing it takes to build a model once with the computing it takes to answer people day after day.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ethics and impact
documents.body: A debate with no judge Picture a class debate about whether your school should start using an AI tutor. One side says a tutor that never gets tired could help students in the evening, after the building closes. The other side asks whose essays the tutor learned from, and whether anyone asked those students first. Now give the debate an unusual rule: there is no judge, and nobody keeps score. Each speaker makes one point, and a note beside it says who would gain or pay if that point is right. That is how this lab works, and its second card is called Tension explorer because it lays out arguments that pull against each other. The analogy stops matching in two places. In a real debate, both teams choose to show up and speak for themselves. Many of the people who bear these costs were never in the room, such as the students whose old essays were used. A debate also ends with a winner, while this one stays open, because the lab cannot decide for the people affected. Four deployments, five claims each The lab offers four made-up deployments, which you choose with the Deployment control: School tutor, Newsroom draft, Clinic intake and Image generator. Each one comes with five short arguments, which the lab calls claims. Some argue for the deployment and some argue against it, so the card sorts them into two columns headed For and Against. Every claim carries three tags, which you can read in Tension explorer once you pick that claim: Theme names what the claim is about, such as access, consent, or energy and labor. Who bears it names the people who carry that benefit or cost, such as students, past students or contractors. Can a benchmark measure it? answers yes, partly or no, and then gives a one-line reason for that answer. Below the two columns, the Deployment card shows four readouts. For claims and Against claims count how many claims the lesson writers put on each side, which is not the same thing as counting votes. A benchmark speaks to counts how many claims a test score could cover fully, and how many it could cover partly. The last readout, Score, always says none, because nothing on the page weights the claims or adds them into a total. Reading one claim, step by step Set Deployment to School tutor, then use the Claim control to pick 2 Against. The claim reads: “The essays used to train it were collected without those students' consent.” Its Theme is consent and Who bears it says past students, while Can a benchmark measure it? says no, with the reason “no leaderboard measures this”. Read those three tags together as one complete thought. The cost is that people's writing was used without their permission, and the people paying it are students who wrote essays in earlier years. No test score could ever show that cost, so however well the tutor scores, those essays were still used without asking. Now step to 3 For: “A published harness shows higher homework completion.” A harness is the setup that runs a test on a model and records its score, so this claim rests on a real number. Its Theme is measured benefit, Who bears it says district, and Can a benchmark measure it? says yes, with the reason “a benchmark number exists for this”. The district is the group of schools that would pay for the tutor. Claim 4 Against answers it right away: “Completion is not learning, and the harness does not represent the district that would pay.” In other words, finishing more homework does not prove that students learned more, and the students in the test may not be like the students in this district. Its tag says partly, because a test could speak to this only in certain cases. It would have to report results for each group of students separately, test students like the ones who will use the tutor, or be built to test this exact case. The costs no leaderboard counts The first goal of this lesson is to name costs that never show up in a test score. The lab's claims raise several of them, and each one below starts in plain words before giving the name the lab's glossary uses. Writing and pictures used without asking The examples a model learns from are called its training data. For chatbots and image generators, much of that data was collected from the web without asking the people who wrote it or appear in it. Permission to use someone's work or likeness is called consent, and a page being public on the web does not automatically mean its author gave consent. Picture a made-up artist who posts drawings on a public art site so that friends can see them. Later a company copies those drawings, along with a huge pile of other people's pictures, to train an image generator. The drawings were public, but nobody asked the artist, and no score the generator ever earns will mention them. The company may attach a license to the finished model, which is a set of rules for how other people may use it. That license covers the finished model itself, though, and it cannot give permission on behalf of the people whose work went in. Hidden human work Behind every polished AI product are people doing slow, careful work by hand. Some label examples with the right answers, while others try to make the model misbehave so its problems can be found and fixed, which is called red-teaming. Others review harmful material so that users never see it, which is called content moderation. Even the data that teaches a model to follow instructions and behave as intended is made this way. All of this is labor, and it is often low-paid and invisible behind the product. In the School tutor list, claim 5 says the labeling work “was billed to contractors”, which means outside workers hired for the job. Energy Training a model takes a huge amount of electricity once, and answering people takes more electricity every day after that. The same School tutor claim says “Serving energy is billed to the school”, where serving means running the model to answer people. The Training versus serving card, covered later in this section, works out how those two costs compare. Costs that land on people who had no say Some costs are paid by people who never chose the deployment. The school pays its own electricity bill, but making that electricity can affect people far away who were never asked. The writers whose work was copied were never asked either. Another example is a task a person used to do that the system now does instead, where the cost lands on that person. These are called externalities, and they never show up in a price or in a loss curve, which is the chart that tracks a model's errors during training. Newsroom draft claim 4 says it directly: “Cheap for the publisher is an externality for the people whose writing was scraped.” Scraped means copied off websites automatically by a program, so the writers paid part of the cost of every cheap article without ever being asked. Mistakes that sound sure of themselves A model's writing can be smooth and convincing even when it is wrong. Newsroom draft claim 2 says “Fluent errors can reach readers in the desk's own voice,” where the desk is the newsroom team that publishes the story. A mistake could go out sounding exactly like the newspaper itself, so the theme is misinformation, meaning false information that spreads, and the people who bear it are readers. Help that can also harm A tool that pulls facts out of a patient's notes can fill in an intake form, which saves the staff time. The same tool could also gather everything about one patient into a single file, which someone could misuse. A skill that can help and harm like this is called dual use, and the tool itself does not choose which way it gets used. Clinic intake claim 5 is the lab's example: “Dual use: the same extractor can compile a dossier on a patient.” An extractor is a tool that pulls facts out of text, and a dossier is a detailed file about one person. Faces and fake photos An image generator can make a realistic picture of a real person without that person's say, which the lab files under the theme likeness, meaning someone's face and appearance. A related problem is that readers may not be able to tell a generated picture apart from a real photograph. A record of where a picture came from, and how it was made or changed, is called provenance. One example is a mark inside the image file that a computer can read, saying the image was generated. A mark like that helps only while it survives editing and someone checks it, so it supports people's judgment instead of replacing it. Nobody to answer for it When something goes wrong, someone should be able to say who decided to use the system, on whom, and how people can get a mistake put right. Being able to answer those questions is called accountability. Newsroom draft claim 5 raises it: “Accountability is unclear when a wrong date ships under a byline,” where a byline is the line naming the reporter who wrote a story. Picture a made-up school newspaper that starts drafting stories with an AI tool. A story about the spring concert goes out under a student reporter's name with the wrong date, and families turn up on the wrong night. Was that the reporter's fault, or the editor's? Was it the teacher who chose the tool, or the company that built it? If nobody can answer, accountability is missing, and the families have nobody to complain to. A model card, which is a document describing a model and how it was tested, does not answer that question by itself. It describes the model, not the people who decided to use it. Who the benchmark represents Picture a made-up teacher who announces that the class averaged 88% on a test, which sounds like great news. Twenty students sat near the front and scored 95%. The other five sat at the back where they could not read the board, and they scored 60%. The average is true, but it hides the five students who were struggling, and you only find them by splitting the results by group. The Who the benchmark represents card applies the same idea to a made-up clinic. When a clinic is busy, staff have to sort patients by how urgent each case is, so that the most serious ones are seen first. That sorting is called triage, and the card's invented model reads each patient's notes and either flags the case as urgent or leaves it alone. The card's small heading calls it a “synthetic triage model”, where synthetic means made up for the lab rather than trained on real patients. The patients belong to two groups, called A and B, and in both groups 1 patient in 5 has a truly urgent case. Group B stands for patients whose notes were under-represented in the labels. That means there were too few notes like theirs among the examples that people had marked with the right answer. The model learned what an urgent case looks like from those marked examples, so it learned much less about how urgent cases look in group B's notes. Working out each group's accuracy A model's accuracy is the share of all its calls, urgent or not, that turn out to be right. Take 1,000 patients from group A and follow them through the model, one step at a time: One patient in five is urgent, which makes 200 urgent patients in the group. The model flags 90% of these urgent patients, which means it catches 180 of them. The remaining 20 urgent patients slip through without being flagged, and these are the misses that matter most in a clinic. The other 800 patients are not urgent, and the model correctly leaves 95% of them alone. Those correct “not urgent” calls come to 760, and adding the 180 urgent patients it caught gives 940 correct calls. That gives group A an accuracy of 94.0%, because 940 out of 1,000 is 94%. Now take 1,000 patients from group B, who also include 200 urgent cases: The model flags only 55% of the urgent ones, which means it catches 110 of them. That leaves 90 urgent patients it misses, which is nearly half of all the urgent cases in the group. Of the 800 patients who are not urgent, the model correctly leaves 93% alone, which is 744 patients. Adding the 110 urgent patients it caught to those 744 gives 854 correct calls, so group B's accuracy is 85.4%. The two accuracies, 94.0% and 85.4%, are less than 9 percentage points apart, since 94.0 minus 85.4 is 8.6. The gap between two percentages is counted in percentage points, often just called points. A gap that small does not sound alarming. The misses tell a very different story from the accuracies. The model misses 10 urgent cases in every 100 for group A, but 45 in every 100 for group B, which is more than four times as often. Accuracy hides most of that difference because urgent cases are only 1 patient in 5. Most of each group's score comes from the other four patients in five, and the model handles those non-urgent patients about equally well for both groups. The test the model passed The model was tested on a holdout, which is a set of cases kept aside for testing instead of being used to build the model. In that holdout, only 10% of the patients were in group B. Out of every 1,000 holdout patients, that makes 900 from group A and 100 from group B. Group A misses 20 urgent cases in every 1,000 of its patients, so its 900 patients produce 18 misses. Group B misses 90 in every 1,000, so its 100 patients add 9 more misses on top of those. That comes to 27 missed urgent cases per 1,000 patients, with an overall accuracy of 93.1%. The clinic that will use it Now suppose the clinic that will really use the model sees half of its patients from group B. Out of every 1,000 patients who walk through its doors: Group A's 500 patients produce 10 missed urgent cases, which is half of the 20 that a full 1,000 would produce. Group B's 500 patients produce 45, which is half of the 90 that a full 1,000 would produce. That comes to 55 missed urgent cases per 1,000 patients, with an overall accuracy of 89.7%. If you compare the two clinics side by side, accuracy slipped only a few points, from 93.1% to 89.7%. Missed urgent cases per 1,000 patients went from 27 to 55, which is roughly double. Most of the extra misses landed on group B. In fact, 45 of the 55 misses, about 82%, are in group B. The accuracy for a mix of patients is a weighted average, where each group's accuracy counts in proportion to how many patients come from that group. With half the patients from each group, it is the ordinary average of the two. Adding 94.0% and 85.4% and dividing by 2 gives 89.7%, which is what the card shows. The holdout works the same way: 90% of 94.0 plus 10% of 85.4 is 84.6 plus 8.5, which rounds to 93.1%. So why does accuracy barely move while the misses double? Accuracy is a weighted average of two numbers that are already close, 94.0% and 85.4%. Missed cases per 1,000 are also a weighted average, but of 20 and 90, which are far apart. Shifting patients from group A to group B moves that average a long way, so the misses jump. Splitting the score by group Reporting a score separately for each group of people is called disaggregated evaluation. The card does this with its bars, under the headings “Patients per 1,000” and “Missed urgent cases per 1,000”. Each heading has one row for the holdout and one for the mix you chose. Group A is drawn as a solid bar, and group B is drawn with diagonal stripes, which the card calls hatched. A single accuracy number cannot show what those bars show. When the test and the real world differ Clinic intake claim 4 puts the problem in one line: “The holdout is last year's clinic, not the patients who walk in tomorrow.” A difference between the people a model was tested on and the people it meets in real use is called distribution shift. A shift like this does not announce itself, because the holdout score stays the same number it always was. Only a split by group shows that the errors have moved onto different people, and that more of them now fall on group B. Beating a lazy guesser Clinic intake claim 3 says “A documented harness beat a majority-class baseline on holdout notes.” A majority-class baseline is a lazy guesser that always gives the most common answer. Suppose 1 patient in 5 is urgent, as in the triage card. A guesser that always says “not urgent” is then right 80% of the time, while catching no urgent case at all. Beating that guesser is worth knowing, but it does not tell you which patients the remaining misses fall on. Accuracy alone can look respectable while the cases that matter most slip through. Two fairness rules, and the one this model breaks The triage card also gives the gap between the groups a name. To see it, you need two rates, and the card shows both of them on its second row of readouts. The true-positive rate is the share of truly urgent cases that the model flags. It is 90% for group A and 55% for group B, which the card shows in True-positive rate, A / B as “90% / 55%”. The gap between them is 90 minus 55, which is 35 points, and the card shows it as Equal-opportunity gap. A fairness rule called equal opportunity asks that the true-positive rate be the same for every group. In plain words, among the people who really need help, each group should be caught at the same rate. A gap of 35 points means the model is far from that, so equal opportunity is the fairness rule the triage gap breaks. The false-positive rate is the share of non-urgent cases the model flags anyway, which are false alarms. It is 5% for group A and 7% for group B, so the False-positive gap is only 2 points. A stricter rule called equalized odds asks for two things at once: equal true-positive rates and equal false-positive rates. The model fails equalized odds as well, almost entirely because of the 35-point gap, since its false-alarm rates are close together. Each rate is worked out inside one group, as a share of that group's own urgent or non-urgent patients. Moving the slider changes how many patients are in each group, but not how the model treats any one of them. In this lab each group's rates are fixed, so both gaps stay the same however you move Group B share of patients. In real use, a group's rates can shift too, for example when its patients change. Accuracy and the number of missed cases do move with the mix, because they depend on how many patients come from each group. Meeting these rules would not settle everything either, because the rates are checked against the labels people wrote. If those labels were wrong, a model could match them equally well for both groups and still be wrong for both. Passing a fairness rule also does not show that using the model is justified. Training versus serving Most of the claims so far were about costs that no test number captures. This card looks at a cost that can be counted, but often is not counted in full. A chatbot reads and writes text in small pieces called tokens, where a token is often a whole word or part of one. Inside, a model is a huge list of adjustable numbers called parameters, and training is the process that sets them. A model with 7B parameters has 7 billion of them. Making a model and using it are two separate jobs. Training means running the model over its training text while the training process adjusts its parameters, which takes an enormous amount of arithmetic, paid once for each training run. Serving means running the finished model to answer people, and every token it reads or writes takes more arithmetic, paid again every day the model is in use. The arithmetic for training is called training compute, while the arithmetic for serving is called inference compute, because running a finished model to get answers is called inference. The lab counts both in FLOP, short for floating-point operations, where one floating-point operation is one arithmetic step on numbers with decimals, such as a single multiplication. The formulas the card shows The note under the card's readouts gives three short formulas. These are rules of thumb, which means quick estimates that researchers use instead of exact counts. They say roughly how many arithmetic steps each parameter needs for each token. In them, N stands for the number of parameters, D stands for the number of training tokens, and the dot means “multiply”: Training takes about 6·N·D FLOP, and that amount is paid once for each training run. Serving takes about 2·N FLOP for each token, and that amount is paid again on every request. The two totals become equal after 3·D ÷ T days of serving, where T is the number of tokens served per day. That day is the break-even point. A worked example at the starting settings The card starts with Parameters at 7B and Training tokens at 2T, which means 2 trillion. Tokens served per day starts at 10B, which means 10 billion tokens a day. For training, multiply the small numbers first: 6 × 7 × 2 is 84. A billion has 9 zeros and a trillion has 12, so multiplying by both adds 21 zeros, which makes 84 followed by 21 zeros. The readout writes big numbers with one digit before the decimal point. 84 is the same as 8.4 × 10, so writing 8.4 instead of 84 adds one more zero to the count. That is why the Training, once readout shows 8.4×10²² FLOP, where ×10²² means “times 1 followed by 22 zeros”. For serving, 2 × 7 × 10 is 140, and the two billions add 9 zeros each, which makes 140 followed by 18 zeros. 140 is 1.4 × 100, which adds two more zeros, so the Serving, per day readout shows 1.4×10²⁰ FLOP each day. For break-even, 3 × 2 trillion is 6 trillion, which is the same as 6,000 billion. Dividing 6,000 billion by 10 billion gives 600. So the Days to break even readout says 600 days at the starting settings. At these settings, serving uses as much compute in 600 days, a little over a year and a half, as training used in one go. After that day serving has cost more than training did, and the difference keeps growing every day the model stays in use. The chart tells the same story, and its dashed line, “one training run”, stays flat because training is paid once. Its solid line, “serving, cumulative”, is a running total that climbs a little every day. The point where they cross is marked break-even, and the note below the chart says “The guide marks day 600, where serving has used as much compute as training.” Why model size cancels out Training costs 6 × N × D, and one day of serving costs 2 × N × T, where T is the number of tokens served per day. To find how many days of serving equal one training run, you divide the first amount by the second. N sits on both the top and the bottom of that division, so it cancels, and 6 divided by 2 is 3, which leaves 3 × D ÷ T. Picture a made-up class trip where the bus costs $30 per student, paid once. Lunch costs $10 per student each day, so lunch spending catches up with the bus fare after 3 days. That is true whether 20 students go or 200, because both costs grow with the number of students. The number of students plays the same part as N, and it cancels for the same reason. The analogy stops matching in what the costs are made of, because compute is arithmetic rather than money. The lab's break-even also depends on two settings, Training tokens and Tokens served per day, instead of two fixed prices. A common mix-up: a bigger model costs far more to train, so it seems serving should take longer to catch up. But a bigger model also costs more to serve every token. A model with twice the parameters costs twice as much to train and twice as much to serve, so the two costs grow together. Move Parameters from 1B to 405B, and both Training, once and Serving, per day grow while Days to break even stays at 600 days. Turning compute into energy The card's note also turns compute into electricity, using two assumptions about the hardware. It assumes the work runs on A100s, a kind of computer chip built for this arithmetic, running at 40% of their top speed and drawing 400 watts each. A watt measures how fast a device uses energy, and a watt-hour is the energy used at one watt for one hour. A megawatt-hour, written MWh, is a million watt-hours, which is enough to keep a 100-watt light bulb lit for 10,000 hours. With those assumptions, the default training run uses about 75 MWh for the chips alone. So 75 MWh would keep that bulb lit for 750,000 hours, which is more than 85 years. Serving at the same efficiency uses about 0.12 MWh a day, which looks tiny next to the training figure. It is paid every day, though, so after 600 days it matches the whole training run. The note adds that real decoding, the step where the model writes its answer, usually runs less efficiently than that. That means the chips stay switched on longer for the same amount of arithmetic, so they use more electricity for it. So serving's energy usually catches up even sooner than the compute chart suggests. What a risk-based law does, and what it leaves open The last goal of this lesson is about how rules handle deployments like these. Think of the safety rules for a school science lab, where a risky experiment needs goggles, gloves and a teacher watching, while reading a thermometer needs none of that. The rules grow stricter as the danger grows, but they do not decide whether a particular experiment is worth doing. Some laws treat AI in the same way, giving more duties to uses that could cause more harm instead of giving every system identical rules. That approach is called risk-based regulation, and the main example is the European Union's AI Act. The European Commission, which runs the EU's day-to-day work, describes four levels of risk under it: Unacceptable risk covers uses that are banned altogether. High risk covers uses that are allowed but bring extra duties with them. Transparency risk brings duties to be open about AI, such as marking content that was generated. Minimal risk covers uses that add no extra rules at all. The Act sorts systems mostly by what they are used for, not by how they are built. Its high-risk list includes emergency healthcare patient triage, which is close to the lab's Clinic intake, and AI that evaluates learning outcomes in education. Whether a particular system falls under that list depends on what it is meant to be used for. A high score does not take a use off the list, because the list is about the use and not about the score. Landing on the list brings extra duties and processes that have to be followed. What the law does not do is decide whether a given deployment is justified. A clinic could follow every duty and still face the lab's open questions: who bears the costs, and who was left out of the benchmark. For a use the law allows, such as triage on the high-risk list, the law says how carefully to go ahead, not whether this particular deployment should go ahead. Only the short list of banned uses gets a flat no. That is where the goggles analogy stops matching, because the Act does ban a few uses outright. Triage is not one of them, so for the clinic the law works just like the goggles rule.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Every test asks one particular question, and its score is an honest answer to that question and to nothing else. The Image generator shows this clearly, because its claim 3 says “A published benchmark rates its images above the previous model's for matching the prompt.” That is a real and useful measurement, since it tells you how well the pictures match what people asked for. The other claims about the same generator ask different questions. Were the training pictures used with the artists' consent? Can the tool fake a real person's face? Can readers tell its pictures from photographs? No amount of skill at matching prompts answers any of those. Picture a made-up website that reviews phones only on battery life. A phone that scores 10 out of 10 really does have a great battery. But the score says nothing about the camera, or about how the workers who built the phone were treated. Nobody would read that number as the final word on buying the phone, yet a top leaderboard score often gets read in exactly that way. This lab follows on from The ecosystem, which showed that a model release is a bundle of separate parts. Those parts include the model's numbers, its code, information about its data, its license and its model card. A download, in other words, is not a finished product. This lab asks the next question: who pays for each of those parts, and who gets left out when the system is measured? The answer is often someone other than the buyer, as you can see by looking at who bears each claim across the four deployments: In School tutor, the district gets the measured benefit, while past students bore the consent cost, contractors bore the labeling work, and the school pays the serving energy. In Newsroom draft, the publisher pays for an API, which is a paid service that lets a program send text to someone else's model and get answers back. One more article looks cheap to the publisher, while scraped writers and misled readers carry the costs. In Clinic intake, the clinic holds the measured benefit, while patients bear the representation gap, the distribution shift and the dual-use risk. In Image generator, the vendor, which is the company selling the tool, holds the benchmark claim, and small studios get the access benefit. Illustrators, photographers, people depicted, readers and newsrooms carry the costs. You might wonder why the lab does not weigh the claims and give each deployment a score. Any weighting would itself be a choice about whose costs count for more, and that choice belongs to the people affected rather than to a formula. So the lab leaves every question open on purpose, because understanding what a score does and does not measure helps you ask better questions. It cannot choose the deployment for you.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Work through the cards in order, because each step builds on the one before it. Pick a deployment Set Deployment to School tutor, and notice that Score reads none. A benchmark speaks to reads “1 of 5, 1 partly”, which means one claim a test fully covers and one it covers only partly. For claims reads 2 and Against claims reads 3, which counts the claims on each side and is not a vote. Walk the claims Move Claim from 1 For through to 5 Against, and read Who bears it and Can a benchmark measure it? each time. You can also click an entry in the For or Against column to pick it. Pay close attention to 3 For, the harness claim, and then to 4 Against, which says what that harness does not represent. Split the benchmark In Who the benchmark represents, the slider starts at 30%. At that setting, Accuracy at 30% B reads 91.4%, and Missed urgent per 1,000 reads “27 → 41”, which compares the holdout with your chosen mix. Try this: In Who the benchmark represents, drag Group B share of patients down to 10%, then up to 50%. At 10%, the readout Accuracy at 10% B matches the holdout's 93.1%, and Missed urgent per 1,000 reads “27 → 27”. At 50%, accuracy reads 89.7%, while Missed urgent per 1,000 reads “27 → 55”, which is roughly double. While the slider sits at 50%, look at the “At 50% B” bar under “Missed urgent cases per 1,000”. The hatched group B part now takes up most of that bar, unlike the holdout bar above it. Then read Equal-opportunity gap, which says 35 points, and False-positive gap, which says 2 points. Move the slider anywhere you like and check that neither gap changes. Weigh serving against training In Training versus serving, leave Parameters at 7B and Training tokens at 2T, so that Days to break even reads 600 days. Next, raise Tokens served per day from 10B to 100B, and Days to break even falls from 600 days to 60. Push it all the way to 1T, and it falls to 6 days. Now drag it down to 1B, and it climbs to 16.4 years. The chart's note then says “Serving does not reach one training run's compute within ten years at this volume.” Set Tokens served per day back to 10B, then change Parameters from 1B all the way to 405B. Training, once and Serving, per day both grow, but Days to break even stays at 600 days. Finally, raise Training tokens from 2T to 4T, and the break-even time doubles to 1,200 days, which the readout shows as 3.3 years. Notice the missing score Switch Deployment to Newsroom draft, then Clinic intake, then Image generator. Switching resets Claim to the first entry, so step through all five claims each time. For each deployment, name two costs that no leaderboard measures and the people who bear them.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ethics and impact
documents.body: At most one claim per deployment is on a leaderboard, and Newsroom draft has none at all, so its A benchmark speaks to reads “0 of 5, 1 partly”. In the other three deployments, claim 4 is an Against line that already answers the one benchmark claim beside it. On Image generator, the only benchmark claim is about matching the prompt. Consent, likeness and provenance are each tagged as either not on a leaderboard or only partly measurable. The costs fall on people other than the buyer, such as past students, contractors, writers, readers and patients. Meanwhile the district, the publisher and the clinic pay for the system, and the vendor profits from selling it. One accuracy number is an average that can hide a group. At the starting setting of 30%, group B makes up 30% of the patients but 66% of the missed urgent cases, which only a disaggregated evaluation shows. The Equal-opportunity gap stays at 35 points and the False-positive gap stays at 2 points at every share. In this lab both are fixed by the model's rates for each group, not by the mix of people who walk in. Training energy is paid once, while serving energy keeps growing with use. At 100 billion tokens a day, a model trained on 2 trillion tokens matches its training compute in 60 days, whatever its size.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ethics and impact
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies The four deployments, their twenty claims and their tags are teaching sentences written for this lesson. They are not findings from a survey or from interviews with the people affected, nothing ranks them, and the counts are not votes. The triage model is invented, so nothing is trained and both groups' rates are made up and fixed. In real life, groups also differ in how often their cases are urgent, and not only in how often a model makes mistakes. Only two fairness rules are named here, although others exist. One called demographic parity asks that each group be flagged at the same overall rate, whether or not its cases are urgent. Different rules can also disagree about the same model, so passing one does not mean passing the others. The compute is an estimate from formulas, not a measurement. The formulas assume a dense model, meaning one where every parameter works on every token. The estimate also counts one training run only, leaving out the experiments and failed runs that came before it. The formulas also leave out the extra arithmetic needed for very long inputs. They also skip models split into many smaller sections, where each token is sent to only a few of them and so uses only some of the parameters. The energy figure covers the chips only, so it ignores cooling and where the electricity comes from. The 40% speed and the 400 watts are assumptions, not readings from a real data center. How hard the chips really run depends on things like batching, which means handling many requests together, so the one fixed 40% figure is only a rough guess. Where the real thing fails A test score still cannot finish the question, however good the score gets. Externalities stay off the loss curve, a public web page is not consent, and a model card is not accountability by itself. Published energy figures often cover only the final training run, leaving out the experiments and failed runs that came before it. Real energy use also depends on the hardware, how hard it runs, how efficient the data center is, and how the local electricity is made. A model tested on last year's patients can be used on a different group next year. Distribution shift and missing groups change who bears the errors, and not only how many errors there are. A provenance mark helps only while it survives editing and someone checks it. Meeting a fairness rule says nothing about whether the labels were right, and a risk-based law sets duties without deciding whether any given deployment is justified. People often treat a top score as a finished ethics argument. The score answered the test, and that answer can be true and useful. It says nothing about who was left out of the test, who labeled the data, whose work was used without asking, or who is accountable when it goes wrong.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Rules and frameworks, checked 30 September 2026 Laws and standards now name deployments like the ones in this lab. Three are worth knowing by name: the EU AI Act, the NIST framework and ISO/IEC 42001. All three set duties and processes without deciding whether a deployment is justified. The EU AI Act's risk levels are the risk-based regulation described above, with four levels running from banned uses down to uses with no extra rules. Its list of high-risk uses sits in a part of the law called Annex III, which includes emergency healthcare patient triage and AI that evaluates learning outcomes in education. The EU AI Act's transparency rules sit in a part of the law called Article 50. It asks the makers of tools that generate audio, images, video or text to mark the results, so that a computer can detect them as generated. Article 50 also says that people who publish deepfakes, which are realistic fake images, audio or video, have to say so. AI-written text published to inform the public must be disclosed too, unless a person has reviewed it and takes editorial responsibility for it. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework comes from NIST, a US standards agency, and it is voluntary rather than a law. Released in January 2023, it is organized around four activities called Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, and a companion guide for generative AI, called a profile, followed in July 2024. Generative AI means AI that makes new text, images or sound. ISO/IEC 42001 is an international standard, published in 2023, that sets requirements for how an organization sets up and keeps improving the way it manages its own AI. It is about an organization's processes, not about how any one model behaves. The transparency rules connect to two of the lab's deployments. A provenance mark is the kind of mark Article 50 asks generator makers to add. The Newsroom draft, meanwhile, raises the question of who reviewed a story and takes responsibility for it. The schedule is the part that keeps moving. As the European Commission's timeline for the Act read on 30 September 2026, its parts apply from these dates: The bans on unacceptable-risk uses applied from 2 February 2025. The rules for general-purpose AI models, meaning large models built to be used for many different tasks, applied from 2 August 2025. Most other rules, including Article 50, applied from 2 August 2026. The Annex III high-risk rules apply from 2 December 2027. That last date was moved later by a change to the law called the Digital Omnibus on AI. Check the current text before relying on any of these dates, because one of them has already moved. More about the fairness rules The names equal opportunity and equalized odds come from a 2016 research paper by Hardt, Price and Srebro. Both rules compare error rates group by group, which is why they can spot a problem that one overall accuracy number hides. Demographic parity is another rule from the same family of group-fairness rules, and because it asks a different question, it can give a different verdict on the same model. More about the compute estimate The 6·N·D and 2·N formulas are rules of thumb for dense models, and real systems can differ from them in several ways. Very long inputs add extra work beyond the formula, and models split into many smaller sections, called mixture-of-experts models, use only some of their parameters for each token. The 40% figure for how hard the chips run is one fixed assumption, and real answering usually runs less efficiently than training, which brings the energy break-even sooner. Where to go next The ecosystem is the lab to read first, because it shows the parts of a release that this lab asks about. How we know a model works and Evaluation explain how a test harness can look fine and still mislead. Failure modes, safety, and security treats dual use as a security problem, while here it stays a question for the people a deployment affects.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Ethics and impact
documents.body: This module is about what a benchmark score can and cannot settle in a deployment decision, and who bears the costs it never records, from past students and contractors to readers and patients. The lab lays out competing claims and leaves them unscored. It does not decide whether any deployment is justified. It builds on The ecosystem and adds two calculations that put numbers on what a score leaves out. Disaggregated evaluation, reporting a metric separately for each group of people, shows whom an average hides. A compute estimate separates training compute, paid once per run, from inference compute, paid on every request served. Where it shows up Benchmarks and leaderboards. A headline accuracy averages over the test set's population. Group-fairness criteria such as equal opportunity and equalized odds (Hardt, Price, and Srebro, 2016) compare error rates group by group. Regulation. The EU AI Act is risk-based regulation, scaling duties with the harm a use could cause. Its high-risk list includes emergency healthcare patient triage and AI that evaluates learning outcomes in education, and Article 50 asks for machine-readable marks on generated content, a form of provenance. Energy reporting. Published energy figures for training often cover only the final run and not the experiments before it. The lab converts its estimate of arithmetic operations to energy with one assumed utilization. Why it matters An average can hide a group. In the lab's synthetic triage model, accuracy falls about 3 points as group B goes from 10% to 50% of patients, while missed urgent cases per 1,000 double, mostly in group B. A single accuracy cannot show where the misses fall; per-group reporting can. Some costs never reach a score. Training text taken without consent, labeling labor, and the energy of serving are costs no score records. Most fall on people who did not choose the deployment, which makes them externalities. A real person's likeness used without their say is only partly measurable, and only by a benchmark whose prompts ask for real people. Serving is the recurring bill. Counting only training misses compute paid on every request, and at high volume serving dominates. A rule is not a verdict. Meeting a risk-based rule's duties still leaves open whether a deployment is justified. What you will be able to explain Name at least two costs that never appear on a leaderboard, and who bears them. Explain why a benchmark score cannot finish an ethics question, using who the benchmark represents. Compare the one-time compute of training with the ongoing compute of serving. Name the fairness criterion the triage gap breaks, and say how a risk-based rule treats a deployment without deciding whether it is justified. What the lab shows Nothing here runs a trained model or measures a real system. Each card is authored text, fixed synthetic rates, or closed-form arithmetic. Deployment switches between School tutor, Newsroom draft, Clinic intake and Image generator, four fictional settings with five authored claims each, tagged by theme, by who bears them, and by whether a benchmark speaks to them. Score stays at none. In Tension explorer, Claim steps through them one at a time. Who the benchmark represents evaluates a synthetic triage model with invented, fixed group rates. The key experiment moves Group B share of patients from 10% to 50%: accuracy barely moves, Missed urgent per 1,000 climbs, and the Equal-opportunity gap and False-positive gap stay put. Training versus serving estimates floating-point operations (FLOP) for a dense model in closed form, about 6 × parameters × training tokens to train and 2 × parameters per token served, driven by Parameters, Training tokens and Tokens served per day. Days to break even, the day cumulative serving compute matches one training run, does not move when Parameters changes. The card's note converts compute to energy in MWh, assuming 40% of an A100's peak throughput and 400 W per GPU.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Ethics and impact
documents.body: A deployment decision has claims for it and claims against it, and they are borne by different people. This lab lays out four fictional deployments, each with five authored claims tagged by theme, by who bears them, and by whether any benchmark number could speak to them. One is an image generator, with claims about consent, likeness, and provenance. The lab never reduces them to a score. Two cards then compute what a leaderboard leaves out. Who the benchmark represents A single accuracy is an average over whoever was in the test set. The synthetic triage model here is 94.0% accurate on group A and 85.4% on group B, whose notes the labels under-represent. It misses 10% of group A's urgent cases and 45% of group B's. On a holdout with 10% group B it scores 93.1%. Move the population to 50% group B and accuracy falls only to 89.7%, while missed urgent cases per 1,000 patients go from 27 to 55. That gap is what disaggregated evaluation exists to show, and what distribution shift hides. The gap has a name. The model flags 90% of group A's urgent cases and 55% of group B's, a true-positive-rate gap of 35 points. Equal opportunity (Hardt, Price, and Srebro, 2016) asks for equal true-positive rates, so the model is far from it. Equalized odds also asks for equal false-positive rates. Those are 5% and 7%, only 2 points apart, so the model fails equalized odds almost entirely because of the first gap. Neither gap moves with the group mix. Training versus serving Training compute for a dense transformer is about 6·N·D operations for N parameters and D training tokens. Inference compute is about 2·N per token served. One is paid once; the other is paid on every request. They are equal after 3·D ÷ tokens served per day days, so model size cancels out. With 2T training tokens and 10B tokens served a day that is 600 days; at 1T tokens a day it is 6.

The ecosystem lab showed that a release is a bundle of parts; this lab asks who pays for each part, and who is left out of the measurement.

documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Deployment · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Four places, five claims each, no score Deployment chooses a school tutor, a newsroom draft, clinic intake, or an image generator. Each has five authored claims, sorted into For and Against, and tagged with a theme, who bears it, and whether any benchmark number could speak to it. Score is fixed at none so a harness number cannot close the question. Deployment, four segments. A ledger: For on the left, Against on the right. Each entry shows its number, theme, who bears it, and a tag: on a leaderboard, partly measurable, or not on a leaderboard. Clicking an entry selects that claim. For claims, Against claims, A benchmark speaks to (how many claims a benchmark covers fully, and how many partly), and Score: none. Every claim and tag is authored. Nothing is computed from a model or a benchmark, and the counts are not votes. "Partly measurable" means a benchmark could speak to the claim only if it were split by group, drawn from the people who will use the system, or built to test that case, such as a prompt set that asks for real people's likenesses. Switching Deployment resets Claim to the first entry. Deployment, and the ledger entries themselves. Comparison worth running: count the "on a leaderboard" tags in each deployment. It is at most one of five. Then read the consent, likeness, and provenance claims on Image generator. The one claim a leaderboard supports in the school, clinic, and image-generator lists is already answered by an Against line beside it. On Image generator the costs are consent of the people whose images trained it, the likeness of people depicted, and whether readers can tell a generated picture from a photograph. The only benchmark claim is prompt match. The costs are borne by people other than the buyer: past students, contractors, writers, readers, patients. In this lab: four fictional deployments, twenty authored claims, and authored tags. There is no survey, no stakeholder interview, and no ranking. In general: a benchmark answers the benchmark. Consent, labor, energy, and accountability stay outside it, however high the score.
documents.title: Four places, five claims each, no score

documents.subtitle: Tension explorer · Ethics and impact
documents.body: One claim at a time, left open Claim steps through the selected deployment's five claims in order. Each is shown with its theme, who bears it, and whether a benchmark can measure it. The page never tallies them into a winner. Claim, a segmented control labeled by number and side. The claim text, bordered green for For and red for Against, with the side also written in the heading. Three tags: Theme, Who bears it, and Can a benchmark measure it, with yes, partly, or no and a one-line reason. Claim is an integer index into the deployment's list; the text and tags are string constants. No weighting, voting, or "ethics score" is applied anywhere on the page. Claim here; Deployment on the card above changes the list. Comparison worth running: on School tutor, claim 3 (the harness) against claim 4 (what the harness does not represent). Two costs that never appear on a leaderboard: labeling labor and training text taken without consent. Accountability shows up as a missing name on a byline, not as a field on a model card. In this lab: the tensions are teaching sentences written for the lesson, not findings. In general: unresolved is the honest state. Understanding the mechanism does not choose the deployment; the people affected should have a say.
documents.title: One claim at a time, left open

documents.subtitle: Who the benchmark represents · Ethics and impact
documents.body: An average over whoever was in the test set A synthetic triage model is evaluated on a holdout where 10% of patients are in group B, whose notes the labels under-represent. Group B share of patients moves the population the model will actually serve. Accuracy is a weighted average of the two groups, so it barely moves, while missed urgent cases pile up in group B. Group B share of patients, from 0% to 60%. Four stacked bars per 1,000 patients: patients in the holdout, patients at your share, missed urgent cases in the holdout, and missed urgent cases at your share. Group A is the left segment and group B the right, each labeled with its count. Accuracy on the holdout, accuracy at your share, and missed urgent cases per 1,000, holdout → yours. A second row of four readouts: the true-positive rate for each group (90% and 55%), the Equal-opportunity gap between them (35 points), the false-positive rate for each group (5% and 7%), and the False-positive gap (2 points). These are properties of the model, so they do not move with the share. Both groups have 20% urgent cases. Group A: sensitivity 0.90, specificity 0.95, accuracy 94.0%. Group B: sensitivity 0.55, specificity 0.93, accuracy 85.4%. The true-positive rate is the sensitivity, the share of truly urgent cases flagged. The false-positive rate is 1 − specificity, the share of non-urgent cases flagged anyway. Equal opportunity asks that the true-positive rates match across groups, and equalized odds asks that the false-positive rates match too (Hardt, Price, and Srebro, 2016). Accuracy at share q = (1 − q)·94.0% + q·85.4%. Missed urgent cases per 1,000 = 1,000·[(1 − q)·0.2·0.10 + q·0.2·0.45]. Holdout (10% B): 93.1% accurate, 27 misses per 1,000. At 50% B: 89.7% and 55, with 82% of the misses in group B. Group B share of patients. Comparison worth running: 10% against 50%. Accuracy drops 3.4 points; missed urgent cases double. Group B is 30% of patients at the default and 66% of the missed urgent cases. A single accuracy number cannot show this. Only a disaggregated evaluation, reported per group, can. The gap in true-positive rates is 35 points, so the model is far from equal opportunity. Its false-positive rates differ by only 2 points, so it fails equalized odds almost entirely because of the first gap. In this lab: the group rates are invented and fixed; nothing is trained, and real groups differ in prevalence as well as error rates. Two criteria are named here; others exist, such as demographic parity. In general: a model evaluated on last year's population can be deployed on a different one. Distribution shift and missing groups change who bears the errors, not just how many there are.
documents.title: An average over whoever was in the test set

documents.subtitle: Training versus serving · Ethics and impact
documents.body: Compute paid once against compute paid every day Training a dense transformer takes about 6·N·D arithmetic operations; serving takes about 2·N per token. The chart compares one training run with the cumulative compute of serving. The two meet after 3·D ÷ tokens served per day, whatever the model size. Parameters (1B to 405B), Training tokens (0.5T to 15T), and Tokens served per day (1M to 1T, on a log scale). Training, once; Serving, per day; and Days to break even. A chart of one training run's compute (dashed, flat) and serving's cumulative compute (solid, rising), with a guide at the break-even day. Training FLOP = 6·N·D. Serving FLOP per day = 2·N·T. Break-even days = 6ND ÷ 2NT = 3D ÷ T, so N cancels. Energy uses 40% of an A100's 312 TFLOP/s and 400 W per GPU, the utilization that reproduces Meta's reported 184,320 GPU-hours for Llama 2 7B. At the defaults that is about 75 MWh for training. At the defaults (2T training tokens, 10B tokens a day) serving matches training after 600 days; at 1T tokens a day, after 6 days. Parameters, Training tokens, and Tokens served per day. Comparison worth running: move Parameters from 1B to 405B. Both costs scale, and Days to break even does not move. A popular service can spend more compute answering questions than it spent learning to answer them. Decoding usually runs at lower utilization than training, so the energy break-even arrives sooner than the compute break-even shown here. In this lab: FLOP arithmetic for a dense model with one utilization figure. It ignores the attention cost of long contexts, mixture-of-experts sparsity, batching, cooling, and the energy source. In general: energy use depends on hardware, utilization, data-center efficiency, and grid mix, and published figures often cover only the final training run.
documents.title: Compute paid once against compute paid every day

documents.subtitle: Rank four checkpoints under three scoring rules with honest error bars, leak the benchmark into training and watch the leaderboard stop measuring ability, then see how the same ideas extend to applications.
documents.body: Rank four checkpoints under three scoring rules with honest error bars, leak the benchmark into training and watch the leaderboard stop measuring ability, then see how the same ideas extend to applications. Score a model with an explicit rule instead of an impression, and see how the choice of rule changes the ranking Read a benchmark score together with its uncertainty Recognize contamination from the gap between benchmark and control Choose what to measure for an application: golden sets for regressions, task metrics for retrieval, agents, and safety, and a checked judge
