documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Evaluation
documents.body: Read the six default items in Benchmark items and note that each distractor is wrong but ordinary, then write one of your own.
documents.title: Write the items

documents.subtitle: Step 2 · Evaluation
documents.body: In Leaderboard, compare each checkpoint's pass rate with its 95% interval, then read the paired leader-versus-runner-up callout to see whether six items can separate them.
documents.title: Read the leaderboard

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Evaluation
documents.body: In Leaderboard, switch Scoring rule to Raw log-probability and compare the pass counts with Length-normalised. Then choose Sample and check and raise Attempts allowed from 1 to 5 to see which checkpoint moves.
documents.title: Change the scoring rule

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · Evaluation
documents.body: In Item-level results, find the items the largest checkpoint gets wrong and read how large each margin is.
documents.title: Inspect the items

documents.subtitle: Step 5 · Evaluation
documents.body: Press Add the benchmark source sentences to the corpus, then compare Margin shift with Control shift.
documents.title: Contaminate it

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: Text excluded from training and used to score the result. Its only property that matters is that no part of it reached the training data.
documents.title: Held-out set

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: The exponential of mean cross-entropy on a corpus. Comparable across models only when the tokenizer and the corpus are identical.
documents.title: Perplexity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: Answering multiple choice by scoring each candidate continuation's log-probability and keeping the highest. No text is generated, so decoding settings cannot move the result. The raw total favours the shorter option, because every extra token multiplies in another probability below one; length normalization divides by the continuation's length, the idea behind acc_norm.
documents.title: Likelihood scoring

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: The correct candidate's score minus the distractor's. It shows how nearly an item was missed, which a pass count hides.
documents.title: Margin

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: A range that would contain the true pass rate in 95% of repeated samples of items. For accuracy p on n items the standard error is the square root of p(1 − p)/n, so six items at 50% give plus or minus 20 points.
documents.title: Confidence interval

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: Evaluation data present in the training data. It raises benchmark scores without raising capability, and usually arrives by duplication rather than intent. Overfitting the benchmark is its slower cousin: choosing data, settings, or checkpoints by one score until the score outruns the ability it was meant to measure.
documents.title: Contamination

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: A second unseen corpus that no leak touches. Without one, a benchmark gain and a contamination artifact look identical.
documents.title: Control

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: The function turning a model's output into a number: raw log-probability, length-normalised log-probability, or sampling answers and checking them are three rules that can order the same checkpoints differently. It is a design decision, so a score is comparable only under the same rule.
documents.title: Scoring rule

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: For sampled answers a checker can verify: the chance that at least one of k samples passes. From n samples with c passing, the unbiased estimate is 1 − C(n − c, k) / C(n, k). It is the ceiling for a perfect checker, and it rewards a model that hedges as much as one that is right first time.
documents.title: Pass@k

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: A fixed list of cases with known good outcomes, drawn from real traffic and past failures. Because it never changes, scores from different versions of a system are comparable, and its size limits how small a difference it can resolve.
documents.title: Golden set

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: A golden set re-run on every change to the model, prompt, retriever, or tools, so a fix in one place cannot silently break another. Compare runs on the same cases and report an interval, not just a count.
documents.title: Regression suite

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: Using a language model to grade outputs against a rubric. Cheap and scalable, and biased toward the first-listed answer, longer answers, and its own style. Check it against human labels on a sample, and swap the answer order to see whether verdicts flip.
documents.title: LLM-as-judge

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: Scoring by people, including arena-style pairwise votes turned into Elo ratings, where the winner gains K times how surprising the win was. It catches what rules miss and has its own taste for length, confidence, and formatting.
documents.title: Human evaluation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Evaluation
documents.body: The share of attack prompts that elicit the prohibited behaviour. Read it with the false-refusal rate, the share of ordinary requests wrongly refused: a model that refuses everything scores 0% attack success and is useless.
documents.title: Attack success rate

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Evaluation · question 1
documents.body: In Leaderboard you switch Scoring rule from Length-normalised to Raw log-probability and several checkpoints gain passes. What is the most likely reason? Raw log-probability favours the shorter option, and two correct answers are shorter than their distractors Raw log-probability removes the model's randomness, so each item is scored more reliably than before Raw log-probability makes each checkpoint train for more epochs before it is scored on the items Raw log-probability counts a tie between the two options as a pass, which the other rule does not Every extra character multiplies in another probability below one, so a total log-probability grows more negative with length and the shorter option wins more often whatever the model knows. Sails against trails and repeats against retreats are the two items here whose correct option is shorter. Dividing by length, the other rule, removes that head start.
documents.title: In Leaderboard you switch Scoring rule from Length-normalised to Raw log-probability and several checkpoints gain passes. What is the most likely reason?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Evaluation · question 2
documents.body: On Sample and check you raise Attempts allowed from 1 to 5, and the least-trained checkpoint climbs from last to first. Why does it gain the most? Each extra attempt trains the checkpoint a little more, so by the fifth it has learned the items Extra attempts average out sampling noise, and noise is what held the least-trained model back A hesitant model gives every item some chance, so a few attempts nearly always include the key Pass@k rewards the checkpoint with the highest chance of being right on its very first attempt Pass@k asks only whether at least one of k samples is right, the ceiling a perfect checker would reach. A model that is unsure spreads probability over both options and hits within a few tries; a model that is confidently wrong on an item stays near zero however many attempts it gets. Pass@1 rewards the opposite. With two options the score is mostly coverage, which is why the rule is a design decision.
documents.title: On Sample and check you raise Attempts allowed from 1 to 5, and the least-trained checkpoint climbs from last to first. Why does it gain the most?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Evaluation · question 3
documents.body: Two checkpoints both pass 3 of 6 items, and the interval for the leader-minus-runner-up margin runs from below zero to above zero. What follows? The two checkpoints are exactly as capable as each other, because their pass counts match These six items cannot say which is better; more items or a bigger gap would be needed The leader is better, because the middle of the interval sits just above zero The interval is too wide to use, so the standard error alone should be reported An interval that includes zero means the data are compatible with either checkpoint being ahead: the gap is unresolved, which is different from the two being equal. Pairing the items removes item difficulty from the comparison, but six items still leave it wide, and the standard error alone would hide that.
documents.title: Two checkpoints both pass 3 of 6 items, and the interval for the leader-minus-runner-up margin runs from below zero to above zero. What follows?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Evaluation · question 4
documents.body: After a data change, the benchmark margin grows five times over while the control corpus perplexity improves by two percent. What is the most likely explanation? The benchmark text, or something close to it, reached the training data The model became better at exactly the skills the benchmark measures and nothing else Margins and perplexity measure different things, so nothing follows The control corpus is too small to move, so its two percent is only noise A real capability gain shows up on unseen text too, roughly in proportion. When the scored items improve far out of proportion to everything else, the most economical explanation is that those items stopped being unseen — which is why a control corpus is not optional.
documents.title: After a data change, the benchmark margin grows five times over while the control corpus perplexity improves by two percent. What is the most likely explanation?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Evaluation · question 5
documents.body: A retrieval-based assistant gives a wrong answer, and the passage that holds the answer was in its prompt. Which reading points at the generator rather than the retriever? Context recall is low, so the retriever never fetched the supporting passage Attack success rate is high, so the generator is easy to push off task Pass@k is low at k = 1, so the generator needs more attempts per question Context recall is full, but answer correctness is low for those questions Context recall asks whether the facts needed reached the prompt; answer correctness asks whether the final answer matches the key. Full recall with a wrong answer means the evidence arrived and the reader failed to use it. Low recall is a retrieval failure, because the generator never saw the evidence. Faithfulness adds a third check, whether the answer's claims are supported by what was retrieved.
documents.title: A retrieval-based assistant gives a wrong answer, and the passage that holds the answer was in its prompt. Which reading points at the generator rather than the retriever?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Evaluation · question 6
documents.body: A safety suite reports an attack success rate of 0% for a model. What must you check before calling it safe to ship? Nothing more: a 0% rate means every attack in the suite failed, so the model is safe to ship as it stands Its false-refusal rate on ordinary requests, because a model that refuses everything also scores 0% Its perplexity on the control corpus, because successful attacks usually raise perplexity first Its pass@k at k = 1, because the first attempt is the one an attacker will use Attack success rate counts only how often the prohibited behaviour appears. A model that refuses everything never produces it, so 0% is also what an unusable model scores; the false-refusal rate on matched ordinary requests measures that cost, and the two are reported together. Neither number covers attacks that are not in the suite.
documents.title: A safety suite reports an attack success rate of 0% for a model. What must you check before calling it safe to ship?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Evaluation
documents.body: Picture two friends arguing about which of them is better at trivia. The fair way to settle it is a quiz, but a quiz only settles anything if the questions are new to both of them. There also have to be enough questions to rule out a lucky guess, and everyone has to agree, before anyone starts, how the answers will be marked. An AI model learns by reading huge amounts of example text, which is called training. AI models get compared much like the two friends, with fixed tests called benchmarks, and a fair test uses questions the model never read during training. This module is about how those tests turn a model's answers into a score, and how that score can mislead you even when nobody is cheating. Where you have met it Whenever you read that one AI model beats another, or that a new model scored higher than an older one on some test, you are reading a benchmark score. Behind each claim sits a list of questions the model was never supposed to see, a rule for marking its answers, and a score worked out from both. The same habits carry over to whole apps built around a model. One example is an assistant that searches through documents before it answers, and another is an assistant that carries out a task step by step, called an agent. Those apps need careful tests too, and the last part of this lesson shows what to measure for them. Why it matters A test score looks like a plain fact, but the number on its own never tells you how it was made. Without careful tests, nobody could tell whether a new model is really better, whether it got lucky on a short test, or whether it saw the test in training. Each of those problems can make a weaker model look stronger, and each one is invisible in the score itself. The lab lets you cause each of them on purpose and watch the numbers change, so you know what to check the next time someone shows you a ranking. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these in your own words: How a model gets a score from a clearly stated marking rule instead of someone's impression, and why switching the rule can change which model comes first. How to read a score together with the range it could really fall in, and why six questions, like the lab's, cannot tell two close models apart. How to spot a test that leaked into a model's training, by comparing how far the test score jumps with how far a score on unrelated text moves. What to measure when you test a whole app. That means a fixed set of known cases rerun after every change, task scores for search, agents and safety, and an AI grader checked against people. What the lab lets you do The lab tests a tiny model that really trains on a few sentences about a harbor. Every score, chart and range you see is worked out from that model's real output. Two parts are kept simple on purpose. The six test questions start out fixed, though you can rewrite them, and the leak is a word-for-word copy, which is easier to spot than real leaks. The lab has four cards: Leaderboard ranks four versions of the model, draws a range beside every score, and lets you change the marking rule with Scoring rule. Item-level results shows how the most-trained version did on each question, and by how much it passed or failed. Benchmark editor holds the six test questions, which you can read and rewrite, along with a slider that sets how long the four versions train. Contamination control has a switch that leaks the test's source sentences into the training text, so you can see what a leak does to every score.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Evaluation
documents.body: The model on test The lab trains a very small language model, which is a program that learns to guess the next character of a piece of text. Here a character means one letter, space or full stop, so “the fog” is seven characters. The model learns from a handful of sentences about harbor weather, such as “the morning fog settles over the harbor and the air feels cool.” This model looks back only one character when it guesses, so when it guesses what follows a space, the only clue it can use is that space. Nothing inside it stands for what a harbor is or what a sentence means, which matters later when you see which questions it gets wrong. The lab saves four versions of the model, each trained for a different amount of time. Training time is counted in epochs, where one epoch is one full pass through the training text, and the four budgets are 3, 10, 30 and 80 epochs. Each saved version is called a checkpoint, which is what the Leaderboard calls its rows. The Training budget multiplier slider in Benchmark editor stretches or shrinks all four budgets together. It runs from a quarter of the default length up to three times it, and it starts at 1.00×, which leaves the four budgets as they are. A test made of two-ending questions In this lab, a benchmark is a short list of fill-in-the-blank questions, which the lab calls items. Each item is one line in Benchmark editor, written in the form context | correct | plausible distractor. That means the start of a sentence, then the right way to finish it, then a wrong ending picked to sound believable, which is called a distractor. Here is one of the six default items: the fog returns in the | morning | evening. “Evening” is wrong only because the harbor notes say the fog comes back in the morning. It is an ordinary word that shares many letter patterns with “morning”, so a model that has not learned this text has no easy way to tell the two apart. For this lab's model, though, learning the text means learning which letters tend to follow which. It cannot connect the fog with the morning, so even when it passes this item, the pass comes from letter patterns, as Item-level results will show. Likelihood scoring: rating the endings instead of writing one The model never writes an answer on this test. Instead, the lab asks how likely the model would be to produce each ending after the context, and the more likely ending wins. This way of marking is called likelihood scoring, and because nothing gets written, the random settings that make a chatbot's replies vary cannot change the result. Rating an ending works one character at a time, with the model giving each character a chance between 0 and 1 of coming next. The chance of the whole ending is all of those chances multiplied together. Every chance is below 1, so the product shrinks with each character you add, and it soon becomes a very tiny number. To keep those numbers manageable, scorers first turn each chance into a log-probability. You do not need to know how the conversion works, only three facts about it. A chance of 1 becomes 0, while smaller chances become negative numbers that sit further below zero: 0.5 becomes about −0.7, and 0.1 becomes about −2.3. Adding log-probabilities together does the same job as multiplying the chances. Every ending is scored with the space in front of it, so “ morning” counts as eight characters, which is the space plus seven letters. Its total log-probability is the sum of eight negative numbers, one per character, and a total closer to zero means a more likely ending. Why length gets in the way Here is the catch: a longer ending adds up more negative numbers, so its total sinks lower even when every one of its characters was a good guess. Picture a made-up model that gives every character in two endings the same log-probability of −2. The ending “ sails” has six characters once you count its space, so its total is −12. The ending “ trails” has seven characters, so its total is −14. Comparing totals hands the win to “sails”, even though this made-up model rated every character in both endings equally well. The shorter ending won for no reason except that it was shorter. The fix is to divide each total by its number of characters, which gives the average log-probability per character. In the example both averages come out at −2, so length gives neither ending a head start, and the winner has to earn it character by character. Dividing by length like this is called length normalization, and it is the lab's default rule. The margin: how close was the call? A pass or a fail hides how close the call was, so the lab also shows each item's margin: the right ending's score minus the wrong one's. A positive margin means the item passed and a negative one means it failed. Because the scores are negative numbers, take care with the subtraction. For example, if the right ending averages −2.0 per character and the wrong one −2.5, the margin is −2.0 − (−2.5) = +0.5, so the item passes. The further the margin sits from zero, the less close the call was. A pass by 0.01 and a pass by 1.2 count the same in a pass count, but as margins they look very different. The scoring rule is a choice Turning a model's output into a number takes a rule, and the rule someone picks is called a scoring rule. It is a decision a person makes, not a fact about the model, and the Scoring rule control on the Leaderboard offers three of them: Length-normalised, the default, compares each ending's average log-probability per character, so a long ending is not punished for its length. Raw log-probability compares the totals instead, which hands the shorter ending a head start whatever the model has learned. Sample and check makes each checkpoint actually pick an ending at random, weighted by how likely it rates each one, and checks whether the pick was right. Switching the rule marks the same four checkpoints a second time, without training them again. Nothing inside the models changes, so any change you see in the ranking comes from the rule alone. Sample and check, and pass@k Under Sample and check, a checkpoint picks between the two endings the way a weighted coin lands. If it rates the whole right ending three times as likely as the wrong one, it picks the right ending about 3 times in 4. The weights come from the whole ending's chance, the same total that Raw log-probability compares, so a shorter right ending gets the same head start here. The lab records 20 picks for every item and reuses the same random numbers each time, so the results come out the same whenever you look. The Attempts allowed (k) slider appears once you choose Sample and check. It runs from 1 to 10 and sets how many tries each checkpoint gets at every item. An item then scores pass@k, the chance that at least one of k tries picks the right ending. So pass@1 is the chance of being right on the first go. To see the idea with small numbers, suppose a checkpoint picks the right ending half the time and gets two tries. It misses both with a chance of 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25, so its pass@2 is 1 − 0.25 = 0.75, or 75%. The lab works out pass@k from the 20 picks it recorded rather than from a shortcut like this one, but it is estimating the same chance. The held-out set and the control A test only measures something if the model has not seen it. The six items were written from the last three sentences of the harbor notes, and the lab removes those sentences before training, so no checkpoint has seen them. Text kept out of training so it can be used for testing is called a held-out set, and you can read these three sentences in Contamination control. The lab also keeps a second piece of text away from training: ten proverbs, such as “the early bird gets the worm”, which have nothing to do with harbors. That text is the control, a yardstick that shares nothing with the test, so a leak of the test copies none of it into training. A real improvement shows up on the control too, roughly in proportion. If the test score jumps far more than the control moves, suspect that the test leaked, even when the control improves a little. Benchmark editor counts the characters in all three texts, under Training characters, Benchmark source and Control. They are three different pieces of text, and only the training text is trained on. When you switch on the leak, the Training characters count grows, because the three source sentences join it. Perplexity: how well does the model fit a passage? Pass counts only look at six items, so the Leaderboard also measures how well each checkpoint fits whole passages of text. It uses perplexity, which you can read as the number of equally likely characters the model is choosing between at each step. Lower is better, because a lower number means the model has narrowed down its guesses. The lab's model can write 30 different characters: the 26 letters, a space, a full stop and two special markers. A model that learned nothing gives all of them the same chance, so it scores a perplexity of 30, like a blind guess every time. A perplexity of 9 means the model is about as unsure as if it were choosing from 9 equally likely characters instead. The table shows two of these numbers for each checkpoint: Benchmark perplexity, measured on the three held-out sentences, and Control perplexity, measured on the proverbs. How sure is a score? Picture a coin that you flip six times and that lands heads three times. That does not prove the coin is fair, because a coin weighted to land heads only 30% of the time could also give three heads in six flips. So could a coin weighted toward 70% heads, which means six flips cannot tell any of these coins apart. Six test items work like six flips, so a score of 3 out of 6 tells you much less than it seems to. The lab measures that wobble with the standard error, using a formula that appears inside the callout at the bottom of the Leaderboard: √(p(1 − p)/n). In it, p is the pass rate and n is the number of items. For 3 passes out of 6, p is 0.5, so p(1 − p) is 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. Dividing by 6 gives about 0.042, and its square root is about 0.20. That is 20 percentage points, which is roughly what Leader's standard error reads at the start, so the leader's score is 50%, give or take about 20 points. The lab turns that wobble into a range. First, a checkpoint's true pass rate is the share of items it would pass on a huge number of similar items, which no six-item test can show you directly. Picture giving the same checkpoint 100 different six-item tests and drawing a range from each one. About 95 of those 100 ranges would contain the true pass rate, and a range built this way is called a 95% confidence interval. A rough version of that range stretches two standard errors either side of the score, which for 3 out of 6 runs from about 10% to 90%. With so few items that rule is only a rough guide. So the chart draws a more careful version called the Wilson interval, which also stays sensible near 0% and 100%. For 3 out of 6, the Wilson interval runs from 19% to 81%, and that is the range to read. Either way, a checkpoint passing 3 of 6 could be weak or could be strong. Comparing two checkpoints item by item Here the coin picture stops matching, because coin flips are all alike while test items are not: some are much harder than others. That difference between items is what makes an item-by-item comparison useful, because both checkpoints answer the same six items. Picture two friends who take the same quiz. Scored separately, each friend's total wobbles with luck, such as whether this quiz happened to be full of easy or hard questions, and that wobble widens each friend's own range. Compare them question by question instead, and a question both of them miss adds nothing to the difference between them. Only the questions where they disagree count, so the range for that difference is usually much narrower than the two separate ranges would suggest. The lab goes one step further than right or wrong, because it compares margins instead. That means every item adds a small difference, not just the ones where the two disagree. Still, an item that is hard for both checkpoints pulls both margins down by about the same amount, so most of its difficulty cancels out in the subtraction. The callout at the bottom of the Leaderboard does exactly this, subtracting the runner-up's margin from the leader's on every item. Under Sample and check it subtracts each item's pass@k instead, because that rule scores items by pass@k rather than by margin. It then averages the six differences and gives that average its own 95% range. When that range runs from below zero to above zero, the items cannot say which of the two is better.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Evaluation
documents.body: Every claim about what a model can do comes down to a score on a test, and that score means something only if three things are true. The test text has to be truly absent from training, and there have to be enough items to separate the models. The scoring rule also has to be stated, so others can use the same one. None of these three conditions shows up in the score. Picture a reading test built on a story that nobody in the class has read, so it checks how well students understand writing that is new to them. If one student happens to have read that exact story at home, their score jumps, even though their reading has not improved at all. The test has quietly stopped measuring what it was built to measure. A second test on a different unread story would reveal the problem, because that student's score there would stay about where it was. That second test plays the same part as the lab's control. In AI this problem is called contamination, which means test text, or the text a test was written from, ending up in a model's training data. The picture stops matching in one way, though. Reading one story does not make a student better at other stories, but a model trained on leaked text usually gets a little better at unrelated text too. So the lab's control moves slightly, and the warning sign is the size of the gap between the two scores, not a control that stays perfectly still. The other two conditions fail as quietly. With only a few questions, luck decides close contests, the way a two-question quiz could rank a lucky guesser above someone who studied. A marking rule that favours short answers can reorder a ranking without anyone getting better or worse.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Evaluation
documents.body: The lab's five steps take you through it in order, and each part below matches one of those steps. Write the items Before writing an item of your own, open Benchmark editor and read the six default items in the Benchmark items box: Every wrong ending is wrong but ordinary, such as “evening” against “morning” or “trails” against “sails”. Each one is a real word that could fit the sentence. So to pick the right ending reliably, a checkpoint has to have learned something from the harbor text, even if it is only the letter patterns. To see why that matters, change morning | evening to morning | xyzzy in the box. The fog item now passes by a wide margin. This model only knows which letter tends to follow which, and pairs like “xy” and “zz” never appear in the training text. An item with a nonsense distractor stops testing anything, so change it back before you go on. When you write an item of your own, take it from the three held-out sentences. An item written from the other harbor sentences is contaminated from the start, because every checkpoint trained on those sentences. Read the leaderboard Now look at Leaderboard at its starting settings, where the chart has one row per checkpoint: a dot for its pass rate and a line showing its 95% range. The leader's range is shaded down the whole chart, so you can see at a glance which other rows fall inside it. The table below the chart gives the same results as numbers, along with each checkpoint's two perplexities. The 80-epoch and 30-epoch checkpoints both pass 3 of 6 items, and both of their ranges run from 19% to 81%. The 80-epoch checkpoint sits on top only because its average margin, in the Mean margin column, is a tiny bit larger: 0.012 against 0.011. The callout under the table says that the leader's margin minus the runner-up's, paired over the same six items, averages +0.002. Its 95% interval runs from −0.220 to +0.224, which crosses zero. So these six items cannot say which checkpoint is better, and the order of the top two is not settled by this test. Change the scoring rule Try this: switch Scoring rule from Length-normalised to Raw log-probability. Every checkpoint gains two passes, and the 80-epoch checkpoint jumps from 3 of 6 to 5 of 6. The 30-epoch checkpoint, also at 5 of 6, now edges ahead of it on mean margin, even though neither one was trained again. Next choose Sample and check, with Attempts allowed (k) at 1. The 10-epoch checkpoint moves into first place, the 80-epoch one drops to third, and the 3-epoch one comes last. Now drag Attempts allowed (k) to 5, and the 3-epoch checkpoint, which trained least of all, takes the lead at 94%. Meanwhile the 80-epoch one falls to last place at 83%. Notice what happened there: the checkpoints and the six items never changed, yet each of the four checkpoints has now had a turn in first place. The only thing that moved was the rule you picked. Inspect the items Open Item-level results, which always shows the most-trained checkpoint, 80 epochs unless you move the multiplier. Each row shows both endings' scores, the margin, and a bar that grows right of centre for a pass and left of centre for a fail. This card follows whichever rule is chosen, so set Scoring rule back to Length-normalised first. Then find “the boats stay in | port | town”, which fails by −0.840. Both endings start with a space, and in the harbor notes a space is most often followed by “t”, as in “the”. So “ town” collects a high score on its first letter, and this model has no way to link “port” with boats, because it only ever looks one character back. Now find “the water stays | warm | wide”, which passes by +1.213, the biggest margin of the six. That win comes from the letters inside “warm” and “wide”, not from any link between water and warmth, so a big margin is not the same thing as understanding. Contaminate it Finally, look at Contamination control and read its two readouts, Margin shift and Control shift, before you press anything. The lab always trains every checkpoint twice, once with the leak and once without, so these readouts compare the two versions whichever way the switch is set. Now press Add the benchmark source sentences to the corpus. Its chip changes from “held out” to “leaking”, and the Leaderboard's badge changes from “clean” to “contaminated”. The scores now come from checkpoints trained with the three source sentences added. The questions themselves never enter training, only the sentences they were written from. Real models train on huge amounts of text collected from websites, so a web page that copies a test's source text can leak a public test in the same way. Then compare how far each score moved, measured against where it started. Margin shift reads +0.519, so the 80-epoch row's Mean margin climbs from 0.012 to about 0.53, more than forty times what it was. Control shift reads −2.8%, a change of under 3 in every 100. To compare like with like, look at the 80-epoch row's two perplexities in the table. Benchmark perplexity falls from 9.33 to 5.83, a drop of more than a third, while Control perplexity drops by that same 2.8%. The test moved far more than the control did, and that lopsided gap is the sign of a leak.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Evaluation
documents.body: Six items cannot rank these checkpoints. Even the paired range for the top two crosses zero, and all three other ranges overlap the leader's, which is what Intervals overlapping the leader's counts. To pin a score down to within 5 points either way at 50%, you would need 385 items, which is what Items for ±5 pts reads. The rule is a choice, not a discovery. The two extra passes under Raw log-probability come from the two items whose right ending is shorter: “sails” against “trails”, and “repeats” against “retreats”. No checkpoint learned anything between the two views, because the rule handed the shorter endings a head start. Pass@k rewards a checkpoint that spreads its chances. The 3-epoch checkpoint has trained so little that it gives both endings a fair share of chance, so a few tries nearly always include the right one. The 80-epoch checkpoint is confidently wrong on “port”, giving nearly all its chance to “town”. Extra tries cannot fix a confident mistake. None of the 80-epoch checkpoint's 20 picks lands on “port”, so its pass@k on that item stays at zero however many tries you allow. No rule settles the ranking, because under all three rules every other range still overlaps the leader's. Changing the rule reshuffles the ranking, and six items are too few to say which order is right. Pairing helps, but not enough here. Because both checkpoints answer the same items, a hard item counts against both and cancels out, yet the paired range for the top two still crosses zero. A leak moves the test a lot: at 80 epochs it raises the margin by +0.519 per item, and that checkpoint passes 6 of 6. The Item-level results callout gives that rise a 95% range of +0.220 to +0.817, well clear of zero, so the jump is very unlikely to be luck. A less-trained checkpoint gains too: at 30 epochs, 3 of 6 becomes 5 of 6. Its benchmark perplexity drops from 10.08 to 6.65, so on the test text it went from choosing among about ten characters to fewer than seven. The control moves a little as well. Control perplexity falls by 2.8% at 80 epochs, because the leaked sentences are ordinary English and help a little with any English text. So the sign of a leak is not a frozen control but the huge difference in size between the two shifts. A perfect score is not a certain score: with the leak on, the leader passes 6 of 6 and Leader's standard error reads ± 0.0 pts. That is because p(1 − p) is 1 × 0 = 0, so the simple formula claims total certainty, while the drawn range still runs from 61% to 100%. A common mix-up: a higher place on the leaderboard means a better model. Here the top two are separated by +0.002, with a range that crosses zero, and a different scoring rule puts them in a different order. A range that crosses zero does not mean the two are equally good either; it means these items cannot tell. A rank printed without its range and its rule can be noise.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Evaluation
documents.body: What this lab simplifies The training, the scoring, the perplexities and the ranges are all really computed from the checkpoints' output, so nothing on the Leaderboard is made up. The simplifications are in what gets tested and how: The model looks back only one character, so words like “water” and “harbor” do not exist for it as words. When it passes an item, it is following patterns of letter pairs, which is not understanding. Each checkpoint comes from one training run with fixed random choices, so its ranges cover which items happened to be picked but not the luck of training. A second run with different random choices could shift every score. The leak is a word-for-word copy of three known sentences, which is the simplest kind of leak to catch. Sample and check picks between the two endings instead of writing free text, because this model almost never writes a whole target word by chance. So its pass@k measures how often a few tries cover the right one of only two choices. The 20 picks per item under Sample and check add their own luck, and the drawn ranges do not include it. Benchmark editor scores only the first 60 lines and cuts each line at 160 characters, so a pasted test cannot freeze the page. Where real benchmarks fail Real leaks rarely arrive as exact copies, and instead come as rewordings, translations, forum posts that discuss the test, and copies of the test posted on other websites. Checks that hunt for exact copies or matching runs of words miss most of them. A benchmark can also be fooled with no leak at all. If a team keeps choosing its training data, settings and checkpoints by whichever gives the best score on one test, the model slowly fits that test's quirks. The score then climbs faster than the ability it was meant to measure, which is called overfitting the benchmark. You saw one rule reorder a leaderboard, and real tests come in more variations than that. Questions with lettered options, written answers checked for an exact match, and grading by another model can each order the same models differently again. So a score means something only when its rule, the testing program that ran it, and that program's version sit beside it.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Evaluation
documents.body: Evaluating applications, not only models A benchmark scores a model on fixed questions, but a real product is a model plus other parts. Those can include a search step that finds documents, tools the model can use, and safety rules. The text the model is handed for each request is called the prompt. Any one of these parts, the search step, the tools, the safety rules or the prompt, can fail on its own. The habits from the lab carry over: fixed cases, a named rule, and a range on every rate. Nothing in this section runs in the lab, because it describes what you would build around a model. Golden sets and regression suites A golden set is a fixed list of cases with known good results, taken from real use and from past failures. Because it never changes, scores from different versions of a system can be compared fairly. When something that used to work stops working after a change, that step backward is called a regression. A regression suite reruns the golden set after every change to the model, prompt, search step or tools, so a fix in one place cannot quietly break another. Picture a homework-help assistant: a change that makes it better at maths questions should not quietly break its spelling answers, and the suite would catch it if it did. Size still limits what a golden set can show: suppose an assistant passes 27 of its 30 golden cases, a score of 90%. The 95% range for that score runs from 74% to 97%, so a small drop between two versions may be luck rather than a real step backward. That is why you compare runs on the same cases, as the lab's paired callout does. Search-based assistants Some assistants search a set of documents first and then write an answer from what they found, and those stages should be graded separately: *Context recall* asks how many of the facts needed for the answer made it into the prompt, alongside the question. *Faithfulness* asks whether every claim in the answer is backed by the text the search found. *Answer correctness* asks whether the final answer matches the known right answer. Picture a school-handbook assistant asked “When does the library close?” Context recall checks whether the search found the page that says the library closes at 4 pm. Faithfulness checks that the reply only says things that page supports, and answer correctness checks that the final reply really says 4 pm. The search step is often called the retriever, and the writing step is called the generator. If recall is full but the answer is wrong, the facts arrived and the generator failed to use them. If recall is low, the retriever is to blame, because the generator never saw the facts. The Retrieval-augmented generation lab in this app computes recall, correctness and a rough support check that stands in for faithfulness, on five questions. Agents An agent is a system in which a model works through a task in steps, such as searching or using a tool, until the job is done. Grade an agent on three things, starting with the *task success rate*: whether the job got done, checked by looking at the end result. The other two are how many *steps* it took and what it *cost*, counted in text processed, tool uses or time. Success without cost hides an agent that loops round and round before it finishes, and cost without success rewards an agent that gives up early. Runs vary from one try to the next, so repeat each task and report the rate with a range. Safety Run a fixed set of prompts written to push the model into something it should refuse. Then report the attack success rate, the share of those prompts that succeed in getting the forbidden behaviour. Pair it with the *false-refusal rate*, which is the share of ordinary, harmless requests the model wrongly refuses. A model that refuses everything scores 0% attack success and is useless, which only the second number reveals. Neither number says anything about attacks that are not in the set, so a kind of attack the set never tried can still work. Judges When answers are free writing, a second model can grade them against a written checklist of what a good answer needs, called a rubric. This is called LLM-as-judge, where LLM stands for large language model, the kind of model behind chat assistants. It is cheap and quick, but it tends to favour the answer shown first, longer answers, and answers in its own style. Picture a friend who marks your essays and always gives the higher grade to the longer one. You would want to check that friend against a teacher before trusting the grades, and an AI judge needs the same check. Have people label a sample of answers, then compare how often the judge agrees with them against how often two people agree with each other. Then swap the order of the two answers and see whether the judge's verdict flips. Trust the judge only where it agrees with people about as well as people agree with each other. People and arenas In human evaluation, people read two anonymous answers and pick the better one. Websites that run these head-to-head votes are often called arenas. The votes become Elo ratings, a points system in which each vote moves points from the loser to the winner. The winner gains K × (1 − E) points. Here K is the most points a single vote can move, and E is the chance of winning that the ratings predicted beforehand. To see the formula with real values, start with two equal ratings, where each side was predicted to win half the time, so E is 0.5. With K = 32, the winner gains 32 × 0.5 = 16 points. A favourite rated 400 points higher was predicted to win about 91% of the time, so E is about 0.91 and 1 − E is about 0.09. A win earns it about 32 × 0.09, which is under 3 points. An expected win barely moves the ratings, while an upset moves them a lot. People catch problems that fixed rules miss, but they also tend to prefer answers that are longer, more confident and neatly formatted. Scoring written answers When a model writes answers that are then checked by an automatic test, success depends on how many tries you allow. Pass@k is again the chance that at least one of k tries passes. Suppose a model wrote 10 answers and 3 of them passed. Rather than run 5 fresh tries, you can estimate pass@5 from the 10 answers you already have. It is the chance that 5 answers picked at random from the 10 include at least one pass. The only way to miss is to pick all 5 from the 7 failures. There are 21 ways to choose 5 answers from those 7, and 252 ways to choose 5 from all 10. You could check these counts by listing every choice, but the next step is what matters. So the chance of missing is 21 in 252, and pass@5 is 1 − 21/252, which is about 0.917, or about 92%. The Reasoning models lab shows how this climbs as you allow more tries. The two kinds of range on the chart The titles above the chart's two columns name the kind of range each one draws. Pass rates get a Wilson interval, because it stays sensible at 0 of 6 and 6 of 6, where the simple formula shrinks to a range of zero width. Averages, such as the mean margin or the mean pass@k, get a t interval, which is built for averages of measurements rather than counts of passes. Keeping tests honest Private test sets never publish their answers, which closes the leak path, but it also means outsiders cannot rerun the test to check the results. Marker strings, which are unusual lines of text planted inside a test set, let you check later whether a model was trained on that test. The name and version of the testing program belong next to any score, because different versions of a rule do not give comparable numbers. Every score should come with a range, and a gap smaller than about two standard errors is not evidence that one model is better. Once the best models all score near the top, the items they still miss are mostly unclear or wrongly labelled. The ranking then measures labelling mistakes more than skill, and that is when a benchmark gets retired.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Evaluation
documents.body: This module is about evaluation: scoring a trained model on items it never saw, under a rule fixed in advance, and reading the score as an estimate with an error bar. The question is when a leaderboard rank reflects what the models learned, and when it is an artefact of the test. It builds on *Train one from scratch*, which judged a run by its held-out loss. The same kind of character bigram is now scored on two-option multiple-choice items, and the lesson then widens from models to applications. Where it shows up Multiple-choice benchmarks. Likelihood scoring is one rule for them: pick the option the model gives the highest log-probability, in total or divided by length, with nothing generated. Lettered options, generated answers, and graders are other rules, and each can order the same models differently. Generated answers checked by tests, scored by pass@k: the chance that at least one of k samples passes. Leak defences against contamination: test text that leaked into training. Real leaks arrive as paraphrases, translations, and scraped mirrors. Private test sets close that path, and canary strings, unique markers planted in a test set, let you check later whether a model ingested it. Applications: regression suites that re-run a golden set (fixed cases with known good outcomes) on every change; task metrics for retrieval, agents, and safety; and LLM judges or human votes for free text. Why it matters Training data, settings, and checkpoints are chosen by scores, so a misread score steers each of those choices. Keep selecting by one benchmark and its score drifts away from the ability it was meant to measure, even with no leak; that is overfitting the benchmark. In a product, scores decide which change ships, and whatever they do not cover can get worse unnoticed. What you will be able to explain How an explicit scoring rule replaces an impression, and why changing the rule can reorder the same checkpoints. How to read a benchmark score together with its confidence interval. How to recognize contamination from a benchmark gain out of proportion to the change on a control, an unseen corpus no leak touches. What to measure for an application: golden sets for regressions, task metrics for retrieval, agents, and safety, and a judge checked against human labels. What the lab shows Nothing on the page is a stored result. The lab trains its own character bigram at 3, 10, 30, and 80 epochs, one seed each, on the harbor corpus minus its last three sentences. Those sentences are the held-out benchmark source, and the Proverbs corpus is the control. Log-probabilities, margins (correct score minus distractor score), and perplexities are measured; standard errors, 95% intervals, and Items for ±5 pts are closed-form. Benchmark editor holds the items, one per line as context | correct | plausible distractor (six fixed defaults you can rewrite), and Training budget multiplier, which scales all four budgets. Leaderboard ranks the four checkpoints under Scoring rule: Length-normalised, Raw log-probability, or Sample and check. Changing the rule re-scores them without retraining. Sample and check adds Attempts allowed (k) and makes 20 seeded draws per item, each a choice between the two options rather than free text. Item-level results shows every item's margin for the largest checkpoint, or its draw count and pass@k under Sample and check. Contamination control holds the switch Add the benchmark source sentences to the corpus, which appends the three held-out sentences to the training text. The key experiment: under the default rule, press that switch, then compare Margin shift with Control shift. The benchmark moves far more than general text does. Nothing in the application half of the lesson runs here.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Evaluation
documents.body: A benchmark is a scoring rule applied to a held-out set, and a score is an estimate with an error bar. This lab makes all three visible, and lets you change the rule. The default rule is likelihood scoring. Each line in Benchmark editor is context | correct | plausible distractor. The model scores the continuation “ candidate” — the space plus every character — and the candidate with the higher mean log-probability per character wins. Nothing is generated, so decoding settings cannot move the result. Dividing by length is length normalization. Raw log-probability favours the shorter candidate, because every extra character multiplies in another probability below one. Dividing by the continuation's length in bytes is the idea behind lm-evaluation-harness's acc_norm. Three scoring rules Scoring rule re-scores the same trained checkpoints without retraining them: Length-normalised is the default above: mean log-probability per character. Raw log-probability compares totals instead of means. Sample and check has each checkpoint answer by sampling one of the two options in proportion to the probability it gives each full continuation, 20 seeded draws per item. An item scores pass@k: the chance that at least one of k attempts picks the key, estimated from those draws. The held-out half The items were written from the last three sentences of the harbor corpus, and those sentences are removed from training. The Proverbs corpus is the control: unrelated text no leak touches. Four checkpoints train for 3, 10, 30, and 80 epochs, scaled by Training budget multiplier. A model that learned nothing scores ln(30) = 3.401 nats per character, a perplexity of 30. The error bar With n items and pass rate p, the standard error is √(p(1 − p)/n). Six items at 50% give ±20 points. The Leaderboard draws each pass rate with a 95% confidence interval (Wilson's, which unlike p ± 1.96·SE does not collapse at 0/6 or 6/6), and each mean margin with a t interval.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Evaluation
documents.body: Every capability claim is a held-out measurement, and it means something only if the held-out text was absent from training and the sample of items was large enough to separate the models. Neither condition shows in the number itself, and neither does the rule that produced it. Here you can break all three on purpose.

documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Evaluation
documents.body: In this lab. Training, scoring, perplexities, and intervals are all computed. The model is a bigram that sees one character of context, so “water” and “harbor” are invisible to it; a pass is not comprehension. Each checkpoint is one run at one seed, so the intervals cover the choice of items, not training noise. The leak is a verbatim copy, the easiest kind to catch. Sample and check draws a choice between the two options, not free text, because this bigram almost never writes a whole target word by chance. Its pass@k therefore measures coverage over two options. The 20 draws per item add sampling noise that the interval does not include. In real systems. Leaks arrive as paraphrases, translations, forum answers quoting the test, and scraped mirrors; exact-match and n-gram checks miss most of them. Overfitting the benchmark needs no leak at all: choosing data, settings, and checkpoints by one score slowly fits the benchmark's quirks. You have just seen the scoring rule change a ranking. Lettered-option prompts, generated answers, and graders each order the same models differently again, so a number means something only with its rule, harness, and version beside it.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Evaluation
documents.body: Evaluating applications, not just models A benchmark scores a model on fixed questions. A product is a model plus retrieval, prompts, tools, and guardrails, and each piece can fail alone. The leaderboard's habits carry over: fixed cases, a named rule, and an interval on every rate. Nothing in this section runs in this lab; it is the mechanism for what you would build around it. Golden sets and regression suites. A golden set is a fixed list of cases with known good outcomes, taken from real traffic and past failures. A regression suite re-runs it on every change to the model, prompt, retriever, or tools, so a fix in one place cannot silently break another. Size still limits resolution: 27 passes out of 30 is 90%, with a Wilson interval from 74% to 97%. Compare runs on the same cases, as the paired callout does. Retrieval pipelines. Score the stages separately. *Context recall* asks what share of the facts needed to answer reached the prompt. *Faithfulness* asks whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved text. *Answer correctness* asks whether the final answer matches the key. Full recall with a wrong answer is a generator failure; low recall is a retrieval failure. The Retrieval-augmented generation lab computes context recall, correctness, and a crude support check that stands in for faithfulness, on five questions. Agents. Score the outcome and the path: *task success rate* over a fixed task set, checked on the end state; *steps* taken; and *cost* in tokens, tool calls, or time. Success without cost hides a looping agent, and cost without success rewards giving up. Runs vary, so repeat each task and report the rate with an interval. Safety. Run a fixed suite of attack prompts and report the attack success rate: the share that elicit the prohibited behaviour. Pair it with the *false-refusal rate*, the share of ordinary requests wrongly refused, because a model that refuses everything scores 0% on the first. Neither covers attacks outside the suite. LLM-as-judge. When answers are free text, a second model grades them against a rubric. That is cheap and scalable, and LLM-as-judge is biased toward the first-listed answer, longer answers, and its own style. To check one, have people label a sample, measure how often the judge agrees with them against how often two people agree, swap the answer order, and see whether verdicts flip. Trust it only where it agrees about as well as humans do. Human and arena evaluation. In human evaluation, people compare two anonymous answers, and pairwise votes become Elo ratings. After each vote the winner gains K × (1 − E), where E is the win chance the ratings predicted, 1 / (1 + 10^((rB − rA)/400)). With equal ratings and K = 32 the winner gains 16 points. A 400-point favourite who wins gains under 3. People catch what rules miss; they also prefer length, confidence, and formatting. Scoring generated answers When answers are generated and checked by tests, success depends on the sampling budget. Pass@k is the chance at least one of k samples passes. From n samples with c passing, the unbiased estimate is 1 − C(n − c, k) / C(n, k). With n = 10, c = 3, k = 5 it is 0.917; the plug-in 1 − (1 − c/n)^k gives 0.832. The Reasoning models lab plots this ceiling. Keeping benchmarks honest Private test sets never publish labels, which closes the leak path and costs reproducibility. Canary strings planted in a test set let you check later whether a model ingested it. Harness name and version belong next to any number, because rule variants are not comparable. And report intervals: a gap smaller than about two standard errors is not evidence. Neither defence helps a saturated benchmark. Once the best models cluster near the ceiling, the remaining items are mostly ambiguous or mislabelled, and the ranking measures label noise. That is when a benchmark is retired.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Leaderboard · Evaluation
documents.body: Four checkpoints ranked, with the uncertainty drawn in The same character bigram trained at four epoch budgets, ranked under a scoring rule you choose: by default how often it gives the correct continuation a higher per-character log-probability than the distractor. Every score carries a 95% interval, and a paired comparison says whether the top two are actually separated by these items. Changing the rule re-scores the checkpoints and can reorder them. A `Scoring rule` selector (Length-normalised, Raw log-probability, Sample and check) and, under Sample and check, an `Attempts allowed (k)` slider from 1 to 10, with a note describing the chosen rule. A forest plot: one row per checkpoint, the headline score with its 95% interval on the left (pass rate with a Wilson interval, or mean pass@k with a t interval), and the rule's second quantity on the right (mean margin, or mean pass@1). The leader's intervals are shaded across all rows, so overlap is visible at a glance. A table sorted by the headline score, then by the second quantity: `Passed` or `Mean pass@k`, `95% interval`, `Mean margin` or `Mean pass@1`, `Benchmark perplexity`, and `Control perplexity`. The leader row is highlighted. Metrics `Leader's standard error`, `Intervals overlapping the leader's`, and `Items for ±5 pts`. A callout with the leader-minus-runner-up margin difference, paired over the same items, and whether its interval excludes zero. Budgets are 3, 10, 30, and 80 epochs times `Training budget multiplier`, each with batch 16, learning rate 0.6, seed 1, on Harbor weather notes minus its last three sentences. Changing the scoring rule never retrains them. Length-normalised: a candidate's score is the mean log-probability of the continuation “ candidate” after the context: the space and every candidate character, divided by that many transitions. Raw log-probability keeps the total instead, so each extra character multiplies in another probability below one and the shorter option gains a head start. Sample and check: the correct option's share is 1 / (1 + exp(distractor total − correct total)). Each item takes 20 draws from a seeded generator, a draw picking the correct option when a uniform number falls below that share. With c correct draws the item scores pass@k = 1 − C(20 − c, k) / C(20, k), and the checkpoint scores the mean over items. The seed depends on the item only, so every checkpoint reuses the same dice. Standard error is √(p(1 − p)/n). The drawn interval is Wilson's, which stays sensible at 0/n and n/n where p ± 1.96·SE collapses to zero width. Margin intervals use Student's t with n − 1 degrees of freedom. `Items for ±5 pts` is ⌈1.96² · p(1 − p) / 0.05²⌉ at the leader's pass rate, clamped to 5–95%: 385 items at 50%. Under Sample and check it uses the per-item variance of pass@k instead, with a floor of two items. `Scoring rule` and `Attempts allowed (k)` re-score every row. `Benchmark items`, `Training budget multiplier`, and the contamination switch retrain every row. Comparison worth running: with the defaults, the 80- and 30-epoch checkpoints both pass 3 of 6 with intervals 19%–81%, and the paired margin gap is +0.002 with an interval from −0.220 to +0.224. The ranking is a coin flip. Then switch to Raw log-probability: every checkpoint gains two passes (80 epochs goes from 3 of 6 to 5 of 6) and the 30-epoch checkpoint edges ahead. Under Sample and check, k = 1 puts the 10-epoch checkpoint first and the 80-epoch one third; at k = 5 the 3-epoch checkpoint leads at 94% and the 80-epoch one is last at 83%. A shaded band covering another checkpoint's point means these items cannot tell them apart. Under all three rules every interval still overlaps the leader's. The two extra raw passes come from the two items whose correct option is shorter, sails against trails and repeats against retreats: the rule, not the model, changed. Pass@k measures coverage. The 3-epoch checkpoint spreads probability over both options, so a few attempts nearly always include the key; the 80-epoch checkpoint is confidently wrong on port against town and stays near zero on it however many attempts it gets. The paired comparison is sharper than comparing two separate intervals, because both checkpoints answer the same items and item difficulty cancels. With contamination on, the leader passes 6/6 and its standard error reads ±0.0 points: the normal approximation claims certainty from six items. The Wilson interval, 61%–100%, does not. In this lab: each checkpoint is one training run at one seed, so the intervals cover item sampling only, not training noise. The model is a 30 × 30 character bigram. Sample and check draws a choice between the two options, not free text, because a bigram almost never writes a whole target word by chance, so its pass@k measures coverage over two options; the 20 draws per item add noise the interval does not include. In general: a scoring rule is a design decision. Likelihood, lettered options, generated answers with exact match, and judge models order the same models differently. A leaderboard gap smaller than about two standard errors is not evidence of a better model, and published comparisons should report the rule, intervals, and paired tests when models share items.
documents.title: Four checkpoints ranked, with the uncertainty drawn in

documents.subtitle: Item-level results · Evaluation
documents.body: Both scores, for every item, at the largest budget The strongest checkpoint scored item by item under the chosen scoring rule, with a bar for each item, so you can see which questions it passed, which it failed, and by how much. The callout restates the contamination experiment as a paired shift against the clean run. A kicker `Largest checkpoint · N epochs`. One row per item: the context, both scores joined by `›` or `‹` (raw totals or per-character means), the signed margin, a verdict, and a bar growing right of centre for a pass and left for a fail. Under Sample and check the row shows how many of the 20 draws picked the key, the item's pass@k, and a bar that grows from the left. Passing and failing rows differ in border colour, bar direction, and the verdict text. Metrics `Pass rate` with its 95% interval, `Mean margin`, and `Control perplexity`. The list always shows the last of the four budgets, not the current leader. Each score is the one the chosen rule uses on the leaderboard (per-character mean, or total log-probability); the margin is correct minus distractor. Under Sample and check the item's value is its pass@k from 20 draws. With contamination on, the callout's margin shift is the paired mean of (leaked margin − clean margin) over the same items at the same budget and seed, with a t interval (pass@k under Sample and check). The control shift compares the two runs' Proverbs perplexity. No controls of its own. The scoring rule, editing items, the multiplier, or the contamination switch rewrites every row. Comparison worth running: “the boats stay in | port | town” fails by −0.840 when clean, because after a space this corpus usually writes “t”. Leak the source and it passes by +0.012. A pass by 0.01 and a pass by 1.2 count the same in `Passed`. The bars show the difference. The biggest margin, +1.213 on “the water stays”, is decided by the letters inside “warm” and “wide”, not by knowing about water. In this lab: only the largest checkpoint is expanded; the others are summarized in the table. Draws under Sample and check are seeded, so the counts are repeatable. In general: item-level inspection is how a benchmark solved by a surface cue — shared characters, a repeated template, a leaked n-gram — gets caught.
documents.title: Both scores, for every item, at the largest budget

documents.subtitle: Benchmark editor · Evaluation
documents.body: Write the items the leaderboard will score The harness: one item per line as `context | correct | plausible distractor`, plus a multiplier that stretches all four training budgets together. The three character counts are the three corpora the page uses. A textarea labelled `context | correct | plausible distractor`. `Training budget multiplier` from 0.25× to 3.00× epochs. Metrics `Training characters`, `Benchmark source`, and `Control`. A line becomes an item when it splits on `|` into at least three non-empty parts. Extra parts are ignored and case is folded. Each candidate is scored as the continuation “ candidate”: log p(space | last context character) plus each candidate character given the one before, divided by the candidate's length plus one. That is per-byte length normalization, the idea behind lm-evaluation-harness's acc_norm. At 0.25× the budgets become 1, 3, 8, and 20 epochs; at 3× they become 9, 30, 90, and 240. `Benchmark items` and `Training budget multiplier`. Comparison worth running: replace `morning | evening` with `morning | xyzzy` and watch the item become an easy pass. The item is only informative when the distractor is a real word. Training, benchmark source, and control are three different texts; only the first is trained on. Writing items from the training sentences instead of the held-out ones contaminates the clean leaderboard from the start. In this lab: scoring is likelihood-based, so a model that would never generate the right word can still pass by ranking it higher. Only the first 60 lines count, and each is cut at 160 characters, so a pasted benchmark cannot freeze the page. In general: likelihood, generation with exact match, and an LLM judge are different scoring rules and can rank the same models differently.
documents.title: Write the items the leaderboard will score

documents.subtitle: Contamination control · Evaluation
documents.body: Leak the source text, not the questions A switch that appends the three held-out harbor sentences to the training corpus, the way a scraped page leaks a public benchmark. Both conditions are always trained, so the leak's effect is measured as a paired shift against the clean run. A pressable row `Add the benchmark source sentences to the corpus` with a `held out` or `leaking` chip. The three held-out sentences. Metrics `Margin shift` (leaked minus clean mean margin, largest checkpoint; `Pass@k shift` under Sample and check) and `Control shift` (percent change in Proverbs perplexity). Off: the training text is the harbor notes without the last three sentences. On: those sentences are appended. The items never enter training. A model that now answers them saw “in winter the same harbor freezes”, not the item line. The shifts compare two runs with the same budget and seed, so they do not change when you flip the switch. The switch. Comparison worth running: at the default budget, Margin shift is +0.519 per item while Control shift is −2.8%. The benchmark moves far more than general text. The control improves a little after a leak. Real English is real English; the signature is the disproportion, not a frozen control. At 30 epochs the leak takes the leaderboard from 3/6 to 5/6 and benchmark perplexity from 10.08 to 6.65. In this lab: the leak is a verbatim copy of three known sentences, the easiest kind to detect. In general: real leakage arrives as paraphrases, translations, and discussions of the test, which exact-match and n-gram checks miss.
documents.title: Leak the source text, not the questions

documents.subtitle: Put developer instructions, user text and a hostile retrieved document into one context window, then test which host controls actually stop a leak — and which failures are about accuracy instead.
documents.body: Put developer instructions, user text and a hostile retrieved document into one context window, then test which host controls actually stop a leak — and which failures are about accuracy instead. Explain prompt injection as untrusted text entering the same context window as trusted instructions, and distinguish direct from indirect injection Show why a pattern filter misses reworded attacks and blocks benign text, and why removing any one of the three leak conditions — private data, untrusted input through a source allowlist, or the outbound channel — closes a leak the filter cannot Separate security failures such as injection and exfiltration from accuracy failures such as hallucination and sycophancy Follow a leak through an output channel that is not a tool, a rendered markdown image, and place poisoning, supply-chain, excessive-agency and output-handling risks on a threat map with one mitigation each
documents.title: Failure modes, safety, and security

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Leave Scenario on Indirect injection. Read who wrote each part, then set View to what the model receives: the attacker's notice is just more text in the same stream.
documents.title: See one context window

documents.subtitle: Step 2 · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Set Keyword filter on retrieved text to on. The notice is removed, and Password in the reply and Password sent by email both read blocked.
documents.title: Filter the literal attack

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Keep the filter on and set Scenario to Paraphrased injection. The reworded notice passes the filter, and both leaks are possible again. In Filter test bench, 1 of 3 attacks is caught and 1 of 2 benign texts is blocked.
documents.title: Reword the attack

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: In Filter test bench, edit Your text. The starter text is caught. Change “all previous” to “the previous”, or “IGNORE” to “Disregard”, and read the filter turn to kept while the simulated assistant still acts: a bypass. Then try a warning that quotes the phrase.
documents.title: Type your own attack

documents.subtitle: Step 5 · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Keep Paraphrased injection. Set Password in the system prompt to kept out, or send_email tool to not offered, and watch the email leak close whatever the filter does.
documents.title: Remove a condition

documents.subtitle: Step 6 · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Put the password back in the prompt, the email tool on automatic and the Keyword filter off, with Paraphrased injection. Set Retrieval sources to allowlist only: the notice is left out, attacker text never reaches the model, and both leaks read blocked. Then pick Direct injection: the allowlist changes nothing.
documents.title: Allowlist the sources

documents.subtitle: Step 7 · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Set Retrieval sources back to any page and Scenario to Image in the reply. Set send_email tool to not offered: Password in a rendered image stays possible, because another channel carries it. Set Images in replies to not fetched, or Retrieval sources to allowlist only, to close it.
documents.title: Close an output channel

documents.subtitle: Step 8 · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Set Scenario to Hallucination, then Sycophancy. No attacker text is present, the host controls change nothing, and the failure is a wrong answer, not a leak. Hallucination points to Grounding check in the Retrieval-augmented generation lab.
documents.title: Separate accuracy from security

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Everything the model reads in one call: system prompt, tool list, user message, retrieved text and tool results, as one token sequence. Role labels are tokens too.
documents.title: Context window

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Text that tries to override the developer's instructions. Models cannot reliably tell instructions they should follow from instructions that merely appear in the data they read. It is direct when the user types it, and indirect when it is planted in content the system retrieves or receives, such as a web page, a document, an email or a tool result, so the attacker never talks to the model.
documents.title: Prompt injection

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: A user's attempt to get a model to break its safety policy, for example by role-play or an instruction to ignore its rules. It is a form of direct prompt injection; success shows a policy failure, not new capability.
documents.title: Jailbreak

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Getting private data out of the system, for example by making the model print a secret, send it with a tool, or put it in the URL of an image the chat window loads. It needs the data to be reachable and a way to send it.
documents.title: Data exfiltration

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Simon Willison's name for the combination that enables exfiltration: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally. Removing any one breaks the path.
documents.title: Lethal trifecta

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: A rule that blocks text matching a pattern. It is cheap and transparent, misses rewordings, case or spelling tricks the pattern does not cover, and blocks harmless text that happens to match.
documents.title: Keyword filter

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Blocking or refusing a benign request because it resembles a harmful one. It is a real cost of crude defenses, not evidence of safety.
documents.title: Over-refusal

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: A list of sources the system may read from; anything else is left out before the model sees it. It removes untrusted input by provenance, whatever the wording, at the cost of the useful content outside the list. It does not touch what the user types.
documents.title: Allowlist

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Passing model output to a browser, database, shell or other component without treating it as untrusted input. Output rendered as HTML or Markdown can run script or load an image whose URL carries data; output placed in SQL or a shell command can run as code. The fix is context-aware encoding and restricting what the output can load or run.
documents.title: Improper output handling

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Giving a model-driven system more functions, permissions or autonomy than its job needs, so one manipulated output can do real harm. Least privilege and a person's approval for high-impact actions limit the damage, and an approval is only a control if the person sees what they are approving.
documents.title: Excessive agency

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Tampering with what a system is built from before any user arrives: training or fine-tuning data, a retrieval corpus, or a downloaded model, plugin or package. The malicious input is already inside, so provenance and integrity checks matter more than filtering later.
documents.title: Poisoning and supply-chain attacks

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Failure modes, safety, and security
documents.body: Fluent output that is not supported by the input or by fact. Training and evaluation that reward a confident guess over “I don't know” make it more likely.
