documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Reusing weights trained on one distribution as the starting point for another. The benefit comes from structure the two distributions share.
documents.title: Transfer learning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Continuing ordinary training on new data with every parameter free to move. Simple, effective, and the most destructive option for prior behavior.
documents.title: Full fine-tuning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Loss on the original data rising while loss on the new data falls. There is one set of weights, and adapting them is the same operation as overwriting them.
documents.title: Catastrophic forgetting

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Excluding parameters from the update. Frameworks usually skip computing their gradients too, which saves optimizer memory; either way it limits how far the model can drift, and also how well it can adapt.
documents.title: Freezing

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: The pretrained model already scoring better than chance on the new corpus before any adaptation, because the corpora share structure.
documents.title: Forward transfer

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Epochs times learning rate, roughly. Forgetting tracks the budget, so the cheapest defense against it is to stop early.
documents.title: Adaptation budget

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Mixing some original data back into the fine-tuning set. The standard practical mitigation, at the cost of a slower fit to the new data. It protects what the replayed examples represent, and little else.
documents.title: Replay

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: The gap between the pretraining and target distributions. Descriptive prose to imperative instructions is a shift in style, not in vocabulary.
documents.title: Domain shift

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Getting the behaviour you want from an unchanged model by changing its input: clearer instructions, worked examples, and what context is supplied. It needs no training data and is undone by editing text, which is why it comes before fine-tuning.
documents.title: Prompt engineering

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Fitting the examples a model trained on more closely than new examples of the same kind. It shows as a gap between trained-on loss and held-out loss that widens with training, and it is largest when the fine-tuning set is small.
documents.title: Overfitting

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Examples held back from training and used to judge a model, covering both the new task and the old behaviour that must not be lost. Without one a fine-tune cannot be checked, so the decision rule counts it as part of being ready to fine-tune.
documents.title: Evaluation set

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Fine-tuning & transfer · question 1
documents.body: Fine-tuning drives the target loss down and the source loss up. What is the mechanism? The model deletes the old corpus from its memory to make room for the new corpus it is learning Every step optimizes only the target data, so the weights that held the source get overwritten Weights that go unused decay a little on every step, the way unrehearsed memories fade over time The source loss rises because the source data is no longer in the validation set Nothing in the objective mentions the original data, so nothing preserves it: the weights that encoded the source distribution are the same weights being overwritten. Freezing and replay both work by making some of the old behavior unavailable for overwriting or by putting the old data back in the loss.
documents.title: Fine-tuning drives the target loss down and the source loss up. What is the mechanism?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Fine-tuning & transfer · question 2
documents.body: With Fine-tune epochs at 0, the pretrained model already beats the from-scratch model on Recipe steps. Why? Recipe steps text was part of the pretraining data, so the model has effectively seen it already The pretrained table has more weights than the zeroed one, so it can fit more of the corpus right away Zero epochs still runs one pass over the target data, which gives the pretrained model a head start Both corpora share character statistics, so a Harbor-fitted table already beats chance on recipes A zeroed table gives every character equal probability, so its loss is exactly the log of the vocabulary size. Harbor and Recipe steps are both English at the character level, with similar letter frequencies and a dominant space, so weights fitted to Harbor already put sensible probability on recipe text. That is forward transfer: both tables hold the same 900 weights and neither has taken a step on recipes.
documents.title: With Fine-tune epochs at 0, the pretrained model already beats the from-scratch model on Recipe steps. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Fine-tuning & transfer · question 3
documents.body: You freeze the blocks labelled ␣abcde and fghijk on Layer freezing and keep the same epochs. What happens to Forgetting and to the transfer run's target loss? Forgetting falls and target loss ends higher: frozen rows keep their Harbor predictions but cannot learn recipes Both improve, because fewer trainable weights means less noise in every update to the table Forgetting is unchanged, because the source loss depends only on the data and not on which weights move The target loss improves and forgetting grows, because the unfrozen rows have to move further to compensate for the frozen ones A frozen row keeps its pretrained next-character distribution, so what it predicted for Harbor survives, and what recipes need after those characters can no longer be learned. Each row's gradient depends only on that row, so the unfrozen rows move exactly as before and nothing compensates. Freezing is a dial between adaptation and forgetting, not a fix.
documents.title: You freeze the blocks labelled ␣abcde and fghijk on Layer freezing and keep the same epochs. What happens to Forgetting and to the transfer run's target loss?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Fine-tuning & transfer · question 4
documents.body: Your assistant answers questions about a policy handbook that is revised every month. Each answer must cite its paragraph, and no special format is needed. What does the lab's rule of thumb recommend, and why? Fine-tuning, because training the handbook into the weights makes answers faster and removes the need for sources A better prompt alone, because the handbook is only text and a prompt can hold any amount of it Retrieval, because a fine-tuned model's facts freeze when training stops and carry no source to cite Fine-tuning every month, because retraining is cheap once you have a few hundred examples Two answers on the decision card point the same way: the knowledge changes often and answers must cite sources. Weights are frozen when training stops, so every revision would need retraining, and a fine-tuned model cannot say which paragraph a fact came from. Retrieval reads the current text and can show the passage. The rule is a rule of thumb, and real decisions also weigh cost, latency, privacy and risk.
documents.title: Your assistant answers questions about a policy handbook that is revised every month. Each answer must cite its paragraph, and no special format is needed. What does the lab's rule of thumb recommend, and why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Fine-tuning & transfer · question 5
documents.body: The Forgetting readout is near zero after a fine-tune. Why can that still hide real damage in a production model? It is computed on the target corpus rather than the source corpus, so it cannot see source behaviour at all It is reported only at the final checkpoint, so damage earlier in training goes unseen It measures how far the weights moved, and weights can move far without changing behaviour It is a loss on one corpus, while instruction following, format and refusals can degrade without moving it Forgetting here is the change in cross-entropy on one source corpus. Real forgetting also shows up in instruction following, output format, tool-call syntax, refusals and calibration, which a loss on generic text can miss, so production fine-tunes are checked against a suite of old behaviours rather than a single loss.
documents.title: The Forgetting readout is near zero after a fine-tune. Why can that still hide real damage in a production model?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Fine-tuning & transfer · question 6
documents.body: On Replay and held-out target you raise Replay share from 0% to 50% and change nothing else. What do you expect to see? Forgetting falls on the replayed sentences but barely moves on the ones not replayed, and trained-on target loss rises Forgetting falls equally on every original sentence, because the weights remember the whole original corpus once any of it is replayed Forgetting stays the same, because replay only adds training steps and leaves the loss unchanged Held-out target loss rises sharply, because replay takes training time away from the target sentences The loss now mentions the replayed sentences, so those are protected: their loss ends below where it started. Sentences that were not replayed are not in the loss, and they forget about as much as with no replay at all. Trained-on target loss rises a little because the weights are also pulled toward the replay, and the run takes twice the steps. Held-out target loss barely moves. Replay protects what it replays, so the replay set has to represent the behaviour you want to keep.
documents.title: On Replay and held-out target you raise Replay share from 0% to 50% and change nothing else. What do you expect to see?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Fine-tuning & transfer · question 7
documents.body: As you add Fine-tune epochs, Trained-on target loss keeps falling while Held-out target loss flattens. What does the widening gap tell you? The fine-tune is fitting the particular sentences it trained on, so the trained-on number overstates what it learned The held-out sentences are corrupted, because a loss that stops falling means the data is bad and should be cleaned The two lines cannot be compared, because held-out sentences are always harder than trained-on ones Falling trained-on loss proves the fine-tune generalizes, so the held-out line is the one to ignore Both lines score recipe sentences, but only one set ever entered a gradient step. The trained-on loss measures memory of those sentences; the held-out loss measures what carried over to new ones. With only a few training sentences the gap opens early and keeps widening. The earlier cards score the target corpus on the sentences it trained on, so their target loss is a training loss too.

documents.subtitle: Plain · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Imagine a small program that has learned to guess the next letter of weather reports, and now you want it to guess the next letter of cooking instructions instead. Training a program like this means letting it practise guessing on a text and adjusting its settings a little after each guess, so its later guesses improve. You could throw it away and train a new one from a blank start, or you could keep it and carry on training it on the recipes. This module is about the second choice, which is called fine-tuning, and about what it gains you and what it quietly costs. Where you have met it Almost no AI model in real use is trained from scratch for its exact job. Instead, people start from a general model that has already learned from a lot of text, and then they adapt it to the job. For example, one step in building the chat model Llama 2-Chat was fine-tuning the general Llama 2 model on 27,540 examples that people had prepared. Fine-tuning is not the only way to adapt a model, and it is often not the first one to try. If you have ever added an example to show a chatbot the format you wanted, you have used the cheapest route. It changes the message you send, called the prompt, not the model itself. Another route lets a system look up documents when you ask a question, so the answer can use the current text and show you the passage it came from. Why it matters If you could not reuse a trained model, every new job would need a model trained from nothing. That would throw away everything an existing model has already picked up, and it hurts most when you have only a little text for the new job. In this lab, a model started from zero begins as a blind guesser, while the model that already trained on weather notes starts well ahead. The catch is that a model like this is really one big table of numbers, and it has only one. Training it on recipes changes the same numbers that handled weather notes, so it can get worse at its old job while it gets better at the new one. If nobody measures that damage, a team can end up with a model that is better at one thing and quietly broken at another. A fine-tuned model can also look better than it really is when you only test it on the sentences it practised on. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these in your own words: why a model that has already learned from one kind of text beats a blank one when the new text is small; how to measure forgetting as a number, instead of assuming that it happens or that it does not; what freezing part of the model does, both to how well it learns the new text and to how much of the old text it loses; when fine-tuning is the right tool, and when a better prompt or a document lookup should come first; how mixing old text back into training protects old behaviour, and why you should judge a fine-tune on new sentences it never trained on. What the lab lets you do Everything in this lab, apart from the last card, is real training that runs live as you move the controls, so every number you see was measured, not made up. Six cards each show one part of the story: Transfer against training from scratch races the model that already trained on weather notes against one that starts from zero, on the same recipe text. Forgetting meter measures that one fine-tuned model on both kinds of text at once, so you can watch it get better at recipes while it gets worse at weather notes. Fine-tuning controls holds the two sliders that decide how hard the training pushes, plus three readouts that sum up the result. Layer freezing lets you lock parts of the model so they cannot change, and shows which parts moved. Replay and held-out target mixes some old text back in and keeps some new sentences out, so you can test the model fairly. Should you fine-tune? Rule of thumb asks four yes-or-no questions and suggests a route, and it is a hand-written guide, not a measurement.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: The model you start from In *Train one from scratch* you met a tiny model that reads one character and guesses the next one. It works with 30 symbols: the 26 letters, the space, the dot that ends a sentence, and two bracket signs, < and >, that never appear in the texts here. All this model holds is a table of 900 numbers, called weights. Picture the table as a notebook with 30 pages, one page for each symbol, where each page lists 30 scores, one for every symbol that might come next. When the model reads t, it opens page t and converts those scores into odds for the next character. Because h so often follows t, page t gives h a high score. This lab trains its own model of that kind once, on a text called Harbor weather notes. It makes a fixed 60 full passes through that text, and each pass is called an epoch, so the model reads all eight Harbor sentences 60 times over. They sound like this one: “the morning fog settles over the harbor and the air feels cool.” This first round of training is called pretraining, and its result is the base model that every fine-tune on this page starts from. It is not the copy you trained in the earlier lab, and no control on this page changes it. How the lab scores a model To judge a model, the lab runs it along a whole text and checks, at every character, what odds it gave to the character that really came next. High odds for the right character earn a small penalty, while low odds earn a big one. The average penalty over the whole text is called the loss, so a lower loss means better guessing. The loss is measured in units called nats per character, and you do not need the math behind the unit, because two landmarks tell you how to read it. A loss of 0 would mean the model gave the right character 100% odds every single time, which no real model manages. A loss of 3.401 is what you get by giving all 30 symbols the same 1-in-30 chance, which is blind guessing. Any loss in between has an everyday meaning too: a loss of 2.556 means the model is, on average, about as unsure as someone choosing among 13 equally likely characters. A loss of 1.921 is more like choosing among 7. Before any fine-tuning, this lab’s base model has a loss of 1.921 nats per character on Harbor. On Recipe steps, the new text you want it to handle, its loss is 2.556. Most charts label the unit nats/char, but the first card says nats/token. For this model a token is one character, so the two labels mean the same thing. Fine-tuning: carry on training on new text Full fine-tuning is the same kind of training that built the Harbor model, except that it starts from the Harbor model’s weights instead of a blank table. You keep those 900 weights and carry on training. This time, every batch of practice comes from Recipe steps, with sentences such as “warm the pan over medium heat and add a spoon of oil.” People often call one run of this training, and the model it produces, a fine-tune. The lab calls Harbor weather notes the source, since it is where the model came from. It calls Recipe steps the target, since that is where you want the model to go. That is why the readouts have names like Source before and Target gained. The training method itself stays the same as before. The trainer takes a small batch of character pairs from the text and works out which way each weight should move to give the real next characters higher odds. That direction is called the gradient. The trainer then nudges the weights a little in that direction, but only on the pages the model opened to make that batch’s guesses. That round of nudges counts as one step. For example, say the batch holds a t followed by an h. The trainer then raises the score for h on page t a little and lowers the other scores on that page. Step by step, this pushes the loss on the practice text down. A page changes only when its own character turns up in the practice text, so a letter that never appears there leaves its page untouched. The part of the trainer that makes these nudges is called the optimizer, so the lab counts them as optimizer steps. The word “full” means that all 900 weights are free to move. Two sliders on the Fine-tuning controls card decide how hard you push. Fine-tune epochs sets how many passes the model makes through the recipe text, from 0 up to 60. Fine-tune learning rate sets how big each nudge is, from 0.05 up to 2.00. Together they make the adaptation budget, how much change you allow, which works out roughly as the number of epochs times the learning rate. Beside the fine-tuned model, the lab trains a second model on the same recipe text, with the same budget and the same random seed. A seed is a number that fixes every random choice in a run, such as the order the practice batches are shuffled into, so both runs make the same choices. The second model starts from a table of zeros, which gives every symbol the same odds, and it appears as the dashed “started from zero” line. Until you freeze anything, the only difference between the two runs is where they began. The Layer freezing card, which comes later, locks parts of the fine-tuned model only, while the model started from zero always trains all 900 weights. The lab calls the fine-tuned model the transfer run and the one started from zero the scratch run, from the everyday phrase “from scratch”, which means from nothing. That is where the readouts Transfer, target loss and Scratch, target loss get their names. What the two texts share, and where they differ Harbor weather notes and Recipe steps are both written in English with the same 30 symbols. A collection of training text like each of these is called a corpus, and two or more are called corpora. The two corpora also share habits. In both of them, about one character in five is a space, e and t are the most common letters, and h is the letter that most often follows t. Weights shaped by Harbor already expect those habits, which is why they are any use for recipes at all. What differs is the style. Harbor weather notes describes what the weather does, while Recipe steps gives orders such as warm, stir, add, pour and simmer. The gap between the old text and the new one is called the domain shift, and here it is a shift in style, not in the alphabet. Reusing weights trained on one kind of text as the starting point for another is called transfer learning, and it pays off because of what the two texts share. Here is a made-up picture of why that head start matters. Picture two friends playing a game where they guess the next letter of a hidden recipe, one letter at a time. One friend has spent weeks playing the same game on weather notes, while the other has never seen English writing and has to treat all 30 symbols as equally likely. Neither has seen a recipe before, yet the weather player already expects h after t and plenty of spaces, so they start far ahead. In this lab, the weather player is the pretrained model and the newcomer is the one started from zero. One notebook, written in pencil Keep the notebook in mind for the rest of the lesson, because it is the main picture here. The weight table is one notebook written in pencil, with a page for each symbol. Learning Recipe steps means erasing and rewriting entries in that same notebook, with no second copy and no blank section set aside for recipes. Take page o as an example, since the two texts disagree about it. In Harbor weather notes, the letter after o is most often r, as in harbor, morning and storm. In Recipe steps it is most often n, as in onions and one. Fine-tuning pencils the score for n up on page o and the score for r down. After the default run, the odds for n on page o rise from about 7% to 24%. The odds for r fall from about 35% to 12%, so harbor, morning and storm become more surprising to the model. Freezing is taping over some pages so nothing can be written on them. A taped page keeps its Harbor scores, which protects what Harbor needs from that page, but it also means the recipe training can never improve it. In large models, freezing works on processing stages called layers. This tiny model has none, so the Layer freezing card tapes over groups of six pages instead. Replay is mixing a few old Harbor sentences into the recipe practice text, so that the pencil edits also have to keep those sentences well predicted. The picture stops matching in a few places. The entries are not facts you could read, like “the harbor is foggy”. Each one is a score for one pair of characters, and it is used every time the page’s character turns up in any word. Nothing is erased in a single stroke, since the scores drift a little at every step and the old text gets worse as a side effect. And in large real models, the weights do not line up with letters at all. The extra card A further card, Replay and held-out target, runs a fine-tune of its own with two changes. Some Recipe steps sentences are kept out of training, or held out, so you can test the model on sentences it never practised on. Some Harbor sentences are mixed back in, which is replay.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: A small text needs a head start A model trained from zero has to learn even the most basic habits of the language from the new text alone. When that text is small, like the eight recipe sentences here, much of the training goes into habits any English text could have taught, such as where spaces go. Transfer gives the model most of those habits for free, because the pretrained weights already carry them, so more of the training budget goes on what is actually new. That is the first problem fine-tuning solves: getting a useful model for a new job out of a small amount of new text. Fine-tuning is one way to turn a general model into a specialist, and it is the way this lab measures. As the help-desk story below shows, though, it is usually not the first route to try. The cost: catastrophic forgetting The other side of the bargain is the part that surprises people. As the model gets better at recipes, its loss on Harbor weather notes climbs, and this is called catastrophic forgetting. Despite the word “forgetting”, it is not wear or decay, and the model does not fade the way an unpractised memory might. The real reason is more direct. The loss that training lowers during fine-tuning is calculated on Recipe steps alone, so nothing in it gives the trainer any reason to protect Harbor. Every step moves the shared weights toward recipes, and those same weights were what made Harbor work, so adapting the weights and overwriting them are one and the same act. Should you fine-tune? Since fine-tuning has real costs, it is worth asking whether you need it at all. Here is a made-up workplace story that maps onto the three routes you can take. Picture a new hire who answers customers at a help desk, and think of three ways to help them do it well. You could leave a clear note on their desk, which is quick to write and quick to take away. You could point them to the current handbook, which keeps their facts fresh and lets them show the customer the page. Or you could send them on a training course, which changes how they work every day. A course takes time, needs good material, and can overwrite habits they already had. Those are the three routes, and the cheaper ones come first. Prompting first is the note, quick to write and quick to undo. Prompt engineering means getting the behaviour you want from an unchanged model by changing what you send it: clearer instructions, worked examples, or the right background. A behaviour you can get from a few example lines is not worth a training run. When a prompt goes wrong, you repair it by editing the text, with no training at all. A model picking up a pattern from examples inside the prompt is called in-context learning, or ICL, and the *ICL & reasoning* lab shows why that works at all. Retrieval is the handbook, which stays current and can be shown. A model’s weights stop changing when training stops, so a fact learned in training goes stale the day it changes. The model also cannot point to where that fact came from. Retrieval looks up the current document when the question arrives and can show the passage it used, and *Retrieval-augmented generation* is the lab for it. Fine-tuning is the course, which changes the habits themselves. Style, format, tone, or one narrow task done the same way every time are habits, and examples teach habits well. It can also save money on a task that runs thousands of times a day. A long prompt has to be processed again with every request. A small fine-tuned model can do the same job with a short prompt instead, or replace a larger, costlier model. The picture stops matching in one important way. A person who took a course can still look things up on their own, but a model cannot look anything up unless you build retrieval around it. The cost side is what the last question on the Should you fine-tune? Rule of thumb card asks about: a fine-tune needs hundreds of good examples that someone wrote or checked. It also needs an evaluation set, which is a collection of examples kept out of training and used only for judging. It covers both the new task and the old behaviour you must not lose. That set shows whether the fine-tune worked and measures what catastrophic forgetting took, which is the same kind of measurement the meter in this lab makes. Finally, a fine-tune needs upkeep. When a newer, better base model comes out, your fine-tune does not carry over to it, so you have to fine-tune the new one all over again.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Step 1: the head start before any training First set Fine-tune epochs to 0, which the slider shows as “no adaptation”. Transfer, target loss reads 2.556 on Recipe steps, while Scratch, target loss reads 3.401, the blind-guess loss of a table full of zeros. That number is exact: it is ln(30), which is what the ln key on a scientific calculator gives you for 30. The third readout, Transfer is lower by, shows a gap of 0.845 nats before a single step of recipe training, and that head start is called forward transfer. The pretrained model already beats chance on the new text, because the two texts share structure. In everyday terms, the pretrained model is about as unsure as someone choosing among 13 characters, while the blank one is choosing among all 30. Step 2: the default run Now return to the defaults, 20 epochs at learning rate 0.6, and the badge on the first card shows that each run took 500 steps. Transfer, target loss reads 2.123 and Scratch, target loss reads 2.247, so the third readout says Transfer is lower by 0.123. The lab subtracts the unrounded losses, which is why it shows 0.123 rather than the 0.124 you get from the rounded readouts. Both models improved a lot, but the one that started from Harbor is still ahead. On Fine-tuning controls, Source before reads 1.921, the base model’s loss on Harbor, and Source after reads 2.065, the fine-tuned model’s loss on that same text. The Forgetting readout on the Layer freezing card is the difference between them, 2.065 − 1.921 = +0.144. In everyday terms, the model slipped from choosing among about 7 characters on Harbor to about 8. Target gained reads 0.433, which is how far the recipe loss fell, from 2.556 to 2.123, shown as a gain. Read it next to Source after, because each one alone tells only half the story of the run. Try this: drag Fine-tune epochs slowly from 0 up to 60 and watch the two lines on the Forgetting meter move toward each other and then cross. Both lines start from the base model, so the solid Recipe steps line begins higher, at 2.556, and the dashed Harbor line lower, at 1.921. At about 25 epochs the two lines meet at the right-hand end of the chart. By 60 epochs the Recipe steps line has fallen to about 1.96 while the Harbor line has climbed to about 2.22. The model now finds weather notes harder than recipes, the reverse of where it began. Every epoch that helps recipes hurts Harbor a little more, and the badge on that card counts the damage. Step 3: freeze some pages Set the epochs back to 20, go to Layer freezing, and click two blocks, ␣abcde and fghijk, so their labels change from trainable to frozen. The ␣ mark stands for the space. Each block covers six pages of the notebook, which the lab calls rows. So Frozen rows reads 12 / 30, and Trainable weights drops from 900 to 540, since 18 pages of 30 scores are left. At the same 20-epoch budget, Transfer, target loss only gets down to 2.345 instead of 2.123, while Source after holds at 1.990 instead of 2.065. On the first card, the third readout even flips to Transfer is higher by. The model started from zero ignores the freeze and still trains every page, so it still reads 2.247. That flip does not mean pretraining hurt. It means the twelve locked pages, which include busy ones such as space, a and e, cost more recipe learning than the head start was worth. Under the grid sits the row strip, with one bar per page showing how far that page’s scores moved. The twelve frozen pages are hatched, which means shaded with diagonal stripes, and they sit at zero. The pages you left trainable show how hard the recipe training pulled on them. Step 4: spend the budget a different way Now test the idea that the two sliders share one budget: unfreeze both blocks, then halve Fine-tune epochs to 10 and double Fine-tune learning rate to 1.20. Since 10 × 1.2 and 20 × 0.6 both make 12, the budget is about the same, and Forgetting lands back near +0.144, within a hundredth of a nat. Fewer, bigger nudges did roughly the same work as more, smaller ones. Step 5: test on sentences it never saw Set the sliders back to 20 epochs and 0.60, then go to Replay and held-out target and leave Held-out target sentences at 3 and Replay share at no replay. This fine-tune trains on the first five recipe sentences and never sees the last three, such as “boil the pasta in salted water until it is tender.” Its table shows Trained-on target at 2.162 and Held-out target at 2.424, a gap of 0.262 nats. The fine-tune looks better on the sentences it saw than on the three it never did, even though all eight come from the same recipe text. This card’s badge reads 320 steps instead of 500, because with three sentences left out, each pass has fewer character pairs to work through. Raise Fine-tune epochs to 60 and the gap widens to 0.472, with 1.927 against 2.399. Meanwhile the Forgetting, all original sentences row climbs to +0.296. Step 6: mix old sentences back in Go back to 20 epochs and raise Replay share to 50%, which mixes the first four Harbor sentences into the training text. A second column, With 50% replay, appears beside No replay, so you can compare the two fine-tunes row by row. In each item below, the first number comes from the No replay column and the second from the replay column. In the No replay column, forgetting reads +0.123, less than the +0.144 on the first cards. That is because training on five recipe sentences instead of eight takes only 320 steps instead of 500, so the weights get fewer nudges away from Harbor. Forgetting, all original sentences falls from +0.123 to +0.042, so far less of Harbor is lost overall. Trained-on target rises from 2.162 to 2.232, which means the model fits recipes a little less closely, because the same pages are also being pulled toward Harbor. More training does not close that gap: at 60 epochs the replay run still reads 2.052 against 1.927 without replay. Optimizer steps doubles from 320 to 640, because every pass now also works through the four Harbor sentences. Those happen to hold about as many characters as the five recipe sentences. Forgetting, the replayed sentences goes from +0.119 to −0.038, a swing of about 0.16 nats. With replay, those four sentences end about where the base model started, or slightly better, because the fine-tune gave them 20 more passes of practice. Forgetting, the sentences not replayed goes from +0.128 to +0.129, which means replay did nothing for them. Push Replay share to 100% and the overall Forgetting row reads +0.001, almost no forgetting, because now every Harbor sentence is part of the training text. Step 7: the decision card Last, on Should you fine-tune? Rule of thumb, leave all four answers on No, and the Recommended route reads Prompt first. Flip only “Do you need a consistent format, style or behaviour?” to Yes and it becomes Prompt with examples, then collect data. Flip “Do you have hundreds of good examples and an evaluation set?” to Yes as well, and it becomes Fine-tune. Now flip “Does the knowledge the answers depend on change often?” to Yes, and retrieval joins the route as Retrieval for the facts, fine-tuning for the style. The rule table under the controls lists all five rows in order, the first row that matches wins, and the winner is marked (matched).
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: On the first four cards The head start is biggest early: at small budgets the two target curves sit far apart, and the longer both run, the more the started-from-zero model catches up. Pretraining mostly buys speed, not a better final result. Forgetting has no safe zone where recipes improve for free. The charts plot the model at saved snapshots along the run, called checkpoints, and at the defaults the Harbor loss rises at every one of them. It goes from +0.144 at 20 epochs to roughly +0.30 at 60, and only the very smallest budgets, which barely help recipes either, keep it near zero. Freezing moves both numbers at once: those 12 frozen rows cost 0.222 nats of recipe learning and save 0.075 nats of forgetting. That makes freezing a trade between the two, not a fix. In this lab, frozen rows still have their gradients worked out and then thrown away, so freezing here saves no computing work. Real training tools usually skip working out those changes, which saves memory, but as the section on real systems explains, it saves computing work only in some cases. The row strip shows which rows really moved: frozen rows sit at zero, and so do j, q, x, z, < and >, even when they are trainable. None of them appears in Recipe steps at all, and the trainer only edits a page when it reads that page’s character, so their pages never get a gradient. Blocks are not equal, since freezing xyz.<> alone changes almost nothing: x, z and the two brackets never appear in Recipe steps, so those rows get no gradient either way. The other two, y and ., are usually followed by a space in both texts, so their Harbor scores already suit recipes. The first block, ␣abcde, is the opposite extreme: freezing it on its own costs 0.146 nats of recipe learning, more than any other block. It holds several pages that recipes both use a lot and need to change, such as a, space and e. How often a page is used is only half of it, because what matters is how far recipes need that page to move. Space is the most common character in the recipe text, yet freezing page a alone costs more than freezing the space page alone. The two lines on the Forgetting meter do not come from two models. They are one model scored on two corpora at every checkpoint, so when the recipe line falls and the Harbor line rises, both changes come from the same moving weights. The Forgetting meter also shows two samples, which are short pieces of text the model writes by itself, picking each next character at random, with likelier characters picked more often. They are labelled Before adaptation and After adaptation. Both start from the same starting text, or prompt, the , with the same random seed, so every difference between them comes from the weights. At the defaults, the before sample contains Harbor fragments such as arbo, while the after sample has picked up fragments such as pan. Neither one is fluent, because a model that sees one character at a time can only learn which letter tends to follow which. Read Source after next to Target gained, because if you pick only one of them, you can tell a flattering story about the very same run. On the replay card A fine-tune can look better than it really is. The first cards score the very recipe sentences the model trained on, so their target loss is really a training loss. Hold three out and the same kind of fine-tune reads 2.424 on the new sentences against 2.162 on the practised ones. That gap grows with the budget: at 10 epochs, it is 0.157; at 20 epochs, it is 0.262; at 60 epochs, it is 0.472. Trained-on loss keeps falling, while held-out loss flattens out near 2.40, because extra training mostly helps with the exact sentences the model keeps seeing. Here is a made-up story that shows the same thing. Picture a classmate who prepares for a quiz by drilling the same five practice questions over and over, until those five feel much easier. They do noticeably better on those five, but on three new questions of the same kind they do only a little better than before. Only the new questions reveal how much they really learned. The picture stops matching in one place. The model never aces anything, and it cannot memorize whole sentences. After 20 epochs it is still about as unsure on its five practice sentences as someone choosing among 9 characters. What it over-fits is how often each letter follows each other letter in those five. Fitting the practised examples much more closely than new examples of the same kind is called overfitting, and small training sets make it worse. Set Held-out target sentences to 4 and Fine-tune epochs to 30, and Held-out target reads 2.541, about its lowest point. Raise the epochs to 60 and it climbs back to 2.570, while Trained-on target keeps falling to 1.865. Only sentences kept out of training can show that rise, which is what makes overfitting measurable here. Replay protects what it replays and little else: at 50% the replayed sentences end 0.038 nats better than they started, while the same sentences with no replay forget +0.119. The sentences that were not replayed get no protection at all, since they forget +0.129 with replay and +0.128 without it. The overall Forgetting number flatters replay, because the replayed sentences are part of what it scores. That is why the card splits it into two rows, and why a replay set has to represent the behaviour you want to keep. Replay costs both fit and computing work, since Trained-on target rises from 2.162 to 2.232 at 50% and the run takes 640 steps instead of 320. Held-out target barely moves, from 2.424 to 2.417. On the decision card Having examples is not a reason to fine-tune by itself. With the format question on No, flipping the examples question changes no route. The data answer only matters once a consistent behaviour is needed, and then it decides whether fine-tuning joins the route. Without retrieval, it turns “Prompt with examples, then collect data” into “Fine-tune”. With retrieval, it turns “Retrieval” into “Retrieval for the facts, fine-tuning for the style”. A Yes to changing facts, a Yes to citations, or a Yes to both gives the same answer: retrieval is part of the route, whatever the other two answers say. A fine-tune can neither show a source nor be updated without training it again.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: In this lab The pretraining, both fine-tuning runs, the freezing and every loss are computed live, but apart from the replay card, nothing on this page is held out. The first cards score Recipe steps in full, which is also the whole fine-tuning set, and they score Harbor in full, which was the whole pretraining set. For measuring forgetting, that is the right comparison, because you want to know whether the old behaviour survived. But none of those numbers tell you how the model does on text it has never seen. Every run on this page also uses a single seed, not an average over several. So you never see how much a different shuffle of the practice batches would move the numbers, including gaps such as the 0.123 head start at the defaults. The Replay and held-out target card holds out at most four of the eight recipe sentences, which is only a few hundred characters. Because these sets are so small, a difference under about 0.05 nats there could come from luck rather than from the setting you changed. The luck could be as simple as the order the batches happened to be shuffled in. Its forgetting rows still score text the model pretrained on, including the replayed sentences, and the replayed sentences are always the first ones of Harbor, not a random pick. The Should you fine-tune? Rule of thumb card is the one exception to “computed live”. Its five rules were written by hand, nothing on it was trained or measured, and it squeezes each situation into four yes-or-no answers. Real choices come in degrees, such as how often facts change or how many examples you have. They also weigh cost, privacy, risk, and latency, which is how long each answer takes to arrive. The Layer freezing grid is the other compromise. Real models are built as a stack of processing stages called layers, but this model has none. So the grid groups the rows of the weight table, the notebook’s pages, into blocks of six symbols, and the lab says so on screen. The freezing itself is real, while the grouping by letters is a stand-in, since a real freeze grid would name layers or the large weight tables inside them. The model is also tiny: it sees one character of context, meaning it looks only at the single character before its guess. It holds 900 weights, trains on eight sentences per corpus, and has none of the attention machinery that large models use to look back over earlier text. Replay is the standard fix for forgetting, and the replay card gives it a control. In large models, replaying a well-chosen sample of old text is meant to protect the old behaviour in general, not only the replayed examples. A model this small can only memorize which characters follow which, so replaying a few sentences protects those sentences and little else. Replaying four Harbor sentences pulls the shared pages toward those sentences’ own letter pairs. That leaves the replayed four slightly better fitted than before. The other four get no help from that pull, so they forget as much as with no replay at all. A few settings are fixed or stretched on purpose. Pretraining is locked at 60 epochs, and Fine-tune learning rate goes up to 2.0, far past anything anyone would use. The “started from zero” model is a table of exact zeros, while a real model trained from scratch starts from small random numbers instead. The starting model also differs between labs. *LoRA & adapters* rebuilds this same 60-epoch Harbor table, but *Model merging* trains its own for 48 epochs, so its base reads 1.953 on Harbor and 2.553 on Recipe steps. Each lab fixes its own epoch count and none of them tests the difference, so compare methods within one lab, not numbers between labs. A common mix-up: the model did not forget Harbor because the Harbor text was deleted, or because the model filled up and ran out of room. Nothing was deleted, and there are still exactly 900 weights: with 100% replay, those same weights keep Harbor almost intact, at +0.001. The only thing that changed is which text the gradient steps came from, and Harbor was never in that text. In real systems Real replay mixes a sample of earlier data into the fine-tuning set, sized so that the old behaviour stays in the loss. Forgetting is then checked on old tasks that were held out, not on the replayed examples themselves. The three routes are not exclusive, and real systems often combine them, but the cheapest route that passes your evaluation set is the right one. Fine-tuning can also teach facts, but it is a weak way to add new knowledge. It also cannot keep those facts current or point to where they came from, which is why the rule sends changing or cited facts to retrieval. Forgetting also shows up in ways a single loss number misses. A model can get worse at following instructions or at formatting its output. It can get worse at writing the exact commands it sends to other programs, such as a calculator or a search tool, or at refusing harmful requests. It can also lose calibration, which is how well its confidence matches how often it is right. All of that can fall apart while its loss on general text barely moves, so a single readout like Source after can understate the damage. In real systems, freezing saves less computing work than you might hope. Picture a real model as an assembly line of stations, called layers. Text goes in at the first station, each station reworks the numbers and passes them on, and the guess comes out at the last one. To work out how to change each station, training starts from the error at the end and traces it back, station by station, toward the start. Tools skip working out changes for the frozen stations themselves, which saves memory. But a frozen late station still has to pass the trace back to any trainable station nearer the start, so freezing only the late layers does not shorten that trace. Freezing the early layers is different. If every station from some point back to the start is frozen, the trace can stop before it reaches them, which saves real computing work. Real domain shift usually changes vocabulary, task and format all at once, not only the style. That usually makes the forgetting bigger than it is here, and how much head start is left depends on how much structure the two kinds of text still share. When they share too little, starting from the old model can even make things worse, which is called negative transfer.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Most defenses put the old data back Every defense that changes the training itself works in the same basic way. It puts the old data, or the old model, back into the loss that training is trying to lower. The old data goes back in as text to practise on, and the old model as a penalty for drifting away from it. Replay mixes original text into the fine-tuning batches, so the loss is calculated on it again. The Replay share slider is that mechanism, and its split rows show the catch: the loss protects only the text it is calculated on. Other methods add a penalty for moving the weights far from where they started, and some make that penalty bigger for the weights that mattered most to the old text. Some later training stages score the model’s answers and reward the good ones. They also add a penalty when the model’s odds drift too far from those of an untouched copy of the starting model. Freezing is the bluntest member of this family, because it acts like a penalty so large that the rows you picked cannot move at all. Why the head start shrinks In this lab, the head start shrinks because both runs keep fitting the same eight recipe sentences. Given enough passes, almost any start ends up close to the same best fit for those sentences, so the gap closes. That is more practice on the same text, not new evidence. The same idea applies to data in general. Think of the pretrained weights as a starting guess and the target text as evidence. With little evidence, the starting guess dominates, so transfer looks decisive, but with plenty of evidence almost any sensible start ends up in a similar place. That is why transfer matters most where data is scarce. How real practice freezes Real practice rarely freezes everything or nothing. Layers can be unfrozen one at a time as training goes on, starting from the output end, or given smaller steps instead of zero steps. The large lookup table at the very start of a model turns each piece of text into numbers, and it is called the embedding table. It is often frozen, because it is huge and general. Still, the cheapest defense is to stop early, because Forgetting grows with the budget. Choosing a route is about testing Choosing between the routes is a testing problem before it is a training problem. Prompt first and score the results on held-out cases. Add retrieval when the failures are missing or stale facts. Fine-tune when the model keeps getting the format or behaviour wrong in a way a set of examples could fix. The *Evaluation* lab shows how to build the score you compare the routes with. A full copy for every job One cost this lab does not charge you for is storage, because full fine-tuning leaves you a whole new 900-weight table for every task. Ten specialized models means ten complete copies to store and load, which is the problem the next lab, *LoRA & adapters*, goes after. Toy versus real Learning rates are not comparable. Llama 2’s fine-tune started its learning rate at 2 × 10⁻⁵, which is 0.00002, and lowered it gradually over 2 epochs, with a batch size of 64. Pretraining its 7B model, the version with about 7 billion weights, used 3.0 × 10⁻⁴, which is 0.0003. Other fine-tunes use other rates. The QLoRA paper’s LoRA fine-tunes, the kind the next lab teaches, used 2 × 10⁻⁴, or 0.0002, for models of 7B and 13B weights. For the larger 33B and 65B models they used half that, 1 × 10⁻⁴. This lab’s slider runs from 0.05 to 2 with a simpler training method, so its numbers are in different units. Data size: the fine-tuning stage of Llama 2-Chat stopped after 27,540 examples prepared by people, and its paper describes tens of thousands as enough for high quality. This lab fine-tunes on eight sentences. Tools: TRL, a collection of ready-made training code from the AI company Hugging Face, includes a trainer for fine-tuning called SFTTrainer. It also has trainers for two other methods, DPO and GRPO, that train a model on feedback about which answers are better. Its documentation lists PEFT, a toolkit for fine-tuning only a small part of a model, among the tools it works with. That means the same training code can train the LoRA adapters of the next lab. Checks: real fine-tunes score held-out sets for the new task and for the old behaviours, while here only the replay card holds anything out. Sources: Touvron and others, *Llama 2* (arXiv 2307.09288), section 3.1 and Table 1; Dettmers and others, *QLoRA* (arXiv 2305.14314), Table 9; the TRL documentation at huggingface.co/docs/trl.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: This module is about transfer learning: reusing weights trained on one distribution as the starting point for another. Full fine-tuning does it by continuing ordinary training on the new data with every parameter free to move. The question is what that buys on the new corpus, and what the same weights lose on the old one. It builds on *Train one from scratch*: the same kind of 900-weight character bigram table, trained by the same minibatch SGD on cross-entropy, except that training now starts from weights already fitted to another corpus. It then adds two levers on the trade, freezing and replay, and the decision that comes first: whether to fine-tune at all. Where it shows up Specializing a pretrained model. Almost no model in production is trained from scratch for its job. Llama 2's supervised fine-tune is one documented case, and Hugging Face TRL provides SFTTrainer for that step. Guarding old behaviour. Replay, the standard mitigation, mixes a sample of earlier data into the fine-tuning set, and forgetting is checked on held-out old tasks. Reinforcement stages add a KL penalty that keeps outputs near a frozen reference model. Next to prompting and retrieval. Production systems often combine fine-tuning with those two routes rather than choosing one. Why it matters Transfer lets a small task dataset go far. Shared structure gives forward transfer, a better-than-chance score on the new corpus before any update, and that head start counts most exactly where data is scarce. The price is catastrophic forgetting: loss on the original data rising while loss on the new data falls. A fine-tune scored only on the target sentences it trained on hides that damage. It also hides overfitting, a fit to the trained-on examples that does not carry to new ones and grows as the set shrinks. Only a separate score on the old data shows the first, and only target sentences kept out of training show the second. What you will be able to explain Why pretrained weights beat a from-scratch start on a small corpus, and why the gap narrows as the budget grows. How to measure catastrophic forgetting rather than assume it. How to predict what freezing parameters does to adaptation and to forgetting. When fine-tuning is the right route, and when prompting or retrieval should come first. How replay protects old behaviour, and why a fine-tune is judged on target sentences it never trained on. What the lab shows Every loss on the page is measured, not closed-form. The lab trains its own 900-weight bigram table once, for a fixed 60 epochs on Harbor weather notes, then fine-tunes it on Recipe steps live. Both corpora are fixed text, eight sentences each, and each run is a single seed, not an average over seeds. Transfer against training from scratch pits the fine-tune against a run from a zeroed table on identical data, seed and budget. Forgetting meter scores that one model on both corpora at every checkpoint. Fine-tuning controls sets the adaptation budget with Fine-tune epochs and Fine-tune learning rate. Layer freezing stops updates to chosen blocks of weight rows. The model has no layers, so the blocks group the table by context character instead. Replay and held-out target runs its own fine-tune with Replay share and Held-out target sentences. Should you fine-tune? Rule of thumb is a hand-written rule table over four yes/no questions. Nothing on it is trained or measured. The key experiment: drag Fine-tune epochs from 0 to 60, and the Forgetting meter shows Recipe steps falling while Harbor climbs, both scored on the same weights.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Full fine-tuning is ordinary training that starts somewhere other than zero. The base model here is a 900-weight character bigram table, the same kind of model as in *Train one from scratch*. It is not the model you trained there: this lab trains its own copy once, for a fixed 60 epochs on Harbor weather notes, and no control changes it. Before anything else happens that base scores 1.921 nats per token on Harbor and 2.556 on Recipe steps. Fine-tuning continues the same minibatch SGD on softmax cross-entropy, but every batch now comes from Recipe steps and the starting weights are the pretrained ones. Fine-tune epochs and Fine-tune learning rate set the adaptation budget. Alongside it the lab trains a second model on identical data, seed, and budget from a zeroed table — the dashed "started from zero" curve. Nothing differs between the two runs except where they started. A further card, Replay and held-out target, runs a fine-tune of its own: some Recipe steps sentences are kept out of training, and some Harbor sentences are mixed back in. What the corpora share, and do not Both are English at the character level, drawn from the same 30 symbols, with similar letter frequencies and the same dominance of spaces, e, and t. The domain shift is stylistic: Harbor weather notes describes, Recipe steps instructs. Shared character statistics are what transfer learning exploits; the style difference is what still has to be learned. There is only one weight table throughout, and the forgetting meter plots that single table scored on both corpora at every checkpoint.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Fine-tuning is one route from a general model to a specific one: the one this lab measures, and not the first one to try. Both halves of its trade become measurable here rather than assumed. Catastrophic forgetting is the half that surprises people, and it is not mysterious decay. The loss being minimized mentions only Recipe steps, so nothing in the objective has any reason to preserve Harbor behaviour. The weights that encoded the source distribution are the same weights being overwritten. Should you fine-tune? Try the routes that are cheaper and easier to undo first. Prompting first. Prompt engineering changes the input to an unchanged model: clearer instructions, worked examples, the right context. A behaviour you can get from a few example lines is not worth a training run, and a prompt is fixed by editing text. *ICL & reasoning* shows why examples in a prompt work at all. Retrieval for facts that change or need sources. Weights are frozen when training stops, so a fact learned in training is stale the day it changes and points to nothing. Retrieval reads the current document when the question arrives and can show the passage it used. *Retrieval-augmented generation* is the lab. Fine-tuning for behaviour. Style, format, tone, or one narrow task done the same way every time are habits, and examples teach habits well. It can also pay for itself at scale: a small fine-tuned model can replace a long prompt or a larger model on a task that runs very often. The cost side is what the rule's last question asks about. A fine-tune needs hundreds of good examples that someone wrote or checked. It needs an evaluation set to show it worked and to measure what catastrophic forgetting took, which is the meter in this lab. And it needs maintenance, because a new base model means doing the work again.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Start by setting Fine-tune epochs to 0. The transfer model already sits at 2.556 on Recipe steps while the from-scratch model sits at 3.401 — a zeroed table gives every character equal probability, so its loss is exactly ln(30). The overall Forgetting readout flatters replay, because the replayed sentences are part of what it scores. That is why the card splits it, and why a replay set has to represent the behaviour you want to keep. Replay costs fit and compute. Both samples use the same prompt and the same seed, so every difference between them comes from the weights. Neither is fluent. Read Source after and Target gained together. Either alone lets you tell a flattering story about the same run. On the decision card, having examples is not a reason to fine-tune. The data answer only matters once a behaviour is needed, and then it separates prompting with examples from fine-tuning. Changing facts and citations give the same route, retrieval, whatever else is true. A fine-tune can neither show a source nor be updated without training again.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Every mitigation for forgetting works by putting the source back into the optimization. Replay mixes original data into the fine-tuning batches, so the loss mentions it again. The Replay share slider is that mechanism, and its split rows show the catch: the loss protects only what it mentions. Weight-space regularizers penalize distance from the pretrained weights, and elastic weight consolidation weights that penalty by how much each parameter mattered before. Reinforcement stages add a KL penalty against a frozen reference model, constraining the output distribution rather than the weights. Freezing is the crudest member of the family: it sets the penalty to infinity for a chosen subset. The shrinking head start has a simple reading. Pretrained weights are a prior and target data is evidence. With little evidence the prior dominates and transfer looks decisive; with enough evidence any reasonable starting point converges to a similar place. That is why transfer matters most exactly where data is scarce, and why gaps between initialization schemes narrow as datasets grow. In practice freezing is rarely all-or-nothing. Gradual unfreezing releases layers from the top down, discriminative learning rates give lower layers smaller steps instead of zero, and embeddings are often frozen because they are large and generic. The cheapest defense remains stopping early, since Forgetting tracks the budget. Choosing between the routes is an evaluation problem before it is a training problem. Prompt first and score it on held-out cases. Add retrieval when the failures are missing or stale facts. Fine-tune when the failures are a consistent format or behaviour gap that examples would close. *Evaluation* is where the score you compare them with comes from. One cost this lab does not charge you: full fine-tuning produces an entirely new 900-weight table per task, so serving ten specializations means storing and loading ten complete copies. That is the problem the next lab attacks. Toy versus real Rates are not comparable.
