Llama 2-Chat's supervised stage stopped after 27,540 annotations, which its paper describes as tens of thousands being enough for high quality. This lab fine-tunes on eight sentences. Tools. Hugging Face TRL provides trainers for supervised fine-tuning (SFTTrainer), DPO and GRPO, and its documentation lists PEFT among its integrations, so the same loop can train the LoRA adapters of the next lab. Checks. Real fine-tunes score held-out sets for the new task and for old behaviours. Here only the replay card holds anything out. Sources: Touvron et al., *Llama 2* (arXiv 2307.09288), section 3.1 and Table 1; Dettmers et al., *QLoRA* (arXiv 2305.14314), Table 9; TRL documentation, huggingface.co/docs/trl.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Transfer against training from scratch · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Same budget, different starting weights Two runs that both spend your fine-tune epochs on Recipe steps: one initialised from a model already trained 60 epochs on Harbor weather notes, one started from a zeroed table. Only the starting weights differ. A kicker `Pretrained 60 epochs on harbor weather notes` and a title that restates the current fine-tune epoch count on recipe steps, plus a badge with the shared step count. A chart of fine-tuning progress against target-corpus loss. Solid `started from pretrained` and dashed `started from zero`, y axis in nats per token from 1.70 to about 3.50. Three metrics: `Transfer, target loss`, `Scratch, target loss`, and either `Transfer is lower by` or `Transfer is higher by` that gap in nats. A footnote: both curves are full-corpus loss on Recipe steps at each saved checkpoint, same seed, same budget. The base model is trained once, cached, on Harbor weather notes for 60 epochs at seed 1. Transfer continues from those weights at seed 2. Scratch starts from zeros at seed 2. Both use your `Fine-tune learning rate` and `Fine-tune epochs`. Each point is `tinyCrossEntropy` on the entire Recipe steps corpus at that checkpoint, not the batch loss of the run. At 0 fine-tune epochs the transfer curve is a single point: the pretrained model's loss on recipes, which is already better than uniform because the alphabets overlap. Scratch at 0 epochs is the uniform 3.401 of a zeroed table. Frozen rows, set on the freeze grid, apply only to the transfer run. Scratch still trains every row. `Fine-tune epochs` and `Fine-tune learning rate` retrain both runs. The freeze grid retrains transfer only, so a large freeze can make transfer lose to scratch — that is the comparison the third metric is willing to flip for. Comparison worth running: at 20 epochs and learning rate 0.60, transfer reads 2.123 against scratch's 2.247. Set Fine-tune epochs to 0 and the gap is 0.845 (2.556 against 3.401): what pretraining bought before any adaptation. The first transfer point is not 3.401. Harbor and recipes share characters and short patterns (`the`, `and`, spaces), so a harbor model is already a better-than-chance recipe model. Scratch can catch up given enough epochs on a corpus this small. Transfer's usual win is speed, not an unbeatable floor. If you freeze every block, transfer cannot move and the solid curve is flat; scratch will pass it. In this lab: both losses are measured, but each run is one seed on two eight-sentence corpora. The gap is real for this page; it is not a claim about ImageNet pretraining. In this lab: the pretrained model is not the one you built in `Train one from scratch`. It is a fresh 900-weight table this lab trains itself, once, for a fixed 60 epochs on Harbor weather notes at seed 1, and nothing you did in an earlier lab carries into it. In this lab: `started from zero` is literally a zeroed 30 × 30 table, which is also a uniform next-character model. A real `from scratch` run still uses random initialisation, not zeros. In general: transfer helps when the source and target share structure. It can hurt when they do not — negative transfer — and nothing on this card searches for that failure except you, by reading the third metric's sign.
documents.title: Same budget, different starting weights

documents.subtitle: Forgetting meter · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: What adaptation costs on the original data The same transfer run scored on both corpora at every checkpoint: Recipe steps falling as it adapts, Harbor weather notes usually rising as it forgets. Two samples, same prompt and seed, sit under the chart so you can hear the style shift. A kicker `Two corpora, one set of weights` and a badge with the signed forgetting in nats, `source_after − source_before`. A chart of fine-tuning progress against loss in nats per character, with the y axis fitted to the two curves. Solid `Recipe steps (adapting)` and dashed `Harbor weather notes (forgetting)`. Two sample panels, `Before adaptation` and `After adaptation`, each 76 characters from prompt `the ` at temperature 0.7, seed 12. Every point is full-corpus cross-entropy of the transfer checkpoint on that corpus. Nothing is smoothed or interpolated. Forgetting is a single number, `CE(harbor, after) − CE(harbor, before)`, printed on the badge and again on the freeze grid. Both samples use the same prompt, temperature, and seed, so a change in the text is a change in the weights. Before is always the frozen 60-epoch harbor model. At 0 fine-tune epochs the two curves meet their starting values and the samples match. This card has no controls of its own. Epochs, learning rate, and the freeze grid all reshape both curves. Comparison worth running: at 20 epochs read the badge, then freeze several early-alphabet blocks and read it again. Forgetting should shrink if those rows were carrying harbor-specific predictions — and target adaptation may shrink with it. At very small budgets the harbor curve can dip by well under 0.001 nats before it rises; at the defaults it rises from the first checkpoint. Forgetting is the harbor curve's net rise, not a requirement that it rise on every step. A 900-weight table only learns which letter follows which, so the after sample is mostly letter fragments, not recipe words, and one draw is not a metric. The chart's loss is what measures the shift. A forgetting badge near 0 with a large target gain is the pleasant case. A large badge with a small target gain is the one the freeze grid exists to mitigate. In this lab: forgetting is training-set cross-entropy on the original eight sentences, not a held-out harbor evaluation. The model can `forget` a memorised weather note and still look fluent. The Replay and held-out target card splits the original corpus into replayed and not-replayed sentences to show how much this one number hides. In this lab: the two corpora are short and stylistically opposite on purpose. That exaggerates the style shift in the samples relative to fine-tuning a model on a nearby domain. In general: catastrophic forgetting is measured on held-out source tasks, often as a suite, and is the reason people freeze layers, replay old data, or use adapters that leave the base weights untouched — the next module.
documents.title: What adaptation costs on the original data

documents.subtitle: Fine-tuning controls · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: How hard to push the pretrained weights The adaptation budget and the step size, plus the three losses that tell you whether the push was worth it: harbor before, harbor after, and how much recipe loss you gained. `Fine-tune epochs` from `no adaptation` at 0 to 60 passes, and `Fine-tune learning rate` from 0.05 to 2.00. Three metrics: `Source before`, `Source after` (loss tone once forgetting exceeds 0.05 nats), and `Target gained` as `CE(recipes, before) − CE(recipes, after)`. The Replay and held-out target card reads these same two sliders for its own fine-tune. Epochs at 0 short-circuits both trainers: transfer keeps the pretrained weights, scratch stays at zeros, and `Target gained` is 0. Both runs use this learning rate with a constant schedule, batch 16, seed 2. The pretrained base used the trainer default of 0.6 for its 60 epochs and is not affected by this slider. `Source before` is a constant for the page: the cached 60-epoch harbor model's loss on harbor. Only `Source after` and `Target gained` move. `Fine-tune epochs` is the honest first knob: 0 is the control, 20 is the default, 60 is enough for scratch to close a lot of the gap on this corpus. `Fine-tune learning rate` at 2.00 will move harbor numbers quickly and usually for the worse. Comparison worth running: hold epochs at 20 and drop the learning rate to 0.05, then raise it to 1.50, reading `Source after` and `Target gained` as a pair each time. `Target gained` stays positive across this page's ranges: even 5 epochs at learning rate 2.00 gains about 0.40 nats. What large rates buy is speed, and they spend it on harbor. `Source after` lighting up as a loss tone at +0.05 nats is a display threshold, not a scientific cutoff. The forgetting meter badge is the same quantity without that threshold. These three numbers describe the transfer run only. Scratch's losses live on the comparison chart. In this lab: the base model is one cached run at seed 1. You cannot change pretraining epochs or the source corpus. In this lab: `Target gained` is training-set improvement on eight recipe sentences. It will look large relative to any real fine-tune gain; the Replay and held-out target card holds some recipe sentences out to show how much. In general: the adaptation budget is chosen against a held-out target metric and a held-out source metric at the same time. One slider that only reports training loss cannot make that trade for you.
documents.title: How hard to push the pretrained weights

documents.subtitle: Layer freezing · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Choose which rows may move A freeze grid over the 30-character vocabulary, in blocks of six. Frozen rows still have gradients computed, then discarded, so they keep their harbor predictions while the unfrozen rows adapt to recipes. Five buttons, each labelled with the six vocabulary characters it covers (`␣abcde`, `fghijk`, …) and a status `trainable` or `frozen`. Three metrics: `Frozen rows` out of 30, `Trainable weights` as `(30 − frozen rows) × 30`, and `Forgetting` with the same +0.05 nats colour threshold as the controls card. A row strip with one bar per context character: the length of that row's change, ‖W_after − W_before‖, scaled to the largest. Frozen rows are hatched; trainable rows that never moved carry a dot. A note stating that this model has no layers, so the grid freezes context rows of the bigram table rather than transformer blocks. Each button toggles a block id in `frozen`. Those row indices are passed to the transfer trainer as `trainableRows`, which computes the gradient for a frozen row and then skips its update. Scratch ignores the grid. Only transfer is affected, which is why freezing every block makes the comparison chart's solid curve go flat. Forgetting on this card is the same `source_after − source_before` as the badge on the forgetting meter. Thirty symbols split into five blocks of exactly six, so each frozen block removes 180 trainable weights. Click a block to freeze or unfreeze it. The pressed/frozen state is visible as `frozen` versus `trainable`. Comparison worth running: freeze nothing at 20 epochs and read Forgetting, then freeze the block that contains space and `e` (the first one) and read it again. Those rows are the most trafficked contexts in English-like text. Freezing a row means `after "x"` keeps its harbor next-character distribution forever. If recipes need a different continuation after `x`, the model cannot learn it. In the row strip, `j`, `q`, `x`, `z`, `<` and `>` never move even when trainable: none of them is ever followed by a character in Recipe steps, so their rows get no gradient. The mechanism, a masked update, is real; the grouping by letters instead of layers is the toy. In this lab: there are no layers. Freezing `␣abcde` is not analogous to freezing layer 0 of a transformer except in the narrow sense that some parameters stop moving. In this lab: frozen rows are still stored, still used at inference, and still have their gradients computed. There is no memory or compute saving, only a training-time mask. In general: people freeze early layers because those layers tend to compute features that transfer, and they leave late layers trainable because those layers tend to be task-specific. A character-row grid cannot show that structure; LoRA is the version that leaves every base weight frozen on purpose.
documents.title: Choose which rows may move

documents.subtitle: Replay and held-out target · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: What replay protects, and what held-out sentences reveal A second fine-tune with two additions the first cards leave out: some original sentences mixed back into the training text, and some target sentences kept out of it. It shows whether a fine-tune generalized, and what replay protects and what it does not. Replay share, a slider from no replay to 100% of the original corpus in notches of 12.5%. Each notch is exactly one of Harbor weather notes' eight sentences, and the readout names the share and the sentence count. Held-out target sentences, a slider from 0 to 4, whose readout says how many of the eight recipe sentences are held out and how many trained on. A chart against fine-tuning progress of three losses in nats per character: the recipe sentences it trained on (solid), the recipe sentences held out (dotted), and Harbor weather notes (dashed, forgetting). With nothing held out the dotted line is absent. A table with a No replay column and, once Replay share is above 0, a With replay column. Its rows are Trained-on target, Held-out target, Forgetting on all original sentences, Forgetting on the replayed sentences, Forgetting on the sentences not replayed, and Optimizer steps. A kicker counting trained-on, held-out, and replayed sentences, and a badge with the optimizer steps of the run. The recipe corpus is split by sentence: the first 8 minus k sentences enter the fine-tuning text and the last k are never trained on. Replay appends the first n sentences of Harbor weather notes, where n is the share times 8, rounded. The optimizer shuffles the pairs of the combined text as usual. The run starts from the same cached 60-epoch Harbor model, uses your Fine-tune epochs and Fine-tune learning rate, and runs at seed 2, batch 16, constant schedule, with every row free to move, so Layer freezing does not apply here. With nothing held out and no replay it reproduces the first card's transfer run exactly. Trained-on target is cross-entropy on the training sentences only. Held-out target is the same on the held-out ones. Each forgetting row is the loss on those Harbor sentences after the fine-tune minus the base model's loss on the same sentences. The No replay column is a second fine-tune with the same epochs, rate, and held-out split, scored on the same two groups of Harbor sentences, so the columns compare like with like. Replayed sentences are extra training pairs, so each epoch is longer and the step count rises with the share. The fine-tune is given epochs, not a fixed number of steps. `Replay share` sets how much of the original corpus is mixed back in. `Held-out target sentences` sets how many recipe sentences are kept out. `Fine-tune epochs` and `Fine-tune learning rate` on the controls card set the budget this card shares. Comparison worth running: at the defaults, 3 held out and no replay at 20 epochs, read Trained-on target (2.162) against Held-out target (2.424). Raise Fine-tune epochs to 60 and the gap widens from 0.262 to 0.472. Comparison worth running: at 20 epochs raise Replay share to 50% and read the two Forgetting rows, then to 100%. The gap between the first two rows is the part of the fit that does not carry to new sentences. It is 0.157 at 10 epochs, 0.262 at 20, and 0.472 at 60: trained-on loss keeps falling while held-out loss flattens near 2.40. Replay protects what it replays. At 50% the four replayed sentences end 0.038 nats better than they started, against +0.119 forgetting for those same sentences without replay. The four sentences not replayed forget +0.129 with replay and +0.128 without: no protection at all. The headline Forgetting falls from +0.123 to +0.042 at 50% and to +0.001 at 100% largely because the replayed sentences are part of what it scores. Only at 100% is there nothing left to compare. Replay costs fit and steps: Trained-on target rises from 2.162 to 2.232 at 50%, and the run takes 640 steps instead of 320. Held-out target barely moves, 2.424 to 2.417. With 4 sentences held out and 60 epochs the held-out line bottoms out at 2.541 and ends at 2.570 while trained-on loss falls to 1.865: small-data overfitting, visible only because those sentences were kept out. In this lab: each corpus is eight sentences, so a held-out set is at most four sentences and a few hundred characters, and every number is one seed. Differences under about 0.05 nats are unresolved. The replayed sentences are simply the first ones of the original corpus. In this lab: forgetting is still scored on text the model pretrained on, and the replayed sentences are part of it. A bigram can only memorize which characters follow which, so replay of a few sentences protects those sentences and very little else. In general: real replay samples a mixture of earlier data, sized so the old behaviour stays in the loss, and forgetting is measured on held-out old tasks and old behaviours, not on the replayed examples. Replay also costs compute, because it adds training data to every epoch.
documents.title: What replay protects, and what held-out sentences reveal

documents.subtitle: Should you fine-tune? Rule of thumb · Fine-tuning & transfer
documents.body: Four yes/no questions, one recommended route A decision table someone wrote by hand. Your four answers pick one of five routes (prompt first, prompt with examples, retrieval, retrieval plus fine-tuning, fine-tuning) and print the reason. It is a rule of thumb, not a measurement: nothing on this card was trained or scored. A badge `rule N of 5 matched` and four fieldsets, each a question with `Yes` and `No` buttons: does the knowledge change often, must answers cite sources, do you need a consistent format, style or behaviour, and do you have hundreds of good examples and an evaluation set. A `Recommended route` box with the route name, the sentence that explains why this rule fired, and a `Next` line saying what to do first. Four printed lines, one per question, each starting with the question's short name and your answer, so you can read what each answer contributed. The whole rule table: five rows in order, the first that matches wins, and the matched row ends with `(matched)` and carries an outline as well as the text. `recommend()` tests the rows in order. Row 1: facts change or need citations, and a consistent format is needed, and you have examples plus an evaluation set. Row 2: facts change or need citations. Row 3: a consistent format is needed and you have the examples and the evaluation set. Row 4: a consistent format is needed. Row 5: none of those. Because the first match wins, retrieval is part of the route whenever facts change or need citations, whatever the other answers say. Fine-tuning is only ever recommended when a consistent behaviour is wanted and you could both train it and check it. All 16 combinations of answers reach exactly one row, so every setting prints a route. The default is four `No` answers, which lands on `Prompt first`. The answers are stored as four true-or-false values in the lab's state, so a reload or a shared link restores them. Each `Yes`/`No` pair is a button group. Use Tab to reach it and Enter or Space to press a button; the pressed button is bold on a raised background, and the printed lines spell each answer out in words, so colour is never the only signal. Comparison worth running: set all four to `No`, then flip only `Do you need a consistent format, style or behaviour?` and note the route. Then flip `Do you have hundreds of good examples and an evaluation set?` as well and see what the second answer changes. Comparison worth running: with a format need and examples both `Yes`, flip `Does the knowledge the answers depend on change often?` and watch the route add retrieval. Having examples does not recommend fine-tuning by itself. The data answer only matters once a format or behaviour is needed, which is the point of asking for it second. A `Yes` to changing facts or to citations gives the same route as both together. The two questions ask for different things, but retrieval answers both. The route that asks for a consistent format without data is `Prompt with examples, then collect data`: the examples you would train on are the same ones you would put in the prompt. In this lab: the mapping from answers to a route is a hand-written rule of thumb. It was not fitted to data or measured on any model, and it is the only card in this lab whose output is not computed from training. In this lab: only four yes/no questions enter the rule, and each is answered in two words. Real situations come in degrees (how often facts change, how many examples) that the rule flattens into a yes or a no. In general: real decisions also weigh cost, latency, privacy and risk. A fine-tuned small model can cut per-request cost or latency at scale, a private corpus may rule out some options, and evaluation and maintenance cost money in every route. The rule leaves all of that to you.

documents.subtitle: Read a confusion matrix on a deliberately imbalanced set and on a population with a realistic share of positives, then watch the precision-recall trade-off, leakage, learning curves, and MSE versus MAE so a tidy number cannot hide the rare class.
documents.body: Read a confusion matrix on a deliberately imbalanced set and on a population with a realistic share of positives, then watch the precision-recall trade-off, leakage, learning curves, and MSE versus MAE so a tidy number cannot hide the rare class. Read accuracy, precision, and recall from the same confusion matrix Explain why accuracy can look fine while the rare class is always missed, and why the same detector's precision falls as positives get rarer Say why choosing a threshold on the test slice is leakage that inflates the held-out score, and how train versus val curves diagnose overfitting Trace the precision-recall trade-off as the decision threshold moves on a population with a realistic share of positives

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: The share of examples the model labeled correctly. On an imbalanced set it can stay high while the rare class is never found.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Accuracy

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: Of the examples the model called positive, the share that truly are: TP over TP plus FP. High precision means few false alarms; it says nothing about the positives you missed, and it has no value (0/0) when nothing was called positive.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Precision

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: Of the examples that truly are positive, the share the model found: TP over TP plus FN. High recall means few misses; it says nothing about how many false alarms you raised, and on a slice with no positives it has no value (0/0), which is not the same as zero.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Recall

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2PR/(P+R), which equals 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN). It stays low unless both are decent, so it follows the precision-recall trade-off as the threshold moves, and it ignores true negatives, so a never-firing rule scores F1 = 0 despite 99 percent accuracy on the 1-in-100 population.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: F1 score

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: A table of true class versus predicted class. Every scalar score on this lab is a way of reading that one table, and the table changes with the decision threshold t: raising t removes false alarms first and then starts removing real positives.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Confusion matrix

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate as the threshold t falls. AUC is the area under it, which equals the chance that a random positive outscores a random negative. It grades the ranking across every t, so it can sit near 1 while the rule you publish at one t never fires.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: ROC curve and AUC

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: Class imbalance is a set where one class is much rarer than another, and the base rate is the share of positives. Majority guessing then looks accurate and still fails the rare class, and the same detector's precision falls as the base rate falls, because its false alarms come from the much larger negative class.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Class imbalance and base rate

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: Held-out data is kept out of fitting so the score is not just memory. The validation set is the slice you may look at while choosing settings such as the threshold t or the stop epoch. The test set is scored once, after those choices are final. Choosing t on the test set turns it into a second validation set, so the number you report stops being a test.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Held-out, validation, and test sets

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: One full pass of training over every training example. The learning-curve card plots loss against epochs 0 to 20 from authored formulas, not from a trained run.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Epoch

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: Using the holdout to make a choice (a threshold, a feature, a stop epoch) and then reporting that same holdout as if it were unseen. It inflates the reported score: the choice was fitted to those rows, so the number overstates what new rows will show.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Leakage

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: A fit that keeps improving on the training slice while the validation slice gets worse. Diagnosed by a diverging pair of curves, not by a low training number alone.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Overfitting

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: A rotation that lets each slice be the holdout once, refitting on the rest, then averages the scores. It still reports whatever metric you chose; accuracy on an imbalanced set remains a trap, and a rare class can miss whole folds unless the folds are stratified.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Cross-validation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: A split that keeps each class's share the same in every slice, so a rare class shows up in train, val, and test alike. It needs at least one positive per slice: with a single positive in 100 rows no split can do it, while the 1-in-5 population here holds 20 percent positives in train, in val, and in test.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Stratified split

documents.subtitle: Glossary · How we know a model works
documents.body: Mean squared error (MSE) is the mean of squared residuals, so large misses dominate. Mean absolute error (MAE) is the mean of absolute residuals and grows linearly with a miss. RMSE is the square root of MSE, which returns to the units of y while still weighting large misses more.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: MSE, MAE, and RMSE

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · How we know a model works · question 1
documents.body: A detector's confusion matrix on 100 rows reads TP 1, FP 1, FN 0, TN 98. Which readings follow? Precision 1.00 and recall 0.50, because one of the two alarms was a real positive Precision 0.50 and recall 1.00: half the alarms are false, no positive is missed Precision 0.99 and recall 0.99, because accuracy sums up all the correct cells Precision 0.50 and recall 0.50, because both read the same two cells of the table Precision is TP/(TP+FP) = 1/2 and recall is TP/(TP+FN) = 1/1, so the one real positive was found but half the alarms were false. Accuracy is (TP+TN)/N = 0.99 and hides both. Precision ignores misses, recall ignores false alarms, and they read different cells of the same table.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: A detector's confusion matrix on 100 rows reads TP 1, FP 1, FN 0, TN 98. Which readings follow?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · How we know a model works · question 2
documents.body: A detector never fires on a set that is 99 percent negative. What is true? Accuracy is about 99 percent while recall of the rare class is exactly 0 Precision and recall are both about 99 percent, since accuracy averages them Accuracy is 0 percent, because the rare class is the one that matters Majority guessing scores high accuracy on an imbalanced set, because the 99 negatives are all counted correct. Recall of the rare class is zero because no true positive was found, and precision has no value at all since nothing was called positive. Accuracy is a legal reading of the matrix that can still be the wrong number to publish.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: A detector never fires on a set that is 99 percent negative. What is true?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · How we know a model works · question 3
documents.body: The same detector, with the same true positive rate and false positive rate, moves from a population where 1 row in 5 is positive to one where 1 row in 100 is. What happens to its precision? It stays put, because precision describes the detector and not the rows it is given to score It rises, because a rarer class is easier to pick out from the crowd of negatives It falls sharply, because that false alarm rate now flags many negatives per positive It falls only a little, because recall is unchanged and precision follows recall Precision is TP/(TP+FP). Holding both rates fixed, TP scales with the number of positives and FP with the number of negatives, so a rarer positive class shrinks TP while the 99 negatives still raise their share of false alarms. At t = 0.50 the 1-in-5 population here reads precision 69.6 percent; the same rates at 1 in 100 give 8.5 percent.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: The same detector, with the same true positive rate and false positive rate, moves from a population where 1 row in 5 is positive to one where 1 row in 100 is. What happens to its precision?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · How we know a model works · question 4
documents.body: On 1 in 5, with Baseline on score ≥ threshold, you raise Decision threshold from 0.40 to 0.60. What happens to precision and recall? Both rise, because a stricter threshold makes the detector more careful about everything Precision rises and recall falls, because weak alarms stop firing before real positives do Both fall, because firing on fewer rows can only lose information about the positives Precision falls and recall rises, because fewer firing rows leaves a larger share of misses The two score distributions overlap, so a higher t drops false alarms first and then starts dropping real positives. From 0.40 to 0.60 the false alarms fall from 22 to 1 while the true positives fall from 19 to 11, so precision climbs from 46.3 to 91.7 percent and recall drops from 95 to 55 percent. Moving t trades one reading for the other and cannot raise both.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: On 1 in 5, with Baseline on score ≥ threshold, you raise Decision threshold from 0.40 to 0.60. What happens to precision and recall?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · How we know a model works · question 5
documents.body: You press Set t from test with Maximize on recall, then report the test recall. Why is that number no longer a test? Recall can only be computed on a validation slice, and never on a test slice at all Choosing a threshold changes the model's weights, which contaminates the test rows The threshold was chosen on the rows it is scored on, so test acted as validation The validation slice is where settings such as the threshold t may be chosen, and the test slice is scored once after every choice is final. Picking t on test lets those rows influence the rule, so the reported recall is optimistic and the holdout badge turns leaked. Setting a threshold does not change the weights.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: You press Set t from test with Maximize on recall, then report the test recall. Why is that number no longer a test?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · How we know a model works · question 6
documents.body: On 1 in 5 you maximize F1, then switch Choose t using from val to test, and Test F1 goes up. What does the Fresh rows reading for that same leaked t show? It equals the leaked Test F1, because one t gives one F1 on every set of rows It is lower than the leaked Test F1, because that t was fitted to the fifteen test rows It is higher than the leaked Test F1, because fresh rows are a larger sample than test It stays blank, because fresh rows cannot be scored until the model is retrained on them Picking the best of 101 thresholds on fifteen rows keeps whatever is lucky about those rows. Scored on 400 rows that took no part in the choice, the leaked t reads 68.8 percent F1 against the 85.7 percent it claimed on test, while the t chosen on val claimed 66.7 and read 77.9. Leakage inflates the claim; it does not improve the detector.

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · How we know a model works · question 7
documents.body: On Learning curves, train loss keeps falling while val loss bottoms out and then rises. What does that show? The model is overfitting, and the best stop is where val loss is lowest The val slice is mislabeled, because val loss should always track train loss The model is underfitting, because val loss sits above train loss Training has broken, because a loss should never rise once it has fallen Overfitting is diagnosed by diverging curves, not by a low training number: the fit keeps improving on rows it has seen while getting worse on rows it has not. Early stopping keeps the weights from the lowest val point. These curves are authored formulas, not a trained run, so they show the pattern, not a real model.

documents.title: On Learning curves, train loss keeps falling while val loss bottoms out and then rises. What does that show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · How we know a model works · question 8
documents.body: A detector's AUC is close to 1, yet at the threshold you published it never fires. What explains both facts? AUC is measured on the training slice, so it cannot describe the rule you published AUC averages accuracy across every threshold, and accuracy on this kind of set is high The model is overfit, so its ranking and its thresholded predictions simply disagree AUC grades the ranking across all thresholds; the published one sits above every score AUC is the chance that a random positive outscores a random negative, so it grades the ranking across every threshold at once. The rule you publish uses one threshold, and if that sits above every score nothing fires and recall is 0. A good ranking is not a good decision rule until a threshold is chosen, on a validation slice.

documents.subtitle: Plain · How we know a model works
documents.body: When someone says a model works, the proof is nearly always a number, such as “99% accurate” or “catches 8 cases in 10”. This module looks at where those numbers come from and what each one really measures, since a perfectly calculated number can still mislead you about a model. A model is a computer program that learns to give answers from examples. Training is that learning: the program sees many examples with known right answers, and it is adjusted little by little until its answers get closer to them. The lab uses a simple kind of model called a detector, which gives every example a score and then answers yes or no. It scores 100 of these examples, and the lab calls each one a row, like a row in a table. The detector works like a smoke alarm, which measures the smoke in the air and rings whenever there is enough of it. Most of this lesson is about judging an alarm like that fairly, so the alarm is the picture you will keep coming back to. In real life, each row might be one email, and the detector’s job might be to spot the rare scam among lots of ordinary emails. The lab’s rows are made up, so they stand for no real thing, but a scam checker is a good picture to hold beside the alarm. There are several ways to turn the alarm’s right and wrong answers into one score, and accuracy is the best known. In this lab, each of those ways is called a reading. Where you have met it When you read that a model scored well on a test, that score came from checking the model’s answers against the right answers on a set of examples. This lab does the same thing on a small scale, where you can see every single answer. The previous lab, The supervised learning loop, already scored a trained model on a holdout, which is a slice of data kept away from training. Later in this app, the Evaluation lab ranks four saved versions of a model on a benchmark, which is a fixed set of test questions. Then it lets the benchmark leak into training so you can watch the rankings stop measuring ability. The leak you will make on purpose in this lab is a small version of that same mistake. Why it matters People use a score to decide whether to trust a model, so a misleading score leads them to trust a model that has not earned it. This lab shows four ways a score can mislead, and each one gets its own card or comparison later on: The wrong reading: an alarm that never rings at all can score 99% accuracy while missing every fire, because fires are so rare. A borrowed precision: where fires are common, an alarm can be right on about 7 of every 10 rings. Where fires are rare, the very same alarm can be right on fewer than 1 in 10. A leaked test: if you use your final test rows to make choices, the score you then report looks better than what the model will do on new rows. Half the evidence: a model that keeps improving on its training rows can be getting worse on everything it has not seen. You only spot that if you track those unseen rows too. What you will be able to explain By the end of this module, you should be able to explain each of these things in your own words: how to read accuracy, precision and recall from the same small table of four counts, and which question each one answers; why accuracy can look great while every rare case is missed, and why the same alarm’s rings become mostly false when real fires get rarer; why choosing the alarm’s cut-off by looking at the test rows is a kind of cheating, called leakage, that pushes the reported score up; how a pair of curves, one for training rows and one for held-back rows, reveals a model getting better on old rows and worse on new ones, called overfitting; how moving the cut-off trades one reading against another when about 1 row in 5 is a real case. What the lab lets you see and try The lab has seven cards, and each one shows a different way a score can be read or misread: Threshold and baseline puts 100 scored rows on a strip, and lets you pick one of two made-up sets of rows and how touchy the alarm is. Train, val, test splits the rows into three slices: one to learn from, one to practise on and one for a final exam. It lets you watch what happens when someone peeks at the exam. Confusion matrix counts the alarm’s catches, misses, false alarms and correct silences. Four readings turns those four counts into four different scores, and draws two charts that show every cut-off at once. Learning curves shows, over time, how wrong a model is on rows it learned from and on rows it never saw. Cross-validation cuts the same 100 rows into five pieces that take turns being held back from the rest. Regression residuals is a separate small example about scoring guesses of a number, such as a price, where one big miss can take over the whole score. Everything here is made up on purpose. The scores were written by hand or drawn at random, and the curves are drawn from formulas, not from a real model in training.

documents.subtitle: Plain · How we know a model works
documents.body: A detector, a score and a cut-off Picture a smoke alarm in a building that almost never has a fire, and think about how touchy you should make it. An alarm that never rings is right on nearly every ordinary day, yet it is useless on the one day that matters. An alarm that rings at every slice of burnt toast is useless in a different way, because soon nobody trusts its ringing. The lab’s detector works in the same way, except that it scores 100 separate examples called rows, giving each one a detector score between 0 and 1. A higher score means the row looks more like the thing the detector is hunting for. Some rows really are that thing, and those are called positive rows, the real fires, while the rest are negative rows, the harmless ones. Here, “positive” does not mean good and “negative” does not mean below zero: they only mean the thing is really there, or it is not. Positive and negative are the two classes of row, and in the lab a positive row is labelled 1 while a negative row is labelled 0. On the score strip, positives are drawn as diamonds and negatives as circles, so you can tell them apart by shape. To turn a score into a yes-or-no answer, you pick a cut-off, called the threshold and written t. The rule named score ≥ threshold makes the alarm ring on every row whose score is at least t. The sign ≥ means “greater than or equal to”, so with t at 0.50, a row scored 0.64 sets the alarm off while a row scored 0.30 leaves it quiet. The lab’s notes call the alarm ringing on a row firing, so be careful with that word. A harmless row can “fire” too, and that is a false alarm, not a real fire. In this lesson, a fire always means a real positive row, whether or not the alarm notices it. When the alarm goes off on a row, this lesson just says the alarm rings. You set t with the Decision threshold slider, which runs from 0.00 to 1.00 in small steps of 0.01. The Baseline control also offers two rules that ignore the scores completely. A baseline is a simple rule to compare against, so any real detector should beat both of them. Always negative never rings, like an alarm with its battery taken out, while always positive rings on every row, like an alarm stuck ringing. You will see that dumb rules like these can still post numbers that look impressive. Two populations The Population control switches between two sets of 100 rows, which differ in their base rate, the share of rows that are really positive. 1 in 100 has a single real fire, row 99, which scores 0.42. One harmless row, row 12, scores a high 0.88, so it sets the alarm off at any cut-off up to 0.88. Every other harmless row scores 0.256 or less, far below both of those rows. 1 in 5 has twenty real fires among its 100 rows, and they score around 0.64 while the harmless rows score around 0.30. Both groups are spread out, though, so they overlap, and some harmless rows score higher than some real fires. The first set is built to show how a single number can hide a total failure, so it is extreme on purpose. The second has a more realistic share of positives, and because its two groups overlap, every choice of t costs you something. The smoke alarm picture stops matching in two places, and both are worth keeping in mind. First, a real alarm sits in one building and takes readings over time, while the lab’s rows are 100 separate examples. Second, no trained model produced the lab’s scores. They were written by hand for 1 in 100. For 1 in 5 they were drawn at random, but from a fixed starting number, so the same “random” scores come out every time. Four outcomes: the confusion matrix Once the alarm has rung or stayed quiet on each row, every row lands in one of four groups. Which group it lands in depends on two questions: was there really a fire, and did the alarm ring? True positive (TP): there was a real fire and the alarm rang, so this is a catch. False positive (FP): there was no fire but the alarm rang anyway, so this is a false alarm. False negative (FN): there was a real fire but the alarm stayed quiet, so this is a miss. True negative (TN): there was no fire and the alarm stayed quiet, so this is a correct silence. Here is a handy way to read the names: the second word is what the alarm said, and the first word says whether it was right. So a false negative is a “no” that turned out to be wrong, which is why it counts as a miss. Count the rows in each group and lay the four counts out in a two-by-two grid, and you have a confusion matrix. It is a table of what each row really was against what the rule predicted, and it is named for showing where the detector mixes the two classes up. On the Confusion matrix card, the grid’s two lines across are labelled True 0 and True 1, which say what each scored example really was. Its two columns, Pred 0 and Pred 1, say what the rule predicted, since “pred” is short for predicted. Here is a real example from the lab: set Population to 1 in 5, Baseline to score ≥ threshold and Decision threshold to 0.50. The matrix then reads 16 TP and 7 FP in the Pred 1 column, which holds the rows where the alarm rang. The Pred 0 column holds 4 FN and 73 TN, the rows where it stayed quiet, and together the four counts cover every row. The coloured grid beside the table shows the same four cells, each shaded by what share of the scored rows it holds. Four readings of one table Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are four different ways of reading those same four counts, and that is the central idea of this module. The Four readings card shows all four, along with a threshold sweep chart that draws each reading for every t from 0 to 1 at once. The Confusion matrix card prints the formula for each one. Below, each one is worked on the example you set up a moment ago, using N for the number of rows being scored. Accuracy asks what share of all the rows the rule got right, and its formula is (TP+TN)/N. On the example that is (16+73)/100, so 89 of the 100 rows were handled correctly and accuracy is 89%. Precision asks how often the alarm was right when it rang, and its formula is TP/(TP+FP). The alarm rang 23 times and 16 of those were real, so precision is 16/23, or 69.6%. Precision never looks at the misses, so an alarm can be very precise while still missing most of the fires. Recall asks how many of the real fires the alarm caught, and its formula is TP/(TP+FN). There were 20 real fires and the alarm caught 16 of them, so recall is 16/20, or 80%. Recall never looks at false alarms, so an alarm that rings on every single row gets a perfect recall of 100%. The F1 score combines precision and recall into one number. The lab writes it as 2PR/(P+R), with P for precision and R for recall, which means 2 × P × R divided by P + R. The same score also equals 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN), where 2TP means twice the TP count, not 2 × T × P. On the example that is 32/(32+7+4), which is 32/43, or 74.4%. F1 is a kind of average called a harmonic mean, and it is dragged toward whichever of the two readings is smaller. On 1 in 5 at t = 0.90, for example, precision is 100% while recall is only 10%. An ordinary average of those would be 55%, which sounds respectable, but F1 is only 18.2%. That lower number is the fairer one, because an alarm that catches only 1 fire in 10 is not a good alarm. F1 also ignores the true negatives completely, so correct silences earn it nothing. A rule that never rings has TP = 0, so its F1 is 0, even when its 99 correct silences give it 99% accuracy. When a reading has no value: n/a Sometimes one of these formulas would mean dividing by zero, and the lab handles that case carefully. If the alarm never rings, TP + FP is 0, so precision becomes 0/0. If the scored rows hold no real fires at all, TP + FN is 0, so recall becomes 0/0. Zero divided by zero has no answer, so the lab prints n/a, short for “not available”, rather than pretending the value is 0% or 100%. That difference matters, because a recall of 0% means there were fires and the alarm caught none of them. A recall of n/a means there were no fires to catch, so those rows cannot tell you anything about recall. Precision and recall by hand Keep Population on 1 in 5 and Baseline on score ≥ threshold, then walk the threshold upward from 0.50 and watch the counts shift. At 0.50, the matrix holds the counts you worked with above, which give a precision of 69.6% and a recall of 80%. At 0.54, two false alarms drop out while no real fire does, which leaves 16 true alarms, 5 false alarms and 4 misses. Precision rises to 16/21, or 76.2%, while recall stays at 80% because no fire was lost. F1 becomes 32/41, or 78.0%, the best F1 on these rows, so this small nudge improved the alarm and cost nothing. At 0.60, the alarm gets pickier, so true alarms fall to 11 and false alarms fall to 1. Precision climbs to 11/12, or 91.7%, but recall drops to 11/20, or 55%, because nine real fires are now missed. This pattern is the precision-recall trade-off, and it comes from how the scores are laid out. At low thresholds, most of the rows sitting just above t are harmless, because there are four times as many harmless rows and they tend to score lower. You can see this by raising t from 0.30 to 0.50. Over that stretch, 40 false alarms go quiet but only 4 fires do. Higher up, more and more of the rows left near the threshold are real fires, so each further step costs recall, as the step from 0.54 to 0.60 showed. Since the two groups overlap, no single t separates them, so moving t trades one reading for the other and can never push both to 100%. Class imbalance: when accuracy looks fine and is useless Now switch Population to 1 in 100 and Baseline to always negative, which turns the detector into a silent alarm. The silent alarm gets all 99 harmless rows right and misses the one fire, which the lab’s note sums up bluntly as “99% accuracy, zero recall.” A set where one class is much rarer than the other has class imbalance. On a set like that, always giving the common answer is called majority guessing, and it looks accurate because the common answer is nearly always right. On 1 in 5, the same silent alarm reads 80% accuracy and 0% recall, which looks less impressive but hides exactly the same total failure. This is why accuracy on its own can be the wrong number to publish, even though the math behind it is correct. The silent alarm really was right on 99 rows out of 100, but if the rare class is the reason the detector exists, that is beside the point. The base rate: the same alarm, fewer fires Precision has a weakness of its own, which is that it depends on how common real fires are, and not only on the alarm. Go back to 1 in 5 with score ≥ threshold at t = 0.50, where the alarm catches 16 of the 20 fires. That is a rate of 0.80, called the true positive rate, which is the same thing as recall. The alarm also rings on 7 of the 80 harmless rows, a rate of 0.0875, or 8.75%. That rate is called the false positive rate, and it is the share of harmless rows that set the alarm off. Now picture the exact same alarm, with those same two rates, in a place where only 1 row in 100 is a fire. To see what happens, imagine 10,000 rows, so that 100 of them are fires and the other 9,900 are harmless: The alarm catches 80% of the 100 fires, which gives 80 true alarms. It also rings on 8.75% of the 9,900 harmless rows, which gives about 866 false alarms. That makes about 946 rings in total, and only 80 of them were real fires. Precision is therefore 80 out of about 946, which works out to about 8.5%. It is the same alarm, yet now about nine rings in ten are false, even though nothing about the alarm itself changed. What changed is that false alarms come from the harmless rows, and when fires are rare there are far more harmless rows around to raise them. The Four readings card does this calculation for you, so you do not have to repeat it by hand. Its two readouts are named Precision if 1 row in 5 is positive and Precision if 1 row in 100 is positive. In its note, the lab borrows the Greek letter π as a name for the base rate, so here π is not 3.14. It also uses a raised dot to mean multiply. The note writes the formula as precision = TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1−π)), with TPR for the true positive rate and FPR for the false positive rate. With π = 0.01, the top of the fraction is 0.80 × 0.01, which is 0.008. The bottom adds that same 0.008 to a false-alarm part, 0.0875 × 0.99, which is about 0.0866. Precision is then 0.008 divided by about 0.0946, which gives the same 8.5% as before. Held-out data: train, val and test So far you have judged the alarm on all 100 rows at once, but real evaluation adds an important rule. You cannot fairly grade a model on rows that were used to build it or tune it, which means choosing its settings, such as t. A score on those rows partly measures memory rather than skill. So you hold some rows back from training, and those rows are called held-out data. In practice they are cut into two slices with different jobs: one you may use while tuning, and one that no choice may touch. Together with the training rows, that makes three slices. The Train, val, test card draws all three as a strip of 100 coloured cells: train, rows 0 to 69, which are the rows a model would learn from; val, short for the validation set, rows 70 to 84, which you may look at while choosing settings such as t or when to stop training; test, the test set, rows 85 to 99, which is scored only once, after every choice is final. The small line above the card’s title sums this up as “70 / 15 / 15”, which is the number of rows in each slice. You can think of val as the practice exams you are allowed to study from. Test is the final exam, which only tells you something true if you have never seen its questions. The Scored split control on the Threshold and baseline card picks which rows the matrix counts, from all 100 down to a single slice. On 1 in 100, the one real fire, row 99, sits in test, so train and val have no positives at all. There, the silent alarm scores 100% accuracy and n/a recall, which looks perfect only because there is nothing to miss. Leakage: choosing t on the test slice Leakage means using the held-out rows to make a choice, such as a threshold, and then reporting a score on those same rows as if they were unseen. It pushes the reported score up, because the choice was made to fit those exact rows. Choose t on test and the test slice quietly becomes a second practice slice, so the number you report is no longer a test at all. Picture a friend who is tuning a cookie recipe for a bake sale by baking batches with slightly different amounts of sugar. She asks the same 15 tasters to score every batch, then announces the top batch’s score as proof of how good her cookies are. The amount of sugar really does matter, but she picked the batch that happened to suit those 15 people. A new crowd at the sale will usually rate it lower than she claimed, because part of her top score was those 15 people’s personal taste. The honest way is to choose the sugar with one group of tasters and then score the final recipe once with a different group. The lab does the same thing with the threshold, using two controls and a button on the Train, val, test card. You pick a slice with Choose t using, and you pick the reading to aim for with Maximize, which offers accuracy, recall and F1. The button then tries 101 thresholds on that slice alone, from 0.00 up to 1.00 in steps of 0.01, and keeps whichever scores best. It is labelled Set t from val or Set t from test, and it shows the threshold it found in brackets. Pressing it switches Baseline to score ≥ threshold and moves Decision threshold to that value, so the other cards update too. A table on the card compares two paths, Intact · t from val and Leaked · t from test, and scores each one twice. Its Test claim column is the number you would publish from the test slice, while Fresh rows scores the same threshold on 400 extra rows. Those fresh rows come from the same random process and took no part in either choice, and the lab can offer them only because it makes its own data. Here is what the table shows on 1 in 5 with Maximize set to F1: Intact: looking only at val, the search picks t = 0.55, which claims an F1 of 66.7% on test and gets 77.9% on the fresh rows. Leaked: looking at test, the search picks t = 0.46, which claims 85.7% on test but gets only 68.8% on the fresh rows. A percentage point, shortened to pts, is the plain difference between two percentages, so going from 66.7% to 85.7% is a rise of 19 points. The Leak inflation readout shows exactly that rise, +19.0 pts. Yet on rows that took no part in the choice, the leaked threshold did worse than the honest one, at 68.8% against 77.9%. The leak changed the number you would report, and it did nothing to make the alarm better. The reason is that the test slice has only 15 rows and only 3 real fires, so the best of 101 tries on it partly fits luck. A threshold chosen that way soaks up quirks, such as which few harmless rows happened to score high, so it looks great there and disappoints elsewhere. The honest claim is off as well, because 15 test rows with only 3 fires make a tiny sample, so one row more or less moves the score a lot. The difference is that the honest number can land too high or too low by luck, and here it landed low. The leaked number was pushed upward by the choice itself. The val search produces a flattering number in exactly the same way, which you can see in the card’s readouts. With Choose t using on val, the readout val F1 at that t shows 100.0%, because 0.55 was picked to suit those 15 val rows. That is why the honest path never publishes the val number and instead scores the untouched test slice once. Overfitting: two curves, not one Training a model means nudging it over and over to lower its loss, a number that measures how wrong its guesses are, where lower is better. One full pass of training over every training row is called an epoch, and a plot of the loss after each epoch is a learning curve. The useful picture always has two of them, one for the training rows and one for the val rows. Because loss measures wrongness, a line going down means the model is getting better, and a line going up means it is getting worse. Picture a student who prepares for an exam by redoing the same practice sheet every night. At first they are learning the subject, so they improve on the sheet and on new questions alike. After a while, though, they are mostly learning that one sheet, so their practice score keeps climbing while their score on fresh questions starts to slip. On a loss chart, that slipping score on fresh questions shows up as the val line rising. That slip is what overfitting looks like: the model keeps improving on the training rows while getting worse on rows it has not seen. On the Learning curves card, with Pattern set to overfit, the solid train line keeps falling all the way to epoch 20. The dashed val line falls until epoch 10, where the Lowest val loss readout shows 0.262, and after that it turns back up. By epoch 20, the Val rise since then readout shows that the val loss has climbed 0.204 above its low point. Meanwhile the train loss has sunk to about 0.06, which would look like a big success if it were the only curve you saw. The vertical guide on the chart marks the epoch with the lowest val loss, which is where early stopping would keep the model. Early stopping means you stop, or roll back, at the point where the model did best on rows it had not trained on. The other two patterns tell different stories, and neither has a val line that turns up. With good fit, both curves fall and stay close together, ending about 0.05 apart at epoch 20. With underfit, both curves flatten early and stay high and close together, because the model is too weak to capture the pattern. In real training, stopping much too early can also leave a model underfit. In this sketch, though, both curves have already flattened, so more epochs would barely help. These curves come from formulas written for the lab rather than from a model trained on the 100 rows, so they show shapes, not a real run. Cross-validation and stratified splits A val slice of 15 rows is small, so one lucky or unlucky slice could mislead you. Cross-validation deals with this by letting the data take turns, so no single slice decides the result. You cut the rows into equal pieces called folds, hold each fold out once while the rest do the training, and then average the scores. The Cross-validation card cuts the 100 rows into five folds of 20 and scores the silent alarm, always negative, on each fold. Nothing is trained on this card, since the silent alarm needs no learning, so each fold is scored in turn and nothing else happens. The Held-out fold slider picks which of the five is held out, and its label tells you which rows that fold covers. On 1 in 100, folds 0 to 3 each score 100% accuracy, while fold 4, which holds row 99, scores 95%. The average is 99.0%, shown as CV mean acc, which is short for the cross-validation mean accuracy. Only fold 4 can measure recall, because the other folds have no fire to miss. On 1 in 5, every fold scores 80% accuracy and 0% recall, so the failure shows up in every single fold. Two lessons come out of this card, and the first is that cross-validation does not repair a bad reading. It averages accuracy more fairly across the folds, and the average still looks fine on 1 in 100. The second lesson is that a rare class can go missing from whole folds or slices. A stratified split fixes that by keeping each class’s share the same in every slice, so a rare class turns up in train, val and test alike. On 1 in 5, the twenty fires were placed so that train holds 14, while val and test hold 3 each. That is exactly 20% of every slice, but on 1 in 100 no split can manage it, because one fire cannot sit in three slices at once. The ROC curve and AUC: grading the ranking Every reading so far judges one threshold, but a different question is how well the detector ranks the rows. Do the real fires tend to score higher than the harmless rows, whatever t you pick? Slide t from 1 down to 0 and two rates climb together, because a lower threshold lets more rows ring. The true positive rate, the share of fires that ring, rises as more fires get caught. The false positive rate, the share of harmless rows that ring, rises as more false alarms creep in. Plot one rate against the other for every t and you get the ROC curve, with false positive rate along the bottom and true positive rate up the side. For example, on 1 in 5 at t = 0.50, the alarm catches 0.80 of the fires and rings on 0.0875 of the harmless rows. That threshold becomes one dot, 0.0875 along the bottom and 0.80 up the side. Every other t gives a dot of its own, and joining them all makes the curve. Both rates run from 0 to 1, so the chart is a square with a total area of 1, and a perfect detector’s curve would fill all of it. The area under the curve is the AUC, a number from 0 to 1 that equals the chance a randomly picked fire outscores a randomly picked harmless row. An alarm that guessed at random would ring on fires and harmless rows at the same rate, so its dots would fall along the dashed diagonal line. That line cuts the square in half, which is why pure guessing gives an area of 0.5. On 1 in 100 with all 100 rows scored, row 99 at 0.42 outscores 98 of the 99 harmless rows, and only row 12 beats it. So the AUC is 98/99, about 0.990, and the What AUC means here readout says “row 99 outranks 98 of 99 negatives”. Yet at t = 0.50 the one real fire does not ring, so recall is 0%. Both facts are true at once because AUC grades the ranking across every possible t, while recall grades the one t you actually chose. So a great ranking can still be shipped with a threshold that never catches anything, which is why AUC alone is not enough. On 1 in 5 the AUC is 0.949, which means 94.9% of the fire-and-harmless pairs are ranked the right way round. Regression: MAE, MSE and RMSE Some models guess a number, such as a price, instead of answering yes or no, and this is called regression. It needs scores of its own, so the Regression residuals card is a separate small example that has nothing to do with the 100 rows. It has five points, each with an x value and a y value, and a very plain model that always guesses ŷ = x. The symbol ŷ, said “y-hat”, means the model’s guess for y, so this model guesses that y equals x. The miss on each point, the real y minus the guess, is written y − ŷ and is called a residual. The first four points sit close to the line ŷ = x drawn on the plot. You move the fifth point, the outlier, up and down with the Outlier y slider, which runs from 3 to 16. Three common scores sum up all five misses in a single number, and each one treats a big miss differently: MAE, mean absolute error, is the average size of the misses with any minus signs dropped. The table writes that size as |y − ŷ|, where the two bars mean “drop the minus sign”. MSE, mean squared error, squares each miss first and then averages them, so a big miss counts far more than a small one. RMSE is the square root of MSE. Squaring also squares the units, so if y were a price in dollars, MSE would be in dollars squared, which is hard to picture. The square root brings RMSE back to plain dollars. Take the default, with Outlier y at 12. The fifth point has x = 4, so the model guesses 4, and the miss is 12 − 4 = 8. The other four misses are small: 0.2, 0.1, −0.1 and 0.2. For MAE, add the sizes, 0.2 + 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.2 + 8, to get 8.6, then divide by 5 to get 1.72. For MSE, square each miss to get 0.04, 0.01, 0.01, 0.04 and 64, which add up to 64.1, then divide by 5 to get 12.82. For RMSE, take the square root of 12.82, which is about 3.58. The outlier’s one squared miss of 64 makes up 99.8% of that total, which is what the Outlier’s share of MSE readout shows. Drag Outlier y from 4 up to 16 and MAE climbs steadily to 2.52, while MSE leaps all the way to 28.82. MSE is the usual training loss for misses like these, yet it is not automatically the number to publish, because one wild point can take it over.

documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · How we know a model works
documents.body: The previous lab ended with a score on a holdout, and the natural next question is whether a published score means what you think it means. The trouble is that a model’s quality has to be squeezed into one number someone can report, and the squeezing is where things go wrong. A score can be calculated with no errors and still be the wrong reading, measured on the wrong rows, or missing the evidence that would expose it. This page pins the published number down as a reading of one matrix, so you can see exactly which counts each number uses and which it ignores. Each of the four traps in the overview comes down to the same thing: a correct calculation that answers a different question from the one you care about. It also separates two kinds of number that often get blurred together, the loss that training lowers and the readings that people publish. A loss shifts a little whenever any score shifts a little. For instance, picture a real fire whose score rises from 0.40 to 0.45 while t stays at 0.50. The loss drops a little, because the model is a bit less wrong about that row. The alarm still stays quiet on that row, though, so accuracy and recall do not move at all. That steady response is what lets the training program tell which way to nudge the model. The readings only change when a row crosses the threshold, so a model can reach a low loss while the reading you publish still hides its failures. Two populations are here on purpose, because each one can show things the other cannot. A single real fire is enough to break accuracy, but with one positive, recall can only ever be 0% or 100%. That is too few to show a trade-off, a base-rate effect, or how much a leak is worth, while twenty fires are enough for all three.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · How we know a model works
documents.body: The lab’s seven steps walk you through the cards in order, and each one sets up a comparison worth making: Keep the never-fire baseline: leave Population on 1 in 100, Baseline on always negative and Scored split on all 100, which is how the lab opens. Then read Accuracy against Recall on the Four readings card, which read 99.0% and 0.0%. Move the threshold: switch Baseline to score ≥ threshold and set Decision threshold to 0.42, where the alarm rings on row 99 and also on row 12, the harmless row. At 0.60 it rings only on row 12, giving a false alarm and a miss, and at 0.90 it rings on nothing at all. Switch to 1 in 5: set Population to 1 in 5 and slide Decision threshold from 0.30 to 0.70. In the matrix, FP drains away first while TP mostly holds, and then TP starts to fall into FN as Precision rises and Recall falls. Change the split: set Scored split to train, then val, then test, on each population and compare the readings. On 1 in 100, train and val hold no fire, so recall reads n/a, while on 1 in 5 every slice holds some fires. Choose t on a slice: with Population on 1 in 5, set Maximize to F1 and press Set t from val. Then set Choose t using to test and press Set t from test, and compare the Test claim and Fresh rows columns for both paths. Watch the Holdout? readout flip from intact to leaked as you do it. Read a learning curve: set Pattern to overfit, then to good fit, and compare where the lowest val loss sits and whether the val line turns up after it. Rotate a fold: move Held-out fold from 0 to 4 on each population and notice which folds can measure recall. Only fold 4 can do it on 1 in 100, but every fold can on 1 in 5. Try this: on 1 in 5 with Baseline on score ≥ threshold, drag Decision threshold slowly from 0.30 to 0.70. Watch the threshold sweep chart on the Four readings card, and guess first whether F1 and accuracy will peak at the same threshold. F1 has one sharp peak, at 0.54. Accuracy reaches its top value of 91% there too, but it comes back to that same 91% several times up to 0.62. The lab’s note reports the last of these, 0.62. By 0.62, F1 has dropped to 71.0%. So a search that chases accuracy can land on a threshold that F1 rates clearly worse, and the “best” threshold depends on which reading you decided to chase. Two more comparisons are worth a minute. First, set Population to 1 in 100, Choose t using to val and Maximize to recall, then press Set t from val. Val holds no fire, so the honest search has nothing to find and falls back to t = 1.00, a threshold where the alarm never rings. Now set Choose t using to test and press Set t from test, which finds 0.42 instead. That catches row 99, but it marks the holdout leaked. Then, on the Regression residuals card, drag Outlier y from 4 to 16 and watch MSE leave MAE far behind.
