documents.subtitle: Plain · How we know a model works
documents.body: 99% accuracy and 0% recall can happen together: on 1 in 100 the silent alarm does exactly that, which is majority guessing. On 1 in 5 the same rule reads 80% accuracy and 0% recall. Each reading has a blind spot: precision ignores misses, recall ignores false alarms, and a slice with no fires cannot measure recall at all, so it prints n/a. The trade-off is gradual on 1 in 5: sliding t from 0.30 to 0.70 moves precision from 29.9% up to 100%. Over the same slide, recall falls from 100% to 45%. F1 peaks at t = 0.54, while accuracy tops out at 91% at several thresholds from 0.54 to 0.62, and the lab reports 0.62. The same alarm is less precise when fires are rare: at t = 0.50 it is 69.6% precise at 1 in 5. At 1 in 100 it would be only 8.5% precise, so most of its rings would be false. On 1 in 100, accuracy barely moves over most of the range: on the threshold sweep chart its line stays near the top for every t above about 0.26. Recall, by contrast, falls off a cliff at 0.42. Below about 0.26, the ordinary harmless rows start ringing and accuracy drops fast. AUC can be near 1 while the alarm never catches a fire: on 1 in 100 the AUC is about 0.99. Yet at t = 0.50 the alarm rings only on row 12, a false alarm, and recall is 0%. Only untouched rows can show how a model does on new data: once you choose the threshold on test, test is no longer untouched. The Holdout? readout then switches to leaked. A leak raises the claim, not the alarm: on 1 in 5 with F1, choosing t on val claims 66.7% and gets 77.9% on fresh rows. Choosing t on test claims 85.7% but gets 68.8%, so the claim rose by about 19 points while the alarm got no better. Overfitting is a val line that turns up: in the overfit sketch, val loss bottoms out at epoch 10 and then rises with every extra epoch. A low train line on its own is not the diagnosis, because train loss keeps falling in all three patterns. Stratifying needs a fire in every slice: one fire in 100 rows is too few for three slices, so only test holds row 99. On 1 in 5, by contrast, train, val and test each hold exactly 20% fires, which makes a stratified split. Cross-validation averages a reading but does not fix it: five-fold accuracy of the silent alarm still looks fine. On 1 in 100 only the fold that holds row 99 can show a miss, while on 1 in 5 every fold can. MSE jumps while MAE walks: drag the outlier and the squared error races ahead, while the absolute error climbs at a steady pace.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · How we know a model works
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies The scores are not from a trained model: on 1 in 100, all 100 scores were written by hand. On 1 in 5 they were drawn from a fixed seed, a starting number that makes the same “random” draw come out every time. Harmless rows centre around 0.30 and real fires around 0.64, but real detectors do not come with tidy, known score patterns like these. The leak was picked to be visible: the seed is the lowest one that shows the leak clearly. Across 400 redraws of the same random process, choosing t on test raised F1 by about 22 points on average. So the direction you see is typical, while the exact size varies a lot, because the test slice has only 15 rows. No model from earlier labs is scored here: nothing from the previous page, The supervised learning loop, is reused, so these scores stand on their own. The learning curves are drawn formulas: no training happens on that card, and nothing in it is random. Cross-validation does not retrain anything: for simplicity its folds also include the test rows, which a real setup would keep out. Zero over zero prints n/a: the lab shows n/a rather than a made-up 0% whenever a reading would divide by zero. There is no calibration plot: calibration asks whether rows scored 0.4 turn out to be fires about 40% of the time. Checking that needs many rows at each score level, which neither population has. Percentages on 100 rows are exact counts: they are not estimates with a margin of error, the way measurements on a sample usually are. The setup is as small as it can be: there are only two classes, and a miss costs no more than a false alarm. The regression card uses ŷ = x: its model is fixed in advance, not a line drawn to fit the five points. Where the real mechanism fails The rare class may be the only class that matters: accuracy can be a perfectly calculated reading of the matrix and still be the wrong number to publish. Nobody hands you 400 fresh rows to expose a leak: in real work, the only protection is a test slice that no choice has seen. Leaks come in many forms: besides choosing a threshold on test, they include building a model’s inputs from numbers taken from the test rows. They also include deciding when to stop training by watching the test curve, and benchmark text that ended up in the training data. The base rate rarely stays put: how common fires are in everyday use seldom matches how common they were in your test set. It might be higher or lower, so precision measured in testing does not carry over. A val slice used for many decisions wears out: every choice made by looking at it fits it a little more, so you still need an untouched test. A good ranking is not a good rule: a high AUC says nothing about whether the threshold you ship catches anything. A common mix-up: people often treat accuracy, precision and recall as one number with three names, or treat a low training loss as proof that a model works. The three readings share a table but ask different questions, and a low training loss says nothing about rows the model has not seen. People also assume that a precise alarm is precise everywhere, when the same alarm is far less precise wherever fires are rarer. The pair of curves, the right reading for the job, and an untouched holdout are how you actually know whether a model works.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · How we know a model works
documents.body: Benchmarks and contamination: later, the Evaluation lab ranks saved versions of a model, called checkpoints, with a scoring rule based on how likely the model thinks each answer is. It then lets the benchmark leak into training, which it calls contamination. That is the same mistake as choosing t on test, made with whole test questions leaking instead of a single threshold. The same honesty, later on: Tokens & embeddings and Attention will hand you tidy numbers too, and the warning carries over. A number can describe a matrix perfectly and still not describe the skill you wanted. Where the 1 in 5 scores come from: each score is drawn from a bell-shaped spread, centred on 0.64 for fires and 0.30 for harmless rows. The fires are spread a little wider, and every score is then kept between 0.02 and 0.98 and rounded to three decimal places. The base-rate formula has a name: it is a form of Bayes’ rule, a general method for working out a chance once you know how common something is. AUC as a count: the lab works out AUC by comparing every fire with every harmless row, counting a tie as half a win. The share of wins equals the area under the stepped ROC curve, which is why the two descriptions of AUC agree. With twenty fires the curve has many small steps, so one row moves it far less than on 1 in 100. There the curve is a single step, and the whole number hinges on row 99. Cross-validation in practice: real cross-validation rotates only inside train and val, keeps the test slice out, and trains the model again for every fold, which this lab skips. Loss versus reading: training works on a smooth loss computed from the scores, such as one called cross-entropy, while the readings in this lab are what gets published.
documents.moduleTitle: How we know a model works
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · How we know a model works
documents.body: This module is about turning a model's scores on held-out rows into a number you can publish, and about the ways that number can mislead. It asks which reading of a detector's performance is honest, and which rows may be used to compute it. It builds on The supervised learning loop, which scored a holdout loss; here the question moves on to a thresholded decision rule and the metric you publish for it. The shared object is the confusion matrix: counts of true against predicted class once a decision threshold t turns each score into yes or no. Accuracy (the share of rows classified correctly), precision (the share of alarms that were real), recall (the share of positives found) and F1 (the harmonic mean of precision and recall) all read that one table. Where it shows up Thresholded detectors. Any rule of the form score ≥ t is scored from a confusion matrix, and someone has to choose t. Model selection. A validation (val) set is held out for choosing settings such as t or the epoch (one full pass over the training rows) at which to stop training, and a test set for one final score. Cross-validation rotates which slice is held out. Deployment. The base rate, the share of positives, seldom matches between production and the evaluation set, so measured precision does not transfer. Regression. MAE (mean absolute error), MSE (mean squared error) and RMSE (its square root) summarize the residuals y − ŷ, each true value minus its prediction; RMSE is back in the units of y. Why it matters A reading of the matrix can be computed correctly and still be the wrong number to publish, and even the right reading misleads when it comes from the wrong rows. Four ways a published number goes wrong: A rare class vanishes behind accuracy. A rule that never fires reads 99% accuracy and recall 0 when 99 rows in 100 are negative. Precision is credited to the detector alone. At t = 0.50 the rule reads 69.6% precision at 1 positive in 5. With the same true and false positive rates (the shares of positives and of negatives it flags), the closed-form precision at 1 in 100 is 8.5%. A leaked holdout overstates the result. Choosing t on the rows you then report as unseen, which is leakage, inflates the score, and nobody hands you fresh rows to expose it. A low training loss passes for success. Only a val curve that bottoms out and turns up shows overfitting. What you will be able to explain How accuracy, precision and recall are each read from the same confusion matrix. Why accuracy can look fine while the rare class is always missed, and why the same detector's precision falls as positives get rarer. Why choosing a threshold on the test slice is leakage that inflates the held-out score, and how train versus val curves diagnose overfitting. How precision and recall trade off as the decision threshold moves on a population with a realistic share of positives. What the lab shows No model is trained or run. The lab scores 100 rows with fixed labels and detector scores: authored constants on 1 in 100 (rare), and bell-shaped draws from a fixed seed on 1 in 5 (about 20%), where the two classes' scores overlap. Counts and percents are exact for those rows. The two base-rate precisions are closed-form, from the current rule's true and false positive rates. On Threshold and baseline, Population picks the set, Baseline picks a constant rule or *score ≥ threshold*, Decision threshold sets t, and Scored split picks the slice that counts. Confusion matrix shows the four counts; Four readings adds Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1, a threshold sweep, precision at two base rates, and an ROC plot of true against false positive rate as t falls, whose area is AUC (ranking). The key experiment is on Train, val, test: on 1 in 5, set Maximize to *F1*, press Set t from val, then switch Choose t using to *test* and press Set t from test. Holdout? turns *leaked*, and a table sets each path's Test claim beside its Fresh rows reading on 400 seeded rows that no choice saw. Learning curves (Pattern) are closed-form sketches. Cross-validation (Held-out fold) rotates five folds and scores the fixed always-negative rule on each, without refitting. Regression residuals (Outlier y) moves one point against the fixed line ŷ = x.

documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · How we know a model works
documents.body: The scored object is a 2×2 of true versus predicted class. Accuracy is (TP+TN)/N. Precision is TP/(TP+FP). Recall is TP/(TP+FN). F1 is their harmonic mean. Class imbalance makes a constant-negative rule look accurate, and the base rate, the share of positives, also limits how precise a detector can be. A held-out set is the slice that must stay out of fitting and threshold choice. Using it to pick t is leakage, and it inflates the score you report. The lab scores two populations of 100 rows. Population 1 in 100 is the deliberate imbalance demo: one positive, so precision can only read 50% or 0%. Population 1 in 5 has twenty positives whose scores overlap the negatives' scores, which is what makes the precision-recall trade-off visible. Held-out data plays two roles. The validation set is where you may look while choosing settings such as the threshold t or the stop epoch. The test set is scored once, after those choices are final. Choose t on test and it quietly becomes a second validation set, so the number you report stops being a test. Overfitting is diagnosed when training loss keeps falling while validation loss turns up. Cross-validation rotates which slice is held out. The ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate as t falls; AUC is its area. For regression, MAE is the mean absolute residual, MSE is the mean square, and RMSE is √MSE, back in the units of y. Precision and recall by hand Set Population to 1 in 5, Baseline to score ≥ threshold, and Decision threshold to 0.50. The matrix reads TP 16, FP 7, FN 4, TN 73. Every reading comes from those four counts, and nothing below needs more. Precision is TP/(TP+FP) = 16/23 = 69.6%: of the 23 rows the rule flagged, 16 were real. Recall is TP/(TP+FN) = 16/20 = 80%: of the 20 real positives, 16 were found. F1 is 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN) = 32/43 = 74.4%, and accuracy is (16+73)/100 = 89%. F1 is a harmonic mean, so it also equals 2PR/(P+R) = 2·0.696·0.80 / (0.696+0.80) = 0.744. Nudge t up to 0.54 and two false alarms drop out while no true positive does: TP 16, FP 5, FN 4, so precision is 16/21 = 76.2%, recall is still 80%, and F1 is 32/41 = 78.0%, the best F1 on these rows. Now raise t to 0.60. TP falls to 11 and FP to 1, so precision climbs to 11/12 = 91.7% while recall drops to 11/20 = 55%. A higher t removes false alarms first and real positives later. Because the two score groups overlap, no t raises both. Precision also depends on how rare positives are. At t = 0.50 the true positive rate is 16/20 = 0.80 and the false positive rate is 7/80 = 0.0875. Keep both and make positives 1 in 100: precision = 0.80·0.01 / (0.80·0.01 + 0.0875·0.99) = 8.5%. The detector did not change; about nine alarms in ten would now be false.

documents.body: Always negative on all 100 of 1 in 100: accuracy 99%, recall 0. On 1 in 5 the same rule reads accuracy 80%, recall 0: it is right on every negative and wrong on every positive. On 1 in 100, train and val contain no positives, so recall is 0/0 there and prints n/a, while accuracy prints 100%. Tuning recall on val therefore cannot find row 99 and falls back to t = 1.00. On 1 in 5 every slice holds positives: 14 in train, 3 in val, 3 in test, exactly 20% each. That is a stratified split, which one positive in 100 rows can never give. Choosing t on val, then scoring test, is the intact path. On 1 in 5, maximizing F1 with t from val claims 66.7% on test and reads 77.9% on fresh rows. With t from test it claims 85.7% and reads 68.8%. Leakage inflated the claim by about 19 points and did nothing for the detector. Maximizing accuracy on the rare set prefers never firing. Maximizing recall prefers a low t that fires on many rows. The sweep shows why: on 1 in 100 accuracy is nearly flat in t and recall is a step at 0.42. AUC on all 100 rows of 1 in 100 is 98/99 ≈ 0.990: only row 12 outranks row 99. AUC grades the ranking across every t, so it can sit near 1 while recall at t = 0.50 is 0. Overfit is a val curve that bottoms out (epoch 10 in the sketch) and turns up, not a low train number. documents.body: In this lab labels and detector scores are authored constants or draws from a fixed seed. On 1 in 5 each score is a bell-shaped draw (positives centred on 0.64, negatives on 0.30), clipped and rounded; real score distributions are neither bells nor known in advance. The seed is the lowest one whose draw shows the leak clearly. Across 400 re-draws of the same process, choosing t on test raised F1 by about 22 points on average, so the direction is typical and the size varies a great deal with 15 test rows. Learning curves are illustrative formulas, not a trained run. Cross-validation does not refit a model, and its folds span all 100 rows, test included. Readings with a zero denominator print n/a. The regression card uses ŷ = x, not a fitted line. There is no reliability diagram for either population. No model from the classical-ML or supervised-loop labs is scored here. In the real mechanism, choosing the threshold on the test split is leakage, and nobody hands you 400 fresh rows to expose it. Accuracy remains a legal reading of the matrix and can still be the wrong published number. documents.subtitle: Threshold and baseline · How we know a model works
documents.body: Two populations, two dumb rules, one threshold One hundred scored rows in two populations. Population 1 in 100 is the deliberate imbalance demo: a single positive at row 99 with score 0.42 and a confident false alarm at row 12. Population 1 in 5 has twenty positives whose scores overlap the negatives' scores, so a threshold has real trade-offs to make. Baseline chooses always negative, always positive, or a threshold on those scores, and Scored split chooses which slice counts. The scores are not a trained loss; the metrics are readings of a thresholded matrix. A kicker with the number of scored rows and how many are truly positive, and a title that names the population. Population with two segments, 1 in 100 (rare) and 1 in 5 (about 20%); Baseline with three segments; Decision threshold from 0.00 to 1.00; and Scored split with all 100, train, val, and test. A score strip: every row as a dot at its detector score, stacked where scores repeat. Positives are diamonds and negatives are circles, so the classes differ by shape and not only by colour. On 1 in 100, row 99 is the diamond at 0.42 and row 12 a ringed circle at 0.88. The shaded side of the t line is what the rule predicts positive; rows outside the scored split are faded. A note that says what fires at the current setting and describes the population. Train is rows 0–69, val 70–84, test 85–99 in both populations. On 1 in 100 the only positive is row 99, so train and val are all negatives. On 1 in 5 the twenty positives are placed four to every block of twenty rows, which leaves 14 in train, 3 in val, and 3 in test: exactly 20 percent in each slice. On 1 in 5 each score is drawn from a bell: positives centre on 0.64 and negatives on 0.30, with spreads of 0.16 and 0.14, clipped to 0.02–0.98 and rounded to three decimals, from a fixed seed. The two bells overlap, so no threshold separates the classes. Always negative predicts 0. Always positive predicts 1. Learned predicts 1 when score ≥ threshold. Threshold is ignored by the two constant rules. Population, Baseline, Decision threshold, and Scored split are the four controls. Comparison worth running on 1 in 100: always negative on all 100, then score ≥ threshold at 0.42, 0.60, and 0.90. At 0.42 both rows 99 and 12 fire; at 0.60 only row 12; at 0.90 nothing. Comparison worth running on 1 in 5: score ≥ threshold at 0.30, 0.50, and 0.70. False alarms leave first and real positives leave later, which is the precision-recall trade-off. Train and val can look perfect for a never-fire rule on 1 in 100 because they contain no positives. On 1 in 5 the same rule scores about 80 percent, because 80 percent of the rows are negative. The threshold only matters when Baseline is score ≥ threshold. In this lab: scores and labels are authored or drawn from a fixed seed, not outputs of the previous lab's classifier. There is no fitted model and no training loss on this card, and no model from the classical-ML or supervised-loop labs is scored. In general: a real holdout must stay unseen, and a real detector's score distributions are neither bells nor known in advance. Tuning the threshold on the test slice is the same leak the Evaluation lab later names contamination.

documents.subtitle: Train, val, test · How we know a model works
documents.body: The strip, and the leak A 100-cell strip: train, val, test. Choose t using picks which slice searches for a threshold that maximizes accuracy, recall, or F1. Set t from that slice writes the threshold. Doing that on test marks the holdout leaked. A table then compares the intact path (t from val) with the leaked path (t from test) on the test slice and on 400 fresh rows from the same scoring process. A 100-cell strip. Train, val, and test use different fills. Positives are outlined; on 1 in 100, row 99 and row 12 have extra marks. Choose t using (train / val / test), Maximize (accuracy / recall / F1), and a Set t button that prints the winning threshold. Metrics t chosen, the goal's value on the tuning slice at that t, Test accuracy, recall, or F1, and Holdout? intact or leaked. A two-row table. Each row gives its threshold, its Test claim (the reading you would publish), its Fresh rows reading, and Claim − fresh, the amount the claim exceeds what fresh rows show. A metric prints Leak inflation: leaked minus intact test reading. The search tries thresholds 0.00, 0.01, …, 1.00 on the chosen slice only, then scores the frozen t on the test slice. Ties go to the highest t. On 1 in 100, train and val have no positives, so recall is 0/0 there at every t, the search finds nothing, and it falls back to t = 1.00. Test contains the only positive; searching there finds t = 0.42 and is leakage. On 1 in 5 every slice has positives, so the val search is meaningful. The table always runs both searches: t from val, and t from test. Fresh rows are 400 more draws from the same scoring process, exactly 20 percent positive, which never take part in either choice. On 1 in 100 there is no fresh batch and the column reads n/a. Choose t using, Maximize, and Set t from … Comparison worth running on 1 in 100: choose t on val for recall (t = 1.00, Test recall 0%), then choose t on test for recall (t = 0.42, Test recall 100%) and watch Holdout? flip to leaked. Comparison worth running on 1 in 5: Maximize F1 with t from val, then with t from test. Test F1 rises, but the Fresh rows reading for the leaked t falls below the claim. Leakage inflates the claim, not the detector. The leaked threshold was fitted to fifteen rows, so its test number is the best of 101 tries on a small sample. Maximizing accuracy on the rare set prefers a t that never fires. Maximizing recall prefers a low t that fires on many rows. F1 balances both. Those are different searches. A leaked test number looks better and is the wrong claim. In this lab: a grid search over 101 thresholds, one authored positive on 1 in 100, and one seeded draw on 1 in 5. The seed was chosen so that the effect is visible; across 400 re-draws of the same process the leaked claim exceeded the intact one in most draws, and the size varies a great deal with fifteen test rows. No model is retrained. In general: leakage also includes features computed with test statistics, early stopping on the test curve, and benchmark text that sat in the training crawl. A fresh batch is a luxury; in practice the cure is to keep a test slice that no choice has seen.

documents.subtitle: Confusion matrix · How we know a model works
documents.body: Four counts the scalars are made from A 2×2 of true class versus predicted class. The heatmap shows each cell as a share of the scored rows so the rare positive does not disappear visually, and the table prints the raw TN, FP, FN, and TP counts. A heatmap with rows true 0 / true 1 and columns pred 0 / pred 1, values as percents of the scored set. A table of the same four cells with integer counts. The true-1 row highlights when the positives are all missed. A note that every scalar on the next card is a reading of this table. TN, FP, FN, and TP are tallied from the current baseline, threshold, and split. Heatmap values are those counts divided by the number of scored rows, so they sum to one. This card has no controls. The previous cards rewrite every cell. Comparison worth running: always negative versus always positive on all 100, and watch which off-diagonal fills. Then, on 1 in 5, slide the threshold and watch FP drain into TN before TP drains into FN. A 99% true-negative cell can hide a single false negative. When the detector never fires, TP is 0 and every positive is an FN: 1 of 1 on 1 in 100, 20 of 20 on 1 in 5. In this lab: two classes, and one authored positive on 1 in 100 or twenty seeded positives on 1 in 5. There is no cost matrix and no confidence interval on a cell. In general: a confusion matrix is still the object. Accuracy, F1, and AUC are different readings of related tables, not separate truths.

documents.subtitle: Four readings · How we know a model works
documents.body: Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 from one table Accuracy is (TP+TN)/N. Precision is TP/(TP+FP). Recall is TP/(TP+FN). F1 is 2PR/(P+R) = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN). A reading whose denominator is 0 prints n/a. On 1 in 100, always negative prints 99% accuracy and 0% recall; on 1 in 5 it prints 80% and 0%. Two further readings hold the detector fixed and change only the share of positives. Four metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1, each as a percent or n/a. A note that names the never-found case, the n/a case, or the two fractions. A threshold sweep: accuracy (solid), precision (dashed), recall (dotted), and F1 (dash-dot) for every t from 0 to 1 on the scored rows, with labelled dots where the current t crosses each line. An ROC plot: true positive rate against false positive rate as t falls, the shaded area under it, the dashed chance diagonal, and a dot at the current t. Metrics AUC (ranking) and what it means for this slice. Two base-rate metrics: Precision if 1 row in 5 is positive and Precision if 1 row in 100 is positive, for the rule currently selected. A note that these scalars are not the training loss. The scalars are computed from the same TP, FP, TN, FN as the matrix. When TP+FP = 0, precision is 0/0 and has no value; when TP+FN = 0, recall is 0/0 and has no value. The card prints n/a instead of pretending either is 0% or 100%. The sweep always evaluates the score ≥ t rule, even while a constant baseline is selected, so you can see what each threshold would give. A gap in a line is a range of t where that reading is 0/0. AUC is the Mann–Whitney probability that a random positive outscores a random negative, ties counting one half; it equals the area under the ROC steps. On 1 in 100 and all 100 rows it is 98/99 ≈ 0.990 because only row 12 outscores row 99. On train or val of 1 in 100 there is no positive and no ROC. The base-rate readings use Bayes' rule on the matrix: TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1−π)), with TPR and FPR taken from the current rule on the scored rows and π set to 0.20 or 0.01. At the rule's own base rate the formula returns its own precision. This card has no controls. Comparison worth running: on 1 in 5 with Baseline on score ≥ threshold, set t to 0.50 and read Precision against Precision if 1 row in 100 is positive. Same rule, same TPR and FPR, far lower precision. Comparison worth running: always negative on all 100 versus the same rule on train of 1 in 100. Both look accurate; only all 100 still has a positive to miss. Precision does not mention the misses. Recall does not mention the false alarms. A split with zero positives cannot measure recall of the rare class; it prints n/a. On 1 in 100 the accuracy line barely moves across t while recall drops off a cliff at 0.42. On 1 in 5 recall falls steadily, precision climbs, and accuracy peaks in the middle. That picture is why accuracy is the wrong headline on a rare class. AUC ≈ 0.99 and 0% recall at t = 0.50 can both be true on 1 in 100: AUC grades the ranking, recall grades one threshold. In this lab: on 1 in 100 one positive makes the ROC a single step and AUC hinges on one row; on 1 in 5 there are twenty positives and the curve has twenty steps. Percents on 100 rows are exact counts, not estimates with error bars. There is no calibration plot: neither population has enough rows to fill reliability bins. In general: the metric you publish is a choice. Accuracy on an imbalanced detector is often the wrong choice, a held-out set is required before any of the numbers mean generalization, and the base rate in production rarely equals the base rate in the evaluation set.

documents.subtitle: Learning curves · How we know a model works
documents.body: Three illustrative pairs of train versus val Pattern chooses underfit, good fit, or overfit. The series are closed-form sketches that all start near the same loss: both flatten high; both fall and stay close; or train keeps falling while val bottoms out and turns up. They are not a model trained on the 100 rows. Pattern, a three-way segmented control. A line chart of train loss (solid) and val loss (dashed) over epochs 0 to 20, with a vertical guide at the epoch of lowest val loss. The legend prints both losses at epoch 20. Metrics Lowest val loss (epoch and value), Val rise since then, and Val − train at 20. A footnote that names the diagnosis, and a note that the curves are illustrative. Underfit: train 0.45 + 0.55e^(−t/3), val 0.04 higher. Good fit: train 0.14 + 0.88e^(−t/5), val 0.19 + 0.86e^(−t/5). Overfit: train 0.05 + 0.9e^(−t/4); val 0.10 + 0.88e^(−t/4) + 0.0009t², lowest at epoch 10. The guide is the argmin of the val series — where early stopping would keep the weights. Nothing is optimized. The 100 detector scores do not enter this card. Pattern is the only control. Comparison worth running: overfit versus good fit. The tell is the val turn, not the final train number. A low training loss is not a diagnosis. The pair of curves is. Early stopping would use the val curve, not the test curve. Using test here would be leakage again. In this lab: three illustrative formulas. There is no optimizer and no random seed. In general: a real run can look like any of the three, and a val curve used for many decisions still needs a final untouched test.

documents.subtitle: Cross-validation · How we know a model works
documents.body: Five folds, one never-fire rule The 100 rows are cut into five contiguous folds of 20. Held-out fold chooses which slice is scored. The rule is always negative. On 1 in 100 four folds print 100% accuracy and fold 4 prints 95%, the fold that contains row 99. On 1 in 5 every fold holds four positives and prints 80%. Held-out fold, a slider from 0 to 4 that names the row range. A strip that marks the held-out fold, a five-row table of always-negative accuracy, recall, and positives in each fold, and metrics for this fold, the CV mean, and this fold's recall. Fold i is rows 20i through 20i+19. Always negative is the constant rule from the first card. CV mean accuracy is the unweighted mean of the five fold accuracies. Recall is 0/0, n/a, on every fold that lacks a positive, and 0% on a fold that has one, because the rule misses it. On 1 in 5 the twenty positives are placed four to a fold, so the folds are stratified by construction and recall is defined on all five. Held-out fold is the only control. Comparison worth running: fold 0 versus fold 4 on each population. On 1 in 100 mean accuracy barely moves and recall only exists on fold 4. On 1 in 5 recall exists on every fold. Cross-validation does not repair a bad metric. It averages that metric more fairly. On 1 in 100 only one fold can see the rare class; on 1 in 5 all five can. In this lab: contiguous folds over all 100 rows, a constant rule, and no model refit per fold. The 1 in 5 folds are stratified by how the positives were placed, and the 1 in 100 folds cannot be stratified at all. The folds include the test slice that a real protocol would keep out. In general: production CV refits the model on each training union. Stratification matters when the rare class can miss a fold entirely, as it does on 1 in 100.

documents.subtitle: Regression residuals · How we know a model works
documents.body: MAE versus MSE on one outlier Five points and the identity model ŷ = x. Outlier y moves the fifth point. MAE is the mean absolute residual; MSE is the mean square. The outlier dominates MSE and barely moves MAE in comparison. Outlier y from 3 to 16, a plot of ŷ = x with a residual tick at each point and the outlier labelled, and a five-row table of residual, absolute residual, and squared residual. Metrics MAE, MSE, RMSE, and the outlier's share of the summed squared error. The first four points are (0, 0.2), (1, 1.1), (2, 1.9), (3, 3.2). The fifth is (4, outlier). Prediction is ŷ = x, not a fitted line. MAE = mean |y−ŷ|. MSE = mean (y−ŷ)². RMSE is the square root of MSE. Outlier y is the only control. Comparison worth running: set the outlier to 4, then to 16, and watch MSE leave MAE behind. MSE is the usual training loss for a squared residual. It is not automatically the number you should publish. This card does not use the 100-row detector. It is a second toy so regression has its own matrix-like object: the residual list. In this lab: five authored points and an identity predictor. No line is fitted, so this is not least squares. In general: a fitted least-squares line would chase the outlier. That is a different demonstration of the same square.

documents.body: Four learning-rate schedules trained side by side on the same data and the same seed, up to the peak rate where a constant schedule stops working. Read a learning-rate schedule as a function of training progress Explain why decay lets you use a larger peak learning rate Tell an overshooting run from a diverging one, and see what a gradient clip changes Judge whether a difference between two runs is larger than the spread that the shuffle seed alone produces Explain how a gradient can explode or vanish with depth, and what a norm clip can and cannot fix
