documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: The multiplier on each gradient step. It is the hyperparameter that most often decides whether a run converges at all.
documents.title: Learning rate

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: A rule setting the learning rate from training progress rather than keeping it fixed. Reported here as a multiplier on the peak rate.
documents.title: Schedule

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: Starting the rate small and ramping it to the peak over the first part of the run. It keeps early steps short while the loss surface is steep and, with Adam, while the running gradient statistics are still built from a handful of batches.
documents.title: Warmup

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: Easing the rate down along half a cosine period, from the peak to a small floor. Small final steps let the model settle rather than bounce around a minimum.
documents.title: Cosine decay

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: Warm up to a peak, then decay below the starting rate. A single rise and fall for the whole run.
documents.title: One cycle

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: Rescaling a batch gradient whose norm exceeds a threshold down to that threshold. The direction is preserved and only the length is capped, so it limits how far one step can move without changing which way it moves.
documents.title: Gradient clipping

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: The length of the gradient vector for one batch. A sudden spike is the signature of an update about to destroy the weights.
documents.title: Gradient norm

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: A pull toward zero, subtracting a small fraction of each weight at every step. For plain SGD this equals an L2 penalty; with Adam the two differ, which is why AdamW applies the decay separately from the adaptive gradient step.
documents.title: Weight decay

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: Taking a step longer than the local slope justified, so the loss rises instead of falling. Repeated overshooting is what a rising loss curve is showing.
documents.title: Overshooting

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: Loss growing without bound, usually ending in non-finite weights. Once weights are not finite, no later step can recover them.
documents.title: Divergence

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: The number fixing every random choice. Here that is only the shuffle order, because the weights start at zero. Holding it constant makes two runs comparable, but one seed is still one sample.
documents.title: Seed

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: The lowest-to-highest range of a result across several seeds of the same recipe. A difference between two runs that is smaller than the band cannot be told from the noise of the shuffle.
documents.title: Seed band

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: A gradient whose length grows layer by layer on the way back because each layer multiplies it by more than one. A norm clip rescales it to a threshold. The opposite case, a vanishing gradient, is not cured by a clip, which can only shorten.
documents.title: Exploding gradient

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Hyperparameters & schedules · question 1
documents.body: At a peak rate of 0.6 the constant schedule wins. At a peak rate of 30 it is the worst of the four. What changed? At a large peak, decay can still settle because its steps shrink, while constant steps keep overshooting Decaying schedules always beat constant ones, so the low-rate result was only a measurement error that a repeat run would remove The higher rate changed which schedule the shuffle seed favours, so the winner is a matter of chance At a small peak rate, decay just wastes budget: the model is still underfit when the steps get small. At a large peak rate, constant steps overshoot for the whole run while decay converts the same aggressive start into a settled finish. Schedules are what make large peak rates usable.
documents.title: At a peak rate of 0.6 the constant schedule wins. At a peak rate of 30 it is the worst of the four. What changed?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Hyperparameters & schedules · question 2
documents.body: You drag Warmup fraction from small to large. Which of the four loss curves can change? All four, because warmup is applied to the rate before any schedule gets to shape it Only One cycle, because it is the only one of the four schedules that has a rising phase Only Warmup + decay and One cycle, because Constant and Cosine decay ignore the setting Only Constant, because it has no decay phase that could hide the effect of the warmup Each schedule is a function of progress through the run. Constant and Cosine decay use only the peak rate and progress, so Warmup fraction never enters them. Warmup + decay and One cycle both ramp up over that fraction, so moving it reshapes their rate curves and therefore their losses.
documents.title: You drag Warmup fraction from small to large. Which of the four loss curves can change?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Hyperparameters & schedules · question 3
documents.body: At a very high peak rate and Batch size 2, the Constant run ends far worse than knowing nothing. You turn on a small Gradient clip. What happens? Nothing changes, because clipping only helps runs whose gradients explode, and the gradients in this model never explode The final loss falls, because the cap limits how far one step can travel even when no gradient was unusual The loss rises, because clipping throws away the gradient's direction along with its length Clipping rescales a batch gradient whose norm exceeds the threshold, keeping its direction and capping its length. That limits how far a single step can travel, which is the damage overshooting does, even though this model's gradients are bounded to begin with. It helps most at Batch size 2, where each batch gives the noisiest estimate of the true gradient.
documents.title: At a very high peak rate and Batch size 2, the Constant run ends far worse than knowing nothing. You turn on a small Gradient clip. What happens?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Hyperparameters & schedules · question 4
documents.body: The lesson says this model cannot produce a gradient explosion. Why, then, does the Constant run at a very high peak rate end worse than chance? Its gradient norm spikes by orders of magnitude within a single step, just as it does in real transformer training Its weights become non-finite, and no later step can recover them, so the loss stays above chance The weight decay pulls the weights toward zero faster than the gradient can fit them Each step is longer than the slope justifies, so it overshoots the minimum while gradients stay bounded With a single linear layer and softmax cross-entropy, each row's gradient is a probability vector minus a one, so its length is bounded at every slider setting. High rates therefore produce repeated overshooting rather than divergence: the weights stay finite and the loss is merely terrible. Real deep networks can multiply many derivatives and genuinely spike, which is what clipping was built for.
documents.title: The lesson says this model cannot produce a gradient explosion. Why, then, does the Constant run at a very high peak rate end worse than chance?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Hyperparameters & schedules · question 5
documents.body: With Five seeds on at the default peak, the table puts One cycle ahead of Cosine decay on average, by far less than the spread across seeds. What should you conclude? One cycle is the better schedule, because its mean is the lower of the two Neither can be ranked, because the gap is smaller than the band the seed alone produces Cosine decay is better, because the simpler schedule wins when the difference is small The ranking is exact, because the seed is fixed and the loss is a precise cross-entropy The two schedules finish about two ten-thousandths of a nat apart on average, while each moves by several thousandths between shuffle orders. A gap that small can flip with the seed, so one run, or five, cannot rank them. The gap between Constant and the decaying schedules at this peak is about fifty times the band, so that ordering is real.
documents.title: With Five seeds on at the default peak, the table puts One cycle ahead of Cosine decay on average, by far less than the spread across seeds. What should you conclude?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Hyperparameters & schedules · question 6
documents.body: In Gradient through depth you set 40 layers and a gain of 0.8, so the first layers receive almost no gradient. What does raising Depth clip do about that? It lifts the early layers' gradients up to the clip value, so that they can start learning again It scales every layer's gradient up equally, until the total reaches the clip value Nothing useful: a clip only shortens gradients, so the early layers still get almost none It makes the shrinking worse, because the clip applies its own gain at every layer A norm clip multiplies the whole gradient by min(1, threshold ÷ length). That factor is never above 1, so it can shorten an exploding gradient but cannot lengthen a vanishing one. At a gain of 0.8 the first layer sees under a thousandth of the output layer's gradient, and the clip leaves that ratio exactly as it was.
documents.title: In Gradient through depth you set 40 layers and a gain of 0.8, so the first layers receive almost no gradient. What does raising Depth clip do about that?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: A brand-new AI model, trained from scratch, starts out knowing nothing. It learns through a training program that has it make guesses and then scores how wrong they were. After each score, the program nudges the model's internal numbers a little so that the next guesses come out slightly better, and the cycle repeats. Each nudge is called a step, and before the first one a person has to choose a handful of settings that the model never learns for itself. How big should each step be, and should that size change as training goes on? How many examples should the model look at before each step, and should any single step be capped? These choices are called hyperparameters, and this module is about making them well. The most important one is the size of each step, called the learning rate. Set it too small and the model creeps along, running out of time before it gets anywhere good. Set it too big and the model keeps leaping past the good answer, and in this lab it can finish worse than a model that never learned anything. A schedule is a plan for changing the learning rate as training goes on, and the usual plan lets the steps shrink toward the end. The same choices are made for large AI models trained on huge amounts of text. The teams behind two well-known ones, GPT-3 and Llama 2, published their settings, and both raised the step size gently over a short opening stretch. After that, both slid it down along a smooth curve, and both put a cap on how big the push behind any single step could be. Getting these settings wrong is costly, and the lab lets you see several of the ways that can happen. Without a schedule, one step size has to suit both the start of training and the end, and no single size does both jobs well. Without a fair way to compare two runs, you can crown a winner that only won by luck. And for the largest models, a wrong schedule cannot be fixed by running it again. A run that big uses so much computer time that it is done only once. By the end of this module, you will be able to explain: how to read a learning-rate schedule, which is a chart of step size against how far through training the model is; why letting the step size shrink toward the end of training makes it safe to start with much bigger steps; how a run that keeps overshooting, stepping past the good answer, differs from one that truly breaks, and what putting a cap on each push, called gradient clipping, changes; how to tell whether one run really beat another, or whether the gap is no bigger than luck. The examples are shuffled into a new order each time, and the order alone can move a result; how big models, built from many stacked stages called layers, pass a message backward that tells each stage how to change. That message can grow huge or fade to almost nothing, and a cap can fix only one of those. The lab gives you five cards to work with, and each one shows a different part of the story: Learning-rate schedule shapes draws four schedules as curves, so you can read how big the step is at every point in a run. Loss for all four schedules trains four real tiny models side by side, one per schedule. It plots how wrong each one is as it learns, a score called its loss. Its Seeds switch retrains every model with five different shuffles, so you can see how much luck alone moves each result. Optimizer controls holds five dials, and the optimizer it is named after is the part of the program that takes the steps. Its Peak learning rate dial sets the top step size, and it can make a run end up worse than knowing nothing. Stability readout shows how big the push behind each step was and whether a cap is cutting it down. It also counts how many runs finished worse than a model that knows nothing and guesses evenly. Gradient through depth is a separate piece of arithmetic, not a trained model, that shows what happens to a message passed back through many layers. The first card draws each schedule straight from its formula, while the loss and stability cards show numbers measured from real training runs. Those runs are retrained every time you move a dial.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: The model and its loss The model in this lab is tiny: it reads a 499-character text called Harbor weather notes, which begins "the morning fog settles over the harbor". Its job is to guess each character of that text from the single character before it. It works with 30 characters: the 26 letters, a space, a full stop and two special marker symbols that never appear in this text. Everything it knows sits in a table of 900 numbers called weights, with one row of 30 scores for each character. To guess what follows a t, the model looks up the t row and turns its 30 scores into chances for the next character, with higher scores getting bigger chances. All 900 weights start at zero, so every score in a row is the same, and the model gives every character the same 1-in-30 chance. The examples it learns from are pairs of neighbouring characters, and the whole text holds 498 of them. The word "the", for instance, gives two pairs: t followed by h, and h followed by e. To learn, the model needs a score for how wrong it is, called the loss. The loss is low when the model gives the real next character a big chance, and high when it gives that character a small one. The lab averages the loss over all 498 pairs and measures it in units called nats per token, where a token here is one character. You will not need to work with the unit itself, because lower is always better, and a few landmarks give the numbers meaning: A loss of 3.401 is what you get by spreading your bets evenly over all 30 characters, which is why the dotted line on the loss chart sits there. The dotted line's label reads "knows nothing · ln 30 = 3.401", where ln is a calculator function that turns 30 into 3.401, and you will never need to work it out. A loss of about 2.08 means the model is, overall, about as unsure as someone choosing fairly among 8 characters each time. A loss of about 1.80 is about as unsure as choosing fairly among 6. That is where the best of the four runs finish when the top step size, the Peak learning rate, is set high. One step of training At each training step, the training program takes a small group of pairs called a batch, 16 pairs by default. For every one of the model's weights, it works out which way to push that weight, and how hard, so that the loss on those pairs would go down. That list of pushes, one for each weight, is called the gradient. The program then moves every weight by its push multiplied by one number, the learning rate, which decides how big each step is. As a worked example, say the gradient's push for one weight is 0.5 and the learning rate is 0.6. That weight then moves by 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3 in the direction that lowers the loss, and doubling the learning rate would double the move. One pass through all 498 pairs is called an epoch. With batches of 16 it takes 32 steps: 31 full batches, plus a last batch holding the 2 pairs left over. A full run of 25 epochs therefore adds up to 25 × 32 = 800 steps. The overall size of the gradient is called its length, or its gradient norm. To find it, you square every push, add the squares together and take the square root of the total. Picture a gradient with only two pushes, 3 and 4, whose squares are 9 and 16. Those add up to 25, and the square root of 25 is 5, so that gradient has a length of 5. It is the same sum you would do on a map: walk 3 steps east and 4 steps north, and you end up 5 steps from where you started. A gradient's length is that straight-line distance, worked out over 900 directions instead of two. It is not the number of pushes in the list. The part of the training program that takes these steps is called the optimizer, which is where the Optimizer controls card gets its name. The picture: walking downhill in fog Picture standing on a hillside in thick fog, trying to reach the lowest point of the valley. You cannot see the bottom, so all you can do is feel which way the ground slopes under your feet, take a stride downhill, and then feel again. Training is that walk: your height is the loss, your position is the set of 900 weights, and the slope you feel is the gradient. The length of each stride is the learning rate times how steep the ground feels, so steep ground and a big learning rate both mean a long stride. Far from the bottom, long strides get you down quickly, but near the bottom a long stride carries you right across the valley floor and up the other side. Then the next long stride carries you back again, and the walk turns into a swing from side to side. That is overshooting: a step so long that it carries the model past the low point instead of down into it, so the loss stops falling or even rises. When a run keeps overshooting, step after step, its loss curve stops falling steadily and starts jumping up and down from one epoch to the next. A schedule: stride length set by the clock A fixed learning rate keeps the same stride multiplier from the first step to the last, so the strides change only with the slope. A schedule changes the learning rate as the run goes on, by taking a top value, the Peak learning rate, and multiplying it by a factor of 1 or less. That factor depends only on how far through the run the model is. The first card, Learning-rate schedule shapes, draws that factor times the peak, with progress through the run along the bottom and the learning rate up the side. Progress is counted in epochs, so the bottom of the chart runs from 0 to 25. Here the valley picture stops matching, because a hiker who sensed the bottom was near could choose to take more careful strides. A schedule never makes that choice: it changes the learning rate by the clock, following its fixed curve whether or not the model is anywhere near a good answer. The ground in this lab also wobbles, because each step feels the slope of only one batch of 16 pairs. That slope is rough and points partly the wrong way. Near the bottom the real slope is gentle, but each batch's rough reading is often much bigger. A big learning rate turns that rough reading into a big hop away from the bottom. Finally, the real valley has 900 directions to move in, one for each weight, while a hillside has only north-south and east-west. The four shapes The four schedules hand out long and short strides at different points in the run, and the falling part of each curve is called its decay: Constant holds the full peak rate from the first batch to the last, which means the same learning rate for the whole walk. Cosine decay starts at the peak and eases down to 3 percent of it, with no slow climb at the start. Its name comes from cosine, a curve from trigonometry, but all you need is its shape: flat at first, steepest in the middle and flat again at the bottom. Warmup + decay climbs in a straight line from near zero to the peak, then falls in a straight line to 5 percent of the peak. How long the climb lasts is set by the Warmup fraction slider. One cycle starts at a tenth of the peak and climbs to the peak over the same warmup stretch, set by the same Warmup fraction slider. Then it curves down to 2 percent of the peak, ending below where it began. The climb at the start of the last two is called warmup. Each stride is the learning rate times how steep the ground feels, and the ground is at its steepest right at the start. The full peak rate there could give an extra-long first stride that throws the model off course. Warmup keeps the rate low for those first steps, then hands over to the long, fast strides. In this lab the start is only a little steeper than later on, so warmup changes the results very little. It matters much more with a different update method called Adam, which comes up under "Where it breaks". Warmup fraction sets the share of the run the climb takes: at its default of 15 percent, warmup lasts 120 of the 800 steps. As a worked example, the default Peak learning rate is 0.6. Take Warmup + decay: by epoch 12 its climb is over and it has come part of the way down, so its factor is 0.63. The learning rate at that moment is then 0.6 × 0.63 = 0.378, which is the number the chart's dot shows at epoch 12. A cap on any single step One more control works on the gradient itself rather than on the clock. Gradient clipping sets a maximum length: whenever a batch's gradient is longer than that cap, every push in it shrinks by the same factor until the length equals the cap. In the valley, clipping means the ground can never count as steeper than a set amount. So at a given learning rate, no stride can be longer than a set distance, however steep the ground feels, while the direction stays the same. Take the gradient with pushes 3 and 4, which has a length of 5, and set the cap at 1. Dividing both pushes by 5 gives 0.6 and 0.8, which still point the same way as before. Their squares, 0.36 and 0.64, add up to 1, so the new length is exactly 1. A gradient already shorter than the cap is left alone, so a cap can be switched on and still do nothing. The lab's Clip readouts say "binding" when the cap shortened at least one gradient, and "never binds" when none was long enough to reach it. Four real runs, one difference The next card, Loss for all four schedules, trains four real copies of the model at once, one for each schedule. All four read the same text, start from the same all-zero weights and see the pairs in the same order, so only the schedule differs. The pairs are shuffled into a new order at the start of every epoch, and a number called the seed fixes how that shuffle comes out. Use the same seed and you get the same order every time. In many models the seed also picks random starting weights, but here every weight starts at zero, so the shuffle order is the only thing the seed changes. Each curve shows the loss on the whole text at the end of each epoch. All four curves start on the dotted "knows nothing" line, because zeroed weights give every character the same chance. The Worse than chance readout on Stability readout counts how many of the four runs finish above that line. Lower loss is better, so finishing above it means doing worse than a model that knows nothing and spreads its bets evenly. That even guessing is the "chance" in the readout's name. A switch and a card for what one run cannot show One run with one seed is one sample, and a different shuffle might have told a slightly different story. Switch Seeds to Five seeds and every schedule is retrained with five shuffles, and the range from its lowest result to its highest, the seed band, is shaded in. The trained model also cannot show one famous way that real training goes wrong, so the Gradient through depth card shows it with plain arithmetic instead. Large models, often called neural networks, are built from many layers, stages of calculation stacked one after another. To work out how to change an early layer, the gradient is passed backward from the output one layer at a time, and each layer multiplies it by some factor. It starts at the output because that is where the guess comes out and the mistake is measured. Picture a line of 24 people passing a message from the front of a hall to the back. The front of the line stands for the output layer, and the back stands for layer 1, where the input comes in. The first person speaks at normal volume, and everyone after that repeats the message 1.2 times as loudly as they heard it. Between 24 people there are 23 hand-offs, and each one multiplies the volume by 1.2. So by the back of the line it is 1.2 × 1.2 × 1.2 and so on, 23 times over, which makes it about 66 times as loud. A gradient that grows like this on its way back is called an exploding gradient. Now make the line 40 people long and turn the factor down to 0.8, so each person repeats the message at 80 percent of what they heard. Over the 39 hand-offs the message fades to under a thousandth of its starting volume, which is called a vanishing gradient. The card lets you cap an exploding gradient and then watch the same cap fail to help a vanishing one. Where the picture stops: in a real network each layer's factor is different, changing with that layer's weights and the input. The card, by contrast, uses one fixed factor for every layer, which its Gain per layer slider sets.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: The learning rate decides whether a run works at all. The sharper lesson is that a schedule is what lets you use a big peak rate without paying for it at the end of the run. One fixed rate has to do two jobs that pull against each other. Early on, the weights are nowhere near good, so long strides make fast progress down the valley. Late in the run, the weights are close to the bottom, and the same long strides keep carrying the model past it and back. Near the bottom the real slope is gentle, but each step sees only a batch of 16 pairs, and that batch's slope is still rough. A big fixed rate turns every rough reading into a big hop, so the model keeps getting knocked away from the bottom. That is also why bigger batches help: at a peak of 30, Constant finishes at 1.883 with batches of 64, but at 3.020 with batches of 16. So a fixed rate forces a trade: pick one small enough to settle at the end, and the start of the run crawls. Pick one big enough for a fast start, and the end bounces around the bottom instead of settling there. Decay gets you out of that trade by letting one run be bold at the start and careful at the end, because shrinking the learning rate shrinks every hop. The trade also runs the other way, because when the peak is small, decay throws away useful steps. The model is still far from the bottom when its steps become tiny. Put together, that is why the winning schedule changes as you move Peak learning rate: at a small peak Constant wins, and at a big one a decaying schedule does. The lab also separates overshooting from two problems that can look similar. One is divergence, where the numbers blow up until the run cannot go on. The other is an exploding gradient, where the push grows layer by layer in a deep model. A cap on the push's length helps with overshooting and with an exploding gradient. No cap can rescue a gradient that has faded away, though. Finally, every training result depends partly on luck, because a different shuffle of the same examples gives a slightly different result. Without measuring how much the shuffle alone moves a result, you cannot tell a real improvement from a lucky draw, so the lab can retrain everything with five seeds.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: Read the schedule before any loss Click through all four Schedule buttons, and at first watch only the schedule chart. The selected schedule is drawn as a thick solid line and the other three as thin dashed or dotted ones, while shaded bands mark its warmup and decay. Pick Warmup + decay and drag Inspect epoch: a dot slides along the curve and reads the learning rate at that moment. Its label looks like "lr 0.378 at step 384", where lr is short for learning rate. Set Inspect epoch to 1 and the rate reads 0.160, then set it to 3 and it reads 0.481, climbing through the shaded warmup toward the peak. Back at epoch 12 it reads 0.378, the example worked out above. Next, drag Warmup fraction on Optimizer controls: only the Warmup + decay and One cycle curves change shape, because Constant and Cosine decay never use that setting. Then move Peak learning rate and watch the schedule chart again: the numbers on its side change, but every shape stays the same. That is because the peak multiplies each schedule's factor, so it stretches every curve by the same amount without bending any of them. Watch the winner change Three readouts sit under the loss chart, and the first is named after whichever schedule you picked. It reads Cosine decay final loss when the page first opens, but Warmup + decay final loss if you still have that schedule picked from the last step. The other two, Best schedule here and Best final loss, always name the winner of all four and its score. Try this: walk Peak learning rate up from 0.6 and watch Best schedule here change hands as the peak rises. At 0.6, the default, Constant finishes at 2.075 and Cosine decay at 2.255, with the other two decaying schedules within a few thousandths of Cosine decay. So at the default peak, Best schedule here reads Constant, and it wins by a wide margin over all three decaying schedules. Somewhere between 4.5 and 5, Best schedule here stops reading Constant. At 6, Constant finishes at 1.880 and Cosine decay at 1.846, so the order has flipped and a decaying schedule now leads. At 12, Constant has gone backwards to 2.093, while Cosine decay has kept improving and reaches 1.816. At 30, Constant ends at 3.020, not far below the dotted line, while Cosine decay reaches 1.802. Between 35 and 38, Constant's final point crosses the dotted line on seed 1, ending at 3.332 at a peak of 35 and at 3.537 at 38. Look at the Constant curve itself at a peak of 30, though. It jumps up and down from epoch to epoch and already pokes above the dotted line at almost half of its points. So 3.020 is only where a jumpy curve happened to stop, which the seed band below will show again. Once the final point crosses, Worse than chance flips to 1 / 4, and the Stability readout names Constant as worse than a model that learned nothing. Meanwhile the three decaying runs, fed exactly the same peak, still finish near 1.80. Break it, then cap it Set Peak learning rate back to 30 and set Batch size to 2, so every step averages over only 2 pairs. A batch that small gives a rough, jumpy push, as the class-poll example under "What to notice" explains. The Constant run now ends at 12.325, far worse than knowing nothing, and its curve runs off the top of the chart, though the legend prints the true number. Now raise Gradient clip to norm ≤ 0.50, so any gradient longer than 0.50 is scaled down to that length before the step is taken. The same run comes back to 6.522, which is a real rescue even though it still sits well above the line. Then compare two more caps, starting with a tighter cap of norm ≤ 0.10, which helps even more and brings the run down to 2.154. The far left of the slider means off, not an even tighter cap. Caps slid up toward 1.40 cut fewer and fewer gradients, and by about 1.0 the rescue is gone. One run there even reads 12.889, slightly worse than no clip. With five seeds, though, the clipped and unclipped results overlap, so that small difference is shuffle luck rather than real harm. Next, set Gradient clip back to norm ≤ 0.50 and click Constant on the Schedule control. The dots on the Stability readout and the caption under them follow whichever schedule is selected. Peak gradient norm, by contrast, is the longest gradient from any of the four runs. Each dot is one step's gradient length, a dashed line marks the cap, and the dots above it are drawn darker. Its Clip readout says "binding", and the caption under the dots counts how many steps the cap rescaled. Set Batch size back to 16 and keep that norm ≤ 0.50 cap: Constant now ends at 2.884, against 3.020 with no cap. The seed band in the next part shows why a change that small might be luck. Read the seed band Put Peak learning rate back to 0.6, keep Batch size at 16, slide Gradient clip back to off, and switch Seeds to Five seeds. Every schedule now gets a shaded band, and a table appears with each seed's final loss and a Spread column, which is the highest minus the lowest. The third readout also changes to Best mean of five seeds, because the winner is now picked by its average over all five shuffles. With five seeds on, the lab trains twenty runs, so the sliders respond more slowly. Read Constant's row first: it runs from 2.075 to 2.077, a band only 0.002 wide. The three decaying rows each move about 0.004 between shuffles, and they finish within 0.004 of each other. So Constant's average beats the best decaying schedule's average by 0.175. That is more than forty times the 0.004 that shuffling alone moves the decaying schedules, and every shuffle agrees that Constant wins at this peak. The decaying schedules are another matter: their order sits inside the band. The boxed note under the table warns that two schedules here cannot be told apart with one run. Raise Peak learning rate to 6, and Constant's band now runs from 1.880 to 2.008. The highest Cosine decay result is 1.847, lower than Constant's lowest, so all five shuffles agree that the order flipped. Raise it to 30, and Constant's band stretches all the way from 2.395 to 4.673. Seed 1's 3.020, the number you saw before, is just one of five results scattered across that wide range, and two of the five shuffles even end worse than chance. Worse than chance still reads 0 / 4, though, because that readout counts only the seed 1 runs. Explode a gradient, then try to rescue a vanished one Last, scroll to Gradient through depth and leave Layers at 24 and Gain per layer at 1.20. That slider reads "×1.20 · grows", meaning each layer multiplies the gradient by 1.20 on its way back. The chart draws each layer's gradient length, with layer 1, the input, on the left and the output on the right. Its side uses a log scale, where each gridline is ten thousand times the one below it: 1e4 means 10,000, 1e0 means 1 and 1e-4 means 0.0001. On this kind of scale, multiplying by the same gain at every layer draws a straight sloping line. So an explosion shows as a steady climb from the output on the right to the input on the left. Input ÷ output gradient, the gradient's length at layer 1 divided by its length at the output, reads 66.2. Whole gradient length reads 120, because it combines all 24 layers the same way you found a gradient's length earlier. You square each layer's length, add the squares and take the square root. The layers near the input are so large that the total comes to 120, more than any one layer. That is over 100 times the output's length of 1, which is the card's test for an explosion. So the boxed note at the bottom of the card says the gradient has exploded. Set Depth clip to 1.0 and look at the table, where the Whole gradient row now reads 1.000 under After the clip. The Whole gradient length readout still shows 120, because it always reports the length before the clip. The clip has multiplied every layer's gradient by the same factor, 1 ÷ 120, which is about 0.0083 and which the Clip readout rounds to 0.008. The first layer still gets 66 times what the output layer gets, because only the overall size changed. The boxed note now says the direction is kept and the whole gradient is scaled down to the threshold, which here means the cap. Then set Layers to 40 and Gain per layer to 0.80, and Input ÷ output gradient now reads 1.66 × 10⁻⁴. That is a short way of writing 0.000166, because × 10⁻⁴ means "move the decimal point four places to the left". So the first layer now gets under a thousandth of the output layer's gradient, and no position of Depth clip lifts it back up. The boxed note says the gradient has vanished before it reaches the early layers, and that a clip cannot bring it back. Here the whole gradient is only about 1.67 long, so a Depth clip of 1.0 multiplies every layer by 1 ÷ 1.67, about 0.600. That makes the faded gradient smaller still, and from 2.0 upward the clip never binds at all.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: On the schedule chart Warmup fraction moves only two of the four curves: Warmup + decay and One cycle read it, while Constant and Cosine decay ignore it completely. None of the shapes here reach zero, since Cosine decay stops at 3 percent of the peak, Warmup + decay at 5 percent and One cycle at 2 percent. How low to go is a real choice: many published training setups stop near 10 percent of the peak, while others slide all the way down to zero. On the loss chart Constant does not get steadily worse as the rate rises, because it first improves from 2.075 at a peak of 0.6 to about 1.86 near a peak of 4. It is already slipping by 6, where it finishes at 1.880. After that it keeps getting worse, through 2.093 at 12 and 3.020 at 30, so the best fixed rate sits in a narrow window. Cosine decay bottoms out near 1.80 around a peak of 30, then creeps back up to 1.809 at the slider's top of 60. So a schedule makes a big peak rate usable, but not free. At a low peak, a decaying schedule can finish behind Constant because it spent the end of the run taking tiny steps, so the run was not unstable, only unfinished. On the stability card Peak gradient norm is the longest gradient any of the four runs produced, and peak here means longest, a different peak from Peak learning rate. It shrinks as Batch size grows. With Peak learning rate at 30, the longest gradient is about 1.41 at a batch of 2 and about 1.00 at a batch of 16. At a batch of 64 it drops to 0.181, smaller still. Picture choosing a film for a class trip by asking classmates: ask 2 people, and the answer swings wildly depending on which 2 you happened to ask. Ask 16, and the strong opinions partly cancel each other out, leaving a steadier answer. A batch works the same way, because pairs from different parts of the text push the weights in different directions. Averaging more of them lets those pushes partly cancel, which gives a shorter and steadier gradient. The dots on the Stability readout show one gradient per step, and at the default settings, with a batch of 16, most of them sit near 0.2. A row of 25 higher dots, one per epoch, spreads from about 0.33 up to 0.8. Those belong to each epoch's last batch, which holds only 2 pairs because 498 does not divide evenly by 16. Gradient clip set above about 1.4 never binds anywhere in this lab, for a reason explained under "Where it breaks". Weight decay is not a schedule Weight decay pulls weights a little toward zero on each step, like a rubber band tied between each number and zero. Despite the shared word, it is a different thing from a schedule's decay, because it shrinks the weights themselves rather than the step size. Here weight decay only makes the result worse: on Constant at a peak of 0.6, a weight decay of 0.02 takes the final loss from 2.075 to 2.664. It also pulls only on the rows used in that step. So a character's row decays only on steps where that character was the first character of a pair in the batch. Weight decay exists to keep weights small, which stops a model from leaning too hard on the quirks of its practice text. That is meant to help it on text it has not seen. This lab never tests the model on such text, so it has nowhere to show that payoff. On the seed table Picture two identical robot students, built exactly alike and starting with empty memories. They study the same deck of flashcards for the same test in exactly the same way, except that each deck is shuffled differently. One scores 41 out of 50 and the other 42, and since nothing else about them differs, that one-point gap came from the order of the cards alone. If one robot later tries a new study method and gains one point, you could not tell that gain from a lucky shuffle. The seed band is the lab's way of measuring that kind of luck. A gap between two runs counts as evidence only when it is bigger than the seed band, the swing the shuffle alone produces. At the default peak, Constant leads by 0.175 against a band of 0.004, which is a real lead. The closest pair, One cycle and Cosine decay, differ by only 0.0002 on average. That is only about a twentieth of their 0.004 spread, so one run cannot say which is better. The band is not the same width everywhere: Constant's is only 0.002 wide at a peak of 0.6, but 0.128 wide at a peak of 6. At a peak of 30 it is 2.278 wide, nearly a thousand times wider than at the default. The decaying schedules stay under 0.011 wide at all of these peaks. For Constant at a high peak, though, the result of a single shuffle is close to a coin flip. The clip's rescue at Batch size 2 is bigger than the band. At a peak of 30, the five unclipped runs end between 9.854 and 12.325. Clipped at 0.50, they end between 6.168 and 6.522, so the two ranges never touch. At Batch size 16 it is a different story, because the clipped runs end anywhere from 2.308 to 3.606, which overlaps the unclipped range. So seed 1's move from 3.020 to 2.884 does not, on its own, prove that the clip helped. On the depth card A clip shrinks the whole gradient by one factor, so every layer keeps its share of the total and only the overall length is capped. A clip can only shorten, so raising Depth clip never lifts a vanished gradient, and a clip set above the whole length does not bind at all. At a gain of exactly 1.00 every layer's gradient has length 1, so the squares are 24 ones that add up to 24. The whole gradient is then the square root of 24, about 4.9. The explosion or the collapse comes entirely from the gain being different from 1, multiplied in once for every layer the gradient passes through.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Four real runs give four real curves, and the single default seed makes sure the only difference between them is the schedule. That same fixed seed is also a limit, because every number you read is one sample from one shuffle. Five seeds adds the missing measure of luck, but five is a small sample. The band is only the lowest and highest of those five results, not a promise about where a sixth shuffle would land. The band also measures the shuffle order and nothing else, so it says nothing about how a different text, model size or set of peak rates would change things. A common mix-up: a rising loss is not an exploding gradient. This model cannot produce an exploding gradient at all, because of the way its pushes are built. Each pair pushes only the row of its first character. On that row, the push for the right next character is 1 minus the model's chance for it. The push for every other character is minus the model's chance for that character. Say the model is reading t and gives h a chance of 0.7 and e a chance of 0.2, spreading the last 0.1 over the other 28 characters. If the right next character is h, the pushes on the t row are 1 − 0.7 = 0.3 for h, −0.2 for e, and tiny negative amounts for the rest. The chances are between 0 and 1 and add up to 1, so these pushes can never get very long. The worst case is a model that is completely sure of a wrong character, say e. Then the push for e is 0 − 1 = −1, the push for h is 1 − 0 = 1, and every other push is 0. Squaring gives 1 and 1, which add up to 2, so the push's length is the square root of 2, about 1.41. A batch averages these pushes, so its gradient can be no longer than that either. An average can never go past its biggest member, in the same way that a class's average test score can never beat the top score. That is why the measured Peak gradient norm stays between about 0.17 and 1.41 at every setting the sliders reach. It is also why the Stability readout draws a dotted line labelled "√2 bound", and why a Gradient clip above that line could never bind. What a high rate causes here is overshooting, over and over, with step after step carrying the model past the low point instead of down into it. Real divergence is something else: the loss grows without limit until the weights become non-finite, values such as infinity that the computer can no longer calculate with. Once that happens no later step can recover them, but divergence never happens inside these slider ranges. So here is how to tell the two apart in this lab: an overshooting run still ends at a number, even a terrible one such as 12.325. A diverged run has no number left, and the legend, the final-loss readout and the seed table print "diverged" in its place. That label never appears here, because the worst run you can build stays finite and performs badly. Gradient clipping still helps, and it is worth being exact about why. It caps how far one step can travel, which limits the damage from a long step even when the gradient behind it was ordinary. It does the most at Batch size 2, where each batch gives the roughest estimate of the real slope. The Gradient through depth card is how this lab shows an exploding gradient, and it is a different kind of thing from the trained runs. It has no weights, no data and no training: each layer multiplies the gradient by the same gain, and the gradient at the output is set to 1. In a real network, each layer's factor changes with its own weights, with the kind of calculation that layer does, and with the input. So the card shows the mechanism, a multiplication that compounds once per layer, and what a clip does to it, but not how any real network behaves. The rest are this model's usual limits, starting with the fact that it sees only one character before each guess and has only 900 weights. It has no hidden layers, the extra stages of calculation that deeper models stack between input and output. It has no tokenizer, the tool real models use to cut text into the pieces they read, and it learns from a text only 499 characters long. Its Peak learning rate slider stops at 60. It also uses plain gradient descent, the simple rule described earlier of moving each weight by its push times the learning rate, instead of Adam. The plotted loss is training loss, measured on the same text the model learns from, so nothing here shows a setting helping the model handle new text. Where the real mechanism fails Deep networks, the ones with many layers, differ in the way that matters most. Their gradients pass back through many layers and get multiplied together, so a small change in each factor compounds. Moving each of 24 factors from 1.20 to 1.25, for example, makes their product about 2.7 times larger. If each factor grows from 1.20 to 1.50 instead, the product grows more than 200 times, and more layers compound it further still. So after one update to the weights, a deep network's gradient norm really can jump tenfold, a hundredfold or more in a single step. A sudden spike like that is the warning sign of a step about to wreck the weights, and those spikes are what clipping was invented for. Both GPT-3 and Llama 2 clip the length of the whole gradient, measured across every weight in the model, at 1.0. This lab never produces one of those spikes from a trained model, so do not read its runs as a demonstration of one. Only the arithmetic on the depth card shows the shape of the problem. A clip also has a hard limit, because it can only shorten, so a gradient that has faded to almost nothing stays faded however you set the clip. Real models need other fixes for that, such as shortcuts that let the gradient skip past layers, called residual connections. Careful starting weights help too, and earlier labs cover both. A schedule is a bet, too, because it assumes the right step size changes in a fixed way as the run goes on. It goes by the clock rather than by how training is going, so the bet can be wrong for a given peak. That is why this lab trains all four schedules instead of trusting the schedule chart, since a curve that looks sensible can still lose. Warmup is also played down here, because it matters much more with Adam. Adam is a more elaborate update method that sizes each weight's step using an average of how big that weight's recent gradients have been. It keeps updating that average as training goes on. In the first few hundred steps, that average is built from almost nothing, so early steps can be large and badly aimed. Warmup holds them back until the average has had time to settle.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: The shape large runs report A common choice is a short straight-line warmup followed by cosine decay down to 10 percent of the peak, which is what both GPT-3 and Llama 2 report. Its drawback is that the curve is drawn to reach its lowest point exactly at the planned last step. So you cannot extend the run later without redrawing the curve and throwing the old plan away. Warmup-stable-decay schedules avoid that by holding a steady rate for most of training and decaying only in a short final stretch. You can keep training as long as you like and add the short decay whenever you decide to stop. This lab does not include one, but on its chart such a schedule would sit between Constant and Warmup + decay. Learning rate and batch size move together A bigger batch gives a steadier gradient, which can support a longer step, so the common rules raise the rate along with the batch. Double the batch, and those rules either double the rate or multiply it by about 1.4, the square root of 2. This lab shows the same link from the other side: hold the rate fixed and shrink the batch, and the run gets much worse. On Constant at a peak of 30, a Batch size of 64 finishes at 1.883, while a batch of 2 finishes at 12.325. Weight decay in large runs There are two ways to add weight decay's pull toward zero: one folds it into each weight's push, so it travels along with the gradient. The other applies it to the weights directly, outside the push. With plain gradient descent, the update rule this lab uses, the two ways give the same step. Adam, though, resizes each weight's push by its own amount, so a pull that travels inside the push gets resized too. That makes the pull stronger for some weights and weaker for others. A version called AdamW keeps the pull outside the push, so every weight is pulled toward zero in the same proportion. One shot at the real thing Picture a baker asked to make one enormous wedding cake, with no chance of a second try. Instead of experimenting on the big cake, they would bake small test cakes first, find the oven settings that work, and use a rule to scale them up. The largest AI training runs, sometimes called frontier runs, work the same way, because each one uses so much computer time that it is done only once. Their settings come from trial runs on much smaller stand-in models, plus a rule for carrying the results across, and a wrong schedule cannot be run again. Toy versus real Peak rate: this lab's default peak is 0.6, and its useful range runs from about 0.5 to 40, using plain gradient descent. Runs that use Adam take far smaller rates, so the two kinds of number cannot be compared directly. GPT-3's published peak rates run from 6.0 × 10⁻⁴, which is 0.0006, for its smallest version with 125 million weights. Its largest version, with 175 billion weights, uses 0.6 × 10⁻⁴, which is ten times smaller. Llama 2's published peak rate is 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ for its 7 billion and 13 billion weight versions. Its 34 billion and 70 billion versions use half that, 1.5 × 10⁻⁴. Warmup: this lab warms up for 15 percent of the run, which is 120 of 800 steps, while Llama 2 warms up for 2,000 steps. Llama 2 trains on 2.0 trillion tokens, the pieces of text such models read, at a batch of 4 million tokens, which makes about 500,000 steps in all. So Llama 2's warmup is roughly 0.4 percent of its run. GPT-3 warms up over its first 375 million of 300 billion tokens, which is 0.125 percent of its run. Both of those percentages are arithmetic on the papers' own figures, not numbers the papers state themselves. The floor: this lab's cosine decay bottoms out at 3 percent of the peak, while both papers decay to 10 percent of it. Both papers also use a weight decay of 0.1 and clip the whole gradient at a length of 1.0. Seeds: this lab can afford five runs per setting, but a frontier run happens once, which is why its settings come from trial runs on smaller stand-in models. The real-world figures come from the GPT-3 paper by Brown and colleagues and the Llama 2 paper by Touvron and colleagues.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: A hyperparameter is a setting chosen before training rather than learned. This module covers the ones that size each update: the learning rate, the schedule that changes it over the run, and the gradient clip, weight decay and batch size around them. It asks how large each step should be at each point in training, and when a gap between two recipes is real. It builds on Anatomy of a training run, which named the stages of one training loop. Here that loop runs four times side by side, changing only the learning-rate rule, so each choice is judged from a measured loss curve. Where it shows up Both GPT-3 and Llama 2 report a short linear warmup followed by cosine decay to 10 percent of the peak, weight decay of 0.1, and a clip of 1.0 on the global gradient norm. Warmup-stable-decay schedules hold the rate constant for most of training and decay only at the end. Clipping exists because the gradient norms of deep networks can spike by orders of magnitude within one step. Why it matters The peak rate can fail both ways. Too small leaves the loss high when the step budget runs out. Too large makes each step longer than the local slope justifies, so it passes the minimum and the loss rises: overshooting. Enough of it can end a run worse than a model that learned nothing. In a deep network a gradient spike can push the weights to non-finite values that no later step recovers: divergence. Judging the result can fail too. One run is one sample of the shuffle order, so a gap smaller than the seed-to-seed spread cannot be told from noise. Frontier settings come from sweeps on small proxy models, so a sweep fooled by seed noise passes the mistake on. What you will be able to explain How to read a learning-rate schedule as a function of training progress. Why decay lets a run use a larger peak learning rate than a constant rate can. How to tell an overshooting run from a diverging one, and what a gradient clip changes. How to judge whether a difference between two runs is larger than the spread that the shuffle seed alone produces. How a gradient can explode or vanish with depth, and what a norm clip can and cannot fix. What the lab shows The lab trains for real: four runs of a tiny 900-weight character model on one 499-character corpus, by plain minibatch gradient descent from the same zeroed weights and seed, differing only in schedule. Loss for all four schedules and Stability readout show measurements from those runs, and every dial on Optimizer controls retrains all four. The model's gradients are bounded, so a high rate makes it overshoot but never diverge; Gradient through depth is where an explosion appears. Four parts are not training results: Learning-rate schedule shapes plots the closed-form rate for each Schedule option (Constant, Cosine decay, Warmup + decay, One cycle), read at one point by Inspect epoch. The dotted "knows nothing" line on Loss for all four schedules is the fixed baseline ln 30 = 3.401. The dotted "√2 bound" on Stability readout, and the note under it, give the closed-form ceiling on every batch gradient norm the trace plots: √2 ≈ 1.41. Gradient through depth is closed-form, with no weights or data: Layers and Gain per layer set a gradient that compounds once per layer, and Depth clip caps its total length. Optimizer controls holds Peak learning rate, Warmup fraction, Gradient clip, Weight decay and Batch size. The key experiment: raise Peak learning rate from 0.6 and Best schedule here flips from Constant to a decaying schedule, then Constant ends above the "knows nothing" line and Worse than chance counts it. Five seeds under Seeds shows whether each gap beats the shuffle spread.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: A schedule sets the learning rate from how far through the run you are, rather than holding it fixed. The top chart plots exactly that: Peak learning rate multiplied by a factor that depends only on progress from 0 to 1. The four shapes differ in where they put the step budget: Constant holds the full peak rate from the first batch to the last. Cosine decay starts at the peak and eases down to 3 percent of it. Warmup + decay ramps from near zero to the peak across the Warmup fraction, then falls linearly to 5 percent. One cycle starts at a tenth of the peak, rises to it over the Warmup fraction, then cosines down to 2 percent. Below that, four separate runs train on the same corpus, from the same zeroed weights, with the same seed — 25 epochs, 800 optimizer steps each. The only difference between them is that factor. The dotted "knows nothing" line sits at ln 30 = 3.401 nats per token, and Worse than chance counts how many of the four runs end above it. Two further controls answer what a single run cannot. Seeds repeats every run over five shuffle orders and shades the spread. Gradient through depth is a closed-form model, not a trained network, of a gradient passing back through many layers, so the explosion that this model cannot produce can be shown and clipped.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: The learning rate decides whether a run converges at all. But the useful claim is sharper than "tune the learning rate": a schedule is what makes a *large* peak rate usable. A single fixed rate has to satisfy two conflicting requirements. Early on the weights are far from anything good, so long steps make progress fast. Late on the weights are near a minimum, so the same long steps overshoot it, and the loss stops falling or rises. Decay lets one run be aggressive at the start and settled at the end, which is why the winning schedule changes as you move Peak learning rate.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Hyperparameters & schedules
documents.body: Click through all four Schedule options and watch only the top chart first: the shaded bands mark the selected schedule's warmup and decay phases, and Inspect epoch moves a dot along the curve that reads the rate at that step. With Warmup + decay at the defaults the warmup lasts 120 of 800 steps, and epoch 12 reads a rate of 0.378. The first metric under the loss chart is named after whichever schedule is selected — Cosine decay final loss on load — while Best schedule here and Best final loss always report the winner of the four. Then compare at rising peak rates: Peak learning rate 0.6, the default: constant 2.075, cosine 2.255, warmup + decay 2.251, one cycle 2.254. Best schedule here reads Constant, and it wins by a wide margin. At 6: constant 1.880, cosine 1.846. The order has flipped. At 12: constant 2.093, cosine 1.816. Constant is going backwards; cosine keeps improving. At 30: constant 3.020, cosine 1.802. Between 35 and 38 the constant run's final loss on seed 1 crosses 3.401 (3.332 at 35, 3.537 at 38) and Worse than chance flips to 1 / 4 while the decaying runs stay near 1.80. Now set Peak learning rate to 30 and Batch size to 2. The constant run lands at 12.325, far worse than knowing nothing. Bring Gradient clip up to norm ≤ 0.50 and the same run returns 6.522. At Batch size 16 that clip moves 3.020 to 2.884. Now set Peak learning rate back to 0.6, Batch size to 16, and switch Seeds to Five seeds. Each schedule gains a shaded band and the table lists the final loss of every seed. Constant spans 2.075 to 2.077, so its lead of 0.175 over the best decaying schedule is about fifty times the band. Cosine decay, One cycle and Warmup + decay each move by about 0.004 between seeds and end within 0.004 of each other, so their order is inside the band. The callout says which pairs fall where. Raise Peak learning rate to 6, then 30, and read Constant's band. At 6 it runs from 1.880 to 2.008 and Cosine decay's top is 1.847, so all five seeds agree that the order flipped. At 30 it runs from 2.395 to 4.673: seed 1's 3.020 is one point inside it, and two of the five seeds already end worse than chance. Last, scroll to Gradient through depth. At 24 layers and a Gain per layer of 1.20, the input layer sees 66 times the length of the output layer and the whole gradient is about 120. Set Depth clip to 1.0: the whole gradient becomes exactly 1.0, every layer scaled by the same factor, 0.0083. Then set 40 layers and a gain of 0.80.
