documents.title: Find where it stops helping

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Adapting behavior from examples in the prompt with no weight update. Nothing persists: clearing the context removes the ability entirely.
documents.title: In-context learning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Supplying a handful of worked examples so the intended task becomes identifiable. Accuracy is sensitive to which examples, their order, and their formatting.
documents.title: Few-shot prompting

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Asking for a task with instructions but no examples. Instruction tuning makes this work far better, though base models can manage some tasks zero-shot.
documents.title: Zero-shot

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: One example pair in the prompt. Min et al. (2022) found that the format and label space of demonstrations can matter more than whether each label is correct.
documents.title: Demonstration

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Treating the examples as evidence about which task is meant. Rules that contradict an example drop out, and several rules can survive when the examples cannot tell them apart.
documents.title: Task inference

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: An attention head that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and predicts the token that followed it. Their appearance during training coincides with a jump in in-context learning (Olsson et al., 2022).
documents.title: Induction head

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: The measurable dependence of accuracy on details that should be irrelevant, including example order, formatting, label wording, and whitespace.
documents.title: Prompt sensitivity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: The maximum number of tokens the model can attend over. It is working space, not memory, and retrieval accuracy can degrade for content buried in the middle of a long context.
documents.title: Context window

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Intermediate tokens generated before the answer, which later tokens can read back. They help most on problems with several dependent steps, because each token gets a fixed amount of computation and a result written down can be built on by the next one.
documents.title: Chain of thought

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Text a model writes for itself before answering. A partial result written there sits in the context, so the next forward pass can start from it instead of recomputing it; padding that carries no partial result adds tokens and no progress.
documents.title: Scratchpad

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Work in which each step needs the result of the one before it, such as following a chain of lookups. A network of fixed depth can chain only so many such steps in one forward pass, and writing intermediate results as tokens lets the chain continue across passes (Li et al., 2024).
documents.title: Serial computation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Whether a stated reasoning trace reflects the computation that produced the answer. Traces can omit the features that actually drove the result. Not the same as circuit faithfulness in Interpretability II: circuits, which asks whether a subgraph of model components reproduces the behavior on its own.
documents.title: Faithfulness

documents.subtitle: Glossary · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Compute spent while answering rather than while training. A scratchpad spends it as extra serial passes; sampling, voting, and verification spend it across several attempts and are priced in Reasoning models.
documents.title: Test-time compute

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · ICL & reasoning · question 1
documents.body: The prompt shows glim → 4, plint → 5, soravel → 7, trelix → 6, then asks letter →. A model that fits every example answers 4. What is the best explanation? It miscounted the word, because the examples clearly define the task as counting every letter Counting distinct letters fits every example as well as counting letters, and letter repeats letters Reading the examples updated its weights, so it switched to a different rule just for this one word It copied the earlier answer 4, because the arrow after letter matches the arrow after the glim line Every example word has no repeated letters, so "count the letters" and "count distinct letters" give identical answers on all four. They only disagree on a word like letter (6 versus 4). The examples underdetermine the task; an example such as ballot → 6, or a stated rule, resolves it. Nothing about the weights changed.
documents.title: The prompt shows glim → 4, plint → 5, soravel → 7, trelix → 6, then asks letter →. A model that fits every example answers 4. What is the best explanation?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · ICL & reasoning · question 2
documents.body: On Copy from context you switch Query from soravel to florin at four examples. What does the induction head do, and what does that show? For soravel it copies the earlier answer; for florin it can only spread its weight over the old answers For florin it computes the letter count from the word, because copying and counting are the same step For both words it learns the rule from the examples and updates its weights to apply it For soravel it fails, because the head only attends to words that have never appeared in the prompt The head finds an earlier line that starts with the same word and copies what followed it. For soravel that line exists, so it retrieves 7. For florin no earlier line starts with that word, so every earlier answer gets similar weight: copying explains the format, a number after the arrow, but not the count. Applying a rule to a new word needs more than this one circuit.
documents.title: On Copy from context you switch Query from soravel to florin at four examples. What does the induction head do, and what does that show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · ICL & reasoning · question 3
documents.body: In Chain-of-thought scratchpad, Hops k is 6 and Per-pass budget b is 3 with Scratchpad off, and the answer is wrong. What does switching Scratchpad on change, and why? The model gets more computation per pass, so it can now chain all six lookups in a single pass The table is stored in the scratchpad, so each lookup becomes free and no extra passes are needed Extra tokens add computation by themselves, whatever they say, so any longer output would also work Pass 1 writes the node it reached, and pass 2 starts from that token and finishes the chain One pass can chain at most b lookups before it must emit a token. With the scratchpad on, pass 1 does three lookups and writes the node it reached; pass 2 reads that token from the context, does the remaining three, and answers. The extra computation comes from carrying a partial result across passes, not from the number of tokens, and padding that carries no result would leave the answer wrong.
documents.title: In Chain-of-thought scratchpad, Hops k is 6 and Per-pass budget b is 3 with Scratchpad off, and the answer is wrong. What does switching Scratchpad on change, and why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · ICL & reasoning · question 4
documents.body: With Per-pass budget b at 3, for which hop counts k does switching the scratchpad on change whether the answer is right? Every count, because a scratchpad always makes a model more accurate, whatever the task is Only counts below 3, because only a short chain is small enough for a scratchpad to store Only counts above 3: up to 3, one pass is already right, and past that only the scratchpad fixes it None, because the budget fixes what any model can compute, with or without a scratchpad at all Up to b hops one pass finishes the chain, so both settings agree and the scratchpad adds nothing. Past b, the single pass stops short and answers wrong, while the scratchpad stays right by spending ceil(k / b) passes, so the benefit comes with a cost in latency that grows with the length of the chain.
documents.title: With Per-pass budget b at 3, for which hop counts k does switching the scratchpad on change whether the answer is right?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · ICL & reasoning · question 5
documents.body: Where does the scratchpad toy stop matching a real model? The limit b is imposed as a clean integer, and the trace is faithful by construction A real model has no limit per pass, so a scratchpad can never help it on any task at all A real model's visible reasoning is always a complete and honest log of everything it computed A real model writes exactly one token for each hop of reasoning, so its cost is always k passes In the toy, b is a number the lab sets, and the next pass reads only what was written, so the written trace has to be what carries the answer. A real model's limit comes from its depth and training and is not a clean integer, and nothing forces its visible reasoning to match what it computed: it can omit the feature that drove the answer. Treat a trace as an output to check, and see faithfulness in the glossary and Reasoning models.
documents.title: Where does the scratchpad toy stop matching a real model?

documents.subtitle: Plain · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: To start, here is a small puzzle: look at these lines and decide which number belongs after the last arrow. Most people answer 6, because each number seems to be the count of letters in the word before it. Nobody told you that rule, though, so you pieced it together from three examples and then used it on a word you had never seen before. A language model, the kind of program behind a chatbot, can often do the same thing. Show it three or four examples of a made-up task and it will often do the task. Yet the settings it learned in training stay exactly the same as it reads them. This module explains how that works, and why a right answer does not always mean the model worked it out, since it may have copied the answer from your message. It also shows what changes when a model is allowed to write out its steps before it answers. Where you have met it If you have ever given a chatbot a couple of examples of the layout you wanted and watched it follow them, you have used this idea. It is the reason that a well-written prompt, the message you send to a model, can get it to do a new job without any extra training. You may also have heard of reasoning models, a newer kind of model that writes out a long chain of steps before it gives an answer. The last part of this module looks at why writing steps down can change whether an answer is right. It also explains why those written steps deserve a careful look rather than blind trust. Why it matters Without this ability to learn from examples in the prompt, every new task would need its own round of training. That would cost time, computing power and a large set of training examples for every single job. Prompting with a few examples, which is the cheapest way to point a model at something new, would not work at all. It also matters that you can tell what kind of success you are looking at. A model that repeats an answer it can already see in your message has not shown that it can handle a new case. In the same way, a tidy list of written steps does not prove that those steps are how the answer was reached. Both are tempting mistakes when you judge what a model can do, and this module shows you how to avoid them. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these ideas in your own words: How a model can pick up a task from the examples in your message by treating them as clues, while the settings it learned in training stay exactly the same. The difference between copying an answer that already sits in the message and working out a rule that also fits a word the message never mentioned. How writing progress down, in what is called a scratchpad, lets a model that does a fixed amount of work per run follow a longer chain of steps. Each step in the chain needs the one before it, and you will see how many extra runs the scratchpad costs. What the lab lets you do The lab has three cards, and each one is a small toy that was built by hand for this lesson: Prompt as context shows the puzzle above with six possible rules beside it. You add examples one at a time and watch the rules that do not fit get crossed out, while a chart shows how the possible answers are shared out. Copy from context shows a copying trick that real models use, and lets you watch it succeed on a word it has already seen. Then you can watch the same trick fail on a word it has never seen. Chain-of-thought scratchpad sets a chain of lookups that is too long to finish in one go. You can switch on a scratchpad to see when writing steps down fixes the answer, and count the extra work it takes. No real model runs anywhere in the lab, so every number you see comes from rules written for the lesson. That makes each result exact and something you can check by hand, while the section "Where it breaks" explains what real models do differently.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Three words you will need A language model reads and writes text in small pieces called tokens, which are whole words or parts of words, and it produces its reply one token at a time. What it does with those tokens is controlled by a huge collection of numbers inside it, called its weights. Those numbers were adjusted again and again while the model was trained, and once training ends they stay fixed while people use the model. The text a model can see at any moment, meaning your message plus everything earlier in the conversation, is called its context. Keep this split in mind for the whole lesson: changing the context changes what the model is reading, while changing the weights changes the model itself. Learning without changing: in-context learning Suppose you send a model a few examples of a task it was never trained on, using words it has never seen. It will often carry on the pattern correctly for the next word. Its weights are exactly the same after it answers as they were before it read your examples, because nothing in the model was adjusted at all. This is called in-context learning, since all of the "learning" lives in the context and none of it reaches the weights. This lesson's puzzle uses letter counting because you can check every answer by hand. Real models are actually weak at counting letters, because they see tokens rather than single letters, so a real chatbot may well miscount florin. On tasks they can see clearly, though, a few examples are often enough for them to pick up a pattern they were never trained on. Nothing is kept afterwards, either, because the examples in the context were the only thing that changed. If you clear the conversation and ask about florin with no examples, the model is back where it started. Three terms describe the different ways of asking a model to do a task: Giving a handful of examples, like the puzzle lines, is called few-shot prompting, where each "shot" is one example. Each example pair in the prompt, such as glim → 4, is called a demonstration. Asking with an instruction and no examples at all, such as "Count the letters in each word" followed by florin →, is called zero-shot. Models that were trained to follow instructions handle zero-shot requests far better, although models without that training can still manage some tasks. So how can a model do a task it was never trained on, without any change to its weights? During training it took in an enormous amount of text and became very good at continuing text in a way that fits what came before. Your examples narrow down what kind of text this is, so the continuation that fits best is the one that carries on the pattern. Carrying on the pattern and doing the task turn out to be the same thing. A game of guess-my-rule Picture a friend who starts a guessing game with you, without telling you the rule. "Glim gives 4, plint gives 5, soravel gives 7," they say, "so what does florin give?" You do not study, and you do not become a different person while you play. Instead you use each clue to throw out the guesses that do not fit, and then you answer with whatever rules are left. The lab plays this game out in the open, so you can watch each guess get thrown out. The game is a way to picture the examples as clues. It is not a picture of what happens inside a real model, and "Where it breaks" explains where the two stop matching. The examples are clues: task inference The Prompt as context card lists six rules that someone might mean by glim → 4. They are "count the letters", "count distinct letters", "consonants + 1", "vowels + 3", "count consonants" and "count vowels". Here "distinct" means that each different letter is counted only once, and the vowels are a, e, i, o and u. Each rule is a real calculation, so the card runs it on every example word and marks the result with a ✓ or an ✗. Watch what the first example, glim → 4, does to the list. Glim has four letters and none of them repeats, so "count the letters" and "count distinct letters" both give 4. It has three consonants and one vowel, so "consonants + 1" and "vowels + 3" also come to 4. Only "count consonants", which gives 3, and "count vowels", which gives 1, miss the answer, so those two rules are out. The next two examples keep cutting the list down, one rule each. Plint has only one vowel, so "vowels + 3" gives 4 instead of 5 and drops out. Soravel has four consonants, so "consonants + 1" gives 5 instead of 7 and drops out as well. That leaves two rules standing: "count the letters" and "count distinct letters". Treating the examples as evidence about which task you mean, and keeping only the rules that fit, is called task inference. The word inference means reaching a conclusion from evidence, which is exactly what you do in the guessing game. Not every example earns its place, though, and the fourth example, trelix → 6, crosses out nothing at all. Trelix has no repeated letters, so both of the rules that survived soravel already give 6 for it. A good example is one that rules something out. From rules to a guess about the answer The card splits 100% equally among the rules still standing, and the Weight column shows each rule's share. This is a different use of the word from the model's weights, the numbers fixed during training, which never change in this lab. With two rules left, for example, each one gets 50%. Each rule then makes its own prediction for the word you are asking about, which the lab calls the Query, and those predictions are added up into the answer bars. Here is how that plays out for florin, a word with six different letters, made of four consonants and two vowels: With no examples, all six rules are still in play and two of them predict 6, so the chance on 6 is two out of six, about 33%. After glim, four rules remain and two of them predict 6, so the chance rises to 50%. After plint, three rules remain and two of them still predict 6, which gives 67%. After soravel, only the two letter-counting rules remain and both of them predict 6, so the chance reaches 100%. The readout P(florin → 6) shows this number as it changes, where the P stands for probability, meaning the chance that something happens. By the third example, something interesting has happened: the card still cannot tell which of the two rules you mean. For florin, though, the two rules agree, so the answer is settled before the task is. When the clues run out Now switch the Query to letter, a word where "count the letters" gives 6 but "count distinct letters" gives only 4, because letter has two e's and two t's. None of the first four example words repeats a letter, so these two rules fit every one of them equally well. With three or four examples the card stays split, 50% on 6 and 50% on 4, because the evidence cannot separate the two rules. In the guessing game, this is the moment when you have two guesses left and both fit every clue so far. You cannot say which one your friend means until a clue arrives that splits them, and the lab offers two ways to provide that clue. The first is the fifth example, ballot → 6, which has two l's, so "count distinct letters" gives 5 and drops out. The other way is to switch Prompt strategy from Examples only to State a rule, which puts an instruction at the top of the prompt. The instruction says "Count the letters in each word", so it gives the whole starting share to the rule "count the letters". The table then marks the other rules as "ruled out by the instruction", unless an example has already knocked them out. In this lab, then, a single stated rule is worth several examples. Copying is not the same as working it out Models also have a much more direct way to produce an answer, which is to copy one. Inside a model, parts called attention heads look back over the earlier text and pull information from the spots that best match what they are searching for. One kind, called an induction head, searches for an earlier spot where the current token appeared and copies whatever came right after it. The Copy from context card runs a hand-built induction head over the puzzle prompt. The last token of the prompt is the arrow after the Query word, so the head looks for earlier arrows. It pays attention to whatever came right after each of those arrows, which is always an earlier answer, and that is what it copies. The head is really looking for the same pair it is sitting on, which is the Query word followed by an arrow. On a line that started with the same word as the Query, the answer comes right after a perfect match of that pair. So that answer gets a much larger share of the head's attention than any other. Watch it work on soravel with at least three examples showing, which means the line soravel → 7 is already in the prompt. The head puts more than 90% of its attention on the 7 at the end of that line and copies it, reaching the right answer without counting a single letter. Switch to florin at four examples and the trick falls apart, because no earlier line starts with florin. With nothing to match, the four earlier answers all tie, and each one's bar sits at about 24%. That is a little under a quarter, because a small amount of attention always leaks onto the other words and arrows. The head has copied the format, a number after an arrow, but nothing in it has looked at how many letters florin has. Push it one step further, and at five examples the bar for 6 climbs to 38%, which looks like progress. It happens only because two of the earlier answers, the ones for trelix and ballot, are both 6. A taller bar for the right answer can be pure luck about which answers sit in the prompt. Picture a classmate who has the practice test's answer sheet lying open on the desk and copies from it instead of solving anything. If a question on the real test matches a line on the sheet, they copy that answer instantly and look like an expert. For a new question, all they can do is hedge between the answers on the sheet, which will sometimes include the right one by luck. Here the picture stops matching. A classmate might remember a few answers after the sheet is gone, but the head keeps nothing. Clear the prompt and the trick is gone. Induction heads are real and well studied, and they make sense for the text models are trained on, which is full of patterns that are set up and then continued. Researchers have found that induction heads appear during training at about the same time as models get much better at learning from examples in the prompt. Copying explains the format and exact repeats, but applying a rule to a brand-new word needs more than this one part. Writing the steps down Each time a model writes one token, it sends the whole context through a fixed stack of processing stages, called layers, from the first to the last. One complete run like this is called a forward pass, and it ends with exactly one new token. Because the number of layers never changes, each pass can do only a fixed amount of work. Some tasks are a chain in which every step needs the result of the step before it, which is called serial computation. In a chain like this, step three cannot start until step two is finished. If one pass can link only so many of these steps, a longer chain does not fit inside it. Picture adding up a long column of numbers in your head, where you can keep a running total for the first few but lose track somewhere along the way. With a pencil, you write the running total down every few numbers and carry on from what you wrote, so the column can be as long as you like. A model can do something similar by writing its partial results as tokens before its final answer, and those in-between tokens are called a chain of thought. The text a model writes for itself before it answers is called its scratchpad. Because the scratchpad sits in the context, the next pass can read the latest partial result and carry on from it instead of starting over. In this way the chain can stretch across as many passes as it needs. Spending extra work while a model answers, rather than while it trains, is called test-time compute. Here "test time" means whenever the model is being used to answer, and compute means the amount of calculating work. Writing a chain of thought is one way to spend it, and a mathematical study published in 2024 showed why it can matter so much. Under some widely used assumptions, a model with a fixed number of layers can solve some step-by-step problems only when it is allowed to write out its steps. The lab's arrow puzzle The Chain-of-thought scratchpad card turns this into a puzzle you can watch, using a table of ten arrows in its prompt. Each arrow, such as C → H or H → A, points from one letter to exactly one other letter. The task is to start at C and follow the arrows a set number of times. Following one arrow is called a hop, and the number of hops is the lab's Hops k. Starting from C, the path through the table runs like this: Each hop is the same find-and-copy step that the induction head performs: find the current letter in the table and copy the letter its arrow points to. You cannot jump ahead, because you only learn the next letter once you have found the current one. To make the limit visible, the lab adds a rule called the Per-pass budget b: one pass can follow at most b arrows before it must write a token. That limit is a rule invented for the lesson, not something measured from a real model. Here is the walk-through the card is built around, with Hops k set to 6 and Per-pass budget b set to 3. If you count six steps along the path above, you land on G, which is the correct answer. With Scratchpad off, the model gets a single pass, which follows C → H → A → J and uses up its budget. It has to write something at that point, so it answers J, which is wrong. With Scratchpad on, pass 1 follows the same three arrows to J, but this time it writes J as a scratch note instead of an answer. Pass 2 reads that J back from the context, follows J → E → B → G, and answers G, which is right. The lookups inside a pass are silent, which means they are never written down. In the lab, the next pass reads only what was written, so the written J is the only thing that carries the progress forward. The letter says where the chain has reached, and the fact that one scratch note is already there tells pass 2 that three hops are done and three are left. You might think any extra tokens would help, since each one gives the model another pass. But filler, such as a row of dots, carries no partial result, so the next pass has nothing to carry on from and the chain does not move forward. What the scratchpad costs The fix is not free, because every pass writes one token and each pass takes its own time to run. The number of passes the scratchpad needs is k divided by b, rounded up to the next whole number. For example, with k at 7 and b at 3, the division gives two and a third. Rounding up makes that three passes, because the last hop still needs a pass of its own. The card's info panel writes the same rule as ceil(k / b), where ceil is short for ceiling and means round up. At the other extreme, with b at 1, every hop needs its own pass, so a chain of eight hops takes eight passes. The pencil-and-paper picture is a good guide to why writing helps, but it stops matching in a couple of places, which "Where it breaks" sets out.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: A new job without new training Changing a model's weights to teach it a task is called fine-tuning, and it means running another round of training with its own examples, time and computing power. If four example lines in the prompt get you the behavior you want, a training run is an expensive way to buy it. That is why "we should fine-tune a model for this" is usually the wrong first instinct. Picture a small team that wants a model to rewrite messy dates into one neat format. One person starts planning a training run, while another pastes four before-and-after examples into the prompt and tries that first. If the examples work, the team has spent a few lines of text rather than a training run. They can also change the format in seconds whenever they change their minds about how the dates should look. Telling copying from working it out You saw that soravel can be answered by copying while florin cannot, and this matters whenever people test a model. A test that shares words with the examples in the prompt will make a model look better than it is, because some of its right answers were copied. A fair test always includes cases the prompt has never shown, like florin rather than soravel. Chains that are too long for one pass A model does a fixed amount of work in each pass, so a chain of dependent steps that is longer than that amount cannot be finished in one go. In the lab, a pass that runs out of budget answers with wherever it got to, and that answer is wrong. Writing partial results down gets around this, which means a chain of thought can change what a model gets right, not only how it explains itself. Steps that look like working The written steps raise a sharper question, because they are text produced in the same way as everything else the model writes, one token at a time. They look like the model showing its working, but how closely they match what really produced the answer has to be checked with evidence, not taken on trust.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Work through the cards from top to bottom, and make a prediction before each change so you can test it. Try this: On Prompt as context, set Examples to 0 with the Query on florin, and read the answer bars. Several answers are still possible at this point, and P(florin → 6) reads only 33%. Now raise Examples one step at a time and watch the table, where each rule that misses says where it went out, such as "out at glim". By the third example, the chance on 6 has climbed all the way to 100%. Set Query to letter and Examples to 4, then read the small badge next to the card's heading, which now says "2 of 6 rules fit". The bars split evenly between the answers 6 and 4, because the two remaining rules disagree. Add the fifth example, ballot, and watch "count distinct letters" drop out of the table for good. Then go back to four examples and switch Prompt strategy to State a rule, which settles the question without the fifth example. Switch Prompt strategy back to Examples only. Then, on Copy from context, keep Examples at 3 or more and set Query to soravel. Read the heading, the shading and percentages under the tokens, and the bars for the "Induction head's predicted next token". Then switch to florin and compare, first at four examples and then at five. On Chain-of-thought scratchpad, set Hops k to 6 and Per-pass budget b to 3 with Scratchpad off. Read Answer, Correct answer and the badge, which should say "answer wrong" because the single pass stopped short. Then switch Scratchpad to on and compare Answer, Passes (one token each) and the scratch line in the context box. Also look at the table of passes beside the context box, where each row is one pass. Its Silent lookups column shows the arrows that pass followed without writing them down. Look at the table of hop counts at the bottom of the card, and compare its No scratchpad and Scratchpad columns while b is 3. Then raise Per-pass budget b one step at a time, and watch the first ✗ in the No scratchpad column move further down the table. The Examples, Prompt strategy and Query controls live on the first card, but they also change the Copy from context card, because both cards read the same prompt. As a reminder, the Weight column shows each rule's share of the 100%, while the Weights changed readout is about the model's own weights, the numbers set during training.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Weights changed always reads 0, because only the prompt ever changes. The confused spread of answers at zero examples and the certain answer at three examples both came from the same fixed calculation. A good example is one that rules something out, and trelix shows the opposite: it adds a column to the table but removes nothing new. An answer can be settled before the task is. For florin, the answer 6 is certain while the card still cannot tell which of the two remaining rules you mean. Copying reproduces the format, a number after an arrow, without working anything out about a new word. A taller bar for the right answer can be a coincidence of which answers happen to be in the prompt. With Scratchpad off, the answer is right exactly when k is at most b. At b = 3, chains of one to three hops are right, while every chain from four to eight hops fails. With Scratchpad on, every chain is right, and the price is paid in passes. At b = 3, chains of up to three hops take one pass, chains of four to six take two, and chains of seven or eight take three. Once b reaches k, both settings answer in one pass, so writing steps down pays off only past the limit of a single pass. The silent lookups in each row of the passes table never reach the next pass, because only the token a pass writes does. That is why a partial result has to be written down before the next pass can build on it.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies On Prompt as context, the six rules, the examples and the Query words were all written for the lesson. The examples never contain a mistake, and every rule starts with an equal share unless you state a rule, which gives it all to one rule. A real model faces a vast range of possible tasks, and which ones it leans toward before seeing any examples comes from its training. Crossing out rules is a clean way to picture a prompt as evidence, but it is not how a real model calculates on the inside. On Copy from context, there is a single induction head whose settings were chosen by hand, and it works on whole words. Nothing was trained, and no tokenizer, the tool a real model uses to chop text into tokens, runs at all. On Chain-of-thought scratchpad, the budget b is a number the lab sets, not something measured from a model. The table, the task and every step are exact, so no pass ever makes a mistake, and no model runs. When a pass runs out of budget, the lab has it answer with wherever it got to, which is the toy's own choice rather than measured behavior. In the lab, the written steps are always honest, because the lab is built so that each pass can read only what was written. The letters on the scratchpad really are what carries the answer, while a real model's written reasoning makes no such promise. Where the two pictures stop matching The guess-my-rule game gives the model too much credit in one way. A person playing it knows they are in a game and remembers the rule afterwards, while a model has no awareness of a task at all. It produces a very good continuation of a pattern, and it keeps nothing once the conversation is cleared. The pencil-and-paper picture also needs a warning, because your limit comes from memory and tiredness, while a model's limit per pass is built into its layers. Your written totals can be wrong, too, and so can a real model's written steps, even though the lab's never are. Where real in-context learning goes wrong Real in-context learning is fussier than the lab suggests, because details that should not matter can still move its accuracy by several percentage points. These include the order of the examples, their formatting, the wording of their answers, and even extra spaces or line breaks. A change of several points means several more or fewer right answers out of every hundred questions, and the effect is called prompt sensitivity. Picture a student whose quiz score changes when the same questions are printed in a different order. The questions did not get harder, yet the result moved, and a model can behave the same way with its examples. Researchers have also found that the layout of the demonstrations, and the set of possible answers they show, can matter more than whether each example's answer is correct. Picture a prompt that labels movie reviews as "happy" or "sad", where some of the labels have been swapped to the wrong one. A model often still does nearly as well, as long as the examples keep the same layout and use the same two labels. The examples seem to tell the model what kind of answer to give more than which answer is right. That sits awkwardly with the neat story that a model learns the rule from its examples, the way the lab's first card does. Piling more text into a prompt has limits too, starting with the context window, which is the most text a model can look at in one go. It is measured in tokens, and it is working space rather than lasting memory. Models can get worse at using information buried in the middle of a long context, and adding more examples eventually stops helping. Where real chains of thought go wrong A real model's limit per pass comes from its depth, meaning its number of layers, and from its training. It is not a clean number like b, and it differs from one task to another. Written steps can be wrong, and one mistake spoils every step that follows. In the arrow puzzle, a wrong letter on the scratchpad would send each later pass down the wrong path. You cannot try this on the card, but a test in the lab's code changes one scratch letter and shows that the final answer changes with it. Studies comparing many tasks found that writing steps down helps most on math and symbol puzzles, and much less on other kinds of task. Every written token costs time, so a long chain of thought makes the answer slower to arrive. A common mix-up: the reasoning a model writes out is not a record of how it got its answer. A model can be swayed by some detail in the prompt and then write a tidy explanation that never mentions that detail. Picture a student who copies an answer from a friend and then writes neat working that leads to it. The working looks convincing, but it is not how the answer was reached. The steps do not have to be deliberately misleading for this to happen. They can simply leave out what actually drove the answer. Whether a written trace matches what produced the answer is called faithfulness, and nothing guarantees it in a real model. Treat the trace as another output to check, not as an explanation to trust.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Other ways to spend time on an answer Writing steps down is one way to spend test-time compute, and there are others that spread the work across several attempts instead of along one chain: Ask the model the same question several times and take a vote on the most common answer. Produce several different answers and let a separate checker pick the best one. This works very well when the checker can tell for certain whether an answer is right, such as running a piece of code to see whether it works. The Reasoning models module works out what each of these costs, including the cases where voting makes things worse. A different idea works during training rather than while the model answers. It rewards each correct step rather than only the final answer, which is called process supervision. Models trained to write long chains Recent reasoning models were trained with reinforcement learning, a kind of training that rewards good behavior. Here the model was rewarded when its final answer could be checked and turned out to be right. As a result, writing long chains of steps became learned behavior rather than something a prompt has to ask for. The Reasoning models module looks at these models, and the Interpretability II: circuits module switches off an induction head and measures what breaks. Interpretability II also uses the word faithfulness, but there it means something different: whether a small group of the model's parts can reproduce a behavior on their own. Three ways to change what a model does Keep these three apart, because they sound alike but do very different things: In-context learning: you put examples in the context. The model's temporary numbers, called activations, change as it reads them, but its weights do not, so nothing about it is permanent. Fine-tuning: this changes the weights themselves, so the change stays with the model after the conversation ends. Retrieval: a search tool finds documents and adds them to the context for you. Like in-context learning, it changes only what the model reads, but it brings in facts rather than examples of a task. Only fine-tuning lasts, and only retrieval gives you a source you can go and check. Where the facts come from The link between induction heads and learning from examples comes from Olsson and colleagues, 2022. The proof about fixed layers and written steps comes from Li and colleagues, 2024. The finding that the layout of demonstrations can matter more than correct answers comes from Min and colleagues, 2022. The comparison showing that chains of thought help most on math and symbol problems comes from Sprague and colleagues, 2024.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: This module is about what a model can do at answer time with its weights frozen. In-context learning adapts to a task from examples in the prompt, with no gradient step. Chain of thought writes intermediate results as tokens so that later forward passes can build on them. Both answer one question: how much can a fixed network get out of its context, and where does that stop? Post-training adapted a model by changing its weights; here every adaptation comes from the text the model reads. The copying mechanism builds on Attention: an induction head is an attention head that finds an earlier copy of the current token and predicts what followed it. Where it shows up Few-shot prompting. Worked examples in the prompt, called demonstrations, make the intended task identifiable, even one the model was never trained on. Induction heads. Trained transformers develop this copying circuit, and its appearance during training coincides with a jump in few-shot ability (Olsson et al., 2022). Reasoning models. Their long traces are trained behavior, not only something a prompt asks for. Test-time compute. This is compute spent while answering rather than while training. A scratchpad spends it as extra passes; sampling and voting spend it across attempts, and the Reasoning models module prices them. Why it matters A fixed network adapts only through its context, and three different things can go wrong there: Examples can underdetermine the task. If every example fits two rules, the prompt does not say which answer is meant where they disagree. Only an example that separates them, or a stated rule, settles it. Copying can pass for inference. Copying reproduces the format and exact lookups, but on a new input it can only offer the old answers, so a well-formatted answer is no evidence of a rule. Some chains do not fit in one pass. A network does a fixed amount of work per forward pass. In serial computation, where each step needs the one before, a chain longer than one pass can follow fails unless partial results are written down, at a cost in passes. What you will be able to explain In-context learning as inference from the prompt, with no weight update. How copying an answer from context differs from inferring a rule from it, and why copying cannot compute the answer for a new word. How a scratchpad lets a fixed per-pass computation follow a longer chain of dependent steps, and what that costs in passes. What the lab shows Nothing here is measured from a trained model: the examples, rules, and lookup table are authored, the induction head is set by hand, and every readout is computed in closed form, with no sampling or noise. Prompt as context builds the prompt from Examples (0 to 5), Prompt strategy (Examples only, or State a rule, which adds an instruction line), and Query (florin, letter, soravel). It checks six rules, each a real function of the word, against the shown examples with noise-free matching. The prior is uniform over the six, or all on "count the letters" when the rule is stated. Rules that miss an example drop out, and Weights changed always reads 0. Copy from context runs the head over the same prompt, split into whole words with no tokenizer. It shades each token by its attention from the final arrow and shows the predicted next token, so soravel, which is in the prompt from three examples on, can be compared with the new word florin. Chain-of-thought scratchpad follows a fixed ten-node lookup table. Hops k sets the chain length, Per-pass budget b caps lookups per pass, a limit the lab imposes rather than measures, and Scratchpad decides whether a pass writes the node it reached for the next pass to start from. The key experiment is k = 6 at b = 3: read the answer with Scratchpad off, switch it on, and count the passes.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Show a model a few examples of a task it was never trained on, and it will often perform the task. No parameter changes and no gradient step: the weights are identical before and after. That is in-context learning, here by few-shot prompting; with instructions and no examples it is zero-shot. Nothing persists. Close the context and the ability is gone. The examples narrowed the model's distribution over "what kind of text is this", and the continuation most consistent with them performs the task. Examples as evidence Prompt as context makes that narrowing explicit with six candidate rules, each a real function of the word. A rule that gets any shown example wrong drops out. This is task inference in its simplest, noise-free form. For florin, the chance on 6 goes 33%, 50%, 67%, then 100% as the first three examples arrive. For letter it stops at 50% on 6 and 50% on 4: no example word repeats a letter, so "count the letters" and "count distinct letters" fit equally well. ballot → 6 settles it. So does stating the rule, which here is worth several examples. Copying is not the same as inferring Pretraining text is full of patterns that are set up and then continued. Induction heads exploit that: they find an earlier copy of the current token and predict whatever followed it. Their appearance during training coincides with a jump in few-shot ability (Olsson et al., 2022). Copy from context runs a hand-set version over the prompt's word tokens. For a word already in the prompt, such as soravel, it retrieves 7 with over 90% weight. For the new word florin it gives each earlier answer 24%. Copying explains the format and exact lookups; applying a rule to a new input needs more. Spending compute at answer time A network does a fixed amount of work per forward pass, and each pass emits one token. A task whose steps depend on one another, such as following a chain of lookups, is serial computation: step three cannot start until step two is done. If one pass can chain only so many steps, a longer chain does not fit. A chain of thought gets around that by writing intermediate results as tokens. The next pass reads that scratchpad from its context and continues from it, so the chain runs across passes. Theory results (Li et al., 2024) show that, under standard assumptions, this separates what a fixed-depth transformer can compute with and without chain of thought. It is one way to spend test-time compute. Chain-of-thought scratchpad makes it concrete. A table of ten arrows sits in the prompt, and the task is to start at C and follow the table k times. Each hop is the find-and-copy step from the previous card, and each needs the hop before it. The lab imposes a per-pass budget b: one pass chains at most b hops. With k = 6 and b = 3 and the scratchpad off, one pass chains three hops and answers J. The correct answer is G. With it on, pass 1 writes J, pass 2 starts from that token, finishes the chain, and answers G, at a cost of two passes. Sampling several answers and voting spends compute across attempts instead; Reasoning models prices that.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: In-context learning is why prompting works at all, and why "just fine-tune it" is usually the wrong first answer. A behavior you can get from four example lines is not worth a training run. The reasoning trace matters for a different reason. It looks like the model showing its work, but it is text produced by the same next-token process as everything else. How far it reflects the computation behind the answer needs evidence, not trust.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Set Examples to 0 and read the answer bars for florin. Add examples one at a time and watch rules drop out of the table. Set Query to letter. At four examples two rules still fit and disagree. Add the fifth example, or set Prompt strategy to State a rule. On Copy from context, compare soravel with florin at four examples. On Chain-of-thought scratchpad, set Hops k to 6 and Per-pass budget b to 3 with Scratchpad off. Switch it on, then raise Per-pass budget b to 6. Read the table under the passes at b = 3. Raise b and watch the first failing row move down.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Weights changed always reads 0. The same fixed function produced the confused zero-example distribution and the certain three-example one. An answer can be settled before the task is. For florin both surviving rules agree, so 6 is certain even though the rule is not. With Scratchpad off, the answer is right exactly when k is at most b. At b = 3 that is k up to 3; k = 4 through 8 all fail. With it on, every k is right, at ceil(k ÷ b) passes. At b = 3 that is 2 passes for k = 4 to 6 and 3 for k = 7 and 8; at b = 1, k = 8 takes 8. Once b reaches k, both settings answer in one pass. The scratchpad earns its cost only past the one-pass limit. The silent lookups never enter the context; only the token a pass writes does. A partial result has to be written to be reused.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: In this lab. The six rules, the examples, and the queries are authored, and the rule weights use a uniform prior with noise-free matching. The induction head is set by hand over whole words; no model or tokenizer runs. The scratchpad card's per-pass limit b is imposed: it is a number the lab sets, not measured from a model. The table and every step are exact, so no step is ever wrong, and the trace is faithful by construction because each pass reads only what was written. In real systems. In-context learning shows prompt sensitivity: details that should not matter, such as example order, formatting, label wording, and even whitespace, can move accuracy by several points. Min et al. (2022) found that the format and label space of demonstrations can matter more than whether their labels are correct, which sits awkwardly with the story that the model learns the mapping from them. A long context window is not free capability. Retrieval accuracy can degrade for information in the middle of a long context, and adding examples eventually plateaus. A real model's per-pass limit comes from its depth and training. It is not a clean integer, and it differs by task. Written steps can also be wrong, and errors compound over a long trace. Published comparisons find that chain of thought helps most on math and symbolic problems and much less elsewhere (Sprague et al., 2024). Every written token costs latency. The largest caution is faithfulness. A chain of thought is not a log of the computation. Models can be swayed by a feature of the prompt and write a trace that never mentions it. Treat the trace as an output to verify, not an explanation to trust.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Sampling, voting, and verifiers spend test-time compute across several attempts rather than along one chain. Reasoning models prices them, including where voting makes things worse. Process supervision rewards each correct step rather than only the final answer. Recent reasoning models were trained with reinforcement learning against checkable answers, so long traces became learned behavior rather than something a prompt requests. Reasoning models covers that; Interpretability II: circuits switches off an induction head and measures what breaks. Keep three things apart. In-context learning changes activations only. Fine-tuning changes weights. Retrieval changes the context by fetching documents. Only the second persists, and only the third grounds an answer in a source you can check.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Prompt as context · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Examples as evidence about the task The literal prompt on the left is all a model gets. On the right, six candidate rules are each run on every example word. A rule that gets any example wrong drops out; the survivors share the weight equally, and their answers for the query become an answer distribution. No weights change anywhere. The prompt text: an optional instruction line, the shown examples, and the query line ending in ?. Examples (0–5), Prompt strategy (Examples only or State a rule), and Query (florin, letter, soravel). A rule table. Each cell is the rule's output for that example word, with ✓ or ✗. The first ✗ is bold. The next column is what the rule would answer for the query, and Weight is its share, or where it dropped out. Answer bars for the query; the letter count is highlighted. Metrics: P(query → its letter count), rules still fitting, and weights changed, which is always 0. The rules are real functions: count the letters, count distinct letters, consonants + 1, vowels + 3, count consonants, count vowels (a, e, i, o, u). Posterior = prior × likelihood, normalized. The prior is uniform over six rules, or all on "count the letters" when the rule is stated. The likelihood is 1 if a rule reproduces every shown example and 0 otherwise. The example answers are the true letter counts: glim 4, plint 5, soravel 7, trelix 6, ballot 6. Examples adds rows to the prompt in order. Prompt strategy adds or removes the instruction line. Query changes the word being asked about. Comparison worth running: florin at 0, 1, 2, and 3 examples gives 33%, 50%, 67%, then 100% on 6. Then Query letter: at 3 or 4 examples it stays 50% on 6 and 50% on 4, because no example word repeats a letter. Ballot, the fifth, settles it. More examples help only when they rule something out. Trelix removes nothing that soravel had not already removed. An answer can be settled before the task is. For florin both surviving rules agree on 6, so the answer is certain while the rule is not. In this lab: six hand-written rules, noise-free examples, and a uniform prior. A real model's space of possible tasks is vast and its prior comes from pretraining. In general: the Bayesian reading of in-context learning is one useful model, not a description of the circuits. Real accuracy also moves with example order, formatting, and label wording.
documents.title: Examples as evidence about the task

documents.subtitle: Copy from context · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: A hand-set induction head over the prompt tokens The last token of the prompt is the arrow. The head attends to tokens that came right after an earlier arrow, prefers the one whose line started with the same word, and copies what it finds. For a word already in the prompt that retrieves the answer; for a new word it can only offer every earlier answer. The prompt split into word tokens, with ⏎ for line breaks. Shading and the percentage under each token are the attention weight from the final arrow, marked now. Bars for the head's predicted next token, highlighting the query's letter count. The heading states whether the query appeared earlier in the prompt. Score for position i: 1 if the token before it equals the current token (→), plus 1 more if the token two back equals the query word. All other positions score 0. Weights are softmax(4 · score) over every earlier position, and the prediction is the attention-weighted vote for the token at each position. With four examples and the new word florin, each earlier answer gets 24%. With soravel and at least three examples, 7 gets over 90%. Query, Examples, and Prompt strategy on Prompt as context. Comparison worth running: soravel, then florin, at four examples. Then florin at five examples, where 6 rises to 38% only because two earlier answers happen to be 6. Copying reproduces the format, a number after the arrow, without computing anything about the new word. A higher bar for the right answer can be a coincidence of which answers appear in the prompt. In this lab: the head's weights are set by hand and there is one head over whole words. Nothing is trained and no real tokenizer runs. In general: induction heads are a real, well-studied mechanism for copying from context, and their emergence in training coincides with a jump in in-context learning. Inferring a new rule relies on more than this one circuit.
documents.title: A hand-set induction head over the prompt tokens

documents.subtitle: Chain-of-thought scratchpad · ICL & reasoning
documents.body: Serial steps that do not fit in one pass The task is to follow a lookup table k times from a start node, where each lookup needs the one before it. In this toy one forward pass can chain at most b lookups, a limit the lab imposes. With the scratchpad off the pass answers with where it got to; with it on, each pass writes the node it reached and the next pass starts from that written token. Hops k (1–8), Per-pass budget b (1–8), and Scratchpad (off or on). The context the model reads: the table and the task, then the tokens written so far. The scratch line holds what the early passes wrote; the answer line is the last token. One row per forward pass: where it starts (the prompt, or a token read back from the scratchpad), its silent lookups, which are never written down, and the one token it writes, marked scratch or answer. Answer, Correct answer from the table, and Passes. Each pass writes exactly one token, so passes and tokens written are the same count. A table of every hop count at the current b: the correct node, the no-scratchpad answer with ✓ or ✗, and the scratchpad answer with its pass count. The table is one cycle through ten nodes, C → H → A → J → E → B → G → D → I → F → C, and every task starts at C. A cycle of ten means a wrong answer is never right by coincidence for k up to 8. A pass starts from C if nothing is written yet, or from the last written token when the scratchpad is on. It counts the tokens written so far, each worth b hops, to know how many lookups remain, chains the smaller of b and what remains, and writes the node it reached. With the scratchpad off there is one pass: it chains the smaller of b and k and answers with the node it reached. That rule is this toy's choice for a pass that runs out of budget, not a measured behavior. With it on, a pass answers when its lookups finish the chain and otherwise writes a scratch token, so passes needed = ceil(k / b). Resuming reads only the written text. A unit test changes one scratch token and confirms the final answer changes with it. Hops k, Per-pass budget b, and Scratchpad. Comparison worth running: k 6 and b 3. Off, the answer is J and wrong, since G is correct. On, pass 1 writes J, pass 2 starts from J and answers G, in 2 passes. Then raise b to 6. Both settings are right in one pass, so the scratchpad adds nothing. The silent lookups are never written. Only the token a pass writes reaches the next one, which is why a partial result has to be written down to be reused. The scratchpad helps exactly where the chain stops fitting in one pass, and its price is passes: ceil(k / b). At b 3, k 4 to 6 takes 2 passes and k 7 and 8 take 3; at b 1, k 8 takes 8. Without a scratchpad the answer is right only while k is at most b. Raising b moves the first failing row of the table down. In this lab: the per-pass limit b is imposed. It is a number the lab sets, not something measured from a model. The table, the task, and every step are exact and deterministic, no pass ever makes an error, and no model runs. In this lab: the trace is faithful by construction, because each pass reads only what was written. A real model's visible reasoning carries no such guarantee. In general: a real transformer's limit per pass comes from its depth and training and is not a clean integer. Theory shows that, under standard assumptions, fixed-depth transformers cannot solve some inherently serial problems in one pass but can with enough chain-of-thought steps (Li et al., 2024). In general: real traces can contain wrong steps that accumulate, can fail to match what the model computed, and cost latency and tokens. Reasoning models covers sampling, voting, and traces that are trained rather than prompted.
documents.title: Serial steps that do not fit in one pass
