documents.body: Learn how generation moves from a parallel prefill to one-token-at-a-time decoding, what caching keys and values saves, and what it costs in memory on a real model. Separate prefill from decode Explain the KV cache memory-speed trade-off Predict how draft length and draft quality set the tokens one verification pass yields in speculative decoding
documents.title: Inference & KV cache

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Set Generated tokens to 0 and change Prompt tokens: the whole lower triangle is computed in one pass, because every prompt position is available at once.
documents.title: Prefill the prompt

documents.subtitle: Step 2 · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Raise Generated tokens one at a time. With Use cache, only the newest row lights up and New Q, K, V stays at 1.
documents.title: Decode one token

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Keep KV cache on Use cache and follow the K and V rows under the triangle: each step writes one slot and only reads the earlier ones.
documents.title: Store keys and values

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Switch KV cache to Recompute and compare Q·K this pass and Q·K whole run, then read Prefill versus decode for the same choice at 8,192 tokens.
documents.title: Compare recomputation

documents.subtitle: Step 5 · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Under Speculative decoding, set Draft quality to 1.00 and read Closed form, tokens per pass, then lower Draft quality, raise Draft length, and compare Simulated, tokens per pass with the closed form and find a pass where the target refused a proposal.
documents.title: Speculate and verify

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: The forward pass that processes every prompt token in parallel and fills the cache. For prompts longer than a few hundred tokens it is compute bound, and its attention cost grows with the square of prompt length.
documents.title: Prefill

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: The phase producing one token per forward pass. At small batch sizes it is limited by memory bandwidth, because every weight and every cached key and value is read to produce one new position per sequence.
documents.title: Decode

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Stored attention keys and values for every earlier position, in every layer and key/value head. The causal mask means later tokens never change them, so they are written once and then only read.
documents.title: KV cache

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Several query heads sharing one key/value head. Llama 3 8B has 32 query heads and 8 key/value heads, which makes its cache four times smaller than one key/value head per query head.
documents.title: Grouped-query attention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Latency before the first output token appears. It is dominated by prefill, and the cache does not shorten it unless the same prompt prefix was already cached.
documents.title: Time to first token

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: The delay between successive output tokens during decode. It sets the perceived streaming speed and is governed mostly by memory bandwidth.
documents.title: Inter-token latency

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Limited by how fast weights and cache entries can be read from memory rather than by arithmetic throughput. This is the normal state of decode.
documents.title: Memory bandwidth bound

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Limited by the hardware's arithmetic units. Long prefills are compute bound because many positions share one read of the weights.
documents.title: Compute bound

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Operations performed per byte of memory traffic. Below the hardware's ridge point, about 295 FLOP per byte for an H100 in bf16, a kernel waits on memory.
documents.title: Arithmetic intensity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: An estimate of a kernel's time as the larger of its FLOPs divided by peak FLOP/s and its bytes divided by peak bandwidth. It gives a lower bound, not a measurement.
documents.title: Roofline model

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Serving many sequences in one pass so a single read of the weights does more work. It raises throughput until cache memory runs out, but each sequence still reads its own cache.
documents.title: Batching

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Admitting and retiring individual sequences at each decode step instead of processing fixed batches, which raises utilization under real traffic.
documents.title: Continuous batching

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Managing the cache in fixed-size blocks with a per-sequence block table, which nearly eliminates fragmentation and lets requests share blocks.
documents.title: PagedAttention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: A small draft model proposes gamma tokens that the large model checks in one pass. A proposal is kept with probability min(1, p over q); the first refused one is replaced by a sample from the leftover difference of the two distributions, so the output distribution is exactly the large model's. With acceptance rate alpha, a pass yields (1 − alpha^(gamma+1)) ÷ (1 − alpha) tokens on average.
documents.title: Speculative decoding

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Reusing cached blocks for a shared prompt prefix across requests, so a long repeated system prompt is prefilled once instead of on every request.
documents.title: Prefix caching

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Storing weights or cache entries at reduced precision. It saves proportional memory and can measurably change output, making it a quality trade rather than free.
documents.title: Quantization

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Inference & KV cache · question 1
documents.body: With Generated tokens at 0 the whole lower triangle is computed in one pass, but each later step lights one row. Why can prefill do the whole prompt at once? Prefill drops the causal mask, so each prompt position can read the whole prompt at once Every prompt token is already known, so all positions can go through each layer together The cache already holds the prompt's results, so prefill only looks them up Prefill and decode use the same model and the same causal mask. The difference is availability: all prompt tokens exist up front, so each layer does one large matrix multiply over every position, while a decode step must wait for the token the previous step produced. The cache is filled by prefill, not used to skip it.
documents.title: With Generated tokens at 0 the whole lower triangle is computed in one pass, but each later step lights one row. Why can prefill do the whole prompt at once?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Inference & KV cache · question 2
documents.body: A user sends a very long prompt. Does turning the KV cache on shorten the wait for the first token? Yes, because the cache stores the whole prompt's results, so the first token needs almost no computation Yes, because cached keys let prefill process the prompt one token at a time instead of all at once No: prefill still processes every prompt token, and the cache saves work only on the later decode steps Time to first token is dominated by prefill, which has to compute every prompt position's keys and values and fill the cache. Its attention cost also grows with the square of prompt length. The cache pays off afterwards: each decode step reads stored keys and values instead of recomputing the prefix.
documents.title: A user sends a very long prompt. Does turning the KV cache on shorten the wait for the first token?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Inference & KV cache · question 3
documents.body: With the KV cache on, what does each decode step still have to read from memory? Every model weight plus every stored key and value for that sequence Nothing but the newest token, because everything else is cached Only the keys and values, because the weights stay in the arithmetic units The cache removes recomputation of past keys and values, not memory traffic. Each step multiplies the new position through every weight matrix and attends over every cached entry, so it reads both. That is why decode is bandwidth bound and why batching helps: one weight read serves many sequences.
documents.title: With the KV cache on, what does each decode step still have to read from memory?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Inference & KV cache · question 4
documents.body: You switch KV cache from Use cache to Recompute during a decode step. What changes in the work for that step? The attention output changes, because recomputed keys differ slightly from the ones that were stored in the cache Nothing changes in the work, because the causal mask already limits every step to a single row of scores Every earlier key and value is projected and scored again, so the pass grows from one row to the full triangle Keys and values depend only on earlier tokens, so recomputing them gives exactly the numbers the cache would have stored and the output is identical. What changes is cost: each step reruns the whole prefix, so per-token work grows with the square of length, which Q·K this pass and Q·K whole run both show.
documents.title: You switch KV cache from Use cache to Recompute during a decode step. What changes in the work for that step?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Inference & KV cache · question 5
documents.body: On Memory budget you double Concurrent sequences. What happens to KV per token and to the KV cache total? KV per token doubles and the total quadruples, because sequences also store each other's keys KV per token stays the same and the total doubles, since each sequence keeps its own cache of keys and values KV per token stays the same and the total stays the same, because the cache is shared across sequences Bytes per token depend only on the model's shape: 2 times layers times key/value heads times head dimension times bytes per value. Each sequence keeps a private cache of its own tokens, so the total scales with sequences times context. Sequences that fit is unchanged, and it is the limit batching runs into.
documents.title: On Memory budget you double Concurrent sequences. What happens to KV per token and to the KV cache total?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Inference & KV cache · question 6
documents.body: In Prefill versus decode you raise Concurrent sequences. Why does total decode throughput rise while each sequence's own tokens per second fall? One read of the weights serves every sequence, but each sequence still reads its own cache Larger batches make the arithmetic units faster, so every sequence's step finishes sooner The sequences share one cache, so each step reads less memory per sequence as the batch grows Decode is memory-bound: the step time is set by bytes read. Weights are read once however many sequences run, so tokens per second in total rise. But every sequence adds its own cache to the bytes, so the step takes longer and each sequence's rate falls. Cache memory is what finally caps the batch.
documents.title: In Prefill versus decode you raise Concurrent sequences. Why does total decode throughput rise while each sequence's own tokens per second fall?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Inference & KV cache · question 7
documents.body: On Speculative decoding you set Draft quality to 1.00 and Draft length to 4. How many tokens does each target pass yield? Five, because all four proposals are kept and the target adds one more token of its own Four, because once every proposal is kept the target has nothing left to add to the text One, because the target must still generate each token itself before any is shown to a reader Two, because a perfect draft is still checked one proposal at a time and kept in pairs At quality 1.00 the draft is the target's own distribution, so every proposal passes the accept test. A pass that keeps all four proposals still ends with the token the target samples at the position after them, so it yields draft length plus one. That is the ceiling: a pass can never yield more.
documents.title: On Speculative decoding you set Draft quality to 1.00 and Draft length to 4. How many tokens does each target pass yield?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Inference & KV cache · question 8
documents.body: At a middling Draft quality, raising Draft length from 1 to 4 adds far more tokens per pass than raising it from 5 to 8. Why? A later proposal counts only if every earlier one was kept, so each extra token is reached less often The target model verifies long drafts more slowly, so every pass with more proposals costs more time to run The draft gets worse the further it writes, so every proposal after the fourth one is refused outright The simulation runs out of passes at long drafts, so the extra tokens are simply lost in sampling noise The expected tokens per pass are 1 plus the chance that the first proposal is kept, plus the chance that the first two are, and so on. Each term is smaller than the last by roughly a factor of the acceptance rate, so the curve flattens toward 1 ÷ (1 − α). The lab counts passes, not time, and every point is a full run.
documents.title: At a middling Draft quality, raising Draft length from 1 to 4 adds far more tokens per pass than raising it from 5 to 8. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Inference & KV cache · question 9
documents.body: Speculative decoding keeps some tokens that a weak draft proposed. How does the text it writes compare with the target model's own? The same distribution, because a refused proposal is replaced from the leftover target probability It is a little worse, because the draft's mistakes sometimes get through the accept test unchanged It is a little better, because two models now effectively vote on every token that is written It matches only at Draft quality 1.00, because any other draft changes what gets written to the text The accept test and the replacement sample are built so that each written token is distributed exactly as the target alone would have written it, whatever the draft. A weaker draft is refused more often and so yields fewer tokens per pass, but the text's distribution does not move. The lab checks this by counting character pairs in a long simulated text.
documents.title: Speculative decoding keeps some tokens that a weak draft proposed. How does the text it writes compare with the target model's own?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: When you send a message to a chatbot, there is usually a short pause before the reply appears a few words at a time, as if someone were typing. This module is about what happens during that pause and that typing. It shows how a trained model reads your message and writes its answer, and how the whole process is kept fast and cheap enough to be useful. The work happens in two stages: first the model reads your entire message in one go, and then it writes the answer one small piece at a time. Every one of those pieces needs another full trip through the model. The pause before the first word comes mostly from the reading, while the speed of the text streaming in afterward comes from the writing. Writing one piece at a time hides a trap. Each new piece looks back at every piece before it, so without a shortcut the model would redo the whole conversation's work every time it added one piece. Long answers would then slow to a crawl. The shortcut is to save some numbers for every earlier piece and reuse them, a store called the KV cache. It saves a huge amount of time but costs memory, and on a real model serving many people, the saved numbers can take more room than the model itself. You have met the effects of these two stages and the cache even if you have never seen the names. The reading stage is the reason a very long document makes a chatbot pause before its first word. The split between reading and writing explains why AI price lists charge less for the words you send than for the words you get back. And the cache's memory decides how many people one machine can serve at the same time. One more trick speeds up the writing stage: a small, quick model drafts a few pieces ahead, and the big model checks the whole draft at once. Keeping the pieces that pass often gets more than one piece of text out of each slow trip through the big model, and the trick is called speculative decoding. By the end of this module you will be able to: tell the reading stage, called prefill, apart from the writing stage, called decode, and say why one can handle the whole message at once while the other cannot; explain what the KV cache saves, what it costs in memory, and why that makes it a trade of memory for speed; predict how many pieces of text one check by the big model produces in speculative decoding, from how long the draft is and how good the drafting model is. In the lab, a small grid shows exactly which pieces of work each step does, with the cache switched on or off. Its counts are exact for that tiny example. Next, a memory bar and a set of timing bars work out estimates for a real model on a real chip. They use the model's published size and the chip's advertised top speeds, so nothing is actually run or timed. There you can watch the saved numbers outgrow the model and see why writing is slow. The last card runs a tiny practice model that writes one letter at a time, so you can watch a drafting model's guesses being kept or refused.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Tokens, layers and passes A chatbot does not write in whole words but in tokens, small chunks of text that are often a whole word and sometimes only part of one. The model itself is a tall stack of layers, and each layer does its own round of arithmetic on the text. That arithmetic uses billions of numbers that were set during training, called weights. One trip of the text through every layer, from the bottom of the stack to the top, is called a pass. Prefill: reading the whole prompt at once Picture your class reading a printed paragraph together: every word is already on the page, so different students can work on different words at the same time. A model reads your prompt, the message you sent it, the same way. Since the prompt is complete before the model starts, all of its tokens travel through each layer together, side by side, in a single pass. This stage, called prefill, ends by predicting the first token of the answer, which is why the first word can appear as soon as prefill is done. In the lab, a prompt of 7 tokens goes through as one pass, and you will see all of its work light up at once. Decode: writing one token per pass Now picture the same class writing a story in a group chat, where each person adds one word and nobody can add the next word until the previous message arrives. However fast everyone types, the story grows by one word per message, because each new word depends on the one before it. Writing an answer works like that group chat, because each new token needs its own full pass through the model. That pass cannot start until the token before it exists, since the newest token is exactly what the next pass takes in. This stage is called decode, and it is why answers stream in piece by piece. A reply of 20 tokens therefore needs the prefill pass, which gives the first token, followed by 19 decode passes, one after another. Where the classroom picture stops matching: prefill and decode are not two different machines. They use the very same layers and the very same rules, and the only difference is whether the tokens already exist when the pass begins. Why writing is slow: a delivery problem The chip that runs the model has two parts that matter here: a calculating section that does arithmetic astonishingly fast, and a large memory that holds the weights. During every pass the weights must travel from memory to the calculators, and the connection between them can carry only so much data per second, a limit called memory bandwidth. Computer memory is counted in bytes, where a byte is a group of 8 tiny on-off switches, each called a bit. The lab's real model, Llama 3 8B, has about 8 billion weights and stores each one in 2 bytes, using a 16-bit number format called bf16. A gigabyte (GB) is a billion bytes, so its weights fill 16.1 GB, and the chip it runs on, an H100 SXM, has 80 GB of memory in total. Picture a delivery truck that has to bring the model's weights to the calculators for every single pass. One part of the weights is a table of about 1 GB that turns each token into its starting list of numbers. A pass only looks up one row of that table for each token, so the truck really carries about 15 GB, the other weights, on every trip. A real chip also usually serves many people's conversations at the same time. One delivery of the weights can then be shared by all of them, as you will see later. During prefill, one delivery serves every token of the prompt, so the calculators have a whole prompt's worth of arithmetic to do, and they become the slow part. For prompts longer than a few hundred tokens, that makes prefill compute bound: its time is set by the arithmetic, and the lab tags it compute-bound. During decode, the same full delivery produces only one new token for each conversation. The calculators finish that small job almost instantly and then sit idle until the next truck arrives. That makes decode memory bandwidth bound: its time is set by how fast memory can deliver, and the lab tags it memory-bound. Writing is slow not because the math is hard, but because every new token needs the weights delivered all over again. The lab's numbers, given in milliseconds (ms), or thousandths of a second, show how lopsided this is. One decode step for one conversation takes 4.8 ms, yet the arithmetic alone would take only 0.02 ms, so almost the whole step is spent waiting for the delivery. Where the truck picture stops matching: nothing gets used up, and the very same weights are fetched again, unchanged, for every pass. One arithmetic step, such as a single multiplication, is called a FLOP. Arithmetic intensity is the number of FLOP the chip does for each byte that memory delivers. This chip can do about 295 FLOP in the time its memory delivers one byte. So it keeps its calculators busy only when the work does at least about 295 FLOP per byte, which the timing card calls the switch point. Decode falls far short of that. Each weight takes 2 bytes to deliver, and for one new token it is used for one multiplication and one addition. That is about 2 FLOP for every 2 bytes, or close to 1 FLOP per byte. Attention's work on the saved notes, which you will meet next, pushes a decode step for one conversation up to about 1.2 FLOP per byte. That is about 250 times too little, which is why the calculators spend most of their time waiting. The KV cache: notes that never change To see what can be saved, you need one idea from attention, the step where tokens gather information from each other. In every layer, each token turns itself into three lists of numbers. A query (Q) describes what the token is looking for, and a key (K) is a label describing what it offers. A value (V) is the information it hands over when it is picked. Each token compares its query with the key of itself and of every earlier token. A comparison multiplies the two lists number by number and adds up the results to give one score, and a high score means a good match. With tiny three-number lists, (1, 2, 0) and (3, 1, 5) give 1 × 3 + 2 × 1 + 0 × 5, which is 5. Real lists in Llama 3 8B hold 128 numbers, so one comparison takes 128 multiplications and the additions that go with them. The lab counts each whole comparison as one Q·K product. The token then blends together the values of the tokens that matched best. There is one strict rule: a token may look only at itself and at tokens before it, never at tokens after it. This backward-only rule is called the causal mask, and it applies during prefill too, which is why the lab's grid only ever fills a triangle. Because of the causal mask, a token's key and value depend only on that token and the ones before it, so nothing that comes later can ever change them. That means they can be worked out once and kept, and the store that keeps one key and one value for every token is the KV cache. The scores are not kept, though: each one is used once and thrown away, since every new token needs fresh scores for its own query. Picture a long meeting where every speaker, on finishing, sticks a note on the wall. The note has a short label saying what they talked about and a summary of what they said. When someone new stands up, they read the wall instead of calling every earlier speaker back to repeat themselves. Nobody ever rewrites a note, because what was said cannot be unsaid. The labels are the keys, the summaries are the values, and the wall is the KV cache. Where the meeting picture stops matching: the notes are lists of numbers rather than sentences, and a real model keeps a separate wall in each of its layers. Llama 3 8B has 32 layers, and each one keeps 8 sets of notes side by side, for a reason explained a little further on. To see the saving in the lab, take 7 prompt tokens and 4 generated ones, so the fourth decode step has 11 tokens in all. With the cache, that step works out a new query, key and value for the newest token only. It compares that query with all 11 keys, its own included, which makes 11 products, and it reads the 10 stored keys and values. Without the cache, the same step reworks all 11 tokens and computes the whole triangle. Token 1 makes 1 comparison, token 2 makes 2, and so on up to token 11. Adding 1 + 2 + 3 and so on up to 11 gives 66 products. The price: memory The cache trades memory for time, and the memory is not small. The lab works out the size for one token of Llama 3 8B with this line: Reading from the left, the 2 counts one key and one value, and the 32 is the number of layers. The 8 needs one more idea. Attention in each layer runs several times side by side, and each copy, called a head, is free to look for a different kind of connection. Llama 3 8B stores keys and values for 8 heads per layer, each key or value is a list of 128 numbers, and each number takes 2 bytes. Multiplying one step at a time, 2 × 32 makes 64, and 64 × 8 makes 512. Then 512 × 128 makes 65,536, and doubling that for 2 bytes per number gives 131,072 bytes. The KV per token readout shows this as 131 kB (128 KiB), two labels for the same amount in slightly different units. A kilobyte (kB) is 1,000 bytes, while a KiB is 1,024 bytes, a size computers like because 1,024 is ten 2s multiplied together. The 8 is smaller than it could have been, because Llama 3 8B actually runs 32 query heads in each layer. Those query heads work in groups of four that share one set of keys and values, so only 8 key and value heads need storing. This sharing is called grouped-query attention, and it makes the cache four times smaller than giving every query head its own keys and values. Without the sharing, each token would need 524 kB. Even so, the notes add up fast, because one conversation of 8,192 tokens holds about 1.1 GB of them. Sixteen such conversations hold 17.2 GB, which is more than the 16.1 GB of weights. The weights stay the same size however busy the chip gets, while the cache grows with every token of every conversation. Speculative decoding: draft, then check Decode's weakness is that each pass produces one token, and each pass needs a full delivery of the weights. Speculative decoding can get more than one token out of each pass of the big model. A small, quick model called the draft guesses the next few tokens, and the big model, called the target, checks all of those guesses in a single pass. The weights are delivered once either way, so checking several known tokens together costs the target about as much as writing one. In this module's lab, each token is a single letter, so the picture below uses letters too. Picture a careful expert writing with a quick helper, who pencils in the next four letters for the expert to read in one look. In that one look, the expert also forms their own opinion about every position, including the spot just after the last guess. So the check always ends with one letter of the expert's own. Starting from the first, the expert keeps letters for as long as they pass. At the first one that fails, the expert crosses it out, writes their own letter in its place, and throws away the rest of the draft. If all four pass, the expert's own letter goes at the end instead. So one check always gives the kept guesses plus exactly one letter from the expert: at least one new token, and at most the number of guesses plus one. Where the expert picture stops matching: the expert does not keep a letter only when it matches the expert's own first choice. A model does not always write its single favorite letter. It gives every possible letter a chance, then picks one at random using those chances, like spinning a spinner whose slices are different sizes. Both models give chances for every possible next letter, and the check compares the two. If the target gives the guessed letter at least as much chance as the draft did, the letter is always kept. If the target gives it less, the letter is kept only part of the time, in proportion. When the target says 30% and the draft said 60%, for example, the letter survives half the time. When a guess is refused, its replacement is picked at random from the target's left-over odds. Those are the share of chance the target gave each letter beyond what the draft gave it. So they come only from letters the target liked more than the draft did. This careful rule has a remarkable result: the finished text follows the target's own odds exactly, as if the target had written every letter by itself. A weak draft gets refused more often, which costs tokens per pass, but it never changes what kind of text comes out. The average chance that one guess is kept is called the acceptance rate, written α (the Greek letter alpha). A later guess counts only if every guess before it was kept, so each extra guess is reached less often than the one before it. That is why making the draft longer helps less and less, which you can test in the lab.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: The problem the cache solves: redoing the past Picture a friend writing an essay who, before adding each new sentence, rereads the whole essay from the first line and rewrites every note in the margin. The first few sentences go quickly, but each one costs a little more than the one before, and a long essay turns into a slog. A model writing without a cache is in exactly that position. Without stored keys and values, the only way to get them back is to run every earlier token through every layer again. Those earlier tokens cannot be skipped, because each layer's results for every token feed the next layer's keys and values. So each decode step redoes a whole triangle of work, and triangles grow fast: ten tokens make 55 comparisons, while twenty make 210. In the grid, doubling the length makes each step's comparisons roughly four times as many. That is what people mean when they say the work grows with the square of the length. With the cache, each step adds a single row, and each new row is only one comparison longer than the last. On a real model, comparisons are not the biggest part of a step without the cache at everyday lengths. Most of the cost is running every earlier token back through the weights, and that part only doubles when the length doubles. In the lab, with one conversation, halving Context length from 8,192 to 4,096 cuts the recompute panel's step from 142 ms to about 67 ms. Even so, every step reruns all the earlier tokens, and a long answer has many steps. Added up over the whole answer, the work without the cache still grows with the square of its length. At real scale the gap is enormous, because at the lab's default settings a decode step takes 9.6 ms with the cache but 2.27 seconds without it. That is more than 200 times longer, paid again for every single new token. The two waits you notice A person using a chatbot feels two different waits. The first is time to first token, the delay before anything appears, which is mostly prefill and grows with the length of the prompt. The second is inter-token latency, the gap between one token and the next while the answer streams in, where latency means waiting time. It is set mostly by how fast memory can deliver the weights and the notes during decode. The cache shortens the second wait enormously but does nothing for the first. The only exception is when the same opening text was already read and stored for an earlier request, which you will meet in "Going deeper". The bill and the crowd The same split explains the prices: sending tokens in costs less per token than getting tokens back, because prefill shares one delivery of the weights across the whole prompt. Every output token, by contrast, needs a pass of its own. It also sets how many people one chip can serve, because a decode step spends most of its time waiting for the weights. The chip can therefore push many conversations through on the same delivery, a trick called batching. Every conversation still brings its own notes, though, so cache memory, not arithmetic, caps how many conversations can run at once. That is the memory side of the trade, and the memory card works it out.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: The triangle Causal attention work shows a grid with one row and one column for each token. Each row is a token's query and each column is a key it might compare against, which the corner label q ↓ k → sums up. Prompt tokens are labeled t1, t2 and so on, generated tokens are labeled +1, +2 and so on, and a dashed line separates the two groups. Cells above the diagonal are faint outlines, because the causal mask stops a query from looking at later keys. Under the grid sit two strips labeled K and V, with one slot per token, which show the cache itself. The controls live on the KV cache controls card, where KV cache switches between Use cache and Recompute. Prompt tokens runs from 3 to 14, and Generated tokens runs from 0 to 10. Try this: set Generated tokens to 0, where the readout says 0 · prefill. The prompt's whole triangle lights up at once, since prefill handles every prompt token in one pass. At the default 7 prompt tokens that is 28 products, because token 1 compares with 1 key, token 2 with 2 keys, and so on up to token 7. Adding 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 gives 28. Now raise Generated tokens one step at a time, keeping KV cache on Use cache. Each step lights only the newest row, and the New Q, K, V readout stays at 1. Meanwhile the K and V strips gain one slot per step, while the older slots are only read. At 1, the caption says the pass "feeds +1 at position 8 and predicts +2". Prefill already produced token +1, so the first decode step feeds that token back in and predicts the one after it. Then switch KV cache to Recompute, and the whole triangle lights up again on every step. The dashed cells are exact repeats of work the previous pass already did. At 7 prompt tokens and 4 generated, Q·K this pass jumps from 11 to 66. Push Prompt tokens to 14 and Generated tokens to 10, and Q·K whole run reads 2,145 without the cache, against 300 with it. The memory bar Memory budget switches from the toy grid to real arithmetic for Llama 3 8B on an 80 GB chip. Context length sets how many tokens each conversation holds, doubling at each step from 512 up to 131,072. Concurrent sequences sets how many conversations, which the lab calls sequences, the chip serves at once, from 1 to 64. The bar shows the weights and the KV cache side by side, with a marker at 80 GB for the chip's memory. At the defaults of 8,192 tokens and 16 conversations, KV cache total reads 17.2 GB, already more than the weights. Sequences that fit reads 59, the number of 8,192-token conversations whose notes would fit in the memory left after the weights. Now push Context length to 131,072 with Concurrent sequences at 1. That single long conversation holds 17.2 GB of notes on its own, and only 3 of them would fit. Finally, set Concurrent sequences to 64 at 8,192 tokens, and the cache runs past the 80 GB marker and turns red. At the same time, Memory left changes into Over by, which reads 4.8 GB. The timing bars Prefill versus decode estimates how long three kinds of pass take on this chip, using the context length and conversation count from the memory card. Each panel has an arithmetic bar, showing how long the calculations alone would take, and a memory bar, showing how long the delivery alone would take. Whichever is longer sets the time and is drawn solid, and the panel is tagged compute-bound or memory-bound to match. The bars use a stretched scale where each equal step along a bar means ten times more time, so compare the printed times rather than the bar lengths. The heading also names the chip's top speeds. For arithmetic it is 989 TFLOP/s, where a TFLOP/s is a trillion FLOP each second. For memory it is 3.35 TB/s, where a TB/s is a trillion bytes each second. Dividing 989 by 3.35 gives the switch point of about 295 FLOP per byte. At the defaults, prefill of one 8,192-token prompt is compute-bound at 142 ms, and the panel notes that this is the time to first token. A decode step with the cache for all 16 conversations is memory-bound at 9.6 ms, and one step writes one new token for each of the 16. Since 1,000 ms ÷ 9.6 ms is about 104 steps a second, each conversation gets about 104 tokens per second. Set Concurrent sequences to 1, and the step drops to 4.8 ms, or about 208 tokens per second. The third panel shows the cost of skipping the cache: at the defaults, a decode step that recomputes everything takes 2.27 seconds. Speculative decoding The Speculative decoding card runs the draft-and-check idea on a tiny model that writes one character at a time, so here each token is a single letter or a space. Draft length sets how many guesses the draft makes per pass, from 1 to 8. Draft quality runs from 0.20 to 1.00, where 1.00 makes the draft the target itself. Lower values make the draft spread its chances more evenly over all letters, as if it were guessing more blindly. Then fewer of its guesses are kept, and the acceptance rate α falls. Seed picks which random draws the simulation uses, so the same seed always replays the same run. The pass lines show the first six checks as text, with each space drawn as ␣. At the defaults, Pass 1 reads: the draft proposed orbs, the target kept 0 of 4, refused o and wrote t instead, for +1 token. Pass 2 goes better, because the draft proposed ␣tha and the target kept 3 of 4, which were ␣th. It then refused a and wrote e instead, for +4 tokens. Together those two passes turn the prompt the␣ into the␣t␣the. The first of the four readouts under the pass lines, Acceptance rate α, reads 0.831, so a single guess is kept about 83 times in 100. Without drafting always reads 1 token per pass, the rate of ordinary decode, for comparison. Closed form, tokens per pass reads 3.57, the prediction from a formula; "closed form" means a formula you can work out directly, without simulating anything. Simulated, tokens per pass reads 3.60 ± 0.02, the average over 4,000 seeded passes. The note under the readouts writes the formula as (1 − α^(γ+1)) ÷ (1 − α), where γ (the Greek letter gamma) is the draft length. Here α^(γ+1) means γ + 1 copies of α multiplied together, so 5 copies when γ is 4. The formula is clearer when you write it out as a sum. Each check gives 1 token for certain, plus 1 more for each guess that is kept, and a guess counts only when every guess before it was kept too. At the defaults, think of 100 checks. The first guess is kept in about 83 of them. Among those 83, the second guess is also kept about 83% of the time, so both survive in about 69 checks out of 100. That is why the chances multiply: 0.83 × 0.83 is about 0.69. Multiplying again gives about 0.57 for the first three and about 0.48 for all four. These steps use the readout's full value of 0.831, so if you multiply the rounded 0.83 four times you get 0.47 instead. A guess kept in 83 checks out of 100 adds 0.83 of a token to each check on average, so adding up the chances adds up the average tokens. That gives 1 + 0.83 + 0.69 + 0.57 + 0.48 = 3.57, the same as the formula. The simulation actually plays out 4,000 random checks, so its average wobbles a little from one seed to another. The ± 0.02 is the typical size of that wobble, called the standard error. Now set Draft quality to 1.00, and every pass yields 5 tokens, because all 4 guesses are kept and the target adds one more. Drop it to 0.30 and the closed form falls to 2.21. The chart below plots tokens per verification pass against draft length γ, with the closed form drawn solid, the simulation dashed, and no drafting dotted.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: With the cache, a whole run costs exactly one triangle, because every product is computed once. Without it, every step pays for a whole triangle again, which comes to 2,145 products instead of 300 at 14 prompt tokens and 10 generated ones. Recompute changes the cost, never the answer: the recomputed keys and values are exactly the numbers the cache would have held. The K and V strips only ever grow, and no slot is ever rewritten. That is the causal mask at work, since later tokens cannot change the keys and values of earlier ones. The cache does nothing for prefill, so at Generated tokens 0 the Use cache and Recompute settings draw the same triangle. Its savings begin at the first decode step. Attention is not the whole job, because even with a perfect cache each decode step still fetches the weights. At one conversation, the 4.8 ms step goes almost entirely on fetching about 15 GB of weights. That is the 16.1 GB minus the lookup table, which is only read one row at a time. The detail line under that decode panel reads 16.1 GB, because it adds the conversation's own 1.1 GB of notes to those 15 GB of weights. It only happens to match the full size of the weights. Prefill is the opposite, with the arithmetic bar as the long one at 142 ms for 8,192 tokens. One delivery of the weights feeds thousands of tokens at once, so the calculators set the pace. Batching shares the delivery of the weights but not the notes. With 16 conversations, the chip writes about 1,665 tokens per second in total, eight times its rate for a single conversation. Yet each of those 16 conversations gets only about 104 tokens per second, half of what one conversation gets alone, because every conversation adds its own notes to each delivery. Each speculative pass yields at least 1 token and at most the draft length plus 1. The extra one is the target's own token, added after the last guess when it keeps them all. Longer drafts help less and less: at the default quality, raising Draft length from 1 to 4 adds almost two tokens per pass, from 1.83 to 3.57. Raising it further, from 5 to 8, adds less than one token per pass, from 3.97 to 4.79. The chart's footnote gives the ceiling: at the default quality the closed form can never pass 5.91 tokens per pass, however long the draft gets. Change Seed and the simulated value moves by about one standard error, while the closed form stays put, because the formula has no randomness in it. The text written follows the target's own odds whatever the Draft quality, so a poor draft costs tokens per pass, not correctness.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: What this lab simplifies The grid is a toy that tops out at 24 tokens and shows one head in one layer. Its counts are exact for that toy, but no scores are actually computed, so the cells carry no values. The real-scale cards use Llama 3 8B's published shape, meaning its numbers of layers and heads. They also use the H100 SXM's advertised top speeds of 989 TFLOP/s for arithmetic and 3.35 TB/s for memory. Nothing is actually run on a chip. Each time on those cards is whichever is longer, the arithmetic time or the delivery time, worked out as if the chip ran at 100% of its top speed. This kind of estimate is called the roofline model. The cards also leave out three things: the in-between results the model produces as it works, the small start-up delay before each calculation, and picking the next token. Real chips never reach their top speed, so treat the times as a best case from a formula, not a stopwatch reading. Sequences that fit ignores those in-between results, the serving software's own memory, and gaps of wasted space, so real capacity is lower. The 80 GB is also the chip's advertised size, not what is free in practice. The Speculative decoding card is a toy too, because its target is a tiny model that predicts each character only from the one before it. Because it only looks at the one letter before, the whole model is a table of odds for each pair of letters, called a character bigram. So checking the guesses "in one pass" is a table lookup, and nothing is timed. The draft is the target with its odds flattened, standing in for a weaker model. The closed form also assumes every guess has the same chance of being kept. Here the chance depends on the letter before it, so the formula is off from the true average by at most about 0.02 tokens. Where the real mechanism struggles The cache shares the chip's memory with the weights and the in-between results. Nobody knows in advance how long a conversation will get. So handing each one a block big enough for the longest possible conversation leaves much of it unused, a problem called fragmentation. A common mix-up: the cache does not make long prompts free. Reading a very long prompt is real work that has to finish before the first token comes out, and prefill's attention work grows with the square of the prompt's length. In this lab's estimate, a prompt of 131,072 tokens takes about 6.5 seconds before the first token can appear. The cache removes repeated work during *writing*, not the one-time cost of *reading*. Storing the notes with fewer bits, such as 8 or 4 instead of 16, is called quantization. Going from 16 bits to 8 halves the cache, but the rounded numbers can measurably change the output. That makes it a trade of quality for memory rather than a free saving. Throwing away the oldest notes to make room is riskier than it looks. Some heads park a large share of their attention on the very first tokens of the text, which act as attention sinks. Deleting those notes makes the output noticeably worse. Real speculative decoding has its own costs. A real draft is a small model, or extra prediction parts added to the big model, and how often its guesses are kept changes with the text. Each pass costs the target's check plus the draft's own steps, one per guess, so tokens per pass is only half of the speed-up story. The other half is how cheap the draft is to run.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Because decode spends most of its time waiting for deliveries, batching raises the total output cheaply until cache memory runs out. Continuous batching goes further by letting new conversations join and finished ones leave at every decode step, instead of waiting for a whole group to finish together. That keeps the chip busier under real traffic. PagedAttention stores the cache in small fixed-size blocks, with a table for each conversation listing which blocks hold its notes, much like the pages of a binder. This nearly removes the wasted gaps, and it lets conversations that start with the same text share the same blocks. That sharing is called prefix caching, where a prefix is the opening part of a text. It is why a long system prompt, the set of instructions a service places at the start of every request, is read by prefill once rather than every time. Other designs shrink the notes directly, as in multi-query attention, where every query head shares one set of keys and values. Grouped-query attention, which Llama 3 8B uses, sits between that and one set per head. Latent-attention designs store a squeezed version of the notes, while sliding-window layers keep notes for only a fixed number of recent tokens. The Modern attention at scale module covers these. Chunked prefill cuts a long prompt into pieces and slips them in between other users' decode steps, so one long prompt does not freeze everyone else's streaming text. The draft-and-check rule, the left-over replacement and the tokens-per-pass formula come from Leviathan, Kalman and Matias (2023, arXiv 2211.17192). They report a speed-up of two to three times on a large model called T5-XXL. The Deployment & serving module uses the same formula and gets 3.36 tokens per pass with an acceptance rate of 0.8 and 4 guesses. Two measurements sum up this whole module: time to first token is set mostly by prefill, and inter-token latency mostly by how fast memory delivers during decode. Structured and constrained decoding adds one more job to every decode step: blocking which tokens are allowed to come next.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: This module is about inference: how a trained language model turns a prompt into text, and what each step costs. Every new token depends on all the earlier ones, so which work can be done once and kept, and which must be paid again for every token? The transformer block traced one token through attention and an MLP. A forward pass runs a stack of those blocks, and generation repeats it in two phases: prefill, one pass over the whole prompt, and decode, one pass per new token. The KV cache stores each position's attention keys and values so decode can skip recomputing the prefix: each step projects only the new position and reads the stored keys and values. Speculative decoding lets one pass of the large model, called the target, accept several tokens that a cheaper draft proposed. Where it shows up Serving engines. Batching runs many sequences through one decode step, and continuous batching admits and retires them at every step. PagedAttention stores the cache in fixed-size blocks, prefix caching shares a cached prompt prefix across requests, and chunked prefill splits a long prompt into pieces between other users' decode steps. Each is built around decode's bandwidth limit, the cache's size, or the split between phases; Going deeper returns to them. Model architecture. Grouped-query attention shrinks the cache: in Llama 3 8B, 32 query heads share 8 key/value heads. Latent-attention schemes store a compressed form of the keys and values, and sliding-window layers keep only a fixed span of recent positions; both attack the same cost. Speculative decoding. A small draft model, or extra prediction heads on the large model that guess tokens further ahead, propose tokens for the large model to check in one pass. Why it matters Without the cache, every decode step reruns the whole prefix, so per-token cost grows with the square of the length. With it, each step computes only the newest position's row against the stored keys, so per-token cost grows only linearly. The price is memory, 128 KiB per token for Llama 3 8B in bf16, and at serving scale cache memory is what caps the batch. The phases also hit different limits. Long prefills are compute bound: every prompt position shares one read of the weights. Decode is memory bandwidth bound: limited by reading weights and cache entries, not by arithmetic. And the cache does not shorten prefill: in the lab's roofline estimate for one H100, a 131,072-token prompt still needs about 6.5 s before its first token. What you will be able to explain Separate prefill from decode, and say why a long prefill is compute bound while decode is memory bandwidth bound. Explain the KV cache memory-speed trade-off: the recomputation it removes and the memory it costs. Predict how draft length and draft quality set the tokens one verification pass yields in speculative decoding. What the lab shows Nothing is measured on hardware. Causal attention work counts the exact query-key products of a toy causal triangle, up to 24 positions in one head and one layer, without computing any scores. KV cache controls set Prompt tokens, Generated tokens (0 is the prefill pass) and KV cache, either Use cache or Recompute. Watch Q·K this pass and Q·K whole run. Memory budget is closed-form arithmetic from Llama 3 8B's published shape against a nominal 80 GB of accelerator memory, and Prefill versus decode adds H100 SXM spec-sheet peaks. Both are driven by Context length and Concurrent sequences. Pass times come from a roofline model, the larger of arithmetic time and memory time at 100% of peak: lower bounds, not measurements. The key experiment: switch to Recompute and see the repeated products in the triangle, then compare the cache-on and recompute decode panels in Prefill versus decode at the default 8,192 tokens. Speculative decoding checks drafts against a target, a character bigram the lab trains in place of the large model; the draft is that bigram with its rows flattened, and Draft quality 1.00 is the target itself. Draft length and Draft quality set Closed form, tokens per pass and Simulated, tokens per pass, a seeded run of 4,000 passes; Seed moves only the simulation. The card counts tokens, not time.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Generation has two phases with different performance characteristics, and most serving decisions follow from that split. Prefill runs the whole prompt through the model in one forward pass. Every position is available at once, so each layer does one large matrix multiply over all of them. For prompts longer than a few hundred tokens it is compute bound. The same pass also produces the first output token. Decode produces one token per forward pass. Each step multiplies a single new position per sequence through every weight matrix, so the limit is how fast weights can be read from memory, not arithmetic. During decode, an accelerator's arithmetic units mostly wait. What the cache stores and why it works Under the causal mask, the key and value at a position depend only on that position and earlier ones. A later token cannot change them, so they can be computed once and kept. That store is the KV cache: one key and one value vector per position, per layer, per key/value head. With the cache, decode step g projects only the newest position and attends over the n stored entries: one row of the causal triangle, n query-key products. Without it, the step reruns the whole prefix and computes all n(n+1)/2 products again. Only keys and values are stored; the attention scores from earlier rows are used once and discarded. The size of the trade The cache is not small. Its size per token is The leading 2 counts keys and values. For Llama 3 8B in bf16 — 32 layers, 8 key/value heads, head dimension 128 — that is 131,072 bytes, 128 KiB per token: 4 GiB for one 32,768-token context. Grouped-query attention keeps it that small: 32 query heads share those 8 key/value heads, a fourfold saving.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: This is where a model becomes a product with a cost and a latency budget, and the split between prefill and decode shapes both. It also explains pricing. Input tokens are cheaper than output tokens because prefill shares one read of the weights across the whole prompt, while every output token needs its own pass.

Speculative decoding Under Speculative decoding, a draft proposes Draft length characters and the target checks them in one pass. The K and V rows only grow. No slot is ever rewritten, which is the causal mask at work. Attention work is not total work. Even cached, a step at one sequence reads about 15 GB of weights to do 19 GFLOP of arithmetic, about 1.2 FLOP per byte, far below the H100's ridge of roughly 295. That is why decode is memory-bound. The trade is memory for time. Batching amortizes the weight read across sequences, but every sequence reads its own cache, and cache memory caps how many can run at once. documents.subtitle: Standard · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: In this lab. The triangle is a toy of at most 24 positions, one head in one layer; its counts are exact, but no scores are computed. The real-scale cards use Llama 3 8B's published shape and H100 SXM spec-sheet peaks (989 TFLOP/s dense bf16, 3.35 TB/s). Their times are a roofline model at 100% of peak, ignoring activations, launch overhead and sampling: lower bounds, not measurements. In real systems. The cache competes with weights and activations for the same memory, and naive per-request allocation wastes much of it through fragmentation. Prefill attention is quadratic in prompt length, so a 131,072-token prompt takes several seconds before the first token appears — about 6.5 s in this model — and caching does not remove that cost. Speculative decoding in the lab and outside it In this lab. The target is also a character bigram, so checking proposals "in one pass" is a table lookup, not a transformer forward pass, and the card counts tokens per pass without timing anything. The draft is the target with its rows flattened, a stand-in for a weaker model. The closed form assumes each proposal is kept independently with the same chance. Here the chance depends on the context, and the formula differs from the exact expectation by at most about 0.02 tokens. In real systems. documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Because decode is bandwidth-bound, batching raises throughput cheaply until cache memory runs out. Continuous batching admits and retires sequences at every step instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish. PagedAttention manages the cache in fixed-size blocks with a per-sequence block table, which nearly eliminates fragmentation and lets requests with the same prefix share blocks. That sharing is prefix caching, and it is why a long system prompt reused across requests is prefilled once. Attention variants attack cache size directly: multi-query and grouped-query attention share key/value heads, latent-attention schemes store a compressed representation, and sliding-window layers bound the cache at a fixed span. Modern attention at scale covers these. Speculative decoding attacks the sequential dependency instead. A small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model checks them in one pass; with the standard acceptance rule the output distribution is exactly the large model's. The rule, the replacement sample and the tokens-per-pass formula are from Leviathan, Kalman and Matias (2023, arXiv 2211.17192), who report a 2X to 3X speed-up on T5-XXL. Deployment & serving states the same formula: 3.36 tokens per pass at α = 0.8 and γ = 4. Chunked prefill interleaves prompt processing with decode steps so one long prompt does not stall other users' streams. Two metrics summarize it all: time to first token, dominated by prefill, and inter-token latency, dominated by decode bandwidth. Structured and constrained decoding adds one more thing that happens at every decode step: masking which tokens may come next.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Causal attention work · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Which query-key products each pass computes The causal attention score matrix for a short sequence, with rows as queries and columns as keys. Prefill fills the whole lower triangle in one pass. With the cache, each decode step adds one row; without it, each step computes the whole triangle again. The counts are exact for this toy sequence. A square grid with one row and one column per position. Prompt positions read `t1`, `t2`…; generated ones read `+1`, `+2`… in the accent colour, split from the prompt by a dashed line. Cells above the diagonal are faint outlines: the causal mask forbids a query from seeing later keys. Solid accent cells are computed in the pass being shown, and the outlined row is the newest position. Pale cells were computed by an earlier pass; their scores were used and discarded, since only keys and values are stored. Dashed red cells are the same products computed again. Two rows under the triangle, `K` and `V`, one slot per position: solid blue is written this pass, pale blue is read from the cache, dashed red is recomputed and then dropped. Readouts: `New Q, K, V` (positions projected this pass), `Q·K this pass`, `K/V read`, and `Q·K whole run`, the products summed over prefill and every decode step so far. Prefill over P prompt tokens computes P(P+1)/2 products and writes P key/value slots. Decode step g feeds token +g at position n = P + g: with the cache it projects one position and computes n products against the stored keys; without it, it projects all n positions and computes n(n+1)/2. Past rows are still needed without a cache, because each layer's outputs for every position feed the next layer's keys and values. The waste is that those numbers are identical to the ones the previous pass produced. Counts are per attention head per layer. Llama 3 8B repeats them across 32 query heads and 32 layers. `Generated tokens` 0 shows the prefill pass; each higher value shows the next decode step. `KV cache` flips between `Use cache` and `Recompute`. At 7 prompt and 4 generated tokens, `Q·K this pass` goes from 11 to 66 and `Q·K whole run` from 66 to 230. With the cache, the whole run costs exactly one triangle: every product is computed once. Without it, the run costs a triangle per step, 2,145 products instead of 300 at 14 prompt and 10 generated tokens. Nothing in the `K` and `V` rows is ever rewritten. Each step appends one slot, which is why the cache is valid. The cache does not change prefill: `Use cache` and `Recompute` draw the same triangle at `Generated tokens` 0. In this lab: the sequence tops out at 24 positions and the grid shows one head in one layer. The counts are exact for that toy, but no attention scores are computed, so the cells carry no values. In general: real kernels such as FlashAttention compute these products in tiles without storing the score matrix, and sliding-window or sparse attention layers skip parts of the triangle altogether.
documents.title: Which query-key products each pass computes

documents.subtitle: KV cache controls · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: The toy sequence and the caching choice Three inputs for the triangle: how many prompt tokens prefill handles in one pass, how many tokens have been generated since, and whether keys and values are kept or recomputed. The real-scale cards below have their own controls. `KV cache`, a two-way switch between `Use cache` and `Recompute`. `Prompt tokens` from 3 to 14 and `Generated tokens` from 0 to 10; at 0 the readout says `prefill`. A note stating what the shown pass reads and projects. `Prompt tokens` and `Generated tokens` set the sequence length n = P + G on the triangle and the cache rows. Prefill also produces the first new token, from the last prompt row. So `Generated tokens` 1 already shows the first decode step, feeding +1 and predicting +2. Set `Prompt tokens` to 14 and `Generated tokens` to 1: the step projects 1 position and reads 14 stored keys and values. Raise `Generated tokens` to 10 under `Recompute` and watch `Q·K whole run` grow to 2,145, then switch to `Use cache` for 300. The cached per-step cost grows by one product per step, linearly with length. The recomputed per-step cost grows with the square of length. `Use cache` changes nothing about the prompt pass. It pays off from the first decode step onward. In this lab: the switch selects which cells are drawn and counted; there is no model running, and the toy stops at 24 positions. In general: real servers never recompute; the practical choices are how much cache to keep, at what precision, and for how many sequences at once.
documents.title: The toy sequence and the caching choice

documents.subtitle: Memory budget · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Weights versus cache on one accelerator Real arithmetic for a named model: Llama 3 8B in bf16 on an 80 GB accelerator. The weights take a fixed 16.1 GB. The cache takes 131,072 bytes per token per sequence, so it grows with both context length and the number of sequences served at once. `Context length`, stepping by powers of two from 512 to 131,072 tokens, and `Concurrent sequences` from 1 to 64. A bar split into weights (solid) and KV cache (hatched), with a marker at 80 GB. If the two exceed it, the cache segment turns red and runs past the marker. `KV per token`, `KV cache total`, `Memory left` or `Over by`, and `Sequences that fit` at this context length. KV bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per value = 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, which is 128 KiB. The leading 2 counts keys and values. Weights are 8.03B parameters × 2 bytes = 16.1 GB. The cache total is sequences × context × 131,072 bytes, and `Sequences that fit` is (80 GB − weights) ÷ (context × 131,072). Llama 3 8B uses grouped-query attention: 32 query heads share 8 key/value heads. With one key/value head per query head the cache would be four times larger, 524 kB per token. At the default 8,192 tokens and 16 sequences the cache is 17.2 GB, more than the 16.1 GB of weights. Push `Context length` to 131,072 with one sequence: that single conversation holds 17.2 GB, and only 3 fit. Raise `Concurrent sequences` to 64 at 8,192 tokens and the bar runs past 80 GB. The weights never change with load; the cache is the part that scales with users and context. That is why serving capacity is usually limited by cache memory, not by weights. Your toy sequence of a couple of dozen tokens needs only a few megabytes. The problem only appears at real context lengths. In this lab: `Sequences that fit` ignores activations, the runtime's own memory, and fragmentation, so real capacity is lower. The 80 GB is nominal capacity. In general: servers shrink this cost with paged allocation, prefix sharing, cache quantization to 8 or 4 bits, sliding-window layers, and latent-attention schemes that store a compressed representation.
documents.title: Weights versus cache on one accelerator

documents.subtitle: Prefill versus decode · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Arithmetic time against memory time A roofline estimate of three passes at the context length and sequence count from Memory budget. For each pass, the arithmetic time is FLOPs ÷ peak FLOP/s and the memory time is bytes ÷ bandwidth; the larger one sets the modeled time. It is a model built from spec-sheet peaks, not a measurement. Three panels: prefill of one prompt, one cached decode step for all sequences, and one recompute decode step. Each has an `arithmetic` bar and a `memory` bar on a log time axis, with the binding one drawn solid and a `compute-bound` or `memory-bound` tag. Under each panel: FLOPs, bytes moved, arithmetic intensity in FLOP per byte, and for cached decode the total and per-sequence tokens per second. Peaks are the H100 SXM spec sheet: 989 TFLOP/s dense bf16 and 3.35 TB/s. Their ratio, about 295 FLOP per byte, is the ridge: below it a pass waits on memory. Matmul FLOPs are 2 × 7.5B per token (all weights except the embedding lookup). Attention adds 4 × layers × heads × head dim × context per token. Prefill of T tokens reads the weights once and writes T cache slots. A cached decode step reads the weights once for the whole batch plus every sequence's cache. A recompute step reruns each sequence's prefix, which is a full prefill per new token. At the defaults, prefill of 8,192 tokens is compute-bound at 142 ms, and a cached decode step for 16 sequences is memory-bound at 9.6 ms, about 104 tokens per second per sequence. Set `Concurrent sequences` to 1: the decode step drops to 4.8 ms and 208 tokens per second, nearly all of it spent reading 15 GB of weights. Decode's arithmetic bar is tiny next to its memory bar: at one sequence the intensity is about 1.2 FLOP per byte, far below 295. Batching amortizes the weight read but not the cache reads, since each sequence reads its own cache. At long contexts the cache reads dominate the step. Recompute turns a memory-bound step into a compute-bound one: 2.27 s per step at the defaults, against 9.6 ms with the cache. In this lab: the model assumes 100% of peak throughput and ignores activations, kernel launch overhead, sampling, and communication, so real times are longer. At very short prompts prefill itself becomes memory-bound, which the model reproduces. In general: production engines split prefill and decode across steps or machines (chunked prefill, disaggregated serving) because the two phases want different hardware balance.
documents.title: Arithmetic time against memory time

documents.subtitle: Speculative decoding · Inference & KV cache
documents.body: Cheap guesses, checked in one target pass A weak draft model proposes `Draft length` characters. The target scores all of them in one pass and keeps a proposal when a random draw falls under p ÷ q; the first one it refuses is replaced by a sample from the probability the target had left over, and a pass that keeps everything adds one more token of its own. The card reports tokens per pass from the SDK's closed form and from a seeded simulation on toy distributions. `Draft length` from 1 to 8 proposals per pass, `Draft quality` from 0.20 to 1.00, and `Seed` from 1 to 999. Six pass lines written as text: what the draft proposed, how many the target kept and which characters, which one it refused and what it wrote instead (or the extra character it wrote when it kept all of them), and the tokens that pass added. Spaces are drawn as ␣. The text those six passes wrote after the prompt `the␣`. Four readouts: `Acceptance rate α`, `Closed form, tokens per pass`, `Simulated, tokens per pass` with its standard error, and `Without drafting`, which is always 1. A note gives the simulation minus the closed form in tokens and in standard errors. A chart of tokens per verification pass against draft length 1 to 8: the closed form solid, the simulation dashed, no drafting dotted. The legend repeats each last value. The target is the lab's character bigram, trained 50 epochs on Harbor weather notes and Recipe steps, with the marker characters removed. The draft raises every target row to the power `Draft quality` and renormalizes, which flattens it: 1.00 is the target itself and 0.20 is close to guessing. A drafted token x after context c is kept when a uniform draw is at most p(x|c) ÷ q(x|c). The first refusal is replaced by a draw from max(0, p − q), renormalized. If all of them are kept, the target draws one more token from its own row. This is Algorithm 1 of Leviathan, Kalman and Matias (2023). α is the sum over tokens of min(p, q), averaged over the contexts the target visits. The closed form is the SDK's `speculativeTokensPerPass`, (1 − α^(γ+1)) ÷ (1 − α), the formula `Deployment & serving` also states. The simulation runs 4,000 passes for each draft length from the prompt, each pass continuing from the last token written. The standard error is the spread of tokens per pass divided by √4,000. At the defaults, length 4, quality 0.70 and seed 7, α is 0.831, the closed form 3.57 and the simulation 3.60 ± 0.02. Set `Draft quality` to 1.00 and every pass yields 5, the draft length plus one; set it to 0.30 and the closed form falls to 2.21. Raise `Draft length` at the default quality: the closed form reads 1.83, 3.57, 3.97 and 4.79 for lengths 1, 4, 5 and 8, and can never pass 1 ÷ (1 − α) = 5.91. `Seed` re-runs every simulation. The simulated value moves by about a standard error and the closed form does not move. A pass always yields at least one token and never more than the draft length plus one. From length 1 to 4 the gain is larger than from 5 to 8: a later proposal counts only if every earlier one was kept. The text written is distributed as the target's own, whatever the draft quality, because a refused proposal is replaced from the probability the target had left over. A poor draft costs tokens per pass, not correctness. `Deployment & serving` states the same formula, 3.36 tokens per pass at α = 0.8 and γ = 4. In this lab: the target is also a character bigram, so checking proposals in one pass is a table lookup, not a transformer forward pass. The card counts tokens per pass and never times anything. In this lab: the draft is the target with flattened rows, a stand-in for a weaker model. The closed form assumes each proposal is kept independently with the same chance; here the chance depends on the context, and the formula is off from the exact expectation by at most about 0.02 tokens across the controls. In general: a real draft is a small model or extra prediction heads, acceptance varies with the text, and a pass costs the target's step plus the draft's γ steps. Tokens per pass is only half of the speed-up.
