documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Next-token training on curated prompt-and-response pairs. The per-token loss is the same cross-entropy as pretraining; what changes is the data, its formatting, and usually a mask that grades only the response.
documents.title: Supervised fine-tuning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: The exact string layout that turns a list of messages into one sequence, including every marker. Two models with different templates need different strings for the same conversation.
documents.title: Chat template

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: A token id reserved for structure, such as a turn marker. It is unforgeable only if the serving stack tokenizes user text so that typing the marker's spelling never yields that id.
documents.title: Special token

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: A leading block of instructions outside the user turn. It is only privileged because the template and the training data agreed to treat it that way.
documents.title: System prompt

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: The marker that tells a decoder to stop generating. Without it a model keeps writing, usually by inventing the next user turn itself.
documents.title: End-of-turn token

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Grading only the assistant's reply and the marker that closes it, while the system and user text is read as context but never graded. Common in SFT recipes and this lab's default; Every character switches it off.
documents.title: Loss masking

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Serving a model with formatting that differs from its training format. It degrades quality quietly, because nothing errors — the model simply sees an unfamiliar string.
documents.title: Template mismatch

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Producing a response to a request instead of continuing the request's text. It is learned from formatted examples, not from more pretraining.
documents.title: Instruction following

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Tags such as user and assistant that wrap each turn so the model can tell whose words are whose. Here they are spelled in letters between reserved angle brackets and share rows with ordinary text; a real tokenizer gives each its own reserved id.
documents.title: Role markers

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Putting several short training examples into one sequence to fill the context window. Unless the attention mask also blocks attention across each boundary, one example can read the one before it.
documents.title: Packing

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: The unit of every loss and surprise readout in this lab: the negative natural log of the probability the model gave the actual next character. A model that spreads probability evenly over the 30 characters scores ln 30, about 3.401.
documents.title: Nats

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Next-token training on a broad corpus with every position graded, which is what the Every character setting reproduces. Supervised fine-tuning keeps the same loss and changes the layout and the mask.
documents.title: Pretraining

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: The proposal, from the LIMA paper, that a model's knowledge and capabilities are learned almost entirely in pretraining, and that alignment mostly teaches which format and style to use with users. It predicts that a small set of high-quality examples can be enough, and it is a hypothesis, not a measured law.
documents.title: Superficial alignment hypothesis

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Training conversations with several user and assistant turns. A model fine-tuned only on single-turn pairs can lose track of the dialogue after a few turns, so multi-turn examples teach it to read earlier turns as context.
documents.title: Multi-turn data

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Instruction tuning & templates · question 1
documents.body: Both models train on the same four pairs for the same number of epochs, one with the chat template and one as plain text. What does the next-character list show after a reply's last character? Only the plain model has learned anything there, because its text is shorter and simpler Only the templated model has learned anything there: it expects the reserved end marker Both models expect a space next, since a space follows most full stops in ordinary text Neither differs, because markers carry no information the letters do not already have The template adds a graded end marker after every reply, so the row for the full stop is trained to point at it. In plain concatenation nothing ever follows a reply's last character within its example, so that row never receives a gradient and stays uniform, one in thirty for every character.
documents.title: Both models train on the same four pairs for the same number of epochs, one with the chat template and one as plain text. What does the next-character list show after a reply's last character?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Instruction tuning & templates · question 2
documents.body: You switch Loss on from Assistant reply only to Every character. What changes in the strip and its metrics? The system and user text stop being read, because they are now graded instead The reply stops being graded, because the mask now covers it The graded count stays the same, but each cell's bar grows taller Every character becomes graded, so no cell is context-only any more The mask decides which characters count in the loss, not which are read. Under the mask the system and user text is still read as context for the next prediction; it just is not graded. Every character removes the mask, which is exactly pretraining's rule.
documents.title: You switch Loss on from Assistant reply only to Every character. What changes in the strip and its metrics?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Instruction tuning & templates · question 3
documents.body: You turn End-of-turn marker off and keep the mask on. What happens to the templated model's next-character list after a finished reply? The marker's share falls to the untrained level, because only the graded end marker taught it The marker's share stays high, because the role markers around each turn still teach where turns end The marker's share rises, because with no closing marker the model is less certain where a reply stops The list is empty, because a turn with no closing marker leaves the model nothing to condition on Under the mask only the reply and its closing end marker are graded, so the row for the full stop is trained only by that end marker. Remove it and the row is never updated, and returns the uniform one in thirty. The role markers sit before the reply, where nothing is graded, so they cannot teach where it ends. A model with no trained stop has no reason to end.
documents.title: You turn End-of-turn marker off and keep the mask on. What happens to the templated model's next-character list after a finished reply?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Instruction tuning & templates · question 4
documents.body: The templated model puts most of its probability on the marker after a full stop. Why is 'it knows the turn ended' too strong a description? The marker's letters never appear in the training pairs, so the probability must have come from the plain model A probability on one character can never show what a model has learned about a whole conversation It sees one previous character, so it has only learned that the row for a full stop points at the marker The angle brackets are stripped from everything typed, so the model has never seen a marker in training The model conditions on exactly one preceding character through a 30 by 30 table, so knowing a turn ended means the full-stop row learned to point at the marker. A real stop is one reserved id predicted from the whole conversation. The lab shows the mechanism that teaches a stop; it cannot show understanding.
documents.title: The templated model puts most of its probability on the marker after a full stop. Why is 'it knows the turn ended' too strong a description?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Instruction tuning & templates · question 5
documents.body: Under Serve with, you pick Chat template. The plain-trained model has never seen a closing bracket in training. What do its next-character bars show? Every character at the same probability, because the bracket's row was never trained The reply's first letters rank highest, because the markers show a model where a reply begins The same bars as the templated model, because both models trained on the same four pairs No bars at all, because a model refuses to continue a string it never saw in training Each model reads one character to choose the next. Plain concatenation never puts a bracket in front of anything, so that row of the plain model's table was never updated and stays uniform. The templated model trained on exactly this row, so the two sets of bars differ. Nothing errors, which is why a template mismatch is silent: the model simply answers from an untrained row.

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Instruction tuning & templates · question 6
documents.body: Chat template and Wrong role marker give identical bars and samples. What does that show about the lab, rather than about real models? Both strings end in the same bracket, and a one-character model cannot see which role came first Role markers carry no information for any model, so a real model would treat the two serves the same Loss masking erased the roles from the weights, so the markers no longer matter to any model Both models were retrained to one table, so every served string now produces the same bars The lab's models condition on a single preceding character, so a served string matters only through its last character. Both serves end in a bracket, so they read the same row. A real model reads the whole marker and would answer as the user. Switching to No template does change the bars, which rules out a retrained shared table.

documents.subtitle: Plain · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: When you type a question into a chatbot, it writes an answer, stops, and waits for your next message. That feels as natural as texting a friend, but the model underneath never sees chat bubbles or a send button. It receives one long line of text, and the one thing it has been trained to do is guess which piece of text comes next. So something has to turn your conversation into that single line, and the line has to show whose words are whose and where each reply ends. This module is about that layout, which is called a chat template, and about the extra round of training that teaches a model to use it. That training is what the module's title calls instruction tuning: practice on hand-picked examples of requests, each paired with a good reply. Where you have met it Each chat model is trained with its own template, which ships with the model so that the software running it can lay out your messages the same way. When a chatbot finishes its answer and stops instead of rambling on, that is because training taught it to write an end marker at that point. A template can also hold a block of instructions that comes before your message, such as "answer briefly and plainly", which is called a system prompt. Why it matters A model that has only learned from web pages is good at continuing text but poor at answering it. Ask it "how long should it simmer" and it may reply with another question, because on web pages one question is often followed by more questions. It also has no signal for when to stop, so it keeps writing and often makes up your next message itself. The template also has to match between training and use, and a mismatch is easy to miss. If an app lays out your messages differently from the way the model was trained, nothing crashes or shows an error, while the model quietly does a worse job. The markers matter for safety as well: a system prompt stays trusted only while ordinary typed text cannot copy the special labels around it. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these ideas in your own words: what a chat template adds to a plain question and answer, and why a model needs it; which part of the long line the model is trained to write, and which parts it only reads; what happens to where a model's replies stop if it trains without an end marker; what a trained model does next when it is given a layout it never trained on. What the lab lets you try The lab trains two tiny models on the same four questions and answers, about fog, a sauce, the weather by noon and how long to simmer something. One model sees them laid out with the chat template, while the other sees each question and answer run together as plain text. You can switch parts of the template on and off, choose which characters the model is graded on during training, and write your own examples. Then you can give both trained models a layout they never saw and watch what each one does next. The models are small enough to train instantly, so every number you see is really measured rather than made up. The four starting examples, the system sentence and one test reply are fixed text written for the lab. The markers are spelled out in letters rather than being special symbols. The models are also far simpler than a real chatbot, and the lesson points out where that changes what the numbers mean.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: One long line of text A chat model never receives a conversation, only one long run of characters, which programmers call a string. The chat template is the rule that decides exactly what that string looks like. Here is the first example in the lab with every part of the template switched on, split over three lines so you can read it: The model gets all of this as one unbroken line of 138 characters. Each of the three switches in Chat template editor adds or removes one kind of piece, and each switch shows in template or off: The System block switch puts <system> and the sentence "answer briefly and plainly." at the front. That sentence is the system prompt, a block of instructions that sits outside the user's turn. The Role markers switch adds labels called role markers, which say whose words each turn holds: <user> goes in front of the question and <assistant> in front of the answer. The End-of-turn marker switch closes every turn with <end>, including the system block when that is on. The question gets its <end> only while Role markers is on too, as step 1 below shows. A radio picture Picture two people talking on walkie-talkies, where only one of them can talk at a time, so they follow a routine. Each turn starts by saying who is talking, such as "this is base", and ends with the word "over" to hand the turn back. Those words carry no news, since their only job is to mark where a turn starts and ends. The markers do the same job, with <user> and <assistant> as the "this is base" part and <end> as the "over". The picture stops matching in two places. First, a person can say "over" in an ordinary sentence, such as "the game is over", and the listener has to work out which meaning was intended. In this lab that cannot happen, because < and > never appear in the lab's example text and are removed from anything you type, so a bracketed marker can only ever mean structure. Second, a radio operator already knows what "over" means, while a model gets nothing from <end> until training has shown it many examples of the marker in use. The tiny models in this lab Real chat models are huge, so the lab uses the smallest kind of model that can still show the idea. It works with only 30 characters: the space, the 26 letters, the full stop, the opening bracket < and the closing bracket >. Each model is a table with one row for each of those characters, and every row holds the odds for which character comes next. To make a guess, the model looks only at the last character and reads that character's row. If the last character is t, it reads the t row, which after training gives h by far the best odds because "the" is so common in the replies. The whole model is 30 rows of 30 numbers, which makes 900 numbers in all, while a real chat model looks back over the whole conversation before every guess. Both models start blank, with every row giving all 30 characters the same chance: 1 in 30, which is about 3.3%. Training changes a row only when the model is graded on a guess made from that row. As you will see below, the lab can choose to grade only some guesses. A row that is never used for a graded guess stays at an even 3.3% for every character. Keep that in mind, because it explains several of the most surprising results in the lab. The lab trains two of these tables side by side on the same four examples. The templated model trains on the chat template, while the plain model trains on each question and answer run together as plain text. Same guessing game, new layout Big language models are first trained on enormous amounts of text by guessing the next piece at every position, which is called pretraining. After each guess, training checks what really came next and gives a penalty that grows with how surprised the model was. That penalty is called the loss, and training works by nudging the model's numbers so that the loss gets smaller next time. The lab measures surprise in a unit called nats, and a perfect guess, which gave the right character a 100% chance, scores 0. Every time that chance is cut in half, the surprise goes up by about 0.69, so the lower the chance the model gave the right character, the higher its surprise. A model that spreads its odds evenly over all 30 characters scores about 3.40, which is the score of a model that has learned nothing at all. Supervised fine-tuning plays the same guessing game with the same penalty, but on a much smaller, hand-picked set of requests paired with good replies. It is called supervised because every example comes with the reply it should get, and fine-tuning because in real life it adjusts a model that pretraining has already trained. Two things change from pretraining: the text is laid out as turns with a chat template, and usually only the reply is graded. Graded, or only read The switch labelled Loss on decides which characters count toward the loss, and with Assistant reply only, the only graded ones are the reply and the <end> right after it. Everything before them, from the system prompt to the question and its markers, is still read, because each next guess is based on it. The model is never graded on guessing those characters, though. This is called loss masking, because a mask covers part of the line so that those guesses do not count. Every character removes the mask and grades every guess, which is exactly the rule pretraining uses. The same switch applies to the plain model, even though its text has no markers. The lab still knows which part of each plain line is the reply, so with Assistant reply only it grades the reply's characters and only reads the question. While the end marker is on, the templated model is also graded on the <end> after each reply, so the two models are not graded on quite the same characters. Picture a worksheet where you copy out each question and then write your answer underneath. You need the question in order to answer it, but only your answer earns marks, and nobody gets points for copying the question neatly. Loss masking grades a model the same way, and for the same reason: the goal is to get better at answering, not at writing questions. The strip under the switches shows the first example with one cell per character. Grey, hatched cells are "context only: read, never graded", while plain cells with a blue underline are "graded: in the loss". A line along the top of each cell shows whose turn the character belongs to. A bar inside the cell shows how surprised the trained model is by that character, on a scale from 0 to 5 nats. At the default settings, Graded characters reads 52 of 137. The total is 137 rather than 138 because the very first character has nothing in front of it to guess from, so it is never predicted. The 52 graded characters are the 47 characters of the reply "the fog settles over the harbor in the morning." plus the 5 characters of <end>. Markers as special symbols Real models do not read one character at a time; instead, they cut text into chunks called tokens, which are often whole words or pieces of words. Each token has its own id number, and a real template gives every marker a reserved id of its own, called a special token. That makes <end> one symbol rather than five characters. In this lab, by contrast, the markers are spelled out in characters, so <end> uses the same e, n and d rows as ordinary words like "the" and "and". Because <end> is graded, the marker and the words compete for those rows. For instance, the d row has to point at a space after "and" but at > inside <end>, so it cannot give either one the full odds. That sharing has a small cost, which you will see in the lab's reply scores.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Look at what the plain model trains on for the first example: "when does the fog arrive the fog settles over the harbor in the morning." Nothing in that line says where the question stops and the answer starts, and nothing comes after the final full stop. Text taken from web pages has the same gap, because it never says whose turn it is. The template adds two things that plain text cannot, and together they make instruction following learnable. Instruction following means writing a reply to a request instead of carrying on with the request's own text. A model picks this up from formatted examples like the ones in this lab, not from more pretraining. A starting line for the reply The first thing the template adds is a clear starting line: after <assistant>, everything is the model's own output, and that is exactly the part the mask grades. When you chat, the app sends your question followed by <assistant>. That puts the model in the same spot where training made it practise writing replies, so a reply is what comes next. A signal to stop The second thing is an end-of-turn token, a marker the model learns to write when a reply is finished. The part of the software that generates a reply, called the decoder, picks one piece of text at a time and keeps going until it reaches a stop signal. If the model never learned to write that signal, the decoder has nothing to stop on, so the model keeps writing and often invents the user's next question itself. Picture two campers on walkie-talkies, and one of them has never learned to say "over". They finish their news, keep holding the button, and then start guessing what their friend might say back, because nothing in their routine tells them to hand the turn over. A model trained without <end> runs on in the same way, because nothing in its training marks the point where a reply ends. The picture stops matching in one way. The camper is guessing on purpose, while a model is not trying to do anything. A real model writes a fake user turn only because, in conversation text, a user's message is what usually comes next. The lab's tiny model cannot show even that: with no <end> and the mask on, its row for the full stop is untrained. So the character it writes right after a reply is a pure guess, with every character equally likely. Why only the reply is graded The mask exists because the model is meant to write replies, not user messages. If every character were graded, the model would also practise writing the questions and markers that the user and the app supply. That practice can then show up in the wrong place, as the lab shows. When every character is graded, the templated model also practises guessing what comes after each >. In its training text, <end> is followed straight away by <user> or <assistant>. So it learns that the closing bracket is often followed by an opening one. A reply starts right after the > of <assistant>, so the model may open its reply with a marker instead of a word.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: The lab follows five steps, and each one below says what to change and what to watch. Edit the template Turn System block, Role markers and End-of-turn marker on and off one at a time, and watch the strip gain and lose structure. For example, turn off only Role markers, and the line becomes this: Now the question runs straight into the answer with a single space between them, so nothing shows where one ends and the other begins. Turn all three switches off, and the strip shows exactly the plain text that the plain model trains on. Watch the count as well: with End-of-turn marker off, Graded characters drops from 52 to 47, since the reply no longer has an <end> after it to grade. Read the loss mask With every switch back on, find <assistant> in the strip, and you will see the graded cells begin right after it, at the t of "the". Try this: switch Loss on between Assistant reply only and Every character, and read the three numbers under the strip. With the mask on, Graded characters reads 52 of 137. Beside it, Mean −log p, graded reads 2.11 nats, while Mean −log p, context reads 2.92 nats. The label "−log p" is the lab's short way of writing the surprise score from earlier, and "mean" means average. Here p is the chance the model gave the right character. Later you will see log-prob, written log p, which is the same number with the sign flipped, so it is negative. A surprise of 2.11 is what you would get if the model gave each right character about a 1 in 8 chance. You can check this with the halving rule, since getting from 100% down to 1 in 8 takes three halvings. Three steps of 0.69 add up to about 2.1. A surprise of 2.92 is closer to 1 in 18, so the context characters are much harder for the model to predict. That makes sense, because the model is never graded on them, so only the letter pairs they share with the replies get any practice. Switch to Every character, and all 137 characters are graded, so Mean −log p, context reads "none" because no character is left ungraded. The graded average becomes 1.99 nats, which is close to a 1 in 7 chance. Set Loss on back to Assistant reply only before you move on, because the numbers in the next steps assume the mask is on. Fine-tune on your pairs In Supervised dataset editor, each line is one example, written as instruction | response. The request goes to the left of the upright line |, and the reply it should get goes to the right. Everything you type is made lowercase. Digits, commas and other symbols turn into spaces, and brackets are removed, because the models only use 30 characters. The editor keeps up to 16 lines of 200 characters each, and a line with no | drops out, which you can spot in the Examples count. The SFT epochs slider (SFT is short for supervised fine-tuning) sets how many times training works through all the examples, and one full pass through them is called an epoch. You can choose anywhere from 1 to 80 passes. Move it and watch the readout “<” after the full stop in Two models, two formats, which gives each model's chance of starting <end> after the reply's last full stop. With the four starting pairs, the templated model gives that marker about a 6% chance at 4 epochs. At the default of 30 epochs that rises to 54%, and at 80 epochs it reaches 88%. The end of a turn is learned gradually, like any other pattern in the examples. The same card shows Reply log-prob per char, templated, the log-prob from step 2. So −2.228 at the defaults means an average surprise of 2.228 per character of the reply, and closer to zero is better. It moves towards zero as the passes rise. At 4 epochs it is about −3.02, close to a 1 in 20 chance for each right character. At 80 epochs it reaches about −1.87, which is nearer to 1 in 6. The chart above it shows each model's loss falling as training goes on. Its bottom axis counts optimizer steps, where each step is a single nudge to the table based on a small batch of graded guesses. Each point on the chart averages a few steps. The two training curves grade different characters, so the chart's own note warns that they are not a ranking of which model is better. The same note gives the counts for one pass over the examples: 191 graded guesses for the templated model against 171 for the plain one. The extra 20 are the five characters of <end> at the end of each of the four replies. Graded targets, in Supervised dataset editor, shows the templated count, and it jumps to 528 when Loss on is set to Every character. Before you move on, delete any line you added and set SFT epochs back to 30. The numbers in the next steps assume the four starting pairs at 30 passes. Break the boundary Turn End-of-turn marker off, keep the mask on, and compare the two lists under What follows the end of a turn. Each list shows the five characters a model gives the best odds right after the full stop that ends the first reply. The templated model is on top, and the plain model is below. With the marker on, the templated model's top bar is < at 54.4%, the first character of <end>. With it off, the upper list goes flat like the lower one. Every character, < included, gets 3.3%, so the list shows only the first five characters in order: space, a, b, c and d. The readout “<” after the full stop drops to 3% for both models. Turn the marker back on before the last step, since its numbers assume the full template. Serve a different format Using a trained model to answer prompts is called serving it, and the card Serve the trained models does that with both of the lab's models. It sends them the first example, cut off right where the reply should begin. The box shows the exact string sent, with its last character highlighted. Each model reads only that last character, so that one character decides what each model does next. Try this: switch Serve with between Chat template, No template and Wrong role marker, and watch the readout First reply character “t”, templated vs plain. Under Chat template, the reply's first letter t gets 18% from the templated model and only 3% from the plain one. The plain model never saw a > in front of anything during training, so its > row was never trained and spreads its odds evenly. No template sends only the question and a space, and then the templated model reads 22% while the plain one reads 25%. The plain model does well here because in its training a single space sat right before every reply. Wrong role marker puts <user> where <assistant> belongs, and you will find it gives exactly the same results as Chat template; "What to notice" explains why. Serving a model with a layout that differs from the one it trained on is called a template mismatch. Above the bars, each model also writes a short piece of text, called a sample, by picking one character at a time, with likelier characters picked more often. A note under each sample says where a decoder watching for markers would stop. Last, set Loss on to Every character and serve Chat template again. The templated model now puts 37% on < right after the closing >, and its sample opens with a marker instead of a reply. A decoder watching for markers would stop at once, leaving an empty reply. This happens because, with every switch on, each training example has two places where a closing bracket is followed by <, inside <end><user> and <end><assistant>. Grading those characters taught the model that a bracket is often followed by another marker.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Where a reply ends With the full template and the mask, the templated model puts 54.4% on < right after a reply's full stop, so its likeliest next step is to start <end>. The plain model gives every character 3.3% at that same spot, because its row for the full stop was never trained. In its training, nothing ever came after a reply's last full stop, so nothing in that row says to stop. Turn End-of-turn marker off with the mask still on, and the templated model drops to 3.3% too. The graded <end> was the only thing teaching it where a reply ends. The role markers cannot do that job, because they sit before the reply, where nothing is graded. Switch to Every character with the end marker still off, and the templated model is back to 55% on <, even with no <end> in its data. It learned that from the system prompt, where "plainly." is followed by <user>, which is a boundary it was never meant to be graded on. The masked result is cleaner, because there the model learns where a reply ends from replies alone. A tall bar for the opening bracket means the model will probably start a marker, not that it will spell <end> correctly. The rest of the marker is still predicted one character at a time. What the mask changes Under the mask, the context characters (the system prompt, the markers and the question) average 2.92 nats, against 2.11 for the graded reply. Nothing trains the model to predict them directly. The question still improves as a side effect. Its characters, spaces included, average about 2.50 nats, well below the 3.40 of a blank model. That is because letter pairs like "th" and "he" in "the fog" also appear in the replies, so the question uses rows that the replies trained. The point of the mask is where the training effort goes: into writing replies, not into writing the user's side of the chat. What the template costs and buys The template costs the reply a little: Reply log-prob per char, templated reads −2.228, while Reply log-prob per char, plain reads −2.168, slightly closer to zero. Both of those scores work out to roughly a 1 in 9 chance per character, so the gap is small. It has two causes in this tiny model. First, the graded <end> uses the same e, n and d rows as the reply's letters, so those rows split their odds between the marker and ordinary words. Second, the reply's first letter is guessed from the > row, which has had far less training than the space row the plain model uses. The <assistant> letters themselves are not graded under the mask, so they train nothing. With Every character, the gap grows to −2.425 against −2.129, because grading the prompt makes the templated model spend more of those shared rows on the markers. What the template buys in return is a known place where every turn starts and ends. The readout “<” after the full stop shows it: 54% for the templated model, against 3% for the plain one, which has never seen <end>. Serving a different format A plain-trained model served the chat template does not crash or show an error. It answers from a row that nobody trained, so all of its next-character bars sit flat at 3.3%. Taking the template away even raises the templated model's score for t, from 18% with the template to 22% with No template. In this toy that is an accident of reading one character, because its space row was trained on the spaces between the replies' own words. It does not mean templates are optional. Chat template and Wrong role marker give identical bars and samples. Both strings end in >, and a model that reads one character cannot tell <user> from <assistant>, while a model that reads the whole marker can. The samples look like scraps of words rather than sentences, because a model that sees one character can only learn which letters tend to follow which. At the defaults, the templated sample writes a few scraps, reaches a full stop, and starts a marker right after it. Held-out reply, log-prob per char, templated vs plain scores a reply that appears in none of the training pairs, "the rain stops before noon." It reads −2.86 for the templated model and −2.87 for the plain one. Compare the templated −2.86 with −2.23, which Reply log-prob per char, templated gives the first trained reply. That gap is roughly the difference between a 1 in 17 chance and a 1 in 9 chance for each character. Scores on training data flatter a model, the same way that grading yourself on the exact questions you practised would flatter you. A common mix-up: the mask does not hide the question from the model. Masked characters are still read, and they are exactly what each next guess is based on; the mask only takes them out of the grade. In the worksheet picture, you still read each question in order to answer it, and the teacher does not mark your copy of it.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Every number in this lab is really trained and measured, so none of it is made up. What is missing is size, and that limits what the numbers can mean. Each model looks at one character to guess the next. So "it knows the turn ended" means only that the row for . learned to point at <, the first character of <end>. A real model predicts a single stop symbol from the whole conversation. Four examples is not a dataset, while real fine-tuning uses thousands to millions of pairs. Both models start from blank tables, instead of from a model that pretraining has already taught. The markers are spelled in letters instead of being single reserved ids, so <end> shares rows with ordinary text. The system prompt is one fixed sentence, the strip shows only the first example, and only the end of the first reply is probed. Serving is tested through one character only, because each model reads the last character of the served string. A template mismatch therefore shows up as one different row of the table. That means the real cost of a mismatch cannot appear here: a real model reads the whole unfamiliar prompt again at every step of its reply. Each sample picks characters at random, with likelier characters picked more often, but the lab reuses the same random numbers every time. A sample therefore changes only when the trained table or the served string changes. Either way, you see one possible reply rather than a typical one, and the held-out reply is one sentence, so neither tells you much on its own. The two reply scores cover the same characters and are divided by the same count, which makes them fair to compare. They still come from two differently laid-out datasets, so treat the gap between them as a hint rather than proof. Where real systems fail Serving a model with the wrong template is a common failure, and it is silent. Nothing errors; the model receives a string unlike anything it trained on, and the quality of its answers sags. Picture a student who practised for weeks with quizzes where every question started with "Q:" and every answer space started with "A:". On test day the paper uses a new layout, so the student still writes answers but makes more slips, and nothing on the paper says the layout caused them. A model served the wrong template is in the same spot, except that it cannot notice the change at all. A serving system that builds prompts by gluing text together can also turn <end> into five ordinary characters instead of the reserved id. The two look identical in the printed record of what was sent, so the bug is hard to spot, but the model never receives the marker it was trained on. Stopping also depends on the serving software, which keeps a list of stop signals to watch for. If the stop id is missing from that list, nothing halts the reply when the marker appears, and the model runs on into an invented next turn. There is a security side as well, since a system prompt only counts as instructions because the template and the training data agreed to treat it that way. If the software turns a marker that a user typed into the real marker id, the user's text can pretend to be a system turn. Picture a group chat where messages from the admin appear in a special gold box. If anyone could type a short code that put their own message in the gold box, the box would stop meaning anything. Reserved ids only protect a system prompt when the serving software keeps them out of user text.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: How real templates ship Real models ship their template as a small piece of code, stored in the settings of the tokenizer, which is the part that cuts text into tokens. The software that runs the model uses it to lay out every conversation. When it is time to write a reply, the template also adds the opening assistant marker after your message, so the model starts writing in the right place. Adding a brand-new marker needs a new token id and a new row of numbers inside the model for that id, so it changes the size of the model itself. Masking is a choice Most fine-tuning recipes grade only the assistant's turns, but some research finds that grading the instructions too can help when replies are short and examples are scarce. So the mask is a setting to test, not a law. What the examples teach The superficial alignment hypothesis is an idea about what this kind of training really does. Here "alignment" means getting a model to behave the way people want when it talks with users, and a hypothesis is an idea that researchers propose and then test. This one says that a model learns nearly all its knowledge and skills during pretraining, and that later tuning mostly teaches it which format and style of reply to use. The idea comes from a 2023 paper by Zhou and colleagues, called LIMA, short for "Less Is More for Alignment". They fine-tuned a large model called LLaMA, with about 65 billion adjustable numbers, on only 1,000 carefully chosen pairs of prompts and replies. For comparison, each model in this lab has 900 adjustable numbers. Smaller tests on a model with 7 billion numbers pointed the same way. The researchers trained it on 2,000 examples from the Stack Exchange question-and-answer sites, picked only from good-quality posts. That raised a helpfulness score by about half a point on a six-point scale, compared with 2,000 examples picked without that quality check. Doubling the amount of data, on the other hand, did not make the replies better. The scores in those tests were given by another AI model, ChatGPT, rather than by people. So treat the results as evidence for the idea about format and style, not as proof that fine-tuning adds no knowledge. Conversations with many turns The lab's examples each have one question and one answer, but real chats go back and forth. In a real chat the template repeats: a user block, an assistant block, then a user block again. The masking rule stretches to fit, because the whole conversation is trained as one string, every assistant turn is graded, and every user turn is read as context. Multi-turn data, meaning training conversations with several turns each, matters because a model tuned only on single questions can lose the thread. In the LIMA paper, one model was tuned on 1,000 examples that each had a single turn. That model stopped following the prompt within three exchanges in 6 of the 10 test chats. Adding only 30 multi-turn conversations raised the share of excellent replies from 45.2% to 76.1%. That is a jump from fewer than half of the replies to about three in every four. Packing Real models read text in windows of a fixed length, called the context window. A short example leaves most of the window empty, and that space is filled with blank filler called padding, which the computer still has to work through. Packing glues several short examples into one sequence to fill the window instead. That can save a lot of work, because Krell and colleagues found that up to half of the tokens in common training datasets can be padding. Packing needs care, though, because each example still needs its own end marker. The model must also be blocked from looking back across the join, or one example can read the one before it as if they were one conversation. In this lab every example is its own sequence, so nothing is packed and no guess ever crosses from one example into the next.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: This module is about the format of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data for chat. SFT keeps pretraining's next-token loss and changes two things: a chat template lays out each instruction and response with markers for the system prompt, each speaker's turn and the end of a turn, and a loss mask decides which parts are graded. The question is what that layout teaches that plain text cannot: where a reply starts, where it stops, and whose words are whose. It builds on *Fine-tuning & transfer*, which trained existing weights on new data, and *Post-training*, where SFT is the first stage after pretraining. Where it shows up Model releases. Models ship their template as code, usually a Jinja chat_template in the tokenizer configuration. SFT recipes. Most grade only the assistant turns, including every assistant turn of a multi-turn conversation. Tokenizers. Each marker gets a dedicated id, a special token, so it can mean only structure as long as the serving stack never produces that id from user text. Serving stacks. Inference libraries render the model's template and append the opening assistant marker, so generation starts in the right place. Why it matters Pretraining teaches a model to continue text, not to take turns, so answering a request instead of extending it has to be learned from formatted examples. The format also has to survive deployment. Serving a model with a format it did not train on raises no error, so the damage is easy to miss, and a marker that user text can forge undoes the system prompt's privilege. What you will be able to explain What a chat template adds to raw completion data. Which part of the sequence the model is asked to produce, and which parts it only reads. What training without an end-of-turn marker does to a model's sense of where a reply stops. How serving a trained model with a format it did not train on changes what it does next. What the lab shows Two tiny models train live on the same pairs, budget and loss rule: one on templated text, one on plain concatenation. Each is a character bigram, a 30 × 30 table of logits trained from zero, so it predicts from one preceding character. Every number is trained and measured. The default pairs, the system sentence and the held-out reply are fixed text, and markers are spelled in letters rather than reserved ids. In Chat template editor, System block, Role markers and End-of-turn marker edit the string, Loss on picks Assistant reply only or Every character, and the strip marks each character as graded or context only. Supervised dataset editor takes your own pairs and SFT epochs, and Two models, two formats compares the two runs. The key experiment is the stop signal. At the defaults, under What follows the end of a turn, the templated model puts most of its probability on < after a reply's full stop, while the plain model's row is untrained. With Loss on at Assistant reply only, switch End-of-turn marker off and the templated row is untrained too. Then, under Serve the trained models, switch Serve with between Chat template, No template and Wrong role marker, remembering that each model sees only the served string's last character.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Supervised fine-tuning is next-token training on curated instruction-and-response pairs. The per-token loss is the same cross-entropy used in pretraining. Two things change: the text is formatted as a conversation, and usually only the reply is graded. A chat template is the exact string a list of messages becomes. The three switches in Chat template editor each add or remove one part: System block prepends a system prompt, Role markers wrap the turns in <user> and <assistant>, and End-of-turn marker closes every turn with <end>. Which characters are graded Loss masking is the second half. With Loss on set to Assistant reply only, the loss counts only the reply and the <end> that closes it. The system text, the user's words and their markers are read as context — they condition the next prediction — but the model is never graded on predicting them. Every character switches the mask off, which is exactly pretraining's rule. The strip draws the first example one character per cell. At the defaults 52 of its 137 predicted characters are graded. The markers are reserved symbols The vocabulary is 30 characters: space, a–z, a full stop, and < and >. The angle brackets appear in no corpus and are stripped from anything you type, so <user> and <end> can only ever mean structure. A real tokenizer gets the same property from dedicated special token ids. Here the markers are spelled in letters, so <end> shares the rows for e, n and d with ordinary text. A real marker is one id with its own row.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Scraped text does not say whose turn it is. Asked "how long should it simmer", a raw predictor may continue with another question, because that is what follows questions on a page. The template supplies two things plain concatenation cannot, and instruction following is the behaviour they make learnable. First, a boundary: after <assistant>, everything is the model's own output, and that is exactly the span the mask grades. Second, an end-of-turn token for the decoder to stop on. Without it generation does not end; the model keeps writing, often inventing the next user turn.

The plain model puts 3.3% on every character there: nothing ever followed a full stop in its data, so that row never trained. Switch End-of-turn marker off, keeping the mask, and the templated model falls to 3.3% too. The only thing that taught it to expect a marker was the graded <end>. With Every character, the end marker off still leaves 55% on <. The model learned it from the system prompt's plainly. followed by <user> — a boundary it was never meant to be graded on. The mask changes what is learned about the prompt. Context characters stay surprising, 2.92 nats against 2.11, because the model is not trained to write user turns. documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: In this lab. Every number is trained and measured. The model conditions on one preceding character through 900 logits, so "knowing a turn ended" means one thing: the row for . points at <. Four examples is not a dataset, both models start from zero rather than from a pretrained base, and markers are characters, not ids. Serving is probed, but only through one character. Each model reads the last character of the served string, so a template mismatch shows up as one different table row. The cost real models pay, reading a whole unfamiliar prompt at every position, cannot appear. Each sample is one seed at one temperature, and the held-out reply is a single sentence. The two reply scores cover the same characters, divided by the same count, each conditioned on its own format. That makes them comparable, but they still come from two differently formatted datasets, so read the gap as a hint. In real systems. Template mismatch is the common failure and it is silent: the model receives a string from a distribution it never trained on, and quality sags. A serving stack that builds prompts by string concatenation can also tokenize <end> as ordinary characters instead of the reserved id, which looks identical in a log. Forgeability is the security version. A system prompt is privileged only because the template and the training data agreed to treat it that way. If the tokenizer turns a typed marker into the real id, user text can claim to be a system turn. Reserved ids close that hole only when the serving stack keeps them out of user text.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Instruction tuning & templates
documents.body: Models ship their template as code, usually a Jinja chat_template in the tokenizer configuration, and inference libraries render it. At generation time the template also appends the opening assistant marker, so the model starts in the right place. Masking is a choice, not a law. Most SFT recipes grade only assistant turns. Some work finds that also grading the instruction helps when replies are short and data is scarce, so treat the mask as a hyperparameter. What SFT data teaches The superficial alignment hypothesis is the proposal that a model's knowledge and capabilities are learned almost entirely in pretraining, and that alignment teaches which format of response to use with users. Zhou et al. (2023, "LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment", arXiv 2305.11206) tested it by fine-tuning a 65B-parameter LLaMA model on 1,000 curated prompt-and-response pairs. Their ablations on a 7B model point the same way. Filtering 2,000 Stack Exchange examples for quality moved a ChatGPT-graded helpfulness score by about 0.5 points on a six-point scale, while doubling the amount of data did not improve response quality. Read this as evidence for a hypothesis about format and style, graded by a model, not as proof that SFT adds no knowledge. Multi-turn data The lab's examples have one instruction and one reply. Real chat data has several turns, and the template repeats: a user block, an assistant block, a user block again. The masking rule extends directly: train the conversation as one sequence, grade every assistant turn, and read every user turn as context. Multi-turn data matters because single-turn tuning can lose the thread. In the LIMA paper, a model tuned on 1,000 single-turn examples failed to follow the prompt within three interactions in 6 of 10 test conversations. Adding 30 multi-turn chains raised the share of excellent responses from 45.2% to 76.1%. Packing Packing fills the context window by concatenating short examples into one sequence. It saves compute: Krell et al. (arXiv 2107.02027) found that up to 50% of the tokens in common NLP datasets can be padding. It also needs care. Each example still needs its own end marker, and unless the attention mask blocks attention across the boundary, one example can read the one before it. Here every example is its own sequence, so nothing is packed and no transition crosses from one example into the next. A new marker needs a new token id and a new embedding row, so adding one resizes the model.

The templated model scores the reply slightly lower even with the mask, because the letters of `<assistant>` and `<end>` compete with the reply's letters for the same rows. With `<end>` in the template, the templated model piles probability on the reserved `<`; the plain model has never seen anything follow a reply. A kicker naming the boundary character, a full stop for the default pairs. Two bar lists of the top five next characters: the templated model above, the plain model below, each with its probability. A note that states what each model saw after that character in training. Both lists softmax one row of the trained table: the row for the reply's last character. Each example is its own sequence, so the plain model's full-stop row receives no gradient and stays uniform, 1/30 per character, unless a full stop also appears mid-reply. Under `Assistant reply only`, only a graded `<end>` can train the full-stop row of the templated model. Turn the end marker off and that row is untrained too. No knobs of its own. The switches, `Loss on`, the pairs and `SFT epochs` retrain both distributions. Comparison worth running: at the defaults the templated `<` reads 54.4%. Turn `End-of-turn marker` off and it falls to 3.3%, the uniform value. With `Every character` and the end marker off it stays at 55%, learned from the system prompt's full stop followed by `<user>`. A high `<` bar means the model wants to start a marker, not that it will spell `<end>` correctly. The rest of the marker is predicted character by character. The masked result is cleaner: the model learns end-of-reply from replies only, not from the system text. If the first reply does not end in a full stop, the probe moves to its last character. documents.body: The same weights, served a string they did not train on Both trained tables are probed with one serving string at a time: the chat template, the bare instruction, or the template with the user marker where the assistant marker belongs. Each model reads one character, so what changes is the table row of the last character sent. Next-character bars, a seeded sample cut at the first marker, and two readouts show what that row holds. `Serve with`, a three-way switch: `Chat template`, `No template` and `Wrong role marker`. A box with the exact string sent, its last character marked, and a line naming the one character each model reads. Two samples, templated above and plain below, at temperature 0.6, length 90 and seed 17 with markers shown. Each has a note on where its first marker falls, because a marker is the stop signal. Two bar lists of the five likeliest next characters, one per model, for the served string. Two readouts written `templated vs plain`: the probability of the first reply character, and the log-probability per character of a held-out reply. The served string is the training prompt cut before the first reply character: `renderExample` with a stand-in reply, so the system block, role markers and closing marker follow the switches. `No template` is the instruction and one space. `Wrong role marker` replaces `<assistant>` with `<user>`, or appends `<user>` when role markers are off. The bars are the softmax row of the string's last character. The first-reply probability reads that row at the reply's first character. The held-out score is the mean log-probability of `the rain stops before noon.` written after the served string, computed by the same function as `Reply log-prob per char`. Both samples use the SDK sampler with reserved characters allowed and the same seed, so any difference comes from the weights and the string. `Serve with` changes only the string. Comparison worth running: at the defaults the first reply character `t` gets 18% from the templated model and 3% from the plain model under `Chat template`, and 22% and 25% under `No template`. Then set `Loss on` to `Every character` and serve the chat template: the templated model puts 37% on `<` after the bracket, because grading the prompt taught it that a bracket is followed by a marker. `Chat template` and `Wrong role marker` give identical bars and samples: both strings end in a closing bracket, which is all either model reads. Dropping the template does not hurt the templated model here, because its space row was trained on the replies' own words. That is a property of the toy, not of templates. documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: A claim that specific components, connected in a specific way, implement a specific behavior. Supporting one requires intervention, not observation.
documents.title: Circuit

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Copying one activation from a clean run into a corrupted run and re-running the rest of the model, to test whether that activation carried the information the behavior depended on.
documents.title: Activation patching

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: A head that attends from the current token to the token after its previous occurrence and copies it, so A B … A predicts B. It relies on an earlier head that writes each token's predecessor into its position.
documents.title: Induction head

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: A head that attends from each position to the token just before it, so the position carries a note of what came before. An induction head in a later layer reads those notes to find the token after an earlier match.
documents.title: Previous-token head

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Removing or zeroing a component and measuring the damage. It answers whether the component is necessary in that setting, not what it computes or where information is stored.
documents.title: Ablation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Replacing an activation with its average over a reference set rather than zero. It reduces the distribution shift that makes zero-ablation overstate damage, though the answer still depends on which reference set is averaged.
documents.title: Mean ablation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Patching a single connection between two components rather than a location, which distinguishes a component mattering from it mattering through a particular route.
documents.title: Path patching

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Estimating a whole patching sweep with a first-order gradient approximation: two forward passes and one backward pass instead of one forward pass per patched location, at some cost in accuracy.
documents.title: Attribution patching

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: The gap between the logits of the right answer and one specific wrong answer. A useful metric moves a lot between clean and corrupted runs; one that barely moves makes every recovery ratio meaningless.
documents.title: Logit difference

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: A pair of minimally different prompts, one producing the behavior and one not. Their contrast is what makes a patching result interpretable.
documents.title: Clean and corrupted run

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Adding a direction to the residual stream during generation to shift behavior. Testing both directions is stronger evidence than a one-sided effect.
documents.title: Steering

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Restating a hypothesis as which computations may be swapped without changing behavior, then performing every permitted swap. It makes circuit claims falsifiable.
documents.title: Causal scrubbing

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Other components compensating when one is ablated, sometimes called backup behavior. It means a small measured effect does not prove a small role.
documents.title: Self-repair

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Whether an identified subgraph reproduces the behavior on its own. Evaluated alongside completeness and minimality when judging any circuit claim. Not the same as reasoning-trace faithfulness in ICL & reasoning, which asks whether a written explanation reflects the computation behind the answer.
documents.title: Faithfulness

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability II: circuits · question 1
documents.body: At period 8 the key an induction head would read is exactly 7 letters back, so a head that always looked 7 back would draw the same map. What tells the two stories apart? The weight on the green key at period 8, since a fixed look-back would not put any weight there The copy accuracy at period 8, since only a content-based head could produce an accuracy that high The stripe at an unseen period such as 13, which moves to the new key, not 7 back The previous-letter column at period 8, since a fixed look-back would leave that column at zero At period 8 the key after the previous occurrence is also 7 back, so both stories draw the same map and both copy well; neither the weight on that key nor the accuracy can separate them. Changing the period moves the previous occurrence but not a fixed distance, so the stories now disagree. At period 13, a length the model's repeated-string training never used, the outlines and the weights both move to 12 back, which is what a content-based head predicts. The previous-letter column measures a different head.
documents.title: At period 8 the key an induction head would read is exactly 7 letters back, so a head that always looked 7 back would draw the same map. What tells the two stories apart?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability II: circuits · question 2
documents.body: L1 H4 puts nearly all its attention on the previous letter, and L2 H3 puts its on the key after the previous occurrence. What do you expect to happen to L2 H3's attention when L1 H4 is switched off? It falls sharply, because L2 H3 reads the notes about each letter's predecessor that layer 1 writes It stays the same, because a head's attention is fixed by its own weights and not by what earlier layers write It moves to the previous letter, because the nearest letter is the next best match for the query It stays the same, because heads in different layers work on separate copies of the sequence Attention in layer 2 is computed from the residual stream that layer 1 leaves behind, not from the raw letters. If L1 H4 no longer writes each letter's predecessor into its position, a layer-2 head has fewer notes to match against and its weight on the green key drops. The lab shows this: at period 8 it falls from about 0.67 to 0.24. L1 H3 is a second previous-letter head, and with both off almost none is left, so no single layer-1 head carries the whole job.
documents.title: L1 H4 puts nearly all its attention on the previous letter, and L2 H3 puts its on the key after the previous occurrence. What do you expect to happen to L2 H3's attention when L1 H4 is switched off?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability II: circuits · question 3
documents.body: With the letter to copy corrupted, restoring the clean vector at that position after block 1 brings back almost all of the gap, while restoring the last position after block 1 brings back almost none. What does that show? Block 1 plays no part in copying, since restoring its output at the last position changes nothing After block 1 the letter is carried at the earlier position, and block 2 reads it from there The earlier position is the only one that matters at any layer, so the recoveries must add to 100% The last position is unimportant, because the model could produce the answer without reading it Patching pastes one clean vector into the corrupted run and measures how much of the metric returns, so a large recovery at one cell says the information the metric needs sits there. Here it sits at the earlier position, where layer 2's induction heads read it; the last position does not hold it yet after block 1. That is a statement about this cell and this prompt pair: it does not say block 1 is idle, and recoveries from different cells need not add to 100%. After block 2 the last position recovers everything by construction, because nothing later reads other positions.
documents.title: With the letter to copy corrupted, restoring the clean vector at that position after block 1 brings back almost all of the gap, while restoring the last position after block 1 brings back almost none. What does that show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability II: circuits · question 4
documents.body: Switching off L1 H2 costs copy accuracy as much as switching off L1 H4, yet L1 H2 attends two letters back, not one. What is the careful conclusion? L1 H2 is the induction head, because whichever head's removal costs the most is the one doing the copying itself L1 H2 must be a second previous-token head after all, because only those heads can hurt copying this much L1 H2 is unrelated to copying, because it does not attend to the previous letter, so the drop must be an artefact L1 H2 is needed for copying here, but this does not show what it computes or that it joins the same route Ablation measures necessity: on these prompts the model copies much worse without L1 H2, and the drop survives mean ablation, so it is not just a zeroing artefact. It does not say what L1 H2 computes, or whether it feeds the induction heads through the same route as L1 H4; the lab even finds that L1 H2's own attention is not on the previous letter. Telling a head that is needed from a head that implements the story takes path patching or a causal test of the whole hypothesis.
documents.title: Switching off L1 H2 costs copy accuracy as much as switching off L1 H4, yet L1 H2 attends two letters back, not one. What is the careful conclusion?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability II: circuits · question 5
documents.body: With L2 H3 switched off, copy accuracy is much lower under zero-ablation than under mean ablation. Why would the two disagree? The mean is taken over the prompt under test itself, so it restores the head's real output at every position Mean ablation leaves the head partly in place, so only zero-ablation really removes it from the model Zero is a value the next layers never saw, so part of the damage is the model reacting to unfamiliar input One of the two is a bug, because removing a head should give the same answer whatever replaces its output Both are interventions with a free choice of what replaces the head's output, and neither is ground truth. Zero is arbitrary and later components may rely on typical values, so zero-ablation can overstate the damage; the mean comes from other random repeats, not the prompt under test, and keeps the head's average contribution. Here L2 H3 costs less under the mean, while L1 H2, L1 H3 and L1 H4 stay costly under both. When the two agree on which heads matter the claim is stronger, and the sizes are not reliable.
documents.title: With L2 H3 switched off, copy accuracy is much lower under zero-ablation than under mean ablation. Why would the two disagree?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability II: circuits · question 6
documents.body: In Activation patching, set Corrupt to An unrelated letter. A few grid cells show large recoveries, though the final answer barely changed. Why should you not read them? Recoveries above 100% mean the patch made the model better than its clean run, which is real evidence of a second route Recovery divides by the gap between the two runs, which is tiny here, so small shifts become huge percentages The grid colour is clipped at 100%, so the large cells are drawing errors, not computed values Patching only works when the corrupted run gets the answer wrong, and with this corruption it still did Recovery is (patched − corrupted) ÷ (clean − corrupted). An unrelated letter moves the metric by well under a logit, so rounding-level changes in the numerator become large ratios, and the cells describe noise rather than a mechanism. The colour does saturate at 100%, but the exact values are printed. Check the gap before reading any cell, and choose a corruption that changes the answer, as the letter to copy does: its gap is several logits.
documents.title: In Activation patching, set Corrupt to An unrelated letter. A few grid cells show large recoveries, though the final answer barely changed. Why should you not read them?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: When you ask a chatbot a question, the reply comes from a language model, a program that writes by predicting text one small piece at a time. Inside it are many small working parts, and nobody gave those parts their jobs by hand, because its internal numbers were set automatically while it learned from example text. So even the people who build a model cannot point to the part that handles a particular task. This module is about finding out which of those parts a behavior really depends on. Looking inside a model shows you which parts are busy while it works, which is useful but not enough. A part can be busy without the answer depending on it at all. To learn what the answer really depends on, you have to change something inside the model on purpose and see whether the output changes too. Researchers run these tests on real models, and one well-known study traced how a model picks which of two names should come next in a sentence. It found a whole team of parts doing the job, including backup parts that step in when the main ones are switched off. The same tests help with safety work, such as finding where inside a model the decision to refuse a request gets made. They can also check whether extra training really removed an ability from a model or only stopped it from showing. This matters because, without these tests, any explanation of a model's insides would be a convincing story with no way to catch it when it is wrong. With them, a story has to predict what will happen when you change something, and a prediction can fail, which is what makes a story worth trusting once it passes. The parts this module studies are called attention heads, small units that each decide, at every letter, which earlier letters to look back at. By the end, you will be able to explain: how two kinds of attention heads, one in each of a small model's two stages, called layers, team up so that the model can copy a repeating pattern; how to spot those heads in a picture of attention, and how to test the idea on a repeat length the model never saw in training; how switching parts off, called ablation, and swapping values between two runs of the model, called activation patching, test what an answer truly depends on; why every claim about the inside of a model comes with limits, and which limits apply to the tests in this lab. The lab runs a real, small language model, the same one the Attention lab uses, on a copying puzzle. The model sees a block of capital letters repeated several times, such as QXZRKWMP three times in a row, and has to guess the letter that comes next. The lab has three cards, which you will work through in order: Copy task and attention shows how well the model copies and where each of its eight attention heads looks. Head ablation lets you switch heads off, one at a time or a whole layer at once, and measures how much worse the copying gets. Activation patching runs the model on a normal prompt and on a broken copy, swaps one piece between them, and measures how much of the right answer comes back. Every number in the lab is measured live from the model as you change the settings, using one fixed puzzle for each repeat length from 6 to 13. There are two exceptions. The third card offers two saved patching results, worked out ahead of time, that you can switch to. And if the model's learned numbers, called its weights, cannot load, the first card's attention grid falls back to a saved example.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: A small model with eight heads The model in this lab reads text one character at a time, and at each character it gives a guess for the character that comes next. It holds about 1.4 million learned numbers, called parameters, which makes it tiny next to the models behind chatbots. It learned from the plays of Shakespeare, mixed with made-up strings of letters that repeat. The model is built in two layers, which the lab also calls blocks, and the first one finishes its work before the second begins. Each layer holds four attention heads, and at every letter a head decides how much to look back at each earlier letter. It then carries information forward from the letters it looks at most. The lab names the eight heads by layer and number, so L1 H4 is layer 1, head 4, and L2 H3 is layer 2, head 3. A head shares out its attention among the letters it can see: each letter gets a share, called an attention weight, and the shares always add up to 1. A weight of 0.67 means about two-thirds of the head's attention goes to that letter, while 0.05 means it barely looks there. The copying puzzle The prompt is always 24 capital letters, made by repeating a short block taken from a fixed list of letters. The length of that block is the Repeat period, the lab's main control. At period 8 the block is QXZRKWMP, so the prompt is that block three times. The model's job is to guess the 25th letter, which should be Q if the model copies the pattern. The lab counts positions from 0, the way many computer tools do, so the first letter sits at position 0 and the last one at position 23. At period 8, each copy of the block fills 8 positions, which puts the third copy at positions 16 to 23. The last letter, at position 23, is a P, and the Q that should come next last appeared at position 16. Two halves of the copying trick How can a model copy a pattern of letters in an order it has never seen before? The standard explanation uses two heads, one in each layer, working one after the other. The first half happens in layer 1, where at every letter a head looks at the letter immediately before it and carries a trace of that letter forward. As a result, each position ends up holding a note that says "the letter before me was …". The piece of text a model reads at each step is called a token, which here is one character. A head that does this job is therefore called a previous-token head. The second half happens in layer 2, where a head at the last letter, P, searches the earlier positions for a note saying "the letter before me was P". Position 16 carries that note, because it comes right after the P at position 15, and the letter stored there is a Q. The head puts much of its attention on position 16, reads the Q, and pushes the model's guess toward Q. A head that works this way is called an induction head, and its rule, in short, is "A was followed by B before, so after A comes B again". Position 8 carries the same note, because it follows the P at position 7, so the head can spread its attention across both earlier copies. The lab outlines the nearer one, position 16, because it is the previous occurrence of the letter to copy. The layer-2 head can find position 16 only because a layer-1 head has already written the note there, which is why the trick needs two layers working in order. Together, the two halves form a circuit: a claim that particular parts, connected in a particular way, produce a particular behavior. In this model, the attention picture points to two previous-token heads, L1 H3 and L1 H4, and two induction heads, L2 H2 and L2 H3. Whether that picture is true, and how far it goes, is what the rest of the lab tests. Watching is not testing A picture of where heads look is a good start, but it is only a picture. To see why, imagine a kitchen where eight helpers work in two shifts to bake a cake, passing ingredients between bowls lined up along a counter. You want to know which helpers and which bowls the cake's sweetness really depends on, and you have three ways to find out. Look: you watch which bowls each helper reaches into, which shows who handles what. But a helper can stir a bowl all afternoon without the cake depending on it.
