Send a helper home: you bake again without one helper and taste the result. If the cake comes out wrong, that helper was needed, at least for this cake. Swap a bowl: you set up a second kitchen where the sugar jar was filled with salt by mistake, so its cake tastes wrong. Partway through, you move one bowl from the good kitchen into the same spot in the salty kitchen and let the baking finish. If the cake now tastes sweet, the sweetness was traveling in that bowl at that moment. In the model, the helpers are the eight heads and the cake is the model's guess for the next letter. The bowls are the lists of numbers the model keeps at each letter, which you will meet properly below. Looking means reading the attention, sending a helper home is called ablation, and swapping a bowl is called activation patching. The analogy stops matching in one important way, because in a real kitchen you can peek into any bowl and ask any helper what their job is. In the model, every bowl is a long list of unlabeled numbers, and no head was ever given a job title. One job can be split across several heads, and one head can help with several jobs, which is exactly why you need tests and not only a look. Ablation: switching a head off When you switch a head off, you have to decide what to put in its place, and that choice changes the result. The plainest choice, called zero-ablation, replaces the head's output with zeros, as if the head had added nothing at all. The trouble is that the parts of the model that come after the head never received a zero from it during training. Some of the damage may therefore come from that strange input, not from the head's missing work. In the kitchen, zero-ablation is like the missing helper's ingredient never landing in any bowl at all, a gap the later work never met during practice. That could throw off what comes next for reasons unrelated to the helper's real job. A gentler choice, called mean ablation, puts in the head's typical output instead: its average over eight other random letter strings that repeat with the same period. That one average is used at every letter, whatever the prompt is. It is like a stand-in who pours the same average scoop into every bowl, whatever this cake needs. The later work gets something familiar, but none of the information the real helper would have added for this cake. The Ablation control in the Head ablation card switches between these two choices, which it labels Zero and Mean. Activation patching: swapping one value At every letter, the model keeps a running list of numbers that sums up the text so far, and each block adds its own results to that list. A list of numbers like this is called a vector, and this particular running one is called the residual, or residual stream. In the kitchen picture, the residual at each letter is one of the bowls on the counter. Patching needs two runs of the model that differ in one small way. The clean run uses the normal prompt, while the corrupted run uses the same prompt with one letter changed to Y, a letter the prompt never uses. Together they are called a clean and corrupted run, and the contrast between them is what gives a patching result its meaning. With the Corrupt control set to The letter to copy, the lab changes the Q at position 16 into a Y. The model then copies what it finds there, so the corrupted run's top guess becomes Y instead of Q. To patch, the lab takes the clean run's residual at one position, right after one block, and pastes it into the corrupted run at the same place. It then lets the corrupted run finish and checks how much of the right answer came back. Each square in the patching grid stands for one experiment of this kind, at one position and after one block. Keeping score: logit difference and recovery Before a model turns its guesses into percentages, it gives every possible next character a raw score, called a logit. A higher logit means the model ranks that character higher, and a logit can be negative. The lab scores each run with a logit difference: the logit of the right letter minus the logit of the decoy Y, read at the last position. At period 8 the card writes it as logit(Q) − logit(Y), so a large positive value means Q is far ahead of Y. A negative value means that Y has pulled ahead instead. At period 8, the clean run scores 10.69, so Q is far ahead, while the corrupted run scores −1.01, so Y is slightly ahead. The distance between those two scores, 11.70, is called the gap, and it is the whole amount a patch could possibly win back. Recovery says what share of the gap a patch wins back, using the rule recovery = (patched − corrupted) ÷ (clean − corrupted). Suppose a patch lifts the corrupted score from −1.01 up to about 10.55. Because the score started below zero, the climb is 10.55 plus 1.01, which comes to about 11.56. Dividing that climb by the full gap of 11.70 gives about 0.988, or 98.8%, which is the recovery you will find in one square of the lab's grid. A recovery near 100% means that one pasted vector brought back almost all of the answer, while a recovery near 0% means it changed almost nothing. A negative recovery means the patch pushed the score even further in the wrong direction.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: The previous lab found features, patterns inside a model that tend to show up alongside an idea such as "this is a name", by noticing what goes along with what. This lab is where the course stops describing and starts testing. Picture a friend who wore the same pair of socks to every game their team won and now believes the socks cause the wins. Watching more games can never settle it, because the socks and the wins keep turning up together. The only fair test is to change one thing on purpose, play a game without the socks, and see what happens. Reading an attention map is like watching the games, so in this lab it runs into three problems that only an intervention can get past. An intervention means changing something inside the model on purpose and measuring what follows. Two stories can draw the same picture At period 8, the letter an induction head should read is always exactly 7 positions back from the letter doing the looking. From the last letter at position 23, for example, the letter to read is the Q at position 16. A head that had learned to always look 7 back, whatever the letters are, would draw the same picture and copy equally well. Attention at period 8 cannot tell these two stories apart, but changing the period can. A new period moves the right letter to a new distance, while a head stuck at 7 back would keep looking at the old distance. Needed is not the same as doing the job A head can be needed for copying without doing what the textbook story says, and a head can show a neat pattern without the answer depending on it. Ablation measures whether the answer gets worse without a part, which tells you the part is needed in this setting, but not what it calculates. Where the information actually travels Attention shows where a head could pull information from, not where the information the answer needs actually travels. Patching answers that second question, because it shows which single position, after which block, carries the letter to copy.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Work through the cards from top to bottom, because each one tests the picture that the one before it draws. Start with Repeat period at 8, the setting the lab opens on, and keep it there until the last step. Step 1: find an induction pattern In Copy task and attention, the prompt appears as a row of letter chips. The Q at position 16 is outlined in green, because it is the previous occurrence of the next letter. Beside the row, a next box shows the letter the pattern calls for, Q?, along with the model's top guess and how much probability it gives that guess. Of the three readouts underneath, Copy accuracy is the average probability the model gives the right next letter, from the start of the second repeat to the end. P(Q) at the end is that probability at the last letter only, and Top 3 next letters lists the model's three highest-scoring guesses there. The lab starts on head L2 H3, and the eight head buttons above the grid let you switch to any other head. The grid shows the chosen head's attention across the whole prompt, with one row and one column for each of the 24 letters. Each row is a letter doing the looking, each column is a letter it can see, and darker purple means more attention. In the Attention lab's words, the letter doing the looking is the query and a letter being looked at is a key. Each row stops at its own letter, because a letter can look at itself and at earlier letters but never at later ones. Solid green outlines mark, in every row from the second repeat onward, the key an induction head would read. An induction head does this lookup at every letter, not only the last one, which is why the outlines run down the grid in a diagonal stripe. The legend under the grid gives the rule as i − 8 + 1, where i is the row's position. Stepping back 8, one whole block, lands on the same letter in the copy before, and stepping 1 forward lands on the letter that came after it. For the last row, 23 − 8 + 1 = 16, which is the Q that follows the earlier P. Dashed amber outlines mark the previous letter, i − 1, which for the last row is position 22. With L2 H3 chosen, the dark cells should sit on the green outlines, and when you choose L1 H4, they should jump to the dashed outlines instead. The line under the grid names the single distance that takes the biggest share of the chosen head's attention, so you can check the picture in words as well. Try L1 H2 too and read where its attention goes, because that head will matter later in the lesson. The table beside the grid scores all eight heads at once. Its previous letter column is each head's average attention on the letter immediately before, and its after previous occurrence column is the average on the green key. Clicking a row in the table also picks that head for the grid, which is a quick way to move between heads. A chip in the corner checks the lab's own arithmetic against a standard program, ONNX Runtime, running the same model file on the same prompt. It first reads Weights loaded, then Matches ONNX followed by a tiny number, the largest difference the check found between the two. The model's learned numbers are also called its weights. If they cannot load, the chip reads Weights unavailable · cached view, and the grid falls back to a saved example at period 13. Step 2: ablate a head In Head ablation, click L1 H4 to switch it off, and its button changes from on to off. The Change readout gives the difference in copy accuracy in percentage points, shown as pts, so a fall from 90% to 10% would read as −80.0 pts. Next to it, the readout Attention on the induction key, L2 H2 · L2 H3 shows how much attention the two induction heads put on the induction key. That key is the green-outlined letter from Step 1. The readout gives the values with every head on, then an arrow, then the values with your chosen heads off. That lets you see whether switching off a layer-1 head disturbs the layer-2 heads. Head switches add up, so click Restore all before each new head to keep only one head off at a time. Restore, then switch off L2 H3, then restore again and switch off L2 H1. Each head's button also shows an alone figure, the change in points when only that head is off, so you can compare all eight heads at a glance. The Ablate layer 1 and Ablate layer 2 buttons switch off a whole layer in one click. With a layer-2 head off, the induction-key readout does not move at all, even when the head you switched off is L2 H3 itself. Switching a head off removes what it writes, not where it looks, and heads in the same layer cannot affect each other. Only switching off a layer-1 head changes where the layer-2 heads look. The bars at the bottom show the probability of the right letter at every scored position, outlined blue for the intact model and solid red with your chosen heads off. The scored positions are every letter from the start of the second repeat on, the same letters that Copy accuracy averages. With L2 H3 off, the red bars collapse almost everywhere. With only L2 H2 off, the losses are partial and uneven, deep at some letters and small at others. Finally, click Restore all, set Ablation to Mean, switch off L2 H3 again, and compare what the copying loses under Mean with what it lost under Zero. Step 3: patch activations In Activation patching, the Sweep control picks where the grid's results come from. Keep it on Live · copy task, which runs the patching on the copy puzzle in front of you, and keep Corrupt on The letter to copy. The clean and corrupted prompts appear as two rows of chips, with the changed position outlined in amber. The readouts give the logit difference for Clean and Corrupted, the Gap between them, and each run's top letter. The grid has two rows, After block 1 and After block 2, and one column for each position. Green squares bring the score back toward the clean run, red squares push it the other way, and the color stops getting darker once it reaches 100%. The exact recovery for whichever square you pick appears in the line under the grid. Above the grid, the letter of the changed column, position 16, is highlighted in amber. Click the square in the After block 1 row under that column, which the lab opens with already selected, and read its recovery. Then click the last square in the same row, position 23, and compare the two. Then set Corrupt to An unrelated letter, which makes the lab change the K at position 4, a letter the answer does not depend on. Read the Gap before anything else, and notice the warning that appears whenever the gap is smaller than 1. The Sweep control also offers two saved sweeps, Cached · speaker and Cached · letters, which were worked out ahead of time and stored with the lab. Cached · speaker uses a short script in the style of the plays: ROMEO: hello, then JULIET: hello, then ROMEO:. In its corrupted prompt the last speaker is JULIET instead, cut to the clean prompt's length, so it ends JULIET with no colon. Cached · letters uses the same period-13 letter puzzle that the live sweep builds at period 13. Both saved sweeps score each run by the right character's logit alone, so their Clean, Corrupted and Gap numbers differ from the live sweep's. The recoveries in the Cached · letters grid still come out almost the same as the live sweep's at period 13. Step 4: try an unseen period The made-up repeating strings in the model's training covered almost every period from 4 to 31. A few were skipped on purpose, including 11 and 13, so the lab marks those two as unseen. Try this: Set Repeat period to 13 · unseen, a length the model's repeated-string training never used. Look again at Copy accuracy, the green outlines, and the L2 H3 row of the table, then go back to 8 and compare what moved with what stayed the same.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: The attention picture matches the textbook At period 8, copy accuracy is 94.5%, which means that on average the model gives the right next letter about a 19-in-20 chance. Across every period the lab offers, copy accuracy stays between 88.0% and 97.2%. That range includes the unseen periods, so the model still copies well at lengths its training skipped. The one weak spot is the guess made at the first letter of the second repeat. That is the very first point where copying is possible, when the pattern has only just started to repeat. From the second letter of that repeat onward, the average is at least 95% at every period. The unseen periods still cost a little. Period 13 gives the lowest copy accuracy of any period, 88.0%, and period 11 gives the next lowest, while every other period scores 93.4% or more. Almost all of that drop comes from the weak first letter, where the model gives the right letter under a 5% chance at period 13. From the next letter on, its average is at least 95% there too. Only two heads put much attention on the green key: L2 H2 and L2 H3, with 0.66 and 0.67 at period 8. No other head puts more than 0.10 there, which is a tenth of its attention. Meanwhile L1 H3 and L1 H4 put 0.98 or more of their attention on the previous letter at every period. Those four heads are the two halves of the textbook picture, found by looking alone. The heads follow the pattern, not a fixed distance Picture a classmate who aces every practice quiz, and you start to wonder whether they learned the topic or only noticed that the answer is always C. Watching them retake the same quiz cannot settle it, because both habits give the same score. You need a new quiz where the right answers sit in different places. Changing the period gives the heads that kind of new quiz. At period 13 the green key moves to 12 back, so a head stuck at 7 back would keep its dark cells at 7 back, off the green outlines. Instead, the distance that takes the largest share of attention for L2 H2 and L2 H3 is always the period minus 1. So at every period, the outlines and the dark cells move together. At period 13, L2 H2 and L2 H3 put 0.82 and 0.80 of their attention on the green key, 12 back. Any period other than 8 already rules out a head stuck at 7 back. The unseen periods 11 and 13 go further, because they rule out a head that only memorized one look-back distance for each period it trained on. Passing both tests is strong evidence that these heads follow the letters, though it does not prove that position plays no part at all. At short periods the prompt holds several earlier copies, and the induction heads spread their attention across them. Take period 6, where the two heads put 0.55 and 0.56 on the green key, the letter after the nearest earlier copy. Counting the matching letter after every earlier copy, their totals rise to 0.89 and 0.93. Single heads are needed At period 8 the intact model scores 94.5%, and switching off one head at a time with Zero sorts the eight heads into three groups: Badly needed: without L1 H2 the score falls to 5.1%, without L2 H3 to 6.0%, and without L1 H4 to 9.9%. Partly needed: without L2 H2 the score falls to 50.2%, and without L1 H3 to 56.6%. Hardly needed: without L1 H1 the score is still 89.2%, without L2 H1 it is 95.8%, and without L2 H4 it is 99.6%. Switching off all of layer 1 leaves 1.9%, and switching off all of layer 2 leaves 0.4%, so the model needs both layers to copy. Notice that switching off L2 H4, and to a lesser degree L2 H1, raises the score above the intact 94.5%. So L2 H4 is not needed for copying here, and it even gets slightly in the way. That does not make it useless, because it may do a different job, such as helping with the Shakespeare text the model also learned from, which this score never checks. An ablation only reports what happened to one score on one prompt, not what a head is for. Layer 1 feeds layer 2, as far as ablation can tell Switch off L1 H4 and watch Attention on the induction key, L2 H2 · L2 H3. With every head on, the two induction heads put 0.66 and 0.67 on the green key. With L1 H4 off, those values fall to 0.19 and 0.24. With L1 H3 and L1 H4 both off, they fall to almost nothing, 0.01 and 0.03. That is what the story predicts, because the layer-2 heads lose their aim when the layer-1 heads stop writing their notes, but the story is not complete. Switching off L1 H2 cuts the same attention to 0.30 and 0.21, even though L1 H2 puts nearly all its attention two letters back. What L1 H2 adds to the copying is not known from this lab. Zero exaggerates, and the layer-1 result holds up Zero is a value the parts after a head never received from it during training, so it can make a head look more important than it is. Each layer has one more step that runs after all four of its heads have finished. So for a layer-2 head, the parts after it are that later step inside its own layer and the final step that turns the model's numbers into a guess. Switch to Mean and switch off L2 H3 alone, and the model keeps 47.9% instead of 6.0%. In the same way, switching off L2 H2 alone keeps 75.9% instead of 50.2%. The layer-1 heads still matter under Mean: without L1 H4 the score drops to 24.3%, and without L1 H2 it drops to 27.4%. Losing L1 H3, the least harmful of the three, still drops it to 48.8%, about half the intact score. So the two ways of switching off agree on which layer-1 heads matter, while they disagree about how much each induction head matters alone. Under Mean, the two induction heads overlap: each does part of the same copying on its own, so losing one leaves the other's share. With both of them off, the score is 2.4%, close to the 1.3% that Zero gives. Because the two heads sit in the same layer, neither can react to the other being switched off, so this is overlap, not one head stepping in for the other. Checks built into the lab's code repeat this comparison on random letter strings at periods 9 and 13, and they find the same split. You do not see those checks on screen. Patching finds one route With Corrupt on The letter to copy, the After block 1 square at position 16 recovers 98.8% of the gap. Every other square in that row stays within 0.6 points of zero, including the last position, which recovers −0.5%. So after the first block, the letter to copy still sits at its own earlier position, where the layer-2 heads can read it, not at the last position. The corrupted run shows that the model copies whatever it finds there, because with Y planted at position 16, its top guess becomes Y. At period 8 the planted Y gets 48% of the probability, about half, and at period 13 it gets 99.5%, nearly all of it. At period 8 an untouched Q still sits at position 8 for the heads to read, while at period 13 the planted Y is the only earlier copy. That fits the idea that the heads read from every copy they can find. The gap is large at every period, between 6.05 and 22.35, so the patching results rest on a big, clear difference between the two runs. In the After block 2 row, every square except the last reads exactly 0%, and the last reads 100%. That pattern is built into the design, because after the last block no layer is left to move information between positions. Only the last position's list can affect the guess at that point. So pasting the clean list at any earlier position changes nothing, which reads 0%. Pasting it at the last position hands the model the clean run's finished answer, which reads 100%. This row is a check that the tool works, not a discovery. A control shows what a bad measurement looks like A control is a run set up so that you already know what should happen, which lets you check the measuring tool itself. Set Corrupt to An unrelated letter, and the model still copies correctly, because the changed letter is not one it needs. Because both runs now give nearly the same answer, the gap between their scores falls to 0.16 at period 8, and the warning appears. Yet the grid still prints percentages, up to 43% in one square, because recovery divides by that tiny gap. A shift of less than a tenth in the score, divided by 0.16, turns into a large-looking percentage like that. Picture two runners who cross the finish line two hundredths of a second apart. If new shoes make the slower one a hundredth of a second faster, someone could say the shoes "closed 50% of the gap". That sounds impressive, yet a hundredth of a second is far too small to matter in a race. The shift is far too small to tell you anything about how the model copies, and dividing by a tiny gap is what makes it look big. The unrelated letter's gap stays under 0.35 at every period, so this control never gives a usable measurement. The lesson for any patching experiment is to check the gap before you read a single square.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: What this lab simplifies The prompts are made-up capital letters from one fixed list, 24 letters long, with one prompt for each period. Checks built into the lab's code repeat the main results on random letter strings, but you do not see those on screen. Repeated capital letters are not a far-out test for this model, because made-up repeating strings were part of its training, even though two of the lab's periods were left out. Ablation switches off a whole head at a time, and patching swaps the whole residual at the end of a block. Neither tool here tests a single connection between two heads, and patching never swaps the output of one head on its own. The score is one logit difference against one decoy letter, Y, which was chosen before the experiment. Mean ablation uses one typical value per head, averaged over eight random repeats. Other ways of choosing the stand-in, such as a separate average for each position, could give different sizes. Nobody here has checked the wiring between the layers directly, which is the job of path patching. That method, described in Going deeper, swaps the signal along one single connection between two heads. The claim that layer 1 feeds layer 2 rests on the induction heads' attention falling when layer-1 heads are off, and L1 H2 shows that other layer-1 heads matter too. This is one small model from one training run, and while a second training run also passed the same induction check offline, only this one is in the lab. A model with 1.4 million parameters says little about the huge models behind chatbots, which have far more layers and heads. The saved Cached · speaker sweep recovers 96% at the last position, but that result is close to built in. Its two prompts differ only in the last speaker's name, right at the end. The final six characters are ROMEO: in one and JULIET in the other, and the lab outlines all six in amber. The last of those six is the very character the guess is made from. Pasting the clean list back at that position restores what the model knows about that character, so a big recovery there could hardly fail to appear. It shows a pattern, not a discovery. Where the real method fails Switching a part off puts the model in a state it never met. Zero is an arbitrary value, and later parts may rely on a head's usual output as a steady background level. That is why, in their 2022 study of names, Wang and colleagues used mean ablation rather than zero. Research papers write this team as Wang et al., where "et al." is Latin shorthand for "and others". A typical value reduces this problem without removing it, as the big change in L2 H3's result from Zero to Mean shows. Other parts can quietly take over: picture a group project where one member is off sick and the others cover their part without saying anything. A teacher who compares the final grade with and without that member might decide the member contributed nothing. Models can do something similar, called self-repair, where other parts make up for a part that has been switched off. In 2023, McGrath and colleagues saw one layer make up for another. They called this the Hydra effect, after a monster in Greek myth that grows new heads when one is cut off. Wang and colleagues found backup heads that took over when the main ones were knocked out, so a small effect does not prove a small role. A circuit may not travel: one found for a single kind of prompt may not hold for a reworded prompt, another model, or another training run. Patching says where, not who: it shows where the needed information passes through, not which head wrote it there. A score can be useless: as the control showed, a score that barely changes between the two runs turns every recovery into a meaningless number. So choose a score that clearly changes between the runs before you start the experiment. A common mix-up: "Every part that matters belongs to the circuit." Switching off L1 H2 hurts copying about as much as switching off L1 H4, yet L1 H2 looks two letters back, not at the previous letter. Being needed shows that the answer depends on a part, not that the part does the job the story describes.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Sharper interventions Ablation and patching each ask about one location at a time, while path patching swaps a single connection between two parts. That separates "this head matters" from "this head matters because it feeds that one". It is the missing test for this lab's claim that layer 1 feeds layer 2. A full patching grid costs one complete run of the model for every square, which gets expensive in large models. Attribution patching estimates the whole grid from two ordinary runs plus one extra calculation that works backward through the model, trading some accuracy for speed. Making claims testable Causal scrubbing turns an explanation into a list of changes that should not matter if the explanation is right, and then tries every one of them. Changing the period in this lab is a small version of that idea. The induction story says changing the period should move where the heads look without breaking the copying, and the outlines and dark cells moved with the period as predicted. Researchers now judge a circuit by three standards, and the first, faithfulness, asks whether the claimed parts can produce the behavior on their own, without the rest of the model. Completeness asks whether the circuit includes everything that matters, and minimality asks whether every part in it is truly needed. Where the idea came from In 2021, Elhage and colleagues showed that induction heads need at least two layers, with a previous-token head feeding an induction head, as in this lab. The following year, Olsson and colleagues argued that induction heads may be behind much of in-context learning, a model's ability to pick up a pattern from the prompt itself. The best-known worked example of a circuit is the 2022 study of names by Wang and colleagues, on a model called GPT-2 small. The researchers mapped 26 heads sorted into 7 groups and scored their circuit on faithfulness, completeness and minimality. They said themselves that those scores also pointed to gaps in their understanding. More recent work, such as Anthropic's circuit tracing by Ameisen and colleagues in 2025, maps how readable features connect rather than mapping raw heads. It builds those maps inside a stand-in model that imitates the original but is built from features like the previous lab's, which makes it easier to read. Steering means turning one feature up or down by hand while the model writes. If turning up a feature labeled "talks about the ocean" makes the model start talking about the ocean, the label has passed a real test of cause. Checking that turning it down has the opposite effect makes the test stronger still. The Attention and The transformer block labs show the heads and the residual stream that this lab switches off and swaps.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: This module is about circuits: claims that specific components of a network, connected in a specific way, implement a specific behavior. It asks which components a behavior actually depends on, and by which route the information it needs travels, which attention maps and correlations alone cannot settle. Where Interpretability I: features found candidate features by correlation, this module intervenes, in two ways. Ablation takes a component out to ask whether the behavior needs it. Activation patching asks where the information an answer depends on sits, using a clean run and a corrupted run: two nearly identical prompts that call for different answers. Both are aimed at one behavior, copying a repeated string, and at its textbook explanation, the induction circuit, in which a previous-token head in layer 1 feeds an induction head in layer 2 so that the model can copy whatever followed the current letter last time. Where it shows up Induction heads in language models. Elhage et al. (2021) showed they need at least two layers, a previous-token head feeding an induction head, and Olsson et al. (2022) argued they may be the source of much in-context learning. Head-level circuits. Indirect object identification in GPT-2 small (Wang et al., 2022) was mapped to 26 heads in 7 classes and scored on faithfulness, completeness and minimality: whether the circuit reproduces the behavior alone, captures everything relevant, and needs every part. Feature-level circuits. Anthropic's circuit tracing (Ameisen et al., 2025) builds attribution graphs over interpretable features in a replacement model, rather than over raw heads. Why it matters Intervention is what lets a circuit claim fail. Ablation can show that a behavior survives without a component, and patching can show that the information an answer needs sits somewhere other than where the story put it. The interventions have failure modes of their own. Zero-ablation feeds later layers a value they never saw, so it can overstate a role. When one component is removed, others can compensate (self-repair), so a small effect can hide a real role. And a patch's recovery, the share of the clean-minus-corrupted gap on a chosen metric that it restores, means nothing when that gap is tiny, because the gap is the divisor. What you will be able to explain Read the two halves of an induction circuit in attention, and say why changing the repeat period, including to one the model never saw, separates a head that follows content from one that reads a fixed distance back. Use ablation to test whether a head is necessary and activation patching to locate the information an answer depends on, and say what causal claim each supports. State the limits of a circuit claim: the ablation's replacement value, self-repair, a gap too small to divide by, and results from one prompt, one metric and one small model. What the lab shows The model is the Attention lab's two-layer, four-head character transformer, run in your browser and checked against ONNX Runtime, so every live readout is measured from its forward passes. The live prompts are synthetic: capitals from one fixed pool, 24 letters long, repeating with the Repeat period you set, from 6 to 13. In Copy task and attention, the head buttons, L1 H1 to L2 H4, choose which head's attention grid to show: solid green outlines mark the key an induction head would read, dashed outlines the previous letter. The decisive test sets Repeat period to 11 or 13, which the repeated-string training never used, and checks whether the induction heads' attention moves with the period. In Head ablation, toggle heads off individually or with Ablate layer 1 and Ablate layer 2, and set Ablation to Zero or Mean; Mean substitutes each head's average over eight random repeats of the same period. Read Change and Attention on the induction key, L2 H2 · L2 H3. In Activation patching, Corrupt replaces one letter with Y: The letter to copy gives the main sweep, and An unrelated letter is a control whose Gap is too small for its recoveries to mean anything. Each grid cell pastes one residual-stream vector, After block 1 or After block 2 at one position, from the clean run into the corrupted one. The live sweep's metric is a logit difference, the right letter's logit minus that of the foil Y. Sweep also offers Cached · speaker and Cached · letters, two sweeps precomputed offline with the target logit alone as the metric. Cached · speaker uses a short ROMEO/JULIET prompt pair rather than the letter pool.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: The previous lab found candidate features by looking at what correlates with what. This lab asks the harder question: does a component actually *cause* a behavior? A circuit is a claim of the form "these components, connected this way, implement this behavior." Supporting one needs intervention, because observation alone cannot separate a component that computes the answer from one that merely correlates with it. The model and the behavior Everything here runs on the course's real two-layer, four-head character transformer, the same file the attention lab uses: 1.4 million parameters, trained on Shakespeare plus synthetic repeated strings. Its weights are read in your browser and checked against ONNX Runtime. The behavior is copying: given QXZRKWMP repeated three times, predict the next letter. The textbook mechanism has two parts. A previous-token head in layer 1 writes into each position a note of the letter just before it. An induction head in layer 2 attends from the current letter to the letter after its earlier occurrence, by matching against those notes, and copies it. This model draws that picture: L1 H3 and L1 H4 look at the previous letter, L2 H2 and L2 H3 at the letter after the earlier match. The lab asks whether the picture is causal, and how far it goes. Three instruments Attention shows where each head looks. It is observation, not intervention. Ablation removes a component and measures the damage: is it *necessary*? You can replace the head's output with zero, or with its average over a reference set (mean ablation). Activation patching runs a clean and corrupted run, two minimally different prompts, pastes one activation from the clean one into the corrupted one, and measures how much of a chosen metric returns: *where is the information?*
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: "Attention was high here" and "the answer depended on this" are different statements, and only the second is a finding. The same tools support practical safety work: localizing where a refusal is decided, and checking whether a fine-tune removed a capability or only its expression.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: In Copy task and attention, choose L2 H3 and read the solid green outlines, the key an induction head would read. Then choose L1 H4 and read the dashed outlines, the previous letter. Compare the table's two columns for all eight heads. In Head ablation, switch off L1 H4, then L2 H3, then L2 H1, reading Change and the attention on the induction key each time. Then set Ablation to Mean and compare what L2 H3 costs. In Activation patching, click After block 1 at the amber position, the letter being copied, and then at the last position. Then set Corrupt to An unrelated letter and read the Gap. Set Repeat period to 11 or 13, which the model's repeated-string training never used, and repeat step 1.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: The attention picture matches the textbook Copy accuracy is 94.5% at period 8 and between 88.0% and 97.2% at every period from 6 to 13, including the unseen 11 and 13. The weak spot is the first letter of the second repeat; from the second letter on, the mean is at least 95% at every period. Only L2 H2 and L2 H3 put much attention on the induction key: 0.66 and 0.67 at period 8, and 0.55 to 0.84 across periods. No other head puts more than 0.10 there. L1 H3 and L1 H4 put 0.98 or more of their attention on the previous letter at every period. At short periods the prompt holds several earlier copies, and the induction heads spread across them. At period 6, L2 H2 and L2 H3 put 0.55 and 0.56 on the nearest copy and 0.89 and 0.93 on the letter after any earlier copy. The period test passes At period 8 the key after the previous occurrence is 7 back, so a head that always looked 7 back would draw the same stripe and copy as well. Changing the period moves the previous occurrence but not a fixed distance. At every period from 6 to 13, the strongest offset of L2 H2 and L2 H3 is the period minus one, and the outlines and the weights move together. That includes 11 and 13, which the training windows never used. This is the test the induction hypothesis had to survive. Surviving it is evidence for content-based heads, not proof that no positional signal also helps. Single heads are necessary At period 8 the intact model scores 94.5%. Zero-ablating one head leaves L1 H2 5.1%, L2 H3 6.0% and L1 H4 9.9%; L2 H2 50.2% and L1 H3 56.6%; and L1 H1, L2 H1 and L2 H4 89.2%, 95.8% and 99.6%. All of layer 1 leaves 1.9% and all of layer 2 leaves 0.4%. Removing L2 H4 raises accuracy. Necessary and useful are different words, and an ablation reports an effect on one metric, not what a head is for. Layer 1 feeds layer 2, as far as ablation can say Switch off L1 H4 and the induction heads' attention on the green key falls from 0.66 and 0.67 to 0.19 and 0.24. Switch off L1 H3 and L1 H4 together and it falls to 0.01 and 0.03. The layer-2 heads' attention depends on what the previous-token heads write, as the induction story predicts. The story is not complete. Switching off L1 H2 cuts the same attention to 0.30 and 0.21, though L1 H2 puts 0.98 or more of its attention exactly two letters back, not on the previous letter. What it contributes is not established here. Zero overstates, and the layer-1 result survives Zero is a value the next layer never saw. With mean ablation, each head's output is replaced by its average over eight random repeats of the same period. L2 H3 then leaves 47.9% rather than 6.0%, and L2 H2 75.9% rather than 50.2%. L1 H2, L1 H4 and L1 H3 still leave 27.4%, 24.3% and 48.8%. Under mean ablation the two induction heads partly overlap: each alone leaves a good share of the copying, and both off leaves 2.4% (1.3% under zero). The same layer-1 heads matter either way; the induction heads' solo roles are smaller than zero suggested. Tests on random strings at periods 9 and 13, which the lab does not show, find the same split. Patching finds one route, with a large gap The metric is logit difference, logit(Q) − logit(Y), where Y replaces the letter to copy. At period 8 the gap between the runs is 11.70 (clean 10.69, corrupted −1.01). Restoring the corrupted letter's own position after block 1 recovers 98.8%; every other position in that row stays within 0.6 points of zero, including the last position (−0.5%). The corrupted run copies the planted letter: its top prediction is Y, at 48% for period 8 and 99.5% for period 13. The gap runs from 6.05 to 22.35 logits across periods 6 to 13, and on 16 random period-13 strings it averages 20.7 and never falls below 15.9. A control shows what a bad measurement looks like Set Corrupt to An unrelated letter. The model still copies correctly, the gap falls to 0.16 at period 8 and stays under 0.35 at every period, and the warning appears. The grid still prints percentages, up to 43% in one cell after block 1, because recovery divides by a tiny number. Check the gap before reading any cell.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: In this lab Prompts are synthetic capitals from one fixed pool, 24 letters long, one prompt per period. Tests repeat the main contrasts on seeded random strings the lab does not show. Ablation is per whole head. Patching is at block outputs in the residual stream, not per head or per path, and the metric is one logit difference against one foil letter. No path patching was run. "Layer 1 feeds layer 2" rests on the induction heads' attention falling when layer-1 heads are off, and L1 H2 shows other layer-1 heads matter too. Mean ablation here is one constant vector per head from eight random repeats. A position-by-position mean or a resample ablation could give different sizes. One trained model. A second training seed also passed the induction check offline, but only this model is in the lab, and a 1.4-million-parameter character model says little about large ones. The cached speaker pair differs in its final character, so its last position recovering 96% is close to built in. It shows a pattern, not a discovery. In real systems Zero-ablation is confounded by distribution shift. Wang et al. (2022) used mean ablation because zero is an arbitrary value and later components may rely on average activations as an implicit bias. Mean and resample ablation reduce the problem and do not remove it, as the L2 H3 result above shows. Self-repair complicates every ablation. McGrath et al. (2023) found that ablating one attention layer can make another compensate, calling it the Hydra effect, and Wang et al. found backup name mover heads that take over when the main ones are knocked out. A small measured effect is not proof of a small role. A circuit found for one prompt template may not transfer to a paraphrase, another model, or another training seed, and patching says where information passes, not which head wrote it.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: More specific interventions Path patching patches a single connection between two components rather than a location, which separates "head A matters" from "head A matters because it feeds head B." It is the missing test for the layer-1 to layer-2 claim here. Attribution patching estimates a whole sweep from two forward passes and one backward pass, instead of one forward pass per cell. Making claims falsifiable Causal scrubbing states a hypothesis as the set of computations that may be swapped without changing behavior, then performs every permitted swap. The period change in this lab is a small version of that idea: the induction hypothesis permits changing the period, and the stripe moved with it. Three criteria are now standard for a circuit: faithfulness (does the subgraph reproduce the behavior alone?), completeness (does it capture everything relevant?), and minimality (is every part necessary?). The field's worked examples Elhage et al. (2021) showed that induction heads need at least two layers, with a previous-token head feeding an induction head, and Olsson et al. (2022) argued that induction heads may be the source of much in-context learning. Indirect object identification in GPT-2 small (Wang et al., 2022) mapped 26 heads in 7 classes, scored by faithfulness, completeness and minimality; the authors say the criteria also point to remaining gaps in their understanding. Current work, such as Anthropic's circuit tracing (Ameisen et al., 2025), builds attribution graphs over interpretable features in a replacement model, in the spirit of the previous lab, rather than over raw heads. Steering along a feature's direction tests whether it has the causal role its label claims. The Attention and The transformer block labs show the heads and residual stream this lab intervenes on.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Copy task and attention · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: An attention map that matches the induction recipe The shipped two-layer, four-head character transformer, run in your browser on 24 letters that repeat with a period you choose. The grid is one head's real attention; solid green outlines mark the key an induction head would read, dashed amber outlines mark the previous letter, and the table scores all eight heads on both keys. `Repeat period`, from 6 to 13 letters. 11 and 13 are marked `unseen`: the model's synthetic training repeats used every period from 4 to 31 except 11, 13, 17 and 19. The prompt as letter chips, with alternate periods shaded and a green outline on the previous occurrence of the next letter, then a `next` box with the letter the repeat calls for and the model's top guess. Three readouts: `Copy accuracy`, the probability of the right letter at the end, and the top three next letters. Eight head buttons and a query × key grid for the chosen head: rows are the letter doing the looking, columns the letters it can see, and darker purple means more attention weight. Solid green outlines mark key i − period + 1 and dashed amber outlines mark key i − 1, for each query in the second repeat. A line under the grid names the one offset that takes the most of the chosen head's attention. A table with each head's mean attention on the previous letter and on the key after the previous occurrence, and a status chip comparing this forward pass with ONNX Runtime. The weights are read straight out of `tiny-transformer.onnx`, the attention lab's model file, and run in TypeScript: token plus learned position embedding, two pre-LayerNorm blocks with four heads of width 64 and causal softmax(QKᵀ / 8), an exact-erf GELU MLP from 256 to 768 to 256, then a final LayerNorm and unembedding. The status chip reruns the prompt through ONNX Runtime in the model worker and reports the largest logit difference it finds. A unit test also matches every attention weight in `interpretability-cache.json`, computed in PyTorch, to within 5 × 10⁻⁵. `Copy accuracy` is the mean softmax probability of the correct next letter over positions period to 23: the second repeat onward, where the current letter has already appeared once. Position period − 1 is left out, because nothing before it can say that the string repeats. The table's columns are mean attention from every query i ≥ period to key i − 1 (the previous letter) and to key i − period + 1 (the token after the previous occurrence). With three or four repeats in the prompt the nearest earlier copy is only one of several, so an induction head spreads its attention over all of them. `Repeat period` rebuilds the prompt from the same pool of letters, `QXZRKWMPJVBH…`. The head buttons and the table rows both choose which head the grid shows. Worth running at period 8: choose L2 H3, then L1 H4, then L1 H2, and read the line under the grid. L2 H3's largest share is 7 back (0.67), the key after the previous occurrence; L1 H4's is 1 back (1.00); L1 H2's is 2 back (0.99). Then set the period to 11 or 13, which the training repeats never used: the green outlines move to 10 or 12 back, and L2 H2 and L2 H3 follow them. Copy accuracy is 94.5% at period 8 and 88.0% to 97.2% at every period from 6 to 13, including the unseen 11 and 13 (88.5% and 88.0%). The first scored letter, the first of the second repeat, is the weak one; from the second letter on the mean is at least 95% at every period. Only L2 H2 and L2 H3 put much attention on the induction key (0.55 to 0.84 across the periods); no other head puts more than 0.10 there. L1 H3 and L1 H4 put 0.98 or more of their attention on the previous letter at every period. Those are the two halves of the textbook induction circuit. The stripe follows the period: the strongest offset for L2 H2 and L2 H3 is period − 1 at every period from 6 to 13. A head that always looked 7 back would draw the same stripe at period 8 and a different one elsewhere; these heads do not. In this lab: the prompts are synthetic capitals from one fixed pool, 24 letters long, one prompt per period. The model was trained mostly on Shakespeare, with about 30% of each batch synthetic repeated strings of period 4 to 31 (minus 11, 13, 17 and 19), so a repeated string of capitals is in-family, not a far-out test. In this lab: the table names two keys, and a head can do something else. L1 H1 puts about 0.5 to 0.6 of its attention exactly 3 back, and L1 H2 about 0.99 exactly 2 back; neither column shows that, and the line under the grid does. In general: attention shows where information could flow, not what it is used for. A previous-token head in layer 1 feeding an induction head in layer 2 is the standard account of induction (Elhage et al., 2021; Olsson et al., 2022); the attention map makes it a hypothesis, and the next two cards test it. In general: passing the period test on unseen periods is evidence that the heads follow content, not a proof that no positional signal also contributes, and one small model says little about what a large model does.
documents.title: An attention map that matches the induction recipe

documents.subtitle: Head ablation · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Necessity, one head at a time, two ways Switch any of the eight heads off, either by zeroing its output or by replacing it with its average over random repeats, then read copy accuracy and the induction heads' attention on the current prompt. Each button also says what removing that head alone costs, so you can compare single and joint ablations and compare the two ways of ablating. An `Ablation` control with `Zero` and `Mean`, which sets what replaces a switched-off head's output. Eight toggles, L1 H1 to L2 H4. Each shows `on` or `off` (struck through, dashed red border when off) and `alone ±x pts`, the change in copy accuracy when only that head is removed, under the chosen ablation. `Ablate layer 1`, `Ablate layer 2` and `Restore all` shortcuts. Readouts: copy accuracy intact, with the chosen heads off, the change in percentage points, and the model's top next letter with those heads off; then `Attention on the induction key, L2 H2 · L2 H3`, the intact values, an arrow, and the values with the chosen heads off. Paired bars for every scored position: outlined blue for the intact model, solid red with the chosen heads off, with the letter and position under each pair. Zero-ablation multiplies that head's attention-weighted values by 0 before the output projection W_O. W_O's bias and every other head are untouched, and the whole forward pass reruns. Mean ablation replaces the head's pre-projection output with one constant vector: its average over the second repeat (positions period to 23) of eight seeded random-letter strings with the same period, not the prompt on screen. The SDK runner can scale a head but not substitute a value, so the lab scales the head to zero and adds mean · W_O to that block's output bias, which is the same forward pass. A unit test checks the construction: replacing a layer-2 head by its own output at the last position leaves that position's logits unchanged. `alone` comes from eight extra forward passes (sixteen for mean, which first averages the reference strings), run just after the prompt or the ablation changes; it is copy accuracy with only that head off minus copy accuracy intact. The induction-key readout is the table's mean attention on key i − period + 1, recomputed on the ablated run. A layer-2 head's attention depends on layer 1's output but not on other layer-2 heads, so switching off layer-2 heads never changes it. The bars are the same per-position probabilities that `Copy accuracy` averages. Click a head to toggle it; the shortcuts set whole layers; `Ablation` switches between Zero and Mean. Worth running at period 8 (intact 94.5%): L1 H4 alone leaves 9.9% under zero and 24.3% under mean, and the induction-key attention of L2 H2 · L2 H3 falls from 0.66 · 0.67 to 0.19 · 0.24 under zero. Switch L1 H3 and L1 H4 off together and it falls to 0.01 · 0.03. Then switch off L2 H3 alone, under Zero and then Mean, and compare: 6.0% against 47.9%. Single heads are necessary here. Zero-ablating one head at period 8 leaves L1 H2 5.1%, L2 H3 6.0% and L1 H4 9.9%; L2 H2 50.2% and L1 H3 56.6%; and L1 H1, L2 H1 and L2 H4 89.2%, 95.8% and 99.6%. Zero overstates. Under mean ablation L2 H3 leaves 47.9% and L2 H2 75.9%, but L1 H2, L1 H4 and L1 H3 still leave 27.4%, 24.3% and 48.8%. The same layer-1 heads matter either way; the induction heads' solo roles shrink, and they partly overlap (both off: 1.3% under zero, 2.4% under mean). L2 H4 off raises accuracy under zero (99.6%) and barely moves it under mean (95.3%). The head is not needed for this task; an ablation reports an effect on one metric on one input, not what the head is for. L1 H2 attends two letters back, not to the previous one, yet removing it costs as much as removing L1 H4 and also cuts the induction heads' attention (0.30 · 0.21 under zero). It is needed; what it computes is not established here. In this lab: one synthetic prompt per period. Offline tests repeat the main contrasts on three seeded random strings at each of periods 9 and 13, and the same layer-1 heads stand out, but the lab does not show those strings. In this lab: the mean is one constant vector per head, averaged over eight random repeats. A position-by-position mean, or a resample ablation that swaps in another prompt's value, is a different replacement and could give different sizes. Zero and Mean disagree on size and agree on which layer-1 heads matter; neither is ground truth. In general: ablation tests necessity, not mechanism, and trained models can repair themselves when a component is removed: McGrath et al. (2023) call this the Hydra effect, and Wang et al. (2022) found backup name mover heads that take over when the main ones are knocked out. In general: no path patching was run, so "layer-1 previous-token heads feed layer-2 induction heads" rests on the induction heads' attention falling when they are off, not on a patched route; L1 H2 shows that other layer-1 heads matter too.
documents.title: Necessity, one head at a time, two ways

documents.subtitle: Activation patching · Interpretability II: circuits
documents.body: Transplant one vector, measure what returns Run the model on a clean prompt and on a corrupted copy, then paste one residual-stream vector from the clean run into the corrupted run and measure how much of the metric comes back. Every cell is one such experiment, run live; two sweeps precomputed in the shipped cache are included for comparison. `Sweep`: the live copy task, or the cached `speaker` and `letters` sweeps from `interpretability-cache.json`. For the live sweep, `Corrupt` chooses which letter is replaced: the letter to copy, or an unrelated one. The clean and corrupted prompts as chips, with the replaced position outlined in amber. The metric, then readouts: its value on the clean run, on the corrupted run, the gap between them and, for live sweeps, each run's top next letter. A warning appears when the gap is under 1 logit. A grid with rows `After block 1` and `After block 2` and a column per position. Green cells recover the metric, red cells push it the other way, and the colour saturates at ±100%. A readout for the selected cell with its exact recovery and, for live sweeps, the metric after patching. Live sweep: the corrupted prompt replaces one letter with `Y`, a letter the prompt never uses. With `The letter to copy` it is the previous occurrence of the next letter (position 24 − period); with `An unrelated letter` it is a letter in the first repeat, half a period from the letter being copied. The metric is logit(right letter) − logit(Y) at the last position. Each cell overwrites the corrupted run's residual vector after block 1 or block 2, at one position, with the clean run's vector, and reruns the blocks after it. Recovery = (patched − corrupted) / (clean − corrupted). Cached sweeps were computed by `precompute_interpretability.py` with the target logit alone as the metric. `letters` is the same period-13 prompt pair the live sweep builds at period 13, so the two compare directly: gaps of 11.99 and 18.43 under the two metrics, and recoveries within 0.006 of each other in every cell. A unit test reproduces the speaker sweep to two decimals. After the last block nothing mixes positions, so in the `After block 2` row every cell but the last is exactly 0% and the last is exactly 100%. Click any cell, or Tab to it and press Enter, to read its value. Worth running at period 8: `After block 1` at position 16, the letter to copy, recovers 98.8%, and at the last position −0.5%. Then set `Corrupt` to `An unrelated letter`: the gap falls from 11.70 to 0.16 and the warning appears. One route, clearly. After block 1 only the corrupted letter's own position recovers (98.8% at period 8) and every other cell in the row stays within 0.6 points of zero. The letter's identity is carried at that earlier position, where layer 2's heads can read it; the last position does not hold it yet. The model copies what it finds there. With `Y` in place of the letter to copy, the corrupted run's top prediction is `Y`: 48% at period 8 and 99.5% at period 13. The gap is large at every period: 6.05 to 22.35 logits across periods 6 to 13, and on 16 random period-13 strings it averages 20.7 and never falls below 15.9. The control shows what a bad measurement looks like. With an unrelated letter replaced, the gap is under 0.35 logits at every period, yet at period 8 a cell after block 1 still reads 43%, because the denominator is tiny. `Cached · speaker` recovers only at the last position (96%): its corrupted prompt is cut to the clean one's length and ends at JULIET with no colon, so the last character is where the runs differ. `Cached · letters` recovers 99.5% at position 11. In this lab: patching is at block outputs in the residual stream only, not per head or per path, and each sweep uses one prompt pair. The metric is a logit difference against one foil letter, `Y`, chosen before the sweep. In this lab: the corruption changes one letter. The cached `speaker` pair differs in its final character, which makes the last position trivially the place the difference enters; it shows a pattern, not a discovery. In general: a patching result supports a claim about this prompt pair and this metric only. A circuit found on one template may not transfer to paraphrases, other models or other seeds, and it says where information passes, not which head wrote it. In general: a full sweep costs one forward pass per cell. Attribution patching estimates the whole grid from two forward passes and one backward pass, at some cost in accuracy.
documents.title: Transplant one vector, measure what returns

documents.subtitle: Run a real sparse autoencoder on a transformer's residual stream, watch a dense vector become 32 active features, test whether a feature's label survives new text and its window position, then steer the model along a feature's direction against a random control.
documents.body: Run a real sparse autoencoder on a transformer's residual stream, watch a dense vector become 32 active features, test whether a feature's label survives new text and its window position, then steer the model along a feature's direction against a random control. Explain superposition and sparse feature extraction Treat feature labels as hypotheses: check where their examples come from and score them as precision and recall Use steering as a causal test of a feature, judged against a random direction of the same length

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: In Residual to sparse code, click positions 0, 1 and 4 of the probe text and compare the 256 dense residual bars with the SAE code's 32 spikes; read the unexplained share and which of the largest features carry a window-start flag.

documents.body: In Sparsity and superposition, move Keep top k features from 1 to 32 and watch the unexplained share fall, then read Most similar pair and its signed cosine.

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: In Feature evidence, keep feature #876, the first in the menu, and read the window position on each of its eight examples; then switch Examples shown to Top 8 from position 4 on and compare the characters and activations.
