documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: Representing more features than there are dimensions by giving them almost-orthogonal, overlapping directions. It works because most features are absent from any single input.
documents.title: Superposition

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A separate model trained on recorded activations that rewrites each one as a few active features out of many more than the activation has dimensions, then reconstructs it. This lab's has 1,024 features for a 256-wide residual, trained on 1,600 text windows.
documents.title: Sparse autoencoder

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A unit that activates on several apparently unrelated things. This is the normal case, and it is the direct consequence of superposition.
documents.title: Polysemantic neuron

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A direction that corresponds to a single recognizable concept. It is the goal of sparse decomposition rather than a property of raw neurons, and many SAE features fall short of it.
documents.title: Monosemantic feature

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: Finding a set of directions such that each input is a sparse combination of a few of them. Sparse autoencoders apply this to a model's internals.
documents.title: Dictionary learning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: The training pressure toward few active features: an L1 penalty, a TopK cutoff, or a learned threshold. This lab's SAE keeps exactly the 32 largest of 1,024 per token and adds a small L1 term.
documents.title: Sparsity penalty

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: The term requiring the decoded output to match the original activation. It trades directly against sparsity, and choosing a point on that curve is a judgment call.
documents.title: Reconstruction loss

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: The way one feature separates into several more specific ones when a wider dictionary is trained, so there is no canonical number of features. This lab trains one width, so it cannot show splitting; its largest overlap is a different effect.
documents.title: Feature splitting

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A dictionary entry that never activates on any input, wasting capacity. Their prevalence is one practical measure of a poorly trained autoencoder; this lab's SAE has none among 1,800 scanned windows.
documents.title: Dead feature

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: Using a language model to read top-activating examples and propose a label. It makes labeling scalable and inherits that model's bias toward tidy explanations.
documents.title: Auto-interpretability

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: The cutoff above which a feature is treated as firing. It is not a neutral choice: a high threshold hides the counterexamples that would disconfirm a label, and a low one lets false alarms in.
documents.title: Activation threshold

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A direction added to a model's activations while it runs, to push its output. With a feature's decoder direction it turns a label from a correlation into a testable causal claim, but only if the effect is compared with a random direction of the same length.
documents.title: Steering vector

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A feature whose largest activations come from the first few positions of the model's window, where the residual depends on almost no context. Its top examples describe the start of a window rather than language, which the cache shows by recording each example's window position.
documents.title: Window-start artefact

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A comparison that should show no real effect, here a random direction of the same length as the steering vector. It sets what a real effect means by showing how much any added vector changes the output.
documents.title: Null control

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability I: features · question 1
documents.body: In Sparsity and superposition you drag Keep top k features from its smallest value to its largest. What happens to the unexplained share, and why? It rises, because each extra feature adds interference from the features already kept It falls steeply at first and then flattens, because the largest features carry most of the vector It stays put, because the autoencoder's weights are fixed and keeping more features changes nothing It reaches exactly zero at the largest k, because the sparse code is a lossless re-encoding of the residual The reconstruction is a sum of decoder directions weighted by the active features, so each added feature typically moves the sum closer to the residual. The biggest few features carry most of the vector and the last ones add little, so the curve drops and flattens. It does not reach zero: the code keeps only a few of the dictionary's many features, so some of the activation stays unexplained.
documents.title: In Sparsity and superposition you drag Keep top k features from its smallest value to its largest. What happens to the unexplained share, and why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability I: features · question 2
documents.body: Why can one neuron respond to several unrelated things, while a feature in the sparse autoencoder's dictionary can be cleaner? The model holds fewer concepts than neurons, so the spare neurons are given arbitrary meanings The autoencoder retrains the transformer so that each neuron ends up holding one concept It packs more features than it has dimensions onto overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions in each layer Neurons respond to everything until training noise has been averaged out of their weights That packing is superposition: it works because most features are absent from any one input, so overlapping directions rarely interfere. A single neuron then mixes several features. The sparse autoencoder is a separate model that rewrites an activation over a wider dictionary of directions; the transformer is untouched, and the dictionary's directions overlap only slightly rather than being exactly orthogonal.
documents.title: Why can one neuron respond to several unrelated things, while a feature in the sparse autoencoder's dictionary can be cleaner?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability I: features · question 3
documents.body: Two decoder directions overlap more than any other pair: they point almost opposite ways, and the two features are never active on the same character. What is the most likely reason? A ReLU feature cannot go negative, so one signed direction in the residual needs a feature for each side of it They are duplicates that training failed to merge, so one of them could be deleted without changing any reconstruction The autoencoder is trained to make every pair of directions orthogonal, and this pair is where that objective failed They label the same concept, and the TopK rule keeps whichever of the two has the smaller activation The encoder passes each value through a ReLU, so an activation is never negative. When a direction in the residual takes both signs, the dictionary can cover it with one feature for the positive side and another, pointing the opposite way, for the negative side, and only one of them is active at a time. Duplicates would tend to be active together, and these two never are. Nothing in training pushes directions toward orthogonality, and TopK keeps the largest activations, not the smaller of a pair.
documents.title: Two decoder directions overlap more than any other pair: they point almost opposite ways, and the two features are never active on the same character. What is the most likely reason?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability I: features · question 4
documents.body: A feature's top examples all show one character. You slide Activation threshold down from a high value. What should you expect for a label that looked perfect? Other characters start to cross the line, so precision can fall and reveal what was hidden Recall falls first, because a lower cutoff misses characters that the label should include Nothing changes, because a label is a property of the feature's direction and not of the cutoff The decoder direction rotates toward the new characters, so the label is updated automatically A feature fires when its activation exceeds the threshold. A high threshold counts only the strongest firings, which are the ones the top examples already showed, so the label looks flawless. Lowering it lets weaker firings on other characters in, and those false alarms lower precision while recall rises. The threshold is not a neutral choice: a high one hides the counterexamples that would disconfirm a label.
documents.title: A feature's top examples all show one character. You slide Activation threshold down from a high value. What should you expect for a label that looked perfect?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability I: features · question 5
documents.body: The sparse autoencoder rebuilds the residual well, with only a small unexplained share. What does that establish about its features? That each feature is monosemantic, since a faithful rebuild needs clean single-concept directions That the transformer computes its answers using exactly these dictionary directions in its layers That the code compresses this activation well, not that its features are the model's concepts That no dictionary entry is dead, since every one of them took part in the rebuild Reconstruction measures how well a few directions rebuild the vector, and a sparse dictionary can do that without matching how the model itself represents anything. Only a few of the dictionary's many features are active at each character, so some may never fire. Meaning has to come from separate evidence: held-out tests of a label and, ideally, interventions such as steering along the direction.
documents.title: The sparse autoencoder rebuilds the residual well, with only a small unexplained share. What does that establish about its features?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability I: features · question 6
documents.body: A feature's eight cached top examples all sit at window position 1 or 2, and it still fires on many later characters. What should you conclude about the label you would write from those snippets? It is unreliable, since those examples describe the window start; check examples from later positions It is reliable, because the largest activations are always the best evidence for what a feature means in text It is wrong only at positions 1 and 2, and every later firing already matches it It cannot be tested, because a window position is not something a probe text can reproduce At window position 1 the residual depends on just two characters and its norm is unusually large, so a feature can win the top-activation ranking there for reasons unrelated to language. The cache records each example's window position so you can see this, and keeps a separate list of examples from later positions. A probe text is itself a window starting at position 0, so you can reproduce the effect by typing text and watching the first characters.
documents.title: A feature's eight cached top examples all sit at window position 1 or 2, and it still fires on many later characters. What should you conclude about the label you would write from those snippets?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability I: features · question 7
documents.body: You add a feature's decoder direction at one position and the label character's log probability rises by about as much as it does when you add random directions of the same length. What follows? Nothing about this feature yet: a random direction does as well, so the change cannot be attributed to it The label is confirmed, because the character became more likely after the feature was added to the residual The label is refuted, because a real feature would have raised the character by far more than that does The strength was too low, and any strength would show the label once the change turns positive Adding any vector of a given length changes the output a little, in either direction, because it shifts the residual before the final normalization. The random directions measure that background. A change inside it is what chance directions produce, so it neither confirms nor refutes the label. Only a change well outside the random spread is evidence about this direction in particular.
documents.title: You add a feature's decoder direction at one position and the label character's log probability rises by about as much as it does when you add random directions of the same length. What follows?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Interpretability I: features · question 8
documents.body: You raise the feature that fires on the letter y, and the next character's probabilities move well outside the random-direction range. What did the lab find, and what does it show? y became less likely and o more likely: a label says where a feature fires, not what adding it writes y became the top prediction, which confirms that the feature stands for the letter y and nothing else Nothing changed, because the transformer ignores any vector it did not produce during its own run y and o rose together, because the feature groups every character that tends to follow a vowel The feature fires on y, but adding its direction made y less likely and o the largest riser; the lab shows that, not why. The label described where the feature fires and did not predict what adding it writes. That is why a label is a hypothesis about where a feature fires, and steering is a separate test of what it does.
documents.title: You raise the feature that fires on the letter y, and the next character's probabilities move well outside the random-direction range. What did the lab find, and what does it show?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A language model, the kind of AI behind a chatbot, works by turning text into long lists of numbers and passing them along from step to step. In the end those numbers decide what it writes next, yet nobody wrote down what any of them means. They were set automatically during training, the long process in which the model learned from example text, rather than chosen by a person. This module is about looking inside those lists and asking what they stand for. That kind of work is called interpretability: trying to explain what happens inside a model, not only what comes out of it. Researchers have already done this with large models. A team at Anthropic found a feature, a pattern inside the numbers, that was linked to the Golden Gate Bridge in a model called Claude 3 Sonnet. When they turned that feature up, the model's replies to most questions began to mention the bridge, even when the question had nothing to do with bridges. Why does this matter? Without a way to read the inside of a model, you can only watch what goes in and what comes out. Its own numbers are too mixed to name one by one, so there is no part you can point to and say what it means. There is also a quieter danger, which this module spends most of its time on. A name for a feature can sound right and still be wrong, so every name needs testing. By the end, you will be able to explain: how a model can carry far more things than it has numbers, an idea called superposition, and why that makes one number react to many unrelated things; how a tool called a sparse autoencoder unpacks those numbers into separate features, with only a few of them switched on at a time; why a feature's name, its label, is only a guess, and how to test it by checking where its examples come from and scoring it with two numbers. Precision is how often the feature is right when it switches on, and recall is how many of the real cases it catches; how steering, turning a feature up on purpose inside the model, tests what the feature does, and why that result has to beat a random push of the same size. The lab runs a real, small model that was trained on text from Shakespeare's plays, along with a real sparse autoencoder that was trained on that model. It has four cards, which you will work through in this order: Residual to sparse code shows the model's list of 256 numbers, called its residual, at any character you click, and the same list rewritten as a few active features. Sparsity and superposition rebuilds that list from fewer features and measures how much the features overlap with each other. Feature evidence shows a feature's best examples, lets you choose a label for it, and scores that label on the lab's text, which you can change. Steer with a feature adds a feature to the model while it predicts the next character, and compares the result with random pushes of the same size. Most of what the cards show is worked out live from the text you type. Two parts were fixed ahead of time, though. A feature's best examples were found in advance and stored for only 128 of the 1,024 features. And the labels you can test are simple rules written by this module's author, not names the model gave itself. On screen, Feature evidence sits above Sparsity and superposition, so you will scroll past it and come back to it.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A list of 256 numbers for every character The model in this lab reads text one character at a time, and at each character it predicts which character comes next. For every character it reads, it keeps a list of 256 numbers that describes the text so far. A list of numbers like this is called a vector. The model is built from two layers, called blocks, and each block reads the list and adds its own changes to it. That running list is called the residual stream, or the residual for short. This lab looks at it after the second and last block, right before the model turns it into a guess about the next character. The model reads text in chunks of up to 64 characters, called windows, and a character's place in its window is its position, counted from 0. So the character at position 4 is the fifth one, and by then the model has read 5 characters. Why reading one number at a time fails The most direct way to understand a model would be to watch its units, the single numbers it computes, which are often called neurons. You would note what makes each one go up and then give it a name. People have tried this, and it works badly, because one unit tends to react to several things that have nothing to do with each other. A unit like that is called a polysemantic neuron, from Greek words meaning "many meanings". This is not a fault in one unlucky model but the normal case, and the reason is a shortage of space. Superposition: a mixing board with too few sliders Picture the 256 numbers as the sliders on a sound mixing board. The model needs those sliders to carry far more than 256 different things about the text. They might need to show that the last character was a space, that a name is being written in capitals, or that a line is about to end. There are not enough sliders to give each thing its own one, so each thing gets its own recipe instead: a pattern of small moves spread across all 256 sliders. One recipe might be "slider 3 up a little, slider 40 down a lot, slider 200 up a bit". Whenever a thing is present in the text, its recipe is added to the board. At any moment, the board shows the total of the recipes for everything present right then. Researchers call a recipe a direction, because turning it up moves the whole board further along the same pattern. To see how two directions can overlap, imagine a board with only two sliders. Each recipe is then an arrow on an ordinary graph, pointing to the spot given by its two slider moves. For example, "slider 1 up 2, slider 2 up 1" is an arrow from the middle of the graph to the point (2, 1). Two directions overlap when their arrows point partly along each other, either the same way or the opposite way. They share nothing when their arrows sit at right angles, which mathematicians call being orthogonal. The simplest case is two recipes that move different sliders, such as "slider 1 up 1" and "slider 2 up 1". Their arrows run along the two edges of the graph. Recipes that move the same sliders can share nothing too. The arrow for "slider 1 up 1, slider 2 up 1" points up and to the right. The arrow for "slider 1 up 1, slider 2 down 1" points down and to the right. The angle between them is a right angle, so these two recipes share nothing, even though both move both sliders. On a flat graph, you can fit only two arrows that are all at right angles to each other. With three sliders, picture the corner of a room, where two edges of the floor meet the upright edge between the walls. Those are three arrows, each at right angles to the other two, and there is no room for a fourth. Each slider is one dimension, so a board with 256 sliders has 256 dimensions. The same rule holds there, so 256 sliders allow at most 256 recipes that share nothing at all. You can fit far more recipes than that, though, if each one is allowed to share a small sliver with the others. The recipes are then nearly orthogonal: almost, but not quite, at right angles. This trick works poorly with two or three sliders, but it works far better as the number of sliders grows. Later, the lab measures 1,024 recipes on these same 256 sliders. They were learned by a second model, introduced in the next section, and on average each pair overlaps by only a small amount. Packing more directions than there are dimensions in this way, keeping them nearly orthogonal, is called superposition. Those slivers of overlap would cause trouble if many things were present at once, because they would pile up into noise. Superposition works because almost none of the things are present at the same time: at any one character only a handful are, so the overlap costs very little. Superposition also explains the problem from the last section, because each slider takes part in many recipes and so moves whenever any of those things is present. Watched on its own, it seems to react to many unrelated things. The same packing happens in the model's neurons, the numbers it computes inside each block. This lab does not show those neurons, though, so it shows the packing in the residual's 256 numbers instead. The analogy stops matching in one important way: on a real mixing board, a person designed every control and labelled it. In the model, nobody designed the recipes or wrote labels for them, because training found them, and they are hidden in the mix of all 256 numbers. Unpacking with a sparse autoencoder If many things are packed on top of each other, the fix is to unpack them. A sparse autoencoder is a second, separate model that is trained to do exactly that. Stay with the mixing board, and picture a much bigger control panel beside it with 1,024 knobs, where each knob moves all 256 sliders by its own recipe. The autoencoder looks at one snapshot of the 256 sliders and uses what it learned in training to work out, in one quick pass, knob settings that recreate it closely. It follows a strict rule: at every character, exactly 32 of the 1,024 knobs are turned, and all the rest stay at zero. Each knob is called a feature, and how far it is turned at a character is that feature's activation. A list that is mostly zeros, like these 1,024 activations, is called sparse. Before it starts, the autoencoder rescales the 256 numbers into its own units. It takes away a typical value for each slider and then divides by one fixed number, so that it always works with numbers of a similar size. After that, it works in two halves: The encoder reads the 256 numbers and gives each of the 1,024 features a score. It turns any negative score into zero, a rule called ReLU, and keeps only the 32 biggest, a rule called TopK, where k is the number kept. The decoder rebuilds the 256 numbers by adding up the recipe of each active feature, scaled by how far that feature is turned. The rebuilt list is called the reconstruction. The whole set of 1,024 recipes is called a dictionary, because every snapshot gets spelled out with a few entries from it. Finding a set like this is called dictionary learning, and a sparse autoencoder is one way of doing dictionary learning on a model's insides. The autoencoder learned its recipes from the model's numbers on 1,600 windows of text, over 10,000 training steps, where each step is one small adjustment to make it better. Two pressures shaped that training, and they pull against each other: The reconstruction loss scores how far the rebuilt list is from the real one, and training pushes that score down. The sparsity penalty is a pressure to keep few features on. Here the TopK rule does nearly all of that job, with a small extra penalty added on top (Going deeper has the details). Fewer features make a rougher rebuild, so choosing a balance between the two pressures is a judgment call. Through all of this the original model is never changed, because the autoencoder only reads copies of its numbers. That makes the autoencoder a measuring tool rather than a change to the model. Measuring a rebuild The lab writes the original list as x and the rebuilt list as x̂, which you say as "x-hat". The leftover is the difference between them, x − x̂. To sum up a whole list in one number, square every number in it and add the squares together, which the lab writes as ‖x‖². Squaring turns every number positive, so a miss in either direction counts. The readout ‖x − x̂‖² / ‖x‖² divides the leftover's sum of squares by the original's sum of squares. The result is the share of the list that the rebuild fails to capture, which this lesson calls the unexplained share. Here is the idea with three sliders instead of 256: Say the original list is 4, −2 and 1, and the rebuild is 4, −1 and 1. The leftover is 0, −1 and 0, so its sum of squares is 0 + 1 + 0 = 1. The original's sum of squares is 16 + 4 + 1 = 21. The unexplained share is 1 ÷ 21, which is about 4.8%, so the rebuild captures all but about 5% of the list. In the lab, at the first space of the default text, all 32 active features together leave only 1.0% unexplained. Labels, examples and the cache Nobody tells you what a feature means, so to find out, you look at where it switches on and propose a name for it. That name is called a label, such as "fires on spaces". A feature fires at a character when its activation rises above a cut-off that you choose, called the activation threshold. The hope is that each feature stands for one clear thing, which would make it a monosemantic feature, from words meaning "one meaning". That is a goal rather than a promise, because many features fall short of it. So a label is a hypothesis: a guess that you can test, and that could turn out to be wrong. To help with labels, the lab scanned 1,800 windows of text, which is 115,200 characters in all. It picked the 128 features that reached the largest activations and stored each one's eight best examples, meaning the characters where its activation was highest. Each example also records its position in the window, and this stored set is called the cache. Three questions about one feature The lab asks three questions about a feature, in order, and each one can come back "no": Where do its examples come from? If its best examples all sit at the start of a window, where the model has read almost nothing, they may say more about the window than about language. Does its label hold up on new text? You turn the label into a rule and score how well it predicts where the feature fires on text that is not in the examples. Does turning it up do what the label says? You add the feature's recipe to the model and compare the change with what a random recipe of the same size does.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A model's residual is a wall of busy numbers. At the first space of the default text, nearly all 256 of them are non-zero, and each one is a blend of many things at once. There is no single number you can point to and say "that one means a space". So you cannot read the residual directly, test an idea about it, or push on one thing without also pushing on others. Rewriting each snapshot as 32 active features out of 1,024 is what makes the three questions above possible. You can read where one feature switches on, test a label for it, and push on it alone. Each of those steps makes a claim, and each claim can be wrong. A good rebuild does not back any of them up, because it only shows that the features can recreate the numbers. It does not show that the model itself is built from those features, since a different set of recipes might recreate the numbers too. Picture a jigsaw puzzle that you could finish with two different sets of pieces cut in different shapes. A finished picture tells you the pieces fit, but not which set the puzzle maker actually cut. In the same way, a good rebuild tells you the features fit the numbers, but not that the model thinks in those features. That is why the lab keeps hunting for evidence that could prove a label wrong. Its first two questions only check what a feature goes along with, which is called a correlation. Only the third tests what the feature causes when you change it, which is a stronger kind of evidence, so it comes last.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: The lab starts with the probe text "hath the king a good horse? KING HENRY: aye, he hath.", which is 53 characters long. You can type your own text into the Probe text box, up to 64 characters, but the lab readouts quoted in this lesson come from the default text. Figures marked as held-out, or taken from the cache, were measured ahead of time on a large batch of Shakespeare text, so typing your own text does not change them. The lab draws a space as ␣ and a line break as ↵, and the steps below take the cards in the same order as the lab's steps. Residual to sparse code In Residual to sparse code, each character of the probe text is a button, and the lab starts on position 4, the first space. Compare the two panels: the top one shows the 256 numbers as bars, with a dash on each bar marking the rebuild. The one below shows all 1,024 feature slots, with a spike for each active feature. Read Active features (L0), which counts the features that are switched on (L0 is the math name for that count). Then read the ‖x − x̂‖² / ‖x‖² readout, which is the unexplained share. Look at the list of the largest active features. A window start mark means at least half of a feature's eight best examples come from the first four positions of a window. At the first space, #121 is the biggest feature, and the second, #499, carries that mark. Now click position 0, the first h, where the six largest features all carry the mark. Then click position 1, the a, where the two largest, #876 and #356, still carry it. Finally, click the K of KING at position 28, where none of the six largest carries the mark. Sparsity and superposition In Sparsity and superposition, drag Keep top k features from 1 up to 32. The lab rebuilds the same snapshot from only the k biggest features and plots how much is left unexplained. Compare the readouts Keep 1 and Keep all 32 under the chart. Lower down, read Most similar pair and Their cosine (signed). They name the two features whose recipes overlap the most and say which way those two recipes point. A cosine is a score for how much two recipes overlap, explained under What to notice, and "signed" means it keeps its plus or minus sign. Feature evidence Try this: In Feature evidence, keep feature #876, the first one in the Feature menu. Each of its eight best examples has a badge giving its position in the window, so read those badges first. Then switch Examples shown to Top 8 from position 4 on, and compare the characters and their activations. Then test a label on another feature: Choose #121 in the Feature menu, or click it in the list in the first card, and set Label to test to Space. Drag Activation threshold from 5 down to 2, then up to 8, and watch Precision and Recall under the text. These are two scores for how well the label fits, explained under What to notice. Choose #511, set Label to test to Same character, which here means the comma, and set Activation threshold to 3. The default text has one comma, and #511 fires on it, so recall is 100%. But it also fires on more than a dozen other characters, so precision drops to about 6%. Raise the threshold to 5, and #511 misses the comma altogether. The line under the controls spells out the hypothesis you are testing, such as "feature #121 fires on spaces", along with the threshold it uses. Steer with a feature In Steer with a feature, keep Feature to steer on #160, Steering position on 43, which is the comma after "aye", and Steering strength on 10. Read the three lists, which show the six most likely next characters before the push, after it, and with a random push instead. The label's character is marked (label). Read Change in log p, which says how much more or less likely the label's character became. Compare it with the range in 20 random: min · median · max, where the median is the middle value. Press Continue 12 characters to see the model write the next 12 characters three ways: without steering, with the feature added, and with a random push. Continue adds the same push again at each new character, so the steered text gets 12 separate pushes, not one that the model carries forward. Move Random control direction to see that the random push shown is one draw out of 20. Choose #683 in Feature to steer, set Steering strength to 5, and compare which characters rise with what its label predicts.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: A few features carry most of the list At the first space, the 32 active features rebuild the residual so well that only 1.0% is left unexplained. With Keep top k features at 1, the single biggest feature leaves 53.5% unexplained, which is more than half. With 8 it leaves 4.6%, so the curve falls steeply at first and then flattens, because the biggest few features carry most of the list. The rebuild is uneven across the text. It runs from 0.0% at the first character to 22.3% at the K of KING, and it averages 7.0% over the default text. On 200 windows that the autoencoder never trained on, called held-out text, it leaves 5.1% unexplained. Held-out text works like a test with new questions rather than the ones you practised. The curve is not perfectly smooth: at the first space, adding the 29th feature nudges the unexplained share up, from 1.00% to 1.03%. That can happen because the 32 features were fitted to work as a team, not to be added one at a time. Overlap: superposition you can measure The lab scores how much two recipes overlap with a number called the cosine, which comes from the angle between their arrows. A cosine of 1 means two recipes point the same way, 0 means they are at right angles and share nothing, and −1 means they are exact opposites. A readout marked |cos| ignores the sign and only asks how big the overlap is. From here on, "overlap" means |cos|: how closely two recipes lie along the same line, in either direction. The readout All: mean · max shows that across all 1,024 recipes, the average overlap is 0.069: close to zero, but not zero. That small overlap is superposition, measured in the autoencoder's own dictionary, and it has to be there because 1,024 recipes cannot all be orthogonal on 256 sliders. The biggest overlap is a surprise: Most similar pair shows #108 and #499, with a |cos| of 0.992, so their recipes lie along almost exactly the same line. Their cosine (signed) is negative, so they point opposite ways along that line, like "slider 3 up" and "slider 3 down". Pairs with |cos| above 0.9 shows that seven pairs overlap by more than 0.9. The lab's measurements find that all seven are negative too, though the card shows the sign only for the top pair. On 768 held-out characters, #108 and #499 are never on together, and one of the two is on for 734 of them. They split the text between them. From position 4 on, away from the window start, #499 is on for 101 of the 111 spaces, while #108 is on for only 6 of them. Among the 181 lowercase vowels the pattern flips, with #108 for 132 of them and #499 for only 41. Why would two features point opposite ways and never be on together? Remember that the encoder turns any negative score into zero, so an activation can never go below zero, and each knob can only turn up from zero. If the model's numbers sometimes move one way along a recipe and sometimes the other way, one knob cannot cover both. The autoencoder needs a "more of this" knob and a "less of this" knob, with recipes pointing in opposite directions. That reading is called a sign split: two features for the two sides of one direction, which is why only one of them is on at a time. It is not feature splitting, which happens when a bigger dictionary breaks one feature into several narrower ones. As a made-up example, a small dictionary might have one feature for punctuation, while a bigger one might split it into separate features for commas, full stops and question marks. Seeing feature splitting needs dictionaries of different sizes, and this lab trains only one. Where a feature's examples come from At the start of a window the model has read almost nothing, so its numbers there look unlike those for running text. A feature can then reach its biggest activations at the window's edge, for reasons that have nothing to do with language. A feature like that is called a window-start artefact, where an artefact is something produced by the way you measure rather than by the thing you are measuring. Picture timing how loud a classroom gets, minute by minute, and keeping the eight loudest minutes. If every one of them is the first minute of a lesson, when everyone is still arriving, your top eight describe the start of class rather than the lessons. The cache marks 21 of its 128 features as window-start artefacts, 18 of them position-0 artefacts, whose best examples are mostly at the very first character. Across all 1,024 features, not only the cached ones, no feature fires only at position 0, but 24 are dominated by it. That means far more of their firing happens at position 0 than chance would give, since only 1 in 64 positions is a first character. The strongest feature in the cache, #876, reaches 56.9 and carries the window start mark. All eight of its best examples sit at positions 1 and 2, and they are a jumble of different characters, from a semicolon to a capital H. What those examples share is their place in the window, so the label First 4 characters matches 8 of 8. Yet #876 is not only a start-of-window feature. It is on for 31.6% of all scanned characters, about 1 in 3, and its biggest example from position 4 on is 36.3, at position 19, on an ampersand (&). On held-out passages it averages 13.3 at position 1 but only 0.64 from position 8 on. It is big at the start and small later, so its best examples describe the window's edge rather than how it behaves in running text. The model's own numbers are unusually large at the start too. You can measure the overall size of the 256-number list, called its length, by squaring each number, adding the squares and taking the square root. It is the same idea as finding the long side of a right-angled triangle. Measured after the autoencoder rescales the numbers into its own units, the length averages 32.5 at position 0 and 21.5 at position 1, against 15.0 from position 4 on. At the very first character, the list is more than twice its usual size. Scoring a label: precision and recall Picture a smoke alarm in a kitchen, which you can judge with two different questions. Of all the times it beeped, how often was there real smoke? And of all the times there was real smoke, how often did it beep? An alarm set to be very sensitive catches every wisp of smoke, but it also beeps at steam from the kettle. One that is hard to trigger rarely gives false alarms, but it can miss a small fire. A feature's label gets the same two questions. Precision asks: of the characters where the feature fires, what share match the label? Recall asks: of the characters that match the label, what share does the feature fire on? The Activation threshold works like the alarm's sensitivity setting, and a lower threshold makes a more sensitive alarm. The default text has 10 spaces. With Label to test on Space and the threshold at 5.0, feature #121 scores 100% precision and 70% recall: it fires on 7 of the spaces and on nothing else. The line under the readouts counts this as 7 hits, 3 misses and 0 false alarms. Lower the threshold to 2.0 and it scores 90% and 90%. It now catches 9 of the 10 spaces, but it also fires on one character that is not a space. On 768 held-out characters, the same label shows the trade-off clearly. Each pair below gives precision first, then recall: At 5.0, it scores 96% and 91%: nearly every firing is a space, and it catches about nine spaces in ten. At 2.0, it scores 63% and 97%: it catches almost every space, but more than a third of its firings are false alarms. At 8.0, it scores 100% and 56%: every firing is a space, yet it misses almost half of them. Lowering the threshold lets false alarms in, while raising it adds misses and can hide the cases that would show a label is wrong. Neither setting is neutral, so when someone reports how good a label is, it is fair to ask what threshold they used. The next feature shows why a feature's best examples can mislead you. Picture a friend who only ever posts photos of their eight best-looking meals. From those photos you would call them a great cook, but you have never seen the burnt toast. Feature #511's eight best examples are all commas, each with an activation of about 14, so "fires on commas" looks like a perfect label. On held-out text at a threshold of 5.0, it fires on 18 of 19 commas, which is excellent recall. But it also fires on 102 other characters. Out of its 120 firings, only 18 are commas, which is 15% precision. The examples looked perfect, and yet the label is poor on ordinary text. The cache has one more trap. Its excerpts show every line break as a space, so feature #53's eight examples all appear to show a space. Yet on held-out text, the Space label scores 0% precision and 0% recall at 5.0, while Line break scores 41% precision and 62% recall. The label that fits the examples you can see scores nothing, most likely because those "spaces" were line breaks in disguise. Steering: does turning a feature up do what its label says? Steering adds a feature's recipe to the model's residual at one position while the model predicts the next character. In mixing-board terms, you reach over and move the sliders along that feature's recipe yourself. The direction you add is called a steering vector, and Steering strength sets how hard the push is. A strength of 10 raises the feature's activation by about 10. At position 43, that push is about 40% as long as the model's own list there, which is a big shove. That share is measured in the model's units, before the autoencoder rescales the list. Keep in mind what the push changes. The residual at a position is about to become the model's guess about the next character, so steering changes that guess. A feature's label, though, describes the character the model has just read, so the two can point to different characters. The lab reports the result as Change in log p, where p is the chance of the label's character. Log is short for logarithm, but you do not need logarithms to read it. A change of 0 means no change, a positive number means more likely, and a negative number means less likely. Each step of +1 multiplies the chance by about 2.7, and each step of −1 divides it by the same amount. Any push this big changes the prediction a little, in some direction, because it shifts the model's numbers right before its final step. So the lab also tries 20 random recipes of the same length, one at a time. The readout 20 random: min · median · max shows the smallest, middle and largest of their effects. This comparison is called the null control: it shows what "no real effect" looks like, so you can see whether the feature beats it. Picture a friend who swears their lucky socks make them play better basketball. In the first game wearing them, they score 14 points instead of their usual 10. Before you believe in the socks, you would want to know how much their score jumps around in ordinary socks. If it often swings between 6 and 15, a score of 14 tells you nothing. Even a 16 would not convince you after only a few games in ordinary socks. Their best so far is only a rough edge, and the next ordinary game might reach 16 too. The same goes for the random pushes: with only 20 tries, the largest random result is a rough edge, not a hard limit. So the lab also gives a second way to judge how far the feature's change sits from the random ones. A standard deviation, or SD, is a common way to measure how spread out a set of results is. Here is an example with made-up numbers. Picture the 20 random changes averaging 0.2, with a typical random change landing about 0.3 away from that average, so that typical distance is one SD. A feature change of 2.3 sits 2.1 above the average, which is 7 of those 0.3 steps, or 7 SDs. That is far outside what random pushes do. A feature change of 0.5 sits only 0.3 above the average, which is 1 SD. Random pushes land that far out all the time. The readout Feature vs random, in SDs counts those steps for the real results. At 3 or more, the lab calls the change far outside the random spread, so it is unlikely to be chance. Between 2 and 3, it calls it weak evidence, and under 2 it cannot be told apart from chance. Feature #160 fires on hyphens. At position 43 and strength 10, the chance of a hyphen goes from 1.3% to 43.0%, which makes it about 34 times as likely and the top choice. Its log probability rises by 3.53, while the random pushes move it by anywhere from −0.53 to +1.36. That is far outside the random range, and Feature vs random, in SDs reads +6.9. Press Continue 12 characters and the three versions differ: without steering, the model follows "aye," with " my lord," and a new line. With #160 added at every new character, it writes a row of hyphens, while random direction 1 writes " where is no". At strength 5, #160 raises a hyphen's log probability by +2.09, more than any other of the 1,024 recipes does. The next best gives +1.68. Feature #683 fires on y, and its eight best examples all show a y. Yet at strength 5, adding it makes a y about a quarter as likely, from 0.55% to 0.14%, while o rises the most. That drop is real, not chance. The log probability of a y falls by 1.38, outside the random range of −0.62 to +0.85 and 3.8 SDs from their average. It is a real effect, just not the one the label seemed to promise. Line up all 1,024 recipes by how much they raise a y, and #683 comes 1,011th of 1,024, near the very bottom. The recipes that raise a y the most belong to features whose examples are b, m and t. Why can this happen? The lab shows the result but not the reason, so here is one possible reading. A feature that fires on y switches on when the character the model has just read is a y. Pushing #683 may be a bit like telling the model "you just read a y", and the next character after a y is rarely another y. That reading would fit o rising, as in "you", and features for b and m raising y, as in "by" and "my". It is still only a reading, and the lab does not test it. Either way, a label tells you where a feature switches on, and steering tests a separate claim about what it does. Feature #122 fires on m. At strength 5 it changes the log probability of an m by +0.39, about one and a half times as likely. That is only just above the largest of the 20 random pushes, which reached +0.37. Like a 16 from the lucky socks, that edge is too thin to trust. The result is only 1.6 SDs from the random average, under 2, so it cannot be told apart from chance. The change looks like an effect but is not evidence of one.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: What this lab simplifies There is one autoencoder, trained once, on one layer of a small model that reads characters and has 1.4 million parameters, the adjustable numbers set during its training. Nothing here shows that a second training run would find the same features. The labels were written by this module's author and checked on 768 held-out characters, which is a small test. Labels here are simple rules, like Same character or First 4 characters, so the lab can score them automatically. A real label such as "speaker names" carries meaning that no rule like that can capture. The cache records each example's window position and flags start-of-window cases across 1,800 scanned windows. It does not promise that an unflagged feature is a good one: #511 is unflagged and still a poor comma label. Only 128 of the 1,024 features have stored examples, and they were picked for their largest activations, not at random. Excerpts also show line breaks as spaces. Your probe text is read as one window starting at position 0, so its first characters are always window-start positions, whatever you type. Keep top k features cuts a finished 32-feature code down to fewer features. That is not the same as training an autoencoder to use fewer, which would learn different, broader features. The sign-split reading of #108 and #499 rests on their opposite recipes and on never being on together. The lab does not test it further, for example by removing one of them and checking the rebuild. Steering here is a direct push only. Because the push is added after the model's last block, the only work left is turning the numbers into next-character chances. So the lab sees what the feature does to one guess, at the position where the push is added. It cannot see how the push might change the model's later thinking, because there is no later block to change. Twenty random pushes are a rough control that is not hard to beat, and a tougher one would compare against other features' recipes. The five features you can steer were also picked because their labels measured cleanly, while most of the 1,024 have no label this good. A feature switching on alongside something is only a correlation, and nothing here shows that the model uses a feature to produce its output. The steering card tests one direct effect at the last layer, not how the model works inside. Where the real technique struggles Train the same kind of autoencoder again from a different random starting point, called a random seed, and you get different features. In one setting with a large model called Llama 3 8B, only about 30% of the features were shared between runs (Paulo and Belrose, 2025). How many features you find depends on how big a dictionary you ask for, because a bigger one splits a feature into narrower ones. That is feature splitting, and it means there is no single correct number of features. Some dictionary entries never fire on any input at all, which wastes space, and these are called dead features. This lab's autoencoder has none in 1,800 scanned windows. A feature can fail to fire where its label says it should, because a narrower feature has taken over that case. This is called absorption (Chanin and colleagues, 2024), and it makes labels harder to trust. A tidy, sparse rebuild does not prove that the autoencoder found the model's own building blocks. Steering with these features is not a settled method. On a standard set of tests called AxBench, steering with autoencoder features did worse than prompting, which means writing instructions into the question itself (Wu and colleagues, 2025). A later paper reports a way of choosing and labeling features with supervision, meaning guidance from examples with known answers (Jørgensen and Hansen). On the same AxBench tests, it gets close to a fine-tuned reference, a model trained further to do that steering job, so the picture is still changing. A common mix-up: A feature's label says where the feature switches on, not what it does when you turn it up. Turning it up changes the guess about the next character, which can be a different character from the one the label names. Feature #683 fires on y, and its eight best examples all show a y, but pushing it makes the model write y less often and o more often. A change also only counts once you compare it with a random push of the same size. Measured that way, the change from #122 looks like an effect but is not evidence of one.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: Other ways to keep features few There is more than one way to enforce "only a few features on at a time", and each one gives a different dictionary from exactly the same snapshots: An L1 penalty adds a cost for the total of all the activations. It pushes most of them to zero, but it also shrinks the ones that stay on, which skews the rebuild. TopK, the method used here, fixes the count directly. Exactly 3.125% of the features, 32 of the 1,024, were on at every logged training step. A third method lets each feature learn its own cut-off. This autoencoder also carries a small L1 penalty, but it barely matters. The loss is the training score of how wrong the autoencoder still is. At the end of training, the L1 term added only 9.7 × 10⁻⁵, which is 0.000097, to a final loss of 0.0471, so the penalty made up about 0.2% of it. From labels to tests of cause Labeling features by hand is slow, so researchers often have a language model read each feature's best examples and propose a label. That label is then scored on held-out text, and the whole method is called auto-interpretability. It makes labeling possible at a large scale, but it carries over the labeling model's leaning toward tidy explanations, and it still only checks where a feature fires. The test of cause is the steering vector: add the feature's direction while the model writes, and check whether its output changes the way the label predicts. The Golden Gate Bridge result from the start of this lesson was a test like this, run on a large model. What makes such a result convincing is the null control, because if a random push of the same size does as much, the feature has earned nothing. Beyond one layer Related tools go further than one layer. A transcoder imitates one of the model's busy layers using a wider layer in which only a few parts are on at a time (Dunefsky and colleagues, 2024). A crosscoder finds features that are shared across several layers, or even across different models (Anthropic, 2024). The next lab, on circuits, asks the same kind of question about the model's own parts: not what goes along with a behavior, but what causes it. Until then, treat every feature label, in this lab and in research papers, as a hypothesis with evidence behind it, not a finished fact.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: This module is about naming the parts of a transformer layer's activation, and how far such a name can be trusted. Neurons are polysemantic, responding to unrelated things, because of superposition: a layer packs more features than it has dimensions onto nearly orthogonal directions. A sparse autoencoder (SAE), a separate model, rewrites an activation as a few active features out of a much wider dictionary; each feature's label is a hypothesis to test, not a finding. The transformer block explained the role of the residual stream, a running sum that every sublayer adds to; this lab's SAE reads it after the last block. Like the VAE in Diffusion & VAEs, an SAE encodes and reconstructs, but its code is wider than its input and almost all zeros. Where it shows up Anthropic amplified a Golden Gate Bridge feature in Claude 3 Sonnet, and its replies to most queries mentioned the bridge, even when irrelevant. Auto-interpretability has a language model read a feature's top examples, propose a label, and score it by how well it predicts activations on held-out text. On the AxBench benchmark, steering with SAE features was not competitive with prompting (Wu et al., 2025); a later paper reports that a supervised pipeline for choosing and labeling SAE features gets close to a fine-tuned reference there. Why it matters Superposition makes the model's own units unreadable, so without a decomposition there is no part with a single meaning to name. With one, each kind of evidence for a label can mislead in its own way: Top examples can come from the first characters of the model's window, where the residual depends on almost no context, and describe the window start rather than language. A feature whose label fits every top example can still fire on many characters the label does not describe. Any added vector shifts the output, so a steering effect counts only when it beats a null control: a random direction of the same length. What you will be able to explain Superposition: why neurons end up polysemantic, and how a sparse autoencoder extracts a few active features from a wider dictionary. Labels as hypotheses: how to check where a feature's examples sit in the model's window, and how to score its label on new text as precision and recall at a chosen threshold. Steering: why adding a feature's direction is a causal test of its label, and why the effect counts only when it beats a random direction of the same length. What the lab shows The lab runs the shipped 1.4-million-parameter character transformer and its SAE through ONNX. Residual to sparse code and Sparsity and superposition compute the residual, its 32 active features of 1,024, the unexplained share, the Keep top k features curve and the decoder overlaps from those weights and your Probe text; only the SAE's training curve is logged. Feature evidence reads fixed top examples, cached for 128 features, each with its window position. It scores author-written rules such as Space on your text at the Activation threshold: precision is the share of firings that match, recall the share of matches that fire. The key experiment is Steer with a feature, for five features whose labels measured cleanly. Steering strength adds a feature's decoder direction at Steering position, and the change in the label character's log probability is set against 20 seeded random directions, one of them shown by Random control direction. Continue writes greedy text three ways: no push, the feature, and that random direction.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: The obvious way to understand a network would be to read its neurons: inspect what activates unit 1,432, name it, repeat. This fails quickly, because individual units respond to collections of apparently unrelated things. They are polysemantic, and that is the normal case rather than an anomaly. Why that happens: superposition A layer has a fixed number of dimensions, and there are far more distinguishable features than that. A model could represent at most d features on orthogonal directions. Instead it represents many more on *almost*-orthogonal directions that overlap slightly. This works because features are sparse: almost none are present in any single input, so the interference between overlapping directions rarely matters. Superposition is a rational use of a dimension budget, and it is exactly what makes single units unreadable. The proposed fix: sparse autoencoders A sparse autoencoder (SAE) unpacks the overlap. It is a separate model trained on recorded activations, here the transformer's residual stream after its last block, which it rewrites as a few active features out of many more, then reconstructs. The transformer itself is untouched. The shipped SAE, from train_sparse_autoencoder.py: normalizes each 256-number residual with a corpus mean and one global scale; encodes it as ReLU(W_enc x + b_enc) over 1,024 features, then keeps only the 32 largest (TopK); decodes with x̂ = W_dec f, where each feature's direction has unit length; trains on reconstruction loss plus a small L1 sparsity penalty (×0.002), for 10,000 steps on 1,600 windows of the corpus's training split. This is dictionary learning applied to a model's internals. Three questions about one feature The lab asks them in order, and each one can come back "no": Where do its examples come from? Every cached example records its position in the model's 64-character window. The first positions are not running text. Does its label survive new text? Score the label as precision and recall at a threshold. Does turning it up do what the label says? Add its direction to the residual and compare with a random direction of the same length.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Interpretability I: features
documents.body: An SAE is one way to ask what a layer represents, and its parts are only as meaningful as their answers to the three questions above. A good reconstruction answers none of them: it says the code rebuilds the vector, not that its parts are the model's own.

Read the window position on each example, then switch Examples shown to the top eight from position 4 on. Choose #121, set Label to test to Space, and move Activation threshold from 5 down to 2 and up to 8. Then choose #511 and test Same character. In Steer with a feature, keep #160 at position 43 and compare its change with the random range. Press Continue, then choose #683 and compare what rises with what its label predicts.
