documents.subtitle: Plain · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: Picture a model that has already been trained on one kind of text, and now you want it to take on a new job, such as writing recipe steps. The most direct way is to keep training every number inside the model on the new text, which is what the *Fine-tuning & transfer* lab did. That works, but every new job then leaves you with a complete new copy of the model, and a large model holds billions of numbers in each copy. This module is about a cheaper method called LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation. LoRA locks the original numbers so that training can never change them, and it trains a small add-on, called an adapter, whose numbers are added on top. You can picture the original model as a printed page and the adapter as a clear plastic sheet laid over it. Whatever is drawn on the sheet changes what you read, while the page underneath stays exactly as it was. Because the add-on stays separate, you can lift it off or swap in another one for a different job. You can also photocopy the page with the sheet on it into one new page for good. Each of those choices has a price, and this lab lets you see every one of them. Where it shows up The calculator in this lab uses the real sizes of three Llama 3 models, which are large language models, the kind of program behind a chatbot. The smallest has about 1 billion learned numbers and the largest about 70 billion. LoRA is built into the free toolkits people use to adapt models like these, and into the software companies run to answer chatbot requests. Because an adapter is small, one computer can keep a single copy of a big model and clip on a different adapter for each request. The researchers who introduced LoRA compared it with retraining every number of GPT-3, an earlier large language model that holds 175 billion of them. They found that LoRA could cut how many numbers you train by 10,000 times. Why it matters Without a method like this, teaching a model ten different jobs would mean storing ten full copies of it. Training each copy would also need extra working memory for every one of its numbers. That is because popular training methods keep notes on each number they are allowed to change. With LoRA, the big model is stored once and each job adds only a small file. For the 8-billion-number model in the calculator, the starting setting gives an adapter of about 84 megabytes. The model’s own numbers, stored the same way, fill about 16,000 megabytes, so the adapter holds about half a percent as many numbers as the model itself. In this lab, the cheap version also fits the new text about as well as retraining everything, which is the result that makes the trade worth making. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these ideas in your own words: what the add-on, written B · A, adds to a table of numbers that stays locked the whole time; how the Rank setting, which decides how many simple patterns the add-on may combine, trades a closer fit against more numbers to train, store and load; what you gain by merging the add-on into the original table for good, and what you give up by doing it; why a brand-new adapter changes nothing at all until it has been trained, and how it still manages to start learning; how to work out an adapter’s size for a real model, as numbers trained, share of the model and file size, and how that compares with the toy. What the lab lets you do The lab runs a real, very small model that guesses the next character of a text. Every score, chance, chart and merge check on its first three cards comes from actually training that model inside the app. The fourth card does arithmetic on the shapes of real models. The low-rank update draws the adapter’s two thin tables and the correction they make, with sliders for Rank and Alpha beside the picture. Adapter training and behaviour lets you train the adapter for longer or shorter, and shows how its guesses about the next character shift as a result. Hot-swap and merge lets you attach and detach the adapter, compare scores on the old and new texts, and then fold the adapter in for good. Adapter size calculator does the same counting for real Llama 3 models, using arithmetic only, since nothing on that card is trained. One surprise to watch for: LoRA keeps the original numbers perfectly safe, yet in this lab the adapter makes the model worse at its old job than full retraining does. Working out how both facts can be true at once is part of the lesson.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: The base model: a table of 900 numbers The model in this lab reads one character and guesses which character comes next. Its alphabet has 30 characters, made up of a space, the 26 letters, a full stop and two spare symbols that never appear in the text. Everything the model has learned sits in one table, with a row for each character it might read and a column for each character that might come next. Each cell holds a score, and a higher score means that pairing is more likely. In the row for t, for example, the cell in the h column holds a high score, because the training text says “the” again and again. To make a guess, the model turns one row of scores into chances that add up to 100%, giving bigger scores bigger chances. These raw scores are called logits, a word the lab uses when it checks a merge. With 30 rows and 30 columns, the table holds 900 numbers, which are called weights or parameters, and the lab calls the whole table W. A table of numbers laid out in rows and columns like this is called a matrix, so you will also see W called a weight matrix. W was trained for 60 passes over a short text called Harbor weather notes, which is eight lines about fog, wind, rain and boats. One full pass over the training text is called an epoch. The lab measures how well a model fits a text with a loss, the average of how surprised the model is by each real next character. The model counts as very surprised when it gave the character that really came next a small chance, and barely surprised when it gave it a big chance. Lower is better, and a model that spread its guesses evenly over all 30 characters would score about 3.4, so anything below that means it has picked up real patterns. The base model scores 1.921 on Harbor weather notes, the text it trained on, and 2.556 on Recipe steps, a short set of cooking instructions it was never trained on. It does worse on recipes because cooking lines such as “simmer the sauce until it thickens” follow different letter patterns from weather notes. This is the same base model that the *Fine-tuning & transfer* lab starts from, rebuilt inside this lab, so the two methods begin from exactly the same place. Locking the table and adding a correction Fine-tuning, in the last lab, let training change all 900 numbers in W on the recipes. Only 720 of them actually move, as the note under the lab’s formula row points out. The recipes never contain some characters, such as j, q, x and z, so the rows for those characters get no push. LoRA takes a different route: it freezes W, which means the model reads the table every time it makes a guess, but training never writes a single change into it. Instead, LoRA learns a separate grid of corrections, the same 30 by 30 size as W, and adds it cell by cell to the table before each guess. The lab calls this grid ΔW, said “delta W”, because the Greek letter Δ is the usual math shorthand for “change in”. The lab’s formula row, Effective weights, shows the table the model actually uses. At the starting settings it reads W + (8 / 4) · B · A, where each dot means “times”. That is W + (alpha / rank) · B · A with the two slider values filled in. B · A is the raw correction, built from two small tables explained below. alpha / rank is a dial that turns the raw correction up or down, set by two sliders you will meet later. ΔW is the correction after the dial. At the starting settings the dial is 8 ÷ 4 = 2, so ΔW is twice B · A. Picture the base table as a printed page and the adapter as a clear plastic sheet laid on top. Ink on the sheet changes what you read, but the page itself is never marked, so when you lift the sheet off, the original is exactly as it was. You can keep a different sheet for each job and swap them in and out, which is called hot-swapping. You can also photocopy the page with a sheet on it into one flat new page, which is called merging. The copy is quicker to read because there is only one layer, but you can never peel the sheet off it again. Building the correction from two thin tables If the correction could be any 30 by 30 grid, it would have 900 numbers of its own, and you would be training as many numbers as before. LoRA saves work by building the grid out of two thin tables, called B and A, in a way that needs far fewer numbers. In the simplest case, B is one column of 30 numbers, one per row of the grid, and A is one row of 30 numbers, one per column. To fill in any cell of the grid, you multiply the B number for its row by the A number for its column. It works exactly like a times table, where every cell is its row heading times its column heading, and that is how 60 numbers can fill all 900 cells. Here is a made-up miniature with three rows and three columns, so you can see the arithmetic. Say A holds the pattern 2, 0, −1 and B holds one number per row, so each row of the grid is its B number times that pattern: Row 1 has a B number of 1, so it reads 2, 0, −1. Row 2 has a B number of 3, so it reads 6, 0, −3. Row 3 has a B number of 0, so it reads 0, 0, 0. Six numbers have filled nine cells, but notice the catch: every row is the same pattern, multiplied by a different amount. A correction built from one pattern can only push every row in that one shared way, harder for some rows and softer for others. A row whose B number is negative gets the pattern in reverse. To allow more variety, LoRA adds several of these times tables together. With two patterns, B gets a second column and A gets a second row, so every row of the correction becomes its own mix of the two patterns. In the miniature, add a second pattern, 0, 1, 1. Then give each row a second B number: 0 for row 1, 1 for row 2 and 2 for row 3. Each cell now adds two products, one from each pattern: Row 1 stays 2, 0, −1, because it takes none of the new pattern. Row 2 becomes 6, 0, −3 plus 0, 1, 1, which is 6, 1, −2. Row 3 becomes 0, 0, 0 plus twice 0, 1, 1, which is 0, 2, 2. The rows no longer all follow one shape, because each one mixes the two patterns in its own amounts. In a grid this tiny, two patterns already cost more numbers than the grid holds. In the lab’s 30 by 30 grid, though, each pattern costs 60 numbers against 900 cells, so a few patterns stay cheap. The number of patterns is the adapter’s rank, written r, and the Rank slider sets it from 1 to 12. So B is 30 tall and r wide, A is r tall and 30 wide, and multiplying them always gives a 30 by 30 grid. In math, the smallest number of patterns needed to build a grid is called its rank. That is where the name comes from, since low-rank adaptation means a correction built from only a few patterns. The lab’s chart calls each pattern a direction, so a rank-4 correction has at most 4 directions. Counting the cost Each pattern costs 30 numbers in B plus 30 in A, so every pattern adds 60 numbers to train. The lab writes this as r · (d + k), where d and k are the height and width of the table, both 30 here. At the starting rank of 4, that is 4 × 60 = 240 numbers to train, a little over a quarter of the 900 that full fine-tuning trains. A higher rank gives the correction more freedom, but it also means more numbers to train, store and load. That trade between fit and cost is what the Rank slider lets you explore. Where the sheet picture stops matching Ink on a real sheet usually marks a few spots and leaves the rest clear, but this sheet is not a small patch. It can change every cell in any row the recipe text uses, which is 24 of the 30 rows here. Only the rows for characters the recipes never contain are left exactly as they were. Nothing on it is a drawing you could read, either, since it is a grid of small positive and negative numbers. And the sheet is not drawn freely, because everything on it must be built from r patterns, which is exactly the limit that rank sets. What the diagram shows The card called The low-rank update draws all of this with the real trained numbers. A runs across the top, labelled A · 4 × 30 · random start, while B runs down the left, and the finished correction ΔW sits where the two meet. The label tells you how A began. Once training starts, A changes too, and after 24 passes most of what you see in it was learned. In the ΔW grid, blue cells raise a score compared with the rest of its row, and red cells lower it. In A and B, blue means a positive number and red a negative one. The deeper the colour, the further that number is from zero, measured against the biggest number in the same grid. Below the diagram, a second map shows the change full fine-tuning made to the table over the same passes. Any grid, even that one, can be broken into patterns like the ones above, up to 30 of them, and some patterns carry much more of the change than others. A chart next to that map asks the same question of both changes: if you kept only the k strongest patterns, how much of the change would you keep? This is the same letter as in the cost formula, but here it means the number of patterns kept. The solid curve is the adapter, and the dashed curve is full fine-tuning. To judge size, the chart squares each number in a change and adds them up, which is why it talks about squared size and update energy. The bottom axis calls each pattern’s strength a singular value, a name from the math used to find the patterns, and you will not need that math here. Because the adapter’s correction is built from exactly r patterns, its solid curve always reaches 100% at k = r and stays flat after that. Why a fresh adapter changes nothing Before any training, B is filled with zeros and A is filled with small random numbers. As in the two-pattern miniature, every cell of B · A is made by multiplying B numbers by A numbers and adding the results, and anything multiplied by zero is zero. So the whole correction is exactly zero, and the effective weights are exactly the base weights. This starting trick is called zero initialization, and it means training begins from the base model’s own behaviour instead of from a copy that random numbers have knocked off course. You might wonder how B ever moves if it starts at zero. Training looks at a small handful of examples at a time, called a batch, and nudges the trainable numbers after each one. Each number gets a push that says which way to move to lower the loss, and that push is called its gradient. Picture one cell made from a B number of 0 and an A number of 0.3, so the cell is 0 × 0.3 = 0. If training nudges the B number up by 1, the cell becomes 1 × 0.3 = 0.3, so a change to B moves the cell by an amount set by A. If training nudges the A number instead, the cell is still 0 times something, which is 0. A change to A cannot help yet, so training gives A no push at first. That is why B starts moving on the very first batch, while A has to wait until B holds something other than zero. It is also why the two cannot both start at zero, since nudging either one alone would leave every cell at zero, and neither would ever get a push. What Alpha does The correction passes through one more control before it is added: a scale equal to alpha / rank, where Alpha is a slider from 1 to 24. At the starting settings, Rank is 4 and Alpha is 8, so the scale is 8 ÷ 4 = 2.00 and ΔW is twice B · A. The card’s top line shows all three at once, as rank 4 · alpha 8 · scale 2.00. Why divide by rank at all? Adding more patterns together tends to make the raw correction bigger. The researchers behind LoRA reasoned that dividing by the number of patterns keeps its size roughly steady, so training settings that worked at one rank still work at another. That reasoning was made for a different training method from the one this lab uses. In this lab, the scale also sets how big every training nudge is, so a smaller scale means smaller nudges. The catch shows up when you hold Alpha at 8 and slide Rank, because the scale moves too. Rank 1 then gets a scale of 8.00, while rank 12 gets only 0.67, so a higher rank also gets a smaller scale. In this lab, that makes each training nudge count for less. At Alpha 8, rank 12’s finished correction ends up a little over half the size of rank 4’s. When alpha equals rank instead, the correction stays roughly the same size from rank 4 to rank 12. Whenever alpha and rank differ, the card shows a warning that the scale has changed. Under it sits a button labelled Set alpha = rank, for a scale of 1, which makes the two equal. From the toy to a real model Real models are built from the same kind of tables, only far bigger and far more of them. A model such as Llama 3 8B, where 8B means about 8 billion numbers, is a stack of 32 layers. The layers are steps that the text passes through one after another, and each layer holds several weight matrices. Four of them sit in the attention part from the *Attention* lab, named q, k, v and o for query, key, value and output. Here k is only the name of a table, the third job this letter has had in the lesson. Three more sit in a second part called the MLP, a block that works on each position of the text after attention has run. The calculator names those three gate, up and down. Every one of these tables has the model dimension, d, as at least one of its sides. The letter d stands for the count of numbers the model uses to describe each piece of text. For Llama 3 8B, d is 4,096. The calculator uses d for this width only, while in the toy’s cost formula d and k were the table’s two sides. The tables are not all square, though. In Llama 3 8B, q and o are 4,096 by 4,096, but k and v are 4,096 by 1,024. The three MLP tables are 4,096 by 14,336, with down turned the other way round, which is why the MLP takes most of the adapter. Choosing which matrices get adapters is called picking the target modules. The calculator’s Target matrices buttons do exactly that, with one button for each attention matrix and one for the whole MLP. For each targeted matrix, the adapter pair costs r · (inputs + outputs), where inputs and outputs are the matrix’s two sides. The calculator’s formula row adds that up over all targeted matrices and layers, writing it as Σ r · (inputs + outputs), where the Greek letter Σ means “add them all up”. As a worked example, the q matrix in Llama 3 8B has 4,096 inputs and 4,096 outputs, so its two sides add up to 8,192. At rank 16, one layer’s pair for that matrix holds 16 × 8,192 = 131,072 numbers. Multiplied across all 32 layers, that comes to 4,194,304, which is the figure the calculator’s bar list shows for q projection. The same steps work for the other tables. For k, the sides add up to 4,096 + 1,024 = 5,120, so 32 layers at rank 16 give 16 × 5,120 × 32 = 2,621,440. Each MLP table has sides that add up to 18,432, so the three of them come to 28,311,552, about two thirds of the whole adapter. Add q and o at 4,194,304 each, k and v at 2,621,440 each, and the MLP. The total is 41,943,040, the count the calculator shows for every matrix at rank 16. From a count to a file size To turn a count into a file size, you need to know how much room each number takes. Computers store everything as bits, each a single 0 or 1, and 8 bits make one byte. At an Adapter precision of 16-bit, each number takes 16 bits, which is 2 bytes. A megabyte, written MB, is a million bytes, so a million numbers stored at 16-bit fill 2 MB. More bits per number keep each number more precise, but they make the file bigger in exact proportion. So the 8B adapter’s 41,943,040 numbers, at 2 bytes each, fill 83,886,080 bytes. That is the 83.9 MB the calculator shows. Why a real adapter is a tiny share Last, the calculator divides the adapter’s count by the number of weights in the whole base model and shows the result as Share of the base model. The badge at the top of the card gives the 8B model’s count, about 8.03 billion, and 41,943,040 ÷ 8,030,000,000 is about 0.00522, or 0.522%. The general name for this is the trainable fraction: how many numbers training is allowed to change, as a share of how many the base model holds. With LoRA, the numbers training changes are the adapter’s. When the lab says the toy “trains 26.7% of its table”, it means the adapter holds that many numbers compared with the table. The table itself still never changes. A pair’s cost grows with the *sum* of a matrix’s two sides, while the matrix itself grows with their *product*. In the times-table picture, 60 headings fill a 900-cell table, but 8,192 headings fill a table of more than 16 million cells. So the bigger the matrix, the smaller the adapter’s share, which you can see by comparing two matrices at rank 4. The toy’s adapter holds 26.7% as many numbers as its 30-wide table, a bit more than a quarter. A 4,096 by 4,096 matrix at the same rank needs 4 × (4,096 + 4,096) = 32,768 adapter numbers, while the matrix itself holds 16,777,216. That makes the adapter only 0.195% of it, or about 1 number in 500.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: With LoRA, the base table stays exactly as it was, byte for byte. The only new thing you keep for each task is the adapter, which is 60r numbers in this lab. The saving reaches training as well as storage. A popular training method keeps two extra numbers of notes for every number it is allowed to change. At rank 4, that bookkeeping covers 240 adapter numbers instead of all 900, and the frozen table needs none at all. Picture a school with one expensive set of science textbooks and three teachers who each want to mark the books up for their own class. If every teacher had to buy and write in a full set, the school would pay for three sets and fill three shelves. If each teacher instead keeps a thin folder of clear sheets that lie over the pages, the school keeps one set of books and three thin folders. A teacher can also lift her sheets off at the end of a lesson, and the next class finds the books exactly as they were. The open question is whether squeezing the correction into a few patterns costs too much accuracy, and in this lab it costs almost nothing. At the same budget of 24 passes, a rank-4 adapter with 240 numbers of its own reaches a loss of 2.077 on Recipe steps. Retraining all 900 weights for the same 24 passes reaches 2.090, so here the adapter does slightly better while training a little over a quarter as many numbers. That is one measurement on one small text, so treat it as an example of the trade rather than a rule. Why might a cheap correction do about as well? LoRA rests on a bet that the *change* a new task needs is simple, even though the table being changed is not. Recipes push the model to favour some letter pairs over others, such as a after s for “sauce” and “salt”. The bet is that a handful of patterns can carry most of a shift like that.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: The lab follows the steps below in order, and each one tells you which control to move and what to compare. Size the update On The low-rank update, drag Rank from 1 to 12 and watch B widen and A grow taller. Each new pattern adds a column to B and a row to A, so the two thin tables grow together. The slider’s label shows the cost as you go, such as 4 · 240 weights. Below it, the bar list called Trainable parameter count compares a bar for LoRA at the current rank with the 900 weights of Full fine-tuning. As you drag, the LoRA bar climbs in steps of 60: At rank 1, the LoRA bar reads 60 weights, which is one fifteenth of the full table. At rank 2, it reads 120, because two patterns cost 60 numbers each. At rank 4, the starting value, it reads 240, a little over a quarter of the table. At rank 8, it reads 480, which is already more than half of the full table. At rank 12, the top of the slider, it reads 720, which is 80% of the full table. The slider stops at 12, well short of rank 15, where the adapter would cost 900 numbers, as many as the whole table. Before moving on, set Rank back to 4, its starting value. Train the adapter Try this: set Adapter epochs to 0, where the slider reads untrained. B and ΔW go blank in the diagram, even though A still shows its random colours, because zero times anything is zero. Target loss, on the Hot-swap and merge card, now reads 2.556, which is exactly the base model’s score. Every pair of bars under Next character after, the base-versus-adapter bars you will explore in a moment, matches too, because an untrained adapter changes nothing at all. Now raise Adapter epochs back to 24 and look at the Adapter training loss chart. Its solid line peels away from the dotted line, which marks the frozen base model’s score on recipes. The solid line is bumpy because each point averages the loss on about a dozen small batches, measured while the adapter was still changing. For a fair score, read the full-text loss in the note under the chart. The chart measures loss in nats per character. A nat is the unit this surprise score is counted in, the way points are the unit of a game score, and every loss in this lesson uses it. Lower is better, and the dotted line at 2.556 is the score to beat. Next, pick s under Next character after, and you will see a row for each of the seven most likely next characters, each with two bars. The upper, hatched bar is the base model, and the lower, solid bar is the base model plus the adapter. Find the row for a, which reads 5% → 29%: the base model gives a a 5% chance after s, and the adapter raises it to 29%. That fits the text, because recipes keep saying “sauce”, “salt” and “salted”. Now pick ␣, the symbol the lab uses for a space, and notice that the most likely next character, t, barely moves, from 22% to 18%. The picker offers five starting characters: ␣, e, s, l and a. If you click through all five, the bars after l change most, since a space after l jumps from 5% to 62%. The bars after s and a change next most, those after e a little less, and the bars after the space barely move. Compare ranks fairly Keep Adapter epochs at 24 and slide Rank again, this time reading the target loss printed on the LoRA bar, where lower is better: Rank 1 scores 2.462, the worst of the five and the closest to the untrained model. Rank 2 scores 2.316, a clear step better than rank 1. Rank 4, the starting value, scores 2.077, beating full fine-tuning. Rank 8 scores 1.990, the best fit of the five. Rank 12 scores 2.059, which is worse than rank 8 even though it has more patterns. That last result looks odd until you read the warning above the bars, which says that with Alpha held at 8, the scale changed every time you moved Rank. At each rank, press Set alpha = rank, for a scale of 1 so that the scale reads 1.00, then read the loss again. With the scale held steady, the extra patterns pay off, and rank 12 comes out slightly ahead of rank 8. Rank 4 is worth a look here too. The button drops its scale from 2.00 to 1.00, and its loss rises to 2.091, level with full fine-tuning’s 2.090. So the adapter’s small win at the starting settings owes something to its scale. The button disappears once the two values match, and it comes back as soon as you move Rank again, because Alpha stays wherever you left it. Before moving on, set Rank back to 4 and Alpha back to 8, the starting values, because the next steps quote the numbers for those settings. Hot-swap it On Hot-swap and merge, flip Serving between Base only and Base + adapter, and watch three readouts move together: Target loss, the score on the recipes, moves between 2.556 and 2.077. Source loss, the score on Harbor weather notes, moves between 1.921 and 2.235. Serving weights moves between 900 and 1140, because keeping the adapter separate means holding its 240 numbers beside the table. The sample text under the readouts changes too, since it is written by whichever table is being served. The model is given the word “the” and a space to start from, but that start is not shown, so the text begins with what it wrote next. It uses a temperature of 0.7, a setting that controls how much randomness goes into picking each character. Merge it Press Merge the adapter into W, and the button changes to Adapter merged into W while Serving shows only one option, Merged — nothing left to swap. Serving weights drops back to 900, because the correction now lives inside the table itself. Target loss stays at 2.077, since the merged table holds the same numbers the adapter was producing. In a real system, an unmerged adapter makes every guess take extra work. The model reads its row of W, builds the matching row of the correction from B and A, and adds the two. After a merge that sum is already done and stored, so each guess reads one table, and that saved work is what merging gains. The callout under the button reports the largest logit gap, at about 4e-7, which is 0.0000004. That is the biggest difference in any score between the merged table and the unmerged path, which keeps W and the adapter apart and adds their effects for each guess. Changing Rank, Alpha or Adapter epochs undoes the merge, because each of them retrains the adapter. Size a real adapter Open the Adapter size calculator, which starts on Architecture Llama 3 8B with every button under Target matrices switched on and Adapter rank r at 16. At those settings, the three readouts across the middle of the card show what the adapter costs: Trainable parameters reads 41,943,040, the count of numbers the adapter would train. Share of the base model reads 0.522%, which is about 1 number in every 190. Adapter size at 16-bit reads 83.9 MB, the size of the file that holds those numbers. Switch the MLP button off, and the count falls to 13,631,488, or 0.170% of the model. Switch the MLP back on, then set Adapter precision to 32-bit to store each number with twice as many bits. The size doubles to 167.8 MB, since each number now takes 4 bytes instead of 2. Then read the callout at the bottom of the card, which uses the Rank from the first card rather than the calculator’s own rank. At the toy’s starting rank of 4, it says the toy trains 26.7% of its table, while the 8B model with every matrix targeted trains 0.131%. That is lower than the 0.522% above because the callout uses rank 4, a quarter of 16, so the share is a quarter as big. Last, switch Architecture between Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3 8B and Llama 3 70B, and watch Share of the base model fall as the model grows.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: The cheap adapter keeps up The headline: 240 trained adapter numbers matched 900 trained weights at the same budget, 2.077 against 2.090. That is the case for adapters, measured once on one small text. Full fine-tuning got there with a change spread over many patterns, not a simple one. On the chart, its first 4 directions hold only 63% of that change. Even its first 8 directions hold only 86%, and its dashed curve does not pass 95% until it reaches 11 directions. A rank-4 adapter can hold at most 4 directions, so at best it could have copied 63% of full fine-tuning’s change. Since it still scored as well, it must have found a different, simpler change that fits recipes about as well. More rank is not automatically better Of the five ranks in the list, the best recipe loss at Alpha 8 came from rank 8, not rank 12. If you stop at every rank, rank 7 is best at 1.977, and rank 12 does worse than every rank from 5 to Two things changed at once, which is the problem: rank 12 had more patterns to work with, but its scale had dropped to 0.67. That smaller scale made every push it took count for less. Picture testing whether bigger study groups score higher on a quiz, while cutting the study time each time you add a member. If the biggest group does worse, you cannot tell whether the size hurt or the shorter session did. The rank sweep at a fixed Alpha has exactly that problem, and setting alpha equal to rank fixes it by holding the scale at 1.00. So a worse score at rank 12 does not prove that extra rank harms the fit. Once the scale is held at 1.00, rank 12 edges ahead of rank 8, so the drop came from the weaker scale, not from the extra patterns. Swapping and merging Taking the adapter off restores the base exactly, because W was never written, so Source loss goes back to 1.921. While the adapter is on, the model does worse on Harbor weather notes than full fine-tuning left it, scoring 2.235 there against full fine-tuning’s 2.088. A scale of 2.00 makes the adapter’s correction bigger, but it is not the main reason. With Rank at 4, set Alpha to 4 for a scale of 1.00. The adapter now fits recipes as well as full fine-tuning, 2.091 against 2.090, yet still leaves Harbor weather notes at 2.208. To reach its recipe score, the adapter’s correction ended up bigger overall than the change full fine-tuning made, and some of that correction also reaches the harbor text. The lab does not pin down the exact cause. Merging matches the unmerged path to within about 4e-7 per score. That difference is rounding, and the recipe loss is the same to four decimal places. The rounding happens because the unmerged path does its sum with extra-precise numbers each time, while the merged table stores every number once in a format that keeps fewer digits. The difference is far too small to change any prediction, which is why the two losses match. Real models The toy makes LoRA’s share look about 200 times bigger than it is on a real model. At rank 4, the toy’s adapter holds 26.7% as many numbers as its table, while the 8B model’s adapter, with every matrix targeted, holds 0.131% as many as the model. The share being compared is the trainable fraction, and it shrinks on big models because pairs grow with the sum of a matrix’s sides while matrices grow with the product. Which matrices you target matters as much as rank. At rank 16, the MLP holds 67.5% of the 8B model’s adapter, because its three matrices are much larger than the attention ones. Starting from q and v alone at rank 16, switching on the MLP as well multiplies the count by 5.15. Size grows in exact proportion to rank, to layers and to bits, so doubling any one of them doubles the file. The share also falls as the whole model grows, as the calculator shows at rank 16 with every matrix targeted: The 1B model’s adapter is 0.912% of the model, a little under 1 number in 100. The 8B model’s adapter is 0.522% of the model, about 1 number in 190. The 70B model’s adapter is only 0.294% of the model, even though it holds 207,093,760 numbers. The same arithmetic also matches a published figure: for Llama 3.2 1B with only q targeted at rank 8, it gives 524,288 trainable parameters. That is the exact count printed by the quick tour of PEFT, a free toolkit for adapting models, for the same setup.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: What this lab simplifies The adapter, its gradients, both losses, the charts and the merge check are all computed for real as you move the controls. The biggest gap is that this model has only one matrix, so the list of target modules has one member. A real LoRA attaches to chosen matrices inside each layer, often q and v, sometimes all four and the MLP, and choosing them well is much of the real skill. Both ΔW maps subtract each row’s average before drawing, which the diagram notes as “each row’s mean removed”. Adding the same number to a whole row of scores changes no prediction, because the chances depend only on how the scores in a row differ from each other. For example, scores of 2, 1 and 0 give exactly the same chances as 5, 4 and 3, because only the gaps between them matter. Full fine-tuning never adds a same-for-the-whole-row amount, but the adapter does, so its raw correction is slightly bigger than its map shows. The hidden part is small: at most about 0.08 per row, next to cells as large as about 4.5. Rank stops at 12, well short of rank 15, where the adapter would cost as many numbers as the whole table. The full fine-tuning bar and map come from one run, with one fixed random order of practice examples. They are a reference point, not a verdict on which method wins. Nothing is held out. Every recipe loss is measured on the same eight recipe lines the adapter trained on, and Source loss on the Harbor lines the base trained on. So a low recipe score shows how well the adapter fits those lines, not how it would handle new ones. Picture a student who is only ever graded on the eight practice questions they studied. A good score there tells you little about how they would do on new questions, and this lab only ever shows you that practice score. The training rule is plain SGD, a basic rule that nudges each number by its gradient times a fixed step size of 0.6. It also uses no dropout, a guard that randomly blanks out some of the adapter’s inputs during training to discourage memorising. Next character after offers five starting characters, chosen because recipes change them visibly, but every row whose character appears in the recipes is trained as well. On Hot-swap and merge, there is no second adapter to swap in, so detaching is the only swap. Merging there is a switch plus a real numerical check, not a new file being written. To keep the lab quick, the Base + adapter setting also reads from a table that was added up in advance. So you never feel the extra work of an unmerged adapter here. The lab does the slower, separate sum only for the merge check. Serving weights still counts A and B, though, because that is the memory a real server pays to keep the adapter swappable. The Adapter size calculator does arithmetic and nothing else. Because it trains and serves nothing, it cannot tell you whether a given rank is enough for a task. Its Custom model follows Llama 3’s proportions and is not a real published model, and its counts leave out anything beyond the LoRA pairs. All three presets come from one family of models, so a model built differently would give different counts. A common mix-up: LoRA does not protect a model from forgetting its old job. The rank-4 adapter leaves Harbor weather notes at 2.235, while full fine-tuning leaves them at 2.088. What LoRA protects is the base *weights file*, which is why you can swap adapters and merge them. In the sheet picture, the page under the sheet is untouched, yet while the sheet is on, the whole page reads differently, including the parts you never meant to change. Whether the old *behaviour* survives depends on the scale, the rank and the training budget, just as forgetting after full fine-tuning depends on how long and how hard it trains. Where real LoRA falls short How close an adapter comes to full fine-tuning depends on the task. Adapters fall behind on big shifts, such as a new language, a new kind of input or genuinely new knowledge. Only testing on examples held back from training tells you which case you are in. An adapter’s training loss can look excellent while the adapter fails on prompts unlike the ones it trained on. The Source loss readout is this lab’s cheap check for side effects on the old job. Serving many unmerged adapters at once needs special code that handles several requests together, so that each request is not slowed down. Merging several adapters into one base makes them get in each other’s way, which is the subject of the next lab, *Model merging*. The file on disk also depends on the number format the adapter is stored in, which can differ from the base model’s. Even when the base model uses 16-bit numbers, PEFT keeps the adapter’s numbers at 32-bit by default, because training is steadier that way. So the 32-bit size is a realistic size during training. A small trainable fraction also says nothing about quality on its own.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: The bet behind the method LoRA’s central bet is that the *change* a fine-tune needs is simple, even when the weights are not. In math terms, the change is close to low rank, so squeezing it into rank r loses little. The squeeze also acts as a brake on overfitting, which means fitting the training text so closely that new text suffers. That is part of why small ranks sometimes do better than large ones on new text. This lab cannot show that, because it scores only the text the adapter trained on. Why Alpha divides by rank The product B · A is a sum of r one-pattern pieces, so its size tends to grow as r grows. The LoRA paper divides by r to hold it roughly steady, so that you can change rank without also changing how hard the adapter pushes. That reasoning was made for the paper’s training method, Adam. It does not hold for this lab’s plain nudges, where alpha equal to rank keeps the size roughly steady, at least from rank 4 to rank 12. Later work called rsLoRA argues that dividing by the square root of r is steadier at large ranks, and PEFT offers that choice as use_rslora. Where the real saving is The biggest saving in real systems is training memory, not prediction speed. The training method with two extra numbers of notes for every *trainable* weight, from *Why it’s here*, is called Adam. No pushes are stored at all for the frozen table, so its memory goes only to holding it. QLoRA QLoRA goes further by storing the frozen base in 4-bit numbers instead of 16-bit, which cuts the base’s memory about four times. Each 4-bit number is expanded back to 16-bit on the fly whenever it is needed for a multiply, while only the 16-bit adapter trains. That was enough to fine-tune a model with 65 billion numbers on one graphics chip, or GPU, with 48 gigabytes of memory, where a gigabyte is a billion bytes. The *Quantization* lab shows the plain version of this storage trick, where the allowed values are evenly spaced. QLoRA’s 4-bit format, called NormalFloat or NF4, spaces its 16 allowed values unevenly to suit weights whose values follow a bell-shaped spread. The QLoRA paper describes this layout as the best possible use of 16 values, in a precise mathematical sense, for weights spread that way. A second trick, called double quantization, squeezes the small helper numbers that the 4-bit format needs, which saves a little more memory. Older adapters Earlier adapter designs slid small extra layers between the frozen ones, and those extra layers stay in every prediction forever. LoRA’s correction is plain addition, so it can be folded into W once and cost nothing extra when the model makes predictions. An adapter that does anything beyond multiplying by fixed numbers and adding, such as cutting off negative values, cannot be folded in this way. Other ways to adapt LoRA is one member of a family called PEFT, short for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, which means training a small set of added or chosen numbers while the base stays frozen. The PEFT toolkit, published free by the company Hugging Face, collects these methods, and they differ in what is trained and where: Prompt tuning trains a few extra lists of numbers, called soft prompts, that are added to the model’s input. Prefix tuning also trains lists of numbers, but slips them into every layer rather than only at the input. IA3 learns numbers that turn the volume up or down on parts of each layer. PEFT’s guide says it trains about 0.01% of a model called T0, where LoRA trains more than 0.1%. DoRA splits each weight into a size and a direction, adapts the direction with LoRA, and learns the size separately. PEFT turns it on with use_dora and recommends merging it before use, because it adds extra work. Serving many adapters Because an adapter is small, one server can hold a single copy of the base model and many adapters, then choose one for each request. This is called multi-adapter serving, and it works like keeping one printed page and a stack of clear sheets beside it. PEFT’s quick tour shows the simplest version, where add_adapter registers a named adapter and set_adapter switches to it. The serving software vLLM runs LoRA adapters when it is started with --enable-lora, and each request names the adapter it wants. A setting called max_loras caps how many adapters run at once. The S-LoRA paper describes a system that keeps every adapter in main memory and moves the ones in use onto the GPU. It reports up to four times the work done per second of vLLM and PEFT setups. It does that while serving several orders of magnitude more adapters, where each order of magnitude means ten times as many. A merged adapter gives all of this up, because each merge is a separate full copy of the weights. Toy versus real Shares: the toy trains 26.7% of its weights at rank 4. The PEFT quick tour prints 524,288 trainable numbers for a rank-8 adapter on the q matrices of Llama 3.2 1B. That quick-tour adapter is 0.0424% of the 1,236,338,688 numbers PEFT counts in total, which is about 1 number in 2,400. GPT-3 is the 175-billion-number model from the start of this lesson. The LoRA paper says that, compared with retraining all of it with Adam, LoRA can cut the numbers being trained by 10,000 times. Settings: the toy uses ranks 1 to 12, Alpha 8 by default and plain SGD. The QLoRA paper used rank 64, alpha 16 and adapters on every matrix, with its own step sizes, called learning rates, that cannot be compared with the toy’s 0.6. The PEFT quick tour’s example uses rank 8 with alpha 32, so its scale is 4. Files: PEFT saves an adapter as two files, a small settings file and a file of numbers in a format called safetensors. Safetensors is built to store tables of numbers safely and load them fast. The quick tour’s adapter for a model called opt-350m is 6.3 MB, against about 700 MB for the model itself. Tools: PEFT’s merge_and_unload folds an adapter into the base, and the training tools in a toolkit called TRL work with PEFT. A tool called mergekit can go the other way: from a fully fine-tuned model, it can pull out a low-rank adapter that approximates the change. The base model here was trained for 60 passes, while the *Model merging* lab trains its own Harbor base for 48 instead. Each lab fixes its own count, and none of them tests the difference. Where these facts come from The facts about tools come from the PEFT documentation, including its quick tour and its guides to LoRA, IA3 and soft prompts, and from the safetensors and mergekit documentation. The research claims come from the LoRA paper by Hu and others (arXiv 2106.09685) and the QLoRA paper by Dettmers and others (arXiv 2305.14314). The model shapes come from the Llama 3 paper (arXiv 2407.21783) and the released settings files of the three Llama models.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, adapts a pretrained model without rewriting it: it freezes a weight matrix W and trains a separate update beside it, ΔW = (alpha / rank) · B · A. B and A are thin matrices whose shared inner dimension is the rank, and alpha / rank sets the update's scale. The question LoRA answers is how much of a fine-tune you can keep while training and shipping only that small update. *Fine-tuning & transfer* kept training a pretrained table's own weights on a new corpus and measured the forgetting that caused. This lab freezes the same Harbor base, compares a low-rank update with full fine-tuning at the same budget, and then follows the update into serving and onto real model sizes. Where it shows up Hugging Face's PEFT library, named for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, implements LoRA among related methods, and TRL's trainers, such as SFTTrainer, integrate with PEFT. In a transformer, adapters often target the query and value projections, sometimes all four attention projections (query, key, value and output) and the feed-forward layers. QLoRA trains a 16-bit adapter on a base stored in 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), which let a 65B-parameter model fine-tune on one 48 GB GPU. vLLM serves LoRA adapters registered by name when started with --enable-lora, and each request selects one. Why it matters Full fine-tuning carries gradients and optimizer state for every parameter, and Adam, for example, keeps two extra values per trainable parameter. LoRA confines both to the adapter. The LoRA paper reports that, compared with fine-tuning GPT-3 175B with Adam, LoRA can cut the trainable parameters by 10,000 times. Because the base is never written, one server can hold a single copy of it and choose among many small adapters per request, instead of a full copy of the weights per task. The price is capacity: whether an adapter matches full fine-tuning depends on the task. What you will be able to explain What the scaled product B · A adds to a frozen weight matrix. How Rank trades fit against parameter count, and why a sweep at a fixed Alpha changes two things at once. What merging an adapter into W gains at inference, and what it forecloses. Why a freshly initialized adapter changes nothing until it is trained. How to compute an adapter's trainable parameters, share of the base model and file size from an architecture, and how they compare with the toy's. What the lab shows The first three cards train a toy live: a 900-weight character bigram model, one 30 × 30 table pretrained on Harbor weather notes, adapted to Recipe steps with plain SGD beside a full fine-tune at the same epochs. Losses, probabilities, spectra and the merge check are measured; the corpora, seeds and learning rate are fixed. The low-rank update: Rank (1 to 12) and Alpha set the update's shape and scale, and a diagram draws the trained A, B and ΔW, each row's mean removed. A warning offers Set alpha = rank, for a scale of 1 whenever they differ. The Trainable parameter count bar list sets Full fine-tuning against LoRA rank r, each with its target loss. A chart compares the directions each update needs, beside a map of the full fine-tune's ΔW. Adapter training and behaviour: Adapter epochs (0 to 48) sets the budget. Next character after picks a context, and paired bars compare base and adapted probabilities. Hot-swap and merge: Serving switches between Base only and Base + adapter, and the card reports Target loss, Source loss and Serving weights. Merge the adapter into W folds the update in and reports the largest logit gap from the unmerged path. Adapter size calculator: closed-form arithmetic that trains nothing. Architecture, Target matrices, Model dimension d, Layers and Adapter rank r drive Trainable parameters and Share of the base model, and Adapter precision also sets the adapter's size. The key experiment runs at the defaults: compare the two target losses in the Trainable parameter count bar list, then flip Serving to see the attached adapter raise Source loss and detaching restore the base exactly.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: LoRA freezes a weight matrix and trains an addition to it. The Effective weights row shows the whole mechanism with the current numbers substituted: W + (alpha / rank) · B · A. W is the base table — the same 900-weight character bigram model, pretrained 60 epochs on Harbor weather notes, scoring 1.921 there and 2.556 on Recipe steps. It is read on every forward pass and written on none. B is 30 × r and A is r × 30, so their product is another 30 × 30 matrix. For a d × k matrix the pair holds r · (d + k) numbers instead of d · k; here that is 60r against 900. Rank sets r, and only B and A receive updates. The base is the identical 60-epoch, seed 1 Harbor table that *Fine-tuning & transfer* starts from, rebuilt inside this lab. *Model merging* trains its own Harbor base for 48 epochs instead. Each lab fixes its own epoch count, and none tests the difference. What the diagram shows The matrix-product diagram on The low-rank update draws the trained numbers: A across the top, B down the left, and ΔW where they meet. Every row of ΔW is a weighted mix of the same r rows of A, so ΔW can have at most r independent directions. The chart beside the full fine-tune's map confirms it: the LoRA curve reaches 100% at k = r exactly. Why an untrained adapter does nothing B starts at all zeros and A starts random, so B · A is exactly the zero matrix. That is zero initialization: adaptation begins from the pretrained behaviour. The gradient reaching B is proportional to A, which is non-zero, so B moves on the first batch; once B is non-zero, A starts receiving gradient too. What Alpha is for Alpha sets the constant alpha / rank that multiplies the product. At the defaults — Rank 4 and Alpha 8 — the scale is 2.00, so the adapter's contribution to each logit is twice the raw product.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: The previous lab left you a whole new 900-weight table per task. LoRA changes the shipping unit: the base stays byte-identical and the per-task artifact is 60r numbers. That separation is what makes hot-swapping and merging possible. The reason anyone accepts the constraint is the measured result. At the same 24-epoch budget, a rank-4 adapter training 240 of 900 weights reaches 2.077 on Recipe steps, while full fine-tuning of all 900 reaches 2.090.

documents.subtitle: Standard · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: Move Rank from 1 to 12. B widens, A deepens, and the bar list reads 60, 120, 240, 480 and 720 trainable weights against 900. Set Adapter epochs to 0. B and ΔW go blank, Target loss reads 2.556, and every pair of bars under Next character after matches. Raise it back to 24 and watch the solid curve leave the dotted frozen-base line. At 24 epochs sweep Rank and read the recipe loss in the bar list: 2.462, 2.316, 2.077, 1.990 and 2.059 for ranks 1, 2, 4, 8 and 12. Then pick s under Next character after: the base gives a 5%, the adapter 29%. Switch Serving between Base only and Base + adapter: Target loss moves between 2.556 and 2.077, Source loss between 1.921 and 2.235. Then press Merge the adapter into W and read the logit gap. Then press Set alpha = rank and repeat the rank sweep at a scale of 1.00. Last, open Adapter size calculator. Switch the MLP off and the count falls to 13,631,488, or 0.170%. Set Adapter precision to 32-bit and the size doubles to 167.8 MB. Then read the callout: at rank 4 the toy trains 26.7% of its table, and the 8B preset trains 0.131%.

The structural gap is that this model has one matrix, so target modules has one member. A real LoRA attaches to chosen projections inside each attention block — often the query and value projections, sometimes all four and the feed-forward layers — and that choice is much of the practical skill. Both ΔW maps subtract each row's mean before drawing, because a softmax ignores a constant added to a whole row. documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: The empirical claim behind the method is that the *update* a fine-tune needs has low intrinsic rank even when the weights do not (Hu et al., 2021). The constraint also acts as a regularizer, which is part of why small ranks sometimes generalize better than large ones. alpha / rank exists so rank and update strength can be tuned separately. The product B · A sums r rank-one terms, so its size tends to grow with r; dividing by r holds it roughly steady, and a learning rate tuned at one rank still works at another. Later work (rsLoRA) argues that dividing by the square root of r is steadier at large ranks. The larger saving is training state, not the forward pass. Adam keeps two extra values per *trainable* parameter, so 240 trainable weights carry optimizer state for 240 rather than 900, and gradients for the frozen matrices are never stored. QLoRA pushes further: the frozen base is stored in 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), dequantized to 16 bits on the fly for each multiply, while the adapter trains in 16-bit precision. That cuts the base's memory about fourfold and let a 65B-parameter model fine-tune on one 48 GB GPU. The *Quantization* lab shows the uniform affine version of this storage trade, with a bit width and a scope. NF4 places its 16 levels non-uniformly, a data type the QLoRA paper describes as information theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights. Double quantization quantizes the quantization constants themselves to save more memory. Earlier adapter designs inserted small trainable bottleneck layers between frozen ones, which stay in every forward pass. LoRA's update is linear in the weights, so it can be folded into W once — which is also why an adapter with a nonlinearity inside cannot be merged. Other ways to adapt LoRA is one member of the family that Hugging Face's PEFT library collects under parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The others change what is trained, and where: Prompt tuning trains soft prompt vectors that are added to the input embeddings of a frozen model. Prefix tuning also trains vectors, but inserts them in every layer rather than only at the input. IA3 learns vectors that rescale the keys, the values, and the intermediate feed-forward activations. PEFT's guide says an IA3 model trains about 0.01% of T0's parameters where LoRA trains more than 0.1%. DoRA splits each weight into a magnitude and a direction, adapts the direction with LoRA, and learns the magnitude as a separate parameter. PEFT turns it on with use_dora and recommends merging for inference, because it adds overhead. PEFT also offers use_rslora, which scales the update by alpha over the square root of rank. Serving many adapters Because an adapter is small, one server can hold a single copy of the base model and many adapters, and choose one per request. PEFT's quick tour shows the in-process version: add_adapter registers a named adapter and set_adapter activates it. vLLM serves LoRA adapters when started with --enable-lora. Adapters are registered by name, a request selects one through its model field, and max_loras bounds how many run at once. The S-LoRA paper describes a system that keeps every adapter in main memory and fetches those used by running requests into GPU memory. It reports up to four times the throughput of vLLM and PEFT baselines while serving several orders of magnitude more adapters. A merged adapter gives all of this up: each merge is a separate full copy of the weights. Toy versus real Fractions. The toy trains 26.7% of its weights at rank 4. The Hugging Face PEFT quick tour prints 524,288 trainable parameters of 1,236,338,688, which is 0.0424%, for a rank-8 adapter on the query projections of Llama 3.2 1B. The calculator gives 0.522% for rank 16 on every matrix of Llama 3 8B. The LoRA paper's abstract says that, compared with fine-tuning GPT-3 175B with Adam, LoRA can cut the trainable parameters by 10,000 times. Settings. The toy uses ranks 1 to 12, alpha 8, and plain SGD at 0.6. The QLoRA paper used r = 64, alpha = 16, adapters on all linear layers, and learning rates of 2 × 10⁻⁴ for 7B and 13B models and 1 × 10⁻⁴ for 33B and 65B. The PEFT quick tour's example uses r = 8, lora_alpha = 32, and 1 × 10⁻³. These rates are not comparable with the toy's. Files. save_pretrained writes the adapter as adapter_config.json plus adapter_model.safetensors. Safetensors is a format for storing tensors safely, as opposed to pickle, while staying fast through zero-copy loading. The PEFT quick tour's opt-350m adapter is 6.3 MB against about 700 MB for the model, and PEFT casts 16-bit adapter weights to float32 by default for stable training. Tools. Hugging Face PEFT provides LoraConfig, get_peft_model, and merge_and_unload to fold an adapter into the base. TRL's trainers, such as SFTTrainer, integrate with it, and the QLoRA recipe stores the base in NF4. mergekit can extract a PEFT-compatible low-rank approximation from a fine-tuned model with mergekit-extract-lora. Sources: PEFT documentation (quick tour; LoRA, PEFT model, IA3 and soft prompt guides); Hu et al., *LoRA* (arXiv 2106.09685); Dettmers et al., *QLoRA* (arXiv 2305.14314), Table 9 and appendix B.2; Hugging Face safetensors documentation; the mergekit README; Llama 3 paper (arXiv 2407.21783), Table 3, and the config.json files of the Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3 8B and Llama 3 70B checkpoints on the Hub (unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B, unsloth/llama-3-8b, NousResearch/Meta-Llama-3-70B).

documents.body: One frozen table plus two thin trainable ones LoRA drawn from the trained numbers: B (30 × r) times A (r × 30), scaled by α / r, is the 30 × 30 update added to the frozen table W. Rank and Alpha sit beside the picture, so you can watch B widen, A deepen, and the update's number of directions follow r. A kicker `rank r · alpha α · scale α/r` and a badge `N of 900 weights train`. `Rank` (1 to 12, printed with r · 60 weights), `Alpha` (1 to 24, printed with the scale), a warning whenever alpha ≠ rank with a button to set them equal, and a bar list comparing `Full fine-tuning` (d · k = 900) with `LoRA rank r` (r · (d + k)), each with its target loss. A matrix-product diagram: A across the top, B down the left, and ΔW = (α/r)·B·A where they meet. Blue cells raise a logit, red lower it, and each matrix is shaded against its own largest entry. A chart of how much of each update's squared size its first k directions hold, for the LoRA ΔW (solid) and a full fine-tune's ΔW at the same epochs (dashed), with a guide at k = r. The full fine-tune's ΔW is drawn beside it. A formula row `W + (α / r) · B · A` and a detail line on how many of the full run's 900 weights actually move. The adapter is `trainTinyLora` on Recipe steps: B starts at zero, A at small random values, batch 16, learning rate 0.6, seed 5, from a base trained 60 epochs on Harbor weather notes. Both ΔW maps have each row's mean subtracted. A softmax row ignores a constant added to all of its logits, so that part changes no prediction; subtracting it cannot raise the rank. The chart uses singular values from a Jacobi eigendecomposition of ΔWᵀΔW. The share at k is (σ₁² + … + σₖ²) / Σσ², the best any rank-k matrix can keep of that update. Trainable count is `r · (d + k)` with d = k = 30, so 60r: 240 at rank 4, 720 at rank 12. At rank 15 it would equal the full table. `Rank` resizes B and A and retrains. `Alpha` changes the scale and retrains. `Adapter epochs`, on the training card, retrains too. Comparison worth running: at 24 epochs, move Rank from 1 to 12. The solid curve always reaches 100% at k = r, while the dashed one needs 11 directions to pass 95%. B is blank at 0 epochs, so ΔW is blank too, whatever A holds. That is zero initialization in one picture. The full fine-tune's update is spread out: its first 4 directions hold 63%, its first 8 hold 86%. The rank-4 adapter still matches its recipe loss, 2.077 against 2.090. The scale α / r is printed in the kicker. Raising rank at a fixed alpha shrinks every update, which is why the warning appears. In this lab: W, A and B are the whole model, one 30 × 30 table. Real LoRA attaches to chosen projection matrices inside attention and the MLP, usually thousands of rows wide. The Adapter size calculator below does the same arithmetic for real architectures. In this lab: the full-fine-tune bar and map are one run at one seed, there to give the parameter count and the spectrum a reference, not to settle which method wins. In general: LoRA bets that the update a task needs is close to low rank. When it is not, as for large shifts in language or knowledge, more rank or full fine-tuning wins, and only held-out evaluation tells you which case you are in.

documents.subtitle: Adapter training and behaviour · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: Only B and A receive gradients How long the adapter trains, its loss while training against the frozen base's recipe loss, and what it does to the next-character distribution after a chosen character. `Adapter epochs`, from `untrained` at 0 to 48 passes. A chart of optimizer step against batch loss on recipes. Solid `LoRA rank r, per-batch`, dotted `frozen base, full corpus` at the base model's recipe cross-entropy, and a footnote with the adapted model's full-corpus recipe loss. `Next character after`, choosing the context `␣`, `e`, `s`, `l` or `a`. The seven most likely next characters after that context, each with a hatched bar for the base model above a solid bar for base plus adapter, and both probabilities printed. The solid curve averages minibatch cross-entropy between history points while A and B train. At 0 epochs the trainer has no history, so the card draws a flat segment at the base loss. The dotted line is `tinyCrossEntropy(base, recipes)`, recomputed rather than trained. Probe bars are the softmax of one row: the frozen table's row, then the same row of `W + (α/r)·B·A`. `Adapter epochs` retrains the adapter and the full-fine-tune comparison. `Next character after` only changes which row is probed. Comparison worth running: at 24 epochs pick `s`. The base puts 5% on `a`; the adapter puts 29%, because Recipe steps says `sauce`, `salt` and `salted`. At 0 epochs every pair of bars matches exactly: an untrained adapter is a no-op. The space row barely moves (`t` 22% → 18%). Of the five probe rows, `l` moves most, then `s` and `a`; `e` and the space row move least. The solid training curve is noisy because it is batch loss. The footnote's full-corpus number is the one to compare with the dotted line. In this lab: the loss is training loss on eight recipe sentences, and the probe shows one row of a bigram model. There is no held-out recipe set. In this lab: five probe contexts are offered, chosen because recipes change them visibly; the other rows are trained too. In general: adapter training loss can look excellent while the adapter fails on prompts unlike its training set. The serving card's source loss is this page's cheap check for side effects.

documents.subtitle: Hot-swap and merge · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: Attach it, detach it, or fold it in The serving choice LoRA exists to give you: run the base, run the base plus adapter, or add (α/r)·B·A into W once. The merge is checked against the unmerged path, logit by logit. A `Serving` control: `Base only` and `Base + adapter`, or a single option `Merged — nothing left to swap` after you merge. Three metrics: `Target loss` and `Source loss` of whatever is being served, and `Serving weights` as 900, 900 + 60r, or 900 once merged. A sample from the served table: prompt `the `, temperature 0.7, seed 12, 76 characters. A button `Merge the adapter into W`, and a callout that reports the largest logit gap between the merged table and the unmerged path, plus the recipe loss through the unmerged path. The unmerged path computes `W[x] + (α/r)·B[x]·A` in float64 for every context row x, never forming B·A. The merged table is `W + ΔW` stored in float32. The gap is float32 rounding, about 4e-7 at rank 4, and the recipe loss agrees to four decimals. At 0 epochs the gap is exactly 0. `Source loss` turns the loss tone when the adapter raises harbor cross-entropy by more than 0.05 nats, a display threshold rather than a standard. `Serving` attaches or detaches the adapter. It does nothing once merged. `Merge the adapter into W` holds until you change Rank, Alpha or Adapter epochs, which clears the merge. Comparison worth running: with a trained adapter, flip Serving and watch Target loss, Source loss and the sample move together. Then merge and confirm Target loss stays at the adapted value while Serving weights drops to 900. Detaching restores the base exactly: Source loss returns to 1.921. The base array was never written. Serving weights reads 1140 at rank 4 unmerged. That is the memory you pay to keep the adapter swappable. Merging an untrained adapter changes nothing: W + 0 is W, and the gap reads 0. In this lab: merge is a flag plus a real numerical check, not a file write, and there is no second adapter to swap in. `Detach` is the only swap. In this lab: while attached, the sample and losses are read from the merged numbers, so you do not pay the extra multiply as you click; the serving-weights metric still counts A and B. In general: servers keep many adapters in memory and apply one per request with batched kernels, or merge one default adapter for a dedicated endpoint. The trade is extra parameters and a matmul against a one-time add you cannot undo.

documents.subtitle: Adapter size calculator · LoRA & adapters
documents.body: What the same idea costs on a real model A closed-form calculator for LoRA's size. Pick an architecture, the matrices to adapt, a rank, and a precision, and it reports the trainable parameters, their share of the base model, and the adapter's size in megabytes. Nothing on it is trained: it is arithmetic on published shapes, set beside the toy's 27%. A kicker naming the architecture with its model dimension d and layer count, and a badge with the base model's parameter count. Architecture, a choice of Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3 8B, Llama 3 70B, or Custom. Target matrices, five toggle buttons: q, k, v, o, and MLP. Model dimension d from 256 to 16,384, Layers from 1 to 126, Adapter rank r from 1 to 256, and Adapter precision of 32, 16, 8, or 4 bits. Three metrics: Trainable parameters, Share of the base model, and Adapter size at the chosen precision in megabytes of 10^6 bytes. A bar list of trainable parameters for each targeted matrix across every layer, a formula row with the live totals, and a callout comparing the toy at its current Rank with this architecture at the same rank and targets. A LoRA pair on a matrix with `inputs` columns and `outputs` rows holds rank × (inputs + outputs) numbers: B is outputs by rank and A is rank by inputs. The query projection is d by heads × head dimension, key and value are d by key-value heads × head dimension, the output projection reverses the query's shape, and the MLP is three matrices between d and the feed-forward width. Trainable parameters sum that over the targeted matrices and every layer. The base count is the embedding table, a separate output table unless it is tied, each layer's four attention matrices, three MLP matrices and two norm vectors, and a final norm vector. Size is parameters times bits divided by 8, in megabytes of 10^6 bytes. It counts weights only, not file metadata. The 8B and 70B presets take layers, d, feed-forward width and head counts from Table 3 of the Llama 3 paper (arXiv 2407.21783). The 1B shape and the 128,256-entry vocabulary come from the released config.json files. Custom keeps Llama 3's ratios: key and value width a quarter of d, feed-forward width 3.5 times d, untied output table. Cross-check: Llama 3.2 1B with q only at rank 8 gives 524,288 trainable parameters, which is the count the Hugging Face PEFT quick tour prints for that configuration. PEFT's own percentage, 0.0424%, divides by the base plus the adapter; this card divides by the base alone, and both round to the same digits. `Architecture` loads a preset's d and layers; moving `Model dimension d` or `Layers` switches to Custom. `Target matrices` toggles q, k, v, o, and the MLP. `Adapter rank r` and `Adapter precision` scale the count and the size. Comparison worth running: on Llama 3 8B at rank 16 with every matrix targeted, switch the MLP off and then back on. Then set Adapter precision to 32-bit and back to 16-bit. Comparison worth running: switch Architecture through 1B, 8B, and 70B at the same rank and targets and read Share of the base model. At rank 16 on every matrix, Llama 3 8B trains 41,943,040 parameters, which is 0.522% of its 8.03 billion, and the adapter is 83.9 MB at 16-bit and 167.8 MB at 32-bit. The MLP holds 28,311,552 of them, 67.5%. With only q and v at rank 8 the count is 3,407,872, 0.0424% of the base. Adding the MLP to q and v at rank 16 multiplies the count by 5.15. The share falls as the model grows: at rank 16 on every matrix it is 0.912% for the 1B model, 0.522% for 8B, and 0.294% for 70B, whose adapter is 207,093,760 parameters or 414.2 MB at 16-bit. Size is exactly linear in rank, in layers, and in bits. Doubling rank doubles the file. The callout compares like with like: at rank 4 the toy trains 26.7% of its table and the 8B preset with every matrix targeted trains 0.131%, about 200 times less. In this lab: every number is closed-form arithmetic. No adapter is trained or served here, so the card cannot say whether a given rank is enough for a task. A custom model follows Llama 3's ratios and is not a published architecture, and the counts leave out anything beyond the LoRA pairs, such as extra saved layers. In this lab: the three presets are one family, with grouped-query attention and a gated MLP. Models with other shapes, or with biases, would change the per-matrix counts. In general: the file on disk depends on the dtype the adapter is stored in, which can differ from the base model's. PEFT, for example, casts 16-bit adapter weights to float32 by default for stable training, so the 32-bit figure is a realistic training-time size. A small share also says nothing about quality.

Interpret loss as an optimization objective Predict a gradient step's direction Explain how the learning rate and curvature decide whether descent settles, overshoots, or diverges

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Loss & gradient descent
documents.body: At step 0, drag Start w and Start b and compare the squared-residual bars on Data and fit with Loss L; the loss is their mean.
