documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: An ordered list of numbers treated as a point or an arrow. In these labs the list is the whole object; there is no extra hidden meaning in the coordinates. The distance between two vectors is the length of their difference, the straight-line gap between their tips.
documents.title: Vector

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: The sum of paired coordinates, equal to the product of the two lengths times the cosine of the angle between them. Read as features times weights, it is the linear score before a bias.
documents.title: Dot product

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: A grid of numbers that transforms a vector by mixing its coordinates. Each output coordinate is a dot product of one row with the input. The same grid can also store a batch of examples as rows.
documents.title: Matrix

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: The map y = Wx + b. W is a matrix of weights, x is the incoming vector, b is a bias. It is affine unless b = 0. A later nonlinearity is what lets a stack bend.
documents.title: Linear layer

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: The local slope of a function: how much the output changes when the input moves a tiny step. For f(x)=x² the finite difference across ε is exactly 2x+ε, which meets 2x as ε shrinks.
documents.title: Derivative

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: The vector of partial derivatives of a scalar. It points in the direction of steepest increase. Gradient descent steps the opposite way.
documents.title: Gradient

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: The update θ ← θ − η ∇L(θ). η is a step size you choose, and too large a step can jump a valley. On a convex bowl every downhill path reaches the one minimum; on a double well a start can settle in a shallower local minimum. The 1-D toy on this page is honest about that and is not a picture of a deep net.
documents.title: Gradient descent

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: A non-negative number assigned to an outcome so the outcomes in a complete set sum to one. Conditional probability P(y|x) is that rule after you restrict to a given x.
documents.title: Probability

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: The probability a model assigns to the data you actually observed, as a function of its parameters. Independent draws multiply. Logs turn that product into a sum.
documents.title: Likelihood

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: Posterior = prior × likelihood / evidence, written P(y|x) = P(y) P(x|y) / P(x). The prior is the belief about y before seeing x, the likelihood is how probable x is if y is true, and the posterior is the updated belief. In odds form, posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio, so a rare class needs strong evidence. Naive Bayes multiplies such likelihoods feature by feature.
documents.title: Bayes' rule

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: The mean is the average of a set of numbers, the center of a distribution. The variance is the average squared distance from the mean, so its square root, the standard deviation σ, is in the units of the data. A Gaussian is the bell curve fixed by these two numbers: μ sets where it is centered and σ² sets how wide. Its height is a density, not a probability; probability is area.
documents.title: Mean and variance

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: The sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^−z) maps any real number, called a logit, to a probability between 0 and 1, with σ(0) = 0.5. The logit is the log-odds ln(p/(1−p)), so the two undo each other. Softmax over two classes is a sigmoid of the logit gap. Logistic regression reports σ(w·x+b) as P(y=1|x).
documents.title: Sigmoid and logit

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: The exponent that produces a number from a fixed base. Logs turn products into sums, which is why loss functions add log probabilities instead of multiplying tiny fractions.
documents.title: Logarithm

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The math you need
documents.body: The expected surprise of a true distribution p if you announced q: −Σ p ln q. It equals the entropy of p only when q = p. A confident wrong q is very expensive.
documents.title: Cross-entropy

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The math you need · question 1
documents.body: On vectors you edit a and b until the arrows point in roughly opposite directions. What happens to a · b and cos θ? a · b stays positive, because it multiplies two lengths that cannot be negative cos θ stays at 1 and only the lengths change, because the arrows share a line Both fall to zero, because opposite arrows cancel each other out completely Both turn negative, because the angle between the arrows is past 90 degrees The dot product is |a||b| cos θ. Opposing arrows have an angle past 90 degrees, so the cosine is negative and the lengths, which are always positive, only scale it. The sum of paired products turns negative, which is why a weight vector can score a feature vector against its direction.
documents.title: On vectors you edit a and b until the arrows point in roughly opposite directions. What happens to a · b and cos θ?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The math you need · question 2
documents.body: On derivatives you shrink Nudge ε toward 0.05 and watch the secant slope. What does it do? It stays fixed at 2x + 1, because f(x) = x² has one slope per point It drifts away from 2x, because a smaller step is a rougher estimate It turns into the value of x², because the nudge cancels in the ratio It closes in on the tangent slope 2x, leaving a gap of exactly ε For f(x) = x² the secant slope is exactly 2x + ε, so shrinking the nudge removes the gap. The derivative is that ratio in the limit as ε goes to zero. A smaller nudge gives a better local estimate here, not a rougher one.
documents.title: On derivatives you shrink Nudge ε toward 0.05 and watch the secant slope. What does it do?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The math you need · question 3
documents.body: Training losses add log-probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities. Why? A log caps the cost of a confident wrong answer, so one miss cannot dominate the total A log turns a product of many tiny probabilities into a sum that stays easy to add A log shrinks the loss so a model looks better without any change to the model itself Probabilities cannot be multiplied until they are first written out as percentages The likelihood of independent draws is a product of probabilities, and a long product of fractions underflows toward zero. Logs make it a sum, which is stable and easy to differentiate. The log does not cap the cost of a confident wrong answer: minus ln q grows without bound as q falls toward zero.
documents.title: Training losses add log-probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The math you need · question 4
documents.body: On optimization with two wells, the run from w = 1.4 settles at a higher loss than the run from w = −1.4. What does that show? Descent follows the local slope, so each start settles in the nearest well Descent always finds the global minimum, so the right-hand run must contain a bug A surface with two wells cannot be trained, so neither run means anything Gradient descent only reads the slope where it stands, so each start rolls into the nearest valley. The right-hand valley is a real local minimum, shallower than the left. That is a fact about this tilted curve. On the convex bowl every start reaches one minimum, and deep networks are not two-well curves.
documents.title: On optimization with two wells, the run from w = 1.4 settles at a higher loss than the run from w = −1.4. What does that show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The math you need · question 5
documents.body: On Bayes' rule you lower Prior P(y=1) from 0.50 toward 0.10 while the count table stays fixed. What happens to P(y=1|x=1)? It stays at 0.75, because the count table fixes the likelihoods and nothing else It rises, because a rarer class makes the same evidence more surprising It falls, because the 3-to-1 likelihood ratio now multiplies smaller prior odds It falls to the prior itself, because x carries no information once the prior changes Posterior odds are prior odds times the likelihood ratio. The ratio stays 3 to 1, but the prior odds drop from 1 to about 0.11, so the posterior falls. The table's 3/4 is the posterior only when the prior is the table's own 0.50. Evidence moves a belief; it does not replace the base rate.
documents.title: On Bayes' rule you lower Prior P(y=1) from 0.50 toward 0.10 while the count table stays fixed. What happens to P(y=1|x=1)?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The math you need · question 6
documents.body: On Probability idea logit to probability you raise Logit A and Logit B by the same amount. What happens to P(A)? It rises toward 1, because e^A grows faster than e^B as both logits increase It rises, because larger logits mean the model is more confident in its choice It stays the same, because two-class softmax depends only on the gap A − B It falls toward 0.5, because both exponentials saturate together as they grow Dividing top and bottom of the softmax by e^A leaves 1/(1 + e^−(A − B)), the sigmoid of the gap. Shifting both logits leaves the gap unchanged, so P(A) does not move. Confidence comes from the size of the gap, not from how large the logits are.
documents.title: On Probability idea logit to probability you raise Logit A and Logit B by the same amount. What happens to P(A)?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The math you need · question 7
documents.body: On mean and variance you raise Variance σ² while the mean μ stays put. What happens to the bell? It moves right, because a larger variance raises the average of the bell It gets taller, because variance measures how much probability there is in total It widens and its peak falls, since the same area spreads over a wider range It only changes the sample table, because variance is a property of the data alone The mean sets where the bell is centered and the variance sets how wide it is. The total area under a density is always 1, so spreading it wider lowers the peak. A density is a height, not a probability: shrink the variance far enough and the peak rises above 1.
documents.title: On mean and variance you raise Variance σ² while the mean μ stays put. What happens to the bell?

documents.subtitle: Plain · The math you need
documents.body: This module is a toolbox for the math that the rest of the app keeps reaching for. It covers six small ideas, one at a time: vectors, which are lists of numbers; matrices, which are grids of numbers; derivatives, which measure how fast one number changes when you nudge another; optimization, which here means walking downhill to the lowest point of a curve; probability, which is the math of chances; logarithms, which count how many copies of a number you multiply together to reach another number. Most of it uses only the arithmetic, fractions, squares and square roots you already know, plus a few new tools, such as logarithms, that the page explains as it goes. Where a step needs a calculator, such as the cosine of an angle or a power of a special number called e, the lab works it out for you. You have already met these ideas inside AI, even if nobody named them. When the model behind a chatbot picks its next word, it reads from a list of chances that add up to 100%, which is probability at work. When a model is trained, its adjustable numbers are moved a little at a time down a slope, so that a score of its mistakes gets smaller. Finding that slope is the job derivatives do. The large models behind chatbots run on this same arithmetic, only with thousands of numbers in each list where this page uses one or two. Without these tools, every later lab would face two bad choices: stop every few minutes to teach the same arithmetic again, or wave its hands. Waving your hands means saying a model “compares” or “learns” without showing what those words mean, and the math is what turns them into steps you can check. The math also protects against real mistakes, because a training program that could not read a slope would have no idea which way to improve. In the same way, a computer that multiplied a long string of small chances together would end up rounding the answer down to zero. And if you forget how rare something was to begin with, a single clue can make it look far more likely than it really is. By the end of this module you will be able to explain: how to score a house for a buyer by multiplying each fact about it by how much the buyer cares, then adding, which is called a dot product; how a grid of numbers called a matrix makes many of those scores at once, in the formula Wx + b; what a derivative tells you, which is how much an answer moves when you nudge a number, and how a downhill step uses it to shrink a score of mistakes; what a “given that” chance does, which is keep only the cases that match what you know, and how a logarithm turns multiplying into adding; how a curve shaped like one bowl, with a single lowest point, differs from a tilted curve with two valleys; why a ball can come to rest in the shallower valley, called a local minimum, and what that does and does not tell you about real models; how to update a guess when a clue arrives, using Bayes' rule; what the center and the spread of a bell-shaped curve, called the mean and the variance, tell you; how the sigmoid squeezes any score into a chance between 0 and 1. In the lab, a Topic control picks one idea at a time, and the Active refresher card turns it into a picture that you can change with your own hands. You can turn two arrows, nudge a point along a curve, roll a ball downhill, lower a starting belief, stretch a bell curve or move a forecast toward the truth. Under the picture, the Worked arithmetic card writes out each step with the live numbers you have set. The Live formula card then prints the exact formula the page computes, so you can check any number by hand. Every number in the lab comes from a formula written into the page, and no model learns anything. The small table of counts and the four-number sample used for the bell curve are made up for the lesson, so nothing here is measured from real data.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · The math you need
documents.body: Think of this page as a cabinet with six labeled drawers, where each drawer holds one idea. Inside each drawer the same number shows up four ways: in words, as a picture, as a short worked calculation, and as a formula. If those four ever disagree, the page has a bug, so you can always check one against another. The page remembers which drawer is open, so a later lab can send you straight to the one you need. The cabinet picture stops matching in one useful way, because real drawers hold separate things while these ideas lean on each other. A matrix is a stack of dot products, a downhill step is built on a derivative, and cross-entropy is built from logarithms, so expect the same pieces to come back. Vectors: a list of numbers you can draw Picture describing a house with two numbers, the way the lab's Worked arithmetic card does. Each number is a made-up score for one fact about the house, and a fact used this way is called a feature. The card calls the two features rooms-like and park-like. The default house scores 1.00 for rooms and 0.40 for parks, so think of it as very roomy and somewhat near a park. The scale is invented for the lab, so only how the numbers compare matters, not what a single number means on its own. A list of numbers kept in a fixed order like this is called a vector, and the order matters because the first number means rooms and the second means park. You can draw a two-number vector as an arrow that starts at the center of a grid. The vector (1, 0.4) means “go 1 to the right and 0.4 up”, so the arrow ends at that point. In the lab this arrow is a, the list of features, and its two numbers are all there is to it, with no hidden meaning tucked behind them. The length of an arrow, written |a|, comes from the right-triangle rule you may know from geometry: square each number, add the squares, and take the square root. For the arrow a, that gives √(1² + 0.4²) = √1.16, which is about 1.08, a little longer than its one step to the right. The dot product: one weighted score Now picture a buyer who cares a little about rooms and a lot about parks. Their wishes form a second list, called the weights, and in the lab they are the vector b: 0.60 for rooms and 1.10 for parks. To score the house for this buyer, you multiply each feature by its matching weight and then add the results together. For the default house, that gives 1.00 × 0.60 + 0.40 × 1.10, which is 0.60 + 0.44 = 1.04. This calculation, where you multiply the pairs and then add, is called the dot product and is written a · b. It is a weighted sum, features times weights added up, and it is the score a model computes before it adds a bias, which the matrix drawer introduces. The arrows give a second route to the same number: the length of a, times the length of b, times a direction score called cos θ. Here θ, the Greek letter theta, is the angle between the two arrows, and cos θ, the cosine of that angle, only cares about direction. It is 1 when the arrows point the same way, 0 when they meet at a right angle, and −1 when they point in exactly opposite directions. You do not need to work out a cosine yourself, because a calculator's cos button does it, and the lab shows the answer in the cos θ readout. Think of it as a direction score that slides down as the arrows turn further apart. For the default arrows, |a| is about 1.08 and |b| is about 1.25. The angle between them is about 40 degrees, which the plot labels as θ, and at that angle the arrows mostly agree, so cos θ is about 0.77. Multiply those three numbers together and you get about 1.04, the same score you found by pairing the numbers up. So a dot product grows for two different reasons: the arrows are long, or the arrows point the same way. Turn b to face away from a and the score goes negative, because cos θ goes negative while lengths can never be negative. With b set to (−0.6, −1.1), for example, the arrows are about 140 degrees apart and a · b becomes −1.04. That is how a set of weights can mark a house down, giving it a negative score when its features point away from what the buyer wants. The lab also draws a dotted line that drops from the tip of a onto the line through b, meeting it at a right angle. The spot where it lands is the point on b's line that is closest to the tip of a. The dashed piece running from the center out to that spot is called the projection of a onto b. The dot product equals the length of b times the length of that projection. For the default arrows the projection is about 0.83 long, which is 1.08 × 0.77, and 1.25 × 0.83 is about 1.04, the same score again. If a points away from b, the projection lands behind the center, so its length counts as negative and the score goes negative too. That gives one more way to see why arrows that line up give a large score, since lining up makes the projection as long as it can be. The lab shows one more measurement, Distance |a − b|, which is the straight-line gap between the two arrow tips. You find it with the same square-and-add rule: the tips differ by 0.4 across and 0.7 up, so the distance is √(0.16 + 0.49) = √0.65, about 0.81. The distance is 0 only when the arrows are identical, and unlike cos θ it changes when you stretch an arrow without turning it. Matrices: many dot products at once One dot product gives one score, but a model usually wants several scores from the same input, each with its own list of weights. Picture scoring one house for two different buyers at once, where each buyer's wishes form their own list of weights. Stack those weight lists as the rows of a grid and you have a matrix, usually written W. The top row is one buyer, and the bottom row is the other. Each row makes its own dot product with the input, so one matrix turns an input vector into a whole new vector of scores. The lab's default matrix has two rows, (1, 0.4) on top and (0, 1) on the bottom. So the first buyer cares mostly about rooms and a little about parks, while the second buyer cares only about parks. The input is the house x = (1, 0.2), which is roomy but not very near a park. The sliders m00, m01, m10 and m11 set the four numbers of W, where the first digit names the row and the second names the column, both counting from 0. That makes m01 the number in row 0 and column 1, which is the top-right number and starts at 0.4. To work out Wx, take one row at a time, multiply each of its numbers by the matching number in x, and add: The top row gives 1 × 1 + 0.4 × 0.2, which adds up to 1.08, the first buyer's score. The bottom row gives 0 × 1 + 1 × 0.2, which adds up to 0.20, the second buyer's score. Next, add a fixed amount to each output, called the bias and written b, which the sliders b0 and b1 set. You can think of it as a starting bonus that each buyer gives every house. This b is a new list, not the weight arrow from the vectors drawer, because math often reuses the same letters. With b = (0.2, 0.1), the outputs become 1.08 + 0.2 = 1.28 and 0.20 + 0.1 = 0.30. The whole calculation is written y = Wx + b, and here it gives (1.28, 0.30), the same pair the W x + b readout shows. Multiplying by a matrix and then adding a bias is called a linear layer, and it is a basic building block of the networks in later labs. Mathematicians save the word linear for maps that keep the center point (0, 0) where it is. Adding b slides everything over, center included, so the Live formula card uses the stricter name, affine layer, and the two names agree only when b is zero. The matrix as a map You can feed any point on the grid into Wx + b as the input x, and it comes out at a new point. So the matrix acts like a map that moves every point of the grid somewhere new. To see how, feed in the point (1, 0) and leave out b for a moment. The top row gives 1 × 1 + 0.4 × 0 = 1, and the bottom row gives 0 × 1 + 1 × 0 = 0. So (1, 0) lands on (1, 0), which is the left column of W. Feed in (0, 1) and it lands on (0.4, 1), the right column. So the two columns of W show where a single step across and a single step up end up. To show what the map does to a whole shape, the lab draws a dashed square with its corners at (±1, ±1). The symbol ± means “plus or minus”, so the corners sit at every mix of 1 or −1 across and 1 or −1 up. The lab feeds those four corners into Wx + b and draws where they land. The shaded shape shows where Wx + b sends that square, and with the default W it leans sideways like a stack of cards with its top slid over. Even so, its area stays exactly the same, because sliding the top of the square sideways does not make it any bigger or smaller. The readout det W · area scale tells you how much every area grows or shrinks when W is applied. It shows the determinant of W: multiply the top-left and bottom-right numbers, then subtract the product of the other two. For the default W, that is 1 × 1 − 0.4 × 0 = 1, so the square keeps its size. A negative determinant flips the square over like a mirror image, and a determinant of 0 squashes it flat onto a line. The Shapes readout, (2×2)(2×1)+(2×1), lists the size of each piece as rows by columns, so W has 2 rows and 2 columns. Both x and b are a single column of 2 numbers, which is what the 2×1 means. The two middle sizes, the columns of W and the rows of x, must match, because each number in a row of W pairs with one number in x. Derivatives: nudge a number and watch the answer move Picture a two-hour car trip with an average speed of 60 kilometers per hour, even though the speedometer showed a different number at each moment along the way. Average speed is a kind of rise over run, the distance gained divided by the time it took, so it blurs a whole stretch of the trip together. If you measure it over shorter and shorter stretches of time, it gets closer and closer to what the speedometer shows at that instant. That speedometer reading is the idea behind a derivative: how fast one number changes as another one moves, measured at a single spot. In math it answers the question “if I nudge this number a little, how much does the answer move?” The lab uses the curve f(x) = x², which squares whatever number x you give it, so at the default x of 1.2 its height is 1.44. To estimate the slope there, nudge x by a small amount called ε, the Greek letter epsilon, and see how much the height changes. The Nudge ε slider sets that amount, and with its default of 0.4 the calculation takes three steps: Move x from 1.2 to 1.6, so the height of the curve goes from 1.44 to 2.56. Subtract to find how much the height rose: 2.56 − 1.44 = 1.12. Divide that rise by the run, which is the size of the nudge: 1.12 ÷ 0.4 = 2.8. That rise over run is the slope of the dashed line through the two points, which is called a secant, and the lab shows it in the secant readout. It plays the part of the average speed over one stretch of the trip. The exact slope of x² at any point is 2x, so at x = 1.2 it is 2.4, shown as slope 2x. The lab draws this exact slope as a solid line called the tangent, which touches the curve at one point and tilts exactly the way the curve tilts there. The tangent plays the part of the speedometer reading, while the secant came out at 2.8, which is the true slope plus the whole nudge of 0.4. On this curve that always holds: the secant's slope is exactly 2x + ε, so the gap between secant and tangent is the nudge itself. Shrink the nudge and the gap shrinks with it, so a nudge of 0.1 makes the secant read 2.5. At the smallest setting, 0.05, it reads 2.45, which is very close to the true slope. The derivative is the number this ratio settles on as the nudge shrinks toward nothing, the same way average speed over a tiny stretch matches the speedometer. In training, the number you nudge is not this x but a parameter, one of the adjustable numbers inside a model. The slope that comes back says which way the model's error changes when that parameter moves, and by how much. Gradient descent: walking downhill To train a model, you first need one number that says how wrong it is, called the loss, where lower is better. The lab draws a loss L(w) that depends on a single parameter w, so the whole training problem fits on one curve. Its derivative is written L'(w) and read “L prime of w”, and it is the slope of the loss curve at the current w. The sign of the slope tells you which way is uphill, because a positive slope means the loss rises as w grows. A negative slope means the loss rises as w shrinks, so either way you should step in the direction opposite to the slope. A real model has many parameters and one slope for each, and the full list of slopes is called the gradient. The gradient points in the direction where the loss climbs fastest, so gradient descent improves the model by stepping the other way. The lab writes one downhill step as new w = w − η × L'(w), where η, the Greek letter eta, is the step size you choose with the Step size η slider. The plot draws this step as a dashed arrow from the current w to the next one. Work one step on the convex bowl, the default Loss surface. Convex is the math word for a curve shaped like a single bowl, with one bottom where every downhill path ends. Its formula is L(w) = (w − 0.8)² + 0.25, so its lowest point sits at w = 0.8 with a loss of 0.25. Start from the default w of −1.4 with the default step size of 0.15, and one step goes like this: The loss starts at (−1.4 − 0.8)² + 0.25, which is 4.84 + 0.25 = 5.09, far above the floor. This bowl is the x² curve from the derivatives drawer slid over so that its bottom sits at 0.8, so its slope follows the same 2x rule measured from 0.8. That gives L'(w) = 2(w − 0.8) = 2 × (−2.2) = −4.4, and the minus sign means the loss falls as w moves right. The step is η × L' = 0.15 × (−4.4) = −0.66, which is the number the η L' readout shows. The new w is −1.4 − (−0.66) = −0.74, because subtracting a negative number moves you to the right, which is downhill here. The loss at −0.74 is about 2.62, roughly half of what it was, so one step already helped a lot. Press Take a downhill step again and w moves to about −0.28, then about 0.05, then closer and closer to 0.8. The steps get shorter as you go, because the slope flattens out near the bottom and each step is the slope times η. The step size matters a lot. On this bowl, each step multiplies your distance from the bottom by 1 − 2η, so at η = 0.15 the multiplier is 0.7 and you keep 70% of the gap each time. Above a step size of 0.5 the multiplier turns negative, so every step jumps past the bottom to the other side. At a step size of 0.7, the multiplier is −0.4, and the first step from −1.4 overshoots all the way to 1.68 on the far side. The next step lands back at 0.45 and the one after that at 0.94, so w zigzags in toward the bottom. Above 1, the multiplier would be bigger than 1 in size, so each jump would land further away than the last, which is why the slider stops at 0.8. Now set Step size η back to 0.15 and switch Loss surface to two wells, a curve with the formula L(w) = (w² − 1)² + 0.35w + 0.6. A well here means a valley, and the extra 0.35w tilts the curve so that the two valleys end up with different depths. The left valley bottoms out near w = −1.04 with a loss of about 0.24, which makes it deeper than the right one. The right valley bottoms out near w = 0.95, where the loss only gets down to about 0.94. Start at w = −1.4 and the steps roll into the deep left valley, but start at w = 1.4 and they settle in the shallow right valley instead. They stay there because the slope at the bottom of that valley is zero, so each update has nothing left to subtract. This curve is much steeper near its edges than the bowl, so it needs a small step size. Trouble starts at step sizes of about 0.2 and above. There the ball can jump between the valleys, swing back and forth without settling, or bounce from edge to edge of the chart. A valley bottom that is lower than every point near it is called a local minimum. The lowest one on the whole curve is also called the global minimum, so the plot labels the shallow valley “local min” and the deeper one “global min”. Picture a hiker caught in thick fog who wants to reach the lowest ground in a range of hills. She can't see anything around her, but she can feel which way the ground tilts under her boots, so she always steps downhill. In a single bowl-shaped valley that plan always works, but in hills with two valleys, where she ends up depends on where she started. From the wrong side of the ridge she will stop at the bottom of the shallower valley, with no way of knowing that a deeper one exists. Gradient descent behaves like that hiker, because it only reads the slope at the spot where it stands. The picture stops matching in one way: the hiker takes tiny steps, but gradient descent jumps a distance of η times the slope. Where the curve is steep, near the edges of the chart, one jump can sail right over the ridge. At the default step size, a start at w = 1.9 lands in the deep left valley, so the starting point and the step size together decide the valley. On the bowl, too, the hiker always reaches the bottom, but gradient descent does so only while the step size stays below 1. You may read online that getting stuck in a local minimum ruins training, or that it never happens at all. This page shows something narrower. On this curve a local minimum is real: it is a point where the slope is zero and every nearby point is higher. Still, that is a fact about one tilted curve with one parameter, not a law about every model you will meet. Probability: shares that add up to one A probability is a share of the possibilities, written as a number from 0, meaning never, to 1, meaning certain. A probability of 0.25 is the same as 25%, or 1 chance in 4, so it sits a quarter of the way from never to certain. The shares for a complete set of outcomes always add up to 1, the way the slices of a pizza add up to the whole pizza. Often you want a chance after you have learned something, such as the chance it rains given that the morning was cloudy. That is a conditional probability, written P(y|x) and read “the probability of y given x”. You find it by keeping only the cases where x happened and then asking what share of those also had y. The lab's count table sums up eight made-up examples, and each one has an input x that is 0 or 1 and a label y that is 0 or 1. The table counts how many examples fall into each mix, and its last column, P(y=1|x), works out the share for you: Of the four examples with x = 0, three have y = 0 and one has y = 1, so P(y=1|x=0) = 1/4 = 0.25. Of the four examples with x = 1, one has y = 0 and three have y = 1, so P(y=1|x=1) = 3/4 = 0.75. You could imagine x as “the morning was cloudy” and y as “it rained”, so that 3 of the 4 cloudy mornings brought rain. The counts are authored, though, which means the lesson's writers chose them, so they are not real weather records. Softmax and likelihood A model does not hand out chances directly: it first produces raw scores called logits, which can be any size. A step called softmax then turns those scores into chances that add up to 1. For two scores A and B, the lab's formula is P(A) = e^A / (e^A + e^B), where e is a fixed number, about 2.718, that is used all over math. Raising e to a power, even a fractional one like 2.4, is a calculator job, so the lab does it for you. What matters is that e to any power is always positive, and a bigger score gives a much bigger result. That is how softmax turns any scores into positive shares that favor the larger score. With the default Logit A of 2.4, the top of the fraction is e to the power 2.4, which is about 11.0. The default Logit B is 1.1, and e to the power 1.1 is about 3.0, so the bottom of the fraction is about 14.0. That makes P(A) about 11.0 ÷ 14.0, which is 0.786 or 78.6%, and it leaves 21.4% for B. The two bars under Model distribution after softmax show those two shares, and they always add up to 100%. Now picture a model that gives team A a 78.6% chance of winning each game against team B. Over the next three games, team A wins, then wins again, and then team B wins, and you want to score the model on those three outcomes. The likelihood is that score: the chance the model gave to exactly what happened. To combine chances in a row, think of a fair coin. The chance of two heads in a row is half of a half, 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25, because only half of the first heads are followed by a second head. If each outcome is independent, meaning one does not affect the next, you multiply their chances in the same way: 0.786 × 0.786 × 0.214, which comes to about 0.132. A higher likelihood means the model gave more of its chance to what really happened, which is why training tries to raise it. The lab shows this number as P(A,A,B), which you read as “the probability of A, A, B”. The readout beside it, ln lik, shows about −2.02, which is the same likelihood after taking its logarithm. Taking the log turns that product of three chances into a sum of three logs, and the logarithm drawer explains how that works. Bayes' rule: updating a belief Picture a big group chat and a friend, call her Jo, who ends 3 out of every 4 messages with three exclamation marks. Everyone else in the chat does that in only 1 message out of 4, so the exclamation marks are a decent clue that Jo wrote the message. A message shows up ending in exclamation marks, but the sender's name is hidden, so how likely is it that Jo sent it? To find out, count messages instead of guessing, starting with a chat where half of all the messages are Jo's. Picture 40 messages, 20 from Jo and 20 from everyone else. Jo's habit gives 15 messages with exclamation marks, while everyone else's gives only 5. That means 15 of the 20 messages with exclamation marks are Jo's, which is a share of 0.75. Now picture a much busier chat where only 1 message in 10 is Jo's, while everyone else keeps their old habits. Out of 40 messages, now only 4 are Jo's, and 3 of those end with exclamation marks. The other 36 messages still produce 9 with exclamation marks, because 1 in 4 of 36 is 9. Now only 3 of the 12 messages with exclamation marks are Jo's, which is a share of 0.25, a third of what it was. The clue is exactly as strong as before, but Jo writes far fewer of the messages, so the clue points to her far less often. That reasoning is Bayes' rule, and the lab's Bayes' rule view uses these same numbers. The lab sorts each example into one of two groups, called classes. Class y = 1 plays the part of Jo, class y = 0 plays everyone else, and x = 1 is the clue, so the four parts look like this: The prior is what you believed before seeing the clue, such as “Jo writes half the messages”. The lab's slider is Prior P(y=1), the share of class 1 before looking at x. The likelihood is how likely the clue is under each explanation: 3 in 4 if it is Jo, and 1 in 4 if it is anyone else. The lab reads these from its table as P(x=1|y=1) = 0.75 and P(x=1|y=0) = 0.25. This is the same idea as the likelihood in the softmax drawer: the chance of what you actually saw under one explanation. Here the explanations are “Jo sent it” and “someone else sent it”. The evidence, shown as Evidence P(x=1), is the total chance of seeing the clue at all: the chance it comes from Jo plus the chance it comes from everyone else. The posterior, shown as Posterior P(y=1|x=1), is the updated belief: the prior times the likelihood, divided by the evidence so that the chances add up to 1. The Live formula card writes this out with the live numbers you set, so you can follow the arithmetic exactly. At a prior of 0.10 it reads P(y=1|x=1) = (0.10 × 0.75) / (0.10 × 0.75 + 0.90 × 0.25), and you can work that out in four steps: Class 1 and the clue, like Jo sending it with exclamation marks: 0.10 × 0.75 = 0.075. Class 0 and the clue, like someone else sending it with exclamation marks: 0.90 × 0.25 = 0.225. The evidence adds up both ways the clue can appear: 0.075 + 0.225 = 0.300. The posterior is the share of that total that belongs to class 1: 0.075 ÷ 0.300 = 0.25. That matches the 3 out of 12 that you counted by hand in the busy chat, which is a good sign that the rule works. The two bars under Weight of each way to see x = 1 are the two weights from the first two steps. There is a shortcut that uses odds, which compare the chance for something with the chance against it. A prior of 0.10 means a chance of 0.10 for and 0.90 against, which works out to odds of 1 to 9. The clue is 3 times as likely when y = 1 as when y = 0, so it multiplies the “for” side of the odds by 3. That turns 1 to 9 into 3 to 9, which is the same as 1 to 3. Odds of 1 to 3 mean 1 chance in 4, which is the same posterior of 0.25 that the four steps gave. The Odds: prior × ratio readout shows the same thing in decimals as 0.11 × 3 = 0.33, since odds of 1 to 9 are about 0.11. Because the clue always multiplies the odds by the same 3, a rare class needs much stronger evidence before it becomes likely. Mean and variance: two numbers that set a bell curve The mean is the ordinary average, and it marks the center of a set of numbers, such as the lab's sample of −1, 0, 1 and 2. The variance measures how spread out the numbers are, because it is the average of the squared distances from the mean, and working it out takes four steps: Find the mean by adding the four numbers and dividing by 4, which gives 2 ÷ 4 = 0.50. Subtract the mean from each number to get its distance from the center: −1.5, −0.5, 0.5 and 1.5. Square each of those distances, which gives 2.25, 0.25, 0.25 and 2.25. Average the squares to get the variance: they add up to 5, and 5 ÷ 4 = 1.25. Squaring does two jobs: it makes every distance positive, so numbers below and above the mean cannot cancel out, and it weighs far-off numbers more heavily. It also leaves the variance in squared units: if the numbers were heights in centimeters, the variance would be in square centimeters. So you take its square root to get back to the units of the data, and √1.25 is about 1.12. That square root is the standard deviation, written σ, the Greek letter sigma, which is why the variance is written σ². Picture the heights of every 15-year-old in a big school. Most are near the average, and fewer and fewer are very short or very tall. A graph of how common each height is rises to a hump in the middle and falls away on both sides. A smooth hump of that shape is called a Gaussian, or a bell curve, and the mean and variance are the two numbers that draw it. The mean, written μ, the Greek letter mu, sets where the center of the bell sits, and the variance σ² sets how wide it spreads. With a bell curve, the chance of landing between two values is the area under the curve between them, and the total area is always exactly 1. The height at one single point is called a density, and it is not a chance. For every Gaussian, about 68% of the area lies within one standard deviation of the center, between μ − σ and μ + σ, and the lab shades that band. So if school heights followed a bell curve, about 68% of students would fall within one standard deviation of the average. Picture pouring the same cup of sand onto a table each time, spreading it into a wide, low mound or piling it into a narrow, tall one. The amount of sand never changes, and the bell works the same way, so a wider bell must have a lower peak and a narrower bell a higher one. At the default variance of 1, the peak of the bell is about 0.40 high, well below 1. Shrink Variance σ² to its smallest setting, 0.10, and the peak climbs to about 1.26, which is fine for a density even though a probability can never go above 1. The sand picture stops matching at the edges, because a bell curve's tails go on forever, getting thinner and thinner without ever reaching zero. A common mix-up: reading the height of a bell curve as a chance, when only area is a chance. Height is a density, and that is why it is allowed to go above 1 when the bell is narrow. The Probe x slider picks one point along the bottom, and the readout z = (x − μ)/σ says how many standard deviations that point sits from the center. With the defaults, the mean is 0 and σ is 1, so a probe at x = 1 sits exactly one standard deviation out. That gives z = 1, and the Density at x readout shows a height of about 0.242 at that point. The Fit μ and σ² to the sample button sets the bell's center and width to the sample's own mean, 0.50, and variance, 1.25. The four sample values also appear as small ticks along the bottom of the plot, so you can see the bell sitting over them. In the Classical machine learning lab, a method called naive Bayes fits one of these bells, with its own mean and variance, for each class and each feature. From logit to probability: the sigmoid A logit can be any number at all, positive or negative, and the sigmoid squeezes it into a probability between 0 and 1. With two options, only the gap between their logits matters, so the sigmoid takes that gap as its single input, called z. The lab shows it as Logit gap z = A − B. The formula is σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^−z), where e^−z means e to the power negative z. A negative power means 1 divided by the matching positive power, so e^−z is always positive but shrinks toward 0 as z grows. Its graph is an S-shaped curve that passes through exactly 0.5 at z = 0 and climbs from left to right. For large positive z it flattens out near 1, and for large negative z it flattens out near 0. Try it with the default logits: the gap is z = 2.4 − 1.1 = 1.3, and e to the power −1.3 is about 0.2725. So σ(1.3) is 1 ÷ 1.2725, about 0.786, which is exactly the softmax P(A) from before, because with two options softmax is the sigmoid of the logit gap. The lab shows Softmax P(A) and Sigmoid σ(z) side by side, so you can see the two numbers match to every decimal place shown. That means only the gap matters: if both logits go up by 1, to 3.4 and 2.1, the gap is still 1.3 and P(A) stays at 0.786. It works like a tug-of-war: give both teams the same extra pull and nothing about the contest changes, because only the difference in pull matters. The picture stops matching in two ways. A rope keeps sliding while one side pulls harder, but P(A) is a fixed number set by the gap. And a tug-of-war ends with a single winner, while the sigmoid gives a chance. You can also run the sigmoid backward, from a chance back to the gap, and the logarithm drawer below finishes that story once it has explained logs. In the Classical machine learning lab, a method called logistic regression builds one logit as z = w·x + b. That is a dot product plus a bias, like the ones in the first two drawers. It then reports σ(z) as P(y=1|x), the chance that the label is 1 given the input, and the Stacking neurons lab uses the same S-shaped curve later on. The letter σ does two unrelated jobs on this page: in the bell-curve view it stands for the standard deviation, while σ(z) here is the sigmoid. The brackets right after the sigmoid's σ are the quickest way to tell the two apart. Logarithms: turning products into sums A logarithm answers the question “how many copies of the base must I multiply together to get this number?”, where the base is a fixed number such as 10. Because 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000, you need three copies of 10 to make 1,000, so the logarithm of 1,000 with base 10 is 3. In the same way, the logarithm of 100 is 2, and numbers between 0 and 1 have negative logs, since 0.1 = 1 ÷ 10 counts as 10 to the power −1. Logs have one property that makes them useful in AI: multiplying numbers matches adding their logs. For example, 100 × 1,000 = 100,000, and on the log side 2 + 3 = 5, which is the log of 100,000. So a log turns a long string of multiplications into a string of additions, which are far gentler to work with. The lab uses the natural log, written ln, whose base is the same number e, about 2.718, that appeared in softmax. The idea is the same as with base 10, and only the base changes, so any chance between 0 and 1 still has a negative log. The lab therefore puts a minus sign in front and calls −ln p the surprise of an event with chance p, which is never below zero. A fair coin landing heads has a chance of 0.5, and its surprise is −ln 0.5, about 0.693. Rarer events surprise you more, so a chance of 0.25 gives a surprise of about 1.386, exactly twice as much. That is because 0.25 = 0.5 × 0.5 is like getting two heads in a row, and the log turns that product into the sum 0.693 + 0.693. These surprises are measured in nats, the unit you get from the natural log. If you used base 2 instead, the unit would be the bit, and one fair coin flip would carry exactly 1 bit of surprise. One bit and 0.693 nats are the same amount measured on different scales, the way 1 hour and 60 minutes are the same length of time. Here is why AI needs this: multiply 0.5 by itself 100 times and the answer has 30 zeros after the decimal point before its first other digit. A computer has a limit on how small a number it can store, and that one is still above the limit, but a longer product soon falls below it. Multiply 0.5 by itself 1,100 times and the answer has more than 330 zeros after the decimal point. That is too small for a computer's ordinary numbers, so it rounds to exactly zero. The sum of the 1,100 surprises is 1,100 × 0.693, about 762, a perfectly ordinary number. That is why training losses add log-probabilities instead of multiplying tiny fractions, and why ln lik in the softmax view adds logs rather than multiplying chances. Logs also finish the sigmoid story from the probability drawer, by running it backward. Start from the odds for A, which are P(A) ÷ P(B) = 0.786 ÷ 0.214, about 3.67, and take their natural log, which is 1.30, exactly the gap you started with. That is why, with two options, the gap z = A − B is also called the log-odds, while Logit A on its own is not. The sigmoid and the log-odds undo each other, and the lab shows the trip back as Log-odds ln(P(A)/P(B)). Surprise, entropy and cross-entropy Picture a weather app that announces a 60% chance of rain every single day, in a town where it really rains on 1 day in 4. Each rainy day then surprises you by −ln 0.60, which is about 0.511, since the app said rain was fairly likely. Each dry day surprises you more, by −ln 0.40 or about 0.916, because the app gave dry weather only a 40% chance. Now average those surprises over the real weather, where 1 day in 4 is rainy and 3 days in 4 are dry. Weighting each surprise by how often it really happens gives 0.25 × 0.511 + 0.75 × 0.916, which comes to about 0.815. That average surprise, when the world follows the true chance p but your forecast said q, is the cross-entropy, written H(p,q). The lab's defaults are this exact case, because True p starts at 0.25 and Model q starts at 0.60. Now suppose the app had told the truth and said 25%, so a rainy day would surprise you by about 1.386. A dry day would surprise you by only about 0.288, and the average comes to 0.25 × 1.386 + 0.75 × 0.288, about 0.562. This is the truth's own average surprise, called the entropy and written H(p), and it is not zero even for a perfect forecast, because the weather really is uncertain. The gap between the two, 0.815 − 0.562 = 0.253, is called KL, and it is the extra surprise you pay for believing q when the world is p. The lab shows it as KL(p‖q), and if you move Model q onto True p the gap closes to 0, while no setting can push it below 0. A confident wrong forecast is very expensive, which you can see by setting True p to 0.02 and Model q to 0.90. That is an app promising rain 90% of the time in a town where it rains on only 2 days in 100. Every dry day now surprises you by about 2.30, so H(p,q) jumps to about 2.26 while H(p) stays under 0.1. Training a model lowers its cross-entropy, which pulls its forecast q toward the true chance p and shrinks the gap.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · The math you need
documents.body: Later labs need one shared set of arithmetic, not a fresh metaphor every time a formula appears. Each drawer is here because some later part of the app runs into a specific problem that this piece of math solves. Comparing two lists of numbers: Tokens & embeddings stores words, or pieces of words, as lists of numbers, and Attention compares those lists to decide which words matter to each other. Both need one number that says how well two lists match. Attention uses the dot product itself, while Tokens & embeddings uses cos θ, the dot product divided by both lengths, so that length does not count. Knowing that the dot product mixes length with direction stops you from reading every large score as a close match. Making many scores at once: a layer of a network needs many weighted sums from the same input. A matrix packs all of their weight lists into one grid, so a whole layer becomes one Wx + b instead of a pile of separate sums. Knowing which way to change: a real model has a huge number of adjustable parameters, and training has to decide which way to move every one of them. The slope answers that question from where the model stands, without trying every possible change first. Seeing a valley for what it is: the two-well curve turns a “local minimum” into a real valley where you can watch a ball settle. It claims nothing about deep networks, and it is still only one dimension. Working with chances: Classical machine learning uses Bayes' rule, the bell curve's two numbers and the sigmoid without stopping to explain them. Naive Bayes multiplies a prior by bell-curve likelihoods, and logistic regression reports σ(w·x + b) as a probability. Adding instead of multiplying: a loss is built from the chances a model gave to many real outcomes. Multiplying all of those chances would shrink toward zero, so losses add log-probabilities instead, and cross-entropy is the result. One drawer at a time: the page stores which Topic is open, so a later lab can link straight to the refresher you need instead of repeating a textbook.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · The math you need
documents.body: Work through the drawers in order, and before each change, say out loud what you expect to happen. Pick a topic Set Topic to vectors, then click through each of the other names one by one. Only one refresher appears at a time in the Active refresher card, and the Worked arithmetic and Live formula cards rewrite themselves to match. The numbers you set in each drawer stay put when you switch away and come back later. Vectors and matrices On vectors, edit the number boxes labeled a features and b weights until the two arrows point in roughly opposite directions. Watch a · b and cos θ both turn negative, then redo the two products in the small table under the arrows by hand, multiplying each pair and adding them up. Switch Topic to matrices and move m01, the top-right number of W, and watch the shaded square lean further over as m01 grows. Even so, det W · area scale stays at 1 while m00 and m11 stay at 1 and m10 stays at 0, because the slant never changes the area. Then set m00 to −1 and watch the determinant turn negative as the square flips over like a mirror image. Derivatives Try this: Switch Topic to derivatives, and before you touch anything, use the rule 2x + ε to predict the secant readout for a nudge of 0.1. Then drag Nudge ε from 0.4 down to 0.05 and watch the dashed secant swing toward the solid tangent. The secant readout should fall from 2.8 through 2.5 to 2.45, while slope 2x stays at 2.4 the whole time. Next, move x to −1, where the slope becomes −2 because the curve falls as you move right at that spot. The secant still sits exactly one nudge above the tangent, so the rule 2x + ε works on both sides of the curve. Optimization Set Topic to optimization and Loss surface to two wells, and leave Step size η at its default of 0.15. Then put Parameter w near 1.4 and press Take a downhill step several times. Watch L(w) and Nearest minimum as you go, and the ball should settle near w = 0.95 with a loss of about 0.94. Now move Parameter w to −1.4 and step again, and this time it settles near −1.04 with a loss of about 0.24. Switch back to the convex bowl and start from either side, and every start reaches 0.8. Then raise Step size η to 0.7, start from −1.4, and watch the dotted path of steps zigzag across the bottom before it settles. Probability Set Topic to probability and use Probability idea to move through its four views: In counts and softmax, read P(y=1|x=1) = 0.75 from the table, then lower Logit A one notch at a time while you watch P(A,A,B). It rises, peaks when P(A) is about 2/3, and then falls again, because two of the three outcomes were A. The score is highest when the model gives A the same share it really got, 2 out of 3. In Bayes' rule, lower Prior P(y=1) from 0.50 to 0.10 and watch Posterior P(y=1|x=1) fall from 0.75 to 0.25, while the table's likelihoods never move. In mean and variance, press Fit μ and σ² to the sample, then raise Variance σ² and watch the bell widen as its peak falls. Then drop the variance to 0.10, move Probe x to the center at 0.5, and watch Density at x climb past 1. In logit to probability, raise Logit A and Logit B by the same amount, and Softmax P(A) and Sigmoid σ(z) both stay put. They stay put because Logit gap z = A − B does not change when both logits move together. Logarithms On logarithms, move Model q onto True p and watch H(p,q) fall to H(p) while KL(p‖q) reaches zero. Then set True p to 0.02 and Model q to 0.90, and see how far KL jumps when the forecast is confident and wrong. Check the arithmetic Finally, pick one line in the Worked arithmetic card and redo it yourself with the live numbers. Then check that the Live formula card prints the same result, because both cards format the numbers the picture was drawn from.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · The math you need
documents.body: A large dot product can come from long arrows or from arrows that point the same way. The cos θ readout separates out direction alone, and the foot of the dotted drop marks the projection of a onto b. Distance |a − b| is the straight-line gap between the arrow tips, and it is 0 only when the two arrows are identical. Unlike cos θ, it changes when you stretch an arrow without turning it. A program that looks for the items closest to a given one, such as similar songs, ranks them by this distance. The shaded shape on matrices is Wx + b applied to the four corners of the square, which is a linear layer in miniature. Under W alone, before the shift by b, the left column of W shows where the point (1, 0) lands, as you worked out in the matrix drawer. The right column shows where (0, 1) lands, and every other point is a mix of those two. On derivatives, the secant slope on x² is always exactly 2x + ε, so the gap to the tangent is always the nudge itself. On the convex bowl, every start reaches w = 0.8 when the step size is small, while a step size above 0.5 overshoots the bottom on every step. On two wells, the starting point and the step size together decide the valley, and the right-hand valley is a real local minimum. Neither curve is a picture of a deep network, though. Two logits become a set of chances only after softmax, and the likelihood of A, A, B then multiplies three of those chances together. Logs turn that product into a sum, which is the number the ln lik readout shows beside it. A rare class stays rare, because at a prior of 0.10 the same 3-to-1 evidence lifts the posterior only to 0.25. A wider bell has a lower peak, because the total area stays at 1. The 68% band holds for every mean and variance, and a height above 1 is fine for a density but impossible for a probability. Raising both logits by the same amount leaves P(A) unchanged, because only the gap between them decides the chances. Cross-entropy equals entropy only when q matches p, and KL can shrink to 0 but never goes below it.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · The math you need
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Every readout here comes from a fixed formula written into the page's code, not from anything learned from data. Most are closed-form, meaning one exact formula you could work out in a single go. Two readouts take a careful search instead. Nearest minimum is found by halving a range over and over until it pins down where the slope is zero. The 68% area is found by adding up many thin slices under the bell. Each readout also works in only one or two dimensions, meaning lists of one or two numbers, where real models use thousands. The curve y = x², called a parabola, is drawn from 81 points, and the two loss surfaces are the formulas printed on the card. There is no automatic differentiation, the method real training software uses to work out slopes through a long chain of calculations. Instead, each slope rule here, such as 2x for the parabola, is written straight into the page. The only number that changes by anything like learning is the w you step by hand on optimization. The count table, its likelihoods and the four-number bell-curve sample are all authored, so none of them is measured from the real world. The dotted path of steps is only a picture of where you have been, so moving Parameter w or switching the surface starts a fresh one. The loss plot also cuts off its top, and it labels the ball when the loss runs off the top of the chart. Where the real ideas run into trouble A real Bayes update multiplies many estimated likelihoods rather than reading one from a tidy table, and the posterior still depends on a prior that someone has to justify. A bell curve is one shape among many, and real data is often not bell-shaped, so a bell can be a poor description of it. Training uses these same ideas in thousands of dimensions, and it needs extra care with two problems that the lab never meets. The first is overflow, which happens when a number grows too large for the computer to store, the opposite of a product shrinking to zero. The second is discrete choices, like picking one word out of many, which jump from one option to the next with no in-between. A jump like that has no slope, so training has to pick a smooth stand-in to measure instead. The loss of a large network is not a one-dimensional double well, so the two-well curve does not support stories about every local minimum in a big model. “All local minima are terrible” is a myth this page refuses, and the curve here does not prove the opposite either. People also slip by treating the logarithm as a way to make numbers smaller, or by treating a local minimum as automatically fatal. The log is here so that products of probabilities become sums that a computer can handle, not to shrink anything. A local minimum is a place where the slope is zero and nearby points are higher, which is real on this curve but not a verdict on deep learning. Another trap is reading the posterior as the likelihood, because the table says 3 in 4 and that looks like the final answer. That number is the posterior only when the prior is the table's own 0.50, and with a rare class the posterior is much smaller, because the prior counts too.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · The math you need
documents.body: Each drawer comes back later in the app, and here is where you will meet each one again: Data, features, and representation builds vectors from the rows of a table on purpose. Classical machine learning uses Bayes' rule and bell-curve means and variances in naive Bayes, and it uses the sigmoid in logistic regression. Stacking neurons uses the sigmoid's S-shaped curve again, so the curve you move here will look familiar there. Tokens & embeddings and Attention reuse the dot product as a way to compare two lists of numbers. Loss & gradient descent takes the slope and the downhill step from this page and applies them to a real parameter. A few extra details Where 2x + ε comes from: multiply out (x + ε)² to get x² + 2xε + ε². Subtract x² to get the rise, 2xε + ε², and divide by the run, ε, to get 2x + ε. As ε shrinks toward nothing, the extra ε fades away and leaves 2x, which is why the secant closes in on the tangent. Many parameters, many slopes: each slope in a gradient comes from nudging one parameter while holding all the others still, and the gradient lists those slopes side by side. Real training software works them all out together with automatic differentiation. Batches: the Worked arithmetic card for matrices mentions stacking several inputs as the rows of a taller grid, which is called a batch. One matrix calculation can then score every input in the batch at once, instead of one at a time. Why layers need a bend: two Wx + b layers in a row, with nothing between them, add up to a single layer of the same straight-line kind. Later labs put a bending step, called a nonlinearity, between the layers so that a stack can bend. Dividing by 4, not 3: some textbooks divide by one less than the count when they estimate a variance from a sample. This lab divides by the full count, 4, which is the version naive Bayes uses. An average given x: the examples with x = 1 have y values that average 0.75, which the lab writes as E[y|x=1]. It is an average over those rows, not a promise about any single one of them. The odds rule in general: posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio. That ratio says how many times more likely the clue is under one explanation than under the other, and on this page it is always 3.

documents.subtitle: Standard · The math you need
documents.body: This module collects the arithmetic later labs lean on: vectors and dot products, matrices and the linear layer Wx + b, derivatives and gradient descent, probability, and logarithms. It answers a practical question: when a later lab says score, layer, slope, distribution or loss, which calculation does it mean? It follows What AI actually is. Each idea is shown four ways that must agree, ending in the exact formula the page evaluates. Where it shows up Dot products. Attention scores each query against each key with one, and Tokens & embeddings compares embeddings by cosine, a dot product divided by both lengths. Data, features, and representation shows where the feature vectors come from. Linear layers. Layers apply Wx + b. A production layer is the same map in thousands of dimensions. Training. Training follows a slope downhill. Loss & gradient descent applies the same update to both parameters, w and b, of a fitted line instead of to one isolated w. Sampling and losses. Sampling reads a distribution, and a loss adds log-probabilities. Classical models. In Classical machine learning, naive Bayes multiplies a prior by Gaussian likelihoods, and logistic regression reports σ(w·x + b) as P(y=1|x). Stacking neurons uses the same sigmoid curve. Why it matters Each calculation guards against a specific misreading: A large dot product can come from length rather than alignment. On the convex bowl, a step size η above 0.5 overshoots the minimum on every step. A likelihood stays a product of tiny fractions until a logarithm turns it into a sum. Reading the likelihood alone misjudges a rare class; Bayes' rule keeps the prior in the answer. A Gaussian's height is a density, not a probability, so it can exceed 1. Descent can settle in a shallower valley rather than the global minimum. What you will be able to explain Read a dot product as a weighted sum of features, and a matrix as the map behind Wx + b. Say what a derivative, a gradient step, a conditional probability and a logarithm each change in a calculation. Tell a convex bowl from a tilted double well without treating local minima as mythology. Use Bayes' rule to turn a prior and a likelihood into a posterior, read a Gaussian's mean and variance, and turn a logit into a probability with the sigmoid. What the lab shows Every readout comes from fixed 1-D or 2-D formulas: no model is trained and nothing is measured. Two quantities are found numerically rather than in closed form: bisection finds the minima shown in Nearest minimum and marked on the plot of L(w), and numeric integration finds the area within μ ± σ. The two loss surfaces are printed formulas, and the probability count table, its likelihoods and the four-number Gaussian sample are authored. A gradient step changes only w, once per press of Take a downhill step. The six-way Topic control on the Topic picker card chooses which widget the Active refresher card mounts, each with its own controls, such as Nudge ε, Loss surface, Probability idea and Model q. Worked arithmetic and Live formula reprint the same live numbers in words and in closed form. The key experiment is on optimization: set Loss surface to *two wells*, leave Step size η at its default 0.15, start Parameter w at 1.4 and then at −1.4, and press Take a downhill step repeatedly. The two starts settle in different valleys; on the *convex bowl* both reach the one minimum.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · The math you need
documents.body: A vector is an ordered list treated as a point or an arrow. The dot product is the sum of paired coordinates, equal to |a||b|cos θ, and it is also the linear score w·x. A matrix is a linear map: each output coordinate is a row dotted with the input. A linear layer is y = Wx + b, affine unless b = 0. A derivative is the local slope. The gradient of a loss is the direction of steepest increase; descent steps the other way. A probability is a non-negative share in a set that sums to one. Conditional probability P(y|x) restricts that set. Likelihood is the probability the model assigned to the data you saw. A logarithm turns a product into a sum. Cross-entropy is expected surprise of p under q. topic selects which identity this page focuses. Four representations, one number Each widget shows the same calculation as words, a picture, a tiny table or walk-through, then a closed form. If those four disagree, the page is wrong. A derivative by hand On f(x) = x² at the default x = 1.2, f = 1.44 and the tangent slope is 2x = 2.4. Nudge by the default ε = 0.4: f(1.6) = 2.56, so the secant slope is (2.56 − 1.44) / 0.4 = 2.8. That is exactly 2x + ε = 2.4 + 0.4. Shrink the nudge to ε = 0.05 and the secant reads 2.45. The gap to the tangent is the nudge itself, so the derivative is the number the ratio settles on as ε goes to zero. In training the thing you nudge is a parameter, and the slope it returns is the gradient. A matrix by hand Take the default W = [[1, 0.4], [0, 1]], x = (1, 0.2), and b = (0.2, 0.1). Row one dotted with x is 1·1 + 0.4·0.2 = 1.08, and adding 0.2 gives 1.28. Row two is 0·1 + 1·0.2 = 0.2, and adding 0.1 gives 0.30. So Wx + b = (1.28, 0.30). The determinant is 1·1 − 0.4·0 = 1, so areas keep their size: this W shears the square sideways rather than stretching it. Each output coordinate is one row of W dotted with x, which is why a linear layer is a bank of dot products. A logarithm by hand Set True p = 0.25 and Model q = 0.60. Under q the two outcomes surprise by −ln 0.60 = 0.511 and −ln 0.40 = 0.916 nats. Weighted by the truth, H(p,q) = 0.25·0.511 + 0.75·0.916 = 0.815. The truth's own entropy is H(p) = 0.25·1.386 + 0.75·0.288 = 0.562. The gap is KL = 0.815 − 0.562 = 0.253, the price of believing q when the world is p. Move q onto p and the gap closes to 0. Because a log turns a product into a sum, a loss adds terms like these instead of multiplying tiny fractions. Bayes' rule: prior, likelihood, posterior Bayes' rule updates a belief: P(y|x) = P(y) P(x|y) / P(x). The prior P(y) is what you believed before seeing x. The likelihood P(x|y) is how probable x is if y holds. The evidence P(x) rescales the result so the posterior sums to one. On the count table, P(x=1|y=1) = 3/4 and P(x=1|y=0) = 1/4. At the table's own prior of 0.50 the posterior is 0.75. Lower the prior to 0.10 and the same evidence only reaches 0.25. In odds form, posterior odds = prior odds × 3, so a rare class needs strong evidence. Mean and variance: the two numbers of a Gaussian The mean is the average, the center of the bell. The variance is the average squared distance from the mean, and its square root σ is back in the units of x. For the sample −1, 0, 1, 2 the mean is 0.50 and the variance is 1.25. A Gaussian N(μ, σ²) is fixed by those two numbers. About 68% of its area lies within one σ of μ, and its height is a density, not a probability. Naive Bayes in Classical machine learning fits one such pair per class and per feature. From logit to probability A logit is any real number z. The sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^−z) maps it to a probability between 0 and 1, with σ(0) = 0.5, and the logit is the log-odds ln(p/(1−p)). With two classes, softmax is the sigmoid of the logit gap: P(A) = σ(A − B), so shifting both logits changes nothing. Logistic regression computes z = w·x + b and reports σ(z) as P(y=1|x). The curve is drawn here before Stacking neurons uses it.

documents.subtitle: Standard · The math you need
documents.body: Cosine isolates angle; the raw dot product still mixes length. The foot of the dotted drop is the projection onto b. Distance |a − b| is the straight-line gap between the two arrow tips, the length of a − b. It is 0 only when a = b, and unlike cosine it changes when you stretch an arrow without turning it. Nearest-neighbor methods rank by it. The columns of W are where (1, 0) and (0, 1) land, det W scales area, and b translates the whole parallelogram. A stack needs a nonlinearity before it can bend. For f(x)=x² the gap between secant and 2x is exactly ε. The tilted well has two valleys of different depth, near w = −1.04 (L ≈ 0.24) and w = 0.95 (L ≈ 0.94). Settling in the shallower one is a real local minimum. On the bowl, L'' = 2, so η above 0.5 overshoots each step. That 1-D picture does not describe a high-dimensional network. Softmax is bookkeeping. Likelihood of A,A,B is P(A)²P(B). Cross-entropy equals entropy only when q = p. A rare class stays rare. At a prior of 0.10 the same 3-to-1 evidence lifts the posterior only to 0.25, because posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. Raising the variance widens the bell and lowers its peak, since the area is fixed at 1. A density can exceed 1 when the variance is small. A probability cannot. Two-class softmax is the sigmoid of the logit gap. Raising both logits by the same amount leaves P(A) unchanged.

A Gaussian is one shape among many, and real features are often not bell-shaped. Automatic differentiation traces a much larger graph. Discrete samples have no derivative until you choose a surrogate. A production layer is the same Wx+b in thousands of dimensions. High-dimensional loss geometry is not a double well, and “all local minima are terrible” is the mythology this page refuses.

A kicker that repeats the topic and a title that names the widget. Vectors: chips a and b, a gridded plane with arrows a and b, the angle θ, the dashed projection of a onto b and the dotted perpendicular drop, a product table with a sum row, and metrics a · b, cos θ, the lengths |a| and |b|, and the distance |a − b| between the two arrow tips. Matrices: sliders for W and b, chip x, the dashed square with corners (±1, ±1) and its shaded image under Wx + b, the input x carried to Wx (dashed) and then shifted by b (dotted), a y₀/y₁ table, and metrics W x + b, Shapes, and det W. Derivatives: sliders x and Nudge ε, a plot of x² with the tangent at x, the dashed secant to x + ε, and the run ε and rise Δf between them, plus metrics x², slope 2x, and secant. Optimization: Loss surface, Parameter w, Step size η, a downhill button, and a plot of L(w) with each minimum marked, the current w as a ball, its tangent, a dashed arrow to the next w, and a dotted path of the steps taken. Metrics L, L', ηL', and the nearest minimum. Probability: a Probability idea control with four views. Counts and softmax shows a 2×2 count table, two logits, softmax bars, and metrics P(A,A,B) and ln lik. Bayes' rule shows the class-by-x count table with P(x=1|y), a Prior P(y=1) slider, two bars for the weight of each way to see x = 1, and metrics for the evidence, the posterior, and the odds. Mean and variance shows a four-number sample table, sliders Mean μ, Variance σ², and Probe x, a Fit button, a bell-curve plot with the mean line, a μ ± σ band, and the four sample values as ticks, and metrics for the density at x, z, and the area within one σ. Logit to probability shows Logit A and Logit B, a sigmoid curve with the current gap marked, and metrics that put softmax P(A) beside σ(z) and the log-odds. Logarithms: sliders True p and Model q, metrics −ln p, H(p), H(p,q), and KL, a surprise curve −ln u with the model's two surprises (filled) and the truth's (rings), and two stacked bars, H(p) and H(p,q), whose gap is KL. Dot product is ax·bx + ay·by. The projection is ((a·b)/|b|²) b. Cosine divides by the two lengths. Distance is the length of a − b, √((ax−bx)² + (ay−by)²). y = Wx + b. The parallelogram applies that affine map to the corners (±1, ±1). Each output coordinate is one row dotted with x, plus a bias. det W = m00·m11 − m01·m10 is the area scale factor. The curve is y = x². The printed slope is 2x. The secant is [f(x+ε)−f(x)]/ε, which equals 2x+ε on this f. Convex L(w)=(w−0.8)²+0.25. Nonconvex L(w)=(w²−1)²+0.35w+0.6. A downhill step writes w ← clip(w − η L'(w), −2, 2). Minima are the roots of L'(w) found by bisection; on the tilted curve they sit near w = −1.04 (L ≈ 0.24) and w = 0.95 (L ≈ 0.94). Empirical P(y=1|x) uses authored counts 3/1 and 1/3. Softmax is e^{logit}/Σ e^{logit}. Likelihood of A,A,B is P(A)²P(B). Bayes' rule reads its likelihoods from the same counts, P(x=1|y=1) = 3/4 and P(x=1|y=0) = 1/4, and weighs them by your prior: posterior = prior × 0.75 / (prior × 0.75 + (1 − prior) × 0.25). At the table's own prior of 0.50 that is 0.75, the conditional the table gives directly. At a prior of 0.10 it is 0.25. In odds, posterior odds = prior odds × 3. The Gaussian view fits the sample −1, 0, 1, 2 by the maximum-likelihood rule: mean = sum / n = 0.50 and variance = mean squared deviation = 1.25 (divide by n, not n − 1). The plotted density is exp(−(x − μ)² / (2σ²)) / √(2πσ²), and the band μ ± σ holds about 68.3% of the area, found by numeric integration. The logit view uses the same two logits as softmax. The gap z = A − B feeds σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^−z), which equals softmax P(A) exactly, and ln(P(A)/P(B)) returns z. Entropy and cross-entropy use the natural log on Bernoulli p and q, so the unit is nats. H(p,q) = p(−ln q) + (1−p)(−ln(1−q)); the bars stack exactly those two terms. KL is H(p,q)−H(p). Edit the chips or sliders that belong to the current topic. The other topic's numbers stay in state. Comparison worth running: on derivatives, shrink Nudge ε and watch the secant meet 2x. On optimization, start the two-well surface at w = 1.4 versus w = −1.4. On probability, set Probability idea to Bayes' rule and compare Prior P(y=1) at 0.50 and 0.10. A large dot product can come from length or from alignment. Cosine isolates the angle. A derivative is local. A local minimum on the tilted well is a real stationary point, not a story about deep nets. In this lab: every readout is a closed-form 1-D or 2-D formula. There is no automatic differentiation and no learned parameter except the w you step by hand. The count table, its likelihoods, and the four-number Gaussian sample are authored. The path of steps is view-only history: moving Parameter w or switching surface starts a new one. The loss plot clips its y-axis and labels the ball when L runs off the top. In general: training uses the same ideas in thousands of dimensions, with care for overflow, batching, and discrete choices that have no slope. High-dimensional loss geometry is not a 1-D double well. A real Bayes update multiplies many estimated likelihoods rather than reading one from a table, and real features are often not bell-shaped.
