documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: Combining the parameters of two or more trained models or adapters into one set of weights with arithmetic alone. No gradient step runs, and no capability is guaranteed.
documents.title: Model merge

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: The fine-tuned weights minus the base weights they started from, one entry per parameter. Merging methods add, scale, trim or drop these vectors and then add the result back onto the base.
documents.title: Task vector

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: The requirement that every model being merged was fine-tuned from the same starting checkpoint. Task vectors from one base live in one coordinate system; two independently trained networks usually do not, because their hidden units can be permuted.
documents.title: Shared base

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: The property that every point on the straight line between two solutions also has low loss. Fine-tunes of one pretrained model often have it, which is why averaging them works at all.
documents.title: Linear mode connectivity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: Taking a weighted mean of checkpoints, one parameter at a time. With a shared base it is exactly base plus the weighted mean of the task vectors, so each task keeps only its share of its own vector.
documents.title: Weight averaging

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: Adding task vectors to the base with a scaling coefficient, and subtracting them to remove a behaviour (Ilharco et al., 2023). The algebra is exact; whether skills add like numbers is an empirical question.
documents.title: Task arithmetic

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: The change in one task's loss caused by adding the other task's vector. Measured by comparing a merge with the same merge where the other vector is set to zero, so shrinkage is not mistaken for it.
documents.title: Interference

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: A parameter that one task vector pushes up and the other pushes down. Averaging a conflict cancels part of both pushes; TIES keeps only the side with more total mass.
documents.title: Sign conflict

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: Trim, elect sign, and merge (Yadav et al., 2023): keep each vector's largest entries, choose one sign per parameter from the summed trimmed values, then average only the entries that agree with it.
documents.title: TIES-Merging

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: Drop And REscale (Yu et al., 2023): zero each task-vector entry with probability p and multiply the survivors by one over one minus p, so every entry keeps its expected value. It relies on the deltas being redundant.
documents.title: DARE

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: Spherical linear interpolation: blend along the arc between two vectors instead of the straight chord, which keeps the blend's length when the vectors point in different directions. It combines exactly two inputs.
documents.title: SLERP

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Model merging
documents.body: A small trained update, such as a LoRA pair, stored apart from the base. Its product is a task vector too, so the same merge arithmetic applies to it.
documents.title: Adapter

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Model merging · question 1
documents.body: A 50/50 average of two fine-tunes is worse on both tasks than either specialist. What is the cleanest test of whether the two task vectors are interfering? Merge again with the other task vector set to zero, so only what remains beyond that is interference Treat any rise above the specialist's loss as interference, so the gap itself is the whole measurement of it Train both fine-tunes for more epochs; if the gap stays after that, the gap was interference Averaging multiplies each task vector by 0.5, and half a fine-tune is worse than a whole one even with no other task present. Comparing against the merge with the other vector removed isolates what the other task actually did. In this lab the average's proverb vector slightly helps recipes; the full sum at scale 1 is where interference shows.
documents.title: A 50/50 average of two fine-tunes is worse on both tasks than either specialist. What is the cleanest test of whether the two task vectors are interfering?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Model merging · question 2
documents.body: This lab merges two fine-tunes of one base, and the merges mostly work. Which common real-world failure can this toy not show, and why? Interference between tasks, because the lab only ever adds two task vectors Sign conflicts, because a 900-weight table is too small for two task vectors to disagree on any entry Averaging nets with different initializations, because a bigram table has no hidden units to reorder Any loss increase from merging, because each specialist is scored on its own training text Merging only makes sense when both fine-tunes start from one base, so that entry 417 means the same weight in both. Two networks trained from different random starts can compute the same function with hidden units in a different order, and averaging them mixes unrelated units. A bigram table has no hidden units, so the lab cannot stage that failure, although it does show interference and sign conflicts.
documents.title: This lab merges two fine-tunes of one base, and the merges mostly work. Which common real-world failure can this toy not show, and why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Model merging · question 3
documents.body: On a weight where the two task vectors disagree in sign, what does TIES-Merging do that a plain average does not? It averages the two entries, so they cancel toward zero and neither task is favoured It elects one sign for that weight and averages only the entries that agree with it It drops both entries and leaves the base value in place for that weight It rotates the pair along an arc so that their combined length is preserved TIES trims each vector to its largest entries, elects a single sign per weight, and averages only entries that agree with the elected sign, so a strong entry is not diluted by a weak opposing one. The plain average lets the two cancel. Rotating along an arc is SLERP, which changes the blend's length rather than resolving signs.
documents.title: On a weight where the two task vectors disagree in sign, what does TIES-Merging do that a plain average does not?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Model merging · question 4
documents.body: Raising DARE's Drop rate p toward 0.9 rescales the surviving entries by 1 / (1 - p). What does that do to both losses in this lab? They fall, because dropping entries removes the interference between the two task vectors for good They are unchanged, because the rescale restores each dropped entry exactly Only the recipe loss changes, because DARE drops entries from one vector only They rise sharply, because rescaling fixes each entry only on average, not individually The rescale makes the surviving sum right on average, not for any single entry, and the deltas of a 900-weight table carry no spare copies to absorb the loss. DARE was designed for large models whose fine-tuning deltas are small and redundant, so this toy tilts against it, and the result varies with the random mask.
documents.title: Raising DARE's Drop rate p toward 0.9 rescales the surviving entries by 1 / (1 - p). What does that do to both losses in this lab?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Model merging · question 5
documents.body: On Task arithmetic you sweep Scale lambda from 0 up to 1.5. Why do both losses first fall and then rise? Small lambda undershoots each task vector; large lambda adds both whole, so interference outgrows the gain Large lambda pushes the merge beyond the base model, so the base's own loss starts to climb again and drags both tasks up Small lambda trains the merged model for fewer epochs, so it is still underfit at that setting The loss rising at large lambda is only noise from the DARE mask seed, which the sweep never fixes Lambda trades two effects. Below about 0.7 to 0.8 the merge is mostly paying the cost of scaling down each task's own vector, which more lambda repairs. Beyond that point both vectors are added nearly whole and the interference from the other task grows faster than the repair. No training happens at any lambda, and the mask seed only matters for DARE.

documents.subtitle: Plain · Model merging
documents.body: Picture a model, a computer program that learns from example text so it can guess what letter or word comes next. Say it has already learned from one kind of text, such as a few lines about the weather. Now picture two copies of it, where one copy practises on recipe steps and the other practises on proverbs, short sayings such as “a stitch in time saves nine”. Training a model a little further like this is called fine-tuning, and each copy is called a fine-tune. Each fine-tune gets better at its own new job, but what you really want is one model that can handle both jobs at once. This module is about model merging, a way to build that one model with arithmetic instead of more training. You work out what each round of extra training changed inside the model, combine those two sets of changes, and add the result back onto the original. The whole merge takes only seconds, and unlike training, it needs no training text at all. Where you have met it Large language models, the kind of program behind a chatbot, are often adapted to a new job by training them a little further on new text. Each adaptation leaves behind its own full set of numbers, and people have built tools to combine several of those sets into one. One of them, mergekit, is described by its makers as “a toolkit for merging pre-trained language models”. The *LoRA & adapters* lab showed a cheaper way to adapt a model, in which each new job is stored as a small add-on file called an adapter. An adapter’s changes can be merged with exactly the same arithmetic, which is why software built for adapters offers the same merge methods you will try here. Why it matters Without merging, there are two ordinary ways to get several skills out of one model, and both of them cost something. You can keep a separate model for every skill and switch between them, or you can gather all the training text and train again on all of it. Merging is a third route, which reuses the training you have already done instead of repeating it. The catch is that a merge is a guess, because nothing checks the combined numbers against either job while the arithmetic runs. A skill can quietly get weaker in the process, and the only way to find out is to test the merged model on every job. This lab runs those tests for you and shows exactly where each merge loses ground, and why. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these three ideas in your own words: why a merge is arithmetic on the changes two fine-tunes made to one shared starting model, rather than a second round of training; how to tell apart two reasons a merge can score worse: each job’s own changes getting watered down, and one job’s changes truly getting in the other’s way; what three methods, called TIES, DARE and SLERP, each do differently from a plain average of the two sets of changes. What the lab lets you do Every number in this lab comes from real training inside the app, using a very small model that guesses the next letter of a text. The texts and training runs are fixed, and every score is measured on the same text the models trained on. The only random part you can redraw is DARE’s, with New random mask. The lab has three cards, and each one shows a different part of the story: Task vectors draws the two lists of changes as two coloured maps, and counts where they agree and where they pull in opposite directions. Merge recipe lets you pick one of five merge methods, prints the exact arithmetic with real numbers, and draws ten of the changes before and after the merge. Two task losses scores every merge on both jobs at once, compares it with the models trained for one job alone, and splits any lost skill into two causes. There is one surprise to watch for: the plainest merge, an even average, ends up worse at recipes than the recipe model and worse at proverbs than the proverb model. Yet in that same merge, each job’s changes actually helped the other job, and working out how both can be true is the heart of this lesson.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Model merging
documents.body: The model: a table of 900 scores The model in this lab reads one character and guesses which character comes next, using an alphabet of 30 characters. Those 30 are a space, the 26 letters, a full stop and two bracket symbols that never appear in the texts. Everything the model has learned sits in one table, with a row for each character it might read and a column for each character that might come next. Each cell holds a score, and a higher score makes that pairing more likely. For example, the cell in row h and column e grows high when the training text keeps putting an e after an h, as in “the”. To make a guess, the model turns one row of scores into chances that add up to 100%, giving bigger scores bigger chances. The raw scores, before they become chances, are called logits, which is the word the lab uses on its maps. The lab names each cell by its pair of characters, so h→a means the score for an a coming right after an h. With 30 rows and 30 columns, the table holds 900 numbers, which are called weights, and the lab’s formulas write the whole set as θ, the Greek letter theta. The starting model The starting model, called the base, was trained on Harbor weather notes, which is eight short lines about fog, wind, rain and boats. It went through that text 48 times, and one full pass over the training text is called an epoch. The lab measures how well a model fits a text with a loss, the average of how surprised the model is by each real next character. If the model gave the real next character a high chance, say 90%, it is barely surprised. If it gave it only 1%, it is very surprised, and the loss goes up. A lower loss is better. The lab measures surprise in units called nats, so it reports each loss in nats per character. You do not need to know how a nat is defined, because one fact is enough to read the numbers. A model spreading its guesses evenly over all 30 characters would score about 3.4, so anything below 3.4 means the model has picked up real patterns from its training text. The base’s loss is 2.553 on Recipe steps and 2.684 on Proverbs, two texts it never trained on, so it already beats even guessing on both. Fine-tuning leaves a list of changes Next, two copies of the base are trained further, one on Recipe steps and one on Proverbs, for 20 epochs each. Recipe steps is eight lines such as “stir the onions until they turn soft and sweet”, and Proverbs is ten sayings such as “the early bird gets the worm”. This is the fine-tuning from the big picture, and the lab calls the two fine-tunes the specialists, since each one is trained for a single job. After training, the recipe specialist’s loss on recipes is 2.123, a clear drop from the base’s 2.553. In the same way, the proverb specialist’s loss on proverbs is 2.169, down from the base’s 2.684. Now compare each fine-tune with the base cell by cell. In each of the 900 cells of the table, subtract the base’s score from the fine-tune’s score. This uses the numbers in the table, not the losses you just read. That gives a list of 900 changes, one for each weight, telling you how far training moved every score up or down. A list of numbers like this is called a vector, so this list of changes is called the fine-tune’s task vector. The Task vectors card writes it as τ = θ_tuned − θ_base, where τ, said “tau”, stands for the task vector. The other two symbols, θ_tuned and θ_base, stand for the fine-tune’s weights and the base’s weights, so the formula reads “tuned minus base”. Here is one real cell, h→a, which is the score for an a coming right after an h. In the proverbs, an a follows an h five times, in words such as “what”, “has” and “than”, while in the recipe steps that never happens. So the proverb fine-tune raised the h→a score by 1.18, and the recipe fine-tune lowered it by 0.89. The two task vectors therefore hold +1.18 and −0.89 in that one spot, which is the kind of disagreement this lesson keeps coming back to. Reading the two maps The card draws each task vector as a 30 by 30 map, τ recipes and τ proverbs, with rows for the previous character and columns for the next. A blue cell means the fine-tune raised that logit, a red cell means it lowered it, and grey means the cell did not change, or changed too little to show. The deeper the colour, the bigger the change, and both maps share one colour scale so that you can compare them fairly. A few rows stay grey on both maps, namely the rows for j, q, x, z and the two bracket symbols. None of those characters appears in either text, so training never gives their rows any reason to move. Every other row changes in all 30 cells, because training on a row nudges every score in it, raising the real next characters and lowering the rest. Both texts use the same set of 24 characters, so both fine-tunes change the same 24 rows. With 30 cells in each row, that makes 720 changed cells out of the table’s 900. A picture to hold on to: two sound engineers Picture a sound desk at a concert, with a long row of sliders that each set how loud one microphone or instrument is. Say this desk has 900 sliders, and think of their starting positions as the base model. Two sound engineers each get an exact copy of that desk, and each one adjusts their copy for a different song. When they finish, each engineer writes down how far they moved every slider, such as “slider 3, up a lot” or “slider 7, down a little”. Each engineer’s list of moves is a task vector, because it records the change from the starting desk rather than the final positions. A merge takes a fresh copy of the original desk and applies some mix of the two lists of moves. The simplest mix moves every slider by half of what the first engineer did, plus half of what the second engineer did. Where both engineers moved a slider the same way, the merge moves it that way too. Where one moved it up and the other moved it down, the two moves partly cancel each other out. That clash is called a sign conflict, because the two changes have opposite signs, one plus and one minus. The picture stops matching in two places, and the first is about labels. On a real desk every slider has a label, such as “drums”, so you can read what each move does. In this tiny model you can read each number too, because each is the score for one pair of characters. In a big model, though, a single number usually has no meaning that anyone could name. The second difference is that on a desk each slider sets its own sound and nothing else. Here the 30 scores in a row share out 100% of the chances between them, so raising one score lowers the chances of every other character in that row. Why both must start from the same base The two lists of moves only make sense together because both engineers started from the same desk. That requirement is called the shared base, which means every model in a merge must have been fine-tuned from the same starting model. Then any one cell, say cell number 417, means the same thing in both task vectors, so adding them cell by cell adds like to like. Now picture two desks that were wired by different people, so slider 417 controls the drums on one desk and the singer on the other. Adding the two engineers’ moves slider by slider would then mix up sounds that have nothing to do with each other. Bigger models have the same problem, because between their input and their output they have inner parts called hidden units. Each hidden unit comes to respond to some pattern during training, and nothing decides ahead of time which unit ends up with which pattern. Before any training, a model’s numbers are set to random values, and training then adjusts them step by step. So two models trained from different random starting points can do the same job with their hidden units in a different order. Averaging them number by number would then mix unrelated units, exactly like the two desks wired by different people. Fine-tunes of one model avoid this problem, because both inherit the same wiring from their base and usually move only a short way from it. Imagine sliding from one fine-tune’s weights to the other’s, with every cell moving at the same steady pace. Say one cell holds 1.0 in the first fine-tune and 3.0 in the second, which are made-up numbers. A quarter of the way along, that cell holds 1.5, halfway it holds 2.0, and three quarters of the way it holds 2.5. Every other cell slides from its first value to its second in the same way, at the same time. Now check the loss at each stop along the way. For fine-tunes of one model, the loss usually stays low at every stop, with no hump in the middle where the model suddenly gets much worse. That property is called linear mode connectivity, and it is why averaging fine-tunes of one model works at all. Two models trained from different random starts usually do not have it, so somewhere between them the loss climbs. Five ways to combine the lists The Merge recipe card offers five methods in its Merge method control, and all five start from the same two task vectors. All five also end the same way: the combined list is added onto the base, and the result is the model you would actually use. The lab calls that result Served weights, and it prints the formula for it with the current numbers filled in. The small line above the card’s title also says “no gradient step”, where a gradient step means one small training update, so merging trains nothing at all. Linear blend Linear blend takes a weighted average of the two fine-tunes, which is an average where each one can count for a different share. This is called weight averaging, and the Blend t slider sets the proverbs’ share, so at 30% the slider reads “70% recipes · 30% proverbs”. At 50% each list counts for exactly half, and the formula reads θ = θ_base + 0.50·τ_recipes + 0.50·τ_proverbs. In words, that means “the base, plus half of the recipe list, plus half of the proverb list”. For the h→a cell, half of −0.89 is about −0.45, and half of +1.18 is about +0.59. Added together, they move that cell up by only about +0.14, so the average gives neither task much of what it wanted. Because both fine-tunes share the base, averaging their task vectors gives exactly the same model as averaging the two fine-tunes’ own weights. A saved copy of a model’s weights is called a checkpoint, which is the word the lab uses when its formula note points this out. Here is why, using a made-up base score of 2.00 for the h→a cell: the recipe fine-tune lowered that score by 0.89, so the recipe fine-tune holds 1.11 in the cell; the proverb fine-tune raised that score by 1.18, so the proverb fine-tune holds 3.18 in the cell; the average of those two scores is 2.145, which is the base’s 2.00 plus 0.145, the same as adding half of each change to the base. Task arithmetic Task arithmetic adds both lists at full strength and then scales the total by one number, written λ, the Greek letter lambda. The Scale λ slider sets that number from 0 to 1.50, and adding task vectors to a base like this is called task arithmetic. At 1.00 the formula reads θ = θ_base + 1.00·(τ_recipes + τ_proverbs), so the h→a cell moves by −0.89 + 1.18, which is +0.29. At a Scale λ of 0.5 it gives exactly the same model as the 50/50 average, since half of the total is the same as half of each list. TIES TIES is short for TIES-Merging, which is named after its three steps of trim, elect sign and merge: Trim: keep only the biggest changes in each list, as a share set by the Keep top slider, and set every other change to zero. Size alone counts here, so −0.89 is a bigger change than +0.5. Elect: for each cell, add up the kept changes from both lists, and whichever sign has the larger total wins that cell’s vote. Merge: average only the kept changes that agree with the winning sign, and then scale the result by λ, the same as in task arithmetic. In sound-desk terms, TIES checks which way each slider got the bigger total push, and then it uses only the moves that went that way. Take the h→a cell again, where both changes are big enough to survive a trim that keeps the top 20% of each list. Their total is +0.29, so plus wins the vote, and the recipe list’s minus change is left out of the average. Only the proverb change is left, so with Scale λ at 1.00 the merged cell gets the full +1.18 instead of the average’s +0.14. Where both lists agree and both changes survive the trim, TIES averages them, much as the plain blend does. Beyond that, TIES differs from the plain blend in three ways: The trim throws away most of each list, so with Keep top at 20%, 678 of the 900 merged cells end up at zero. In a cell where only one list’s change survives the trim, that change goes in at full strength instead of half, and the lab has 84 cells like that. In a conflict cell where both changes survive, the losing side is left out instead of cancelling the winner, as h→a showed. Those full-strength cells help explain why TIES with Scale λ at 1.00 lands close to plain task arithmetic at the same setting, as you will see in the lab. DARE DARE stands for Drop And REscale, and it works by making a random draw for every change in each list. Each change is thrown away, meaning set to zero, with a chance of p, which you set with the Drop rate p slider. The changes that survive are then multiplied by 1 / (1 − p) to make up for the missing ones. At p = 0.5, each change has a 50% chance of being dropped, and the multiplier is 1 divided by 0.5, which is 2. So every kept change is doubled, which is why the slider reads 50% dropped · ×2.00 at that setting. After that, the two thinned lists are added together and scaled by λ, the same way task arithmetic does it. To see why doubling makes up for the losses on average, picture one change of +0.6, which is a made-up size. Half the time it is dropped to zero, and half the time it is doubled to +1.2, so over many draws it averages out to the original +0.6. In any single merge, though, that change is either zero or +1.2, and never the +0.6 it started as. The random choice of which changes to drop is called a mask, and the New random mask button draws a fresh one each time you press it. SLERP SLERP stands for spherical linear interpolation, and it blends along a curve instead of a straight line so that the blend does not shrink. To see what shrinking means here, you first need a way to measure the length of a list of numbers. Think of a list of two numbers, 3 and 4, as an arrow on graph paper that goes 3 squares across and 4 squares up. Its length is the square root of 3² + 4², which is the square root of 25, so the arrow is 5 squares long. That is the same rule you would use for the long side of a right-angled triangle. The same rule works for 900 numbers: square each one, add up all the squares, and then take the square root of the total. You cannot draw an arrow that needs 900 numbers to describe it, but its length, and the angle between two such arrows, still work exactly as they do on paper. The lab prints each task vector’s length under its map as ‖τ‖, where the double bars mean “length of”, and both lengths are about 10. The badge on Task vectors reads cosine 0.34, where the cosine is a score for how closely two arrows point the same way. A cosine of 1 means the same direction, 0 means a right angle, and −1 means opposite directions. So a cosine of 0.34 means the two task vectors point partly the same way, at an angle of 69.9°, a little less than a right angle. The cosine on the badge and that angle are the same fact written in two different ways. Now picture two friends who start at the same lamp post and each walk a little over 10 steps, in directions about 70° apart. If you stand halfway along the straight line between where they stop, you are only about 8.5 steps from the lamp post. That is because cutting across the corner brings you back toward the start, which is exactly how an average shrinks. If you walk around the lamp post instead, on a curve that keeps your distance, you stay a little over 10 steps away the whole time. A plain average takes the straight line between the two arrows, while SLERP takes the curve. In the lab, the halfway point of the plain average has a length of only 8.46, which is shorter than either task vector. SLERP’s halfway point has a length of 10.32, and you can read both numbers on the ‖τ_merged‖ badge of Merge recipe. At the halfway point, SLERP points in exactly the same direction as the average, and the only difference is that its arrow is longer. You can check this with the formula the lab prints, which uses sin, the sine key on a calculator. At Blend t 50%, the formula reads θ = θ_base + (sin(0.50Ω)·τ_recipes + sin(0.50Ω)·τ_proverbs) / sin Ω. Here Ω, the Greek letter omega, stands for the angle between the two lists, which is 69.9°, so half of it is 34.95°. Each list is multiplied by sin 34.95°, which a calculator gives as about 0.57. The total is then divided by sin 69.9°, which is about 0.94. Since 0.57 divided by 0.94 is about 0.61, SLERP takes about 0.61 of each list. The plain average takes only 0.50 of each list, and that bigger share is what keeps SLERP’s arrow long. So at the halfway point, SLERP gives the same model as Task arithmetic with Scale λ at about 0.61, and the curve does nothing more than set that bigger share. SLERP can only combine two lists at a time, so it cannot merge three models in one go.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Model merging
documents.body: As the big picture said, merging gives you one fixed model with both skills from two fine-tunes you already have. It works even when you no longer have the text to train again. The trouble is that nothing tunes the merged numbers for either job, so whether both skills survive the arithmetic has to be measured. Measuring has a trap in it, though, because a merged model can score worse than a specialist for two quite different reasons. The first reason is shrinking, which happens when a method uses less than all of each job’s own list. The 50/50 average, for example, uses only half of the recipe list, so the recipe skill gets watered down even if the proverbs did nothing. The second reason is interference, which is the harm one job’s list does to the other job when both lists are added together. That is the real clash between the two skills, and it is a separate thing from shrinking, even though both make the score worse. The water test Picture a friend who makes a strawberry and banana smoothie with half a cup of each fruit, instead of her usual full cup of strawberries. She complains that it tastes less of strawberry than usual, and she blames the banana for spoiling it. Before she blames it, she can make one more smoothie, with half a cup of strawberries and half a cup of water in place of the banana. The water version shows how much flavour she lost by halving the strawberries, and comparing it with the banana version shows what the banana really did. The lab runs that same test on every merge, and to measure interference on recipes it reruns the merge with the proverb list set to zeros. That list of zeros plays the part of the water, and the difference between the two scores is the interference. The picture stops matching in one way: the water smoothie is a real drink she could pour, while the lab’s water version is only a check it works out. Nobody would ever use it as a model. Here is the test with real numbers for the 50/50 average, scored on the recipe text: The recipe specialist, which uses the whole recipe list, scores 2.123 on recipes. Half the recipe list on its own, with zeros in place of the proverbs, scores 2.294, which is 0.171 worse, and all of that comes from shrinking. Half the recipe list plus half the proverb list scores 2.257, which is 0.037 *better* than the water version’s 2.294. So the interference is −0.037, and the minus sign means the proverb list helped the recipes. On Two task losses, the Gap column shows the total change from the specialist, which is 2.257 minus 2.123, or +0.134. The Interference column shows the part caused by the other list, and whatever is left of the gap is the cost of shrinking. The two parts add up to the gap: 0.171 of shrinking plus −0.037 of interference gives 0.134. Because the proverbs helped a little, the total gap is smaller than the shrinking on its own.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Model merging
documents.body: Read the two task vectors Start on Task vectors, with Task vectors from left on Full fine-tunes and Recipe epochs and Proverb epochs both at 20. Each of those two sliders reads “20 passes” at that setting, since an epoch is one pass through the text. Under the maps, Recipe specialist, recipes shows 2.123 and Proverb specialist, proverbs shows 2.169, the two specialists’ scores on their own texts. Overlapping entries reads 720 of 900, which counts the cells that both fine-tunes changed, and the badge above the maps reads cosine 0.34. Sign conflicts reads 96 (13%), so about 1 in 8 of those shared cells were pushed in opposite directions by the two fine-tunes. Look for the cells with a thin diagonal line through them, because those are the 96 conflicts, and they are marked on both maps. Then drag Recipe epochs down to 0, and watch the slider change to read untrained · τ = 0 as the recipe map turns grey. Every merge now works with the proverb list alone, because an untrained fine-tune has a task vector made entirely of zeros. The one exception is SLERP, which needs two non-zero lists to measure an angle, so its row falls back to the base model’s losses. Set the slider back to 20 before you go on, so the numbers match the rest of this lesson. Average, then split the cost On Merge recipe, leave Merge method on Linear blend with Blend t at 50%, where the slider reads “50% recipes · 50% proverbs”. The Served weights formula shows the arithmetic, and under it you can read the merged model’s loss on each of the two texts. Now go to Two task losses, whose plot puts the recipe loss along the bottom and the proverb loss up the side. Lower and further left is better on both jobs, so you want a merge’s point as close to the bottom left corner as it can get. The fixed markers are the harbor base, the recipe specialist, the proverb specialist, and a cross for two separate models. That cross sits at each specialist’s score on its own job, which is what you would get by keeping both models. The large filled circle is the merge you picked, while small hollow circles show the other four methods, each tagged with a short name: Lin, TA, TIES, DARE or SL. If a point would fall off the edge of the plot, it is drawn at the edge with a dashed outline and labelled with its true losses. In the table below the plot, the Linear blend row shows 2.257 on recipes and 2.330 on proverbs. Both are worse than the Specialists row, so the merge loses to each specialist at its own job, by gaps of +0.134 and +0.161. Then read the two Interference columns, which show −0.037 and −0.055, and notice that both of them are negative. The note under the table puts this into words, saying that adding each list helped the other task rather than hurting it. Try this: switch Merge method to Task arithmetic and set Scale λ to 1.00, which makes the losses 2.279 and 2.258. Interference now turns positive, at +0.156 on recipes and +0.089 on proverbs, so this time each list is hurting the other job. Then drag Scale λ slowly from 0 up to 1.50, and watch the large circle travel along the dashed line that the legend calls “task sum, λ from 0 to 1.5”. The dotted line beside it is the linear blend’s path. When you finish, set Scale λ back to 1.00, because TIES and DARE use the same slider and this lesson’s numbers assume 1.00. Resolve sign conflicts Switch Merge method to TIES, where Keep top starts at 20% of each vector. Move it up to 100% first, and then slide it slowly down to 10% while you watch the strip of bars on Merge recipe. The strip shows ten cells, with the five biggest sign conflicts on the left and the five biggest agreements on the right. Each cell has three bars: the recipe change on the left, the proverb change in the middle, and the merged value on the right, with that value printed underneath. With TIES selected, any change that was trimmed away turns into a dashed outline, and the winning sign is printed as ▲ + above the merged bar or ▼ − below it. Find the conflict cell named h→a, whose merged bar reads +1.18, the full proverb change, where Linear blend gave only +0.14. Drop and rescale Switch Merge method to DARE, then sweep Drop rate p from 0 up to 0.9 and watch the large filled circle, which now stands for DARE. In the strip, dropped changes become dashed outlines. A short tick, which the legend calls “height before rescaling”, marks how tall each kept change was before it was multiplied. On the way up, stop at 0.50 and read the DARE row in the table, which shows 2.762 on recipes and 2.602 on proverbs. Those numbers belong to the starting mask, and once you draw a new one you cannot get that mask back, so read them first. Then carry on to 0.9 and press New random mask a few times. The button starts out reading New random mask · #4, and the number goes up by one with each press, as each press draws a fresh mask. Curve instead of line Switch Merge method to SLERP, keeping Blend t at 50%, and look at the ‖τ_merged‖ badge, which now reads 10.32 instead of 8.46. The note under the formula gives the angle between the two lists as Ω = 69.9°, which matches the cosine of 0.34 on the first card. In the table, SLERP’s Interference cells show a dash, because SLERP has no version with one list taken out. It needs two arrows to measure an angle, so the lab cannot run its water test on it. Compare SLERP’s point with the Linear blend point at the same Blend t instead, which is what the lab’s note suggests. Switch to LoRA task vectors Last, switch Task vectors from to LoRA rank 4, so that each task vector comes from a small adapter like the one in *LoRA & adapters*. The 4 is the adapter’s size setting from that lab, and a smaller number means a smaller add-on. Read Sign conflicts again, which should now read 331 (46%), and the cosine badge, which should read 0.19. Then set Merge method back to Linear blend at 50% and read the two Interference columns, which now sit close to zero. Finally, pick Task arithmetic with Scale λ at 1.00 and read the Interference columns again. They show about +0.51 on recipes and +0.38 on proverbs, roughly three to four times the full fine-tunes’ values.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Model merging
documents.body: Shrinking, not clashing, explains the average The average’s gap is mostly shrinking, because the recipe list at half strength, alone, scores 2.294, and adding half the proverb list *improves* that to 2.257. Both texts are ordinary English, so the two lists point partly the same way, which is what the positive cosine of 0.34 tells you. The proverbs help here because the recipe list is only at half strength, so the recipe model still has room to improve. Half the proverb list supplies some of that missing push. At full strength the recipe list has already done its job, so the same overlapping push overshoots and the interference turns positive, as the next section shows. The cosine is 0.34 in both cases, so the cosine alone cannot tell you whether the other list will help or hurt. How strongly each list is added matters just as much. About 87% of the 720 shared cells agree in sign, so two lists can overlap almost everywhere without being in conflict. Full strength is where they collide Task arithmetic at full strength is where the lists collide, costing recipes +0.156 and proverbs +0.089 against the same merge without the other list. In that row the Gap and Interference numbers match. With the proverb list removed, the merge is exactly the recipe specialist, so the whole gap comes from the other list and none from shrinking. Scale λ has a sweet spot, since both losses fall until λ is about 0.7 to 0.8 and then both rise as the dashed path bends back. At λ = 0.8, the losses are 2.218 on recipes and 2.241 on proverbs, which beats the 50/50 average on both jobs. Below the sweet spot each list is too weak, so turning λ up repairs the shrinking, while above it the interference grows faster than the repair. TIES picks a winner in each conflict TIES changes the conflict cells most: in h→a, recipes wrote −0.89 and proverbs wrote +1.18, and TIES keeps +1.18 where the average keeps +0.14. At Keep top 20%, only 38 of the 96 conflicts survive the trim on both sides, so only those 38 need a vote. In the other 58, at least one side was trimmed away first, so there was nothing left on that side to vote with. With 20% kept, TIES lands at 2.273 on recipes and 2.280 on proverbs, which is close to plain task arithmetic in this lab. DARE breaks this model At p = 0, DARE drops nothing and multiplies by 1, so it gives exactly the same numbers as Task arithmetic at the same Scale λ. At p = 0.5, with the starting mask, DARE scores 2.762 on recipes and 2.602 on proverbs, worse than every other method here. At p = 0.9, nine in ten changes are dropped and each kept change is multiplied by 10, and the losses climb to nearly 6. That is 5.967 and 5.661, far worse than the score of about 3.4 for a model that spreads its guesses evenly over every character. The multiplying keeps each change right on average but not in any single draw, and this tiny model has no spare copies of its changes to fall back on. Losing changes alone would only drift the model back toward the base, with losses close to the base’s own. Going far past even guessing comes from the other half of the rule. Each surviving change is multiplied by 10, so those scores land ten times too far, and the model becomes confidently wrong. Each press of New random mask moves the DARE point, because a different set of changes is thrown away each time. SLERP keeps its length SLERP at 50% scores 2.226 on recipes and 2.284 on proverbs, which beats the plain average on both jobs. The two lists are 69.9° apart, so the straight-line halfway point is only 8.46 long, while the curve’s halfway point is 10.32 long. Since both halfway points face the same direction, keeping more of each list’s strength is what makes SLERP the better blend here. SLERP at 50% is the same model as Task arithmetic at Scale λ about 0.61. The slider moves in steps of 0.05, but at 0.60 the losses come out at 2.229 and 2.287, almost the same. Task arithmetic at 0.80 does better still, so the curve is not special in itself. LoRA lists clash far more With LoRA rank 4, Sign conflicts reads 331 (46%), out of the same 720 shared cells, so nearly half the shared cells are pushed in opposite directions. That is far more than the roughly 1 in 8 for full fine-tunes, and the cosine drops to 0.19, so the two LoRA lists point in less similar directions. At the 50/50 average the LoRA interference stays near zero, while each list is only at half strength. The clash shows up once both lists are added whole: Task arithmetic at Scale λ 1.00 gives interference of about +0.51 and +0.38, against +0.156 and +0.089 for full fine-tunes. One file has a price No merge reaches the two separate models cross, and that leftover gap is the price of serving one model instead of keeping two.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Model merging
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Every task vector, merge and loss in this lab is computed live from real fine-tunes, so nothing is recorded in advance or made up. The limits come instead from how small and narrow the experiment is, and each one is worth keeping in mind. There are only two tasks, and each fine-tune runs once with one seed, the starting number for its random choices. A different seed could give somewhat different lists. The model is also tiny, with only 900 weights, and its texts hold only eight recipe lines and ten proverbs. This lab’s base is its own 48-epoch run, not the 60-epoch Harbor model from the *Fine-tuning & transfer* and *LoRA & adapters* labs. That is why its loss on recipes is 2.553 rather than the 2.556 you may remember. The difference is only 0.003, far smaller than the gaps between a merge and a specialist that this lesson studies, though no lab tests whether it matters. Each merge is also scored on the very sentences the fine-tunes trained on, so nothing is held back for a fair test. Picture a student who practises with the exact questions that will be on the exam, so a high mark shows only that they learned those questions. In the same way, these scores say which merge fits these sentences, not which one would do best on new recipes or proverbs. The strip shows only 10 of the 900 cells, picked because they are the biggest conflicts and agreements, while the other 890 cells still count in every loss. SLERP is applied here to the task vectors rather than to whole models, which lets you see the curve clearly. Real tools such as mergekit apply SLERP to whole models instead. Think of each whole model as one long arrow, made of the long base arrow plus a short arrow of changes. Two such arrows almost overlap, so there is hardly any corner to cut. In real use, SLERP on two fine-tunes of one base therefore gives nearly the same result as a plain blend. This model is a single table with no hidden units, so it cannot show what goes wrong when two models lack a shared base. Every task vector in the lab starts from the same base on purpose, so you only meet that failure in this lesson’s words. The lab also tilts against TIES and DARE, which were designed for huge models whose changes are small and highly repetitive. In such models most changes can be trimmed or dropped at little cost, while here every one of the 900 numbers matters. Picture a school play run by a crew of 900, where each person has a different job that nobody else knows how to do. If you send half the crew home at random and ask the rest to work twice as hard, the total effort might stay the same. Yet if the one person who knew the lights went home, nobody can work them. Now send nine in ten home, as DARE does at p = 0.9, and ask the rest to work ten times as hard. Worse than the missing jobs, each person who stays now overdoes their own job, so the sound person turns the music up far too loud. That is what DARE does to this lab’s tiny model. A huge model is more like a crew where many people can cover each job, which is the setting DARE was built for. DARE also uses a single random mask for each setting, and the lab never averages its results over many masks. New random mask shows you how far one fresh draw can move the result, which is the only spread you get to see. The LoRA maps carry one extra quirk, because adding the same amount to every score in a row changes no guess at all. If every score in the h row went up by 1, the gaps between them would stay the same, so the chances for the next character would not change. The model only cares how the scores in a row compare with each other, and full fine-tunes never add a shift like that. LoRA adapters do add such shifts, so part of what the LoRA maps and cosine show makes no difference to any prediction. A common mix-up: a merged model that loses to each specialist at its own job is not proof of interference. Averaging halves each task’s own list, and half a list scores worse even when nothing else is added at all. Only the Interference columns, which rerun the merge with the other list set to zero, measure what the other task really did. Where real merging falls short Real merges are tuned and judged on held-out tests for every task at once, which means tests built from examples the models never trained on. The scale λ is tuned on those tests too, and choosing it well matters as much as choosing the method. Interference grows as you merge more tasks, and also as the tasks become more different from each other. Two tasks that share a lot, like the two English texts here, clash less than tasks that pull a model in very different directions. A merged model can keep its test scores while losing behaviour that no single score captures, such as the way it lays out its answers. It might also lose its habit of refusing requests it should refuse, or its calibration, which is how well its confidence matches how often it is right. No merge comes with a promise, because merging runs no training step, so nothing guarantees that any skill survives until you test it. Licences also travel with the weights, and a licence sets the rules for how a model may be used. So a merged model inherits every rule from every model that went into it.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Model merging
documents.body: Subtracting a task Task arithmetic works in reverse too, so you can subtract a task vector instead of adding one, written θ_base − λ·τ. This has been used to remove a behaviour that a fine-tune taught, such as writing toxic text, meaning text that is rude or hurtful. Adapters are task vectors too An adapter, such as the LoRA add-on from *LoRA & adapters*, is a small trained update that is stored apart from the base. Its correction, written (α / r)·B·A in that lab, is a list of changes to the base’s weights, which makes it a task vector too. That is why the software built for adapters offers the same merge methods that you have tried in this lab. The LoRA rank 4 option here uses adapters with a rank of 4 and an alpha of 8, as the line of text above the maps says. So each adapter’s correction is its two small tables multiplied together and then doubled, since 8 divided by 4 is 2. Methods stack The methods can also be combined, and DARE is often used first to thin out the lists before they are merged with TIES. SLERP takes exactly two models, so merges of many models use the linear, TIES or DARE methods instead. Tools such as mergekit apply these rules to one block of weights at a time. They sometimes use a different blend for each layer, which is one of the stages a big model passes its input through. The cosine, worked out The cosine on the badge comes from a short calculation that you could do by hand for a small list. Multiply the two lists cell by cell, add up all the products, and divide the total by the two lengths multiplied together. Take two short lists, 3 and 4, and 4 and 3, which are both arrows 5 squares long. Multiplying cell by cell gives 12 and 12, which add up to 24. Dividing 24 by 5 times 5, which is 25, gives a cosine of 0.96, so those two arrows point almost the same way. Lists that rise and fall together give a cosine near 1, unrelated lists give one near 0, and lists that move in opposite ways give one near −1. Other ways to combine skills *LoRA & adapters* made the kind of lists this lab combines, and *Distillation & pruning* takes a different route to a similar goal. It reaches one smaller model with many behaviours by training rather than arithmetic, which costs computer time but actually tunes the result for the job. Merge, or serve the adapters side by side Merging is not the only way to get several tasks out of one base, and *LoRA & adapters* ends on the other route. That route keeps one copy of the base and many adapters, and it picks the right adapter for each request as it arrives. Serving software called vLLM does this when it is started with the --enable-lora option. A research paper called S-LoRA describes serving thousands of adapters at the same time from one shared base. The two routes trade differently, because serving keeps each task’s adapter exact but costs effort in scheduling requests and managing memory. A merge costs nothing extra when the model runs, but, as this lab measures, it can add interference between the tasks. How much depends on the method and the scale. Serve the adapters separately when tasks must never interfere, or when you need to add and remove them while the system is running. Merge them when one fixed model is enough and your held-out tests show that the interference is small. Toy versus real Tools: mergekit, from Arcee AI, describes itself as “a toolkit for merging pre-trained language models”. You describe a merge in a short settings file, written in a format called YAML, that names the models and the method. Methods: mergekit’s methods include Linear, SLERP, Task Arithmetic, TIES, DARE and DELLA, among others, and this lab rebuilds the first five on a table of 900 numbers. Memory: mergekit works through a model one piece at a time instead of loading it all at once, so a merge can run on a computer’s main processor alone. It can also use a graphics card with as little as 8 GB of its own memory. A gigabyte, or GB, is about a billion bytes, and one byte holds about one letter of text. Testing: here a merge is arithmetic on 900 numbers and the check is two losses, while a real merge is judged on held-out tests for every task. On those tests, one score can hold steady while another slips, so every task needs checking. Adapters: in Hugging Face’s PEFT library, merge_and_unload() folds one adapter into its base for good. The mergekit tool can go the other way with mergekit-extract-lora, building an adapter that comes close to a full fine-tune’s changes. Side by side: several adapters can also stay unmerged and be served side by side, as the section above describes. Where these facts come from The facts about tools come from the mergekit README (github.com/arcee-ai/mergekit) and the PEFT LoRA reference (huggingface.co/docs/peft/package_reference/lora).
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Model merging
documents.body: A model merge turns separate fine-tunes of one pretrained model into a single set of weights by arithmetic alone, with no training data and no gradient step. The question this module asks is whether skills learned in separate runs add together, and what each merging rule costs each task. Its unit is the task vector: the change a fine-tune made to its base's weights, entry by entry. *Fine-tuning & transfer* rewrote a base table's own weights, and *LoRA & adapters* left you one low-rank adapter per task; both changes are task vectors. This lab builds two from one Harbor base, for Recipe steps and Proverbs, and combines them five ways. Where it shows up mergekit, from Arcee AI, merges pretrained language models from a YAML configuration, and its methods include all five this lab runs. Adapter libraries apply merge methods to LoRA adapters too, because the low-rank update a LoRA adapter adds, (α / r)·B·A, is itself a task vector. Hugging Face PEFT can also fold a single adapter back into its base weights with merge_and_unload(). Subtracting a scaled task vector instead of adding it has been used to remove a behaviour a fine-tune taught, such as toxic generation. Why it matters Serving many tasks otherwise means keeping one model or adapter file per task, or training one model again on all the data. A merge combines the files you already have, in seconds, with no training data, and costs nothing extra at inference. It assumes a shared base: every input was fine-tuned from the same checkpoint, so each entry means the same weight in all of them. What you will be able to explain How a merge works as arithmetic on task vectors that share one base, not as a second training run. How to separate the cost of shrinking each task vector from true interference: the change in one task's loss caused by adding the other task's vector. What TIES, DARE and SLERP each change about a plain average. What the lab shows Nothing is synthetic. The app trains a 900-weight character bigram base and two fine-tunes of it, full or LoRA rank 4; every merge is exact arithmetic on their task vectors, and every loss is measured on the full Recipe steps and Proverbs corpora. Corpora, training seeds and learning rate are fixed, nothing is held out, and DARE's drop mask is the only random draw you can change, with New random mask. Task vectors: Task vectors from (Full fine-tunes or LoRA rank 4), Recipe epochs and Proverb epochs shape the two vectors, mapped cell by cell with sign conflicts struck through. Under the maps, Overlapping entries counts the entries both vectors changed, and Sign conflicts how many of those disagree in sign. Merge recipe: Merge method picks Linear blend, Task arithmetic, TIES, DARE or SLERP and shows only its own controls among Blend t, Scale λ, Keep top, Drop rate p and New random mask. Served weights prints the operation with current numbers. Two task losses: every merge plotted by recipe and proverb loss against the base, the specialists and the two separate models cross, with a table of each method's Gap and Interference. The key experiment changes only how much of each vector is added: compare Linear blend at Blend t 50% (each vector at half strength) with Task arithmetic at Scale λ 1.00 (both whole), and read the Interference columns.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Model merging
documents.body: A model merge combines trained weights with arithmetic and no gradient step. The unit it works on is the task vector: fine-tuned weights minus the base they started from, τ = θ_tuned − θ_base. Every method in this lab builds one combined vector from two task vectors and serves θ_base + τ_merged. The base is the 900-weight character bigram table, trained 48 epochs on Harbor weather notes. It scores 2.553 nats per character on Recipe steps and 2.684 on Proverbs. Two full fine-tunes start from it, 20 epochs each. The recipe specialist reaches 2.123 on recipes; the proverb specialist reaches 2.169 on proverbs. That base is this lab's own run, not the 60-epoch Harbor table of *Fine-tuning & transfer* and *LoRA adapters*, which reads 2.556 on recipes. Each lab fixes its own epoch count, and none tests the difference. Why a shared base matters Both task vectors are differences from the same checkpoint, so entry 417 means the same weight in both. That shared base is what makes adding them meaningful. Two networks trained from different random initializations can compute the same function with their hidden units in a different order, and averaging them entry by entry mixes unrelated units. Fine-tunes of one pretrained model tend to share a low-loss basin, a property called linear mode connectivity. The five recipes Weight averaging (Linear blend): θ_base + (1 − t)·τ_r + t·τ_p, the same as averaging the two fine-tuned checkpoints. Task arithmetic: θ_base + λ·(τ_r + τ_p). At λ = 0.5 it is the average. TIES-Merging: trim each vector to its largest entries, elect one sign per weight, average only the entries that agree. DARE: drop entries at random with probability p, rescale survivors by 1 / (1 − p), then add. SLERP: blend along the arc between the two vectors rather than the chord.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Model merging
documents.body: The cost of skipping training is that a merge is a guess. Nothing optimizes the combined weights for either task, so whether two skills survive the addition has to be measured. This lab measures it on both tasks at once, and separates two reasons a merge can lose: the method shrinking each task's own vector, and genuine interference from the other task.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Model merging
documents.body: Start on Task vectors. At 20 epochs each, the cosine badge reads 0.34, Overlapping entries reads 720 of 900, and Sign conflicts reads 96 (13%). Struck-through cells on both maps are those conflicts. On Merge recipe, leave Merge method on Linear blend with Blend t at 50%. The table on Two task losses reads 2.257 on recipes and 2.330 on proverbs: gaps of +0.134 and +0.161 over the specialists. Now read the interference columns: −0.037 and −0.055. Switch to Task arithmetic at Scale λ 1.00: 2.279 and 2.258, and interference turns positive, +0.156 and +0.089. Sweep Scale λ and watch the dashed path on the plane. Pick TIES and move Keep top from 100% down to 10%. Pick DARE, sweep Drop rate p from 0 to 0.9, and press New random mask a few times. Finally switch Task vectors from to LoRA rank 4 and repeat the average.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Model merging
documents.body: Task arithmetic also subtracts: θ_base − λ·τ has been used to remove a behaviour, such as toxic generation, learned by a fine-tune. The same algebra works on an adapter: a LoRA product (α / r)·B·A is a task vector, which is why adapter libraries offer the same merge methods. TIES and DARE compose. DARE is a pre-processing step, and its sparsified vectors are often merged with TIES rather than summed. SLERP combines exactly two inputs, so multi-model merges use linear, TIES or DARE variants instead. Tools such as mergekit apply these rules tensor by tensor, sometimes with a different t per layer. Merging sits beside two neighbours in this track. LoRA adapters produced the vectors this lab adds. Serve separately when tasks must never interfere or must be added and removed live. Merge when one fixed model is enough and your held-out evaluations show the interference is small. Toy versus real Tools. mergekit, from Arcee AI, is "a toolkit for merging pre-trained language models". A merge is a YAML configuration that names the models and the method. Its methods include Linear, SLERP, Task Arithmetic, TIES, DARE and DELLA, among others; this lab reproduces the first five on a 900-number table. documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Task vectors · Model merging
documents.body: Two fine-tunes, written as differences from one base A harbor base is trained once. Two fine-tunes start from that same base, one on Recipe steps and one on Proverbs. Each task vector is the fine-tuned table minus the base table, and the two maps draw both vectors cell by cell. A kicker naming the base and where the vectors came from, and a badge with the cosine similarity of the two task vectors. `Task vectors from` (`Full fine-tunes` or `LoRA rank 4`), `Recipe epochs`, and `Proverb epochs`, each 0 to 40 in steps of 2. Two 30 × 30 maps, `τ recipes` and `τ proverbs`. Rows are the previous character, columns the next character. Blue raises that logit, red lowers it, colour depth is |entry| on one shared scale, and grey means unchanged. A diagonal strike marks every entry whose sign disagrees with the other vector. Four metrics: each specialist's loss on its own corpus, how many of the 900 entries both vectors changed, and how many of those disagree in sign. The base is `trainTinyModel` on Harbor weather notes for 48 epochs at seed 1. Full fine-tunes continue from it at learning rate 0.6, seeds 3 and 4. The LoRA option trains a rank-4, alpha-8 adapter instead and uses its product `(α / r)·B·A` as the task vector. `τ = θ_tuned − θ_base`, entry by entry. A specialist is `θ_base + τ`, scored with full-corpus cross-entropy. Rows for characters a corpus never uses as context (`j`, `q`, `x`, `z`, the brackets) receive no gradient, so they stay grey. That holds for LoRA too: the row of B for an unused context never receives gradient and stays at zero. Sign statistics count an entry as changed when |τ| > 1e-6. Cosine is the ordinary normalized dot product of the two 900-entry vectors. `Task vectors from` swaps the fine-tuning method. `Recipe epochs` and `Proverb epochs` set how far each fine-tune travels from the base. Comparison worth running: at 20 epochs each, read Sign conflicts with `Full fine-tunes` (96 of 720, 13%), then switch to `LoRA rank 4` (331 of 720, 46%). Both fine-tunes touch the same 720 entries, because both corpora use the same 24 context characters. Overlap alone does not mean conflict: 87% of those entries agree in sign. The cosine of 0.34 is positive. The two tasks share English structure, so part of each vector helps the other task. Set one epoch slider to 0 and that map goes grey: an untrained fine-tune is a zero task vector, and every merge reduces to the other task alone. In this lab: the model is a 30 × 30 bigram table with no hidden units, so the permutation problem that breaks merges of independently trained networks cannot occur here. Every vector shares the base on purpose. In this lab: a softmax row ignores a constant added to all its logits. Full fine-tunes never add one, since each row's gradient sums to zero, but LoRA products do, so LoRA maps and cosines include direction that changes no prediction. In general: merging assumes the checkpoints share a base, or at least sit in one linearly connected basin. Fine-tunes of one pretrained model usually do; two models trained from different random seeds usually do not.
documents.title: Two fine-tunes, written as differences from one base

documents.subtitle: Merge recipe · Model merging
documents.body: The merge as arithmetic you can check Pick a method and its knobs. The formula prints the exact operation with current values, and the strip shows ten real coordinates: the two inputs, what each method keeps or discards, and the merged value. `Merge method`: `Linear blend`, `Task arithmetic`, `TIES`, `DARE`, `SLERP`. Below it, only that method's controls: `Blend t`, `Scale λ`, `Keep top`, `Drop rate p`, and `New random mask`. A `Served weights` formula with the current numbers substituted, and both merged losses as its result. A badge reports the merged vector's length. A strip of ten coordinates named `previous→next`: the five largest sign conflicts, then the five largest agreements, ranked by |τ_recipes| + |τ_proverbs|. Each has three bars in a fixed order, recipes, proverbs, merged, on one symmetric scale, with the merged value printed. For TIES, trimmed inputs are dashed outlines and the elected sign is printed above or below the merged bar. For DARE, dropped inputs are dashed outlines and a short line in the text colour marks each survivor's height before rescaling. Linear blend: `θ_base + (1 − t)·τ_r + t·τ_p`, which equals averaging the two fine-tuned checkpoints. Task arithmetic: `θ_base + λ·(τ_r + τ_p)`. TIES: keep each vector's top `Keep top` share by magnitude, set each entry's sign to the sign of the summed kept values, average only kept entries with that sign, then scale by λ. DARE: drop each entry of each vector with probability p using a seeded mask, multiply survivors by `1 / (1 − p)`, add both, then scale by λ. SLERP: `(sin((1 − t)Ω)·τ_r + sin(tΩ)·τ_p) / sin Ω`, where Ω is the angle between the two task vectors. mergekit applies SLERP to whole checkpoints; this lab applies it to the task vectors so the curvature is visible. `Merge method` swaps the rule. `Blend t` moves along the recipes-to-proverbs line. `Scale λ` stretches the combined vector. `Keep top` sets the TIES trim. `Drop rate p` and `New random mask` set DARE's mask. Comparison worth running: pick TIES and move `Keep top` from 100% to 10%. With 100% kept, every conflict column is resolved by sign election alone; with fewer kept, small opposing entries are trimmed first. In a conflict column, Linear blend leaves the merged bar between the two inputs, partly cancelled. TIES leaves it at the size of the winning side, because the losing side is excluded from the mean. At `Keep top` 20% with the default vectors, 38 of the 96 conflicts survive trimming in both vectors and need an election; in the other 58, at least one side was trimmed away first. DARE's survivors grow by `1 / (1 − p)`. At p = 0.5 each kept entry doubles, which is why the strip's scale jumps. In this lab: two task vectors only, one seed each, and the strip shows 10 of 900 coordinates chosen for size. The other 890 still count in every loss. In this lab: SLERP is applied to task vectors, not to full checkpoints. With a shared base, full checkpoints are nearly parallel and SLERP on them is almost the same as a linear blend. In general: TIES and DARE were designed for many large fine-tunes whose small deltas are largely redundant. Their published gains come from that regime, with λ tuned on held-out data.

documents.body: Where each merge lands on both tasks Every merge scored on both corpora at once, plotted against the base, the two specialists, and the corner you would reach by keeping two separate models. A table lists every method at the current settings and splits each gap into interference and shrinkage. Recipe loss on the x axis and proverb loss on the y axis, both in nats per character. Lower and further left is better on both. Fixed markers: `harbor base` (hollow circle), `recipe specialist` (square), `proverb specialist` (triangle), and `two separate models` (cross), which sits at each specialist's own loss. The selected merge as a large filled circle, the other four methods as small hollow circles tagged Lin, TA, TIES, DARE, SL, a dotted line for Linear blend from t = 0 to 1, and a dashed line for Task arithmetic from λ = 0 to 1.5. A table with each method's recipe and proverb loss, its gap to the specialist, and its interference. A note below states what the other task did to each loss. Each point is `tinyCrossEntropy` of `θ_base + τ_merged` on the full Recipe steps and Proverbs corpora. Interference on recipes is `loss(merge(τ_r, τ_p)) − loss(merge(τ_r, 0))`: the same method re-run with the proverb vector set to zero. Proverbs is scored the same way with the recipe vector removed. Gap minus interference is the cost of the method shrinking, trimming or dropping a task's own vector. SLERP has no one-vector version, so its interference is left blank. The plot stretches to hold the anchors, the linear path and the selected merge. Any other merge further out is pinned to the edge, drawn with a dashed outline, and labelled with its true losses. No controls of its own. Every control on the two cards above moves these points. Comparison worth running: on Linear blend at t = 0.5, the gaps are +0.134 and +0.161 while interference is −0.037 and −0.055. Switch to Task arithmetic at λ = 1 and interference turns positive, +0.156 and +0.089. Negative interference means the other task vector helped. In the 50/50 average, both gaps come from halving each task vector, not from the other task. The dashed Task arithmetic path bends back: both losses fall until about λ = 0.7 to 0.8, then both rise. Too much of both vectors overshoots. No merge reaches the `two separate models` cross. That gap is the price of serving one file instead of two. In this lab: the losses are training-set cross-entropy on eight-to-ten sentence corpora, with no held-out split. They say which merge fits these sentences, not which generalizes. In this lab: one DARE mask per setting. `New random mask` shows how much a single draw moves the point; at p = 0.5, masks #1 to #5 put recipe loss anywhere from 2.50 to 3.11. In general: merges are judged on held-out benchmarks for every task at once, and the scaling coefficient is tuned there. A merge that wins on two losses can still lose formatting, safety, or calibration behaviour that no loss here measures.

Separate the attention scoring rule from the memory layout used to compute it Explain what grouped-query and sliding-window attention trade away Explain why FlashAttention gives the exact same output, and which costs it leaves in place Read rotary position embedding as a rotation whose query-key score depends only on the distance between positions

documents.body: In FlashAttention tiles, step Tiles processed from 0 to the end and watch a new running max rescale the earlier weights; at the end the gap to the full softmax is at rounding level.
