documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Several attention heads computed in parallel, each with its own query, key, and value projections. At decode time every head's keys and values must be cached.
documents.title: Multi-head attention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Query heads split into groups that share one key-value head, so the cache holds only as many K and V heads as groups. Memory falls in proportion; the grouped queries must read the same stored keys.
documents.title: Grouped-query attention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: The extreme of grouped-query attention: every query head shares a single key-value head. It gives the smallest cache and the most quality risk.
documents.title: Multi-query attention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: The stored keys and values of tokens already processed, reused while decoding. Its size is 2 times layers times KV heads times head dimension times bytes per value, per token.
documents.title: KV cache

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Each query attends only to the most recent W keys. Cost and cache stop growing past W, and longer-range information must hop through layers.
documents.title: Sliding-window attention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: How far back information can reach. With a window W and L stacked layers it is up to L times W, but only by relaying through intermediate positions.
documents.title: Receptive field

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: An exact attention kernel that tiles queries, keys, and values through fast on-chip memory and never writes the full score matrix to main memory. It changes memory traffic, not the result.
documents.title: Flash attention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Computing softmax in one pass over tiles by keeping a running maximum and running sum, and rescaling earlier partial results by exp of the old maximum minus the new one. The result equals the ordinary softmax.
documents.title: Online softmax

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: A GPU's large, slower high-bandwidth main memory and its small, fast on-chip memory. Attention at long lengths is often limited by traffic between them rather than by arithmetic.
documents.title: HBM and SRAM

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: RoPE rotates each pair of query and key dimensions by the token's position times a per-pair frequency. The query-key dot product then depends only on the distance between the two positions.
documents.title: Rotary position embedding

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: The constant that sets RoPE's frequencies, theta i equals base to the power minus 2i over d. A larger base makes the slow pairs rotate more slowly; Llama 3 uses 500,000.
documents.title: RoPE base

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: How many tokens the model is trained to condition on. Memory for the KV cache, attention's quadratic cost, and the positions seen in training decide whether a length works.
documents.title: Context length

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Stretching a trained model to longer inputs by rescaling RoPE, as in position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, or YaRN, usually with some further training. Plain RoPE degrades beyond the trained length.
documents.title: Context extension

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Modern attention at scale · question 1
documents.body: On KV cache budget you set KV heads from 32 to 8. What happens to the cache, and to the attention arithmetic on Quadratic cost? Both fall to a quarter, because there are a quarter as many key-value heads doing the attention work The cache is unchanged, because its size follows the number of query heads rather than key-value heads The cache falls to a quarter; the arithmetic barely moves, since every query head still scores every key The cache stores one key and one value per key-value head, so 8 of 32 heads is exactly a quarter of the bytes. Each of the 32 query heads still computes scores against every key, so the n-squared work is the same, and only the key and value projection weights shrink. Grouped-query attention trades memory, not scoring.
documents.title: On KV cache budget you set KV heads from 32 to 8. What happens to the cache, and to the attention arithmetic on Quadratic cost?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Modern attention at scale · question 2
documents.body: A sliding window of 4,096 stops the cache growing at 128K tokens. What does a window give up? Direct access to older tokens, which must now be relayed through intermediate positions across layers Nothing, because the window only drops keys the model was never going to attend to in the first place Exactness of the softmax over the keys it keeps, because a window only approximates the weights Each query still gets an exact softmax over its window, so the keys kept are scored normally. But a token older than the window cannot be read directly, and information from further back survives only by hopping through intermediate positions, up to layers times window, and it degrades on the way. That is why some models mix windowed and full layers.
documents.title: A sliding window of 4,096 stops the cache growing at 128K tokens. What does a window give up?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Modern attention at scale · question 3
documents.body: You switch a model's attention kernel to FlashAttention. What changes? The attention output, because tiles only approximate the full softmax and lose a little accuracy How the same scores are computed: in tiles, never storing the full score matrix in main memory The KV cache size, because FlashAttention stores fewer key-value heads than the standard kernel FlashAttention computes exactly the same softmax attention. Online softmax rescales earlier tiles when a larger score arrives, so the final output matches to rounding, as the tiles card shows. It saves memory traffic and the n-squared score matrix, not the KV cache, which only fewer KV heads or a window shrink.
documents.title: You switch a model's attention kernel to FlashAttention. What changes?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Modern attention at scale · question 4
documents.body: In FlashAttention tiles you step Tiles processed and a later tile brings a larger score. What happens to the bars for the earlier keys? They stay where they are, because earlier tiles are finished and their results are never revisited They grow, because a larger score adds weight to every key that was already seen in earlier tiles They shrink, because the running max rose and earlier partial results are rescaled Online softmax keeps a running max, sum and output. When a tile raises the max, everything accumulated so far is multiplied by exp of the old max minus the new one, which is below one, so the earlier shares shrink. After the last tile the output equals the ordinary softmax to rounding.
documents.title: In FlashAttention tiles you step Tiles processed and a later tile brings a larger score. What happens to the bars for the earlier keys?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Modern attention at scale · question 5
documents.body: On Quadratic cost, attention's share of FLOPs grows with sequence length. Does FlashAttention flatten that curve? Yes: tiling skips the lower-scoring keys, so far fewer query-key pairs are computed per query No: it drops the stored score matrix and most memory traffic, but the arithmetic stays quadratic Yes: it caches keys, so each query-key product is computed only once and reused for later tokens FlashAttention is exact, so it still scores every causal query-key pair. What it removes is the stored n-squared score matrix and the traffic to main memory. Only a sliding window changes how many pairs each query scores, which is what bends the curve. Caching keys is a separate idea, the KV cache.
documents.title: On Quadratic cost, attention's share of FLOPs grows with sequence length. Does FlashAttention flatten that curve?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Modern attention at scale · question 6
documents.body: In RoPE rotation you press Shift both +16. Both vectors turn, but the Score stays the same. Why? The dot product depends only on the position difference, so shifting both positions cancels out The score is computed from the unrotated vectors, so position never reaches it Rotations change the vectors' lengths in equal amounts, so the score is rescaled back to the same value Each pair is rotated by position times its frequency, and a rotation preserves length. The dot product of a rotated query and a rotated key then contains the angle difference, which is the position difference times the frequency. Moving both by 16 leaves that difference unchanged, so the Score is unchanged.
documents.title: In RoPE rotation you press Shift both +16. Both vectors turn, but the Score stays the same. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Modern attention at scale · question 7
documents.body: RoPE makes the score depend on relative distance. Does that let a model trained on 8K tokens handle 128K at inference? Yes: because the score depends only on the distance between positions, any length behaves the same way No: RoPE keeps a table of absolute position vectors, so every position beyond 8K has no vector at all No: unseen distances still degrade attention unless the frequencies are rescaled and the model is retrained RoPE has no table of positions, but the angles for distances beyond the training range were never seen, and the model's attention degrades there. Context extension methods such as position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN rescale the frequencies, usually with some further training. Relative encoding is necessary for extension, not sufficient.
documents.title: RoPE makes the score depend on relative distance. Does that let a model trained on 8K tokens handle 128K at inference?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: This module is about what happens to attention when a model reads a very long text. In the Attention lab you met the rule itself. Each piece of text checks how well it matches the earlier pieces, then takes in a blend of information from the best matches. That rule stays exactly the same here. What changes is everything around it: how much gets stored, what gets thrown away, the order of the work, and how the model tracks each piece’s position. Language models read text in small pieces called tokens, where a token is usually a word or part of a word. Suppose you paste a long document into a chatbot and ask about something near the start. The model has to hold on to information about every earlier token while it writes its reply. This lab works out the costs for one real model’s shape, up to 131,072 tokens. It writes that as 128K, because in computing a K often means 1,024 rather than 1,000. Where you have met it Each idea you will try in this lab is used in real models today: Inside attention, many small units work side by side. Many recent models let groups of these units share one set of stored notes. They usually keep 4 to 8 shared sets rather than just one, because quality drops as more units share each set. Some models built for long texts, such as Gemma 2 and Gemma 3, mix layers that only look at recent tokens with layers that can look at everything. FlashAttention, a method published in 2022, changes the order of the work on the chip that does the arithmetic, so that far less has to be written to memory. Llama 3 marks each token’s position by turning its numbers through an angle. Why it matters Long texts are expensive in two ways, and both get worse as the text grows. First, the model keeps notes on every earlier token so it never has to reread the whole text. For a text the length of a book, those notes can take more memory than the model itself. Second, every token is compared with every token before it, so doubling the length of a text roughly quadruples the comparisons. While the model reads a long prompt, there comes a length where that comparing work catches up with everything else each layer does, and after that it takes over. Without the tricks in this module, a long conversation would need far more memory and far more time. Every trick has a price as well, though, so a large part of this lesson is about what each one gives up in exchange for its savings. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these ideas in your own words: how the rule attention uses for scoring differs from the way the work is stored and ordered, which can change while the rule stays fixed; what a model gives up when groups of attention units share their stored notes, and what it gives up when it keeps only the most recent 4,096 tokens; why FlashAttention produces exactly the same answer as ordinary attention, and which costs it leaves in place; how rotary position embedding marks position by turning numbers through an angle, so that the score between two tokens depends only on how far apart they are. What the lab lets you see and try The lab has four cards, and nothing in it is trained or timed, so you can change any setting and see the result at once. The first two cards, KV cache budget and Quadratic cost, calculate memory and arithmetic with exact formulas for one real model’s shape. Every number on them is a calculation rather than a measurement taken on a real chip. You choose how many sets of notes are kept, whether old tokens are dropped, and how long the text is. The other two cards use small made-up numbers so that you can follow every step by eye. FlashAttention tiles works through one row of 16 scores a few at a time and lands on exactly the same answer as doing them all at once. RoPE rotation turns two short lists of numbers by their positions, and a button moves both positions together so that you can check whether the score changes. The key experiment is to stretch the text to 128K tokens and then tell the model to keep only the last 4,096 tokens. When you do, watch how far both the memory and the share of arithmetic spent on attention fall.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: One rule for scoring Inside a model, each token is stored as a long list of numbers, and a list like this is called a vector. Attention makes three vectors from every token, and each one has its own job. The query describes what this token is looking for, while the key works like a label saying what the token can offer. The value holds the information that the token can hand over to any other token that finds its label useful. Each token compares its query with the key of every token it is allowed to see. The comparison multiplies the first number in the query by the first number in the key, the second by the second, and so on. Adding up all of those results gives one score for each key, and this step is called the dot product. A tool called softmax then turns the scores into shares that add up to 100 percent. Finally, the token takes in a blend of the values, in which each value counts as much as its share. Together these steps make up the scoring rule, and that rule never changes anywhere in this module. What can change is the memory layout, meaning which keys and values are kept, where they are kept, and in what order the computer works through them. Two very different layouts can give exactly the same scores and the same blend, so the first skill this module asks for is keeping these two ideas apart. Of the four tricks below, only the third, working in small pieces, keeps the answer exactly the same. Two others, sharing stored keys and values among groups of heads and throwing old ones away, keep the rule too. But they change what it is applied to: fewer different keys, or fewer keys in view. So their answers can change a little. The fourth trick, RoPE, is different again, because its whole job is to change the scores on purpose by building in each token’s position. The library picture To picture all this, think of the model as a library in which every token it has read leaves a folder behind. The label on the front of the folder is the token’s key, and the papers inside are its value. A reader arrives with a question, which is a query, and checks the label on every folder. The reader then copies out a blend of the papers, taking more from the folders whose labels fit the question best. A real model has many readers working side by side, and each one asks its own kind of question. Each reader is called an attention head, and running several heads side by side is called multi-head attention, or MHA. In the model this lab uses, every layer has 32 of these query heads, and in plain multi-head attention each head has a shelf of its own. That means each token leaves 32 different folders, one written for each reader, because every head makes its own key and value from the token. The model is also built from 32 layers stacked on top of each other, and each layer runs attention again on what the layer below produced. So the library really has 32 floors, and every floor has its own readers and its own shelves. The picture stops matching in two places, and the first is that the labels and papers are lists of numbers rather than words. A reader also never picks a single folder, because it always takes a blend from every folder it can see, even when some of them count for almost nothing. Trick 1: sharing shelves The first trick keeps fewer shelves by letting a group of readers share one shelf, instead of each reader having its own. As a result, each token leaves one folder for each group rather than one for each reader. Every reader still writes its own question and still checks every label on its group’s shelf, so the scoring rule is untouched. Each shelf holds keys and values, so it is called a key-value head, or KV head for short. Letting groups of query heads share KV heads is called grouped-query attention, or GQA. The most extreme version, where all 32 readers share one single shelf, is called multi-query attention, or MQA. With 32 query heads, the lab lets you keep 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 or 1 KV heads, since each of those numbers divides 32 evenly. The real model whose shape the lab uses, called Llama 3 8B, has 8 KV heads, so each shelf serves a group of 4 readers. The saving is exact, because 8 shelves instead of 32 means a quarter of the folders and therefore a quarter of the memory. The price is that the readers in a group must all read the same folders, so those folders cannot be shaped to suit each reader’s question. That usually costs the model a little quality, and the cost grows as the groups get bigger. Trick 2: throwing old folders away The second trick limits how far back a reader may look, and it is called sliding-window attention. Each token may only see the most recent tokens, up to a limit called the window size, and older keys and values are thrown away. In this lab the window holds 4,096 tokens, and that count includes the token that is doing the looking. So a token at position 10,000 can see back as far as position 5,905, but nothing before that. The sum 10,000 − 4,096 gives 5,904, and the window starts one later because it counts position 10,000 itself. As the text grows, the window slides forward with it, like a frame moving along a long strip of film, which is where the name comes from. Because only the last 4,096 tokens are ever kept, the memory stops growing once the text is longer than that. Each token also scores at most 4,096 keys, so the scoring work grows in a straight line instead of curving upward. Older text is not completely out of reach, and the reason is the layers. On layer 1, a token can only collect information from the tokens inside its own window, as described above. On layer 2, it reads tokens that have already collected information from their own windows, so information can now arrive from up to twice as far back. After all 32 layers, information can in principle travel up to 32 × 4,096 tokens, which is 131,072. How far back information can reach in this way is called the receptive field. Picture a group chat that only lets you see the last 50 messages. You cannot scroll up to something said two days ago, but if a friend quoted it recently, you still find out about it, secondhand and maybe shortened. A sliding window behaves the same way, because old information reaches the present only when it has been passed along through newer tokens. A little of that information is lost on each hop, so what arrives from far back is weaker and less exact. The group chat stops matching in two ways. In the model, nothing deliberately saves a fact for later, so old information survives only if newer tokens picked it up through their attention, layer after layer along the way. And each hop uses up one layer, so with 32 layers it can travel at most 32 windows back. Trick 3: working in small pieces The third trick changes the order in which the work is done, while the keys and values that are kept stay exactly the same. To see why order matters, you need one fact about the chip that does a model’s arithmetic, which is called a GPU. A GPU has a large main memory that takes a while to reach, and a tiny memory built right into the chip that is extremely fast. These two are called HBM and SRAM, where HBM, short for high-bandwidth memory, is the large main store and SRAM is the small fast one. In the library picture, HBM is a huge storeroom and SRAM is a small reading desk. Carrying folders back and forth between them takes much longer than reading at the desk, so for long texts the carrying often decides how fast the work goes. The ordinary way to run attention calculates every score for a query and writes the whole row of scores out to the storeroom. Later it comes back to read them all again and turn them into shares. Done for every token at once, that makes a grid with one score for every pair of tokens, which is called the score matrix. For a long text this grid is enormous, and moving it in and out of HBM uses up much of the available time. Flash attention, usually written FlashAttention, carries a few keys and values to the desk at a time, and each small piece of the work is called a tile. It scores the keys in that tile, folds them into a few running totals, and moves on to the next tile. Because each tile is finished before the next one arrives, the full score matrix is never written to the storeroom at all. The hard part is softmax, so start with how softmax turns scores into shares. Recall from the Attention lab that softmax raises a special number, about 2.718, to the power of each score. This number is called e, and the lab writes “e raised to a power” as e^ followed by the power in brackets. Softmax then adds up all of these numbers, and each key’s share is its own number divided by that total. Raising 2.718 to a big score gives a huge number, and at a score of 100 the answer has 44 digits. Numbers that big can be too large for the space a GPU sets aside for each number. So softmax first subtracts the top score from every score, which keeps every result between 0 and 1. Subtracting the same amount from every score never changes the shares, because every number shrinks by the same factor, and so does the total. After that subtraction, each key’s number says how far behind the leader it is. The leader gets exactly 1, a key one point behind gets about 0.37, and a key two points behind gets about 0.14. If those three were the whole row, the total would be 1.51, so the leader’s share would be 1 ÷ 1.51, about 66 percent. Here is the problem for the desk. Each share depends on the total over every score and on the top score, but the desk has only seen some of the scores so far. FlashAttention handles this with online softmax, which keeps three running numbers as it goes: the highest score seen so far, which is called the running max m and marks the current leader; a running sum ℓ, which will become the total that the shares are divided by; a running blend of the values, called the output o, which becomes the final blend at the end. Each key’s number is measured against the best score seen so far. When a new tile brings a score higher than the running max, every key already counted is suddenly further behind the new leader, so its number is now too big. The fix is to multiply the running sum and the running blend by the same factor, which is 2.718 raised to the old max minus the new max. The lab’s example shows why that factor is the right one. A key that scored 2.4 led the first tile, so its number was 1. Then a 3.1 arrives, and the 2.4 key is now 0.7 behind the new leader, so its number should be what a key 0.7 behind gets, which is 0.4966. Multiplying its old 1 by the factor, 2.718 raised to 2.4 − 3.1, gives exactly that, because that power is −0.7. A negative power gives a number below 1, so the factor always shrinks whatever it multiplies. The same factor works for every earlier key. A key that was 1 point behind the old leader is now 1.7 behind the new one. Multiplying its 0.37 by 0.4966 gives the right number for 1.7 behind, too. One multiplication of the running sum and blend fixes every earlier key at once, without going back to the storeroom. So each correction turns every earlier key’s number into exactly what it would have been if it had been measured against the new top score from the start. By the end, each key’s number is what it would have been if the whole row had been done at once against the true top score. The total is identical, so every share is identical too, and so is the final blend. FlashAttention is exact rather than an estimate, because it reaches the same answer by doing the work in a different order. What FlashAttention leaves alone matters as much as what it changes, because it still scores every pair of tokens. So the arithmetic stays the same, and the stored folders are not touched at all. Trick 4: position as a rotation The scoring rule compares the contents of a query and a key, so on its own it has no sense of how far apart two tokens sit. The fourth trick builds position into the query and the key themselves, by turning them. Rotary position embedding, or RoPE, splits each query and each key into pairs of numbers. You can draw a pair of numbers as an arrow from the centre of a graph. Use the first number as x and the second as y, the same way you would plot a point. RoPE turns each arrow around the centre by an angle that grows with the token’s position, so a token at position 20 turns further than one at 7. Turning an arrow around a fixed centre like this is called a rotation, which is where the word rotary in the name comes from. Each pair rotates at its own speed, meaning the angle it turns for every step in position, and the lab calls this speed θ, the Greek letter theta. Angles here are measured in radians instead of degrees, and a full turn of 360 degrees is about 6.28 radians, so one radian is about 57 degrees. In the lab’s small example, with the base at 10,000, pair 0 turns one radian per position. Each later pair turns ten times more slowly than the pair before it. Here is the reason only the distance matters, and it comes from how the dot product treats a pair of arrows. For each pair, the dot product depends only on how long the query arrow and key arrow are, and on the angle between them. It is largest when they point the same way, zero when they are at right angles, and negative when they point in opposite directions. Rotating an arrow never changes its length, so the only thing a rotation can change is the angle between the two. Try it with three simple pairs of arrows, using the multiply-and-add rule from earlier: The arrows (1, 0) and (1, 0) point the same way, and 1 × 1 + 0 × 0 = 1. The arrows (1, 0) and (0, 1) are at right angles, and 1 × 0 + 0 × 1 = 0. The arrows (1, 0) and (−1, 0) point opposite ways, and 1 × −1 + 0 × 0 = −1. Turn both arrows of the first pair a quarter turn and you get (0, 1) and (0, 1). Their dot product is 0 × 0 + 1 × 1 = 1, the same as before, because neither the lengths nor the angle between the arrows has changed. Suppose the query sits at position m and the key sits at position n, where m and n stand for the two position numbers. The query’s arrow turns m steps and the key’s arrow turns n steps, so the angle between them shifts by m − n steps. Their actual positions drop out of the score completely, and only the distance between the two tokens is left. Picture two hands on a clock face: if you turn the whole clock, both hands move, but the angle between them stays exactly the same. Take pair 1 in the lab, which rotates 0.1 radians for every step in position: With the query at position 20, its arrow rotates 20 × 0.1 = 2 radians away from where it started. With the key at position 7, its arrow rotates 7 × 0.1 = 0.7 radians, which is a much smaller rotation. The angle between the arrows therefore shifts by 2 − 0.7 = 1.3 radians, which is the distance of 13 positions times 0.1. Move both 16 places later and the rotations become 3.6 and 2.3 radians, so the shift is still 1.3. Pairs that rotate quickly change a lot between neighbouring tokens, so they can tell apart tokens that are close together. Pairs that rotate slowly hardly change between neighbours, but they keep changing over long distances. This is a bit like the second hand and the hour hand on a clock. Here, though, the two hands stand for two different pairs, not for a query and a key. The setting that decides how slowly the slowest pairs rotate is called the RoPE base, and a bigger base means slower rotation. The clock picture stops matching in one way that matters, because the length of each arrow counts toward the score as well as the angle between them. The full score also adds up the parts from every pair, and each pair has its own query arrow and key arrow rotating at its own speed. The model behind the numbers Every memory and arithmetic number in the first two cards is calculated for one real model shape, called Llama 3 8B. The 8B in its name stands for about 8 billion learned numbers, which were adjusted during training. It has 32 layers and 32 query heads, and each head’s query, key and value hold 128 numbers. Every stored number takes 16 bits, where a bit is a single 0 or 1. Eight bits make one byte, so each stored number takes 2 bytes.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Each of the four tricks answers a specific problem, and three of those problems are costs that grow more serious as a text gets longer. The fourth is a gap in the scoring rule itself, which cannot tell near from far without help. A stack of notes that grows with every token A model writes its reply one token at a time, and every new token needs the keys and values of all the earlier tokens. Calculating them from scratch for every new token would repeat an enormous amount of work, layer after layer. So instead, the model calculates them once, stores them in memory, and reuses them for every token that follows. That store is the KV cache, which is the stack of folders in the library picture. The Inference & KV cache lab split a model’s work into two phases, and both of them matter here. Reading your whole prompt at once is called prefill, and writing the reply one token at a time is called decode. The cache is filled during prefill, then read in full for every new token during decode, and each new token adds its own key and value to it. Memory is counted in bytes, where a byte is roughly the space one letter of plain text takes up. The bigger units in the lab go up in steps of 1,024. A KiB, or kibibyte, is 1,024 bytes, which is roughly a thousand letters of plain text. Each bigger unit is 1,024 of the one before, so a MiB, or mebibyte, is about a million bytes. A GiB, or gibibyte, is about a billion bytes, and a TiB, or tebibyte, is about a trillion. The KV cache row on the first card shows the formula 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 B × 8,192 with its values filled in. Read from left to right, it starts with 2, because every token leaves two vectors, one key and one value. The next two numbers are the 32 layers and the 8 KV heads, since every layer and every shelf keeps its own folders. Then come the 128 numbers inside each vector and the 2 bytes, written 2 B, that each 16-bit number takes up. The last number is the 8,192 tokens that have been read so far, since every one of them leaves its own folders. Multiplying everything except the last number gives 131,072 bytes, which is exactly 128 KiB for each token. The Per token readout shows that figure, and multiplying it by 8,192 tokens gives the 1.00 GiB in the Cache readout. The cache grows in a straight line with the length of the text, so doubling the number of tokens doubles the memory. At 128K tokens it reaches 16 GiB, which is more than the model’s own learned numbers take up, at about 15 GiB. Size is not the whole problem, because the cache also slows the model down while it writes. For every new token, the model must read its learned numbers and its whole cache out of memory, which usually takes longer than the arithmetic. So a bigger cache also means slower writing, which is why shrinking the cache is often the saving that matters most. How many tokens a model is trained to handle at once is called its context length. Three things decide whether a long context works, and the first two are the memory for the cache and the cost of comparing every pair. The third is whether the model saw distances that long while it was being trained. Comparisons that grow with the square The second cost is the arithmetic of scoring, where each token scores itself and every earlier token but never a later one. A model that writes from left to right must not peek ahead, so later tokens are blocked. This rule is called the causal mask, and it appears in the small heading of the Quadratic cost card. Count the pairs for a short text of 4 tokens to see how fast they pile up: The first token scores only 1 key, which is itself, because nothing comes before it. The second token scores 2 keys, itself and the first, and the third token scores 3. The fourth token scores 4 keys, so the total is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 pairs. With 8 tokens, adding up the whole numbers from 1 to 8 gives 36 pairs. So doubling the length of the text took the count to nearly four times as many pairs. Picture a party where every guest who arrives shakes hands with everyone already in the room. The first few arrivals are quick, but the hundredth guest has 99 hands to shake, so the total speeds up as the room fills. Attention grows the same way, since each new token has to be scored against everything already there. One difference is that a token also scores itself, so the hundredth token makes 100 comparisons, not 99. When a count grows roughly with the square of the length like this, the growth is called quadratic, which is where the Quadratic cost card gets its name. A text 16 times longer has about 256 times as many pairs, because 16 × 16 = 256. The card measures arithmetic in FLOPs, where one FLOP is a single multiplication or addition of decimal numbers. Its chart counts in TFLOP, where a TFLOP is a trillion FLOPs, because the totals for long texts are so large. In this model, each pair of tokens costs 512 FLOPs in each head, with half going on the score and half on blending in the value. Everything else in the layer grows in a straight line instead, because each token passes once through the layer’s grids of learned numbers. These learned numbers are called weights, and the card calls this work the Weight matmuls, short for multiplications by a matrix, which is a grid of numbers. The lab called The transformer block showed the arithmetic inside one layer, and this card prices that same layer. Doubling the text doubles the weight work but roughly quadruples the attention work, so attention’s share keeps climbing. At the starting length of 8,192 tokens, attention is 13.3 percent of one layer’s arithmetic while the model reads the prompt. At 128K tokens it is 71.1 percent, and the Crossover readout shows that the two are equal at 53,247 tokens. The hidden cost of moving numbers A third cost hides behind the other two, and it comes from writing scores down. If attention wrote down every score before turning them into shares, the score matrix for one layer would need room for every pair in all 32 heads. The Score matrix if stored readout shows that this would take 4.00 GiB at 8K tokens. At 128K tokens it would take 1.00 TiB for a single layer, which is far more than the whole model needs. Even when a chip has room for that grid, writing it to HBM and reading it back often takes longer than the arithmetic itself. FlashAttention never writes that grid at all, which is the whole point of working in tiles. The FlashAttention keeps readout shows what it saves instead: one small summary number for each row in each of the 32 heads, which comes to 1.0 MiB at 8K tokens. Those summaries matter during training. While a model is being trained, it needs the shares a second time to work out how to adjust its learned numbers. FlashAttention recalculates the scores from the queries and keys, then uses the summary numbers to turn them straight back into shares, rather than keeping the whole grid. Position has to reach the scores The last problem is order, because the scoring rule on its own cannot tell near from far. Without help, two tokens would get the same score whether they sat side by side or thousands of tokens apart. That is because the score compares only what the tokens contain, not where they are. RoPE fixes this by turning each query and key according to its position, in a way that makes only the distance between them matter. Which trick answers which problem Fewer KV heads shrink the cache in exact proportion. The scoring arithmetic does not change at all, and the layer’s total arithmetic barely moves. A sliding window shrinks both the cache and the arithmetic, but it gives up direct access to old tokens. FlashAttention removes the stored score matrix and most of the carrying between memories, while the arithmetic and the cache stay the same. RoPE puts position into the scores, and it saves no memory or arithmetic at all.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Each part below matches one of the four steps listed in the lab, in exactly the same order. The first two cards share their controls, so the settings you pick on KV cache budget also drive Quadratic cost. Share key-value heads Try this: On KV cache budget, set KV heads to 32 · MHA, then 8 · GQA, then 1 · MQA, while leaving Sequence length at 8,192 tokens. As you switch from one setting to the next, watch how the Per token and Cache readouts change. The vs MHA readout shows your cache as a percentage of the cache with all 32 KV heads. At 32 · MHA, Per token reads 512 KiB and Cache reads 4.00 GiB. At 8 · GQA, they read 128 KiB and 1.00 GiB, and vs MHA reads 25.0%. At 1 · MQA, they read 16 KiB and 128 MiB, which is about 3 percent of the full cache. Watch the head diagram on the same card as you switch, because it draws the sharing for you. The row of 32 small squares, the query heads, never changes, while the blocks underneath, the KV heads, merge into fewer and wider blocks. At 8 · GQA its caption reads 8 KV heads cached · 4 query heads each. The bar chart lists the cache for all six settings at the current length, with your selection highlighted. Each step down the list halves the bar, because halving the shelves halves the folders. Now look at Quadratic cost while you switch between the same settings. Its three curves are the solid Weight matmuls line, the dashed full-span attention line and the dotted window line, and you will see that they barely move. Crossover only shifts between about 51,000 tokens with one KV head and about 59,000 with all 32. That small shift has a simple cause. With fewer KV heads, the layer makes fewer keys and values, so its weight work shrinks a little. Attention then catches up with that smaller weight work slightly sooner, which moves the crossover earlier. The scoring work itself stays put, because all 32 readers still check every label. Stretch the sequence Set KV heads back to 8 · GQA, then drag Sequence length all the way to the right, to 131,072 (128K) tokens. Cache now reads 16.00 GiB, which is sixteen times the cache at the starting length. In Quadratic cost, the dashed Attention, full span line has curved up well above the solid Weight matmuls line, and Attention share reads 71.1%. Step the length back down one notch at a time and watch Attention share fall: At 64K tokens, attention is 55.2% of the layer’s arithmetic, so it still does a little over half the work. At 32K tokens, its share drops to 38.1%, which is somewhat more than a third of the work. At 16K tokens, its share drops to 23.5%, which is a little under a quarter of the work. At 8K tokens, its share is back down to 13.3%, which is a little over one eighth. The share itself does not halve, because it is attention’s part of the total. Compare attention with the weight work instead. Halving the length cuts attention’s work to about a quarter but the weight work only to a half, so attention’s work divided by the weight work halves each time: At 128K tokens, attention does about 2.5 times the weight work, and at 64K about 1.2 times. At 32K it does about 0.6 times the weight work, and at 16K about 0.3 times. At 8K it does about 0.15 times the weight work, a little under one sixth. That halving is the square growth showing itself, because attention grows with the square of the length while the weight work grows only in a straight line. Now go back to 128K tokens and set Attention span to Sliding window 4,096. Cache drops to 512 MiB, which is one thirty-second of what it was, and Attention share falls to 13.2%. The KV cache formula now multiplies by 4,096 tokens instead of 131,072, because only the last 4,096 tokens are kept. The note under that formula calls this a rolling buffer, as in a model called Mistral 7B, which means each new token pushes out the oldest one. It also says that a token reaches 4,096 tokens back directly, and up to 131,072 back by hopping through 32 layers. In Quadratic cost, follow the dotted Attention, window 4,096 line, which runs almost straight while the dashed line curves upward. Once the text is longer than the window, each new token adds the same 4,096 pairs, so the cost grows in a straight line. Finally, keep the window on and shorten the text to 4,096 tokens or fewer, where the window changes nothing at all. The whole text already fits inside the window, so no tokens are thrown away. Tile the softmax FlashAttention tiles follows the scores of one query against 16 keys, and each key’s score sits in its own box. Its caption says the keys wait in HBM, the outlined tile is the one loaded into SRAM, and shaded tiles are done. Under each key are two marks that you will compare at every step of the walk-through. A dashed outline shows the key’s full softmax weight, which is its true final share of the row. Here “weight” means the key’s share, not the learned weights from the Quadratic cost card. A filled bar shows the share the key would get using only the tiles that have been seen so far. Walk through it one tile at a time with Tile size on 4 keys: Drag Tiles processed all the way down to 0 of 4, so that no tile has been loaded yet. The table then reads m = −∞, ℓ = 0, where minus infinity is a starting value lower than any real score. Step Tiles processed to 1 of 4, which loads the first four keys into SRAM. Their highest score is 2.4, so Running max m becomes 2.4, and Running sum ℓ reads 1.3729. The 2.4 key’s number is 1, and 1 ÷ 1.3729 is about 0.73, so its share is about 73 percent at this point. Its filled bar towers over its outline, because it is sharing with only three other keys. Step to 2 of 4, and the new tile brings a 3.1, which beats 2.4 by 0.7. The running max jumps to 3.1, and the column headed Rescale e^(m_old − m) shows 0.4966. Here m_old is the old running max, 2.4, and m is the new one, 3.1, so the column shows e^(2.4 − 3.1), which is e^(−0.7). That factor shrinks the stored running sum and the 2.4 key’s own number by the same amount, so on its own it would leave the share unchanged. The share drops to about 25 percent because the new leader joins the total at a full 1, and its three tile-mates add about 0.28 more. Everything counted before now adds up to only 0.68, measured against that new leader, so the new total is about 1.96, and 0.4966 ÷ 1.96 is about 0.25. Step to 3 of 4, then to 4 of 4, and notice that neither tile beats 3.1, so the rescale stays at 1.0000. Nothing is multiplied down, but each tile still adds more keys to the running sum, so every share slips a little lower. At 4 of 4, the 2.4 key’s share settles at 14.0 percent, exactly on its outline, and every other bar lands on its outline too. At the end, the Online vs full row compares the tiled answer with the all-at-once answer and reads 8.3e-17. That is computer shorthand for 0.000000000000000083, a difference in the 17th decimal place. The tiny gap comes from floating-point rounding, because a computer keeps only a fixed number of digits for each decimal. Adding the same numbers in a different order can change the very last digit, and nothing more. Then pick a different Tile size, such as 2 keys or 16 keys, and the card jumps to the finished result. The final output is the same every time, because tiling changes only the order of the work. With 2 keys, step through again from 0 of 8. The first tile sets a starting max, and later tiles raise it twice, first to 2.4 and then to 3.1, with a rescale each time. Rotate by position On RoPE rotation, the starting settings put Query position at m = 20 and Key position at n = 7, so m − n reads 13. The Score row, which adds up the dot product over all four pairs after rotation, reads 2.0865. The card starts on pair 1, the same pair as the worked example, and the circle shows its two arrows before and after rotation. Dashed lines are the arrows before rotation, and solid lines are the arrows after, with a round dot for the query and a square for the key. Press Shift both +16, and both solid arrows swing round, because the query is now at 36 and the key at 23. Even so, Score still reads 2.0865, and Pair angle, the angle between the two rotated arrows, stays at 1.88 rad, where rad is short for radians. The m − n readout stays at 13 as well, since both positions moved by the same amount. That 1.88 is the 1.3 radians of rotation from the worked example, plus the 0.58 radians that the two arrows were already apart before any rotation. Shift both −16 moves both positions back again, and it stays greyed out until both positions are at least 16. Now move only Key position, and this time the score changes, because the distance between the two tokens changes. Set the two positions equal, and the score becomes 2.8200, which is the score the two vectors have with no rotation at all. With a distance of 0, the angle between each pair of arrows shifts by 0, so it is as if nothing was rotated. If you drag the key past the query, m − n goes negative, because the key now sits later in the text. The lab then adds a note that a causal model would mask that key. Next, step Dimension pair from 0 to 3 and read Wavelength 2π/θ, which is how many tokens one full turn of that pair takes. Here π is the number pi, about 3.14, so 2π is one full turn, about 6.28 radians. For pair 1, θ is 0.1, so one full turn takes 6.28 ÷ 0.1, or about 63 tokens. With the base at 10,000, the four pairs give these wavelengths: Pair 0 makes a full turn in about 6 tokens, so it changes a lot between neighbouring tokens. Pair 1 takes 63 tokens to make one full turn, so it changes more gently from one token to the next. Pair 2 takes 628 tokens, which is ten times longer again, so neighbours look almost alike to it. Pair 3 takes 6,283 tokens, so it barely moves between neighbours but keeps changing over long stretches. Last, set Dimension pair back to 1 and switch RoPE base from 10,000 to 500,000, so that pair 1 rotates more slowly. Its wavelength stretches from 63 tokens to 167 tokens, so it now needs more than twice the distance to make one full turn. The chart below the circle shows the distance between the two tokens along the bottom. Up the side it shows how much the selected pair adds to the score at that distance. Its side label for pair 1 reads dims 2,3 share of q·k. Here dims is short for dimensions, meaning places in the list of numbers counted from 0, and q·k means the query-key dot product. As the distance grows, the angle between the arrows keeps turning, so this part of the score rises and falls in waves. The chart always draws both bases for the selected pair, so you can compare them without switching. The dashed base 500,000 curve rises and falls more slowly than the solid base 10,000 curve. On pair 0 the two curves sit on top of each other, because the fastest pair rotates at the same speed whatever the base is.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: On KV cache budget The cache follows the number of KV heads, not the number of query heads. With 8 KV heads it is exactly 25.0% of the full multi-head cache at every length, which you can check by moving Sequence length while you watch vs MHA. Changing KV heads barely moves the curves on Quadratic cost, because every one of the 32 readers still checks every label. Fewer shelves mean fewer folders to store, but the scoring work stays exactly the same, and only the layer’s weight work shrinks a little. This is the difference between the scoring rule and the memory layout, showing up in numbers. On Quadratic cost Attention’s share climbs from a small slice to most of the layer’s arithmetic as the text grows. The number of pairs grows with the square of the length, while the weight calculations grow in a straight line. The window turns that curve back into a nearly straight line, though only once the text is longer than 4,096 tokens. The Score matrix if stored readout also grows with the square, until it reaches 1.00 TiB at 128K tokens. FlashAttention keeps grows only in a straight line, and it reaches 16 MiB at the same length. On FlashAttention tiles Each tile adds keys to the running sum, so the filled bars of the earlier keys shrink. They shrink most when a tile brings a new running max, because the new leader joins the total at a full 1. The rescale shows how much further behind the new leader every earlier key has fallen, which is the same extra amount for all of them. Before the last tile, the filled bars sit above their outlines, since the running sum has not seen every key yet. At the end they land exactly on the outlines, whatever tile size you choose. On RoPE rotation Shifting both positions together rotates both arrows but leaves Score and Pair angle unchanged, while moving one position alone changes them. That is the sign that only the distance m − n reaches the score, which is exactly what RoPE was designed to do. A bigger RoPE base slows the slower pairs, so their part of the score changes more gently as the distance grows.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: What this lab simplifies The first two cards count bytes and FLOPs with formulas for one text: the cache across all 32 layers, and the arithmetic for one layer. Nothing runs on a GPU and nothing is timed. Real speed also depends on how much data moves between memories, on how well the program is tuned, and on whether it skips pairs the causal mask blocks. Quadratic cost shows only prefill, the reading of the prompt, and leaves out decode. During decode, each new token is scored against the whole cache, and speed is mostly limited by reading memory. A real server handles many conversations at once, which multiplies the cache. Storing each cached number in fewer bits, such as 8 instead of 16, or in fixed-size blocks called pages, also changes the totals. You cannot take a model trained with 32 KV heads and switch it to 8, because GQA models are trained that way or converted and then trained further. FlashAttention tiles uses one query and 16 fixed teaching scores, and each value is a pair of numbers. The real method also handles many queries at once and is tuned to the size of the chip’s SRAM. RoPE rotation uses a toy head of 8 numbers and two fixed vectors, not numbers taken from a trained model. Real Llama heads have 128 numbers, which makes 64 pairs, each rotating at its own speed. Where the real tricks fail Sharing shelves has a price, because the readers in a group must all use the same stored keys and values. Those folders cannot fit every reader’s question at once, and that usually costs the model a little quality. MQA forces all 32 readers onto one shelf and carries the most risk, which is why many recent models keep 4 to 8 KV heads rather than 1. Picture four friends working on different parts of a history project who agree to keep one shared notebook instead of four. They save a lot of paper, but the notes have to serve all four topics at once. So each friend sometimes finds less detail on their own topic than a private notebook would have held. A window forgets, because a token further back than 4,096 tokens cannot be read directly at all. Its information reaches the present only by being relayed through the layers, and it gets weaker on the way. That is why several long-context models, such as Gemma 2 and Gemma 3, mix windowed layers with layers that see the full text. A common mix-up: FlashAttention is not a new or approximate kind of attention, and it does not shrink the KV cache. It reaches the same answer by working in a different order, and it still scores every pair, so its arithmetic still grows with the square of the length. Of the tricks in this lab, only fewer KV heads or a sliding window make the cache smaller. RoPE also has a limit, because it tells the model how far apart two tokens are without making every distance familiar. A model trained on texts of 8,000 tokens has never seen larger distances, so its attention gets worse beyond them. Stretching a trained model to longer texts by changing RoPE’s rotation speeds, usually with a little extra training, is called context extension. Without it, plain RoPE becomes less reliable past the length the model was trained on.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: FlashAttention on a real chip FlashAttention was published in 2022, and it was designed around the gap between HBM and SRAM. It loads blocks of queries, keys and values into SRAM and calculates their scores there. It then writes only the output and one summary number per row in each head back to HBM. During training it recalculates the scores from the queries and keys, and uses those summary numbers to turn them straight back into shares, instead of storing the whole grid. Later versions split the work better across the chip and support smaller number formats, and the result stays exact. RoPE’s rotation speeds The lab’s heading writes the rule for each pair’s speed as θᵢ = 10,000^(−2i/8), where i is the pair number and 8 is how many numbers the toy head holds. Here is the rule worked out in steps for pair 1, the pair the lab starts on: For pair 1, the power is −2 × 1 ÷ 8, which works out to −1/4. A power of 1/4 means the fourth root, and the fourth root of 10,000 is 10, because 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10,000. The minus sign means one over that number, so θ = 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1, which matches θ = 0.10 in the Dimension pair readout. A real Llama head holds 128 numbers instead of 8, so it has 64 pairs instead of the toy head’s 4. At base 10,000, its fastest pair makes a full turn every 6.3 tokens, much like pair 0 in the lab. The slowest pair takes about 54,000 tokens to make a single full turn. Llama 3 raised the base to 500,000, which stretches that slowest turn to about 2.6 million tokens. Stretching the context Context extension methods change these rotation speeds, and each of the three named in the lab does it differently: Position interpolation squeezes the positions, so a longer text fits inside the range of angles the model already saw in training. NTK-aware scaling raises the base, which makes the slow pairs rotate even more slowly, much like switching the lab’s RoPE base to 500,000. YaRN treats fast and slow pairs differently, and it also adjusts how sharp the softmax shares are. Other labs Inference & KV cache covers this cache while a model serves many people, including grouping requests together and storing the cache in pages. Why GPUs explains why moving bytes, rather than doing arithmetic, often sets how fast a model can write. The architecture zoo covers state-space models, which replace the growing cache with a summary of fixed size and give up exact lookup of old tokens in exchange.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: This module is about running attention at long context lengths. The scoring rule stays the one from the Attention lab; each technique here changes what is cached, which keys a query can see, how the work is scheduled, or how position enters the scores. As a context grows to 128K tokens, which costs grow, and what does each way of cutting them give up? It builds on The transformer block, whose layer is costed here, and on Inference & KV cache, which covered the KV cache: earlier tokens' keys and values, stored for reuse during decoding. Grouped-query attention (GQA) shrinks that cache by sharing key-value heads among query heads. Sliding-window attention caps the cache and each query's work, so attention's arithmetic grows linearly with the sequence length n rather than with n². FlashAttention cuts memory traffic without changing the output. Rotary position embedding (RoPE) encodes position as a rotation of queries and keys, so a score depends on the distance between positions. Where it shows up Many recent models use 4 to 8 KV heads rather than the single shared head of multi-query attention (MQA), since the quality cost grows as more query heads share each KV head. Several long-context models, such as Gemma 2 and 3, interleave sliding-window and full-attention layers. FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) is a GPU kernel that computes attention in tiles in fast on-chip SRAM instead of writing the score matrix to the GPU's large, slower high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Llama 3 uses RoPE with a base of 500,000. Position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN extend context by changing RoPE's frequencies. Why it matters The figures here are for one sequence and a model with Llama 3 8B's shape: 32 layers, 32 query heads of width 128, and 16-bit values. At 128K tokens, a cache with 8 KV heads needs 16 GiB, more than the model's own 16-bit weights, and multi-head attention (MHA), with all 32 KV heads, would need four times that. At that length, a stored score matrix would take 1.00 TiB per layer. With 8 KV heads, attention's arithmetic in one layer's prefill (one pass over the whole prompt) passes the weight matmuls at 53,247 tokens. Each technique has a limit. Shared heads usually cost a little quality, a window of W recent keys gives up direct access to older tokens, FlashAttention leaves the n² arithmetic and the cache in place, and RoPE alone does not extend a model past its training length. What you will be able to explain Separate the attention scoring rule from the memory layout used to compute it. Explain what grouped-query and sliding-window attention trade away for their savings. Explain why FlashAttention gives the exact same output, and which costs it leaves in place. Read rotary position embedding as a rotation whose query-key score depends only on the distance between positions. What the lab shows Nothing is trained or timed. Cache sizes and FLOP counts are closed-form arithmetic for that same sequence and model shape. KV cache budget sets KV heads (32 · MHA to 1 · MQA), Attention span (Full or Sliding window 4,096) and Sequence length (1K to 128K tokens). These also drive Quadratic cost, one layer's prefill FLOPs. FlashAttention tiles runs online softmax, a one-pass softmax that rescales earlier partial results when a larger score arrives, over one query row of 16 fixed scores. Set Tile size, step Tiles processed and compare Online vs full. RoPE rotation rotates fixed vectors in an 8-dimensional toy head; Shift both +16 moves query and key together while you watch Score. The key experiment: at 128K tokens, switch Attention span to Sliding window 4,096 and watch Cache and Attention share fall.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: The scoring rule is unchanged from the Attention lab: softmax(QKᵀ/√d + M) V. What changes at scale is how keys and values are stored, which keys each query may see, how the computation is scheduled on the hardware, and how position enters the scores. GQA and MQA cache fewer key-value heads than query heads. Sliding-window attention limits each query to the last W keys. FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles with an online softmax. RoPE rotates query and key pairs by position so scores depend on relative distance. Every count in the lab uses Llama 3 8B's shape: 32 layers, 32 query heads, head dimension 128, model width 4,096, a SwiGLU MLP of width 14,336, and a 16-bit cache.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Two costs grow with the context. The KV cache grows linearly, 2 × layers × kv_heads × d_head × bytes per token, and full attention's arithmetic grows with n². Decoding speed is mostly set by how many bytes must be read per token, so cache size is often the binding constraint. Inference & KV cache already separated prefill from decode (one token at a time, reading the stored keys and values) and sized this cache for Llama 3 8B.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Set KV heads to 32, 8 and 1. Per token the cache is 512 KiB, 128 KiB and 16 KiB; at 8,192 tokens that is 4.00 GiB, 1.00 GiB and 128 MiB. At 128K tokens, 8 KV heads need 16 GiB, more than the model's own 16-bit weights. Drag Sequence length to 128K and read Quadratic cost. Attention is 13.3 percent of one layer's prefill FLOPs at 8K tokens and 71.1 percent at 128K; it equals the weight matmuls at 53,247 tokens. Switch Attention span to Sliding window 4,096: the cache stops at 512 MiB and attention's share at 128K falls to 13.2 percent. In FlashAttention tiles, step Tiles processed through the row. In RoPE rotation, press Shift both +16 and compare the Score before and after.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: The cache scales with KV heads, not query heads. GQA with 8 KV heads is exactly a quarter of MHA at every length, while the attention FLOPs barely move, because every query head still scores every key. Online softmax keeps a running max m, sum ℓ and output o. A tile with a larger score rescales the old ℓ and o by exp(m_old − m_new), 0.4966 for tile 2 with 4-key tiles. The final output matches full softmax to 8.3e-17. A stored score matrix would be 4.00 GiB per layer at 8K tokens and 1.00 TiB at 128K. FlashAttention keeps one log-sum-exp per row: 1 MiB and 16 MiB. RoPE's score depends only on m − n: 2.0865 at positions (20, 7) and at (36, 23).
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: In this lab. Byte and FLOP counts are closed-form for one sequence and one layer; nothing is timed. The FlashAttention card processes a single query row of 16 fixed scores, and the RoPE card uses an 8-dimensional toy head with fixed vectors. Real kernels also tile queries, skip fully masked tiles, and recompute scores in the backward pass. In the real mechanisms. GQA forces each group of query heads to read the same stored keys and values, and MQA forces all of them to. Both usually cost a little quality, which is why many recent models use 4 to 8 KV heads rather than 1. A sliding window removes direct access beyond W tokens. Information from further back must be relayed through intermediate positions across layers, up to L × W tokens, and it degrades on the way. Several long-context models, such as Gemma 2 and 3, interleave windowed and full-attention layers for that reason. FlashAttention is exact but still quadratic in arithmetic. It removes the n² memory and most of the memory traffic, not the n² work, and it does nothing for the KV cache. RoPE encodes relative position but does not by itself extend a model past its training length. Plain RoPE degrades on unseen distances unless its frequencies are rescaled and the model is trained further.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) is IO-aware: a GPU's HBM is large but slow relative to on-chip SRAM, so the kernel loads blocks of Q, K and V into SRAM, computes their scores there, and writes only the output and per-row statistics back. Later versions improve parallelism and low-precision support; the result stays exact. RoPE (Su et al., 2021) sets θᵢ = base^(−2i/d). For a 128-dimensional head the fastest pair turns once every 6.3 tokens and the slowest once every 54,000 at base 10,000. Llama 3's base of 500,000 stretches the slowest wavelength to about 2.6 million tokens. Context-extension methods change these frequencies: position interpolation scales positions down, NTK-aware scaling raises the base, and YaRN treats fast and slow pairs differently and adjusts the softmax temperature. Inference & KV cache covered this cache during serving, including batching and paging. Why GPUs explains why bytes moved, not FLOPs, often set decoding speed. The architecture zoo covers state-space models, which replace the growing cache with a fixed-size state and give up exact retrieval of arbitrary old tokens.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: KV cache budget · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: How many keys and values you must keep The decode-time KV cache for a model with Llama 3 8B's shape: 32 layers, 32 query heads of width 128, 16-bit values. Sharing key-value heads across query heads (GQA, MQA) or keeping only a window of recent tokens shrinks it; the attention scores are computed the same way. KV heads: 32 is multi-head attention, 16 to 2 are grouped-query attention, 1 is multi-query attention. All six divide the 32 query heads evenly. Attention span: Full keeps every token's K and V; Sliding window 4,096 keeps only the most recent 4,096. A head diagram: 32 query-head squares linked to the KV-head blocks they share. Bars for all six KV-head settings at the current sequence length, with the selected one highlighted, and a formula row that multiplies the terms out. Metrics: bytes per token across all layers, total cache, and the cache as a percentage of MHA's. KV cache = 2 (K and V) × 32 layers × KV heads × 128 × 2 bytes × cached tokens. Cached tokens are the sequence length, or min(sequence length, 4,096) with the window. With 8 KV heads that is 128 KiB per token, the figure for Llama 3 8B. At 8,192 tokens: 4.00 GiB for MHA, 1.00 GiB for 8 KV heads, 128 MiB for MQA. `KV heads` picks the number of cached key-value heads. `Attention span` switches between Full and Sliding window 4,096. `Sequence length` steps through powers of two from 1K to 128K tokens. The cache is proportional to KV heads: 8 KV heads cost exactly a quarter of MHA at any length. At 128K tokens, 8 KV heads need 16 GiB, more than the model's own 16-bit weights (about 15 GiB). The window caps it at 512 MiB. With the window, a token reaches 4,096 back directly and up to 131,072 back only by relaying through 32 layers. In this lab: counts are closed-form for one sequence. Batching multiplies the cache by the batch size, and paged or quantized caches change the constant. In this lab: a model trained with 32 KV heads cannot simply be switched to fewer; GQA models are trained that way or converted and fine-tuned. In general: sharing KV heads forces the grouped query heads to read the same stored keys and values, a quality cost that grows as groups get larger. A window drops direct access to older tokens.
documents.title: How many keys and values you must keep

documents.subtitle: Quadratic cost · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: When the n² term takes over Prefill FLOPs for one layer of the same model as the prompt grows: the weight matmuls grow linearly with tokens, full causal attention grows with the square, and a 4,096-token window grows linearly again. Three curves in TFLOP against sequence length in thousands of tokens: weight matmuls (solid), attention with the full span (dashed), and attention with a 4,096 window (dotted). A vertical line marks the current length. Metrics: attention's share of the layer's FLOPs at the current length and span, the crossover length where attention equals the weight matmuls, the memory a stored score matrix would take, and what FlashAttention keeps instead. Weight matmuls: 2 FLOPs per weight per token, over the layer's 218,103,808 weights with 8 KV heads (Q and output projections, K and V projections, and a SwiGLU MLP of width 14,336). Attention: 4 × 32 heads × 128 FLOPs per causal query–key pair, half for q·k and half for mixing values. Full causal attention has n(n + 1)/2 pairs; a window caps each query at 4,096 keys. Score matrix if stored: 32 heads × n² × 2 bytes. FlashAttention keeps one 4-byte log-sum-exp per row per head: 32 × n × 4 bytes. This card has no controls of its own. `Sequence length`, `KV heads`, and `Attention span` on the KV cache budget card drive it. At 8K tokens attention is 13.3% of the layer's FLOPs; at 128K it is 71.1%. The crossover is 53,247 tokens with 8 KV heads. KV heads barely moves the curves: every query head still scores every key. Only the K and V projection weights shrink. A stored score matrix would be 4.00 GiB per layer at 8K tokens and 1.00 TiB at 128K. FlashAttention keeps 1 MiB and 16 MiB. In this lab: FLOPs are counted, not timed. Real speed also depends on memory traffic, kernel efficiency, and whether the kernel skips masked tiles. In this lab: only prefill is shown. During decoding each new token does 2 × weights FLOPs plus attention over the whole cache, and speed is limited by reading the weights and, at long context, the cache from memory. In general: sub-quadratic alternatives such as sliding windows, sparse patterns, linear attention, and state-space layers trade away some direct long-range access for lower cost.
documents.title: When the n² term takes over

documents.subtitle: FlashAttention tiles · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Exact softmax without the whole row One query's attention over 16 keys, processed in tiles the way FlashAttention does: keep a running max, a running sum, and a running output, and rescale them whenever a tile brings a larger score. After the last tile the output equals the ordinary softmax to rounding. A row of 16 keys with their scores q·k. Finished tiles are shaded, the tile currently in fast on-chip memory (SRAM) is outlined, and waiting tiles are grey. Weights below each key: a dashed outline for the full softmax weight and a filled bar for exp(s − m) ÷ ℓ using the statistics so far. A table with one row per processed tile: tile max, running max m, rescale factor, running sum ℓ, and the normalised output o ÷ ℓ. A final row comparing the online output with the full softmax output. For each tile: m_new = max(m, tile max); scale ℓ and o by exp(m − m_new); add exp(s − m_new) to ℓ and exp(s − m_new)·v to o. The output is o ÷ ℓ. Because every earlier term was rescaled to the same final max, it equals Σ softmax(s)ᵢ vᵢ exactly, apart from floating-point rounding (8.3e-17 here with 4-key tiles). Scores and values are fixed teaching numbers; values are 2-dimensional unit vectors. `Tile size` picks 2, 4, 8, or 16 keys per tile and shows the finished result. `Tiles processed` steps from none to all of them. When a tile raises the running max, the filled bars of earlier keys shrink: the rescale factor, 0.4966 for tile 2 with 4-key tiles, multiplies everything seen so far. Before the last tile the partial bars overshoot the outlines, because ℓ has not seen every key. They land on the outlines exactly at the end. Every tile size gives the same final output. Tiling changes the order of work, not the answer. In this lab: one query row and 16 keys. The real kernel tiles blocks of queries too, runs the backward pass by recomputing scores from the saved log-sum-exp, and is tuned to a GPU's SRAM size. In general: FlashAttention cuts memory traffic and the n² score matrix, which makes long contexts affordable, but it still does quadratic arithmetic and does not shrink the KV cache.
documents.title: Exact softmax without the whole row

documents.subtitle: RoPE rotation · Modern attention at scale
documents.body: Relative position from absolute rotations Rotary position embedding rotates each pair of query and key dimensions by position × θ for that pair. Rotating q by m and k by n makes their dot product depend only on m − n. The lab uses a toy 8-dimensional head so every pair is visible. A unit circle for the selected pair: dashed rays are the unrotated q and k, solid rays are q rotated by m·θ (round dot) and k rotated by n·θ (square). Controls for query position m, key position n, both shifted together, the dimension pair, and the RoPE base. A Score row with the full 8-dimensional dot product after rotation, and the same score after shifting both positions. A chart of the selected pair's share of q·k against distance, for base 10,000 and base 500,000. θᵢ = base^(−2i/8) for pair i. Each pair (x, y) becomes (x cos a − y sin a, x sin a + y cos a) with a = position × θᵢ. Rotations preserve length, and rot(q, m)·rot(k, n) = Σᵢ |qᵢ||kᵢ| cos(φᵢ + (m − n)θᵢ), so absolute positions cancel. Wavelength 2π/θ is how many tokens one full turn of that pair takes. q and k are fixed teaching vectors, not weights from a model. `Query position` and `Key position` run from 0 to 96. `Shift both −16` and `Shift both +16` move both positions together. `Dimension pair` selects dims 0,1 through 6,7; `RoPE base` switches between 10,000 and 500,000. Shift both +16 turns both rays but leaves the Score unchanged: 2.0865 at m = 20, n = 7 and at m = 36, n = 23. Pair 0 turns a full circle every 6.3 tokens; pair 3 takes 6,283 with base 10,000. Fast pairs resolve nearby order, slow pairs change over long distances. Raising the base to 500,000 stretches pair 1's wavelength from 63 to 167 tokens. In this lab: 8 dimensions and one q, k pair. Llama heads have 128 dimensions, 64 pairs, whose slowest wavelength is about 54,000 tokens at base 10,000 and 2.6 million at 500,000. In general: RoPE encodes relative distance but does not make a model generalise past the lengths it was trained on. Beyond that, attention degrades unless the frequencies are rescaled (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) and the model is usually trained further.
documents.title: Relative position from absolute rotations

documents.subtitle: Cut an image into patches, project each patch into a token vector, place those tokens beside words, count what the same cut costs at real resolutions, and see why a contrastive loss makes matched images and captions score highest.
documents.body: Cut an image into patches, project each patch into a token vector, place those tokens beside words, count what the same cut costs at real resolutions, and see why a contrastive loss makes matched images and captions score highest. Compute how many patch tokens an image becomes from its size and the patch size, including the optional CLS token Describe a patch embedding as a linear map from a patch's pixels to a vector, plus a position code Compare what CLIP, LLaVA-style and Flamingo-style designs hand on — one pooled vector, projected tokens inside the text sequence, or 64 resampled vectors read by cross-attention — and what each costs in context Explain how a contrastive loss over a batch of image–caption pairs rewards the labelled pairs and penalizes the other pairings, and how the temperature sharpens or flattens each softmax
