Vocabularies hold tens of thousands of subword tokens, contexts run to thousands of tokens, and even at temperature 0 output is not perfectly reproducible across hardware, because floating-point reduction order can flip near-ties. Two conceptual limits matter more. Nothing in the loop revisits an earlier token, so an unlucky draw becomes context and errors compound. And per-token probability is not a calibrated statement about truth; a model can be confident across an entirely fabricated sentence. The logit lens has its own limit. It applies a readout trained for the last layer to states that were never trained to be read that way, so an early stage's distribution can look like noise.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Next-token prediction
documents.body: Other decoding tools restrict or rescore the candidates: Min-p is a recent adaptive cut: Nguyen et al. (ICLR 2025) define it as p_scaled = p_base × p_max, keeping every token at least that likely. Beam search keeps several partial sequences and scores them jointly. It suits translation and short constrained outputs, and tends to flat, repetitive text when open-ended. Repetition penalties lower the logits of tokens already in the context before the draw. Penalties exist because greedy and low-temperature decoding loop. In the lab's greedy run the transformer gives its chosen character 83% on average over the first 22 characters and above 96% over the last 22, once the phrase repeats. The repeated text is the context that makes the repeat likely, so the loop feeds itself. A penalty breaks it, at a cost: it also discourages repetition that is correct, such as a name that has to recur. Hugging Face's repetition_penalty is one: 1.0 means off, and above 1.0 penalizes tokens already seen, the prompt included. Training differs from generation. During training the model is fed the true previous tokens, called teacher forcing, so it never practises recovering from its own mistakes. The surprisal bars on the tape are teacher-forced: one forward pass scores every character at once. Cross-entropy exponentiated gives perplexity, the effective number of equally likely choices per token: 2^2.23 ≈ 4.7 characters for the transformer on held-out text, and 2^3.04 ≈ 8.2 for the GRU. It measures distribution quality and predicts usefulness only weakly, which is why the post-training lab exists. The logit lens was introduced by nostalgebraist in 2020. Belrose et al. (2023) call their tuned lens a refinement of that technique, which they describe as often brittle. A check from outside the lab: switching off layer-2 heads 2 and 3 on the Jason prompt puts u back on top at 82%. That is evidence, not proof, that those heads supply the copied a. The Attention and Interpretability II: circuits labs open this same transformer, and Inference & KV cache shows how production systems avoid recomputing the whole prefix at every step of this loop.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Generation loop · Next-token prediction
documents.body: Predict, draw, append, repeat The autoregressive loop run by real character models. The selected model predicts the next character from the text so far, the sampler draws one with a seeded random number, the character is appended, and the longer text is fed back in for the next prediction. A Prompt box and a tape of every character so far. Spaces show as ␣ and newlines as ↵; sampled characters are boxed and bold. Two buttons under the prompt, Unseen line (default) and Line from the training text, and a Seen in training? line. The default prompt is not in Tiny Shakespeare; the other button loads a line that is. Under each character, a bar whose height is its surprisal under the selected model, −log2 p from 0 to 10 bits, measured teacher-forced on the text as it stands. Characters the model cannot see are faded (all but the last for the bigram, all but the last 64 for the transformer). A dashed slot at the end showing where the next draw would land with the current seed and settings. Buttons Sample next token, Sample 10 more, Undo, and Clear continuation; metrics for the last draw; and a log of the five most recent draws. One token is one character from a 66-symbol vocabulary: the 65 characters of Tiny Shakespeare plus <unk>. Characters outside it become <unk>. Each draw uses u = a deterministic hash of (Seed, draw number) in [0, 1) and picks the first kept character whose running sum of q passes u. The same prompt, seed and settings always reproduce the same text. Last draw records p, the model's probability at T = 1 with nothing cut, and q, the probability the sampler actually used. Surprisal is −log2 p; Mean over draws averages it and ppl = 2 to that power. Seen in training? is not a search. The corpus is not shipped with the app, so the lab recognises only its two preset lines (both checked against the corpus offline) and says Unknown for anything else you type. Prompt (up to 120 characters; editing it clears the continuation), the two preset buttons, Sample next token, Sample 10 more, Undo, Clear continuation. Comparison worth running: load each preset line and compare the transformer's Mean surprisal on this text. Then, with the RNN, set Top-k to 1 on the default prompt and sample 30 characters: it repeats itself, and the lab does not stop it. Low temperature produces text the model itself finds unsurprising; high temperature produces text it finds surprising. Neither is a measure of truth. A drawn character is never revisited. An unlikely draw stays in the tape and conditions everything after it. The text ends only at the 120-character cap or when you stop. The model never signals that it is finished. In this lab: character-level models trained on Tiny Shakespeare, about 1.1 million characters, so continuations are Shakespeare-flavoured spelling, not sense. The vocabulary has no end-of-sequence token, so nothing but the 120-character cap ends a continuation. In general: production models predict subword tokens from vocabularies of tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand entries, condition on thousands of tokens, and are trained on trillions of tokens. The loop is the same, but it ends when the model draws an end-of-sequence token, reaches a maximum length, or the output contains a stop sequence the caller chose.
documents.title: Predict, draw, append, repeat

documents.subtitle: Next token distribution · Next-token prediction
documents.body: The model's odds, before and after the sampler The selected model's real next-character distribution for the text on the tape, next to the distribution the sampler actually draws from after temperature, top-k, top-p and min-p. The strip below lays the kept characters end to end so you can see where the seeded number u lands. A status line that reports loading, running, or failure for the selected model, and which runtime ran it. The 10 most likely next characters. The outlined bar is p, the model's probability at T = 1; the filled bar is q, what the sampler uses. Cut characters read cut · top-k, cut · top-p or cut · min-p. A final row sums the other 56. An inverse-CDF strip of the kept characters with a marker at u; the highlighted segment is the next draw. Metrics Model entropy, Sampler entropy, Kept, and Kept mass. Bigram: logits are the logarithms of the row of bigram.json for the last character. RNN: character-rnn.onnx, a two-layer GRU, runs on the whole text. Transformer: the attention lab's tiny-transformer.onnx runs on the last 64 characters, its trained block size. Both ONNX models run in a background worker. p = softmax(z). q = softmax(z / T) restricted to the kept set and renormalised. Entropy = −Σ p log2 p in bits. Kept mass is the tempered probability of the kept set before renormalising. Bars are scaled so the longest shown value fills the track; the percentages are exact. This card has no controls of its own. Model, Temperature, Top-k, Top-p, Min-p and Seed live on Sampler controls. Comparison worth running: on the default prompt, Bigram puts U first (33%) because it only sees J, and 125 of the corpus's 320 capital Js are followed by U, the start of the speaker name JULIET. The RNN, which sees the whole line, puts o first (26%). The Transformer puts u first (99%). The order of the outlined p bars never changes with temperature, top-k, top-p or min-p. Only the filled q bars move. A confident step has low model entropy and top-p keeps few characters; an uncertain step, such as right after a space, keeps many. In this lab: the full 66-entry distribution is computed, and the top 10 are drawn. Models are tiny: the GRU trained for 240 steps and the transformer for 8,000. If the worker cannot run ONNX, the RNN and transformer report an error and the bigram still works. In general: probabilities are over tokens, not meanings, and a model's probability is not a calibrated statement that a continuation is true.
documents.title: The model's odds, before and after the sampler

documents.subtitle: Sampler controls · Next-token prediction
documents.body: Reshaping real logits before the draw The model produces logits; decoding decides how to draw from them. Temperature rescales the logits, top-k, top-p and min-p cut the tail, and the seed fixes the random numbers. None of these changes what the model computed or the order of its candidates. Model: Bigram, RNN, Transformer. Temperature 0.10 to 2.00, Top-k 1 to 66 (66 reads off, 1 reads greedy), Top-p 0.05 to 1.00 (1.00 reads off), Min-p 0.00 to 0.50 (0.00 reads off) and Seed 1 to 64. A formula row with the top candidate's logit z, z / T, and its final q. When Min-p is on, a second row shows its cut-off: p_min times the top character's probability, and how many characters clear it. Order of operations in this lab: divide logits by T; keep the k highest; of those, keep the smallest most-likely prefix whose renormalised mass reaches p; drop any survivor whose probability is below p_min times the top probability; renormalise; draw by inverse CDF. Min-p keeps a character when its tempered probability is at least p_min × p_max (Nguyen et al., ICLR 2025, section 3.1). The test is a ratio to the top character, so renormalising does not change it, and the top character always passes. Temperature divides every logit, so it scales the gaps between them: below 1 the distribution sharpens, above 1 it flattens toward uniform. Rescaling cannot reorder. Seed feeds the hash that makes u for each draw number; changing it changes future draws, not past ones. Model, Temperature, Top-k, Top-p, Min-p, Seed. Comparison worth running: Min-p 0.10 with the RNN keeps about seven characters at Temperature 1.00 and about nineteen at 2.00, because a flatter distribution leaves more characters above a tenth of the top one. With the Transformer on the default prompt it keeps one at every temperature. Temperature 0.10 against 2.00 with nothing cut. Then set Top-k to 1: every draw is the top character, the pick a very low temperature makes almost every time. Top-p and min-p both adapt to confidence. At Top-p 0.50 the RNN keeps one or two characters in the middle of a word and about six right after a space. Lower temperature is lower variance, not higher accuracy. If the top candidate is wrong, it becomes reliably wrong. In this lab: there is no repetition penalty, stop sequence or beam search; those are described in the lesson only. Min-p is applied last, after top-k and top-p. In general: temperature 0 is not perfectly reproducible on real hardware, because floating-point reduction order can flip near-ties. Truncation settings also interact with temperature, as the Min-p comparison above shows.
documents.title: Reshaping real logits before the draw

documents.subtitle: Three models, one context · Next-token prediction
documents.body: What each wiring sees, and how well it was trained All three models read the same 66-symbol vocabulary and come from the same Tiny Shakespeare text. The bigram sees one character, the GRU sees everything through a fixed-size state, and the transformer attends directly to the last 64. The columns compare their next-character guesses and their measured loss, and the training behind each number. One column per model, the selected one outlined: what it sees, its top three next characters, the entropy of its next-character distribution, and its mean surprisal on the tape's text. Held-out loss and Whole-corpus loss, in bits per character, from language-models.metadata.json: consecutive non-overlapping 64-character windows over the last 10% of the corpus and over all of it. The note under each says what that model trained on. Size and training: 66 × 66 table entries, the parameter counts from the metadata file, and the number of training steps. Mean surprisal on this text = the average of −log2 p(character | preceding characters) over every character the model can score, computed from one forward pass (teacher forcing). Held-out loss is the same average over the last 10% of the corpus. The transformer trained only on the first 90%. The GRU trained on random windows of the whole corpus for a third of an epoch, so its tail figure is nearly, not strictly, held out. The bigram figure comes from a table fitted on the first 90%; the table in this lab was fitted on all of it, so its whole-corpus figure is the one that describes it. Nats convert to bits by multiplying by log2 e ≈ 1.443. This card has no controls. Edit Prompt or generate text to change the context; Model on Sampler controls chooses the outlined column. Comparison worth running: load Line from the training text and back to the default, and compare each model's Mean surprisal. Then read the Held-out and Whole-corpus rows for the transformer. On held-out text the transformer scores lowest, the GRU next and the bigram highest. On the whole corpus the order is the same. The transformer's whole-corpus figure is lower than its held-out figure because 90% of the corpus is text it trained on. The GRU and bigram figures barely differ between the two. In this lab: the transformer trained for 8,000 steps and the GRU for 240, so the ordering is not a comparison of architectures. The lab cannot say how much of the gap is wiring and how much is training. The transformer's training also replaced about 30% of each batch with synthetic repeated strings, for the attention and circuits labs. In general: at scale, transformers beat recurrent nets and n-gram tables by a wide margin, largely because attention trains in parallel over long contexts. Comparing architectures fairly needs matched training budgets and text none of the models trained on.
documents.title: What each wiring sees, and how well it was trained

documents.subtitle: Layer by layer · Next-token prediction
documents.body: The whole model, read one stage at a time The path from characters to one sampled character: ids, embeddings plus position, two transformer layers, a final norm and unembedding, softmax, a draw. The logit lens applies the model's own last two steps to the stream after the embeddings, after layer 1 and after layer 2, so you can see what each stage would predict. A numbered strip of the seven steps with their sizes. Three carry a lens reads here tag: after the embeddings, after layer 1 and after layer 2. Three panels, one per tap. Each lists the five most likely next characters with their probabilities as text and as bars (all panels share one scale, so a full bar is 100%), the entropy of that readout in bits, and the rank and probability it gives the character the finished model ranks first. A sentence and four metrics: the finished model's first choice, the first stage at which it heads the list, the entropy at each stage, and how many characters the model read. The page runs the transformer in plain TypeScript on the weights read out of tiny-transformer.onnx, on the last 64 characters of the tape. The residual stream at the last position is taken after the embeddings (token embedding plus position embedding) and after each layer. Each tap goes through the same readout as the model's own output: final LayerNorm, then multiplication by the 256 × 66 unembedding matrix, which has no bias. Softmax turns the 66 logits into probabilities and entropy = −Σ p log2 p. The last tap equals the model's output logits to rounding error, so the third panel is the answer the Transformer column of Three models, one context would give. This card has no controls of its own. Edit Prompt, press Sample next token, or use the preset buttons; the lens reads the last character of whatever is on the tape. Comparison worth running: on the default prompt, note where u ranks in each panel. Then change both Juliets to Jason and see which character layer 2 puts on top. On the default prompt the entropy is about 4.9, 4.5 and 0.1 bits: nearly all of the drop is in layer 2, and the answer first heads the list there. The pattern is not always so sharp. For the prompt “To be, or not to be, that is the question” the readout after layer 1 is less certain than after the embeddings. The after-embeddings panel depends on the last character and its position alone, so it cannot depend on the earlier words. Anything the finished model does with those words happens in the layers. In this lab: only three taps, not each attention head or MLP step, and only the last position. The weights are the shipped 2-layer, 256-wide model. The finished model's choice is one character from one prompt, so a pattern across stages here does not show how the model works in general. In general: the logit lens applies a readout that was trained for the last layer to earlier states, which were never trained to be read that way, and it shows what is linearly readable, not what caused it. Its author (nostalgebraist, 2020) found early layers can look like nonsense, and Belrose et al. (2023) call their tuned lens a refinement of it because the plain lens is often brittle. Real models have dozens of layers.

documents.body: Read the base bars in Post-training pipeline: the pretrained model favors A, another exam question. Raise SFT steps from 0 to 8 and watch mass move to the demonstrations B and F.
documents.title: Fine-tune on demonstrations

documents.subtitle: Step 2 · Post-training
documents.body: In Preference pairs, click the response you prefer in each pair, then read the three weights and Agrees with gold in Reward model fit.
documents.title: Label preferences

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Post-training
documents.body: Move KL coefficient β from 20 down to 0.02 and watch Reward-model score climb while Gold score rises, peaks, and falls.
documents.title: Optimize with a KL leash

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · Post-training
documents.body: Label Pair 5 for B, the short answer that names the mechanism, then sweep KL coefficient β again and compare the Words ÷ 10 weight and the gold curve.
documents.title: Break the length shortcut

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: Supervised fine-tuning: ordinary next-token cross-entropy on curated prompt-and-response demonstrations, usually counted only on the response tokens. The loss is the pretraining loss; the data is what changed.
documents.title: SFT

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: A learned function that maps a prompt and response to one scalar, trained on human comparisons and also called a preference model. Because it is an approximation fitted to limited comparisons, optimizing it hard rewards its mistakes along with the intended behavior.
documents.title: Reward model

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: fit a reward model to human comparisons, then optimize the language model to score well on it while a KL penalty keeps it near the fine-tuned starting point.
documents.title: RLHF

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: Direct preference optimization: it uses the closed-form optimum of the KL-regularized objective to turn the reward-model loss into a loss on the policy itself, so it trains on preference pairs with no separate reward model and no sampling loop.
documents.title: DPO

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: The expected log-ratio between two distributions: the sum over outcomes of P times the natural log of P over Q, weighted by P. It is never negative, zero only when the two are identical, and not symmetric, so KL of P from Q differs from KL of Q from P. In nats when natural logs are used.
documents.title: KL divergence

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: A term, weighted by beta, that charges the policy for moving away from a reference model, usually the SFT model. It limits drift and slows reward hacking; it does not prevent it.
documents.title: KL penalty

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: The pairwise model behind most reward-model training: the probability that A beats B is the sigmoid of r(A) minus r(B). Only reward differences matter, so adding a constant to every reward changes nothing.
documents.title: Bradley-Terry

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: Raising a learned or written reward without raising the quality it was meant to measure, an instance of Goodhart's law. Against a held-out gold scorer the proxy keeps rising while the gold score peaks and falls; a verifiable reward from a real checker, such as unit tests, removes the learned scorer as a target but exists only for checkable tasks.
documents.title: Reward hacking

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: A method in which a model critiques and revises its own outputs against written principles to make fine-tuning data, then judges pairs of outputs against those principles to make preference data. Human effort shifts from labeling to writing the principles.
documents.title: Constitutional AI

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: Getting a model's behavior to match what its developers and users intend, when intent can only be reached through proxies such as demonstrations, comparisons, and scores. Outer alignment asks whether the specified objective is the right one; inner alignment asks whether the trained model actually pursues it. Alignment training can also cost some benchmark performance, an alignment tax.
documents.title: Alignment

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: A trained policy that pursues a different goal from the intended one while still matching the training reward on every training situation, so the difference only shows in new situations. It is documented in small reinforcement-learning environments; how far it explains the behavior of large language models is an open question.
documents.title: Goal misgeneralization

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: Methods for supervising outputs that people cannot easily check, such as long programs or subtle arguments, for example with model-written critiques for raters, debate between models, or feedback against written principles. It is active research: some methods help in controlled studies, and none is established as enough for a model more capable than its overseers.
documents.title: Scalable oversight

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: Agreeing with the user against the evidence, including abandoning a correct answer after mild pushback. It is a measured behavior of preference-trained models: studies found that people and reward models sometimes rate agreeable answers above correct ones, so optimizing against them can raise it.
documents.title: Sycophancy

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Post-training
documents.body: A test, run before release, of whether a model can do something seriously harmful if misused or if it acted on its own, such as giving real uplift toward weapons or carrying out cyber operations. Developers' safety frameworks tie the results to safeguards; failing a test under one attempt shows the model did not do it then, not that it cannot.
documents.title: Dangerous-capability evaluation

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Post-training · question 1
documents.body: You raise SFT steps from 0 to 8 and change nothing else. What moves? Probability shifts toward the demonstrations B and F, away from the base model's favorite, A The reward model's three weights shift toward whatever the demonstrations prefer The gold score of each response rises, because SFT re-grades the responses against the demonstrations KL coefficient β falls, because SFT sets how far the policy may drift from the base model SFT is ordinary next-token cross-entropy on the demonstrations, so each step moves probability toward B and F and away from A. It never looks at a reward: the reward model is fitted separately from your comparisons, gold is an authored grade, and β is a setting for the later optimization stage. SFT changes the starting point, π_SFT, that the KL leash later holds the policy near.
documents.title: You raise SFT steps from 0 to 8 and change nothing else. What moves?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Post-training · question 2
documents.body: You label Pair 5 for B, the short answer that names the mechanism, and leave the other labels alone. What happens to the Words ÷ 10 weight, and why? It rises, because one more label is more evidence that longer answers are better in general It falls, because a longer response now loses a comparison and length stops explaining every win It stays the same, because the reward model reads only whether an answer names the mechanism at all It turns negative, because the reward model now treats length as something that it should avoid Bradley–Terry fits whatever feature differences separate winners from losers. In the default labels every winner is also the longer response, so length explains every pair. Pair 5 puts a longer, empty answer against a shorter, correct one, so length stops being a reliable reason to win and its weight falls, though it stays positive because other pairs still reward it.
documents.title: You label Pair 5 for B, the short answer that names the mechanism, and leave the other labels alone. What happens to the Words ÷ 10 weight, and why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Post-training · question 3
documents.body: Every pair you labeled put the longer response on top, and the reward model gives words a large positive weight. You lower KL coefficient β until KL from the SFT model is large. What happens to the gold score? It keeps rising, because the reward model was fit to your own preferences and so tracks them It falls from the start, because any move away from the SFT model must lower the quality of answers It stays where it was, because β only changes the reference model and leaves the policy alone It rises at first as junk answers lose mass, then falls once the policy piles onto the long, empty answer Lowering β lets exp(r/β) dominate the reference probabilities. Early on that removes mass from A and D, which both scorers dislike, so gold rises. Past the peak the policy piles onto E, the long response with no mechanism, because length was the feature your labels could not separate from quality. The proxy keeps rising; the gold score falls.
documents.title: Every pair you labeled put the longer response on top, and the reward model gives words a large positive weight. You lower KL coefficient β until KL from the SFT model is large. What happens to the gold score?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Post-training · question 4
documents.body: In this lab the tuned policy is the exact optimum of the reward model. Which alignment problem therefore cannot appear in it? A reward model that overrates length, so the proxy keeps rising while the gold score falls A policy that drifts far away from the SFT model when the KL coefficient is small A policy that learned a goal of its own, matching the training reward on training prompts only A reward model that fits your labels but disagrees with the careful rater's grades on other pairs Everything the lab shows is a failure of the objective: the policy does exactly what the proxy says and the proxy is wrong. A policy that internalized a different goal, called goal misgeneralization, needs a learned policy whose behavior can agree with the reward on training inputs and part from it on new ones. The lab's policy is defined by the reward, so it has no goal of its own that could diverge.
documents.title: In this lab the tuned policy is the exact optimum of the reward model. Which alignment problem therefore cannot appear in it?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Post-training · question 5
documents.body: Why can preference training encourage sycophancy, as the lesson describes it? SFT demonstrations are full of users who are wrong, so the model learns to confirm whatever they say A KL penalty pays the policy for repeating whatever the user has just said to it in the prompt Reward models cannot read the user's message, so they score every possible reply as equally good People and reward models sometimes rate agreement above correctness, so optimizing the reward favors agreement It is the length shortcut again with a different feature. If raters or a reward model score agreement slightly higher than correctness, optimizing against that score moves the model toward agreeing, and the proxy rises while quality falls. Studies measured this behavior in preference-trained assistants. The KL penalty only limits drift, and a reward model does read the prompt.
documents.title: Why can preference training encourage sycophancy, as the lesson describes it?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Post-training · question 6
documents.body: A developer's dangerous-capability evaluation finds that a model fails a test of a harmful skill. What does the result establish? That the model cannot do it, because a model that could would always succeed on the test That the model did not do it on this attempt, and a stronger attempt might still draw it out That the skill is safe to ship, because such evaluations are run only on models known to be risky That the model is deceptive, because failing a test on purpose shows an intent to hide a skill A failed test is evidence about one attempt, not a proof of absence. Weak prompting, missing tools, or a model that underperforms on purpose can all produce a failure, so evaluators also try fine-tuning and scaffolding to draw the skill out. Safety frameworks use these results to decide which safeguards a developer commits to, but they are commitments, not guarantees.
documents.title: A developer's dangerous-capability evaluation finds that a model fails a test of a harmful skill. What does the result establish?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Post-training
documents.body: Type "Explain why the sky is blue." into a chatbot, and you expect a short answer about sunlight and air. A model that has only had its first round of training might reply with more questions instead, such as "Why is the sunset red?" and "Why is grass green?" That model is not broken. Its first round of training, called pretraining, taught it to continue text by guessing what comes next. Your line looks like a question from a homework sheet. On the web, a question like that is usually followed by more questions from the same sheet, so more questions are a good guess. A freshly pretrained model is great at continuing text but poor at helping you. Post-training is the name for the stages that come next, and their job is to turn that text continuer into an assistant that answers you. Where you have met it Every modern AI chatbot built on a large language model goes through post-training. Much of what feels like a chatbot's personality was set in these stages, not in pretraining. That includes how helpful it is, how much it hedges, what it refuses to do, and whether it admits when it does not know something. It is also why two chatbots built on the same pretrained model can feel completely different to talk to. Why it matters Without post-training, a model would keep adding to your text instead of answering it, so there would be no assistant to talk to. Post-training is also where one of the biggest problems in AI is clearest to see. To train a model toward good answers, you need a number that a computer can push up, and that number always stands in for what people really want. If you push hard on a stand-in, the model gets better at the number rather than at the thing you meant. In this lab, you will watch that happen with a set of starting clicks, and then fix it with one click of your own. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these ideas in your own words: how the four stages differ: pretraining, copying good answers, training a scorer on people's picks, and tuning the model toward that scorer on a leash; how a scorer learns from your picks between pairs of answers, using a rule called Bradley-Terry, and how to check what it really learned; how to spot reward hacking, where a stand-in score keeps going up while the real quality of the answers goes down; what alignment means, which is the gap between what people can measure and what they really want, and which problems this training does not fix. What the lab lets you do The lab shrinks the whole process down to one prompt, the sky question, and six possible answers labeled A to F. With only six answers, you can see how likely the model is to give each one, and watch every number change as you work. You will train the model on two good example answers, judge six pairs of answers yourself, and watch a scorer learn from your clicks. The leash is a limit on how far the model may move away from where copying left it. At the end, you will loosen that leash and watch the model chase the scorer. Next to all of this sits a separate grade called the gold score. The lesson's authors wrote it to stand for what a careful human rater would give, and it plays no part in training. It is there so you can tell whether the answers are really getting better or only scoring higher. With the picks the lab starts with, the answers really do get a little better at first. Then, as the leash loosens, they only score higher, because the model ends up favoring a long, flattering answer that never explains anything. Working out why, and then fixing it with one click, is the heart of this module. Some parts of the lab are real and some are made up. The six answers, the model's starting chances and the gold scores were written by the lesson's authors. So were the yes-or-no flags that say whether an answer explains why the sky is blue. Each answer's word count, and whether it opens with praise, are measured from its text instead. The copying stage and the scorer really learn, step by step. The final tuned model is worked out with an exact formula instead of being trained, so you see each result the moment you move a slider.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Post-training
documents.body: The model in this lab A real language model writes an answer one small piece at a time, choosing each piece from a long list of options. That is far too much to watch, so this lab shrinks the model to one prompt, "Explain why the sky is blue.", and six whole answers it could give. The model is nothing more than six chances, one for each answer, saying how likely it is to give that answer, and the six always add up to 100%. Each whole answer counts as one choice, which is the setup that Reinforcement learning foundations calls a bandit, after slot machines: you pick one option and get one score back. In that kind of learning, whatever makes the choices is called the policy. That is why the last stage in the strip across the top of the lab is labeled Policy + KL, where KL is the leash you will meet in Stage 3. Here are the six answers, with the short tags the lab gives them: A (tagged "another exam question") lists three more exam questions, starting with "Why is the sunset red?", so it never answers the prompt at all. B (tagged "short, names scattering") explains in 25 words that air scatters blue light far more than it scatters red light. C (tagged "praise, then scattering") opens with "Great question!" and then gives the same explanation in more detail, using 52 words. D (tagged "short, wrong") claims in 9 words that the sky reflects the blue of the oceans, which is not the reason. E (tagged "praise, long, no mechanism") opens with "Great question!" and spends 59 words on how fascinating the sky is without ever saying why it is blue. F (tagged "medium, names scattering") explains the scattering in 39 words and also says why sunsets look red. The real reason the sky is blue is that the gas molecules in air scatter blue light much more strongly than red light. Blue light travels in shorter waves, and shorter waves get scattered far more. An answer that explains this "names the mechanism", which means it gives the how-it-works reason rather than only describing the result. B, C and F name it, while A, D and E do not. Each answer also carries a gold score from 0 to 1, written by the lesson's authors to stand for the grade a careful human rater would give. F gets 1 and B gets 0.95, while E, the long empty answer, gets only 0.1. Gold is never used to train anything, because its only job is to grade how well the training turned out. The one exception is a button you will meet later, Label like the gold rater. It copies gold's rankings into your picks, to show what perfectly careful picks would teach the scorer. A picture to keep in mind Picture a trainee cook who is learning to run a kitchen and starts by copying a mentor's plates, dish by dish. Next, tasters try pairs of dishes and pick the better dish in each pair, and a judge studies all those picks until it can score any dish on its own. Finally the cook adjusts their cooking toward whatever the judge scores highly. Meanwhile the head chef keeps them on a short leash, so they cannot stray too far from how they cooked right after copying the mentor. Behind all of it sits the diner, whose real appetite is what the kitchen is meant to serve, even though nobody in it can measure that appetite directly. Each of those steps matches one stage of post-training, and the picture also shows where things can go wrong. If the bigger dish happened to win every tasting, the judge learns to score big portions highly, whether or not the food is any better. Keep that in mind, because the lab's scorer is about to learn the same taste for big portions from the picks it is given. Stage 1: copy good answers The first stage is the cook copying the mentor. The model trains on examples of a prompt followed by a good answer, and each round of training nudges its chances toward those answers and away from everything else. The examples are called demonstrations, and the stage is called supervised fine-tuning, or SFT. It uses the same kind of training as pretraining, which makes the right next piece of text more likely. What has changed is the text itself, which is now a set of hand-picked answers instead of ordinary pages from the web. In the lab, B and F are the demonstrations, and their cards are marked SFT demo. Before any SFT, the pretrained model gives about 50% of its chance to A, the exam question, while B gets about 8%. Move SFT steps from 0 to 8 and A's share falls to about 9%. Meanwhile B climbs to 38% and F to 36%, so the two demonstrations now hold nearly three quarters of the chance between them. Notice what SFT never does: it never looks at a score. It only knows which answers were demonstrated, so it can make the model more like its examples, but it cannot say what makes one answer better than another. Even so, SFT does most of the visible work of turning a continuer into an assistant. Stage 2: let people compare Writing a perfect answer by hand is slow, while picking the better of two answers is fast and gives more consistent results. So the second stage collects many picks and uses them to train a separate program, a scorer that gives any answer a single number. The scorer is called the reward model, and the number it gives an answer is that answer's reward, shown as r on each answer card. In the cook picture the people making picks are the tasters and the reward model is the judge. In the lab you are the taster, and you supply the picks on the Preference pairs card. That card shows six pairs of answers, and each click records which answer in a pair you prefer. Each recorded pick is called a label. So that you have something to start from, the lab comes with five of the six pairs already labeled, and these are the starting labels. What the scorer can see A real reward model reads every word of an answer, while the lab's much cruder scorer sees each answer as only three numbers, called its features: Words ÷ 10 is the answer's word count divided by 10, so E's 59 words become 5.9. Names mechanism is 1 if the answer explains the scattering and 0 if it does not. Opens with praise is 1 if the answer starts with "Great question!" and 0 if it does not. The scorer gives each feature a weight, multiplies each feature by its weight, and adds up the three results to get the reward. The Reward model fit card shows the three weights as bars, and a weight above zero means that feature raises the reward. With the starting labels, the weight for Words ÷ 10 comes out at +1.255, the largest of the three by far. The Names mechanism weight comes out at about +0.47, and the Opens with praise weight at about +0.14. Here is the arithmetic for E, the long answer that never explains anything: Its 59 words become 5.9, and 5.9 times the words weight of 1.255 is about 7.4. E does not name the mechanism, so the weight for that feature adds nothing. E does open with praise, so the praise weight of 0.142 adds a little more. The total is about 7.5, which matches the r of 7.54 on E's card once you allow for rounding. Now run the same steps for F, the answer with a perfect gold score: Its 39 words become 3.9, and 3.9 times 1.255 is about 4.9. F names the mechanism, so the mechanism weight adds about 0.47. F does not open with praise, so the praise weight adds nothing. The total is about 5.4, which matches the r of 5.36 on F's card. So the scorer rates E, which explains nothing, well above F, which a careful rater gives full marks, and nearly all of the difference comes from word count. Turning picks into chances: Bradley-Terry The scorer still needs a rule that links its numbers to your picks. The usual rule is called Bradley-Terry: the chance that one answer beats another depends only on the gap between their two rewards. If the rewards are equal, each answer has a 50% chance of being preferred, and as the gap grows the chance climbs toward 100% without ever quite reaching it. The lab writes this rule as P(A ≻ B) = σ(r_A − r_B), where A and B stand for any two answers, not only answers A and B. In that line, P means "the chance that", the symbol ≻ means "is preferred to", and r_A and r_B are the two rewards. The symbol σ, the Greek letter sigma, stands for a curve that turns any gap into a chance between 0 and 1. A gap of 1 gives about 73%, and a gap of 3 gives about 95%. Pair 1 shows the rule at work: B has a reward of 3.61, while D has only 1.13. That makes the gap between them about 2.5, and the σ curve turns that gap into 0.92. That is the P(B ≻ D) = 0.92 printed under Pair 1, which means the scorer predicts about a 92% chance that you would pick B over D. Because only the gap matters, adding the same number to every reward changes nothing: if every reward went up by 10, every gap and every chance would stay the same. How the scorer learns The scorer starts with all three weights at zero, so every pair looks like a coin flip. It then adjusts the weights 200 times, and each adjustment makes the picks you actually made a little more likely under the Bradley-Terry rule. The line chart on Reward model fit tracks a number called the training loss, which measures how badly the scorer's chances fit your picks, so lower is better. It starts at 0.693, which is the value this measure always gives when every pair is a 50-50 guess. The exact number comes from a piece of math called a logarithm, which you do not need here. The loss then falls as the scorer learns to put your winners on top. Stage 3: tune toward the scorer, on a leash The last stage is the cook adjusting toward the judge. The model is tuned so that answers with higher rewards get more of its chance, while a leash stops it from wandering too far from where SFT left it. Measuring how far the model moved To build a leash, you first need a way to measure the distance between two sets of chances. KL divergence is a number for how far one set of chances has moved from another. For each answer, it looks at how many times bigger or smaller the new chance is than the old one. Then it averages those comparisons, giving more weight to the answers that the new model picks more often. KL divergence has three properties worth knowing: it is never negative, it is zero only when the two sets of chances are identical, and it is not symmetric. Not symmetric means that measuring from the new chances back to the old ones gives a different number from measuring the other way. That is why the lab always names the direction, measuring the tuned model against the SFT model. The lab reports this distance as KL from SFT, in units called nats. A nat is the unit KL comes in, the way a meter is a unit of length. Its name comes from a piece of math called the natural logarithm, which you do not need here. What matters is that 0 nats means the tuned model matches the SFT model exactly, and bigger numbers mean it has moved further away. Here is a feel for the size of these numbers. After SFT, the model gives E about 11% of its chance. If tuning pushes E to nearly 100%, E's chance has grown about 9 times, the new chances look nothing like the old ones, and KL reaches about 2.2 nats. That is the biggest reading you can reach with the starting labels. At the other end, if tuning leaves every chance where SFT put it, KL is 0. In between, at a β of 3.5, the chances shift a fair amount but nothing piles up on one answer, and KL is about 0.2 nats. For example, A's chance there is cut in half, from about 24% to about 12%. The leash itself The leash is a KL penalty, which charges the tuned model for every nat of distance from the SFT model. A setting called β, the Greek letter beta, sets the price per nat. The lab's slider for it is called KL coefficient β, where a coefficient is a number that multiplies something else. A large β makes distance expensive, so the model stays close to SFT, while a small β makes distance cheap, so the model can chase the scorer much further. Put together, the tuning tries to make the average reward as high as possible after subtracting β times the distance. The lab prints this target at the top of its last card as maximize E[r] − β·KL(π‖π_SFT). In that line, E[r] means the average reward, where E stands for "expected" rather than for answer E. It is the reward the model would earn on average if it answered the sky question many times, picking each answer as often as its chances say. The letter π stands for the tuned model's chances rather than the number 3.14, π_SFT stands for the chances after SFT, and KL(π‖π_SFT) is the distance between them. The double bar ‖ only separates the two sets of chances being compared. The recipe the lab uses This target has an exact solution, so the lab can calculate the tuned model directly instead of training it. It takes each answer's chance after SFT and multiplies it by a boost that grows very fast as the reward goes up. Then it rescales all six results so that they add up to 100% again. For answer E, the formula card writes this as π(E) ∝ π_SFT(E) · exp(r / β). The card always works through whichever answer the tuned model currently favors, so if you change β and a different answer takes the lead, the letter in the card changes too. In that line, ∝ means "is in proportion to", and exp(x) means a special number called e, about 2.72, raised to the power x. When x is a whole number such as 2, that means e times e. When x is not a whole number, a calculator handles it, and all you need to know is that a bigger x gives a much bigger result. At the default settings, where β is 2.0 and E is the model's favorite, the card works through E like this: E's chance after SFT is 0.108, or about 11%, and its reward is 7.54. Dividing the reward by β gives 3.77, and exp(3.77) is about 43, so E's chance gets multiplied by about 43. That makes E's boosted value about 0.108 × 43, which comes to about 4.7. F starts with a bigger chance, about 0.20, but its lower reward earns a boost of only about 15, which gives F about 3. Once all six answers are boosted, their values add up to about 11.9, and E's share of that total is 4.7 ÷ 11.9, or about 39%. That 39% is the result shown on the formula card. E, an answer that explains nothing, is now the model's favorite, because the scorer's taste for length has been turned into chance. Making β smaller makes every boost bigger, and halving β squares each boost. At β 1, E's boost jumps from about 43 to about 1,900. F's boost grows too, but E's lead widens from about 3 times F's boost to about 9 times. That is why sliding β down hands more and more of the chance to whichever answer the scorer likes best. Where RLHF fits Stages 2 and 3 together are called RLHF, short for reinforcement learning from human feedback. Reinforcement learning means learning from a score that arrives after acting, like a game that awards points after each move instead of telling you the right move in advance. In RLHF, people's comparisons train the scorer, and the scorer's rewards then steer the model. What AI actually is introduced this reward-after-acting kind of learning, and Reinforcement learning foundations runs the basic version on a small bandit. A real model cannot list every possible answer the way this lab lists six, so real RLHF cannot use the exact recipe above. Instead, it has the model write answers, scores them with the reward model, and adjusts the model a little at a time. Step by step, that moves the model toward the same target by trial and error. Where the cook picture stops The analogy stops at intent, because a cook knows they are trying to please a judge, while the model has no idea it is pleasing anyone. Its chances shift toward higher numbers only because the math moves them there. The judge is different too, since in real systems it is a program built from many people's picks. As the lab shows, that program can end up rewarding things that nobody meant to reward.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Post-training
documents.body: Copying is not enough SFT can only copy, so it shows the model what a good answer looks like but cannot rank two decent answers against each other. Writing perfect example answers by hand for every kind of question would also take an enormous amount of work. Comparisons fill that gap, because judging is much faster than writing. A scorer trained on comparisons can then rate answers that nobody has ever judged, which lets training reach far beyond the examples people wrote. Why the leash is needed The reward model is fitted to a limited set of picks, so it is only an approximation, and it has mistakes. Pushing hard on it rewards those mistakes along with the things it gets right. Without a leash, the tuned model would pile all of its chance onto whichever answer the scorer rates highest, however that answer earned its score. The leash keeps the model near the SFT model. SFT never saw a score, so it has no special liking for the answers the scorer wrongly loves. It gives E, the long empty answer, only about 11% of its chance. So the model can move away from the junk answers that the scorer rightly dislikes, without running all the way to the scorer's mistakes. The trap of pushing on a measurement Post-training is the clearest example in this course of a general trap, known as Goodhart's law. Push hard on a measure of what you want, and it stops tracking what you wanted, so you start getting the measurement instead of the thing. Picture a class where the teacher, short on time, starts giving higher marks to longer essays, because the longer ones have usually been the more careful ones. One student notices and begins padding every essay with sentences that say nothing new. Their marks go up while their essays get worse, so the marks have stopped measuring what the teacher cared about. In the lab, the scorer plays the teacher and the tuned model plays the student. The model is not scheming, though, since the math pushes it toward whatever scores higher. Raising a score without raising the quality it was meant to measure is called reward hacking, and the lab's last chart is a picture of it. That gap between a measurement and what you meant is also the core of the alignment problem. This lab shows one small piece of it, and the subsection on alignment under Where it breaks says which pieces it leaves out.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Post-training
documents.body: The lab has four cards, and they follow the stages in order. At the top of the first card, a strip of five stages runs Pretrained → SFT → Preferences → Reward model → Policy + KL. Each stage shows a short live readout, and the highlighted stage follows the lesson step you are on. Watch SFT move the chances On the Post-training pipeline card, each of the six answer cards shows three bars. The base bar shows the pretrained model's chance of giving that answer, the SFT bar shows the chance after fine-tuning, and the tuned bar shows the final chance. Each card also shows r, the scorer's reward, and gold, the careful rater's score. Set SFT steps to 0, and the base and SFT bars match, with A out in front at about 50%. Now raise SFT steps to 8, and watch A's SFT bar shrink while the bars for B and F, the two demonstrations, grow. Then set it back to 3, the starting value, so the numbers you see match the ones in this lesson. Be the judge On Preference pairs, each row is one pair, and the pressed button shows which answer is preferred. The starting labels already pick a winner in five pairs and leave Pair 5 unlabelled. Under each row, the lab prints the scorer's predicted chance that the first answer beats the second, and it shows this even for a pair that nobody has labeled. Click an answer to pick it, and click a pressed button again to clear that label. Below the rows, three buttons change every label at once: Restore default labels, Label like the gold rater and Clear all. Read what the scorer learned On Reward model fit, read the three weight bars, each marked "raises reward" or "lowers reward". Below the loss chart, three readouts sum up the fit. Pairs used counts your labels, and Labels fitted counts how many of those pairs the scorer now ranks the way you did. Agrees with gold goes further, because it checks all 15 ways of pairing up the six answers, most of which you never labeled, against the gold scores. With the starting labels, Labels fitted reads 5 of 5, while Agrees with gold reads only 9 of 15. Loosen the leash On Optimize against the reward model, the KL coefficient β slider runs from 20 down to 0.02. Each notch multiplies or divides β by the same amount, so the stretch from 0.02 to 0.2 takes up as much room as the stretch from 2 to 20. Under the slider, Reward-model score shows the tuned model's average reward, the same E[r] as in the target, and Gold score shows the same kind of average for gold. KL from SFT shows how far the tuned model has moved from the SFT model, in nats. The chart plots both scores against KL from SFT, and a marker shows where your current β sits. To fit both lines on one chart, the reward-model line is rescaled so that the worst answer counts as 0 and the best answer counts as 1. Try this: Leave the default labels, push KL coefficient β up to 20, and then drag it all the way down to 0.02. The Reward-model score keeps climbing the whole way. On the chart, the gold curve starts at 0.49 at a KL of 0, where the model still equals the SFT model. Even β 20 lets the model move a little, so there the Gold score readout already shows about 0.51. The curve rises to a peak of about 0.56 near β 3.5. At that peak, KL from SFT reads about 0.20 nats. After that the gold score collapses to 0.10, because the tuned model has piled onto E, the long answer that never explains anything. On the first card, an outline marks the tuned model's favorite answer, and you can watch it move from B to F and then to E. Break the length shortcut Now give the scorer the one comparison it was missing. On Preference pairs, label Pair 5 for B, the short answer that names the mechanism, over E, the long one that does not. On Reward model fit, Words ÷ 10 falls from +1.255 to +0.456. Meanwhile Names mechanism rises to about +1.86 and becomes the biggest weight, and Opens with praise slips a little below zero. Agrees with gold climbs to 12 of 15 at the same time. Sweep KL coefficient β down again, and this time the gold score peaks at about 0.91. It ends at 0.85, on C, a correct answer padded with praise, instead of collapsing onto E. Compare with the gold rater Finally, press Label like the gold rater, which labels every pair the way the gold scores would. Agrees with gold reaches 13 of 15, and Opens with praise drops far below zero, to about −0.93. That happens because Pair 4 now prefers the plainer B over C, which opens with "Great question!". Even these perfect labels cannot reach 15 of 15. The scorer sees only three numbers per answer, and no choice of three weights puts all six answers in exactly gold's order.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Post-training
documents.body: In the default labels, the preferred answer is always the longer one. Pairs 1 to 3 also favor the answer that explains the scattering; in Pair 4 both answers explain it, and in Pair 6 neither does. Length is the only feature that sides with the winner in all five labeled pairs, while naming the mechanism explains only Pairs 1 to 3. So the scorer leans on length. A gap of 40 words also becomes a gap of 4 in Words ÷ 10, far bigger than the gap of 1 that naming the mechanism can make. That means a modest weight on length already buys a large difference in reward. Labels fitted can be perfect while Agrees with gold is poor, because matching your clicks is not the same as learning what you meant by them. Before Pair 5 is labeled, the scorer already puts P(E ≻ B) at 0.98, even though nobody compared those two answers. It has carried its taste for length over to a pair it never saw. The reward-model curve never bends down, and it cannot, because for each β the tuned model is built to push that score as high as the leash allows. Only an independent score, like gold, can reveal reward hacking. One extra comparison, Pair 5, does more for the final answers than any setting of β. With the starting labels no β gets gold above about 0.56, but with Pair 5 labeled the gold score peaks near 0.91. That is because β never changes what the scorer learned. The leash, β, decides how far along the curve the model goes, but it cannot change the curve itself. Without a gold score you could not see where the peak is. A larger β keeps the model close to SFT and gives up part of the gain, so choosing β is a trade-off with no setting that is right in general.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Post-training
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies Six fixed answers stand in for everything a model could write, while a real model builds its answers piece by piece from a huge range of possibilities. The starting chances, the "names mechanism" flags and the gold scores were all written by the lesson's authors. The word counts and the praise check, by contrast, are measured from the text. Gold is an authored score standing in for a careful rater, not the result of a study with real people. The scorer sees three numbers instead of the words, so it cannot notice anything else about an answer. The tuning is calculated exactly rather than learned by trial and error, so none of the randomness or extra machinery of real training appears here. Your labels are one person's six clicks on one prompt, while real preference data pools the picks of many people on many prompts. Because the lab changes six chances for a single prompt, it cannot show how training on some prompts changes a model's answers to others. Because the tuned model is calculated straight from the scorer, the lab cannot show a model that learned a goal of its own. The alignment subsection below covers that problem separately. Where the real thing fails Real reward models read the whole answer and still pick up shortcuts, and they have been measured favoring longer answers, confident wording and agreement with the user. That last habit drives sycophancy, where a model drops a correct answer as soon as you push back. Picture a friend in your group chat who always ends up agreeing with whoever spoke last. Ask whether a film was good and they say yes, but tell them you hated it and suddenly they hated it too. Their replies please you in the moment but tell you nothing, and a model trained to win people's approval can drift toward the same habit. Pushing hard against a scorer like that produces the same curve you saw in the lab. A 2022 study by Gao and colleagues measured it by using a much bigger reward model to play the part of the careful rater. The stand-in score kept rising, while the gold score rose, peaked and then fell. A KL penalty slows that slide, but it does not remove it. A common mix-up: people assume that if the reward number goes up, the model is getting better. Past a point, the scorer's number keeps rising while a careful human's rating falls, because the model has found a loophole in the scorer. That is reward hacking, and the lab's last chart shows it happening. Post-training has other limits too, because it can teach a model not to *say* certain things without removing the ability underneath. That is why a jailbreak, a cleverly worded prompt that gets around that training, can work. Alignment training can also cost a model some performance on benchmarks, the shared tests researchers use to compare models, and that cost is called the alignment tax. Finally, preference data reflects whoever produced it. The instructions the raters were given, who the raters are and how they are rewarded for the work all shape what "better" means. So no set of preferences is free of someone's choices. What alignment is, and what RLHF does not fix Alignment means getting a model to do what its makers and users actually want, but a model never sees what you want directly. It only sees stand-ins, such as example answers, which of two answers people picked, a written rule, or a score. In the cook picture, the cook only ever meets the judge's scores, never the diner's real appetite, and the alignment problem is the gap between the two. Researchers ask two separate questions about that gap. The first is whether the stand-in is the right thing to aim at, which is called outer alignment. The second is whether the trained model really aims at that stand-in, which is called inner alignment. The coin game described below, under goal misgeneralization, is an example of the second question going wrong. What this lab shows about alignment In this lab, the scorer is a stand-in built from your clicks, and the gold score stands in for what you meant. When you drag KL coefficient β down, the scorer's number rises the whole way. Meanwhile the gold score peaks, near 0.56 at 0.20 nats on the default labels, and then falls to 0.10. A measure pushed hard stops tracking what it measured, which is Goodhart's law again. The leash only limits how far the model goes, and it does not fix the stand-in. Every failure in this lab sits in the stand-in itself. The tuned model does exactly what the scorer says, so the lab shows the first question, outer alignment, and only that one. What this lab does not show Four problems sit outside this lab, and because the evidence for each one is uneven, each comes with a status that says how well it is established. Goal misgeneralization is when a model learns a goal that matches the training reward everywhere it was trained, yet differs from the intended goal in new situations. In a 2022 game study by Langosco and colleagues, a game-playing program was trained on levels where a coin always sat at the far right. When the coin was moved, the program kept running right, as if its goal had been "go right" rather than "get the coin". In training, both goals always led to the same place, so the reward never told them apart. *Status:* shown in small game worlds, while whether it explains chatbot behavior is still open. This lab cannot show it, because its model is defined directly by the scorer and has no goal of its own that could differ. Scalable oversight covers ways of supervising answers that are hard for people to check, such as a long program or a subtle argument. Every pick in RLHF needs a person who can tell which answer is better, and for answers like these they may not be able to. Picture judging two answers to a hard chess puzzle when you only know how the pieces move: you could pick one, but your pick would mean very little. Ideas for helping include a second model that points out flaws to the human judge, debates between models, and feedback against written principles. *Status:* these give some help in small studies, but none is proven enough for a model that does better than its judges. Sycophancy, agreeing with the user against the evidence, differs from the others because it has been measured. Studies by Perez and colleagues in 2022 and by Sharma and colleagues in 2023 looked at assistants trained on human feedback. They found that these assistants sometimes tailor their answers to a view the user has stated, or drop a correct answer after pushback. They also found that people and scorers sometimes rate agreeable answers above correct ones, so it is the length shortcut again, with agreement taking the place of length. *Status:* established as a behavior, while how much each training stage adds to it is still being worked out. Deceptive behavior is the worry that a model might behave well when it seems to be watched and differently when it seems not to be. It might also do badly on a test on purpose to hide a skill, which is called sandbagging. The evidence comes from set-ups built on purpose to study it. In a 2024 study by Hubinger and colleagues, models were trained to carry a hidden trigger, a secret cue that switches on a different behavior. The models kept that trigger through safety training. Another 2024 study, by van der Weij and colleagues, showed that models can be prompted or trained to do worse on tests than they are able to. *Status:* whether this arises on its own during ordinary training is open. How developers check before release Before releasing a model, developers run dangerous-capability evaluations, which are tests of whether it can do something seriously harmful. The worry is harm if someone misused the model or if it acted on its own, such as giving real help toward weapons or carrying out cyber attacks. Published frameworks, such as Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework, tie the results to safeguards each developer promises to apply. A failed test shows that one attempt failed, not that the skill is missing. Picture a friend who cannot solve a riddle on the first try: that tells you about one try only, and with a hint they might well get it. For the same reason, testers also try extra training aimed at the skill, and extra tools, to draw it out. The tests, and the scores that count as a warning sign, are each developer's own promises, and they are still new and changing. Where this leaves RLHF RLHF is the best-tested way to make a model behave as intended on the cases people can check. The problems above are mostly about the cases people cannot check, or about what a stand-in leaves out. As you read about any of them, keep three kinds of statement apart: what this lab computes, what has been measured elsewhere, and what is still open.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Post-training
documents.body: Less human labeling In Constitutional AI, a model critiques and rewrites its own answers against a list of written principles, and those rewrites become fine-tuning data. The model then judges pairs of answers against the same principles to make preference data, so people write the principles instead of clicking pairs. No scorer where a checker exists Answers in math and code can be checked, because a program can be run against its tests and a math answer can be compared with an answer key. Training against a real checker, called a verifiable reward, removes the learned scorer and its loopholes, but it only works for tasks that can be checked. Simpler machinery DPO, short for direct preference optimization, skips the separate scorer and trains the model directly on the preference pairs. It does this by rearranging the same target that this lab computes. Group-based methods such as GRPO, short for group relative policy optimization, have the model write several answers to the same prompt and score those answers against each other. Preference optimization in practice runs DPO on a tiny model you can watch. How real RLHF reaches the target Real systems approximate the lab's exact recipe with a method called PPO, short for proximal policy optimization. PPO has the model write answers, scores them and updates the model in small, limited steps. Because it learns from whatever answers the model happens to write, its progress is noisy, and that noise is one of the things this lab leaves out. More on KL divergence The comparison inside KL divergence uses the logarithm of the new chance divided by the old chance, which is a tool you may meet in later math classes. That is also where nats come from, since using the natural logarithm gives distances in nats. More on SFT Real SFT also teaches a chat template, a set of special markers showing where the instructions, the user's message and the reply each begin. Those markers let the model tell instructions apart from the text it is working on, and Instruction tuning & templates builds that stage on a real tiny model. Small open models, whose trained numbers are published for anyone to download, are also often trained on a larger model's answers, which is why they inherit its habits and mistakes. Neighboring modules Failure modes, safety, and security covers attacks on deployed systems, and Ethics and impact asks who bears the costs and how rules and laws treat them. Both sit beside alignment rather than inside it.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Post-training
documents.body: This module covers post-training, the training that follows pretraining and shapes a base model into an assistant. Every stage of it faces one question: how do you move a model toward what people intend, when intent only arrives through proxies such as demonstrations, comparisons, and scores? The module runs all three stages on one prompt: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated demonstrations, a reward model (a learned scorer) fitted to pairwise comparisons, and optimization against that scorer under a KL penalty, a charge for drifting from the SFT model. In real systems, SFT reuses the next-token cross-entropy loss from Next-token prediction, and optimization usually treats each sampled response as one action that gets one score, the bandit setup from Reinforcement learning foundations. Where it shows up Post-training sits between a pretrained base model and the assistant people talk to. RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) optimizes against a reward model with PPO (proximal policy optimization), a policy-gradient method that clips each update so the policy moves in small steps. DPO (direct preference optimization) trains on preference pairs with no separate reward model. Why it matters A base model predicts how a page continues, and the continuation of a question is often not an answer. Demonstrations move it toward answering, but they are expensive to write and comparisons are cheap, so the pipeline turns next to comparisons and a scorer learned from them. That scorer is a proxy, and optimizing hard against it rewards its mistakes along with the intended behavior. The proxy score keeps rising while true quality falls. This failure, reward hacking, shows up only against an independent score, and a KL penalty slows it but does not stop it. What you will be able to explain How pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and KL-regularized policy optimization differ. How a Bradley–Terry reward model is fitted from pairwise preferences, and how to read what it actually learned. Why reward hacking shows up as a proxy score rising while true quality falls. Alignment as the gap between what can be measured and what is wanted, and the problems RLHF does not fix. What the lab shows Everything runs on one prompt, "Explain why the sky is blue," and six fixed responses, A to F, so every distribution in the lab, SFT's included, is over six whole responses rather than over tokens. Post-training pipeline shows each response's base, SFT, and tuned probability; SFT steps takes real cross-entropy gradient steps toward the demonstrations B and F. Preference pairs holds six comparisons. Five come labelled by default, and in each one the preferred response is also the longer one. Pair 5, a long answer that never names the mechanism against a short one that does, starts unlabelled. Reward model fit refits a three-weight Bradley–Terry scorer to the current labels, the defaults or yours, with 200 gradient steps. The key experiment is on Optimize against the reward model. With the default labels, lower KL coefficient β from 20 to 0.02 and watch Reward-model score rise the whole way while Gold score peaks and falls. Then label Pair 5 for B, the short answer that names the mechanism, and sweep again. The tuned policy is the exact closed-form optimum, with no sampling and no PPO. Word count and praise are measured from the text; the base logits, the "names mechanism" flag, and the gold scores are authored, and gold stands in for what you meant.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Post-training
documents.body: Pretraining produces a text predictor, not an assistant. Given "Explain why the sky is blue," a raw predictor's likely continuation might be more exam questions, because that is what follows such a line in web text. It is behaving correctly and uselessly. Post-training is the set of stages that turn that predictor into something that answers. This lab runs all of them on one prompt with a deliberately tiny policy: a probability distribution over six complete responses. Each response is one action, the bandit view from Reinforcement learning foundations. Stage one: supervised fine-tuning SFT is ordinary next-token cross-entropy on curated demonstrations, usually counted only on the response tokens. The loss is the pretraining loss; the data changed. Here the authored base model puts 50% on A, another exam question. SFT steps takes real gradient steps toward the demonstrations B and F; eight steps move them to 38% and 36%. Real SFT also teaches the chat template: special tokens that delimit system, user, and assistant turns, so the model can tell instructions from content. Stage two: a reward model from comparisons Writing an ideal response is slow; choosing the better of two is fast and more consistent. Those choices train a reward model with the Bradley-Terry objective: P(A ≻ B) = σ(r_A − r_B). Here r(y) = w·φ(y), where φ is three numbers: words ÷ 10, whether the response names the scattering mechanism, and whether it opens with praise. Reward model fit runs 200 gradient steps on the pairs you label. Stage three: optimize under a KL leash The policy is then tuned to maximize E[r] − β·KL(π‖π_SFT). The KL penalty charges it for drifting from the SFT model. KL divergence is that drift, measured: It is the expected log-ratio of the tuned probabilities to the SFT probabilities, averaged over the tuned policy's own responses. It is never negative, it is zero only when the two distributions are identical, and it is not symmetric: swapping the arguments gives a different number. The lab's KL from SFT readout is this sum in nats; with the default labels the gold score peaks near 0.20 nats. The full objective has an exact optimum, π(y) ∝ π_SFT(y)·exp(r(y)/β), which this lab computes directly. RLHF approximates the same optimum by sampling responses and updating with PPO. That reward-after-acting signal is the reinforcement learning that What AI actually is sorted from labels and raw text, and Reinforcement learning foundations runs the basic policy-gradient update on a bandit. DPO rearranges the optimum so the reward is β·log(π/π_SFT) plus a constant, and trains the policy on pairs directly.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Post-training
documents.body: Most traits people call a model's personality are set here: helpfulness, verbosity, hedging, formatting habits, refusals, and willingness to say "I don't know." Two products built on the same base model can feel completely different. It is also where a model is optimized directly against an imperfect measurement, so the reward hacking previewed above is post-training's case of Goodhart's law: push hard on a measure, and it stops tracking what you wanted. That gap between a measure and what you meant is the alignment problem. This lab shows one small piece of it, and the subsection under Where it breaks says which pieces it leaves out.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Post-training
documents.body: Move SFT steps from 0 to 8 and watch A's base-model lead collapse as B and F grow. Read the default labels on Preference pairs. Pairs 1 to 3 prefer the answer that names the mechanism; pair 4 prefers the longer of two answers that both name it, and pair 6 the longer of two that neither names. Pair 5 starts unlabelled, and every preferred answer is also the longer one. Reward model fit reports Words ÷ 10 at +1.255 and Agrees with gold at 9 of 15. Move KL coefficient β from 20 to 0.02. Gold score starts at 0.49, peaks at 0.56 near KL 0.20 nats, then falls to 0.10 as the policy moves onto E. Reward-model score rises the whole way. Label Pair 5 for B and sweep β again. Words ÷ 10 falls to +0.456, and gold now peaks at 0.91.
