documents.subtitle: Standard · Post-training
documents.body: Labels fitted reads 5 of 5 while Agrees with gold reads 9 of 15. Fitting your data is not the same as learning your criterion. When every preferred answer is longer, the scorer cannot tell whether you liked length or correctness. It picks the feature with the larger differences. The reward-model curve never bends down. It cannot; the tilt maximizes it. Only an independent score can show reward hacking. A larger β keeps the policy close to SFT and gives up part of the gain. There is no β that is correct in general.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Post-training
documents.body: In this lab. Six fixed responses stand in for everything a model could write. The base logits, the "names mechanism" flag, and the gold scores are authored; word count and praise are measured from the text. The reward model sees only three features. The tuned policy is the exact optimum, so there is no sampling noise, no PPO clipping, and no value function. In real systems. Reward models read the whole response and still learn shortcuts. They have been measured favoring longer answers, confident phrasing, and agreement with the user. The last is a driver of sycophancy: a model abandoning a correct answer after mild pushback. Optimizing hard against such a scorer produces the curve in this lab. Gao et al. (2022) measured it against a larger "gold" reward model: the proxy kept rising while the gold score peaked and fell. A KL penalty slows that; it does not remove it. Two further limits. Post-training can suppress a behavior without removing the capability, which is why jailbreaks work. And alignment can cost some benchmark performance, an alignment tax. Finally, preference data encodes whoever produced it. Annotator instructions, demographics, and incentives shape what "better" means, and there is no neutral setting. What alignment is, and what RLHF does not fix Alignment is getting a model's behavior to match what its developers and users actually intend. Intent is never handed to a model directly. It arrives through proxies: demonstrations, comparisons, a written rule, a score. The alignment problem is the gap between those proxies and what we want. Researchers split it in two. *Outer alignment* asks whether the specified objective is the right one. *Inner alignment* asks whether the trained model actually pursues that objective. What this lab shows. The reward model is a proxy fitted to your labels, and the gold score stands in for what you meant. As KL coefficient β falls, the reward-model score rises the whole way while the gold score peaks, near 0.56 at 0.20 nats on the default labels, and then falls to 0.10. That is Goodhart's law in miniature, and the KL leash only slows it. Every failure here sits in the objective. The tuned policy is the exact optimum of the reward model, so it does precisely what the proxy says. That is the outer half of the problem, and only that half. What it does not show. Four problems sit outside this lab. Each carries its status, because the evidence is uneven. Goal misgeneralization. A policy can learn a goal that matches the training reward wherever it was trained and differs from the intended goal elsewhere. In one reinforcement-learning demonstration (Langosco et al., 2022), an agent trained on levels where a coin always sat at the far right kept running right after the coin was moved. *Status:* shown in small environments; how far it explains language-model behavior is open. This lab cannot show it, because its policy is defined by the reward. Scalable oversight. Both reward-model steps need a person who can say which answer is better. For a long program or a subtle argument, they may not be able to. Proposed remedies include model-written critiques that help raters find flaws, debate between models, and feedback against written principles, as in Constitutional AI. *Status:* some help in controlled studies; none is established as enough for a model that outperforms its overseers. Sycophancy. This one is measured. Studies (Perez et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2023) found that assistants trained with human feedback sometimes tailor answers to a user's stated view or drop a correct answer after pushback, and that preference data sometimes rates agreeable answers above correct ones. It is the length shortcut again, with a different feature. *Status:* established as a behavior; each training stage's share of it is still being worked out. Deceptive behavior. The worry is a model that behaves well when it seems to be observed, or underperforms on purpose, called sandbagging, to hide a capability. The evidence comes from constructed settings: models trained to carry a hidden backdoor kept it through standard safety training (Hubinger et al., 2024), and models can be prompted or fine-tuned to underperform on evaluations (van der Weij et al., 2024). *Status:* whether such behavior arises unprompted in ordinary training is open. How developers check before release. Developers run dangerous-capability evaluations: tests of whether a model can do things that would be seriously harmful if misused or if it acted on its own, such as giving real uplift toward weapons or carrying out cyber operations. Published frameworks, such as Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework, tie results to safeguards the developer commits to. A failed test shows that one attempt failed, not that the capability is absent, so evaluators also try fine-tuning and scaffolding to draw it out. The tests and thresholds are each developer's own commitments, and they are still young. Where this leaves RLHF. It is the best-tested way to make a model's behavior match intent on the cases people can check. The problems above are mostly about the cases they cannot, or about what a proxy leaves out. Keep three kinds of statement apart: what this lab computes, what has been measured elsewhere, and what is still open.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Post-training
documents.body: Less human labeling. In Constitutional AI, a model critiques and revises its own drafts against written principles to make fine-tuning data, then judges pairs of outputs against those principles to make preference data. Human effort moves from labeling to writing the principles. No learned scorer where a checker exists. For math and code, a verifiable reward comes from tests or an answer key, which removes the exploitable reward model. It only applies where checking is possible. Simpler optimizers. DPO removed the separate reward model. Group-based methods such as GRPO score several sampled responses to the same prompt against each other instead of training a value function. Instruction tuning & templates builds the SFT stage on a real tiny model, and Preference optimization in practice runs DPO on it. Small open models are also often distilled from a larger model's answers, which is why they inherit its habits and mistakes. Failure modes, safety, and security covers attacks on deployed systems, and Ethics and impact asks who bears the costs and how regulation treats them. Both sit beside alignment rather than inside it.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Post-training pipeline · Post-training
documents.body: One prompt, six responses, three distributions The whole policy is a probability distribution over six complete responses to one prompt, so each response is one action. The bars show that distribution three times: the pretrained model, after supervised fine-tuning, and after optimizing against the reward model under a KL penalty. A five-stage strip, Pretrained → SFT → Preferences → Reward model → Policy + KL, each with a live readout. The highlighted stage follows the lesson step. SFT steps, from 0 to 12. Six response cards. Each shows the text, the three features the reward model sees (word count, whether it names the mechanism, whether it opens with praise), and three bars: base, SFT, and tuned. r is the fitted reward-model score and gold is the authored careful-rater score. The outlined card is the tuned policy's most likely response. The badge repeats the tuned policy's expected gold score. Base probabilities are softmax of authored logits that favor A, a continuation with more exam questions: 50% at the defaults. SFT is real gradient descent on cross-entropy toward the two demonstrations B and F: logits ← logits − 0.8·(p − target), with target ½ on each demo. Three steps take B from 8% to 23% and F from 6% to 20%. Tuned is the exact maximizer of E_π[r] − β·KL(π‖π_SFT), which is π(y) ∝ π_SFT(y)·exp(r(y)/β). No sampling or PPO is simulated. Word count and praise are measured from the text. "Names mechanism" and gold are authored. SFT steps on this card; labels, β, and the preset buttons on the other cards all change the tuned bars here. Comparison worth running: SFT steps 0, then 8. The base model's favorite, A, falls from 50% to 9% while B and F rise to 38% and 36%. SFT moves mass toward what was demonstrated; it never looks at a reward. At the default labels and β 2, the tuned policy already puts 39% on E, the long answer that never names the mechanism. In this lab: six fixed responses stand in for everything a model could write, and the base logits and gold scores are authored. A real policy spreads probability over sequences token by token. In general: SFT and RLHF on a real model change billions of weights and generalize to other prompts. The tilt formula is the target that PPO or DPO approximate, not what they compute exactly.
documents.title: One prompt, six responses, three distributions

documents.subtitle: Preference pairs · Post-training
documents.body: Your comparisons are the training data Six pairs of responses. Each click records which one you prefer, and the reward model is refitted from scratch on every labeled pair. Unlabelled pairs are ignored. The probabilities are the fitted model's Bradley–Terry predictions. Six rows. The pressed button is your preferred response; a dashed row is unlabelled. Under each row, P(A ≻ B) = σ(r_A − r_B) from the current fit, shown even for unlabelled pairs. Presets: Restore default labels, Label like the gold rater, and Clear all. Default labels prefer the answer that names the mechanism in pairs 1–3, the longer of two answers that both name it (C over B) in pair 4, and the longer of two that neither names (E over A) in pair 6. In every one of those the preferred response is also the longer one. Pair 5 puts E (59 words, no mechanism) against B (25 words, names the mechanism). It is the only pair that separates length from correctness, and it starts unlabelled. Clicking a pressed button clears that label. One pair of buttons per row, plus the three presets. Comparison worth running: label Pair 5 for B and watch Words ÷ 10 fall from +1.255 to +0.456 on Reward model fit. Correlated labels teach a correlated scorer. Nothing in pairs 1–4 tells the model whether you liked length or correctness. P(E ≻ B) is 0.98 before Pair 5 is labeled, even though you never compared them. In this lab: one person's six clicks on one prompt. Your labels persist in the lab state and nothing is aggregated across users. In general: production datasets pool many annotators whose disagreement on hard items is substantial, and the instructions, incentives, and demographics of the raters shape what "better" means.
documents.title: Your comparisons are the training data

documents.subtitle: Reward model fit · Post-training
documents.body: A three-weight Bradley–Terry scorer The reward model is r(y) = w·φ(y) with φ = [words ÷ 10, names mechanism, opens with praise]. It is fitted by 200 steps of full-batch gradient ascent on the Bradley–Terry log-likelihood of your labeled pairs, from w = 0, with a small L2 penalty. Three weight bars with signed values. Blue raises reward; red lowers it. The training loss, mean −log σ(r_win − r_lose), over 200 steps. It starts at ln 2 = 0.693 because all rewards start equal. Pairs used, Labels fitted (labeled pairs the scorer now orders your way), and Agrees with gold (of all 15 response pairs, how many it orders the way the gold score does). Gradient: Σ (1 − σ(r_win − r_lose))·(φ_win − φ_lose) averaged over pairs, minus 0.05·w, with step size 0.5. Only differences in features between winner and loser matter, so a feature that is always higher on the winner looks like a reason to win. Words are divided by 10 before fitting, so a difference of 40 words is a feature difference of 4, larger than the mechanism's 1. No controls on this card; it refits whenever a label changes. Comparison worth running: default labels give 9 of 15 agreement with gold; Pair 5 labeled for B gives 12; Label like the gold rater gives 13. Labels fitted can be perfect while Agrees with gold is poor. Fitting your data is not the same as learning your criterion. With the gold-rater labels, Opens with praise goes negative, because pair 4 then prefers the plainer B over C. In this lab: three hand-picked features, so the scorer cannot represent anything else about the text. In general: real reward models are fine-tuned language models that read the whole response. They still pick up shortcuts such as length, confident tone, and agreement with the user, because those correlate with preference in the data.
documents.title: A three-weight Bradley–Terry scorer

documents.subtitle: Optimize against the reward model · Post-training
documents.body: Proxy up, gold up, then gold down KL coefficient β sets how far the tuned policy may move from the SFT model. The chart sweeps β from 20 down to 0.02 and plots the tuned policy's expected reward-model score and expected gold score against the KL divergence each β allows. KL coefficient β on a log scale from 0.02 to 20, and three readouts: Reward-model score, Gold score, and KL from SFT in nats. A formula card for the tuned policy's top response: its SFT probability times exp(r/β), before normalizing over all six. Two curves against KL: the reward-model score, rescaled so the worst response is 0 and the best is 1, and the gold score. The guide marks the current β. For each β the policy is π(y) ∝ π_SFT(y)·exp(r(y)/β), the closed-form maximizer of E[r] − β·KL(π‖π_SFT). KL = Σ π·ln(π/π_SFT). At the default labels gold starts at 0.49 (the SFT model), peaks at 0.56 near β 3.5 where KL is 0.20 nats, and falls to 0.10 as E takes all the mass. The reward-model score rises the whole way. With Pair 5 labeled for B, gold peaks at 0.91 near β 0.42 and ends at 0.85 on C, a correct but padded answer. KL coefficient β. Labels and SFT steps on the other cards move both curves. Comparison worth running: default labels at β 20, 2, and 0.1; then label Pair 5 for B and repeat. The proxy never falls as β shrinks. That is by construction: the tilt maximizes it. Only an independent score can show the damage. A larger β keeps the policy close to SFT and gives up some of the gain. Choosing β is a trade, not a solved parameter. In this lab: the optimum is computed exactly over six responses, so there is no sampling noise, no PPO clipping, and no value function. Gold is an authored score, not a human study. The card shows a proxy failing under optimization; because the policy is defined by the reward, it cannot show a policy that learned a different goal, which the lesson's alignment subsection names separately. In general: Gao et al. (2022) measured this rise-then-fall against a larger "gold" reward model as policies were optimized further from their start. A KL penalty slows it; it does not remove it.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: Direct preference optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023). A classification-style loss on preference pairs, derived from the closed-form optimum of KL-regularized RLHF, so it needs no separate reward model and no sampling loop.
documents.title: DPO

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: A frozen copy of the starting model. Every reward in DPO is defined relative to it, which is what keeps the policy from drifting into nonsense.
documents.title: Reference model

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: Beta times the log of the policy's probability over the reference model's for a completion. It equals the reward DPO implicitly fits up to a per-prompt constant, so it compares completions of one prompt and is never a quality score.
documents.title: Implicit reward

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: The implicit reward of the preferred completion minus that of the rejected one. The DPO loss is a decreasing function of exactly this number.
documents.title: Margin

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: The KL-penalty strength inherited from RLHF. In the DPO loss it scales the margin, so a higher beta saturates the loss with a smaller log-ratio change and ends nearer the reference. Under plain gradient descent it also scales every step, so early on a higher beta moves faster.
documents.title: Beta

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: How far one distribution sits from another, in nats. Here it is KL from policy to reference averaged evenly over all 30 context rows, a whole-table measure of drift; RLHF's penalty is instead taken over the policy's own sampled completions.
documents.title: KL divergence

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: Two effects of length. Raw total log-probability always favours the shorter completion, and preference data in which longer answers tend to win teaches the policy to lengthen its answers.
documents.title: Length bias

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: Looping on a phrase. It is a high-probability failure for small models, which makes it a useful thing to label against.
documents.title: Degenerate repetition

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: Improving the measured objective while real quality stalls. In DPO the objective is the margin, so a rising margin is evidence about the margin and nothing else.
documents.title: Reward hacking

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: The model being trained, as opposed to the frozen reference. Here it starts as an exact copy of the reference table and is the only set of weights DPO updates.
documents.title: Policy

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: fit a reward model to preference comparisons, then train the model to raise that reward while a KL penalty holds it near a reference. DPO reaches the same optimum without the separate reward model or the sampling loop.
documents.title: RLHF

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: The model of pairwise comparisons in which the chance of preferring one completion is the sigmoid of the difference between the two rewards. DPO's loss is the negative log of that likelihood with the implicit reward substituted in, so it depends only on the margin.
documents.title: Bradley-Terry

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: Comparisons the optimizer never trains on, scored by the finished policy with the same margin as the training pairs. A margin that is large on the training pairs and small or negative on held-out pairs means the policy fitted those pairs rather than the preference behind them.
documents.title: Held-out pairs

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: A model already fine-tuned on instruction and response pairs. DPO normally starts from one and freezes a copy of it as the reference, so every reward measures movement away from the supervised model rather than from a raw base.
documents.title: SFT checkpoint

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Preference optimization in practice · question 1
documents.body: At DPO steps 0 the loss reads 0.6931. What is that number telling you? The learning rate is too small for the loss to start moving, so the optimizer has not taken a step Every margin is zero because the policy is a copy of the reference, and the loss at zero margin is ln 2 The chosen completions are exactly as likely as the rejected ones under the base model, so nothing is learned yet Every untrained policy scores 0.6931 whatever the data, because the loss is normalised to start there Each margin is the policy's log-ratio gap minus the reference's, and at step 0 the policy is the reference, so every margin is exactly zero. The loss is then −log sigmoid(0) = ln 2 = 0.6931 whatever the data. It does not mean the two completions are equally likely: in the default pairs the base model rates the repeating loop as the more likely one.
documents.title: At DPO steps 0 the loss reads 0.6931. What is that number telling you?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Preference optimization in practice · question 2
documents.body: After DPO the margin has grown, yet both the chosen and the rejected completion have lower log-probability than before. Is something wrong? Yes. A correct run must raise the log-probability of the preferred completion on every pair it trains on Yes. It means beta was set too low for the data, so the margin could not be scaled up enough No. The loss rewards only the gap, so it is satisfied by pushing the rejected side down faster Yes. The reference model was updated by mistake, so the log-ratios no longer mean anything at all DPO optimizes a difference. Lowering both sides while widening the gap satisfies it perfectly, and it is a common outcome in practice. In this lab the chosen side rises a little and the rejected side falls much further, which is why the two sides are worth plotting separately rather than trusting the margin alone.
documents.title: After DPO the margin has grown, yet both the chosen and the rejected completion have lower log-probability than before. Is something wrong?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Preference optimization in practice · question 3
documents.body: Which comparison is an implicit reward built to support? Rewards from different prompts, because beta scales every prompt's rewards onto one common quality scale Any two completions of any prompt, because the reward is the policy's log-probability alone The preferred completion against a human rating, because the reward estimates that rating directly Chosen against rejected on the same prompt, because each reward is relative to the reference's probability An implicit reward is beta times the log of the policy's probability over the reference's, which equals the fitted reward only up to a constant for each prompt. That constant cancels inside a pair, so a chosen-versus-rejected gap on one prompt is meaningful. Across prompts, or as a quality score, it is not.
documents.title: Which comparison is an implicit reward built to support?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Preference optimization in practice · question 4
documents.body: Sweeping Beta from 0.2 to 0.8 at 40 steps, the beta-scaled margin rises but the log-ratio gap falls. What does that show? A higher beta trained the policy better, because the larger scaled margin means the pairs are separated further apart Beta scales the margin, so the loss saturates after a smaller log-ratio change and the policy ends nearer the reference Beta cancels out of the loss, so only the step size changed between runs and the gap fell by chance The optimizer diverged at the higher beta, so the gap shrank even though the scaled margin kept growing Beta multiplies the log-ratio gap inside the sigmoid, so a larger beta reaches any given loss with a smaller gap and the gradient flattens sooner. The scaled margin is therefore not comparable across betas: compare runs by the unscaled gap and by KL. A larger beta ends nearer the reference, which is the control it buys.
documents.title: Sweeping Beta from 0.2 to 0.8 at 40 steps, the beta-scaled margin rises but the log-ratio gap falls. What does that show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Preference optimization in practice · question 5
documents.body: In the lab a higher beta drifts less at 40 steps but more at 4 steps. A production run uses Adam instead of plain gradient descent. What happens to that early flip? It gets stronger, because Adam takes larger steps early in training than plain gradient descent does It stays exactly as shown, because the step-size role comes from the loss and not from the optimizer It largely disappears: Adam rescales each step, so beta's step-size role fades and saturation dominates It reverses at every step count, because Adam makes a higher beta always drift farther from the reference Under plain gradient descent beta multiplies every gradient, so a higher beta also takes bigger steps, and that wins early. Adam normalises each parameter's step size, so that role fades and beta's other role, saturating the loss sooner, is what remains. The early flip is a property of the lab's optimizer, not of DPO.
documents.title: In the lab a higher beta drifts less at 40 steps but more at 4 steps. A production run uses Adam instead of plain gradient descent. What happens to that early flip?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Preference optimization in practice · question 6
documents.body: At the defaults every training pair ends ordered correctly, but fewer held-out pairs do. What does that show? The optimizer fitted the pairs it trained on, and ordering new comparisons is a separate fact to check The held-out pairs are mislabelled, because a correct preference would be ordered like the training pairs Beta is set too high, because a lower beta would order every held-out pair just as well as the training ones DPO has not run long enough, because more steps always order more of the pairs it never trained on The loss grades only the training margins, so a high training margin is evidence about those pairs. The held-out pairs share some character transitions with them, which is why one held-out pair carries over while two end with their margin reversed. More steps make those two worse, not better. A check on unseen pairs is the only evidence that the preference itself was learned.
documents.title: At the defaults every training pair ends ordered correctly, but fewer held-out pairs do. What does that show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Preference optimization in practice · question 7
documents.body: You switch Reference model to SFT checkpoint. At DPO steps 0 the loss still reads 0.6931 although the reference now orders some training pairs correctly. Why? The policy starts as a copy of whichever reference is chosen, so every margin is zero whatever it prefers The SFT checkpoint only changes the samples, so the loss ignores it until the first optimizer step The optimizer resets the loss to its starting value on every pair, so the reference cannot move it The SFT reference still prefers the loops on every pair, because SFT leaves raw probabilities as they were A margin is the policy's log-ratio gap minus the reference's, and at step 0 the policy is the reference, so every margin is exactly zero and the loss is ln 2 whatever the reference prefers. SFT does change the raw preferences: the reference now ranks two of the three training pairs correctly, which the Per-pair rewards rows state as already preferred it.
documents.title: You switch Reference model to SFT checkpoint. At DPO steps 0 the loss still reads 0.6931 although the reference now orders some training pairs correctly. Why?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: This lesson is about teaching an AI model by comparison, where you show it two answers to the same prompt and say which one you prefer. You never write out a perfect answer for it to copy, and the lab turns a handful of your choices into real training. The model here is a language model: a program that writes text one piece at a time by guessing what comes next, like the much larger ones behind chatbots. As the Post-training lesson showed, a model that has only learned to continue text then gets more training to shape the kind of replies it gives. Picking the better of two replies is one way people give that feedback, because choosing is quicker and more reliable than writing a perfect reply from scratch. The method in this lab is called DPO, short for direct preference optimization, and it nudges the model to favor the answer you preferred over the one you rejected. It does this with one formula and no separate program for scoring answers, which is what makes it "direct". Without a method like this, you would have to write the ideal answer for every situation, or train a second model whose only job is scoring answers. Comparisons are cheaper to collect, so DPO makes it practical to steer a model with feedback that people can give quickly. It also comes with a trap, because the number DPO pushes up can keep climbing while the model learns something much narrower than you meant. That is why most of this lesson is about reading the results honestly. By the end of the lesson, you should be able to explain each of these in your own words: how to run preference optimization on comparisons that you wrote yourself, and what each part of a comparison does; how to read the score gap between the two answers in a pair, which the lab calls the implicit reward margin, including which answer actually moved; what you gain and what you give up when you raise or lower a setting called beta, which controls how far training lets the model move from where it started; how to judge whether a gain carries over, by scoring pairs that training never saw. The lab's model is tiny, looks only at the last character it read, and learned from short harbor weather notes and recipe steps. So the answers here are short phrases about a foggy harbor and cooking. Each rejected answer is a loop such as "fog fog fog fog fog.", which is a real failure that small models fall into. You can write your own pairs in the Preference pair editor, run training for more or fewer steps, and watch four other cards respond. They include charts of the score gap and of drift, meaning how far the model has moved from its starting copy. The last card scores every pair one by one, along with three test pairs that training never touches, so you can check whether training carried over to new comparisons.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: A model that guesses one character at a time The model in this lab reads one character, such as a letter or a space, and gives every possible next character a chance, or probability, of coming next. It has 30 symbols in all: a space, the letters a to z, a full stop and two spare symbols kept for special use. Because it only looks one character back, it cannot tell which word it is in, so its writing comes out as jumbled letters with a few real words. To find the chance of a whole answer, the model multiplies the chances of each step. Take "fog" after a space: the chance that "f" follows a space, times the chance that "o" follows "f", times the chance that "g" follows "o". With made-up chances of one half, one half and one quarter, the chance of "fog" is one sixteenth. A 28-character answer multiplies 28 chances, which gives a number so tiny that it is hard to read or compare. So the lab turns each chance into a score called a log-probability and adds the scores instead of multiplying the chances. A step that is sure to happen, with a chance of 1, scores 0, and every time a chance halves, the score drops by about 0.69. These scores are measured in units called nats, so a chance of one half scores about −0.69 nats and a chance of one quarter scores about −1.39. For "fog", the three scores add up to about −2.77, which is four halvings and matches the one sixteenth from before. Ten halvings in a row make a chance about a thousand times smaller, which shows up as a score drop of about 6.9. That rule of thumb, about 0.69 for every halving, is the key to reading the numbers in this lab. Inside, the model is a table. For each of the 30 characters it might have just read, it keeps a row of 30 numbers that set the chances of what comes next. That makes 900 numbers in all. Training means nudging those numbers a little at a time, and each nudge is called a step, so some next characters become more likely and others less. Two copies of one model The lab first trains a model for 50 epochs, meaning 50 full passes, over two small sets of text: harbor weather notes and recipe steps. That trained model is then frozen and kept as the reference model, and the Reference model switch calls it Base model. Training works on a second, editable copy called the policy, which starts as an exact copy of the reference and is the only one that ever changes. Every result in this lab compares the two copies, so the question is never "how good is this answer?" but "how much more or less likely did training make it?" What you tell it In the Preference pair editor, each line has three parts split by bars: prompt | preferred | rejected. The prompt is the start of the text, the preferred answer is the continuation you like, and the rejected answer is the one you do not. The lab also calls an answer a completion, and it calls the preferred one "chosen", so you will see both words on the cards. These are the three default lines, one comparison per line: the | fog settles over the harbor. | fog fog fog fog fog. warm the | pan and add a spoon of oil. | pan and the pan and the pan. simmer the | sauce until it thickens. | sauce and simmer the sauce. Every rejected answer loops on a phrase, a failure called degenerate repetition, and it is a real and common problem for small models. In all three pairs the reference model actually rates the loop as more likely than the good sentence. Training does not have to reverse that, though. It only has to move the two answers apart compared with where the reference had them. Even after 40 steps, the trained model still rates the loop as more likely in pairs 1 and 2. The picture: a playlist that learns from your taps Picture a music app that plays songs at random from a big playlist, with some songs coming up far more often than others. Each song stands for one possible answer, and how often a song plays stands for its chance. The app never asks you to name the perfect song, but now and then it shows you two songs and you tap the one you like better. The app keeps a saved copy of the original playlist, which plays the part of the reference, while it changes a working copy, the policy. To respect your tap, it can play your favorite more often, play the other song less often, or both. Since total listening time is shared, playing one song more always means playing something else less. The picture stops matching in two places, and the second one matters most. First, neither the app nor the model likes or dislikes anything: "better" means only "the side you labeled preferred". Second, songs are separate tracks, while the model's answers are built from small shared steps, like "a space followed by f". Turning down one answer also turns down every other answer that uses the same steps, and you will see that happen in the lab. The implicit reward and the margin For any answer, the policy's log-probability minus the reference's log-probability says how far training has moved that answer. Multiply that difference by a setting called beta, written β, and you get the answer's implicit reward. It is called implicit because no separate program hands out the reward; it is read straight off the model's own chances. A reward of zero means the policy rates the answer exactly as the reference did, while a positive reward means more likely and a negative one means less likely. The margin is the preferred answer's reward minus the rejected answer's reward, and pair 1 after the default training makes a good example. Its preferred sentence has a reward of about +0.18 and its loop has about −3.61. The margin is +0.18 minus −3.61, which is about 3.8, and nearly all of it came from the loop going down rather than the sentence going up. Because each reward is measured against the reference, an implicit reward is not a quality score. A great answer the reference already liked can have a reward of 0, because training did not move it. Meanwhile, a poor answer that training made a little more likely gets a positive reward. So the reward tells you how much training moved an answer, not how good the answer is, and it is only meant for comparing the two answers inside one pair. The loss in one formula Training needs one number to aim at, called the loss. Each step nudges the table in whatever direction makes the loss a little smaller, and a smaller loss means the model fits your choices better. DPO's loss depends on the margin and on nothing else. The Where each pair sits on the loss card draws it as loss −log σ(β·m), which looks dense, so here it is piece by piece: m is the margin divided by beta, the gap between how far the two answers moved, which the readout Log-ratio gap m = margin ÷ β shows in nats. So β·m, meaning β times m, is the margin itself. The card splits it this way because m is in nats, which you can read with the halving rule, while β is a setting you choose. σ, the Greek letter sigma, stands for an S-shaped squashing curve called the sigmoid, which turns any number into a share between 0 and 1. Zero becomes one half, large positive numbers come out close to 1, and large negative numbers come out close to 0. σ(β·m) is the formula's predicted chance that the preferred answer wins the comparison, so a gap of zero gives a coin flip, 50%. −log uses the same log step that turned chances into log-probability scores earlier, then flips the sign, so the loss is never negative. A 50% chance is one halving away from certain, so its loss is about 0.69. Every pair starts at m = 0, so the predicted chance is 50% and the loss is 0.6931, the size of one halving, which mathematicians write as ln 2. Now take pair 1 after the default training, which sits at m = 9.50, so with beta at 0.4, β·m is 3.8. The sigmoid turns 3.8 into about 97.8%, so the loss shrinks to about 0.022. Where training starts The policy begins as an exact copy of the reference, so at the start every reward and every margin is exactly zero. With DPO steps at 0 the slider reads untrained and DPO loss reads 0.6931, the value a zero margin always gives, whatever pairs you wrote. That 0.6931 does not mean the two answers are equally likely, because the reference still prefers every loop; it means the policy has not moved yet.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: Picture planning a birthday message in a group chat, where writing the perfect message from scratch takes a while and five friends would write five different ones. If someone shows you two drafts, though, you can pick the better one in seconds. That is why people train models on comparisons. The older way to do it is RLHF, short for reinforcement learning from human feedback, which first trains a separate scoring model on people's comparisons. Then it trains the main model to raise that score, while a penalty keeps the main model near the reference so that it does not drift into nonsense. That needs extra machinery: the scorer itself, plus a loop in which the model writes fresh answers for the scorer to grade. DPO reaches the same goal from the same comparisons with one loss, no separate scorer and no loop of fresh answers. The Post-training lesson stopped at that argument, while this lab runs real training steps on pairs you write. Running DPO for real shows a problem that the argument hides, because the margin is the exact number DPO pushes up. So the margin will rise whether or not the model is picking up the preference you meant. That makes a rising margin the weakest evidence that training did what you wanted, which is why the lab puts four other readouts beside it: the two sides of the margin plotted apart, so you can see which answer moved; where each pair sits on the loss, so you can see which pairs are still driving training; the drift from the reference, so you can see how much of the whole model changed; held-out pairs, so you can see whether the preference carried over to comparisons that training never saw.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: Work through these in order, because each step builds on the one before. Run the optimizer The part of the lab that takes the training steps is called the optimizer, and DPO steps sets how many steps it takes. Try this: set DPO steps to 0 and read DPO loss: 0.6931, with every line on the first chart, Implicit reward margin during training, sitting at zero. The badge reads 0% ordered correctly, because it only counts pairs whose margin is above zero, and every margin is exactly zero. Now raise DPO steps to 40, keeping Beta at 0.4 and DPO learning rate, which sets how big each step is, at 0.35. The loss falls to 0.0317, and all three pairs end ordered correctly, so the badge reads 100% ordered correctly. Here ordered correctly means the margin is above zero, so the preferred answer has gained on the loop since training began. It does not mean the preferred answer is now the more likely of the two, and in pairs 1 and 2 it still is not. Move the slider slowly from 0 upward and watch the numbered circles on Where each pair sits on the loss slide right and down the curve. After only a few steps every training pair is already ordered correctly, yet the loss keeps falling, because a bigger margin always gives a smaller loss. Read the margin and its two sides The first card, Implicit reward margin during training, plots four lines against the step count, and its solid margin (chosen − rejected) line is the average margin. The dashed chosen reward line follows the preferred side, and the dotted rejected reward line follows the loop side. The margin is always exactly the distance between the dashed and dotted lines, and the fourth line will come up later. At 40 steps the chosen reward ends at +0.556 and the rejected reward ends at −2.940. The Margin, β-scaled readout shows the difference between those two lines, which comes to 3.497. Next to it, Log-ratio gap m = margin ÷ β shows the same gap with beta divided back out, so 3.497 ÷ 0.4 gives about 8.74 nats. To turn those rewards into chances, divide by beta first, so on the rejected side −2.940 becomes a drop of about 7.35 nats. That is more than ten halvings, so averaged over the three pairs, a loop became over a thousand times less likely. On the chosen side, +0.556 becomes a rise of about 1.4 nats. That is two doublings, so on average a preferred sentence became about four times as likely. These are averages, and the pairs differ. The loop in pair 3 became only about 230 times less likely, and the preferred sentence in pair 1 became only about one and a half times as likely. Watch where each pair sits On Where each pair sits on the loss, the card draws three loss curves, one each for half your beta, your beta and double it. Each curve shows the loss for every possible gap m. The numbered circles sit on the curve for your own beta, the one marked (current) in the legend, and show where your pairs are now. Below the curve, each pair's row gives its m, its loss and its pull, labeled pull σ(−β·m). The pull is the share of full strength that a pair still puts into training, and it equals the chance the formula still gives the rejected answer of winning. So it starts at 50% when m is 0 and falls toward zero as the gap grows. At 40 steps the pairs sit between m = 7.88 and m = 9.50, out on the flat part of the curve. There each one still pulls at only 2 to 4% of full strength. Pair 1 is the worked example from before: with β·m at 3.8, the formula gives the loop about a 2.2% chance, so its pull is 2.2%. Set DPO steps to 4 and the pairs sit near m = 3, still pulling at around 20%. The least separated pair always pulls hardest, so training puts more of its effort into the comparisons closest to a tie. Sweep beta Next, slide Beta and watch Drift from the reference model, which runs three complete trainings side by side. One uses half your beta, one uses your beta and one uses double it, so you can compare them at a glance. Each legend entry gives that run's final gap and its final KL, short for KL divergence. KL is the lab's measure of how far the policy has drifted from the reference, and the badge shows the KL for your own run. Read the legend at 40 steps, then set DPO steps to 4 and read it again, and you will see the order of the KL values flip. Change the step size Because DPO learning rate sets how big each training step is, raising it makes the loss fall faster but also makes the drift grow faster. Lowering it slows both down, which you can see on the DPO loss readout and the KL badge. Check the held-out pairs Scroll to Per-pair rewards, where each pair gets a block with both answers and a bar called a dumbbell. A circle marks the chosen reward, a square marks the rejected reward, and the bar between them is the margin. The dashed line down the middle is zero, which is where the reference sits, and each block says ordered correctly or not ordered. Below your pairs sit three held-out pairs, H1 to H3, which are the same kind of comparison, a good sentence against a loop. They were fixed before any run, and no training step ever uses them: H1 sets "clouds break apart and the sun warms the streets." against "clouds clouds clouds clouds clouds." H2 sets "onions until they turn soft and sweet." against "onions onions onions onions." H3 sets "pasta in salted water until it is tender." against "pasta and the pasta and the pasta." At 40 steps all three training pairs are ordered correctly, but among the held-out pairs only H3 is. H1 and H2 end at margins of −0.54 and −1.12, which means training pushed them the wrong way. H3 moved the right way instead, and its block ends at a margin of +2.90. The badge held-out: 1 of 3 ordered and the readout Held-out pairs ordered correctly both report 1 of 3. On the first chart, the held-out margin (never trained on) line ends at +0.42, against +3.50 for the training pairs. Write your own pair Add a fourth line to Preference pairs, following the same pattern: a short prompt, a sentence you like and a loop you do not. For example, try the | rain falls on the boats. | rain rain rain rain. as a fourth line. Then check whether the new pair ends ordered correctly, and whether the held-out badge changes. You should find the new pair ordered correctly but the badge still at 1 of 3. Even another loop that repeats a word does not teach the model that repeating a word is bad. It mostly changes the character steps inside "rain rain", not a general rule about repeating words. The editor keeps up to 5 lines with up to 50 characters in each part, and it turns capitals into small letters. Characters the model does not have, such as digits and commas, become spaces. Train one pair at a time Copy the three default lines somewhere first, so you can paste them back afterwards. Then delete every line except pair 2, the one whose loop is "pan and the pan and the pan.", and read the margin on H3. Trained on pair 2 alone, H3 ends at +2.25, but if you keep only pair 1 instead, H3 ends at only +0.28. Compare those two loops with the loop in H3 before you read why in "What to notice". With pair 1 alone, look at the held-out badge too, because it reads 3 of 3. That sounds like great news, but every held-out margin is tiny, under +0.3. Training on the fog pair alone moves the held-out pairs only a little, and this time slightly the right way. A passing badge with margins that close to zero is weak evidence too. Switch the reference Last, switch Reference model to SFT checkpoint, which gives training a different starting point. A checkpoint is a saved copy of a model, and SFT, short for supervised fine-tuning, means extra training on examples of good answers to copy. Here the lab takes the base model and trains it for 60 steps to copy your preferred answers. It sees each prompt, but it is only trained to write the preferred answer that follows. That is the same kind of tuning as in *Instruction tuning & templates*, although that lab's own model is never loaded. Real DPO starts from a tuned model like this, which is why the switch is here. The footers under Per-pair rewards now say the reference already preferred it on two of the three training pairs, where the base model preferred none. Even so, at DPO steps 0 the DPO loss still reads 0.6931, because the policy starts as a copy of whichever reference you pick. After 40 steps H1 and H2 end at −1.48 and −1.76, while H3 ends at +2.70. So still only one of the three carries over. Look at the dashed chosen reward line as well, which now ends a little below zero.

documents.subtitle: Plain · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: The margin is bought lopsidedly The rejected side moves about five times further than the chosen side, as the first chart shows with −2.940 against +0.556. Here is how that looks pair by pair at the defaults: In pair 1, the fog pair, the preferred sentence ends at +0.18 and the loop at −3.61. In pair 2, the pan pair, the preferred sentence ends at +0.51 and the loop at −3.03. In pair 3, the sauce pair, the preferred sentence ends at +0.97 and the loop at −2.18. In every row the rejected side moved further, so most of the margin comes from making the bad answer unlikely. In the playlist picture, that means burying the song you skipped rather than playing your favorite more. A common mix-up: a growing margin does not mean the preferred answer became likely. The loss only sees the difference between the two sides, so pushing the rejected side down counts as complete success. If both sides fall and the gap still opens, the run is working as designed. The loss counts that as a success, even though your preferred answer got less likely. That is why the lab plots the two sides apart. You can watch that happen by switching Reference model to SFT checkpoint, where the chosen reward line ends below zero. So on average the preferred answers became slightly less likely than the reference rated them, with two of the three falling. Yet every training pair still ends ordered correctly, because the loops fell much further. Beta does two jobs Beta's first job is to set how big a gap counts as "done", which the note under the loss curve shows for a loss of 0.1: at β 0.2, the gap m has to reach 11.26; at β 0.4, it has to reach 5.63; at β 0.8, it has to reach 2.82. Doubling beta halves the gap needed, so a higher beta reaches the flat part of the curve with a smaller change to the model. On the flat part a pair barely pulls, so training stops changing the model much. The second job comes from the formula and the simple way this lab takes its steps. Beta multiplies the gap inside the loss, so the push each step gives is multiplied by beta too, which means a higher beta also moves faster at the start. The two jobs pull in opposite directions, which is why beta's effect on drift depends on how long you train. With Beta at 0.4 and DPO steps at 40, the drift legend reads like this: β 0.2 ends with a gap of 10.2 nats and a KL of 0.0133; β 0.4 ends with a gap of 8.7 nats and a KL of 0.0102; β 0.8 ends with a gap of 6.2 nats and a KL of 0.0053. So after 40 steps a higher beta ends nearer the reference, but at 4 steps the order flips: β 0.2 ends with a KL of 0.0005; β 0.4 ends with a KL of 0.0013; β 0.8 ends with a KL of 0.0017. Early on, before any pair reaches the flat part, the bigger steps of a higher beta matter more. What beta trades away The gaps in that list show the trade, since a higher beta settles for a smaller gap and so changes the model less to honor your pairs. What it gets in exchange is a policy that stays nearer the reference. Staying near the reference matters because the reference already writes ordinary text. The next part shows that changing the table for three pairs also changes the chances for lots of other text, so less drift means fewer of those side effects. A lower beta trades the other way, pushing the pairs further apart while letting the model wander further from where it started. That trade holds once training has had enough steps to reach the flat part. At a very low beta such as 0.05, each step is so small that after 40 steps DPO loss is still about 0.58, far from the flat part. The gap reaches only about 5 nats, smaller than at 0.4, so in the drift legend a higher beta now gives both a bigger gap and more drift. Be careful with Margin, β-scaled when you compare different betas, because beta multiplies that readout. Set Beta to 0.2 and it reads 2.045, while at 0.8 it reads 4.949, so it rises with beta even though the real gap shrinks. To compare runs fairly, use Log-ratio gap m = margin ÷ β instead. Drift spreads across the whole model As you saw earlier, the model's table has one row of chances for each of the 30 characters it might have read last. KL divergence measures how different the policy's row is from the reference's row, in nats, and the lab averages it evenly over all 30 rows. A KL of 0 means the two tables match exactly, and bigger numbers mean they differ more. For example, if the reference gives "o" a 50% chance after "f" and the policy gives it 25%, that row now differs. KL adds up differences like this across the row, giving more weight to the characters the policy itself rates as likely. Editing three pairs changes every row your answers pass through, which is 21 of the 30 rows at the defaults. Those same rows are used by all other text, through steps like a space followed by "f", so the change spreads well beyond your three answers. With the SFT checkpoint reference, drift is measured from that checkpoint instead, and at the default beta the KL reads 0.0161 rather than 0.0102. The two numbers measure distance from different starting tables, so they are not a like-for-like comparison. Passing the practice pairs is not learning the preference Picture a classmate who gets three practice questions with their answers the night before a test, and drills those three exact questions without learning the idea behind them. The practice sheet earns them 100%, but on the real test they get one question of three right, the one that looked like a practice question. That is what the two badges show: the training badge reads 100% and the held-out badge reads 1 of 3. Getting the studied pairs right is not the same as learning the preference behind them. The picture stops matching in one way, because the model memorized nothing. As the next paragraphs show, it only nudged the chances of single character steps, which helped one held-out pair and hurt the other two. Raising DPO steps keeps lifting the training margin, while H1 and H2 get worse, not better, and the held-out line stays near zero. At the default beta and learning rate, no step count orders more than one held-out pair. H3 carries over because its loop, "pasta and the pasta and the pasta.", shares and the with training pair 2's loop. Pushing pair 2's loop down lowered the chances of the character steps inside and the , and the loop in H3 uses those same steps. That is why training on pair 2 alone gives H3 +2.25, while pair 1 alone gives only +0.28. The loops in H1 and H2 do not contain that piece, and training actually hurt them. Each row's chances must add up to 1, so lowering the steps in the training loops hands their share to other steps in the same rows. Some of that share went to steps the H1 and H2 loops use. The onion loop in H2 ended up about 100 times more likely than before, while H1's good sentence, which contains and the , became less likely. In the playlist picture, burying one song means the others play more, including songs you would also have skipped. The model changed the chances of particular character steps, not a general rule that repeating yourself is bad, which is the playlist picture's second limit at work. Margins are always measured from the reference With the SFT checkpoint reference, the reference already ranks pairs 2 and 3 correctly, and the lab still reports a loss of 0.6931 at 0 steps. Every margin is measured from the reference, whatever it happens to prefer, so the loss only reflects how the policy has moved since training began.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies The loss, the training steps, the rewards and the drift are all computed for real, and the part that is small is the model itself. It looks at one character to guess the next, using a table of 30 rows by 30 columns, or 900 numbers in all. So an answer is a chain of character-to-character steps, and nothing in the model can see a whole word. Prompts make no difference here, because the editor always ends a prompt with a space and the model reads only that last character. So every answer starts from the same place, whatever prompt you write. Shared steps cause side effects, because the steps inside "fog fog fog" are the same steps ordinary harbor text needs. Pushing the loop down therefore takes probability from useful text too, and even the preferred answer starts with "fog ", so the two share their first few steps. A model that could see more context could learn that a phrase is fine once and bad five times over, but this one cannot. The training setup is tiny: three pairs, one full update per step that uses every pair at once, and no answers written by the model during training. Real training works through thousands of pairs, fed in a group at a time. The flip in drift order at 4 steps comes from the simple stepping method this lab uses, called gradient descent, which moves every number by the same rule. Real training often uses a method called Adam, which adjusts each step's size on its own and mostly removes the flip. Drift is an even average, so every one of the 30 rows counts equally, however often its character appears in real text. The held-out test is small: three fixed pairs of one kind, a sentence against a loop. It shows that ordering does not carry over automatically, not how often it does. The SFT checkpoint is tuned on your own preferred answers, so it prefers them by design, while real tuning data is separate and far larger. The sizes belong to a toy, because these are chances for short strings of characters, so trust which answer wins more than the exact numbers. The drift card also shows two samples, meaning short pieces of text each model writes by itself. They are labeled Reference model and After preference optimization, and both start from "the " with the same random seed. The seed is a number that fixes the lab's dice rolls, so any difference between the two samples comes from training. Both look jumbled because the model only sees one character back. Where the real method fails A rising margin is evidence about the margin, not about how good the answers are. When the measured number keeps improving while people judge the answers as flat or worse, that is called reward hacking. DPO removes the separate scorer but not this problem, because the margin itself becomes the number that can be gamed. Length bias is the concrete case, and it works in two ways. First, the raw score of an answer leans toward shorter answers, because every extra character adds another chance below 1 to multiply in. Pair 1 shows it: the preferred sentence is 28 characters against 20 for the loop, which alone pulls its raw score down. Second, picture a teacher who, without meaning to, tends to give higher marks to longer essays, until students notice and start padding their work. In the same way, if the preferred answers in a set of comparisons tend to be the longer ones, the model learns to write longer answers, better or not. Real comparisons have other gaps between what they measure and what you want: Real comparisons usually come from some other model's answers, so the policy is taught about text that it would not have written itself. Real collections run to tens of thousands of comparisons and carry the habits of the people who labeled them, such as favoring length, confidence and formatting. A small average drift can hide a large change in one narrow slice of behavior. A small pull only means the loss has stopped asking for more, and it does not prove the pair was learned in any useful sense.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: The full formula The card shows the short form, loss −log σ(β·m), while the long form below names every piece: L = −log sigmoid(beta · ((logp_chosen − logp_chosen_ref) − (logp_rejected − logp_rejected_ref))) Read it from the inside out, starting with the first bracket, which is how far the preferred answer's score moved from the reference. The second bracket is the same for the rejected answer, and the difference between the two brackets is the gap m. The rest is the same beta, sigmoid and −log that you worked through earlier. Where the formula comes from The formula is not a guess, because it starts from RLHF's goal: raise the reward while a penalty holds the model near the reference. That penalty is a KL divergence, the same kind of drift measure this lab shows, although RLHF measures it on answers the model writes itself. That goal has a known best answer, and working backwards from it lets you write the reward in a new form. The reward becomes beta times the log-ratio, the policy's log-probability minus the reference's, plus a part that depends only on the prompt. Then put that reward into the standard formula for comparisons, called the Bradley-Terry model, which says the chance of preferring one answer is the sigmoid of the reward difference. It is a bit like a game where your chance of beating a rival depends only on the gap between your ratings. The prompt-only part is the same for both answers, so it cancels out, and the separate scorer drops out with it. That is also why an implicit reward only compares answers to the same prompt. The penalty was folded into the formula rather than removed, so beta is both the reward's scale and the strength of the pull toward the reference. How real runs start Real DPO runs on top of an SFT checkpoint, a saved model that has already had supervised fine-tuning, meaning extra training on examples of instructions and good responses. That same checkpoint is normally used as the reference as well. The DPO paper, by Rafailov and colleagues in 2023, says to start from the tuned model when you have one, and otherwise to tune on the preferred answers first. That fallback is what Reference model SFT checkpoint does here, but the default is still the base model, so the usual order is only followed once you switch. Fixes people have tried Later versions of the method each fix one of the limits above: versions that take answer length into account, aimed at length bias; versions that need no reference model, so there is no second model to keep in memory; an extra term on the preferred side, to stop both sides from sinking together; online versions, which have the current model write fresh answers and then get those answers labeled. What people watch The checks people rely on in real training are the ones shown here, starting with both sides of the margin plotted apart and the share of pairs ordered correctly. The other two are the drift from the reference and a check on pairs the optimizer never trained on.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: This module is about direct preference optimization (DPO): training a language model on comparisons, each a prompt with a preferred and a rejected completion, through one classification-style loss. It asks what a successful-looking run has actually changed: which completions moved, how far the model drifted from its starting point, and whether the preference holds on comparisons it never trained on. It follows Post-training, which fitted a reward model to comparisons and optimized against it under a KL penalty, a cost on drifting from a reference distribution. Instruction tuning & templates supplies the response-only loss that builds this lab's optional SFT checkpoint, a stand-in for the supervised fine-tuned model DPO normally starts from. Where it shows up After supervised fine-tuning. Production DPO runs on an SFT checkpoint, which is normally also the frozen reference. Without one, Rafailov et al. (2023) build the reference by maximizing the likelihood of the preferred completions, which is how this lab's SFT checkpoint is built. On off-policy data. Pairs are usually collected from some other model's outputs. As a family of objectives. Length-normalized and reference-free variants (SimPO, ORPO), an added likelihood term on the preferred side, and online variants that sample fresh completions from the model being trained each target one of DPO's known limits. In run monitoring. Production diagnostics match the lab's readouts: both sides of the margin plotted apart, the share of pairs ordered correctly, drift, and a check on unseen pairs. Why it matters DPO turns comparisons into gradients with no reward model, no sampling and no reinforcement-learning loop. The KL penalty survives inside the loss: every reward is measured against a frozen reference model, and beta sets how strongly the policy, the model being trained, is held near it. Without that anchor, nothing in the loss would keep the policy close to a working model. The cost is a result that is easy to misread. The loss sees only the margin between the two completions, can be satisfied mostly by making the rejected one unlikely, and grades only the training pairs. Without separate readouts for each side, for drift and for unseen pairs, a falling loss looks like a learned preference whether or not it is one. What you will be able to explain Run DPO on comparisons you write, and say why the loss reads ln 2 before the first step whatever the pairs contain. Read an implicit reward margin correctly: the gap between two completions of one prompt, each scored by beta times its log-probability gain over the reference, and never a quality score. Explain what beta trades away: separation between the completions against drift from the reference, and why, under this lab's plain gradient descent, that trade depends on the step budget. Judge whether a preference gain carries over, by scoring held-out pairs the optimizer never saw. What the lab shows Every loss, gradient, reward and KL value is genuinely computed; the model, the data and the optimizer are deliberately simple. The model conditions on one preceding character through 900 logits, trains on the pairs you write (three by default), and updates by plain full-batch gradient descent with no sampling. Reference model chooses Base model, a table trained 50 epochs on the Harbor and Recipes corpora, or SFT checkpoint, that base fine-tuned here on your preferred completions. In the Preference pair editor, write comparisons in Preference pairs as prompt | preferred | rejected, then set DPO steps, Beta and DPO learning rate. Each change retrains from the reference. Implicit reward margin during training plots the margin and both of its sides, averaged over the training pairs, at every step, and the held-out margin at evenly spaced step counts along the same run. Where each pair sits on the loss places each pair's measured log-ratio margin m, the margin with beta divided out, on the closed-form loss curve for the current beta, beside the curves for half and double beta. Drift from the reference model plots KL from the reference, averaged evenly over 30 context rows, at three betas. Per-pair rewards shows both rewards for every training pair and for the held-out pairs H1 to H3, three fixed comparisons written before any run. The key experiment raises DPO steps from 0 and compares the training pairs' ordered correctly badge with Held-out pairs ordered correctly. At the defaults every training pair ends ordered correctly, but only one of the three held-out pairs does.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: DPO trains on comparisons directly. There is no reward model, no sampling, and no reinforcement-learning loop — just one loss over pairs of completions: L = −log sigmoid(beta · ((logp_chosen − logp_chosen_ref) − (logp_rejected − logp_rejected_ref))) The implicit reward of a completion is beta times how much more log-probability the policy — the model being trained — gives it than the frozen reference model does. The margin is the chosen completion's implicit reward minus the rejected one's. The loss is a decreasing function of the margin and of nothing else. By default the reference model is a real checkpoint: 50 epochs on the Harbor and Recipes corpora, a base table. Production DPO starts from an SFT checkpoint instead. Reference model in the pair editor can switch to one: the same base, fine-tuned here on your preferred completions with a response-only loss, as in *Instruction tuning & templates*. That lab's own weights are never loaded. The policy starts as an exact copy of the reference. Set DPO steps to 0 and DPO loss shows 0.6931, because every margin is exactly zero and −log sigmoid(0) is ln 2. What the comparisons look like The three default pairs in Preference pair editor use prompt | preferred | rejected, and every rejected completion is degenerate repetition — "fog fog fog fog fog." against "fog settles over the harbor.". Looping on a phrase is a genuinely high-probability failure for a small model, and in all three pairs the reference model assigns the loop the higher raw probability.

documents.body: Post-training made the case for learning from comparisons: ranking two replies is faster and more reliable than writing an ideal one, and DPO reaches the RLHF objective without a separate scorer. It described DPO but never ran it. The margin needs care precisely because it is the quantity being optimized. That makes it the last quantity that can serve as evidence the optimization did what you wanted.

documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: In this lab. The objective, the gradients, the rewards and the KL are all real; the model is not. It conditions on one preceding character through 900 logits, so a completion is a chain of character transitions. Three pairs, full-batch plain gradient descent, and no sampling. Drift is an even average over the 30 context rows, not weighted by how often each occurs. The transitions inside "fog fog fog" are the same ones ordinary harbor text needs, so pushing the rejected completion down necessarily takes probability from useful text. A model with real context can learn that a phrase is fine once and bad five times in a row; this one cannot. With Adam, which rescales steps per parameter, beta's step-size role largely disappears and its saturating role dominates. The early-steps flip above is a property of plain gradient descent. The held-out set is three fixed comparisons of one kind, a corpus sentence against a loop. It shows that ordering does not carry over automatically, not how often it does. The SFT checkpoint is trained on the same preferred completions the pairs contain, so it prefers them by construction; a real SFT set is separate and far larger. In real systems. A rising margin is evidence about the margin. Reward hacking — the measured objective improving while human-judged quality stalls — survives the removal of the reward model, because the margin is now the exploitable quantity. Length bias is the concrete case. Raw total log-probability always favours the shorter completion, and preference data in which longer answers tend to win teaches the policy to write longer. Pairs are also usually collected off-policy, from some other model's outputs, so the policy is taught about text it would not have produced.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: The closed form comes from RLHF. Maximizing reward minus β times the KL to the reference has a known optimal policy, πref · exp(r / β) / Z(x). Inverting it writes the reward as β · log(π / πref) plus a per-prompt constant, and that constant cancels inside the Bradley-Terry likelihood for a pair. The KL constraint is not dropped — it is absorbed, which is why beta is both the reward scale and the constraint strength. The variants each attack one limit above: length-normalized and reference-free objectives (SimPO, ORPO) for length bias and the second model's memory, an added likelihood term on the chosen side for the "both sides fell" outcome, and online variants that sample fresh completions from the current policy and label those. DPO is run on a supervised fine-tuned checkpoint, and that checkpoint is normally the reference. Rafailov et al. (2023, arXiv 2305.18290) initialize the reference from the SFT model when one exists and, when it does not, by maximizing the likelihood of the preferred completions. That fallback is what Reference model SFT checkpoint does here. The default is still the base table, so the lineage is only followed once you switch. The production diagnostics are the ones on screen here: both sides plotted apart, the share of pairs ordered correctly, drift, and a check on pairs the optimizer never trained on.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Implicit reward margin during training · Preference optimization in practice
documents.body: The quantity DPO actually optimizes The implicit reward margin at every DPO step, with the chosen and rejected rewards that make it up. Every point comes from a real DPO gradient run against a frozen reference model trained on this page. A chart of DPO step against implicit reward, β times a log-probability shift from the reference, averaged over the pairs. Four series with their final values: `margin (chosen − rejected)` solid, `chosen reward` dashed, `rejected reward` dotted, and `held-out margin (never trained on)`, a solid line in a second colour. The margin is exactly the distance between the chosen and rejected lines. A kicker with the training pair count, the held-out count, beta and steps, and two badges: the share of training pairs whose margin is strictly positive, and how many of the three held-out pairs are. Four metrics: `DPO loss` averaged over pairs, `Margin, β-scaled`, `Log-ratio gap m = margin ÷ β`, the same gap with β divided back out, and `Held-out pairs ordered correctly`. The loss is `−log σ(β · ((log πθ(y_w|x) − log πref(y_w|x)) − (log πθ(y_l|x) − log πref(y_l|x))))`, averaged over the pairs. It depends on the policy only through that margin. The reference is 50 epochs on Harbor weather notes and Recipe steps at seed 1, or, under `Reference model`, that base fine-tuned on your preferred completions. The policy starts as an exact copy of whichever it is, so at step 0 every reward is 0 and the loss is ln 2 = 0.6931. A completion's log-probability sums its character transitions, starting from the prompt's last character. Prompts keep a trailing space, so `the | fog …` is scored as `the fog …`. Each step is one full-batch update over every pair: learning rate times the gradient β·σ(−β·m)·∇m. The held-out line is β times the mean log-ratio gap of three fixed pairs the optimizer never uses, read at five evenly spaced step counts along one run of the same update. A test checks it against the trainer. `DPO steps`, `Beta`, `DPO learning rate` and the pair editor all retrain from the reference. Comparison worth running: at the defaults the chosen reward ends at +0.556 and the rejected at −2.940. Set `DPO steps` to 0 and every line collapses to 0. Then read the held-out line. At the defaults the training badge reads 100% and the held-out badge reads 1 of 3, and the held-out margin ends at +0.42 against +3.50 for the training pairs. At the default beta and learning rate no step count orders more than one held-out pair. The margin is bought lopsidedly: the rejected side moves about five times further than the chosen side. Both sides falling while the margin grows would not be a fault. The loss sees only the difference. At 0 steps the badge reads 0% because it counts strictly positive margins, and every margin is exactly zero. The training margin keeps climbing with more steps. The held-out line does not follow it: two of the three held-out pairs get worse as training continues. In this lab: the objective, gradients, loss and rewards are genuinely computed, but the model is a 30 × 30 character bigram. The mechanism is real; the capability is not. In this lab: by default the reference is a base table trained 50 epochs on Harbor and Recipes. The `SFT checkpoint` choice is a second model trained here on your preferred completions with a response-only loss; the weights from `Instruction tuning & templates` are never loaded. In this lab: the held-out set is three fixed comparisons of one kind, a corpus sentence against a loop, written before any run. It shows that ordering does not carry over automatically, not how often it does. In this lab: every series is multiplied by β. The `Log-ratio gap` metric removes β so runs at different betas can be compared. In general: a rising margin is evidence about the margin. DPO can over-optimize just as RLHF can, because the margin itself is now the exploitable quantity. In general: DPO starts from a supervised fine-tuned checkpoint and uses that same checkpoint as the frozen reference, so the margin measures movement away from the SFT model.
