documents.body: A table of scores Start with the table that the lab rounds, which comes from a tiny model that reads one character at a time and guesses the next one. Its alphabet has 30 characters: the 26 letters, a space, a full stop and two spare symbols. For each character it could have read last, the model keeps a row of 30 scores, one for every character that could come next. That makes a 30 by 30 table of 900 numbers, and those numbers are the model’s weights. A higher score means that a character is more likely to come next, and a lower score means it is less likely. The biggest score in the table is 5.93, for a space right after a full stop. The model learned from its training text that a space nearly always follows a full stop, so every other character in that row scores only about −0.20. The lab’s chart calls each weight a logit, which is the name for a raw score before it is turned into a probability. It also calls the whole thing a bigram table, meaning a table about pairs of characters that sit next to each other. The model was trained on a short collection of harbour weather notes for 80 epochs, where an epoch is one full pass through the training text. Its quality is measured by perplexity, which says how unsure the model is, on average, about each next character in that text. A model guessing at random among all 30 characters would score 30, while this table scores 6.600. That is as unsure as choosing among about 6.6 equally likely characters, and lower is better, so watch this number rise as the rounding gets rougher. Short codes instead of long numbers Each extra bit doubles the number of different patterns you can make, because every old pattern can now end in either a 0 or a 1. One bit gives two patterns, 0 and 1, while two bits give four: 00, 01, 10 and 11. Keep doubling and you find that 4 bits gives 16 patterns, while 8 bits gives 256 of them. A group of eight bits is called a byte, which is the unit that file sizes are usually counted in. The original table stores each weight in 32 bits, which is enough to write a number like 1.0174948 with about seven digits of detail. Quantization replaces those 32 bits with a much shorter code, such as 4 bits, plus a little shared information that turns the codes back into numbers. The rebuilt weight keeps its meaning but loses some detail, in the same way that 165 keeps the meaning of 164.73. Rounding onto a ruler Picture a ruler laid along the number line beneath the weights, with a fixed number of evenly spaced tick marks. Each weight slides to its nearest tick, and instead of storing the weight itself, you store only which tick it landed on, counting up from the start. That tick number is the weight’s code, a small whole number such as 0, 5 or 15. To turn a code back into a number later, you also need to know where the ruler starts and how far apart its ticks are. The gap between neighbouring ticks is the scale, and the lab’s readout for it is called Step in this block. The value where the ruler starts is the zero point, which is the value that code 0 stands for. The lab calls the ruler a grid and its ticks levels, so a 16-level grid is a ruler with 16 ticks. Bit width sets how many ticks there are, since every tick needs its own pattern of bits, and 4 bits gives 16. Fewer ticks means wider gaps between them, so each weight has to move further, on average, before it reaches one. A worked example from the lab Take the whole table at 4 bits with one ruler, which is what you get when Scaling granularity is set to Per tensor. That is the lab’s name for one ruler for the whole table, explained below. The smallest weight is −1.71 and the largest is 5.93, so the ruler has to stretch across a distance of 7.64 to cover them both. Sixteen ticks leave 15 gaps between them, so each gap is 7.64 ÷ 15, which is about 0.51. Under the chart, the lab writes this rule as scale = (max − min) / 15, where max and min are the largest and smallest weights that the ruler has to cover. Now round a weight of 1.00, which sits 2.71 along the ruler, because 1.00 minus −1.71 is 2.71. Dividing 2.71 by the gap of 0.51 gives about 5.3, so the weight sits about 5.3 gaps along. The nearest tick is tick 5, and the number 5 is the code that gets stored. To rebuild the weight, start at −1.71 and add 5 gaps of 0.51 each, which lands on about 0.84. The rebuilt weight is 0.84 where the original was 1.00, so rounding has moved this weight by about 0.16. No weight on the ruler can move by more than half a gap, since a weight halfway between two ticks is as far from both as it can be. Here half a gap is about 0.25, and the Largest error readout shows a value a hair under that. Measuring the damage How far a weight moves is called its rounding error, and the lab writes it as w′ − w, which you read as “w prime minus w”. It means the rebuilt weight minus the original one, so a positive error means the weight was rounded up and a negative one means it was rounded down. The lower strip of the Rounding grid and per-weight error card draws one dot for every weight. Each dot sits left or right according to the weight’s original value, and up or down according to its error. To boil all 900 errors down to one number, the lab uses RMS rounding error, where RMS stands for “root mean square”. You square every error, find the average of those squares, and then take the square root of that average. Suppose one weight moved up by 0.1 and another moved down by 0.3, so that squaring makes both positive and gives 0.01 and 0.09. Their average is 0.05, and the square root of 0.05 is about 0.22, which is a little more than the plain average size of 0.2. The squaring gives a bigger miss more say than a small one, so a few large errors push RMS up quickly. What matters in the end, though, is not how far the weights moved but how much worse the model writes as a result. The Quality against bits per weight card measures that by running the rounded table over the training text and reading its perplexity again. Its Full precision readout shows the original 6.600, and Quantized shows the perplexity of the rounded table. Quality cost then shows how much higher the second number is than the first, as a percentage of the first. At 4 bits with one ruler, Quantized reads 6.662, which is 0.062 above the original perplexity of 6.600. Since 0.062 is 0.94% of 6.600, Quality cost reads +0.94%, which means the perplexity has gone up by a little less than 1 part in 100. Where the ruler picture stops matching A real ruler’s ticks cost nothing, because they are printed once and the same ruler can be used for years. Here, every ruler has to be written down and stored beside the codes, or the codes could never be turned back into numbers. On the default setting, every ruler costs 32 bits to store: 16 bits for its start and 16 bits for its gap. That cost is the central tension of the whole lab, since more rulers fit the weights better but each one adds to the bill. Two ways to lay the ruler The Range mapping control decides where each ruler sits on the number line, and it has two settings. Asymmetric · min/max is the default, and it starts the ruler at the smallest weight it covers and ends it at the largest. Every tick then sits over real data, so none is wasted, but the ruler must store both its start and its gap, which costs 32 bits. Symmetric · absmax centres the ruler on zero and stretches it the same distance in both directions, out to the weight that sits furthest from zero. The “absmax” in its name means the largest absolute value, which is the biggest distance from zero on either side. Because the middle tick is always exactly zero, this ruler does not need to store its start, so it costs 16 bits instead of 32. This layout is called symmetric quantization, and it is cheaper to store and simpler to compute with. To stay balanced around zero, a symmetric 4-bit ruler uses the codes from −7 to +7, which makes 15 ticks rather than 16. These codes count outward from the middle tick instead of up from the start, so code 0 stands for exactly zero and there is no separate zero point to store. You can see this in the Bit width label, which reads “4 bits · 15 levels” whenever the symmetric setting is on. The trouble starts when the weights lean to one side, as they do here, since this table runs from −1.71 up to 5.93. A symmetric ruler has to stretch from −5.93 all the way to +5.93, so every tick below −1.71 sits over empty space where no weight will ever land. With 7 ticks above zero, the ruler needs 7 gaps to climb from 0 to 5.93, so each gap is 5.93 ÷ 7, or about 0.85. That is much coarser than the 0.51 of the asymmetric ruler. One ruler or many The Scaling granularity control decides how many weights share one ruler, and the lab calls a set of weights that share a ruler a block. Per tensor gives all 900 weights a single ruler, and since a whole table of weights is called a tensor, this is per-tensor scaling. Per row gives each of the 30 rows its own ruler, so there is one ruler for each character the model could have read last. Per group gives each short run of neighbouring weights its own ruler, which is called group scaling, and the run length is set by the Group size slider. The Group size slider only appears in Per group mode, and it runs from 2 up to 30 weights per ruler in steps of two. A ruler that covers fewer weights only has to stretch across their range, which is usually narrower than the range of the whole table. A narrower range means smaller gaps and smaller gaps mean smaller errors, so going from one ruler to many usually makes the rounding far more accurate. The danger with a shared ruler is a single extreme weight, which is called an outlier because it lies far outside the range of its neighbours. Picture a class lining up for a photo beside a height chart with 16 marks, spread evenly from the shortest student to the tallest. Then a visiting basketball player joins the end of the line, far taller than anyone else in the class. The chart has to stretch up to reach them, so its marks spread apart and every ordinary student ends up crowded around the bottom few marks. Weights behave in the same way, since one far-out weight stretches any ruler it shares. The more weights share that ruler, the more of them get stuck with its wide gaps. The story stops matching this table in one place, though, because the table has no single giant. Several rows hold big scores of their own, such as 5.61 and 5.42, not far below the 5.93. So the one shared ruler is wide because the whole table is spread out, not because of one weight, and taking away the 5.93 alone would barely narrow it. Smaller blocks help here mainly because each row or group covers a much narrower range than the whole table. They also stop any one big score from widening everyone else’s gaps. Inside its own row, though, the 5.93 really is an outlier, since every other score after a full stop is about −0.20. You will see what it does to that row’s ruler in How to play with it. Bits per weight: the real bill Bit width counts the bits in each code, but each weight also has to pay for its share of a ruler. That true cost is called bits per weight, and it adds each ruler’s 32 bits, shared out evenly among the weights that use the ruler. Here is how the three choices work out at 4 bits, where every code takes 4 bits before the rulers are added: Per tensor: one 32-bit ruler shared by 900 weights adds only about 0.04 bits to each one, so Bits per weight reads about 4.04. Per row: 30 rulers cost 960 bits in total, which comes to about 1.07 extra bits for each weight, so the readout is about 5.07. Per group with a Group size of 8: each ruler is shared by only 8 weights, so its 32 bits add 4 more bits to each, for about 8.02. That last figure sits slightly above 8 because 900 does not split evenly into groups of 8, which leaves a final group of only 4 weights. At groups of 8, about half of all the storage goes on rulers rather than on codes, and the note under the readouts spells out the same sum. Push Group size down to 2 and each ruler is shared by only two weights, adding 16 bits to each, for a total of 20 bits per weight. The rounding error drops to zero, because a ruler for two weights starts on one of them and ends on the other. But 20 bits is more than the 16 bits of the half-precision format you will meet later, so the “shrunk” table is now bigger than a plain 16-bit copy. The same card also turns bits into a size, using the Model size readout, which gives the whole table’s size in bytes. At 4 bits per tensor, 900 codes of half a byte each make 450 bytes, and the single ruler adds 4 bytes. So the readout says 454 B, where B stands for bytes. Against 32-bit compares that with the original table, which takes 4 bytes per weight or 3,600 bytes in all, so it reads 12.6%. Real formats have names Programs that run models on ordinary computers do not let you pick any ruler size you like, because they use fixed recipes called block types. The ones in this lab come from llama.cpp, a program for running language models on your own computer. It is also the engine behind this app’s optional local model. Each block type fixes how many weights share a ruler, how many bits each code gets, and how the ruler itself is stored. The number after the Q in a block type’s name is the code width in bits, so Q4_0, Q4_1 and Q4_K all store 4-bit codes. The rest of the name tells you how the rulers are stored, and the Published quantization formats card lists each layout in detail: Q4_0 gives every 32 weights one symmetric ruler with a 16-bit gap, so its ruler adds 16 ÷ 32 = 0.5 bits to each weight, for 4.5 in total. Q4_1 adds a 16-bit start to each ruler so that it can sit off-centre, which doubles the ruler cost to a whole bit per weight, for 5.0 in total. Q4_K puts 256 weights in one big block and splits it into eight groups of 32, then squeezes each group’s ruler into small 6-bit numbers. That last layout is a K-quant. Each group’s start and gap take 6 bits each, so the eight groups need 8 × 12 = 96 bits. The whole block then adds two 16-bit numbers that turn those small numbers back into real ones. That makes 128 bits of ruler for 256 weights, or half a bit per weight. So a K-quant spends half a bit per weight on rulers instead of one, and Q4_K costs 4.5 bits per weight, the same as Q4_0. Yet it keeps the off-centre rulers that make Q4_1 accurate. A whole model contains many tensors, and one file can mix block types across them, which is what a file name like Q4_K_M describes. It is a recipe built around Q4_K that keeps some sensitive tensors in larger types such as Q5_K or Q6_K. An ending of S, for small, keeps fewer tensors in the larger types, and M, for medium, keeps more. Some types, such as Q3_K, also come in an L version, for large, that keeps more still. All of this travels in a single file called a GGUF file. It holds the tensors in their block types, along with the information that turns codes back into numbers. The file also holds the tokenizer, the part that splits text into the pieces that a model reads. The file begins with a header, a short description of what is inside, which a program checks before it trusts the rest of the file. This app does the same kind of check for its own local engine before starting it. Predicting a file’s size and rough quality To predict a file’s size, multiply the number of weights by the bits per weight, and then divide by 8 to turn bits into bytes. File sizes are often given in GiB, short for gibibytes, where one GiB is 1,024 × 1,024 × 1,024 bytes, a little over a billion. The model this app downloads has 1,881,825,088 weights, which the lab calls parameters, so you can try this prediction on a real file. If every one of those weights were stored as Q4_K at 4.5 bits, the file would come to about 0.99 GiB. The real file is 1.19 GiB, which is 21.0% bigger than that prediction, because its recipe keeps many tensors in larger types. Dividing the real file’s size in bits by its number of weights gives its Effective bits per weight, 5.445, the true average cost. Rough quality is harder to read from a name, but it follows a pattern that the formats table makes clear. More bits per code usually means smaller gaps and less damage, so Q8_0 costs almost nothing on this table, while Q3_K and Q2_K cost noticeably more. The RMS error column is not perfectly in order, though, because the way a type stores its rulers matters too. Q3_K uses symmetric rulers that waste ticks on this lopsided table, so its RMS error is slightly larger than that of Q2_K, even though Q2_K still costs more in quality. Among types with the same code width, the cleverer ruler storage of Q4_K buys the accuracy of Q4_1 for half a bit less. Still, a name is a promise about storage rather than quality, which always has to be measured on the task you care about. How computers write ordinary numbers Everything so far started from weights stored in 32 bits, but those 32 bits do not use a ruler at all. They use a different layout called a floating-point format, or a float for short, and the Float formats card compares five of them. You may have seen big numbers written in scientific notation, such as 6.5 × 10,000 for 65,000, which splits a number into two parts. The first part holds the digits, here 6.5, and the second is a power of ten that sets how big the number is. Picture a friend’s old calculator that shows every number as three digits times a power of ten. It can show 1.23 or 1,230, but it has to round 1,234, since that would need a fourth digit. If the largest power it allows is 1,000, it cannot show 50,000 at all, however you round it. The first problem is about precision, meaning how finely numbers can be told apart, and the second is about range, meaning how big a number can be. A float works the same way, except it uses powers of two, the numbers you reach by doubling again and again from 1. Its bits split into three parts: one sign bit, which says whether the number is positive or negative, so that the rest of the bits only have to describe its size; exponent bits, which pick the power of two and so set the format’s range, meaning how big or small a number it can hold; mantissa bits, which hold the digits and so set its precision, meaning how finely it can tell nearby numbers apart. Each exponent value picks one stretch of the number line, running from a power of two up to the next one, such as from 2 to 4. The mantissa bits split that stretch into equal steps, one for each pattern they can make, so a format with 10 mantissa bits makes 1,024 steps in every stretch. In the stretch from 1 to 2, each of those steps is about 0.001 wide, which is what the Spacing at 1.0 column shows for such a format. The column writes it as 2^−10, meaning 1 divided by 2 ten times over, which is 1 ÷ 1,024. Higher stretches are wider but still have the same number of steps, so the steps grow as the numbers grow. That is why a float keeps about the same number of digits of detail whether a number is tiny or huge. The exponent bits decide how many stretches there are, and so they decide the largest number the format can write. Take fp16, which has 5 exponent bits and 10 mantissa bits. Its 5 exponent bits make 32 patterns. Roughly half of them pick stretches below 1, for tiny numbers, and a couple are kept for special jobs. So the highest stretch starts at 32,768, which is 1 doubled 15 times, and runs up to 65,536. Each of its 1,024 steps in that stretch is 32 wide, so the largest number fp16 can write is one step short of 65,536, which is 65,504. Anything bigger than that does not fit at all, however it is rounded, and the lab marks such a number as overflow. The lab lines up five formats, from the most bits to the fewest, and writes each one as sign plus exponent plus mantissa bits: fp32 is 1 + 8 + 23 bits, which is the full precision that this lab starts from and compares everything else against. fp16, also called half precision, is 1 + 5 + 10 bits, so it has fewer exponent bits than fp32 and far fewer mantissa bits. bf16 is 1 + 8 + 7 bits, so it keeps all of fp32’s exponent bits and its huge range, but it has fewer mantissa bits than fp16. fp8 E4M3 is 1 + 4 + 3 bits, where the name means 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits. fp8 E5M2 is 1 + 5 + 2 bits, which gives it more range than E4M3 but even less precision. So a number can go wrong in a float format in two separate ways, and the lab shows you which one is happening. It can be too big for the exponent bits, which is a range problem, and then the lab marks it overflow. Or it can fit but land between two of the format’s values, which is a precision problem, and the Error column shows how far off it ends up. Very small numbers have a problem of their own, which shows up in the Smallest normal to largest column. As numbers get smaller, the stretches get shorter and the steps inside them shrink too, but the exponent bits eventually run out of smaller stretches. The first number in that column is the smallest normal value, the smallest number where the usual pattern still works. Below that number, the steps stop shrinking and stay the size they were in the lowest stretch, so tiny numbers keep fewer digits of detail. The lab calls a number stored down there subnormal. A number smaller than half of one of those steps has nowhere to go but zero, which is called underflow, and the lab says it “underflows to zero”.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Quantization
documents.body: The problem: every token reads every weight A model writes text one token at a time, where a token is a small piece of text such as a word or part of a word. For every token, the model reads all of its weights out of memory once. A long answer runs to hundreds of tokens, so that reading happens again and again. A model stored in half the bits has half as much to read each time, which is why bits per weight affects speed as well as size. That is also why the Deployment & serving lab, later in this app, counts a model’s weights in bits. It uses them to work out how much memory a model needs, including the file this app downloads. Why plain rounding is not enough Rounding with one ruler for everything works well at 8 bits, but it falls apart quickly as you take bits away. At 2 bits per tensor the ruler has only four ticks, about 2.55 apart, and the model’s perplexity rises by almost a quarter. The tools in this module are the fixes for that problem: where each ruler starts, how far apart its ticks are, and how many weights share it. Each of those fixes costs something, because a ruler with its own start takes more storage than one centred on zero, and more rulers take more storage still. Real formats such as Q4_K are the result of balancing those costs carefully, and this lab lets you see each part of that balance on its own. Rounding after training is finished Everything in this lab happens after training is over, so nothing is retrained and the model’s weights are only rounded. Quantizing a finished model like this is called post-training quantization, and it is cheap enough that anyone can apply it to a model whose weights have been released. The downside is that plain rounding looks only at the weights themselves and not at how the model uses them. Better methods first run some sample text through the model to measure which weights matter most, and then use that to round more carefully. That step is called calibration, and the file this app downloads records that it was calibrated in this way. Why number formats belong here too The 32-bit starting point is a choice as well, and smaller float formats such as bf16 and fp8 save space in a different way from integer codes. Instead of sharing one ruler, they keep a separate exponent for every number, which lets each number carry its own sense of size. The Float formats card shows what each format gives up, so you can tell when a value runs out of range and when it only loses precision.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Quantization
documents.body: Work through the cards in order, since each step builds on the one before, and remember that the lab opens at 4 bits with groups of 8. Round the weights Try this: Set Scaling granularity to Per tensor and pull Bit width from 8 down to 2. Watch the dots in the lower strip of Rounding grid and per-weight error line up into a sawtooth, which is a row of slanted teeth. Each tooth is one gap of the ruler: as a weight slides from one tick towards the next, its error grows steadily until it reaches half a gap. Then the weight snaps to the next tick and its error flips to the other side, so each tooth is exactly one gap wide. As you take bits away, the gaps widen, so the teeth get wider. They get taller too, but the strip rescales to fit them, so read the numbers on its left edge: about +0.015 at 8 bits, and about +1.27 at 2 bits. The top half of the same card is a histogram, a bar chart that counts how many weights fall in each small range of values. The ruler’s ticks are drawn over it as vertical lines, solid where at least one weight landed and dashed where none did. Its bars use a square-root scale, which squashes the tallest bars so that the few large weights still show up beside the big pile near zero. At 7 and 8 bits there are too many ticks to draw, so the chart prints a note instead, and the lines appear once you reach 6 bits. Here is what the readouts show at each width, with RMS rounding error rounded to three decimals and Quality cost as the lab prints it: 8 bits: the error is 0.008 and the cost is +0.01%, which is too small to matter. 5 bits: the error is 0.074 and the cost is +0.14%, which is still a small change. 4 bits: the error is 0.147 and the cost is +0.94%, a little under one percent. 3 bits: the error is 0.353 and the cost is +5.03%, which is now clearly visible. 2 bits: the error is 0.967 and the cost is +23.90%, so perplexity is almost a quarter higher. Below 5 bits, each bit you remove multiplies the cost by roughly five to seven, so losing bits is cheap at first and then suddenly very expensive. While you are at 2 bits, look at the two text samples on Quality against bits per weight, which show what each version of the model writes. Both start from the prompt “the ” and write 76 characters at temperature 0.7, a setting for how much chance goes into picking each character. Both panels also roll the same dice, so any difference between the full-precision text and the rounded text comes from the rounded weights. Change the granularity Set Bit width back to 4 and click through the three Scaling granularity choices while you watch RMS rounding error. It falls from 0.147 with one ruler to 0.031 with a ruler per row, and then to 0.027 for groups of 8. Now read Bits per weight for the same three settings, which come to about 4.04, 5.07 and 8.02. Shorter rulers fit better, but every ruler costs 32 bits to store, so the storage bill climbs as the error falls. Then pick Per row and look at Inspect block, the slider that chooses which block’s ruler is drawn on the chart. It starts on the block that holds the largest weight, the row for the full stop, where Step in this block reads 0.41. That is because the 5.93 score has stretched this ruler far above the rest of the row. Levels used in this block reads 2 of 16. The 5.93 takes the top tick, and the other 29 weights in this row are all the same, about −0.20, so they share the bottom tick and lose nothing. The real damage is the gap. A gap of 0.41 is wide, and in a row with varied weights it would blur neighbouring weights together onto the same few ticks. Drag Inspect block to other rows and the step is smaller in every one. Rows with big scores of their own, such as the rows for h and v, still come close to 0.41. A few rows show a step of exactly 1, and they belong to characters that never appear in the training text, such as the two spare symbols. All the weights in those rows are equal, so they need no gaps at all, and the lab shows a stand-in step for them. Move the zero point Go back to Per tensor at 4 bits and switch Range mapping to Symmetric · absmax, then look at the grid lines on the chart. The ruler now runs from −5.93 to +5.93, but no weight is below −1.71, so most of the negative ticks are wasted. The dashed lines mark ticks that no weight landed on, and Levels used in this block reads 10 of 15. Quality cost rises from +0.94% to +2.33%, so the cheaper ruler has more than doubled the damage. Now drop Bit width to 2 with the symmetric ruler still on, which leaves only three ticks, at −5.93, 0 and +5.93. Almost every weight now rounds to zero, and Quantized jumps to about 22.55, which is more than three times the original perplexity. Price the tradeoff Switch Range mapping back to Asymmetric · min/max and look at the chart on Quality against bits per weight, where each point is one setting. A point sits left or right according to its bits per weight with the rulers included, and up or down according to its quality cost. Down and to the left is better, because a point there means less space and less damage at the same time. The upward direction uses a log scale, which means each equal step up multiplies the cost by ten instead of adding to it. So the gap from 0.1% to 1% looks the same as the gap from 1% to 10%, which lets tiny costs and huge ones share one chart. Points at 0.01% or below cannot go any lower, so they sit on the floor of the chart as hollow markers. The chart draws three lines, and each has its own marker and line style so you can tell them apart without relying on colour. Circles on a solid line mark per tensor, squares on a dashed line mark per row, and triangles on a dotted line mark per group of 8. Find the 4-bit point on each line and compare them, starting with per tensor at about 4.04 bits and +0.94%. Per row sits further right, at 5.07 bits, but far lower, at +0.17%, so one extra bit per weight cuts the damage to under a fifth. The diamonds are the real llama.cpp block types, and a ring marks your current setting so you can always find it. The Q4_K diamond sits at 4.5 bits and +0.19%, about as low as the per-row point but well to its left. It gets about the same quality for less storage because it stores its rulers more compactly, at 0.5 bits per weight instead of 1.07. If you set a very small Group size, some points land beyond 17 bits per weight, and the chart leaves those off and tells you how many it skipped. Read the format names Open Published quantization formats, where each row is a block type and the columns include Bits per weight, Toy perplexity and RMS error. The Toy perplexity column gives the perplexity measured on this table, with its percent cost printed underneath, so you can compare it with the chart. Rows whose code width matches your Bit width are highlighted, so at 4 bits you will see the 4-bit types light up. Compare the three types that all use 4-bit codes, since they differ only in how they store their rulers: Q4_0 costs 4.5 bits per weight, with an RMS error of 0.127 and a cost of +0.20%. Q4_1 costs 5.0 bits per weight, with an RMS error of 0.063 and a cost of +0.16%. Q4_K costs 4.5 bits per weight, with an RMS error of 0.062 and a cost of +0.19%. Q4_0 has about double the error of the other two, because its symmetric ruler wastes ticks on this lopsided table. Q4_K matches Q4_1 while spending half a bit less per weight, which is the whole point of squeezing its rulers. Notice too that all three costs are small and close together, a reminder that double the rounding error does not always mean double the damage. The last column, llama.cpp file, Llama-3-8B, lists the file sizes that llama.cpp reports for a model with about 8 billion weights. Its Q4_K_M file is 4.58 GiB, which works out to about 4.90 bits per weight rather than the 4.5 of a single block. Weigh the file you downloaded Now open The file you downloaded, which weighs the model file this app downloads in the same way as the toy table: File size reads 1.19 GiB, and the note below the bars gives the exact count, 1,280,835,840 bytes. Parameters in the file reads 1.88 B, where the B means billion rather than bytes, so this is the number of weights. Effective bits per weight reads 5.445, which is the file’s size in bits divided by its number of weights. Share of the F16 size reads 34.0%, so the file is about a third of the size of a plain 16-bit copy. So a file built from 4-bit blocks really costs 5.445 bits per weight, which is 0.945 above the 4.5 of a Q4_K block. To find where those extra bits go, switch Group tensors by from Block type to Role in the network, which sorts the model’s parts by the job each one does. Each bar is then one part of the model, sized by its share of the file’s bytes, with its own bits per weight written beside it. The token embedding costs 6.56 bits per weight, while the feed-forward layers cost 4.84. A model is built as a stack of repeated steps called layers. The feed-forward parts of those layers, added together, hold more weights than any other part of the model. The token embedding is the table that turns each token into a list of numbers the model can work with. This recipe keeps it in the larger Q6_K type, which is why it costs so much per weight. Bars above 5 bits per weight are drawn in a warning colour, so you can spot the expensive parts quickly. Back on Block type, the Q6_K bar holds 35.3% of the parameters but 42.9% of the bytes, because each of its weights costs more to store. Climb the float ladder Last, open Float formats, where the Example value control jumps to a few preset numbers and the Value to store slider reaches anything from 0.000001 up to 1,000,000. Set Example value to 100,000, and you will see that only fp32 and bf16 can write it, because only they have 8 exponent bits. The fp16 row shows overflow because fp16 stops at 65,504, and the fp8 rows overflow too, since E5M2 stops at 57,344 and E4M3 at 448. Even bf16 cannot store the number exactly, so it rounds it to 99,840, which is 0.16% low because bf16 has few mantissa bits. Set it to 0.02, which fits in every format, and read the Error column to see how close each one gets. The fp16 row is off by 0.021% and the bf16 row by 0.098%, while both fp8 formats are off by 2.3%. Here the problem is precision rather than range, because fewer mantissa bits mean wider steps, so the stored value lands further from 0.02. Try 300 as well, which fits in every format, although fp8 E4M3 stores it as 288 and fp8 E5M2 stores it as 320. Between 256 and 512, three mantissa bits make steps that are 32 wide, while two mantissa bits make steps that are 64 wide. Finally, try 0.001. E4M3’s smallest normal value is about 0.0156, so 0.001 sits down in the subnormal zone, where every step is about 0.00195 wide. That means the nearest values E4M3 can write are 0 and about 0.00195. The number 0.001 is a little closer to 0.00195, so it rounds up. The fp8 E4M3 row shows this as 1.9531e-3, meaning 1.9531 ÷ 1,000, or about 0.00195, and marks it subnormal. The stored value is nearly double the real one, which shows how little detail is left down there. The last two columns round the whole trained table through each format, and Toy table RMS error is 0.0002 for fp16 but 0.0017 for bf16. So fp16 keeps the weights more than eight times closer, because its 10 mantissa bits make steps 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times finer than the 7 of bf16. The table never comes near the fp16 limit of 65,504, so the extra range of bf16 buys nothing here.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Quantization
documents.body: The bit width is not the size, because at 4 bits, groups of 8 cost 8.02 bits per weight once the rulers are counted. A group of 2 costs 20 bits per weight, which is more than the 16 bits of half precision, even though every code is only 4 bits. One huge weight bends its whole ruler: the 5.93 score stretches its row’s 4-bit gap to 0.41, which would blur any varied weights that shared that row. A weight like that is called an outlier, and smaller blocks keep its stretch inside its own block instead of widening the gaps for the whole table. On the chart, down and to the left is better, and Q4_K sits left of the per-row line at about the same cost. That is because Q4_K stores its rulers more compactly, at half a bit per weight instead of about one. A ruler centred on zero wastes ticks on lopsided data, which is why the symmetric Q4_0 has double the error of Q4_1 on this table. Each bit you remove below 5 bits multiplies the per-tensor cost by roughly five to seven, so the savings get expensive fast. The label on the box is not its weight: the downloaded Q4_K_M file averages 5.445 bits per weight. That is because about 51% of its parameters sit in larger types such as Q5_K or Q6_K. The biggest of those larger parts is the token embedding table, which has a row of numbers for each of its 248,320 tokens. The header of that file adds only 0.047 bits per weight, so almost all of the gap comes from the recipe itself. A float is like a number written as digits times a power. Mantissa bits are the digits and set precision, while exponent bits are the power and set range. The fp16 and bf16 formats both use 16 bits but split them differently, so on the trained table fp16’s error is 0.0002 against bf16’s 0.0017. Yet bf16 holds 100,000 while fp16 overflows, because bf16 spent its bits on range instead. An 8-bit float with no ruler is rougher than an 8-bit integer code with one: fp8 E4M3 costs +0.17% and fp8 E5M2 costs +0.36% on this table. Meanwhile Q8_0 costs below 0.01%, although its ruler raises its storage to 8.5 bits per weight, so the better result is not quite free. A common mix-up: many people read “4-bit” as exactly 4 bits of storage per weight, but it is always more, because the rulers are stored too. That is why Q4_0 costs 4.5 bits per weight, and why llama.cpp’s own Q4_K_M file for an 8-billion-parameter model averages about 4.9. The app’s own 2B file averages 5.445, because some of its tensors are kept in Q5_K, at 5.5 bits per weight, or in Q6_K, at about 6.56. Picture a friend who downloads a “4-bit” model and expects it to be a quarter of the size of the 16-bit version, since 4 is a quarter of 16. The Share of the F16 size readout says 34.0% instead, which is about a third, and now you can explain the difference to them. A common mix-up: because bf16 shares fp32’s exponent bits, it can seem like the more precise of the two 16-bit formats, but it is the other way around. Exponent bits buy range rather than precision, so near 1.0 the steps in bf16 are about 0.008 apart, while the steps in fp16 are about 0.001 apart.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Quantization
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Every card except The file you downloaded is really computed, including the rounding, the errors, the bit counts and every perplexity. The one other exception is the llama.cpp file, Llama-3-8B column, which copies the file sizes that llama.cpp itself reports. What is missing is size and structure, because the lab rounds one small 30 by 30 table and the model behind it looks back only one character. Only the stored weights are rounded, and not the numbers that flow through a model while it runs. Perplexity here is measured on the same text the table was trained on, so it tells you how closely the rounded table matches the original. It does not tell you how well the model would handle new text that it has never seen. When you use the Quantization controls, the lab counts 16 bits for each start and each gap, but it rebuilds the weights with the exact, unrounded start and gap. So its errors can differ very slightly from what a real 16-bit ruler would give. The controls also count every bit with none wasted, while real files sometimes leave a few spare bits to keep the codes lined up. The Published quantization formats rows, by contrast, do round their stored rulers the way the real files do. The histogram on Rounding grid and per-weight error sorts the weights into narrow bins for display. So its bars are a slightly blurred picture of the table rather than an exact one. The Published quantization formats rows copy each llama.cpp block’s layout, but they run it along the table as one long line of 900 weights. The real tool rounds each row separately, searches for better rulers, and needs rows that are a multiple of 32 or 256 weights long. Because the lab skips that search, its errors for those formats are an upper limit, and the real tool’s errors may be lower. With only one tensor, the lab also cannot show how the _S, _M and _L recipes mix block types across a model. The file you downloaded shows one file’s labels, read from its header on 30 September 2026 and typed into the lab. Nothing is downloaded or measured again when you open the card, and it tells you the file’s size, not its quality. Float formats rounds the table straight into each format with no ruler or scaling step first, which is not how real 8-bit setups work. Its perplexity is also measured on the training text, like the rest of the lab, so it shares the same blind spot. Where real quantization runs into trouble In real models the weights are not the hardest part. While a model runs, it passes lists of numbers from step to step, called activations, and these are harder still to round. In large models, a few positions in those lists, called channels, carry values far larger than their neighbours. One shared ruler has to stretch to reach those big values, so every other value gets coarse steps. Rounding error is not the same as quality loss, so real recipes try to keep the model’s outputs close on sample text, not only its weights. Better methods than plain rounding use calibration to find and protect the weights that matter most, as the Going deeper section describes. Perplexity is a weak final test, because a format can keep its perplexity on ordinary prose and still get worse in other places. It may slip on very long inputs, on computer code, or on languages that were rare in the training text. A format only helps if fast software exists to do its arithmetic, so an unusual layout can make a file smaller and the model slower at once. Effective bits per weight only measures storage, so it says nothing about quality and leaves out the extra memory a model uses while it runs. That extra memory includes the saved keys and values that you met in the Inference & KV cache lab. When a number is too big for a float format, what happens next depends on how the conversion is set up. The number might be clipped to the largest value, or it might be turned into a special marker that means infinity or “not a number”.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Quantization
documents.body: Reading the names in full A block type such as Q4_K is a storage layout that holds 256 weights in a super-block, split into eight groups of 32. Each group’s gap and start are squeezed into 6-bit numbers, and two 16-bit numbers for the whole super-block turn those small numbers back into real ones. Altogether that is 144 bytes for every 256 weights, which works out to 4.5 bits per weight. Q4_0 is the older layout, with 32 weights sharing one 16-bit gap, and it also lands on 4.5 bits per weight. A file name such as Q4_K_M is a recipe across tensors, and for Llama-3-8B it is mostly Q4_K. Parts of two kinds of layer, along with the final output layer, are kept in Q6_K. The llama.cpp project reports this file at 4.58 GiB, which is about 4.90 bits per weight. The file you downloaded The app’s local model is Qwen3.5 2B, as a Q4_K_M file from the unsloth/Qwen3.5-2B-GGUF repository. It is pinned to one exact version with a known fingerprint, a SHA-256 hash, which lets the app check that it has exactly that file. The counts in the lab were read from the file’s own header on 30 September 2026. Hugging Face, the site that hosts the file, reports the same parameter total. According to its model card, the model has 24 layers. Six of them use full attention, the method from the Attention lab where every token looks back at every earlier token. The other 18 use a cheaper kind of layer called Gated DeltaNet. The recipe keeps the big token embedding table at the larger Q6_K size, and that table has a row of 2,048 numbers for each of its 248,320 tokens. The lab calls it “shared with the output” because the same table is used again at the very end, to score each possible next token. In a small model that table makes up 27.0% of all the parameters, so keeping it wide moves the average a lot. The Deployment & serving lab turns this same file into a memory budget, so you will meet these numbers again there. The float ladder in more detail Each step down the ladder halves the bits and gives something up, and the two 16-bit formats give up different things. The bf16 format keeps fp32’s 8 exponent bits and cuts the mantissa to 7 bits, while fp16 trades the other way, with 5 exponent bits and 10 mantissa bits. The lab also lists a bias for each format. This is a fixed number subtracted from the stored exponent, so that the exponent can reach small numbers as well as big ones. The two fp8 formats come from a 2022 paper by Micikevicius and colleagues, who suggest E4M3 for weights and activations and E5M2 for gradients. Gradients are the nudges that training applies to the weights, so they matter while a model is being trained rather than when it is used. E4M3 gives up its patterns for infinity and keeps only one for “not a number”, which stretches its largest value up to 448. The paper describes scaling each tensor first so that its biggest value lands near the format’s maximum, which is a step this lab does not take. Calibration methods Plain rounding looks only at the weights, while calibration also runs sample text through the model. In a real model each weight is multiplied by numbers that come from the text. A weight that is always multiplied by large numbers matters more than one that is always multiplied by tiny ones. These are the published claims, not measurements from this lab, and the sources were checked on 30 September 2026. They are the papers’ summaries and the documentation for llama.cpp version b10991, which is the version this app pins. llama.cpp can compute an importance matrix for a model from a text file and then use it to improve the quality of quantizing. This app’s own file records that it used one, built from a dataset called unsloth_calibration_Qwen3.5-2B.txt in 80 chunks. GPTQ (2022) rounds the weights in order and adjusts the ones not yet rounded to make up for each error. It reports 3 or 4 bits per weight with very little loss on models of 175 billion weights. AWQ (2023) finds that protecting about 1% of the weight channels, the ones that matter most, greatly reduces the error. AWQ picks those channels by watching the activations rather than the weights, and it protects them by scaling instead of by retraining. LLM.int8() (2022) sends the few outlier channels through 16-bit arithmetic, while more than 99.9% of values go through 8-bit arithmetic. SmoothQuant (2022) instead moves the difficulty of activation outliers into the weights, so that both the weights and the activations can use 8 bits. Quantizing the cache While a model writes, it saves keys and values from earlier tokens in a KV cache, as the Inference & KV cache lab shows, and these can be rounded too. The llama.cpp server has a setting for the type of each, --cache-type-k and --cache-type-v, with f16 as the default and q8_0 and q4_0 among the other choices. A 2024 paper, KIVI, rounds them to 2 bits and reports 2.6 times less peak memory, counting the weights, and the Deployment & serving lab prices this lever. What comes after rounding A barely trained model hardly cares about rounding, which is why this lab trains for 80 epochs first. A well-trained table spreads its scores apart and stores information in the differences between them, which rounding can damage. On a fresh table, by contrast, even 2 bits would look free, so the lab would teach you nothing about the real cost. Training with the rounding switched on is called quantization-aware training, and it teaches a model weights that survive rounding. It costs a whole training run, and it is most useful at 4 bits and below.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Quantization
documents.body: A trained model is mostly a large array of floating-point weights that must be stored and read to run it. Quantization asks how few bits each weight can keep, and at what cost in quality. Its answer is a grid: each weight becomes a small integer code, and per-block metadata, a scale and sometimes a zero point, turns the codes back into approximate values. Two questions stay separate throughout: how much error the rounding adds, and what storage really costs once the metadata is counted, the bits per weight. The float ladder from fp32 down to fp8 shrinks numbers another way: each format keeps one sign bit and splits the rest between exponent (range) and mantissa (precision). It builds on Inference & KV cache, which priced decoding in memory, and Train one from scratch, which trained the kind of logit table rounded here. Where it shows up Local model files. llama.cpp loads GGUF, a single-file model container. A name such as Q4_K_M is a recipe across tensors: mostly Q4_K blocks, with some tensors kept wider. This app. Its local model is a 1.19 GiB Q4_K_M file of Qwen3.5 2B, quantized with an importance matrix, which llama.cpp computes by running sample text through the model and uses to steer the rounding. The KV cache. The llama.cpp server can store keys and values as q8_0 or q4_0. Large models. GPTQ and AWQ calibrate on sample text; LLM.int8() and SmoothQuant were built around outlier channels in the activations. fp8. Two 8-bit float formats split the same bits differently: after the sign bit, E4M3 has 4 exponent and 3 mantissa bits, E5M2 has 5 and 2. Micikevicius et al. (2022) propose the first for weights and activations, the second for gradients. Why it matters Quantization lets a model run in a fraction of the memory its floating-point weights would take. The file this app downloads averages 5.445 bits per weight; stored as fp16, the same weights would take about three times the space. It is also easy to misjudge. The code width is not the storage cost, one outlier coarsens a whole block, a format can hold perplexity on prose yet lose ground on code or long contexts, and a format helps only where a fast kernel exists for it. What you will be able to explain What a scale and a zero point do, and when a symmetric grid wastes levels. How bit width trades against scaling granularity in real bits per weight. What a GGUF block type or file name predicts about size and rough quality. How fp32, fp16, bf16, and fp8 split exponent and mantissa bits, and whether a value runs into range or precision. What the lab shows The lab rounds a real trained model: a 30 × 30 character-bigram logit table of 900 weights, trained for 80 epochs. Every setting re-rounds it and re-measures rounding error against the original weights and perplexity on the training corpus, so perplexity shows reconstruction, not held-out quality. Bits per weight is closed-form accounting: the code bits plus 16 bits charged per block for the scale, and 16 more for an asymmetric grid's zero point, spread over the 900 weights. Quantization controls sets Bit width, Scaling granularity, Group size, and Range mapping. Rounding grid and per-weight error draws every weight's error, and Quality against bits per weight plots measured cost against storage. The key experiment: at Per tensor, drag Bit width from 8 to 2 and watch Quality cost climb, then cycle the granularity at 4 bits. Published quantization formats emulates llama.cpp block layouts on the same table: each layout fixes its bits per weight; error and perplexity are measured on the table; the Llama-3-8B file sizes are quoted from llama.cpp. The file you downloaded is fixed data typed in from one GGUF header, so it reports size, not quality. Float formats computes each format's range in closed form, then rounds one number, set with Example value or Value to store, and the trained table through each format.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Quantization
documents.body: Quantization stores each weight as a small integer code plus per-block metadata that turns codes back into numbers. The weight keeps its meaning and loses resolution. The weights here are the real 900-entry logit table from the tiny language-model labs, trained for 80 epochs to perplexity 6.600; every setting re-rounds them and re-measures. Two ways to place the grid Asymmetric · min/max stretches the grid over the block's own range. The Scale is one step and the Zero point is the offset code 0 decodes to — here the block minimum, stored as a float, the way llama.cpp's Q4_1 and K-quants do it. Symmetric · absmax is symmetric quantization: the grid is centred on zero and only a scale is stored. Where the blocks come from Scaling granularity chooses how many weights share one grid. Per tensor is per-tensor scaling: one grid for all 900 weights. Per row gives each of the 30 context rows its own grid — per-channel scaling. Per group is group scaling: one grid per Group size consecutive weights. For a weight inside its grid, the error w′ − w is at most half a step. The Rounding grid and per-weight error card draws both: the grid over the weight histogram, and every weight's error underneath. Beyond the toy table Two cards step off the toy. The file you downloaded weighs the model file this app installs, in the same bits per weight. Float formats lays out fp32, fp16, bf16, and the two fp8 formats as sign, exponent, and mantissa bits, and rounds one value and the trained table through each.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Quantization
documents.body: Decoding reads every weight for every token, so bits per weight sets what fits in memory and how fast a model answers. That is why the Deployment & serving lab prices its weights in bits, including for the file this app downloads. This is post-training quantization: the checkpoint is finished and nothing is retrained. It is cheap enough to apply to anyone's released model, which is also why it is only as good as plain rounding unless calibration data is used.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Quantization
documents.body: Set Scaling granularity to Per tensor and drag Bit width from 8 to 2. The error strip turns into a sawtooth whose teeth are the grid. RMS error runs 0.008, 0.074, 0.147, 0.353, 0.967 at 8, 5, 4, 3, 2 bits, and Quality cost runs +0.01%, +0.14%, +0.94%, +5.03%, +23.90%. At 4 bits, cycle the granularity. RMS error falls from 0.147 per tensor to 0.031 per row to 0.027 for groups of 8, while Bits per weight rises from 4.04 to 5.07 to 8.02. The accuracy was bought with metadata: each asymmetric block stores two 16-bit numbers. Now switch Range mapping to Symmetric · absmax at 4 bits per tensor. The grid now spans −5.93 to +5.93, but the table only reaches −1.71, so Levels used in this block reads 10 of 15 and the cost rises from +0.94% to +2.33%. At 2 bits symmetric per tensor, three levels (−5.93, 0, +5.93) leave perplexity at 22.55. Finally read Published quantization formats. Q4_0, Q4_1, and Q4_K all use 4-bit codes: 4.5, 5.0, and 4.5 bits per weight, RMS error 0.127, 0.063, and 0.062, cost +0.20%, +0.16%, and +0.19%. Open The file you downloaded. The app's local model is 1,280,835,840 bytes, 1.19 GiB, over 1,881,825,088 parameters, so Effective bits per weight reads 5.445: not 4, and 0.945 above a Q4_K block's 4.5. Switch Group tensors by to Role in the network: the token embedding costs 6.56 bits per weight, the feed-forward layers 4.84, the Gated DeltaNet layers 5.34, and the full-attention layers 4.60. In Float formats, set Example value to 100,000. Only fp32 and bf16 hold it: fp16 stops at 65,504, E5M2 at 57,344, and E4M3 at 448. Set it to 0.02 and read Error: fp16 is off by 0.021%, bf16 by 0.098%, and both fp8 formats by 2.3%.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Quantization
documents.body: The code width is never the storage cost. Groups of 8 at 4 bits cost 8.02 bits per weight, and a group of 2 costs 20 — more than F16 — while storing every pair exactly. One outlier sets its block's scale alone. The largest logit, 5.93 for “.” followed by a space, stretches its row's 4-bit step to 0.41; that row uses 2 of its 16 levels. On Quality against bits per weight, down and left is better. The Q4_K diamond sits left of the per-row series at about the same cost, because its quantized scales cost 0.5 bits per weight rather than 1.07. Symmetric grids waste levels on lopsided data. Q4_0 is symmetric and has double the RMS error of Q4_1 here. Both sample panels share a seed, so any difference in the text is the rounded weights. A file's bits per weight is a recipe's average. The downloaded Q4_K_M file is 5.445, not 4.5, because 51% of its parameters sit in Q5_K or Q6_K tensors, led by the 248,320-token embedding table at Q6_K. Its header adds only 0.047 bits per weight. Exponent bits set the range; mantissa bits set the precision. On the trained table fp16's RMS error is 0.0002 against bf16's 0.0017, yet bf16 holds 100,000 and fp16 does not. Eight float bits with no scale are not eight integer bits with one: E4M3 costs +0.17% perplexity here, E5M2 +0.36%, and Q8_0 at 8.5 bits less than 0.01%.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Quantization
documents.body: In this lab. Rounding, errors, bits, and perplexities are computed on the trained table. What is missing is scale and structure: one 30 × 30 matrix, weights only, no activations or KV cache. Perplexity is measured on the training corpus, so it reports reconstruction, not held-out quality. The llama.cpp rows emulate each block layout in flattened order; real llama.cpp quantizes row by row, searches for better scales, and needs rows that are a multiple of 32 or 256 weights. The teaching quantizer charges 16 bits per scale but keeps it at full precision. The file card is one file's header, read on 30 September 2026 and typed in: nothing is downloaded or re-measured, and it reports size, not quality. The float card rounds the stored table with no per-tensor scale, and its perplexity is again measured on the training corpus. In real systems. Weights are the easy half. Activations in large transformers carry outlier channels far larger than their neighbours, which is what LLM.int8() and SmoothQuant were built around. Weight-only methods also do better than rounding, by calibrating on sample text: see Calibration methods below for GPTQ, AWQ, and the importance matrix this app's own file used. Perplexity is a weak acceptance test. A format can hold perplexity on prose and lose ground on long contexts, code, or under-represented languages. And a format only helps if a fast kernel exists for it; an exotic layout can be smaller and slower at once.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Quantization
documents.body: Reading the names A block type such as Q4_K fixes the storage: 256-weight super-blocks, eight 32-weight sub-blocks, and each sub-block's scale and min quantized to 6 bits against fp16 super-scales — 144 bytes per 256 weights, 4.5 bits per weight. That is a K-quant. Q4_0 is the older 32-weight block with one fp16 scale, also 4.5 bits. A file name such as Q4_K_M is a recipe across tensors. It is mostly Q4_K, with parts of the attention value and feed-forward down projections, and the output layer, kept in Q6_K. llama.cpp reports its Llama-3-8B file at 4.58 GiB, about 4.90 bits per weight. _S and _L keep fewer or more tensors wide. GGUF is the container: named tensors in their block types, metadata, and the tokenizer in one file with a header a loader checks before trusting the bytes. This app does that for its own optional engine before starting llama-server on a loopback port. The file you downloaded The app's local model is Qwen3.5 2B as a Q4_K_M file from the unsloth/Qwen3.5-2B-GGUF repository, pinned to one revision with a known SHA-256. The counts above were read from that file's own GGUF header on 30 September 2026, and Hugging Face's API reports the same 1,881,825,088 parameters. They cover the text model only: 24 layers, six of them full attention and 18 Gated DeltaNet (linear attention), per the model card. The recipe keeps the 248,320 × 2,048 token embedding, shared with the output, at Q6_K. In a small model that table is 27.0% of the parameters, so the recipe's average moves a lot. The Deployment & serving lab turns the same file into a memory budget. The float ladder Each step down halves the bits and gives something up. Floating-point formats split their bits three ways: one sign bit, exponent bits for the range, and mantissa bits for the precision. bf16 keeps fp32's eight exponent bits and cuts the mantissa to seven; fp16 trades the other way, five exponent bits and ten mantissa bits. The two fp8 formats are from Micikevicius et al. (2022), who recommend E4M3 for weights and activations and E5M2 for gradients. E5M2 follows IEEE 754; E4M3 has no infinities and one NaN pattern, which stretches its largest value to 448. The paper describes scaling each tensor so its largest magnitude lands near the format's maximum, which this lab does not do. Calibration methods Plain rounding looks only at the weights. Calibration also runs sample text through the model, because which weights matter depends on the activations that multiply them. These are the published claims, not measurements from this lab. Sources checked 30 September 2026: the arXiv abstracts and the llama.cpp b10991 documentation, which is the engine version this app pins. Importance matrix. llama.cpp's llama-imatrix computes an importance matrix for a model from a text dataset, and llama-quantize --imatrix uses it to improve quantization quality. This app's file records one: dataset unsloth_calibration_Qwen3.5-2B.txt, 80 chunks, 186 entries. GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) quantizes weights in one shot using approximate second-order information, and reports 3 or 4 bits per weight with negligible accuracy loss on models of 175 billion parameters. AWQ (Lin et al., 2023) finds that protecting about 1% of salient weight channels greatly reduces error. It picks them from activation statistics rather than weights and protects them by scaling, with no backpropagation. LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al., 2022) sends the outlier feature dimensions through a 16-bit multiply while more than 99.9% of values multiply in 8-bit. SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2022) instead moves the difficulty of activation outliers into the weights, so both can be 8-bit. Quantizing the cache The KV cache can be stored in fewer bits too. The llama.cpp server exposes --cache-type-k and --cache-type-v, with q8_0, q4_0 and other types and f16 as the default. KIVI (Liu et al., 2024) quantizes keys per channel and values per token down to 2 bits, and reports 2.6 times less peak memory including the weights. The Deployment & serving lab prices this lever. What comes after rounding A well-trained model spreads its logits apart and stores information in the differences, which is why the lab pretrains for 80 epochs: on a fresh table, 2 bits would look free. Beyond post-training methods, quantization-aware training exposes the rounding during training; it costs a training run and is most useful at 4 bits and below.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Quantization controls · Quantization
documents.body: Bit width, block size, and where the grid sits The three decisions a weight quantizer makes: how many integer codes each weight gets, how many weights share one grid, and whether that grid is centred on zero (symmetric) or stretched over the block's own range (asymmetric). Every other card re-quantizes the same trained table when these change. `Bit width` from 2 to 8, printed with the number of levels: 2^b for asymmetric grids, 2^b − 1 for symmetric ones. `Scaling granularity`: `Per tensor` (one grid for all 900 weights), `Per row` (30 grids, one per context character), or `Per group`. `Group size` from 2 to 30, shown only in per-group mode. `Range mapping`: `Asymmetric · min/max` or `Symmetric · absmax`. Three metrics: `Bits per weight` including metadata, `Model size` in bytes, and `Against 32-bit` as a share of 900 × 4 bytes. Asymmetric: scale = (max − min) / (2^b − 1), code = round((w − min) / scale), w′ = min + code × scale. The block stores an fp16 scale and an fp16 min: 32 bits. Symmetric: scale = max|w| / (2^(b−1) − 1), code = round(w / scale) clamped to ±(2^(b−1) − 1), w′ = code × scale. The block stores one fp16 scale: 16 bits. Bits per weight = b + blocks × metadata bits / 900. Model size is that times 900 / 8, rounded up. `Bit width`, `Scaling granularity`, `Group size`, and `Range mapping`. Comparison worth running: at 4 bits, read Bits per weight for Per tensor (4.04), Per row (5.07), and Per group of 8 (8.02). Then set Group size to 2: 20 bits per weight, more than F16. Symmetric metadata is half the size of asymmetric, which is why the same granularity costs fewer bits per weight on the symmetric setting. A group of 2 stores two weights exactly with an asymmetric grid, because each pair's min and max are its two weights. The error is zero and the storage is absurd. In this lab: the scales are kept at full float precision while being charged 16 bits each, and bits are assumed to pack with no padding. In general: real formats pick block sizes that divide a row (32 or 256 weights in llama.cpp) and quantize the scales themselves to shrink this overhead.
documents.title: Bit width, block size, and where the grid sits

documents.subtitle: Rounding grid and per-weight error · Quantization
documents.body: The grid each weight snaps to, and what it cost Top: the 900 trained weights as a histogram, with one block's rounding grid drawn over it. Bottom: every weight's rounding error w′ − w, plotted at its original value. Under per-tensor scaling the errors trace a sawtooth that is the grid itself; under finer scaling each block has its own, smaller teeth. A histogram of the original weights on a square-root count axis, so the few large logits stay visible beside the pile near zero. Vertical lines at the inspected block's levels. Solid lines are levels at least one of the block's weights landed on; dashed lines are levels nobody used. Above 64 levels the lines are too dense and a note says so. A shaded band covering the inspected block's grid, and a marker at the table's largest weight (the logit for “.” followed by a space, 5.93). An error strip: grey dots for every weight, accent dots for the inspected block, and dashed lines at ± half of that block's step. `Inspect block` when there is more than one block, and metrics `RMS rounding error`, `Largest error`, `Step in this block`, and `Levels used in this block`. The weights are a 30 × 30 character bigram trained for 80 epochs on Harbor weather notes at seed 1, perplexity 6.600. Nothing is retrained after rounding. For a weight inside its block's grid, the error is at most half a step. That is why the dots stay between the dashed lines for the inspected block. `Inspect block` starts on the block that contains the largest weight. `Levels used` counts distinct codes in that block. `Inspect block` picks which block's grid is drawn; all quantization dials live on the controls card. Comparison worth running: at 4 bits per row, the “.” row uses 2 of 16 levels because one 5.93 logit stretches its step to 0.41; drag Inspect block to another row and the step shrinks. Switch Range mapping to Symmetric at 4 bits per tensor: the grid spans −5.93 to +5.93, the table only reaches −1.71, and 10 of 15 levels are used. The sawtooth is exact, not noise: per tensor, every weight with the same value gets the same error. In this lab: one small weight matrix, weights only. Activations and the KV cache are not quantized, and the histogram is binned for display. In general: rounding error is not quality loss. The next card measures perplexity, and production recipes minimize output error on calibration data rather than weight error.
documents.title: The grid each weight snaps to, and what it cost

documents.subtitle: Quality against bits per weight · Quantization
documents.body: Measured quality cost against the real storage bill Each point re-quantizes the trained table at one bit width and granularity, re-measures perplexity on the harbor corpus, and plots the percent increase over full precision against bits per weight including scales. The llama.cpp block types from the table below are plotted as diamonds. A log-scale y axis of perplexity increase, from ≤0.01% to 1000%. Points at or below 0.01% (including tiny negative changes) sit on the floor as hollow markers. Three series for the current range mapping: `per tensor` (circles, solid), `per row` (squares, dashed), `per group of G` (triangles, dotted), each at 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8 bits. Diamonds for Q8_0, Q6_K, Q5_K, Q4_K, Q4_1, Q4_0, Q3_K, and Q2_K, and a ring on the current setting. Metrics `Full precision`, `Quantized`, and `Quality cost`, and two samples at temperature 0.7 from the same seed. Cost = (quantized perplexity / 6.600 − 1) × 100%. The x position is the same bits per weight the controls card reports. Points beyond 17 bits per weight (small asymmetric groups) are left off the axis and counted in the caption. Both samples use prompt “the ”, 76 characters, seed 5, so a different string means a different next-character table. `Bit width` moves the ring; `Scaling granularity` moves it between series; `Group size` and `Range mapping` redraw every series. Comparison worth running: find 4-bit per tensor (4.04 bpw, +0.94%) and 4-bit per row (5.07 bpw, +0.17%), then the Q4_K diamond at 4.5 bpw and +0.19%. Down and to the left is better. The Q4_K diamond sits left of the per-row series at the same cost, because its quantized scales cost 0.5 bits per weight instead of 1.07. Per-tensor cost grows about fivefold or more for each bit removed below 5 (6.6×, 5.3×, then 4.8×): +0.14%, +0.94%, +5.0%, +23.9%. In this lab: perplexity is measured on the training corpus of a 900-weight bigram, so it measures reconstruction of this table, not held-out quality. In general: quality should be checked on held-out tasks, and low-bit formats can hold perplexity while losing ground on long contexts, code, or rare languages.
documents.title: Measured quality cost against the real storage bill

documents.subtitle: Published quantization formats · Quantization
documents.body: The block layouts behind GGUF names Nine llama.cpp block types applied to the same table in storage order: the exact bits per weight from each block's struct, the perplexity and rounding error measured here, and llama.cpp's own file size for Llama-3-8B where a file mix is built on that block. Columns `Block type` (with the byte layout and a one-line description), `Bits per weight` (with a bar out of 16), `Toy perplexity` (with its percent cost), `RMS error`, and `llama.cpp file, Llama-3-8B`. Rows whose code width matches the Bit width slider are highlighted. A note decoding a file name like Q4_K_M as a mix of block types. Q8_0: 32 int8 codes plus an fp16 scale, 34 bytes, 8.5 bpw. Q4_0: 32 4-bit codes plus an fp16 scale, 4.5 bpw. Q4_1 adds an fp16 min, 5.0 bpw. K-quants use 256-weight super-blocks whose sub-block scales are quantized: Q4_K and Q5_K store 6-bit scales and mins for eight 32-weight sub-blocks (4.5 and 5.5 bpw); Q6_K and Q3_K store signed scales for sixteen 16-weight sub-blocks (6.5625 and 3.4375 bpw); Q2_K stores 4-bit scales and mins (2.625 bpw). The emulation follows those layouts and rounds every stored scale to fp16, but skips llama.cpp's search for the best scale, so its errors are an upper bound. The file column converts llama.cpp's reported GiB for Llama-3-8B, whose mixes keep some tensors in a larger type. This card has no controls. `Bit width` only moves the highlight. Comparison worth running: Q4_0, Q4_1, and Q4_K all use 4-bit codes. Read their bits per weight (4.5, 5.0, 4.5) against their RMS error (0.127, 0.063, 0.062). Q4_0 is symmetric and pays for it on this lopsided table: double the RMS error of Q4_1 at the same code width. Q4_K matches Q4_1's error while spending half a bit less, which is the whole point of quantizing the scales. In this lab: llama.cpp quantizes each row separately and needs rows that are a multiple of the block size; this 30-wide table is quantized in flattened order instead, and the _S / _M / _L mixes need more than one tensor. In general: the name is a contract about storage, not quality. Quality still has to be measured on the task and model you care about.
documents.title: The block layouts behind GGUF names

documents.subtitle: The file you downloaded · Quantization
documents.body: What a Q4_K_M file really costs per weight The model file this app downloads, weighed the way the rest of the lab weighs a table: its bytes over its parameters give effective bits per weight, set against the nominal Q4_K rate and against F16. The bars show which tensors carry the extra bits. Metrics `File size` (1.19 GiB), `Parameters in the file` (1.88 B), `Effective bits per weight` (5.445), and `Share of the F16 size` (34.0%). `Group tensors by`: `Block type` (Q6_K, Q4_K, Q5_K, Q8_0, F32) or `Role in the network` (embedding, feed-forward, Gated DeltaNet, full attention, norms). One bar per group for its share of the file's tensor bytes, with its tensor count, its share of the parameters, and its own bits per weight. Groups above 5 bits per weight are drawn in the loss colour. A note with the exact byte and parameter counts, the gap to Q4_K, the header's cost, and the calibration the file's metadata records. Effective bits per weight = 8 × file bytes / parameters = 8 × 1,280,835,840 / 1,881,825,088 = 5.445. A group's figure is 8 × its bytes / its parameters, and each block type reproduces its layout rate: Q4_K 4.5, Q5_K 5.5, Q6_K 6.5625, Q8_0 8.5, F32 32. The tensor bytes sum to 1,269,873,920; the header (metadata, the 248,320-token vocabulary, the chat template) is the other 10,961,920, which is 0.047 bits per weight. Q4_K_M is a recipe across tensors: the token embedding (27.0% of the parameters, tied to the output) is Q6_K at 6.5625; feed-forward layers average 4.84, Gated DeltaNet layers 5.34, full-attention layers 4.60. Source and date: the counts were read on 30 September 2026 from the GGUF header of the pinned revision (unsloth/Qwen3.5-2B-GGUF at f6d5376, the file Settings downloads); Hugging Face's API reports the same 1,881,825,088 parameters. `Group tensors by` switches the bars between the two groupings; the metrics do not change. Comparison worth running: by `Block type`, Q6_K holds 35.3% of the parameters but 42.9% of the bytes. By `Role in the network`, the token embedding costs 6.56 bits per weight while the feed-forward layers cost 4.84. The file is 0.945 bits per weight above a Q4_K block, 21.0% more bytes than a file stored entirely as Q4_K, because about 51% of the parameters are held at Q5_K, Q6_K, or wider. The header explains under 1% of the file. This 2B model averages 5.445 where llama.cpp's Llama-3-8B Q4_K_M file averages 4.90: the embedding table is a much larger share of a small model, so a recipe's average depends on the model it is applied to. In this lab: the numbers are one file, authored from its header on 30 September 2026. Nothing here is downloaded or re-measured when you open the card, and the quality of the file is not measured, only its size. In general: effective bits per weight is a storage figure. It ignores the runtime cost of the KV cache and recurrent state, and says nothing about quality, which depends on the model, the recipe, and the calibration text.
documents.title: What a Q4_K_M file really costs per weight

documents.subtitle: Float formats · Quantization
documents.body: From fp32 to fp8: range from exponent bits, precision from mantissa bits Five floating-point formats laid out as sign, exponent, and mantissa bits, with their range and spacing computed from those layouts, one value you choose rounded into each of them, and the trained 900-weight table rounded through each to see what it costs. `Example value` (0.001, 0.02, 300, 100,000) and `Value to store`, a log slider from 1e-6 to 1e6 that sets the number rounded in every row. Per format: sign, exponent, and mantissa bits and the exponent bias; the smallest normal and largest finite value; the spacing at 1.0 as 2 to the minus the mantissa bits, with the worst relative rounding error; what your value is stored as and its percent error, or `overflow`. Toy columns: RMS rounding error of the 900 trained weights through each format, and the perplexity against the full-precision 6.600. Largest finite value = (2 − 2^(−mantissa bits)) × 2^(top exponent − bias): 65,504 for fp16, 448 for E4M3, 57,344 for E5M2. E4M3 gives its top exponent to numbers and keeps one mantissa pattern for not-a-number; the others reserve that exponent for infinity and not-a-number. Rounding finds the value's binade, takes the spacing 2^(exponent − mantissa bits), and rounds to the nearest multiple with ties to even. Below the smallest normal value the spacing stops shrinking, so values go subnormal and then to zero; a result past the largest finite value overflows. The toy columns round each float32 weight this way and re-measure perplexity on the harbor corpus. No per-tensor scale is applied. `Example value` jumps to a preset; `Value to store` moves the number by a twentieth of a decade, about 12%, per step. Comparison worth running: at 100,000 only bf16 and fp32 hold the value; fp16 stops at 65,504 and the fp8 formats at 57,344 and 448. At 0.02, fp16 is off by 0.021%, bf16 by 0.098%, and both fp8 formats by 2.3%. bf16 and fp16 are both 16 bits. bf16 keeps fp32's eight exponent bits and so its range, and is eight times coarser than fp16 at 1.0; on this table fp16's RMS error is more than eight times smaller than bf16's. Eight bits per weight with no scale and no blocks costs +0.17% (E4M3) or +0.36% (E5M2) perplexity here, while Q8_0 spends 8.5 bits for a change below 0.01%: integer blocks with a scale spend their bits on precision, float formats on range. In this lab: rounding is applied to a stored weight table with no per-tensor scale and no accumulation, and perplexity is measured on the corpus the table was trained on. In general: formats are used differently. Training keeps fp32 or bf16 accumulators and often scales fp8 tensors so their largest value lands near the format's maximum; overflow handling (saturate, infinity, or not-a-number) depends on the conversion mode.
documents.title: From fp32 to fp8: range from exponent bits, precision from mantissa bits

documents.subtitle: Train a toy reasoning policy against a checker, then price the two kinds of test-time compute: a longer trace, and more samples with a vote or a verifier.
documents.body: Train a toy reasoning policy against a checker, then price the two kinds of test-time compute: a longer trace, and more samples with a vote or a verifier. Contrast a reasoning model, whose long traces come from reinforcement learning against a checker, with in-context chain-of-thought prompting Explain how group-relative training against a verifiable reward lengthens traces, and why a missing length cost lets them pad Treat test-time compute as extra generated tokens or search, not as proof of inner thoughts Predict when majority voting helps and when only a verifier does

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Reasoning models
