documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: Intermediate tokens generated before an answer. They can be trained, prompted, or distilled. Visible steps are not a window into a separate mind.
documents.title: Chain of thought

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: Extra work spent while answering: a longer trace, or several sampled traces plus a way to pick one. It costs tokens and latency; it does not rewrite the weights.
documents.title: Test-time compute

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: A next-token predictor post-trained, typically with reinforcement learning against a checker, to write long intermediate traces before answering. The architecture is unchanged; the post-training recipe is different.
documents.title: Reasoning model

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: A reward computed by a program rather than a learned judge: an exact-match check on a final answer, or unit tests on code. It is cheap and hard to argue with, and it can only reward what the program can tell apart.
documents.title: Verifiable reward

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: sample several traces, score each with a checker, and make the traces that pass likelier. No human labels each trace, but the policy learns only what the checker distinguishes.
documents.title: RLVR

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: A policy-gradient method that samples a group of G traces for one prompt and scores each against its group: advantage is reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation. The group is the baseline, so no value network is needed; a group with equal rewards gives zero advantage and no update.
documents.title: GRPO (group-relative advantage)

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: Trace length beyond what the answer needs. With a pure verifiable reward nothing penalises extra steps, and spare steps can still raise the pass chance a little, so length keeps drifting up. A per-step cost or a length budget trims it; the extra tokens are latency, not understanding.
documents.title: Overthinking

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: Scoring each step rather than only the final answer, usually with a trained process reward model. It can catch a wrong step that happens to reach a right answer, and it can still reward a fluent but unused step.
documents.title: Process supervision

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: Sampling several traces and returning the most common final answer, also called self-consistency. It needs no checker, and it amplifies whichever single answer is most likely, right or wrong.
documents.title: Majority vote

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: A verifier checks a candidate answer: an exact-match test, unit tests, or a learned reward model. Best-of-n samples n candidates and keeps the one it scores highest; a perfect verifier succeeds whenever any sample is right, which is pass@n, while a learned one can be gamed.
documents.title: Verifier / best-of-n

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: Training a smaller or faster model to imitate traces from a stronger one. The student copies the text of the steps, not a guaranteed algorithm.
documents.title: Distillation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: The chance that at least one of n independent samples is correct, 1 minus (1 minus p) to the n for per-sample accuracy p. It is the ceiling for any way of choosing among the samples and what a perfect verifier reaches.
documents.title: Pass@n

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: A trace step that restates or recalls something the answer never uses. It adds tokens and latency without changing the answer; this lab places it by hand, where a real sampler interleaves it with useful steps.
documents.title: Padding

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reasoning models
documents.body: A trace step that does not match the work the answer needs, such as naming an unused fact, the wrong operation, or an invented rule. The lab labels these by hand; in real models faithfulness is tested by editing or truncating a trace and checking whether the answer changes.
documents.title: Unfaithful step

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reasoning models · question 1
documents.body: A base model writes a chain of thought when two worked examples sit in its prompt. A reasoning model writes longer ones with no examples. What differs? Prompting updates the weights a little for that one answer, while training updates them far more A reasoning model has an extra reasoning layer in its architecture that a base model lacks Prompting changes only the context; training changes the weights so long traces become likelier A prompted chain is a faithful record of the work, while a trained chain is only decoration A prompt changes what the model reads and leaves the weights alone. Reinforcement learning against a checker changes the weights so that traces which end in a passing answer become likelier; that is why the Train card's policy moves and a prompt could not move it. The architecture is unchanged, and neither kind of trace is guaranteed to be faithful.
documents.title: A base model writes a chain of thought when two worked examples sit in its prompt. A reasoning model writes longer ones with no examples. What differs?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reasoning models · question 2
documents.body: In Train against a checker (k = 3, Length cost off) the pass rate is already close to 100% by update 50. What does Mean length do after that? It keeps rising: nothing penalises extra steps and each one still adds a little pass chance It falls back toward k, because the checker only rewards the steps the task actually needs It stops moving, because a group where every trace passes always has zero advantage It falls, because every extra step is another chance to slip and fail the checker Advantage is measured against the group, so once almost every trace passes, the rare failures carry the signal and they tend to be the shorter traces. With no cost term the steps beyond k are free, and each still raises the chance that at least k of them land, so length creeps up. That drift is overthinking. Groups where every trace passes do give zero advantage, but not every group is like that.
documents.title: In Train against a checker (k = 3, Length cost off) the pass rate is already close to 100% by update 50. What does Mean length do after that?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reasoning models · question 3
documents.body: With Length cost on and Group size 8, seed 1 collapses to one-step answers and a pass rate near zero. Why? The cost per step is bigger than the reward for passing, so every trace scores below zero The checker gets stricter when the cost is on, so fewer traces pass at every length Eight traces are too few to estimate a standard deviation, so every advantage comes out as zero No early group contains a pass, so cost is the only difference between traces and shorter wins Advantages are rewards relative to the group. When no trace in a group passes, the only thing that differs is the length cost, and dividing by the group standard deviation scales that small difference up to full-size advantages, so the update favours the shortest traces before any passing length has been found. The cost is 0.05 per step, so it never outweighs a pass; the failure is what normalisation does when there is no pass to compare against.
documents.title: With Length cost on and Group size 8, seed 1 collapses to one-step answers and a pass rate near zero. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reasoning models · question 4
documents.body: A model writes numbered steps and then an answer. What is safe to conclude? The numbered steps are a faithful record of the algorithm it actually ran It was trained or prompted to emit intermediate tokens before the answer In-context prompting and training a reasoning model are the same recipe Writing more steps always raises accuracy, so longer traces are always better Visible steps are generated tokens. They can be useful, because later tokens can read what earlier ones wrote, and still be unfaithful. Extra steps cost latency and help only where later steps need earlier results, so more is not always better. Prompting and training are different recipes for getting those tokens.

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reasoning models · question 5
documents.body: At p = 0.40 with 16 samples you switch Wrong answers from Split over 3 to Always the same one. What happens? Majority vote and Verifier picks both drop, because every wrong sample now counts against both Majority vote rises, because the wrong answers agree and the vote becomes more stable Majority vote falls below One sample, but Verifier picks does not change Neither changes, because both depend only on how many samples are drawn and on p A verifier needs only one correct sample, so its accuracy depends on p and n and not on how the wrong answers are spread. A vote needs the right answer to out-poll every wrong one: when all wrong samples are the same answer it collects about 60% of the votes against 40%, so more samples make the vote converge on the wrong answer.

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reasoning models
documents.body: When you solve a hard math problem, you probably do not write the answer straight away. You fill some scratch paper with working, check each line, and only then copy a final answer into the box. Some AI models have been trained to do something similar, writing out a long stretch of steps before they answer, and they are called reasoning models. This module looks at where that habit comes from, what it costs, and what the written steps do and do not prove. Where you have met it If you have ever asked a chatbot to show its working, you have seen one way to get steps out of a model, which is to ask for them. A reasoning model gets there by a different route, because it was trained to write long working without being asked. That training uses a program that checks final answers, such as an answer key for math questions or a set of automatic tests for computer code. The same ideas turn up in other places too. Smaller models are sometimes trained to copy the long working of a stronger model. AI agents, which are programs that take actions such as running a search, spend extra time and computing power on those actions instead of on writing more working. Why it matters A program that checks answers is what lets this training run without a person grading every try, and understanding how it all works protects you from three tempting mistakes: Reading working as a true record: long working looks like careful thought, so it is tempting to treat it as the real story of how the answer was reached. It is generated text, and some lines can be filler or even wrong while the final answer is right. Paying for length that does little: every extra line costs time and computing power, even when it adds nothing to the answer. If training never puts a price on length, the working keeps growing even when each extra line makes the answers only a tiny bit better. Trusting the wrong way to pick an answer: another way to spend extra effort is to make several tries and pick one of them. Picking by a vote can leave you right less often than a single try would, while a perfect checker never can, and you need to know when each one applies. What you will be able to explain By the end, you should be able to explain each of these in your own words: Why a reasoning model is different from a model asked for steps in a prompt, since a prompt changes only what the model reads. Training against a checker changes the model itself, so that long working becomes its habit. How comparing a group of tries against a checker makes the working longer, and why, when nothing charges for length, it keeps growing past what the task needs. Why extra working, or extra tries, is extra generated text and extra searching, not proof of thoughts going on inside the model. When taking a vote among several tries helps, and when only a checker can find the right answer. What the lab shows The lab has five cards, and each one is honest about what is real and what was set up by hand: Problem picks one of three practice questions, Sunday hours, 17 + 28 or Dog on the ferry, and shows the question in full. Train against a checker really runs a tiny training session of 100 updates. Each update is one round of making a group of tries, checking them and nudging the learner. You can step through the updates one at a time with a slider. What it trains is a single number, the length of working the toy likes best, and the checker is a rule written by hand, so no language model is involved. Thinking budget and Inspectable trace reveal working one step at a time, labelling each step useful, padding or unfaithful. Those steps, their labels and the final answer were all written in advance, so no model produces them. Sampling and voting works out exactly how often a vote or a checker picks the right answer, based on an accuracy you choose rather than a measured one.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reasoning models
documents.body: Working, one piece at a time A language model writes text one small piece at a time, and each piece, a word or part of a word, is called a token. For every new token it reads everything written so far, picks the next piece, adds it to the end, and repeats. The steps a model writes before its final answer are called a chain of thought, because each step links to the next like the links of a chain. Here is the working the lab shows for the question "What is 17 + 28?": Each line is ordinary text, written one token at a time like any other sentence, and the final answer comes only after the working. Two ways to get working: ask for it, or train for it Inside every model is a huge set of adjustable numbers, called weights, which training sets and which decide what the model tends to write. There are two quite different ways to get a model to write working, and the difference is whether those weights change. The first way is to ask: you put a couple of worked examples in your message, which is called the prompt, and the model tends to copy their style. This is in-context prompting, which the ICL & reasoning lab covers (ICL is short for in-context learning). It leaves every weight exactly as it was, because only what the model reads has changed. The second way is to train: after its main training, the model gets extra training, called post-training, that changes its weights. That makes long working likely even when nobody asks for it, and a model trained this way is called a reasoning model. Its design is the same as any other language model's, so it still writes one token at a time, and only the training recipe is different. Training against a checker The recipe is a kind of reinforcement learning, which means learning by trial and score: the model makes tries, and each try gets a score. The weights then shift so that the high-scoring kind of try becomes more likely next time. Here the score comes from a program that checks the final answer, which for 17 + 28 means comparing it with 45. For computer code the program might run small automatic checks, called unit tests, that confirm the code gives the right outputs. A score that a program can compute like this is called a verifiable reward, and training with it is called RLVR, short for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Each round of RLVR has three steps, and the lab's training card runs a tiny version of the same loop: The model writes several tries at the same question, each with its own working. A checker program marks each final answer as a pass or a fail, without looking at the working. The weights are nudged so that the working in the passing tries becomes a little more likely, and the working in the failing tries a little less likely. No person has to grade any try, which makes the method cheap, but the model can only learn what the checker can tell apart. Since the checker looks only at the final answer, it rewards the working that comes before a pass, whether every line of it was needed or not. Grading on a curve: GRPO One way to do the nudging, and the one this lab copies, is called GRPO, and it never judges a try on its own. Instead it compares each try with the other tries in its group, much like a test graded on a curve, where your mark depends on the class average. Each try's score is turned into an advantage, a number that says how much better or worse the try did than its group's average. Tries above the average get pushed up and tries below it get pushed down, and the size of each push is scaled by how spread out the scores are. That scaling makes the pushes come out at about the same size, whether the scores in a group differ a lot or only a little. Because the group itself is the yardstick, nothing else has to judge what counts as a good score. To measure how spread out a group's scores are, take each score's distance from the average and square it. Then average those squares and take the square root. A try's advantage is its distance from the average divided by that spread. Here is a small example with a group of four tries, where a pass scores 1 and a fail scores 0: If half the group passes, the average score is 0.5 and every score sits 0.5 away from it, so the spread is 0.5. Each passing try gets 0.5 ÷ 0.5 = +1, and each failing try gets −0.5 ÷ 0.5 = −1. If only one try passes, the average is 0.25 and the spread works out to about 0.43. The lone pass sits 0.75 above the average, so it gets 0.75 ÷ 0.43, or about +1.73. Each of the three failures sits 0.25 below, so it gets a small −0.58. A rare success is pushed up hard, because it stands out so clearly from the rest of its group. If all four pass, or all four fail, every score equals the average, so every advantage is 0 and that group teaches nothing at all. Keep that last case in mind, because the lab's Groups with no signal readout counts exactly those groups. Test-time compute Everything so far happens during training, while test-time compute is the extra work a model spends later, while it is answering you. It comes in two kinds: a model can write longer working before its answer, or it can make several separate tries and use some way to pick one. A bigger version of the second kind, called search, judges working that is still half-written and keeps going only with the most promising tries, which Going deeper describes. Every kind costs more tokens and more waiting time, but none of them changes the weights, so the model itself is no different afterward. The scratch-paper picture, and where it stops Picture a student who sits test after test where the teacher marks only the answer box and never looks at the scratch paper. Every right answer earns a gold star, and the papers that earn stars tend to be the ones with more working above the answer. Test after test, the student drifts toward whatever habits came with stars, so their scratch paper slowly fills up, even though nobody ever marks the working itself. Training against a checker works in a similar way: long working appears because it is more often followed by a right answer. The picture stops matching at the student, who can decide to show more work because they understand why it helps. The model decides nothing, and nobody shows it a method. Training only makes whatever working came before a pass a little more likely, and long working comes along because it is more often followed by a pass.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reasoning models
documents.body: Reasoning models deal with two separate problems, one about how a model computes and one about how it can be trained, and this lab connects them. A fixed amount of work per token To choose each token, the model pushes everything written so far through the same set of weights once. That is a huge sum, and it grows a little as the text gets longer. But the sum always passes through the same fixed number of stages, one after another. So the model can chain together only about the same amount of work for every token, however hard the question is. Picture being allowed exactly three seconds of thinking before every word you say. Some problems need a chain of steps where each step uses the result of the one before, and a long chain may not fit into three seconds. In 17 + 28, for example, you cannot finish the tens until you know whether adding the ones produced a carry. On a sum this small you would manage. But a model that had to produce the answer to a long problem in one go would need to squeeze the whole chain into a single fixed-size calculation. Writing working changes that, because if you can write a note after each three seconds, you can carry on from the note. Once the model has written "write 5 carry 1", the carry sits in the text where the next step can read it. In this way, working spreads a long chain of steps across many tokens and each token's calculation handles only a small part. That is the real reason working can help, and it is also why working helps most on problems where later steps depend on earlier results. Building the habit without a human grader A prompt cannot build the habit of long working into the weights, so you need a training signal. The Reinforcement learning foundations lab showed a learner improving against a reward. The hard part is finding a reward, and a checker program fits well because it is cheap to run and hard to argue with. That means it can score a huge number of tries without anyone having to read them. This lab joins the two ideas, because the reward is the checker and the learner is something that writes working. The sampling card adds one more idea, the chance that at least one of several tries works, which the Evaluation lab also uses.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reasoning models
documents.body: Work down the cards from top to bottom, following the steps below, which match the lab's own step list. Pick a practiced problem In the Problem card, choose Sunday hours, 17 + 28 or Dog on the ferry, and notice that switching Problem also resets Thinking budget to 3. Each one stands for a question the model met during its training, not an example pasted into a prompt, and the card's note spells out that difference. Train against a checker Start the Train against a checker card at its default settings, which are listed here along with what each control means in this toy: Steps the task needs (k) is 3, the number of steps that must succeed for an answer to be right. In this toy, each step comes out right by chance, 4 times out of 5. Group size (G) is 16, the number of tries that each update makes and compares with one another. Learning rate is 0.3, which sets how big each push is, so a higher rate makes the run change faster. Seed is 1, which decides which random tries get drawn, so the same seed always gives exactly the same run. Length cost is Off, so steps are free and only the checker's pass or fail counts. The bar chart under the line charts shows how likely the toy is to write each length of working, and the lab calls those odds the policy. Outlined bars show where the policy started, and the dashed line shows how often the checker passes working of each length. Training update does not retrain anything, because the whole run of 100 updates has already happened, and the slider lets you look at any point along it. Try this: with Length cost set to Off, drag Training update from 0 to 100 and watch both line charts. Mean length climbs from 1.8 steps to 7.1, well past the 3 steps the task needs. Over the same run, the pass rate rises from 10% to 99%, and the solid bars slide from short lengths over to long ones. Add a length cost Set Length cost to On · 0.05 per step, which charges 0.05 points for every step, while a pass is worth a whole point. Now the run ends at 5.3 steps with a 93% pass rate, which is shorter than before while still passing almost every time. A dashed line called Mean reward after cost also appears on the first chart, showing the average score after the cost of the steps is taken off. Keep the cost on and set Group size to 8, and this time the run collapses to one-step answers. It ends at 1.2 steps with a 1% pass rate, because the policy has settled almost entirely on 1-step and 2-step working, which can never pass. Then set Seed to 4 with everything else the same, and watch a run that finds a passing length before the collapse can set in. It ends near 4 steps with a 78% pass rate, which shows how much one run can depend on its random draws. Raise the budget Set Problem to Sunday hours, which asks "When does the north dock close on Sunday?" Then in the Thinking budget card raise Thinking budget one step at a time from 3 up to 6, and watch the readouts under the slider. At 4, Padding goes up to 1, and at 5, Unfaithful goes up to 1. Useful stays at 3 at budgets 3, 4 and 5, and goes up to 4 at budget 6, when the last line, "Commit to 16:00", gives the answer. Padding means a line that adds nothing the answer uses, and Unfaithful means a line that pretends to be part of the work when it is not. What to notice explains both. Inspect the extra tokens Set Problem to 17 + 28 and read the first two lines in the Inspectable trace card. The first line writes the carry, and the second line uses that carry to add the tens. Now drop Thinking budget to 0, and the trace reports that no intermediate tokens ran. Answer (authored) still shows 45 anyway, because the lab wrote that answer in advance instead of working it out. While you are here, try Dog on the ferry at a budget of 4 and then 5. The fourth line is padding about ticket prices, and the fifth invents a leash rule that the harbor notes never mention. Sample and vote In Sampling and voting, leave Single-sample accuracy at p = 0.40 and Wrong answers on Split over 3. That means each try is right 40% of the time, and the wrong tries spread evenly over three different wrong answers. Majority vote keeps whichever answer comes up most often, and Verifier picks keeps any try that a perfect checker accepts; What to notice explains both. Set Samples to 16, and Majority vote reads 70.8% while Verifier picks reads 99.97%. Now set Wrong answers to Always the same one, and Majority vote falls to 21.3%, below the 40% that One sample shows. Verifier picks does not move at all, because it needs only one right try out of the 16. Decode cost, the lab's name for how much text gets written, reads 16× tokens the whole time, a reminder that every extra try costs as much text as the first.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reasoning models
documents.body: Length grows because the checker rewards it In this toy, every step of the working lands, meaning it comes out right, with a chance of 0.80, which is 4 times out of 5. The answer passes when at least k steps land, so with k = 3, any try shorter than 3 steps can never pass. A try of exactly 3 steps passes only when all three steps land, and 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.512, so it passes about 51% of the time. Think of this rule as standing in for "is the final answer right?" The answer comes out right when enough steps landed, and the checker sees only that pass or fail, never which steps slipped. Longer tries have spare steps that can cover a slip, which is why the dashed line on the bar chart climbs fast as the length grows. A try of 4 steps passes about 82% of the time, and a try of 6 steps passes about 98%. The checker never rewards length directly, but longer tries pass more often, so they earn more reward and the policy drifts toward them. With no price on length, it keeps growing Once nearly every try passes, you might expect the length to stop growing, but it does not. With the cost off, nothing pushes back, and each extra step still adds a sliver of pass chance. In the groups that still contain a failure, that lone failure gets a large negative advantage. It works like the +1.73 a lone pass got in the four-try example, but it points down, and in a group of 16 it is even bigger, about −3.87. That failure is usually one of the shorter tries. So each of those groups pushes the policy longer, and the length keeps creeping up. At update 100, Steps past k still reads 4.1, which means the average try is about four steps longer than the task needs. This drift is called overthinking: working beyond what the answer needs, which adds waiting time without adding understanding. In this toy the extra steps are not pure waste, since each one still buys a sliver of pass chance. But that sliver gets smaller with every step, while the time each step costs stays the same. The length cost below trims away the steps whose sliver is worth less than their cost. The Groups with no signal readout shows why training slows down while the length keeps drifting, because it reads 51 of 100 at the end of the run. In 51 of the 100 updates every try in the group got the same score, mostly because they all passed, so those groups taught nothing. Only the other updates, the ones with a rare failure, kept pushing. Picture a class where long answers are never marked down, and an answer with extra lines is very slightly less likely to lose a mark. Week by week the answers that keep full marks are the longer ones, so answers drift longer while marks creep up only a hair. Unlike the students, the model is not choosing to be careful: longer tries simply passed a little more often, so they became a little more likely. A price trims length, but not down to k With Length cost on, each step costs 0.05, so a step is worth adding only if it raises the pass chance by more than 5 percentage points. That is because a pass is worth 1 point, so raising the pass chance by 5 percentage points earns 0.05 points on average, exactly what the step costs. Adding a fifth step raises the pass chance from about 82% to 94%, a gain of 12 points, so that step pays for itself. A sixth step raises it only from 94% to about 98%, a gain of about 4 points, so that step costs more than it earns. That is why the run with the cost hovers around 5 steps, ending at 5.3 on this seed. That is 2.3 steps past k rather than right at 3, but well short of the 7 you saw without the cost. The spare steps still protect against a slip, and the cost removes only the steps that no longer pay for themselves. Why a small group collapses The collapse at Group size 8 comes from grading on a curve when nobody passes. At the start, about 4 in 5 tries are shorter than 3 steps, so they can never pass. A small group often contains no pass at all, and every group like that pushes the policy shorter, which makes the next pass even less likely. When every try fails, the only difference between them is the length cost. Say a group holds four failed tries, two with 1 step and two with 2 steps. The 1-step tries lose 0.05 each for their cost, while the 2-step tries lose 0.10 each. So the scores are −0.05 and −0.10, the average is −0.075, and every score sits 0.025 from it, which makes the spread 0.025. That gap is tiny, but dividing by a spread of 0.025 blows it up, so the short tries get an advantage of +1 and the long tries get −1. That is the same size of push that a pass gets over a fail, so the policy learns "shorter is better" before it has ever seen a pass. Picture a quiz where every paper in the class fails, but the teacher still has to grade on a curve. If the only difference between the papers is how much scratch paper each one used, the shortest papers get the top marks. Week after week, the class learns to write less and less, and nobody ever gets close to a right answer. That is why Group size matters, because a group of 16 is much more likely to catch at least one pass early on. A single pass is worth far more than any cost difference, so it points the run toward longer working instead. Working helps most where a later step needs an earlier result On 17 + 28, the first line writes the carry and the second line reads it, so the working acts as memory. On Sunday hours the steps mostly look facts up. Only the third one leans on the others, picking the Sunday slot from the two facts the first two steps wrote down. After the useful steps, the trace shows two kinds of extra text that add tokens without helping the answer. Padding restates or recalls something the answer never uses, and it is harmless filler that does not pretend to be part of the work. An example is "Note that addition is associative, which is unused here." That line states a true fact, that it does not matter which pair you add first when you add three numbers, but this sum never needs it. An unfaithful step does not match the work the answer needs, yet it presents itself as part of that work. It might use the wrong operation, invent a rule, or drag in a fact as if it mattered. On 17 + 28 it reads "Check 17 × 28 as if the task were a product", which multiplies when the question asked for addition. That is why an unfaithful step misleads anyone who reads the working as a record of how the answer was found. The lab puts a right answer next to the unfaithful step on purpose, to show something real models do too. A right answer and working that honestly matches it are two separate things, and a model can produce one without the other. A checker needs only one right try A program or model that checks a candidate answer is called a verifier. When it is perfect, such as an exact answer key or a full set of tests, you can make n tries and keep any try it accepts. You succeed whenever at least one try is right, and that chance is called pass@n. Keeping the try that the verifier scores best is called best-of-n, and with a perfect verifier it succeeds exactly as often as pass@n says. The lab's chart labels the formula as 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ, where p is the chance a single try is right and n is the number of tries. To work it out with p = 0.40, notice that a single try is wrong 60% of the time. Two tries are therefore both wrong 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36 of the time, or 36%. So at least one of the two is right 1 − 0.36 = 0.64 of the time, which is 64%. With eight tries the chance reaches 98%, and with 16 tries it reaches the 99.97% you saw on Verifier picks. A vote follows the most popular answer A majority vote needs no checker at all, because it makes several tries and returns whichever final answer comes up most often. That works well when the right answer is the single most common answer, and badly when one particular wrong answer is more common than the right one. Picture a group chat settling 17 + 28 by poll, where everyone who gets it wrong made the same slip of forgetting the carry and answered 35. If 40% of the chat answers 45 while the other 60% all answer 35, the poll picks 35. Adding more people only makes that wrong result more certain, which is exactly what the Always the same one setting shows. There the vote falls to 21.3% at 16 samples, and adding more tries never lifts it back up, so by 32 samples it is lower still. It is not 0%, because with only 16 tries, luck sometimes gives 45 more votes than 35. Now picture the wrong answers scattered evenly across 35, 44 and 46, which is what Split over 3 means. Each wrong answer then gets only about 20% of the votes, so 45 with its 40% is the most popular single answer, and more voters help. The bar chart in the card shows this directly, with one bar for each possible number of right tries out of n. The height of a bar is the chance of getting that many right tries, and its solid part is the chance that the vote then picks the right answer. One more thing to check is that at 2 samples, Majority vote always equals One sample, whatever the other settings are. When the two tries disagree, the vote is a tie settled by a coin toss, so a second try cannot help a vote. With p = 0.40, both tries are right 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16 of the time. They split one right and one wrong 0.48 of the time, and the coin toss wins half of those, which adds 0.24. That totals 0.40, the same as one try.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reasoning models
documents.body: What this lab simplifies or fakes The learner in Train against a checker is one number, the length the toy most likes to write. The policy is a hump of odds over working of 1 to 8 steps, centred on that number, so training slides the hump rather than setting each bar separately. It is not a language model, so it learns how long to write and never what to write. The checker is a rule written by hand, in which every step lands with a fixed chance of 0.80, and no real checker works that way. There is one question instead of many, and each group of tries is used for one push and then thrown away. There is also no reference model and no clipping, two parts of real training that Going deeper explains. The curves and bars are exact averages for the policy at each update, but its path comes from randomly drawn groups, so another seed gives another path. The working, the labels and the answers on the Thinking budget and Inspectable trace cards were all written by hand, and no model writes them. The order of useful, then padding, then unfaithful is set by hand too, while a real model mixes them together. The answer prints at every budget, even 0, so the lab cannot show that cutting real working short usually costs accuracy on hard problems. Process supervision, which means grading each step of the working instead of only the final answer, is named here but never computed. In Sampling and voting, p is a number you choose rather than a measured model, every try is independent of the others, and the verifier is perfect. Where real reasoning models fail The collapse you saw is real, because with a length cost and no passing try in the early groups, the cost is the only signal. Scaling by the spread makes that small signal look large. Real training softens the problem by mixing many questions into each batch, which is the set of tries used for one round of training. A checker sees only the final answer, so it cannot tell a needed step from a wasted one. Padding and unfaithful steps that end in a right answer get rewarded along with everything else. Real tries from one model are not independent, because they tend to repeat the same mistakes. The lab's math treats every try as separate, so real extra tries can help less than it suggests. Best-of-n with a learned grader, which is a second model trained to score answers, can pick an answer that fools the grader instead of one that is right. Process supervision can catch a wrong step that happens to reach a right answer, but it can still reward a smooth-sounding step that the answer never uses. Even working that looks useful and leads to a right answer may not be the real route the model took. So working is not a window into how the answer was produced. A common mix-up: people often read a model's numbered steps as a faithful record of how it reached its answer. The steps are generated tokens, though. Researchers have tried changing or cutting lines of a model's working and letting it carry on, and sometimes it gives exactly the same answer. If changing the steps does not change the answer, those steps cannot be the full story of how the answer was reached. So the steps are not a window into a hidden mind. A second mix-up is to think that asking for steps in a prompt and training a reasoning model are the same thing. A prompt changes only what the model reads, while training against a checker changes the model's weights.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reasoning models
documents.body: Real RLVR and GRPO add four things that this toy leaves out on purpose, to keep the lab small enough to follow: A policy over every token: the push reaches the odds of every token the model writes, so a real model learns what to write, not only how long. A penalty for drifting: a penalty called the KL penalty (KL comes from the names of Kullback and Leibler, the two mathematicians behind it) works like a leash. It measures how far the model's writing has moved from a reference model, the version it started from, and charges for the distance. That charge keeps the model from drifting into strange text that games the checker instead of solving the problem. Clipping: real training reuses each batch of tries for several pushes, and clipping stops the model from moving too far from the version that made those tries. That keeps the reuse safe. Many questions per batch: mixing many questions into each batch averages out the noise, and groups whose tries all scored the same matter less. That is because the other questions in the batch still give a push. Published versions of GRPO differ in how they size each push, by dividing by the length of each answer and by how spread out the group's scores are. Those choices matter, because each one changes how long the answers grow as training goes on. On hard problems with many steps, reported accuracy rises when models get a bigger thinking budget, and it falls when they are forced to stop early. Search goes further than voting, because instead of only comparing finished answers, it also judges working that is still half-written. A system makes several tries, scores the unfinished working with a trained model that grades each step, called a process reward model, and continues only the best. Distillation trains a smaller or faster model to copy the long working of a strong reasoning model. It is a bit like copying a classmate's homework, because the student model copies the text of the steps, not a guaranteed method for solving the problem. Unlike copied homework, though, the student model learns to write similar working on new questions it never saw. What it does not get is any guarantee that the method behind that working is sound. Related recipes live in the Preference optimization in practice and Post-training labs, which cover other ways to train a model after its main training. The Agents lab shows a similar budget being spent on tool calls, which are actions such as running a search, instead of on extra tokens.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reasoning models
documents.body: This module is about reasoning models, which write a long chain of thought, the intermediate tokens generated before an answer. It asks where those traces come from, and when test-time compute, extra work at answer time spent on a longer trace or on several samples, buys accuracy. Those traces come from training, not prompting: RLVR (reinforcement learning with a verifiable reward, one computed by a program that checks answers) changes the weights, while a prompt changes only what the model reads. The module builds on *ICL & reasoning*, *Reinforcement learning foundations* and *Preference optimization in practice*. Where it shows up Post-training. Reasoning models are typically post-trained with RLVR, and published variants of GRPO, the group-relative method the lab imitates, differ in how they normalise the loss. Thinking budgets. On hard multi-step problems, reported accuracy tracks how long the model may think. Several samples. Majority vote (self-consistency), best-of-n with a verifier or a learned reward model, and search guided by a process reward model (a learned model that scores each step) all spend compute on more than one sample. Distillation and agents. Smaller models are trained to imitate a strong model's traces, and agents spend a similar budget on tool calls. Why it matters A trace lets later tokens read results that earlier tokens wrote down, so it helps where later steps need earlier results. Training for traces and spending extra compute also have specific limits: With only a pass-or-fail reward, nothing prices length, so traces pad past what the task needs (overthinking): each spare step adds latency and only a little pass chance. A checker sees only the final answer, and a visible chain can be useful yet unfaithful (with steps that do not match the work the answer needs), so a trace is no proof of inner thoughts. A vote amplifies the most common answer, even a wrong one; only a perfect verifier succeeds whenever any sample is right. What you will be able to explain How a reasoning model, whose long traces come from reinforcement learning against a checker, differs from in-context chain-of-thought prompting. How group-relative training against a verifiable reward lengthens traces, and why a missing length cost lets them pad. Why test-time compute is extra generated tokens or search, not proof of inner thoughts. When majority voting helps, and when only a verifier does. What the lab shows The training card is a seeded simulation of a toy policy, the traces are authored, and the voting card is closed-form arithmetic. Train against a checker runs 100 GRPO-style updates on a one-parameter policy over trace lengths of 1 to 8 steps. The checker is a hand-written rule, and no language model is involved. Its controls are Steps the task needs (k), Group size (G), Learning rate, Seed, Length cost and Training update. Curves and bars are exact expectations, but the policy's path comes from sampled groups, so the seed matters. Problem picks *Sunday hours*, *17 + 28* or *Dog on the ferry*; Thinking budget reveals up to six authored steps in Inspectable trace, each labelled useful, padding or unfaithful by hand, and the Useful, Padding and Unfaithful tiles count them. Answer (authored) prints at every budget. Sampling and voting computes Majority vote and Verifier picks exactly from Samples, Single-sample accuracy (an assumed p) and Wrong answers, with independent samples and a perfect verifier. Key experiments: drag Training update from 0 to 100 with Length cost *Off*, then *On · 0.05 per step*, and compare Mean length with k. Then set Wrong answers to *Always the same one*: Majority vote falls below One sample, while Verifier picks holds.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reasoning models
documents.body: A reasoning model is a next-token predictor post-trained to write a long chain of thought before it answers. A prompt can ask any model for steps and leaves its weights alone; this recipe changes the weights. It is RLVR, reinforcement learning with a verifiable reward: sample several traces for one prompt, let a program check each final answer, and make the traces that pass likelier. GRPO scores each trace against its own group: advantage = (reward − group mean) / group standard deviation. The group is the baseline, so no separate value network is needed. Longer traces tend to emerge because they pass more often. Test-time compute is the extra work spent while answering. This lab shows two kinds: a longer trace (the authored Thinking budget cards) and several sampled answers with a way to choose among them (Sampling and voting, exact arithmetic). The toy in the first card Train against a checker trains one number, the typical trace length, with exactly that update. The policy is a bump over 1 to 8 steps. The checker is a hand-written rule: a trace passes when at least k of its steps land, and each step lands with probability 0.80. It is a one-parameter policy and a rule, not a language model.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reasoning models
documents.body: In-context learning showed chains prompted with worked examples. Reinforcement learning foundations showed a policy improving against a reward. This lab joins them: the reward is a checker, and the policy is a trace writer. The sampling half also sets up an idea the Evaluation lab uses: how often at least one of n tries succeeds.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reasoning models
documents.body: In Train against a checker, keep k = 3, a group of 16, learning rate 0.3, and seed 1. With Length cost off, drag Training update from 0 to 100. Mean length climbs from 1.8 steps to 7.1, well past the 3 the task needs, while the pass rate goes from 10% to 99%. Turn Length cost on and the length ends at 5.3 steps with a 93% pass rate. Now set Group size to 8: the policy collapses to one-step answers, with a 1% pass rate. Problem and Thinking budget slice an authored trace. On 17 + 28, the first step writes the carry and the second reads it. In Sampling and voting, leave p = 0.40 and Split over 3, and set Samples to 16. Majority vote reads 70.8% and Verifier picks 99.97%. Now set Wrong answers to Always the same one: the vote drops to 21.3%, below a single sample.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reasoning models
documents.body: Length emerges because the checker rewards it. A trace shorter than k never passes, and a trace of exactly 3 steps passes only 51% of the time, because every step must land. Longer traces earn more. With the cost off, nothing pushes back. After the pass rate saturates, Steps past k still reads 4.1 at update 100: overthinking. In 51 of the 100 updates every sampled trace had the same reward, so the group taught nothing. The cost trims length but not to k. It ends 2.3 steps past k, because spare steps still insure against a slip. A trace helps where later steps need earlier results. Past the useful steps, padding and unfaithful steps add latency and nothing else. With a perfect checker, or verifier, success is 1 − (1 − p)^n: pass@n. At p = 0.40 it passes 98% by eight samples. Majority vote (self-consistency) needs no checker but returns whichever answer is most common. When one wrong answer is likelier than the right one, more samples make it worse.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reasoning models
documents.body: In this lab. The policy is one number over eight lengths, and the checker is a hand-written rule with a fixed step success of 0.80. There is one prompt, one gradient step per sampled group, no reference model, and no clipping. The curves are exact expectations of a policy whose path came from sampled groups, so another seed gives another path. The traces and the answer slot on the other cards are authored; process supervision is named, not computed; the sampling card treats p as your assumption. In real systems. The collapse you saw is real: with a length cost and no passing trace in the early groups, cost is the only signal, and normalisation scales it up. Real runs dilute it with many prompts per batch. A checker sees only the final answer, so it cannot tell a needed step from a wasted one. Samples from one model are correlated, and best-of-n with a learned reward model can pick an answer that games the reward. Visible chains can be useful and still unfaithful.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reasoning models
documents.body: Real RLVR and GRPO add what the toy leaves out: A token-level policy. The gradient reaches every token's probability, so the model learns what to write, not only how long to write. A KL penalty to a reference model. It keeps the policy near the model it started from, so it cannot drift into text that games the checker. Clipped ratios. Several gradient steps can reuse one batch without moving too far. Many prompts per batch. Noise averages out, and groups with equal rewards matter less. Published GRPO variants change how the loss is normalised by length and by group standard deviation, because both choices affect how long responses grow. On hard multi-step problems, reported accuracy rises with the thinking budget, and forcing an early stop lowers it. Search goes further than voting: sample, score partial traces with a process reward model, and extend the promising ones. Distillation copies long traces from a strong reasoning model into a smaller one; the student copies the text of the steps, not a guaranteed algorithm. Preference optimization and post-training are where related recipes live, and Agents spend a similar budget on tool calls instead of tokens.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Problem · Reasoning models
documents.body: A question the policy already practiced Problem chooses Sunday hours, 17 + 28, or a dog on the ferry. They stand for items a reasoning model met during post-training, not few-shot examples pasted into a prompt. The contrast with the ICL lab is the recipe, not the harbor facts: a prompt changes what the model reads, while training against a checker changes its weights. Problem, three segments, and the question text. A note contrasting the two recipes: examples in a prompt (no weight change) and post-training with reinforcement learning against answers a program can check (weights change). Switching Problem writes problem and resets Thinking budget to 3. No prompt with worked examples is built. The traces are authored to look like trained behaviour. Problem. Comparison worth running: Sunday hours against 17 + 28. The arithmetic trace has a step whose result the next step reads (the carry); the lookup trace mostly does not. The harbor facts match other labs so the course stays one world. Neither the Train against a checker card nor the sampling card depends on which problem is selected: one trains a toy policy over trace length, the other is arithmetic on an assumed accuracy. In this lab: three authored problems. No model samples the steps. In general: a reasoning model is still a next-token predictor with a different post-training recipe, not a new layer type.
documents.title: A question the policy already practiced

documents.subtitle: Train against a checker · Reasoning models
documents.body: A toy policy learns from a checker to write longer traces A one-parameter policy over trace length (1 to 8 steps) is trained by a group-relative policy gradient, GRPO-style, against a hand-written checker: a trace of L steps passes when at least k of its steps land, each landing with probability 0.80. It shows a verifiable reward making traces longer, an unpriced length drifting past what the task needs, and a per-step cost trimming it. It is not a language model. Controls Steps the task needs (k) from 1 to 4, Group size (G) from 2 to 32, Learning rate from 0.1 to 1.0, Seed, Training update (a scrubber over the 100 updates), and Length cost Off or On. Two learning curves with a marker at the chosen update: Checker pass rate (plus Mean reward after cost when the cost is on), and Mean trace length against a dotted line at k. Bars for the policy over trace length at that update: solid bars now, outlines for the starting policy, a dashed line for the checker's pass chance at each length, and a vertical rule left of which a trace is too short to ever pass. Metrics Checker pass rate, Mean length, Steps past k, Mean reward after cost, and Groups with no signal (updates so far whose sampled group had identical rewards). Policy: a softmax over lengths 1 to 8 with logits −(L − μ)² / 2. The single trained number is μ, which starts at 1.5, so short traces dominate and the mean length is 1.8 steps. Checker: pass chance for length L is P(at least k of L steps land) with each step landing at 0.80. Reward is pass minus 0.05 × L when Length cost is on, and pass alone when it is off. Each of the 100 updates samples G lengths, runs the checker on each, and sets advantage = (reward − group mean) / (group standard deviation + 1e-6). Then μ += rate × (1/G) × Σ advantage × (L − mean length). A group with identical rewards has zero advantage and changes nothing. The curves and bars are exact expectations of the current policy. The path μ takes comes from the sampled groups, so a run is deterministic in the seed and the controls and a different seed gives a different path. Steps the task needs (k), Group size (G), Learning rate, Seed, Training update, and Length cost. Comparison worth running: with the defaults (k = 3, group of 16, rate 0.3, seed 1) and Length cost Off, mean length ends at 7.1 steps and the pass rate at 99%. Turn Length cost On: the length ends at 5.3 steps and the pass rate at 93%. Then set Group size to 8 with the cost on: the policy collapses to one-step answers (1.2 steps, 1% pass rate). Length emerges because the checker rewards it. A trace shorter than k never passes, and a trace of exactly 3 steps passes 51% of the time, so longer traces earn more. With the cost off, length keeps rising after the pass rate saturates: Steps past k reads 4.1 at update 100, and in 51 of 100 updates the sampled group had identical rewards and taught nothing. That is overthinking. The cost trims length but not to k. It ends 2.3 steps past k, because spare steps still insure against a slip. On a hard task (k = 4) with the cost on, no early group contains a pass, so the cost is the only difference between traces and length collapses. In this lab: the policy is one number over eight lengths, not a language model. The checker is a hand-written rule with a fixed step success of 0.80. There is one prompt, one gradient step per sampled group, no reference model, and no clipping. The traces on the other cards are not produced by this policy. In general: real RLVR and GRPO train a token-level policy over a language model, add a KL penalty to a reference model, clip probability ratios, average over many prompts per batch, and face checkers that can be gamed. Longer traces there help on some problems and are wasted tokens on others.
documents.title: A toy policy learns from a checker to write longer traces

documents.subtitle: Thinking budget · Reasoning models
documents.body: How many authored steps are revealed Thinking budget reveals 0 to 6 authored steps, useful first, then padding, then an unfaithful step, then a final useful one. The answer slot is authored and prints at every budget. Extra tokens are test-time compute, not a weight update. Thinking budget, a slider whose maximum is the trace length. Metrics Useful, Padding, Unfaithful, and Answer (authored). A note on why a trace can help: each token is another forward pass that can read what earlier steps wrote. visible = trace.slice(0, budget). The three counts filter the kind field. Answer (authored) always prints the problem's canned answer. It is not computed from the visible steps. Thinking budget. Comparison worth running: 3 against 6 on Sunday hours, then 0 on 17 + 28. Padding does not change the answer. Unfaithful steps name unused facts or the wrong operation. On real hard problems, forcing a short trace usually lowers accuracy. This lab does not model that, which is why the answer is labelled authored. In this lab: the order useful → padding → unfaithful is authored. A real sampler interleaves them. In general: a fixed-depth transformer does a bounded amount of computation per token; a chain lets it spread serial work across many tokens, and that is where long traces help.
documents.title: How many authored steps are revealed

documents.subtitle: Inspectable trace · Reasoning models
documents.body: Tokens labelled useful, padding, or unfaithful Each revealed line is a generated-looking sentence with a label this lab assigns. The labels are teaching marks, not a probe of an inner algorithm. A process reward model would score these steps; this page only displays them. An ordered list; an empty budget prints that no intermediate tokens ran. Each row has a kind label and the sentence. The list is the prefix of the authored trace. Distillation, if this were production, would copy these strings into a student. The student would copy text, not an algorithm. This card has no controls. Comparison worth running: budget 4 on Dog on the ferry (padding about ticket price) against budget 5 (an invented leash rule). An unfaithful step can sit beside a correct answer. Faithfulness is a separate claim from accuracy. On 17 + 28, the first line writes the carry that the second line uses: the trace is working memory. In this lab: the trace is a template. No model writes it, and no process reward is computed. In general: visible steps can be useful and still unfaithful. Studies that edit or truncate a model's trace find the final answer sometimes ignores it.
documents.title: Tokens labelled useful, padding, or unfaithful

documents.subtitle: Sampling and voting · Reasoning models
documents.body: More samples, and two ways to pick one The other kind of test-time compute: draw n independent answers, each right with probability p, then either keep the most common answer (majority vote) or keep any answer a perfect checker accepts (verifier picks). Both curves are exact binomial arithmetic. Controls Samples (1 to 32), Single-sample accuracy (p from 0.05 to 0.95), and Wrong answers: Always the same one, Split over 3, or All different. A chart of accuracy against n: dotted one sample (flat at p), solid majority vote, dashed verifier picks, with markers at the current n. Bars for the binomial probability of k correct samples out of n. The solid part of each bar is the chance the vote then picks the right answer. Metrics One sample, Majority vote, Verifier picks, and Decode cost in multiples of one sample's tokens. Verifier picks = 1 − (1 − p)^n, the chance at least one sample is right. That is pass@n, the ceiling for any way of choosing among the samples. Majority vote = Σₖ P(k correct) × P(the right answer wins the plurality | k), with ties broken at random. Wrong samples are spread evenly over 1 or 3 wrong answers, or are all different; the win probability is computed exactly by counting how the wrong votes can fall. Samples, Single-sample accuracy, and Wrong answers. Comparison worth running: at p = 0.40 and 16 samples, Split over 3 gives a majority vote of 70.8% against a verifier's 99.97%. Switch to Always the same one and the vote falls to 21.3%, below one sample. Voting amplifies whichever single answer is most likely. If one wrong answer beats the right one, more samples make the vote worse. Two samples never beat one under voting: a split vote is a coin toss. In this lab: p is your assumption, samples are independent, and the verifier is perfect. Real samples from one model are correlated, and learned verifiers make mistakes that selection can exploit. In general: sampling more helps only with a way to choose. Unit tests, proof checkers, and exact answer keys are the checkers that make best-of-n reliable.
documents.title: More samples, and two ways to pick one

documents.subtitle: Chunk a small corpus, retrieve with BM25, a dense encoder or both, assemble the prompt, score the pipeline to see whether each confident wrong quote is a retrieval failure or a reader failure, and add a grounding check that abstains when the best match scores too low.
documents.body: Chunk a small corpus, retrieve with BM25, a dense encoder or both, assemble the prompt, score the pipeline to see whether each confident wrong quote is a retrieval failure or a reader failure, and add a grounding check that abstains when the best match scores too low. Describe RAG as chunk, retrieve, assemble a prompt, then generate — a pipeline over your index, not a model that looked something up by itself Explain how chunk size and overlap decide whether an answer can be retrieved whole Name three retrieval failures — a split answer, a stale index, a vocabulary mismatch — and why each still yields a fluent, cited answer Compare BM25, dense and hybrid retrieval by what each misses — synonyms for BM25, words the encoder has no vector for for dense — and how reciprocal-rank fusion keeps either one’s hit Score a pipeline with context recall, a support check and correctness, and use recall to tell a retrieval failure from a reader failure Use a retrieval-score threshold to make a pipeline abstain, and read the coverage and precision trade-off — a score measures how well a chunk matches the question, not whether it answers it
documents.title: Retrieval-augmented generation

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Leave Question on North dock, Sunday. Find the answer span on the Harbor handbook ruler, the [1] chunk in Retrieval, the same text in Assembled prompt, and 16:00 in Reader output.
documents.title: Follow one question

documents.subtitle: Step 2 · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Set Chunk size to 12. The answer span now straddles two chunks, the ruler shows no whole-answer chunk, and the reader quotes 18:00 — the weekday time.
documents.title: Cut the answer in half

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Keep Chunk size at 12 and raise Overlap to 7. A window now starts at “north”, the reader returns 16:00 again, and Chunks in index rises from 8 to 15.
documents.title: Overlap the windows

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Set Chunk size to 20, Overlap to 0 and Question to Afternoon ferry. Built before the June notice, the index yields the stale 15:40. Switch Index built to after, then set Top-k to 2 and read the conflict check.
documents.title: Refresh the index

documents.subtitle: Step 5 · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Set Question to Dog on the ferry, then to Closed for wind now, with Retriever on BM25. Read which chunk wins in Retrieval and what the reader quotes when the right passage never arrives.

documents.subtitle: Step 6 · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: With Chunk size 20 and Overlap 0, set Index built to before, Question to Dog on the ferry and Top-k to 2, then switch Retriever from BM25 to Dense: the pets chunk arrives as [2]. Next set Index built to after and Question to Changed in June, and compare BM25, Dense and Hybrid.
documents.title: Switch the retriever

documents.subtitle: Step 7 · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Set Chunk size to 20, Overlap to 0, Index built to after and Top-k to 3, with every Abstain below slider off. In Score the pipeline compare the Mean context recall and Answers correct rows across the three retrievers, read which failures sit on the reader side, and find the wind row: it reads wrong because no answer exists.
documents.title: Score the pipeline

documents.subtitle: Step 8 · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Keep those settings, choose Retriever BM25 and Question Closed for wind now?, then raise Abstain below in Grounding check from off to 2.4. Wind turns to correctly abstained, but Changed in June (best score 1.87, under wind’s 2.28) turns to wrongly abstained. Switch Retriever to Dense, set 0.9, and compare Handled correctly in Score the pipeline.
documents.title: Set an abstention threshold

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: A pipeline that retrieves passages from an index and places them in the prompt before the model generates. The model is unchanged; only its input is.
documents.title: Retrieval-augmented generation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: A window of text stored and retrieved as one unit. Here a chunk is a fixed number of words (Chunk size) and consecutive windows share Overlap words. Too small a window cuts one fact across chunks, too large a window mixes topics, and more overlap stores and scores more chunks for a likelier whole fact. Real systems often split on sentences, headings or tokens.
documents.title: Chunk

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: The stored, searchable chunks. It is a snapshot of the documents at build time; a document added later is invisible until the index is rebuilt.
documents.title: Index

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: The component that scores chunks against the question and returns the top-k. If it misses, nothing downstream can recover the fact.
documents.title: Retriever

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: A keyword score that sums, over query terms in a chunk, a rarity weight (IDF) times a saturating term count, discounted for long chunks. It cannot match synonyms it never sees.
documents.title: BM25

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Ranking chunks by the cosine between the question's embedding and each chunk's embedding, so a chunk can match without sharing a word. It is only as good as the encoder: words the encoder has no vector for add nothing, and exact names, codes and dates can blur together.
documents.title: Dense retrieval

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Running a keyword retriever and a dense retriever and merging their rankings, so a chunk that either one finds can reach the prompt. Production systems usually follow the merge with a reranker.
documents.title: Hybrid retrieval

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: A way to merge ranked lists: each chunk scores the sum of 1 divided by (60 plus its rank) over every list that contains it. It uses ranks, not scores, so BM25 scores and cosines need no common scale.
documents.title: Reciprocal rank fusion

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: How many retrieved chunks go into the prompt. A larger k raises the chance of including the answer and also adds distractors and conflicting passages.
documents.title: Top-k

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: The token budget the generator reads at once. The instructions, retrieved chunks and question all share it.
documents.title: Context window

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: A pointer from the answer back to a numbered passage. It shows which passage was quoted, not that the passage was correct, current or the right one.
documents.title: Citation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: The share of the gold evidence that reached the prompt. Here it counts the answer-span words that sit inside a retrieved chunk. A wrong answer with low recall points upstream, at chunking, the index or the retriever; a wrong answer with full recall points at the reader.
documents.title: Context recall

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Whether an answer is supported by the retrieved context, which is what grounding an answer means. This lab checks only that the quoted sentence appears word for word in the passage it cites. Support is not correctness: a supported quote can answer a different question, and checking a real generator's claims takes a judge model or a person.
documents.title: Faithfulness

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Declining to answer: here the pipeline says the sources do not say. The grounding check abstains when nothing was retrieved or the best retrieved chunk scores below a threshold. A score measures how well a chunk matches the question, not whether it answers it, so a threshold can withhold right answers and let wrong ones through.
documents.title: Abstention

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Coverage is the share of questions the pipeline answers; precision is the share of those answers that are right. Raising the abstention threshold can only lower coverage; precision rises when the answers it drops were wrong and falls when they were right.
documents.title: Precision and coverage

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Retrieval-augmented generation
documents.body: Text that was true when indexed and is no longer. Ranking has no notion of date unless the system adds one, for example as metadata.
documents.title: Stale data

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Retrieval-augmented generation · question 1
documents.body: At Chunk size 12 and Overlap 0, North dock, Sunday is answered with 18:00 and a handbook citation. What went wrong? The handbook states the wrong Sunday time, and the reader copied it faithfully A window edge split the sentence, so the Sunday clause was never retrieved BM25 ranked a ferry timetable chunk first, so the handbook never reached the prompt The source is correct and the right document was retrieved. At Chunk size 12 “north dock closes at 18:00 on weekdays” and “and at 16:00 on Sundays” land in different chunks, and at Top-k 2 only the first one is retrieved. The quote is fluent, cited and wrong. Overlap or a larger window keeps the span in one chunk.
documents.title: At Chunk size 12 and Overlap 0, North dock, Sunday is answered with 18:00 and a handbook citation. What went wrong?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Retrieval-augmented generation · question 2
documents.body: Switching Index built from before to after changes the Afternoon ferry answer from 15:40 to 16:10. What changed in the pipeline? The notice became searchable, so a chunk holding 16:10 could reach the prompt The reader learned the new time from the notice and stopped trusting the timetable The retriever noticed that the 2025 timetable was out of date and demoted it Nothing about the reader or the retriever's scoring changed. The index is a snapshot, so a document added later is invisible until the index is rebuilt. Once the notice is in it, its short chunk outranks the timetable on the same question words. BM25 has no notion of dates, which is why Top-k 2 puts both times in the prompt.
documents.title: Switching Index built from before to after changes the Afternoon ferry answer from 15:40 to 16:10. What changed in the pipeline?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Retrieval-augmented generation · question 3
documents.body: With Retriever on BM25, Dog on the ferry retrieves only timetable chunks. Why is the pets sentence never retrieved? No word in it matches the question, so its chunk scores 0 under BM25 Chunk size 20 is too large for any chunk to hold a whole sentence about pets BM25 skips handbook chunks whenever the question mentions a ferry or a boat “Pets may travel on a leash with a tag” has no word in common with “Can I bring my dog on the ferry?”, so its chunk scores 0 and a timetable chunk wins on “ferry”. At Chunk size 20 a chunk holds the whole sentence, and BM25 has no rule about documents. The failure is vocabulary: dog and pets are different strings.
documents.title: With Retriever on BM25, Dog on the ferry retrieves only timetable chunks. Why is the pets sentence never retrieved?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Retrieval-augmented generation · question 4
documents.body: With Index built after the notice, Changed in June retrieves the notice under BM25 and nothing under Dense. Why? The notice’s vector points in a different direction from the question’s vector The notice is too short to be embedded, so Dense search skips it The question has no vector at all, because the encoder knows none of its words The toy encoder has no vector for “changed” or “June”, so the question’s vector is all zeros and every cosine is 0. Nothing is retrieved, while BM25 weights the rare word “june” most and finds the notice at once. Real encoders are not blind to rare words, but dates, names and codes are where dense scores are least reliable.
documents.title: With Index built after the notice, Changed in June retrieves the notice under BM25 and nothing under Dense. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Retrieval-augmented generation · question 5
documents.body: BM25 misses the pets chunk for Dog on the ferry and Dense misses the notice for Changed in June. Why can Hybrid retrieve both? It runs BM25 first and falls back to Dense only when BM25 returns nothing It averages the BM25 score and the cosine, so one high score carries a chunk Each list gives its chunks 1/(60 + rank), so a chunk in one list scores Reciprocal-rank fusion adds 1/(60 + rank) for every list that contains the chunk, so a chunk found by only one retriever still scores and a chunk found by both scores about double. It fuses ranks, not scores, because BM25 scores and cosines live on different scales. It is not a fallback: for Dog, BM25 does return something, so a fallback would never call Dense.
documents.title: BM25 misses the pets chunk for Dog on the ferry and Dense misses the notice for Changed in June. Why can Hybrid retrieve both?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Retrieval-augmented generation · question 6
documents.body: Dog on the ferry, Retriever Dense, Top-k 2, index before: context recall reads 100% and the answer is still wrong. Where did it fail? In retrieval, because the pets chunk was ranked below a timetable chunk In the reader, which skipped the pets sentence although it was in the prompt In the support check, because the quoted sentence is not in any retrieved chunk The pets chunk arrives as [2], so every answer-span word reached the prompt. The reader quotes the piece that shares the most words with the question, and “Pets may travel on a leash with a tag” shares none, so it quotes the ferry sentence. Full recall with a wrong answer is a reader failure. A language model could use the pets sentence; this stand-in cannot.
documents.title: Dog on the ferry, Retriever Dense, Top-k 2, index before: context recall reads 100% and the answer is still wrong. Where did it fail?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Retrieval-augmented generation · question 7
documents.body: In Score the pipeline almost every quote is marked supported, yet many answers are wrong. What does that show? The scorer is broken, because a supported quote must be a correct answer Retrieval worked for those questions, so every remaining failure is in the reader The support check tests whether the cited passage holds the quote, not the answer The reader only quotes, so its quote is always inside the passage it cites, whatever the question. Support says nothing about whether that passage was the right one, current, or complete, so it cannot separate a correct answer from a wrong one. Correctness against the gold fact and context recall do that, and only a real generator can fail the support check.
documents.title: In Score the pipeline almost every quote is marked supported, yet many answers are wrong. What does that show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Retrieval-augmented generation · question 8
documents.body: Retriever BM25, Index built after, Top-k 3. You raise Abstain below until Closed for wind now? turns to correctly abstained. What does Changed in June do? It turns to wrongly abstained, because its best chunk scores lower than the wind question’s It stays answered correctly, because the June notice is the only chunk that holds the answer It turns to correctly abstained, because the index was rebuilt after that notice arrived The check reads only the best chunk’s score. Wind’s best chunk, the 40-knot rule, matches “harbor” and “wind” and scores 2.28; the June notice matches only the rare word “june” and scores 1.87. Any threshold that drops wind drops June too, although June’s answer is in the corpus. A score measures how well words match, not whether a passage answers.
documents.title: Retriever BM25, Index built after, Top-k 3. You raise Abstain below until Closed for wind now? turns to correctly abstained. What does Changed in June do?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Retrieval-augmented generation · question 9
documents.body: In Grounding check you keep raising Abstain below. Which statement about coverage and precision holds every time?
