The slider cannot abstain on wind without also abstaining on June, so Handled correctly stays at 3 of 5 while precision reaches 100% and coverage falls to 40%. Under Dense the same idea works on these five questions: wind scores 0.843, below Sunday and ferry (0.981 and 1.000), so a threshold at 0.9 lifts Handled correctly from 2 to 3. That is a feature of five hand-written questions, not a rule: 0.843 is still a high cosine, and the check cannot tell that nothing here reports today's wind. Hybrid scores sit at 2.00 for almost every question, because the best chunk is first in both lists. Wind's best chunk is first in one list and second in the other (1.984), so only a threshold of 2.00 separates it, and that also drops Changed in June (1.00). A stale answer is not caught: with Index built before, the 15:40 chunk scores 4.38 under BM25, far above wind, because it matches the question as well as a right source would. In this lab: five questions and one corpus, with the scores of the three toy retrievers, so a threshold is tuned on the questions it is graded on. The reader is extractive, the abstention line is fixed text, and nothing judges whether a passage answers the question. Hybrid's scale is the fused rank score times 61, which this card invents to make it readable. In general: a retrieval score measures similarity, not truth or relevance to the question, and it is not calibrated across queries, retrievers or index versions. Production systems calibrate a threshold on labelled questions and re-tune it when the index or the encoder changes, and add a verifier (an entailment check or a judge model) or a model trained to say “I do not know”. Abstaining too often is itself a failure that users feel.
documents.title: Say “the sources do not say” when the best match is weak

documents.subtitle: Solve a tiny gridworld with real Bellman backups, watch value flow backward from a delayed reward, and see an exploit become the optimal policy, so RLHF later reads as one use of the same loop.
documents.body: Solve a tiny gridworld with real Bellman backups, watch value flow backward from a delayed reward, and see an exploit become the optimal policy, so RLHF later reads as one use of the same loop. Identify state, action, reward, policy, and discounted return in a small episode Use the Bellman backup to explain credit assignment as value flowing backward from a delayed reward Explain why learning from samples needs exploration, and why a misspecified reward is maximized anyway Explain how a policy-gradient update turns sampled rewards into a better policy, and what a baseline and the learning rate change
documents.title: Reinforcement learning foundations

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: On Return along the episode, move Episode step from 0 to the end and compare Reward this step with Return so far and Full return G₀.
documents.title: Read one episode

documents.subtitle: Step 2 · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Set Value-iteration sweeps to 0, then raise it one sweep at a time and watch value spread backward from G until V(S) stops changing.
documents.title: Sweep the backup

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Move Discount γ from 0.95 down to 0.50 and read V(S), then set Slip chance to 20% and watch the arrows beside T turn away from it.
documents.title: Change the discount

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: On Explore versus exploit, set Exploration ε to 0, then 0.10, then 0.50, and compare Best-arm share, 300 runs with Same, ε = 0.
documents.title: Explore or exploit

documents.subtitle: Step 5 · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Set Bonus tile H to on at Discount γ 0.95 and watch the episode circle H, then lower Discount γ to 0.85 and watch it walk to G again.
documents.title: Turn on the bonus

documents.subtitle: Step 6 · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: On Policy gradient on the bandit, leave Baseline on at Learning rate α 0.20 and read Best-arm probability, 300 runs, 92.1%. Switch Baseline off and compare it with 84.9%, and Runs below 50% on best arm, 2 against 29 of 300.
documents.title: Follow the policy gradient

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: The information the policy is allowed to see before it acts. Here that is the cell index. If a needed fact is outside the state, no amount of training recovers it.
documents.title: State

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: The choice the policy emits, here one of up, right, down, or left. In language-model training each generated token can be treated as an action.
documents.title: Action

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: A scalar the designer chose to pay for a transition. It is not an objective fact about goodness, and a misspecified reward is maximized as faithfully as a good one.
documents.title: Reward

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: A rule, often a probability distribution, that maps each state to an action. Here it is the greedy action with respect to the current value table.
documents.title: Policy

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: One run from the start state until a terminal state or a step cap. This lab caps episodes at 24 steps so a loop cannot run forever.
documents.title: Episode

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: The discounted sum of rewards from a time step onward, G = r1 + γ r2 + γ² r3 and so on. One episode's return is a single sample, not an average.
documents.title: Return

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: The number γ between 0 and 1 that shrinks a reward k steps away by γ to the k. It sets how far ahead the agent cares, and keeps an endless stream of rewards finite.
documents.title: Discount factor

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: V(s), the expected return from state s when following a policy. With slip on it is an average over outcomes, so a single episode's return can land above or below it.
documents.title: Value function

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: The recursion V(s) = max over actions of the expected immediate reward plus γ times V of the next state. It turns a long-horizon question into a one-step lookup.
documents.title: Bellman equation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Applying the Bellman backup to every state repeatedly, starting from zero. It needs the full transition table, and each sweep shrinks the worst error by at least a factor of γ.
documents.title: Value iteration

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Deciding which earlier actions earned a later reward. In value iteration the answer travels backward one cell per sweep; with sparse, delayed rewards that is the hard part.
documents.title: Credit assignment

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Trying actions whose value is uncertain, at a short-term cost. An agent that learns only from its own samples cannot improve its estimate of an action it never takes.
documents.title: Exploration

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Policy gradient nudges a policy's parameters along the gradient of ln π(action) times (reward − baseline), so an action that beat the baseline becomes more likely and one that fell short less likely. REINFORCE is the basic form. It needs only sampled rewards, not a transition table. A baseline that ignores the current action leaves the expected update unchanged and reduces its noise.
documents.title: Policy gradient and baseline

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: A policy scoring highly on the written reward by a route the designer did not intend. It is correct optimization of the wrong scalar, not a bug in the optimizer.
documents.title: Reward hacking

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reinforcement learning foundations · question 1
documents.body: With no slip, you lower Discount γ from 0.95 to 0.50 on Return along the episode. What happens to Full return G₀ and to the path the policy takes? G₀ falls and the path bends toward T, because a short horizon makes the −1 look closer G₀ rises because a smaller γ also shrinks the −0.04 cost that every move pays along the way G₀ stays the same because the six rewards are unchanged and only V(S) depends on the discount G₀ falls because the final +1 is shrunk by γ to the fifth power, and the path still ends at G A return weights the reward k steps ahead by γ to the k. The six rewards are the same, but at γ 0.50 the +1 at the end keeps only about 3% of its face value, less than the step costs paid on the way, so G₀ drops below zero. The greedy path does not change, because every alternative is worth even less.
documents.title: With no slip, you lower Discount γ from 0.95 to 0.50 on Return along the episode. What happens to Full return G₀ and to the path the policy takes?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reinforcement learning foundations · question 2
documents.body: At the defaults, V(S) is not positive until Value-iteration sweep 6. What is the best explanation? Each sweep carries the +1 back one move, and S is six moves from G Value is learned from experience, and the agent needs six episodes to reach G once The discount shrinks the +1 below the step costs until the sixth sweep The backup uses a small learning rate, so each sweep adds a fraction of the reward The Bellman backup reads only neighbours' current values, so the +1 at G reaches a cell one sweep per move of distance. S is six moves away, so V(S) first sees the reward at sweep 6. Value iteration reads the known transition table rather than learning from episodes, and γ is the same at every sweep.
documents.title: At the defaults, V(S) is not positive until Value-iteration sweep 6. What is the best explanation?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reinforcement learning foundations · question 3
documents.body: On Explore versus exploit you set Exploration ε to 0 and step through several Bandit seeds. What do you see? Every run finds the 0.70 arm in the end, because greedy always follows the highest estimate Runs pull all four arms about equally, because nothing yet favors any arm Average reward is highest at ε = 0, because no pulls are wasted on random arms Each run locks onto whichever arm paid first, so the best arm is often never found Estimates start at 0, so the first arm that pays beats every untried arm and keeps winning. Averaged over 300 runs the best arm then gets only about a third of the pulls, against about 72% at ε 0.10, and average reward is lower too. A little exploration costs a few pulls and buys information the agent cannot get any other way.
documents.title: On Explore versus exploit you set Exploration ε to 0 and step through several Bandit seeds. What do you see?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reinforcement learning foundations · question 4
documents.body: With Bonus tile H on at Discount γ 0.95, the greedy policy circles H and never reaches G. Which diagnosis is right? Value iteration has not converged yet, so a few dozen more sweeps will eventually send the agent to G The reward pays more for circling than for finishing, so the policy is maximizing it correctly The agent has not explored enough to find out that G exists, so it settles for the nearby tile H The discount is too small, so the +1 at G is too far away to count for anything at all At γ = 0.95, stepping into H every other move is worth about (0.3γ − 0.04) / (1 − γ²) ≈ 2.5 from H, more than the single +1 at G. Value iteration reads the full transition table, so it is not missing information and more sweeps only confirm the loop. The scalar was misspecified; lowering γ to 0.88 or below makes finishing worth more again.
documents.title: With Bonus tile H on at Discount γ 0.95, the greedy policy circles H and never reaches G. Which diagnosis is right?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reinforcement learning foundations · question 5
documents.body: Value iteration solves this gridworld exactly. Why can't the same method train a language model? It needs a table of every state and transition, and text has far too many states to list The Bellman equation only holds on deterministic grids, and generated text is random from token to token A language model gets no reward signal at all, so there is no return to back up through the tokens Value iteration needs γ = 1, which would make the return of a long text infinite Value iteration sweeps every state using P(s′|s,a) as a lookup. A language model's state is the prompt plus the tokens so far, which cannot be enumerated, and its transitions are not given as a table, so it learns from sampled returns instead. The Bellman equation itself holds with randomness, as the slip chance shows, and rewards come from a reward model or a checker.
documents.title: Value iteration solves this gridworld exactly. Why can't the same method train a language model?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reinforcement learning foundations · question 6
documents.body: On Policy gradient on the bandit, Learning rate α is 0.20 and Baseline is on. You switch Baseline off. What happens to the 300-run results? The policy ends less sure of the best arm and more runs lock onto a worse one: any reward lifts the arm pulled The policy stops improving, because without a baseline the update cannot tell a good reward from a bad one at all The policy improves faster, because rewards that are not shifted down make every step larger than before Nothing changes on average, because subtracting a baseline cannot alter what the update does in expectation here A baseline that ignores the current action leaves the expected update the same but removes much of its noise. Without it, every reward of 1 raises the probability of whichever arm was pulled, so an arm that pays early can run away before the better arm is sampled. At α 0.20 the average probability on the best arm is 92.1% with the baseline and 84.9% without, and 2 of 300 runs end below 50% on it against 29.
documents.title: On Policy gradient on the bandit, Learning rate α is 0.20 and Baseline is on. You switch Baseline off. What happens to the 300-run results?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Reinforcement learning foundations · question 7
documents.body: With Baseline on, you raise Learning rate α from 0.20 to 1.00. What do the 300 runs show? The policy commits sooner, but more runs commit to a worse arm, so the average ends less sure of the best arm The policy gets steadily better, because a bigger step always finds the best arm in fewer pulls without overshooting The policy stops learning, because a step that large cannot be applied to a softmax over only four arms Nothing changes, because the baseline cancels the learning rate out of every update the policy takes A larger α moves the policy further on every sampled reward. After 50 pulls the average probability on the best arm is 65.1% at α 1.00 against 40.1% at 0.20, so it commits sooner. But a few early lucky pulls can then push it onto a worse arm for good: 33 of 300 runs end below 50% on the best arm, against 2, and the average final probability falls from 92.1% to 88.3%.
documents.title: With Baseline on, you raise Learning rate α from 0.20 to 1.00. What do the 300 runs show?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Many models in this course learn from examples with the right answer attached, such as a photo labelled "cat" or a sentence whose next word is already known. This module is about a different way to learn, called reinforcement learning, where the learner acts first and gets a score afterward. Nobody tells it which move was right, so it has to work that out from the score alone. Picture a video game level that gives you no points along the way. You only see your score at the very end, and the game never says which of your turns helped. Figuring out which early choices earned that late score is the main puzzle of this module, and the lab lets you watch a computer solve it. Where it shows up Chat assistants are trained in several stages, and in a later stage another program can score each answer the model writes. The model is then nudged toward answers that score well. The next lab, Post-training, runs that loop on a language model, and a later lab, Reasoning models, looks at models trained further to write out extra steps before they answer. When those scores come from people's choices about which answers are better, the method is called reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF. Every word you learn on this page, from state to reward, comes back in those labs with the same meaning. Why it matters A score tells you how things turned out but not which move was right, and that leaves three problems for the lab to show you: The score arrives late, so the learner must trace it back to the moves that earned it, or it cannot tell a good first move from a bad one. You only learn about what you try, so a learner that keeps repeating whatever worked first may never discover that a better option was there all along. The score is a number someone wrote, and a learner chases whatever that number pays for, so a carelessly written reward produces behaviour nobody wanted. That last problem has really happened, and a 2016 write-up from OpenAI described a computer player in a boat-racing game that ran into it. The player learned to circle a lagoon hitting targets instead of finishing the race, because the score paid for hitting targets rather than for crossing the finish line. This module also builds on How we know a model works, which showed how one tidy score can hide a failure. Here the stakes are higher, because the score is also the thing the learner is trained to push up. What you will be able to explain By the end of this module, you will be able to explain: which part of a short run on the board is the state, the action, the reward and the policy; how the rewards add up into a return, where rewards that come later count for a little less; how a one-step lookahead rule, the Bellman backup, passes a late reward backward one square at a time, so the early moves get their share of the credit; why a learner that learns only from its own tries has to explore, and why it will chase a badly written reward anyway; how a policy gradient update turns the rewards from those tries into better choices, and what a baseline and the learning rate change. What the lab shows The lab has five cards, and it moves from planning, where the computer knows every rule, to learning, where it has to find things out by trying: Gridworld is a 5 by 4 board with a start S, a goal G worth +1 and a trap T worth −1. You choose how many rounds of calculation run, how much the future counts, how often moves slip sideways, and whether a bonus tile H is switched on. Bellman backup opens up one square and writes out the arithmetic for each of its four possible moves. Return along the episode replays one run and adds up its rewards step by step. Explore versus exploit has a learner choosing among four machines whose payout chances it does not know. Policy gradient on the bandit has a second learner that adjusts its chance of picking each machine after every try. Nothing here comes from a trained network or a real system, because the board, its rewards and its rules were all written for this lesson. The lab works out every value on the board exactly. The slips on the board and the payouts from the machines are random, but the lab's random choices all start from a fixed number called a seed. The same seed always gives the same random choices, so every number you see, including averages over many repeated runs, comes out the same each time you visit.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: A tiny game with a late score The Gridworld card is a board 5 squares wide and 4 squares tall, so it has 20 squares, which the lab calls cells. S, the start, is in the bottom-left corner and G, the goal, is in the bottom-right corner, while a trap T sits in the middle of the bottom row. The player that moves around the board is called the agent, and every move earns it a number called a reward. Stepping into G pays +1 and ends the run, while stepping into T scores −1 and ends it too. Every other move costs 0.04 of a point, like a small fee for each step, which pushes the agent to finish rather than wander. Bumping into the edge of the board leaves the agent where it was and still charges the fee. These are the words reinforcement learning uses for the parts of this game: The state is the information the agent gets to see before it moves, and here that is only which cell it is on. If something the agent needs is missing from the state, no amount of training can make up for it. For example, picture a board with a locked door and a key, where the state shows only which cell the agent is on. However long it trained, the agent could never tell whether it was carrying the key. An action is one move the agent can make, and on this board there are four: up, right, down and left. A reward is the number paid for a move, chosen by whoever built the game, so it is a design decision rather than a fact about what is good. An episode is one complete run from S until it ends at G or T. The lab also stops any run after 24 steps, so a run that goes in circles cannot last forever. In the run you see when the lab opens, the agent moves up once, right four times, then down into G. That makes six moves and six rewards: five fees of −0.04, then +1 at the end. It goes over the top of T because T blocks the bottom row, and the badge on the card reads "reaches G in 6 steps". The policy is the arrows A policy is the agent's rule for choosing an action in each state, and you can see it on the board as the arrow in each cell. In this lab, the rule is to pick whichever move looks best according to the numbers in the cells, worked out in a way the Bellman backup section below explains. Always taking the best-looking option like this is called being greedy, a word you will also see in the lab's notes and charts. When two moves look equally good, the cell shows more than one arrow, and the agent breaks the tie in a fixed order: up, then right, then down, then left. The next few sections explain where the numbers in the cells come from, because they are what the arrows follow. Adding up the score: return and discount The total score of an episode is called its return, and you could find it by adding the six rewards straight up. However, reinforcement learning usually counts a reward that arrives later as worth a little less than one that arrives now. The number that sets how much less is the discount factor, written γ, the Greek letter gamma, and the Discount γ slider starts at 0.95. The rule works like this: the first reward counts in full, the second is multiplied by γ once, the third by γ twice, and so on down the line. At γ 0.95 the second reward keeps 95% of its size, and by the sixth reward only about 77% is left. Written as a formula, the return is G₀ = r₁ + γ·r₂ + γ²·r₃ + …, where r₁ is the first reward, r₂ the second, and so on. You can read it aloud as "the first reward, plus γ times the second, plus γ squared times the third, and so on". Apply it to the opening run: each fee is 0.04, shrunk a little more at every step, so the five fees add up to about −0.181. The +1 arrives on the sixth move, so it is multiplied by 0.95 five times and counts as 0.774. The two parts add up to a return of 0.593, which is the number on the Full return G₀ readout. Here the letter G stands for the return, not the goal cell, and the small 0 means it is counted from step 0, the start. Shrinking later rewards does two jobs, and the first is setting how far ahead the agent looks, because a smaller γ makes the far future count for less. At γ 0.50 each step halves a reward, so the +1 at the end of six moves keeps only 0.031 of its face value, about 3%. The second job is to stop an endless stream of rewards from adding up to an endless total. Each later reward keeps the same fraction, γ, of the one before it, so the shrinking pieces add up to a fixed amount. At γ 0.50, a +1 reward every step adds up to 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.125 and so on, and however long it runs, that total never passes 2. That second job matters later in the lab, when the bonus tile offers the agent a reward it can collect again and again. Value: how good is it to stand here? Now ask one question about every cell at once: if the agent started here and played as well as it could, what return would it get? That number is the cell's value, and the rule that gives every cell its value is called the value function, written V. Each cell shows its value in its top-right corner, and the V(S) readout shows the value of the start cell, S. Values are easiest to follow close to G, and with the starting settings, where γ is 0.95 and nothing slips, they work out like this: The cell right above G is one move away, and stepping down pays +1 and ends the episode, so its value is 1.00. The cell above that one is two moves away, so its first move costs 0.04 and lands on a cell worth 1.00. That 1.00 counts 95% because it comes one step later, so the value here is −0.04 + 0.95 × 1.00 = 0.91. One more step back gives −0.04 + 0.95 × 0.91, about 0.82, and the values keep shrinking like this all the way back to S, which is worth 0.593. V(S) is the same 0.593 as the return you added up for the opening run, and that is no accident. With nothing random and the values settled, the run can only go one way, and it reaches G. So the value of S and the return of that one run agree. When moves can slip, the value becomes the average return over all the ways a run could turn out, which is why the glossary calls it the expected return. The Bellman equation: one step of lookahead You do not have to play a whole game from a cell to find its value, because looking one move ahead is enough. For each of the four moves, take the reward for that move, add γ times the value of the cell it lands in, and keep the biggest total. That rule is the Bellman equation, and working it out once for one cell is called a Bellman backup. The Bellman backup card does this for one cell at a time, and you can click any cell on the board to choose it. Each row of the card's table is one action, and the Q column gives that action's total, which is the value of taking that move from this cell. The best row is marked max, its Q becomes the cell's new value, and its move becomes the cell's arrow. The card starts on cell r2c2, which means row 2, column 2, with rows counted down from the top and columns counted from the left, both starting at 0. That puts it right above T, and with the starting settings its four rows work out like this: right steps onto a cell worth 0.91, so it scores −0.04 + 0.95 × 0.91 = 0.824, the biggest of the four, and its row is marked max; down steps into T, which scores −1 and ends the episode, so it is worth −1.000; up and left each step onto a cell worth 0.743, so each scores 0.666. So r2c2 is worth 0.824 and its arrow points right. G and T are called terminal cells, because the episode ends there. Their +1 or −1 is paid on the move that enters them, and since nothing comes after, the cell itself counts as 0.00. That is why the down row works out to −1 + 0.95 × 0.00 = −1.000. When Slip chance is above zero, a move can land in three different places, and the card writes out all three landings. At 20%, a move goes where the agent meant 80% of the time and slides off to each side 10% of the time. So each row becomes a weighted average, where the score for the intended landing counts 80% and each sideways landing counts 10%. Take the right row from r2c2 at 20%. Most of the time the agent reaches the cell on its right. But 1 time in 10 it slides up, and 1 time in 10 it slides down into T and loses a whole point. Mixing those three scores 80, 10 and 10 gives the right row a Q of about 0.58, well below the 0.824 it had with no slips. This also means an arrow does not always point at the biggest neighbouring number. It follows the biggest Q, which counts the fee, the discount and any slips as well as the number where the move lands. Value iteration: passing the good news backward At the start the lab knows no values at all, so it sets every cell to 0. Then it runs a sweep, in which every cell does one Bellman backup at the same moment, using its neighbours' numbers from before the sweep. Repeating sweeps until the numbers stop changing is called value iteration, and the Value-iteration sweeps slider sets how many sweeps have run. Because each backup looks only one move ahead, the good news from G can travel only one cell per sweep: After sweep 1, only the two cells touching G, the one above it and the one to its left, have learned about it, so they show 1.00. Every other cell has seen nothing but a fee so far, so each of them shows −0.04. After sweep 2, the cells two moves away from G show 0.91, because they can now see a neighbour worth 1.00. After sweep 3, the cells three moves away show 0.82, and the ring of good news keeps growing by one cell with every sweep. S is six moves from G, because T blocks the short way, so V(S) stays negative through sweep 5 while the fees pile up. It sinks to −0.181 by then, and on sweep 6, when the news from G finally arrives, it jumps to 0.593. That delay is credit assignment at work, which means deciding which earlier moves earned a later reward. In value iteration, the credit for the +1 flows backward from G, one cell per sweep, until it reaches the very first move. Picture labelling a maze backward from its exit, starting in the first round with the squares that touch the exit. In the second round you mark the squares that touch those, and the marks keep spreading one ring per round. A far corner stays blank until the ring reaches it, and value iteration spreads its numbers across the board in the same way. The picture breaks down in two places: a cell's number is an expected score that includes fees, the discount and slips, rather than a count of steps. Also, the computer fills in the whole map from the rules, without ever walking through it to find out. The Residual readout tells you when the work is done, because it shows the biggest change any cell made in the last sweep. It stays large while news is still spreading, and with no slip and the bonus off, it drops to zero once every cell has heard from G. At that point the values have converged, which means they have settled and will not change again. The chart on the Bellman backup card plots the residual for every sweep up to 60. Learning from tries: the bandit and exploration Value iteration only works because the lab hands it the full rulebook, which says where each move from each cell can land and what it pays. That rulebook is called the transition table, and working out the best moves from it is planning. A learner without the rulebook has to find things out by trying actions and seeing what happens, and that brings a new problem. The Explore versus exploit card shows that problem with a simpler game called a bandit, which you can picture as four arcade machines that each have a lever. The name comes from an old nickname for slot machines, "one-armed bandits", because each has one lever and tends to take your money. The lab calls each lever an arm, and each pull either pays 1 point or pays nothing, which is what the word Bernoulli on the card means. Arm 4 is the best, paying 70% of the time, while the other three pay between 30% and 55% of the time. The agent does not know those chances, so for each arm it keeps the average of what that arm has paid so far, called its estimate. The greedy choice is then to pull whichever arm has the highest estimate. Using what you already know to pick the best-looking option is called exploiting, and trying something else to learn more is called exploring. Pure greed has a trap, because every estimate starts at 0, so the first arm that happens to pay jumps ahead of all the others. A greedy agent then keeps pulling that arm for the rest of the run, since the other arms never get another chance to prove themselves. Even if that arm misses many times afterward, its average stays above 0 because it paid once. Every untried arm is still sitting at 0, so the paying arm always looks best. With Exploration ε at 0 and Bandit seed at 3, the run spends all 400 pulls on Arm 3, which pays only 45% of the time. The fix is exploration: with a chance of ε, the Greek letter epsilon, the agent ignores its estimates and pulls a random arm instead. One run of 400 pulls can be lucky or unlucky, so to check that a result is not luck, the lab replays the whole 400-pull game 300 times. Each replay is called a run, and each one gets different random payouts. The readouts that say "300 runs" average over all of them, and the bars show a single run, chosen by Bandit seed. Averaged over 300 runs, the best arm gets 33% of the pulls at ε = 0 and 72% at ε = 0.10. Exploring too much wastes pulls on arms the agent already knows are worse, so at ε = 0.50 the share falls back to 56%. Picture a friend who tries a sandwich on the first day at a new school, finds it fine, and orders it every single day for the rest of the year. They never learn that the soup beside it was much better, because they never tried it once. Ordering something different now and then costs a few so-so lunches, but it is the only way to find out. Policy gradient: nudging the probabilities The Policy gradient on the bandit card plays the same four arms in a different way. Instead of keeping an average for each arm, this agent keeps a chance of picking each one, which the card calls a probability. That list of four probabilities is the agent's policy, and all four start at 25%, so at first it picks completely at random. Every pull then follows the same four-step loop, repeated 400 times: Pick an arm at random, using the current probabilities, so a likelier arm gets picked more often. See whether it paid 1 or 0, which is the reward, written r. Compare the reward with a baseline, written b, which here is the average reward of all the earlier pulls. If the reward beat the baseline, make that arm a little more likely next time, and if it fell short, make it a little less likely. Over 400 pulls, those small nudges shift the probabilities toward the arms that tend to pay more. The word gradient comes from slopes: picture standing on a hill in fog and feeling with your foot which way is uphill. Unlike your foot, one pull gives only a rough guess of the slope, so a single nudge can point the wrong way even though the nudges point uphill on average. A policy gradient update is the step that, on average, moves the probabilities uphill toward more reward. The Learning rate α slider, where α is the Greek letter alpha, sets how big each nudge is. To see why the comparison helps, picture scoring 70 on a test and deciding whether that is good news. If you usually score 50, it is great news, but if you usually score 90, it is a warning sign. A score only means something next to what you normally get, and the baseline is the agent's version of "what you normally get". With Baseline off, b is 0, so every payout counts as good news and every miss counts as no news. A reward of 1 always raises whichever arm was pulled, even a weak one, while a reward of 0 changes nothing at all. That makes learning without a baseline jumpy. A weak arm that pays early can grab most of the probability before the best arm has been pulled often enough to show that it pays more. With the baseline on, a single nudge can point a different way than it would without it. Averaged over every pull the agent might make, though, the nudge still leans the same way with or without the baseline, toward the arms that pay more. What the baseline changes is how much the nudges jump around. Hits push the arm up by less, and misses push it down instead of doing nothing. So the nudges stay closer to their average, and lucky early pulls do less damage. That steadiness still changes where runs end up. Each nudge changes which arms get pulled next, so a few noisy nudges early on can send a whole run somewhere else. That is why the results over 300 runs differ. With α at 0.20 and the baseline on, the 300 runs end with an average probability of 92.1% on the best arm. Only 2 of the 300 end up stuck, meaning they finish with less than half their probability on the best arm. With the baseline off, the average falls to 84.9%, and the number of stuck runs jumps from 2 to 29. At the starting Policy seed of 3, switching the baseline off leaves the run with 92% of its probability on Arm 2, which pays only 55% of the time. The learning rate trades speed against safety, because a tiny step barely moves anything while a big one moves fast but can lock in early luck. At α 0.02, the policy has only 37% on the best arm after 400 pulls, not far from the 25% it started with. At α 1.00, learning is fast: after only 50 pulls, the average run already has 65.1% on the best arm, compared with 40.1% at α 0.20. The cost shows up later. 33 runs in 300 end up stuck, and the final average on the best arm drops to 88.3%.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Many learning signals hand the learner a right answer for every example, so it can be corrected one example at a time. A reward does not work like that, which is why What AI actually is sorted it apart from labels and raw text. A reward scores how things turned out after a whole string of choices, and it never says which choice was the right one. This is the late-score puzzle from the big picture, the credit assignment problem, and on the grid value iteration answers it by passing value backward, one cell per sweep. Language models face the same problem on a much bigger scale, and in the Post-training lab every word from this page takes on a new job: the state is the prompt plus the text the model has written so far; an action is the next token, a small piece of text such as a word or part of a word; the policy is the language model itself, which gives a probability to every possible next token; the reward is a score for the finished answer, from another model trained to judge answers, called a reward model, or from a program that checks the answer. One score for a whole answer is the late reward from the grid, spread across many tokens. A language model also cannot plan the way the grid does, because there are far too many possible texts to write out a table of every state and move. So it must learn from its own tries, and that is where exploration and policy gradients come in. That is why this page uses a board small enough to solve exactly, where you can watch each word do its job. After you watch an agent chase the bonus tile here, the reward model in the next lab reads as what it really is. It is one number that someone designed, and training will follow that number wherever it leads.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Work through these six steps in order, because each one builds on the one before. Read one episode On Return along the episode, drag Episode step from 0 to the end and watch the readouts. Reward this step shows −0.04 for each of the first five moves and +1 for the last one. Return so far sinks a little further below zero with each fee, reaching −0.181, then jumps to 0.593 when the agent enters G. That final 0.593 matches both Full return G₀ and V(S), because nothing in this run is random. In the bar chart, each outer bar is one raw reward, and the inner bar is the same reward after the discount has shrunk it. Look at the last pair of bars to see the +1 losing almost a quarter of its size. Sweep the backup Try this: Set Value-iteration sweeps to 0, then raise it one sweep at a time. Watch the green shading and the numbers spread backward from G, one ring per sweep, while V(S) stays negative until sweep 6, because S is six moves from G. Keep going, and Residual drops to zero by sweep 8, once even the far top-left corner has heard the news. Then set Value-iteration sweeps back to 30 before going on, because the steps below assume the values have settled. Change the discount, then let moves slip Move Discount γ from 0.95 down to 0.50 and watch V(S) fall to −0.046, below zero, even though the path still ends at G. At 0.50, the +1 is worth only 0.031 by the time it arrives, which is less than the 0.078 that the fees cost on the way. G is still the best choice, though, because never finishing would cost even more, and T costs a whole point. Set γ back to 0.95 and move Slip chance to 20%, and V(S) drops to 0.314 because some runs now slide into T. Now look at the cell between S and T, whose arrow used to point up but now points left, away from T. Going up from there now risks a 10% slide sideways into the trap, so the policy steps back onto S instead. Then click r2c2, right above T, and compare Slip chance at 0% and at 30%. At 30%, moving right carries a 15% chance of slipping down into T, so on the Bellman backup card the up row wins and is marked max. With Slip chance at 20%, change Episode seed to draw a different set of slips. The Full return G₀ changes from seed to seed while V(S) stays at 0.314, because V(S) is the average over all possible runs and G₀ is one run. Seed 10, for example, slips once and falls into T, so its return is about −0.97. Explore or exploit On Explore versus exploit, set Exploration ε to 0, then 0.10, then 0.50, and each time compare Best-arm share, 300 runs with Same, ε = 0. The second readout always shows the pure greedy result, so it works as a fixed point of comparison. With ε back at 0, step through a few Bandit seed values and watch the bars. Each run piles almost all its pulls onto whichever arm paid first, and that is often not Arm 4. Turn on the bonus Set Bonus tile H to on with Discount γ at 0.95, which puts a bonus in the top-right corner. H pays +0.3 every time the agent steps into it, and stepping into it never ends the episode. The path now climbs to the top row, walks across to H, and then steps out and back in, over and over. The badge reads "circles H · 9 visits in 24 steps", and the agent never reaches G. Then lower Discount γ to 0.85 and watch the agent walk to G again. Follow the policy gradient On Policy gradient on the bandit, leave Baseline on with Learning rate α at 0.20 and read Best-arm probability, 300 runs, which shows 92.1%. Switch Baseline off and compare that with 84.9%, then compare Runs below 50% on best arm, which goes from 2 of 300 to 29 of 300. Finally, turn Baseline back on and try α at 0.02 and then at 1.00. Watch the solid line on the first chart, which shows the average probability on the best arm before each pull, and see how fast it climbs.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Good news moves one cell per sweep, so a far cell cannot know about G until the ring of value reaches it. A value is an average, but a return is one try. With Slip chance at 0 every try is identical, so once the values settle, V(S) and Full return G₀ match exactly. With slips, they stop matching, because each run has its own luck. The discount can shrink the prize below the costs: at γ 0.50, the +1 at the end of six moves keeps only 0.031 of its size. Slips make the agent careful: at 20%, the arrow beside T turns away from it, and V(S) drops because some runs end in the trap. A discount near 1 settles slowly: each sweep shrinks the biggest gap on the board, between any cell's number and its final value, to γ times what it was, or less. So at γ 0.99, a sweep may close only 1% of the gap. With no slip and no bonus you never notice, because the news reaches every cell within 8 sweeps. With the bonus on, the loop around H keeps adding value, so the residual is still well above zero after 60 sweeps. No exploration means no discovery: averaged over 300 runs, the best arm gets about 33% of the pulls at ε = 0, against 72% at ε = 0.10. The baseline makes learning steadier, because without it every payout lifts the arm that was pulled, so an arm that pays early can take over. The numbers show it: 84.9% on the best arm against 92.1%, and 29 stuck runs in 300 against 2. The learning rate trades speed for safety: a tiny rate learns almost nothing in 400 pulls, while a large one commits fast but locks in early luck. At α 1.00, 33 runs in 300 end up stuck, against 2 at α 0.20. The bonus becomes a loophole: with Bonus tile H on, circling H is the best policy at γ 0.89 and above, and walking to G wins at 0.88 and below. A stuck run, as before, is one that ends with less than half its probability on the best arm, which is what Runs below 50% on best arm counts. At α 0.02 with the baseline on, that readout counts all 300 runs, but only because those runs have barely moved away from 25%, so they are slow rather than stuck. The loop wins because each round trip, out of H and back in, costs a 0.04 fee and earns 0.3. That nets about +0.26 every two moves, with no end in sight, while finishing at G pays +1 only once. At γ 0.95 the later loops still count for a lot, so at the default 30 sweeps the number on H is already past 2, well above the +1 at G. It keeps climbing toward about 2.5 as you add sweeps, so more sweeps never send the agent back to G. At γ 0.88 or below, later loops shrink so fast that finishing is worth more. The agent is doing exactly what the numbers reward, and that is called reward hacking.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: What this lab simplifies The grid has only 20 cells and the lab knows its full transition table, so value iteration can sweep every cell and get exact answers. The rewards, the +0.3 bonus and the 24-step limit were all written for this lesson. The episode on the grid always follows the greedy arrows, so slips are its only randomness, and there is no exploring on the grid at all. A run that loops is cut off at 24 steps, so its Full return G₀ undercounts what the loop is worth. With the bonus on at γ 0.95 and the default 30 sweeps, the looping run's G₀ is 0.979, while V(S) shows 1.341. V(S) is also not settled yet, so it keeps rising as you add sweeps, to about 1.67 at 60 sweeps and about 1.76 once fully settled. The lab stops at 60 sweeps, which is not enough for the values to settle at γ 0.95 or higher with the bonus on. The bandit has one situation, four arms whose payout chances never change, and one way of exploring, called ε-greedy: greedy, except for a random pull with chance ε. Smarter strategies, such as ones that deliberately favour arms the agent is still unsure about, usually do better. The policy-gradient card is the simplest version that works, with one situation, four arms, a plain running average as its baseline and a fixed 400 pulls. Real training methods, with names like PPO and GRPO, add pieces that this card leaves out. They swap the plain average for a smarter baseline, such as a learned value estimate or a group average, and they limit how far one update can move the policy. They can also add a penalty for drifting too far from the model they started with. Where the real thing struggles A language model cannot use value iteration, because there are far too many possible texts to list. No table of every state and every move could ever be written out and swept. Instead, it has to learn from samples, one response at a time. Those samples are noisy, because one answer might score well partly by luck, so the nudges jump around much as they did on the baseline card. That noise, and the unsteady training it causes, is the main practical difficulty when real models learn this way. A behaviour the model never produces can never be rewarded, so exploration matters for language models too. A reward that can be pushed up in a way nobody intended will be pushed up that way, and more training makes that worse, not better. A common mix-up: people read the reward as a measure of what is good, when it is really a number the designer chose. The agent circling H is not broken, because the +0.3 bonus made circling worth more than finishing, and the agent followed the numbers exactly. Picture a teacher who gives one point for every page of homework handed in. Before long, someone starts writing in giant letters, and the points go up while the homework gets no better. Nobody broke the rule, because the rule paid for pages rather than for good work, and that is reward hacking in a classroom. The story stops matching in one way: unlike the student, the agent is not trying to cheat. It has no idea what the designer meant and follows whichever path the numbers make biggest.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: The official name for the board A setup with states, actions, a rulebook for where moves lead, rewards and a discount is called a Markov decision process, or MDP. You will see the short name MDP in the info panel of the Gridworld card. The −0.04 charge per move, often called a living cost, comes from a small 4 by 3 grid in a well-known AI textbook by Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig. Learning without the rulebook One family of methods, called Q-learning, learns the value of each move, the Q from the Bellman backup card, from the agent's own tries instead of from the table. Basic policy-gradient methods need no value table, because they nudge the policy toward actions whose return beat a baseline. Bigger methods often learn a value estimate to use as that baseline. REINFORCE, described by Williams in 1992, is the basic form, and the Policy gradient on the bandit card runs it. PPO, from Schulman and others in 2017, limits how far each update can move the policy, so the policy changes in small steps rather than lurching. How the probabilities are stored The policy-gradient agent keeps a hidden score for each arm, called a preference, and a recipe called softmax turns the four scores into four probabilities that add up to 100%. That is the softmax in the card's heading, "A softmax policy that learns from sampled rewards". Equal scores give equal probabilities, which is why every arm starts at 25%, and raising one arm's score raises its probability while the others fall. The nudge, worked out The note under the card gives the exact rule: each arm's preference moves by α·(r − b)·(1[arm] − π). In that rule, 1[arm] is 1 for the arm that was pulled and 0 for the others, and π is each arm's current probability. The key part is r − b, the reward minus the baseline, which is positive when the pull did better than usual and negative when it did worse. To see it with round numbers, say every arm is at 25%, α is 0.20 and the baseline is 0.5, because half the earlier pulls paid. The agent pulls Arm 4, which pays 1, so r − b is 0.5. Arm 4's score then rises by 0.20 × 0.5 × 0.75 = 0.075, where 0.75 is 1 minus Arm 4's probability of 0.25. Each other arm's score falls by 0.20 × 0.5 × 0.25 = 0.025. If Arm 4 had paid 0 instead, every sign would flip, so its score would fall by 0.075 and the others would rise. With the baseline off, b is 0, so a payout of 0 moves nothing and a payout of 1 always lifts the pulled arm, here by 0.15. The bandit is closer to chatbot training than the grid The InstructGPT paper, from Ouyang and others in 2022, describes the environment for its reinforcement learning stage as a bandit. It shows a random prompt, gets one response, and gives it one score. That is why the arcade machines' exploration problem carries over to language models. The bonus tile has a real ancestor In the boat-racing game from the big picture, the targets kept coming back after being hit, so circling the lagoon earned more points than finishing the race. It is the same story as circling H instead of walking to G. Where to go next Post-training runs this loop on a language model, with a learned reward and a leash that keeps the model from drifting too far from where it started. Preference optimization in practice trains a tiny model with a method called DPO, which learns from comparisons between answers. Reasoning models looks at models trained further to write out extra steps before they answer.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: This module is about reinforcement learning (RL): learning a policy, the rule that picks an action in each state, from a scalar reward paid after acting instead of a label for each output. The reward can arrive many steps late. The question RL answers is which actions, in which states, earn the largest return, the discounted sum of the rewards that follow. The module moves from planning to learning. On a small gridworld with a known transition table, which says where each move can land, value iteration computes every state's value with no trial and error: each sweep updates every cell from its neighbours' current values. On a four-armed bandit, a one-state problem whose arms pay at unknown rates, the agent learns from its own samples: first by averaging each arm's rewards, then with a policy gradient that shifts probability toward arms whose reward beat a baseline, here the running average reward. It builds on How we know a model works, which showed how a single tidy score can hide a failure. Here the score is also the training target. Where it shows up Language-model post-training. The next module, Post-training, follows how a language model is tuned against a reward model learned from human preferences: reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). Reasoning models covers tuning one against a checker that grades its answers. Policy-gradient methods. The lab runs REINFORCE, the simplest one. Proximal policy optimization (PPO) builds on the same update and clips it so the policy moves in small steps. Reward hacking. A boat-racing agent once circled for points instead of finishing, and Post-training shows a reward-model score rising while true quality falls. Why it matters A reward scores what happened, not which move was right. That leaves three problems, and the lab shows each one: Credit assignment. A late reward must be traced back to the moves that earned it. In value iteration, value reaches the start one sweep per move of distance from the reward. Exploration. An agent cannot improve its estimate of an action it never takes. With no random pulls (ε = 0), the bandit agent keeps whichever arm paid first. Reward specification. An optimizer picks whatever earns the most return, intended or not. The lab's Bonus tile H pays +0.3 on every entry and does not end the episode. Value iteration avoids sampling only because it reads a known table. A language model has none, so it learns from noisy sampled returns. A baseline cuts that noise without changing the expected update. What you will be able to explain Identify the state, action, reward, policy and discounted return in one small episode. Use the Bellman backup, the one-step update value iteration repeats, to explain credit assignment as value flowing backward from a delayed reward. Explain why learning from samples needs exploration, and why a misspecified reward is maximized anyway. Explain how a policy-gradient update turns sampled rewards into a better policy, and what a baseline and the learning rate change. What the lab shows No network is trained and no real-system data appears. The 5×4 gridworld, its rewards, the +0.3 bonus tile and the 24-step episode cap are authored. Value iteration computes each sweep's values exactly from the known table, with no sampling. The episode follows the greedy policy; a slip, set by Slip chance, sends a move sideways, and slips are drawn from a seeded generator. The bandit's four arms pay 1 or 0 at fixed rates, and the 300-run averages use fixed seeds, so the same settings always give the same averages. On Gridworld, set Value-iteration sweeps, Discount γ, Slip chance and Bonus tile H, and read V(S), the start cell's value after that many sweeps (the expected return once it converges). Click a cell to see its four action values on Bellman backup. Return along the episode scrubs one episode with Episode step, resamples its slips with Episode seed, and totals it as Full return G₀. Explore versus exploit sets Exploration ε, the chance of a random pull, and Bandit seed for the single run shown in the bars. Policy gradient on the bandit sets Learning rate α, Baseline and Policy seed. The key experiment raises Value-iteration sweeps one at a time from 0. At the default γ 0.95, with no slip and the bonus off, V(S) starts at 0, is negative on sweeps 1 to 5 and turns positive on sweep 6, when the +1 has travelled the six moves back from the goal G. At γ 0.95, Bonus tile H makes the optimal policy circle H instead of finishing. At Learning rate α 0.20, switching Baseline off raises Runs below 50% on best arm from 2 to 29 of 300.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: A Markov decision process has states, actions, a transition rule P(s′|s,a), a reward r(s,a,s′), and a discount factor γ. A policy chooses actions. The return from time t is G = r₁ + γ·r₂ + γ²·r₃ + …, and the value function V(s) is the expected return from s. This lab's MDP is a 5×4 grid. Entering G pays +1 and ends the episode. Entering T pays −1 and ends it. Every other move costs −0.04, the living cost from Russell and Norvig's classic 4×3 world. Slip chance sends a move sideways. The Bellman equation The optimal value satisfies one recursion: V(s) = maxₐ Σₛ′ P(s′|s,a) · [ r(s,a,s′) + γ·V(s′) ] Value iteration applies that backup to every cell at once, starting from V = 0. The Bellman backup card writes out the four action values for one cell. The largest is exactly what the next sweep stores there. Credit assignment, made visible A backup reads only the neighbours' current values. So the +1 at G can reach S only one move per sweep. S is six moves from G, and at the defaults V(S) stays negative through sweep 5, then jumps to 0.593 on sweep 6. That delay is credit assignment: deciding which early moves earned a late reward. A policy gradient on the bandit Value iteration needs the transition table. When the rules are unknown, an agent can learn a policy directly from sampled rewards. Policy gradient on the bandit runs REINFORCE on the four-armed bandit. A softmax policy starts at 25% on each arm, samples an arm and a reward r, and moves each preference by α·(r − b)·(1[arm] − π). The bracket is the gradient of ln π(arm), so an arm becomes likelier when its reward beat the baseline b and less likely when it fell short. Here b is the average reward so far. At α 0.20 with the baseline on, the average over 300 seeded runs ends with 92.1% of its probability on the best arm, and 2 runs in 300 end below 50% on it. With the baseline off, those are 84.9% and 29.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Post-training reuses these words. The state is the prompt plus the tokens so far, an action is the next token, the policy is the language model, and the reward is a score from a reward model or a checker. This is the reward-after-acting signal that What AI actually is sorted from labels and raw text. This page makes each word concrete on a problem small enough to solve exactly. Then the next lab's reward model reads as what it is: one designed scalar that an optimizer will follow.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Set Value-iteration sweeps to 0 and raise it one sweep at a time. Watch the shading spread backward from G and read V(S) and Residual. On Return along the episode, scrub Episode step. At the defaults the six rewards give Full return G₀ = 0.593, equal to V(S). Move Discount γ from 0.95 to 0.50. V(S) falls to −0.046, yet the path still ends at G. Set Slip chance to 20%. V(S) drops to 0.314 and the arrow on the cell left of T turns away. On Explore versus exploit, compare Exploration ε at 0, 0.10, and 0.50. Set Bonus tile H to on at γ 0.95, then lower γ to 0.85. On Policy gradient on the bandit, compare Baseline on and off at Learning rate α 0.20, then try α 0.02 and 1.00.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Value arrives at a cell one sweep per move of distance from the reward. The Residual hits exactly 0 once every cell has heard from G, because the grid with no slip is deterministic. V(S) is an average over slips; G₀ is one sampled episode. They agree only when nothing is random and V has converged. A discount below 1 shrinks the final +1 by γ⁵ over six moves. At γ 0.50 that is 0.031, less than the step costs on the way. On the bandit, best-arm share averaged over 300 seeded runs is 33% at ε = 0, 72% at ε = 0.10, and 56% at ε = 0.50. With no exploration, the agent keeps whichever arm paid first. Subtracting a baseline leaves the expected policy-gradient update unchanged and cuts its noise. At α 0.20 that is 92.1% against 84.9% on the best arm, and 2 against 29 stranded runs in 300. The learning rate trades speed for lock-in. At α 1.00 with the baseline on, the policy has 65.1% on the best arm after 50 pulls against 40.1% at 0.20, but 33 runs in 300 end below 50%. At α 0.02 it has learned almost nothing after 400 pulls: 37%. With Bonus tile H on, circling H is optimal at γ 0.89 and above. That is reward hacking: correct optimization of a scalar that says the wrong thing.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: In this lab. The transition table is known and has 20 states, so value iteration can sweep all of them. The rewards, the +0.3 bonus, and the 24-step episode cap are authored. The gridworld episode follows the greedy policy, so slips are its only randomness. A looping episode's G₀ is cut at 24 steps and undercounts V(S). The bandit has one state, four stationary Bernoulli arms, and ε-greedy only. Better strategies, such as upper-confidence bounds, usually beat it. The policy-gradient card is the simplest estimator, with a running-average baseline and a fixed 400 pulls. It has no value function, no clipping, and no KL penalty, so it is not PPO or GRPO. In real systems. A language model has far too many states to enumerate and no known transition table. It cannot run value iteration. It learns from sampled returns, which are noisy, so variance and instability dominate practical training. The baseline card shows that noise in miniature. A reward that is easy to maximize in an unintended way will be maximized that way. More optimization makes that worse, not better.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: Learning without the table. Q-learning estimates Q(s,a) from sampled transitions instead of the table. Policy-gradient methods skip values altogether and nudge the policy toward actions whose sampled return beat a baseline: ∇J = E[∇ log π(a|s) · (G − b)]. REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) is the basic form, and the Policy gradient on the bandit card runs it. PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) clips each update so the policy moves in small steps. The bandit is closer to RLHF than the grid. The InstructGPT paper (Ouyang et al., 2022) describes its RL environment as a bandit that presents a random prompt and expects a response. One sampled response gets one score, so exploration matters there too: a behavior the model never samples cannot be rewarded. The bonus tile has a famous ancestor. In OpenAI's 2016 "Faulty reward functions in the wild" write-up, a boat-racing agent learned to circle a lagoon hitting respawning targets instead of finishing the race, because the score paid for targets. Post-training applies this loop to a language model with a learned reward and a KL leash. Preference optimization in practice runs DPO on a tiny model, and Reasoning models looks at policies post-trained to spend extra tokens before answering.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Gridworld · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: A 5×4 MDP solved by value iteration Twenty cells, four actions, rewards paid on entering a cell. The shading and numbers are V after the chosen number of synchronous Bellman backups from V = 0, and the arrows are the greedy action for that V. The agent's path is a rollout of that greedy policy from S. S (start, bottom left), G (+1, terminal), T (−1, terminal), and H when the bonus tile is on. Every other move costs −0.04. Each cell's top-right number is V(s). Tint strength is |V| relative to the largest |V| on the grid; greener is higher, redder is lower. Arrows are argmax over actions of Q(s, a). Two or more arrows mean a tie within 10⁻⁹; the rollout breaks ties up → right → down → left. The dark line is the episode up to Episode step; the faint line is the rest of it. "slip" marks a move that went sideways. The badge reports the episode outcome; V(S) and Residual repeat the start value and the last sweep's largest change. V_{k+1}(s) = max_a Σ_{s′} P(s′|s,a)·[r(s,a,s′) + γ·V_k(s′)], applied to all 18 non-terminal cells at once. Terminal cells stay at 0. P(s′|s,a) sends the agent the intended way with probability 1 − slip and to each perpendicular neighbour with slip/2. A move into the wall leaves it in place and costs −0.04. The bonus tile pays +0.3 each time it is entered and does not end the episode, so stepping in and out of it is an endless stream of rewards. The rollout samples slips from a seeded generator and stops at G, at T, or after 24 steps. Value-iteration sweeps (0–60), Discount γ (0.50–0.99), Slip chance (0–30%), and Bonus tile H (off or on). Each change replays the episode to its end. Click a cell, or focus the grid and use the arrow keys, to inspect it on Bellman backup. Comparison worth running: sweeps 0 through 6 at γ 0.95. V(S) stays negative until sweep 6, when the +1 has traveled the six moves back to S. Value arrives at S exactly one sweep per move of distance from G. That is credit assignment made visible. At Slip chance 20% the arrow on the cell left of T turns away from it, and V(S) falls because some episodes now end in T. With the bonus on, the policy circles H at γ 0.89 and above and walks to G at 0.88 and below, at the default 30 sweeps with no slip. In this lab: the transition table is known and tiny, so value iteration can sweep every state. The rewards, the 24-step cap, and the +0.3 bonus are authored. In general: language models have far too many states to enumerate and no known transition table, so they are trained with sampled policy-gradient methods rather than value iteration. The vocabulary carries over; the algorithm does not.
documents.title: A 5×4 MDP solved by value iteration

documents.subtitle: Bellman backup · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: The one-step lookahead every sweep repeats For the inspected cell, each row evaluates Q(s, a) = Σ P(s′|s,a)·(r + γ·V(s′)) with the current V. The largest Q is exactly what the next sweep writes into that cell. The chart shows how fast the largest change across the grid shrinks. A four-row table: the action, the expectation written out with the live probabilities, rewards, γ, and neighbour values, and the resulting Q. The best row is marked max. A formula card repeating the winning action's terms, its value, and the number the next sweep writes into this cell. A line chart of the measured residual max_s |V_k(s) − V_{k−1}(s)| for k = 1 to 60, a dotted γ^(k−1) × first-residual reference, and a guide at the current sweep. Rewards depend on the cell entered: +1 for G, −1 for T, +0.3 for H when on, −0.04 otherwise, and −0.04 for bumping a wall. Value iteration is a γ-contraction: each sweep can shrink the worst-case error by at least a factor of γ. The dotted line is that reference, drawn from the first residual. With no slip the grid is deterministic and the residual drops to exactly 0 once value has reached every cell. Click any cell on Gridworld. Value-iteration sweeps, Discount γ, Slip chance, and Bonus tile H all change the numbers here. Comparison worth running: inspect cell r2c2, directly above T, at Slip chance 0% and then 30%. Right wins at 0%; at 30% a 15% chance of slipping down into T makes up the better move. The backup reads only neighbours' current values. Nothing looks further ahead, which is why a long corridor needs many sweeps. At γ 0.99 with the bonus on, the residual is still well above zero after 60 sweeps. A discount near 1 converges slowly. In this lab: the expectation is exact because P(s′|s,a) is a three-entry table. A 60-sweep cap is short enough that γ ≥ 0.97 with the bonus on has not converged. In general: deep RL replaces the table with a neural network and the exact expectation with sampled transitions, which brings bias, variance, and instability that exact value iteration does not have.
documents.title: The one-step lookahead every sweep repeats

documents.subtitle: Return along the episode · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: A single sampled return, term by term The bars are this episode's rewards r₁, r₂, … in order. The inner bars are the same rewards multiplied by γᵗ, which is what the discounted return adds up. With no slip and a converged V, G₀ equals V(S) exactly. Outer bars: raw rewards, +1 up to −1. Inner bars: γᵗ·r, green above zero and red below. Bars left of the cursor are counted in Return so far. Episode step (0 to the episode length) and Episode seed (1–20, which draws a different sequence of slips). Reward this step, Return so far, Full return G₀, and V(S) at the current sweep. G₀ = Σₜ γᵗ·r₍ₜ₊₁₎ over the rewards actually received. The +1 at the end of a six-move episode is worth γ⁵ of its face value. V(S) is an expectation over all slip outcomes, while G₀ is one draw, so they differ whenever Slip chance is above zero. A looping episode is cut at 24 steps, so its G₀ undercounts the infinite-horizon value. Episode step scrubs the return; Episode seed resamples the slips. The Gridworld controls regenerate the episode. Comparison worth running: Slip chance 20%, then seeds 1 to 5. G₀ scatters around V(S) = 0.314. Most of an early step's contribution is the −0.04 step cost. The payoff that justifies the whole path arrives last and discounted. The note under the chart tells you why G₀ and V(S) do or do not agree for the current settings. In this lab: the episode follows the greedy policy, so the only randomness is slipping. There is no exploration inside the gridworld. In general: a real agent sees only sampled returns like this one and must average many of them, which is why return variance is the central practical difficulty of policy-gradient training.
documents.title: A single sampled return, term by term

documents.subtitle: Explore versus exploit · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: ε-greedy on a four-armed Bernoulli bandit Four arms pay 1 with probabilities 0.30, 0.55, 0.45, and 0.70. The agent does not know them. It keeps a sample-average estimate per arm, pulls the best estimate, and with probability ε pulls a random arm instead. Without exploration it keeps the first arm that happens to pay. Bars: how many of 400 pulls each arm got in one seeded run, with its final estimate and its true mean. A line chart of mean reward so far, averaged over 300 seeded runs, for your ε and for ε = 0, with the best arm's 0.70 as a dotted ceiling. Best-arm share for this run, averaged over 300 runs, and the same average for ε = 0. Estimates start at 0 and update as Q ← Q + (r − Q)/n. Greedy ties are broken uniformly at random. The 300 runs use fixed seeds, so the averages are deterministic. At ε = 0.10 the best arm gets about 72% of pulls; at ε = 0 about 33%; at ε = 0.50 about 56%. Exploration ε from 0 to 0.50, and Bandit seed for the single run in the bars. Comparison worth running: ε = 0 across several Bandit seeds. The run locks onto whichever arm paid first. Exploration has a price and a payoff: too little and the agent never learns the 0.70 arm; too much and it keeps pulling arms it already knows are worse. Value iteration on the gridworld never needed this, because it read the transition table directly instead of learning from its own samples. In this lab: one state, four arms, stationary Bernoulli payoffs, and ε-greedy only. Upper-confidence and Thompson-sampling strategies usually do better. In general: RLHF on a single prompt and response is close to a contextual bandit, so the same trade appears there; a model that is never sampled into a behavior cannot be rewarded for it. The next card replaces the value estimates with a learned policy.
documents.title: ε-greedy on a four-armed Bernoulli bandit

documents.subtitle: Policy gradient on the bandit · Reinforcement learning foundations
documents.body: REINFORCE on four arms The same four Bernoulli arms, but the agent now keeps a softmax policy instead of value estimates. Each pull samples an arm from the policy and a reward from the arm, then nudges the policy toward arms that paid more than a baseline expects. The charts average 300 seeded runs; the bars show one run. `Learning rate α` (0.02 to 1.00), `Baseline` (off, so b = 0, or on, so b is the running average reward), and `Policy seed` (1 to 20). Bars: the policy's probability on each arm after 400 pulls in one seeded run, with the arm's true mean and how often it was pulled. Every arm starts at 25%. Two charts over 300 seeded runs, baseline on solid and off dashed: the probability on the best arm before each pull, and the mean reward so far with the best arm's 0.70 as a dotted ceiling. Their legends print the final values. Three metrics: the best-arm probability in this run, its average over 300 runs for your Baseline setting, and how many of the 300 runs end with less than half their probability on the best arm. The policy is `π = softmax(θ)` over four preferences θ, all 0 at the start. Each pull samples an arm from π and a reward `r` of 0 or 1 from that arm's Bernoulli. The update is `θ_i ← θ_i + α·(r − b)·(1[i = arm] − π_i)`. The bracket is exactly `∂ ln π(arm) / ∂θ_i`, so this is REINFORCE (Williams, 1992): a sampled estimate of the gradient of expected reward. A unit test checks the bracket against finite differences, and checks that the expected update is that gradient for any constant baseline. The baseline `b` is the mean reward of the earlier pulls, or 0 when off. It does not depend on the current arm, so it leaves the expected update unchanged and changes only its noise. Both curves use the same 300 seeded runs that `Explore versus exploit` uses, so the only difference between them is b. `Learning rate α`, `Baseline`, and `Policy seed` on this card. Comparison worth running: α 0.20 with Baseline on, then off. Then Baseline on at α 0.02, 0.20, and 1.00. At α 0.20 the baseline-on policy ends with 92.1% on the best arm on average and 2 of 300 runs below 50%. With the baseline off, 84.9% and 29 of 300. With the baseline off a reward of 0 changes nothing and a reward of 1 raises the arm just pulled, so an arm that pays early can run away. At the default seed 3 the run without the baseline ends with 92% on arm 2, whose mean is 0.55. α 0.02 barely moves in 400 pulls: 37% on the best arm either way. α 1.00 commits fastest, with 65.1% after 50 pulls against 40.1% at 0.20, but 33 of 300 runs end below 50%. In this lab: one state, four stationary arms, a fixed 400 pulls, and a running-average baseline. There is no value function, no clipping, and no KL penalty, so this is the simplest policy-gradient estimator, not PPO or GRPO. In general: a language model's policy gives a probability to every possible response, and its rewards come from a learned reward model or a checker. Practical methods subtract a learned value estimate or a group average, and clip the step. The noise this card shows is the reason they do.

Read the compute-optimal frontier as a power law: a straight line on log-log axes once the floor is removed, with steady and slow returns Describe compute-optimal model and data balance Estimate N from a transformer's layer count and width, and say what that estimate leaves out
