documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: An empirical fit relating loss to parameters, data and compute, here a floor plus two decaying power-law terms. It holds within the range of runs it was fitted on, for one architecture, dataset and tokenizer.
documents.title: Scaling law

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: The split of a fixed training budget between parameters and tokens that minimizes predicted loss. It is optimal for training cost only, not for serving cost.
documents.title: Compute-optimal

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: Predicted loss against model size with training compute held fixed, so every larger model sees fewer tokens. Its lowest point is the compute-optimal size for that budget.
documents.title: IsoFLOP curve

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: A relationship of the form y = a times x to a fixed power. Loss minus its floor falls as a power of compute, so it plots as a straight line on log-log axes, with steady and slow returns.
documents.title: Power law

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: The constant E in the fit, which no amount of scale removes. It is often read as the entropy of the text, but it is a fitted number and also absorbs limits of the model family.
documents.title: Irreducible loss

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: The rule of thumb of about 20 training tokens per parameter, from Hoffmann et al. 2022, who trained Chinchilla with 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens. The same paper's printed parametric fit puts the optimum at a higher ratio.
documents.title: Chinchilla ratio

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: Floating-point operations, the unit of training cost. For a dense transformer, training compute is approximately 6 times parameters times tokens: about 2 per parameter per token forward and 4 backward. A fixed compute budget is therefore one isoFLOP curve, and the choice is where on it to sit.
documents.title: FLOPs

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: N, the number of learned weights. For a dense transformer it is about 12 times layers times width squared with embeddings left out. Fits differ on embeddings: Kaplan et al. fitted non-embedding parameters and Hoffmann et al. total parameters, so a rule of thumb for one does not carry straight to the other.
documents.title: Parameter count

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: Training tokens divided by parameter count. It locates a run between a large model starved of data and a small model fed far more data than it can use.
documents.title: Token-to-parameter ratio

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: Training a smaller model well past its compute-optimal token count so it is cheaper to serve. It costs a little extra loss per training FLOP and is standard for widely deployed models.
documents.title: Overtraining

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: A capability that seems to appear abruptly with scale. Many reported cases depend on a thresholded metric such as exact match, while the underlying loss improves smoothly.
documents.title: Emergent ability

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: Scaling behavior when unique high-quality text runs short. Up to about four epochs, repeated tokens are nearly as useful as fresh ones; beyond that their value decays.
documents.title: Data-constrained scaling

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: Using a fit beyond the range it was measured on. It is the main practical use of scaling laws and also their largest assumption.
documents.title: Extrapolation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Scaling laws
documents.body: Compute spent at answer time through longer reasoning, multiple samples or verification. It has its own scaling behavior and trades against training compute.
documents.title: Test-time compute

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Scaling laws · question 1
documents.body: On Frontier power law the compute-optimal line is straight on log-log axes. What does that say about the returns on more compute? Returns accelerate with scale, because each extra decade of compute removes more loss than the last Each tenfold increase in compute removes the same fraction of the reducible loss: steady, slow returns Returns hit a threshold budget, after which the loss drops sharply and then flattens at the floor A straight line on log-log axes is a power law: multiplying compute by a fixed factor multiplies the reducible loss by a fixed fraction. There is no point where improvement accelerates or collapses, and halving the reducible loss takes about ninety times the compute under the printed fit. The slope is the exponent.
documents.title: On Frontier power law the compute-optimal line is straight on log-log axes. What does that say about the returns on more compute?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Scaling laws · question 2
documents.body: Even at the largest sizes the fit predicts a loss above E. What does E stand for, and why does the frontier look straight only after subtracting it? The text's entropy, measured directly, so the loss above it is the model's remaining error The loss of the largest model trained so far, so the line is drawn downward from that point A fitted floor no scale removes, so only the loss above it falls as a pure power of compute E is the constant in L = E + A/N^α + B/D^β. Both power-law terms shrink toward zero, so loss bends toward E and looks like diminishing returns on raw axes. Subtracting E leaves a pure power law. E is a fitted number, often read as the text's entropy but also absorbing limits of the model family.
documents.title: Even at the largest sizes the fit predicts a loss above E. What does E stand for, and why does the frontier look straight only after subtracting it?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Scaling laws · question 3
documents.body: Your compute budget is fixed. Why not spend it all on the largest model you can build? Fixed compute means fewer tokens for a bigger model, and past the minimum that data term outgrows the size term Large models cannot learn from more than 20 tokens per parameter, so any extra tokens would be wasted on them Predicted loss does not depend on model size once compute is fixed, so a larger model would gain nothing at all C = 6ND ties the two together: at fixed C, doubling N halves D. Past the bottom of the isoFLOP curve the B/D^β term rises faster than the A/N^α term falls, so loss goes up. The 20:1 figure is a rule of thumb, not a limit on learning.
documents.title: Your compute budget is fixed. Why not spend it all on the largest model you can build?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Scaling laws · question 4
documents.body: With Budget on Hold compute you drag Parameters well past the diamond. What happens to Training tokens and to Predicted loss? Tokens stay put and loss keeps falling, because a bigger model is always better at any budget Tokens fall to keep compute fixed, and loss rises once the dot passes its curve's bottom Tokens and loss both stay put, because Hold compute freezes the dot at the point you left it Hold compute keeps N times D constant, so the other slider moves with the one you drag and the dot slides along one isoFLOP curve. Beyond the minimum the starved data term grows faster than the size term shrinks, so Predicted loss and Gap to optimum rise while Compute C stays fixed.
documents.title: With Budget on Hold compute you drag Parameters well past the diamond. What happens to Training tokens and to Predicted loss?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Scaling laws · question 5
documents.body: Loss breakdown shows the hatched data term larger than the solid size term. Where should the next doubling of compute go? Mostly to more parameters, because the larger term should be fed with a bigger model each time Equally to both, because compute-optimal always means exactly twenty tokens for every parameter Mostly to more training tokens, because doubling D would lower the loss by more than doubling N The Doubling D and Doubling N readouts say which resource buys more loss per unit of compute. When the data term dominates, extra tokens help more; at the optimum the two gains match. The 20-to-1 ratio is a rule of thumb that only approximates where that balance falls.
documents.title: Loss breakdown shows the hatched data term larger than the solid size term. Where should the next doubling of compute go?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Scaling laws · question 6
documents.body: Labs often train a smaller model on far more tokens than the compute-optimal count. Why accept that? The fit is wrong beyond the optimum, so extra tokens lower loss by more than the formula predicts Compute-optimal covers training cost only, and a smaller model costs less to serve per answer Smaller models cannot overfit, so they always gain from seeing the same data many more times over The optimum is defined for training compute alone. A model served to millions of users spends more on inference than on training, so a smaller model trained past its optimum costs a little extra loss per training FLOP but far less per answer. This is overtraining, and the fit still describes its predicted loss.
documents.title: Labs often train a smaller model on far more tokens than the compute-optimal count. Why accept that?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Scaling laws · question 7
documents.body: Under N from dimensions, you double Width d and leave Layers L alone. Compared with doubling Layers L instead, what happens to N? It grows fourfold, against twofold for doubling layers, since every matrix has d × d entries It grows twofold, the same as doubling layers, because both simply count the number of blocks It grows eightfold, against twofold for doubling layers, because width enters N as a cube It stays the same, because N depends on how many layers there are and not on how wide they are Per block, attention has four d × d matrices and the MLP has d × 4d and 4d × d, so 12d² weights, and N is that times the layer count. Doubling d multiplies every matrix by four; doubling L multiplies the number of blocks by two.
documents.title: Under N from dimensions, you double Width d and leave Layers L alone. Compared with doubling Layers L instead, what happens to N?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Scaling laws · question 8
documents.body: A small model's N from 12 × L × d² sits well below its total parameter count, while a large model's sits close to it. Why? The rule leaves out embeddings, and the embedding table is a much larger share of a small model The rule counts only the attention matrices, and attention is a much larger share of a small model Small models store their weights at higher precision, so each one of their parameters counts for more The rule double-counts the layers, and that double count matters less once there are many of them The embedding table has one row per vocabulary entry, so its size is the vocabulary times d, while the blocks grow with d squared times the layer count. For GPT-2 small the table alone is 38.6M against 84.9M in the blocks. The blocks grow with d squared while the table grows only with d, so its share falls as models widen. Hoffmann et al. count total parameters, so for small models the rule undercounts their N.
documents.title: A small model's N from 12 × L × d² sits well below its total parameter count, while a large model's sits close to it. Why?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Scaling laws
documents.body: The AI models behind chatbots learn by reading huge amounts of text, and training a large one costs so much computing power that a team gets only one try. Before that run starts, someone has to make two choices that cannot be undone: how big the model will be, and how much text it will learn from. This module is about the patterns that guide those two choices and predict how good the model will be before anyone pays for it. These patterns are called scaling laws. Researchers found them by training hundreds of models of different sizes on different amounts of text and scoring how far off each one's guesses were. The scores follow smooth curves that one formula can describe, so a team can test ideas on small models and read the curve forward to plan a big one. The chatbots you may have used were planned with the help of patterns like these. In 2022, a study that trained a model called Chinchilla suggested that many of the biggest models of the time had read too little text for their size. Today, many widely used models are deliberately made smaller than the formula's best choice and taught with extra text, because a smaller model costs less every time it answers you. Why does this matter? Without scaling laws, picking a model's size would be a very expensive guess, because nobody could tell in advance which way of splitting the budget would work best. Put too much into size and the model is starved of text, while putting too much into text leaves a model too small to use it all. Either mistake is locked in once the run ends, and the money spent on it is gone. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain: why the best results form a straight line on a special graph once you remove a floor the score never drops below, and why that means slow, steady progress; how to split a fixed budget between model size and training text so that neither one is wasted; how to estimate a model's size from how many layers it has and how wide they are, and what that estimate leaves out. The lab never trains anything: it runs a published formula, so every number you see is a prediction. You set a model size and an amount of text on the Scaling law controls card, and three more cards show what the formula predicts for that choice: IsoFLOP curves shows how good every possible split of one budget would be, and where the best split sits. Loss breakdown shows which part of the formula is holding the score up, the model's size or its text. Frontier power law shows the best result at every budget, lined up on that special graph. The controls card also holds a small calculator, N from dimensions, which counts a model's size from its shape.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Scaling laws
documents.body: A library on a fixed budget Picture a town that has saved up enough money to build one library, with no second chance. If it spends most of the money on shelves, it gets a huge building with almost nothing to read. If it spends most of the money on books, they end up stacked on the floor with nowhere to go. Somewhere between those two mistakes is the split of shelves and books that gives the best library for that budget. Training a language model, the kind of AI behind chatbots, involves the same kind of choice. The model's size plays the part of the shelves and its training text plays the part of the books, with both paid from one bill for computing power. A scaling law is a formula that predicts, for any split you choose, how good the finished model will be. Three words you need first The lab's labels lean on three ideas, so it helps to pin them down before going further. A model is a huge collection of adjustable numbers, and training nudges each one, over and over, so that the model's guesses get better. Each of those numbers is a parameter, also called a weight, and the letter N stands for how many a model has, which is its parameter count. The lab writes big counts with a letter on the end, M for million, B for billion and T for trillion, so 3.2B means 3.2 billion parameters. Models read text in small pieces called tokens, where a token is usually a whole word or part of one. The letter D counts the tokens a model reads in training, so 28B means 28 billion pieces of text, far more than anyone could read in a lifetime. During training, the model guesses each next token and gets a score, called loss, for how far off its guess was, so lower is better. The lab measures loss in nats per token, a unit of surprise that grows when the model gave the real next token a low chance. As a sense of scale, a model that gave the correct token a 1-in-11 chance every single time would score about 2.4 nats per token. A model that was sure of the right token, and correct, would score 0, while a 1-in-2 chance scores about 0.7. Each time the chance the model gives the right token halves, the loss rises by about 0.7 nats. So the differences you will meet in this lab, often a few hundredths of a nat, are small but real edges. The bill multiplies Here the library picture needs a fix, because a library's bill adds the cost of shelves to the cost of books, while a model's bill multiplies size by text. It multiplies because every token of training text has to pass through every parameter. For each token, each parameter takes part in about 6 small calculations: 2 while the model makes its guess, and 4 while training works out how to adjust it. Each of those small calculations is one step of arithmetic on decimal numbers, called a floating-point operation, so training cost is counted in FLOPs, short for floating-point operations. The total cost of a run, called its compute and written C, is therefore about 6 × N × D, which the lab shows as Compute C = 6ND. Here is the bill for the run the lab starts on, which has 3.2B parameters and 28B tokens. Multiply 6 × 3.2 billion × 28 billion and you get about 5.4 × 10²⁰ FLOPs, where 10²⁰ means a 1 followed by 20 zeros. In other words, the run takes roughly 540 billion billion small calculations. Because the bill multiplies, a fixed budget fixes the product N × D. A model twice as big can read only half as many tokens for the same money, and that trade is the whole puzzle this lab is about. The formula: a floor plus two shrinking parts The formula comes from those hundreds of training runs, where researchers measured each model's loss and found the formula that best matched the results. It is a bit like drawing the line that best fits a scatter of dots on a graph. The lab prints that formula at the top of its IsoFLOP curves card: Here L is the predicted loss, and N and D are the parameter and token counts from before. The letters E, A, B, α and β stand for numbers the researchers chose so that the formula matches their results. Choosing numbers this way is called fitting, and one chosen set of numbers is called a fit. The sign ^ means "raised to the power", so N^α is N raised to the power α. The lab offers two fits under Fit, and the main one, Hoffmann 2022, is the set printed in the 2022 Chinchilla paper. Each of the formula's three parts has its own job: E is a floor that no amount of size or text gets below, called the irreducible loss, and in the lab's main fit it is 1.69. A/N^α is the size term, which shrinks as the model gets bigger, because a bigger model can pick up more patterns from the same text. B/D^β is the data term, which shrinks as the model reads more tokens, because more text gives it more examples to learn from. Loss breakdown works the formula out for your run, and at the starting run of 3.2B parameters and 28B tokens it shows this line: The size term adds 0.238 on top of the floor, while the data term adds 0.488, about twice as much, and the total is the Predicted loss. The lab also works out that doubling the text here would lower the loss by 0.086, while doubling the size would lower it by only 0.050. So this model is short of text more than it is short of size. The Greek letters α (alpha) and β (beta) are powers, like the 2 in a square, but they are small: 0.34 and 0.28 in the main fit. A power of one half is the same as taking a square root, so a power of 0.34 grows even more slowly than a square root does. Here is what that means for a model ten times bigger. N^α grows by 10 to the power 0.34, which is only about 2.2, and because N^α sits on the bottom of the fraction, the size term gets divided by 2.2. At the starting run, that takes the size term from 0.238 down to about 0.109. Another tenfold step takes it to about 0.050, so the second step removes less than half as much as the first, at ten times the price. Ten times more tokens works the same way, but it divides the data term by only about 1.9. That is why each improvement costs more than the one before. The floor needs care, because people often describe it as the truly unpredictable part of text, like the next word in a sentence where several words fit equally well. But E is a number the fit chose to match the results, not something anyone measured. So it also includes whatever this design of model, trained this way, never learns, and a different design might have a lower floor. Within this formula, though, no run ever reaches E. Even at the far end of both sliders, 1T parameters on 30T tokens, the formula predicts a loss of 1.793, which is still above the floor of 1.69. The library picture stops matching in two places. Books sit on shelves as whole copies, but a model does not keep copies of its text, because training only adjusts its numbers to pick up patterns. And while a library's hundredth shelf holds as many books as its first, each extra step of size or text lowers the loss less than the last. The best split for one budget Now put the bill and the formula together by fixing the budget and trying every model size. Each bigger model must read fewer tokens, so its size term falls while its data term rises. Plot predicted loss against model size and you get a U-shaped curve, which the lab calls an IsoFLOP curve. The name comes from "iso", which means "same", because every point on the curve costs the same number of FLOPs. The lowest point of the U is the best split for that budget, and a run sitting there is called compute-optimal. To the left of the bottom, the model is too small to make full use of its text. To the right, it is so big that it reads too little text to fill it. At the bottom, doubling the size or doubling the text would each double the bill and lower the loss by about the same amount. Since neither is a better buy than the other, moving money from one to the other cannot help, which means neither resource is being wasted. Notice that the bottom is where the two doubling gains match, not where the two terms are equal. Doubling the size cuts the size term by about 21%, while doubling the text cuts the data term by only about 18%, because α is bigger than β. So at the best split the data term is still a little bigger. At the starting budget's best split, the data term is 0.385 while the size term is 0.317. The bigger term is only a rough guide to what a model is short of, and the doubling gains are the real test. Here is one budget worked out, where two runs that each cost 1.2 × 10²⁰ FLOPs sit on the same U: 10B parameters on only 2B tokens, a giant library with almost no books, has a predicted loss of 2.873. 200M parameters on 100B tokens, a tiny library buried in books, has a predicted loss of 2.643. The two runs sit on opposite sides of their curve's bottom, which reaches 2.575 at about 700M parameters, so each one wastes a good part of the same budget. The number of training tokens divided by the number of parameters is called the token-to-parameter ratio, and the lab shows it as Tokens per parameter. A low ratio means a big model starved of text, while a very high one means a small model fed more text than it can use. A popular rule of thumb, the Chinchilla ratio, says to aim for about 20 tokens per parameter. It is named after the Chinchilla model, which its makers trained with 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens, exactly 20 tokens for every parameter. A straight line on a special graph Find the bottom of the U for every budget and join them up, and you get the compute-optimal frontier, the lowest loss the formula allows at each budget. To show its shape, the lab uses a graph whose axes grow by multiplying instead of adding, so each equal step along an axis means ten times more. These are called log-log axes, from logarithm, a piece of math you will not need here. The IsoFLOP chart's size axis works the same way: it runs 100M, 1B, 10B, 100B and 1T. Now take the frontier's loss and subtract the floor E, and what is left, written L − E, is the part that more compute can still remove. On log-log axes it falls along a perfectly straight line, which is the sign of a power law. In a power law, each tenfold step in compute multiplies the loss above the floor by the same fraction, which is about 70% under the main fit. Here is that rule at work along the frontier, read from the formula: Start at a budget of 10²⁰ FLOPs, where the best possible run sits 0.910 above the floor. Ten times that budget, 10²¹ FLOPs, brings it down to 0.639, which is 70% of what was there. Ten times again, 10²² FLOPs, brings it to 0.449, which is once more 70% of the step before. Why does that draw a straight line? On the loss axis, which also grows by multiplying, keeping 70% is the same-sized step down wherever you start. On the lab's frontier chart, the space from 2 down to 1 is as tall as the space from 0.2 down to 0.1, because each one is a halving. Each tenfold budget is also the same-sized step across. The same step down for every step across is exactly what a straight line is, so a power law always draws one on these axes. This is what steady but slow means. Every tenfold budget buys the same share of progress, with no sudden jumps or stalls, yet that share is small. Two tenfold steps, 100 times the compute, keep 70% of 70%, which is 49%, a little under half. So halving the loss above the floor takes a bit less than 100 times the compute, about 90 times. The floor has to come off first, because with it left in, the loss bends and flattens as it nears E, as if progress were dying out. With the floor left in, the frontier losses at those three budgets are 2.600, 2.329 and 2.139. Each keeps about 90%, then 92%, of the one before, so the drops seem to fade, even though the part that can still shrink keeps the same 70% every time. Only once E is removed does the straight line appear, which is why the lab's chart plots L − E instead of the loss itself. Counting N from a model's shape The formula needs N, and for the most common kind of language model you can estimate N from the model's shape. These models are transformers, built as a stack of repeated blocks called layers, and inside each layer every token is carried as a list of numbers. The length of that list is the model's width, written d, and the number of layers, sometimes called its depth, is written L. (The letter L does double duty in this lab: next to Layers L it counts layers, while in the formula it means loss.) Each layer keeps its weights in grids of numbers, called matrices. A grid d numbers by d numbers holds d × d numbers, written d², so a grid 8 by 8 holds 64. The attention part of a layer, where tokens gather information from one another, has four of these square grids, so it holds 4 × d². The feed-forward part, which works on each token by itself, has two wide grids, one d by 4 × d and one 4 × d by d. Each of them holds 4 × d² numbers, so together they hold 8 × d². Adding 4 × d² and 8 × d² gives 12 × d² weights per layer, so the whole stack holds about 12 × L × d². The lab's calculator starts at 32 layers of width 4,096, which is the shape of one of the LLaMA models. Each of those layers holds 12 × 4,096² weights, about 201 million, so 32 layers hold about 6.44B in total. Because the width is squared, it adds to N far faster than the number of layers does. Double the width and every grid gets four times as many entries, so N grows fourfold, to 25.8B. Double the layers instead and you only get twice as many grids, so N doubles, to 12.9B. This count is an estimate that leaves some things out, and the biggest is the embeddings, a lookup table that turns each token into its starting list of numbers. It has one row of d numbers for every token in the model's vocabulary, which is the full list of tokens the model can read. The count also skips small extras, such as the numbers each layer uses to shift and rescale its values. It assumes the feed-forward part is exactly four times as wide, too, which not every model follows. So a real model's total usually comes out a little higher, and for small models it can be a lot higher, as Going deeper shows.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Scaling laws
documents.body: Picture a baker asked to make one enormous cake for a wedding, with enough ingredients for exactly one attempt. She cannot practise on the real thing, so she bakes small cakes at several sizes and writes down how the baking time grows with size. Then she draws a curve through her notes and reads it forward to plan the big cake. The biggest AI training runs are planned the same way, because nobody can afford to try one of them twice. A team trains many small models, fits the scaling-law formula to them, and reads it forward. That way the budget, the model size, the amount of text and the expected loss are all chosen before the expensive run starts. Using a formula beyond the range it was measured on is called extrapolation, and it is both the main use of scaling laws and their biggest assumption. Like the baker's curve, the pattern might not hold at a size nobody has tried. The formula also settles a question that people have gotten wrong before, which is how to split the budget. An earlier study, from 2020, concluded that model size should grow much faster than the amount of text. The 2022 Chinchilla study made several changes. One was to match each run's learning-rate plan, which sets how the size of each adjustment step shrinks over time, to how long that run would last. That way every run, short or long, could finish as well as it was able to. Compared fairly like this, the runs showed that size and text should grow at roughly the same pace. Going deeper shows that the two studies also counted parameters differently, which explains much of the gap too. The two crosses on IsoFLOP curves show what that change meant for the biggest models of the time. Gopher had 280B parameters and read 300B tokens, while Chinchilla had 70B parameters and read 1.4T tokens, and the two used similar amounts of compute. The main fit predicts that the smaller model, which read more text, comes out ahead, at 1.937 against 1.993 for Gopher. Scaling laws also help explain the AI industry, since a company will spend huge sums on a training run only if it can predict what the money buys. Returns that are steady and predictable, even if slow, justify that spending in a way that surprises could not.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Scaling laws
documents.body: The Scaling law controls card holds everything you can change, starting with Parameters, which runs from 100M to 1T, and Training tokens, which runs from 1B to 30T. Both sliders move by multiplying, like the log axes, so each notch along them is the same percentage change rather than the same amount. Fit picks which published set of numbers the formula uses, and Budget decides whether the two sliders move on their own (Free) or together (Hold compute). Under the sliders, Fit optimum here names the best split at your current budget, in parameters, tokens and tokens per parameter. Read the starting run Before you touch anything, read the four readouts under IsoFLOP curves: Predicted loss is 2.416, the average score per token that the formula expects for your run. Compute C = 6ND is 5.4 × 10²⁰ FLOPs, the size of the bill for training this model on this much text. Tokens per parameter is 8.8, well below the rule of thumb of 20, so this model reads little text for its size. Gap to optimum is 0.023 nats, which is how far your loss sits above the best split at the same budget. Your run is the filled dot on the thick curve, and the diamond on that same curve marks the formula's best split for the same budget. The legend calls it Fit optimum, same C, and it sits at 1.38B parameters on 65B tokens, with a loss of 2.393. The hollow square marks the 20-tokens-per-parameter split, called 20 tokens/param, same C, at 2.12B parameters on 42.3B tokens. Loss breakdown tells you which way to move, because Doubling N lowers L by shows 0.050 while Doubling D lowers L by shows 0.086. So at this run more text is the better buy, and the sentence under the readouts says the data term dominates. Change the size, change the budget With Budget on Free, drag Parameters and leave Training tokens alone. Your dot moves across the thin curves, and the thick curve moves with it. That happens because a bigger model on the same text costs more compute, which is a different budget. Each thin curve is one fixed budget, labelled from 10¹⁹ to 10²⁵ FLOPs where it leaves the chart, while the thick curve is always the budget of your current run. Feed the model more text Bring Parameters back near its starting 3.2B, then drag Training tokens upward while you watch Loss breakdown. The hatched bar is the data term and the solid bar is the size term, and the hatched bar shrinks as the text grows. Keep an eye on the two doubling readouts as well. At around 190B tokens, Doubling N lowers L by catches up with Doubling D lowers L by, and past that point it is the bigger of the two. The bottleneck has moved, so now the model is short of size rather than text. The bars themselves only cross later, past 360B tokens, because the size term shrinks faster with each doubling. Two bad splits on one curve Try this: Set Parameters to 10B and Training tokens to 2B, and Predicted loss reads 2.873, a huge library with almost no books. Now set 200M and 100B, and the loss is 2.643, a tiny library buried in books. Compute C = 6ND reads 1.2 × 10²⁰ FLOPs both times, so both dots sit on the same curve, on opposite sides of its low point. Fit optimum here tells you where that low point is, at about 700M parameters. Walk one curve Switch Budget to Hold compute, and the box under it now says the budget is held. Moving one slider now moves the other, so your dot slides along one curve instead of jumping between them. Drag Parameters toward the diamond, and watch Training tokens move the opposite way while Gap to optimum shrinks. Stop when it reads 0.000, because then you are on the diamond, the best split this formula allows for that budget. Keep dragging past the diamond and the gap grows again. On the left of the diamond, the model is too small for its text. On the right, the model is so big that it is starving for text. Drag across the whole curve and watch the gap grow on both sides of the bottom. Near the bottom, the two doubling readouts in Loss breakdown nearly match, and its sentence changes to say that doubling either resource buys about the same. Each slider stops where the other would run off its range, so the budget never changes by accident. Read the frontier On Frontier power law, the dashed line is the compute-optimal frontier, drawn on log-log axes with the floor already removed, while the dotted line follows the 20-tokens-per-parameter rule. Your dot sits on or above the dashed line, higher by however far your run is from its best split. Read Slope, which shows −0.154, and 10× compute keeps, which shows 70% of L − E. The frontier has its own power, which comes from combining α and β, and the lab shows it as the slope, so it says how steeply the line falls. A minus sign on a power means dividing: ten to the power −0.154 is 1 divided by ten to the power 0.154. Ten to the power 0.154 is about 1.43, and 1 ÷ 1.43 is about 0.70, which is where the 70% comes from. Then switch Fit to Epoch 2024 refit, and the line stays straight while the slope steepens to −0.178. Ten to the power 0.178 is about 1.51, and 1 ÷ 1.51 is about 0.66. So each tenfold budget now keeps 66% of the loss above the floor, a slightly faster pace than before. Build N from dimensions Find N from dimensions at the bottom of the controls card, where Layers L runs from 1 to 128. Width d runs from 64 to 16,384 in steps of 64, and the line below them works out 12 × L × d² for you. At the starting 32 layers of width 4,096 it reads 6.44B weights, and Use as Parameters moves the Parameters slider to that count. Budget may still be on Hold compute from walking the curve, so switch it back to Free first. Under Hold compute, the button would also move Training tokens to keep the bill the same. It could even stop short of the count, because the held budget runs out of room before the slider does. Press it, then double Width d to 8,192 and watch N become 25.8B, four times as many. Put the width back and double Layers L to 64 instead, and N becomes 12.9B, only twice as many. If a shape gives a count outside the slider's 100M to 1T range, the line says so and the button stops at the nearest end.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Scaling laws
documents.body: The bottom of the U is flat At the starting budget, the square for 20 tokens per parameter sits only 0.006 above the diamond, even though it uses a model 54% bigger. Getting the balance roughly right matters a lot, while getting it exactly right barely matters. That flatness is also why the dotted 20:1 line and the dashed frontier nearly overlap on Frontier power law. The bottleneck moves instead of vanishing Push one resource far enough and the other becomes the one worth buying, which Loss breakdown shows when its doubling readout takes the lead. You never escape both terms by piling everything onto one slider, because the term you ignore stops shrinking. Loss has a floor Even at 1T parameters and 30T tokens, the largest run the sliders allow, the formula predicts 1.793 against a floor of 1.69. The size and data terms keep shrinking toward zero as you add more, but E stays put however much you spend. Width grows N faster than depth N follows the square of the width but only the plain count of layers, so widening a model adds parameters much faster than adding layers does. Doubling the width multiplies N by four, while doubling the layers multiplies it by two. This is only about the count, and it says nothing about whether a wide model or a deep one learns better. Straight, steady and slow On Frontier power law, every tenfold budget keeps the same 70% of the loss above the floor. No point on the line speeds up or suddenly drops, so progress is predictable, but halving the loss above the floor costs about 90 times the compute. The two fits agree on shape, not on the bottom Switch Fit at the starting run and Fit optimum here moves from 1.38B parameters on 65B tokens to 2.02B on 44.3B. Under Hoffmann 2022, the diamond pulls further from the square as budgets grow, toward smaller models fed more text. Under Epoch 2024 refit, the two stay close together, near 20 tokens per parameter. The crosses are predictions The crosses marked Chinchilla and Gopher stand for real models, and the legend lists their sizes as Real runs (70B/1.4T, 280B/300B). But each cross sits at the loss this formula predicts for that size, not at the loss the real model actually reached.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Scaling laws
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Nothing in this lab is trained. Every readout is the published formula worked out with your numbers, so the lab shows what the formula predicts, not what a real model would do. The sliders also reach far past the runs the formula was fitted on. Those runs went from about 70M to 16B parameters, trained on 5B to 500B tokens, while the sliders reach 1T parameters and 30T tokens. Most of the chart is therefore extrapolation, like the baker reading her curve past the biggest cake she has ever baked. The loss is in the formula's own units, measured on one particular collection of text cut into tokens one particular way. So a loss from this lab cannot be compared with a loss reported for some other model. The bill, 6 × N × D, is a shortcut too, because it leaves out some of the work in attention, which adds up when a model reads very long passages. Real runs also lose time when machines wait on each other or restart, so the true cost is higher. The frontier line is perfectly straight here because it is worked out from the formula itself. A real frontier is fitted to a few dozen training runs, so it comes with uncertainty that grows with each tenfold step past them. Last, N from dimensions is a calculator, not a fit, and it skips the embeddings and small extras. For large models it lands a few percent under the real count. For small ones it lands much further under, because the embedding table is a big share of them, as Going deeper shows. When the fit and the rule of thumb disagree A common mix-up: "20 tokens per parameter" is a rule of thumb, not what the Chinchilla formula says at every budget. With the formula's numbers as the paper printed them, the best split at Chinchilla's own budget is 32B parameters on 3.0T tokens, about 93 tokens per parameter. The Chinchilla paper worked out the best split in three different ways, and the printed formula was only one of them. A 2024 study by Epoch AI, which redid the Chinchilla paper's analysis, found that the formula's numbers did not agree with the other two ways. So it fitted the data again. Switch Fit to Epoch 2024 refit and that same optimum moves to about 73B parameters on 1.34T tokens, about 18 tokens per parameter, which is close to 20. The powers α and β are touchy as well. That study also lists the original powers with two more decimal places, so 0.34 becomes 0.3392 and 0.28 becomes 0.2849. That tiny change moves the same optimum from 32B to about 40B parameters, which shows how much large-scale predictions hang on small details of a fit. Where real scaling laws fail Scaling laws are trends inside a tested range, not laws of nature, so they only describe the kind of model and training they were measured on. Every part of the formula depends on the model's design, the mix of training text, the way text is cut into tokens, and the training recipe. Change any of these and the whole curve shifts, so a fit made for one setup cannot be carried over to another. Lower loss is also not the same as being more useful. Picture a spelling bee where you score a point only if you spell the whole word right, with no credit for being close. A student who gets a few more letters right each week scores zero for weeks, then suddenly starts scoring, even though the student improved steadily all along. Some AI tests work the same way, giving credit only for a fully correct answer. A smooth loss curve can sit under a test score that jumps, and a skill that seems to appear suddenly at some size is called an emergent ability. Many reported emergent abilities depend on whether the test gives partial credit or counts only exact answers. Good text also runs out, and how scaling behaves when it does is called data-constrained scaling. One study found that reading the same text up to about four times is nearly as good as reading fresh text, though each pass after that is worth less.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Scaling laws
documents.body: From dimensions to N The 12 × L × d² rule comes from counting one layer's grids, the way The transformer block lab does. There, the toy block has a width of 8, so it holds 12 × 8² = 768 such weights, or 840 once you count its small extras. The rule holds up well at large scale, which you can check against the LLaMA paper. LLaMA's 6.7B model has 32 layers of width 4,096, so the rule gives 6.44B, about 4% under the paper's count. Its 65.2B model has 80 layers of width 8,192, and the rule gives 64.4B, about 1% under. The missing part is what the rule leaves out: the embeddings, the small extras, and the exact shape of the feed-forward part. Small models are where the rule falls furthest short, and GPT-2 small shows why. According to its published settings, it has 12 layers of width 768 and a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens. Its layers hold 84.9M weights, yet its token table alone holds 38.6M, nearly half as much again on top. The table grows only with the width, while the layers grow with the width squared, so the table's share falls as models get wider. For a model with the LLaMA shape above, a table of the same 50,257 tokens would add only about 3% to the count. Papers even disagree about whether N should include that table, since an early study from 2020 left it out while the 2022 Chinchilla study counted it. A 2024 paper traced much of the gap between their two answers on how to split a budget to that one choice. Both fits in this lab follow the 2022 study's form. Inference & KV cache looks at the same two numbers when a model is answering people rather than training. While it writes an answer, the model saves a few notes for every token so far, and those notes grow with the number of layers and with the width. Some models share notes between parts of a layer to save space, so for them the notes grow more slowly than the full width. So layers and width set both what a model costs to train and what it costs to run. Training cost is not the whole bill Picture a bakery choosing between two ovens. One is cheap to buy but uses a lot of power on every loaf, while the other costs more up front but uses far less per loaf. If you plan to bake millions of loaves, the second one comes out cheaper in the end, even though it cost more on the first day. Models face the same trade, because compute-optimal means best for the training bill only. A model served to millions of people runs up a new bill on every answer, and those bills can add up to more than training cost. So labs deliberately train a smaller model on far more text than the formula's best split, which is called overtraining. For a model, the up-front price is paid in training, and here the oven picture stops matching. The oven's extra cost is only money, but the smaller model pays in quality too. At the same training budget it ends with a slightly higher loss, or it needs extra training compute to reach the same loss. Set Budget back to Free, then set Parameters as close to 8B and Training tokens as close to 15T as the sliders allow, which is about 7.94B and 15.1T. That is roughly the recipe for Llama 3 8B. The printed fit charges about 0.026 of extra loss compared with its best split at that budget, which is a model of about 36B parameters. In return, the 8B model is several times cheaper to run on every answer it gives. Under Epoch 2024 refit, the extra loss is about 0.054, measured against a best split of about 81B. Inference & KV cache showed where that running cost comes from: every new token makes the model read through all its weights and its saved notes again. That bill comes back on every answer, for as long as the model is in use. Other ways to scale Some models send each token to a few internal specialists, called experts, instead of through the whole model. Their total size can grow while the work per token stays the same. So fits for these models track three things separately: the total size, the part actually used for each token, and the number of experts. Spending more compute at answer time has its own curves too. Sampling several answers, writing out longer reasoning, or checking an answer before giving it are all kinds of test-time compute. To reach a given accuracy, a lab can spend less on training and more at answer time, or the other way around. The same curve-fitting trick also helps choose training settings for a big run. Labs fit how the best learning rate and the best batch size, the number of examples a model learns from in one step, shift as compute grows. Another approach sets up the model so those best settings stay the same as it gets wider.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Scaling laws
documents.body: This module is about scaling laws: empirical curve fits that predict a language model's loss from its parameter count N and its number of training tokens D. They answer a budgeting question. With a fixed amount of training compute, how large should the model be, how many tokens should it see, and what loss should it reach? Training dynamics followed loss within one run; a scaling law is fitted to the measured losses of many runs. The transformer block counted one block's weights, which this module scales up to a whole model's N, and Inference & KV cache showed the serving cost that a training-only optimum leaves out. Compute is counted in FLOPs, floating-point operations. An isoFLOP curve holds the compute budget fixed and trades model size against tokens; its lowest point is the compute-optimal split. Where it shows up The model-to-data ratio. Hoffmann et al. (2022), the Chinchilla paper, found that model size and data should grow roughly in proportion; their headline rule of thumb is about 20 training tokens per parameter. The earlier fits of Kaplan et al. (2020) had favored growing model size much faster than data. Models built to be served. Labs deliberately overtrain smaller models, training them on far more tokens than the compute-optimal count, because smaller models are cheaper to serve. Roughly 8B parameters on 15T tokens is Llama 3 8B's recipe. Other axes. Mixture-of-experts models use only some of their parameters for each token, so their fits separate active from total parameters. Test-time compute, spent at answer time on sampling, longer reasoning or verification, has its own scaling behavior. Scaling fits also track how the best learning rate and batch size shift with compute. Why it matters Training compute is roughly proportional to parameters times tokens, so on a fixed budget a bigger model sees fewer tokens. Lean too far either way and loss rises: a large model is starved of tokens, and a small one is limited by its size. The fit also makes returns predictable. Once the irreducible loss, a fitted floor that no amount of scale removes, is subtracted, the compute-optimal frontier is a power law: each tenfold budget removes the same fraction of the reducible loss, the loss above that floor. The fitted constants hold only for the architecture, data mix, tokenizer, optimizer and schedule they were fitted with, and a lower loss does not guarantee a better score on a given task. What you will be able to explain Read the compute-optimal frontier as a power law: a straight line on log-log axes once the floor is removed, with steady and slow returns. Describe the compute-optimal balance of model size and data, and why a bigger model is not automatically better at fixed compute. Estimate N from a transformer's layer count and width, and say what that estimate leaves out: embeddings, norm scales and the exact MLP shape. What the lab shows Nothing is trained. Every readout is closed-form arithmetic: a published loss fit, C = 6ND, the ratio D/N, or 12·L·d². Fit chooses Hoffmann 2022, the constants Hoffmann et al. printed, or Epoch 2024 refit, Besiroglu et al.'s refit of them. The Chinchilla and Gopher crosses are the fit's predictions for their sizes, not their reported results, and most of the (N, D) plane the sliders reach is extrapolation beyond the fitted runs. On Scaling law controls, Parameters and Training tokens set N and D. IsoFLOP curves draws one thin U-shaped curve per budget, each with a small dot at its minimum. The thick curve is your own budget: your run is the filled circle on it, a diamond marks the fit's optimum and a square the 20:1 split. The card reads out Predicted loss, Compute C = 6ND, Tokens per parameter and Gap to optimum. The key experiment sets Budget to Hold compute and drags Parameters, so the filled circle slides along the thick curve until Gap to optimum reads 0.000 at the diamond. There the two doubling readouts on Loss breakdown nearly match: doubling either resource buys about the same. Frontier power law plots loss above the floor against compute on log-log axes and reads out its Slope. N from dimensions turns Layers L and Width d into a parameter count, which Use as Parameters puts on the Parameters slider, clamped to its 100M to 1T range.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Scaling laws
documents.body: Scaling laws are empirical curve fits. Train many models at different sizes on different amounts of data, measure their loss, and fit a formula. The fit then predicts the loss of runs you have not done. The lab uses the parametric form from Hoffmann et al. (2022), the Chinchilla paper: N is parameter count and D is training tokens, both as raw counts. E is the irreducible loss, a floor no amount of scale removes. The two power-law terms shrink with size and with data. In the printed fit, E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, α = 0.34 and β = 0.28, with loss in nats per token on the paper's own data. Why a budget must be split Training compute is approximately C ≈ 6ND FLOPs for a dense transformer: about 2 operations per parameter per token in the forward pass and 4 in the backward pass. Because the product ND is what costs money, a fixed budget is one isoFLOP curve. Along it, a bigger model means fewer tokens. Each isoFLOP curve is U-shaped. Too small a model and the size term dominates. Too large and the data term dominates. The bottom is the compute-optimal split, and at that point the marginal returns match: α·A/N^α = β·B/D^β. The ratio that changed The first influential fits (Kaplan et al., 2020) concluded that model size should grow much faster than data. Hoffmann et al. used learning-rate schedules matched to each run's length and found the two should grow roughly in proportion. Their headline recipe, about 20 tokens per parameter, implied that the largest models of the time were undertrained.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Scaling laws
documents.body: Scaling laws are why large training runs can be planned at all. You cannot afford to try a frontier configuration twice, so the configuration is chosen by fitting curves on small runs and extrapolating to the large one. They also explain the shape of the industry. Steady, predictable, sublinear returns justify large capital spending in a way that unpredictable returns would not.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Scaling laws
documents.body: Start on IsoFLOP curves. The default run is 3.2B parameters on 28B tokens: Predicted loss 2.416 at 5.4 × 10²⁰ FLOPs, only 8.8 tokens per parameter. The diamond on your curve is the fit's optimum at the same compute, 1.38B on 65B tokens at 2.393. Two failures on one curve Set Parameters to 10B and Training tokens to 2B: loss 2.873. Then set 200M and 100B: loss 2.643. Both runs cost 1.2 × 10²⁰ FLOPs, so they sit on the same curve, on opposite sides of its minimum at 2.575. Walk the curve Switch Budget to Hold compute and drag Parameters. Now the other slider moves with it, the dot slides along one curve, and Gap to optimum falls to 0.000 at the diamond. Loss breakdown shows why: Doubling N lowers L by and Doubling D lowers L by meet there. Build N from dimensions Under N from dimensions, set Layers L and Width d. The defaults, 32 layers of width 4,096, give 12 × 32 × 4,096² = 6.44B weights. Press Use as Parameters to put the slider there. Then double Width d: N becomes 25.8B, fourfold. Double Layers L instead and it is 12.9B, twofold.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Scaling laws
documents.body: The bottoms are flat. At the default budget the 20:1 square is 0.006 above the diamond while using a 54% larger model. Roughly right matters; exactly right barely does. The bottleneck moves rather than disappearing. Push one resource and the other term becomes the one worth buying. Loss has a floor. Even at 1T parameters and 30T tokens the printed fit predicts 1.793 against E = 1.69. N follows the square of the width but only the first power of the layer count. Doubling the width quadruples N; doubling the layers doubles it. On Frontier power law, L − E along the frontier is a straight line on log-log axes with slope −0.154. Each tenfold budget keeps 70% of the reducible loss.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Scaling laws
documents.body: In this lab. Nothing is trained. Every readout is the published formula evaluated in closed form, and the crosses for Chinchilla and Gopher are the fit's predictions for their sizes, not their reported results. The sliders reach 1T parameters and 30T tokens, far beyond the fitted runs (about 70M to 16B parameters, 5B to 500B tokens), so most of the plane is extrapolation. The fit and the rule of thumb disagree Under the printed constants, the optimum at Chinchilla's own budget (5.76 × 10²³ FLOPs) is 32B parameters on 3.0T tokens, about 93 tokens per parameter, not 70B on 1.4T. Besiroglu et al. (2024) found the printed estimates inconsistent with the paper's other two methods. Their refit, the Fit option Epoch 2024 refit, puts that optimum at 72B on 1.33T, about 18 per parameter. The exponents are fragile too. With the more precise α = 0.3392 and β = 0.2849 listed in that replication, the same optimum moves to about 40B. Small changes in α and β move large-scale predictions a lot. Limits of the mechanism Every term is conditional on architecture, data mix, tokenizer, optimizer and schedule. Loss is not capability: a smooth loss curve can sit under a metric that jumps, and much of the "emergent ability" literature turns on whether the metric is continuous or thresholded. The token supply is finite: Muennighoff et al. (2023) found about four epochs of repeated data nearly as good as fresh data, with value decaying after that.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Scaling laws
documents.body: From dimensions to N The fit's N is a parameter count, and for a dense transformer two numbers nearly set it: the layer count L and the width d. The transformer block counts a block's weights as 4d² for attention (queries, keys, values, output) and 8d² for a classic MLP, so 12d² per block and 12·L·d² for the model, with embeddings left out. Its toy block has d = 8: 12 × 8² = 768 weights, or 840 with biases and norm parameters. The same formula works at scale. LLaMA's 6.7B model has 32 layers of width 4,096 (Touvron et al., 2023, Table 2), so 12 × 32 × 4,096² = 6.44B, about 4% under the paper's count. Its 65.2B model has 80 layers of width 8,192, giving 64.4B, about 1% under. The shortfall is what the rule leaves out: embeddings, norm scales and the exact MLP shape. Embeddings matter more for small models. GPT-2 small has 12 layers of width 768 and a 50,257-token vocabulary (its Hugging Face configuration): the blocks hold 12 × 12 × 768² = 84.9M weights and the token table alone holds 50,257 × 768 = 38.6M. The blocks grow with d² and the table only with d, so the share falls as models widen. Which count a fit uses is part of the fit. Kaplan et al. fitted non-embedding parameters and Hoffmann et al. total parameters, and Pearce and Song (2024) attribute much of the gap between the two fits to that choice. Both fits in this lab are of Hoffmann et al.'s form. Inference & KV cache uses the same two numbers from the serving side. Its cache holds 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim values per token, which is 2·L·d when every query head has its own key and value head. So layers and width set both what a model costs to train and what it costs to serve. Overtraining and serving Compute-optimal is optimal for training only. A model served to millions of users spends more on inference than on training, so labs deliberately overtrain smaller models. Set 8B parameters on 15T tokens, roughly Llama 3 8B's recipe: the printed fit charges 0.026 extra loss against a 36B optimum, and the refit 0.054 against an 81B one, for a model several times cheaper to serve. Inference & KV cache showed where that serving cost comes from: every generated token re-reads the weights and the cache, and that bill recurs on every answer. Mixture-of-experts models scale along a third axis: total parameters can grow while per-token compute stays fixed, so fits separate active parameters, total parameters and expert count. Test-time compute — sampling several candidates, longer reasoning, or verification — has its own scaling behavior and trades against training compute for a target accuracy. Scaling fits are also used to set hyperparameters, by fitting how the best learning rate and batch size shift with compute, or by using a parametrization such as μP that keeps them stable as width grows.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Scaling law controls · Scaling laws
documents.body: Two resources, one compute bill Two log-scale sliders set the parameter count N and the training-token count D. Training compute is C = 6ND, so every choice of the pair is also a choice of budget. Budget can hold that product fixed, and Fit picks which published constants the loss formula uses. `Parameters` from 100M to 1T and `Training tokens` from 1B to 30T, both on logarithmic tracks so each notch is the same percentage change. `Fit`, a two-way switch between `Hoffmann 2022` (the constants printed in the Chinchilla paper) and `Epoch 2024 refit` (the replication by Besiroglu et al.). `Budget`, with `Free` and `Hold compute`. The box under it states what the sliders are doing in words, and `Fit optimum here` names the best split at your current compute. `N from dimensions`: `Layers L` from 1 to 128, `Width d` from 64 to 16,384 in steps of 64, a line reading `12 × L × d² = N weights` with the weights per block, and a `Use as Parameters` button. Compute is `C = 6ND` FLOPs: about 2 operations per parameter per token in the forward pass and 4 in the backward pass of a dense transformer. Under `Hold compute` the product N·D is kept fixed. Moving `Parameters` sets D = C / 6N, and the moving slider stops where the other would leave its range, so the budget never changes silently. `Fit optimum here` is the closed-form minimum of the loss formula along your isoFLOP curve: N* = G·(C/6)^a with a = β/(α+β) and G = (αA/βB)^(1/(α+β)), and D* = C/(6N*). `N from dimensions` evaluates 12 · L · d². Attention has four d × d matrices and a classic MLP has d × 4d and 4d × d, so a block holds 12d² weights and L blocks hold 12·L·d². `Use as Parameters` sets the `Parameters` slider to that count, clamped to 100M to 1T; under `Hold compute` the `Training tokens` slider moves with it. `Parameters` and `Training tokens`: set 10B and 2B, then 200M and 100B. Both cost 1.2 × 10²⁰ FLOPs, so they sit on the same curve, on opposite sides of its minimum. `Budget`: switch to `Hold compute` and drag `Parameters`; the dot slides along one curve instead of jumping between curves. `Fit`: switch fits at the default run and watch `Fit optimum here` move from 1.38B on 65B tokens to 2.02B on 44.3B tokens. `N from dimensions`: the defaults, 32 layers of width 4,096, give 6.44B. Double `Width d` and N becomes 25.8B, fourfold; double `Layers L` instead and it becomes 12.9B, twofold. Under `Free`, every slider move changes the budget. Under `Hold compute`, the only question left is the split, which is what compute-optimal means. The two fits agree on the shape and disagree on where the minimum sits, most sharply at large budgets. N follows the square of the width and only the first power of the layer count, so a wider model grows much faster than a deeper one. In this lab: nothing is trained. Every number is the published formula evaluated in closed form; the sliders reach 1T parameters and 30T tokens, far past the runs either fit was measured on (up to about 16B parameters and 500B tokens). In general: C = 6ND ignores attention FLOPs, which matter at long context, and real runs lose efficiency to communication and restarts, so the FLOPs actually paid are higher than 6ND. In this lab: `N from dimensions` leaves out embeddings, biases, norm scales and any other MLP shape, so it lands a few percent under a real model's total: 4% under LLaMA's published 6.7B shape and 1% under its 65.2B shape. It is a calculator, not a fit. In general: fits differ on what N counts. Kaplan et al. fitted non-embedding parameters and Hoffmann et al. total parameters, and Pearce and Song (2024) attribute much of the gap between the two fits to that choice. Both fits in this lab are of Hoffmann et al.'s parametric form.

documents.subtitle: IsoFLOP curves · Scaling laws

Every curve is U-shaped, and its lowest point is the compute-optimal size for that budget. The thick curve is your own budget. The x-axis is parameters N on a log scale from 100M to 1T; the y-axis is predicted loss in nats per token. Thin curves are budgets from 10¹⁹ to 10²⁵ FLOPs, labelled where they leave the plot. A small dot at the bottom of each thin curve, joined by the dashed compute-optimal frontier. The dotted line joins the points that spend each budget at 20 tokens per parameter. Your run is the filled circle on the thick curve. On that curve the diamond is the fit's optimum and the hollow square is the 20:1 split. Two crosses mark Chinchilla (70B on 1.4T tokens) and Gopher (280B on 300B tokens) at the loss this fit predicts for them. Readouts: `Predicted loss`, `Compute C = 6ND`, `Tokens per parameter`, and `Gap to optimum`, the loss above the diamond at the same compute. The legend repeats each marker's size, tokens and loss as text. Loss is `L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β` with N and D as raw counts. `Hoffmann 2022` uses E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, α = 0.34, β = 0.28 (eq. 10 of the paper). `Epoch 2024 refit` uses E = 1.8172, A = 482.01, B = 2085.43, α = 0.3478, β = 0.3658. An isoFLOP curve evaluates L(N, C/6N) across N. Its minimum has the closed form above, and the frontier is that minimum traced across budgets. Chinchilla and Gopher used almost the same compute (5.9 and 5.0 × 10²³ FLOPs). Under the printed fit Chinchilla scores 1.937 and Gopher 1.993: the smaller model trained on more tokens wins at equal cost. Drag `Parameters` with `Training tokens` fixed: the dot changes curve because compute changes. Set `Budget` to `Hold compute` and drag `Parameters` until `Gap to optimum` reads 0.000; the dot is then on the diamond. Switch `Fit` and watch the diamond, the frontier and the gap move while the square stays on the same N. The bottoms are flat. At the default budget the 20:1 square sits only 0.006 above the diamond although it uses a 54% larger model. Getting the ratio roughly right matters; getting it exactly right barely does. Under `Hoffmann 2022` the diamond drifts right of the square as compute grows: at Chinchilla's budget the printed fit prefers 32B parameters on 3.0T tokens (93 per parameter). Under `Epoch 2024 refit` the two nearly coincide, near 20 per parameter. Loss never reaches the floor: even at 1T parameters and 30T tokens the printed fit predicts 1.793 against E = 1.69. In this lab: the curves are a formula, not measurements, and the Chinchilla and Gopher crosses are what the fit predicts for their sizes, not their reported losses. Loss is in the fit's own units (nats per token on the MassiveText data and tokenizer), so it does not transfer to another model's loss. In general: Besiroglu et al. 2024 found the printed constants inconsistent with the paper's other two estimation methods and refitted them. Rounding alone matters: their table lists Hoffmann's estimates to more digits (α = 0.3392, β = 0.2849), which put the optimum at Chinchilla's budget near 40B rather than 32B. Fits also shift with architecture, data mix and learning-rate schedule.
documents.title: Loss against model size at fixed compute

documents.subtitle: Loss breakdown · Scaling laws
documents.body: Which term is holding the loss up The same formula split into its parts: the floor E, the size term A/N^α and the data term B/D^β. The bars compare your run with the optimum at the same compute, and the readouts say how much each resource would buy if you doubled it. A worked line: the formula, your N and D in scientific notation, then the evaluated terms, with the size term in the forward colour, the data term in the gradient colour, and the total. Two bars, `Your run` and `Optimum, same C`, showing loss above the floor. The solid segment is the size term and the hatched segment is the data term; each segment prints its value and the row ends with their sum. `Doubling N lowers L by` and `Doubling D lowers L by`, with a sentence naming which one is larger. Doubling N multiplies the size term by 2^−α, so it lowers L by (A/N^α)·(1 − 2^−α). Doubling D lowers L by (B/D^β)·(1 − 2^−β). Either doubling doubles C. At the optimum the marginal returns per log step match: α·(A/N^α) = β·(B/D^β). Because α and β differ, the two terms are not equal there; under the printed fit the size term is β/α ≈ 0.82 times the data term. At the default run (3.2B on 28B tokens) doubling tokens buys 0.086 and doubling parameters 0.050, so the next compute should go to data. Raise `Training tokens` until the two doubling readouts meet; `Gap to optimum` on the isoFLOP card falls toward zero at the same time. The bottleneck moves rather than disappearing. Push one slider far enough and the other term becomes the one worth buying. Both terms shrink slowly. With β = 0.28, ten times more tokens divides the data term by only 10^0.28 ≈ 1.9. In this lab: the terms come from a formula fitted to one family of runs. The split between size term and data term is only as trustworthy as that fit. In general: real models are not described by two knobs alone. Data quality, repetition, architecture and schedule all move the terms, and a lower loss does not guarantee better scores on a specific task.
documents.title: Which term is holding the loss up

documents.subtitle: Frontier power law · Scaling laws
documents.body: A straight line once the floor is removed Along the compute-optimal frontier, loss minus the floor E falls as a pure power of compute. On log-log axes that is a straight line, which is what lets labs extrapolate from small runs to large ones. The x-axis is training compute from 10¹⁸ to 10²⁶ FLOPs; the y-axis is L − E. Both are logarithmic. The dashed frontier is straight. The dotted 20:1 line nearly overlaps it. Your run is the dot, with a short dashed drop to the frontier at the same compute. `Slope` and `10× compute keeps`, which is 10 to the power of the slope, written as the share of reducible loss that survives a tenfold budget. At the optimum both reducible terms scale as C^(−αβ/(α+β)), so L*(C) − E is an exact power law. The slope is −0.154 under the printed fit and −0.178 under the refit. A slope of −0.154 means each tenfold increase in compute keeps 70% of the reducible loss; it takes about 90 times the compute to halve it. Drag either slider: the dot moves right with compute and sits above the line by your `Gap to optimum`. Switch `Fit` to see the slope and the floor change together. Straight on log-log axes means steady, predictable and slow returns. There is no point on the line where improvement accelerates. Loss itself, with the floor left in, would bend toward E and look like diminishing returns. The straight line only appears after subtracting E. In this lab: the line is exact because it is derived from the formula. Real frontiers are fitted to a few dozen runs and carry error bars that widen with every decade of extrapolation. In general: a smooth loss line can sit under a benchmark that jumps, because a thresholded metric such as exact match turns steady gains into sudden-looking ones. Loss is not capability.
documents.title: A straight line once the floor is removed

documents.subtitle: Carry one small model through adapting, aligning, compressing and serving, and let a release gate decide whether it ships.
documents.body: Carry one small model through adapting, aligning, compressing and serving, and let a release gate decide whether it ships. Trace one model through adapt, align, compress and serve, and name what each stage costs Gate a release on held-out loss for the target task and for a control task, and explain what a six-item benchmark cannot settle Fit the artifact you would ship to a memory and concurrency budget before calling it ready

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Ship it
documents.body: In Stage by stage, compare Recipe-text loss and Harbor-text loss from Base model to After adapting, then to As shipped.
documents.title: Run the pipeline

documents.subtitle: Step 2 · Ship it
documents.body: In Eval gate, read which of the two checks fails and by how many nats, then compare it with the benchmark line underneath.
documents.title: Read the gate

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Ship it
documents.body: Raise Replay sentences from none, one step at a time, and watch the Harbor check in Eval gate turn from fail to pass while recipe loss still falls.
documents.title: Fix the regression

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · Ship it
documents.body: In Compress and serve, try each Weight format, then drag Prune toward 90% and watch As shipped drift away from After aligning.
