documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: A pass-or-fail check run on the artifact you would actually ship, with thresholds set before looking at the result. It decides whether a model goes out, so a gate that is loosened until it passes has stopped being a gate.
documents.title: Release gate

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: Held-out text from a task the adaptation was not meant to change. It exists to catch what the target metric cannot see: a model can improve on the new task while quietly getting worse at the old one.
documents.title: Control set

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: Loss of earlier ability when a model is trained on new data alone. Here it shows as harbor-text loss rising after the adapter trains on recipes only.
documents.title: Catastrophic forgetting

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: Mixing some of the old data back into the adaptation data so the update has to keep serving it. It costs training signal for the new task and is the cheapest defence against forgetting.
documents.title: Replay

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: Ability lost to preference training. Here, DPO raises the margin between the chosen and rejected answers while the held-out loss on both texts rises slightly.
documents.title: Alignment tax

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: Mean cross-entropy, in nats per character, on text the model never trained on. It is continuous and uses every character, so it separates close candidates that a handful of benchmark items cannot.
documents.title: Held-out loss

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: A stage that makes something measured worse than the stage before it. The report lists every stage-to-stage rise above 0.02 nats so a loss does not hide inside a net gain.
documents.title: Regression

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: A benchmark difference whose 95% intervals overlap. Six items per benchmark means a real change of several items can still be inside the noise.
documents.title: Not decisive

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: A low-rank update added into the base weights, so the shipped model is one table and costs nothing extra at inference. The adapter cannot be swapped out afterwards.
documents.title: Merged adapter

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: Storing weights in fewer bits per value. It shrinks the file and the memory read per token, at a rounding error that this lab measures through the gate.
documents.title: Quantization

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: Setting the smallest-magnitude weights to zero. Unstructured pruning keeps the file shape, so it saves speed only on hardware that skips zeros.
documents.title: Pruning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Ship it
documents.body: Weights plus the KV cache for every concurrent stream plus runtime overhead, set against accelerator memory. The model fits only if all three do, at the load you actually expect.
documents.title: Serving budget

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Ship it · question 1
documents.body: With Replay sentences at none, the recipe text improves but the gate fails. What does the failing check catch? The adapter made it worse on the harbor text it handled before The base model was trained for too few epochs to be a fair baseline The quantization format dropped too many bits to keep the recipe text The control check compares harbor-text loss with the base model's. Adapting on recipes alone moves the shared table away from harbor text, which is forgetting, and no target-task number would show it. The gate's second check exists for exactly this.
documents.title: With Replay sentences at none, the recipe text improves but the gate fails. What does the failing check catch?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Ship it · question 2
documents.body: Why does the gate read held-out loss rather than the count of benchmark items answered correctly? Loss cannot be gamed, but a benchmark can always be gamed by the tuner Loss is continuous and uses every character; six items jump and overlap A quantized model cannot be scored on a benchmark, so loss is the only option A six-item benchmark can show the same count before and after a real improvement, and its 95% intervals overlap. Loss averages over every held-out character, so it separates close candidates. Loss can still be gamed by tuning on the held-out text, which is why that text is never trained on.
documents.title: Why does the gate read held-out loss rather than the count of benchmark items answered correctly?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Ship it · question 3
documents.body: A recipe passes the gate with 4-bit weights at the starting load. What must you still check before calling it ready to ship? Whether the 4-bit file is smaller than the base model's file at full precision Whether the DPO margin is larger than the number of replay sentences used Whether weights, KV cache and overhead fit in memory at the load you expect Passing the quality gate says nothing about memory. The KV cache grows with users and context, so a model that fits at eight users can fail at sixty-four. The serving budget is a separate pass-or-fail condition on the same release.
documents.title: A recipe passes the gate with 4-bit weights at the starting load. What must you still check before calling it ready to ship?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Ship it · question 4
documents.body: You raise the Prune slider to 90% and the gate fails on both checks. Which explanation matches what the lab shows? Pruning only changes file size, so the gate failed because the control set was small Both losses rise, and recipe loss ends up nearly back at the base model's Pruning deletes the adapter first, which resets the model to the base exactly Magnitude pruning zeroes the smallest weights without regard to which text they serve. At 90% both losses rise, and the recipe gain nearly disappears. Pruning acts on the merged table, so it does not remove the adapter as a unit.
documents.title: You raise the Prune slider to 90% and the gate fails on both checks. Which explanation matches what the lab shows?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ship it
documents.body: This module is the last stop on the training path, where everything the earlier labs taught comes together in one place. Each earlier lab studied one step on its own, such as teaching a model a new job or squeezing it into a smaller file. Here you carry one small model through all of those steps in a row. At the end you make a single decision about it: is it ready to go out, or should it wait? Releasing a finished model so that people can use it is called shipping it, which is where the module gets its name. The steps always come in the same order, and each one changes the model in its own way. First the model learns to write one kind of text, which becomes its old job, and next it learns a second kind of text, its new job. Then it is tuned toward the kind of answers people prefer, and after that it is squeezed into a smaller form. Last of all, you check whether a machine has enough memory to run it for many people at the same time. The catch is that any step can have a price, and some of those prices hide in places where nobody is looking. A step studied on its own can look almost free, but when you chain the steps together, their costs add up. This lab turns each of those costs into a number that you can read and compare. Where you have met it This app can download a program called llama.cpp and use it to run a small model on your own computer as its guide. In this lab you will pick a format for storing the model’s numbers, with names such as Q4_K_M. These are formats that llama.cpp uses to fit a model into a smaller file. Every other step in this lab also has a full-size version that people use on real models, and the last section of this lesson names those tools. Real releases make the same ship-or-wait decision that you make here, but with much bigger tests and more care afterwards. They test with thousands of questions across many topics, give the new model to a small share of users first, and keep watching the numbers after launch. Why it matters Without a careful check at the end, a change that helps a model with its new job can quietly hurt it at its old one. Nobody notices, because nobody tested the old job again. The starting settings in this lab make exactly that kind of change, and here it is the gate’s check on the old job that catches it. A model can also pass every quality test and still run out of memory on its first busy day. So a release decision has to check both quality and memory, and it has to check the version that will actually go out. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these ideas in your own words: how one model, once it has had its first training, moves through four more stages, called adapting, aligning, compressing and serving, and what each of those stages costs it; how to decide on a release using scores on text the model never trained on, for both its new job and an old job you meant to keep; why a quiz with only six questions cannot settle a close call between two versions of a model; why the exact version you would release has to fit in a machine’s memory, with as many people using it as you expect, before you can call it ready. What the lab shows The lab really trains a tiny model while you watch, and it trains the whole thing again from the start whenever you move a setting. Every quality score you see is measured on that tiny model. Its texts, its pairs of better and worse answers, and its quiz questions are fixed, so the same settings always give exactly the same numbers. The lab lays all of this out across five cards: Training recipe holds the settings for the first three stages, which train the model and then adapt and tune it. Stage by stage shows the model’s scores after each stage, so you can see what every step did to it. Eval gate runs two pass-or-fail checks on the finished model, with pass marks that you can move yourself. Compress and serve shrinks the model and then works out whether it fits in a machine’s memory. Release report gives the final answer, ship or hold, along with the reasons behind it. The memory check works differently from everything else, because it is arithmetic about an imagined model of about 8 billion numbers. That imagined model runs on one imagined machine, so none of the memory figures come from real hardware.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ship it
documents.body: A picture to hold on to Picture a small studio getting ready to release an update to a game that people already play. The update adds a new level, gets polished using players’ votes on which of two versions they like better, and is shrunk so the download takes less space. Before it goes out, the team works through a checklist that was written in advance. The new level has to be clearly better, the old levels must still play as well as before, and the servers must cope with the crowd on launch day. If any one item fails, the update waits, however good the rest of it looks. This lab follows the same plan with a model, and each part of the update has a match: the old levels are the model’s first job, which is writing harbor weather notes; the new level is the second job you want to add, which is writing recipe steps; the polish is the preference step, and the smaller download is the compression step; launch day is serving many people at once, and the checklist is the release gate. The picture stops matching in one important way, because in a game, programmers change the code on purpose and can read exactly what they changed. Training nudges many of a model’s numbers at once, and nobody chooses any single number, so the only way to find out what got worse is to measure it. A broken level is also usually plainly broken, while a model slips by degrees, which is why the gate uses scores and pass marks instead of a quick play-through. The model: a table of 900 numbers The model is the same kind of tiny model as in the Train one from scratch lab, and its only job is to guess the next character. Here a character means a letter, a space or a full stop, and the model works with 30 of them in all. Those are the 26 letters, the space, the full stop and two special marks that never appear in its text. For each character, the model keeps a row of 30 scores, one for every character that might come next, and turns that row into chances that add up to 100%. That gives 30 rows of 30 scores, or 900 numbers in all. The numbers a model learns are called its weights, so this is the 900-weight table that the lab keeps mentioning. Because each row belongs to one character, the model only ever looks at the single character just before the one it is guessing. The lab calls this tiny model the toy, which is why some of its readouts begin with the word Toy. After its first training, for example, the row for t makes h by far the likeliest next character, because the word “the” turns up in every sentence of both texts. That one row serves both texts at once, which will matter a great deal later on. Two jobs: harbor text and recipe text The lab uses two short texts with eight sentences each, and the model learns them one after the other. The first is harbor weather notes, such as “the morning fog settles over the harbor and the air feels cool.” The second is recipe steps, such as “warm the pan over medium heat and add a spoon of oil.” Because the model learns harbor text first, that is its old job, and recipe text is the new job you want to add. The last two sentences of each text are kept away from every stage of training, and text kept back like this is called held-out text. For recipes, the held-out text is “drain the pasta and toss it with the warm sauce. finish the dish with fresh basil and a little cheese.” The lab writes all of its text in lowercase, which is why “finish” has no capital letter. Testing on sentences the model trained on would reward it for repeating them, while held-out text shows how it does on writing it never trained on. Scoring the model: held-out loss To score the model, the lab walks through a held-out sentence one character at a time and looks at each of the model’s guesses. At each step it checks the chance the model gave to the character that really came next. A big chance means little surprise and a small chance means a lot, and the average surprise over every character is the model’s loss. So a lower loss is better, because it means the model was less surprised by real text. The unit of surprise is called the nat, which is why the lab reports loss in nats per character. You will not need the formula, only one rule of thumb: every time the chance given to the right character halves, the surprise goes up by about 0.69 nats. That gives a few landmarks to read the numbers by: a model that was always certain and always right would score exactly 0; a model that gave the right character a 1-in-8 chance every time would score about 2.08. Going from a sure thing to 1 in 8 takes three halvings, and 3 × 0.69 is about 2.08; a blind guess, which gives all 30 characters the same 1-in-30 chance, scores 3.401. Small changes in loss read almost like percentages. When the loss drops by 0.03, the model is giving the right characters roughly 3% more chance on average. When it rises by 0.10, it is giving them roughly 10% less. At the start, the base model scores 2.098 on held-out harbor text, which is about as surprised as a steady 1-in-8 guess. On held-out recipe text it scores 2.540, nearer a 1-in-13 guess, because it has never trained on a single recipe. Loss measured on held-out text like this is called held-out loss, and both of the gate’s quality checks run on it. The five stages The lab runs one model through five stages. Stage 1 builds the starting model, and the four stages after it are the ones whose costs this lesson tracks. The Stage by stage table has a row for the model after each of the first four stages. The fifth, serving, is worked out on the Compress and serve card instead. The Training recipe card holds the settings for the first three stages, and the Compress and serve card holds the rest. Stage 1: pretrain The empty table trains on the six harbor training sentences, and the result is the row called Base model. Base training epochs sets how many times it reads through those sentences, where one full pass through them is called an epoch. Stage 2: adapt The model then learns recipe text through a small add-on called an adapter. It uses a method called LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, which the LoRA & adapters lab covers. Rather than retrain all 900 numbers freely, the adapter builds a correction to the table out of a few simple patterns, which keeps the add-on small. Each pattern is one list of 30 numbers, one for each row, and another list of 30, one for each column. Every cell of the pattern is the number for its row times the number for its column. LoRA rank sets how many patterns get added together, from 1 to 12. At rank 4 the adapter learns 4 × 60 = 240 numbers instead of 900, so it can only change the table in a limited, regular way. In a big model, that saving is what makes adapters cheap to train and store. Adapter epochs sets how long the adapter trains, while Replay sentences can mix some harbor sentences back in, which the part called Replay, under Why it’s here, explains. When training ends, the correction is added into the table for good, which makes it a merged adapter and gives the row called After adapting. Merging means the shipped model is still one table and costs nothing extra to run, but the adapter can no longer be lifted off or swapped for another. Stage 3: align Next the model is tuned toward answers people prefer, using a method called DPO, which is short for direct preference optimization. DPO works from three pairs, and each pair gives two endings for the same opening, one preferred and one rejected. For the opening “stir the”, for example, the preferred ending is “onions until they turn soft.” and the rejected one is “onions onions onions onions.” DPO nudges the table so that each preferred ending gains on its rejected partner, which means the gap between how likely the two endings are grows wider. To see how far each ending has moved, DPO compares the model with a frozen copy, a saved copy of the model from just before this stage that never changes. DPO steps sets how long this runs, with 0 switching it off, and the result is the row called After aligning. DPO beta sets how big a gap counts as good enough. Once training has run long enough, a higher beta settles for a smaller gap and keeps the model nearer the frozen copy. A lower beta pushes the pairs further apart and lets the model wander further, which the Preference optimization in practice lab explores. Preference pairs ordered, on the Stage by stage card, gives the share of pairs where the preferred ending gained on the rejected one, compared with the frozen copy. Reward margin shows how far ahead the preferred endings have pulled on average. DPO beta scales that readout too, so compare it only between runs that use the same beta. Stage 4: compress The computer stores each weight as a string of bits, where a bit is a single 0 or 1, and 8 bits make one byte. Storing each weight in fewer bits is called quantization, and the Weight format control picks how many bits each weight gets. With 16 bits a number can be stored very precisely, but 4 bits can only be set in 16 different ways. So in a 4-bit format, every weight has to be rounded to the nearest value the format allows, which loses a little detail. The formats run from F16, which uses 16 bits per weight, down to Q4_0, and the lab starts at Q4_K_M. Apart from F16, each format uses roughly the number of bits after its Q, plus a little extra for bookkeeping. Pruning is a second kind of squeezing, which sets the smallest weights, the ones closest to zero, to exactly zero. The Prune slider picks what share of all the weights to remove, anywhere from 0% up to 90%. The hope is that a table full of zeros can be stored in less space or run faster, on software and chips built to skip over the zeros. In this lab it does not make the file any smaller, as Where it breaks explains, so here you only see what it costs. The result of both steps is the row called As shipped, which is the version that would actually go out. That finished version, after every stage has changed it, is called the artifact, and the first line of the Release report describes it. At the start it reads Q4_K_M, not pruned, merged adapter of rank 4, which names its format, its pruning and its adapter. Stage 5: serve The last stage asks whether the model fits on a machine at the load you expect, and here the lab switches to an imagined model. A table of 900 numbers fits anywhere, so the card imagines a model of about 8 billion weights instead, which the lab calls 8B-class. It runs on one accelerator, a chip built to run models quickly, which has 24 GiB of memory. A GiB, short for gibibyte, is a little over a billion bytes, so 24 GiB is room for about 26 billion bytes. A full-size model writes one small piece of text at a time, called a token, which is often a short word or part of a longer one. For each token it saves notes about the text so far, so it does not have to redo that work every time it writes a new token. A store of saved work like this is called a cache. These notes are the KV cache, named after the two kinds of note it keeps, which are known as keys and values. Every conversation needs its own notes, and the lab calls each conversation it serves a stream. So the cache grows with Concurrent users, the number of people served at once, and with Context length, the number of tokens each conversation can hold. The weights, every stream’s notes and 1 GiB of working space all have to fit inside the machine’s 24 GiB. Adding those three up and checking the total against the machine’s memory is called the serving budget. The release gate Once the stages are done, the Eval gate card runs two pass-or-fail checks, always on the As shipped row and never on an earlier one: Gains on the recipe text passes only if recipe loss has fallen below the base model’s by at least Required recipe-loss gain, which starts at 0.030 nats. Keeps the harbor text passes only if harbor loss has not risen above the base model’s by more than Allowed harbor-loss rise, which starts at 0.100 nats. The Release report then adds the serving budget as a third condition, so the verdict depends on quality and memory together. Its badge reads Verdict: ship only when both checks pass and the budget fits, and in every other case it reads Verdict: hold. A set of checks like this, with pass marks fixed before the run and applied to the version you would actually release, is called a release gate.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ship it
documents.body: Chaining the steps together creates problems that no single lab could show, and each part of the release gate is there to catch one of them. Getting better at one job can mean getting worse at another Picture a friend on a soccer team who spends a whole month practising nothing but penalty kicks. Her penalties get sharp, but at the first real match her passing has gone rusty, and nobody saw it coming because nobody watched her pass all month. The adapter in Stage 2 can do something similar, because with Replay sentences at none it trains on recipe sentences only. Yet harbor text and recipe text lean on the very same table, since both use letter pairs such as t followed by h. When training bends those shared numbers toward recipes, the harbor guesses move with them, and at the starting settings harbor loss rises by 0.150 nats during adapting. Losing an old skill when a model trains on new data alone is called catastrophic forgetting. The name sounds dramatic, but what matters is whether the old skill got worse and by how much, and the lab shows you that number. The soccer story stops matching in one way, because her passing fades from lack of use. The model’s harbor guesses, by contrast, are pushed away by the very same changes that teach it recipes. Replay: practising the old job alongside the new one In the soccer story, the fix would be to mix a few passing drills into every practice session. The model’s version is called replay, which mixes some of the old harbor sentences back into the adapter’s training. Every change then has to keep working for harbor text as well as recipe text, and Replay sentences sets how many of the six harbor training sentences join in. In general, replay has a price, because one small update now has to serve two texts at once. The push that training gives toward the new job is called the training signal. It is now shared with the old job, so the update cannot bend as far toward the new one. In bigger jobs that cost is real, and it is worth watching for. In this lab, though, you will not see it. With four replayed sentences, recipe loss ends at 2.367, lower than the 2.497 it reaches with no replay at all. One likely reason is that the adapter trains for a set number of epochs, so adding harbor sentences also gives it more practice steps in total. Here, replay is the cheapest defence against forgetting, and it leaves the recipe text better off. You only see what you measure: the control set If the gate checked recipe text alone, the starting model would pass, because its recipe loss falls by more than the bar. The damage to harbor text would go out with the release, and nobody would find out until people started using it. So the gate also reads a control set, which is held-out text from a job that the adapting was not meant to change. Here the control set is the two held-out harbor sentences, and the check called Keeps the harbor text reads them. In the game picture, this is the item on the checklist that says to re-test the old levels before the update goes out. Test the version you ship, not the one you trained Compression comes after training, and it changes the numbers, so a gate that read the After aligning row would be grading a model that never goes out. With four replayed sentences and Prune at 90%, for example, After aligning would pass both checks with room to spare, while As shipped fails both. That is why the gate always reads the last row, the artifact itself, and never the model as it left training. A six-question quiz cannot settle a close call The lab also runs a short quiz, called a benchmark, with six questions for each of the two texts. Each question gives the start of a sentence and two possible next words, one right and one wrong, where the wrong one is still a normal English word. The model passes a question if it scores the right word higher than the wrong one. One recipe question, for example, asks whether “season the soup with salt and a pinch of” should go on with “pepper” or with “rain”. The Recipe items and Harbor items columns count how many of the six questions the model passes at each stage. Picture a friend who makes 1 of 6 free throws on Monday and 4 of 6 on Tuesday. She may really have improved overnight, or Monday may have been an unlucky day, and six shots cannot tell you which. The quiz has the same weakness, so the lab puts a range around each count, called a 95% interval. If you built ranges this way for many different tests, about 95 in every 100 of them would contain the model’s true pass rate. That true pass rate is the share it would get right on a huge number of similar questions, which is what you really want to know. For 1 of 6 the range runs from 3% to 56%, while for 4 of 6 it runs from 30% to 90%. Both ranges include everything from 30% to 56%, so they overlap. When two ranges overlap, the quiz cannot say whether the model really changed, so the lab calls the difference not decisive. Held-out loss suffers much less from that problem, because it scores every character, which comes to about a hundred in each held-out text. It can also move by a thousandth of a nat at a time, instead of jumping a whole question. That is why both gate checks read held-out loss, while the quiz appears beside them only as extra evidence. Held-out loss is still a small test, though, since it reads only two sentences per text. A gap of a few hundredths of a nat can be luck too, as Where it breaks explains. A model that does not fit is not ready Passing on quality says nothing about memory, and in the game picture, a great update that crashes the servers on launch day has still failed. The model’s weights take the same space however many people use it, but every conversation adds its own notes, and longer conversations add more. A release has to fit at the load you actually expect, which is why the Release report adds the serving budget to the two quality checks. Pass marks have to come first Picture a class where the pass mark is chosen after the tests are marked, and it keeps sliding down until everyone passes. Everyone does pass, but the result now tells you nothing about who actually learned the material. A gate works the same way, because if you loosen the pass marks after seeing the results, any model can pass. A real release gate writes its marks down before the run and then leaves them alone, whatever the results turn out to be.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ship it
documents.body: The lab’s five steps walk you through one full release, and each part below matches one of them. Begin at the starting settings, and read each card in turn before you move anything. Run the pipeline Read Stage by stage from the top row down, comparing the recipe and harbor columns at each step. Going from Base model to After adapting, recipe loss improves from 2.540 to 2.461, which the table marks −0.079 better. Harbor loss gets worse, from 2.098 to 2.248, marked +0.150 worse, and that rise is catastrophic forgetting caught in the act. The next row, After aligning, nudges both losses up a little, by 0.035 on recipe text and 0.042 on harbor text. As shipped then barely moves, because rounding the weights to Q4_K_M costs almost nothing. Under the table, Recipe loss, base to shipped reads −0.043 and Harbor loss, base to shipped reads +0.194. The box under those numbers lists every rise bigger than 0.02 nats from one stage to the next, and each one is called a regression. A regression is any stage that made a loss more than 0.02 nats worse than it was after the stage before, even if the model ends up better overall. Read the gate Open Eval gate, where the badge reads Gate: fail and the two checks sit underneath it. Gains on the recipe text passes, because recipe loss fell by 0.043 against a bar of 0.030. Keeps the harbor text fails, because the shipped model is 0.194 worse than the base on harbor text, while 0.100 is the most allowed, so the release is on hold. Now read the benchmark line under the two checks, which gives the quiz results for the same comparison. The recipe count went from 1 to 4 correct and the harbor count fell from 5 to 1, yet both are marked “overlapping, so not decisive”. Even a drop from 5 correct to 1 cannot be called decisive with only six questions, while the loss check shows a 0.194 rise, nearly twice the allowance. Fix the regression Try this: raise Replay sentences one step at a time, starting from none, and watch Keeps the harbor text in Eval gate. At 1 of 6 harbor sentences it already passes, because harbor loss now rises by only 0.057, which is under the 0.100 limit. The badge turns to Gate: pass, and since the budget already fits, the Release report now reads Verdict: ship. Keep going until the slider reads 4 of 6 harbor sentences, and watch both losses as you go. Harbor loss now ends at 2.086, a hair better than the base model’s 2.098, so the forgetting is gone. Recipe loss ends at 2.367, so the recipe text actually gained more with replay than it did without it. Compress Leave Replay sentences at 4, then step Weight format through every option from F16 down to Q4_0. While you do, watch Recipe loss, as shipped and Harbor loss, as shipped in the first row of numbers on Compress and serve. Across all five formats, neither one moves by as much as 0.02 nats, while Toy bits per weight falls from 16.04 to about 5. Then set Weight format back to Q4_K_M, the starting format, and drag Prune to 50%. Recipe loss, as shipped moves only from 2.367 to 2.372, so cutting half the weights costs almost nothing here, and the model still ships. Now drag Prune all the way to 90%, and recipe loss jumps back to 2.530, nearly the base model’s 2.540. Almost all of the recipe training is undone, and the gate fails on both of its checks. Budget and decide Set Prune back to 0%, and look at the second row of numbers on Compress and serve. At the starting load of 8 users and 4,096 tokens, 8B-class weights reads 4.58 GiB and KV cache for all streams reads 4.00 GiB. Add the 1 GiB of working space and you get 9.58 GiB, and the box below confirms that this fits in 24 GiB with 14.42 GiB to spare. Now set Concurrent users to 64 and Context length to 32,768, then read the Release report. The model still passes both quality checks, but the verdict is hold, because the budget has grown to 261.58 GiB, more than ten times the machine’s memory. Last, bring the two sliders down until the budget fits again, and read the verdict and its reasons once more. More comparisons worth running With Replay sentences at none, slide Adapter epochs from 8 up to 40 and watch the harbor column. Harbor loss ends worse than the base at every setting. Past about 25 epochs, recipe loss also ends worse than the base at most settings, including 40, and it jumps up and down from one setting to the next. Long training on six recipe sentences pushes the shared table hard, and the lab shows the result without pinning down the exact cause. Repeat with replay at 4, and harbor never rises more than about 0.03 above the base. Recipe loss stays below the base at every setting, by more than 0.1 nats from 14 epochs on. Set DPO steps to 0 to switch the preference step off, and After aligning becomes identical to After adapting. The cost of aligning vanishes, and Preference pairs ordered reads DPO off, because no preference training ran. With replay at 4, set LoRA rank to 1, which gives the adapter only one pattern to build its correction from. The adapter is now too weak to move the model much, so the recipe check fails, which is a different kind of failure from forgetting.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ship it
documents.body: Replay buys back the old job: at the starting settings, the shipped model is 0.194 worse on harbor text and 0.043 better on recipe text. With four replayed sentences it is 0.173 better on recipe and no worse on harbor, so in this lab replay helped both texts. Aligning has a price: with four replayed sentences, going from After adapting to After aligning raises recipe loss by 0.030 and harbor loss by 0.040. Meanwhile Preference pairs ordered reads 100%, so in all three pairs the preferred ending has gained on the rejected one. Ability lost to preference training like this is called the alignment tax, and it shows up here because DPO edits the same 900 numbers both held-out texts rely on. DPO only cares about the gap inside each pair, not about making real recipe text likelier. The rejected endings, such as “onions onions onions onions.”, are built from everyday letter pairs, so pushing them down can make ordinary text a little less likely too. The report keeps every cost on the record: those two rises are regressions, and the Release report lists them under Cost of getting here even though the model ships. The recipe text still improved overall, so listing each stage stops a loss from hiding inside an overall gain. The quiz barely notices: with four replayed sentences, the recipe quiz reads 1 of 6 before and 1 of 6 after, though recipe loss fell by 0.173. The ranges overlap, so the quiz is not decisive, while held-out loss shows a clear gain because it counts every character. Shrinking is nearly free, but pruning is not: these numbers use four replayed sentences. The shipped model is 0.022 worse on recipe text than After aligning at 50% pruning, and 0.180 worse at 90%. Rounding to Q4_K_M causes 0.017 of that first rise on its own, so pruning half the weights adds only about 0.005. Pruning 90% adds about 0.163, so removing a little under twice as much does about thirty times the damage. The harm grows much faster than the amount removed. Memory fails in a different place: at the heaviest load the sliders allow, the imagined 8B-class budget is 261.58 GiB at Q4_K_M and 271.96 GiB at F16. Switching formats saves only about 10 GiB, because the notes alone take 256 GiB, so the KV cache, not the weights, is what runs out of room. A common mix-up: “The recipe count went from 1 to 4, so the model clearly got better at recipes.” At the starting settings the count did jump from 1 to 4, while recipe loss fell by only 0.043. With four replayed sentences the count stayed at 1, while recipe loss fell about four times as far. Six questions move in jumps that can point the wrong way, which is exactly what “not decisive” warns you about. Working out the memory At 4,096 tokens, each conversation’s notes take half a GiB, which is why 8 users need 4.00 GiB of cache. To find Streams that fit, start from the 24 GiB and subtract the 4.58 GiB of weights and the 1 GiB of working space. Then divide the 18.42 GiB that is left by half a GiB per conversation, which gives 36.84. A conversation cannot be split into pieces, so the lab rounds down and shows 36. Raising Context length to 32,768 makes each conversation eight times as long, so its notes grow eight times bigger, to 4 GiB each. With 64 users that comes to 64 × 4 = 256 GiB of notes, before the weights are even counted. Adding users also slows each person down, because every step of writing has to read through more notes. You can see this in Per user, the number of tokens each person gets per second, which reads 43.4 tok/s at the starting load. The bill, stage by stage Putting it all together, here is what each stage of the journey costs the model in this lab: Adapting can cost the old job through forgetting, unless replay mixes some of the old text back in. Replay asks one update to serve both texts. In general this costs some of the training signal for the new job, though in this lab four replayed sentences left the recipe text better off. Aligning costs a little loss on both texts at once, which is the alignment tax. Quantizing costs almost nothing here, while pruning costs more and more the harder you push it. Serving costs memory, mostly in notes that grow with every user and every token of context.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ship it
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies A tiny model makes the costs look bigger: the model has only 900 weights, and the adapter and the preference step both edit that one table. So forgetting and the alignment tax are bigger here than they would be in a large model. The tests are tiny: twelve quiz questions and two held-out sentences per text cannot tell close models apart. The toy also looks back only one character, so for a quiz word it sees only the space in front and the word’s own letters. The start of the sentence, which is what a reader would use to choose, barely matters to it at all. The pass marks are sliders: that lets you do exactly what the pass-mark story warned against, so try it once to see. Drag Allowed harbor-loss rise to the top at the starting settings, and the forgetful model ships, while a real gate fixes its marks before the run. The memory numbers are arithmetic, not measurements: the quality numbers come from the toy, while the budget describes an imagined 8B-class model that is not in the lab. That arithmetic treats every conversation’s notes as full length from the start and adds a flat 1 GiB of working space. It also works out speed only from how fast memory can be read. Pruning saves nothing here: pruning that removes weights wherever they sit, called unstructured pruning, keeps the table the same size. So in this lab Prune changes neither Toy file at this format, the toy’s file size, nor the memory budget, and it only adds damage. The toy is not a chatbot model: it reads one character at a time rather than words or pieces of words, and it looks back only one character. It was also never trained to follow instructions, and eight sentences per text stand in for what would really be a huge collection of training data. Nothing in this lab is measured on a real model or on real hardware, even where the numbers look precise. Where the real mechanism fails Passing is evidence, not proof: a gate shows that a model cleared the tests you chose, and it cannot speak for the tests you never ran. Real tests are far bigger: releases of real models use thousands of test questions across many topics, and they check that those questions never slipped into the training data. They also test the whole product, such as search, tools and safety, and re-run a set of old cases after every change. A test can be worn out: if you keep adjusting a model until the same held-out text scores well, the model ends up tuned to that one text. That is called overfitting, and a gate tuned against its own test text can be overfit like any other test. Compression depends on the model: how much quality a format loses depends on the model and on the sample text used to tune the rounding. Unstructured pruning saves time only on hardware that can skip over the zeros it leaves behind. Real speed depends on more than memory: the software that does the math, how requests are grouped and how chips are linked all matter, and this arithmetic skips them. People make the final call: real release decisions weigh quality, safety, cost, speed and risk, usually with people who answer for the choice. A verdict from a script like this one is only one input to that decision. A common mix-up: “It passed the gate, so it is safe to ship.” The gate here is two held-out texts and one imagined machine, which is far too little to vouch for a real release. A pass says nothing about a real model’s safety, its accuracy on real tasks, or how it behaves under real traffic.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Ship it
documents.body: What a real release adds A bigger, fresher test: hundreds to thousands of questions for each skill, kept away from the model, with the uncertainty written down beside every score. Tests for the whole product: these check whether search finds the right passage and whether the answer sticks to what it found. For a model that carries out tasks on its own, called an agent, they check whether it finishes and what each task costs. Safety tests count how often attacks succeed and how often harmless requests get refused by mistake. A careful rollout: a small share of users goes first, with an automatic way back if a watched number moves. The team also keeps a record of which model, data and pass marks produced the release. Watching after launch: people type things nobody tested, and the world changes, so the gate is the start of the evidence, not the end. Behind the numbers The ranges in the benchmark line are Wilson intervals, the same kind the Evaluation lab draws, and they stay sensible even at 0 of 6 or 6 of 6. The weight sizes in the memory check come from the file sizes llama.cpp reports for a real model of this size, and everything built on them is arithmetic. For the imagined model, every token of every conversation needs 128 KiB of notes, where one KiB is 1,024 bytes. The Deployment & serving lab shows step by step where that figure comes from. Where to go next Every piece of this lab has a full-size version that you can download and run on your own computer: Training and adapting: Hugging Face Transformers, with PEFT for LoRA adapters and TRL for preference training such as DPO. Squeezing and running a model on your own computer: llama.cpp, the same engine this app downloads for its guide. Serving many people at once: vLLM, which groups many people’s requests together so they share the work. Testing: EleutherAI’s lm-evaluation-harness for standard tests, plus your own held-out set for the job you care about. Four research papers cover most of what the labs touched, and two of them describe stages in this lab directly: *Attention Is All You Need*, by Vaswani and colleagues in 2017, which introduced the design behind most of today’s chatbots; *LoRA*, by Hu and colleagues in 2021, which describes the adapter method used in Stage 2; *Direct Preference Optimization*, by Rafailov and colleagues in 2023, which describes the preference method used in Stage 3; *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, by Hoffmann and colleagues in 2022, which works out how big a model should be for a given amount of training. A good first project is to repeat this lab’s loop on a small real model of your own choosing. Pick one job, hold out a control set, adapt the model, and write your gate down before you run anything.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Ship it
documents.body: This module carries one model from training to a release decision. A single small model is pretrained, adapted, aligned and compressed in order, and a memory budget for serving is checked at the same weight format. The question is whether this exact artifact should ship. The artifact is the file that would go out, after the training and compression stages have changed it. The module builds on the earlier labs rather than reteaching them. The model is the 900-weight character table from *Train one from scratch*. *LoRA & adapters* supplies the low-rank adapter, *Preference optimization in practice* the DPO (direct preference optimization) step, *Quantization* and *Distillation & pruning* the compression, *Evaluation* the intervals around a small benchmark, and *Deployment & serving* the memory arithmetic. Where it shows up Release evaluation. A real release is scored on far larger, contamination-checked suites, and on the whole application rather than the model alone. Rollout and monitoring. A release reaches a small share of traffic before everyone else, can be rolled back automatically, and is watched after launch because inputs drift. Production tools. Most stages have a production counterpart you can run on your own machine: Hugging Face Transformers with PEFT for LoRA and TRL for DPO, llama.cpp for GGUF quantization (the engine this app downloads for its guide), vLLM for serving at scale, and EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness for benchmarks. Why it matters Unless the artifact that ships is itself measured, no one can say whether the release is better than the model it started from. A score on the new task cannot detect catastrophic forgetting, the loss of earlier ability when a model is trained only on new data. A six-item benchmark can read the same before and after a real improvement. And a bar chosen after seeing the result can be loosened until a bad model passes. Memory fails separately. The KV cache, the keys and values stored for every token of every conversation being served, grows with each concurrent user and each token of context. A deployment that fits a light load can run out of memory at the load it will actually serve, and then the cache, not the weights, is what overflows. What you will be able to explain How one model changes as it is adapted, aligned and compressed on its way to serving, and what each stage costs. How a release gate reads held-out loss on the target task and on a control task, and what a six-item benchmark cannot settle. Why the artifact you would ship must fit a memory and concurrency budget before it counts as ready. What the lab shows Every training and compression stage runs in the app. Training uses fixed text, harbor and recipe sentences plus three preference pairs, and is deterministic, so the same controls always give the same model. Recipe text is the target task. Harbor text, which the base model learned first and the adapter is not meant to change, is the control. Every loss is read from the last two sentences of each corpus, which no stage trains on. Twelve fixed benchmark items, six per text, are scored alongside the losses. Training recipe sets Base training epochs, LoRA rank, Adapter epochs, Replay sentences, DPO steps, and DPO beta. Stage by stage tabulates both losses, in nats per character, and the benchmark counts from Base model to As shipped. Eval gate applies two thresholds you choose, Required recipe-loss gain and Allowed harbor-loss rise, to the shipped model. In Compress and serve, Weight format sets both how the toy's weights are rounded and how much memory the budget's weights take. Prune zeroes a fraction of the toy's weights only, and the toy's losses are measured again. Concurrent users and Context length size the budget, which is closed-form arithmetic for an imagined 8B-class model on one 24 GiB accelerator. That model is never run, and its per-user speed is computed, not timed. Release report joins gate and budget into Verdict: ship or Verdict: hold. The key experiment: at the defaults the harbor check fails. Raise Replay sentences, which mixes harbor sentences back into the adapter's training data, until the harbor check passes, then drag Prune to 90% and watch both checks fail.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Ship it
documents.body: This lab carries one small model along the path the previous labs taught one piece at a time: pretrain a base table, adapt it with a low-rank adapter, align it with DPO, quantize and prune it, then decide whether it ships. The decision is a release gate: two pass-or-fail checks on held-out loss, plus a memory budget, all read from the artifact that would actually go out. The model is the 900-weight character table from the training labs. Stage 1 trains it on harbor sentences. Stage 2 trains a rank-r adapter on recipe sentences and folds it in as a merged adapter. Stage 3 runs DPO on three preference pairs. Stage 4 quantizes and prunes the result. The last two sentences of each corpus are held out of every stage, and every loss in the lab is read from them.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Ship it
documents.body: Each earlier lab measured one stage in isolation, so each stage looked cheap. Shipping is where the costs add up, and where a gain on the task you cared about can hide a loss somewhere you stopped looking. Adapting for recipes can make the model worse at harbor text; aligning can cost a little of both; compressing can undo the rest. A control set is what makes that visible: held-out text from the task the adaptation was not meant to change. The gate checks the new task and the control together.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Ship it
documents.body: Read Stage by stage at the defaults. The adapter improves recipe text, from 2.540 to 2.461 nats per character, and harbor text gets worse, from 2.098 to 2.248. That second change is catastrophic forgetting: the adapter trained on recipes alone, and the shared table moved. Open Eval gate. The recipe check passes, with a gain of 0.043 against a bar of 0.030. The harbor check fails: the shipped model is 0.194 nats worse than the base against an allowance of 0.100. The verdict is hold. Now raise Replay sentences to 1, then 4. One sentence is enough to pass; four leaves harbor loss at 2.086, slightly better than the base, with recipe loss at 2.367. Then compress, with replay at 4. Step Weight format from F16 to Q4_0 and the losses barely move. Drag Prune to 90% and they jump: recipe loss returns to 2.530, almost the base model's 2.540, and the gate fails on both checks. Finally set Concurrent users to 64 and Context length to 32,768 and read the Release report.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Ship it
documents.body: Replay trades signal for memory. At the defaults the shipped model is 0.194 nats worse on harbor and 0.043 better on recipe. With four replayed sentences it is 0.173 better on recipe and no worse on harbor. Alignment has a price here. Going from After adapting to After aligning raises recipe loss by 0.030 and harbor loss by 0.040 with four replay sentences, while the three preference pairs end up ordered correctly. That is the alignment tax in miniature. It is a regression, and the report lists it even though the model still ships. The benchmark barely sees it. With four replay sentences the recipe benchmark reads 1 of 6 before and after, though recipe loss fell by 0.173. The intervals overlap, so the difference is not decisive. That is why the gate reads held-out loss: it averages over every character. Quantization is nearly free; pruning is not. Against After aligning, 50% pruning raises recipe loss by 0.022 and 90% by 0.180. The harm is not proportional to the amount removed. The budget has a different failure. At 64 users and 32,768 tokens the imagined 8B-class budget is 261.58 GiB at Q4_K_M and 271.96 GiB at F16. The cache, not the weights, overflows.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Ship it
documents.body: In this lab. The model has 900 weights, and adapting and aligning edit the same table, so forgetting and the alignment tax are exaggerated by the architecture. Twelve benchmark items and two held-out sentences per text cannot separate close models. The thresholds are sliders, which lets you loosen the gate until a bad model passes: drag Allowed harbor-loss rise to its maximum and the defaults ship. A real gate fixes its bars before the run. The quality columns come from the toy; the budget is arithmetic about an imagined 8B-class model. No figure is measured on a real model or real hardware. In general. Passing a gate is evidence, not proof. Release evaluation uses thousands of items across several domains, checks for contamination, and covers the application as well as the model: retrieval, tool use, safety, and regression suites that re-run on every change. A gate tuned against its own held-out text can be overfit like any other test set.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Ship it
documents.body: What a real release adds Larger, fresher evaluation. Hundreds to thousands of items per capability, refreshed so the model has not seen them, with the uncertainty reported. Application tests. Context recall and faithfulness for retrieval, task success and cost for agents, attack success and false refusals for safety. A staged rollout. A small share of traffic first, with automatic rollback if a monitored metric moves, and a record of which model, data, and thresholds produced the release. Monitoring after release. Inputs drift and users find prompts you did not test, so the gate is the start of the evidence, not the end. Where to go next The pieces in this lab have production counterparts you can run on your own machine: Training and adaptation: Hugging Face Transformers with PEFT for LoRA and TRL for DPO and other preference methods. Compression and local inference: llama.cpp for GGUF quantization and CPU or GPU inference, the same engine this app downloads for its guide. Serving at scale: vLLM for batching and paged attention. Evaluation: EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness for standard benchmarks, and your own held-out sets for the task you care about. Four papers cover most of the mechanisms the labs touched: Vaswani et al., 2017, *Attention Is All You Need*; Hu et al., 2021, *LoRA*; Rafailov et al., 2023, *Direct Preference Optimization*; and Hoffmann et al., 2022, *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*. A good first project is to repeat this lab's loop on a small real model: pick one task, hold out a control, adapt, and write down the gate before you run it.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Training recipe · Ship it
documents.body: The first three stages, as six controls The knobs for pretraining a base table, adapting it to a second task with a merged low-rank adapter, and aligning it with DPO. Each one changes what the later cards measure. `Base training epochs`, `LoRA rank`, `Adapter epochs`, `Replay sentences`, `DPO steps`, and `DPO beta`, each with its current value beside the label. A note listing which sentences each stage trains on and which two sentences of each corpus are held out. Stage 1 trains the 900-weight character table on six harbor sentences with minibatch SGD (seed 1). Stage 2 trains a rank-`r` adapter on the first six recipe sentences plus the first `k` replayed harbor sentences, then merges it into the table. Stage 3 runs DPO on three preference pairs, with the adapted table as the frozen reference. Every run is deterministic in the controls, so the lab stores controls only and recomputes all four stages whenever one changes. Shared state from a link is clamped to the slider ranges before anything trains. Comparison worth running: with `Replay sentences` at none, raise `Adapter epochs` from 8 to 40. Harbor loss in `Stage by stage` rises at every setting, while recipe loss gains little and ends worse than the base model. Then set replay to four and repeat: harbor loss barely moves and recipe loss falls. `DPO steps` at 0 makes After aligning identical to After adapting, so the cost of alignment is one slider away. Replay and adapter epochs pull in opposite directions: more epochs fit the new task harder, more replay keeps the old one in the update. Rank 1 barely moves the model at all, which fails the gate for a different reason than forgetting does. In this lab: the model is a single table of 900 logits, so adapting and aligning edit the same weights, and a corpus of eight sentences stands in for a dataset. Nothing here is a transformer, a tokenizer, or an instruction-following model. In general: a real pipeline pretrains for weeks on trillions of tokens, adapts on curated data with a held-out split per task, and runs preference training against a reward signal collected from people or a verifier.
documents.title: The first three stages, as six controls

documents.subtitle: Stage by stage · Ship it
documents.body: What each stage did to both texts Held-out loss on the recipe text and the harbor text after each of four stages, the six-item benchmark counts for both, and the preference-pair result from DPO. Changes between stages are written in words, not only signs. A table with a row per stage (Base model, After adapting, After aligning, As shipped) and columns for recipe-text loss, harbor-text loss, and benchmark items answered correctly out of six. Small notes beside each loss: the change from the stage above, labelled `worse` or `better` when it moves by more than 0.02 nats. Four metrics: base-to-shipped change in each loss, the share of preference pairs ordered correctly, and the reward margin. A callout listing every stage-to-stage rise above 0.02 nats, or saying there was none. Loss is mean cross-entropy over the held-out characters, in nats. The two held-out texts are the last two sentences of each corpus, which no stage trains on. The benchmark scores each candidate as its continuation after the context, per transition, and counts an item correct when the right word outscores a wrong but ordinary one. All twelve items are held-out or freshly written phrases, and a test checks that none appears in a training text. `Preference pairs ordered` is the share of the three DPO pairs whose reference-relative reward margin is positive; `Reward margin` is the mean scaled margin. Adapting without replay for 16 epochs or more costs harbor loss more than it gains recipe loss. Aligning then raises both losses a little, which is the alignment tax in this toy. A stage can improve the benchmark count while worsening held-out loss, or the reverse. Six items move in jumps. In this lab: twelve benchmark items and two held-out sentences per text are far too few to separate close models, and a bigram reads each candidate only through its own characters and the space before it, so context barely matters. In general: release evaluation uses thousands of items, several domains, and checks for contamination, because a single pair of held-out texts can be overfit by the person tuning against it.
documents.title: What each stage did to both texts

documents.subtitle: Eval gate · Ship it
documents.body: A bar set in advance, run on the shipped artifact Two checks decided by held-out loss, read on the model as it would ship: the recipe text must improve by at least a set amount, and the harbor text may not get worse by more than a set amount. The benchmark appears beside them as advisory evidence. A `Gate: pass` or `Gate: fail` badge, two sliders for the thresholds, and one line per check with `Pass` or `Fail`, the loss it measured, and the base model's value. A note giving each benchmark's counts before and after, their 95% intervals, and whether the intervals overlap. Target check: `base recipe loss − shipped recipe loss ≥ Required recipe-loss gain`. Control check: `shipped harbor loss − base harbor loss ≤ Allowed harbor-loss rise`. The gate passes only if both do. The intervals are Wilson 95% intervals for the item counts, from the same helper the Evaluation lab uses. They are advisory because six items cannot settle a close call. The gate reads the last stage, after quantizing and pruning, not the model you trained. Comparison worth running: with the default thresholds, find the smallest `Replay sentences` that passes the harbor check, then drag `Allowed harbor-loss rise` to its maximum and notice that a gate loosened until it passes decides nothing. The benchmark counts often fail to move while loss moves by tenths of a nat; that is the case for gating on loss at this scale. Both thresholds are yours, and that is the weakness: nothing stops you setting them after seeing the result. In this lab: the thresholds are sliders so a learner can feel how much the verdict depends on them. A real gate fixes them before the run and keeps them under review. In general: a gate is one layer. Releases also run safety and regression suites for the application, human review for high-stakes changes, and a staged rollout with monitoring.
documents.title: A bar set in advance, run on the shipped artifact

documents.subtitle: Compress and serve · Ship it
documents.body: Shrink the weights, then fit the load Quantize the aligned table to a named format and optionally prune it, which changes the model the gate reads; then size an imagined 8B-class deployment for the format, user count, and context length chosen. A segmented control for `Weight format` (F16, Q8_0, Q5_K_M, Q4_K_M, Q4_0), and sliders for `Prune`, `Concurrent users`, and `Context length`. A first row of metrics from the toy: its file size and bits per weight at that format, and the recipe and harbor loss as shipped, coloured by whether they moved more than 0.02 nats from After aligning. A second row for the imagined deployment: 8B-class weights, KV cache for all streams, streams that fit, and tokens per second per user. A callout stating the headroom or the overshoot against a 24 GiB accelerator. The toy is quantized with the format's block layout (bits, scope, group size) and its error is the rounding to that grid; pruning then zeroes the smallest-magnitude weights, a fraction of all 900. The deployment arithmetic is the serving lab's: weights = parameters × bits per weight ÷ 8, using the published whole-file size for each format; KV cache = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × 2 bytes × context × users; per-user speed = 1 ÷ ((weights + cache) ÷ memory bandwidth) for a batched step. Comparison worth running: at a passing recipe, step `Weight format` from F16 to Q4_0 and watch the toy's losses barely move, then drag `Prune` to 90% and watch them jump. Set `Concurrent users` to 64 and `Context length` to 32,768 and switch between F16 and Q4_K_M: the cache, not the weights, is what overflows. Quantization at 4 bits or above costs almost nothing here; pruning is what hurts, and not gradually. A smaller format helps the budget twice: fewer bytes of weights, and fewer bytes read per decode step. In this lab: the quality numbers come from the toy and the budget from arithmetic about a different, imagined model, so no figure on this card is a measurement of a model that runs. The 8B shape is a stand-in for a real size. In general: compression quality depends on the model and the calibration data, and unstructured pruning saves time only on hardware that skips zeros. Real throughput also depends on kernels, batching policy, and the interconnect, which this arithmetic leaves out.
documents.title: Shrink the weights, then fit the load

documents.subtitle: Release report · Ship it
documents.body: The decision, and what it cost to get there One verdict that combines the quality gate and the serving budget, the artifact it applies to, every stage that made something worse, and, when the answer is hold, which condition failed and what to try. A `Verdict: ship` or `Verdict: hold` badge and a headline. A summary of the artifact (format, pruning, adapter rank), the gate result, the serving budget, and the stage-to-stage regressions. On hold, a callout with each failing condition's measured numbers and a suggested next move. The verdict is `ship` only if both gate checks pass and the imagined deployment fits in memory at the chosen load. The regressions list is every stage-to-stage rise in either held-out loss above 0.02 nats, so a loss cannot hide inside a net gain. A hold with a one-line reason is usually cheaper to fix than a ship with a regression nobody read. Changing the thresholds changes the verdict without changing the model, which is why they belong in the plan, not in the run. In this lab: a pass means the toy cleared two held-out texts and fitted one imagined machine. It says nothing about a real model's safety, accuracy on real tasks, or behaviour under real traffic. In general: release decisions weigh quality, safety, cost, latency, and risk, usually with people accountable for the call. A verdict from a script is an input to that decision.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: A learned multiplier controlling how much one input contributes to the sum. Its sign says for or against; its size says how strongly.
documents.title: Weight

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: A learned constant added to the weighted sum. It slides the decision boundary without turning it, so the neuron can fire, or stay silent, when every input is 0.
documents.title: Bias

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: The pre-activation value z = w·x + b. Every dense layer, attention projection, and MLP in this course is built from this one operation.
documents.title: Weighted sum

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: The sum of element-wise products of two vectors. It measures alignment, which is why it appears in both neurons and attention scores.
documents.title: Dot product

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: The weights written as one arrow, w = (w₁, w₂). It is perpendicular to the decision boundary, points toward growing z, and its length sets how fast z grows away from the line.
documents.title: Weight vector

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: The scalar function applied to the weighted sum. It introduces the nonlinearity that makes stacked layers more expressive than one layer.
documents.title: Activation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: An activation squashing any input into the open range 0 to 1. Its slope peaks at 0.25 at z = 0 and falls below 0.05 once z is beyond about ±2.9.
documents.title: Sigmoid

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: An activation passing positive values unchanged and returning 0 otherwise. Its slope is 1 above zero and 0 below, so a unit that is negative for every input stops learning.
documents.title: ReLU

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: An activation returning a hard 0 or 1. Its derivative is 0 everywhere except at the jump, where none exists, so gradient descent gets no signal from it.
documents.title: Step function

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: The set of inputs where the weighted sum equals zero. For a single neuron it is always a straight line, plane, or hyperplane, perpendicular to the weight vector.
documents.title: Decision boundary

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: The property that a single straight boundary can split two classes. Exclusive-or is the standard pattern that lacks it, which is why depth is needed.
documents.title: Linear separability

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: The flat region of an activation where large changes in input barely change the output. It reads as a near-zero gradient during training.
documents.title: Saturation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · A single neuron
documents.body: Any number learned from data rather than supplied as input. In this lab only the two weights and the bias are parameters.
documents.title: Parameter

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · A single neuron · question 1
documents.body: Set Weight w₁ to 1.2, Weight w₂ to −0.8 and Bias b to −0.1, then Input x₁ to 1.00 and Input x₂ to 0.50. What does Weighted sum z read? 1.1: only the first product counts, because a negative weight cancels its input 0.8: both products are added, with the bias left out of the sum 0.7: both products are added, then the bias is added once 1.5: the negative weight is counted as positive, then the bias is added z = x₁w₁ + x₂w₂ + b = 1.00 × 1.2 + 0.50 × (−0.8) + (−0.1) = 1.2 − 0.4 − 0.1 = 0.7. A negative weight subtracts its input's contribution instead of removing it, and the bias is added once after the products.
documents.title: Set Weight w₁ to 1.2, Weight w₂ to −0.8 and Bias b to −0.1, then Input x₁ to 1.00 and Input x₂ to 0.50. What does Weighted sum z read?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · A single neuron · question 2
documents.body: Compare z = 3 with z = 6 on the Activation curve. Which description of the three outputs is right? Sigmoid barely moves because it has flattened near 1, ReLU doubles, and Step stays at 1 All three roughly double, because a bigger weighted sum always gives a proportionally bigger output Sigmoid roughly doubles while ReLU stays flat, because ReLU only reacts to values near zero Step climbs smoothly from 0.5 toward 1, while sigmoid jumps straight to 1 once z passes zero Sigmoid is already close to 1 at z = 3 and flattens further, so doubling z hardly changes it. ReLU returns z itself on the positive side, so its output doubles with z. Step is 1 for every positive z. The three functions disagree most near z = 0 and in how they treat large values.
documents.title: Compare z = 3 with z = 6 on the Activation curve. Which description of the three outputs is right?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · A single neuron · question 3
documents.body: A unit's Slope f′(z) reads about 0 for every training input, either a saturated sigmoid or a ReLU with z below zero. What does that do to learning? Its weights get larger corrections to make up for the flat part of the curve, so it learns faster than its neighbours Almost no gradient flows through it, so its weights barely change and it learns slowly or not at all Nothing: slope is only a display value, and the weights are updated from the loss alone Training updates a weight by multiplying the loss's slope by the activation's slope at that unit. When the activation's slope is about 0 the whole product is about 0, so the unit's weights stop moving. That is the cost of saturation and of a dead ReLU, and why a step function, with slope 0 almost everywhere, cannot be trained by gradient descent.
documents.title: A unit's Slope f′(z) reads about 0 for every training input, either a saturated sigmoid or a ReLU with z below zero. What does that do to learning?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · A single neuron · question 4
documents.body: You double w₁, w₂ and the bias together. What happens? The boundary moves closer to the origin, as it does when only the weights are doubled The boundary moves twice as far from the origin, because every one of the three parameters doubled Nothing changes at all, because only the ratio of the weights matters The boundary stays where it is, and off the line the sigmoid output moves further from 0.5 Doubling every parameter doubles z at every input. Its sign, and so the line z = 0, is unchanged, but |z| grows, so σ(z) moves toward 0 or 1. Doubling only the weights would move the line, because b would no longer scale with them.
documents.title: You double w₁, w₂ and the bias together. What happens?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · A single neuron · question 5
documents.body: With Corner task on XOR the best score is 3 / 4. Would Weight and Bias sliders that reached beyond ±2 get 4 / 4? No: one neuron draws one straight line, and no line has both 1-corners on one side and both 0-corners on the other Yes: larger weights would make the line steeper, so it could squeeze between the diagonal corners Yes: a large enough bias would slide the line to a spot that separates both diagonal pairs of corners The boundary z = 0 is a single straight line. XOR needs the two 1-corners on one side and the two 0-corners on the other, but each pair sits on a diagonal and the two diagonals cross, so any straight line leaves at least one corner on the wrong side. Scaling the weights does not move the line and a bias only slides it, so a wider slider range cannot help; XOR needs a second neuron.
