documents.subtitle: Plain · A single neuron
documents.body: Picture deciding whether to go to the beach on Saturday. You look at a few things, like how sunny the forecast is and how much homework you still have, and some of them count for more than others. Sunshine pulls you toward going while homework pulls you back, and you weigh it all up into one answer: go, or stay home. This lab is about the smallest working part of an AI model, a single artificial neuron, which does a stripped-down version of that using only numbers. It takes a few numbers in, scales each one by how much it counts, adds them up, and turns the total into one answer. No thinking is involved, only multiplying and adding, but that small recipe is the brick the later models in this course are built from. Where it shows up Every model in the rest of this course, including the kind of text-writing model behind a chatbot, is built from huge numbers of copies of this one piece. A layer is a row of neurons that all read the same inputs but count them differently, and a deep network is layers feeding their answers into more layers. In the last lab, Tokens & embeddings, text became lists of numbers, and a neuron is the kind of piece that reads a list like that and returns one number. Even the attention scores you will meet later come from the same multiply-and-add. Why it matters When a model learns, a process called training adjusts the few numbers inside each neuron, so one neuron shows you what learning actually changes. The neuron's last step, the activation, is what makes stacking neurons worth doing, because without it a tall stack of neurons would be no better than one. Its biggest limit is that it can only sort inputs into yes and no by drawing one straight line between them. That is why real models need many neurons working together. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lab you will be able to: work out a neuron's total by hand, by multiplying each input by how much it counts, adding the results, and adding one fixed nudge; describe how the three answer-shaping curves in the lab turn that same total into three different kinds of answer, and why the flat parts of a curve slow learning down; explain how the neuron's numbers turn and slide the line where its answer flips from no to yes, and why one neuron can never solve a small puzzle called XOR. What the lab shows The lab has three cards, and the same sliders drive all of them. Decision boundary and controls shows a square map of every possible pair of inputs, coloured by the neuron's answer, with the line where that answer flips. Neuron equation writes out the arithmetic with your current numbers, while Activation curve shows where your total lands on the chosen curve and how steep the curve is there. A Corner task setting also puts a small four-corner puzzle on the square, where you try to get the neuron to say yes at the right corners. Every number on screen is worked out exactly from the neuron's formula, so nothing is guessed or measured from a real model. Nothing is trained either: you set by hand the numbers a real network would learn, and the four-corner puzzle is a tiny made-up test rather than real data.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · A single neuron
documents.body: A neuron does two small jobs in a row: it weighs and adds up its inputs, then passes the total through a curve that shapes the answer. Job one: weigh and add Go back to the beach decision and turn each thing you look at into a number from 0 to 1. Call the sunshine forecast x₁, where 0 means pouring rain and 1 means a clear sky. Call the homework you still have x₂, where 0 means none left and 1 means all of it. These are the neuron's inputs, and in the lab they are the Input x₁ and Input x₂ sliders. Each input gets a multiplier that says how much each unit of that input counts and in which direction, called a weight. Sunshine pulls you toward going, so its weight w₁ is positive, starting at 1.2 in the lab. Homework pulls you back, so its weight w₂ is negative, starting at −0.8, which means "the more of this, the less likely yes." The neuron then adds one fixed amount that does not depend on any input, called the bias. You can think of it as your mood before you even check the forecast, and the lab starts it at −0.1, a slight lean toward staying home. When every input is 0, the bias is the only thing left in the total, so it alone decides which way the neuron leans. Multiply each input by its weight, add the results, then add the bias, and you get the weighted sum. The lab writes it as z = x₁ × w₁ + x₂ × w₂ + b, where z is the total and b is the bias. Here it is with the lab's starting numbers, a fairly sunny forecast of 0.70 with about a third of your homework, 0.35, still to do: The sunshine part is 0.70 × 1.2 = 0.84, a push toward going. The homework part is 0.35 × (−0.8) = −0.28, a pull toward staying home. Adding both parts and the bias gives 0.84 − 0.28 − 0.10 = 0.46. So z is 0.46, a small positive total, which means the neuron leans toward yes. The Neuron equation card shows exactly this arithmetic, with each line into the middle circle carrying its weight and the product it adds. Its Weighted sum row prints the whole sum with your current numbers, so you can check every step. Multiplying two lists of numbers pair by pair and adding up the results has its own name, the dot product. Here one list holds the two inputs and the other holds the two weights, so the weighted sum is their dot product plus the bias. You will meet the dot product again in later labs, because attention uses the same move to score how well two lists of numbers line up. The weights and the bias are the neuron's adjustable settings, called parameters. In a real network nobody sets them by hand. Training shows the network many examples with known right answers and nudges the parameters a little at a time until it makes fewer mistakes. The inputs are not adjusted, because they arrive fresh with each example, the way each Saturday brings a new forecast. In this lab you set the parameters yourself with the Weight w₁, Weight w₂ and Bias b sliders. Job two: the activation The weighted sum can be any number, large or small, positive or negative, so the neuron's second job is to turn it into a useful answer. The curve that does this is called the activation, and the Activation control in the lab offers three of them. Picture a graph with the total z along the bottom and the answer up the side. Find your z on the bottom, go straight up until you hit the curve, and read across: that height is the neuron's answer. The Activation curve card draws exactly this picture for whichever curve you pick. Sigmoid squashes any total into a number between 0 and 1 along a smooth S-shaped curve. A total of 0 gives exactly 0.5, big positive totals creep toward 1, and big negative totals creep toward 0, though it never quite reaches either end. The lab prints its recipe as 1 / (1 + e^−z), where e is a fixed number a little over 2.7. You never need to work that out by hand, but one case is quick. At z = 0 the e^−z part becomes e^0, which is 1, because any number to the power 0 is 1. That leaves 1 ÷ (1 + 1), which is 0.5. The Neuron equation card shortens sigmoid to σ, which is the Greek letter sigma. ReLU passes a positive total through unchanged and turns any negative total into 0. Its recipe is max(0, z), which means "whichever is bigger, 0 or z", so a total of 0.46 stays 0.46 while a total of −2 becomes 0. Step, known in full as the step function, gives a flat yes or no with nothing in between. It answers 1 when z is above 0 and 0 otherwise, which includes the case where z is exactly 0. With the starting total of 0.46, the three activations give three different answers: Sigmoid gives 0.613, a mild lean toward yes that sits about 61% of the way from 0 to 1. ReLU gives 0.460, which is the total itself, because the total is positive. Step gives 1, a flat yes, because the total is above 0. The activation never changes z, only what the neuron does with it. Each of these curves bends somewhere, which a plain multiply-and-add can never do, and Why it’s here explains why that bend matters so much. The line where the neuron is undecided Now picture every possible Saturday at once, laid out on the big square of the Decision boundary and controls card. Sunshine x₁ runs from 0 on the left to 1 on the right, while homework x₂ runs from 0 at the bottom to 1 at the top. Each point is one pair of inputs, and the dark dot, called the probe, marks the pair your Input x₁ and Input x₂ sliders are set to. Every point on the map has its own total z. Points where z is positive are shaded green, and points where it is negative are shaded red, or grey when ReLU is picked. How deep the shading looks depends on the activation. Between them runs a solid dark line made of every point where z is exactly 0, which is called the decision boundary. These are the Saturdays where the pushes and pulls cancel out, so the neuron is perfectly undecided. With the starting numbers, the line runs from near the bottom-left corner up to the top edge. One point on it is a forecast of 0.75 with all your homework still to do, and the sum shows why it sits there: 0.90 − 0.80 − 0.10 = 0. To see why the boundary is always straight, imagine z as a height above each point of the map. With the starting weights, every step of 0.1 to the right raises z by the same 0.12, wherever you start. Every step of 0.1 upward lowers it by the same 0.08, and that happens because z only ever multiplies and adds. A surface that rises by the same amount for every equal step, with no bumps or dips, is a perfectly flat, tilted sheet, like a ramp. The decision boundary is where the ramp crosses floor level. A flat ramp always meets a flat floor along a straight line, so one neuron's boundary is straight whatever numbers you choose. The weights set which way the ramp tilts and how steeply. Changing them turns the line, and it can shift the line too, because a new tilt changes where the ramp crosses the floor. The bias raises or lowers the whole ramp without tilting it, so changing the bias slides the line to a new spot without turning it. The arrow and the distance The lab also draws the two weights together as one arrow, labelled w. The first weight says how far the arrow goes across and the second says how far it goes up. With the starting weights of 1.2 and −0.8, the arrow points to the right and somewhat downward. A list of numbers drawn as an arrow like this is called a vector, and this one is the weight vector. The arrow always points straight uphill on the ramp, toward bigger z and the green "yes" side. You can check it with the starting weights, where moving right raises z by 1.2 for each full step and moving down raises it by 0.8. So the fastest climb heads right and somewhat down, exactly where the arrow points. Any part of a step that runs along the line is wasted, because z does not change along it. So the steepest climb cuts straight across the line at a right angle. The thin dashed lines join points at the same height, like the height lines on a hiking map. They mark where z is 1 or 2 on the green side, and −1 or −2 on the red side. The true length of w measures how steep the ramp is, and the lab prints it as ‖w‖, which you can read as "the length of w". The drawn arrow gets longer as ‖w‖ grows, but it is resized to fit the picture. You find ‖w‖ the way you find the long side of a right triangle: square each weight, add the squares, and take the square root. With the starting weights the squares are 1.44 and 0.64, which add to 2.08, and the square root of 2.08 is about 1.442. That is how much z rises when you walk one full unit in the arrow's direction, which is why it measures steepness. Distance to boundary tells you how far the probe sits from the line along the shortest path, which the lab draws as a short dotted line from the probe. The lab works it out as z / ‖w‖, which is the probe's height divided by how steep the ramp is. To see why that gives a distance, picture a ramp that rises 2 metres for every metre you move across the floor toward its high side. If you are standing 1 metre up, the floor line is half a metre away across the floor, which is 1 ÷ 2. In the lab, at the start, that is 0.460 ÷ 1.442, or about 0.319, which is a bit under a third of the square's width. The sign only tells you which side you are on: positive on the side the arrow points to, and negative on the other side.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · A single neuron
documents.body: Every model needs a way to turn many incoming numbers into one useful signal, and that way of combining them has to come with knobs that learning can adjust. A neuron does both with very few moving parts. Each weight decides how much one input counts and whether it pushes toward yes or toward no, while the bias sets the starting lean before any input arrives. Why the bias is there You can see the bias earn its place on the map, because without it a neuron whose inputs are all 0 would have a total of exactly 0. That would force the decision boundary to pass through the bottom-left corner every single time. Step would always say no there, and Sigmoid would always say exactly 0.5. With a bias the line can sit anywhere, so the neuron can choose its own answer even when every input is 0. Why the bend matters A model gets its power from stacking neurons in layers, but stacking only helps if each layer adds something the others cannot. Without an activation every neuron is a multiply-and-add, and a multiply-and-add fed into another multiply-and-add collapses into a single multiply-and-add. Here is a tiny example with one input, where the first neuron doubles its input and adds 1, and the second neuron triples that answer and subtracts 4. Feed in 5 and the first neuron gives 11, and then the second neuron turns that 11 into 29. Now picture a single neuron that multiplies by 6 and subtracts 1, which also turns 5 into 29. In fact it matches the pair for every other input you try, so the two-neuron stack was one neuron in disguise all along. A hundred layers would collapse the same way, which would make all that depth useless. The reason is that graphing any multiply-and-add, like 6 × x − 1, always gives a straight line, and two straight-line steps in a row still give a straight line. An activation stops the collapse because its curve bends: ReLU has a sharp corner at 0, sigmoid flattens out at both ends, and step jumps. To see a bend at work, let a first neuron give x − 2, and then let ReLU turn anything negative into 0. Inputs 0, 1 and 2 all come out as 0, then 3 gives 1 and 4 gives 2. That graph is flat and then climbs, a bent line that no single multiply-and-add can draw. With a bend between layers the stack can no longer be squeezed into one neuron, so each extra layer can add new shapes. The next lab, Stacking neurons, tests this directly. Why one neuron is not enough The flat ramp also explains the neuron's biggest limit, because a boundary that is always one straight line can only sort inputs that a straight line can split. Real tasks are rarely that tidy, so models use many neurons that each draw their own line, and later neurons combine those lines into more complicated shapes. The last step of this lab, with Corner task set to XOR, shows you exactly where one neuron runs out.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · A single neuron
documents.body: Work through these five steps in order, since each one builds on the last. Move the inputs Move Input x₁ and Input x₂ and watch the probe travel across the square. The Weighted sum and Activation rows on the Neuron equation card update as you go, and so does the z badge on the Decision boundary and controls card. Notice that moving the inputs never moves the line, because the inputs are data, not parameters. Turn and slide the line Try this: Hold the inputs still, push Weight w₁ up to 2, and then drag it slowly down toward The line turns around a point a little below the bottom-left corner and lies flatter as you go. Meanwhile the arrow w swings with it, always at a right angle to the line, though all you changed was how much the sunshine counts. Bring it down to 0.1 and the solid line leaves the square altogether, because now no point on the map has a positive total. Even the best Saturday, full sun and no homework, now gives at most 0.1 − 0.1 = 0. The arrow keeps turning, though, so you can still see which way the ramp tilts. Now set Weight w₁ back to 1.2 and move Bias b, and this time the line slides without turning, staying parallel to where it was. The worst corner, no sun and all the homework, gives −0.8 plus the bias, and the best corner, full sun and no homework, gives 1.2 plus the bias. So push the bias up to 0.8 and the whole map turns green, while pulling it down to −1.2 turns it all red. Either way, the line has slid right off the square and left only one colour behind. One total, three answers Return the two weights to 1.2 and −0.8 and the bias to −0.1, which are the lab's starting values. Then set Input x₁ to 0.75 and Input x₂ to 1.00. That puts the probe exactly on the decision boundary, so the z badge on the Decision boundary and controls card reads 0.000. Flip Activation between Sigmoid, ReLU and Step, and read the output each time: Sigmoid gives 0.500, exactly halfway between no and yes, which is what it gives anywhere on the line. ReLU gives 0.000, because a total that is not positive becomes 0. Step gives 0, because it only says yes when z is above 0, and 0 is not above 0. Keep an eye on the Activation curve card as you switch, where the solid violet curve is your pick and the faint dashed ones are the other two. The dot on the solid curve marks where your z lands, which right now is the centre line of the plot, z = 0. It sits halfway up for Sigmoid, and down at 0 for ReLU and Step. Double everything Put the inputs back at their starting values, 0.70 and 0.35, and set Activation to Sigmoid. Set the three parameters to the first values below and note what z and Distance to boundary say, then double all three: Weight w₁: first 1.0, then double it to 2.0 Weight w₂: first −0.5, then double it to −1.0 Bias b: first −0.2, then double it to −0.4 Before doubling, z reads 0.325, and after doubling it reads 0.650, which is twice as much. Yet the solid line does not budge, and Distance to boundary reads 0.291 both times. The dashed lines for z = 1 and z = −1 do move, though. Before doubling they sit outside the square, and after doubling they slide into view, closer to the solid line. A ramp twice as steep reaches a height of 1 in half the distance. In ramp terms, doubling all three makes the ramp twice as steep while it still crosses the floor in the same place. The height doubles and the steepness doubles, so height divided by steepness, which is the distance, stays the same. The corner puzzle Set Corner task to AND, and four marks appear at the corners of the square. A filled circle wants the neuron to answer 1 and an open square wants 0, while the ✓ or ✗ beside each mark scores the current setting. A corner counts as a yes when its z is above 0, which is the same rule Step uses, whichever activation you picked. AND wants a yes only at the top-right corner, where both inputs are 1, like a game that starts only when both players press ready. With the lab's starting sliders the Corners correct readout shows 3 / 4. See if you can find a setting that scores 4 / 4 before checking the answer in What to notice. Then switch to OR, which wants a yes whenever at least one input is 1. Last, switch to XOR and try to get all four corners right, giving it a real try before you read Where it breaks.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · A single neuron
documents.body: The three activations differ near the line and far out on the green side. Right on the line they give 0.5, 0 and 0. Just past it, Step jumps to 1, while sigmoid is still near 0.5 and ReLU is still near 0. Far out on the red side all three settle near 0 and agree. Far out on the green side, sigmoid creeps up to 1 and step is already at 1, while ReLU keeps climbing with z, so there the gap grows. Switching Activation never moves the line. It changes the shading and the output, but the line, the arrow and the corner marks stay put. They come from z and the weights alone, before the activation is applied. The line is where z = 0, the arrow is the two weights, and a corner counts as yes when its z is above 0. Each activation shades the map its own way. Sigmoid is pale near the line and deepens further out, while Step splits the square into two flat regions, one on each side of the line. ReLU paints the whole negative side grey, because every output there is exactly 0. A negative weight is not a mistake, because it means "the more of this, the less likely yes." The Neuron equation card draws it as a dashed red line instead of a solid green one, and the thickness of each line shows the size of its weight. Doubling all three parameters makes sigmoid more sure of itself, because z doubles while the line stays put. With Sigmoid selected, the output in step 4 rose from 0.581 to 0.657, moving further from the undecided halfway point. Doubling only the weights does move the line. If you leave the bias at −0.2 while the weights double, the line slides toward the bottom-left corner, because the bias no longer keeps pace. The flat zone Push z as high as it can go by setting both inputs to 1 and both weights and the bias to 2. Now z is 6, and with Sigmoid selected the output reads 0.998, which is almost exactly 1. The Slope f′(z) readout tells you how steep the curve is at your dot. Its label f′(z) is maths shorthand for "the slope of the curve at z". The short pink line on the Activation curve card shows the same slope as a picture. Both answer the question "if z moved a tiny bit, how much would the output move?" Sigmoid is steepest at z = 0, where its slope is 0.25. That means nudging z by 0.1 there moves the output by a quarter as much, about 0.025. At z = 6 the slope reads 0.0025, a hundred times smaller, and the readout turns red because it is below 0.05. The shaded bands on the sigmoid plot, labelled slope < 0.05, mark where z is beyond about 2.9 in either direction. This flat stretch, where big changes in z barely change the output, is called saturation, and it comes back in the training labs. Solving AND and OR AND reaches 4 / 4 with both weights at 1 and the bias at −1.5, and adding up each corner shows why: At the bottom-left corner both inputs are 0, so the total is −1.5, a no. At the two side corners one input is 1, so the total is 1 − 1.5 = −0.5, also a no. At the top-right corner both inputs are 1, so the total is 2 − 1.5 = 0.5, a yes. OR reaches 4 / 4 with the same weights and the bias at −0.5 instead, which makes every corner except the bottom-left one positive. XOR, by contrast, never gets past 3 / 4 whatever you try, and Where it breaks explains why.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · A single neuron
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Nothing is trained: you set by hand the numbers a real network would learn. There is no data, no running score of mistakes, and no rule for improving the weights. The inputs only run from 0 to 1, and the weights and bias only run from −2 to 2, so z always stays between −6 and 6. The four corners are a truth table, a short list of the right answer for every combination of inputs, rather than a real collection of examples. The arrow's direction is exact, but its drawn length is scaled so that it fits the picture. The neuron has only two inputs, which is what lets its whole map fit on a flat square. The beach picture stops matching You know what sunshine and homework mean, but a neuron does not know what its inputs stand for. It receives plain numbers with no labels, and in a real network its weights come from training rather than from anyone's reasons. The beach decision is a way to picture the arithmetic, not a description of what a neuron is doing. A weight is not an importance score Picture two friends who each build the same beach neuron, except that one measures homework in hours and the other measures it in minutes. Every homework number in the minutes version is 60 times bigger, so its weight has to be 60 times smaller to give the same answers. Both neurons behave identically, yet one weight looks tiny, which shows that a small weight does not mean an input matters less. So a weight tells you how much one unit of its input counts, and that depends on what unit the input is measured in. One straight line is all it gets XOR wants a yes when exactly one input is 1 and a no when both inputs match. Picture a hallway light with a switch at each end, wired so the light is on when exactly one switch is up. Both switches down means off, one up means on, and both up means off again. On the lab's square, that puts the two yes corners at the top-left and bottom-right, diagonally across from each other, with the two no corners on the other diagonal. Any straight line you draw leaves at least one corner on the wrong side, which is why Corners correct never passes 3 / 4. You can check why with a pencil. Add up the totals at the two yes corners: the top-left gives w₂ + b and the bottom-right gives w₁ + b, so together they make w₁ + w₂ + 2b. Now add up the two no corners: the bottom-left gives b and the top-right gives w₁ + w₂ + b, which together also make w₁ + w₂ + 2b. To score 4 / 4, both yes totals must be above 0, so their sum is above 0. Both no totals must be 0 or below, so their sum is 0 or below. One number cannot be both, so some corner is always wrong, whatever the sliders say. On the map, the two diagonals cross at the centre of the square, and the centre's total is exactly half of that shared sum. So the centre would have to sit on both sides of the line at once. A computer search through every setting of the three sliders agrees. Wider sliders would not help either, because bigger numbers can only turn or slide the line, never bend it. A pattern that one straight line can split, like AND or OR, is said to have linear separability. XOR is the classic pattern that lacks it, because no single line can split its corners. Solving it takes more than one neuron: two that each draw a line, and one more that combines their answers, which is where the next lab begins. Flat zones stall learning Training improves a network by nudging each weight in whichever direction makes its mistakes smaller, and it finds that direction by following slopes. The usual method is called gradient descent, where the gradient is the collection of all those slopes. A slope of about 0 gives training almost nothing to follow, so the weights behind that neuron barely move. Picture a class test with questions so basic that everyone scores 99 or 100. Studying harder barely changes anyone's score, so the test cannot tell the teacher who improved. A saturated sigmoid works the same way, because its output sits so close to 0 or 1 that changing the weights hardly shows. Here the test picture falls short, because everyone in that class is already right. A saturated neuron inside a network can also be stuck near the wrong end, say near 1 when the right answer is 0. It is then badly wrong, but because its slope is about 0 it gets almost no push to change. That is when saturation hurts most. ReLU has its own version of this problem, because its slope is 0 whenever z is negative. A ReLU neuron whose total is negative for every example therefore gets no signal at all, and it may never recover. Step is worse still: its slope is 0 everywhere except at the jump, where there is no slope at all, so gradient descent cannot train it. Real neurons live in bigger spaces A real neuron usually has many more than two inputs. With three inputs, the square becomes a box and the boundary becomes a flat wall cutting through it. With more inputs the same idea continues in more directions than anyone can draw, so only two or three inputs can be pictured the way this lab does. Inside a trained network, one neuron's line is also only one of many lines that later layers combine. Reading a single neuron's boundary on its own tells you much less about the whole model than it seems to. A common mix-up: The name comes from nerve cells in the brain, but an artificial neuron is not a tiny brain cell making a decision. It is one multiply-and-add followed by one bending curve, and it remembers nothing it saw before.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · A single neuron
documents.body: Real models mostly use smoother activations called GELU and SiLU in their hidden layers, which are the layers between the input and the final output. Both are close relatives of ReLU that keep a gentle slope near zero and allow slightly negative outputs, which makes training steadier than with ReLU's sharp corner. Sigmoid still shows up where a model gives a final yes-or-no answer. It also works inside parts called gates, where a value between 0 and 1 sets how much of a signal gets through. Its relative for choosing among many answers, called softmax, appears in every attention head, a part of the attention step you will meet later. Deep stacks of sigmoids have a further problem, because training multiplies the slopes of one layer after another and even sigmoid's steepest slope is only 0.25. Multiply ten of those together and you get less than one in a million, which is one reason the learning signal can fade to almost nothing. To avoid flat zones, starting weights are sized so that z lands in the responsive middle part of the activation rather than at its flat ends. Inside deep models, extra steps called normalization keep z in that range as more layers are added. With Step as its activation, this neuron is the perceptron that the researcher Frank Rosenblatt described in 1958. In 1969 the researchers Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert showed what one layer like this cannot compute, with XOR among the examples. The next lab, Stacking neurons, puts two of these lines together and solves XOR.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · A single neuron
documents.body: This module is about a single neuron: a unit that multiplies each input by a learned weight, adds a learned bias, and passes the resulting weighted sum z through an activation, a fixed scalar function. *Tokens & embeddings* turned text into vectors; a neuron reads a vector of inputs like those and returns one number. The question it answers is what a few learned numbers can decide about an input, and what they cannot. The answer is geometric. The inputs where z = 0 form the decision boundary, a straight line in this lab's two-input plane and a hyperplane in general. The weights and bias place that boundary; the activation sets how the output changes across it. Where it shows up Layers in this course. Dense layers, attention projections, and MLP blocks are all built from this one weighted sum. Transformers. Attention scores, MLP hidden units, and output logits are all weighted sums with a nonlinearity nearby. Activation choices. Hidden layers in production mostly use smooth relatives of ReLU, and sigmoid remains at binary outputs and gates. Why it matters A neuron decides from its inputs using only numbers that training can change: its parameters, the weights and the bias. Three ingredients are there because leaving any one out causes a specific failure: Without the bias, the decision boundary is forced through the origin. Without a nonlinear activation, extra layers add no expressive power. Without a usable slope in the activation, gradient descent has nothing to follow, which is why step units cannot be trained by it. Even so, one neuron draws one straight boundary. A pattern is linearly separable when a single straight boundary splits its classes; one that is not is out of reach. XOR is the standard example, and the reason *Stacking neurons* comes next. What you will be able to explain Compute a weighted sum z = x₁w₁ + x₂w₂ + b by hand, and check it against the lab's Weighted sum readout. Describe how sigmoid, ReLU and step shape the output from the same z, and how each one's slope decides whether gradient descent gets a signal. Relate the weights and bias to the position of the decision boundary: the direction of the weight vector w = (w₁, w₂) turns it, the ratio |b| / ‖w‖ sets how far it sits from the origin, and scaling all three together leaves it in place. What the lab shows Nothing trains and there is no dataset. Every number is closed-form maths for one two-input neuron, evaluated exactly from the inputs and parameters you set by hand. Decision boundary and controls. The input square, shaded by the neuron's output, with the boundary, the weight vector drawn as the w arrow, and a probe at the current input. Controls: Activation (Sigmoid, ReLU, Step), Input x₁, Input x₂, Weight w₁, Weight w₂, Bias b, and Corner task (Off, AND, OR, XOR). Readouts: ‖w‖, Distance to boundary, and Corners correct. Neuron equation. The forward pass with every product shown, and the Weighted sum and Activation rows evaluated live. Activation curve. The chosen function for z from −6 to 6, with the current z, the tangent where one exists (never for Step), and Slope f′(z). The w arrow points exactly along w, but its length is resized to fit the plot, and the four corners are a fixed truth table with no loss. The key experiment: set Corner task to AND or OR and find weights that score 4 / 4, then switch to XOR. No setting of the three sliders gets past 3 / 4.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · A single neuron
documents.body: A neuron is two operations in sequence: an affine map, then a scalar activation. For the two inputs in this lab the affine part is z = x₁w₁ + x₂w₂ + b and the output is a = f(z). Only the weights and the bias are learned; the inputs arrive from data or a previous layer. At the defaults, z = 0.70 × 1.2 + 0.35 × (−0.8) + (−0.1) = 0.460, and σ(0.460) = 0.613. The geometry of z = w · x + b Written for any width, z = w · x + b. The weight vector w is the gradient of z with respect to the input, so it is perpendicular to every level line of z, including the decision boundary z = 0. Its direction sets the boundary's orientation. Its length sets how fast z grows: the lines z = ±1, ±2 sit 1 / ‖w‖ apart. The bias sets the offset. The signed distance from an input to the boundary is z / ‖w‖, which the lab prints as Distance to boundary: 0.319 at the defaults, where ‖w‖ is 1.442. Without a bias the boundary would be forced through the origin. What the activation adds Sigmoid maps any z into the open interval (0, 1). Its slope σ(1 − σ) peaks at 0.25 at z = 0 and falls below 0.05 beyond |z| ≈ 2.89. ReLU returns max(0, z). It is unbounded above, and its slope is exactly 1 on the active side and 0 on the other. Step returns 1 when z > 0 and 0 otherwise. Its slope is 0 everywhere except the jump, where no derivative exists, so it gives gradient descent nothing to follow.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · A single neuron
documents.body: This is the smallest unit that learns, and the rest of the course is built from copies of it. A layer is many neurons reading the same inputs with different weights; a deep network is layers of those. Two affine maps composed are still one affine map, so without a nonlinearity any stack collapses to a single linear function. The next lab tests that claim directly.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · A single neuron
documents.body: Move Input x₁ and Input x₂ and watch the probe cross the plane while Weighted sum and Activation update. Hold the inputs and sweep Weight w₁ from -2 to 2: the boundary rotates and the w arrow stays perpendicular. Bias b translates it. With the default parameters, set the inputs to 0.75 and 1.00 so z = 0, then switch Activation: Sigmoid gives 0.500, ReLU 0.000, Step 0. Finally set Corner task to AND, OR, and XOR and try to score 4 / 4 on each.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · A single neuron
documents.body: Scaling w₁, w₂, and b by the same factor leaves the boundary and the distance in place while z scales. From (1.0, −0.5, −0.2) to (2.0, −1.0, −0.4), the default probe's z goes from 0.325 to 0.650 and its distance stays 0.291. Scaling only the weights moves the boundary toward the origin, because b did not scale. The three activations disagree most near z = 0. At the lab's maximum, z = 6, sigmoid reads 0.998 with slope 0.0025, step reads 1, and ReLU reads 6. AND and OR reach 4 / 4, for example w = (1, 1) with b = −1.5 or b = −0.5. XOR never passes 3 / 4.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · A single neuron
documents.body: In this lab Nothing trains. The parameters are hand-set, the inputs are clamped to the unit square, and the four corners are a truth table, not a dataset with a loss. The w arrow's drawn length is scaled for display; its direction is exact. In real systems One neuron draws one hyperplane, so any pattern that is not linearly separable is out of reach. XOR is the standard example: an exhaustive search over this lab's slider grid finds no setting above 3 / 4. Step units cannot be trained by gradient descent. Sigmoid units in deep stacks slow learning through saturation, and ReLU units can die: once z is negative for every example, the gradient is zero and the unit may never recover. A weight is also not an importance score. Rescale an input feature and its weight compensates, with no change in behaviour.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · A single neuron
documents.body: Production hidden layers mostly use GELU or SiLU, smooth relatives of ReLU that allow small negative outputs and keep a usable slope near zero. Sigmoid survives at binary outputs and inside gates; its multi-class relative, softmax, appears in every attention head. Initialization scale keeps z in the responsive part of the activation at the start of training, and normalization layers keep it there as depth grows. With a step activation, this unit is Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958). Minsky and Papert's 1969 analysis of what one layer cannot compute, XOR among it, is answered by Stacking neurons, the next lab.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Decision boundary and controls · A single neuron
documents.body: The line where z = 0, and every knob that moves it The input square shaded by the neuron's output at each point, with the line z = 0, the weight vector w drawn perpendicular to it, and all six controls. Every mark is computed from the same `z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b` the Neuron equation card prints. A 30 × 30 grid of cells over x₁ and x₂ from 0 to 1, shaded by the current activation's output: graded for Sigmoid, a grey zero side and a growing green side for ReLU, two flat halves for Step. Green is z > 0 and red is z < 0. A solid dark line, the decision boundary z = 0, and thin dashed lines at z = ±1 and ±2. They are parallel and spaced 1 / ‖w‖ apart. A blue arrow labelled w, starting on the boundary. It is perpendicular to the line and points toward growing z. Its drawn length grows with ‖w‖ but is scaled for display. The probe (dark dot) at `Input x₁`, `Input x₂`, and a dotted segment from it to the nearest point on the line. With `Corner task` on, the four corners (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1): a filled circle wants output 1, an open square wants 0, and each carries ✓ or ✗ for the current prediction. `‖w‖`, `Distance to boundary`, and `Corners correct` under the plane, plus a note that changes with the task. Each cell's centre is evaluated with `z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b` and then `f(z)`. The boundary is where z = 0, clipped to the square; it disappears when both weights are 0. The gradient of z with respect to the input is (w₁, w₂), which is why w is perpendicular to every level line and why the z = k lines are 1 / ‖w‖ apart. `Distance to boundary` is `z / ‖w‖`, the signed Euclidean distance from the probe to the line, positive on the side w points to. A corner counts as predicted 1 when its z is strictly positive, the same rule as Step. For Sigmoid that is σ(z) > 0.5; for ReLU, an output above 0. An exhaustive search over the slider grid (steps of 0.1) finds settings that score 4 / 4 on AND and OR, and none better than 3 / 4 on XOR. That search is a unit test. `Activation` (Sigmoid, ReLU, Step) changes only the shading and the output. The line, the arrow, and the corner marks do not move, because they depend on the sign of z alone. `Input x₁` and `Input x₂` (0 to 1) move the probe only. They are data, not parameters. `Weight w₁` and `Weight w₂` (−2 to 2) turn the line: sweep `Weight w₁` from −2 to 2 and the arrow swings with it, always perpendicular. `Bias b` (−2 to 2) slides the line without turning it. At w = (1.2, −0.8), a bias above 0.8 or below −1.2 pushes the line out of the square. `Corner task` (Off, AND, OR, XOR) overlays the four truth-table corners and scores them. Scaling w₁, w₂ and b together keeps the line in place: at (1.0, −0.5, −0.2) and at (2.0, −1.0, −0.4) the probe's `Distance to boundary` is 0.291 in both, while z doubles from 0.325 to 0.650. Scaling only the weights does move the line, because b no longer scales with them. At the defaults AND and OR both score 3 / 4, and XOR 2 / 4. AND reaches 4 / 4 at w = (1, 1), b = −1.5; OR at w = (1, 1), b = −0.5. XOR never passes 3 / 4. The regions are always two half-planes. No setting of the three sliders bends the line. In this lab: nothing is trained. You set the weights by hand, and the four corners are a truth table, not a dataset with a loss. In this lab: inputs stay in 0 to 1 and the parameters in −2 to 2, so z stays between −6 and 6. In general: a real boundary lives in as many dimensions as there are inputs, so it can be drawn only for two or three of them. In general: one neuron inside a trained network is one of many half-planes that later layers combine. Reading its boundary alone over-explains the model.

documents.subtitle: Neuron equation · A single neuron
documents.body: One weighted sum, then one activation The forward pass of a two-input neuron with every intermediate number shown: each input times its weight, the sum plus the bias, and the activation of that sum. Two input circles with their values. Each line into the sum carries `× w = product`: the weight and that input's contribution to z. Line thickness grows with |w|. Positive weights are solid green lines; negative weights are dashed red lines, so sign is not shown by colour alone. The z circle holding the weighted sum, a dotted bias line from below, an activation box with a sketch of the chosen function, and the output a. Two formula rows: `Weighted sum`, written out with the current numbers, and `Activation`, naming the function and applying it. `z = x₁ × w₁ + x₂ × w₂ + b`, evaluated exactly as printed. At the defaults: 0.70 × 1.2 + 0.35 × (−0.8) + (−0.1) = 0.840 − 0.280 − 0.100 = 0.460. Sigmoid computes `1 / (1 + e^−z)`, ReLU computes `max(0, z)`, and Step returns 1 when z > 0 and 0 otherwise, including at z = 0. Written for any width this is `z = w · x + b`, the dot product that appears in every attention projection and MLP later in the course. This card has no controls. The sliders and `Activation` on Decision boundary and controls drive it. Comparison worth running: with the default weights and bias, set `Input x₁` to 0.75 and `Input x₂` to 1.00 so z reads 0.000. Sigmoid gives 0.500, ReLU 0.000, Step 0. A negative weight turns a large input into a negative contribution. At the defaults x₂ subtracts 0.280 from z. Switching `Activation` changes a but never z: the three functions read the same weighted sum. Only w₁, w₂ and b are parameters. x₁ and x₂ are one example's features. In this lab: two inputs and hand-set parameters. There is no data, loss, or update rule. In general: a weight is not an importance score. Rescale an input feature and its weight compensates with no change in the neuron's behaviour. In general: production hidden layers mostly use GELU or SiLU, smooth relatives of ReLU. Sigmoid survives at binary outputs and inside gates.
documents.title: One weighted sum, then one activation

documents.subtitle: Activation curve · A single neuron
documents.body: Where this z sits on f, and how steep f is there The chosen activation plotted for z from −6 to 6, the lab's full reachable range, with the current z marked and its tangent drawn. The slope readout is the number backpropagation would multiply by at this point. The selected function as a solid violet curve, and the other two as faint dashed curves for comparison. Step's curve breaks at the jump rather than drawing a vertical line. A dotted vertical guide and a dot at the current z, and a short pink tangent line whose steepness is f′(z). Step has no tangent. For Sigmoid, two shaded bands beyond z = ±2.89 labelled `slope < 0.05`: the saturated regions. `z`, `f(z)`, and `Slope f′(z)`. The slope turns red when it is below 0.05. Sigmoid's slope is `σ(z)(1 − σ(z))`: 0.25 at z = 0, 0.2372 at the default z = 0.460, and 0.0025 at z = 6. ReLU's slope is 1 for z > 0 and 0 for z < 0. At exactly 0 the kink has no derivative; training libraries use 0 there by convention. Step's slope is 0 everywhere except the jump, where no derivative exists, so the readout shows 0.0000, or `none at z = 0` exactly on the jump. ReLU's kink at z = 0 reads the same way. `Activation` switches the solid curve. Push z to its extreme with `Input x₁` and `Input x₂` at 1 and `Weight w₁`, `Weight w₂`, `Bias b` at 2: z = 6, Sigmoid reads 0.998, and its slope 0.0025. The three functions disagree most near z = 0 and least far from it, except that ReLU keeps climbing. In the shaded bands Sigmoid barely moves: pushing z a further 1 unit outward shifts the output by less than 0.05. A slope of 0 means gradient descent gets no signal through this unit at this input, which is the whole case against Step. In this lab: the plot shows one neuron's activation for one z. No gradient flows anywhere, because nothing is trained. In general: saturation in deep sigmoid stacks multiplies many small slopes together, which is one reason gradients vanish. Normalization and careful initialization keep z in the responsive range.
