documents.title: Hold data out

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: A set of neurons reading the same inputs with different weights, written h = f(Wx + b). Its output is consumed by the next layer, not by the user.
documents.title: Hidden layer

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: The vector a layer hands forward: a rewritten version of the input that later layers find easier to use. It is a means, not an answer.
documents.title: Representation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: Width is the number of units in a layer; depth is the number of stacked hidden layers. Width adds parallel detectors at one level and drives most of the parameter count; depth adds stages of composition, letting later layers build on features earlier layers invented. Which one wins at equal size depends on the task, the activation, and the training budget.
documents.title: Width and depth

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: The activation placed between layers. Without it, any stack of linear layers collapses algebraically into a single linear map.
documents.title: Nonlinearity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: The result that one sufficiently wide hidden layer with a non-polynomial activation can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain. It proves existence, not trainability or efficiency.
documents.title: Universal approximation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: The observed progression from simple to composite features across depth, such as edges to object parts in vision or surface form to syntax in language.
documents.title: Feature hierarchy

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: An encoding spread across many units rather than stored one concept per unit. It is why single hidden units rarely have a clean human label.
documents.title: Distributed representation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: How complex a function a network could express, set mainly by depth and width. High capacity permits good fits and also permits memorizing noise.
documents.title: Capacity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: The total learned numbers in the model. Each layer contributes width-times-input weights plus one bias per unit, so adjacent wide layers dominate the total. Different shapes can share a count: one layer of 21 units and two layers of 7 both have 85.
documents.title: Parameter count

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: The forward pass is one left-to-right evaluation that turns an input into a prediction, each layer consuming the previous layer's output. Backpropagation runs back through the same layers with the chain rule to get the gradient for every weight; here it is exact, and it is taught in the lab Backpropagation.
documents.title: Forward pass and backpropagation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: The loss for a yes-or-no output: the average of minus the log of the probability the network gave the correct label, so a confident wrong answer costs a lot. Answering 0.5 everywhere scores ln 2 = 0.693. It is taught in the lab Loss & gradient descent.
documents.title: Binary cross-entropy

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: Training repeatedly nudges every weight against the gradient of the loss, and momentum adds a running velocity so steps build along a steady slope. This lab uses a fixed learning rate of 0.5 with momentum 0.9 over the whole training set, so one epoch, a complete pass of the optimizer over the training set, is one full-batch step. Both ideas are taught in the lab Loss & gradient descent.
documents.title: Gradient descent, momentum, and epochs

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: The random starting weights. Different seeds can end in different solutions, and with only two hidden units some seeds get stuck below 100% on XOR. The scale of the starting weights also sets how large gradients are at the start, which the Backpropagation lab's Gradient flow card measures.
documents.title: Initialization

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Stacking neurons
documents.body: Held-out data are points the network never trains on. Overfitting is fitting the training points, including any wrong labels among them, better than the pattern behind them, so accuracy on held-out points falls behind training accuracy. Label noise, wrong labels in the training set, gives a high-capacity network something to memorize that will not repeat.
documents.title: Overfitting and held-out data

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Stacking neurons · question 1
documents.body: Set Dataset to Ring with one hidden layer of 2 neurons, then raise Neurons per layer to 3. What changes, and why? Accuracy rises only slightly, because extra neurons in the same layer mostly repeat one another's cut Accuracy reaches 100%, because three straight cuts can enclose the inner disc and two can only carve a wedge Accuracy stays the same, because only an extra layer can add a new kind of boundary Accuracy falls, because more neurons mean more weights to tune on the same few points Each first-layer neuron contributes one straight line, and the output unit combines them. Two lines can bound a wedge but not a closed region, while three can wall off the inner disc, so the number of units limits what a single hidden layer can express. Width adds more parallel detectors at one level.
documents.title: Set Dataset to Ring with one hidden layer of 2 neurons, then raise Neurons per layer to 3. What changes, and why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Stacking neurons · question 2
documents.body: With Hidden layers at 2, the second-layer tiles in Network builder have bent edges while first-layer tiles have one straight edge. Why? Later layers are trained for more epochs, and the extra training curves a unit's boundary away from a line Every extra input to a unit adds one bend, so units that read more inputs end up bending more Deeper units use a different activation function, and the shape of that function bends the edge First-layer units read x₁ and x₂ directly; second-layer units read the curved outputs of first-layer units A first-layer unit is a weighted sum of x₁ and x₂ followed by an activation, so its zero line is straight. A second-layer unit takes a weighted sum of those units' outputs, which are already bent responses over the square, so its zero line bends. This is what depth adds here: composition of earlier units, not extra straight cuts.
documents.title: With Hidden layers at 2, the second-layer tiles in Network builder have bent edges while first-layer tiles have one straight edge. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Stacking neurons · question 3
documents.body: At the defaults, set Probe x₁ and Probe x₂ to (0.6, 0.6), then to (−0.6, −0.6): two far-apart points with the same label. What do h1 and h2 do? They swap signs, so the output unit has to learn a separate rule for each corner They change by as much as the inputs did, so the output unit sees two distant clusters to handle Both points land near the same values, so the output unit can treat them alike with one rule They both drop to zero, because these corners lie on the first-layer lines The trained hidden layer rewrites the input: both label-0 clusters land near the same corner of the (h1, h2) space, while the two label-1 clusters land in other corners. In that rewritten space one straight line separates the classes, and that line is the output unit. A hidden layer helps because it moves points into a layout the next layer finds easy, not because it labels them.
documents.title: At the defaults, set Probe x₁ and Probe x₂ to (0.6, 0.6), then to (−0.6, −0.6): two far-apart points with the same label. What do h1 and h2 do?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Stacking neurons · question 4
documents.body: Set Hidden activation to none (linear) and train XOR with 3 hidden layers of 6 neurons. What happens, and why? Accuracy stays at chance and Training loss stays at 0.693, because the stacked layers compose into one linear map Accuracy still reaches 100%, only more slowly, because 18 neurons give far more capacity than 2 Training blows up, because every extra linear layer multiplies the signal until the loss grows without any bound Only depth is wasted: with 6 neurons per layer the extra width still carves enough cuts to reach 100% here W₂(W₁x + b₁) + b₂ is still one affine map, so a linear stack draws one straight boundary however deep or wide it is. The loss stays at 0.693 = ln 2, the value for answering 0.5 for every point. The activation is what lets one layer's output be a bent function of the input, so width and depth both add nothing without it.
documents.title: Set Hidden activation to none (linear) and train XOR with 3 hidden layers of 6 neurons. What happens, and why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Stacking neurons · question 5
documents.body: Set Dataset to Checkerboard, Hidden activation to tanh, and Training epochs to 300. In Depth against width the two networks have the same number of parameters. What do you see? Two layers of 7 fit most of the board while one layer of 21 stays near chance, with the same budget Both fit about equally well, because any two networks with the same parameter count have the same capacity One layer of 21 fits better, because a single wide layer holds more detectors than two narrow layers can Neither learns anything, because a checkerboard needs far more than 85 parameters for any network to fit it Both networks have 85 parameters. At seed 2 the one-layer network ends at 56.3% and the two-layer network at 87.5%; across seeds 1 to 6 the first never passes 58% and the second never falls below 81%. The lab cannot say whether the wide layer could ever fit the board, only that in 300 epochs of this optimizer it does not, while the stacked layers do.
documents.title: Set Dataset to Checkerboard, Hidden activation to tanh, and Training epochs to 300. In Depth against width the two networks have the same number of parameters. What do you see?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Stacking neurons · question 6
documents.body: Which claim about the checkerboard result does the lab itself support? With tanh and 300 epochs two layers beat one wide layer of equal size, but with ReLU the wide layer ties or wins Depth beats width at any equal size, because stacking layers always adds more than adding units to one layer does A single layer of 21 tanh units cannot represent a checkerboard, so no amount of training could ever make it fit Depth wins on every dataset in the lab, because XOR and the ring also pull the two shapes apart by accuracy here On XOR and the ring both shapes reach 100% on every seed, so there is no depth advantage there. On the checkerboard with tanh the stacked network wins, but switch Hidden activation to ReLU and the one-layer network fits at 86% to 100% across seeds 1 to 6. The advantage belongs to this task, activation, and training budget. It is not a law, and the lab does not show that a wide layer is unable to represent the board.
documents.title: Which claim about the checkerboard result does the lab itself support?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Stacking neurons · question 7
documents.body: In Held-out data with Training labels at 20% flipped and Training epochs at 300, the large network scores far higher on the training points than on the held-out points. What does that gap show? It has fit some flipped labels, which do not repeat on new points, so training accuracy overstates what it learned The held-out points are harder than the training points, so every network scores lower on them whatever it learned It learned the ring better than the narrow network, because more units find the pattern in noisy labels more reliably Training corrected the flipped labels, so the training points became easier than the held-out points for the network A label that is wrong in training tells the network nothing about new points. The large network has the capacity to bend around those points, so its training accuracy climbs while its held-out accuracy and loss get worse; at seeds 1 to 6 the gap is at least 15 points, against 7 or fewer for the narrow network. Training accuracy alone would have hidden this, which is what the held-out points are for.
documents.title: In Held-out data with Training labels at 20% flipped and Training epochs at 300, the large network scores far higher on the training points than on the held-out points. What does that gap show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Stacking neurons · question 8
documents.body: Switch Training labels to Clean. What happens to the gap between the large network's training and held-out accuracy at epoch 300? It nearly vanishes, because with clean labels everything the network fits also holds on new ring points It gets larger, because a bigger network always memorizes its training points whatever the labels say about them It stays the same, because the gap comes from the network's size and not from the labels it trains on It reverses, because clean labels make the held-out points easier than the training points it sees With clean labels the large network reaches 100% on both the training and the held-out ring points at seeds 1 to 6, so the gap is zero. Capacity alone does not overfit: it needs something in the training set that will not repeat, such as wrong labels. That is why the gap grows only once 12 of the 60 labels are flipped.
documents.title: Switch Training labels to Clean. What happens to the gap between the large network's training and held-out accuracy at epoch 300?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Stacking neurons
documents.body: In the last lab you worked with a single artificial neuron, which multiplies each input by a dial setting and adds up the results. However you set its dials, it can only ever draw one straight line between "yes" and "no". This module connects many of those neurons, some side by side and some one after another, so that together they form a small neural network. The big question is how a team of these simple parts can draw shapes that no single part can, such as a bent boundary or a closed ring. The module also asks when adding more parts helps, and when it quietly makes things worse. Where it shows up Stacking layers of neurons is the basic plan behind the models in the rest of this course. Models that work with pictures and models that work with language both pass their input through many layers, each building on what the one before it produced. Even the transformer block, which later labs build on, is a stack of layers with some extra structure added. Why it matters Without stacking, a network would be stuck drawing one straight line, which sounds like a small limit until you meet a puzzle like XOR. XOR has four clumps of dots, one near each corner of a square, yet a single neuron can sort at most 3 of the 4 correctly. Two more lessons sit inside this one, and the first is that stacking only helps if each layer bends its numbers before passing them on. Without that bend, a hundred layers collapse into one plain multiply-and-add, which can never do better than a single straight line. The second is that bigger is not automatically better, since a large network can memorize mistakes in its practice data, which you only catch by testing it on fresh examples. What you will be able to explain By the end of this module you should be able to explain: how adding neurons to a layer lets a network draw more complicated shapes; a real case in this lab where two narrow layers beat one wide layer that has exactly the same number of dials; what a hidden layer hands to the next one, which is a new description of each input; why the bend between layers has to be there for extra layers to add anything at all; how comparing a network's score on its practice dots with its score on fresh dots tells memorizing mistakes apart from learning the real pattern. What the lab shows The lab trains a real, tiny network right in front of you, and it trains a new one every time you change the network's shape. Every color, score and curve you see is measured from that training, not drawn by hand. The data, on the other hand, is made up: three fixed sets of dots on a square, called XOR, Ring and Checkerboard, with 48 to 64 dots in each. Each of the lab's five cards shows a different side of the experiment: Decision surface colors every spot on the square by the network's answer, so you can see the shape it has drawn. Network training controls let you pick the puzzle and the network's shape, then train it and replay the training round by round. Network builder shows each neuron's own map of the square, and the numbers flowing through the network at one point you choose. Depth against width trains two networks with the same number of dials side by side, one wide and one deep. Held-out data scores two networks on fresh dots they never practiced on, and lets you flip the labels on some practice dots to see which network memorizes them.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Stacking neurons
documents.body: One neuron, one straight line Start with a quick reminder of how a single neuron works on this lab's square of dots. Each dot is described by two numbers: x₁ says how far left or right it sits, and x₂ says how far up or down. Both numbers run from −1 to 1, so the middle of the square is the point (0, 0). A neuron multiplies x₁ and x₂ by its own dial settings, called weights, adds them, and then adds one more fixed nudge called a bias. It then passes that total through an activation, a small rule that reshapes the number before handing it on. Every spot where the total comes out exactly zero lies on one straight line across the square. On one side of that line the total is positive, leaning "yes", and on the other side it is negative, leaning "no". However you set the dials, one neuron gives you one straight cut. Three puzzles made of dots Every dot in the lab has a label, 1 or 0, which you can read as "yes" or "no". On the Decision surface, filled circles are label 1 and open squares are label 0. The network's job is to color the square so that each dot sits on the side that matches its label. The background is shaded by the network's answer: green where it leans toward "yes", red where it leans toward "no", and pale where it is unsure. A dot the network gets wrong has a red ring drawn around it. The Dataset control offers three sets of dots, each laid out so that no single straight line can split it: XOR has 48 dots in four clumps of 12, with one clump near each corner of the square. A dot is "yes" when exactly one of its two numbers is positive, so the two yes clumps sit diagonally across from each other. Ring has 24 "yes" dots packed into a small disc in the middle, and 36 "no" dots in a band around them. Checkerboard splits the square into a 4 × 4 grid of small squares that alternate between yes and no, with 4 dots in each, so 64 in all. The name XOR is short for "exclusive or", which is the kind of "or" on a menu that says a meal comes with soup or salad. You get one or the other, but not both and not neither. In the XOR puzzle, "x₁ is positive" and "x₂ is positive" play the parts of soup and salad, so the yes clumps are the top-left and bottom-right corners. A hidden layer: neurons side by side Now put several neurons side by side and give them the same two inputs, while each one keeps its own dial settings: that group is a hidden layer. Each neuron in it draws its own straight line, which shows up on the Decision surface as a dashed line. The lines are labeled h1, h2 and so on, where the h stands for hidden. The layer is called hidden because you never read its outputs as the answer. Its numbers go to the next layer instead, and at the very end one more neuron, the output neuron, turns them into the network's answer. That answer is written ŷ, said "y-hat", and it is always a number between 0 and 1: near 1 means "yes" and near 0 means "no". A dot counts as correct when ŷ lands on its label's side of 0.5, so a "yes" dot needs an answer of at least 0.5. An assembly line of neurons Picture a network as an assembly line in a furniture workshop, where logs come in at one end and a chair comes out at the other. The first station turns logs into planks, the next turns planks into frames, and the last turns frames into a chair. The plank station never makes a chair, and nobody there is told about chairs, because its job is to hand the next station better raw material. In a network, each station is a layer and each worker is a neuron, which gives two separate ways to grow: Making a layer wider adds more workers at the same station, and in the lab you do that with Neurons per layer, from 1 to 6. Making the network deeper adds more stations, each building on what the last one made, and in the lab you do that with Hidden layers, from 1 to 3. These two numbers, how many neurons sit in each layer and how many layers there are, are the network's width and depth. The picture gets one thing right: each station only hands its work forward, and the whole line is judged by the finished chair. It gets one important thing backwards, though. A real plank station is told to make planks, but a hidden neuron is told nothing at all about what to make. Its dials are tuned only by how good the final answer turns out to be, so whatever in-between material it ends up producing is whatever happened to help. The picture gets a few more things wrong, which "Where it breaks" comes back to. Capacity: what a network could draw More workers at one station means more straight cuts for the next station to combine. How complicated a shape a network could draw is called its capacity, and it is set mainly by width and depth. The Ring puzzle shows this clearly, because two neurons give the output neuron only two straight lines to work with. Two crossing lines make an X, and the space between two arms of an X is a wedge that stays open at its far end. In the lab the two lines may meet outside the square, so you see a funnel rather than an X, but it is still open on one side. Two lines can fence off a wedge but never a closed area. So with the Ring chosen and the other settings left at their starting values, the network gets 86.7% of the dots right and stops there. A third neuron adds a third line, and three lines can form a triangle that walls in the middle disc on every side, so the score climbs to 100%. Counting the dials Every number that training can adjust is called a parameter, and the Parameters readout counts them for you. That total is the network's parameter count, and you can work it out by hand. Each neuron has one weight for every number it reads, plus one bias of its own. Here is the count for the lab's starting network, which has one hidden layer of two neurons: Each hidden neuron reads x₁ and x₂, so it has 2 weights, one for each input, plus a bias, which makes 3 dials. Since there are two hidden neurons, together they hold 6 of the network's dials. The output neuron reads the two hidden numbers and has its own bias, which adds 3 more. That makes 9 in total, which is exactly the number the Parameters readout shows at the start. With 3 hidden layers of 6 neurons, the count climbs all the way to 109. That is because every neuron in a later layer reads all six neurons of the layer before it, so each one carries 7 dials. Layer by layer, the count goes like this: The first hidden layer has 6 neurons with 3 dials each, which makes 18. The second and third hidden layers each have 6 neurons with 7 dials each, which makes 42 apiece. The output neuron reads 6 numbers and adds a bias, which makes 7. Adding 18, 42, 42 and 7 gives 109. Between two layers of 6, every neuron reads every neuron before it, so 6 × 6 = 36 weights sit between them. Make both layers 12 wide and that becomes 144, four times as many, which is why width drives most of the total. Representation: a new description of each dot Now for the central idea of the module: the list of numbers a layer hands forward, one from each neuron, is that layer's representation of the input. A representation is not an answer, but a new description of the dot, written in a form the next layer finds more useful. At the lab's starting settings, the hidden layer has two neurons using tanh, an activation that keeps every output between −1 and 1. That gives each dot two new numbers, h1 and h2, and here is where the four XOR corners end up after training: The "no" dot at the top right, (0.6, 0.6), becomes about (1, 1). The "no" dot at the bottom left, (−0.6, −0.6), also becomes about (1, 1). The "yes" dot at the top left, (−0.6, 0.6), becomes about (1, −1). The "yes" dot at the bottom right, (0.6, −0.6), becomes about (−1, 1). Look at what happened to the two "no" corners, which sat at opposite ends of a diagonal on the original square. In the new description they land almost on top of each other, while each "yes" dot gets one number close to −1. Now add up each dot's two new numbers. Both "no" corners give about 1 + 1 = 2, while both "yes" corners give about 1 + (−1) = 0. So the output neuron only needs one cut somewhere between 0 and 2. After training, it says "yes" when h1 + h2 comes out below about 0.9, a value set by its own dials, which the next section reads. If you drew h1 and h2 as a new square, every spot where h1 + h2 equals 0.9 would sit on one straight line. Among the four corners, a sum that small only happens when one of the two numbers is near −1. That is true for both yes dots and for neither no dot. This is the whole trick behind solving XOR, and it shows that the hidden layer never answers the question itself. Instead, it moves the dots into a new layout where the output neuron's one straight line is enough. Reading the output neuron's sum Network builder prints this last step as a formula, in the row called "Output unit at the probe". The probe is a point you place with Probe x₁ and Probe x₂, and it starts at the bottom-right corner, (0.6, −0.6). The lab starts at seed 2 and epoch 150. The seed picks which random starting dials the network gets, and the epoch counts how many rounds of training it has had so far. "What training does here" explains both more fully. At those starting settings, the row reads ŷ = σ((−6.39)·(−1.00) + (−6.36)·1.00 + 5.74). If you have already changed things, press Reset interactive to get back to that starting point. In each product, the first number is one of the output neuron's weights and the second is h1 or h2 at the probe, while 5.74 is the output neuron's bias. The σ, a Greek letter called sigma, stands for the sigmoid from the last lab, which squashes any total into a number between 0 and 1. Big positive totals come out near 1 and big negative ones near 0. Here is the sum at the starting probe, step by step: The first product, −6.39 times −1.00, is +6.39, because a negative times a negative is positive. The second product, −6.36 times 1.00, is −6.36, since multiplying by 1 changes nothing. Those two nearly cancel, so the total, which the lab calls z, lands close to the bias. The lab shows z = 5.73 because it adds up the exact values, not the rounded ones printed in the row. The sigmoid turns 5.73 into 0.997, which is very close to 1, so the answer is "yes". Now move Probe x₂ up to 0.6, so the probe sits on the top-right "no" corner. Both hidden numbers are now close to 1, so the products come out at about −6.2 and −6.3, and together they outweigh the bias. The total z drops to about −6.8, and the sigmoid turns that into 0.001, a clear "no". Working out an answer this way, layer by layer from the inputs to ŷ, is called the forward pass. The number under each tile in Network builder is one step of it, read at the probe. The bend between layers Every hidden neuron passes its total through an activation before handing it on, and the Hidden activation control offers three choices: tanh squashes any total into a number between −1 and 1, passing small totals through almost unchanged and flattening big ones. A total of 3, for example, comes out as about 0.995. ReLU keeps a positive total as it is and turns any negative total into 0. none (linear) passes the total through untouched, so the neuron only multiplies and adds. Drawn as a graph, neither tanh nor ReLU is a straight line. For ReLU, the inputs −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2 give 0, 0, 0, 1 and 2. Plot those points and you get a flat line along the bottom that turns a corner at 0 and then climbs. That corner is the bend, and tanh has a smooth version of it, flattening out at both ends. An activation that bends like that is called a nonlinearity, and stacking only pays off because of it. To see why, picture a friend who doubles a cookie recipe for a party, and a second friend who then triples that doubled batch. Together they have multiplied the original by 6, which one person could have done in a single step. Layers without a bend behave the same way, because each one only multiplies and adds. Now try it with actual numbers: say one layer doubles its input and adds 1, and the next layer triples the result and subtracts 4. Feed in 5, and the first layer turns it into 11, which the second layer turns into 29. But multiplying 5 by 6 and subtracting 1 also gives 29, and that shortcut works for every input you try. So however many multiply-and-add layers you stack, they collapse into a single multiply-and-add, which can only ever draw a single straight line. A bend breaks the shortcut, and you can check this with ReLU between two layers. Feed in −2, 0 and 2, and ReLU turns them into 0, 0 and 2. Any single multiply-and-add, graphed, is a straight line, and no straight line passes through all three of these results. It would have to stay flat at 0 for −2 and for 0, and then rise to 2 at 2. That corner is something no multiply-and-add can copy, so the next layer receives something genuinely new to work with. That is what lets each new layer add something the last one could not. A stack with no bend at all actually does worse on XOR than a single tanh neuron. One tanh neuron can still sort 3 of the 4 clumps, because it flattens out and can say a firm "no" on one side of its line. A plain multiply-and-add never flattens out, so its total keeps changing at the same steady rate across the whole square. Since the two "yes" corners sit opposite each other, any tilt that pushes one of them toward "yes" pushes the other one just as far toward "no". Those pushes cancel out, so the best training can do is answer 0.5 everywhere, which scores 50%. What training does here The network starts with random dial settings, called its initialization. Each random start has a number, called its seed, so the same seed always gives the same start. The note under the loss chart shows which seed you are on. Each press of New initialization moves to the next seed and so draws a fresh random start. From there, training repeats one loop: measure how badly the network misses on the practice dots, then nudge every dial a little to shrink that miss. The miss score is the Training loss, which this lab measures with binary cross-entropy, a score for yes-or-no answers that punishes confident wrong answers heavily. A network that shrugs and answers 0.5 for every dot gets a loss of 0.693. That is why the loss chart has a dotted line marked "0.693 = always 50%". Nudging every dial in the direction that lowers the loss is called gradient descent. This lab adds momentum, which lets the nudges build up speed while they keep pointing the same way. One full round of practice over all the dots is an epoch, and here every epoch is exactly one nudge of every dial. Working out how far each dial should move is the job of backpropagation, which runs backward through the same layers after the forward pass. You do not need the details of any of these yet, because the next two labs, Loss & gradient descent and Backpropagation, take them apart. For now, read training as nudging every dial to shrink one miss number. Each run lasts 300 epochs, and the lab keeps the dials from every one of them, so the Training epochs slider replays the run instead of training again. Dragging it to 0 shows the random start, and dragging it to 300 shows the end. Two cards that run extra networks Two more cards train networks of their own beside the main one, and each is built to answer one question. Depth against width uses the same puzzle, activation and seed as the main controls, and compares two shapes with the same budget of 85 dials. One has a single hidden layer of 21 neurons, and the other has two hidden layers of 7 each, which you can count the same way as before: One wide layer: each of the 21 neurons has 3 dials, which makes 63. The output neuron reads all 21 numbers and has a bias, which adds 22, for a total of 85. Two narrow layers: the first 7 neurons have 3 dials each, which makes 21. Each neuron in the second layer reads all 7 numbers from the first layer and has a bias, so it has 8 dials, and seven such neurons make 56. The output neuron adds 8 more, for a total of 85. Since the size is the same, any difference between the two comes from shape alone. Held-out data asks a different question: did the network learn the pattern, or did it memorize its practice dots? It trains two networks on the Ring's 60 dots, then scores them on 120 fresh ring dots that they never practice on. One is a narrow network with a single hidden layer of 3 neurons, which has 13 dials. The other is a large network with two hidden layers of 6 neurons, which has 67 dials, so it is bigger in both width and depth. Dots kept out of training like this are called held-out data, because they are held back from practice. On the card, the practice dots are called training points and the fresh dots are called held-out points. The card can also flip the labels on 12 of the 60 practice dots, turning some "yes" dots into "no" and the other way around. Those flipped labels, 20% of the practice set, are called label noise, and since they do not repeat in the fresh dots, memorizing them gains nothing. When a network fits its practice dots so closely that it copies their mistakes too, and so does worse on fresh dots, that is called overfitting. Picture a classmate who studies for a quiz from a practice sheet where a few answers in the key were misprinted. If they memorize the sheet word for word, misprints included, they ace the sheet, but on the real quiz the misprints are useless or worse. A classmate who learns the method instead answers the misprinted questions correctly, so the sheet's key marks them wrong. They score a little lower on the sheet but just as well on the quiz. The memorizer is the one whose sheet score is much higher than their quiz score, so the gap between the two scores is what gives them away. In a network, memorizing a flipped label means curving the boundary around that one dot. The curve then gets nearby fresh dots wrong, because their labels follow the real ring.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Stacking neurons
documents.body: The puzzle one neuron could not solve The single neuron lab ended on XOR, whose "yes" clumps sit in opposite corners, top left and bottom right, while the "no" clumps fill the other two. Try placing one straight line across the square so that both yes corners fall on the same side. Wherever you put it, at least one "no" corner lands on that side too, so the best one line can do is 3 clumps out of 4. You can watch this happen here: with Neurons per layer at 1, the network stalls at 75%, which is 3 clumps out of 4. Stacking more layers after that one neuron does not help, because Neurons per layer sets every layer to 1. Each later layer only reshapes that same single number again, which can never turn the one straight cut into a bend. Nobody tells the hidden neurons what to look for Look again at the trained XOR network at the starting settings, where h1 is negative only on the bottom-right side of its dashed line. That side holds only one clump of dots, the bottom-right "yes" clump. In the same way, h2 is negative only on the top-left side of its line, which holds only the top-left yes clump. You could call h1 a "bottom-right corner" detector, though that name is only a story people put on it. Its tile in Network builder shows what it actually does across the whole square. Nobody wrote those jobs into the network, since the dials started out random and the only pressure on them was that the final answer be right. A pair of corner detectors happened to make the final answer right, so that is where training ended up, unlike a real workshop, where someone decides each station's job. This is what people mean when they say a network learns its own features: useful in-between quantities that nobody asked for by name. A different random start can split the work differently, and some starts never find a good split at all. With two neurons on XOR, one press of New initialization takes you from seed 2 to seed 3. That start ends at 68.8% after 300 epochs, even though a perfect answer exists. The note under the chart says its best was 75%, a score it reached early on before slipping lower. That is worse than a single neuron's 75%, which seems strange at first. Training works to lower the miss score, not to raise the number of dots it gets right. From this start, lowering the miss score meant becoming more sure about most dots while giving up a few. The two lines settled in an unhelpful place, and training had no way to climb back out. Why both width and depth matter A wider layer gives the next layer more straight cuts to combine, which is how three neurons close the Ring. A deeper network lets later layers combine the shapes that earlier layers made, rather than only straight cuts. That lets their boundaries bend in ways that one layer would need many more straight cuts to copy. The Checkerboard gives one way to picture this, though the lab does not prove it is what the trained network does. On a checkerboard, the answer flips every time you step one square across or one square up, which makes it like XOR repeated all over the board. A first layer could draw straight cuts along the grid lines. A second layer could then combine those cuts to keep track of the flips, the same way the XOR network's output neuron combined h1 and h2. One wide layer has to do all of that in a single step, with nothing but straight cuts to combine. With tanh, training in this lab did not manage that. Which one helps more at the same size depends on the puzzle, the activation, and how long training runs. The Checkerboard in Depth against width is the one place in this lab where the two shapes come apart. There, depth wins clearly with tanh, while with ReLU the wide layer ties or wins. The same plan in bigger models Every later design in this course answers the question "what should the layers be?", including the transformer block that later labs build on. That block is a small stack of layers with extra structure: one part mixes information between the words in a text, and another reworks each word on its own. Underneath that extra structure, the stacking works the same way as in this lab. Checking on fresh dots This is also the first lab in the course that scores a network on dots it never practiced on. That habit matters because a score on practice dots can look perfect while hiding memorized mistakes, and later labs, starting with Training dynamics, build on it.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Stacking neurons
documents.body: The numbers below come from the lab's starting seed, which is 2, and the note under the loss chart always tells you which seed you are on. After a press of New initialization your exact numbers will differ, and a few runs may get stuck. Reset interactive always takes you back to the starting settings. Solve XOR Try this: With Hidden layers at 1, set Neurons per layer to 1, and the network scores 75% and stalls, because one neuron gives one straight cut. Now set it to 2: two dashed lines, h1 and h2, appear on the Decision surface, and the red band between them catches both "no" clumps. Every dot is on the correct side from epoch 28 onward, which the green dashed line on the loss chart marks. Next, drag Training epochs to 0 to see the random start, where only about half the dots are right. Then press Train 50 epochs a few times and watch the loss fall while the boundary forms. Press New initialization a few times as well, since each press draws a new random start and sends you back to epoch 0. Train each one forward, and you will find that some starts get stuck below 100%. Look inside If you pressed New initialization above, press Reset interactive first to get back to seed 2 at epoch 150. With one hidden layer of two neurons, move Probe x₁ and Probe x₂ to each XOR corner in turn, such as (0.6, 0.6) and then (−0.6, −0.6). Read h1 and h2 under the tiles in Network builder, where, at the starting seed, both "no" corners should give numbers near 1 for both neurons. Then raise Hidden layers to 2 and compare the columns of tiles, where each tile shows one neuron's number over the whole square. Look for how the tiles in the second column differ from the ones in the first. Remove the bend Set Hidden activation to none (linear), then try any mix of Hidden layers and Neurons per layer, even 3 layers of 6. Keep an eye on the Accuracy readout and the Training loss as you change them. Need more width Set Dataset to Ring, put Hidden activation back to tanh, and set Hidden layers to 1. Compare 2 neurons per layer with 3, and watch whether the green "yes" area closes around the middle disc. Match the size Set Dataset to Checkerboard, keep tanh, and drag Training epochs to 300. Then, in Depth against width, compare one layer of 21 neurons with two layers of 7, which both have 85 dials. Next, switch Hidden activation to ReLU and press New initialization a few times. Each press resets Training epochs to 0, so drag it back to 300, or read the chart's legend, which always gives each network's score at epoch 300. Hold data out On Network training controls, drag Training epochs to 300. Then, in Held-out data, switch Training labels between Clean and 20% flipped. Then set Curves to Loss and watch the large network's dashed line, which tracks the fresh dots while the solid line tracks the practice dots.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Stacking neurons
documents.body: Each tile in Network builder is one neuron's view of the whole square, shaded green where its number is positive and red where it is negative with tanh. First-layer tiles are always split by one straight edge, because those neurons read x₁ and x₂ directly. Second-layer tiles can have curved edges, because they read the already-bent outputs of the first layer. At the starting settings, the hidden layer moves both "no" corners to about (1, 1), so one straight rule can separate them from the "yes" corners. You can check every corner yourself by moving the probe and reading h1 and h2. With none (linear), adding layers or neurons stops helping, and XOR stays at 50%, the score of guessing at random (often called chance), however big you make the network. The loss sits at 0.693, the score for answering 0.5 everywhere. The stacked layers collapse into one multiply-and-add with no flat part, and on XOR no tilt beats answering 0.5. On Ring, two neurons carve a wedge and reach 86.7%, while a third neuron closes the circle and gets every dot right from epoch 74 onward. Width also changes what training manages to find, because with two neurons on XOR some starts get stuck. With three or more neurons, every seed from 1 to 6 solves it. On the Checkerboard with tanh, the two narrow layers beat the one wide layer at every seed from 1 to 6. At the starting seed, the two narrow layers finish at 87.5% while the wide one stops at 56.3%. With ReLU, though, the one wide layer does at least as well as the two narrow ones, so the winner depends on the activation. The badge at the top of Depth against width shows "two layers minus one layer" in percentage points, which means the plain difference between the two scores. With tanh at the starting seed and Training epochs at 300, it reads about 31 points in favor of the two layers. Adding layers in the main controls also adds dials, so it is not a fair test of depth. At the starting seed on the Checkerboard, three layers of six neurons beat one layer of six, but they also carry more than four times as many dials. With Clean labels, both networks score about the same on fresh dots as on practice dots, so the Gap readout sits near zero. With 20% flipped, the large network scores 96.7% on its practice dots but only 79.2% on fresh ones. The narrow network scores 90.0% and 91.7%, so its two scores stay close. A network that followed only the true ring could score at most 80% on these flipped practice dots, since 12 of the 60 labels are wrong. The narrow network's 90% means it has fitted some mistakes too, but with only three straight cuts it cannot curve far, so its score on fresh dots holds up. Across the first six seeds, the large network's gap is always at least 15 points, while the narrow network's never passes 7. With Curves on Loss and labels flipped, the large network's training loss keeps falling, down to 0.07. Its held-out loss, though, bottoms out near 0.28 around epoch 71. After that it climbs all the way to 0.99, a rise the training loss alone would never show you.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Stacking neurons
documents.body: What this lab simplifies The main network is tiny, with two inputs, at most 64 practice dots, and at most 3 layers of 6 neurons. Even the biggest network anywhere in the lab has only 109 dials. The Decision surface can only be drawn because there are two inputs, while a real model reads far more numbers at once than any flat picture can show. Training always uses the same size of nudge, called the learning rate, with the same momentum, for 300 epochs. Different settings would change which random starts succeed and how quickly they get there. The Decision surface and Network training controls score only the practice dots, so a 100% there says nothing about how the network would do on new dots. Held-out data is the only card that uses fresh dots, and it works only on the Ring, always with tanh neurons. It also flips the same 12 labels every time, and flipping a different 12 would change how big the gap is. Depth against width has only one puzzle where the two shapes come apart. Depth wins there only with tanh, within 300 epochs, and a longer run might close the gap. With ReLU the result flips at some seeds, where the wide layer wins by up to 31 points, so read it as one case, not a rule. That card also does not prove that one wide layer is unable to draw a checkerboard, only that this training method, in this much time, did not find a way. Stacking layers after a single neuron adds nothing here, because Neurons per layer sets every layer to 1. Each later layer only reshapes the same single number again, so the cut stays one straight line. The dots are made up and fixed, and the fresh dots come from the same made-up ring as the practice dots, with every label correct. Real fresh data may have wrong labels too, and may not look like the data a model practiced on. Where real networks struggle The assembly-line picture is too tidy, because workers on a real line each have one clear job. Real hidden neurons are messier: one neuron often responds to several unrelated things at once, and a single idea is usually spread across many neurons. That spreading is called a distributed representation, and it is why a single hidden neuron rarely has a clean human label. The XOR network's neat corner detectors are the exception that a tiny toy allows, and the interpretability labs take up the harder real case. More capacity does not mean more learning, because past a point a network starts fitting the noise in its practice data, as the large network does on Held-out data. A held-out set also stops being held out once you use it again and again to choose between models, because your choices slowly start to fit it too. Picture checking dozens of study methods against the same practice quiz and keeping whichever scores best. In the end you have picked the method that suits that one quiz, not one that works on any quiz. Deep stacks bring a training problem too, because backpropagation works out each dial's share of the blame by passing it backward through every layer. In a deep stack, that blame signal can fade away or blow up on its way back. In the Backpropagation lab's Gradient flow card, twelve sigmoid layers with sensible starting dials leave the first layer's nudges millions of times weaker than the last layer's. Very deep stacks were hard to train until extra design pieces, called normalization and residual connections, became standard. A common mix-up: Bigger is not reliably better, and adding layers is no exception. On Held-out data, the large network has both more layers and more dials. With flipped labels, it memorizes more of the mistakes and does worse on fresh dots than the narrow one. Adding layers also does not rescue a bad start. With two neurons per layer on XOR, seed 3 gets stuck whether there is one hidden layer or two, even though a perfect answer exists. And very deep stacks bring the fading-blame problem above, which makes them harder to train at all.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Stacking neurons
documents.body: A mathematical result called universal approximation says that one hidden layer, made wide enough and given a bend like tanh, can copy any shape that has no sudden jumps. The copy can be as close as you like, as long as you stay within a limited area of inputs. The result is true but not very useful in practice, because it says nothing about how wide the layer must be. It also says nothing about whether training will ever find the right dials, and the Checkerboard with tanh may be a small example of that second gap. The lab does not show that one wide tanh layer is unable to draw the board, only that this training method did not find a way in 300 epochs. With ReLU, though, the same 21-neuron layer gets 86% to 100% of the board across seeds 1 to 6. That hints that the hard part is finding the dials rather than having too few. Depth is often the practical shortcut, because later layers reuse what earlier layers built. For many shapes, a deep network needs far fewer neurons than a shallow one would, and the Checkerboard card is one small case of this, with the limits above. That reuse is why the layers of big models tend to form a progression from simple to complex, called a feature hierarchy. In image models, early layers react to edges and later ones to parts of objects. In language models, early layers handle surface form, meaning the exact words and how they look, later ones the grammar, and later still the structure of the task. Some layer designs go further, sharing or routing their dials in special ways: A convolution layer slides one small set of dials across every position of its input, reusing the same dials everywhere. A recurrent layer reuses one layer again and again, once at each step of a sequence. A mixture-of-experts layer sends each token, a small piece of text, to only a few of its many smaller layers. The next lab, Loss & gradient descent, opens up the training step that this lab ran for you.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Stacking neurons
documents.body: *A single neuron* showed one unit splitting its input with one straight boundary. This module stacks units: side by side in a hidden layer, all reading the same inputs with their own weights, and layer on layer, each reading the one before. Width is the number of units in a layer; depth is the number of hidden layers. The question is what a stack can compute that one neuron cannot. Each hidden layer rewrites its input into a representation, a vector the next layer finds easier to use, and a nonlinear activation keeps the stack from collapsing into one affine map, a linear map plus a constant. The module also asks whether the shape of a fixed parameter budget matters, and how to tell learning a pattern from memorizing labels. Where it shows up Every later architecture answers "what should the layers be?" A transformer block is a hidden layer with structure: one sublayer mixes information across positions, one transforms each position independently. Convolutional, recurrent, and mixture-of-experts layers are hidden layers that share or route their weights. Feature hierarchies form across depth: edges then object parts in vision models, surface form then syntax in language models. Interpretability has to work with distributed representations: a hidden vector spreads its encoding across many units, so single units rarely mean one clean concept. Why it matters One neuron gives one straight cut, so XOR, where each class holds one diagonal's pair of opposite corners, is out of reach. A hidden layer lets the next unit combine several cuts into a bent boundary, but only through a nonlinearity: without one, linear layers compose into one affine map however many you stack. Capacity, how complex a function a network can express, cuts both ways. Given enough epochs, a large network can fit wrong training labels along with the pattern, and training accuracy alone cannot tell memorized labels from a learned pattern. What you will be able to explain How width limits what one hidden layer can express and find, and a measured task where depth beats width at the same parameter count. What a hidden representation is, and how a trained hidden layer moves XOR's points so one straight line separates them. Why depth adds nothing without a nonlinearity between layers. How comparing training and held-out accuracy separates memorized noisy labels from a learned pattern. What the lab shows A two-input network trains in the app for 300 epochs of full-batch gradient descent with momentum. Every accuracy and loss on every card is measured from real training on small, fixed synthetic datasets; the lab's seed, which New initialization changes, sets only the starting weights. Accuracy is on training points everywhere except Held-out data. Network training controls: Dataset, Hidden activation (tanh, ReLU, none (linear)), Hidden layers, Neurons per layer, Training epochs (replays the saved run), Train 50 epochs, and New initialization. Decision surface and Network builder: the output across the input square, and one tile per unit, with Probe x₁ and Probe x₂ tracing the forward pass at one point. Depth against width: two fixed 85-parameter shapes, one wide and one deep. Held-out data: a narrow and a large network trained on the Ring and scored on 120 points they never train on, with Training labels set to Clean or 20% flipped and Curves set to Accuracy or Loss; these networks always use tanh units. The key experiment: on Checkerboard with tanh and 300 epochs, two layers of 7 fit most of the board while one layer of 21 stays near chance. Switch to ReLU and the wide network ties or wins, so the result belongs to this task, activation, and training budget, not to depth in general.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Stacking neurons
documents.body: A hidden layer is a set of neurons reading the same inputs in parallel, each with its own weights and bias. A layer of m units over n inputs is h = f(Wx + b), with W of shape [m, n]. Its output vector is the layer's representation: a rewriting of the input that the next layer finds easier to use. What this lab runs A real network: 2 inputs, 1 to 3 hidden layers of 1 to 6 units, and one sigmoid output. It trains by full-batch gradient descent with momentum on mean binary cross-entropy, and every epoch's weights are kept so the Training epochs slider replays the run. Backpropagation is exact and checked against finite differences. Three datasets are available: XOR, Ring, and a 4 × 4 Checkerboard of 64 points. Two more cards train fixed networks beside it. Depth against width compares two shapes with the same number of parameters. Held-out data scores networks on points they never trained on. Those training terms are defined in the glossary and taught in the next labs: Loss & gradient descent covers the loss, the step, and momentum, and Backpropagation covers where each weight's gradient comes from. Until then, read the training step as nudging every weight to lower one loss number. Why the activation is load-bearing Compose two affine maps and you get W₂(W₁x + b₁) + b₂ = W'x + b', still one affine map. Without a nonlinearity, depth buys nothing. In the lab, none (linear) leaves XOR at 50% and the loss at 0.693 = ln 2, the loss of answering 0.5 everywhere, even at 3 layers of 6. How two units solve XOR At the defaults (one layer of 2 tanh units, seed 2) the trained units are h1 = tanh(−4.11x₁ + 4.20x₂ + 1.97) and h2 = tanh(4.46x₁ − 3.82x₂ + 2.79). Both label-0 clusters map near (h1, h2) = (1, 1); the label-1 clusters map to (1.00, −0.97) and (−0.99, 1.00). In that space one line separates them: the output σ(−6.39h1 − 6.36h2 + 5.74) fires only when h1 + h2 is below about 0.9. Depth against width at the same size Width alone solves XOR and Ring, so neither can separate depth from width. The Checkerboard can. Depth against width trains two fixed networks with 85 parameters each: one hidden layer of 21 units, and two hidden layers of 7. With tanh units, at seed 2 and 300 epochs, the one-layer network ends at 56.3% and the two-layer network at 87.5%. Across seeds 1 to 6 the first ends between 46.9% and 57.8%, the second between 81.3% and 100%. On XOR and Ring both shapes reach 100% at every seed. The claim is narrower than it looks. Switch Hidden activation to ReLU and the order turns around: the one-layer network ends between 85.9% and 100%, level with or ahead of the two-layer network (68.8% to 100%) on every seed. Nor does the lab show that one wide layer cannot represent the board. It shows that this optimizer, in 300 epochs, did not find it with tanh units. Held-out data and label noise Every number above is scored on the points the network trained on. Held-out data are points it never trains on. The Held-out data card keeps the Ring's 60 training points and adds 120 fresh ring points. Training labels can be Clean or 20% flipped: 12 of the 60 labels are swapped, the same 12 every time. That is label noise. A narrow network (1 layer of 3 units, 13 parameters) and a large one (2 layers of 6, 67 parameters) train on it. With clean labels both reach 100% on the training points and at least 99% on the held-out points at seeds 1 to 6. With flipped labels, at seed 2 and epoch 300, the large network scores 96.7% on its training points and 79.2% on the held-out points. Its training loss falls to 0.07 while its held-out loss bottoms out near 0.28 at epoch 71 and climbs to 0.99. The narrow network scores 90.0% and 91.7%. Across seeds 1 to 6 the large network's gap between the two is at least 15 points; the narrow network's is at most 7. That gap is overfitting: fitting wrong labels, which do not repeat on new points.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Stacking neurons
documents.body: This is where "learning features" becomes concrete. A single neuron matches one template. A stack discovers intermediate quantities nobody specified, because the only pressure on them is that the final output be correct. It is also where the course first scores a network on points it did not train on, the habit that Training dynamics builds on.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Stacking neurons
documents.body: Set Neurons per layer to 1: XOR stalls at 75%. Set it to 2: the two first-layer lines appear on Decision surface and every point is correct from epoch 28. Drag Training epochs to 0 and press Train 50 epochs to watch the loss fall. Raise Hidden layers and compare tiles in Network builder. Move Probe x₁ and Probe x₂ and read each unit's value. Then try Hidden activation none (linear), New initialization, and Dataset Ring. Set Dataset to Checkerboard and Training epochs to 300. In Depth against width, compare the two 85-parameter networks, then switch Hidden activation to ReLU and press New initialization through a few seeds. In the main controls, try 1, 2, and 3 Hidden layers of 6 neurons: at seed 2 with tanh they end at 54.7%, 93.8%, and 100%, with 25, 67, and 109 parameters. In Held-out data, drag Training epochs to 300 and switch Training labels between Clean and 20% flipped. Set Curves to Loss and watch the dashed held-out curve of the large network turn upward.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Stacking neurons
documents.body: First-layer tiles are always split by one straight edge; second- and third-layer tiles bend. Composition is visible. Width changes what is expressible. On Ring, one layer of 2 units reaches 86.7% at seed 2; 3 units reach 100% from epoch 74. Width also changes what is findable. With 2 units, seeds 1 and 3 stick at 62.5% and 68.8% (loss about 0.35); with 3 or more, seeds 1 to 6 all solve XOR. At the same size the shape can matter. On the Checkerboard with tanh, 2 × 7 beats 1 × 21 at every seed from 1 to 6; with ReLU, 1 × 21 does at least as well. With clean labels the gap between training and held-out accuracy is about zero. With 20% flipped, the large network's training accuracy rises while its held-out accuracy falls behind. Parameters counts n_in × n_out + n_out per layer: 9 at the default, 109 at 3 layers of 6.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Stacking neurons
documents.body: In this lab The network has two inputs, at most 64 training points, a fixed learning rate of 0.5 with momentum 0.9, and 300 epochs. Decision surface and the training controls report training accuracy only. Held-out points are scored only on Held-out data, on the Ring, with tanh units and one fixed set of 12 flipped labels; flipping a different 12 changes the size of the gap. The decision surface is drawable only because there are two inputs. Depth against width has one dataset where the shapes come apart, only with tanh, and only within 300 epochs. A longer run might close the gap, and with ReLU the wide network does. Depth stacked on a one-unit layer does nothing, because every layer after it receives a single number. In real systems More capacity does not reliably mean better results: past a point the network fits noise in its training set, which Held-out data shows and Training dynamics shows with polynomial fits. A held-out set also stops being held out once you use it again and again to choose models. Depth adds an optimization problem as well as expressive power. Gradients multiplied through many layers decay or blow up: in the Backpropagation lab's Gradient flow card, twelve layers of sigmoid units with sensible starting weights leave the first layer's gradient at 1.2e-7 of the last layer's. Plain deep stacks were hard to train until normalization and residual connections became standard. A hidden vector is a distributed representation. Unit 3 rarely means one clean concept; units often respond to several unrelated features, the superposition problem the interpretability labs take up.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Stacking neurons
documents.body: Universal approximation results say one hidden layer of sufficient width, with a non-polynomial activation, can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain. They are existence proofs, silent on width, trainability, and data. For many functions a deep network needs far fewer units than a shallow one, because it reuses intermediate results; the Checkerboard comparison is one small case, with the caveats above. That reuse makes a feature hierarchy possible: edges then object parts in vision models, surface form then syntax then task structure in language models. Specialized layers share or route weights: convolutions reuse a filter across positions, recurrent layers reuse a layer across time, and mixture-of-experts layers send each token to a few of many sublayers. Loss & gradient descent, next, opens up the training step this lab ran for you.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Decision surface · Stacking neurons
documents.body: What the trained network answers, everywhere The network's output ŷ evaluated on a 40 × 40 grid over the input square, with the training points and the straight line each first-layer unit draws. Every shade comes from a real forward pass through the weights at the selected epoch. Background cells shaded by ŷ: green toward 1, red toward 0, pale near 0.5. The axes are x₁ and x₂ from −1 to 1. Training points: filled circles are label 1, open squares label 0. A red ring marks a point whose prediction (ŷ ≥ 0.5 means 1) is wrong. Dashed lines h1 … hN: where each first-layer unit's weighted sum `w·x + b` is zero. Each is a straight line, like the single neuron's boundary. A cross at the probe from Network builder, and a badge with the percentage of training points classified correctly. Each cell centre is fed forward: `h = f(W₁x + b₁)` for every hidden layer, then `ŷ = σ(w·h + c)`. f is tanh, ReLU, or the identity for `none (linear)`. The weights are those after the selected number of epochs of full-batch gradient descent on mean binary cross-entropy (learning rate 0.5, momentum 0.9), starting from Glorot-uniform weights for the chosen seed. Datasets are fixed: XOR is 48 points in four clusters at (±0.6, ±0.6) with the diagonal pair labelled 0; Ring is 24 points inside radius 0.4 labelled 1 and 36 on a band from 0.66 to 0.9 labelled 0; Checkerboard is 64 points, four in the middle half of each cell of a 4 × 4 grid, with the label alternating from cell to cell. Everything on Network training controls changes this picture. `Training epochs` scrubs through the saved run without retraining. `Probe x₁` and `Probe x₂` on Network builder move the cross. At the defaults (one layer of 2 tanh units, seed 2) the two dashed lines run parallel to the diagonal, and the red band between them holds both label-0 clusters. Every point is correct from epoch 28. With `Neurons per layer` at 1 there is a single line and the best the network reaches is 75%: one unit, however deep the stack after it, gives one straight cut. With `Hidden activation` set to `none (linear)`, the shading becomes one faint straight split and accuracy sits at 50%. On Ring, two units can only carve a wedge (86.7% at seed 2); three can enclose the disc. On Checkerboard at seed 2 with tanh, one layer of 6 units ends at 54.7%, two layers of 6 at 93.8%, and three layers of 6 at 100%. Those networks have 25, 67, and 109 parameters, so the fair test of depth against width is the Depth against width card. In this lab: two inputs, at most 64 points, and training accuracy only. This card never scores a point the network did not train on, so 100% here says nothing about generalization; the Held-out data card does that for the Ring. In this lab: only first-layer boundaries are drawn as lines. Deeper units have bent boundaries, which Network builder shows as tiles. In general: real inputs have hundreds or thousands of dimensions, so a decision surface can be drawn only as a slice or a projection.

documents.body: Change the architecture, then train it for real Dataset, hidden activation, depth, width, and a real training run you can scrub through epoch by epoch. `Training loss`, `Accuracy`, and the curve are measured on the training set after each full-batch gradient step. `Dataset` (XOR, Ring, Checkerboard) and `Hidden activation` (tanh, ReLU, none (linear)). `Hidden layers` (1 to 3), `Neurons per layer` (1 to 6), and `Training epochs` (0 to 300). `Train 50 epochs` and `New initialization`, then `Training loss`, `Accuracy`, and `Parameters`. A loss curve for all 300 epochs with a marker at the selected epoch, a dotted line at 0.693, and, when reached, a green dashed line at the first epoch with every point correct. Changing dataset, activation, depth, width, or seed retrains from scratch: 300 epochs of full-batch gradient descent with momentum, `v ← 0.9v − 0.5∇L`, `θ ← θ + v`. The weights after every epoch are kept, so the epoch slider replays the run. The loss is mean binary cross-entropy `−[y ln ŷ + (1−y) ln(1−ŷ)]`. The gradient is exact backpropagation; a unit test checks it against finite differences. `Parameters` is `Σ (n_in × n_out + n_out)` over the layers: 9 for 2 → 2 → 1, 109 for three layers of 6. 0.693 is ln 2, the loss of answering 0.5 for every point. A linear stack on XOR settles exactly there. `New initialization` increments the seed, which redraws the random starting weights and resets to epoch 0. `Neurons per layer`: at 1, XOR stalls at 75% (loss 0.482 at epoch 150). At 2, seed 2 reaches 100% by epoch 28. `Hidden activation`: `none (linear)` at any depth and width leaves XOR at 50% and loss 0.693. `Training epochs` and `Train 50 epochs`: drag to 0 to see the initial random surface (47.9% correct at the default seed), then step forward. `New initialization`: at one layer of 2, seeds 1 and 3 get stuck near 0.35 loss with 62.5% and 68.8% correct. The loss falls steeply then flattens, and a stuck run flattens early, well above zero. More width makes training more reliable here: with 3 or more tanh units per layer, every seed from 1 to 6 solves XOR. Depth trains too: 2 layers of 3 reach 100% by epoch 10 at seed 2. Depth also adds ways to get stuck, which `New initialization` exposes. In this lab: the numbers on this card are training accuracy and training loss. Held-out points are scored only on the Held-out data card, which uses its own fixed networks. In this lab: one fixed learning rate, momentum, and 300 epochs. Other settings would change which seeds succeed and how fast. In general: real networks train on mini-batches with optimizers such as Adam, and deep stacks rely on normalization and residual connections to train at all. The Backpropagation lab's Gradient flow card measures why. In general: universal approximation says one wide enough layer can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain. It proves existence, not that gradient descent will find those weights.

documents.body: Every unit's map of the input, and the forward pass at one point The network drawn as columns of tiles. Each tile shades one unit's output over the whole input square, edges show the real weights, and the numbers under the tiles are the forward pass at the probe. Columns labelled input, hidden 1 … hidden 3, output. The two input tiles are x₁ (left to right) and x₂ (bottom to top). Each hidden tile shades that unit's activation over [−1, 1]²: green for positive, red for negative with tanh or none (linear, scaled to the tile's largest value), and grey for ReLU's zero region. The output tile shades ŷ. Edges from every unit to every unit in the next column. Thickness grows with |w| (capped at |w| = 3); positive weights are solid green, negative weights dashed red. Under each tile, the unit's name and its value at the probe. The small dot inside each tile marks the probe. `Probe x₁`, `Probe x₂`, and a formula row showing the output unit's weighted sum at the probe. Each tile is a 14 × 14 grid of forward passes through the network at the selected epoch. A first-layer tile always has one straight edge between its green and red halves, because it is one neuron reading x₁ and x₂ directly. Later layers read earlier units, so their edges bend. The formula row is the output unit exactly: `ŷ = σ(Σ wᵢ·hᵢ + c)` with the trained weights and the last hidden layer's values at the probe. `Probe x₁` and `Probe x₂` (−1 to 1) move the probe; every value under a tile updates. The architecture and epoch come from Network training controls. At the defaults the hidden layer rewrites the input: both label-0 clusters land near (h1, h2) = (1, 1), while (−0.6, 0.6) lands at (1.00, −0.97) and (0.6, −0.6) at (−0.99, 1.00). In that new space one straight rule separates the classes: the output unit, σ(−6.39·h1 − 6.36·h2 + 5.74), fires only when h1 + h2 is below about 0.9. With three layers, compare columns: first-layer tiles are split by straight lines, later tiles by bent ones. That is composition, visible. In this lab: tiles make each unit legible because there are only two inputs. With real inputs, a unit's response can only be probed, not drawn whole. In this lab: the edge thickness cap hides differences between very large weights; read the formula row for exact values. In general: hidden units rarely have clean single meanings. Individual units often respond to several unrelated features, the superposition problem the interpretability modules take up. In general: specialized layers share or route weights: convolutions reuse one small filter across positions, recurrent layers reuse one layer over time, and mixture-of-experts layers send each token to a few of many sublayers.

Under each surface: `Accuracy`, `Training loss`, and `Parameters` at that epoch. A badge in the heading gives the two-layer network's accuracy minus the one-layer network's, in percentage points. A chart of training accuracy for epochs 0 to 300 for both networks, the one-layer curve dashed, with a guide at the current epoch. The legend prints each curve's accuracy at epoch 300, which is the chart's text alternative. Parameters are `Σ (n_in × n_out + n_out)`: 2 → 21 → 1 is 63 + 22 = 85, and 2 → 7 → 7 → 1 is 21 + 56 + 8 = 85. Each network trains exactly as on Network training controls: full-batch gradient descent, learning rate 0.5, momentum 0.9, Glorot-uniform starting weights (He-uniform for ReLU), 300 epochs. Only the shape differs. The two runs depend on `Dataset`, `Hidden activation`, and the seed, which `New initialization` increments. On XOR and Ring both shapes reach 100% at every seed from 1 to 6, so those datasets cannot tell width from depth. On Checkerboard with tanh the one-layer network ends between 46.9% and 57.8% across seeds 1 to 6 and the two-layer network between 81.3% and 100%. At seed 2 they end at 56.3% and 87.5%. With ReLU the order turns around: the one-layer network ends between 85.9% and 100% and is level with or ahead of the two-layer network (68.8% to 100%) on every seed. With none (linear) both networks stay at 51.6%, the share of the more common label, because each is one linear map. It does not show that one wide layer cannot represent the checkerboard, which universal approximation says a wide enough layer can. In this lab: surfaces are drawn over training points only. No held-out point is scored on this card. In general: whether depth or width wins at a fixed size depends on the task, the activation, the initialization, the optimizer, and how long training runs. Depth can make some functions far cheaper to represent, but a trained network of equal size does not always show the gain.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Choosing each next token only from the set a grammar still allows. The model proposes a distribution; the mask removes illegal continuations before sampling or greedy choice.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: A set of rules for which strings are legal, such as balanced braces or a function-call syntax. It is a filter, not a knowledge source.
documents.title: Grammar

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: A description of fields and types, often JSON Schema, compiled into a grammar. A free string or number field still admits fluent nonsense.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: A per-step yes-or-no over the whole vocabulary. Illegal tokens get probability zero, which is the same as setting their logits to minus infinity before the softmax.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Dividing the surviving probabilities by their sum Z so they add to one again. It keeps the model's ratios among legal tokens and adds no new information.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Text that can still be completed into a legal string. The mask checks whether the prefix plus a candidate token is still a valid prefix.

documents.body: Where one vocabulary token ends and the next begins. Tokens rarely line up with grammar symbols, so a correct mask checks a token character by character, and a token may span two symbols.
