documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Structured and constrained decoding · question 1
documents.body: On Masked distribution the model's favourite token is masked. What happens to the probabilities of the tokens that survive? The masked token's probability is shared out equally among the legal tokens, whatever their ratios were They stay as they were, so the legal tokens now sum to less than one and the rest is simply ignored Each is divided by Z, the total the legal tokens had, so they sum to one and keep their ratios Masking sets illegal tokens to zero, equivalent to setting their logits to minus infinity before the softmax. Dividing the survivors by Z restores a total of one, and because every survivor is divided by the same number the model's ratios between legal tokens are unchanged. The removed mass is not redistributed evenly.
documents.title: On Masked distribution the model's favourite token is masked. What happens to the probabilities of the tokens that survive?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Structured and constrained decoding · question 2
documents.body: A token such as { followed by a quote opens the object and starts the key in one step. How does the mask decide whether it is legal? It allows only tokens that equal a single grammar symbol, so a token that spans two symbols is always masked It runs the token's characters through the matcher and checks the text is still a valid prefix It asks the model whether the token fits the format, and masks the ones the model scores below a threshold Tokens rarely line up with grammar symbols, so a correct mask checks character by character whether prefix plus token can still be completed into an accepted string. A mask limited to whole-symbol tokens would forbid common spellings the model rarely saw in training. The check is a matcher, not a judgement by the model.
documents.title: A token such as { followed by a quote opens the object and starts the key in one step. How does the mask decide whether it is legal?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Structured and constrained decoding · question 3
documents.body: A constrained decoder returns valid JSON for your schema. What did the constraint guarantee? Every token kept the text a valid prefix, so a finished output is guaranteed to fit the grammar The values inside the object are true, since the schema fixes each field's meaning The model's probabilities are unchanged by the mask, because only the output text is filtered The mask only removes tokens that would leave the grammar, so the text stays a valid prefix and can only end once it is complete. It says nothing about truth: a free string field accepts hello as a city. And the mask does change probabilities, both by renormalizing each step and by distorting which whole strings come out.
documents.title: A constrained decoder returns valid JSON for your schema. What did the constraint guarantee?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Structured and constrained decoding · question 4
documents.body: The function-call grammar allows any letters for the city. What does that mean for get_weather(city="Os")? It cannot be produced, because a legal token is always a token the model believed was correct about the city It is guaranteed to parse, but nothing checks that Os is a real place, so the host must still validate it It will be rejected by the matcher, because a city that is not in the vocabulary is an illegal string Legality means the text is still a valid prefix of the grammar, and a free string field accepts any letters, so the call parses, runs, and asks about the wrong city. The grammar checks shape, never truth. Tools and agents therefore still validate arguments on the host side, as for any untrusted input.
documents.title: The function-call grammar allows any letters for the city. What does that mean for get_weather(city="Os")?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Structured and constrained decoding · question 5
documents.body: In Mask distortion you drag P(slo" after "O) from 10% to 90%. What happens to the two bars? Both bars rise together, because both read the same probabilities from the slider control The per-step bar rises and the conditioned bar stays, because the mask uses the slider's probability The per-step bar does not move, while the conditioned bar rises until the two bars meet Per-step masking renormalizes over the legal first tokens and then over a single legal continuation, so the slider never enters it and it stays put. The conditioned bar multiplies the first-step probability by the slider's value, so it rises as that continuation becomes likely. At 90% both branches keep the same share legal and the bars meet.
documents.title: In Mask distortion you drag P(slo" after "O) from 10% to 90%. What happens to the two bars?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Structured and constrained decoding · question 6
documents.body: Why can masking token by token sample different strings than the model conditioned on producing valid output? It commits to a prefix before seeing whether the model could continue it legally, over-weighting branches that are dead ends Masking nudges the model's weights a little at every step, so later tokens come from a slightly different model Renormalization shuffles the order of the legal tokens, so the draw no longer follows the ranking the model gave The mask looks one token ahead. A branch whose valid continuations are unlikely still gets its full share at the first step, because that step only compares legal first tokens, so such branches are over-represented. Weights never change and renormalization keeps the order and the ratios. Exact conditioning would need every legal future, which is intractable.
documents.title: Why can masking token by token sample different strings than the model conditioned on producing valid output?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: When a person reads a chatbot's answer, a friendly "Sure!" at the start or an extra sentence at the end does no harm. Sometimes, though, the reader is another computer program, and programs are far less forgiving. A program may need the answer in an exact format, with every bracket and quotation mark in place, and one stray word can make it fail. This module is about constrained decoding, a way to keep a language model's output inside a required format. As you saw in Next-token prediction, a model writes text one small piece at a time, and those pieces are called tokens. Picking the tokens one by one to write the answer is called decoding, and *constrained* means held inside limits. Before each token is picked, the model gives every possible token a chance of being picked, such as 40% for one and 2% for another. Constrained decoding adds a rule check at that moment, so any token that would break the format gets a chance of zero and can never be picked. Where it shows up When a chatbot app shows you a neat weather card instead of a paragraph, a program had to read the model's answer first. That program needed the answer in an exact format. A program that needs data from a model can ask for the answer in JSON, a common text format that programs use to share information. JSON writes labels and values inside curly brackets, like {"ok":true}, and constrained decoding keeps the answer in the exact shape the program expects. An AI system that uses a tool, such as a weather lookup, has to write an instruction called a function call, like get_weather(city="Oslo"), for a program to run. Read it as: do the action get_weather, and fill in the blank called city with the text Oslo. The quotation marks go around the city name, and the closing bracket ends the call. The Tools and function calling lab later in this guide runs calls like this one, and the Agents lab runs them again and again in a loop. Why it matters A model's favourite next token is not always one the format allows. In this lab's JSON example, the token the model rates most likely at the very first step is Sure, which starts a chatty reply instead of a JSON object. If Sure were picked, the program reading the answer would fail on the very first word. Constrained decoding blocks it, along with every other token that would break the format, so the shape no longer depends on what the model rates highest. The promise is narrow, though, and a good part of this lesson is about where it ends. It covers the shape of an answer, not whether the answer is true, so a perfectly formatted weather request can still name the wrong city. A length limit can still cut an answer off before its closing bracket. And blocking tokens one at a time changes how often each whole answer comes out, in a way that can be surprising the first time you see it. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these in your own words: How constrained decoding uses a token mask at every step. Tokens that would break the format are blocked, and the chances of the tokens that are left get scaled up to add to 100% again. Why an answer can be valid JSON, with every bracket in the right place, and still be the wrong answer. Why blocking tokens one at a time can give whole answers in different proportions from the model's own odds once its invalid answers are thrown out. What the lab lets you try No trained model runs in this lab. A small pretend model, which this lesson calls the toy model, stands in, with scores for its 24 tokens set by hand and then turned into chances. Everything the lab does with those chances is real, though. The rule check, the blocking and the rescaling are worked out exactly, and they give the same results a real system would. The lab is built from four cards, each with its own job: Grammar lets you pick one of two formats, a tiny JSON answer or a weather tool call, and shows exactly which outputs each one allows. Prefix walk builds the answer one token at a time with the numbered Decode step buttons. It shows the model's top choice next to the token it was allowed to pick. Masked distribution lists each token's chance before and after the blocking, and it works out the rescaling with real numbers. Mask distortion is a separate small example about two city names. Its slider shows how blocking one token at a time can give a different result from the model's own odds for whole answers.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: A stencil for text Picture a stencil held over a spray can, so that paint lands only where the stencil has holes. The letters come out the right shape however wobbly your hand is, but the stencil does nothing about the colour, because its only job is the shape. Constrained decoding is a stencil for text, and here is how the pieces match up. At every step, the model gives a chance to every token in its vocabulary, the full list of tokens it can pick from. These are the same kind of odds you worked with in Next-token prediction. A set of rules for which texts are allowed, called a grammar, then marks the tokens that could still lead to an allowed answer. Those tokens are the holes in the stencil, and everything else is covered up. The stencil is cut fresh at every step, because what is allowed next depends on what has been written so far. At the very start of the JSON example, the only allowed tokens are ones that begin with a curly bracket. Once the text reads {"ok":, the only allowed tokens are true and false. Blocking tokens: the token mask At each step, the lab marks every one of its 24 tokens as legal, meaning allowed, or masked, meaning blocked. This yes-or-no list over the whole vocabulary is called the token mask, and a masked token gets a chance of exactly zero, so it can never be picked. Here is the first step of the JSON example, where the prompt asks whether the service is up and says to answer as JSON. Four tokens get most of the model's probability, and the mask splits them into two pairs: Sure at 41.5% and The at 18.6% are masked, because a JSON object cannot start with a word. {" at 22.8% and { at 9.3% are legal, because both of them start with a curly bracket. So the two legal tokens held only about 32% of the model's probability between them, while the other 68% sat on tokens that are now blocked. Rescaling what is left: renormalization After the mask, the legal chances no longer add up to 100%, so they have to be rescaled. Picture letting the model write its first token 1,000 times, picking at random with these odds each time. About 320 of those starts would be legal, and about 228 of the legal ones would be {". If you count only the legal starts, {" makes up roughly 71% of them. The lab does the same thing with one division, after adding up the chances of all the legal tokens and calling the total Z. At this step Z is 0.320, which is 32% written as a decimal, and the Masked distribution card shows the division for the token that gets picked: Read it like this: the new chance of {", written p′ and said "p prime", equals its old chance, written p, divided by Z. The result is 0.711, which means {" now has a 71.1% chance of being picked. If you try the division on a calculator you get 0.7125, a hair different, because the lab divides the unrounded numbers and rounds only at the end. The other legal token, {, rises from 9.3% to 28.9% the same way, so together the two legal tokens now hold all of the probability. This rescaling step is called renormalization, and it is worth noticing what it keeps. Before the mask, {" was about two and a half times as likely as {, and after the mask it still is. Every legal token is divided by the same number, so the model's ratios between legal tokens stay exactly as they were. That means the mask adds no new information about which allowed token is the better one. How the mask decides what is legal The rule check works on single characters, meaning single letters, digits and symbols, and it asks one question about each token. If this token were added to the text so far, could the result still be finished into an allowed answer? A beginning of text that can still be finished that way is called a valid prefix. In the JSON grammar, {"ok":tru is a valid prefix because adding e} completes it, while {"ok":x is not, because no allowed answer has an x in that spot. Checking character by character matters because tokens do not line up neatly with the pieces of the grammar. The token {" opens the object with its curly bracket and also starts the label "ok" with a quotation mark, so it covers two grammar pieces at once. The token ": also covers two pieces, because it closes the label and adds the colon that follows it. Both are ordinary ways to write JSON, and both are legal because every one of their characters fits. The place where one token ends and the next begins is called a token boundary. Token boundaries rarely fall exactly where the grammar's pieces start and end, so a correct mask lets a token cross from one piece into the next. In Masked distribution, a legal token that crosses like this carries a ↔ tag naming the two pieces it joins, such as { and "ok". Knowing when to stop The grammar also decides when the answer ends, using a special token that means "the end". In this lab it appears as ⟨eos⟩, short for end of sequence, and it is legal only once the answer is complete. At step 5 of the JSON walk the text reads {"ok":true, and the model gives ⟨eos⟩ a 22% chance. The mask blocks it anyway, because stopping there would leave the object without its closing bracket. Picking a token: greedy decoding After the mask and the rescaling, something still has to choose one token. A chatbot often picks at random, using the rescaled chances as its odds, the way the Next-token prediction lab draws its characters. The Prefix walk in this lab always takes the single most likely legal token instead, which is called greedy decoding. That is why its heading says "greedy constrained decoding", and an automatic check in the app's code confirms that every step of both walks really is the top legal token. Where the stencil picture stops matching The stencil captures the blocking well, but two points need care. First, a paper stencil is cut once, while this mask is worked out again after every token, from the text written so far. Second, a stencil says nothing about how likely each shape is, and the mask has the same blind spot. It checks only whether an allowed ending still exists, and never how likely the model is to write that ending. That shared blind spot turns out to matter a great deal, and the Mask distortion card shows why.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Programs read text with no room for error A program that receives a model's answer usually hands it to a parser, which reads text in a fixed format and turns it into data. A parser is strict on purpose, so if a bracket is missing or an extra word appears, it stops with an error instead of guessing what was meant. Picture a friend who builds a small app that asks a chatbot whether a game server is up, then shows a green or red light. The app expects {"ok":true} or {"ok":false} and nothing else, and for weeks that is what it gets. Then one day the reply comes back as a friendly sentence that starts with "Sure!" and says the server looks fine. That reply makes sense to a person, but the parser finds no curly bracket, so it throws an error and the app shows a crash screen. Any JSON is not enough: the schema Your friend's app also needs more than valid JSON, because some valid JSON would still confuse it. The text {"ok":null}, where null is JSON's word for "no value", is valid JSON. So is {"ok":"yes"}, where the quotation marks make yes a piece of text. The app, though, needs the label ok followed by true or false and nothing else. A value that can only be true or false is called a boolean, and a label in a JSON object is called a key. A labelled spot that the model has to fill in, such as ok here or the city in the weather call, is called a field. A description of which keys an answer must have, and what kind of value each one holds, is called a schema. Real systems often write schemas in a standard format called JSON Schema, and then turn each schema into a grammar for the mask. That makes the mask stricter than JSON itself, because it enforces this app's rules and not only the basic rules of JSON. Why not fix the model instead? There are other ways to get the right format, but they do not come with a guarantee. You can describe the format in the prompt, which helps a lot, yet the model can still slip. You can also train the model further on examples, which changes its weights, the numbers it learned in training. Training changes the odds rather than setting rules, though, so a slip is still possible. Constrained decoding takes a different route, because it leaves the model's weights alone and edits each step's chances while the answer is being written. No retraining is needed, and the shape is guaranteed even for a model that would otherwise slip, as long as the answer is allowed to finish.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Work through the cards from top to bottom, using the steps below to see what to click and what to look for. Step 1: choose a format on Grammar Start by setting Grammar to JSON object and reading the lines under it. The Prompt line shows the request the toy model is answering, which asks whether the service is up and asks for the answer as JSON. The Allowed output line shows {"ok":true} or {"ok":false}, and the Rule line says the object's only key is a required boolean called "ok". It also notes that spaces are left out to keep the example small. Then set Grammar to Function call, whose prompt asks for the weather in Oslo and whose allowed output is get_weather(city="…"). In that pattern the city can be any run of one or more letters. Switching Grammar always sends Decode step back to the first token, so each walk starts from the beginning. Step 2: step through on Prefix walk Go back to JSON object and click the numbered Decode step buttons in order. Each button shows its step number and the token that step ends up picking. The tokens written so far, called the prefix, appear as chips followed by a ? for the spot being decided. Above the buttons, the line Grammar accepts next says in words what the rules allow at that spot, such as "true or false". Under the buttons sit three readouts, which compare the model's top choice with the token the mask allows: Unconstrained pick is the token the model rates most likely before any blocking, with a ✗ after it if the mask blocks it. Pick after mask is the token actually chosen, which is the most likely legal one. Legal tokens counts how many of the 24 tokens are allowed at this step. Step 3: read the numbers on Masked distribution This card lists tokens from most to least likely, and its model p column shows each token's chance before the mask. The mask column says ✓ legal or ✗ masked, and the after mask column shows the rescaled chance. The heading calls Z the "legal mass", meaning the total chance held by legal tokens, and it also shows the share of the model's probability that was removed. The formula under the table works out the picked token's new chance. Try this: With Grammar on JSON object, click Decode step button 1. Unconstrained pick shows Sure ✗, the model's top token marked as blocked, while Pick after mask shows {". On Masked distribution, Sure drops from 41.5% to 0 in the after mask column. Meanwhile {" rises from 22.8% to 71.1%, the same numbers you worked through above. Then click button 4 and find ", the quotation mark that would start a text value like "yes", at 27.9%. It is masked because the schema demands true or false, and false keeps 21.4% after the mask. Step 4: compare with the function call Switch Grammar to Function call and click button 5, where the city name starts. Legal tokens jumps to 11 / 24, because almost any token made of letters is allowed inside the city. That includes hello, which gets 11.2% after the mask, so the model could ask for the weather in a city called hello. Click button 6 next: after Os, the closing token ") keeps 6.3%, which would finish the call as get_weather(city="Os"). Step 5: drag the slider on Mask distortion The last card is a separate example, which the next section explains in full. Drag P(slo" after "O) from 10% to 90% and watch the two bars, Per-step mask and Model, conditioned on a valid string. The slider's label means the chance that the model writes slo", finishing Oslo, after it has already written "O. One bar never moves while the other climbs, and they meet only when the slider reaches 90%.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: The mask keeps the model's ratios Renormalization divides every legal chance by the same number, so it never changes which legal token is ahead or by how much. Before the mask at JSON step 4, true has 37.6% while false has 10.3%. That makes true a bit more than three and a half times as likely, and after the mask, at 78.6% to 21.4%, it still is. Nothing in the mask checks whether the service is actually up, because the mask only makes sure the answer is one of the two allowed words. The model and the mask mostly agree On most steps, Unconstrained pick and Pick after mask show the same token. The mask makes its biggest difference at the edges of the answer, where the model's top token is often a chatty word such as Sure. At step 6 of the JSON walk, once {"ok":true} is finished, the model's top token is The at 40.7%. That would start a sentence after the object, so the mask blocks it and allows only ⟨eos⟩. Constrained decoding works best when the model already leans toward the format, because then the mask has less to block, and "Going deeper" shows how real systems use that. The rules can be stricter than JSON At JSON step 4, the mask blocks both null and ", even though each could appear in some other JSON object. This schema needs a boolean in that spot, so the grammar rules them out, which shows the mask enforcing the schema and not only the basic rules of JSON. Some legal tokens cross grammar pieces At JSON step 1, {" is legal even though it covers the curly bracket and the start of the label. At step 3, ": is legal even though it closes the label and adds the colon. Look for the ↔ tags on Masked distribution, which show the mask checking each token character by character. A free text field lets almost anything through Legal tokens swings from 1 to 13 as you step through the walks, depending on what kind of spot is being filled. At punctuation, often only one token fits, but inside the city name almost any word-like token is legal, including hello, Sure and true. The grammar only asks for letters, so any letters will do. The setup on Mask distortion The Mask distortion card gives the most surprising result in the lab, so it is worth going through slowly. The card's answer starts with {"city": and then needs a city name to fill that field, and the schema allows only two values, "Oslo" or "Bergen". A field whose value must come from a short fixed list like this is called an enum field, which is what the card's heading means. Each city name takes two tokens, and the tree on the card shows the model's chances: For the first token, "O gets 55% and "B gets 30%. The other 15% goes to "P, which is masked because no allowed city starts with P. After "O, the model can write slo" to make Oslo, or ttawa" to make Ottawa, which is masked. The slider sets the chance of slo", and it starts at 10%, so the other 90% goes to Ottawa. After "B, the model writes ergen" nine times in ten to make Bergen. The rest of the time it writes ern" to make Bern, which is masked. What the per-step mask does Unlike Prefix walk, this card assumes the model picks at random using the masked odds, the way a chatbot often does. Both bars show how often each city would come out. At the first step, the mask blocks "P and rescales "O and "B, which gives "O about 65%. The caption under the bar shows this as 55% ÷ 85%, where 85% is what "O and "B held together. At the second step each branch has exactly one legal token left, which renormalizes to 100%, so every "O becomes Oslo. The Per-step mask bar therefore shows Oslo at 65%, wherever you put the slider. What the model's own odds say Now picture letting the model write the city 1,000 times with no mask, with the slider at its starting value of 10%: About 550 answers start with "O, but only a tenth of those, about 55, go on to spell Oslo, while the rest spell Ottawa. About 300 answers start with "B, and nine in ten of those, about 270, spell Bergen, while the rest spell Bern. About 150 answers start with "P and never become an allowed city. Throw away every answer that is not allowed, and about 325 valid answers remain. Only 55 of them are Oslo, which is about 17%, while the rest are Bergen. Keeping only the valid answers and rescaling the model's own chances for them is called conditioning the model on valid output. That is what the Model, conditioned on a valid string bar shows. Why the two bars differ The mask asks only whether "O *can* still end as an allowed city, and it can, through Oslo. It never asks how *likely* the model is to end it that way, so it cannot see that most of the model's "O answers go on to Ottawa. It commits to "O first and then forces slo", so every one of those Ottawa-bound starts is turned into Oslo. This gap between the two bars, caused by committing to a start before seeing where it leads, is called distribution distortion. For a single token, as at JSON step 1, masking and throwing away bad answers give the same numbers, which is what the 1,000-starts picture showed. The gap appears only once an answer takes more than one token, because the mask throws away bad endings one step at a time instead of throwing away whole answers. Picture a phone keyboard that only lets you type two city names, Oslo and Bergen. A friend starts typing Ottawa, and the keyboard accepts the O, because Oslo starts with O too, then fills in "slo" for them. The message says Oslo, a city your friend never meant, and if lots of people start typing Ottawa, the keyboard sends far more Oslos than anyone intended. The friend is where this picture stops matching. A model has no word in mind when it writes "O. It only gives the next token its odds, and after "O most of those odds happen to point to ttawa". Watching the slider As you drag P(slo" after "O) up, more of the "O answers really do spell Oslo, so the conditioned bar climbs while the per-step bar stays at 65%. At 90%, both branches keep the same share of legal endings, nine in ten, so the two bars match. Past 90%, the conditioned bar edges slightly beyond the per-step bar, because then the "O branch has the larger share of legal endings. The distortion comes from starts that differ in how often the model finishes them with an allowed city, which a mask that decides one token at a time cannot see.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies No trained model runs here, so the chances are made up. At each step every token starts on the same low score, −2, and a few get higher scores set by hand. The lab then turns those scores into chances, the same way the Next-token prediction lab does. The vocabulary has only 24 tokens, while a real model's vocabulary can hold 100,000. Both grammars are tiny patterns with no spaces, no objects inside other objects, and no special codes for putting a quotation mark inside a piece of text. Prefix walk always takes the top legal token, so you never see a random pick. The distortion tree has only two levels, so the lab can list every answer and work out the conditioned bar exactly, which is out of reach for a real model. Everything the lab does with those made-up chances is real, though. The character-by-character check, the mask and the rescaling are real calculations that give the same results a real system would get. The difference is that real systems prepare most of the check ahead of time. Where the real mechanism fails A common mix-up: it is tempting to treat valid JSON as a correct answer, but passing the parser only checks the shape. Picture a multiple-choice test marked by a machine that first checks that every row on the answer sheet has exactly one bubble filled in. A sheet can pass that check perfectly and still get every question wrong, because filling one bubble per row says nothing about filling the right one. Constrained decoding is like an answer sheet that physically lets you fill only one bubble per row. The shape is guaranteed, but the sheet still says nothing about which bubble is right, and the function-call walk shows this clearly. The call get_weather(city="Os") parses perfectly and asks for the weather in a place called Os. At step 6, the token ") that would end the call right there still keeps 6.3% after the mask. A free text or number field also lets fluent nonsense through, so hello is a perfectly legal city. If a format had a number field for a temperature, any number at all would be legal there, even one far hotter than any real day. Even a strict enum cannot rescue a misunderstood question, because if the person really asked about Ottawa, every answer the Oslo-or-Bergen schema allows is wrong. So the program that runs a function call still has to check its inputs, the way it would check any input it cannot trust. Length limits can still break the shape, because real systems set a maximum number of tokens for each answer. If that limit is reached before the closing bracket, the answer is cut off mid-object and the parser fails anyway. The guarantee holds only when the answer is allowed to finish. Forcing the text can make it poor, because when the mask removes most of the probability, the tokens that survive may all be ones the model rated unlikely. The output can then be valid and still poor, so the share removed, shown in the heading of Masked distribution, is a warning sign worth watching. It reaches 75% at the first step of the function call, even though the surviving token there, get, happens to be a good one. Per-step masking distorts whole answers, and the Oslo-and-Bergen gap is not a quirk of this lab. Any per-step mask commits to the start of an answer before finding out whether the model would finish it legally, and real formats branch far more than twice. Getting the exact conditioned answer for a real model would mean adding up the chances of every possible legal ending, which is far too much work. Park and colleagues pointed out this problem for grammar-based masking in 2024, and they proposed a corrected way to pick tokens. A badly built mask can hurt quality too, if it allows only tokens that match one whole grammar piece. Such a mask would block {" and ":. The same text can be cut into tokens in more than one way. In the text the model learned from, an opening like {"ok" usually came with {" as one token. A mask that forces { then " then ok gives the model a spelling it rarely saw, and its later guesses can get worse after an opening that looks strange to it. That is why a correct mask checks each token character by character.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: How real systems make the mask fast Real engines turn full JSON Schemas, or bigger kinds of grammar, into a state machine, a rule-following machine that tracks where the text is inside the format. Each possible position is called a state, and for each state they work out most of the list of allowed tokens ahead of time. Checking a 100,000-token vocabulary character by character at every step would be far too slow, so this preparation is what makes masking cheap. Outlines and XGrammar are two well-known engines of this kind. The same result, done earlier The note under the formula on Masked distribution says masking gives the "same result as setting illegal logits to −∞ before the softmax". In Next-token prediction, a model's raw scores are called logits, and the softmax step turns them into chances. The symbol −∞ means minus infinity, and a score that low becomes a chance of exactly zero. The softmax then shares the probability among the remaining tokens in the same ratios that dividing by Z gives. So you can mask the scores first or the chances afterwards, and you get the same numbers either way. A safety net, not a steering wheel The usual pattern in practice is to describe the format in the prompt and use a mask as well. The prompt makes the model's own chances favour the format, so little probability gets removed and the mask acts as a safety net rather than a steering wheel. Token healing Token boundaries can cause trouble at the other end of the text too, where your prompt stops and the model's answer begins. Suppose your prompt ends with {, but the model almost always writes {" as one token. A lone { at the end of the prompt is unusual for it, so its next guess can be odd. A fix called token healing removes the prompt's last token, here the {, then masks the next pick so that it must begin with the removed text. That lets the model choose {" as it normally would. Where these calls go next The Tools and function calling lab runs calls like the get_weather one you built here, and the Agents lab runs them over and over in a loop. The program that runs them still has to check the inputs, because the grammar checked the brackets, not whether get_weather should run for that city. Constrained decoding is also a decode-time technique, meaning it changes how text is produced without changing the model, like the techniques in Inference & KV cache.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: This module is about constrained decoding: keeping a language model's output inside a required format, such as a JSON object that matches a schema or a tool call with a fixed syntax. It asks how a decoder can guarantee that a finished output has the right shape, and what that guarantee leaves unchecked. It builds on Next-token prediction, where a model emits one token at a time from a softmax over its vocabulary. Constrained decoding edits each step's distribution: a grammar, a set of rules for which strings are legal, decides which next tokens are still allowed, and the rest are removed before the choice. Where it shows up Structured output. A JSON schema, a description of fields and types, is compiled into a grammar, so an answer meant for a program comes out in the shape that program expects. Function calls. A grammar keeps a call such as get_weather(city="…") parseable before the host runs it, the step that Tools and function calling and Agents rely on. Inference engines. Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar run the mask inside the decoding loop, so a request can carry a schema and every finished output fits it. Why it matters A model's most probable token can fall outside the format. At the first step of this lab's JSON example the favourite is Sure, the opening of a prose reply rather than an object. A mask removes that token and every other one that would leave the grammar, so the shape no longer depends on what the model happens to prefer. The guarantee is narrow. It covers shape, not truth: a parseable function call can name the wrong city, and a free string field admits fluent nonsense. A length limit can still cut the output off mid-object. And masking one token at a time can change how often each whole string comes out, compared with the model's own probabilities restricted to valid strings. What you will be able to explain How constrained decoding applies a token mask at each step, removing illegal tokens and rescaling the rest so they sum to one (renormalization). Why a valid JSON string can still be a wrong answer. Why masking one token at a time can sample different strings than conditioning the model on valid output, a gap called distribution distortion. What the lab shows No trained model runs here: each step's distribution is a softmax over authored logits, a baseline of −2 plus a few hand-set values, across 24 tokens. The softmax, the character-level matcher, the mask and the renormalization are real computations, and a test checks that each walk is the greedy constrained path, taking the most probable legal token at every step. Grammar switches between *JSON object*, which accepts only {"ok":true} or {"ok":false}, and *Function call*, get_weather(city="…") with a free-string city. On Prefix walk, each button of Decode step is one step of the greedy decode, labelled with the token it picks; readouts give Unconstrained pick, Pick after mask and Legal tokens. Masked distribution lists token probabilities before and after the mask, the legal mass Z, and the share removed. The key experiment is Mask distortion, a separate two-step example with an enum field (a closed list of values) that allows only Oslo or Bergen. Its probabilities are authored, and both bars are computed exactly from them. Drag P(slo" after "O) from 10% to 90%: the Per-step mask bar stays at 65% Oslo, while Model, conditioned on a valid string rises from 17% until the two meet.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Constrained decoding restricts each next token to those a grammar still allows. At every step the model produces a distribution over its whole vocabulary, the logits and softmax from Next-token prediction. A token mask sets illegal tokens to zero, and renormalization divides the survivors by Z, the probability they had together: That is the same as setting illegal logits to −∞ before the softmax. Sampling or greedy choice then proceeds as usual. How legality is decided A grammar (often compiled from a JSON schema) is turned into an automaton over characters. A token is legal when the prefix plus that token is still a valid prefix: some accepted string starts with it. End of sequence is legal only once the string is complete. Tokens do not line up with grammar symbols. {" opens the object and starts the key in one token; ": closes the key and adds the separator. A correct mask walks each token's characters through the automaton, so these token boundary crossings are allowed.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Tools, APIs and agents consume model output with a parser. A decode that drifts from the format breaks the pipeline. Constrained decoding guarantees the shape at decode time, with no change to the weights, which is why it is a decode-time technique like those in Inference & KV cache.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Grammar selects a JSON object with schema {"ok": boolean} or a tool call get_weather(city="…"). Prefix walk steps through the greedy constrained decode; each button of Decode step is one token. At JSON step 1 the model's favourite token is Sure at 41.5%. It is illegal, so Masked distribution shows Z = 0.320 and the pick {" rising from 0.228 to 0.711. At step 4 the model's second choice is ", a string, which the boolean field forbids. Mask distortion is a separate two-step example. Drag P(slo" after "O) from 10% to 90% and compare the two bars.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: The model's ratios among legal tokens survive the mask exactly. Renormalization is bookkeeping, not new knowledge. The schema is stricter than the syntax: null is valid JSON but masked for a boolean field. A free string field lets almost anything through. At function-call step 5, 11 of 24 tokens are legal, including hello. At step 6, ") keeps 6.3%, which would call the tool for city Os. In the distortion example, per-step masking picks Oslo 65% of the time whatever the slider says. The model's own probabilities, restricted to valid strings, give 17% at the default.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: In this lab. The logits are authored, not produced by a trained model: a baseline of −2 plus a few hand-set values per step. The grammars are two tiny patterns with no whitespace, nesting or escapes, and the vocabulary has 24 tokens. The softmax, the mask, the matcher and the renormalization are real computations. In the real mechanism. Constrained decoding guarantees shape, not truth. A parseable function call can name the wrong city, and a schema with free strings and numbers admits fluent nonsense. The guarantee also needs the run to finish: a length limit can still cut a string off mid-object. Distortion Masking one token at a time does not sample from the model's distribution conditioned on valid output. It commits to a prefix before learning whether the model would continue it legally; Park et al. (2024) call this out for grammar-constrained decoding and propose a corrected sampler. When a large share of mass is removed, the survivors may all be tokens the model thought unlikely. Tokenization A mask that allowed only tokens matching whole grammar symbols would forbid {" and ": and force spellings such as {, ", ok that the model rarely saw in training. Prompt boundaries have a similar issue: a prompt ending mid-token pushes the model toward odd continuations, which "token healing" fixes by backing up one token and constraining the next.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Production engines compile full JSON Schema or context-free grammars into finite-state or pushdown automata and precompute, for each automaton state, most of the allowed-token set. Outlines and XGrammar are well-known examples; the precomputation is what makes masking a 100,000-token vocabulary cheap at every step. The practical pattern is to describe the schema in the prompt as well, so the model's unconstrained distribution already favours the format and little mass is removed. The mask then acts as a safety net rather than a steering wheel. Tools and function calling executes objects like the one this lab builds, and Agents loops that execution. The host still has to validate arguments: the grammar checked the shape, not whether get_weather should run for that city.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Grammar · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Which language the mask enforces Grammar picks one of two small output languages: a JSON object that must match a schema, or a Python-style tool call. The lab compiles the chosen pattern into a character-level matcher, and that matcher, not a list of hand-picked tokens, decides which tokens are legal at every step. `Grammar`, a two-way switch between `JSON object` and `Function call`. Switching resets `Decode step` to the first token. `Prompt`, the request the toy model is answering; `Allowed output`, the strings the grammar accepts; `Rule`, where the pattern comes from; `Vocabulary`, the 24 tokens the model can emit. `JSON object` accepts exactly `{"ok":true}` and `{"ok":false}`: a JSON Schema with one required boolean key and no others, with whitespace dropped to keep the toy small. `Function call` accepts `get_weather(city="…")` where the city is one or more letters. The pattern becomes a small automaton over characters. A token is legal when the text so far plus that token is still a prefix of some accepted string; end of sequence is legal only when the text is complete. `Grammar` is the only control here. Compare the two at step 1: the JSON walk allows `{"` and `{`, the call walk allows only `get`. The JSON schema is stricter than JSON syntax: `null` and a string are valid JSON after the colon but illegal for a boolean field. The call's free string field accepts any letters, so `hello` or `Sure` would be a legal city. Parseable is not the same as correct. In this lab: two tiny patterns with a finite, hand-picked vocabulary. There is no JSON Schema compiler for arbitrary schemas, and no whitespace, nesting or escapes. In general: production engines compile full JSON Schema or context-free grammars into automata and precompute which vocabulary tokens each state allows, because checking 100,000 tokens character by character at every step would be too slow.
documents.title: Which language the mask enforces

documents.subtitle: Prefix walk · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: The mask depends on the prefix The walk is the greedy constrained decode: at each step the lab takes the most probable legal token. The emitted text so far is the prefix; the matcher's state after that prefix is what decides the next mask. Unconstrained pick shows what the model would have emitted without the mask. The emitted tokens as chips, followed by a dashed `?` for the position being decided. `Grammar accepts next` states the matcher's state in words, such as `true or false` or `more letters or ")`. `Decode step`, a step controller whose buttons are the tokens of the walk, including the end-of-sequence token `⟨eos⟩`. `Unconstrained pick` (the model's top token before masking, marked ✗ if illegal), `Pick after mask`, and `Legal tokens` out of 24. Each step's model distribution is a softmax over authored logits. The mask is computed by running prefix plus token through the matcher, and the pick is the largest probability that survives. A test checks that the authored walk is exactly this greedy path, so the buttons are not a canned script. `Decode step`: at step 1 of the JSON walk the model's favourite is `Sure` (41.5%), which is masked, so the pick is `{"`. At the last step of either walk only `⟨eos⟩` is legal: the grammar also decides when generation stops. The number of legal tokens swings from 1 to 13. Inside a free string almost every word-like token is legal; at punctuation often only one is. The model's top choice and the pick agree on most steps. Constrained decoding works best when the model already wants to produce the format, which is why schemas are also described in the prompt. In this lab: the walk always follows the greedy pick, and the logits are authored per step rather than produced by a trained model. In general: the mask is applied to whatever the model proposes. It does not teach the model the schema, and a model that has never seen the format can be forced through it into low-probability, low-quality text.
documents.title: The mask depends on the prefix

documents.subtitle: Masked distribution · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Zero the illegal mass, then renormalize The model's next-token probabilities before and after the mask. Illegal tokens drop to zero, and each legal token's probability is divided by Z, the total probability the legal tokens had. The result sums to one and keeps the model's ratios between legal tokens. Rows sorted by the model's probability. `model p` is the softmax over all 24 tokens; the bar is hatched red when the token is masked. `mask` says `✓ legal` or `✗ masked`, and a masked token's chip is struck through. `after mask` is the renormalized probability. The outlined row is the pick. A legal token that spans two grammar symbols carries a `↔` tag naming them, such as `{ and "ok"`. Tokens that are illegal and below 1% are folded into a final `+N more tokens` row with their combined mass. The formula line evaluates the pick: `p′ = p ÷ Z`. The kicker gives Z and the share of probability removed. p = softmax(logits) over the whole vocabulary. Z = Σ p over legal tokens. p′ = p ÷ Z for legal tokens and 0 otherwise. This equals setting illegal logits to −∞ and taking the softmax again. Legality is checked on characters, so `":` is legal after `{"ok` although it closes the key and starts the separator in one token. A mask that only allowed tokens matching whole grammar symbols would forbid it. This card has no controls; `Grammar` and `Decode step` set it. At JSON step 1, Z = 0.320: 68% of the model's probability was on illegal tokens, mostly `Sure` and `The`. At JSON step 4, the model's second choice is `"` (27.9%), a string, which the boolean field forbids; `false` keeps 21.4% after the mask. Renormalization adds no information. Whatever ratio the model had between `true` and `false` is exactly the ratio after the mask. At function-call step 6, `")` keeps 6.3%: `get_weather(city="Os")` would parse, run, and ask for the wrong city. In this lab: the logits are authored to tell a clear story, a baseline of −2 plus a few hand-set values per step. No trained model runs here. In general: when most of the mass is removed, the survivors may all be tokens the model found unlikely, so the output can be valid and poor. Mass removed is a useful warning signal.
documents.title: Zero the illegal mass, then renormalize

documents.subtitle: Mask distortion · Structured and constrained decoding
documents.body: Per-step masking is not conditioning A separate two-step example with an enum field that allows only Oslo or Bergen. Masking token by token commits to a prefix before seeing whether the model would continue it legally, so it samples whole strings in different proportions than the model's own probabilities restricted to valid strings. A token tree: the first value token splits into `"O` 55%, `"B` 30% and a masked `"P` 15%. After `"O` the model continues with `slo"` or the masked `ttawa"`; after `"B`, with `ergen"` 90% or the masked `ern"`. Dashed red branches are masked. `P(slo" after "O)`, a slider for the model's probability of the legal continuation after `"O`. Two bars: `Per-step mask`, the share of Oslo and Bergen that token-by-token masking produces, and `Model, conditioned on a valid string`, the share the model itself assigns once invalid strings are ruled out. Per-step: the first step renormalizes over `"O` and `"B`, so Oslo gets 0.55 ÷ 0.85 = 65%. Each branch then has one legal continuation, which renormalizes to 100%. The slider cannot change this. Conditioned: P(Oslo) = 0.55 × q and P(Bergen) = 0.30 × 0.90, divided by their sum. At q = 10% that is 0.055 ÷ 0.325 = 17% Oslo. Drag `P(slo" after "O)` from 10% to 90%. The conditioned bar moves from 17% to 65% Oslo and meets the per-step bar, because both branches then keep 90% of their mass legal. The distortion comes from branches that differ in how much of their future is legal. The mask sees only one token ahead. Neither answer is guaranteed right. If the user meant Ottawa, the enum makes every valid output wrong. In this lab: the probabilities are authored and the tree has two levels, so the conditioned answer can be computed exactly by enumerating every string. In general: exact conditioning needs the probability of every legal future, which is intractable. Methods such as grammar-aligned decoding (Park et al., 2024) and sequential Monte Carlo approximate it at extra cost; most production systems accept the distortion.
documents.title: Per-step masking is not conditioning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The supervised learning loop
documents.body: The family of functions you are willing to search. Here that is a linear score, a logistic sigmoid of that score, or an axis-aligned tree. Changing H is a different search, not a different dataset.

documents.body: The number the fit actually drives down on the training slice: mean squared error or mean log-loss. It is not automatically the number you should publish.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The supervised learning loop
documents.body: The procedure that searches inside H. Linear and logistic take real full-batch gradient steps on the mean training loss from (w,b) = 0. A tree grows greedy Gini or entropy splits. The holdout is never used to choose a step.
