documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Synthetic data · question 4
documents.body: Under Synthetic only, a Real words verifier lifts Real words close to 100% yet leaves fewer Transitions than no filter at all. What does that show? Quality and variety are separate: a verifier only removes text, so it can raise one and lower the other The verifier is broken, since higher quality must also mean more variety Real words measures transitions indirectly, so the two lines should have risen together The verifier just needs a higher sampling temperature, which would let it restore the pairs that went missing A verifier moves probability toward outputs that pass; it cannot restore a pair the generator never writes. A spelling check also rewards repetition, since the the the is all real words, so it keeps the loop clean while the set of distinct pairs shrinks. Variety has to come from the seed, the prompts, or fresh human data.
documents.title: Under Synthetic only, a Real words verifier lifts Real words close to 100% yet leaves fewer Transitions than no filter at all. What does that show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Synthetic data · question 5
documents.body: You set Generator to A stronger teacher, Training data to Real + synthetic, and Measure to Unseen text, then drag Generation from 0 to 10. What happens to the line? It falls, because any model trained on generated text loses patterns, whoever happened to write it It rises, because the teacher writes pairs the seed lacked and the seed stays in every round It stays flat, because a student can never produce a pair that its human seed text lacked It rises, but only if Filter is Real words only, since only verified text can add anything The collapse in the self loop comes from each generation sampling its own table, so a missed pair is gone for good. A fixed teacher is not refitted, so it keeps writing pairs the seed never had, and the student counts them. Keeping the seed in every round also stops any loss, so coverage of unseen harbor text climbs toward the teacher's. A seed-bound verifier would remove exactly those new pairs.
documents.title: You set Generator to A stronger teacher, Training data to Real + synthetic, and Measure to Unseen text, then drag Generation from 0 to 10. What happens to the line?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Synthetic data · question 6
documents.body: With A stronger teacher and Filter set to Real words only, Unseen text hardly improves, though the teacher knows far more than the seed. Why? The verifier keeps only words from the seed, so it discards the new text the teacher adds A teacher cannot improve a student once the data has been filtered by any check at all The filter retrains the teacher on the seed each round, so its extra knowledge is overwritten The student already covers all of the unseen text, so there is nothing left for it to gain A verifier accepts or rejects drafts against its own standard, here the seed's 57 words. Text full of words the seed never used fails that test, so the verifier throws away the very patterns that make the teacher stronger. A filter only removes text, and a filter written from the seed can only keep what the seed already contains.
documents.title: With A stronger teacher and Filter set to Real words only, Unseen text hardly improves, though the teacher knows far more than the seed. Why?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Synthetic data
documents.body: Some of the text that AI models learn from was never written by a person at all, because another AI model wrote it. This module is about what happens when one model's writing trains the next model, whose writing then trains the model after that, round after round. If you have used a chatbot, you have seen how quickly it can fill a page. Text like that is cheap to make and there is no limit to it, while more of the web is written by models every year. So the text future models learn from will include model-written text, sometimes by accident when text is gathered from the web. Sometimes it is on purpose, when people use one model to write practice examples for another. This matters because, done carelessly, the loop quietly drains away the rarest patterns in the text, a little more each round, and nothing inside it can bring them back. The writing can even look cleaner while this happens, which makes the damage hard to spot. Done with care, model-written text can genuinely help, and the lab shows what that care looks like. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain: what synthetic data is: text that a model wrote, which then becomes the training text for another model; why models trained on their own writing, round after round, lose their rarest patterns first, which is called model collapse; how to judge a filter that checks model-written text, by asking what it keeps and what it can never bring back; what changes when a fixed, stronger model does the writing: the loop breaks and new patterns can come in, but only patterns that the stronger model has. In the lab, a very small model learns which letter tends to follow which, using eight short sentences that people wrote about the weather in a harbor town. You run ten rounds of the loop and watch three things change. A chart shows how much variety is left, a grid crosses out the letter pairs that are lost, and a sample shows what each round writes. You can also keep or drop the human sentences, switch on a spelling filter, and make the model lean harder on its likeliest letters or spread its picks out. Other controls change how much text each round writes and hand the writing job to a stronger model. Every number in the lab is worked out for real, and the chart shows eight separate runs for each setting along with their average. A few parts of the lab are fixed and kept small on purpose. The stronger model is the same kind of tiny letter-pair table, trained once on about four times as much harbor text and never changed. The spelling filter only checks words against the 57 different words in the human notes. One measure tests each model on extra harbor sentences that no model ever trains on. The model is tiny, but the reason it loses patterns carries over to much larger models.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Synthetic data
documents.body: Text that a model wrote Synthetic data is training text that a model wrote rather than text that people wrote and someone collected, and the word "synthetic" means made rather than found. This lab is built around a loop: train a model, let it write the training text for the next model, train that one, and repeat. Repeating this round after round is called recursive training, and the lab runs ten rounds of it. Each model in the chain is called a generation, and the lab counts them from 0. The first model, the one that learns from human writing, is generation 0. The model trained on its writing is generation 1, the model trained on generation 1's writing is generation 2, and so on up to generation 10. The lab's Generation slider picks which one you are looking at. The loop has to start somewhere, so the first model learns from human writing. Here that is 499 characters of harbor notes, where a character is any single letter, space or full stop. The notes are eight short sentences, and the first one reads "the morning fog settles over the harbor and the air feels cool." This starting text is called the seed data, because every later round grows out of it, the way a plant grows from a seed. The model: a table of letter pairs The model in this lab is about as simple as a model of language can be. It reads the seed one character at a time and counts, for every character, which character came straight after it. In the seed, t is followed by h 21 times, which makes sense in text full of the word "the". The letter q shows up only once, in the word "quiet", so the pair q then u was seen exactly once. Those counts go into a grid with one row for each character and one column for each character that might come next. The lab's alphabet has 30 symbols: the 26 letters, the space, the full stop, and two spare symbols that never get used. That makes a 30 × 30 grid with 900 boxes, and a grid like this, built from pairs, is called a bigram table, where "bi" means two. The grid you see on screen later leaves out the two spare symbols, so it has 28 rows and 28 columns. To turn counts into chances, which the lab's notes call probabilities, the model divides each box by the total for its row. After q, the only thing the seed ever shows is u, so the chance of u after q is 1 out of 1, which is 100%. In the t row, h holds 21 of the 46 counts, which gives h a probability a little under half, while e, o and others share the rest. Building a table this way from some text is what the lab calls fitting a model to that text. Each different pair, such as t then h, is called a transition, and the seed holds 157 different ones. The chart's Transitions measure counts how many different pairs are still in a round's training text, which tells you how much variety that round's model has left. How the model writes To write, the model acts as if it has just seen a space, and it picks the next character from the space's row. The pick works like a spinner whose slices are sized by the probabilities. A likely letter has a big slice and gets picked often, while a rare one has a thin slice and is easy to miss. Then the model moves to the row for the character it picked and picks again, so it builds text one character at a time. Because it only ever looks one character back, it often glues pieces of real words together into words that do not exist. For example, it can write theze, even though that word appears nowhere in the notes. Every step in it is a real pair from the seed: t then h, h then e, e then z from "freezes", and z then e. That is why only about 7% of the words the first model writes are real words from the seed, even though every pair it writes is real. One rule follows from all this, and it drives everything that happens in the lab. If a pair never appears in a model's training text, its box holds a count of zero, which gives it a probability of zero. A model can never write something it gives zero probability, so a table built by counting can only write pairs that its training text showed it. A table trained in a different way, like the teacher you meet below, works a little differently, as the lab will show. The marble jar picture Picture a jar of coloured marbles, where each colour stands for one letter pair and common pairs have many marbles. You draw a handful, then fill a fresh jar with marbles in the same colours and the same mix as your handful, then repeat with each new jar. A colour that misses one handful is gone from every jar after it, and rare colours with only a marble or two are the likeliest to miss. Here is where the picture stops matching: a model does not copy its handful of text letter for letter. Instead, it learns the odds of what follows each character and writes fresh text from those odds. So it can invent new words, but it can never invent a new pair, and that is the part of the picture that matters here. Two ways to build each round's training text The Training data control decides what each new model is fitted to, and it has two settings. Synthetic only: each round's training text is only the newest batch, the one the previous model wrote, while the human notes train only generation 0 and are then dropped. Real + synthetic: each new batch is added to the human notes and to every earlier batch, instead of replacing them. Keeping the original data and adding to it like this is called data accumulation. In the marble picture, Real + synthetic means pouring the original jar's marbles into every new jar as well, so no colour from the original jar can ever disappear. Who does the writing The Generator control decides who writes each round's text, and it also has two settings. With The model itself, each round's model writes the next round's text, which is the loop described above. With A stronger teacher, a separate model does all the writing instead, and a model used like this is called a teacher model. The teacher is the same kind of letter-pair table, but it learned from much more text. On top of the 499 characters of human notes, it learned from 1,515 more characters of harbor notes that the student never sees. That makes 2,014 characters in all, about four times as much as the seed. The teacher was trained once and is never changed after that. Instead of counting, it was trained with a method the lab calls SGD, which improves a table's numbers in many small steps. One side effect of training this way matters later: SGD never gives any pair a chance of exactly zero. The student is the same counting table as before, and it never sees the teacher's extra notes. It only sees the text the teacher writes, along with the human notes when Training data is on Real + synthetic. In the marble picture, the teacher is a much bigger jar that every handful comes from, and it is never swapped for a jar built from a handful. A colour missing from one handful can still turn up in the next.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Synthetic data
documents.body: The problem this lab is built around is what happens to rare patterns when each model learns from a limited amount of another model's writing. Small samples miss rare things Every batch of text has a fixed length, and a sample of fixed size can miss rare things purely by chance. Think back to the pair q then u, which the seed contains only once. A pair that rare turns up about once in every 500 characters the first model writes, so a 500-character batch often misses it. The common pair t then h turns up about 20 times in a batch that size, so it is almost never missed. The gap between the true odds and what a limited sample happens to contain is called finite-sample error, where "finite" means limited. If you drew a bar graph of the seed's pairs from most common to least common, the rare ones would form a long, low stretch at the end. That stretch of rare patterns is called the tail, and it is where finite-sample error does its damage. One miss is forever Under Synthetic only, each new model is fitted to the last batch and nothing else. If a batch misses q then u, the next table has a zero in that box, so the next model can never write that pair. From then on, that pair is missing from every batch that follows, however many rounds you run. One unlucky miss becomes permanent, while every round gives the remaining rare pairs another chance to be missed. This slow, one-way loss of variety, with the rarest patterns going first, is called model collapse. Picture a family that makes a fresh recipe book every year by copying only the recipes it cooked that year. Pancakes are made every week, so they always make it into the new book. A plum cake that someone bakes only now and then might skip a year by chance. If it does, it is missing from the next book, so nobody bakes it the year after either. It is gone for good, and the books get a little plainer each time this happens. Unlike the family, a model does not copy whole recipes. It mixes pieces it has seen into new ones, but it still cannot bring back a piece that went missing. The same thing carries over to real models, although their tail is not rare letter pairs but rare facts, uncommon dialects and unusual cases. A model trained only on another model's limited output ends up with too few of exactly those things. The same rule points to the fixes The same zero-chance rule also tells you what can stop the slide, and the lab tries out two ways of doing it. If the human notes stay in every round's training text, their pairs always keep a count above zero, so none of them can be lost. If the writer is instead a fixed model that covers more pairs than the student, the student's misses never reach the next round, because the student never writes anything. Meanwhile, the writer's extra pairs can flow into the student's training text. Picture two different ways you might practise speaking a new language. In the first, a chain of learners each learns only from the one before. Any word that one learner happens never to say is never heard by the next, so it is gone from the chain for good. In the second, everyone practises with a fluent speaker who never changes, so a word you happen to skip can still come up in the next conversation. You can also pick up words you never heard before, though only words that speaker uses. The rule also shows the limit of filters, which are checks that throw away bad-looking text before it is used for training. A filter can remove text, but it cannot add a pair the writer never writes, so it can make the text look cleaner without bringing back any lost variety. The lab lets you test all three of these ideas for yourself, one control at a time.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Synthetic data
documents.body: When the lab opens, it is set up like this: Generation is at 5, on a slider that runs from 0 to 10. Training data is on Synthetic only, and Measure is on Transitions. Generator is on The model itself, and Filter is on No filter. Temperature, which controls how boldly the model picks its letters, is at 1.0, which the slider labels "as fitted". Step 4 explains it. Sample size, how much text each round writes, is on 500 chars, where "chars" is short for characters. The five steps below follow the lab's own steps and walk through its comparisons in order. Step 1: read one generation Set Generation to 0 and look at the card called What a generation writes. It shows the first 240 characters that one run of the model writes, and at generation 0 that is the model fitted to the human seed. Even this first model mostly writes made-up words, because it only looks one character back. The Real words here readout shows how few of its words are real seed words. Now set Generation to 1 and compare the new sample with the one from generation 0. The Trained on readout changes from 499 human characters to 500 synthetic ones. This model learned only from text the first model wrote, and it never saw a word of the human notes. Step 2: let the loop run on synthetic text only Keep Training data on Synthetic only, then drag Generation slowly from 0 to 10 while you watch the chart on the Recursive training card. Its line counts the different letter pairs left in each generation's training text, averaged over eight runs. At these settings, the line starts at 157 pairs at generation 0, which is every pair the seed contains. After one round it drops to 125, and after two rounds it is down to 105. The fall then slows down, and the line reads 75 at generation 5. By generation 10, only 51 pairs are left, about a third of where it started. The biggest drops come first, because that is when there are the most rare pairs left to miss. The chart draws each of the eight runs as a thin line and their average as a thick line. Each run makes its own random picks, so the eight runs come out a little different. The legend calls the eight thin lines "sampling seeds", because each run uses its own sampling seed, a number that decides which random picks that run makes. It has nothing to do with the seed data. The eight thin lines end between 46 and 58 at generation 10, so the drop is not the bad luck of one run. Both settings are always on the chart: Synthetic only is drawn as a solid line and Real + synthetic as a dashed one. Training data only changes which one is drawn more strongly and which setting the grid and sample cards follow. So for now, the dashed line sitting flat at 157 is the other setting, which Step 3 explains. Below the chart, the Seed (generation 0) readout shows the starting value, while the two readouts that begin with "Gen" show each line's average at the generation you picked. Now look at the card called Which transitions survive, which shows the same loss pair by pair. It is a grid with one row for each current character and one column for each next character, with the space shown as ␣. It has 28 rows and 28 columns, and it draws only the 157 pairs that appear in the seed, so pairs the seed never used are left blank. A filled box is a pair that is still present, and darker boxes are pairs the seed used more often. A box with a line through it is a pair that is lost, which the key below the grid marks as "crossed". Hover over a box to see its pair and how often the seed used it. The box for t then h, for example, says it was seen 21× in the seed. As you step from generation 1 to 10, watch the crossed boxes spread from the pale ones toward the dark ones. Two more views of the same loss The Measure control changes what the chart's line shows, and two of its options look at the same loss in other ways. Coverage asks how much of the seed text the model could still write. Here a common pair counts many times, once for every time it appears in the seed. So t then h counts 21 times, while q then u counts just once. Under Synthetic only, Coverage starts at 100% and falls to 58.9% by generation 10. That is far less of a drop than the Transitions line shows, which keeps only 51 of its 157 pairs, about a third. The reason is that the pairs lost first are rare ones, and rare pairs fill only a small slice of the text. Entropy measures how unpredictable the next character is, which is another way to see how much choice the model still has. It is counted in units called nats, and two everyday examples give a feel for the scale. A fair coin flip has about 0.69 nats of uncertainty, while a roll of a fair six-sided die has about 1.79. The first model scores 1.787, which is about as unpredictable as a die roll. By generation 10 under Synthetic only, entropy is down to 0.912, closer to picking between two or three equally likely options. The full spread of chances across all the possible next characters is called a distribution. When entropy falls like this, the chances are bunching up on fewer and fewer likely letters, which is called distribution narrowing. Step 3: keep the real data Try this: set Measure back to Transitions, then switch Training data to Real + synthetic, where each round adds to the human notes instead of replacing them. Drag Generation from 0 to 10 again. With The model itself writing, the line stays flat at 157 in every round and every run, while Coverage, if you check it, stays at 100%. Because the seed is part of every round's training text, each of its pairs always has a count above zero, so none can be lost. Now switch Measure to Entropy while staying on Real + synthetic. Here entropy still drifts a little, from 1.787 down to 1.713. Each new batch is a small sample, so its mix of pairs is a little off from the model's odds. A rare pair that should turn up about once in a batch is missed completely about a third of the time, and now and then it shows up twice. Its share of the growing pile wobbles up and down, and round after round these random wobbles tend to leave the odds leaning toward the common pairs. Keeping the seed stops pairs from being lost, but it does not stop the odds from tilting slowly toward the common ones. Step 4: filter and sharpen Next, on the Generator and filter card, set Filter to Real words only. That switches on a verifier, a check that accepts or rejects pieces of model-written text before they are used for training. This one keeps a word only if it is one of the 57 different words in the seed, and throws everything else away. In the What a generation writes card, the words it would reject are struck through, and the Filter keeps readout shows what share of the characters survive. Then set Measure to Real words, which shows what share of each round's own writing is made of real seed words. Drag Generation under both Training data settings, and then switch Measure back to Transitions to see what the filter did to the variety underneath. Now, with the filter still on, lower Temperature to 0.6 and watch Transitions under both Training data settings again. Under Synthetic only, Transitions crash to just 4 by generation 5, while Real words reaches 100%. Under Real + synthetic, all 157 survive. Temperature controls how the model picks from its odds, and the note on the Generator and filter card gives the rule. When the model picks its next character, the lab raises every probability to the power 1/T, where T is the temperature. Then it rescales them all so they add up to 100% again. Here is a worked example with made-up odds, where after some letter the table gives e a 75% chance and a a 25% chance. Suppose you set Temperature to 0.5, so 1/T is 2, which means every chance gets squared. As decimals, the chances are 0.75 and 0.25. Squared, they become 0.5625 and 0.0625. Those add up to 0.625, so you divide each one by 0.625 to make them add up to 1 again. That gives 0.9 and 0.1, so e now gets 90% of the picks and a gets only 10%. So a temperature below 1 makes the likeliest letter even likelier, which the slider labels "sharper". At exactly 1, the odds are used as fitted, and above 1 they are evened out, which the slider labels "flatter". To see the flatter case, imagine a temperature of 2, which is past the slider's top setting of 1.2. Then 1/T is 1/2, which means taking square roots. The chances 0.75 and 0.25 become about 0.87 and 0.5, and after rescaling they are about 63% and 37%, so the odds are closer together than 75% and 25% were. A chance of zero stays zero at any temperature, because zero raised to any power is still zero. So temperature changes which text gets written, but it never adds a pair that the table lacks. Step 5: bring in a stronger teacher For the last step, set Temperature back to 1.0, Filter back to No filter, and Measure to Unseen text. The numbers below were measured at those settings, so your screen will only match them if you reset all three. This measure tests each round's model on 586 characters of extra harbor sentences that no model in the lab ever trains on, not even the teacher. One of them reads "the fog lifts from the bay and the boats leave the harbor one by one." The measure asks what share of the letter pairs in those sentences the model could write at all. That score is called held-out coverage, where "held out" means kept out of training. The model fitted to the human seed scores 92.6%, because a few pairs in the test sentences never appear in the seed. With The model itself writing and Synthetic only, the score falls to 55.6% by generation 10. Now switch Generator to A stronger teacher and Training data to Real + synthetic, then drag Generation again. This time the line rises instead of falling, because the teacher keeps writing pairs that the seed never had. It reads 96.2% after the first round and passes 98% by generation 3, and it ends at 99.4% at generation 10. Switch Training data to Synthetic only. Now the teacher's line dips at generation 1, to about 88%, and then stays level instead of sliding further. Then set Sample size to 2000 chars and compare the two writers at generation 10 by switching Generator back and forth. The teacher's student reaches 97.5% without any human text in any round, while the model itself, on the same settings, has decayed to 80.7%. Last, set Sample size back to 500 chars, keep the teacher, and set Filter to Real words only. Then watch what the filter does to the teacher's gain under both Training data settings.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Synthetic data
documents.body: The rare pairs go first, as the three bars under the grid in Which transitions survive show by grouping pairs by how often the seed used them. The grid shows run 1 of the eight. At generation 10 with the other settings at their defaults, that run has lost 63 of the 72 pairs the seed used only once. Of the 58 pairs seen 2–4 times, it has lost 35. Of the 27 pairs seen five or more times, it has lost only 8, so finite-sample error is eating away the tail first. With the model itself writing, nothing new ever shows up, so the grid only loses boxes and, under Synthetic only, the Transitions line never rises in any run. Every pair a model writes had to be in its own training text, so this loop can lose pairs but can never gain them. Bigger samples slow the loss down, but they cannot stop it. Under Synthetic only, about 34 transitions are left at generation 10 when Sample size is 250 chars. With 2000 chars, about 109 are left, because a bigger batch gives each rare pair more chances to be drawn. Lower temperature speeds the loss up. It makes the likeliest letters even likelier, which leaves the rare pairs with even thinner chances, so each batch misses more of them. With Filter on No filter, the average at generation 10 falls to about 11 transitions at Temperature 0.8. At 0.6, every run ends up writing the the the by generation 6. That loop uses only four pairs: t then h, h then e, e then a space, and a space then t. That is distribution narrowing taken all the way to its end. At 1.2, the loss slows to 73 pairs, but it still does not stop. A filter can make the text look better while making it worse. Under Synthetic only, the Real words verifier throws away about 95% of the first round's draft. It then pushes Real words above 99%, while Transitions fall to 16, fewer than the 51 left with no filter at all. That sounds odd, since real words are made of real pairs. But a model that picks one letter at a time gets a word right mostly by luck. So nearly everything the filter keeps is short, common words such as the, a, in and by. Longer words like quiet or freezes almost never come out spelled right, so the pairs inside them never reach the next model, and it loses them at once. The text the the the scores 100% on Real words, which shows how a word check rewards repetition. Keeping the human text in every round is what protects the variety. Under Real + synthetic, the same filter lifts Real words from about 7% to 82%, and all 157 transitions survive. Filtered model-written text plus the original data is the combination that helps. A fixed writer stops the slide, even with no human text in the mix. With the teacher on Synthetic only, Unseen text stays level from generation 1 instead of falling. The teacher is never refitted to a student's mistakes, so a pair that one student misses can still turn up in the next batch. A level line is not the same as a high line. At the default sample size, the teacher's Synthetic only student sits near 87%, below the 92.6% of the model fitted to the human notes. That is because a single batch from the teacher, like any limited sample, still misses some of the pairs the teacher could write. At 2000 chars the same student reaches 97.5%, higher than the seed model's own score, with no human text in any round. A filter built from the human notes throws the gain away. With the teacher writing and Real words only on, Synthetic only scores 42.2% on Unseen text at generation 1. Real + synthetic, which reached 99.4% without the filter, now ends at 93.0%. The teacher's extra pairs show up inside words, mostly made-up ones. A word that holds a pair the seed never had cannot be one of the seed's 57 words. So a filter built from the seed rejects the very text that carries the teacher's gain. A teacher can pass on only what its own training gave it. The human notes plus the teacher's extra notes cover 99.5% of the pairs in the test sentences, which is roughly the most this teacher can pass on. Under Real + synthetic, Transitions can even climb past the 258 pairs in the teacher's data, to 275 at generation 10. These extra pairs are not knowledge. SGD never pushes a chance all the way to zero, so the teacher spreads about 1% of its odds across the pairs its data never contained. Some of them leak into its writing. With big samples, a few of those happen to match test pairs by luck. That is why Real + synthetic at 2000 chars can edge just past 99.5%, to 99.7%. Picture a writing contest where the judge scores essays only on spelling. An essay that says "the the the" all the way down the page would get full marks, while a lively essay with one typo would lose points. That is the Real words filter: it measures one narrow kind of quality, and it can push that score up while the variety underneath drains away.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Synthetic data
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Everything on screen is computed rather than faked, from real random sampling, real refits and eight runs per line, so the lab's limits come from its small size. The model looks one character back and holds 900 numbers, while the seed is 499 characters long and the loop runs for only ten rounds. Real words is a spelling check against the 57 words in the seed, not a measure of quality. It cannot tell a sensible sentence from nonsense made of real words, and as the the the shows, it rewards repetition. This model is fitted by counting, so a missed pair drops to exactly zero. A table trained step by step with SGD keeps at least a tiny chance on every pair, so it never reaches exactly zero. Retrained on its own writing, a table like that drifts toward random jumble instead, writing pairs the seed never had while getting worse at predicting the real text. That is a second way the same loop goes wrong, and this lab does not show it. The teacher is a letter-pair table too, trained on four times as much text as the seed. It is stronger only in which pairs it covers, and in nothing like understanding. Unseen text asks only whether a pair can be produced at all, not how likely it is, so it rewards covering pairs rather than getting their odds right. The test sentences were written by hand in the seed's style and share its theme, as the teacher's extra notes do, so the test stays on familiar ground. The grid and the sample card show only run 1, and the sample is a single 240-character excerpt, while the chart averages eight runs over longer samples. A single run or excerpt can look better or worse than the average. Where the real mechanism fails Real models have no letter-pair tails, but they do have a tail of rare facts, uncommon dialects, unusual styles and edge cases. The mechanism is the same: what a limited sample misses, the next model does not learn. Making model-written data look "clean" by favouring the likeliest words, which is what a low temperature does, speeds that loss up. Other settings that cut off unlikely words do the same. A common mix-up: "If model-written data is causing trouble, filter it harder." A filter can only throw text away, so it cannot bring back a pattern the model stopped writing, and a strict filter can make the loss faster. In the lab, the Real words filter left 16 transitions where no filter left 51. What protects variety is keeping the real data in every round, which is what Gerstgrasser and colleagues found in 2024 for the real models they tested. There is a second risk, called contamination, which involves benchmarks: standard tests that people use to score and compare models. A model that saw a benchmark's questions during its own training can write them back out in its synthetic text. Private text from the model's own training data can reappear in the same way. A copied test question reads perfectly well, so it passes any filter that only checks for fluent writing. A model trained on that text has then seen the test before taking it, so its score on that test means less. That is why model-written data needs the same checks for leaked test material, called decontamination, as text gathered from the web. Picture a class whose practice worksheets were written by someone who had seen the final exam. If a few exam questions slip onto the worksheets, a high score on the exam says less about what the class can really do.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Synthetic data
documents.body: Where synthetic data works The success stories pair a strong writer with a checker that can tell right from wrong. Computer code is kept only if it runs and gives the right results on a set of test cases, and math is kept only if the answer is right. Worked reasoning can be kept only when it reaches a correct result, which a 2022 method called STaR did. Drafting many attempts and keeping only those that pass is called rejection sampling, and the share you throw away is its cost. In this lab, at generation 1, the Real words filter keeps only about one character in twenty. What a verifier can and cannot do A verifier shifts the kept text toward outputs that pass its check, but it cannot restore an output that the writer never produces. Variety has to come from somewhere else, such as the requests the writer is given, the seed data, or fresh human writing. A stronger model as the writer Training a smaller model on a larger model's writing is also synthetic data, with the larger model as the writer, which is what the Generator control acts out. A well-known example is Stanford's Alpaca, whose team started from a LLaMA model labelled 7B, meaning it holds about 7 billion adjustable numbers. By comparison, this lab's whole table holds only 900 numbers. The Alpaca team trained that LLaMA model further on 52K, or about 52,000, examples of following instructions, each one a request paired with a reply. OpenAI's text-davinci-003 model wrote those examples, and paying to use it cost the team less than $500. As in the lab, the student can reach only as far as its teacher. Whose rules the student inherits The Alpaca authors released it for academic research only, and they gave two reasons. They pointed to LLaMA's non-commercial licence, which ruled out using it to make money, and to text-davinci-003's terms of use. Those terms forbid developing models that compete with OpenAI (Stanford CRFM, 2023). Synthetic data carries the licence and rules of the model that wrote it. Keep the original Adding new text to the old instead of replacing it is data accumulation, and it is the whole difference between the two lines on the chart. Shumailov and colleagues showed that the rare parts of the original data disappear when models train on model-written text. Their 2024 paper in the journal Nature uses the name model collapse. Gerstgrasser and colleagues found that keeping and adding to the original data avoided it in the models they tested. Connections The Building a dataset lab covers removing repeated text and leaked test material, and both apply to model-written text too. Train one from scratch trains the same kind of table with SGD instead of counting. The Distillation & pruning lab trains a small model against a large model's full odds rather than its sampled text. Evaluation is where a leaked benchmark question would show up. Toy versus real Scale: The lab writes 250 to 2000 characters per round, for ten rounds. Alpaca's data was 52K instruction-following examples, written by text-davinci-003 for less than $500 (Stanford CRFM, 2023). The teacher: The lab's teacher is a letter-pair table trained on four times as much text as the seed. A real teacher is a far larger model, and the student's gain is limited by what the teacher has, as the roughly 99.5% limit shows here. Collapse: The lab loses 106 of 157 pairs under Synthetic only and none under Real + synthetic. Shumailov and colleagues report that rare parts of the original data disappear when models train on model-written text. Gerstgrasser and colleagues found that accumulating data avoids this in their models. Checkers: The lab's checker is a list of 57 words that keeps about 5% of the first round's draft. Real checkers run code on test cases, or compare answers with known right answers.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Synthetic data
documents.body: This module is about synthetic data, training text a model wrote rather than a person. It asks what survives when models learn from models: which patterns a model fitted to generated text keeps, which it loses for good, and what a filter, the original data, or a stronger writer changes. *Building a dataset* cleaned scraped text with deduplication and decontamination, and both apply to generated text unchanged. What is new here is the loop, recursive training: each model is fitted to text the previous one wrote, starting from human-written seed data. Where it shows up The web crawl. Generated text is cheap and unlimited, and a growing share of the web is already model-written, so the next crawl contains text a model produced. Verified training sets. Many training sets are generated on purpose. The ones that work pair a strong generator with a check, such as a code test or a matching math answer. Distillation. A large model writes a smaller one's training data, as OpenAI's text-davinci-003 did for Stanford's Alpaca. Data governance. Generated text carries the licence and policy of the model that wrote it. Why it matters Synthetic data can only contain what its generator produces, so careless use fails in ways that can look clean: Replacing the data loses the tail. A model trained only on the last model's output loses the rarest patterns first (in real systems, rare facts, dialects, and edge cases), then variety. That is model collapse. Sampling sharpened toward likely text, at low temperature or with top-p, speeds it. Filtering can trade variety for quality. A verifier, a check that accepts or rejects generated examples, raises quality but can only remove text. Leaks pass fluency checks. A generator that saw a benchmark can write its items back out. What helps is verified synthetic data added to the original data. New patterns need a writer that knows more than the student. What you will be able to explain What synthetic data is: model-generated text that becomes another model's training set. Why model collapse happens: models trained on finite samples of their own output lose rare patterns first, and the losses compound. How to judge a filter or verifier by what it keeps, and why it cannot restore what the generator no longer writes. What a fixed, stronger teacher changes: it breaks the loop and can add patterns the seed lacked, but only patterns it knows. What the lab shows Every generation is the track's 30 × 30 character-bigram table, which predicts each character from the one before it and is fitted in closed form by counting. Generation 0 is fitted to a fixed seed of 499 characters of harbor notes, and ten generations follow. Sampling is real. The Recursive training card plots two regimes at once, each as eight runs with different sampling seeds plus their mean: Synthetic only, where each batch replaces the data, and Real + synthetic, where it joins the seed. Training data highlights one regime and picks which one's run 1 feeds Which transitions survive and What a generation writes, the cards that show that run's pairs and text. Measure picks Transitions, Coverage, Entropy, Real words, or Unseen text, and Generation steps from 0 to 10. Generator and filter sets Generator (The model itself or A stronger teacher), Temperature, Filter, and Sample size. The key experiment: at the defaults, under Synthetic only, drag Generation to 10 and watch Transitions, the number of distinct character pairs the table has seen, fall from 157 to about 51, while the Real + synthetic line stays at 157. On Unseen text, the model itself decays under Synthetic only, and the teacher with Real + synthetic climbs. Some parts are fixed or simplified. The teacher is a bigram too, trained once by SGD on the seed plus 1,515 characters of extra notes the student never sees. The Real words measure and the Real words only filter, the lab's verifier, are both a spelling check against the seed's 57 words. Unseen text asks only whether the pairs in 586 characters of hand-written held-out sentences can be produced.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Synthetic data
documents.body: Synthetic data is training text a model wrote. This lab runs the loop that question raises: fit a model, let it write the next model's training text, and repeat for ten generations of recursive training. The model is the 30 × 30 character-bigram table used across this track, fitted exactly by counting what follows each character. Generation 0 is fitted to 499 characters of harbor notes, the seed data. Its table holds 157 distinct character pairs, which the chart calls Transitions. Each later generation drafts text at a chosen Temperature, an optional Verifier keeps what it accepts, and the next table is fitted to the result. Training data decides what that fit sees: Synthetic only: the latest generated batch replaces the data. Real + synthetic: every batch is added to the human seed, which is data accumulation. Generator decides who does the writing. The model itself is the loop above. A stronger teacher is a fixed teacher model: a bigram trained with the track's SGD trainer on the seed plus 1,515 characters of extra harbor notes, 2,014 characters in all. It writes every generation's data. The student is the same counting table as before and never sees those notes.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Synthetic data
documents.body: What survives when models learn from models turns on one mechanism. A model fitted to a sample gives probability zero to anything the sample missed, and it can never write what it gives zero. Losses compound across generations, and the first things lost are the rarest. This is the model collapse named in Shumailov et al. (Nature, 2024). The same mechanism explains the success case. When the writer is a fixed model that knows more than the student, nothing the student misses can reach the next round, and what the writer knows can flow in.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Synthetic data
documents.body: Start at Generation 0 and read what the seed-fitted model writes, then step to 1. Keep Training data on Synthetic only and drag Generation to 10. At the defaults (temperature 1.0, no filter, 500 characters per generation) the mean of eight runs reads: Transitions: 157, 125, 105 at generations 0, 1 and 2, then 75 at 5 and 51 at 10. The eight runs end between 46 and 58. Coverage: 100% falls to 74.1% at generation 5 and 58.9% at 10. Entropy: 1.787 nats falls to 0.912. Switch to Real + synthetic. Transitions hold at 157 and Coverage at 100% at every generation; Entropy only drifts to 1.713. Now set Filter to Real words only and Measure to Real words. Then lower Temperature to 0.6 and compare both regimes again. Last, set Filter back to No filter and Measure to Unseen text. It asks what share of the character pairs in 586 characters of held-out harbor sentences a generation can produce at all. The seed-fitted model scores 92.6%. With The model itself and Synthetic only it falls to 55.6% by generation 10. Switch Generator to A stronger teacher with Real + synthetic, and the line rises instead: 96.2%, 98.1%, 98.8%, and 99.4% at generations 1, 3, 5, and 10. With Synthetic only it stays level.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Synthetic data
documents.body: The tail goes first. In Which transitions survive, run 1 at generation 10 has lost 63 of the 72 pairs the seed used once, 35 of 58 used 2–4 times, and 8 of 27 used five or more times. That is finite-sample error: a once-seen pair appears about once per 500 characters and is often simply missed. Nothing new appears. The grid only ever loses cells. Under Synthetic only the Transitions line can never rise, in any run. Sample size is the brake. At generation 10, Synthetic only keeps about 34 transitions with 250 characters per generation, 51 with 500, and 109 with 2000. Temperature is the accelerator. At 0.8 the generation-10 mean is about 11; at 0.6 every run has fallen into the four-pair the loop by generation 6. That is distribution narrowing taken to its end. At 1.2 the loss slows to 73 but does not stop. Quality and variety come apart. Under Synthetic only the verifier keeps about 5% of drafted characters at generation 1, pushes Real words above 99%, and leaves 16 transitions, fewer than with no filter. the the the is 100% real words. Keeping the seed is what works. Under Real + synthetic the same verifier raises Real words from about 7% to 82% while all 157 transitions survive. Verified synthetic data plus the original data is the combination that helps. A fixed writer stops the compounding. With the teacher on Synthetic only, Unseen text is level from generation 1 instead of decaying, because the teacher is never refitted to a student's mistakes. A level line is not a high line. At 500 characters per generation the teacher's Synthetic only student sits near 87%, below the seed-fitted model's 92.6%: one finite sample of the teacher still misses pairs. At Sample size 2000 it reaches 97.5% with no human text in any round, where the model itself has decayed to 80.7%. A verifier built from the seed throws the gain away. With the teacher and Real words only, Synthetic only scores 42.2% at generation 1, and Real + synthetic ends at 93.0% instead of 99.4%. The teacher's extra knowledge is mostly words the seed never used, which the verifier rejects. A teacher can only teach what it knows. The seed plus the extra notes cover 99.5% of the held-out pairs, the most this teacher's data can offer. Transitions can pass the data's 258 pairs, reaching 275 at generation 10, because SGD leaves about 1% of the teacher's probability on pairs its data never contained.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Synthetic data
documents.body: In this lab Every number is computed from real sampling and exact refits, averaged over eight sampling seeds. What is small is everything else: one character of context, 900 numbers, a 499-character seed, ten generations. Real words is a spelling check against 57 seed words, not a quality score, and it rewards repetition. The fit is by counting, so a missed pair is exactly zero. A table trained by SGD from zero weights never reaches zero; retrained on its own samples it drifts toward noise instead, emitting pairs the seed never had while its loss on the real text rises. That is a second face of the same loop, and this lab does not show it. The teacher is a bigram too, fitted to four times the text, so it is stronger in coverage and in nothing like understanding. Held-out coverage asks only whether a pair can be produced, not how likely it is. The held-out sentences were written by hand in the seed's style and share its theme, as the teacher's extra notes do. In real systems The mechanism carries over: rare facts, dialects, and edge cases are the tail, and a model trained only on another model's finite output under-represents them. Low-temperature or top-p sampling for "clean" data accelerates it. Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) found that accumulating synthetic data alongside the original, rather than replacing it, avoids the collapse in the models they tested, which is what the Real + synthetic line shows. Contamination is the other risk. A generator that saw a benchmark can write its items back out, and the leak passes any fluency filter. Synthetic data needs the same decontamination checks as scraped data.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Synthetic data
documents.body: Where synthetic data works. Its successes pair a strong generator with a check: code kept only if its tests pass, math kept only if the answer matches, reasoning traces kept only when they reach a correct result (Zelikman et al., STaR, 2022). That is rejection sampling, and the acceptance rate is its cost. A stronger model as the writer. Distilling a large model's outputs into a smaller one is also synthetic data, with the teacher as the generator, which is what the Generator control stages. Stanford's Alpaca fine-tuned a 7B LLaMA model on 52K instruction-following examples generated by OpenAI's text-davinci-003, for less than $500 of API use. What a verifier can and cannot do. A verifier moves probability toward outputs that pass. It cannot restore an output the generator never writes, so diversity has to come from the prompts, the seed data, or fresh human data. Whose terms the student inherits. The Alpaca authors released it for academic research only. They cited LLaMA's non-commercial licence and the terms of use of text-davinci-003, which prohibit developing models that compete with OpenAI (Stanford CRFM, 2023). Synthetic data carries the licence and policy of the model that wrote it. Connections. Building a dataset covers deduplication and decontamination, which apply to generated text unchanged. Train one from scratch trains the same table by gradient descent. The Distillation & pruning lab trains a student against a teacher's probabilities rather than its sampled text, and Evaluation is where a leaked benchmark item would show up. Toy versus real Scale. The lab writes 250 to 2000 characters per generation for ten generations. Alpaca's data was 52K instruction-following examples, generated from text-davinci-003 for less than $500 (Stanford CRFM, 2023). The teacher. The lab's teacher is a bigram trained on four times the seed. A real teacher is a far larger model, and the student's gain is bounded by what it knows, as the 99.5% ceiling is here. Collapse. The lab loses 106 of 157 pairs under Synthetic only and none under Real + synthetic. Shumailov et al. report that tails of the original distribution disappear when models train on model-generated content (arXiv 2305.17493), and Gerstgrasser et al. that accumulating data avoids it in their models (arXiv 2404.01413). Verifiers. The lab's is a 57-word list that keeps about 5% of the first generation's draft. Real ones are test suites and answer checkers.

documents.subtitle: Recursive training · Synthetic data
documents.body: Ten generations, each fitted only to the last one's text Generation 0 is the character-bigram table fitted to 499 characters of human harbor notes. Every later generation is fitted to text that a generator wrote: by default the previous generation, or with the Generator control a fixed stronger teacher. The chart tracks what that loop keeps, for two regimes: synthetic text replacing the data, or synthetic text added on top of the human seed. The x axis is generation, 0 to 10. The y axis is whichever Measure is selected: Transitions (distinct character pairs with evidence), Coverage (share of the seed's character pairs still producible), Entropy (next-character uncertainty in nats), Real words (share of the generation's own writing that is seed words), or Unseen text (share of the character pairs in 586 characters of held-out harbor sentences that the generation can produce). Two families of lines. Synthetic only is drawn solid in the loss tone; Real + synthetic is drawn dashed in the forward tone. Each family has eight thin lines, one per sampling seed, and a thick line through their mean. The selected Training data family is drawn stronger. A dashed guide and enlarged dots at the Generation you selected. The legend and the three metrics repeat the generation-0 value and both means at that generation. Each model is fitted exactly: row c holds the count of each character that followed c in the training text, divided by the row total. That is the maximum-likelihood bigram table, the optimum SGD would approach. To build generation g's data, generation g−1 drafts text at the chosen Temperature, the Filter keeps what it accepts, and drafting continues until Sample size characters are kept. Synthetic only fits generation g to that text alone; Real + synthetic fits it to the seed plus every batch kept so far. A pair the training text never contains gets probability zero, and a model cannot write what it assigns zero. So under Synthetic only the transition count can never rise. Under Real + synthetic the seed keeps every original pair in the counts. Entropy is each row's entropy weighted by how often the seed uses that character as context. Real words samples 2000 characters from the generation at the chosen temperature and counts tokens that are one of the seed's 57 words. Unseen text counts every adjacent pair in the held-out harbor sentences and asks whether the generation's training counts contain it. Those sentences are in no training text, the teacher's included. The seed-fitted model scores 92.6%. With Generator set to A stronger teacher, the draft in step 2 is written by a fixed teacher table instead of by generation g−1. Everything else is unchanged, so the only difference is who writes. The Transitions axis runs to 160 for the model itself, and grows to the next multiple of 40 when a teacher lifts a line past it. `Training data` switches which family is emphasised and which run feeds the sample and grid cards. Both families are always computed. `Measure` changes the y axis. `Generation` moves the guide and every per-generation readout on the page. `Generator` on `Generator and filter` chooses who writes the data. Both families recompute. Comparison worth running: at the defaults read Transitions at generation 10 for both families (51 against 157), then set Measure to Entropy and compare 0.912 with 1.713. Then set Measure to Unseen text and switch Generator to A stronger teacher with Real + synthetic: the line rises from 92.6% to 99.4% instead of staying flat. At the defaults the Synthetic only mean falls 157, 125, 105 over the first two generations and reaches 51 by generation 10; the eight runs end between 46 and 58. The drop is largest at first, when the rarest pairs are the easiest to miss. Real + synthetic holds Transitions at exactly 157 and Coverage at 100% at every setting, yet Entropy still drifts: from 1.787 to 1.713 at temperature 1, and to 1.341 at temperature 0.8. Keeping the seed stops loss, not narrowing. Real words can rise while Transitions collapse. Repeating `the the the` scores 100% real words with four transitions. Under Synthetic only the model itself loses Unseen text, from 92.6% to 55.6% by generation 10. A teacher stops that decay: its line is level from generation 1, because a fixed source cannot compound anyone's errors. A level line is not a high line. At 500 characters per generation the teacher's Synthetic only student sits near 87%, below the seed-fitted model's 92.6%, because one finite sample of the teacher still misses pairs. At 2000 characters it reaches 97.5%, above the seed, with no human data in any round. In this lab: every value is computed from real sampling and exact refits, and each line is eight seeds, not one. But the model has one character of context and 900 numbers, the seed is 499 characters, and there are only ten generations. In this lab: the fit is by counting, so an unseen pair is exactly zero. An SGD-trained table from zero weights keeps some probability on every pair and instead drifts toward noise when retrained on its own samples. That is a different face of the same loop, not shown here. In this lab: the held-out sentences were written by hand in the seed's style and share its theme, as the teacher's extra notes do. Unseen text asks whether a pair can be produced, not how likely it is, so it rewards covering pairs, not getting their odds right. In general: published collapse results come from repeatedly retraining language models and image generators on their own outputs (Shumailov et al., 2023), and accumulating synthetic data alongside the original real data avoided it in the models Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) tested. Real pipelines mix synthetic data with fresh human data, deduplicate it, and filter it with verifiers, which is why synthetic data can help rather than harm.

documents.body: The text the next generation will be fitted to The first 240 characters that the selected generation writes, from run 1 of 8, at the chosen temperature. With the real-words verifier on, each token is marked kept or struck through, which is exactly what the filter does to drafts before they become training data. A kicker naming the run, the Training data regime, and the temperature, and a title naming the generation. Generation 0 is the model fitted to the human seed. The sample in monospace. When Filter is Real words only, rejected tokens are struck through and dimmed, so the verdict does not depend on colour. Three metrics: `Real words here` (the share of tokens in this excerpt that are seed words), `Filter keeps` (the share of this excerpt's characters the verifier would keep), and `Trained on` (how many human and synthetic characters this generation was fitted to). The sample is drawn one character at a time from the generation's fitted row for the previous character, with every probability raised to the power 1/T and renormalized. It starts after a space. The verifier splits on spaces and keeps a token only if, ignoring full stops, it is one of the 57 words in the seed. It never edits a token and never adds one. Under Real + synthetic, `Trained on` adds the seed's 499 characters to every synthetic batch kept so far; under Synthetic only it is the latest batch alone. The card follows `Generation` and `Training data` on the chart and the three controls on `Generator and filter`. Comparison worth running: with Training data on Synthetic only, read generation 0, 5 and 10 at temperature 0.6. By generation 6 every run is writing `the the the`. Generation 0 is already mostly non-words: a bigram joins real fragments into invented words, so about 7% of its tokens are seed words at temperature 1. The loop starts from that, not from the human text. Later Synthetic only samples repeat a shrinking stock of fragments. Nothing new appears, because every pair the model writes had to be in the text it was fitted to. With the verifier on, early generations lose most of their draft. That discarded text is the price of rejection sampling. In this lab: one run and one 240-character excerpt are shown; the chart averages eight runs over 2000-character samples. A single excerpt can look better or worse than the mean. In general: a real synthetic-data pipeline samples prompts as well as completions, often from a stronger model than the one being trained, and checks outputs against far richer verifiers than a word list.

documents.subtitle: Generator and filter · Synthetic data
documents.body: Sharpen, verify, and size each round Four settings that decide what each generation writes and keeps: who writes the data (the model itself or a fixed stronger teacher), the sampling temperature, whether a real-words verifier filters the drafts, and how many characters each generation is fitted to. `Generator`: The model itself, where each generation is drafted by the previous one, or A stronger teacher, a fixed model that writes every generation's data. With the teacher on, a note says how it was trained. `Temperature` from 0.5 to 1.2, labelled sharpened below 1, flattened above 1, and the model as fitted at exactly 1. `Filter`: No filter keeps every drafted character; Real words only keeps tokens that are one of the seed's 57 words. `Sample size`: 250, 500, or 2000 characters of kept text per generation. The seed itself is 499 characters. The teacher is a character bigram trained by the track's SGD trainer, `trainTinyModel`, for 40 epochs at batch 16 and learning rate 6, seed 5, on the 499 seed characters plus 1,515 characters of extra harbor notes that the student never sees: 2,014 characters, about four times the seed. Its rows are softmaxed, the two reserved angle brackets are masked, and each row is renormalized. It is trained once and reused. SGD never drives a probability exactly to zero, so the teacher keeps about 1.0% of its probability, averaged over the rows its data uses, on pairs its data never contained. Its data holds 258 distinct pairs, and a student fed 10 generations of its text can list more, up to 275 at the defaults. Temperature raises each probability to 1/T before renormalizing, so a pair with probability zero stays zero at any temperature. Below 1 the likeliest continuation gains share each round, and the loss compounds. With the verifier on, drafting repeats in chunks until the kept text reaches Sample size, up to 40 times the sample size in drafts. The accepted share is recorded for every generation. Sample size sets how many draws each generation gets. A pair with probability 0.2% appears about once in 500 characters, so it is often missed at 250 and usually caught at 2000. `Generator`, `Temperature`, `Filter`, and `Sample size` each recompute all sixteen chains, eight per Training data regime. Comparison worth running: with Synthetic only and Measure on Transitions, read generation 10 at Sample size 250, 500 and 2000: about 34, 51 and 109. Then set Measure to Unseen text and Generator to A stronger teacher, and read the same three sizes again. Comparison worth running: with the teacher on and Real + synthetic, switch Filter to Real words only and watch Unseen text at generation 10 fall from 99.4% to 93.0%. Temperature 0.8 takes the Synthetic only mean at generation 10 from 51 transitions to about 11, and 0.6 reaches the four-pair `the ` loop by generation 6. Temperature 1.2 slows the loss (73 at generation 10) but cannot undo it. The verifier keeps about 5% of drafted characters at generation 1. Under Synthetic only it pushes Real words above 99% while Transitions fall to 16, fewer than with no filter at all. Under Real + synthetic the same verifier lifts Real words to 82% by generation 10 while all 157 transitions stay: verified synthetic data plus the original data is the combination that helps. The teacher's extra knowledge is mostly words the seed never used, so the seed-word verifier rejects it. With the verifier on, Synthetic only with the teacher scores 42.2% on Unseen text at generation 1, and Real + synthetic ends at 93.0%, close to the seed's 92.6%. A stronger teacher is not a free pass: it can only teach what it knows. The seed plus extra notes cover 99.5% of the held-out pairs, which is the most this teacher's data can offer a student. In this lab: the verifier is a 57-word list, a stand-in for a checker. It measures spelling against the seed, not truth or usefulness. In this lab: the teacher is a bigram too, only fitted to four times the text, so it is stronger in coverage and not in any kind of understanding. It is not the Distillation & pruning lab's setup, where a student is trained against the teacher's probabilities rather than its sampled text. In general: verifiers such as unit tests, proof checkers, or answer matching are what make synthetic data useful for code and math. They filter the generator's output; they do not extend what the generator can write. In general: a stronger model writing a weaker one's training data is common. Stanford's Alpaca fine-tuned a 7B LLaMA model on 52K instruction-following examples generated by OpenAI's text-davinci-003, for less than $500 of API use, and its authors restricted it to academic research partly because the data inherits the teacher's terms of use. The data's licence is part of what the student inherits.

Lost cells cluster among the pairs the seed used least. A 28 × 28 grid: rows are the current character, columns the next one (space is shown as ␣). Only pairs that occur in the seed are drawn. A filled cell is a pair still present; darker means the seed used it more often. An outlined cell with a diagonal stroke is a pair that is gone. The title counts how many of the seed's 157 pairs remain. Three bars below split the lost pairs by how often the seed used them: once, 2–4 times, or 5+ times. A cell is present when the selected generation's training counts contain that pair at least once. Under Real + synthetic the seed is part of those counts, so no cell can be lost. The grouping reads the seed's own counts: 72 pairs occur once, 58 occur 2–4 times, and 27 occur 5 or more times. The grid follows `Generation`, `Training data`, and the three generator settings. Hover a cell for the pair and its seed count. Comparison worth running: at the defaults step Generation from 1 to 10 with Synthetic only and watch the crossed cells spread from the pale ones toward the dark ones. At the defaults, run 1 at generation 10 has lost 63 of the 72 once-seen pairs, 35 of 58 pairs seen 2–4 times, and 8 of 27 common pairs. The tail goes first. No cell outside the seed ever appears. The loop can only lose pairs, never invent them, because a zero-probability pair cannot be sampled. In this lab: the grid shows one run of eight, so its counts can differ from the chart's mean. In general: a language model's tail is not a grid of character pairs but rare facts, dialects, styles, and edge cases. documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: A model trained for a general objective such as next-token prediction, before assistant or domain adaptation. It is a starting point, not a finished product.
documents.title: Base model

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: A further training run on a narrower dataset. The name does not tell you whether the data were public, licensed, or synthetic, and the base model's license usually still applies.
documents.title: Fine-tune

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: A file of parameters you can download and run. It does not by itself include training data, training code, or permission for every use.
documents.title: Open weights

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: Under the Open Source Initiative's definition (OSAID 1.0, October 2024): the weights, the complete training and inference code, and data information detailed enough to build a substantially equivalent system, all under terms that allow any purpose.
documents.title: Open source AI

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: A hosted interface that runs a model for you. You get behavior, not weights, and the terms of service decide what you may do with outputs, such as whether they may train a competing model.
documents.title: API

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: The legal terms on weights, code, data, or outputs. A research-only clause can sit on otherwise downloadable files, and a license cannot grant rights its authors never had.
documents.title: License

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: A license such as Apache-2.0 or MIT that allows any use, including commercial, with light conditions such as keeping notices. On weights alone it still does not make a release open-source AI.
documents.title: Permissive license

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: A list of banned uses attached to a license or an API. It makes the grant conditional, which is one reason custom model licenses do not meet the Open Source Definition.
documents.title: Acceptable-use policy

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: A structured document describing a model's intended uses, training data, evaluation, and limitations, proposed by Mitchell et al. (2019). It is only as good as what its authors chose to disclose.
documents.title: Model card

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: Where training data came from and under what terms or consent. Permission to use the weights does not repair missing provenance.
documents.title: Data provenance

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: A scripted set of tasks and scoring rules used to compare models. A leaderboard position is a score on that harness, not a complete quality claim.
documents.title: Evaluation harness

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The ecosystem
documents.body: The spread a measured score has from sampling alone: the square root of p(1 − p)/n for accuracy p on n items. On 40 items at 70% it is about 7 points.
documents.title: Standard error

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The ecosystem · question 1
documents.body: A model ships its weights under Apache-2.0, with no training code and no information about its training data. Which description is accurate? Open source AI, because Apache-2.0 is an open-source license and the weights are public Closed, because a release that gives no data information cannot be reused in any way API-only, because training code that stays private means the model can only be reached remotely Open weights under a permissive license, but short of open-source AI as OSAID 1.0 defines it Apache-2.0 lets you use, modify, and redistribute the weights for any purpose, so they are permissively licensed open weights. OSAID 1.0 also asks for the complete training code and data information detailed enough to build a substantially equivalent system. The weights are downloadable, so it is not API-only, and a permissive license is exactly what lets you reuse them.
documents.title: A model ships its weights under Apache-2.0, with no training code and no information about its training data. Which description is accurate?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The ecosystem · question 2
documents.body: You set License to Apache-2.0 and Intended use to Hosted product, and License match says yes. What has that settled? That the product is safe to launch, because the license answers every legal question about the model That the training data was gathered with permission, since a license could not be granted otherwise That commercial use is allowed, while where the training data came from is still unknown That the release is open-source AI, because the license now allows any purpose License match looks up the clauses the use needs, here commercial use, and Apache-2.0 grants it. It cannot answer where the data came from or whether the people in it consented, because a license cannot grant rights its authors never had; Still unknown depends only on Data information. A permissive license on the weights also does not by itself make a release open-source AI.
documents.title: You set License to Apache-2.0 and Intended use to Hosted product, and License match says yes. What has that settled?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The ecosystem · question 3
documents.body: Model A scores 73% and model B scores 70% on the card's 40-item harness. What does the card's own arithmetic say about that 3-point gap? It settles the ranking, because both models were scored on exactly the same 40 test items It is inside the harness's standard error of about 7 points, so this harness cannot rank them reliably It would become reliable once either score passes 80%, because noise vanishes near the ceiling It is a real difference, because a computed score has no sampling error to worry about A score measured on n items has a standard error of the square root of p(1 − p)/n, about 7 points at 70% on 40 items. Resampling the items would move either score by about that much, so a 3-point gap is inside the noise even though both models saw the same questions. The error shrinks only slowly near the ceiling (about 6 points at 80%) and mainly with more items.

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The ecosystem · question 4
documents.body: A real model card lists a strong harness score but says nothing about its training data. What is the sound way to read the omission? As neutral, because a card only has to report scores and the data is the developer's own business As a gap in what you know: provenance, consent, and leakage cannot be judged from this card As reassurance, because developers are happy to disclose their data whenever it is clean As harmless, because OSAID 1.0 never asks for any information about how the data was built A card is only as good as what its authors chose to disclose, so a missing field is information, not a blank to fill with hope. Without data information you cannot check provenance or consent, and you cannot rule out that benchmark items leaked into training and inflated the score. OSAID 1.0 does ask for data information, though not necessarily the data itself.
