documents.subtitle: Plain · The ecosystem
documents.body: Training an AI model is the long process in which it learns from huge amounts of text. When a company or a research group finishes training one, it has to decide what to hand to everyone else. That decision is called a release. Some releases come with a download button, some only let you type into a website, and many sit somewhere in between. This module takes a release apart piece by piece, the way you might unpack a delivery to check that everything on the packing slip is really in the box. Taking it apart answers three questions that a download button hides. What did you actually receive? What are you allowed to do with it? And how far can you trust the numbers printed about it? People often talk as if the word "open" answers all three, but you will see that it does not answer any of them on its own. Where you have met it Every AI model you have heard of was released in one of these ways, and the ways differ a lot. When GPT-4 came out in 2023, you could only use it through OpenAI's own apps and its online service, so nobody outside the company could download the model itself. That same year, Meta's Llama 2 and a model called Mistral 7B came out as files anyone could download. The two came with quite different rules, though, about what you could do with them. Releases also come with a written description, a bit like the label on a box, and with test scores that people use to rank models on a leaderboard. This module builds on three earlier labs: Post-training, which showed how a raw starting model gets adapted into other models; Scaling laws, which linked a model's size to its training text and computing cost; How we know a model works, which showed that one headline score can hide what matters. Why it matters If you read one part of a release as if it were the whole thing, you can make real and costly mistakes, such as these: building a paid app on a model whose rules allow research only; training a model of your own on another model's answers when its rules forbid that; assuming that generous rules on the download mean the training data was gathered fairly, with the agreement of the people who wrote it; declaring one model better than another because of a 3-point gap on a test whose scores can wobble by about 7 points from luck alone. What you will be able to explain By the end of this module, you should be able to explain these things in your own words: how a raw starting model, called a base model, differs from a version adapted from it, called a fine-tune; how using a model through a company's online service, called an API, differs from downloading the model itself, called open weights; why a download with generous rules still falls short of open-source AI, which also needs the code that built the model and a detailed description of its training data; how to check a planned use against a license, the legal rules attached to a model, one rule at a time, and why the strictest rule decides; why that permission still says nothing about where the training data came from, or whether its writers agreed; how to read the numbers on a model card, the description that comes with a model, starting with how much a test score could wobble by chance; what an estimate of the electricity used in training counts, and what it leaves out. What the lab lets you see and try Nothing in this lab is trained, and no model actually answers anything. The model, called harbor-lm-7b, is made up for this lab, and so are its test and its three licenses. Each kind of rule in those licenses is borrowed from real ones, though. When the lab says a use is allowed or not, it is looking that use up in the made-up rules, so it is never legal advice. Two numbers on the card are worked out with fixed formulas from the card's own figures. One is how much the test score could wobble, and the other estimates the electricity the chips used for one training run. The lab has three cards, and they work together: Sample model card shows the model's description. Its License control sets the rules, while its Training code and Data information controls set what comes with the model. A badge names the kind of release you have made. Release spectrum has no controls of its own. It is a table of four kinds of release, running from API only to open-source AI, with the column for the model on the Sample model card highlighted. Is this use allowed lets you pick an Intended use and checks it against the license, then reports License match, Clauses checked and Still unknown. The most important experiment comes last. You give the model its most generous license, ask about selling a product built on it, and get a yes. Meanwhile, Still unknown keeps showing you what the license could never answer.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · The ecosystem
documents.body: A release is a bundle of parts Picture a bakery that has made a remarkable cake and now has to decide what to give away. It could serve you a slice across the counter or hand you the whole cake in a box. It could add the recipe card, list every ingredient and where each one came from, and print rules on the box about what you may do with the cake. Each of those is a separate choice, and getting one of them tells you nothing about the others. An AI model release works the same way, because it is a bundle of parts that can each be shared freely, held back or shared only with rules attached: the weights, the file that is the trained model itself, which is the cake; inference code, the program that uses the weights to turn your typed text into the model's answer; training code, the program that made the weights, which is the recipe; data information, a description of the text the model learned from, which is the ingredient list; the license, the legal terms that say what you may do, which are the rules printed on the box; evaluation results, the model's scores on tests; cost figures, such as how much computing and electricity training used. The weights need a word of explanation, because everything else hangs off them. A model is a huge collection of adjustable numbers, called parameters or weights, and training is the long process of nudging each number until the model's guesses improve. When training stops, those numbers are the finished model, so the weights file is the model you would download. The lab's made-up model, harbor-lm-7b, has 7 billion of them, which is what the "7B" on its card means. The bakery picture stops matching in two places. A cake gets eaten once, while a weights file can be copied endlessly at almost no cost, which is why licenses have rules about passing copies on. And even with the full recipe and ingredient list, rebuilding the model would take a huge amount of computing power, the kind few people have. A home baker with a recipe faces no such barrier, and later in this module you will see just how large that amount is. Base model and fine-tune The first model a big training run produces is called a base model. It was trained on a huge pile of text to do one job, which is to guess the next small piece of text. That small piece is called a token, and it is usually a word or part of a word. A base model is good at continuing text but is not yet an assistant, so if you type a question, it might add more questions instead of answering. A fine-tune is a second, narrower training run on top of a base model. It uses a smaller set of examples chosen for one purpose, such as answering questions politely, and it adjusts the model to suit that purpose. The name "fine-tune" does not tell you whether those extra examples were public, paid for or written by another model. Because a fine-tune starts from the base model's weights, it usually carries along the base model's license and any problems hidden in its training data. You can see both ideas on the lab's Sample model card. Its Base model row reads "7B parameters, next-token pretrained on 2T tokens. Not an assistant." In everyday words, it has 7 billion weights and learned by guessing the next token across 2 trillion tokens, but nobody trained it to be a helper. "Pretrained" is the name for that first big training run, the one that comes before any fine-tune. The Fine-tunes row reads "None from the authors. Community adapters exist, unreviewed." That means the makers built no fine-tunes, while other people have trained small add-on pieces, called adapters, that have not been reviewed. Open weights and the API There are two very different ways to let people use a model. With open weights, you can download the weights file and run the model on your own computer. Your copy then keeps working the same way, even if its makers later change their own service. That is all the phrase promises, though, because it says nothing about training code, data information or permission for every use. The other way keeps the model on the company's own computers. You send your text over the internet, the company runs the model, and it sends back the answer. The doorway that lets one program send requests to another like this is called an API. With an API you can use what the model does, but you never get its weights. The company's terms of service, the rules you accept to use it, decide what you may do with its answers, such as training a rival model on them. The company can also change the model behind the API whenever it likes, and your app will feel that change without you choosing it. Back at the bakery, open weights are like the whole cake in a box, while an API is like a café that serves slices but keeps the cake. On the Release spectrum card, the API only column is the only one where the "Run on your own hardware" row, meaning on your own computers, says "no". Open source AI: the full kit You may have heard "open source" used for apps whose code anyone may read, change and share. For AI, a group called the Open Source Initiative, or OSI, published a definition of open source AI in October 2024. It is called the Open Source AI Definition 1.0, which the lab shortens to OSAID 1.0, and it asks for three things together: the weights; the complete code used to train the model and to run it; information about the training data detailed enough that a skilled person could build a substantially equivalent system, meaning one close enough to do the same job about as well. On top of that, all three must come under terms that allow use for any purpose, including making money. Notice what is missing from the list: the training data itself. The definition asks for detailed information about the data rather than always the data, which is why the last row of Release spectrum says "not always required" for open-source AI. In that table, "not required" or "not always required" means that kind of release does not promise the item. Open source AI is like getting the cake, the full recipe and an ingredient list precise enough to shop from, all with permission to sell whatever you bake. The bakery still does not have to hand over its own sacks of flour. A permissive license is one that allows any use, including selling, with only light conditions such as keeping the original notices attached. Those notices are the short lines that say who made the work and under what license. Apache-2.0 and MIT are two examples, and Apache-2.0 is one of the three choices in the lab. Even so, a permissive license on the weights alone leaves a release short of open source AI, because the training code and data information can still be missing. A common mix-up: people often call any downloadable model "open source". Under the definition this lab uses, a download on its own is only open weights. It becomes open source AI only when the complete code, detailed data information and any-purpose terms come with it. The license, one rule at a time A license is the set of legal terms attached to weights, code, data or answers, and it works like a list of separate rules called clauses. Each use you might plan needs particular permissions, such as these: permission to make money from the model, called commercial use; permission to change the model, such as by fine-tuning it; permission to pass copies on to other people, called redistributing; permission to use the model's answers to train another model. The lab's Intended use menu offers four plans. A Research paper means studying the model and writing up what you find. A Hosted product is an app or website you charge for that runs the model on computers you control, so customers use it without getting a copy. Fine-tune and ship means changing the model and handing out the result. Train on its outputs means training another model on its answers, which the lab calls its outputs. The Is this use allowed card checks a use in three steps. First it lists each clause the use needs, and then it looks up each one in the license and marks it ✓ allowed, ◐ allowed with conditions or ✗ not allowed. Finally it reports the strictest of those marks, because one refusal is enough to block the whole use. Think of a school trip that needs a yes from your parent, your teacher and the coach. If any one of them says no, you stay home, however keen the other two are. If one says yes only if you bring a packed lunch, then you go only with the lunch. A license check works the same way, so a use is only as allowed as its strictest clause. Here is a worked example from the lab. Set License to Apache-2.0 and Intended use to Fine-tune and ship, which needs three clauses because you would be selling, changing and handing out the model. Commercial use shows ✓ "granted for any purpose", and Modify or fine-tune shows ✓ "allowed; modified files must say they were changed". That row gets a ✓ even though it carries a small duty, because the lab treats labelling your changes as part of the permission itself. Redistribute the weights shows ◐ "allowed with a copy of the license and the notices", because the lab counts passing the license on with every copy as a real condition. In real licenses both are light duties. The strictest mark is the ◐, so License match reads "if conditions met" and Clauses checked reads 3, even under the most generous license in the lab. Some licenses attach an acceptable-use policy, a list of banned uses, so your permission only holds while you stay away from them. In the lab, the Custom community license allows commercial use "below a monthly-user cap, subject to an acceptable-use policy". That means you may sell a product only while fewer than a set number of people use it each month. Even then, your product must stay clear of every use on the banned list. Conditions like these are one reason custom model licenses do not meet the OSI's definition of open source, which asks for freedom to use something for any purpose. What a license cannot settle The word provenance means where something came from and how it got here, the way a museum tracks who owned a painting before it arrived. Data provenance is the same idea for training data, covering where the text came from, on what terms it was collected, and whether its writers agreed, which is called consent. A license can only give away rights that its authors actually had. Picture a classmate who makes a poster from photos found online and writes "free for anyone to use" across the bottom. That note can let you reuse the classmate's own layout and lettering, but it cannot give away the photographers' rights, because the classmate never had them. A model license works the same way: it can let you use the weights, but it cannot promise that the training text was collected fairly or with consent. The match is not exact, because a model's weights are adjusted numbers rather than a folder holding the original texts. The point is only that whoever writes a license cannot give away rights to material they never owned. You can watch this in the lab's Still unknown readout. With Data information set to not published, the card says only "Web crawl and licensed books" and notes that there are no sources, mix or consent log. That describes text gathered automatically from websites plus books the makers got permission to use, but it names no actual sources, so Still unknown reads "data sources, consent". Now set Data information to published. The card then says three things have been published: the sources, the filtering steps used to clean the text, and how much text came from each source. It adds that these are detailed enough to rebuild a similar set. It still says "No consent log", though, so Still unknown shrinks to "consent" but never disappears. Changing License never moves this readout, because it depends only on Data information. Reading a model card A model card is a structured document that describes a model: what it is meant for, what it was trained on, how it was tested and where it falls short. It is the label on the box, and like any label, it is only as good as what its authors chose to put on it. Nothing forces a card to be complete or accurate, so a missing field tells you something too. Two rows on harbor-lm-7b's card are worked out from the card's own figures rather than typed in, and reading them well is the third skill this module teaches. How much a test score could wobble An evaluation harness is a fixed set of test questions, called items, along with rules for scoring the answers. A program runs it, so every model is tested in exactly the same way. A place on a leaderboard is a score on one such harness, not a full verdict on how good a model is. The card says harbor-bench has 40 items and the model scored 70%, which means 28 right answers out of 40. Picture a student who has learned about 70% of a history chapter and sits a 40-question quiz on it. If the quiz happens to lean toward the parts they know, they might get 31 right, and if it leans the other way, they might get 25. Their knowledge did not change between those two quizzes; only the luck of which questions were picked did. The amount a score spreads out from that luck alone is called the standard error. Going from 28 right to 25 or 31 is 3 questions either way. Since 3 out of 40 is 7.5% of the quiz, that is close to the standard error you are about to work out. The card's info panel shows the formula: standard error = √(p(1 − p)/n), where p is the score written as a decimal and n is the number of items. Here is the calculation with the card's numbers, one step at a time: The score is 70%, so p is 0.7, and 1 − p is 0.3. Multiplying gives 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.21. Dividing by the 40 items gives 0.21 ÷ 40 = 0.00525. The square root of 0.00525 is about 0.072. Because p was a decimal, multiply by 100 to turn the answer back into percentages, which gives about 7.2 percentage points. A percentage point is the plain gap between two percentages, so 7.2 points is the distance from 70% to 77.2%. That is why the card says "One standard error is ±7.2 points", where ± means "plus or minus". The card then gives a 95% interval, a range wide enough that the model's true score, the one it would earn on a huge test, very likely sits inside it. The "95%" says how likely: a range built this way catches the true score about 95 times in 100. To build it, you go about two standard errors either side of 70%, which is roughly 14 points each way, so the card shows "about 56–84%". That range changes how you should read a leaderboard. Suppose another model gets 29 of the 40 items right, which is 72.5%, or 2.5 points higher. That gap is smaller than one standard error, so fresh questions could easily flip which model comes out ahead. More items help, but slowly. With 160 items, four times as many, step 3 becomes 0.21 ÷ 160, which is a quarter of 0.00525. The square root of a quarter is a half, so the wobble only halves, to about 3.6 points. To cut the wobble in half, you need four times as many questions. What the energy figure counts The Training energy (estimated) row reads "6 × 7B × 2T = 8.4×10²² FLOP". It comes from a standard rule of thumb: training takes about 6 arithmetic operations per weight for every token of training text. A single multiplication or addition of two decimal numbers is called a FLOP, short for floating-point operation, because computers call decimal numbers floating-point numbers. Here is the chain of steps the card follows: Multiply 6 by 7 billion weights and then by 2 trillion tokens. The result is about 84,000 billion billion FLOP, which the card writes as 8.4×10²², meaning 8.4 with its decimal point moved 22 places to the right. Training runs on graphics chips, called GPUs, which are built to do enormous numbers of these operations at once. The card assumes a chip called the A100, whose top speed is 312 trillion FLOP per second, written 312 TFLOP/s. Chips in real training rarely run at top speed, so the card assumes they average 40% of it, which is about 125 trillion FLOP per second. Dividing 8.4×10²² FLOP by that speed gives about 673 million seconds of work for one chip. There are 3,600 seconds in an hour, so that is about 187,000 GPU-hours, where one GPU-hour is one chip working for one hour. Each chip draws about 400 watts, a unit for how fast electricity is used. One chip running for an hour therefore uses 400 watt-hours, and 187,000 chip-hours use about 75 million watt-hours. "Mega" means million, so 75 million watt-hours is 75 megawatt-hours, written 75 MWh. To feel the size of 187,000 GPU-hours, imagine one chip doing all the work alone, which would take about 21 years. Spread across 1,000 chips, the same work would take about 8 days. Now read the end of that row: "one run, not serving". The estimate counts only the chips' own power for one successful training run. It leaves out cooling, the computers' other parts, the network between them, failed runs and the experiments before the final run. It also leaves out serving, the energy used every time someone asks the finished model a question, so the true total is larger.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · The ecosystem
documents.body: A download feels like a product off a shop shelf: once it is yours, you expect to use it however you like. AI releases do not work like that, because three separate questions decide whether you can safely build on one, and each answer lives in a different part of the release. Nobody gathers the answers for you, and the download button answers none of them. Picture a friend who finds harbor-lm-7b, likes its 70% test score, and builds a homework-helper app that charges a small monthly fee. Each part of the card has something different to tell them: License answers the legal question. Under Research only, the Commercial use clause says "no commercial use of the weights or a hosted service", so the app is blocked before cost or quality even come up. Data information answers the data question, but only partly. Even with the most generous license, the card cannot say whether the people whose writing trained the model ever agreed, so that risk travels into the app. Evaluation harness answers the quality question, but only together with its standard error. If your friend picked this model over a rival because it scored 3 points higher, the card's own arithmetic says that gap is smaller than the wobble from luck alone. The same problem repeats down the chain. If your friend fine-tunes harbor-lm-7b first, the new model usually inherits the original license and any gaps in the original data, whatever the new name says. That is why this module trains you to read every part separately rather than trusting the part you looked at first. The Ethics and impact lab builds on these same distinctions, because it asks who pays the costs that a model card only hints at.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · The ecosystem
documents.body: Work through the cards in this order, and predict what will change before each click: Read Sample model card top to bottom before changing anything, paying special attention to the License, Data information, Evaluation harness and Training energy (estimated) rows. With the starting settings, the badge reads "Open weights, restricted license". Set License to Apache-2.0, then Training code to released, and then Data information to published. After each click, read the note under the controls and watch the highlighted column in Release spectrum. The column moves from restricted to permissive after the first click, stays put after the second, and jumps to Open source AI after the third. Until then, the note lists what is still missing for OSAID 1.0. After the third click, it stops listing missing pieces and says the card has the components OSAID 1.0 asks for. It adds that OSI's own review would also check the exact terms. Set Intended use to Hosted product, then to Train on its outputs. Try each under Research only and then under Custom community, and read which clause row carries the ✗ or ◐ that decides the result. Set License to Apache-2.0 and Intended use to Hosted product. License match says yes, so now read Still unknown and ask yourself why switching licenses never changed it. For the step 3 comparison, here is what to expect. A Hosted product needs only commercial use, so Research only gives "no" while Custom community gives "if conditions met". Train on its outputs needs commercial use plus the outputs clause, and under Custom community that second clause says "outputs may not be used to improve another model family". So License match turns to "no", even though the commercial clause on its own would have been allowed with conditions. Under Research only, both rows of Train on its outputs show ✗, so either one alone would block it. The lab assumes you train the new model to use it to make money, which is why this use also needs the commercial clause. Try this: With Training code at released and Data information at published, switch License back to Research only. Every file is still on offer, yet the Release spectrum title drops back to "This card sits in: Open weights, restricted license". The note now lists only one missing piece: "terms that allow any purpose".
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · The ecosystem
documents.body: Terms matter as much as files. Research only with the training code and data information both released is still restricted open weights, because the rules do not allow every purpose. Permissive weights are not the full kit. Under Apache-2.0 with nothing else released, the badge reads "Open weights, permissive license", and it only reaches "Open source AI (OSAID 1.0 components)" once code and data information arrive too. The strictest clause decides. One ✗ row turns License match to "no", however many ✓ rows sit beside it, and one ◐ row with no ✗ gives "if conditions met". Permission and provenance are different questions. Under Apache-2.0 the hosted product is allowed, and the data's consent is still unknown, while its sources are unknown too unless Data information is published. Forty items make a small test. At 70%, one standard error is about 7 points, so the true score very likely sits somewhere from about 56% to 84%. A 3-point gap between two models means little. The energy figure is a calculation, not a meter reading. For comparison, Meta reported 184,320 GPU-hours to train Llama 2 7B on the same 2 trillion tokens, which is close to the card's estimate of about 187,000.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · The ecosystem
documents.body: What this lab simplifies The model harbor-lm-7b, its harness and all three licenses are made up for this lab, although the kinds of clauses come from real licenses. Each verdict is a lookup in those made-up clauses, and none of it is legal advice. The four columns in Release spectrum are categories, not products, and they squeeze a smooth range into four boxes. Real releases mix their parts in many ways, and OSI's own review of a release would also weigh its exact terms. "Not required" or "not always required" in a column means that kind of release does not promise the item, while some real releases in that column include it anyway. The energy figure uses fixed guesses, 40% of top speed and 400 watts per chip, and counts only the chips' own power for one successful run. It leaves out cooling, the other computer parts, networking, failed runs, experiments and serving. The standard error only covers the luck of which questions were picked. It cannot catch a score pushed up by other problems, such as the ones in the next list. Where the real thing goes wrong Licenses change between versions and differ from country to country, and custom model licenses often change from one release to the next. An API's terms of service can limit what you do with its answers even though you never see the weights. A fine-tune usually inherits its base model's license, along with any problems in the base model's data. A real model card can be wrong or silent, and a missing field is information rather than a blank to fill with hope. A test score can be inflated when test items leak into the training data, so the model has effectively seen the answers before the test. OSAID 1.0 is one definition of openness. Other groups define it differently, and some releases that their makers call "open" do not meet it. A common mix-up: people treat a download button as permission. Permission lives in the license, and even the most generous license cannot promise that the training data was collected fairly or with consent.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · The ecosystem
documents.body: Here are real examples of where releases sat when they came out, though later versions may have changed: GPT-4 (2023) was offered only through OpenAI's API and apps, and its weights were not released. Llama 2 (2023) came out as open weights under a custom license with an acceptable-use policy. Services with more than 700 million monthly users needed a separate license, and the OSI said Llama 2 is not open source. Mistral 7B (2023) came out as weights under Apache-2.0, without its training data. EleutherAI's Pythia (2023) and AI2's OLMo (2024) released their weights, their training code and their training data. The rule of 6 operations per weight per token counts two kinds of work in training. One pass runs forward through the model to make a guess, and a second pass runs backward to work out how each weight should change. Meta's reported 184,320 GPU-hours for Llama 2 7B is less than 2% away from the card's estimate. So the card's simple rule, with its guess of 40% of top speed, lands close to a real reported figure. The idea of a model card was proposed by Mitchell and colleagues in 2019, as a structured way to describe a model's intended uses, training data, testing and limits. Ethics and impact compares the energy used in training with the energy used in serving, and asks who is represented in a benchmark. Evaluation shows how a harness gets contaminated when its test items leak into training data, and Deployment & serving follows the hosted-product path from a model to a working service.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · The ecosystem
documents.body: This module takes a model release apart. It answers three questions a download button hides: what you actually received, what you may do with it, and how far its reported numbers can be trusted. The word "open" settles none of them on its own. It builds on *Post-training*, which separated a base model from the models adapted from it; *Scaling laws*, which related parameters, tokens and compute; and *How we know a model works*, which showed that one headline score can hide what matters. Where it shows up A model's release page or download, which lists or leaves out each part: weights, code, data information, license, evaluation results and cost figures. The model card, the structured document describing a release, and leaderboard scores from an evaluation harness, a scripted set of test items and scoring rules. At release, GPT-4 (2023) was API-only, Llama 2 (2023) shipped open weights under a custom license, Mistral 7B (2023) shipped weights under Apache-2.0 without its training data, and Pythia (2023) and OLMo (2024) released weights, training code and training data. The Open Source Initiative's Open Source AI Definition 1.0 (OSAID 1.0, October 2024), the definition of open source AI this module uses. Why it matters Reading one part of a release as the whole, or a reported score as exact, leads to concrete mistakes: shipping a hosted product on weights licensed for research only; training another model on outputs that a license or an API's terms of service forbid; taking a permissive license as clearance for training data whose origin and consent are unknown; ranking two models on a 3-point gap from a 40-item harness, where a score of 70% has a standard error of about 7 points (the spread a score has from sampling its items alone). What you will be able to explain How a base model, a fine-tune, an API, open weights and open-source AI differ, and why permissively licensed weights alone fall short of open-source AI. How to check a proposed use against a license clause by clause, why the strictest clause decides, and why that permission says nothing about data provenance. How to read a model card's numbers critically: the standard error on a harness score, and what an estimated training-energy figure counts and leaves out. What the lab shows Nothing is trained or run. harbor-lm-7b, its harness and its three licenses are fictional, with clause types drawn from real licenses. Every verdict is a lookup of those clauses, not legal advice. Two card fields are closed-form: the standard error for 40 items at 70%, and the training energy from 6 × parameters × tokens at a fixed A100 peak of 312 TFLOP/s, 40% utilization and 400 W per GPU. Sample model card: License sets the terms, and Training code and Data information set what ships beside the weights. A badge names the release tier, and a note lists what is still missing for OSAID 1.0. Release spectrum: no controls. Four columns run from API only to Open source AI, and the card's column is highlighted. Is this use allowed: Intended use picks one of four uses, and the card lists each clause that use needs as allowed, allowed with conditions, or not allowed. License match reports the strictest, beside Clauses checked and Still unknown. The key experiment sets License to Apache-2.0 and Intended use to Hosted product. License match says yes, but Still unknown keeps listing what the license cannot answer, because that readout depends only on Data information.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · The ecosystem
documents.body: A model release is a bundle of separable parts: weights, inference code, training code, data or information about the data, a license, evaluation results, and cost figures. Each part can be shipped, withheld, or restricted on its own. A base model is next-token pretrained and is not yet an assistant. A fine-tune is a further, narrower run on top of one. An API sells access to behavior without the weights. Open weights means you can download the parameters, and nothing more is implied. Open weights are not open source The Open Source Initiative published version 1.0 of its Open Source AI Definition in October 2024. It asks for the parameters, the complete code used to train and run the system, and data information detailed enough that a skilled person could build a substantially equivalent system. All of it must come under terms that allow use for any purpose. So open source AI differs from open weights on code, data information, and terms. A permissive license such as Apache-2.0 on the weights alone still leaves a release short. The definition does not require publishing all training data in every case. Permission is per use A use needs specific permissions: commercial use, modification, redistribution, or using outputs to train another model. The strictest clause it touches decides. An acceptable-use policy makes a grant conditional, which is one reason custom model licenses do not meet the Open Source Definition. A license only settles what its authors could grant. Data provenance, where the training data came from and on what terms, is a separate question.

documents.body: Examples at release, which later versions may change: GPT-4 (2023) was offered only through OpenAI's API and apps; its weights were not released. Llama 2 (2023) shipped open weights under a custom license with an acceptable-use policy and a separate-license requirement above 700 million monthly active users. OSI said it is not open source. Mistral 7B (2023) shipped weights under Apache-2.0, without its training data. EleutherAI's Pythia (2023) and AI2's OLMo (2024) released weights, training code, and training data. Ethics and impact compares training energy with serving energy and asks who is represented in a benchmark. Evaluation shows how a harness gets contaminated, and Deployment & serving is the hosted-product path.

documents.subtitle: Sample model card · The ecosystem
documents.body: A fictional 7B release with real-shaped fields harbor-lm-7b is authored for this lab, but every field is one a real model card should make you read. Three release choices, License, Training code, and Data information, decide which kind of release it is. Two fields are computed from the card's own numbers: the evaluation error and the training energy. Rows for base model, fine-tunes, weights, training code, data information, license, evaluation harness, and training energy. Red and green text marks what is missing or present. License (Research only, Custom community, Apache-2.0), Training code (not released or released), and Data information (not published or published). A badge naming the release tier, and a note listing what is still missing for the Open Source AI Definition. Evaluation harness: standard error = √(p(1 − p)/n) = √(0.7 × 0.3 / 40) ≈ 0.072, so ±7.2 points, and a 95% interval of about 56–84%. Training energy: compute ≈ 6·N·D = 6 × 7×10⁹ × 2×10¹² = 8.4×10²² FLOP. At 40% of an A100's 312 TFLOP/s dense BF16 peak that is about 187,000 GPU-hours; at 400 W per GPU, about 75 MWh. The tier is computed: a license that is not any-purpose makes it restricted open weights; Apache-2.0 without training code or data information makes it permissive open weights; Apache-2.0 with both has the components OSAID 1.0 asks for. License, Training code, and Data information on this card. Intended use is on Is this use allowed. Comparison worth running: Apache-2.0 with nothing else released, then with Training code and Data information. The tier changes; the weights file does not. For scale, Meta reported 184,320 A100 GPU-hours to pretrain Llama 2 7B on 2T tokens, close to this 6ND estimate at 40% utilization. Forty items cannot separate two models whose scores differ by a few points. In this lab: the model, the harness, and the licenses are fictional. The energy figure counts GPU board power only, for one successful run, with no cooling overhead, failed runs, or experiments. In general: a real card can omit the field you need. A missing field is information, not a blank to fill with hope, and nothing forces a card to be accurate.
documents.title: A fictional 7B release with real-shaped fields

documents.subtitle: Release spectrum · The ecosystem
documents.body: Four kinds of release, six things you might get Columns are categories of release, from API-only to open-source AI as the Open Source Initiative defines it. Rows are what you might need. The column this card falls into is highlighted and moves as you change License, Training code, and Data information. A table with columns API only, Open weights with a restricted license, Open weights with a permissive license, and Open source AI (OSAID 1.0 components). The current card's column is shaded and marked this card. Cells read yes, no, limited, required, not required, or not always required, colored and worded so color is never the only signal. OSAID 1.0 (Open Source Initiative, October 2024) requires the model parameters, the complete code used to train and run the system, and data information detailed enough that a skilled person could build a substantially equivalent system, under terms that allow any purpose. It does not require releasing all training data in every case, which is why the last row says "not always required". "Not required" in an open-weights column means the category promises nothing; individual releases sometimes include more. No controls on this card. The highlighted column follows Sample model card. Comparison worth running: Research only with everything released still sits in the restricted column, because the terms are not any-purpose. Open weights and open source differ on code, data information, and terms, not on whether you can download a file. Only the API column withholds the weights entirely, and it is the only one where the provider can change behavior under you. In this lab: four columns simplify a continuum. Real releases mix components, and OSI's own review weighs the exact terms. In general: OSAID 1.0 is one definition. Other groups define openness differently, and some prominent releases called open by their authors do not meet it.

documents.subtitle: Is this use allowed · The ecosystem
documents.body: A use needs clauses; the strictest one decides Each intended use needs one or more permissions. The lab looks up each needed clause in the card's license and reports the strictest outcome. A separate readout keeps what the license cannot answer, where the data came from, in view. Intended use: Research paper, Hosted product, Fine-tune and ship, or Train on its outputs. One row per clause the use needs, marked ✓ allowed, ◐ allowed with conditions, or ✗ not allowed, with the clause text. License match, Clauses checked, and Still unknown. Needs: research paper → research use; hosted product → commercial use; fine-tune and ship → commercial use, modification, redistribution; train on outputs → commercial use and use of outputs to train another model. Verdict = worst outcome among the needed clauses. Apache-2.0 redistribution is conditional because the license and notices must travel with the copy. Still unknown depends only on Data information, never on the license. Intended use here; License, Training code, and Data information on Sample model card. Comparison worth running: Train on its outputs under Custom community, then under Apache-2.0. A download button is not a grant. Research only blocks the hosted product before any cost or quality question arises. Under Apache-2.0 the hosted product is allowed, and consent for the training data is still unknown. In this lab: three fictional licenses with clause types drawn from real ones. This is not legal advice, and real terms vary by jurisdiction and version. In general: API terms of service also govern outputs, and a fine-tune usually inherits the base model's license along with any data problems the name "fine-tune" does not mention.

documents.subtitle: Watch a real byte-pair tokenizer turn text into IDs one merge at a time, then query real word vectors for neighbours, analogies, and a flat map that distorts them.
documents.body: Watch a real byte-pair tokenizer turn text into IDs one merge at a time, then query real word vectors for neighbours, analogies, and a flat map that distorts them. Explain why models process tokens rather than words Trace how byte-pair merges turn bytes into token IDs Interpret distance in an embedding space Explain why an embedding is one vector per token and where word order has to come from
documents.title: Tokens & embeddings

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Keep the default sentence and drag Vocabulary size from 512 down to 69. Compare the Tokens count: the text is unchanged, only the merge budget shrank.

documents.body: Select the ␣king chip and read Merge trace from bytes to the final token. Then set Vocabulary size below 345 and watch the last rung fade and the chip split.
documents.title: Replay the merges

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Compare the IDs on The, ␣the and ␣king, and note that the two ␣the chips in the default sentence share ID 82: one row, wherever the word sits. Then pick the sample 2024 was 33 years and find the <unk> chips with ID 0.
documents.title: Inspect token IDs

documents.subtitle: Step 4 · Tokens & embeddings
