documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: A chunk of text drawn from a fixed vocabulary. It may be a whole word with its leading space, a word fragment, punctuation, a single byte, or a reserved special token.
documents.title: Token

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: The integer address of a token in the vocabulary. It only selects one row of the embedding matrix and is never used in arithmetic. In this BPE vocabulary IDs follow merge order, but the model attaches no meaning to that order.
documents.title: Token ID

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: The fixed set of tokens a tokenizer can emit: 512 in this lab, usually 32,000 to about 256,000 in production. It is set before training; adding entries later means adding and training new embedding rows.
documents.title: Vocabulary

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: A token smaller than a word, used so a fixed vocabulary can still spell rare words, names, and typos by combining pieces.
documents.title: Subword

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: A tokenizer training method that starts from single bytes or characters and repeatedly adds the most frequent adjacent pair as a new token, so frequent words become one token and rare words decompose.
documents.title: Byte-pair encoding

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: One learned pair, such as i + n becoming in, stored with its rank. Encoding replays the rules in rank order, and a smaller vocabulary is the same list cut short.
documents.title: Merge rule

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: The split into word-like chunks before any merge runs. Merges never cross these boundaries, which is why a leading space stays attached to the word after it.
documents.title: Pre-tokenization

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: A reserved ID with a structural meaning, such as end-of-text, padding, or a chat role marker. Whether the literal string in user text becomes one is an encoder setting; this lab's tokenizer allows it.
documents.title: Special token

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: The learned vector a token ID is replaced with. It is the model's entire representation of that token before any layer runs, and it is the same in every context.
documents.title: Embedding

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: The lookup table of shape vocabulary-by-width holding one trainable row per token. It is often the largest single tensor in a model. Selecting a row equals multiplying a one-hot vector by the matrix.
documents.title: Embedding matrix

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: The width of each vector, written d: 50 for the GloVe vectors here, several hundred to over 16,000 in production models. More dimensions give more directions but raise the cost of every later operation.
documents.title: Embedding dimension

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: The cosine of the angle between two vectors, from −1 to 1, ignoring their lengths. High similarity means used in similar contexts, which includes opposites: the two nearest words to hot here are cool and cold.
documents.title: Cosine similarity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Adding and subtracting word vectors, as in king − man + woman, then taking the nearest remaining word. It works for some relations and fails for others, and the famous answers depend on excluding the input words.
documents.title: Analogy arithmetic

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: A reduction of high-dimensional vectors to two or three dimensions for display. It keeps some neighbourhoods and distorts most distances, and how much depends on the method.
documents.title: Projection

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: A vector that depends on a token's slot, added to its embedding or applied inside attention, because the embedding itself is the same wherever the token appears. Learned, sinusoidal, relative and rotary schemes exist.
documents.title: Positional encoding

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Tokens & embeddings · question 1
documents.body: The sample 2024 was 33 years shows <unk> chips in this lab, but a production byte-level tokenizer would never produce one. Why not? Its vocabulary holds every word that could ever appear, so no text arrives that it lacks an entry for It starts from all 256 byte values, so any text can be spelled out, at the cost of more tokens It skips characters it has not seen, so they cost no tokens and never reach the model at all This lab's alphabet is the 65 byte symbols Tiny Shakespeare happens to use, with no byte fallback, so a digit it never saw becomes <unk>. A production byte-level tokenizer begins from every possible byte, so rare text just splits into many small tokens. Vocabularies hold tens of thousands of entries, far from every word.
documents.title: The sample 2024 was 33 years shows <unk> chips in this lab, but a production byte-level tokenizer would never produce one. Why not?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Tokens & embeddings · question 2
documents.body: In this lab ␣king is one token but ␣queen is three (␣qu, e, en). What explains the difference? Queen is less important to the model, so the tokenizer spends fewer IDs on it than on king Longer words are always cut into more pieces, and queen is longer than king in letters The merge table learned a chain of merges that completes ␣king but never completes ␣queen Merges follow pair frequency in the tokenizer's training text, Tiny Shakespeare. There, merges #8, #44, #91 and #275 build ␣king; ␣queen only reaches ␣qu, e, en. Length and meaning play no direct role: ␣speak is five letters and one token.
documents.title: In this lab ␣king is one token but ␣queen is three (␣qu, e, en). What explains the difference?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Tokens & embeddings · question 3
documents.body: You drag Vocabulary size from 512 down to 69 and leave the text alone. What happens to the Tokens count? It rises, because with fewer merges words fall back to the smaller pieces they are built from It stays the same, because the text is unchanged and each word is still one token It falls, because a smaller vocabulary has fewer entries to emit for the sentence A smaller vocabulary is the same merge list cut short, so the later merges that glued letters into words are missing. Encoding replays only the merges that remain, and each word stays in more pieces. Nothing about the text changed, only how many glue steps were allowed.
documents.title: You drag Vocabulary size from 512 down to 69 and leave the text alone. What happens to the Tokens count?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Tokens & embeddings · question 4
documents.body: In Nearest neighbours, the two closest words to hot are cool and cold. What does a high cosine similarity between two word vectors tell you? The words mean the same thing, so the model treats them as interchangeable The words have nearby token IDs, because similar words are numbered together The words are used in similar contexts, which includes opposites such as hot and cold Training pushes tokens that appear in similar sentence frames toward similar vectors, and hot and cold fill the same frames. Cosine similarity measures that overlap, not agreement in meaning. Token IDs are only shelf addresses assigned in merge order, so they carry no similarity at all.
documents.title: In Nearest neighbours, the two closest words to hot are cool and cold. What does a high cosine similarity between two word vectors tell you?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Tokens & embeddings · question 5
documents.body: On the Embedding projection map, some of a word's true 50-dimensional neighbours sit far from it. What does that tell you? Those words were never really neighbours, so the cosine list in Nearest neighbours is wrong The 2-D map had to discard distance information, so the real cosines are the better guide to use The map is correct and the vectors are noisy, so far-away dots mean the vectors were poorly trained Two directions cannot hold the neighbourhoods of ten thousand words in fifty dimensions, so any projection keeps some neighbours and pulls others apart. The badge counts how many survive: it differs between UMAP and PCA on the same word. Use the map to find a region, then check it against the cosines.
documents.title: On the Embedding projection map, some of a word's true 50-dimensional neighbours sit far from it. What does that tell you?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Tokens & embeddings · question 6
documents.body: In the default sentence both ␣the chips show ID 82. What does the embedding lookup return for them, and what follows from that? A different vector each time, because the lookup reads the words around the token The same vector both times, which is enough because the IDs themselves are numbered in word order The same vector both times, so something else must tell the model which came first An embedding is one row per token ID, chosen without looking at the context, so identical tokens get identical vectors. IDs here follow merge order, not position in the text. Order has to be added separately, as a positional encoding added to the embedding or applied inside attention.
documents.title: In the default sentence both ␣the chips show ID 82. What does the embedding lookup return for them, and what follows from that?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Before a chatbot can do anything with your message, it has to turn your words into numbers, because the program inside it, a language model, works only with numbers. It never sees letters the way you do. This module is about the two steps that turn text into numbers, which run before any of the model's other work begins. In the first step, the text is cut into small pieces called tokens, and each piece gets a number. A token is often a whole word, but not always, because a common word can be one token while a rarer word is built from two or three smaller pieces. In this lab, "king" is a single token, while "queen" is made of three. In the second step, each token's number is swapped for a long list of numbers, called an embedding, and that list is what the model works with from then on. The lists are learned during training, a long practice run in which the model reads huge amounts of text and keeps guessing the next token. Words that are used in similar ways end up with similar lists, which is how plain numbers come to reflect the way words are used. If you have done the Data, features, and representation lab, you looked words up in a fixed list of eight slots. You also saw a map whose points were placed by hand, not learned. Here both of those jobs are learned instead: the list of pieces is worked out from real text, and so are the numbers for each piece. Where you have met it Every message you have typed to a chatbot, and every reply it wrote back, went through these steps, because a chatbot reads and writes tokens rather than letters. That one fact explains some odd behaviour you may have run into: A chatbot can miscount the letters in a word, because the whole word may arrive as one token with no letters inside it. Sums with long numbers can go wrong, partly because long numbers get split into tokens in odd places. The same paragraph can take more tokens in one language than in another, which matters because a model can only take in a fixed number of tokens at once. Why it matters Without the first step, a model would have no fixed set of pieces to work with. A list of every possible word could never be finished, because people keep inventing new names, slang and typos. Reading text one letter at a time would avoid that problem, but it would make every sentence much longer. Tokens sit in between those two choices, and the lab lets you watch how they get chosen. Without the second step, a model would be left holding only the token numbers, which are labels rather than amounts. So 344, the number for "king", is not "more" than 82, the number for "the". The lists of numbers give the model something it can compare, combine and adjust while it learns, and every later lab in this course works on lists like these. This module also covers one more catch, which is that each token gets the same list wherever it appears in a sentence. Nothing in that list says whether the token came first or last, so the order of the words has to be added in a separate step. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these in your own words: Why a model reads text as tokens from a fixed list, rather than as whole words or single letters. How a tokenizer, the program that cuts text into tokens, builds its tokens by gluing pairs of smaller pieces together, one step at a time. How each token ends up with its number. What it means when two words get similar lists of numbers, so that they sit close together in the lab's word space, and what that closeness does not mean. Why each token gets one fixed list of numbers wherever it appears, and where the order of the words has to come from instead. What the lab lets you do The lab has five cards, and none of them runs a language model. The top two, Tokenizer workbench and Merge trace, run a real tokenizer, which is the program that cuts text into tokens. It is a very small tokenizer that learned from a collection of Shakespeare's plays, but you can type any text you like into it. A slider shrinks its list of pieces, and the second card replays how any word was put together, one step at a time. The lower three cards, Nearest neighbours, Vector arithmetic and Embedding projection, use real embeddings for 10,000 common English words, each one a list of 50 numbers. These lists come from a published set called GloVe, which was learned from Wikipedia and news articles. You can find the closest words to any word, add and subtract words as if they were numbers, and see all 10,000 words squeezed onto a flat map. The cards work everything out live, except the flat maps, which were made once, when the lab was built. One honest warning before you start: the word lists in the lower cards come from a separate table, not from the tokenizer above. No model in this lab was trained on the tokenizer's pieces, and the lesson points out each place where that matters.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Cutting text into tokens Imagine a set of building bricks that comes with a numbered parts list. The smallest bricks each carry one byte, a small unit of stored text, which for plain English is a single letter, a punctuation mark or a space. Bigger bricks carry chunks that were glued together ahead of time, such as ing or a whole common word. You can build a sentence only from the bricks in the set, so a word with no big brick of its own has to be put together from smaller ones. A tokenizer works the same way: it cuts text into pieces taken from a fixed list, called the vocabulary, and each piece is a token. A token might be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a special marker. A token that is smaller than a word is called a subword, and subwords are what let a fixed list still spell out rare words, names and typos. Here is the lab's default sentence, "The king and the queen read the attention paper", cut into tokens: The symbol ␣ stands for a space. In this sentence, the space in front of each word ends up inside that word's first token, so ␣king is one token that includes its space. Some words, like "king", "and" and "the", became single tokens, while "queen", "read", "attention" and "paper" were built from smaller pieces. The Tokens readout on the Tokenizer workbench counts these 18 pieces, for a sentence that is 47 characters long. Giving each token a number Every entry in the vocabulary has a number, called its token ID, which works like the number next to each brick in the parts list. In this lab, ␣king is token 344 and ␣the is token 82. The workbench shows each token as a small box, called a chip, with its ID as a small number above its text. An ID is only an address, so token 344 is not worth more than token 82, and a model never does arithmetic with IDs. It uses an ID for one thing only, which is finding that token's row in a big table that you will meet further down. Bytes, the smallest bricks The tokenizer's smallest bricks are bytes, which are the small units a computer uses to store text, and each byte is one of 256 possible code numbers. For example, a capital A is stored as the code number 65 and a space as 32. A plain English letter, digit, space or punctuation mark takes one byte, while an accented letter such as é takes two. This lab's tokenizer started with only the 65 byte symbols that appear in its Shakespeare text. Those are the capital and small letters, the space, the line break, a handful of punctuation marks and, oddly, the digit 3. Any byte outside those 65 becomes <unk>, short for "unknown", which has ID 0. That is why the sample 2024 was 33 years turns each digit of the year into a red <unk> chip, while each 3 keeps its own ID, which is 11. How the tokenizer learned its bricks Picture a friend who has to spell out the same long story again and again using single-letter bricks. To save time, they find the two letters that sit side by side most often in the story and glue them together wherever they appear. Each glued pair becomes a new brick in the set, and then they count again, treating each glued piece as one brick, and glue the next most common pair. After many rounds the set has bricks for chunks like "ing" and even whole common words, while rare words still have to be spelled out from small bricks. The lab's tokenizer was built by this same recipe, which is called byte-pair encoding, or BPE for short. It started from its 65 byte symbols and a collection of Shakespeare's plays called Tiny Shakespeare. It counted every pair of neighbouring pieces in the text, glued the most common pair into a new token, and added that token to the vocabulary. Then it counted again, because each new piece changes which pairs are most common, and it repeated the whole process 443 times. Each glue step is a merge rule, such as "i + n becomes in", and its place in the order of learning is its rank. Counting starts at 0, so the very first rule learned has rank 0 and the last of the 443 has rank 442. Some of the earliest rules joined a space with t to make ␣t (rank 2), and h with e to make he (rank 3). At rank 13 the tokenizer glued ␣t and he into ␣the. Adding it all up, the vocabulary holds 4 special tokens, 65 byte symbols and 443 merged tokens, which makes 512 entries in all. That total appears in the badge "512 entries" at the top of the workbench. Now the IDs make sense, because they follow a simple pattern. IDs also count from 0. The 4 special tokens, which are markers explained further down, take IDs 0 to 3, and the 65 starting symbols follow at IDs 4 to 68. Every glued token comes after those 69 entries, so its ID is 69 plus its rank. For example, ␣the was glued at rank 13, so its ID is 69 + 13 = 82, and ␣king was glued at rank 275, so its ID is 69 + 275 = 344. The last rule, rank 442, gets ID 511, which is the 512th entry because counting began at 0. Replaying the merges on new text When you type text, the tokenizer learns nothing new, and instead it replays the merge rules it already has, in three stages: Pre-tokenization: The text is first split into word-sized chunks, each keeping the space in front of it, and the lab calls each chunk a pre-token. A space goes at the front of the chunk for the word after it, and merges never reach across from one chunk into the next. So a space can only ever be glued to the word after it, never to the word before it, and only if a merge rule allows it. The workbench draws a coloured bracket under the chips that came from each chunk. Bytes: Each chunk is broken into its bytes, so the chunk ␣king starts out as five pieces, ␣, k, i, n and g. Merges: The tokenizer looks at every pair of neighbouring pieces in the chunk and picks the pair whose merge rule has the lowest rank, meaning the rule learned earliest. It glues that pair everywhere it appears. Then it looks again, and it stops when no neighbouring pair has a rule. Going in learning order means each word gets built up in the same order the rules were first learned. Here is ␣king going through the merges, the way the Merge trace card shows it, with the pieces left after each step on the right. The number after # is the rule's rank. At the start, the lowest-ranked pair is i + n, at rank 8, so it joins first. Next, in + g at rank 44 beats ␣ + k at rank 91, and once both of those are done, the rule at rank 275 joins ␣k and ing. The ranks only ever go up as you read down a trace, for two reasons. Any pair that was waiting from the start has a higher rank than the one just picked, or it would have been picked first. Any new pair that uses a freshly glued piece, such as ing, must have been learned after that piece was made, so its rank is higher too. The word ␣queen goes differently, as its own trace shows: No rule in the table joins ␣qu, e and en, so even with all 512 entries the word stops at three tokens. It never becomes a single token at any vocabulary size. At smaller sizes it breaks into even more pieces. Length and meaning have nothing to do with it, since ␣speak has five letters, just like queen, and is a single token. What matters is which pairs were most common in the Shakespeare text the tokenizer learned from. This also explains how the Vocabulary size slider works, since a smaller vocabulary is the same list of merge rules cut short, as if training had stopped earlier. With fewer rules to replay, words fall back to the smaller pieces they were built from. Special tokens Four IDs are kept aside for special tokens, which are markers with a job to do rather than pieces of text. In ID order, they are <unk>, which stands in for any byte the vocabulary lacks, then <pad>, then <bos> and <eos>, which mark the start and end of a text. The <pad> token is filler, used to make a short text as long as the others when several texts are handled together. On the workbench, special tokens such as <eos> (ID 3) get a double border, while <unk> chips (ID 0) are red and dashed. If you type the characters <eos> yourself, this tokenizer turns them into the real end-of-text token, as the sample the end<eos> shows. That choice matters more than it looks, and "Going deeper" explains why. From a number to a list of numbers The second lookup is where the numbers a model really uses come from. Think of a huge table with one row for every token in the vocabulary, where each row is a long list of decimal numbers. A token's ID says which row to read, and nothing else about the token is used. A list of numbers like this is called a vector, and the row for a token is that token's embedding. The whole table is the embedding matrix, where "matrix" is the name for a grid of numbers arranged in rows and columns. How many numbers each row holds is the embedding dimension, often written as d, and it is 50 for the word lists in this lab. When you select ␣king on the workbench, the line under the readouts ends with "The model would read row 344 of a 512-row embedding matrix." That sentence describes what a real model built on this tokenizer would do. No such model exists in this lab, though, so the lower cards use a separate table of whole words instead. After the lookup, the model holds only that list of numbers for the token. The letters are gone and so is the ID, and every later step in the model works on lists like this one. Where the numbers come from Nobody types the numbers into the table by hand, because in a language model every row starts out as random numbers. Training then shows the model real text again and again and asks it to guess the next token, a bit like your phone's keyboard suggesting the next word. After each guess, every number that played a part, including these rows, is nudged a tiny bit so that the next guess is better. Picture a friend who texts you about something called florp, a word you have never seen. First they spilled florp on their shirt, then they said it was too warm to drink, and later they asked you to grab one from the fridge. Nobody told you what florp means, yet you would place it near juice or soda because of the words around it. Training reaches a similar result, though nothing in it guesses or reasons the way you did. Words that fill the same gaps in sentences get their numbers nudged up and down in the same ways while the model learns, so their lists drift close together. The GloVe word lists in the lower cards were learned separately, from Wikipedia and news text, with their own training method, but they show the same pattern. In the Nearest neighbours card, the closest words to queen are princess, lady and elizabeth. Reading a list of numbers as a point A pair of numbers, such as (3, 2), marks a point on a graph: three steps across and two steps up. A list of 50 numbers marks a point in the same way, but in a space with 50 directions instead of two. Nobody can picture 50 directions, but distances and angles work there the same way they do on a flat graph. So every word becomes a point, and the space they all sit in is called the embedding space. Interpreting distance in that space means asking which points sit close together, and what that closeness tells you. To measure closeness, picture an arrow from the centre of the graph, the point (0, 0), out to each word's point. Cosine similarity measures how closely two arrows point in the same direction, while ignoring how long they are. A score of 1 means they point exactly the same way, 0 means they sit at a right angle, and −1 means they point in opposite directions. Three small examples on an ordinary graph show how this works: The first pair scores 1 even though one arrow is longer than the other, because cosine similarity looks only at direction. So in this lab, two words count as close when their arrows point the same way, not when their points are a short ruler distance apart. Two points can sit far apart on the graph and still count as close, as long as they lie along the same line out from the centre. In the lab, the closest word to queen is princess, with a cosine similarity of 0.852. The bars in Nearest neighbours run from 0 to 1, so a long bar means two arrows point in nearly the same direction across all 50 numbers. Close arrows mean the words are used in similar sentences, which is not the same as meaning the same thing, as "Where it breaks" shows with the word hot. Adding and subtracting words Because each word is a list of numbers, you can add and subtract words, which is called analogy arithmetic. The famous test is king − man + woman: start from king, take away man, add woman, and see which word lands closest to the result. Here is a made-up example with only two numbers per word, so you can follow it in your head: Going from man to woman means one step up, and adding that same step to king lands exactly on queen. Real lists of 50 numbers never line up this neatly, so the lab looks for the word whose arrow points closest to the result. Before adding, the lab stretches or shrinks every word's arrow to a length of 1, so that a word with a long arrow cannot drown out the others. That is what "unit-length vectors" means in the heading of the Vector arithmetic card, and "3CosAdd" in the same heading is the name of this add-then-compare method. With the real GloVe lists, king − man + woman does come out as queen, with a cosine of 0.852, but only after the three input words are ruled out. It is a coincidence that this matches the 0.852 between queen and princess in Nearest neighbours. If the three input words are allowed to win, king itself comes out on top at 0.885, because the result still points mostly in king's direction. Squeezing 50 numbers onto a flat map To draw 10,000 words on a flat screen, the lab has to squeeze 50 numbers down to 2, which is called a projection. If you hold your hand between a lamp and a wall, its shadow is flat, so it loses one direction. Two fingers that are far apart from front to back can land right on top of each other in the shadow. A flat map of 50-number lists loses far more than a shadow does, because it drops 48 directions instead of one. The lab offers two methods for making the map, and the one called PCA works most like a shadow. It finds the two directions in which the words spread out the most, and it drops all the rest. The other method, UMAP, builds a new flat layout that tries to keep each word near its closest neighbours, at the cost of bending the larger distances. The Embedding projection card shows how much each method keeps, using a badge that checks the ten closest words to queen. It counts how many of those ten true neighbours are also among queen's ten nearest dots on the flat map. UMAP keeps 5 of them, while PCA keeps none. One list per token, wherever it sits In the default sentence, ␣the appears twice, once after "and" and once after "read", and both chips show ID 82. Since the ID decides which row is read, both copies get exactly the same list of numbers. Nothing in that list says whether its token is the 4th piece of the sentence or the 10th. Picture a friend who writes each step of a recipe on its own card: "crack the eggs", "stir in the flour", "bake". If the cards get shuffled, each card still says exactly the same thing, and nothing on any of them tells you which step comes first. To keep the order, you would have to write a step number on every card. Language models face a similar problem, even though the tokens do arrive in order and nothing really gets shuffled. A later step called attention lets each token look at the other tokens around it and borrow information from the most useful ones. Attention compares tokens by their numbers, so unless position has been mixed into those numbers, it can tell very little about which slot each token sits in. So the order has to be added on purpose. A positional encoding is a second list of numbers that depends on a token's slot in the text. It is either added to the token's embedding right after the lookup, before attention or any other step has run, or mixed in later, inside attention itself. Unlike a step number in the corner of a card, it is blended into the token's numbers rather than kept separate. Here is a made-up example with two numbers per list. If ␣the has the embedding (0.4, 1.2) and slot 4 has the position list (0.1, −0.3), the model works with (0.5, 0.9). Slot 10 has a different position list, so the two copies of ␣the no longer look identical. The transformer block lab shows a part of a model that cannot tell two word orders apart until position is added, while Attention compares ways of adding it. The same rule has a second effect, which is that a token gets one list for all of its meanings. So bank starts out with the same numbers in "river bank" and in "bank account", and working out which meaning is meant happens later, in attention.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: A model needs numbers it can work with A language model is a huge pile of arithmetic: multiplying, adding and comparing numbers over and over. Token IDs cannot take part in that, because they are only addresses. If a model added ␣king (344) and ␣the (82), the answer would mean nothing, any more than adding two phone numbers gives you a useful phone number. An embedding solves this by giving each token a list of numbers that training can shape. Because the lists are learned, tokens used in similar ways can end up with similar numbers, which lets the model's arithmetic treat them in similar ways. A bare label becomes something the model can measure, compare and change. A fixed list has to cover every possible text The vocabulary is fixed before training starts, and adding an entry later means adding a new row to the table and training it. So the list has to cope with any text a person might type, and the two obvious choices both fail. A list of whole words could never be complete, because people keep writing new names, slang and typos, and any word missing from the list would turn into an unknown. A list of single bytes could spell anything, but it would make every text much longer, so the default sentence would take 47 tokens instead of 18. A model can only take in a fixed number of tokens at once, so a text that long would use up that space more than twice as fast. Subword tokens are the middle ground, because common words become one token each while rare words are spelled from a few smaller pieces. That keeps common text short without leaving anything unknown. Most tokenizers used in real systems include all 256 possible bytes, so any text at all can be spelled out, even if rare text takes many tokens. Everything later is built on these lists Every later part of a language model works on the lists this step produces. A language model is built from a stack of repeated units called transformer blocks. Inside each block, attention compares the lists for different tokens, and another part reshapes each token's list on its own. At the very end, the model scores its final list against every row of the vocabulary to rank which token should come next. It explains behaviour you can see How text gets cut into tokens explains several things language models get wrong: Counting letters: If a word arrives as one token, the model receives one list of numbers for it, and the letters themselves are not part of what it receives. In this lab, ␣king is a single token, so k, i, n and g never reach a model as separate pieces. Different languages: A vocabulary is fitted to the text it was trained on, so the same sentence can cost different numbers of tokens in different languages. This lab's tokenizer is an extreme case, since it learned from English alone and turns accented letters like the ï in naïve into <unk>. Markers: Markers such as end-of-text are whole tokens, so a model ends its reply by producing that one token, not by spelling out the letters of <eos> one by one.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Work through the cards from top to bottom, since each step below matches one step in the lab's own guide. Split text Try this: Leave the sentence alone and drag Vocabulary size from 512 down to 69. The Tokens readout climbs from 18 to 47, while Characters stays at 47 the whole time. The text never changed, only the number of merge rules the tokenizer may use, which the slider's label also shows, starting at 512 · 443 merges. At 69 there are no merges left, so every character becomes its own token and Characters per token reads 1.00. Drag back up slowly and watch the chips join into bigger pieces as the merge rules come back. You can also type your own text into Text to tokenize, up to 200 characters, and the chips, the readouts and the merge trace all update as you type. The sample buttons next to the word "Try" swap in texts chosen to show one behaviour each. Replay the merges When the lab opens, the ␣king chip is already selected, so the Merge trace card shows its four merges, from the bytes row down to #275. Read it from top to bottom and match each row to the walk-through in "What it is". Then set Vocabulary size to 344, though anything from 161 to 344 gives the same result. IDs start at 0, so keeping ID 344 needs 345 entries, and at 344 the last one is cut. The last row fades with the note needs vocabulary ≥ 345, and the ␣king chip on the workbench splits into ␣k and ing. The badge at the top of the trace drops from "4 of 4 merges in budget" to "3 of 4 merges in budget". Go lower still and the earlier rows fade too. Click any of the four chips that make up "attention" (␣at, t, ent or ion) as well, and the trace follows the whole word. You can watch "attention" being built by six merges into the four pieces ␣at, t, ent and ion. Inspect token IDs Start by comparing the small numbers on the chips, where The with a capital is 167 and ␣the is 82. Both ␣the chips in the default sentence share that ID, because they are the same token. Click any chip and the line under the readouts explains where its ID comes from, such as "created by merge rank 275, so its ID is 69 + 275". A single-letter chip is described instead as part of the starting alphabet, which holds IDs 4 to 68. Next, pick the sample the The ␣the, which shows three spellings of one word. The first the, which has no space in front of it, splits into t and he, while the capital The is 167 and ␣the is 82. You will also see two lone ␣ chips. The one before The stayed alone because no rule joins a space to The. The extra space in the double space was split off as its own chunk before any merge ran, so no rule could reach it. Then pick 2024 was 33 years, find the red, dashed <unk> chips with ID 0, and check the Unknown bytes readout. The sample naïve café shows two <unk> chips for each accented letter, because each of those letters takes two bytes. Map meaning The lower cards need the word lists to load first, so wait until the small label on Nearest neighbours says Loaded. Type a word into Query word, and the card lists its ten closest words, each with its cosine similarity. Click any bar to make that word the new query, which lets you walk from word to word. Try queen, hot, apple and bank in turn, and notice how different their neighbourhoods look. Under the bars you will also see the first 6 of the word's 50 numbers. For queen they start with ordinary decimals such as 0.38 and 1.82, and none of them has a label saying what it means. Two readouts sit below those numbers: Frequency rank shows how common the word is in GloVe's list, where the is number 1 and queen is number 1,939. Vector length ‖v‖ shows how long the word's arrow is, which is the one thing cosine similarity ignores. Then scroll to Embedding projection and switch Projection between UMAP and PCA while queen is the query. Dashed lines, called spokes, join queen to its ten true neighbours, so a long spoke means the map pulled a real neighbour far away. Watch the badge change between "keeps 5 of 10 neighbours" and "keeps 0 of 10 neighbours". Under PCA, queen's real neighbours spread out across the map, and the badge reads 0. That is the shadow effect at work. Many unrelated words, such as miami and grabbed, land almost on top of queen, closer than even princess, so they fill all ten of its nearest dots. The Frame control switches between Fit highlights, which zooms in on the marked words, and All words, which shows all 10,000 dots. Try vector arithmetic In Vector arithmetic, start with the preset king − man + woman and switch Input words between Excluded and Allowed to win. With Excluded, queen tops the list at 0.852, but with Allowed to win, king itself moves to the top at 0.885. In that mode, king is greyed out and tagged "input word", so you can tell it was one of the three words you started from. Then pick bigger − big + small and read the honest top answer, which is larger, not smaller. Try paris − france + italy and tokyo − japan + germany as well, or type your own words into the A, B and C boxes. Finally, pick the king − man + woman preset again in Vector arithmetic, then scroll to Embedding projection and set Highlight to Analogy words. The boxes stand for A − B + C, so here A is king, B is man and C is woman. A solid arrow runs from man to king, and another runs from woman to queen, the top answer once the inputs are ruled out. A dashed arrow copies the man-to-king arrow and starts it at woman. If the flat map had kept the analogy, that dashed arrow would end right on queen. Try the other presets too, and you will see that the dashed arrow rarely ends on the answer.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: The text stays the same, but the count changes: The default sentence takes 18 tokens at full size and 47 with no merges at all. A shorter list of merge rules leaves words in smaller pieces. IDs are addresses, not amounts: ␣king gets ID 344 only because it was made by the merge ranked 275. A model never treats a bigger ID as "more" of anything. Spaces and capitals change the tokens: One word gets three encodings in the sample the The ␣the. The is 167 and ␣the is 82, while a the at the very start splits into t and he. Frequency, not length, decides what becomes one token: ␣king and ␣speak are one token each, while ␣queen needs three and ␣attention needs four. Shrinking the vocabulary never changes a surviving token's ID: It only removes the latest merges, so words fall back to shorter pieces. Repeated tokens share one row: Both ␣the chips in the default sentence show 82, so a model would read exactly the same list for each of them. Close means "used in similar sentences": The nearest words to queen are princess, lady and elizabeth, a mix of royalty, women and particular queens. One list covers every meaning of a word: In news text apple is mostly the company, so its neighbours are chips, microsoft and pc. The neighbours of bank are all about money, with nothing about rivers. The famous analogy needs help: king − man + woman lands on queen at 0.852 only when the inputs are excluded, and otherwise king wins. Most published tests of analogy arithmetic rule the inputs out in the same way. The flat map keeps only some neighbours: UMAP keeps 5 of queen's 10 nearest words close on the map, and PCA keeps none. Under UMAP, elizabeth and victoria land far from queen even though their cosine scores are 0.787 and 0.729.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Where the brick picture stops matching The brick picture works for cutting and gluing, but it stops at meaning. A brick has nothing inside it, while a token's embedding is a list of many numbers, and none of those numbers comes with a label saying what it stands for. The pattern that looks like meaning lives in how the learned lists relate to each other, not in the token itself. The picture also suggests a builder who chooses which bricks to use. A tokenizer has no choice at all, because it replays the same merge rules in the same order every time, so the same text always gives the same tokens. Limits of this lab The tokenizer is tiny: It has 512 entries and learned from Shakespeare alone, so modern words break into many pieces. Most digits, accented letters and emoji become <unk> because it cannot fall back on raw bytes, so its coverage is nothing like a real tokenizer's. The two halves use different tables: The word lists are GloVe, looked up by whole lowercase word, not rows for the tokenizer's IDs. No model here was trained on the tokenizer's pieces, so the workbench's line about "row 344 of a 512-row embedding matrix" describes a model that is not present. The word table is small: It holds only 10,000 words with 50 numbers each, so rare words are missing, and the neighbourhoods are rougher than in bigger tables. The maps were made in advance: Both were worked out once, when the lab was built, so they show only the 10,000 words. They can never show the point where A − B + C lands, because the lab saved only the 10,000 finished positions, not a way to place new points on the map. On a UMAP map, the exact positions, the sizes of clusters and the gaps between them carry no meaning. Every flat map loses most of the distances: Squeezing 50 numbers into 2 always throws information away. Use a map to find a region worth looking at, and then check it against the real cosine scores. A common mix-up: Being close does not mean "means the same thing"; it means "shows up in similar sentences". The two nearest words to hot in this lab are cool and cold, even though cold means the opposite. All three fit into the same sentences, such as "the water is too hot" and "the water is too cold", so training pulled their lists together. Limits of the real mechanism One list per token, whatever the context: A token gets the same embedding in every sentence and position, so bank starts out identical in "river bank" and "bank account". Sorting out the meaning happens later, in attention, and word order has to come from the positional encoding. Word arithmetic is fragile: bigger − big + small lands on larger before smaller, and tokyo − japan + germany lands on frankfurt before berlin. Results depend on details like ruling out the inputs, and many relationships fail completely. A working analogy proves less than it seems: When king − man + woman does land on queen, it shows that some directions in the space are consistent. It does not show that the lists store facts as neat, reliable steps. Closeness is not agreement: Cosine similarity also scores opposites and loosely related words as close. A high score is a hint worth checking, not proof that two words mean the same thing. Some mistakes start at the cut: Counting letters, sums with long numbers and languages the tokenizer rarely saw all get harder because of where token edges fall.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Real tokenizers Most modern tokenizers work the same way at a much larger scale, with vocabularies of roughly 32,000 to 256,000 entries built from tens of thousands of merge rules. Most include all 256 possible bytes from the start, so no text is ever unknown, and rare text takes more tokens instead. Before any merges, this lab's tokenizer tidies the text into a standard form, so a character that can be stored in several ways is always stored the same way. It then splits the text into chunks using a common pattern known as the GPT-2 pattern. In the tokenizer's own file, the space byte is written as Ġ, which the lab shows as ␣. Not every tokenizer uses merges, since some, such as SentencePiece's unigram models, score each possible way of cutting a word and keep the highest-scoring one. Special tokens and safety Tokenizers disagree about what to do when a user types a special token's text. A library here means a ready-made package of code that programmers reuse. This lab, like the default in Hugging Face's library, turns a typed <eos> into the real end-of-text token, while the tiktoken library refuses such text by default. Chat systems have to choose carefully, because if typed text can become a real marker, a user could fake the structure of a conversation, such as where one message ends. Why a lookup counts as arithmetic Reading a row from the table can also be written as a multiplication. Make a list of 512 numbers that are all 0 except for a single 1 in the spot for token 344, which is called a one-hot vector. Multiply each row of the table by the matching number in that list, which means multiplying every number in the row by it, then add all the rows together. Here is the same idea with a tiny table of three rows: (2, 5), (7, 1) and (4, 4). The one-hot list (0, 1, 0) picks the second row: The real table works the same way, with 512 rows instead of three. Every row gets multiplied by 0 except row 344, so the result is exactly that row. Real code skips the multiplying and reads the row directly. Writing it as a multiplication still matters, because it shows the lookup is ordinary arithmetic, so the table can be trained like every other part of the model. Cosine similarity with real numbers The info panel on Nearest neighbours gives the formula as cos(u, v) = u·v / (‖u‖‖v‖). Here ‖u‖ is the length of arrow u, the same thing the Vector length ‖v‖ readout shows, and u·v means "multiply the matching numbers and add the results". Try it with two arrows, one to (3, 4) and one to (4, 3): The two arrows point in nearly the same direction, so the score comes out close to 1. The lab does the same sum with 50 numbers instead of 2, and to save time it divides every word's list by its length once, in advance. The same table, at the other end At the very end of a model, the process runs in reverse. The model's final list is scored against every row of the vocabulary to rank which token comes next, and many models reuse the same table for both jobs. A tokenizer is built once, before the model is trained, and then kept. Swapping it afterwards would make every learned row meaningless, because each row belongs to one particular token. Bigger tables in real models Real models use far longer lists than the 50 numbers here, since their embedding dimension runs from several hundred to over 16,000. More numbers give the lists more directions to spread out in, but they also make every later step cost more. With a vocabulary of tens of thousands of tokens on top of that, the embedding matrix is one of the largest single tables of numbers in a model. Tokens per word across languages The average number of tokens a tokenizer needs for each word is called its fertility, and it varies from language to language. Since a model can take in only a fixed number of tokens at once, the same content can use up very different amounts of that space depending on its language. Next up The next lab, A single neuron, shows the first thing a model does with numbers like these: multiply, add, and squash. It uses two plain numbers as its inputs instead of a full list, so you can follow every step by hand.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: This module covers the conversion that runs before a language model's first layer, from a string to one learned vector per token, a piece of text drawn from a fixed vocabulary. It has two halves: a tokenizer cuts text into tokens and numbers each with an integer token ID, and an embedding matrix maps each ID to a vector, which is all the model holds about that token before any layer runs. Data, features, and representation looked words up in a fixed eight-word list and placed points on a map by hand. Here both halves are learned: the vocabulary by byte-pair encoding (BPE), which repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair in a corpus, and the vectors by gradient descent. The question is what that conversion keeps and what has to be added back. Where it shows up The first step of every language model. The embedding lookup is the first operation applied to every token ID, and every layer after it works on its output. Production tokenizers. Byte-level BPE tokenizers in production start from all 256 byte values, so no input is unknown. Chat systems. Special tokens such as end-of-text mark structure, and encoders disagree on whether user text may produce them: the Hugging Face default allows it, tiktoken refuses by default. The output layer. The unembedding maps the final vector back to one score per vocabulary entry, and many models tie it to the input embedding matrix. Why it matters A network has parameters for a fixed set of inputs, but text is open-ended. A vocabulary of subwords, pieces that may be smaller than a word, closes that gap: rare words are spelled from several common pieces, and a vocabulary that keeps all 256 byte values can spell any input. An ID, though, is only an address. The embedding row gives it a geometry, in which tokens used in similar contexts lie close together. The tokenizer is trained once, before the model, and changing it invalidates the learned rows. The lookup also carries no position: a token gets the same row wherever it sits. Without a causal mask, a transformer block cannot tell two orderings of the same tokens apart; the mask, which hides later tokens, leaks only some order. So most models add a positional encoding, a vector that depends on the token's slot. What you will be able to explain Why models process tokens from a fixed vocabulary rather than whole words. How byte-pair merges, replayed in rank order, turn a word's bytes into token IDs. What distance means in an embedding space, read as cosine similarity: the cosine of the angle between two vectors. Why an embedding is one vector per token, and where word order has to come from instead. What the lab shows The lab runs no language model. Tokenizer workbench encodes your Text to tokenize with the real BPE tokenizer shipped with the module, 512 entries trained on Tiny Shakespeare, and computes the chips, IDs and Tokens count exactly. Its alphabet is only the 65 byte symbols Tiny Shakespeare uses, with no byte fallback, so any other byte becomes <unk>. The key experiment: hold the text fixed and drag Vocabulary size from 512 toward 69. Only the earliest merges remain, so words fall back to their pieces and the token count rises. Merge trace lists every merge that builds the word containing the selected chip, one rung per merge, and fades the rungs the current Vocabulary size cuts. The embedding cards query real GloVe vectors, 10,000 English words by 50 dimensions, from a word-level table not indexed by the BPE IDs. Nearest neighbours computes cosines live for a Query word, and Vector arithmetic ranks words against A − B + C, with Input words set to Excluded or Allowed to win. Embedding projection reduces the vectors to two dimensions for display. Its UMAP and PCA layouts, chosen with Projection, are fixed, computed once when the asset was built. A badge counts how many of the query's ten nearest words by 50-D cosine are still among its ten nearest dots on the map.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: A language model never sees text. Two lookups stand between a string and the first arithmetic operation: a tokenizer cuts the string into pieces drawn from a fixed vocabulary and numbers them, and an embedding matrix replaces each number with a learned vector. The two lookups Each token ID selects one row of an embedding matrix of shape [V, d], where V is the vocabulary size and d the model width. Nothing else about the piece survives: after the lookup the model holds d numbers per position. Production vocabularies hold roughly 32,000 to 256,000 entries, which makes this matrix one of the largest single tensors in a model. The lookup is a one-hot vector times a matrix: a vector of length V with a single 1 at the token's ID, multiplied by the [V, d] matrix, returns exactly that row. Implementations skip the multiplication and index the row directly. Byte-level BPE, step by step The lab runs the real tokenizer shipped with this module, a byte-level byte-pair encoding trained on Tiny Shakespeare with 512 entries. Encoding has three stages: Pre-tokenization. The text is NFKC-normalized and split by the GPT-2 pattern into word-like chunks, each keeping its leading space. Merges never cross these chunks. Bytes. Each chunk becomes its UTF-8 bytes, drawn as printable symbols; a space byte is Ġ in the file and ␣ in the lab. Merges. Repeatedly join the adjacent pair with the lowest merge rank until none applies. Training produced those ranks greedily: each merge was the most frequent adjacent pair at that moment. So ␣king is assembled as i + n (#8), in + g (#44), ␣ + k (#91), and ␣k + ing (#275), and its ID is 69 + 275 = 344. What the vectors hold Embedding rows begin as random noise and are updated by gradient descent like every other weight. Because the objective rewards predicting real text, tokens used in similar contexts drift toward similar vectors. The geometry is a consequence of the training task. The lab's vectors are GloVe: 10,000 English words by 50 dimensions, trained on Wikipedia and news text. They are a separate word-level table, used because no model here was trained on the 512-token vocabulary. Where order comes from An embedding is one vector per token, chosen without looking at its neighbours. In the default sentence ␣the appears twice, after and and after read, and both chips show ID 82: the same row is read both times. Nothing in a row says whether its token came second or ninth. So order has to be added separately. A positional encoding is a vector that depends on the slot, added to each embedding before the first block or applied inside attention. The transformer block shows a block that cannot tell two orderings apart until it is added, and Attention compares the schemes.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: From the first block on, attention compares the embedded vectors and the MLP transforms them. No layer reads the characters directly, only what the embedding rows encode. Tokenization also explains visible behaviour. Digit grouping affects arithmetic reliability. Letter counting fails when a word is one opaque token. The same sentence costs different amounts in different languages because vocabularies are fit to their training mix. Stop sequences and special markers operate on token boundaries, not characters.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: On Tokenizer workbench, keep the default sentence and move Vocabulary size from 512 to 69. Only the merge budget changes, yet the count rises from 18 tokens to 47. Select ␣king and read Merge trace; below 345 entries its last rung fades. Pick the sample the The the to compare case and spacing, and 2024 was 33 years to find <unk>. Then type a word into Query word, switch Projection between UMAP and PCA, and run the presets in Vector arithmetic with Input words set both ways.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: IDs are addresses, not magnitudes. In this vocabulary a merged token's ID is 69 plus its merge rank, but the model attaches no meaning to that order. The (167), ␣the (82), and a leading the (t + he) are three different encodings of one word. Case and spacing are part of the token. queen's nearest words are princess (0.852), lady (0.805), and elizabeth (0.787). king − man + woman gives queen at cosine 0.852, but only with the inputs excluded. If they may win, king scores 0.885. UMAP keeps 5 of queen's 10 cosine neighbours as 2-D neighbours; PCA keeps none.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: In this lab The tokenizer has 512 entries and saw only Shakespeare. Its alphabet lacks most digits, accents, and emoji, which become <unk> because it has no byte fallback. The word vectors are GloVe, looked up by whole lowercase word, not rows indexed by the BPE IDs above. The workbench's line about an embedding row describes a model that is not present. The projections were computed once when the asset was built. They cannot place the analogy target itself, only the words. In real systems High cosine similarity means "appears in similar contexts", which includes antonyms: the two nearest words to hot here are cool and cold. Analogy arithmetic is fragile: bigger − big + small returns larger before smaller, and tokyo − japan + germany returns frankfurt before berlin. An input embedding is static, one vector per token regardless of context or position. Separating the senses of bank, and knowing which word came first, is work done later: by attention, and by the positional encoding added alongside the embedding.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Production byte-level BPE tokenizers start from all 256 bytes, so no input is unknown; rare text simply costs more tokens. Encoders differ on special tokens. This one, like the Hugging Face default, turns a literal <eos> in the text into the real end-of-text ID; tiktoken refuses such strings by default. Chat systems must decide, or user text can forge structure. The unembedding step at the end of the network reverses this one, projecting a d-vector back to V logits. Many models tie the two matrices. A tokenizer is trained once, before the model, and effectively frozen: changing it invalidates the learned rows. Fertility, the average number of tokens per word, varies across languages, so the same content spends different amounts of a fixed context window. The next lab, A single neuron, shows what a layer does with numbers like these, using two scalar inputs in place of a full embedding: one weighted sum and one activation.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Tokenizer workbench · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Your text through a real byte-level BPE tokenizer The text is split, turned into bytes, and merged by the 443 learned rules in `bpe-tokenizer.json`, giving the same IDs Hugging Face `tokenizers` produces. `Vocabulary size` keeps only the first merges, which is the tokenizer a shorter training run would have learned. `Text to tokenize` and a row of sample texts. Each sample is chosen to show one behaviour: whole-word tokens, spacing and case, missing digits, accented letters, and a literal special token. `Vocabulary size`, printed as entries and merges. 69 entries means 4 special tokens plus 65 byte symbols and no merges; 512 means all 443 merges. One chip per token. The small number is the token ID; `␣` marks a leading space that belongs to the token. A coloured bracket under a group of chips marks one pre-token, a chunk merges never cross; the selected chip's bracket is thicker. Dashed red chips are `<unk>` (ID 0): a byte this vocabulary never saw. Double-bordered chips are special tokens such as `<eos>`. `Tokens`, `Characters`, `Characters per token` and `Unknown bytes`, then a line explaining where the selected chip's ID comes from. The text is NFKC-normalized and split by the GPT-2 pattern, which keeps a leading space with the word after it. Each chunk becomes its UTF-8 bytes, shown as printable symbols (a space byte is `Ġ` in the file, `␣` here). Within each chunk, the adjacent pair with the lowest merge rank joins, and this repeats until no ranked pair remains. A byte missing from the 65-symbol alphabet becomes `<unk>`, since this tokenizer has no byte fallback. IDs are addresses: 0 to 3 are specials, 4 to 68 are byte symbols, and a merged token's ID is 69 plus its merge rank. `␣king` is merge 275, so its ID is 344. A literal `<eos>`, `<pad>`, `<bos>` or `<unk>` in the text is matched before normalization and becomes that special token, as in the Hugging Face encoder. The implementation was checked against Hugging Face `tokenizers` 0.23.2 on 316 strings with no differences; a subset is a unit test. `Text to tokenize`: edit freely, up to 200 characters. The chips, counts, and merge trace update on every keystroke. Sample buttons replace the text. `the The the` shows `The` (167), `␣the` (82), and a leading `the` that splits into `t` + `he`. `Vocabulary size` (69 to 512): drag from 512 to 69 on the default sentence and the count rises from 18 tokens to 47, with the text unchanged. Click a chip to select it. The explanation line and the Merge trace card follow the selection. Frequent Shakespeare words are one token (`␣king`, `␣and`, `␣the`), while `␣queen` needs three and `␣attention` four. Frequency in the tokenizer's training text decides this, not length or meaning. `The` is ID 167 and `␣the` is ID 82. At the start of the text, with no leading space, `the` becomes `t` + `he`. Case and spacing change the tokens. In `2024 was 33 years`, the digits 2, 0 and 4 are `<unk>` but 3 is kept (ID 11). Tiny Shakespeare contains the digit 3 and not the others. Shrinking the vocabulary never changes a surviving token's ID. It only removes the latest merges, so words fall back to shorter pieces. The default sentence has `␣the` twice, after `and` and after `read`, and both chips show ID 82. A model would read the same embedding row at both places, so the row carries no information about position: order has to be added separately, as a positional encoding. In this lab: the tokenizer is tiny (512 entries) and trained only on Tiny Shakespeare, so modern words fragment heavily and most digits, accents, and emoji are `<unk>`. Its coverage should not be compared with a production tokenizer. In this lab: no model reads these IDs. The line about an embedding row describes what a model would do; the vectors in the cards below come from a separate word-level table. In general: production tokenizers have 32,000 to about 256,000 entries, and most modern ones cover all 256 bytes, directly or as a fallback, so no text is `<unk>`; rare text just costs more tokens. In general: segmentation explains visible model behaviour. Digit grouping affects arithmetic, letter counting fails when a word is one opaque token, and languages underrepresented in tokenizer training spend more tokens on the same content. In general: encoders differ on special tokens. This one, like the Hugging Face default, turns a literal `<eos>` in user text into the real end-of-text token; tiktoken refuses such strings by default. Accepting them lets user text forge structure.
documents.title: Your text through a real byte-level BPE tokenizer

documents.subtitle: Merge trace · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: The merge sequence for one word, rung by rung The selected chip's pre-token replayed through the merge table one rule at a time: start from bytes, join the lowest-ranked adjacent pair, repeat. Faded rungs are merges the current `Vocabulary size` does not contain. A heading naming the pre-token (for example `␣king`) and a badge counting how many of its merges fit in the current vocabulary. The first rung, `bytes`: one box per UTF-8 byte of the pre-token, before any merge. One rung per merge. Left to right: the merge rank (`#275`), the rule (`␣k + ing → ␣king`) with the new token's ID, and the word's pieces after that merge, with the newly joined piece outlined. Faded, dashed rungs with a note such as `needs vocabulary ≥ 345` when the slider has cut that merge. `×2` marks a rule that joined two places in one word. At each step every adjacent pair is looked up in the merge table, and the pair with the lowest rank joins everywhere it occurs, left to right. The process stops when no adjacent pair has a rank. A merge can only use pieces that earlier merges created, so the ranks along a word always increase. That is why a smaller vocabulary simply cuts the list from the bottom. The trace always shows every merge in the full 512-entry table. The chips on the workbench use only the merges below the slider's budget, so the two agree on every rung that is not faded. Byte-pair encoding was trained greedily: each merge was the most frequent adjacent pair in the training text at that moment. Rank order is therefore the order in which the merges were learned. Select a chip on Tokenizer workbench to trace its pre-token. Selecting any chip of `␣attention` traces the whole chunk. `Vocabulary size` on the workbench: set it below 345 with `␣king` selected and the last rung fades, and the chip splits into `␣k` and `ing`. `␣king` is built in four steps: `i + n` (#8), `in + g` (#44), `␣ + k` (#91), `␣k + ing` (#275). Common fragments such as `in` and `ing` were learned long before the whole word. `␣queen` stops at `␣qu`, `e`, `en`: no merge in the table joins those three, so the word stays in pieces at every vocabulary size. A word with no rungs, such as a run of unknown bytes, received no merges at all. In this lab: the table has only 443 merges learned from one small corpus, so the traces are short and the word pieces are unlike those in production tokenizers. In this lab: the trace follows one pre-token. Merges never cross pre-token boundaries, so the rest of the sentence cannot change it. In general: production tokenizers use the same rank-ordered replay, but with tens of thousands of merges and optimized data structures. Some, such as SentencePiece unigram models, choose segmentations by likelihood instead of merge order. In general: merge order reflects pair frequency during tokenizer training, not meaning. A word that sits in one token carries no extra meaning because of it.
documents.title: The merge sequence for one word, rung by rung

documents.subtitle: Nearest neighbours · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Cosine similarity over real word vectors The query word's 50-number GloVe vector compared with all 10,000 rows by cosine similarity, listing the ten highest. Every value is computed live from the 2 MB vector file, loaded on first use. A status pill: `Loading…`, `Loaded`, or `Unavailable` with a retry button. The embedding cards wait for it; the tokenizer cards do not. `Query word`, which accepts any of the 10,000 lowercase words. An unknown word is flagged and the last valid word stays in use. Ten bars, one per neighbour, with the cosine printed to three decimals. The bar length runs from 0 to 1. Click a bar to make that word the query. The first 6 of the query's 50 raw numbers, then `Frequency rank` (its position in GloVe's frequency-ordered list) and `Vector length ‖v‖`. Each row is divided by its length once, so the cosine of two words is the dot product of their unit vectors: `cos(u, v) = u·v / (‖u‖‖v‖)`. The query is compared with every other row and the ten largest cosines are kept. The query itself is skipped. The vectors are GloVe 6B 50-dimensional vectors, trained on Wikipedia and Gigaword news text. The first 10,000 purely alphabetic ASCII words in GloVe's frequency order were kept. `Query word`: type a word. The list updates as soon as the typed text is one of the 10,000 words. Click a neighbour to walk the space. Try `queen`, then `hot`, then `apple`. `queen` → princess 0.852, lady 0.805, elizabeth 0.787, king 0.784: royalty, women, and specific queens mixed together. `hot` → cool 0.861, cold 0.801. Words used in the same sentence frames end up close even when they mean opposite things. `apple` → chips, microsoft, pc. In news text the company sense dominates, and a word gets one vector for all its senses. In this lab: these are word-level GloVe vectors looked up by whole lowercase word, not rows for the BPE token IDs above. A real model keeps one row per token ID; no model here was trained with this tokenizer. In this lab: only 10,000 words and 50 dimensions ship, so rare words are missing and neighbourhoods are coarser than in larger tables. In general: cosine similarity measures shared contexts, not shared meaning. Antonyms, co-hyponyms, and topical associations all score high. In general: a transformer's input embedding is static like this one, but every later layer rewrites the vector using context, so `bank` in two sentences ends up different after attention.
documents.title: Cosine similarity over real word vectors

documents.subtitle: Vector arithmetic · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: Analogies as vector offsets, with the honest answer The 3CosAdd analogy test: normalize A, B and C to unit length, form `A − B + C`, and rank all words by cosine to that target. The result is reported as computed, including when it is not the textbook answer. Three word fields laid out as `A − B + C`. Each accepts any of the 10,000 words. Preset analogies, and `Input words` with `Excluded` or `Allowed to win`. Five result bars with their cosines. The top result is bold. When inputs are allowed, an input word is greyed and tagged `input word`. A sentence stating the top answer and, when inputs are excluded, what would have won otherwise. `target = unit(A) − unit(B) + unit(C)`, then every row is scored by `cos(target, row)` and the five best are kept. With `Excluded`, A, B and C are skipped when ranking, which is how most published analogy benchmarks score. With `Allowed to win`, nothing is skipped. Nothing is tuned toward an expected answer. Whatever word ranks first is shown. Edit A, B or C, or pick a preset. `Input words`: switch on `king − man + woman` and watch the winner change from queen (0.852) to king (0.885). `king − man + woman` → queen at 0.852 only once the inputs are excluded; allowed to win, `king` itself scores 0.885. `paris − france + italy` → rome at 0.847, one of the relations this space encodes well. `bigger − big + small` → larger (0.924), with smaller second (0.885), and `tokyo − japan + germany` → frankfurt (0.889) ahead of berlin (0.868). The offset lands near the right region, not always on the right word. In this lab: the space is the same 10,000-word, 50-dimensional GloVe subset. Larger vocabularies and dimensions change which analogies succeed. In general: analogy arithmetic is fragile. Results depend on normalization, word frequency, and excluding the inputs, and many relations fail. It shows that some directions are consistent, not that the space stores facts as clean offsets. In general: a transformer's own embeddings are rarely queried this way. Its useful structure appears after attention and MLP layers mix in context.
documents.title: Analogies as vector offsets, with the honest answer

documents.subtitle: Embedding projection · Tokens & embeddings
documents.body: A 2-D map of 50-D vectors, and what it loses All 10,000 words placed by one of the two precomputed projections in the asset file, UMAP or PCA, with the query's true 50-D neighbours or the analogy words highlighted. A readout counts how many 50-D neighbours survive as 2-D neighbours. A grey dot for every word inside the frame, drawn at its projected position with the same scale on both axes. The axes carry no units. In `queen + neighbours` mode: the query in the accent colour, its ten nearest words by 50-D cosine in violet, and dashed spokes from the query to each one. In `Analogy words` mode: solid arrows from B to A and from C to the top answer, and a dashed arrow that copies the B→A offset onto C. A `keeps k of 10 neighbours` badge, a caption counting the words in view, and leader lines where a label had to move off its dot. UMAP was fit with cosine distance, 18 neighbours, and minimum distance 0.12. PCA takes the two directions of greatest variance after standardizing each of the 50 dimensions. Both were computed once when the asset was built, not in the browser. The badge compares two lists: the query's ten nearest words by 50-D cosine, and its ten nearest dots by 2-D Euclidean distance. `keeps` is the size of their overlap. `Fit highlights` frames the highlighted words with padding; `All words` shows the whole projection. `Projection`: switch UMAP and PCA with `queen` selected. UMAP keeps 5 of 10 neighbours; PCA keeps 0. `Highlight`: switch between the query's neighbours and the analogy words from Vector arithmetic. `Frame`: zoom to the highlighted words or show all 10,000. Under UMAP most of queen's neighbours cluster, but elizabeth and victoria land far away: their spokes are long even though their cosines are 0.787 and 0.729. Under PCA the same neighbours scatter across the map. Two directions of variance cannot hold ten thousand words' neighbourhoods. In analogy mode the dashed arrow rarely ends on the answer. An offset that works in 50 dimensions need not survive a 2-D projection. In this lab: the projections were computed when the asset was built and cannot place a new vector such as the analogy target. The map shows words only, never `A − B + C` itself. In this lab: the same scale on both axes keeps shapes honest, but the absolute positions, cluster sizes, and gaps in UMAP carry no meaning. In general: every 2-D view of high-dimensional vectors discards most distance information. Use a projection to find neighbourhoods to inspect, then check them with the real cosines.
documents.title: A 2-D map of 50-D vectors, and what it loses

documents.subtitle: Parse a model's tool call, validate it against a JSON schema, apply host policy, and return the result as a message — then watch a failed call come back as data and get corrected on the next turn. The model only writes text; the host runs everything.
documents.body: Parse a model's tool call, validate it against a JSON schema, apply host policy, and return the result as a message — then watch a failed call come back as data and get corrected on the next turn. The model only writes text; the host runs everything. Separate what the model does (emit text naming a tool and arguments) from what the host does (parse, validate, decide, execute, report) Use a JSON schema to name distinct failures — unparseable text, unknown tool, missing field, wrong type, bad enum, extra field — and what the host returns for each Explain why a call that passes every schema check can still need a policy decision, and why constrained decoding cannot provide one Trace an error-then-retry loop: the host returns the failure as data, the next call reads it and corrects its arguments, and the host validates the corrected call from scratch
documents.title: Tools and function calling

documents.subtitle: Step 1 · Tools and function calling
documents.body: Leave the preset on valid call. In Schema check read get_dock_hours: dock and day are required, each limited to an enum, and no other fields are allowed. Then follow stages 1–10 in Host pipeline.
