documents.title: Read the model card

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Starting from initialized weights rather than someone else's trained ones. Everything the model knows has to come from the corpus you chose.
documents.title: From scratch

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: The inner dimension of a factorized weight matrix. Here it is the capacity dial: parameters are two times rank times vocabulary.
documents.title: Rank

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Storing a large matrix as the product of two thin ones. Cheaper to store and train, and unable to express every matrix the full version could.
documents.title: Factorization

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: How much structure a model can represent at all. Too little and it cannot fit the data; too much and it can fit noise.
documents.title: Capacity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: A training loss that stays high because the model cannot represent the data's structure, or has not trained long enough. More capacity fixes the first kind; more steps fix only the second.
documents.title: Underfitting

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Fitting the training text more closely than text of the same kind that was held out. It shows up as a held-out curve that stops falling, or rises, while the training curve keeps dropping.
documents.title: Overfitting

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Cross-entropy on text kept out of training. The gap between it and the training loss is the only honest signal of generalization here.
documents.title: Held-out loss

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Held-out loss minus training loss. It tends to grow with capacity and with epochs, though on 119 held-out characters it moves unevenly from one setting to the next.
documents.title: Generalization gap

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: The exponential of cross-entropy in nats: the number of equally likely options that would leave the model as uncertain. Uniform guessing over 30 symbols scores 30.
documents.title: Perplexity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: The record of what was trained on what, with which recipe, and how it scored. It documents scope and limits, not quality.
documents.title: Model card

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Text generated by repeatedly drawing from the model's next-token distribution. Samples show what the loss number feels like, and are not themselves a measurement.
documents.title: Sample

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Everything about a run apart from the architecture: which text it reads, epochs, peak learning rate, schedule, batch size, gradient clip, and seed. A model card records it so the result can be reproduced.
documents.title: Training recipe

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: How the step size changes over the run: constant, cosine decay, warmup then decay, or one cycle. The schedule multiplies the peak learning rate, so the best peak depends on the schedule chosen.
documents.title: Learning-rate schedule

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Scaling down any batch gradient whose norm exceeds a threshold before the step. It keeps one oversized step from wrecking the weights. When the rate is too large for the whole run it only contains the damage, because every step still overshoots, and it does not make the rate a good one.
documents.title: Gradient clipping

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Train one from scratch · question 1
documents.body: At rank 1 the loss flattens out well above the full-table run, and thirty epochs barely move it. What is the plateau telling you? The learning rate is wrong for rank 1, and a larger one would close the gap with the full table The corpus is too small for any model to fit, so the full table would plateau just as high Rank 1 cannot express most of the structure in the data, so longer training cannot reach it A rank-1 factorization can only express one outer product: every row of scores is the same pattern, scaled or reversed. Most of the bigram structure is unreachable no matter how long it trains. That is an underfitting plateau: more steps do not help, more capacity does. You can check the first option on the Training recipe card: no learning rate, schedule, or clip setting brings rank 1 close to the full table.
documents.title: At rank 1 the loss flattens out well above the full-table run, and thirty epochs barely move it. What is the plateau telling you?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Train one from scratch · question 2
documents.body: You switch the corpus from Harbor weather notes to Proverbs and leave Model size and Epochs where they were. Which readout stays the same? The trained weight count, because only Model size sets it The held-out loss, because the recipe is unchanged The sample text, because the seed is unchanged The number of optimizer steps, because the epochs are unchanged Model size alone sets the weight count, 60 for every unit of rank. The corpus decides the training text and the held-out sentences, so training loss, held-out loss, samples and the step count all follow it. That is why a comparison between runs has to name all four choices: corpus, size, budget and what you report.
documents.title: You switch the corpus from Harbor weather notes to Proverbs and leave Model size and Epochs where they were. Which readout stays the same?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Train one from scratch · question 3
documents.body: With the recipe at its defaults, on Proverbs at rank 12 and 30 epochs, training loss keeps falling while held-out loss turns upward. What does that show about the Epochs choice? The held-out text gets harder as training continues, so the two curves cannot be compared The model is underfitting, so more epochs or a larger rank would close the gap Both curves score the same sentences, so a rising one must be a plotting error Past some epoch it fits quirks of its training sentences that do not carry to new text That is overfitting: held-out loss bottoms out around epoch 18 and climbs back while training loss keeps falling, because later updates fit the particular training sentences rather than structure shared with new text. How long to train is a decision, not a free setting, and the held-out curve is what tells you where to stop.
documents.title: With the recipe at its defaults, on Proverbs at rank 12 and 30 epochs, training loss keeps falling while held-out loss turns upward. What does that show about the Epochs choice?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Train one from scratch · question 4
documents.body: The model card lists training loss, held-out loss, and perplexity for your run. What does it promise? That the model will score about the same on any other English text, since the card covers the language How the model scored on sentences it never trained on, for this corpus and recipe, and nothing wider That the samples shown are a measurement of quality, since they came from the final weights That the model is safe to use, because a low held-out loss rules out bad behaviour A model card documents scope: which corpus, which recipe, and how the model scored on text outside its training. It promises nothing about other text, about behaviour such as refusals, or about the samples, which only illustrate the loss. The gap between the two losses is the card's honest half.
documents.title: The model card lists training loss, held-out loss, and perplexity for your run. What does it promise?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Train one from scratch · question 5
documents.body: With the default recipe and 20 epochs on Harbor weather notes, a middle-rank model finishes below the full 900-weight table on both training and held-out loss. What does that show? More weights always fit better, so a result like this must be a plotting error The factored model can express matrices the full table cannot, so it fits the data more closely Parameter count is not capacity: shared structure lets each example move more of the model The held-out split is easier for small models, so the comparison is unfair to the full table In the full table an example moves only its own 30-weight row. In the factored model it moves its row of the input factor plus the output factor every character shares, so at this data scale each example does more work per weight. The result is conditional on plain SGD, a small corpus and this budget; at real data scale the usual finding runs the other way.
documents.title: With the default recipe and 20 epochs on Harbor weather notes, a middle-rank model finishes below the full 900-weight table on both training and held-out loss. What does that show?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Train one from scratch · question 6
documents.body: You raise Learning rate to 4 and leave the rest of the recipe at its defaults. Constant ends far above Cosine decay at that same peak rate. What is the most likely reason? Cosine shrinks its steps late in the run, so it settles where constant keeps overshooting Cosine decay makes extra passes over the text, so it has simply trained for more epochs Constant cannot update the shared output factor, so only a decaying schedule trains both factors A rate of 4 is too small for a constant schedule to move the weights at all The two runs read the same text for the same epochs and take the same number of steps; only the step size over time differs. At a peak of 4 a constant step is big enough to overshoot the low point and keeps doing so to the end, while cosine uses the same peak early and then shrinks the step so late updates settle. At the default rate of 0.5 the order reverses and Constant wins, because decaying wastes steps when no step was too large. A schedule has to be judged together with the rate.
documents.title: You raise Learning rate to 4 and leave the rest of the recipe at its defaults. Constant ends far above Cosine decay at that same peak rate. What is the most likely reason?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Train one from scratch · question 7
documents.body: At Learning rate 8 on the Constant schedule the factored run halts with a diverged loss. You set Gradient clip to 0.50 and change nothing else. What do you expect? It finishes with a finite loss, because any batch gradient above 0.50 is scaled down to that size It still halts, because clipping only changes the number shown as Peak gradient norm It matches the default recipe, because clipping cancels out the effect of the larger learning rate It still halts, because clipping takes effect only after the schedule has decayed the rate Clipping rescales any batch gradient whose norm exceeds the threshold to exactly that norm, so no step can be longer than the learning rate times 0.50. At rate 8 it fires on nearly every step, 459 of 480, and the run finishes. It still ends well above the default recipe, because clipping contains a step that is too large without making the rate a good one. The full table never needed it: its batch gradient norm cannot exceed the square root of 2, while the factored model multiplies two matrices, so each one's gradient grows with the other and the norm can climb far past that.
documents.title: At Learning rate 8 on the Constant schedule the factored run halts with a diverged loss. You set Gradient clip to 0.50 and change nothing else. What do you expect?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Train one from scratch · question 8
documents.body: You change Batch size from 8 pairs to 64 and leave Epochs at 20. What happens to the run? It takes about eight times fewer steps and ends higher, because the same passes buy fewer updates It takes the same number of steps, because Epochs alone fixes how many updates the run makes in total It takes fewer steps but ends lower, because a larger batch always gives a better gradient It takes more steps, because each larger batch needs extra updates before it is used up An epoch is one pass over the training pairs, so the step count is the number of pairs divided by the batch size, times the epochs: 960 steps at batch 8 and 120 at batch 64. A bigger batch averages away gradient noise, but with a fixed epoch budget it buys far fewer updates, and at this size the missing updates cost more than the cleaner gradient gains. Batch size and learning rate are chosen together, not one at a time.
documents.title: You change Batch size from 8 pairs to 64 and leave Epochs at 20. What happens to the run?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Train one from scratch · question 9
documents.body: You switch Training text from Cleaned scrape to Raw scrape and change nothing else. Which readouts move clearly, and which barely move? Steps and Footer lines move clearly while Held out stays close, so held-out loss alone would not flag the junk Held out rises sharply, because boilerplate and repeats poison every row the held-out sentences rely on, and little else changes Nothing moves, because both scrapes hold the same training sentences and the same held-out text The trained weight count rises, because the raw scrape has more characters for the model to store The raw scrape adds footer lines, two exact repeats, a misspelled copy, and two fragments to the same sentences, so each epoch has more pairs and the run takes more steps. The model learns the footers: its loss on those lines drops by more than half a nat. Held-out loss, which scores different sentences, barely changes and changes sign from seed to seed, so it would not have told you to clean. Cleaning here saves compute and keeps page furniture out of the model rather than lowering the held-out score.
documents.title: You switch Training text from Cleaned scrape to Raw scrape and change nothing else. Which readouts move clearly, and which barely move?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Picture a friend reading a sentence to you one letter at a time, pausing before each new letter so that you can guess it. If they stop at the harbo, you would bet on r, and after a q you would bet on u. You can do this because you have seen those letters follow each other many times before. In this module you build a tiny program that plays a simpler version of this guessing game, and you build it starting from nothing at all. A program that guesses the next piece of text is called a language model. The large language models behind chatbots do this same job at an enormous size, while yours works one character at a time on a few hundred characters of text. Your model starts from scratch, which means its numbers begin as meaningless starting values that carry no information about any text. Everything it can predict by the end has to come from the text you chose for it, and from nothing else. The lab lays out a training run in four stages, where the first three are decisions you make and the fourth is a report on them: The text the model learns from, which you pick from three short choices in the lab. The size of the model, meaning how many adjustable numbers, called weights, it gets to tune while it learns. The recipe, which covers how long training lasts, how big each learning step is, and how many examples the model studies before each step. The report at the end, on a page called a model card, which the lab fills in to record what you built and how it scored. Where you have met it The chatbots you may have used rest on language models trained through these same kinds of decisions, only with vastly more text and weights. The team behind Llama 2, a family of large language models, trained one version with 7 billion weights. It learned from 2 trillion tokens, where a token is a word or a piece of a word. That is far more text than a person could read in many lifetimes. The Llama 2 recipe used ideas you will try in this lab, such as a step size that shrinks during training and a limit on oversized steps. Real model cards exist too, and they list much more than yours will, such as where the data came from and what the model is meant for. Why it matters Without a training run there is no model at all, but a run can also go wrong in ways that are hard to spot. To see how a model is doing, you measure its error with a number called the loss, where lower means better guessing. The loss on the model's own practice text flatters it, since it has already studied that text, so you need a second loss measured on text it has never seen. A recipe whose steps are too large can wreck the whole run, while one with too few steps stops well short of where it could get. This module also holds a result you might not expect: with the lab's starting recipe, a smaller model beats a bigger one. Working out why will show you that the number of weights a model has does not, on its own, decide how well it learns. And unless you write down what you did and how it scored, nobody else can tell what your numbers mean or whether they apply to anything they care about. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these ideas in your own words: how the text, the size and the recipe together define a training run, and how each of them changes the result you get; why giving a model more weights does not automatically make it fit its text better, and what decides how well it fits instead; what a model card promises about a model, and the much longer list of things it does not promise; how four recipe settings work together, and why you judge the whole recipe by how well the model does on text it never trained on. Those four settings are: the learning rate, which is the size of each learning step; the schedule, which is the plan for changing that step size during the run; the batch size, which is how many examples the model studies before each step; the gradient clip, which is a limit on oversized steps. What the lab lets you do The lab trains two real models from scratch every time you move a control. One is yours, and the other is a plainer comparison model, called the full table, that stores its numbers in the simplest possible way. Because both are really trained, every curve, loss and sample you see is computed, not drawn by hand. You pick the text, slide the model's size up and down, and choose how many times it reads through the text. Then you watch two losses fall as the model trains, one on its practice text and one on text it never saw. Along the way, you can read three samples of the model's writing, from before training to the very end, and watch random letters turn into rough word shapes. The Training recipe card lets you change how the model learns, and even break a run on purpose to see how a safety limit contains the damage. The Model card then sums up your whole run, with both losses side by side. A few things are fixed rather than computed: the three texts, and the random choices training makes, so the same settings always give the same result. The messy "raw scrape" version of a text is built by the lab from that text's own sentences plus made-up junk, rather than collected from the web.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Train one from scratch
documents.body: The guessing game, as numbers Your model reads one character and guesses the next one, and that single character is all the context it ever gets. So at the harbo it bets using the o alone, not the whole word, which makes its game much narrower than the one you played above. Its alphabet has 30 symbols: a space, the letters a to z, and a full stop, plus two angle brackets. Those two are kept back for a later lab, which uses them as special markers, and none of the three texts here contains them. Every character in the practice text, together with the character right after it, makes one practice pair. One of the lab's three texts, Harbor weather notes, has a sentence that begins the morning fog. That gives the pairs t then h, h then e, and e then a space, and so on through the whole text. A model that learns from pairs of characters like this is called a character bigram, since "bi" means two, and the Model card uses that name under Architecture. In this lesson, the character the model is looking at is called the current character. For each of the 30 characters that could be current, the model keeps a row of 30 scores, one for each character that could come next. A step called softmax turns each row of scores into chances that add up to 100 percent, and the highest scores get the biggest chances. For example, if a row had only three scores, 2, 1 and 0, softmax would turn them into chances of about 67, 24 and 9 percent. A score can even be negative, and it still gets a chance, only a small one. After training, you would expect the row for t to give h a large share of the chances, because th turns up again and again in the practice text. Measuring surprise: the loss To improve, the model needs a single number that says how badly it is doing, and that number is the loss from the big picture. For each pair, the lab looks at the chance the model gave to the character that really came next. A big chance means little surprise while a small chance means a lot, and the loss is the average surprise over every pair, so lower is better. The surprise for a chance of 1 in N is written ln N, where ln is the natural logarithm key on a scientific calculator. You do not need to know how ln works inside, only how it behaves for a few chances: A sure thing, which is a chance of 1 in 1, gives a surprise of 0, because there is nothing to be surprised by. A chance of 1 in 8 gives a surprise of about 2.08, which is a moderate amount. A chance of 1 in 30 gives a surprise of 3.401, which is what a completely blind guess gets here. A chance that is not a whole "1 in N" works the same way. A 40 percent chance is 1 in 2.5, so its surprise is ln 2.5, which is about 0.92. So the surprise climbs as the chance shrinks, but it climbs slowly, since going from 8 choices to 30 adds only about 1.3. The unit of this surprise is called the nat, which is why the chart measures loss in nats per token. A token is the piece of text a model reads at a time. Large models use words and pieces of words, while in this lab every token is one character. Now picture a model that has learned nothing and spreads its bets evenly, giving each of the 30 symbols a chance of 1 in 30. Its surprise is ln 30 = 3.401 on every character, so its loss is 3.401 as well. The chart draws this as a dotted line labelled knows nothing, which is the number to beat, since any model that has learned a pattern should land below it. When a model's loss on a text is low, people say the model fits that text well, and the lower the loss, the closer the fit. How training works Training from scratch begins with those meaningless starting values and then repeats one small routine hundreds of times. First, the model takes a handful of practice pairs, called a batch, and measures its loss on them; at the default settings a batch holds 16 pairs. Then it works out, for every weight, how steeply the loss would rise or fall if that weight moved a little. That steepness is called the weight's slope, just like the slope of a hill on a graph. The full list of those slopes is called the gradient. It points the way that would raise the loss, so each weight steps the opposite way, downhill, and this lesson calls that downhill direction the push. The learning rate sets how big each step is. Repeating this routine is called gradient descent, because each step heads downhill on the loss, the way a ball rolls toward the lowest point of a valley. To work one push through, picture the weights for now as the 900 scores in the rows, since the Model size section below shows a cheaper way to store them. Suppose a batch holds the pair t then h, and the model gives h only a 10 percent chance after t. The push then says to raise the score for h in t's row by a lot. It also says to lower the other 29 scores in that row by a little, so that h gets a bigger share next time. Each weight's part of the push says which way that weight should move, and how strongly. One full pass through all the practice pairs is called an epoch, and the default run makes 20 of them. The pairs are shuffled into batches, the pushes are actually calculated rather than made up, and the whole run starts again from the beginning each time you move a control. Because the model is so small, that takes only milliseconds, which are thousandths of a second. The four choices The first card, Build a model in four choices, lays the run out as a strip of four stages, and each stage stands for one part of the run: Corpus is the text the model reads, since a corpus is the usual name for a body of text used for training. Size is how many weights the model gets, which you set with the Model size slider. Recipe is how the model trains, which you set with Epochs and the Training recipe card. Model card is the report the lab fills in on what you built, so it is a summary of the other three rather than a fourth choice. Clicking a stage only moves the Choice N of 4 marker at the top of the card, since no choice is locked behind another. Every control stays live the whole time, so you can change any choice in any order you like. What Model size does The most direct way to store the scores is a full grid, with a row for each current character and a column for each next character. That grid holds 30 × 30 = 900 numbers, and this lab calls it the full table. Each of its rows is completely separate, so learning something about t changes nothing in the row for s. Picture a coach who has to rate how well each of 30 players suits each of 30 positions on a team. One way is to write all 900 ratings by hand, one for each player and position, with no link between them, and that is the full table. A cheaper way is to give each player a short stats card, with one number for speed and one for strength. Each position then gets a matching card that says how much speed and strength it needs. To rate a player for a position, the coach multiplies the matching numbers on the two cards and adds up the results. Model size swaps the full table for this cheaper version, so each character, as the current one, gets a short list of r numbers. Each possible next character gets a matching list of r numbers, and the score for a pair is the two lists multiplied number by number, then added up. Storing a big grid as two thin sets of lists that multiply together like this is called a factorization. The length of each list, r, is called the rank, and it is the number that the Model size slider sets. Here is one score worked through at rank 2, using made-up numbers. Suppose the list for t, as the current character, is 2 and −1, while the list for h, as a possible next character, is 1.5 and 0.5. Multiplying the matching numbers and adding gives 2 × 1.5 plus −1 × 0.5, which comes to 3 − 0.5 = 2.5, the score for h after t. Counting the weights uses the same kind of arithmetic, because each of the 30 characters gets r numbers on the current side and r more on the next side. So the model stores 2 × r × 30 weights in all, and at the default rank of 8 that is 2 × 8 × 30 = 480. The slider shows this as rank 8 · 480 weights, and the other sizes you will try in this lesson follow the same rule: rank 1 stores 60 weights, which makes it the smallest model the slider allows; rank 4 stores 240 weights, which is about a quarter of the full table's size; rank 12 stores 720 weights, which makes it the largest model the slider allows. The lab trains your factored model and the full table side by side. Because both models use the same text and the same recipe, the only difference between them is how the weights are stored. On the chart, the thick curves are your model and the thin curves are the full table. The coach picture stops matching in one important way, because a coach chooses what each stat means, while nobody chooses what the model's r numbers mean. They end up wherever training happens to leave them, so you usually could not put a name such as "speed" on any one of them. Capacity: the ceiling that rank sets How much pattern a model can represent at all, however long it trains, is called its capacity, and the rank puts a hard ceiling on it. Rank 1 shows that ceiling most clearly, because each list then holds a single number, so every score is one number multiplied by another. Take a small case with only three possible next characters, where the next-side numbers are 3 for h, 2 for e and 1 for u. A current character whose number is 2 gets scores of 6, 4 and 2, so h comes first. One whose number is 0.5 gets 1.5, 1 and 0.5, which is the same order but flatter. One whose number is −1 gets −3, −2 and −1, so the order flips and u comes first. So at rank 1, every row follows one shared order of next characters or its exact reverse. Each row's favourite must be either the top or the bottom of that order, so there can only ever be two different favourites. A rank 1 model can never expect u after q, h after t and t after a space all at once, because that needs three. Real text needs far more than three. In the coach picture, that is like rating everyone on speed alone. Every player gets the same order of positions, only more or less extreme, or flipped end to end for a player whose number is negative. That limit is built into the model's shape, so extra training cannot remove it. What the recipe changes The size decides what the model could represent, while the recipe decides how training gets there, much like a set of cooking instructions. With the same ingredients and the same pan, how hot you cook, for how long and how much at a time can change the dish completely. The Training recipe card holds the settings that the earlier labs kept fixed, now turned into controls. The cooking picture stops matching at one point: a cook can taste the dish, but a model's loss on its own practice text is a poor guide. You judge a recipe mainly by the held-out loss, which the Why it’s here section explains. The training recipe, then, is everything about the run apart from the model's shape. It covers which version of the text the model reads and how many epochs it runs, along with the learning rate and how it changes. It also covers the batch size, the gradient clip and a fixed seed, and each of these gets its own part below. The training text A program that copies text off web pages is called a scraper, and the pile of text it collects is called a scrape. A scrape picks up junk along with the writing you wanted, such as the repeated notices at the bottom of every page, which are called boilerplate. The Training text switch chooses between a Raw scrape, junk included, and a Cleaned scrape, which is the default. The lab builds the raw scrape from the corpus's own training sentences by slotting extra lines in at fixed places: footer lines of the kind found at the bottom of web pages, such as click here to subscribe to our newsletter.. Harbor gets three of these, and Proverbs gets four because it has one more training sentence; two exact repeats of sentences that already appeared earlier in the scrape; one copy of a sentence with a spelling mistake in it, such as cllouds in place of clouds; two tiny fragments, ok. and yes., which carry almost no useful text at all. Cleaning uses the stages from *Building a dataset*, in order, dropping lines with a boilerplate phrase, lines under 12 characters, exact repeats, and near-repeats such as the misspelled copy. For Harbor weather notes, the raw scrape has 14 lines and 696 characters, and cleaning removes 8 of those lines: 3 boilerplate lines, which are the three footers; 2 lines that are too short, which are the two fragments; 2 lines that repeat an earlier line exactly; 1 near-repeated line, which is the misspelled copy. That leaves 6 lines and 379 characters, and those 6 lines are exactly the original training sentences. So the Cleaned scrape is the very same text that this lab has always trained on. Learning rate and schedule Learning rate sets how far each weight moves for a given push, and its slider has eight notches that each double the one before. The notches run from 0.125 up to 16, and the default is 0.5. For the same push, a rate of 4 moves every weight eight times as far as the default rate does. Schedule changes the step size over the course of the run, and its four buttons give four different shapes: Constant keeps the same step size from the first batch of the run to the last. Cosine decay starts at full size and eases down along the smooth curve that gives it its name, ending at 3 percent of where it began. Warmup + decay starts near zero and ramps up to full size over the first 15 percent of the steps. Then it shrinks in a straight line to 5 percent of full size. One cycle also warms up to full size, then eases down along a smooth curve until it ends below where it began. Every schedule works by multiplying the learning rate, so the rate you set is the peak, and the schedule decides how much of that peak each step uses. With the rate at 4 and Cosine decay, for example, the first step uses 4 and the last uses about 0.12, which is 3 percent of 4. A plan like this for the step size across a run is called a learning-rate schedule. Batch size Batch size is how many pairs the model studies before each update, from 2 up to 64, and the default is 16. The number of updates, which the card shows as Steps, is the number of pairs divided by the batch size, rounded up, and then multiplied by Epochs. Harbor's training text gives 378 pairs, shown at the top of the Training progress and samples card, and the default run turns them into steps like this: 378 pairs ÷ 16 pairs per batch = 23.6, which rounds up to 24 batches in each epoch; 24 batches × 20 epochs = 480 steps, which is the number the Steps readout shows. Gradient clip The push has an overall size, which is one number for how strong it is across all the weights together. To find it, square each weight's part of the push, add up the squares, and take the square root. That size is called the gradient norm, and the Peak gradient norm readout shows the largest one in the whole run, measured before any clipping happens. Putting a limit on that size is called gradient clipping, and the Gradient clip control sets the limit. Whenever a push is bigger than the limit, the lab shrinks every part of it by the same fraction, so that its size drops to exactly the limit. Here is a small example with only two weights. A push of 0.6 on one weight and 0.8 on the other has a size of the square root of 0.36 + 0.64, which is 1. With the clip at 0.50, the lab halves both parts to 0.3 and 0.4, so the size drops to 0.5. The two weights still move in the same proportion to each other, which is what people mean when they say clipping keeps the push's direction. A push whose size is already under the limit, such as 0.3, passes through untouched. The clip is off by default and can go up to 1.50, while the Clipped steps readout counts how many steps it had to shrink. The seed, and sharing your recipe Training your factored model uses random numbers twice, once for its starting values and once for shuffling the pairs into batches. The full table needs them only for shuffling, since it starts with every number at zero. A seed is a number that fixes those random choices, so the same recipe always gives the same result, and this lab always uses seed 9. Your recipe is saved in the lab's state, so the Copy a link to this state button in the header shares it with the rest of your work. Copy my recipe writes every setting out as one line of text that starts with tiny-lm-recipe v1, and Load this recipe reads a line like that back in. The model card The last stage is a report rather than a choice, because the Model card writes down the run that the other three stages defined. It lists the corpus and how it was split, the architecture and the recipe. Then come the Training loss and the Held-out loss, with a number called perplexity that the What to notice section explains. Its last row gives the full table's two losses for comparison, and under the rows sit three readouts, Train, Held out and Gap, which the next section explains.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Train one from scratch
documents.body: The flattering loss and the honest one Picture a friend who gets ready for a test by memorising the answer key to the practice test. They score 100 percent every time they retake the practice test, yet that says little about how they will do on the real test, which asks new questions. Training loss has the same weakness, because it measures the model on text it has already studied many times over. So the lab holds back about the last quarter of each corpus's sentences, which never enter a single training step, and measures the model's loss on those sentences as well. That second loss is the held-out loss, and it is the honest one, because it shows how well the model predicts text it has never seen. For Harbor weather notes, the held-out text is the final two sentences of the corpus, which come to 119 characters, against 379 for training: in summer the harbor fills with sails and the water stays warm. the fog returns in the morning and the pattern repeats. How well a pattern learned from one text carries over to new text is called generalization. The chart draws both losses after every epoch, with a solid line for training and a dashed line for held out, and it shades the space between them. The size of that space is the generalization gap, which is the held-out loss minus the training loss. The Gap readout on the Model card shows that difference at the end of the run, and the chart prints it beside the curves as well. The readout subtracts the losses before they are rounded to three decimals, so your own subtraction can differ from it by 0.001. Extra capacity usually lowers the training loss, and the gap shows how much of that gain fails to carry over to new text, which training loss alone never shows. Two ideas that usually travel together The number of weights, often called the parameter count, and capacity usually rise together, so people tend to treat them as one idea. They are not the same thing. A rank 15 model would store 900 weights, the same as the full table. Yet every row of its scores would still be a mix of only 15 shared patterns, so it could build only some of the grids the full table can. This lab adds a second surprise, which What to notice unpacks: even the model with more of both can end up fitting worse after a short run. The run that is yours From here on, every lab in the track starts from weights that somebody else trained, and you adapt them. This is the one run you own from start to finish, and the model card is the claim you have to stand behind afterwards. A model card works a bit like the label on a food packet. It lists what went in and a few measured numbers, but it does not tell you whether the food tastes good or suits your plans. The comparison stops there, because a food label's numbers hold for every packet, while a model card's losses hold only for the text and recipe it names. Where the first half of the track meets *Building a dataset* asked which text is worth training on, and *Hyperparameters & schedules* asked how to spend each step. In this lab both questions land in one run. The Held out readout judges the recipe, but it barely tells raw text from cleaned text. The difference cleaning makes shows up instead in Footer lines, a readout on the Training recipe card that gives the model's loss on the footer junk.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Start with every control at its default, which is Harbor weather notes, Model size at rank 8, Epochs at 20, and the Training recipe card untouched. Compare the three texts Click each of the three corpus buttons and read the character count on it, which is the size of the whole corpus. Harbor weather notes has 499 characters, roughly one short paragraph of a school book, and the other two are shorter still. The Model card then shows how the text splits, and for Harbor that is 379 characters for training and 119 held out. The one character left over is the space where the two parts meet. Notice how little text that is, since every pattern the model ends up with has to come from those few sentences. Each button also describes its corpus, and Harbor is repetitive description. Recipe steps is a list of cooking instructions, which has nothing to do with the training recipe apart from the word. The Proverbs button calls it short unrelated sentences that are hard to fit. You will see below what that means here: the text is small enough to memorise, so its training loss can fall low, while its held-out loss stays high. Walk Model size up Leave Epochs at 20 and move Model size from 1 up to 12, stopping at these ranks to read the Model card each time: At rank 1, the training loss ends at 2.925 and the held-out loss ends at 3.025. Rank 4 brings the training loss down to 2.208 and the held-out loss down to 2.246. Rank 8 brings them lower again, to 2.039 for training and 2.117 for held out. Rank 12 barely changes the training loss, at 2.038, but the held-out loss rises to 2.165. Now read the thin lines, which belong to the 900-weight full table and end at 2.283 for training and 2.302 held out. So with this recipe, the 240-weight model at rank 4 has already beaten a table almost four times its size. The boxed note under the two sliders on the Size and epochs card, which this lesson calls the callout, explains why. Hit the wall at rank 1 Try this: put Model size back to 1 and drag Epochs all the way to 30. The training loss ends at 2.852, and the callout reports that the full table is ahead by 0.688 nats. Look at the thick solid curve, too: from about epoch 10 to epoch 22 it hardly moves, staying between about 2.92 and 2.96. Now set Model size to 8, and its training curve drops below 2.852 by epoch 4, while even the slow full table passes that mark by epoch 5. Changing the learning rate or the schedule on the Training recipe card does not rescue rank 1 either. With or without the clip, it never gets within a third of a nat of the full table. That is a wall, not a slow start. Read the samples Below the chart on the Training progress and samples card sit three samples, labelled A, B and C. Each one is also marked on the solid curve at the point where it was written. A sample is text that the model generates one character at a time, starting after the and a space. The model only uses that last space, and the sample shows only the characters it adds. Each next character is picked at random, with the likelier characters picked more often. The samples use a fixed seed of their own, so they come out the same each time for the same weights. Sample A comes from before any training, B from halfway through, and C from the end, and each one shows the loss the model had at that moment. At the defaults, sample A is letter soup, because the untrained model sits at a loss of 3.40, right on the knows nothing line. By sample C, at a loss of 2.04, you can see word-shaped pieces such as the in a stream that is still not real English. Moving Model size changes all three samples, because they come from your factored model rather than from the full table. Watch overfitting happen Pick Proverbs, set Model size to 12 and Epochs to 30, and keep your eyes on the dashed held-out line. It falls for a while, bottoms out, and then turns back up, while the solid training line keeps going down the whole time. The What to notice section explains what that turn means. Set the recipe Go back to Harbor weather notes, rank 8 and 20 epochs, and open the Training recipe card with its defaults. There, Held out reads 2.117 and Peak gradient norm reads 0.95, and from that starting point you can work through these comparisons one at a time: Raise Learning rate to 4 with Schedule on Constant, and Held out jumps to 3.016, which is much worse than before. Switch Schedule to Cosine decay at the same rate, and Held out falls to 2.054, which is better than the default. Return the rate to 0.5 and compare the two schedules again, and the order flips, with Constant at 2.117 and Cosine decay at 2.251. Break the run, then rescue it Set Learning rate to 8 with Schedule on Constant, and the run halts at step 154 with a warning that it diverged. Diverging means the weights grew so large that the computer could no longer store the loss as an ordinary number, so training could not go on. Now turn Gradient clip up to 0.50, and the same run finishes, with 459 of its 480 steps clipped. It ends with a held-out loss of 3.089, which is far worse than the default's 2.117 but is at least a real number. Change the batch size Return the rate to 0.5 and the clip to off, then set Batch size to 8, 16 and 64 in turn while you watch Steps and Held out: batch 8 gives 960 steps, and its held-out loss ends at 2.089; batch 16 gives 480 steps, and its held-out loss ends at 2.117; batch 64 gives only 120 steps, and its held-out loss ends clearly highest, at 2.618. Feed it junk Last, note Held out and Footer lines with Cleaned scrape, then switch Training text to Raw scrape and see how much each one changes. The Footer lines readout is the model's loss on the three footer lines, so a low number there means the model has learned to predict the junk. Save your recipe When you find a recipe you like, press Copy my recipe and paste the line somewhere safe, or send it to a friend. They can paste it into the box labelled Load a recipe someone sent you and press Load this recipe to set up exactly the same run.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Train one from scratch
documents.body: The smaller model wins, and sharing is the reason At the default recipe, the full table only updates the row for the current character, so each practice pair moves 30 weights. In the factored model, the same pair moves that character's own list of r numbers plus the whole next side, which every character shares. At rank 8 that is 8 + 240 = 248 weights moved by a single pair. The letter q shows how uneven this gets, since it appears only once in Harbor's training text, in the word quiet. So the full table's q row learns from that one pair in each pass. Over 20 epochs that row gets only 20 updates, while every weight on the shared side of the factored model is updated on every one of the 480 steps. In the coach picture, one game showing that player t suits position h changes only t's own 30 ratings in the full table. With stats cards, the coach updates t's card and also every position's card, and those position cards are used to rate every other player too. With only 378 pairs to learn from, that sharing gets far more out of each example. More weights is not more fitting power The full table has more weights than any rank 8 model, and more capacity too. Every grid that a rank 8 model can build is also a possible 900-number grid. Yet after 20 epochs at the default recipe it fits worse. Capacity is only a ceiling, the most a model could ever fit with unlimited training. The full table has the higher ceiling, but after 20 epochs it is still far below it, because each of its rows gets so little practice. So a parameter count tells you at best about the ceiling, not how close a given run gets to it. You can check that the full table was short of practice rather than capacity. At a rate of 4 on Constant, its training loss in the Model card's comparison row reaches 1.872. That is far below the 2.039 your rank 8 model reaches at the default. Read the Gap as a trend The Gap tells the other half of the story. The full table has the smallest gap, only 0.019, although the next part explains why that is not the win it looks like. Among the factored models, the gap tends to grow with rank past rank 4, but it grows in a bumpy way: at rank 4, the gap is 0.038, so the two curves almost touch; at rank 6, the gap jumps to 0.095, more than twice as wide; at rank 8, the gap dips back down to 0.077; at rank 12, the gap reaches 0.128, the widest of these four. The held-out text is only 119 characters, which is two sentences. So the held-out loss can shift by a few hundredths through small accidents, such as which letters happen to land in those sentences. Random ups and downs like these are called noise. Ranking rank 6 against rank 8 on so little text is like ranking two basketball players on two free throws each. A single step such as rank 6 to rank 8 is mostly noise, so it is the overall trend that counts. A small gap can still be bad news A gap only means something when you read it next to the loss itself. At the very start of training, the two curves begin at the same point, a gap of about 0.001, yet the model knows nothing. The full table's gap of 0.019 is small for a similar reason. Its training loss of 2.283 is worse than any rank from 4 up, so it has fit its practice text too loosely to have much to lose on new text. Train it at a rate of 8 on Constant, and the Model card's comparison row reads 1.853 for training and 2.066 held out, a gap of 0.213. A loss that stays high because the model cannot represent the pattern, or has not trained long enough, is called underfitting. The full table at the default recipe shows the second kind, since bigger steps let it fit much better. Rank 1 shows the first kind. Its gap of 0.100 is no comfort, because its training loss of 2.925 is not far below the 3.401 of a model that learned nothing. However you train it, it stays well behind the full table. When a model is stuck like this, more capacity would help and more steps would not. Overfitting on Proverbs On Proverbs at rank 12 and 30 epochs, you can watch the opposite failure happen. The dashed held-out line bottoms out at 2.668 around epoch 18, then climbs back to 2.818. Meanwhile the solid training line keeps dropping, all the way down to 1.865. Past epoch 18, extra practice made the model worse at new text, because it was fitting quirks of its training sentences that new sentences do not share. Fitting the training text more closely than new text of the same kind is called overfitting. Picture the friend with the answer key again, but now they have memorised it so firmly that they write the practice answers down on new questions too. The model does the same, making confident bets on patterns from its training sentences. Each confident wrong bet costs a lot of surprise on new text, so the held-out loss rises. Enough, then too much Rank 8 and rank 12 train to almost the same place, 2.039 against 2.038, and rank 12 does no better on the held-out text. Its 2.165 against rank 8's 2.117 is a difference of 0.048, which is inside the noise, and at 30 epochs the two swap places. So the extra 240 weights bought nothing here, which is the shape to look for when you size a model: more capacity helps only until the model has enough. For a clear case of too much capacity costing you on new text, look back at Proverbs. Perplexity turns the loss into a count The Model card shows perplexity beside the held-out loss, and it turns the loss back into a number of choices. At the defaults, the held-out loss of 2.117 becomes a perplexity of 8.31. That means the model is about as unsure as if it were picking among 8 equally likely characters, which is a big drop from the 30 it started with. On a scientific calculator, the eˣ key undoes ln, and e to the power 2.117 is about 8.31. You can check this against the surprise scale from earlier, where a 1 in 8 chance gave a surprise of about 2.08. By the same logic, a model that learned nothing would have a perplexity of exactly 30. Samples follow the loss The samples improve as the loss falls, from letter soup before training to word-shaped pieces such as the in a stream that is still not fluent. A sample shows you what a loss number looks like as text, but it measures nothing, so never judge a run by its samples alone. Rank 15 is where the saving ends Past rank 15, the factored model saves nothing at all, because 2 × 15 × 30 is already 900, the size of the full table. Model size stops at 12, so you cannot reach that point in this lab. The best learning rate depends on the schedule Picture adjusting the hot tap in a shower that is slow to respond. If you make big turns the whole time, you keep overshooting, too hot and then too cold, and you never settle. If you start with big turns and switch to tiny ones near the end, you get close quickly and then settle on the right temperature. A learning rate of 4 behaves like those big turns, because on Constant every step stays large right to the end. The run keeps overshooting and finishes at 3.016 held out. Under Cosine decay, the same peak reaches 2.054, better than the default's 2.117, because the decay hands back small steps for the end of the run. At a rate of 0.5, though, no step is too big to begin with, so shrinking the steps only wastes the later part of the run. That is why Cosine decay ends worse there, at 2.251 against 2.117 for Constant. A schedule only makes sense when you judge it together with the rate it multiplies. Why only the factored model can blow up The full table cannot explode, because of how its push is built. For one pair, the push lowers each character's score by the chance the model gave it. The one exception is the character that really came next, which is raised by 1 minus its chance. The worst case is a model that is 100 percent sure of a wrong character. Then the wrong character is lowered by 1, the right one is raised by 1, and the rest do not move. The size is the square root of 1 + 1, which is about 1.41. Every other case is smaller, and averaging over a batch cannot make it bigger. So at a learning rate of 8 on Constant, the full table trains normally to 2.066 held out, and its biggest push has a size of only 0.34. The factored model is different, because it multiplies two sets of numbers together, so the push on each side grows with the size of the other side. A big step can make one side larger, which makes the next push on the other side larger, which makes the next step larger still. On Constant at a rate of 8, the factored run halts before the end, so this comparison uses Cosine decay, where the run does finish. With no clip, its Peak gradient norm reaches about 1.2e+12, which is calculator shorthand for 1.2 trillion. The run ends at a held-out loss of 22.245, far worse than the 3.401 of a model that learned nothing. With a clip of 0.50, the same run ends at 2.065. That even beats the default, because Cosine decay shrinks the steps late in the run: the clip held the early, oversized steps in check, and the schedule did the rest. Clipping contains a bad rate without fixing it On Constant the clip gets no such help, so at a rate of 8 it lets the run finish, but only at 3.089 held out, against the default's 2.117. The steps are shorter, but they are not better aimed, because the rate is still too large for every step of the run. Clipping is a safety limit that stops one oversized step from wrecking the weights, not a cure for a learning rate that is wrong. Batch size trades steps against noise Picture two teachers marking the same pile of homework over the same number of weeks. One gives feedback after every 8 questions, while the other waits until 64 questions are done. The second teacher's feedback is based on more work each time, so it is steadier, but the student hears it far less often. Batch size works the same way when Epochs is fixed, because a bigger batch averages over more pairs and smooths out the random wobble in each push. The catch is that bigger batches leave fewer updates, so batch 64 makes only 120 of them and ends clearly highest, at 2.618. Batch 8 makes 960 updates and ends at 2.089, which is within noise of batch 16. So the clear lesson is at the large end: on this text, with the epochs fixed, too few updates cost more than steadier pushes gain. Junk text: the footers notice it, the held-out loss does not The raw scrape adds steps, 880 against 480, because it has more pairs in each pass. It also lowers Footer lines from 3.090 to 2.509, which shows that the model has learned to predict the footer junk. Yet Held out barely moves, 2.105 against 2.117, and with other seeds the difference sometimes goes the other way, although this lab keeps the seed fixed at 9. So the held-out loss alone would never have told you to clean the text, while the Footer lines loss does. In this lab, cleaning keeps junk out of the model and saves training steps rather than lowering the held-out loss.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Train one from scratch
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Nothing in the training is faked: the pushes, all four curves, the held-out losses and the samples are all worked out live. The one made-up part is the raw scrape, described below. Each point on a curve is the loss of the weights saved at that epoch, measured on the whole split rather than on one noisy batch. What is missing is size and context, since the model sees exactly one character back, so t predicts the same thing in the as in it. A real model has many layers, which are stages that each rework every token's list of numbers. This model has none, and no attention either, which is the part of a real model that lets it look back across many earlier tokens. Nothing sits between the two halves of the factored model, the current-character lists and the next-character lists, while a real model does its main work in the layers between them. Because the held-out text is only 119 characters, treat any difference under about 0.05 nats as noise. It is also taken from the end of the document rather than picked at random, so it may not be typical of the rest. The three samples come from the factored model you sized, so they change when you move Model size. The thin curves belong to the full table, which has no samples of its own. Epochs stops at 30 and Model size stops at 12, and the three corpora are fixed, so you cannot paste in your own text. The scrape is synthetic, meaning the lab made it up from the corpus's own sentences with fixed junk slotted in, rather than collecting it from real web pages. The step method is the plainest kind, called stochastic gradient descent or SGD, where "stochastic" means random, because each batch is a shuffled handful of pairs. Real models use step methods with momentum, which carries part of each step into the next, and with a separate step size for each weight. So a rate of 0.5 here and a rate of 0.0003 in a real model are on different scales and cannot be compared, as Toy versus real explains. The clip shrinks the push on both halves of the factored model together, and only the factored model can explode. Every recipe result comes from one seed on about 380 characters, so differences under about 0.05 nats are noise there too. Weight decay, a real-world extra described below, is not offered, and the warmup always takes 15 percent of the steps. The callout on the Size and epochs card is written with the default recipe in mind. Raise the rate to 2 or 4 on Constant and the full table pulls ahead, and the callout then blames capacity. There the factored model is really overshooting, since the same rank 8 reaches a lower loss at the default rate. Where the real mechanism fails "Smaller fits better" is a real result, but it depends on this setup, with plain SGD, 379 characters of training text, and a full table whose rows share nothing. It also depends on the default learning rate and short run. On Constant at a rate of 2 or more, the full table pulls ahead. Bigger steps let its rarely updated rows catch up, while the factored model starts to overshoot. Step methods that give each weight its own step size also shrink that advantage. They give weights that rarely get practice, such as the q row, bigger steps to make up for it, and this lab has no switch for them. Scaling laws are patterns that describe how loss falls as models and data grow. With real amounts of data, bigger models usually do better, and scaling laws say to grow the weights and the text together rather than pushing either one alone. A held-out loss is only honest while the split is honest. Suppose near-copies of the same sentence land on both sides of a real split between training text and test text. Then the model has partly seen the test already, so its loss looks better than it deserves, which is one more reason the near-repeat stage in cleaning matters. A real recipe also leans on tools that this lab leaves out, such as a step method that gives each weight its own step size. It also uses weight decay, which gently shrinks every weight a little at each step so that none grows too large. Real runs also use mixed precision, which does some of the arithmetic with shorter, less exact numbers to save time and memory. A common mix-up: a low loss is not a capable model. Loss only says how well the model predicts the next character on this kind of text. It promises nothing about following instructions, refusing what it should refuse, citing sources or getting facts right. A model card records which model was trained on which text, with which recipe, and how it scored. It is a statement of scope, not a quality rating, and its job is to let someone else judge whether your number applies to their problem.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Train one from scratch
documents.body: The same two halves sit inside real models The two thin halves of your factored model are not a toy shortcut, because every real language model has these same two pieces at its two ends. One turns each token into a list of numbers, and the other scores every possible next token against that list. These two pieces are usually called the embedding and the unembedding. In a real model each list is thousands of numbers long, and much of the interesting work happens in the many layers stacked between the two ends. Your model has no layers there, and no attention to look further back. It only ever sees one character, which is why it can only learn which character tends to follow which. Two reasons the small model wins The first reason is uneven practice, which the letter q showed in What to notice. A rare character's row in the full table barely gets updated, while the shared side of the factored model learns from every step. What matters is how much practice each weight gets, not how many weights there are. The second reason is that the factorization is a constraint, since it forces characters to share structure whether the text calls for it or not. That keeps the factored model from bending each row to fit its few training pairs exactly, which helps it on new text. The full table's tiny gap at the default recipe has a different cause, as you saw earlier. It learns so slowly that it has fit its training text only loosely, so it has little to lose on new text, and once it trains harder its gap grows. What real model cards add Real model cards go much further than this one, recording where the data came from and under what licence, along with the exact recipe. They also list which tests were run on which version, the failure modes people already know about, and what the model is meant to be used for. None of that is a quality rating either, because a card describes what a model covers rather than how good it is. Your card does the smallest version of the same job, because it reports two losses that disagree instead of only the one that looks good. Toy versus real Learning rates do not carry over from this lab to real models, because this lab uses plain SGD with rates from 0.125 to 16. The Llama 2 paper trained its models of 7 billion and 13 billion weights with a method called AdamW, which rescales each weight's own step. The peak learning rate for those Llama 2 models was 0.0003, which the paper writes in scientific notation as 3.0 × 10⁻⁴. The Llama 3 paper lists the same rate for its 8 billion weight model. Since AdamW gives every weight its own step size, its rates and this lab's rates cannot be compared. The same three ideas show up at full size in Llama 2. It used a schedule that warmed up over 2,000 steps and then followed a cosine curve down to 10 percent of the peak. It also used weight decay of 0.1 and clipped its gradients at 1.0. Cosine decay, warmup and a clip are three of this lab's recipe settings, although the lab's cosine ends at 3 percent of the peak rather than 10. The scale is wildly different, since the Llama 2 paper reports 2.0 trillion training tokens for its 7 billion weight model. Each of its batches held 4 million tokens, while this lab works through 16 pairs at a time. The same paper reports 184,320 hours of work on GPUs, which are chips built to do huge amounts of arithmetic at once. That adds up to about 21 years if a single chip had done all the work alone, while this lab trains on about 380 characters in milliseconds. Cleaning is a chain of steps in real data work, using the same kinds of stages as this lab's cleaning step: filtering junk and removing near and exact repeats. It runs those stages over collections of text vastly larger than this one, and it judges the results on large held-out tests rather than on one small split. These facts come from two sources, both cited in the Standard lesson: Touvron and co-authors, *Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models* (arXiv 2307.09288), section 2.2 and Tables 1 and 2. Llama Team, AI @ Meta, *The Llama 3 Herd of Models* (arXiv 2407.21783), Table 3.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Train one from scratch
documents.body: This module puts a whole training run in your hands. You choose the text, the model's size, and the training recipe, train a character-level language model from initialized weights, and read a model card that records what you built and how it scored. The question is which of those decisions helped, judged on text the model never trained on. Along the way, with plain SGD on a few hundred characters of text, a model with fewer parameters can fit better, and the best learning rate depends on the schedule. This module brings the first half of the track together, building on two prerequisites. *Building a dataset* asked what text is worth training on, and *Hyperparameters & schedules* asked how to spend a step. Here both land in one run. The model card's Held out readout judges the recipe, but it barely separates training on the raw scrape (the corpus with footer lines and repeats mixed in) from training on the cleaned one. The difference cleaning makes shows up in Footer lines on the Training recipe card, the model's loss on the three boilerplate lines the raw scrape contains. Where it shows up Pretraining recipes. Llama 2 used three of the Training recipe card's ideas (cosine decay, warmup, and gradient clipping), with AdamW instead of plain SGD. Data pipelines. The lab's Cleaned scrape comes from a small version of the stages that production pipelines run over web crawls many orders of magnitude larger: filtering, exact deduplication, and near deduplication. Model cards. Real cards add data provenance and licence, versioned evaluation suites, known failure modes, and intended use. The ends of a language model. The lab's factored model stores its 30 × 30 table of next-character scores as a 30 × r matrix times an r × 30 one, where r is the rank. The first factor is an embedding matrix, mapping each character to r numbers, and the second is an unembedding, scoring every candidate next character against them. Real language models have these two matrices at their ends. Why it matters Training loss can keep falling while a model gets worse on new text, so without a held-out score you cannot tell useful capacity from overfitting. Without the data and recipe written down on a card, nobody can reproduce the run or judge whether its number applies to their problem. The settings also interact: a learning rate that ruins one schedule can beat the default under another. What you will be able to explain Which decisions define a training run (text, size, and recipe) and what each one changes. How parameter count relates to fit, and why a smaller factored model can beat the full table here. What a model card promises (scope and measured scores) and what it does not. How learning rate, schedule, batch size, and gradient clip interact, and why held-out loss judges the recipe. What the lab shows The lab trains two real character bigrams with minibatch SGD on the same text and recipe, retraining whenever you move a control: the factored model you configure and the full 900-weight table for comparison. Every curve, loss, perplexity, gradient readout, and step count comes from those runs, and the samples are drawn from the factored model's checkpoints. The weight and character counts are exact arithmetic, and the dotted "knows nothing" line at ln(30) is closed-form. The inputs are fixed: three short built-in corpora (Harbor weather notes, Recipe steps, and Proverbs), a held-out split taken from the end of each, and seed 9. The Raw scrape option is synthetic, the corpus's own sentences with footer lines, repeats, and fragments slotted in. The corpus buttons sit on Build a model in four choices, and Size and epochs holds Model size (the factored model's rank) and Epochs. Training recipe holds Training text, Learning rate, Schedule, Batch size, and Gradient clip. That card's readouts are Held out, Footer lines, Steps, Peak gradient norm, and Clipped steps, and Copy my recipe saves the settings as one line of text that Load this recipe reads back. Training progress and samples plots the curves, and Model card reports Train, Held out, and Gap. The key experiment is the Model size sweep on Harbor weather notes at 20 epochs and the default recipe: from rank 4 up the factored model beats the full table on both losses, and held-out loss bottoms out at rank 8 (2.117), with ranks 7 to 11 all within about 0.03 of it. Rank 1 stalls well above the table. On Proverbs at rank 12 and 30 epochs the factored model's dashed held-out curve turns upward. On Training recipe, a rate of 8 on Constant makes the factored run diverge until Gradient clip contains it, while the full table trains normally at the same rate.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Training from scratch means starting from initialized weights, so everything the model knows has to come from the corpus you picked. Four decisions define the run — which text, how many weights, which training recipe, and what you report — and the wizard stages are those decisions. The recipe is everything about the run except its architecture: epochs, peak learning rate, schedule, batch size, gradient clip, and a fixed seed. The model is a character bigram. The vocabulary is 30 symbols: a space, a–z, a full stop, and two reserved angle brackets that occur in no corpus. For each possible preceding character it keeps a row of 30 logits, and a softmax over that row is the next-character distribution. Loss is mean cross-entropy in nats per token. A model that has learned nothing spreads probability evenly across 30 symbols and scores ln(30) = 3.401, the dotted "knows nothing" line. Training is minibatch SGD on that loss, recomputed whenever you move a control. What Model size changes The full logit table holds 30 × 30 = 900 numbers. Model size replaces it with a factorization: a 30 × r matrix times an r × 30 matrix, whose product is the logit table. That trains 2 × r × 30 = 60r weights, and r is the rank — 60 at rank 1, 240 at rank 4, 480 at rank 8, 720 at rank 12. The lab trains the factored model and the full 900-weight table on the same text with the same recipe — by default batch 16, learning rate 0.5, a constant schedule, no clipping, and seed 9 — so the only difference between the thick factored curves and the thin full-table curves is how the weights are stored. Rank is a hard ceiling on capacity, and rank 1 makes that concrete. With r = 1 every logit is u[row] · v[next], so every context row produces the *same* shaped distribution scaled by a single number. Sharper, flatter, or reversed — never a different ordering of characters. What the recipe changes The Training recipe card carries the settings the earlier labs fixed. Training text chooses between a raw scrape and a cleaned one. The lab builds the scrape from the corpus's own training sentences by slotting in footer lines, two exact repeats, a misspelled copy, and two fragments. Cleaning uses the stages from *Building a dataset*: a boilerplate phrase, a length floor, an exact duplicate, a near-duplicate. Cleaned is the default, and it is exactly the text this lab always trained on. Four settings come from *Hyperparameters & schedules*: Learning rate is the peak step size, in eight notches that double from 0.125 to 16. Schedule multiplies that peak over the run: Constant, Cosine decay, Warmup + decay, or One cycle. This is the learning-rate schedule. Batch size is the number of pairs per update, from 2 to 64. Steps equal the pairs divided by the batch, rounded up, times Epochs. Gradient clip scales any batch gradient whose norm exceeds it down to that norm, which is gradient clipping. It is off by default. The recipe is saved in this lab's state, so the *Copy a link to this state* button in the header shares it with the rest of your work. Copy my recipe writes only the recipe, as one line, and Load this recipe reads such a line back.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Train one from scratch
documents.body: Every later lab adapts weights someone else trained. This is the run you own end to end, and the model card is what you have to defend afterwards. It also pulls apart two ideas that usually travel together: capacity is what a model can represent at all, parameter count is how many numbers it stores. Here they come apart on screen. And it puts the honest number beside the flattering one. Training loss covers text the model has already seen; held-out loss is scored on the last 25% of sentences, which never enter a gradient step. The chart plots both at every epoch — solid for training, dashed for held out, with the band between them shaded — and the Gap between them is what extra capacity buys and what it costs.

documents.body: Click each of the three corpora and read the character count on the button, which is the whole corpus. documents.body: The smaller model fits better, and the reason is the update rule. The full table only touches the row for the character it just saw, so each example moves 30 weights. In the factored model it moves that character's r weights in the input factor plus the whole r × 30 output factor, which every character shares: 31r weights, 248 at rank 8. At 379 characters, shared structure beats independent rows. So parameter count is not capacity. The full table can express strictly more matrices than any rank-8 product and still loses on this data at this budget. The Gap readout tells the other half. The full table has the smallest gap, 0.019, but because it fits its training text loosely (2.283), not because it generalizes better: at rate 8 on Constant it trains to 1.853 and its gap grows to 0.213. Rank 12 sits at 0.128. Among the factored runs the gap trends up past rank 4 but not smoothly: 0.038 at rank 4, 0.095 at 6, 0.077 at 8, 0.128 at 12. With 119 held-out characters, single steps like 6 to 8 are noise; the trend is the signal. A gap is only readable next to a loss. Rank 1's gap is 0.100, larger than rank 4's, and means nothing good: 2.925 against 3.401 for knowing nothing. That is underfitting. Rank 1 is an underfitting plateau, not a slow start — thirty epochs buy 0.073 nats. Rank 8 and rank 12 train to almost the same place (2.039 against 2.038) but rank 8 holds out better, which is the shape of "enough capacity, then too much". Overfitting is visible on the harder corpora. More epochs made the model worse on new text. Perplexity on the model card is the held-out loss on a friendlier scale: 8.31 at the defaults, so 30 equally likely options narrowed to about 8. Samples track loss. The untrained checkpoint is letter soup; by the end there are word-shaped fragments like the and and in a stream that is still not fluent. A sample illustrates the loss and measures nothing. Past rank 15 the factorization saves nothing, since 2 × 15 × 30 is already 900. The lab notes this, and Model size stops at 12 so you cannot reach the crossover. The best learning rate depends on the schedule. Rate 4 ruins a constant run at 3.016 held out, yet under cosine decay the same peak reaches 2.054, below the default's 2.117, because the decay hands back small steps for the end. At rate 0.5 nothing overshoots, so decay only wastes steps. The full table cannot explode. Its batch gradient norm cannot pass the square root of 2, so at rate 8 on Constant it trains normally to 2.066 held out with a peak norm of 0.34. The factored model can. It multiplies two matrices, so each factor's gradient grows with the other. At rate 8 on Cosine decay with no clip its Peak gradient norm reaches about 1.2e12 and it ends at 22.245; with a 0.50 clip it ends at 2.065. Clipping contains a bad rate without fixing it. At rate 8 on Constant the clip lets the run finish, but at 3.089 against 2.117 for the default: the steps are shorter, not better chosen. Batch size trades step count against noise when Epochs is fixed. Batch 64 makes only 120 updates and ends highest at 2.618; batch 8 makes 960 and ends lowest at 2.089.
