documents.subtitle: Plain · Training dynamics
documents.body: Picture two classmates who both score 100% on every practice quiz in the back of their maths textbook. On the real test, though, one of them does well and the other falls apart. The first one had learned how to solve the problems, while the second one had memorized the answers to those exact questions. If all you ever saw were their practice scores, you could never tell the two of them apart. Training an AI model has the same trap, since a model learns by adjusting the numbers inside it until it does well on a pile of examples. It can get there by picking up the real pattern behind the examples, or by memorizing the examples themselves, odd details and all. This module is about telling those two apart, catching the moment a model starts sliding from one to the other, and knowing what to do about it. The main idea fits in one sentence: keep some examples out of training, and score the model on those as well. Training only ever looks at the score on its own examples, so the score on the held-back ones is your honest check on what the model really learned. Where you have met it Whenever you read that a new AI model did well on a test, often called a benchmark, that score was measured on questions held back from its training. The score only means something if those questions were truly kept out, since otherwise it measures memorizing instead of skill, and nobody can tell from the number alone. The chatbots you may have used face the same risk at one stage of their training. The large models behind them are first trained on huge amounts of text, and can then be trained again on a much smaller set of examples, called fine-tuning. That smaller round is one of the places where memorizing becomes a real danger. The checks you will practise in this lab are the ones people use to catch it. Why it matters Without a held-back score, a training error that keeps shrinking looks like progress even while the model is busy memorizing its examples. You could end up with a model that shines on its practice examples and fails on everything new, without finding out until it meets real inputs. You would also have no good way to choose a model’s size or when to stop training, because the practice score keeps improving almost whatever you do. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these ideas in your own words: how a model’s score on the examples it trained on differs from its score on examples it never saw, and why only the second one shows real learning; how to spot the moment a model starts memorizing, which is called overfitting, and two ways to respond: keeping its numbers small and stopping at the right time; what happens to a training run when you make the model more or less flexible, or change how hard its numbers are pulled toward zero; what happens when you change how big each training step is, called the learning rate, and how many examples feed into each step, called the batch size. What the lab lets you do The lab trains a real, tiny model right inside the app, and its only job is to draw a curve through 16 dots. Another 16 dots are kept back to score that curve, so you can see how it does on dots it never trained on. Nothing on the screen is a pre-drawn animation. Every line and number comes from real training runs, one for each model size. The app runs them again in a split second whenever you change a training setting or the noise draw, and records them as they go. Moving Epoch or Polynomial degree retrains nothing. It only picks which saved run, and which moment in it, to show. The lab is split into four cards, and each one lets you see or change a different part of the run: watch the two scores move together or drift apart over 10,000 rounds of training on Training curves; see the actual curve the model has drawn so far, next to both sets of dots, on Fitted function; change the model’s size and each of its training settings, one at a time, on Training dynamics controls; compare every model size at the same moment of training, side by side, on Capacity sweep. The lab is unrealistic in one way, on purpose: it makes its own dots from a curve it chose, then nudges each dot up or down at random. Because it made the data itself, it can show you the true curve behind the dots, which no real project ever gets to see. The badge that calls a run “fitting” or “overfitting” uses cut-off points that the lab picked, and they are not rules that every project follows. The lab also leaves out a third set of examples, a kind of final exam that real projects keep, which you will meet further down.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Training dynamics
documents.body: Go back to the two classmates for a moment, because there are two very different things you can measure about any student. One is how well they do on practice problems they have already worked through, and the other is how well they do on brand-new problems. You can measure a model in the same two ways, and this lab draws both measurements as lines on one chart so that you can compare them. Two scores from one model The examples a model trains on are called the training set, and they are like the practice problems with the answers in the back of the book. During training, the model is adjusted over and over to do better on exactly these examples and no others. Its score on them is the training loss, where “loss” means how far wrong the model is, so a lower loss is a better score. A second pile of examples is kept out of training on purpose, or “held out”, and it is called the validation set. The model is never adjusted to fit these examples, so they work like a quiz full of brand-new problems. The score on them is the validation loss, and it tells you how well whatever the model learned carries over to examples it has not trained on. Doing well on new examples like these is called generalization, and it is the only real evidence that a model picked up a pattern. A memorized answer is no help on a question you have never seen, so a model that only memorized its practice set will do badly on new examples. The difference between the two scores, the validation loss minus the training loss, is called the generalization gap, and the lab shows it as Gap (val − train). Neither line tells you much on its own, because the useful information is in how far apart the two lines sit and whether that distance keeps growing. How a miss is scored The model in this lab draws a curve, and its loss measures how badly that curve misses the dots it is being scored on. For each dot, the lab measures the up-and-down distance between the dot and the curve, squares that distance, and then averages the squares over all 16 dots. That average is called the mean squared error, and it is the loss on every chart in the lab. Here is a small worked example that uses three dots instead of 16, with the curve missing each dot by a different amount: The curve passes 0.1 above the first dot, and that miss squares to 0.01. It passes 0.3 below the second dot, and squaring that miss turns it into a positive 0.09. It passes 0.2 above the third dot, and that miss squares to 0.04. The squares add up to 0.14, so their average over the three dots, which is the loss, comes to about 0.047. Squaring does two useful jobs: it turns misses below a dot into positive numbers, so they cannot cancel out misses above another dot. It also makes big misses count far more than small ones, since a miss that is three times bigger counts nine times as much. To turn a loss back into a distance, take its square root, which gives you the size of a typical miss. For example, a loss of 0.0625 means a typical miss of about 0.25. That is because 0.25 squared is 0.0625, and you will meet this exact number again in a moment, when the lab measures its noise. The model in this lab The “student” in this lab is a small model whose only job is to draw a curve that fits a set of dots. The lab starts from a smooth wave that tilts upward from left to right, which it calls the true curve, and places 32 dots along it. It then nudges each dot up or down by a random amount, so the dots sit near the wave but not exactly on it. Those random nudges are called the noise, and in the textbook picture they are like misprints in the answer key. They are part of what the student studies, but they are not part of the method the student should learn, so memorizing them can only hurt. Counting from left to right, every other dot goes into the training set and the rest go into the validation set, which gives each pile 16 dots. Because the two piles alternate, both of them are spread across the whole width of the chart. The model only ever trains on the 16 training dots, and it never sees the true curve at all. The lab chose the size of the nudges itself, so their average size is known exactly, something real data never offers. A typical nudge is about 0.25, so the average squared nudge is 0.0625, and the lab calls this the noise variance. It is written σ² and read as “sigma squared”, and it appears as a dotted line on both loss charts. That dotted line matters because no curve can predict random nudges, so even the true curve misses the dots by that much on average. On this lab’s 16 training dots, the true curve scores 0.081, a little above 0.0625, because these particular nudges happen to run on the large side. The true curve is the best any curve can do by following the pattern alone. So when a model’s training loss sinks well below the dotted line, it can only have got there by bending toward some of the random nudges in its own dots. Those nudges will not be there on any new dot, so matching them can never help on new examples. Weights, degree and capacity The model builds its curve by adding together a set of simple building-block curves of different shapes. The first block is a flat line, the next is a sloping line, and each block after that bends one more time than the block before it. Each block comes with its own number, which says how much of that block goes into the mix, and these numbers are called weights. Training a model means adjusting its weights until the blocks add up to a curve that matches the training dots well. A curve built from blocks like these is called a polynomial, and its degree counts how many blocks come after the flat one. The Polynomial degree control runs from 1 to 13, and next to the degree it shows how many weights that gives. At degree 1 there are two weights, one for the flat block and one for the sloping block, so the model can only ever draw a straight line. At degree 11 the control reads 11 · 12 weights, and a curve built from that many blocks can bend as many as 10 times. How flexible a model is, meaning how many different shapes it can draw, is called its model capacity, and in this lab capacity is the polynomial degree. Turning up the degree gives the model more freedom to bend, and in the much larger models behind chatbots, capacity grows with the number of weights. How training moves the weights Training starts with every weight set to zero, so the first curve is a flat line across the middle of the chart. From there, training repeats the same move thousands of times, and each repeat is called a step. In each step it looks at the training dots, works out which small change to each weight would lower the training loss fastest, and makes that change. One full pass through all 16 training dots is called an epoch, and the Epoch slider in the lab runs from 0 to 10,000 of them. The lab recorded both losses 83 times along the way, so dragging the slider shows you the model at any of those moments. Two settings on Training dynamics controls decide how each step is made, and each one comes with an everyday picture below: Learning rate sets how big each step is, and the lab writes it with the Greek letter η, read as “eta”, set to 0.1 unless you change it. A bigger learning rate gets somewhere faster, but a step that is too big can jump past the best values for the weights and land somewhere worse. Batch size sets how many training dots the model looks at before each step. At 16 (full) it uses every dot and takes one step per epoch, while at 4 it takes four quicker but less reliable steps per epoch. Picture a group chat of 16 friends trying to pick a place for lunch, where you can either wait for everyone or decide as the replies come in. If you wait for all 16 replies, you make one well-informed choice, but it takes a while to arrive. If you decide after every 4 replies, you make four quick choices in the same time, but each one leans toward whichever friends happened to answer first. Smaller batches work the same way: more steps per epoch, each pointing a little away from the direction that all 16 dots would agree on. The picture stops matching in one way. Lunch choices replace each other, but the four small steps add up, each one starting from where the last one left off. Over an epoch every dot still gets its say, and the lean only makes the path wobble. Overshooting deserves its own picture, so imagine someone in a shower who turns the knob a long way every time the water feels wrong. The water goes from too cold to too hot, so they swing the knob hard the other way, and each correction overshoots by more than the last. A training run with too big a learning rate can do the same thing, with its loss swinging wider and wider instead of settling down. On the chart you will see a steady climb rather than visible swings, because the lab only records the loss now and then. Once the loss passes 10⁶, which is a 1 followed by six zeros, the lab stops the run and marks it as diverged. Two more controls round out the card: Weight decay, a fix for memorizing that you will try further down, and Noise draw. Noise draw picks one of four random draws of the dots, labelled seed 1 to seed 4. It lets you check whether a result depends on the luck of the draw. A seed is the starting number the lab feeds into its random-number maker, so the same seed always gives the same dots. A different seed changes both the up-and-down nudges and exactly where each dot sits from left to right. Three ways a run can go As you drag Epoch, a badge on Training curves names the situation the run is in, and there are three main situations to know: Underfitting means both losses stay high, because the model is too simple to follow the pattern or has not trained long enough yet. A straight line at degree 1 settles at a training loss of 0.322 and never improves, because no straight line can follow a wave. Fitting means both losses fall together and then hold fairly steady, which is what you want to see. At the default degree 5, validation reaches its lowest point at epoch 11, then creeps up only slightly and holds steady for the rest of the run. Overfitting means the training loss keeps falling while the validation loss turns around and climbs. The model is now matching the random nudges in its 16 training dots, which helps on those dots but hurts on every new one. The badge also has a fourth reading, diverged, for a run whose steps overshoot so badly that its loss explodes, as in the shower story. In the textbook picture, overfitting is the student who has memorized the answer key, misprints and all, so their practice score is perfect for the wrong reason. Three piles, not two The validation set has a weakness of its own, because you also use it to make choices about the model. You check it to decide how big a model to use, how big a learning rate to pick, and when to stop training. Every time you keep whichever option scored best on it, you are choosing partly on luck, so your final choice’s score looks a little better than it really is. Picture a student who tries ten different ways of studying and keeps whichever one earns the best mark on the same practice quiz. Part of that winning mark is real, and part of it is luck, because one method happened to suit those particular questions. To get an honest number, the teacher needs a final exam that played no part in any of the choosing. That final pile is called the test set, and a real project locks it away and scores it only once, at the very end. It stays honest only until someone starts tuning against it, because at that point it has turned into one more validation set. This lab does not draw a test set. The split strip is the row of all 32 dots at the top of Training dynamics controls. The note under it says so in plain words: “No test split is drawn.”
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Training dynamics
documents.body: The last few labs in this course worked on making a loss go down, and this one asks which loss, measured on which examples. It also asks when to stop pushing that loss down, which is the difference between just running training and ending up with a model you can trust. Training cannot tell pattern from noise Training can only push down the score it can see, and the only score it sees is the training loss on its own dots. From inside that score, a random nudge in a dot looks exactly like part of the real pattern, so there is no signal that says “ignore this one”. Bending the curve toward a noisy dot lowers the training loss as surely as following the true wave does. So training does both whenever the model has enough weights to bend that far, and a high degree gives it plenty. Nothing in the process is trying to cheat, and nothing in it can tell the difference between a pattern and an accident. The validation dots are the only outside check, because their nudges are different random amounts from the nudges in the training dots. A curve that bent toward the training noise has no reason to pass near the validation dots. So it misses some of them, most of all where no training dot holds it in place. Why the damage shows up late Training does not learn every part of the curve at the same speed, and that turns out to matter a great deal. Big, smooth changes to the curve lower the loss a lot with each step, so training makes them first, mostly within the first dozen or so epochs. Fine, wiggly changes lower the loss only a tiny bit with each step, so training gets to them slowly, over hundreds and then thousands of epochs. The real pattern here is mostly smooth, while the noise mostly looks like fine wiggles from one dot to the next, so useful learning arrives first. The harmful fitting creeps in afterwards, which is why, at degree 11, the validation line falls quickly at the start and only later begins to climb. Picture a friend who studies the same practice book every night for a month, hoping to do well on the end-of-term test. In the first few sessions they pick up the methods, and their marks on new problems improve quickly. Weeks later they have started remembering particular answers, misprints included, so their practice marks keep creeping up while their marks on new problems slowly slip. This ordering is the reason that stopping early works, because there is a moment between the two stages when the pattern is learned but little noise is matched. At degree 11 in this lab, that moment comes at epoch 13, long before the thousands of epochs in which the damage builds up. Why it matters for every score you read Any claim that a model is good rests on a held-out score of some kind, and a benchmark score is one of these. So a benchmark score can only be trusted when you know how its test questions were kept apart from the training data. Going deeper shows two ways that can fail.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Training dynamics
documents.body: The lab’s four guided tasks walk you through this in order: Split the data, Watch the curves, Trigger overfitting and Regularize. The parts below follow the same path, after a quick tour of what each card shows and how to read its axes. Reading the cards Training dynamics controls holds every control, and at its top is the split strip, which lines up all 32 dots in a row. Filled dots above the line are training dots and hollow dots below it are validation dots. The strip’s note sums this up as “Hollow only scores it.” In other words, hollow dots are only used to score the curve and are never used to train it. Training curves plots both losses against the epoch, with a solid blue line for training, a dashed orange line for validation, and a shaded band for the gap. A green ring marks the lowest validation loss of the whole run, and a dotted upright line shows the epoch you have picked. Fitted function draws the model’s curve, labelled ŷ and read as “y-hat”, over the filled training dots and the hollow validation dots. The dashed line is the true curve, which the legend reminds you is hidden from the model. Capacity sweep shows training and validation loss for every degree from 1 to 13 at the epoch you have picked, each trained with the same settings. The degree runs along the bottom and the loss up the side, so each line runs from simple models on the left to flexible ones on the right. Both loss charts use a log scale on the up-and-down axis, which works differently from the axes you usually see in maths class. On an ordinary axis, each grid line adds the same amount to the one below it, such as going up by 1 each time. On a log scale each grid line is ten times the one below, so a tiny loss like 0.007 and a huge one like 8.63 both fit on one chart. The epoch axis on Training curves works the same way. After 0 at the corner, each labelled mark is ten times the one before, from 1 up to 10k, which means 10,000. One handy result follows from this: a run that does the same things, only ten times later, slides about one mark to the right. Split the data Pick the third filled dot from the left on the split strip, then count across to the third filled dot from the left on Fitted function. Do the same with a hollow dot. Because the split alternates along the line, both piles cover the whole width, so the validation dots test every part of the curve. Watch the curves Start at the default degree 5, and drag Epoch back to 0 and then slowly all the way up to the end. Both lines drop fast in the first few epochs and then level off, with validation sitting a steady distance above training. The green ring sits at epoch 11, where validation reaches its lowest value of 0.100. The Lowest validation readout shows this as 0.100 @ 11, where the @ sign means “at epoch”, and the button under the slider names the same epoch. Its label reads Stop at lowest validation (epoch 11) for now, and it changes whenever the ring moves. Now go back to epoch 100, where the slider sat when you first opened the lab, and look at the readouts under the chart. Training reads 0.017 and validation reads 0.111, and the badge says fitting. Their difference shows up in Gap (val − train) as 0.093, and the readouts are rounded, so the subtraction can look off by 0.001. The gap barely moves for the rest of the run. Notice that 0.017 is already well below the dotted line, so even this model has matched a good share of the noise. What makes the run healthy is that it stops there. With only 6 weights it cannot bend any further, so the gap holds steady and validation does not climb. Trigger overfitting Try this: Set Polynomial degree to 11, which gives the model 12 weights to turn, then drag Epoch to 10,000 and watch the two lines part ways. As soon as you set the degree to 11, the green ring and the stop button jump to epoch 13, the lowest point of the new run. Here is what you should see, in order, as the slider moves: Validation drops to its best value, 0.098, at epoch 13. After that, validation turns around and climbs, and the badge switches to overfitting at epoch 215. By the last epoch, validation has climbed to 8.63, which is 88 times worse than the best it reached. Meanwhile, the training loss keeps falling the whole way down to 0.007, which is far below the dotted noise line. Now look at Fitted function at epoch 10,000, where the curve has stopped following the dashed true curve and bends toward individual filled dots instead. Near the right edge, the last hollow dot sits beyond the last filled dot, so no training dot holds the curve in place there. The curve swings so far that it leaves the chart, which only runs from −2 to 2, and a red note reports a peak of about 24. That one hollow dot at the right edge accounts for almost all of the 8.63. The curve misses it by about 11.7, which squares to about 136. The other 15 hollow dots have squared misses that average only about 0.14, so most of the curve still passes fairly close to them. This is the squaring rule from earlier at work, because one huge miss can outweigh everything else in the average. Regularize Any rule that makes it harder for a model to bend toward noise is called regularization, and the lab gives you two kinds to try at degree 11. First, raise Weight decay to 0.03, which makes every step pull each weight except the flat block’s a little toward zero, as well as toward a better fit. The lab writes the strength of that pull with the Greek letter λ, read as “lambda”, so the control now shows λ 0.03. Each building block on its own only rises and falls a modest amount. Bending sharply toward one dot and back before the next takes large amounts of the bendiest blocks, some pushing up and some pushing down. Swinging far off near an edge takes the same. So wild swings need large weights, and a steady pull toward small weights keeps the curve smoother and calmer between the dots. Drag Epoch to 10,000 again and read the validation loss, which now sits much closer to the best this model ever reached. It reads 0.135 instead of 8.63, while the training loss ends a little higher than it did without weight decay. That trade is the whole idea: the model gives up a little fit on its own dots in exchange for a curve that works on new ones. Second, set Weight decay back to λ 0 (off) and press Stop at lowest validation, which jumps the slider back to the ring at epoch 13. Validation there reads 0.098, and this move is called early stopping: same model, same settings, but you keep the version from the best epoch instead of the last. More comparisons to run Once you have seen the main story, these comparisons show how the other settings change a run: Learning rate: at degree 11, move Learning rate from 0.1 down to 0.01 and look at where the green ring lands. The best validation loss is almost the same, at 0.097, but it arrives about ten times later, at epoch 147. The whole run slides about one mark to the right on the log scale, and it still overfits afterwards. Batch size: go back to degree 5, set Learning rate to 0.3, and try each Batch size in turn. With 16 or 8 dots per step, the run trains normally from start to finish. With only 4 dots per step, the loss explodes and the badge reads diverged at epoch 22. What to notice explains why. Model size and learning rate: put Batch size back to 16 (full) and set Learning rate to 0.6, then compare two degrees. At degree 5 the run still trains normally, but at degree 11 it diverges at epoch 562, so a bigger model can need a smaller learning rate. The training loss bottoms out near 0.03 in the first few epochs, then climbs steadily for hundreds of epochs before the run is stopped. One reason is that the bendiest blocks reach their biggest values near the edges of the chart. A small change in their weights moves the curve a lot there, so the loss reacts more sharply. A step size that is safe at degree 5 then overshoots at degree 11, like turning a more sensitive shower knob just as far. Capacity sweep: with every setting back at its default, drag Epoch and watch the dashed validation line on Capacity sweep change shape as training goes on. At epoch 13 the line is nearly flat from degree 5 up. At epoch 10,000 it rises steeply after degree 8 and peaks at degree 12. Degree 13 lands back near 1.0, because on this draw its swing at the right edge happens to miss the last hollow dot by less. That dip is the luck of the draw, not the strange pattern described at the end of Where it breaks. Noise draw: at degree 11, try each seed. Seed 1 is the most dramatic, ending at 8.63. Seeds 2 and 3 overfit far less, ending near 0.12 and 0.34. With seed 4 the run barely overfits at all. Its best validation comes late, at epoch 909, and it ends at 0.078, only a little above that best of 0.073. How badly a model overfits depends on which dots it happened to get, especially near the edges. In both runs that end in diverged, the badge reads overfitting for a while first, because validation has passed 1.5 times its best. Look at the training line, though. It is climbing, not falling, so this is an unstable run, not a model memorizing its dots.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Training dynamics
documents.body: A common mix-up: Validation loss sitting above training loss does not, by itself, mean that the model is overfitting. The model was adjusted to fit the training dots and has never seen the validation dots, so on only 16 points some gap is expected from the start. What signals overfitting is a gap that keeps growing while training goes on, not a gap that holds steady. With that in mind, here are the signals worth watching as you move the controls: A steady gap is healthy: at degree 5 the gap settles near 0.09 and stays there for thousands of epochs, while at degree 11 it keeps widening. Falling training loss proves nothing by itself: at degree 11 it falls at every one of the 83 recorded moments. That includes the ones where validation is 88 times worse than its best. It is the cheapest number to improve, because memorizing noise lowers it as well as learning the pattern does. Training loss far below the dotted line means noise is being matched: even the true curve scores 0.081 on the training dots. At degree 5 the training loss settles near 0.017, so it has matched a good share of the noise. It cannot bend any further, though, and validation holds steady near 0.111. At degree 11 the training loss ends at 0.007, only a little lower, yet validation ends 88 times worse than its best. How far training sinks below the line tells you noise is being matched, but only the validation line tells you how much that hurts. Being consistently bad is not the same as generalizing: at degree 1 the losses sit close together, 0.322 for training and 0.279 for validation. Validation even lands a little lower here, by the luck of which dots fell into each pile. Yet both are poor at every epoch, so a small gap only counts as good news when both losses are also low. Capacity matters differently at different times: at epoch 13, Capacity sweep shows every degree from 5 upward scoring about the same on validation. Let training run to the last epoch and they spread far apart, with degree 7 holding at 0.100 and degree 12 climbing past 10. Memorizing depends on model size, the amount of data and the length of training, all acting together. A smaller learning rate tells the same story, only slower: cutting the learning rate to a tenth gives about the same best score, reached roughly ten times later. The run still overfits afterwards, so smaller steps buy you time to stop, but they do not prevent the memorizing. Batch size and learning rate work together: picture the loss as a valley, with the best weights at the bottom. With all 16 dots the valley has gentle sides, so a step at learning rate 0.3 moves most of the way down toward the bottom without crossing it. The loss on just 4 dots can make a much narrower, steeper valley. A step at the same learning rate then jumps clean over the bottom and lands higher up the far wall. The next step overshoots even more, like the shower knob, which is how the batch-4 run above diverged. This is a different problem from the wobble in the lunch picture. Weight decay shows up in the weights: the Weight size ‖θ‖ readout on Fitted function gives one number for the size of all the weights together. It squares every weight, adds the squares up and takes the square root, where θ, read as “theta”, stands for the whole list of weights. At degree 11 and the last epoch, it reads 2.48 with no weight decay at all. Raising Weight decay to 0.03 brings it down to 0.74, which makes the weights about three times smaller overall. One noise draw is one roll of the dice: changing Noise draw changes how badly each degree overfits. A single run shows you one roll of the dice, so try a few seeds to see what is typical.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Training dynamics
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Everything is real, but unusually visible: the model, the data, the training and every loss are real, and the same seed gives the same run every time. What is unrealistic is how much you can see: the true curve, the exact noise level, and a simple model. It takes in just one number, how far left or right a dot sits, so it fits on a flat chart. The split is unusually even: half the dots are held out, so that the validation line is not decided by a few unlucky points. Real projects usually hold out far less than half, often somewhere between 10 and 20 percent of their data. The badge uses the lab’s own cut-offs: it reads overfitting once validation is 1.5 times the best it reached earlier in the run. It reads underfitting while the training loss is above 0.125, which is twice the noise variance, and these are sensible choices rather than laws. Overfitting here is slow: it spreads over thousands of epochs because a polynomial picks up fine wiggles very slowly. Other models overfit on their own schedules, and some do it within a few epochs of fine-tuning. Only one fix is built in: weight decay is the only regularizer the lab offers, and early stopping is something you do yourself with the Epoch slider. The lab has no dropout and no extra data, which are other fixes you will meet in the last section. The capacity sweep stops early: the highest degree, 13, has 14 weights, which is fewer than the 16 training dots. In general, a curve needs as many weights as there are dots to pass exactly through every one of them. A straight line, with its two weights, can always pass through two dots but usually not through three. So here the curve can never pass exactly through every training dot, which keeps the lab away from a stranger pattern described at the end of this section. Real models cannot be drawn: a model with one input can be shown as a curve, but a real model takes in thousands of numbers at once. Nobody can look at a curve like that, so in real projects overfitting is spotted from held-out loss and never seen directly. Where the textbook picture stops matching The textbook picture suggests deliberate cheating, but nothing in a model is choosing to memorize anything. Fitting the noise is one more way to lower the training score, and the training process has no way to tell noise from pattern. A student could also look at a misprint and notice that it is wrong, while the model has nothing to compare its dots against except the dots themselves. Where the real thing gets harder Real validation curves are bumpy: in real projects the validation score jumps around from one check to the next, so a single upward point is not a verdict. People smooth the curve, wait for several worse checks in a row before stopping, or average over several runs started from different random seeds. Loss and the score you care about can disagree: picture a model answering multiple-choice questions. Instead of naming one answer, it gives each choice a percentage, such as “95% sure it is B.” The loss for this kind of model punishes being confidently wrong very hard, so being 95% sure of a wrong answer costs far more than being 60% sure of it. A model can get more answers right while growing too sure about the few it gets wrong, which is called overconfidence. Its validation loss then rises even as its share of right answers improves. Overfitting is also not the main worry when a large language model, the kind behind a chatbot, is first trained. Those runs often see most of their text only about once, so there is little chance to memorize by repetition and the two curves stay close. Overfitting comes back later, when a model is fine-tuned on a small set of examples or when the same data is repeated many times. It also returns when a model is trained against an automated judge, itself a model that scores answers, until it exploits a weakness in that judge. The model ends up learning the judge’s quirks instead of the real skill, which is memorizing the judge rather than learning the pattern. There is also a genuinely strange pattern called double descent, which shows up in very large models and runs against the tidy story of this lab. Held-out error can get worse as a model gains enough capacity to pass exactly through every training point. Then, once the model grows far beyond that size, the error can start improving again, and a similar rise and fall can even appear as training runs longer. This lab stops at degree 13, below the 16 training dots, so it never gets there, and its tidy story describes one situation, not a law of nature.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Training dynamics
documents.body: How the weight decay penalty works Weight decay adds a penalty to the loss that training pushes down, equal to λ times the sum of the squared weights. It leaves out the flat block’s weight, which only shifts the whole curve up or down and cannot make it swing. The info panel on Training dynamics controls writes this as λ Σ θₖ², where Σ means “add them all up” and θ stands for the weights. Here is one worked example, using made-up numbers that are small enough to check in your head: Suppose the penalty counts only two weights, 0.5 and −1, and λ is set to 0.1. The squares of the two weights are 0.25 and 1, which add up to 1.25. The penalty is λ times that total, so 0.1 times 1.25 gives 0.125. The training line on the chart leaves this penalty out, so both loss lines still measure plain misses on the dots. Because big weights make a big penalty, training now has two goals at once: fit the dots well, and keep the weights small. A weight that is twice as big adds four times the penalty, so the largest weights get pulled down the hardest. Wild swings in the curve need large weights, so they become expensive, and the curve that wins is a calmer one. Other tools against memorizing Weight decay is one of several real tools for the same problem, and all of them count as regularization: Dropout is used in neural networks, which are built from many small parts that each pass a number along to the next. During training, dropout switches off a random handful of those parts on every step, so no part can count on one particular partner and backup routes have to form. More or more varied data attacks the real cause, because memorizing is hardest when there is too much to memorize. One way is to make extra examples by changing existing ones without changing their answers, such as flipping a photo of a cat. Early stopping is regularization by budget, because fewer steps leave less time to fit noise. Label smoothing stops a model that answers multiple-choice questions from pushing its percentage for one choice all the way to 100%. Two readouts about the steps Training works out each step from a list of slopes, one for each weight, called the gradient, and Training dynamics controls has two readouts about it. Each slope says how fast the loss changes as that weight changes, so together they show which way lowers the loss fastest. Full-batch |∇L| shows how big the whole list of slopes is when all 16 dots are used, and ∇L is shorthand for the gradient of the loss. Minibatch noise shows how far, typically, the slopes from a smaller batch stray from the full-batch ones, and at 16 (full) it reads 0 (full). Once the big, smooth part of the fit is done, after the first dozen or so epochs, the second readout can be several times the first. You can see this at degree 11 with Batch size set to 4. At epoch 100 in that run, Minibatch noise reads 0.199, while Full-batch |∇L| reads only 0.051. By that point, most of each small-batch step is noise rather than real direction, because the full slope has already become small. Problems in the real world Distribution shift: a model can do well on held-out data from the same source as its training data and still fail on real inputs that look different. It is like practising only with one teacher’s quizzes and then sitting an exam written by someone with a very different style. That is why where the validation set came from matters as much as how big it is. Data leakage: sometimes near-copies of one example land on both sides of the split, or the test questions were quietly in the training data all along. The held-out line then stays reassuring while measuring nothing, like a final exam whose questions were printed in the practice book by mistake. Everyone aces that exam, and the score tells you nothing about what anyone learned. For the curious If you have met the sine function in maths class, the true curve in this lab is y = 0.8 sin(4x) + 0.4x. The random nudges are drawn so that their typical size, which statisticians call the standard deviation, is 0.25. Later in the course, Anatomy of a training run returns to batch size on a real model that writes text one character at a time. Hyperparameters & schedules trains four learning-rate schedules side by side, so you can compare ways of changing the learning rate during a run.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Training dynamics
documents.body: This module is about how a training run unfolds over time, and how to tell a model that is learning structure that transfers from one that is memorizing its sample. *Loss & gradient descent* and *Backpropagation* built the machinery that fits parameters to data. Here it runs for thousands of epochs, and the question is when more fitting stops helping on data the model has not seen. The answer takes two measurements. Training loss is scored on the examples the optimizer fits and validation loss on held-out examples it never fits, so only the second shows generalization. Whether the two curves stay together or part depends on model capacity (the flexibility of the model family), on data size and training time, and on regularization. Learning rate and batch size mostly set the pace of the run and whether it stays stable or diverges. Where it shows up Training pipelines. Data is split three ways: one set to fit, one to choose settings and when to stop, and a test set scored once at the end. Large language models. Pretraining often sees most data about once, which keeps the two losses close. Overfitting returns instead in fine-tuning on small datasets, in data repeated many times, and in optimization against a learned reward model. Regularizers. Weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, label smoothing, and early stopping all discourage brittle fitting. Evaluation. Data leakage between training and evaluation data, or distribution shift between held-out data and real inputs, can make a healthy-looking held-out score misleading. Why it matters Training loss is the cheapest number to improve and the least informative on its own. With enough capacity, a model keeps lowering it by fitting noise in its sample, which is overfitting, while held-out loss rises. Plotted alone, that failure looks like progress. Too little capacity underfits, leaving both losses high. Choosing model size, learning rate, and the epoch to keep all depend on the held-out curve. What you will be able to explain What training and validation loss each measure, why the generalization gap between them is the diagnostic, and why a separate test set is still needed. How overfitting shows up as a widening gap, and how early stopping and weight decay respond to it. How capacity, weight decay, learning rate, and batch size change a run, so you can predict whether it will underfit, fit, overfit, or diverge. What the lab shows The model, its training, and every loss are real and computed in the browser. The data is generated from a known curve plus noise rather than collected, so the true curve and the noise variance are known, which no real project offers. Polynomials of degree 1 to 13 are each trained by minibatch gradient descent on 16 of 32 noisy samples and scored on the other 16, with both losses measured at 83 checkpoints over 10,000 epochs. Training curves: both losses by epoch, a ring at the lowest validation loss, and a status badge. Training dynamics controls: Epoch and Stop at lowest validation choose the moment to read, and Polynomial degree picks which of the 13 trained degrees to display. Changing a run setting (Weight decay, Learning rate, Batch size, or Noise draw) retrains all 13. Fitted function: the model's curve over the data and the true curve. Capacity sweep: both losses for every degree at the current epoch. The badge applies thresholds the lab chose, and no test set is drawn. The key experiment: at Polynomial degree 11, drag Epoch to 10,000, then compare raising Weight decay with setting it back to 0 and pressing Stop at lowest validation.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Training dynamics
documents.body: Two losses, measured on different data. Training loss is the error on the examples the optimizer fits. Validation loss is the error on examples held out from that fitting. Their difference, the generalization gap, is the diagnostic. Neither curve alone tells you much. The run in this lab is real The lab draws 32 noisy samples of a known curve, y = 0.8 sin(4x) + 0.4x, with noise of standard deviation 0.25. Alternate samples form a 16-point training set and a 16-point validation set. A polynomial of the chosen degree, ŷ = Σ θₖ φₖ(x), starts at zero and is trained by minibatch gradient descent for 10,000 epochs. Both losses are recorded 83 times. Because the noise is known, the chart can also show what no real project has: the noise variance σ² = 0.0625, the average loss of a perfect model. The three regimes Underfitting. Both losses stay high. A straight line (degree 1) settles at 0.322 on training and 0.279 on validation by about epoch 24 and stays there. It cannot bend to follow a sine. Fitting. Both losses fall together. At degree 5, validation reaches 0.100 by epoch 11 and ends at 0.111. Overfitting. Training loss keeps falling while validation turns up. At degree 11, validation bottoms at 0.098 at epoch 13 and ends at 8.63, while training loss falls to 0.007. The true curve itself only scores 0.081 on those training points. Why the damage arrives late Gradient descent fits the smooth, strongly curved directions of the loss first, and the wiggly, weakly curved directions last. The noise lives mostly in the wiggly directions. So the useful fit happens in the first dozen epochs and the harmful fit creeps in over thousands. That ordering is why early stopping works as a regularizer. Three splits, not two The training set fits parameters. The validation set chooses capacity, learning rate, and when to stop. Because you make decisions with it, its number becomes mildly optimistic. A third test set, touched once at the end, gives the honest estimate. This lab does not draw one.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Training dynamics
documents.body: Held-out measurement is the difference between a training loop and an engineering practice, and it underlies every capability claim. A benchmark score is a held-out measurement, and it means something only if the test data was absent from training. When it was not, the score measures memorization, and the failure looks like the gap in this lab, except nobody plotted the second curve.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Training dynamics
documents.body: Read the split strip on Training dynamics controls: filled dots train the model, hollow dots only score it. Find the same dots on Fitted function. Drag Epoch from 0 to 10,000 at the default degree 5. Both losses fall together, and the green ring marks the lowest validation loss, 0.100 at epoch 11. Set Polynomial degree to 11 and drag Epoch to 10,000. The status reads overfitting from epoch 215. On Fitted function the curve bends toward individual training dots and swings to about 24 near the right edge. Now regularize two ways. Raise Weight decay to 0.03, and validation at epoch 10,000 drops from 8.63 to 0.135. Or set it back to 0 and press Stop at lowest validation. Then try Learning rate and Batch size, and watch Capacity sweep as you move Epoch.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Training dynamics
documents.body: Falling training loss proves nothing by itself. At degree 11 it falls at every checkpoint, including the ones where validation is 88 times worse than its best. A steady gap is normal on 16 points. At degree 5 the gap settles near 0.09 and stays there. A widening gap is the signal. A ten times smaller learning rate gives almost the same run, slower. At degree 11, η 0.01 reaches its best, 0.097, at epoch 147 instead of 13. On the log axis the curves slide one decade to the right. Learning rate and batch size interact. At degree 5, η 0.3 trains normally with batch 16 or 8 but diverges at epoch 22 with batch 4. The loss on 4 points can curve far more sharply than the average over 16, so the same step overshoots. On Capacity sweep, capacity barely matters at epoch 13 and matters enormously at epoch 10,000. Overfitting depends on capacity, data, and training time together.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Training dynamics
documents.body: In this lab. The model, the data, the training, and every loss are real and reproducible from the seed. What is unrealistic is how much you know: the true curve, the noise level, and a one-dimensional input you can plot. Half the data is held out so the validation curve is not decided by a few points; real projects usually hold out 10 to 20 percent. The status label applies fixed thresholds the lab chose: 1.5 times the best validation loss so far, and training loss above 2σ². The overfitting here is also slow, spread over thousands of epochs, because a polynomial's wiggly directions are weakly curved. Networks overfit on their own schedules, sometimes within a few epochs of fine-tuning. In real systems. Validation curves are noisy, so one upward point is not a verdict. Practitioners smooth, average over seeds, or wait several evaluations before stopping. Loss and the metric you care about can disagree: validation loss can rise from overconfidence while accuracy still improves. The classical picture also does not transfer cleanly to large language model pretraining. Those runs often see most data about once, so training and held-out loss stay close for the whole run. Overfitting returns in fine-tuning on small datasets, in data repeated many times, and when a model is optimized against a reward model until it exploits it. Large models can also show double descent: held-out error rises as capacity approaches the point of fitting the training set exactly, then falls again well beyond it. This lab stops at degree 13, below the 16 training points, so it never reaches that regime.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Training dynamics
documents.body: Weight decay is one regularizer among several: Weight decay adds λ times the sum of squared weights to the objective, pulling weights toward zero. At degree 11 and epoch 10,000 it holds the weight size at 0.74 instead of 2.48. AdamW applies it directly to the parameters. Dropout zeroes a random fraction of activations on each step, so no unit can rely on one partner. Data augmentation enlarges the dataset with label-preserving transformations. It attacks the cause: too little data for the capacity. Early stopping is regularization by budget. Label smoothing stops a classifier from pushing its confidence all the way to 1. Two concerns show up in production. Distribution shift means a model that generalizes to held-out data from the same source can still fail on real traffic, so the validation set's provenance matters as much as its size. Data leakage, such as near-duplicates across the split or evaluation text inside pretraining data, makes the validation curve look healthy while measuring nothing. Later in the course, Anatomy of a training run returns to batch size on a real character model, and Hyperparameters & schedules trains four learning-rate schedules side by side.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Training curves · Training dynamics
documents.body: Two losses from one real run A polynomial model trained by gradient descent on 16 noisy points and scored on 16 held-out points after every checkpoint. The two curves, the gap, the lowest-validation marker, and the status are all measured from that run; none is a drawn shape. The horizontal axis is the epoch: 0 at the axis, then 1 to 10,000 on a log scale, so each labelled tick is ten times the last. The vertical axis is mean squared error on a log scale from 0.003 to 30. The solid blue line is training loss and the dashed orange line is validation loss. The shaded band between them is the gap. The dotted line is the noise variance σ² = 0.0625, the expected loss of the true curve itself. A green ring marks the lowest validation loss in the run, and the dotted vertical marker with two dots is the current `Epoch`. A red note appears if the run diverges. Metrics: training loss at the current epoch, `Validation`, `Gap (val − train)`, and `Lowest validation` with its epoch. The badge is the status: fitting, underfitting, overfitting, or diverged. At the defaults (degree 5, η 0.1, full batch, λ 0, seed 1) and epoch 100 the metrics read 0.017, 0.111, 0.093, and 0.100 at epoch 11, and the status is fitting. The model is `ŷ = Σ θₖ φₖ(x)` with φₖ the Legendre polynomial of degree k scaled by √(2k+1), starting from θ = 0. Each epoch shuffles the 16 training points and takes 16 / batch steps of `θ ← θ − η(∇L + 2λθ)`, with the constant term left undecayed. Both curves are plain mean squared error. The training curve leaves out the weight-decay penalty, so the two lines measure the same thing on different points. Losses are recorded at 83 checkpoints: epoch 0 and about 24 per decade up to 10,000. Between checkpoints the chart draws straight segments. Status is a rule on measured values: overfitting once validation is 1.5 times the best it reached earlier in this run; underfitting while training loss is above 2σ² = 0.125; diverged once training loss passes 10⁶; fitting otherwise. The thresholds are the lab's choice. This card has no controls of its own. Everything is on `Training dynamics controls`. Comparison worth running: set `Polynomial degree` to 11 and drag `Epoch` to 10,000. Validation falls to 0.098 at epoch 13, turns up, reads overfitting from epoch 215, and ends at 8.63 while training loss keeps falling to 0.007. Second comparison: at degree 11 move `Learning rate` from 0.1 to 0.01. The lowest validation is almost the same, 0.097, but it arrives at epoch 147 instead of 13. On a log axis the whole run slides one decade to the right. The signal is the gap widening, not the gap existing. With 16 points some gap is normal from the first epochs. Training loss below the dotted noise line means the model is fitting the noise in its 16 points: the true curve itself only scores 0.081 on them. Early stopping is a reading of this chart: the ring marks the epoch you would keep. In this lab: a 1-D polynomial on 32 seeded samples of a known curve, so the noise level and the true curve are known, which real data never offers. Half the samples are held out so the validation curve is not decided by a few points; real projects usually hold out 10 to 20 percent. In this lab: the overfitting here is slow and grows over thousands of epochs because the wiggly directions of a polynomial are weakly curved. Other models overfit on other schedules. In general: validation curves are noisy, so practitioners smooth them, wait several evaluations before stopping, and average over seeds. Loss and accuracy can also disagree: validation loss can rise from overconfidence while accuracy still improves. In general: large-model pretraining often sees most data about once, so training and held-out loss stay close for the whole run. Overfitting returns in fine-tuning, in data repeated many times, and when a model is optimized against a learned reward.
documents.title: Two losses from one real run

documents.subtitle: Training dynamics controls · Training dynamics
documents.body: The knobs that change the run The data split, which moment of training to inspect, and the four settings that change the run itself: model capacity, weight decay, learning rate, and batch size, plus which noise draw to use. Changing any run setting retrains all 13 degrees from scratch in the browser. A split strip: all 32 samples along x, filled dots above the line for training and hollow dots below for validation. `Epoch` (0 to 10,000 in 83 checkpoints) and `Stop at lowest validation`, which jumps to the ring on the curve chart. `Polynomial degree` (1 to 13, printed with its weight count), `Weight decay` (λ 0 to 0.1), `Learning rate` (η 0.003 to 0.6), `Batch size` (4, 8, or 16 = full), and `Noise draw` (seed 1 to 4). Two gradient readouts at the current epoch: `Full-batch |∇L|` and `Minibatch noise`, the root-mean-square distance between each minibatch's gradient and the full one. The generator draws 32 points on a jittered grid over [−1, 1] with y = 0.8 sin(4x) + 0.4x plus Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.25. Alternate points go to training and validation, so both splits cover the whole range. `Epoch` only chooses which checkpoint to read. The four run settings and `Noise draw` retrain every degree; the sweep takes a few tens of milliseconds. Weight decay adds `λ Σ θₖ²` for k ≥ 1 to the training objective, so each step also pulls every weight toward zero by `2ηλθₖ`. A smaller batch means more steps per epoch: 4 steps at batch 4, 1 at the full 16. Each of those steps follows a noisier gradient. Comparison worth running: at degree 11 set `Weight decay` to 0.01, 0.03, and 0.1 and read validation at epoch 10,000: 0.310, 0.135, and 0.102, against 8.63 with no decay. Second comparison: at degree 5 set `Learning rate` to 0.3 and `Batch size` to 4. The run diverges at epoch 22. Batch 8 at the same rate trains normally. Third comparison: at degree 11, η 0.6 diverges at epoch 562 while degree 5 at η 0.6 is stable. A bigger model can need a smaller learning rate. Two different fixes reach almost the same validation loss at degree 11: stopping at epoch 13 gives 0.098, and training to epoch 10,000 with λ 0.1 gives 0.102. `Minibatch noise` is several times `Full-batch |∇L|` once the full gradient is small: at degree 11, batch 4, epoch 100 they read 0.199 and 0.051. Late in training, minibatch steps are mostly noise. Changing `Noise draw` changes how badly each degree overfits. One seed is one sample of a noisy process. In this lab: weight decay is the only explicit regularizer, and early stopping is something you do with `Epoch`. There is no dropout, augmentation, or learning-rate schedule, and no test split is drawn. In general: choosing capacity, learning rate, or stopping point from the validation set spends its independence, so serious pipelines keep a third, test split touched once at the end. Distribution shift and data leakage can make a healthy-looking validation curve meaningless.
documents.title: The knobs that change the run

documents.subtitle: Fitted function · Training dynamics
documents.body: The model the curves are scoring The fitted curve at the current epoch drawn over the data it was trained on and the data it was scored on, with the true curve the data came from. It shows what overfitting looks like in the function itself, not just in the loss. x from −1 to 1 and y from −2 to 2. Filled blue dots are the 16 training points; hollow orange dots are the 16 validation points. The dashed green line is the true curve, 0.8 sin(4x) + 0.4x, which the model never sees. The purple line is the model's ŷ at the current epoch. A red note gives the peak |ŷ| when the curve leaves the plot. Metrics: `Weights`, the degree plus one, and `Weight size ‖θ‖`, the length of the weight vector. The purple line evaluates `Σ θₖ φₖ(x)` at 161 points using the weights stored at the current checkpoint, the same weights that produced the losses on the curve chart. Validation loss is the mean squared vertical distance from the purple line to the hollow dots; training loss uses the filled dots. Driven by `Epoch`, `Polynomial degree`, and the other run settings on `Training dynamics controls`. Comparison worth running: at degree 11 move `Epoch` from 13 to 10,000. The curve stops following the dashed line and bends toward individual blue dots, and near x = 1, where the last validation point sits beyond the last training point, it swings to a peak |ŷ| of about 24. Overfitting shows first at the edges and between training points, where nothing pins the curve down. Weight decay keeps `Weight size ‖θ‖` small: at degree 11 and epoch 10,000 it reads 2.48 with no decay and 0.74 with λ 0.03. In this lab: one input, so the whole function can be drawn. Wild swings between samples are typical of high-degree polynomials in particular. In general: a network's function has thousands of input dimensions and cannot be drawn. Overfitting is inferred from held-out loss, not seen.
documents.title: The model the curves are scoring

documents.subtitle: Capacity sweep · Training dynamics
documents.body: Capacity matters differently at different times Training and validation loss for every degree from 1 to 13 at the current epoch, all trained with the same settings. Moving `Epoch` shows the classic U-shape of validation loss against capacity forming as training goes on. The horizontal axis is polynomial degree 1 to 13; the current degree is shaded and its tick is bold. The vertical axis is mean squared error on the same log scale as the curve chart. Blue dots and line: training loss at the current epoch. Orange dots and dashed line: validation loss. The green ring marks the degree with the lowest validation loss, and a red × at the top marks a degree whose run has diverged. Metrics: `Best degree now` with its validation loss, and `Diverged runs`. Each point reads the checkpoint at the current epoch from a full training run for that degree. There are 13 separate runs; none is interpolated. Each degree's model family contains the one below it, so at convergence training loss cannot rise with degree. Validation loss has no such guarantee, and at an early epoch neither does training loss, because descent has not finished. Driven by `Epoch` and the run settings on `Training dynamics controls`. `Polynomial degree` only moves the shaded band. Comparison worth running: at epoch 13 validation sits between 0.096 and 0.117 for every degree from 5 to 13. At epoch 10,000 it climbs from 0.100 at degree 7 to 0.246 at degree 9, 8.63 at degree 11, and 10.6 at degree 12. Degrees 1 and 2 stay high at every epoch: a line or a parabola cannot follow a sine. That is underfitting. Early in training, extra capacity costs little because the wiggly directions have not been fitted yet. That is why early stopping works as a regularizer. In this lab: degree stops at 13, below the 16 training points, so the model never has enough weights to pass through every training point exactly. In general: very large models can show double descent, where held-out error rises as capacity approaches the point of fitting the training set exactly and falls again well beyond it. This sweep does not reach that regime.
documents.title: Capacity matters differently at different times

documents.subtitle: Dataset, batch, forward, loss, backward, step, checkpoint — running for real on a character model small enough to retrain every time you move a control.
documents.body: Dataset, batch, forward, loss, backward, step, checkpoint — running for real on a character model small enough to retrain every time you move a control. Name each stage of a training loop and what it produces Distinguish an epoch, a step, and a batch Use a checkpoint to inspect a model partway through training Read what one optimizer step changes: which rows move, and how the loss on its own batch differs from the whole-corpus loss Estimate training memory from parameters, precision, and optimizer, and say why large runs split it across devices

documents.subtitle: Step 3 · Anatomy of a training run
