documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: One complete pass over the training data. It is a bookkeeping unit, not a unit of learning: the same epoch count means very different amounts of learning at different batch sizes.
documents.title: Epoch

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: One optimizer update. Steps, not epochs, are what actually change the weights, which is why the step count is the number to compare across runs.
documents.title: Step

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: The group of examples averaged together before one update. Larger batches give a less noisy gradient estimate and fewer updates per epoch.
documents.title: Minibatch

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: The component that shuffles, batches, and feeds examples to the model. Shuffling makes each batch a fair sample of the whole corpus, so consecutive updates do not all pull toward one passage.
documents.title: Dataloader

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: Running inputs through the model to produce logits, then probabilities. No parameter changes during it.
documents.title: Forward pass

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: The negative log-probability the model assigned to the token that actually came next, averaged over the batch. Reported here in nats per token.
documents.title: Cross-entropy

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: The exponential of cross-entropy. Read it as the effective number of options the model is choosing between, so lower is better.
documents.title: Perplexity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: The sweep that computes one gradient per parameter from the loss. For softmax cross-entropy the gradient of a row is the predicted distribution minus one at the true token. The length of the whole batch gradient is its gradient norm.
documents.title: Backward pass

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: Subtracting the scaled gradient from each parameter. Everything else in the loop exists to produce the numbers this step consumes.
documents.title: Optimizer step

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: A saved copy of the weights at a point in the run. Checkpoints make training inspectable and recoverable; a checkpoint meant for resuming also stores optimizer state, the data position, and random state.
documents.title: Checkpoint

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: Cross-entropy measured with natural logarithms. A drop of ln 2, about 0.69 nats, means the probability given to the correct token doubled, as a geometric mean over the tokens scored.
documents.title: Nats per token

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: What the optimizer remembers between steps. Plain SGD keeps nothing; momentum keeps one value per parameter and Adam keeps two, a running mean and a running variance of the gradient, usually in fp32.
documents.title: Optimizer state

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: Running the forward and backward passes in 16-bit numbers while the optimizer keeps an fp32 master copy of the weights. It speeds up the arithmetic but does not shrink the model state, because the master copy and the optimizer state stay at 4 bytes.
documents.title: Mixed precision

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: Splitting weights, gradients, or optimizer state across devices so none holds a full copy. ZeRO partitions all three across data-parallel workers, and PyTorch's FSDP, motivated by ZeRO, shards the parameters. Data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism split the work instead.
documents.title: Sharding

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Anatomy of a training run · question 1
documents.body: You keep the epoch count fixed and raise the batch size from 4 to 64. What happens to the number of optimizer steps? It stays the same, because the epoch count alone decides how many updates the run takes It rises, because a larger batch means more work to be done in every single epoch It falls about sixteen times, because each step consumes sixteen times more pairs Steps per epoch equal the number of pairs divided by the batch size. Epochs count passes over the data; steps count updates. That gap is why two runs with identical epoch counts can end at very different losses.
documents.title: You keep the epoch count fixed and raise the batch size from 4 to 64. What happens to the number of optimizer steps?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Anatomy of a training run · question 2
documents.body: Walking the loop from Dataset to Checkpoint, which stage is the first one to change a weight? Optimizer step, which subtracts the learning-rate-scaled gradient from each weight Backward, which writes a finished gradient into every weight that it reaches in the table Loss, which pulls the predicted probabilities toward the character that really came next Forward, which turns the row for the current character into probabilities Forward turns a row of weights into probabilities, Loss scores them, and Backward computes one gradient per weight; all three only read the weights. The optimizer step is where the gradient, scaled by the learning rate, is subtracted, so every earlier stage exists to produce the numbers this one consumes.
documents.title: Walking the loop from Dataset to Checkpoint, which stage is the first one to change a weight?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Anatomy of a training run · question 3
documents.body: The lab prints sample text from the middle of the run after training has finished. What makes that possible? Training reruns from step 0 up to the chosen stop every time the Checkpoint slider moves A checkpoint is a saved copy of the weights, so that earlier model can be loaded and sampled Only the final weights exist, and the earlier text is blended toward them just for display The sampler stored every string it printed during training and replays the one nearest the stop The run saves nine genuine copies of the weights, including the untrained one. Scrubbing loads one of those copies, so its loss, its sample text and its next-character ranking all come from exactly that model; nothing is replayed, blended or recomputed.
documents.title: The lab prints sample text from the middle of the run after training has finished. What makes that possible?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Anatomy of a training run · question 4
documents.body: At 60 epochs the final loss is lower than at 12 epochs. Which question about that lower number can this lab not answer? Whether the extra epochs really took more optimizer steps, since the lab never counts them Whether the saved checkpoints are real copies of the weights or only a drawing of them Whether it learned the language or memorised the text, since loss is scored on the training text Whether a larger batch would have taken the same number of steps, since batch size has no control Every loss in this lab is cross-entropy on the same text the weights were fitted to, so a lower number can mean better prediction of the language or tighter memorisation of those sentences, and nothing on screen separates the two. A held-out set, as in Building a dataset, is what does.
documents.title: At 60 epochs the final loss is lower than at 12 epochs. Which question about that lower number can this lab not answer?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Anatomy of a training run · question 5
documents.body: From the untrained checkpoint you press Step one batch once. The loss on that batch falls by about 0.04 nats, but the whole-corpus loss falls by about 0.005. Why the gap? The step is fitted to the pairs its batch averaged and moves only their rows, while the corpus loss counts every pair The corpus loss is computed on different text, so a step cannot change it and the small drop is only rounding The step moves all 900 weights by the same amount, and the smaller batch simply makes that shared move look bigger The batch loss was measured after the weights moved and the corpus loss before, so the two are not comparable The batch gradient has entries only in the rows of the characters that began a pair in that batch, so exactly those rows move. The batch is scored on the pairs the step just fitted; the corpus loss spreads the same small improvement across all 498 pairs, most of which sit in rows that did not move. Both losses are computed on the same text with the same weights.
documents.title: From the untrained checkpoint you press Step one batch once. The loss on that batch falls by about 0.04 nats, but the whole-corpus loss falls by about 0.005. Why the gap?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Anatomy of a training run · question 6
documents.body: At Batch size 2 you pick the checkpoint at step 1492 and press Step one batch again and again. What do the two losses do? The batch loss falls on every press, but the whole-corpus loss rises on many of them Both losses fall on every press, since each step follows the gradient downhill The batch loss rises on many presses, because two pairs are too few to give a gradient Both losses wander up and down, since a batch of two has no reliable direction A step is computed from the pairs in its batch, so it lowers the loss on those pairs every time at this learning rate. With two pairs, a step can fit them while nudging shared structure the other pairs relied on, so the whole-corpus loss rises on most presses from that checkpoint. It still falls over the run on average; a larger batch makes each step a fairer sample and removes most of the rises.
documents.title: At Batch size 2 you pick the checkpoint at step 1492 and press Step one batch again and again. What do the two losses do?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Anatomy of a training run · question 7
documents.body: With Adam selected at 7.5 billion parameters you switch Precision from fp32 to Mixed 16-bit. What happens to Total, and why? Total halves, because every number in the model is stored in two bytes where fp32 uses four, whatever the optimizer is Total stays the same, because the fp32 master copy and the optimizer state take back what the 16-bit parts save Total rises, because mixed precision stores every weight twice, once in each format, and the copies add up Total falls by a quarter, because only the gradients switch to the smaller format and everything else stays the same In fp32, Adam costs 4 bytes of weights, 4 of gradients and 8 of momentum and variance. In mixed precision the weights and gradients take 2 bytes each, but the optimizer keeps a 4-byte master copy next to the 8 bytes of state. Both come to 16 bytes per parameter. Mixed precision speeds up the arithmetic and shrinks activations; it does not shrink model state.
documents.title: With Adam selected at 7.5 billion parameters you switch Precision from fp32 to Mixed 16-bit. What happens to Total, and why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Anatomy of a training run · question 8
documents.body: Weights, gradients and Adam's state for a 7.5 billion parameter model need 120 GB. What does sharding such as ZeRO or FSDP do about that? It compresses the optimizer state so that one device can hold all of it It splits the training text across devices, so each one works through its own share of the data It keeps only a slice of the state on each device, so no device has to hold a full copy It skips the gradient for most parameters, so the optimizer has less to store The 16 bytes per parameter are needed somewhere, so the fix is to divide them rather than shrink them. ZeRO partitions optimizer state, gradients and parameters across data-parallel workers, and each worker keeps one slice and fetches the rest when it needs it. Splitting the text is data parallelism, which on its own leaves a full copy of the state on every device.
documents.title: Weights, gradients and Adam's state for a 7.5 billion parameter model need 120 GB. What does sharding such as ZeRO or FSDP do about that?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: The language model behind any chatbot you have used was made by a training run. A program showed the model a huge amount of text, checked its guesses about what comes next, and adjusted its numbers by a tiny amount. That cycle repeated many thousands of times, and this module takes one training run apart so you can watch every piece of it at work. The model in this lab is tiny on purpose. It is a table of 900 numbers that guesses the next character of a text from the one character before it. It learns from a short passage of notes about the weather in a harbor town, which is only 499 characters long. Because the model is so small, the lab retrains it from scratch whenever you change a training setting. Every number on the first four cards therefore comes from a real run, not from a drawing. The fifth card, about memory, is different. It works out its totals by multiplying, because no model with billions of numbers is trained here. A few things also stay fixed. The learning rate, a number that scales how big each adjustment is, is always 0.6. Every score is measured on the same text the model learned from. Where you have met it Every trained model came out of a loop like this one, including the very large models behind chatbots. Their runs are vastly bigger, often use a different adjusting rule called Adam, and save their progress more carefully. Even so, they go through the same seven stages in the same order. One published run, for a family of models called Llama 2, made about 500,000 adjustments, and each one was based on about 4 million pieces of text. Size is where the difference shows most: the largest model on this lab's memory card has 70 billion numbers. Training it with Adam needs room for those numbers plus several extra numbers about each one. That comes to more than a trillion bytes, where one byte is about the space a single letter of text takes. The card counts how many memory chips that would fill if each chip holds 32 billion bytes, and it calls each such chip a "device". The answer is 35 devices. Why it matters Without this loop, a model's numbers would stay where they started, and its guesses would be no better than picking a character at random. The loop is what turns a pile of text into better guesses, one small correction at a time. Knowing how the loop works also protects you from three common mistakes. You might compare two runs by how many times they read the text, when what actually counts is how many times they adjusted their numbers. You might trust a single adjustment because it helped the examples it was built from, even though it can make everything else worse. And you might plan a run around the size of the model alone, when the extra numbers kept for training take several times more memory than the model does. Saved copies of the model, called checkpoints, made along the way, matter too, because they let you look inside a run partway through. They also let a run that crashes start again from the last copy instead of from nothing. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these ideas in your own words: the seven stages of a training loop, in order, and what each stage hands on to the next one; the difference between a batch, a step and an epoch, and why two runs with the same number of epochs can end up far apart; how to load a saved copy of the model from partway through a run and test what it had learned by then; what one single update changes, meaning which rows of the table move, and why it helps its own small group of examples far more than the entire text; how to estimate a run's memory from three things: the model's size, how many bytes it uses for each number, and which adjusting rule it uses. You will also be able to say why big runs spread that memory across many chips. What the lab lets you do The lab has five cards, and each one shows a different side of the same run: One pass through the training loop walks through the seven stages and prints real numbers from the run at each one. Measured training loss draws how the model's error score fell from the first update to the last one. Run controls and checkpoint timeline lets you change how the run is set up, then reload a saved copy of the model and read some text that it writes. Step one batch replays a single real update and shows which rows of the 900 numbers moved. Where the memory goes calculates how much computer memory training needs, for models from this lab's size all the way up to 70 billion numbers.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: The model: a sheet of guesses The model works with 30 symbols: the space, the letters a to z, a full stop, and two angle brackets, < and >, that only a later lab uses. Its job is to guess which of those symbols comes next in a text. It does that with a grid of numbers that has one row for each symbol, so you can think of it as a printed sheet of guesses. Each row answers a single question: if the last character was this one, how likely is each character to come next? A row holds 30 raw scores, one for every possible next character, and these scores are called logits. A higher logit means a likelier guess, and to read a row the model turns its 30 logits into 30 chances, or probabilities, that add up to 100%. The rule that does this conversion is called softmax, and it always gives the highest probability to the highest logit. Thirty rows of 30 numbers makes 900 numbers, and those 900 numbers are the entire model. The numbers a model learns are called its weights, or its parameters, and training a model means changing them until its guesses improve. Here is one row at work: after the text the fo, the model looks only at the last character, o, and reads the o row. At the end of the default run, that row gives r a probability of 23.5%. That is because the training text has words like harbor, morning, storm and before, where r follows o. A model that looks back only one character is called a bigram model, from "bi", meaning two, because it works with pairs of characters. It cannot use the word or the sentence that the character sits in, which is the main reason its guesses stay rough. The training loop as a study session Training is one cycle repeated over and over, and the lab's Training loop stages strip shows the seven stages of one trip around it. Before looking at each stage, it helps to have a picture of the whole cycle. Picture the guess sheet on a desk, next to a big stack of flashcards made from the training text. Each card shows one character on the front and, on the back, the character that came right after it, so making the deck is the job of the Dataset stage. Making the deck happens once, before the first round. At the start of each pass through the deck, you shuffle it once. A single round of study, which is one trip around the loop, then goes like this: Deal yourself the next small handful of cards from the top of the shuffled deck, which is what the Batch stage does. When the deck runs out, that pass is over, and you shuffle again. For each card, find the row for the front character and read off the sheet's guesses, which is the Forward stage. Flip each card over and mark how badly the sheet did on the real answer, which is the Loss stage. Calculate how each number on the sheet should change so that it would do better next time, which is the Backward stage. Rub out the old numbers on the sheet and pencil in the new ones, which is the Optimizer step stage. Every so often, photocopy the whole sheet and file the copy away somewhere safe, which is the Checkpoint stage. The picture stops matching in two places. A person studying these cards would use the whole word and its topic, but the guess sheet only ever looks at the single character on the front. You would also use judgement to fix the sheet, whereas the training program calculates every correction by exact arithmetic, the same way every time. The seven stages, one at a time Dataset turns the text into flashcards, which the lab calls training pairs, where each pair is one character plus the character that followed it. The lab draws a space as ␣, so the words "the fog", which have seven characters counting the space, give six pairs: t→h, h→e, e→␣, ␣→f, f→o and o→g. Every character except the very last one starts a pair, so there is always one pair fewer than there are characters. That is why the stage displays Characters 499 and Training pairs 498, while Vocabulary counts the 30 symbols. Batch shuffles the pairs once at the start of every pass, then deals them out in handfuls in order. A handful is called a minibatch, or a batch for short. The Batch size slider sets how many pairs each handful holds, starting at 16, and the part of the training program that shuffles and deals is called the dataloader. The shuffle matters because the text runs in order, so without it a string of updates could all come from the sentence about winter. Those updates would drag the model toward that one passage, while a shuffled handful is a fair mix of the entire text. The stage's readouts are Batch size, Batches / epoch and Total steps, and the counting part below explains how they fit together. Forward takes each pair in the handful, reads the row for its first character, and turns that row's 30 logits into 30 probabilities. Nothing in the model changes here, because this stage only reads, and it is called the forward pass. Its readouts show the Top prediction and Runner-up after the fo, plus Row width, which is 30 logits. Loss checks each guess against the back of the card by looking at the probability the model gave to the character that actually came next. It turns that probability into a penalty and averages the penalties over the handful, and that average is called the cross-entropy. The next part explains how the penalty is scored, and the stage's readouts are Loss at this checkpoint, Its perplexity and the Uniform baseline. Backward calculates, for every one of the 900 weights, how the penalty would change if that weight went up a little. A positive number means raising the weight would make the penalty worse, while a negative number means raising it would make the penalty smaller. That list of 900 numbers is called the gradient, and the stage that works it out is called the backward pass. Like the forward pass, the backward pass only reads the weights and does not change anything yet. Optimizer step is the stage that finally changes the model, by multiplying each weight's gradient by the Learning rate and subtracting the result from that weight. Subtracting moves every weight the opposite way to its gradient, which is the direction that lowers the penalty, and the learning rate is fixed at 0.6 in this lab. The learning rate sets how big each change is: a larger one makes bigger jumps, and a smaller one makes more careful ones. For example, picture a weight of 0.50 with a gradient of +0.10. The step takes away 0.6 × 0.10 = 0.06, so the weight becomes 0.44. If the gradient were −0.10 instead, taking away −0.06 would raise the weight to 0.56. The rule that applies these changes is called the optimizer, and one use of it is one optimizer step, or one step for short. This lab uses the plainest optimizer there is, called SGD, which is short for stochastic gradient descent, where "stochastic" means working from randomly chosen handfuls. The word "descent" fits if you picture the penalty as your height on a hill. Each step moves the weights a little way downhill for the handful it was calculated from. As you will see later, that is not always downhill for the whole text. Checkpoint saves a copy of all 900 weights so that you can come back to them later. At the default settings the run saves nine copies (some settings save ten), including the untrained model at step 0, and the stage displays Checkpoints, Selected step and Its loss. Scoring a guess: cross-entropy and nats The penalty follows one rule: the smaller the probability the model gave to the right answer, the bigger the penalty. Every time that probability is cut in half, the penalty grows by the same amount, about 0.69. Here is the ladder that rule builds, from a perfect guess down to a blind one: Giving the right character 100% costs nothing, since the model could not have done any better. Giving it 50% costs about 0.69, which is one halving away from being certain. Giving it 25% costs about 1.39, which is two halvings away from being certain. Keep halving: 12.5%, then 6.25%, then about 3.1% after five halvings, which costs about 5 × 0.693, or 3.47. (The 0.69 above is 0.693 rounded off.) Giving it 1 in 30, about 3.3%, sits just above that 3.1%, so it costs a little less: 3.401, which is what blind guessing scores. The unit of this penalty is called the nat, so the lab reports the loss in nats per token. A token is one piece of text the model reads, and in this lab every token is a single character. Nats per token therefore means the average penalty for each character the lab scores. The Loss stage's title calls the penalty the "negative log-probability", which is a name from a part of maths you may meet later. The halving ladder above is all you need to read the numbers this lab displays. Lower is better, as in golf, and a model that has learned nothing spreads its guesses evenly across the symbols, so it scores 3.401 on every character. That score is the Uniform baseline, and the loss chart draws it as a dotted line labelled "knows nothing, ln 30". The ln there is a button on a scientific calculator, and ln 30 works out to 3.401. Read the ladder backwards and you get a handy rule that the Loss stage mentions. Whenever the loss falls by about 0.69 nats, the probability given to the right character has doubled, on average across the characters scored. The loss has a friendlier twin called perplexity, which turns the penalty back into a number of options. It asks this question: if the model were choosing evenly among some number of characters, how many would give this same score? Blind guessing among 30 symbols has a perplexity of 30, since that is exactly the situation the question describes. The default run ends at a loss of 2.277, which matches choosing evenly among 9.75 characters, so Perplexity reads 9.75. You can check that with the ladder. Three halvings, or 1 in 8, cost about 2.08, and four halvings, or 1 in 16, cost about 2.77. A score of 2.277 sits between them, so it matches choosing among a number of options between 8 and 16, which works out to 9.75. In everyday terms, the trained model's guesses are about as spread out as a multiple-choice question with ten options instead of thirty. Better than chance by says the same thing a third way, by measuring how far the loss has come down from blind guessing toward a perfect zero. The default run brought the loss from 3.401 down to 2.277, a drop of 1.124. That drop is 33% of the full 3.401, so the readout displays 33%. It is not the share of guesses the model gets right, which is a different measurement that this lab does not show. One more detail matters when you read these numbers, because the lab scores the loss in two different ways. During training, each handful's loss is averaged over its own pairs, and each point on the chart's thin, jagged line is the average of a few handfuls' losses. The Loss stage instead scores the checkpoint you picked on all 498 pairs. The whole body of training text is called the corpus, so the lab calls that score the whole-corpus loss. Calculating the gradient: the backward pass For this kind of model and this kind of penalty, the backward pass follows a rule short enough to do by hand. For each of the 30 logits in a row, take the probability the model gave that character, written as a decimal. Then subtract 1 from the probability of the character that actually came next, and the 30 results are that row's part of the gradient. The Backward stage draws this for one real pair from the text, o followed by g, from the words "the fog". At step 0, before any training, the model gives every character the same probability of 1 in 30, which is about 0.033. So every other bar stands the same small height, +0.033, above the line, while the bar for g drops below it. Only the g bar carries a printed number, which is 0.033 minus 1, or −0.967. The strip has its own key: a bar above the line means that logit will be pushed down, while a bar below it means the logit will be pushed up. That is because the optimizer step subtracts the gradient, so taking away −0.967 raises the score for g. Taking away each small +0.033 lowers every other score a little, and raising the right answer while lowering the others is the whole of what learning means for this row. On the Run controls and checkpoint timeline card, move Checkpoint to the end of the run, step 384, and the g bar still reads −0.957. That is 0.043 minus 1, because the trained model gives g only 4.3% after o. In this text, r follows o much more often than g does. The strip shows one pair, but a real step uses a whole handful. Each pair's gradient is added into the row for its first character, and then the total is divided by the number of pairs in the handful. For a full handful that number is 16. A shorter handful, like the one you will meet at the end of each pass, is divided by its own smaller count, so each of its pairs counts for more. A row that starts three of the pairs can therefore get up to three times the push of a row that starts one. A row gets nothing at all unless at least one pair in the handful starts with its character. The stage also measures how big a gradient is overall, as one number called the gradient norm. To calculate it, square every number in the gradient, add up the squares, and take the square root. For the o→g strip at step 0, each of the 29 small bars of 0.033 squares to about 0.001, and together they add up to about 0.03. The g bar of −0.967 squares to about 0.94. The total is about 0.97, and its square root is about 0.98. A bigger norm means the step built from that gradient changes the weights more. This pair's gradient norm measures the strip, and Last batch gradient norm measures the run's final handful. Peak batch norm in the run displays the largest gradient norm that any handful in the run produced. Three ways to count: batch, step and epoch A training run has three counts that sound alike but measure different things: A batch is one handful of pairs dealt out together, and the Batch size slider sets how many pairs each handful holds. A step is one update to the weights, calculated from one batch, and steps are the only thing that actually changes the model. An epoch is one complete pass through all 498 pairs, and the Epochs slider sets how many complete passes the run makes. Plain division ties the three counts together, as you can see with the default setting of 16 pairs per handful. One pass through 498 pairs needs 498 ÷ 16 = 31.125 handfuls, and since you cannot deal part of a handful, that rounds up to 32. Thirty-one full handfuls use 496 pairs, which leaves 2 for a small last handful. That is why Batches / epoch reads 32, and why the last handful of each pass holds only those 2 pairs. The default run makes 12 passes, and 12 × 32 = 384 steps, which is what Total steps displays. Two cards that zoom in Below the loop, two more cards show what the stages hide, and Step one batch is the first. It replays one real optimizer step from the checkpoint you pick. It shows how many weights moved and lists the rows that moved most. The second, Where the memory goes, calculates how much memory a training run needs for a model of any size, and the next part explains what it adds up. What training has to hold in memory Computers store every number as a pattern of 0s and 1s, where each 0 or 1 is called a bit. Eight bits make a byte, which is about the space one letter of plain text takes up. A KB is a thousand bytes, a GB is a billion bytes, and a TB is a trillion bytes, which is the same as 1,000 GB. To take a step, training has to keep three things in memory for every weight: the weight itself, which the forward pass reads every time it makes a guess; its gradient, which is the number that the backward pass calculated for it; its optimizer state, meaning any extra numbers the optimizer remembers about that weight from one step to the next. How much each of these costs depends on two choices, and the first is Precision, which means how many bytes each number gets. The full-size choice, fp32, gives every number 4 bytes, which is 32 bits. The letters "fp" stand for floating point, the normal way computers store numbers with decimals. The other choice on the card, Mixed 16-bit, stores the weights and gradients in 2 bytes each, which speeds up the arithmetic. More bytes let a number keep more digits, which is why this choice is called precision. A 2-byte number keeps only about three digits or fewer, so a tiny update, like adding 0.0001 to 1.5, gets rounded away and lost. So the optimizer also keeps a full 4-byte copy of every weight, called the master copy, where those tiny updates can build up. Doing the arithmetic in 16-bit numbers while keeping that 4-byte master copy is called mixed precision. The second choice is the Optimizer, and SGD, the kind this lab trains with, remembers nothing at all between steps. The Momentum optimizer keeps one extra 4-byte number for each weight. That number is an average of the weight's recent gradients, updated after every step, and it helps the weight keep moving in a steady direction. Adam keeps that same number, which the card's table also calls momentum. It adds a second number, called variance, which tracks how big the recent gradients have been. Add up the bytes that one weight needs, multiply by the number of weights, and you have the memory training needs before anything else is counted. That multiplication is all that the Where the memory goes card does.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: Each stage feeds the next The seven stages come in this order for a reason: each one uses exactly what the stage before it produced. The dataset makes pairs, the batch picks a few of them, the forward pass turns them into guesses, and the loss scores those guesses. The backward pass turns the score into a gradient, and the optimizer step uses it to change the weights. Every stage before the optimizer step only reads the weights, so that one stage is the only place where the model changes. Bigger runs change the scale, the optimizer and the plumbing around saving, but they do not change this order. Why handfuls, and not the entire text Why not update the weights from all 498 pairs at once, or from one pair at a time? Using the entire text for every update would give the steadiest direction, but the model would change only once per pass. Using a single pair would change the model often, but every update would chase whatever that one pair happened to contain. A handful sits between these two extremes, and the Batch size slider lets you move along that trade-off and measure what happens. Counting passes is not counting learning The loop is also where two counts get mixed up. Picture two friends studying the same deck of 498 flashcards, and both of them go through the whole deck 12 times. One friend stops to fix their notes after every 2 cards, which adds up to 2,988 rounds of fixes. The other fixes their notes only after every 64 cards, which adds up to 96. Both can honestly say they went through the deck 12 times, yet one of them corrected their notes about 30 times as often as the other. The lab works the same way, since twelve epochs at a Batch size of 2 make 2,988 steps, while the same twelve epochs at 64 make only 96. The two runs end at very different losses, which is why Total steps is the honest number to compare between runs, and Epochs is not. One step is only a rough guess A step is built from one handful, not from the entire text, so it is only a rough estimate of what would help everywhere. The lab measured this in its 12-epoch runs at batch sizes 2, 16 and 64. Every step lowered the loss on its own handful, but some steps made the model worse on the rest of the text. Picture a teacher who rewrites the class study guide after marking only two quizzes. The changes lean the guide toward the mistakes those two students made, but they might confuse everyone else in the class, who never had those problems. Marking sixteen quizzes first would give a fairer picture of what the whole class needs. Training has the same problem, but its steps point the right way on average, so the run still improves over many steps even when single steps misfire. The picture stops matching in one way: a teacher can rewrite anything, while a step only nudges the numbers a small, calculated amount toward the pairs in its handful. Checkpoints let you look back Picture a long video game that only lets you save at the very end. If the power cuts out halfway, you lose everything, and you can never go back to see how you played on an earlier level. A training run without checkpoints is like that, because it reports one number at the end and nothing else. Saved copies fix both of those problems, because you can load the model from partway through and test it, which shows you when and how it improved. In a large run, a crash far into the run would otherwise throw away all of that work. With a recent saved copy, the run loses only the steps taken since that copy was made. Memory is more than the model The last problem is space, because to take a step, training must hold the weights, the gradient and everything the optimizer remembers, all at the same time. Under Adam, the weights themselves take up only a small fraction of that total memory. For a large model the total is far more than one of the card's 32 GB devices can hold, so large runs have to plan carefully where every byte goes.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: Walk the loop Start with the Training loop stages strip and click all seven stages in order, reading the title, the explanation and the three readouts that each one prints. At Backward, look at the strip of 30 bars for the pair o→g and find the one long bar, which belongs to g. The default run makes 12 passes at Batch size 16, which gives 32 Batches / epoch and 384 Total steps. Over on the Measured training loss card, Final loss reads 2.277 nats per token, while Perplexity reads 9.75. On that same card, compare the three lines that the chart draws, and notice how differently they behave. The thin line is the loss on handfuls, the thick line is the whole-corpus loss at each checkpoint, and the dotted line is the "knows nothing" baseline at 3.401. Resize the batch Try this: leave Epochs at 12 and drag Batch size from one end to the other, watching Total steps and Final loss as you go. Before you drag, predict which end of the slider will finish with the lower loss, and decide why you expect it. At a batch size of 2, the run takes 2988 steps and lands at a final loss of 1.877 nats. At a batch size of 16, the run takes 384 steps and lands at a final loss of 2.277 nats. At a batch size of 64, the run takes only 96 steps and lands at a final loss of 2.808 nats. The text and the learning rate never changed between these runs, so the difference in final loss comes mainly from the number of updates each run was allowed to make. Each small-batch update is also noisier, as the backfire experiment below shows. Then set Batch size back to 16 and drag Epochs on its own to watch the same effect from the other side. One epoch ends at 3.166 nats, while sixty epochs reach 1.921. Reload a checkpoint Set the run back to 12 epochs at Batch size 16, then scrub Checkpoint from step 0 to step 384. Four separate readouts move together as you scrub, because all of them come from the same saved copy. They are Its loss on the Checkpoint stage, the big dot on the loss chart, the sample text, and the Next character after "the fo" at this checkpoint list. At step 0 every option in that list reads 3.3%, and by step 384 r leads with 23.5%. The stages card shows one stage at a time, so scrub once with the Checkpoint stage open. Then scrub again with the Backward stage open, and watch the g bar move from −0.967 at step 0 to −0.957 at step 384. It barely changes, because g is not what usually follows o in this text. The sample is 96 characters that the lab writes by picking each next character at random, weighted by the model's probabilities. A setting called temperature, fixed at 0.8 here, tilts each pick a little toward the likelier characters. The picks also use a fixed seed, which is a starting number that makes the computer's random choices come out the same every time. That means any change between checkpoints comes from the weights and not from luck. Step one batch Now set Checkpoint on the Run controls card to step 0, scroll to Step one batch, and press the Step one batch button once. This applies the run's very first handful of 16 pairs to the untrained model. The pairs appear as small labels, such as o→r and e→a, drawn from all over the text. Then read the four readouts on the card, which report what that single update did: Batch loss, before → after goes from 3.401 to 3.362, measured only on the 16 pairs in that handful. Batch gradient norm reads 0.2567, which measures how big that handful's whole gradient is. Whole-corpus loss, before → after moves only from 3.401 to 3.396, because it is measured across all 498 pairs in the text. Weights changed reads 270 of 900 in 9 rows, one row for each character that started a pair in the handful. The count of 270 comes from whole rows, because every weight in a touched row moves. Softmax gives every character some probability, so all 30 logits in that row get part of the gradient. Nine rows of 30 weights is 270, and the other 630 weights stay exactly as they were. Now look at the gap between the two losses. The step was calculated to fit those 16 pairs, so it helps them a lot. But 16 pairs are only about 3% of the 498, so their gain shrinks a lot once it is averaged over the whole text. The nine rows that moved also hold 308 of the 498 pairs, and inside them the effect is mixed. About 78 pairs, including the handful's own, get a little better, because they ask for the same next character as the handful. About 230 that needed a different next character get slightly worse. The other 190 pairs sit in rows that did not move, so they do not change at all, and the whole-corpus average barely moves. The table below the readouts lists up to eight rows with the biggest gradients, and its top row is s. It started 3 of the 16 pairs, and two of them asked for a space, so their pushes add up. The space row also started 3 pairs, but they asked for f, m and r, so their pushes partly cancel and its gradient is smaller. The Target column displays the next character a row was asked for most often, which for s is a space. Target probability shows the space's probability in the s row rising from 3.3% to 3.6%. On this first press nine rows moved, so the caption mentions one more row that changed less. Press twice more, and a different set of rows moves each time, because each press applies the next handful the run actually used. Back to the checkpoint returns you to the saved copy whenever you want to start over. Watch a step backfire Now set Batch size to 2, put Checkpoint at step 1492, and press Step one batch again and again, up to its limit of 24 presses. Batch loss still falls on every press, but Whole-corpus loss rises on 17 of the first 24. For comparison, at Batch size 16, 24 presses from the checkpoint at step 192 never raise it. Here is how a tiny handful can backfire, using a made-up example. Picture a handful of two that holds the pair e→a, from a word like "sea". The step raises a in the e row, and because the probabilities in a row always add up to 100%, every other choice in that row loses some probability. That includes the space after e, which the text needs after every "the". The two pairs in the handful improve, while the many other pairs that need that space get a little worse. (Your 24 presses hold other e pairs, such as e→v and e→r, and they make the same kind of trade.) Every step makes this kind of trade, so why does it backfire so often here? By step 1492, the e row already gives a about 7%, which is close to its share of the text: 4 of the 55 pairs that start with e. A full push for one e→a pair overshoots that share. In a handful of two, that one pair also drives half the step, eight times the share it would get in a handful of 16. Count the memory Last, scroll to Where the memory goes, which starts at Model size 7.5 billion, with Precision set to Mixed 16-bit and Optimizer set to Adam. Here is what a single weight costs at those settings: The weight itself takes 2 bytes, because Mixed 16-bit stores it in 16 bits. Its gradient also takes 2 bytes, because the backward pass stores it in the same 16-bit format. The optimizer state takes 12 bytes: the 4-byte master copy, plus 4 for momentum and 4 for variance. That adds up to 16 bytes, which is what Bytes per parameter displays. Multiply 16 bytes by 7.5 billion weights and you get 120 billion bytes, or 120 GB. Weights and gradients take 15 GB each, and the optimizer state takes the other 90 GB. That is six times as much as the weights, which is what Optimizer state ÷ weights reports. A device here means one chip with its own memory, like the graphics chips, called GPUs, that big runs train on. Here the card uses the word "state" for everything training holds for each weight: the weight, its gradient and its optimizer state together. The card assumes each device holds 32 GB, and 120 GB ÷ 32 GB is 3.75, which rounds up to 4 whole devices. So 32 GB devices for state alone reads 4 for this model. Now switch Precision to fp32 and predict the new total before you look. It stays at 120 GB. The weight and its gradient each grow from 2 bytes to 4, which adds 4 bytes, but fp32 needs no separate master copy, which takes 4 away. Each weight now costs 4 + 4 + 8 bytes, where the 8 is Adam's two 4-byte numbers, so the total is still 16. Only the split between the parts changes. A common mix-up: "16-bit" sounds as if it should halve the memory, but it does not shrink what Adam needs at all. In both precisions each weight costs 16 bytes. Mixed precision only moves bytes. The weight and the gradient each shrink from 4 bytes to 2, and the 4 bytes saved go into the master copy in the optimizer state. Its gain is faster arithmetic, not a smaller total on this card. Then switch Optimizer to SGD, and momentum and variance disappear, so the total falls to 8 bytes per weight, or 60 GB. With fp32 still selected, the optimizer-state segment vanishes from the bar completely. Switch back to Mixed 16-bit and that segment returns at 30 GB, half the bar, because SGD in mixed precision still needs the 4-byte master copy. That copy is twice the size of the 2-byte weight, so each weight costs 2 + 2 + 4 = 8 bytes. Finally, switch Optimizer back to Adam and set Model size to 70 billion, then watch the total climb to 1.12 TB while the device readout jumps to 35.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: The thin batch-loss line on the chart stays jagged while the thick whole-corpus line drops smoothly. Each point on the thin line averages only a few handfuls of 16 pairs, so it wobbles with whichever pairs those handfuls happened to hold. The last handful of each pass holds only 2 pairs, so it is the noisiest of all. The small ticks under the chart mark where each pass ends, which is every 32 steps at the default setting. Scrub through the nine checkpoints and the loss reads 3.401, 3.068, 2.816, 2.641, 2.530, 2.438, 2.374, 2.320 and then 2.277. The first 48 steps cut it by about 0.33, while the last 48 cut it by only about 0.04. Each stretch of steps buys less than the one before, right from the start. Rows updated on the Optimizer step stage reads 26 / 30, because four symbols never start a pair in this text. Those four are j, x and the two angle brackets, so their rows are never changed at all. Peak batch norm in the run reads 0.749 at Batch size 16, but that peak comes from one of the 2-pair handfuls left over at the end of a pass. No full handful of 16 reaches even half of that. At a batch size of 2 every handful has 2 pairs, and the peak reaches about 1.09. Averaging over more pairs makes each gradient shorter and steadier. Each pair supplies only one sixteenth of a 16-pair gradient, and because the pairs push on different rows and characters, their pushes add up only partly. Pairs in the same row that ask for different next characters also partly cancel. Better than chance by reads 33%, which is the same fact as Perplexity falling from 30 options to 9.75. The Forward stage prints "the fo" but uses only the final o, because a bigram throws the rest away. Top prediction is r at 23.5%, from words like harbor, morning, storm and before, while at step 0 every option reads 3.3%. The sample uses the same seed at every checkpoint, so early checkpoints print almost the same string, and later ones still share their opening letters. Any change comes from the weights, not from luck. Even at step 384, most of it is gibberish with real fragments inside, such as the, and and thin. One sample is not a measurement, so a 96-character sample can look worse at a later checkpoint even while the loss fell. Trust Its loss over your eyes when the two seem to disagree. One step helps its own handful far more than it helps the entire text: 0.039 against 0.005 nats at step 0. Only rows that started a pair in the handful move, so 630 of the 900 weights are not touched. The nine rows that did move still cover most of the text. A step can make the entire text worse, and the smaller the batch, the more often it happens. At Batch size 2, the whole-corpus loss rose on 1,174 of the 2,988 steps in the 12-epoch run. At 16 it rose on 5 of 384 steps, and at 64 it rose on none of the 96. The loss on each step's own handful fell every single time, so the run improves on average, not at every step. Mixed 16-bit does not shrink what Adam needs, which is 16 bytes per weight in both precisions. In mixed precision the optimizer state is six times the weights, and in fp32 it is twice the weights. At 70 billion weights, the weights, gradients and optimizer state together come to 1.12 TB, which fills 35 devices of 32 GB before a single activation is stored. The optimizer state on its own is 840 GB of that. An activation is an in-between result that a large model calculates during the forward pass and keeps for the backward pass.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Everything on screen is computed for real: the pairs, the shuffle, the probabilities, the loss, every gradient, every update and every saved copy of the weights. The run saves nine copies at the default settings and ten at some others. What is missing is structure, because the model sees one character of context and has only 900 numbers. It has no hidden layers, which are the extra stages of number-crunching that real models run between reading and guessing. It also has no tokenizer to split text into word pieces, and its training text is only 499 characters long. The Learning rate is stuck at 0.6, and there is no control to change it. Keep in mind that the stages do not all describe the same moment in the run. The Forward and Loss stages, and the Backward strip, describe the Checkpoint you picked. The counts, the batch gradient norms and the step totals describe the whole finished run. The loss is also measured on the training text itself, and there is no held-out text, meaning text the model never trained on. Nothing in this lab can therefore tell real learning apart from memorising these exact sentences, and the next lab, Building a dataset, adds that check. Step one batch is a replay, not a second run, because it rebuilds the handful that the run's seeded shuffle dealt at that step. It applies the trainer's own arithmetic, so pressing it again always gives the same numbers. Like the run itself, its update leaves out three extras that big runs use: momentum, gradient clipping and weight decay. The "Toy versus real" list at the end of the lesson explains the last two. A press past the final checkpoint deals the next pass's handful, which is a step the saved run never took, and the card says so. The Backward strip shows one pair's gradient at a saved checkpoint, which is not the same as the full handful's gradient that the optimizer applied at that step. Where the memory goes is multiplication, since nothing is set aside or measured. Activations are left out on purpose, so each total is the least a run could need rather than a forecast. The only real memory in this lab belongs to its own trainer: 3,600 bytes of weights and 3,600 bytes of gradient, with no optimizer state under plain SGD. Splitting a run across devices is described here but not simulated, so the card never shows how the bytes would be divided between chips. More epochs is not the same as more learning. Epochs count passes through the text, and only steps change the weights. Twelve epochs at Batch size 64 make 96 updates, while twelve at 2 make 2988 and end nearly a whole nat lower. Small batches win here by updating more often per pass, but the cost is that each update comes from fewer pairs. That is why, at Batch size 2, the whole-corpus loss rose on 1,174 of the 2,988 steps. Where real training runs break Real runs differ in ways this one cannot show, starting with how they count. They count tokens seen rather than epochs, and the biggest make only one pass through their text, so the epoch stops meaning much. The dataloader also becomes a real bottleneck, meaning it can turn into the slow part that holds the whole run back. A run that restarts must carry on exactly as before, and Adam's remembered numbers shape every step it takes. So a checkpoint that can restart a run must save the optimizer state as well as the weights. That optimizer state can be twice the size of the weights, or six times in mixed precision. The checkpoint also needs the dataloader's place in the text and the state of the random shuffles. Memory is also more than the three parts of the card's bar, as a research paper called ZeRO points out, and the card's numbers follow that paper. It looks at a 1.5 billion weight model reading 32 examples at a time, each 1,000 tokens long. In that case the activations take about 60 GB, which is more than twice the 24 GB of weights, gradients and optimizer state. Working the activations out again during the backward pass, instead of storing them, cuts them to about 8 GB. The paper also names short-term scratch space and wasted gaps in memory as costs that appear at large scale. Real loss curves also throw sudden spikes that a small, smooth toy run like this one never produces. The usual fix is to roll back to the last checkpoint and skip the handfuls that caused the spike, which only works if someone saved one.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: Adam and the optimizer step Adam divides each weight's gradient by a running estimate of how large that weight's gradients usually are. That lets one learning rate work for weights whose gradients differ enormously in size, at the cost of two extra numbers to remember for every weight. Building big batches Big batches are usually built by adding up: the run does several forward and backward passes, adds their gradients together, and then takes one optimizer step. This is called gradient accumulation, and the loss curve responds to the number of steps, not to how many smaller handfuls were added together for each one. Saving checkpoints at scale At large scale, saving happens in the background and is split across many machines. Stopping everything to write out a huge optimizer state would leave every machine in the run sitting idle. Deciding how many checkpoints to keep becomes a policy: a few for restarting, a thin history for study, and a record of which one a released model came from. Memory and parallelism The 16 bytes per weight have to live somewhere, so big runs divide them up rather than shrink them. Real models are built from many layers stacked one after another, each with its own grids of numbers, and there are three main ways to split the work across chips: Data parallelism gives each chip a different handful of examples to work through. Tensor parallelism splits each layer's grids of numbers into pieces held by different chips. Pipeline parallelism gives each chip a different slice of the stack of layers, like stations on an assembly line. A paper by Narayanan and colleagues shows how the three combine to train on thousands of GPUs. Data parallelism on its own still leaves every chip holding a full copy of the 16 bytes per weight. Sharding Sharding is the fix for that wasted space, because it stops every chip from storing the same full copy. Picture a group project where, instead of everyone printing the whole binder of notes, each member keeps one chapter and borrows the others when needed. Sharding works the same way, because each chip keeps only a slice of the weights, gradients and optimizer state, and fetches the rest when it needs them. A method called ZeRO splits all three across the chips, and FSDP, a feature of the PyTorch training toolkit inspired by ZeRO, does the same kind of splitting. The card's 120 GB for 7.5 billion weights is the ZeRO paper's own example. Why this matters for LoRA Fine-tuning means training an already trained model further on new examples, and only the weights that are being trained need a gradient and optimizer state. Training a small add-on, called an adapter, beside weights that stay frozen, meaning unchanged, therefore removes most of those two costs. The LoRA paper compares this with fine-tuning all of GPT-3, a 175 billion weight model, with Adam. It reports 10,000 times fewer trained numbers and 3 times less GPU memory. A related method, QLoRA, also stores the frozen weights in 4 bits each. Its paper reports fine-tuning a 65 billion weight model on a single 48 GB GPU, and the LoRA & adapters lab trains one of these adapters. Toy versus real Updates: this lab's default run takes 384 steps of 16 pairs each, which is tiny next to a published run. Llama 2 reports 2.0 trillion training tokens at 4 million tokens per batch, which works out to about 500,000 updates. Step size: this lab uses plain SGD at a learning rate of 0.6, while runs that use Adam pick far smaller rates. An Adam rate and an SGD rate work differently, though, so the two cannot be compared directly. GPT-3's published rates run from 0.0006 for its smallest model down to 0.00006 for its largest. Llama 2 used 0.0003 for its two smaller models, and half that for its two largest. Memory: the lab's whole model is 3.6 KB, which is 900 weights at 4 bytes each. At 16 bytes per weight, 7.5 billion weights take the card's 120 GB, before any activations are counted. What the loop adds: the GPT-3 and Llama 2 papers both wrap these seven stages in three extras that this lab leaves out. A warmup-and-decay schedule starts the learning rate small, raises it, and then lowers it again over the run. Gradient clipping shrinks any gradient whose norm is over 1.0 back down to a length of 1.0. Weight decay, set to 0.1, pulls every weight a little toward zero at each step.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: A training run cuts text into training pairs, then turns untrained weights into a model by repeating one cycle over them: draw a batch, predict, score the prediction, compute a gradient, update the weights, and now and then save them. This module names those seven stages and asks what each hands to the next, how many updates a run really makes, and what it costs in memory. It builds on Next-token prediction, which showed what a trained character model outputs, and Training dynamics, which showed how loss curves respond to settings. Here the loop underneath both is taken apart one stage at a time. Where it shows up A frontier run keeps the same stage order as the lab's toy run, plain SGD on a 900-weight character model, and differs from it in scale, in the optimizer, and in the machinery around checkpointing. Pretraining. Llama 2 reports 2.0 trillion tokens at a global batch of 4 million tokens, which works out to about 500,000 updates. Runs that large are counted in tokens seen, not epochs (passes over the data). Memory. Under Adam, weights, gradients and optimizer state (what the optimizer keeps between steps) cost 16 bytes per parameter: 120 GB at 7.5 billion parameters in the ZeRO paper. ZeRO shards all three across devices so each holds a slice, and PyTorch's FSDP, motivated by ZeRO, shards the parameters. Recovery. When a production loss curve spikes, the standard response is to roll back to the last checkpoint and skip the offending batches. Fine-tuning. LoRA and QLoRA, which train a small adapter beside frozen weights, follow from the same accounting: only parameters that are trained need a gradient and optimizer state. Why it matters The optimizer step, which uses the gradient to update each weight (in this lab, by subtracting the gradient times the learning rate), is the only stage that changes the weights. A final loss does not say how many updates produced it; that takes the step count, not the epoch count. Without checkpoints, a run that fails has nothing to roll back to. Without a memory estimate, you cannot tell in advance whether a run fits: at 70 billion parameters under Adam, model state alone is 1.12 TB. What you will be able to explain The seven stages of a training loop, from Dataset to Checkpoint, and what each produces. How an epoch, a step and a batch differ, and how Batch size links epochs to steps. How a checkpoint lets you inspect a model partway through training. What one optimizer step changes: which rows move, and how the loss on its own batch differs from the whole-corpus loss. How training memory follows from parameters, precision and optimizer, and why large runs split it across devices. What the lab shows The lab trains a real character bigram, which predicts each character from the one before it: a 30 by 30 table of next-character scores, 900 weights, fitted by minibatch SGD to the 499-character Harbor weather notes corpus at a fixed Learning rate of 0.6. Changing Batch size or Epochs retrains it. Every loss is scored on the training text; there is no held-out set. One pass through the training loop walks the Training loop stages; click each stage to read what it reports for this run. Measured training loss plots the batch loss, the whole-corpus loss, and the dotted "knows nothing" line at ln 30. Run controls and checkpoint timeline holds those two sliders and Checkpoint, which reloads a saved copy of the weights and samples text from it. Step one batch applies one real optimizer step to that checkpoint's weights, using the batch the run drew next. From the final checkpoint, the default, it draws the next epoch's batch, a step the saved run never took. Where the memory goes is closed-form arithmetic over Model size, Precision and Optimizer: nothing is allocated or measured, activations are left out, and sharding is described, not simulated. The first four cards are computed from the run, not illustrated. The key experiment holds Epochs at 12 and moves Batch size: across its range, a larger batch generally means fewer Total steps and a higher Final loss, though neighbouring sizes can tie on steps.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: A training run is one cycle repeated until you stop it. The Training loop stages flow walks that cycle once: Dataset, Batch, Forward, Loss, Backward, Optimizer step, Checkpoint. Each stage consumes exactly what the stage before it produced. The model is a character bigram — a 30 by 30 table of logits, where the row for the current character holds the scores for the character that comes next. Weights reads 900, and that is the entire model. Dataset cuts text into pairs: one context character, and the character after it. Characters and Training pairs differ by exactly one, because every character except the last begins a pair. Batch shuffles the pairs with a seeded generator and slices them. That is the dataloader's work. The shuffle makes each batch a fair sample of the whole text, so consecutive updates do not all pull toward one passage. Forward reads one row and softmaxes it into 30 probabilities. A forward pass changes nothing. Loss averages the negative log-probability of the character that actually followed over the minibatch. That is cross-entropy, reported in nats per token. Backward produces one number per weight. For softmax cross-entropy a row's gradient is the predicted distribution minus a one at the correct character. The Backward stage draws it for one real pair, o followed by g in "the fog". Optimizer step subtracts that gradient scaled by the Learning rate, held at 0.6. Checkpoint copies the weights so you can return to them. Vocabulary is 30 symbols: space, a to z, a full stop, and two reserved angle brackets that only a later lab uses. Spread probability evenly across 30 and you score ln 30 = 3.401 nats per token — the Uniform baseline and the dotted "knows nothing" line. Two cards below the loop zoom in on what the stages hide. Step one batch replays a single real optimizer step from the checkpoint you select and shows the rows it moved. Where the memory goes counts the bytes a training run needs per parameter, for a model of any size.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: Every claim about a trained model rests on this loop having run. The loop is also where two units get conflated. An epoch is one pass over the data; a step is one weight update. Steps per epoch are the pair count divided by Batch size, so the same Epochs setting buys very different amounts of learning at different batch sizes. Total steps is the number worth comparing across runs. Checkpoints matter for a separate reason: without them a run reports one number at the end and nothing else. Two more facts about the loop get lost at scale. A step is a noisy estimate built from one batch, so it can help the batch and hurt everything else. And the bytes a run needs are set by the optimizer as much as by the model: the weights are the smallest part of what training holds.

documents.subtitle: Standard · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: In this lab. Everything on screen is computed: the pairs, the shuffle, the softmax, the cross-entropy, every gradient, every update, and nine genuine copies of the weights. What is missing is structure — one character of context, 900 parameters, no hidden layers, no tokenizer, a 499-character corpus. The Learning rate is fixed at 0.6 and has no control. Read the stage panel with the timeline in mind: the Forward and Loss stages both describe the Checkpoint you selected, while the counts, gradient norms and step totals describe the whole run. And the loss is measured on the training text: there is no held-out set here, so nothing in this lab separates learning from memorizing. Step one batch is a replay, not a second run. It rebuilds the batch the seeded shuffle gave the run at that step and applies the trainer's own arithmetic, so pressing it again gives the same numbers. The update has no momentum, no clipping, and no weight decay. Where the memory goes is multiplication. Nothing is allocated or measured, and it leaves out activations on purpose, so its totals are a floor. The only real buffers here are the trainer's own: 3,600 bytes of fp32 weights and 3,600 bytes of gradient, with no optimizer state under plain SGD. Data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism and ZeRO sharding are described, not simulated. In real systems. Large runs are counted in tokens seen rather than epochs, and the largest make a single pass, so the epoch stops being a useful unit. The dataloader becomes a real bottleneck. Memory is more than the three bars. The ZeRO paper counts the activations of a 1.5 billion parameter model at sequence length 1,000 and batch size 32 at about 60 GB, more than twice its 24 GB of model state, and about 8 GB with activation recomputation. It also names temporary buffers and memory fragmentation as costs that appear at scale. Optimizer state can be twice the size of the weights, or six times in mixed precision, so a checkpoint that can restart a run must save the optimizer, the dataloader position, and the random state, not just the parameters. Production loss curves also throw spikes no smooth toy run reproduces; the standard response is to roll back to the last checkpoint and skip the offending batches, which is only possible because checkpoints exist.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: Optimizer step. Adam divides each coordinate by a running estimate of its own gradient magnitude, which makes a single learning rate workable across parameters whose gradients differ by orders of magnitude, at a cost of two extra numbers per weight. Batch. A large effective batch is usually assembled by gradient accumulation: several forward and backward passes, gradients summed, then one optimizer step. The loss curve responds to the step count, not to how many passes fed it. Checkpoint. At scale, saving is asynchronous and sharded across ranks, because a synchronous write of a large optimizer state would stall every accelerator in the job. Retention becomes policy: a few for restart, a sparse history for analysis, and a record of which one a released model came from. Memory and parallelism. The 16 bytes per parameter are needed somewhere, so large runs divide them rather than shrink them. Data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism split the work: the batch, each layer's matrices, or the stack of layers. Narayanan and colleagues show how the three compose to reach thousands of GPUs (arXiv 2104.04473). Data parallelism on its own leaves each worker with a full copy of the state. Sharding. ZeRO partitions the optimizer state, gradients, and parameters across the workers (arXiv 1910.02054), and PyTorch's FSDP, motivated by ZeRO, shards model parameters (arXiv 2304.11277). The per-parameter figures above follow the ZeRO paper, which gives 120 GB for 7.5 billion parameters, the number the card reproduces. Why this justifies LoRA. Only parameters that are trained need a gradient and optimizer state. Training a small adapter beside frozen weights removes most of those two rows. The LoRA paper reports 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters and 3 times less GPU memory than fine-tuning GPT-3 175B with Adam (arXiv 2106.09685). QLoRA also stores the frozen weights in 4 bits, and its paper reports fine-tuning a 65 billion parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU (arXiv 2305.14314). The LoRA & adapters lab trains one. Toy versus real Updates. This run takes 384 steps of 16 pairs. Llama 2 reports 2.0 trillion pretraining tokens at a global batch of 4 million tokens (Touvron et al., arXiv 2307.09288, Table 1), which is 2.0 trillion ÷ 4 million, about 500,000 updates of that size. Step size. The toy uses plain SGD at 0.6. Adam-style runs use far smaller rates, and they are not comparable with SGD's. GPT-3 lists learning rates from 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ at 125 million parameters to 0.6 × 10⁻⁴ at 175 billion, with batches of 0.5 to 3.2 million tokens (Brown et al., arXiv 2005.14165, Table 2.1). Llama 2 lists 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ for its 7B and 13B models and 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ for its 34B and 70B models. Memory. The lab's whole model is 3.6 KB. At 16 bytes per parameter, 7.5 billion parameters is the card's 120 GB, before activations. What the loop adds. Both papers wrap these seven stages in a warmup-and-decay learning-rate schedule, gradient clipping at a norm of 1.0, and weight decay of 0.1.

documents.subtitle: One pass through the training loop · Anatomy of a training run
documents.body: The same loop, named one stage at a time A walkthrough of one training iteration on the bundled Harbor weather notes character bigram: dataset, batch, forward, loss, backward, optimizer step, checkpoint. Every metric on this card is measured from the run the sliders on the right just defined. A kicker `Stage N of 7` and a badge naming the corpus `Harbor weather notes`. A looping stage strip: Dataset, Batch, Forward, Loss, Backward, Optimizer step, Checkpoint. The current stage is marked; earlier ones are marked done. A title and a paragraph that change with the stage, plus three metrics that belong to that stage only. Dataset reports Characters, Training pairs, and Vocabulary 30. Batch reports batch size, batches per epoch, and total steps. Forward reports the top two next-character predictions after `the fo` and the row width. Loss reports this checkpoint's loss, its perplexity, and the uniform baseline 3.401. Backward reports the gradient norm of one real pair, the last logged batch norm, and the peak batch norm, and draws that pair's gradient as a strip of 30 bars. Optimizer step reports the fixed learning rate 0.6, how many of the 30 rows actually moved, and steps taken. Checkpoint reports how many snapshots were saved, the selected step, and its loss. The model is a 30 × 30 logit table: the row for the previous character is softmaxed to get the next-character distribution. Training is minibatch SGD on cross-entropy at learning rate 0.6, seed 1. Text is encoded into ` abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz.<>`. Adjacent encoded characters become (context, next) pairs. The pair count is one less than the encoded length. A model that has learned nothing scores `ln 30 ≈ 3.401` nats per token, because that is the cross-entropy of the uniform distribution over 30 symbols. The forward, loss, and checkpoint stages, and the Backward strip, read the checkpoint selected on the right, not the end of the run. The batch norms and the optimizer stage quote the last recorded history point of the finished run. The Backward strip is the exact gradient of −log p(g | o) with respect to the 30 logits in row `o`: each character's predicted probability, minus 1 at `g`, because the corpus continues `the fo` as `the fog`. The strip is an indicator. Clicking a stage changes which explanation you see and nothing about the weights. Click a stage on the strip to change which part of the loop is described. The lesson stepper does not move this strip. `Batch size`, `Epochs`, and `Checkpoint` on `Run controls and checkpoint timeline` retrain the run or reload a snapshot, and every metric here follows. Comparison worth running: open Dataset and read Training pairs, then open Batch and raise `Batch size` from 16 to 64. Batches per epoch falls; total steps falls; the pair count does not. Forward's top prediction is the row for `o` — the last character of the probe `the fo` — taken from the selected checkpoint. It will not match a sample drawn from a different snapshot. A fall of `ln 2 ≈ 0.693` nats means the probability given to the correct next character doubled, as a geometric mean over the pairs. That conversion is why the Loss stage mentions 0.69. In the Backward strip the one large bar points down at `g`; every other bar is small and points up, the largest on the model's current favourite. The update raises `g` and lowers everything else, which is all learning means for this row. Only rows that appeared in some batch receive gradient. The optimizer stage's `Rows updated` reads 26 / 30 on this corpus: `j`, `x`, and the two reserved angle brackets never appear as a context character, so their rows stay at zero. In this lab: every count, loss, and gradient norm is measured from a real training run in the browser. The model is still a character bigram — one previous character of context, 900 weights, no layers. In this lab: the stage walkthrough is a labelling of one already-finished run. It does not pause mid-batch or show a live tape; the Backward strip is one pair's gradient at a saved checkpoint, not the batch gradient the optimizer actually applied at that step. The `Step one batch` card is where a single real update is replayed. In general: a production step also does mixed precision, gradient accumulation, data-parallel all-reduce, and an optimizer with per-parameter state. The seven names stay the same; the engineering around each one does not.
