documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: The shared vector channel running the full depth of the model, one per position. In a pre-norm block every sublayer reads it and adds an increment; nothing overwrites, so contributions accumulate.
documents.title: Residual stream

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: The position-wise network that transforms each token's features independently: widen, apply a nonlinearity, project back. It holds about two-thirds of a block's parameters.
documents.title: MLP

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: Rescaling a vector by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation across features, then applying a learned scale and shift.
documents.title: Layer normalization

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: A cheaper normalization that divides by the root-mean-square without subtracting the mean, with a learned scale but no shift. It performs comparably and is standard in recent models such as Llama.
documents.title: RMSNorm

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: Normalizing a copy of each sublayer's input rather than the stream after the addition, leaving the residual path unnormalized. It is the standard placement because deep stacks train stably with it.
documents.title: Pre-norm

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: One component inside a block, either attention or the MLP. Each is wrapped in a normalization and a residual addition.
documents.title: Sublayer

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: The addition that carries the input around a sublayer. It preserves information and gives gradients a direct path to earlier layers.
documents.title: Skip connection

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: The ratio by which the MLP widens the representation before projecting back: four times the model width in a classic MLP, about 8/3 in SwiGLU.
documents.title: Feed-forward expansion

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: A gated MLP that multiplies one up-projection by the Swish of another, then projects down. Its hidden width near 8/3 of the model width keeps three matrices at the cost of a classic MLP's two.
documents.title: SwiGLU

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: Applied to each position independently with shared weights. The MLP is position-wise, which is why attention is the block's only cross-position step.
documents.title: Position-wise

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: Removing or zeroing a component to observe the effect. In a trained model it produces a distribution-shifted state, so damage overstates the component's isolated role.
documents.title: Ablation

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: Replacing one MLP with many and routing each token to a few of them, decoupling total parameter count from the compute spent per token.
documents.title: Mixture of experts

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: Information about each token's slot, added to its input vector or applied inside attention, because attention alone cannot tell order. Learned, sinusoidal, relative and rotary schemes exist; this lab adds a sinusoidal vector of amplitude 0.5.
documents.title: Positional encoding

documents.subtitle: Glossary · The transformer block
documents.body: The property that reordering the input words only reorders the outputs the same way. Attention without position information has it: a word's output depends on which words are present, not where they sit. The causal mask breaks it slightly, because a word can still count how many came before.
documents.title: Permutation equivariance

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The transformer block · question 1
documents.body: In a pre-norm block you switch Self-attention off. What happens to one token's output when the other words in the sentence change? It still changes, because the MLP mixes information across positions It still changes, because Layer norm averages over all the words in the sentence Nothing, because the norms and the MLP each work on a single position at a time Attention is the block's only cross-position step. Layer norm normalizes across one token's features, and the MLP applies the same weights to each position separately, so with attention off the lab's output shift is exactly 0.000 while the residual stream still carries the token's own vector through.
documents.title: In a pre-norm block you switch Self-attention off. What happens to one token's output when the other words in the sentence change?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The transformer block · question 2
documents.body: In a pre-norm block you switch the MLP off. What does the block output for that token equal in the Residual stream card? Only the attention write, because each sublayer replaces the stream with its own result The input plus the attention write, because the MLP now adds zeros to the stream Zeros, because the MLP is the last stage and the output is its write alone The stream is a running sum: output = input + attention write + MLP write. A sublayer adds its increment and never overwrites, so switching one off removes only its own lane and the diamond lands at the end of the remaining ones. That additive path is also why gradients reach early layers.
documents.title: In a pre-norm block you switch the MLP off. What does the block output for that token equal in the Residual stream card?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The transformer block · question 3
documents.body: In the Position card you swap cat and mat and set Position information to Off. What do the block's six output vectors do? They are the same six vectors, just sitting in the other words' slots, so the block cannot tell the sentences apart They change, because each word's attention weights depend on which of the other words came before and after it Only cat and mat change, because the other four words kept their slots and so have the same inputs as before Attention scores depend only on the vectors being compared, and without a position vector a word's vector is the same wherever it sits. Each word therefore gets the same output in both orders. Position information makes the input depend on the slot, which is what lets later layers use order.
documents.title: In the Position card you swap cat and mat and set Position information to Off. What do the block's six output vectors do?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · The transformer block · question 4
documents.body: Ablating a sublayer in this untrained block is exact. What goes wrong when you ablate one in a trained model and read the drop in quality as that sublayer's own effect? The skip connection replaces the removed write, so the measured drop is exactly its own contribution Later layers expected its writes, so removing it also hands them inputs they never saw in training The other layers retrain their weights around the gap, so the measured drop is too small In this untrained block nothing downstream expected the sublayer, so ablation is exact. In a trained model every later layer learned to read the sublayer's contribution. Removing it hands them an input they never saw, so the damage mixes the sublayer's role with that distribution shift, and no weights change.
documents.title: Ablating a sublayer in this untrained block is exact. What goes wrong when you ablate one in a trained model and read the drop in quality as that sublayer's own effect?

documents.subtitle: Plain · The transformer block
documents.body: When you send a message to a chatbot, the program behind it, called a language model, first turns each word into a list of numbers. Those numbers then climb through a tall stack of steps, and at the top the model scores every piece of text that could come next. The surprising part is that almost the whole stack is one design, copied over and over again. That repeated design is called the transformer block, and in this module you take one apart and watch every piece of it work. Where you have met it The language models behind today’s chatbots are built from this block, stacked dozens of times, with a word lookup at the bottom and a next-word scorer at the top. The lab names two real models whose sizes you can check for yourself: GPT-2 small stacks 12 blocks, while Llama 2 7B stacks 32 of them. The 7B in that name means the model holds about 7 billion adjustable numbers, which you will meet in a moment. Bigger models stack even more, since Llama 2 70B uses 80 blocks and Llama 3.1 405B uses Inside every one of those blocks, the same few steps run in the same order. That is why understanding one block, even the tiny one in this lab, takes you a long way toward understanding the whole model. Why it matters A block has several jobs to do at once, and each job would fail in a clear way without its part: First, words have to share information. In “the animal did not cross the street because it was tired”, the word it stands for the animal, so that word needs information from several words back. Without a sharing step, called attention, every word would be processed on its own and could never pick anything up from its neighbours. Second, each word’s information has to be reworked, because whatever a word has gathered still has to be combined and turned into something more useful for the next block. Third, the stack has to survive being repeated dozens of times. In this design, each step adds a correction to a word’s numbers instead of replacing them. Without that rule, information from the bottom of a deep stack would get scrambled on the way up. Training would stall too. That is the long practice stage where a model guesses next words over and over. After each guess, its adjustable numbers are nudged a little so that the next guesses improve. Fourth, word order has to count. Picture a block in which every word may read every other word. Without extra position information, it cannot tell “the cat sat on the mat” from “the mat sat on the cat”, even though they mean very different things. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these three ideas in your own words: how information travels through one block, step by step, from the moment a word’s numbers enter to the moment they leave; what the residual stream is, a running list of numbers that every step adds to and no step erases, and why that one rule lets models stack so many blocks; why attention, the only step where words share information, cannot tell word order by itself, and what adding position information changes. What the lab lets you do The lab runs a real transformer block right in the page, and it lets you switch its parts on and off while you watch the numbers change. It is organised into four cards, and each one shows a different side of the block: Transformer block shows one word’s numbers at every stage of the block, with an on and off switch for each working part. Residual stream shows how each part’s changes pile up for that word, and its Input scale slider makes the incoming numbers bigger or smaller. Parameter count counts the adjustable numbers inside a block, the settings that training tunes, and adds them up for two real models to match their published totals exactly. Position reorders the words of a sentence and checks whether the block’s outputs change. Nothing in the lab has been trained, so its adjustable numbers are still random rather than tuned by practice. It shows you the plumbing of a block rather than anything a block has learned. That turns out to be enough to see why each pipe is there.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · The transformer block
documents.body: Words as lists of numbers A computer cannot do arithmetic on the letters c, a and t, so a language model starts by swapping each word for numbers. It uses a list of numbers that describes the word, and a list like this is called a vector. The swap uses a word lookup table, which stores one starting list of numbers for every word the model knows. Each piece of text the model handles is called a token, and in this lab every token is a whole word. Real models use hundreds or thousands of numbers for each token: 768 in GPT-2 small and 4,096 in Llama 2 7B. The lab uses just 8, so that you can see every one of them. The lab labels those eight places d0 to d7, and the number of places is the model’s width, written d, so in this lab d is 8. The lab’s sentence is “the cat sat on the mat”, six tokens sitting in slots numbered 0 to 5. The Token buttons at the top of the Transformer block card choose which word that card and the Residual stream card describe. The lab starts on mat in slot 5. The card draws each vector as eight small bars, with positive numbers rising above a middle line and negative numbers dropping below it. For mat, the first bar dips a little below the line and the second rises well above it. The bars carry no number labels, but the lab computes them as −0.45 and 1.70. Beside each row, the card also prints a single number called the norm, which measures the overall size of the whole list. You find it the way you find the long side of a right-angled triangle: square each number, add up the squares, then take the square root. For a short list such as 3 and 4, that gives 9 plus 16, which is 25, so the norm is 5. Doing the same with mat’s eight starting numbers gives a norm of 2.93, which the top row of the card prints as norm 2.93. If you picture a list as an arrow, its norm is the arrow’s length. Keep the two meanings of “norm” apart as you read on, because this norm measures size, while the Layer norm step you are about to meet changes the numbers. A conveyor belt that only adds Picture a factory conveyor belt that carries one tray for each word, with all six trays riding side by side. In each tray sits a card with that word’s 8 numbers, and specialists stand at stations along the belt. A specialist never takes a card away and never rubs out a number. Instead, it photocopies the card, works on the copy, and writes down a change for each of the 8 numbers. A change might say “add 0.58” or “take away 0.66”, and since a change can be negative, adding it can lower a number as well as raise it. The changes are added onto the card, and the tray rolls on to the next station carrying everything it already had plus the new changes. The belt is the model’s residual stream: one running list of numbers for each word, travelling the full height of the model. Each block is one stretch of the belt with two specialists along it, and each specialist is called a sublayer: Self-attention is the specialist that can look into other trays, copying information from the cards of other words. It is the only step in the block where one word’s numbers can affect another word’s. The MLP, short for multilayer perceptron, an old name for a small network built in layers, works on one tray at a time. It has no way of seeing that other words exist, and it reworks the numbers already on that card. The path that carries a card around a specialist, straight to the point where the change is added, is called a skip connection. It is the reason the belt never breaks, even when a specialist is switched off. Each specialist also has its own set of numbers, like the dials on a machine, which decide exactly how it turns a copy into a change. These are not the word’s numbers. They belong to the specialist, and it uses the same ones for every word. Training tunes them, so they are called adjustable numbers, or parameters. One trip through the block The Transformer block card lists the stages from top to bottom in the order the numbers meet them, and the six stages below follow mat along that path. Rows on the left rail are the belt itself, while indented rows work on a copy. A Layer norm row tidies the copy, and the specialist row below it writes its change back at the next plus sign. Stage 1: tidy a copy (Layer norm) Numbers on a card can drift very large or very small on their way up a model, but a specialist works best on input of a steady size. So, before each specialist reads its copy, a tidying step resizes the copy in two moves. First, it subtracts the average of the eight numbers from each of them, so that the new numbers average zero. Second, it divides each number by how far the numbers typically sit from their average, a kind of spread called the standard deviation. That leaves eight numbers whose typical size is 1, and this two-move step is called layer normalization, which the lab’s button shortens to Layer norm. Here is a small example you can check by hand, using the list 2, 2, 6 and 6, whose average is 4. Subtracting 4 gives −2, −2, 2 and 2, and since every number now sits exactly 2 away from the average, the spread is 2. Dividing by 2 then gives −1, −1, 1 and 1. Now make the list 8 times bigger, so that it reads 16, 16, 48 and 48. The average is now 32 and the spread is 16, so the tidied copy comes out as −1, −1, 1 and 1 once again. That is the key property: however big or small the numbers on the card are, the tidied copy comes out at the same size. In the conveyor-belt picture, the tidying step is a photocopier with an automatic zoom that always prints the copy at one standard size. For mat, the Layer norm row reads (x − 0.05) ÷ 1.03, which means subtract an average of 0.05 and then divide by a spread of 1.03. The tidied copy’s norm is 2.83, the square root of 8, because eight numbers with a typical size of 1 have squares that add up to about 8. Only the copy is tidied, so the card on the belt keeps its own size. Tidying a copy before each specialist reads it is called pre-norm, and it is the placement that GPT-2 and Llama use. Stage 2: share between words (Self-attention) This is the step you met in the Attention lab, and here each word again makes three lists of numbers from its tidied copy. A query describes what the word is looking for, a key advertises what it can offer, and a value holds the information it hands over. The word compares its query with the key of every word it may read, and it turns those match scores into shares that add up to 100 percent. It then takes a blend of their values, where each word’s value counts as much as its share. In this block, a word may read itself and the words before it but never the words after it, a one-way rule called the causal mask. The rule is there because the model’s job is to guess the next word, and reading later words would be peeking at the answer. The block runs two of these searches side by side, and each search is called a head and has its own adjustable numbers. In a trained model, that lets each head learn to look for a different kind of match, such as one finding the action and another the thing being acted on. The Self-attention row shows both heads’ shares for the chosen word, and for mat, head 1 gives 29 percent to sat and only 3 percent to cat. Head 2 also leans toward sat, giving it 31 percent. The two blends are then combined into one list of 8 numbers, which is the change this specialist writes back, called the attention write. For mat, its size measured as a norm is 1.57, which the Residual stream card shows as Attention write. Stage 3: add (the first Residual add) The skip connection carries the original card around the specialist, and at the plus sign the attention write is added to it. For mat, d1 starts at 1.70 and the attention write for d1 is −0.66, so after the addition d1 reads 1.04. The Residual add rows have no switch, because removing the addition would remove the belt itself. Stage 4: tidy again (the second Layer norm) The updated card is copied and tidied in exactly the same way as in stage 1, so that the next specialist also reads numbers of a standard size. Stage 5: rework each word alone (MLP) The MLP is a small network built from the kind of artificial neurons you met in earlier labs. It first widens the 8 numbers into 32, then passes each of the 32 through a bending rule called GELU, and finally squeezes the result back down to 8 numbers. Each of the 32 new numbers is a mix of the 8 old ones. To make one, multiply each old number by its own adjustable number, then add up the eight results. Squeezing back down to 8 works the same way, with each final number a mix of the 32. GELU passes large positive numbers through almost unchanged and squashes negative numbers to nearly zero, with a smooth bend in between. That bend matters, because two multiply steps in a row can always be replaced by one. Multiplying by 3 and then by 2 is the same as multiplying by 6. Without the bend in between, the widening and the squeezing would do no more than one plain mixing step, and the extra room would be wasted. For mat, the row reads 8 → 32 (GELU, 16 positive) → 8, meaning 16 of the 32 in-between numbers came out positive. How much the MLP widens the list, 4 times here, is called the feed-forward expansion. The MLP uses the same adjustable numbers for every word, handling one word at a time, and it never looks at another slot. A step that works like this, separately on each slot with shared adjustable numbers, is called position-wise. Layer norm is position-wise too, because it averages across one word’s 8 numbers and never across different words. That leaves attention as the only step in the whole block that crosses between slots. Stage 6: add again (the second Residual add) The MLP’s change, called the MLP write, is added to the belt, and the result is the block’s output for this word. For mat’s d1, the MLP write is 0.57. The lab does not print values for a single place like d1, but here is the arithmetic it does for the whole trip: In a pre-norm block, every one of the 8 numbers follows the same pattern: the output equals the input plus the attention write plus the MLP write. Nothing was replaced along the way, and the Residual stream card draws exactly this sum for all eight places. Pre-norm and post-norm The order above, which tidies a copy before each specialist, is pre-norm, but the original Transformer from 2017 used a different placement, called post-norm. Post-norm tidies the belt itself right after each addition, so in the photocopier picture it resizes the card on the belt instead of the copy. The specialists then read the belt directly, with no tidied copy in between. In this one-block lab, that means attention reads the raw input card, because nothing has tidied it yet. The Placement control switches between Pre-norm and Post-norm, and in post-norm the Layer norm rows move onto the rail. Post-norm also puts a tidying step across the belt itself, so the route from the top of a stack back to the bottom is no longer only plus signs. That is part of why deep post-norm stacks are harder to train, as the next section explains. Where order comes from Look again at how attention works, and you will find a gap. Its match scores depend only on the numbers being compared, and nothing on a card says which slot its tray rides in. So, when every word may read every other word, swapping two trays changes nothing about the work. Each card receives exactly the same changes as before, and the outputs come out the same, only in the swapped slots. Walk one word through both sentences to see why, with every word allowed to read every other word and no position information yet. Take sat. In “the cat sat on the mat”, it compares its query with all six cards, including cat in slot 1 and mat in slot 5. In “the mat sat on the cat”, sat meets the very same six cards, only cat and mat have swapped trays. The match scores are the same, so the shares and the blend are the same, and sat gets exactly the same change. Attention cannot tell a word next door from a word five trays away, because distance is written on no card. The same goes for cat itself. Its card gets the same change in slot 5 as it did in slot 1, so the six outputs are identical to before, and only their slots have swapped. This property has a long name, permutation equivariance, which makes sense once you split it in two. A permutation is a reordering, and equivariance means the outputs change in the same way as the inputs, so reordering the words going in reorders the outputs coming out. Layer norm and the MLP never look at slots either, so the whole block shares this property. The fix is a positional encoding: information about each word’s slot. The simplest kind, used in this lab, is a list of numbers that depends only on the slot, added to each word’s vector before the first block. Other kinds work inside attention instead, as Going deeper describes. In the conveyor-belt picture, it is like stamping each card with its seat number, where the stamp is a set of small numbers added onto the card’s own 8 numbers. This lab uses a wave pattern, called sinusoidal, whose numbers swing between −0.5 and 0.5. Slot 0’s pattern is 0, 0.5, 0, 0.5 and so on, while slot 1’s pattern begins 0.42 and then 0.27. The first numbers of the pattern change quickly from slot to slot while the later ones change slowly, so every slot gets its own mix. It works like the hands of a clock. The second hand moves fast and the hour hand moves slowly, so together they give every moment of the day its own reading. In the same way, the fast-changing first numbers and the slow-changing later ones give every slot its own pattern. The label on the Input x row says the same thing, describing the input as the word’s embedding, meaning its starting numbers, plus the position. So the in slot 0 and the in slot 4 enter the block as two different vectors, with first numbers of −1.48 and −1.86. They are the same word, but the block no longer receives them as the same input. The one-way rule gives away a little order on its own, because the first word sees only itself and the last word sees all six. To keep its test about order alone, the Position card switches that rule off, so that every word reads all six words. What is actually running The lab computes a real transformer block in your browser, only a very small one. Each word is a list of 8 numbers, attention has two heads that each work with 4 numbers, and the MLP widens to 32 numbers and back. Altogether, the block has 840 adjustable numbers, which the Parameter count card lists as This lab’s toy block. Those adjustable numbers are random rather than trained, because they come from a random number generator that always starts from the same value, called a seed. That is why you see the same numbers every time you open the lab. The arithmetic is honest, but the numbers carry no meaning, so the lab shows how information flows through a block, not what a trained block does with it.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · The transformer block
documents.body: Earlier labs gave you separate pieces: attention showed how words share information, and the neuron labs showed how a small network reworks numbers. A useful model needs both jobs done many times over, one layer after another. The transformer block wires the two together into a single unit that you can repeat, and the hard part is making that repetition work. Deep stacks lose their signal Picture a game of telephone with 32 players, where each player whispers the message to the next one. Every whisper loses a little, so by the last player the message has turned into nonsense. Now change one rule: the original note travels down the line too, and each player may only stick a short correction onto it. The last player still holds the original note, plus every correction made along the way. A deep stack built without the belt would be like the first game, because every layer would have to pass on a whole new version of every word. With the belt, each specialist only adds a correction, so the original information survives all the way to the top. It also lets each specialist focus on one kind of correction, since none of them has to rebuild the whole card. The same path also helps in the other direction, during training, when a correction signal travels backward from the model’s answer down through every layer. The signal tells each adjustable number which way to move, and the plus signs give it a direct route all the way down to the lowest layers. Here is why the plus sign matters. A block’s output is its input plus the changes, so if the input rises by 1, the output rises by 1 as well, plus whatever the changes do. A message such as “move this number up” therefore passes back through each plus sign at full strength. The route through a specialist is different, because a specialist can shrink the message as it passes. Picture a stack where each specialist halves it: after 10 layers, less than a thousandth is left, and after 32 layers almost nothing. The plus-sign route still carries the message whole, and that direct route is what made very deep stacks trainable. Together with the tidying step described next, this path is what lets real models repeat their block dozens of times. Information does not fade on the way up, and the training signal does not die on the way down. There is one more benefit, which the interpretability labs, about explaining what goes on inside a model, build on. Because the stream is a sum of many separate changes, the numbers at the top can, in principle, be pulled apart into the pieces that each specialist added. Numbers that drift out of range Without the tidying step, the size of the numbers drifts as they pass through layer after layer. Attention is especially sensitive to this, because its match scores come from multiplying numbers from two words together. You will see the result in the lab: make the input large with Layer norm off, and each head gives 100 percent of its share to a single word. Where the tidying happens matters as much as whether it happens, and pre-norm is the standard choice today because deep stacks train steadily with it. Post-norm usually needs extra care before a deep stack will train, such as a slow warm-up with small training steps at the start and carefully chosen starting numbers. Order carries meaning Order changes more than which sentence sounds sensible. Picture a model reading “the dog chased the cat up a tree, and then the” and guessing what comes next. To guess well, it has to know which animal did the chasing and which one is now stuck in the tree, and only the order of the words says so. Swap the two animals and the same words describe a different story, with a different likely next word. Since attention alone cannot see order, a position signal has to be added. Without one, a block where every word reads every other word hands back the same numbers for both stories, only shuffled between the slots. Reading a model’s spec sheet Knowing the block’s shape also helps you read the short descriptions that are published for real models, called model cards. The width, the number of layers, the type of MLP and the size of the vocabulary almost fix how many adjustable numbers a model has. The Parameter count card shows how, and it does the counting for you.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · The transformer block
documents.body: Switch off the only step that crosses words Try this: In the Transformer block card, click the Self-attention button so that it reads off. Then read Output shift if other words change in the Residual stream card, and watch it drop from 0.900 to exactly 0.000. That readout comes from a small experiment the lab runs for you. It runs the block a second time with the other five words replaced, so “the cat sat on the mat” becomes “a dog ran to a mat”. Only mat stays the same, and the lab measures how far its output moved between the two runs. With attention on, the output moves by 0.900, because mat reads the other words. With attention off, nothing else in the block can see another word, so the output does not move at all. The belt still reaches the output, though, and Output norm stays well above zero, because the card’s own numbers pass straight through. Now switch Self-attention back on and pick the the button at slot 0. Its shift is 0.000 even with attention on, because under the one-way rule the first word has no earlier words to read. Its Self-attention row shows both heads giving 100 percent to the word itself. Make the input huge Click the mat button again, turn Layer norm off, and then drag Input scale from 1× up to 8× while you watch the Self-attention row. Both heads now give 100 percent of their share to sat, so mat reads one word and ignores the rest. Match scores come from multiplying numbers from two words together, so when every number is 8 times bigger, each score becomes 64 times bigger. Gaps between scores that were small turn huge, and the top score takes everything. The changes the specialists write grow about five times bigger, which you can read in the Attention write as it climbs from 1.83 to 9.18. The MLP write climbs in the same way, from 2.25 to 11.19, so a block without tidying lets every size run away. Now turn Layer norm back on, and the attention write drops to 1.57 and stays exactly there wherever you drag the slider. Making every number on every card the same amount bigger leaves the tidied copies unchanged, as the 2, 2, 6, 6 example showed, so attention reads exactly the same input. The MLP’s copy is taken after the attention write has been added, and that write tilts a small card more than a large one. So the MLP write drifts a little as you drag, staying between about 1.9 and 2.2. Then look at cos(output, input), where cos is short for cosine. Picturing each list as an arrow again, the cosine scores how closely the two arrows point the same way. It runs from 1 for exactly the same direction down to −1 for opposite directions. With Layer norm on and the input at 8×, it reads 0.995, so the output is almost the same as the input. At 0.25× it falls to 0.178, so the output is mostly the specialists’ changes. The changes are about the same size in both cases, so what differs is the size of the stream they land on. Two spoonfuls of sugar change a cup of tea a lot, while in a swimming pool you would never taste them. Watch the additions line up First set Input scale back to 1×. In the Residual stream card, each of the eight rows, d0 to d7, has three lanes. The top lane runs from zero to the input value, and the middle lane adds the attention write, starting where the top lane ended. The bottom lane adds the MLP write in the same way, and a diamond marks the block’s output for that place. In pre-norm, every diamond sits exactly at the end of the bottom lane. Find the d1 row for mat, where the middle lane points left, because the attention write there is negative, and the bottom lane points back to the right. Now switch the MLP off in the Transformer block card, and the bottom lanes vanish. Each diamond lands at the end of the middle lane instead, because the output is now the input plus the attention write. Switch the MLP back on and compare the two writes, which for mat read 1.57 for Attention write and 2.00 for MLP write. Move the tidying onto the belt In the Transformer block card, switch Placement to Post-norm, and the Layer norm rows jump onto the rail, because they now resize the belt itself. In the Residual stream card, the diamonds no longer sit at the end of the lanes, since the output is resized after every addition. Watch Output norm while you drag Input scale from 0.25× to 8×. With Layer norm on, it reads 2.83 the whole time, the square root of 8, because every card is resized to the same standard size. Post-norm erases the stream’s own size at every addition, while pre-norm keeps it. Now look at the Self-attention row with the slider at 8×. Both heads again give 100 percent to sat, even with Layer norm on, and the Attention write reads 9.18. In post-norm, attention reads the raw input card, which nothing has tidied yet, so its huge numbers reach the match scores unchanged. Count where the parameters live As you saw earlier, the adjustable numbers in a model are called parameters, and the main ones are also called weights. In the Parameter count card, click GPT-2 small, and the bar splits one block’s parameters into attention, the MLP (hatched) and a thin sliver for the norms. MLP share reads 66.6%, so two out of every three adjustable numbers in a block belong to the MLP. The note under the card adds up all the blocks, the word lookup tables and the final norm. It arrives at 124,439,808, which is exactly the published count for GPT-2 small. Click Llama 2 7B instead, and the MLP share reads 66.8%, with a total of 6,738,415,616, or about 6.7 billion. Next, drag Model width from 768 to 1,536, which doubles d, and watch the Block row grow about four times bigger. It goes from about 7.1 million to about 28.3 million parameters, because a block’s size grows with d squared, and 2 squared is 4. Going deeper shows where the square comes from. Then switch Norm between LayerNorm and RMSNorm, a cheaper tidying step described in Going deeper, and notice that the total barely moves. Test word order The Position card runs the block with the settings from the Transformer block and Residual stream cards, so start by resetting them. Set Placement back to Pre-norm, make sure Layer norm, Self-attention and MLP are all on, and set Input scale to 1×. Open the Position card, then set Word order to Swap cat ↔ mat and Position information to Off. The two rows of word chips show “the cat sat on the mat” and “the mat sat on the cat”, and Words whose output changed reads 0 of 6. Every Output shift in the table is 0.000, and every Result says “same output”. The block hands back the same six outputs, only in each other’s slots, so it cannot tell the two sentences apart. Switch Position information to On, and all six words change output, with cat moving by 1.565 and mat by 1.286. Those two move the most because their own slots changed. The four words that stayed put move less, by about 0.4 each. Their own cards did not change, but the cat and mat cards they read now carry different seat-number stamps. Try Shuffle all next, which turns the sentence into “mat on cat the the sat”. With position information off, the result is again 0 of 6, while with it on all six change and Largest output shift reads 1.391. Finally, go back to the swap with position information on, and turn Self-attention off in the Transformer block card. Now only cat and mat change output, because without attention a word’s output depends only on its own input.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · The transformer block
documents.body: Each specialist adds a nudge rather than rewriting the card, so in the Residual stream card the pre-norm diamond lands exactly at the end of the three lanes. Switching a specialist off does not cut the block, because the skip connection still carries the stream to the output. That is why blocks built around a residual stream get gradually worse when a part is removed, instead of breaking outright. Attention is the only step where words affect each other, so with Self-attention off the output shift is 0.000 for every word. With it on, the first word still reads 0.000, because it has no earlier words to read. In pre-norm, Layer norm hides the stream’s overall size from the specialists, so with it on the attention write stays at 1.57 at every Input scale. That keeps their work in a sensible range however large the stream has grown. The same change matters less on a bigger stream, so as you raise Input scale, the cosine between output and input climbs toward 1. Pre-norm keeps the stream’s own size, while post-norm erases it, which is why the post-norm output norm reads 2.83 at every input scale. Most of a block’s parameters live in the MLP, which the Parameter count card shows as about two-thirds for both presets. In the Position card, only position information supplies order, because the card lifts the one-way rule. With position information off, the card shows zero change at every setting of the other switches. Tidying, the MLP and the input size cannot supply order, because none of them looks at slots.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · The transformer block
documents.body: What this lab simplifies Nothing here has been trained, because the adjustable numbers are random values from a fixed seed. The arithmetic is honest, but no vector means anything, so the lab shows the plumbing rather than learned skill. The block is tiny, with 8 numbers for each word where real models use hundreds or thousands, and it runs one block where real models run dozens. One switch stands in for two, since the single Layer norm button turns both tidying steps off together, while a real block has two separate ones. Real tidying steps also end by multiplying by a learned scale and adding a learned shift. Here the scale is fixed at 1 and the shift at 0, so those last moves change nothing. Some parts are missing, since attention here has no biases, the extra adjustable numbers some steps add on at the end of their arithmetic. There is also no dropout, a training trick that randomly blanks out some numbers. Switching a part off is exact here, in one sense: nothing later in this block was trained to expect that part’s changes. So no step is thrown off by an input unlike anything it saw in training, which stops being true in a trained model, as the mix-up below explains. Later steps still react to a part being switched off, though. Switch Self-attention off and the MLP reads a different card, so for mat the MLP write changes from 2.00 to 1.89. The output then moves by more than the attention write alone. The Position card lifts the one-way rule, which matters because with the rule in place, the first word sees only itself and the last sees all six. So even a block with no position numbers leaks a little order, although the last word still cannot tell in which order the five words before it came. The position pattern is fixed: it is a wave pattern of size 0.5 added to the input of an untrained block. The card shows that the block’s outputs can depend on position, not that the block makes any use of order. The parameter counts assume every head has its own keys and values, which Smaller attention below explains. Outside the two presets, the card also counts the main weights only, with no biases and no word lookup tables. Where the conveyor belt stops matching The belt picture makes a real model look tidier than it is, in three ways. First, the picture suggests that each specialist’s changes stay neat and separate on the card. In a real model, every specialist at every level writes into the same fixed list of numbers, as long as the model’s width. With hundreds of specialists, that list runs out of room, so their changes end up crowded on top of each other. The interpretability labs return to this problem. Second, the tidying step is not neutral bookkeeping. It has its own adjustable numbers, a scale and a shift, which training tunes. And the size it hides from each copy still matters. A word with large numbers on the belt is changed less by the same write, as the sugar example showed. Trained models make use of effects like these. Third, the specialists are not workers who choose what to write, since each one does fixed arithmetic with its learned numbers, and its change is whatever that arithmetic produces. What goes wrong in real models A common mix-up: Switching a specialist off in a real, trained model is not a clean experiment. Picture a school band that has rehearsed for months with a drummer, and on concert night the drummer is sick. The band sounds noticeably worse, but not only because the drum part is missing, since the other players were counting on the beat to keep time and they stumble too. Judging the drummer’s job by how bad the band sounds would overstate it. A trained model works the same way, because every later layer learned to expect that specialist’s changes. Removing it hands those layers inputs they never saw in training, and nothing retrains to make up for the gap. The damage you measure therefore mixes the specialist’s own job with the shock to everything after it. Removing a part like this is called ablation, and getting an honest answer from it takes the more careful methods in the circuits lab. Position has real-world limits as well, because adding position information is necessary but not enough, and a trained model still has to learn to use it. How well a model copes with texts longer than the ones it trained on also depends on which position scheme it uses. Finally, for most models the parameter count tracks both the memory a model needs and the work it does for each word. Some designs separate the two, because they hold many MLPs per block but run only a few of them for each word, as Going deeper explains.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · The transformer block
documents.body: Counting a block from its shape You can work out a model’s size from its shape, because most of its adjustable numbers sit in grids that turn one list into another. Each new number is a mix of all d old ones, and each mix needs d adjustable numbers of its own, one for each old number. So a grid that turns a list of d numbers into a new list of d numbers needs d × d entries, written d². Attention needs four of these grids, one each to make queries, keys and values and one to combine the heads’ results, which is the Attention row’s 4 · d². With d = 768, one grid holds 589,824 numbers, so the four of them together hold 2,359,296. The MLP needs two bigger grids, one that widens the list to 4d and one that squeezes it back. For GPT-2 small the widened list has 3,072 numbers, which is 4 times 768. So the MLP row reads 2 · d · 3,072, which comes to 4,718,592, twice the attention count. The MLP’s two grids hold 8 · d² between them, so adding attention’s 4 · d² gives about 12 · d² for a whole block. That is why the Block row compares the total with this rule of thumb, and why two-thirds of every block is MLP. The two tidying steps add only a scale and a shift for each of the d places. At d = 768 they make up about 0.04% of a block, so choosing between LayerNorm and RMSNorm affects speed and steadiness rather than size. Because the count grows with d², doubling the width makes each block four times bigger. Load GPT-2 small, and the lab adds its 12 blocks to a word lookup table for 50,257 tokens. It also counts a table of positions, the biases and a final norm, and it reproduces the published 124,439,808 exactly. Newer MLPs Newer designs mostly change the MLP rather than attention, and one such design, SwiGLU, splits the widening step into two branches that are multiplied together. One branch acts a little like a dimmer switch on the other. Since SwiGLU uses three grids instead of two, it narrows the middle to about 8/3 of the width, which keeps its total close to the classic MLP’s. It is the SwiGLU ≈8/3× choice in the MLP control, and Llama 2 7B uses it with a middle width of 11,008. With it, the preset still adds up to Llama 2 7B’s published 6,738,415,616. A mixture of experts goes further by keeping many MLPs in each block but sending each word to only a few of them. A model can then have an enormous total size while each word still pays only a small bill in work. Smaller attention Grouped-query attention, covered in Modern attention at scale, lets several heads share the same keys and values. That shrinks two of attention’s four grids, so real attention often costs less than 4 · d². A cheaper tidying step RMSNorm skips subtracting the average and has no learned shift, so it only divides by the typical size of the numbers and then applies a learned scale. It is cheaper to compute, works about as well in practice, and is the standard in recent models such as Llama. Other ways to supply order Real models handle order in several ways, and some of them add a learned list of position numbers for each slot. Others add a fixed wave pattern, as this lab does, while others lower the match score between two words the farther apart they sit, a scheme called ALiBi. Many current models, Llama among them, add nothing at the input at all. Instead, they twist each query and key by an angle that depends on its slot, a scheme called rotary embeddings. Modern attention at scale shows it at work, and the Attention lab lines the schemes up. A model that only reads earlier words can pick up a little order from that rule alone. Even so, most models still supply position information on purpose, either at the input or inside attention. Peeking partway up At the very top of the stack, one more tidying step and a word-scoring layer turn each word’s list of numbers into odds for the next token. You can also apply that scoring layer to the residual stream partway up the stack. That gives a rough peek at which next token the model was leaning toward at that depth, a tool researchers call the logit lens. Specialists that read and write in the same space Because every specialist only adds to a shared stream, you can picture each part of attention, and each neuron in the MLP, as reading certain mixes of the stream’s numbers. Each part also writes its own mix back, and two parts at different depths work together when what one writes overlaps with what the other reads. The circuits lab is built on that way of looking at a model.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · The transformer block
documents.body: This module is about the transformer block, the unit a language model repeats. It answers a structural question: how can attention and a per-position network form one layer that stacks without losing each token's information? The answer is the residual stream, a running vector per token position. Each sublayer, attention or the per-position network, reads the stream, usually through a normalization, and adds its result to it. It builds on Attention, which studied self-attention alone. Here attention sits beside an MLP (multilayer perceptron) that transforms each position separately. The module ends on word order: attention by itself cannot tell it, so a positional encoding, a vector that depends on the slot, supplies it. Where it shows up Language models. GPT-2, Llama and their relatives are stacks of this block or a close variant, with an embedding layer below that turns tokens into vectors and an unembedding layer on top that turns the final vectors into scores over the vocabulary. Variants. The original 2017 Transformer normalized after each addition (post-norm); the standard choice now is pre-norm, which normalizes each sublayer's input. Blocks also swap in RMSNorm (a cheaper normalization), a gated SwiGLU MLP, mixture-of-experts layers that send each token to a few of many MLPs, or grouped-query attention, in which several query heads share each key and value head. Position. Order enters as a vector added before the first block, as in this lab, or inside attention, as the rotary scheme in Modern attention at scale does. Interpretability. In a pre-norm stack, a late representation is the input embedding plus every earlier sublayer's write, so it can in principle be split into per-component writes, the premise the interpretability and circuits labs build on. Why it matters Each piece has a distinct job: Attention is the only step where a token's vector depends on other tokens' content. The norms and the MLP are position-wise: applied to each position alone, with shared weights. The MLP is the block's main position-wise computation, a nonlinear transformation of each vector, and it holds two-thirds of a classic block's parameters. Residual additions overwrite nothing, so each sublayer only supplies a correction and gradients keep an additive path to early layers. Normalization fixes the scale each sublayer reads in pre-norm. In the lab's pre-norm block, without it an 8× input collapses each head's attention onto a single token. Position information breaks a symmetry. Without it, an unmasked block given reordered words returns the same outputs reordered, so it cannot tell *the cat sat on the mat* from *the mat sat on the cat*. What you will be able to explain Trace one token through a block, and say which step reads other positions. Explain the residual stream as a running sum that sublayers add to but never overwrite. Explain why attention alone cannot tell word order, and what a position vector adds. What the lab shows The lab computes a tiny block exactly in the page: width 8, two causal attention heads (each token reads only itself and earlier tokens), a GELU MLP and LayerNorm. Its input is the fixed sentence *the cat sat on the mat*, each word a seeded vector plus a sinusoidal position vector. The weights are seeded and untrained, so the values show data flow, not learned features. On the Transformer block card, Placement (Pre-norm or Post-norm) and the Layer norm, Self-attention and MLP switches set what runs, and Token picks which of the six positions this card and the Residual stream card describe. The Residual stream card draws the token's input, attention write and MLP write as lanes per dimension, sets Input scale, and reads Output shift if other words change. The Parameter count card is closed-form arithmetic for full-size blocks: Model width, Layers, MLP, Norm, and GPT-2 small and Llama 2 7B presets. The key experiment is on the Position card, which runs the block on the sentence and on a reordering, with the causal mask lifted. Set Word order to Swap cat ↔ mat and Position information to Off: Words whose output changed reads 0 of 6. With the other cards at their default settings, switch it to On and all six outputs change.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · The transformer block
documents.body: The block is the unit that gets repeated. A modern language model is essentially one of these stacked dozens of times, with an embedding layer before and an unembedding layer after. In its pre-norm form it is two lines: Each line reads the stream, normalizes a copy, computes something, and *adds* the result back. The original x is never overwritten. This is the structural fact everything else depends on. The residual stream Think of x as a shared bus running the full depth of the model, one copy per token position. Every sublayer reads from it and writes an increment into it. Nothing deletes; contributions accumulate by addition. This has three consequences. Gradients reach early layers through the additive path even when the sublayers attenuate them, which is what made very deep stacks trainable. Sublayers can specialize, because each only needs to supply a correction. And because the stream is a sum of many contributions, a late representation is decomposable in principle, the premise the interpretability labs build on. The two sublayers do different jobs Attention moves information between positions. It is the only place in the block where one token's vector is affected by another token's content. The MLP transforms each position independently. The same weights apply at every position. The classic MLP expands the width by a factor of four, applies a nonlinearity such as GELU, and projects back down. That expansion holds two-thirds of each block's parameters. Where order comes from Attention compares vectors and mixes values. Nothing in that arithmetic mentions where a word sits, so when every word may read every other, it is permutation equivariant: reorder the input words and the outputs are the same vectors, reordered the same way. The norms and the MLP are position-wise, so the whole block inherits this. A positional encoding fixes that. A vector that depends on the slot is added to each word's embedding before the first block, or applied inside attention, as the rotary scheme in Modern attention at scale does. The lab's input is a seeded token vector plus a sinusoidal position vector. Normalization Layer normalization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation across the feature dimension, then applies a learned scale and shift. RMSNorm skips the mean subtraction and the shift and divides by the root-mean-square, which is cheaper and works as well in practice. Placement matters more than the variant. Pre-norm normalizes the input to each sublayer and leaves the residual path unnormalized, and is the standard choice because deep stacks train stably with it. Post-norm, used in the original 2017 Transformer, normalizes after each addition and typically needs learning-rate warmup and careful initialization to converge at depth. What this lab computes A real block runs in the page: width 8, two causal attention heads of width 4, a GELU MLP of width 32, and LayerNorm, with seeded random weights. It is untrained, so its vectors show the data flow and the algebra, not learned features. The Position card runs the same block with the causal mask lifted, so that only word order is being tested.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · The transformer block
documents.body: From Attention came routing and from Stacking neurons the transformation; stacking the pair is where depth becomes the problem. Llama 2 7B, Llama 2 70B and Llama 3.1 405B repeat the block 32, 80 and 126 times, and only the residual path and normalization keep the signal and the gradients usable at that depth. It also gives you the right mental model for reading model cards. Width, layer count, MLP type, and vocabulary size nearly determine the parameter count, as the Parameter count card shows.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · The transformer block
documents.body: Turn Self-attention off and read Output shift if other words change. The lab runs the block a second time with the other five tokens swapped, and the selected token's output moves by 0.900 with attention on and exactly 0.000 with it off. The norms and the MLP are position-wise. Turn Layer norm off and set Input scale to 8×. Both heads' weights collapse to 100 percent on one token, and the attention and MLP writes grow from 1.83 and 2.25 at 1× to 9.18 and 11.19. With the norm on, the attention write is 1.57 at every scale, because LN(s·x) = LN(x). Switch Placement to Post-norm and watch the norm rows move onto the rail. The output norm is now 2.83, which is √8, at any input scale: post-norm rescales the stream itself. In the Position card, set Word order to Swap cat ↔ mat and Position information to Off. Words whose output changed reads 0 of 6: the block returns the same six vectors in the other words' slots, so it cannot tell *the cat sat on the mat* from *the mat sat on the cat*. Switch to On and all six outputs move. Cat moves by 1.565 and mat by 1.286; the four words that kept their slots move by 0.389 to 0.465.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · The transformer block
documents.body: In pre-norm, each sublayer's output is an *addition*. The Residual stream card shows every dimension as input plus attention write plus MLP write, with the output diamond exactly at the sum. Turning off a sublayer does not sever the block. The skip path still carries the stream, which is why residual architectures degrade gracefully. Scale matters. For mat at 8× input with the norm on, cos(output, input) is 0.995: the same writes that dominate a small stream are a small nudge on a large one. Pre-norm keeps the stream's own scale; post-norm erases it at every addition. With position information off, the Position card's shifts are zero at every setting of the other cards. Norms, MLP, placement and input scale cannot supply order, because none of them looks at slots.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · The transformer block
documents.body: In this lab. The weights are random, so no vector means anything beyond the arithmetic. One Layer norm switch disables both norms at once, attention has no biases, and there is no dropout. Ablation here is exact, because nothing downstream was trained to expect the ablated sublayer. The Position card also lifts the causal mask. Under the mask the first word sees only itself and the last sees all six, so a masked block with no position vector already leaks some order. In real systems. Ablating a sublayer in a trained model is not a clean subtraction. The remaining layers were trained expecting its contribution, so removing one produces a distribution-shifted state, and the observed damage overstates what that component did in isolation. Mean-ablation and activation patching, in the circuits lab, exist to reduce this confound. Order has its own real-world caveat. A decoder-only model can recover some position from the causal mask alone, yet most models still supply explicit position information, and the scheme chosen affects how well they handle lengths beyond training. Attention compares the schemes, and Modern attention at scale shows rotary embeddings at work. Two further caveats. Layer normalization is not a passive rescaling: its learned scale parameters and its per-token statistics both carry information that downstream layers use. And the residual stream is a fixed-width channel shared by every sublayer at every depth, so capacity is contended, one mechanism behind the superposition problem in the interpretability labs.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · The transformer block
documents.body: Parameter accounting falls straight out of the structure. Per block, attention has four d × d matrices for queries, keys, values, and the output projection, 4d². A classic MLP has 2 × d × 4d = 8d². So a block is about 12d² weights, two-thirds in the MLP. With the GPT-2 small preset, 12 such blocks plus biases, embeddings and a final norm give exactly 124,439,808. SwiGLU splits the up-projection into a gate and a value branch, multiplies the value by the Swish of the gate, and uses a hidden width near 8d/3 so three matrices still cost about 8d². The Llama 2 7B preset uses 11,008 = 8·4096/3 rounded up to a multiple of 256, and adds up to 6,738,415,616. Mixture-of-experts blocks replace the single MLP with many and route each token to a few, decoupling total parameters from per-token compute. Grouped-query attention, covered in Modern attention at scale, shrinks the key and value matrices, so production attention is often below 4d². The stack ends with one more normalization and the unembedding projection to vocabulary logits. Reading the residual stream at intermediate depths through that unembedding, the logit lens, gives a rough view of the model's evolving prediction. Because sublayers only add to a shared stream, you can think of attention heads and MLP neurons as reading from and writing to subspaces of it. Composition between components at different depths then becomes overlap between what one writes and what another reads, the vocabulary the circuits lab uses.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Transformer block · The transformer block
documents.body: One block, computed stage by stage A real, tiny transformer block running in the page: width 8, two causal attention heads of width 4, a GELU MLP of width 32, and LayerNorm. Each row shows the actual vector for one token at that stage, and the residual stream runs down the left rail. Rows in data order. Rows on the rail are the residual stream itself; indented dashed rows are sublayers that read a copy of the stream and write back at the next `+`. Each row's 8-dimensional vector as diverging bars (positive up, negative down) on one shared scale, plus its Euclidean norm. On the Self-attention row, both heads' weights from the selected token to every earlier token, as percentages that sum to 100 per head. On the MLP row, how many of the 32 hidden GELU units are positive for this token. An `on`/`off` pill on each switchable row. Switched-off rows fade and write zeros. Pre-norm, as in GPT-2 and Llama: `h = x + Attn(LN(x))`, then `out = h + MLP(LN(h))`. Post-norm, as in the 2017 Transformer: `h = LN(x + Attn(x))`, then `out = LN(h + MLP(h))`. The norm rows move onto the rail because they rescale the stream itself. Attention: q, k, v = x·W, scores q·k ÷ √4 over positions up to this one, softmax, weighted sum of v per head, concatenate, then the output projection. MLP: x·W₁ (8 → 32), GELU (tanh approximation), then ·W₂ (32 → 8). LayerNorm subtracts the mean, divides by the standard deviation (ε = 1e-5), then applies a scale of 1 and shift of 0. Inputs are a seeded vector per token plus a sinusoidal position vector, multiplied by Input scale. Weights are seeded Gaussians with standard deviation 1/√fan-in. `Placement` switches between Pre-norm and Post-norm. `Token` picks which of the six positions the rows describe. `Layer norm`, `Self-attention`, and `MLP` switch their rows. The Layer norm button switches both norms together; `Residual add` rows cannot be switched, because removing the addition removes the stream. With Layer norm on in Pre-norm, the Self-attention and MLP writes keep the same size at any Input scale: LN(s·x) = LN(x). Turn it off and push Input scale to 8×: attention weights collapse to 100% on one token. Self-attention is the only row that mentions other positions. The first token, `the` at position 0, can only attend to itself. In Post-norm the output norm is always √8 ≈ 2.83 with the norm on, whatever the input: the stream's own scale is erased at every addition. In this lab: the weights are random and untrained, so the vectors show the plumbing, not learned features. One shared Layer norm switch stands in for two independent norms, and there is no dropout, no biases in attention, and a width of 8 instead of thousands. In this lab: switching a sublayer off here is exact, because nothing downstream was trained to expect it. In general: ablating a sublayer in a trained model leaves the later layers in a state they never saw, so the damage overstates that component's isolated role. Mean-ablation and activation patching in the circuits lab reduce that confound. In general: production blocks vary what this one fixes: RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm, a gated SwiGLU MLP, grouped-query attention, and mixture-of-experts layers that route each token to a few of many MLPs.
documents.title: One block, computed stage by stage

documents.subtitle: Residual stream · The transformer block
documents.body: The sum every sublayer writes into One token's residual vector decomposed dimension by dimension into the input and the two sublayer writes. In a pre-norm block the output is exactly their sum, which is what makes the stream a shared, additive channel. Eight rows, one per dimension d0–d7, on a shared horizontal axis centred at zero. Three lanes per row: the top lane runs from 0 to the input value, the middle lane adds the attention write, and the bottom lane adds the MLP write, each starting where the previous one ended. A diamond at the block's output value for that dimension. Input scale, and metrics for the input, attention write, MLP write, and output norms, the cosine between output and input, and how far this token's output moves if the other five words change. Lane ends are x_i, x_i + a_i, and x_i + a_i + m_i, where a and m are the attention and MLP writes from the Transformer block card. Pre-norm: the diamond equals x_i + a_i + m_i exactly. Post-norm: the diamond is LN(LN(x + a) + m)_i, so it generally sits elsewhere. Output shift if other words change: the block is run a second time with every other position swapped (the cat sat on the mat → a dog ran to a rug, keeping this token), and the lab prints the distance between the two outputs at this position. Input scale multiplies every input vector before the block runs. `Input scale` runs from 0.25× to 8×. Compare Layer norm on and off at 8×. The sublayer switches, Placement, and Token live on the Transformer block card and change this card too. Turn Self-attention off and the output shift is exactly 0.000: the norms and the MLP work on each position alone. For `mat` in Pre-norm with the norm on, cos(output, input) is 0.995 at Input scale 8×: the writes are a small nudge on a large stream. At 0.25× the same writes dominate and the cosine falls to 0.178. Switch to Post-norm and the diamonds leave the end of the lanes. The output is no longer the input plus a correction. In this lab: one token of one untrained block. A real stream passes through dozens of blocks, and each one's writes accumulate on top of the last. In general: the stream is a fixed-width channel shared by every sublayer at every depth, so writes compete for the same directions, one mechanism behind superposition in the interpretability labs. In general: layer normalization is not passive. Its learned scale and its per-token statistics carry information that later layers use.
documents.title: The sum every sublayer writes into

documents.subtitle: Parameter count · The transformer block
documents.body: Counting a block from its shape Weight counts for one block at a chosen width, split into attention, MLP, and norms, compared with the 12·d² rule of thumb, and multiplied by the layer count. Presets reproduce GPT-2 small's and Llama 2 7B's published totals. Preset buttons, Model width, Layers, and choices of MLP and Norm. A bar split by parameter share: attention, MLP (hatched), and a sliver for the norms. Formula rows with the exact counts, the block total against 12·d², and metrics for all blocks, the MLP share, and the toy block's 840 parameters. Attention: four d × d matrices for Q, K, V, and the output projection, 4d². GELU MLP: up d × 4d and down 4d × d, 8d². SwiGLU: gate, up, and down with hidden width 8d/3 rounded up to a multiple of 256, also about 8d². Norms: two per block. LayerNorm has a scale and a shift (2d each); RMSNorm has only a scale (d each). GPT-2 small preset: 12 blocks with biases, plus 50,257 × 768 token and 1,024 × 768 position embeddings and a final LayerNorm, gives 124,439,808. Llama 2 7B preset: 32 blocks, plus untied 32,000 × 4,096 input and output embeddings and a final RMSNorm, gives 6,738,415,616. `GPT-2 small` and `Llama 2 7B` load published configurations. `Model width` (256 to 8,192) and `Layers` (1 to 128) change the shape; `MLP` and `Norm` change the block's recipe. The MLP holds two-thirds of every block with either MLP type: 66.6% for GELU 4×, 66.8% for Llama's SwiGLU at d = 4,096. Norm parameters are about 1/(3d) of a block, 0.04% at d = 768, so LayerNorm versus RMSNorm matters for speed and stability, not size. Doubling Model width quadruples the block: parameters grow with d². In this lab: counts assume standard multi-head attention. Grouped-query attention shrinks the K and V matrices, so a GQA block has fewer than 4d² attention weights. In this lab: outside the presets the card counts weights only, with no biases or embeddings. In general: parameter count sets memory, not compute per token alone. Mixture-of-experts models hold many MLPs per block but run only a few for each token.
documents.title: Counting a block from its shape

documents.subtitle: Position · The transformer block
documents.body: Why a block needs position information The same six words are run through the lab's block in their original order and in a reordering, with every word allowed to read every other. Without position information each word gets the same output in both orders, so the block cannot tell the sentences apart. With it, the outputs differ. `Word order`: Original, `Swap cat ↔ mat` (the cat sat on the mat becomes the mat sat on the cat), or `Shuffle all` (mat on cat the the sat). Two rows of numbered chips show both sentences, with the slot of each word. `Position information`: Off feeds the block each word's own vector; On feeds it the same vector plus a sinusoidal position vector, exactly the input the other cards use. A table with one row per word of the original sentence: its slot before and after (`1 → 5`), the output shift (the distance between that word's block output in the two orders, with a bar), and a text verdict, `same output` or `different output`. Metrics for how many of the six words changed output and the largest shift. A note below states the result in words. The block runs twice, once on the original word list and once on the reordered one, using the Layer norm, Self-attention, MLP, Placement and Input scale settings from the other cards. Each word's output in the first run is compared with the output of the same word in the second. Without position information, the input is the seeded token vector alone. Every step of the block is then either position-wise (norms, MLP) or attention, whose scores depend only on the vectors being compared. So a word's output depends on which words are present and not where they sit, and reordering only reorders the outputs. With position information the input is `embed(word, slot)`: the token vector plus a position vector built from sines and cosines of the slot. The same word in a different slot now enters the block as a different vector. The card runs attention without the causal mask, so each word reads all six. That isolates order from the mask. `Word order`: pick `Swap cat ↔ mat`, then set `Position information` to Off. Every shift reads 0.000 and Words whose output changed reads 0 of 6, though the sentence now says something different. Switch `Position information` to On with the swap. At the default settings all six words change output: cat and mat move most because their own slots changed, and the other four move less because only their neighbours moved. Turn `Self-attention` off on the Transformer block card with Position information On and the swap selected: only cat and mat change output, because without attention a word's output depends on its own input alone. With position information off, the shifts are zero at every setting of the other cards: Layer norm, MLP, Placement and Input scale cannot supply order, because none of them looks at slots. `Shuffle all` moves every word, and the result is the same: identical output vectors in new slots with position information off, six different ones with it on. Position information does not tell a word what is near it. It makes the input depend on the slot, and attention then has to learn to use that signal. In this lab: the position vector is a fixed sinusoidal pattern of amplitude 0.5 added to an untrained block's input. Nothing here learns to use order, so the card shows that the block can be sensitive to position, not that it understands it. In this lab: the card lifts the causal mask. Under the mask a word can still tell how many words precede it, because the first word sees only itself and the last sees all six, so a masked block leaks some order even with no position vector. In general: this block adds a sinusoidal vector to the embedding. Learned absolute vectors, relative biases such as ALiBi, and rotary embeddings supply order differently; many current models, Llama among them, rotate queries and keys inside attention (see Modern attention at scale) instead of adding any position vector at the input. In general: position information is necessary but not sufficient. A trained model has to learn to use it, and how well it handles positions beyond those seen in training depends on the scheme chosen.
documents.title: Why a block needs position information

documents.subtitle: Treat AI as a family of function-approximators, nest the modern methods, and name what the word does not claim.
documents.body: Treat AI as a family of function-approximators, nest the modern methods, and name what the word does not claim. Place machine learning, deep learning, and large language models inside AI rather than treating them as synonyms Name the learning problem as a hypothesis class, a loss, a search over parameters, and a generalization gap Separate symbolic methods, statistical fitting, and deep stacks, and say what those objects are not Name where a model's training signal comes from (human labels, structure in raw data, labels made from the data itself, or reward) and tell classification from regression by the kind of output
