documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: Any method that performs a task that used to need human judgment. The label names a goal, not a single algorithm, so a rule list and a neural net can both count. Symbolic AI, which runs on written rules, search, or logic, is AI but sits outside machine learning because nobody estimated θ from a table. AGI, artificial general intelligence, is the hoped-for or feared goal of a system that could do any cognitive task a person can; it is defined in different ways and has no agreed test, so it is not a measured property, and nothing in these labs claims it.
documents.title: Artificial intelligence

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: A method that fits parameters from examples instead of writing the decision rule by hand. The fit is only as good as the data and the objective you chose.
documents.title: Machine learning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: Machine learning that stacks differentiable layers so later layers can reuse earlier features. Depth is a wiring choice, not a guarantee of understanding.
documents.title: Deep learning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: A generative model is trained to produce new samples from a distribution, such as text, images, or audio. The Gen ring in the diagram holds the neural ones; an n-gram is generative without being deep and sits outside it. A large language model is a generative model trained to predict the next token in text, then often adapted into an assistant. Generating a fluent sample is not the same as checking that the sample is true.
documents.term: Generative model and large language model
documents.title: Generative model and large language model

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: The set of functions you are willing to search, written H. On this page H is every line ŷ = wx + b. A different H (a tree, a deep net) is a different search.
documents.title: Hypothesis class

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: A number that says how wrong the current parameters are on the data you are fitting. Training searches for parameters that make this number small. It is not automatically the number you should publish.
documents.title: Loss

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: Low error on new examples drawn from the same process as the training data. A small training loss does not, by itself, measure it.
documents.title: Generalization

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: A model is a fixed function f_θ: once its numbers θ are set, each input x maps to one output ŷ, or to one distribution p_θ(y|x). Training searches for θ by lowering the loss on examples; inference runs the finished model on a new input with θ held still. Finding θ so that f_θ(x) is close to a target y is function approximation, which is most of modern AI and not a model of a mind.
documents.title: Model, training, and inference

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: A parameter is a number inside the model that training sets from data. Here w and b in ŷ = wx + b are the parameters; a large language model has billions. A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before the search starts, so training does not learn it. Here the 0.12 step size is one; later labs add learning rate, batch size, and epoch count.
documents.title: Parameter and hyperparameter

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: Fitting a model on input-output pairs that someone labeled. The labels decide what counts as correct, so a biased label set becomes a biased rule. Semi-supervised learning is the same idea when only a few examples carry labels and many do not.
documents.title: Supervised learning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: Learning from data that has no answer column. The model finds structure in the inputs themselves, such as clusters of similar records or readings far from the usual pattern. With no target there is nothing to score accuracy against, so a person still has to judge whether the structure means anything.
documents.title: Unsupervised learning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: Learning where the label is made from the data itself: hide part of the data, such as the next word of a sentence or a blanked patch of a photo, and ask the model to restore it. The model still trains against labels, but they come free, so the training set can be as large as the raw collection. This is how large language models are pretrained.
documents.title: Self-supervised learning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: Learning from a reward received after acting, with no example of the right action. The learner tries actions, sees the reward or penalty, and has to work out which earlier choices earned it. A reward scores an outcome; it is not a label for each step.
documents.title: Reinforcement learning

documents.subtitle: Glossary · What AI actually is
documents.body: Two kinds of output for a model that predicts a target. Classification returns one category from a fixed set, such as spam or not spam, or the next word out of a vocabulary. Regression returns a number on a scale, such as a price or a pixel value. The output type is a separate axis from the learning signal: next-word prediction is self-supervised classification.
documents.title: Classification and regression

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · What AI actually is · question 1
documents.body: A GAN draws new face images from a learned distribution. Which placement in the rings is correct? Generative and deep learning, but not an LLM, since it does not predict the next token An LLM, because every generative model is trained to predict the next token in text Machine learning but not deep learning, because drawing samples needs no stacked layers Outside machine learning, because nobody wrote a label for each generated face The rings nest the common modern stack, but a GAN is generative without being an LLM: an LLM's training job is predicting the next token in text. A GAN's generator is a stack of differentiable layers, so it sits in deep learning, and fitting parameters from examples is what makes it machine learning. Labels are not required for that.
documents.title: A GAN draws new face images from a learned distribution. Which placement in the rings is correct?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · What AI actually is · question 2
documents.body: On Learning problem you start at Weight w = 0 and Bias b = 0 and press Take a downhill step several times. What happens? The three data points slide toward the line, which is what makes the residuals shrink The dot jumps straight to the bottom of the bowl on the first press, whatever the step size L stays the same until the slopes are exactly zero, then drops all at once L falls and the dot walks toward the bottom as the slopes flatten toward zero A downhill step moves (w, b), the dot on the parameter map, by minus 0.12 times the gradient of L. The data never move. Each press shrinks the squared residuals, so L falls, and the slopes flatten as the dot nears the bottom of the bowl. A fixed small step means several presses, not one jump.
documents.title: On Learning problem you start at Weight w = 0 and Bias b = 0 and press Take a downhill step several times. What happens?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · What AI actually is · question 3
documents.body: A line ŷ = wx + b is fitted by making mean squared error small on three points. What is still not guaranteed? That the mean squared error is a well-defined number on these three points That a new x from the same process will also have a small prediction error That the hypothesis class contains at least one straight line through them Training loss is a reading of the fitted sample. Generalization is error on new draws from the same process. A small L on three authored points does not measure that, and nothing in the search requires consciousness or folk understanding.
documents.title: A line ŷ = wx + b is fitted by making mean squared error small on three points. What is still not guaranteed?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · What AI actually is · question 4
documents.body: A hand-written checker applies a fixed list of rules to a chess position. How does it differ from fitting a line to data? It must be machine learning, because any program that decides has learned from experience It is deep learning, because several rules are applied one after another It generalizes to new positions by construction, because written rules cannot be wrong It can be AI with no fitted parameters, because nobody estimated θ from examples Artificial intelligence names a goal, so a rule list counts. Machine learning means parameters fitted from examples, and a rule list has no θ to fit. Applying rules in sequence is not stacking differentiable layers, and a rule can still fail on a position its author never imagined.
documents.title: A hand-written checker applies a fixed list of rules to a chess position. How does it differ from fitting a line to data?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · What AI actually is · question 5
documents.body: Next-word prediction can train on a huge pile of raw text that nobody labeled. Why? It is unsupervised, so no target exists and the model only clusters similar words The next word is already in the text, so each sentence supplies its own answer key It is reinforcement learning, because the reader rewards each word after it appears Hiding the next word turns the text into labeled pairs for free: the context is x and the word that follows is y. That is self-supervised learning, and it scales with the amount of raw text rather than with the number of annotators. Unsupervised methods have no target at all, and no reader supplies a reward here.
documents.title: Next-word prediction can train on a huge pile of raw text that nobody labeled. Why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · What AI actually is · question 6
documents.body: A model fills in photo patches that were blanked out by predicting the hidden pixel values. Which pair of descriptions fits? Self-supervised signal and a regression output, since the answer is hidden numbers Supervised signal and a classification output, because a person labeled each patch Unsupervised signal and a regression output, because no target is being predicted Reinforcement signal and an action output, because a good repair earns a reward The hidden pixels are part of the original photo, so the data supplies its own label: that is the self-supervised signal. The output is a number for each pixel, so the task type is regression. The signal says where the target comes from; classification and regression say what kind of answer it is, and the two are separate choices.
documents.title: A model fills in photo patches that were blanked out by predicting the hidden pixel values. Which pair of descriptions fits?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · What AI actually is · question 7
documents.body: On Era timeline, the perceptron (1958) and the expert systems of 1980 both count as AI. What separates them? A perceptron is the only one that is AI, since a rule list has no parameters and so cannot count Expert systems run rules people wrote, while a perceptron fits weights from labeled examples Both fit parameters from examples, and they differ only in the hardware they ran on Expert systems are deep learning, because several rules are applied in sequence and stacked An expert system such as XCON holds specialist knowledge as written rules, so no parameters are fitted and it is AI without being machine learning. A perceptron learns weights from labeled examples, which makes it machine learning. Applying rules in sequence is not a stack of differentiable layers, and AI names a goal, so a rule list counts.
documents.title: On Era timeline, the perceptron (1958) and the expert systems of 1980 both count as AI. What separates them?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · What AI actually is · question 8
documents.body: A chat assistant answers questions on many topics fluently. What do these labs say about calling it AGI? It qualifies, because training on text from many topics makes a model skilled at every task It cannot qualify, because every large language model is narrow by definition and always will be It is a broad tool; AGI is a goal with no agreed test, and fluency does not measure it It qualifies, because answering any question in words is the definition of general intelligence AGI names a system that could do any cognitive task a person can, and people define it differently, so it is a goal rather than a measured property. A wide interface such as language makes a model look general; its training job is still next-token prediction plus later wraps. The rings do not contain AGI, and these labs neither claim it nor rule it out forever.
documents.title: A chat assistant answers questions on many topics fluently. What do these labs say about calling it AGI?

documents.subtitle: Plain · What AI actually is
documents.body: People use the word “AI” for many different things, from a chatbot that writes a poem to a filter that sorts email into spam or not spam. A chess program that follows rules a person typed in gets called AI as well, even though it works in a completely different way from the other two. Calling all three by one name hides more than it tells you, because the name says nothing about how each one actually works. This module sorts out those words, starting with the idea that AI is a large family of methods with smaller groups nested inside it. Those groups fit together the way your street sits inside your town, and your town sits inside your country. The module also shows you what “learning from examples” really means, by letting you fit a straight line to three dots on a graph, one step at a time. Where you have met it If you have ever typed a question into a chat assistant, you have used the smallest and most specific group in this module, called a large language model. That assistant also belongs to every larger group around it, all the way out to AI itself, which is the largest group of all. Some of the lab’s other examples are close to everyday tools, such as sorting emails into spam or not spam, or predicting a house’s sale price from past sales. Others are less familiar, such as repairing a photo that has a patch blanked out, but all of these are jobs a model can learn from examples. A list of chess rules typed in by a person counts as AI too, even though it never learned anything at all. Why it matters When these words get mixed up, claims about AI turn into mush, because you can no longer ask the questions that matter. Those questions include which numbers inside the model were adjusted, which examples they were adjusted to match, and where the right answers came from. Asking them is how you check a claim about a model instead of taking it on trust. There is a second reason, which is that smooth, confident writing can make a program seem as if it has a mind of its own. This module shows you what is actually inside “learning”: a handful of numbers being adjusted to shrink a score for how wrong the answers are. Once you have seen that, you can separate what the math really does from things it never claims, such as having a mind. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain each of these ideas in your own words: Why AI, machine learning, deep learning and large language models are not four names for one thing, and how each one fits inside the one before it. What “learning from examples” means, broken into four parts that you will name and try for yourself. Those parts are a menu of allowed rules, a score for how wrong a rule is, a search for better numbers, and a gap that practice scores cannot show. How three families of methods differ, from rules people wrote to numbers fitted to examples to deep stacks of layers. You will also say what none of them claims, such as having a mind. Where a model’s right answers come from while it trains. They can be answers people wrote down, patterns found in data that has no answers, answers hidden inside the data itself, or a reward for how things turned out. You will also tell apart a model whose answer is a category from one whose answer is a number. What the lab lets you do The lab has six cards, and each one lets you try out a different piece of the idea for yourself: Nested methods draws the five groups as rings, one inside the next, so you can select each ring and read what it adds. Learning problem gives you three dots and a straight line with two sliders, plus a button that nudges the line toward a better fit. What the word hides cuts the word “AI” five different ways and shows you what the math does not claim. Era timeline walks through eleven moments from 1956 to 2022, and for each one it names the big idea and the reason that idea stalled. Sort leftover terms asks you to place five kinds of systems in the smallest ring that still fits each of them. What is the learning signal asks you to sort eight training situations by where their right answers come from. Almost everything on these cards was written by hand for teaching, including the three dots, the eras, the scenarios and the correct answers. The one thing the lab really works out as you go is the line fit, where the score and the downhill steps come from actual arithmetic.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · What AI actually is
documents.body: Five rings, one inside the next Think about how a mailing address works: your home is on a street, the street is in a town, and the town is in a country. Your home is in all of those places at once, but the most useful part of the address is the smallest one, because it says the most. The Nested methods card draws AI in the same way, as five rings nested one inside the next, and here is what each ring adds from the outside in: AI, short for artificial intelligence, is the outer ring, and it names a goal rather than one particular method. That goal is getting a machine to do a task that used to need human judgment, so even a list of written rules can count. ML, short for machine learning, is the part of AI where nobody writes the rule by hand. Instead, the method keeps adjusting some numbers to fit a set of examples. Often that means making its answers match the answers the examples came with, but it can also mean grouping similar examples together. DL, short for deep learning, is the part of machine learning that stacks many layers of adjustable steps, so later layers can build on what earlier ones picked out. Gen stands for generative models, which are trained to produce new samples, meaning new text, pictures or sounds that resemble the examples they learned from. In this lab, the Gen ring holds only the generative models that are also deep learning models. LLM, short for large language model, is the innermost ring, a generative model trained to predict the next token. A token is a small piece of text, such as a whole word or part of a word. A layer in the deep learning ring is one step that turns a list of numbers into a new list of numbers, using adjustable numbers of its own. To see why that helps, think about a photo, which reaches a computer as a long list of numbers. Each number gives the brightness of one tiny colored dot in the photo, called a pixel. In a model that sorts photos, the first layer might turn those numbers into a list that marks where the edges are. The next layer might combine edges into shapes such as circles and corners, and a later one might combine shapes into something like an eye or a wheel. Nobody tells the layers to look for edges. Training adjusts their numbers, and looking for edges turns out to help. The lab also calls these stacked-layer models neural networks, or neural nets for short, which is why it describes the Gen ring as holding neural generative models. On its own, an LLM is not yet the chat assistant you talk to, because people train it further afterward so that it answers in a helpful style. That is why the lab’s note for the LLM ring says assistant behavior is added later. One product, several rings Because the rings nest, one product can sit in several of them at once, the same way your home is in your street and in your country. A next-token chat assistant is an LLM, so it is also generative, deep learning, machine learning and AI, all at the same time. The smallest ring that still holds a method is called its tightest ring, and it is the ring that tells you the most about how the method works. Here are the five systems the lab asks you to sort, with the tightest ring for each one: Hand-written chess rules belong in AI and nowhere smaller, because a person wrote every rule and nothing was fitted from examples. Linear regression on house prices belongs in ML, because it fits a straight-line rule to past sales, much like the line you will fit below. It has no stack of layers, though, so it is not deep. The Convolutional image classifier belongs in DL. A classifier sorts things into categories, here photos into labels such as cat or dog. “Convolutional” means its stacked layers slide small learned filters across the photo, each one looking for a pattern such as an edge or a stripe. It labels pictures rather than making new ones, so it is not generative. A GAN that samples faces belongs in Gen. GAN is short for generative adversarial network, a deep learning model that learns to draw new pictures, and this one draws faces. It is not an LLM, though, because it never predicts the next token of text. A next-token chat assistant belongs in LLM, because predicting the next token is its training job, and the assistant style comes from further training added afterward. Where the rings stop matching The address picture works because every street lies inside exactly one town, and every town lies inside exactly one country. Now think about a label such as “by the sea”, which is true of some towns in one country and some towns in another. You cannot draw “by the sea” as one ring inside a single country, because the label cuts straight across the borders. The word “generative” cuts across the rings in the same way, and an older method called an n-gram shows why. An n-gram counts which words tend to follow which, and then picks each next word from those counts. Those counts are numbers it gets from example text rather than rules a person wrote, so it belongs in machine learning. It makes new text, so it is generative, but it has no stack of layers, so it is not deep learning. The Gen ring sits entirely inside DL, so putting the n-gram there would wrongly claim that it is deep. Instead, the lab marks the n-gram with a small dot inside the ML ring and outside the DL ring, and a note under the rings explains why. The rings are a common way to describe today’s methods, then, and not a law of nature. Learning from examples, with one straight line In science class you may have drawn a line of best fit, which is the straight line that passes as close as it can to some plotted dots. Machine learning does the same job, but instead of judging by eye, it scores how wrong the line is and then searches for a better score. The Learning problem card gives you three dots, at (0.5, 1.4), (1.5, 2.1) and (2.5, 3.2). Each dot is one example, made of an input x and its right answer y, and you fit them with a straight line written as ŷ = wx + b. Here ŷ, read “y-hat”, is the line’s guess for y, so the line does well when ŷ comes out close to y. In math class you may have seen this written as y = mx + b, where m is the slope. Here the slope is called w, the weight, and the height of the line where x is 0 is called b, the bias. This use of “bias” only means a starting height, and it has nothing to do with the unfair kind of bias you will meet later. You set these two numbers with the sliders labeled Weight w and Bias b, and the line on the left-hand plot moves as you drag them. The menu of allowed rules Every line those two sliders can draw is one possible rule, and the full set of them is called the hypothesis class. A hypothesis here is one guess about the rule, so the hypothesis class is the menu of every rule the method is allowed to pick. On this card the menu is every straight line, which means no setting of the sliders can ever bend the line into a curve. A different menu, such as curves or a tree of yes-or-no questions, would be a different search with different possible answers. Scoring a line To score a line, you first measure how far it misses each dot, which is ŷ − y, the line’s guess minus the right answer. The lab calls this miss a residual, and it draws each one as a short vertical stroke from the dot up or down to the line. Then you square each miss, which makes every miss positive and makes a big miss count far more than a small one. A miss of 2 becomes 4, while a miss of 1 stays 1, so the bigger miss now counts four times as much instead of twice. The average of the three squared misses is the loss, written L. This kind of loss is called the mean squared error, or MSE for short, and “mean” is another word for average. The card draws each squared miss as a shaded square beside its dot, so L is the average area of those three squares. A smaller L means the line fits these three dots better, and a perfect fit would make L zero. Under the plots, a table has one row for each dot. It lists the dot’s x, its right answer y, the line’s guess ŷ, the miss ŷ − y and the squared miss, so the worked example below matches its rows. Here is the score worked out for the line the card starts with, where w is 1.00 and b is 0.90: For the first dot, at x = 0.5, the line’s guess is 1 × 0.5 + 0.9, which works out to 1.4. That matches the right answer of 1.4 exactly, so this miss is 0 and so is its square. For the second dot, at x = 1.5, the line guesses 2.4, but the right answer is only 2.1. That is a miss of 0.3, and squaring it gives 0.09, which is the area of the second shaded square. For the third dot, at x = 2.5, the line guesses 3.4, but the right answer is 3.2. That is a miss of 0.2, and squaring it gives 0.04, a smaller square than the second one. Adding up the three squares gives 0.13, and dividing by 3 gives about 0.043, which is the L the card shows when it opens. Model, training and inference The two numbers w and b are the line’s parameters, which are the numbers inside a rule that training sets from data. This line has only two parameters, while a large language model has billions of them, but the idea is the same. A model is the rule with its parameters fixed, so that every input x gets exactly one answer ŷ. Training is the search that picks the parameters by shrinking the loss on examples. Inference is using the finished rule on a new input, while its numbers stay fixed. For example, suppose training settled on the best line, which you will meet below, where w is 0.90 and b is about 0.88. If you then asked that line about a new input of 2, it would answer about 2.68, and asking would not change w or b at all. In math, a rule that turns each input into exactly one output is called a function, so a model is a function with its numbers set. Searching for numbers that make a function’s answers land close to the right answers is called function approximation. Most of modern AI is this kind of search, and none of it is a model of a mind. A setting you choose before the search starts, which training never changes, is called a hyperparameter. On this card the step size of 0.12 is a hyperparameter, and it sets how far each downhill step moves, as you will see shortly. The map seen from above The right-hand plot, labeled “Parameter space · every point is a line”, shows the same search from above. Each spot on this map is one pair of numbers, with w across and b up, so each spot stands for one whole line on the left-hand plot. A filled dot on this map shows where your current line sits, like a “you are here” pin on a mall map. It moves whenever you drag a slider or press the downhill button. This you-are-here dot is a different thing from the three data dots on the left-hand plot. Now imagine working out L for every spot and treating it as a height, like the height of the ground on a map. You would get a bowl-shaped valley, high at the edges where the lines miss badly and low in the middle where they fit well. The map draws that valley the way a hiking map shows hills and valleys, using contour lines. Each oval line joins all the spots that share the same L, and the number printed on it tells you that L. The green × marks the bottom of the bowl, which is the best line these three dots allow, at w = 0.90 and b ≈ 0.88. The Minimum L readout shows that this best line still has a loss of about 0.0089, which is small but not zero. Even the best line misses a little, because the three dots do not lie on one straight line. Walking downhill Picture standing on a hillside in thick fog, where you cannot see the bottom of the valley but can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. You take a small step downhill, feel the slope again, and repeat, and the Take a downhill step button does exactly that on the map. The two readouts ∂L/∂w and ∂L/∂b are the slopes under your feet, one for each parameter. You can read ∂L/∂w as “how fast L changes when you nudge w up a tiny bit”. If it is negative, raising w lowers L, so the step raises w, and if it is positive, the step lowers w instead. Together the two slopes are called the gradient, which the lab writes as ∇L. The Optimization stage of the card prints the rule for one step as θ ← θ − η ∇L. Here θ, the Greek letter theta, is a short way to write both parameters at once, and η, the letter eta, stands for the step size of 0.12. The arrow means “becomes”, so in words, each parameter becomes its old value minus 0.12 times its own slope. That moves it downhill as long as the step size is small enough, and 0.12 is small enough for this bowl. With too big a step size, a step could jump right past the bottom and land higher up the other side. Here is one step worked out, starting from the flat line where w is 0 and b is 0: That line lies along the bottom of the graph and misses all three dots badly, so L reads about 5.54. The slope ∂L/∂w reads −7.900, and because it is negative and large, raising w would lower L quickly. The step changes w to 0 − 0.12 × (−7.9), and since subtracting a negative number adds, that comes to about 0.95. The ∂L/∂b readout shows about −4.47, so the same rule gives b = 0 − 0.12 × (−4.47), which comes to about 0.54. With this new line, L drops to about 0.086, so a single press has taken the you-are-here dot most of the way down the bowl. The step is set by a formula rather than by guessing, and this nudge of two numbers is the whole of what “learning” means on this card. The fog picture stops matching in one way, because this card can draw the whole map for you. That works only because there are two numbers, one for across and one for up. A model with billions of numbers would need a map with billions of directions, which nobody can draw or fill in. Real training therefore feels its way by the slopes alone, just like the hiker in the fog. Practice scores and new examples Picture a friend who memorizes the answer key to a practice quiz, all ten answers in order. On that exact quiz they score perfectly, but the moment the teacher swaps in new questions, the memorized answers are no help at all. A model can fall into the same trap, which is why the score that really matters is how it does on examples it has never seen. Doing well on new examples that come from the same source as the training examples is called generalization. The difference between how a model does on its training examples and how it does on new ones is the generalization gap. The Learning problem card names this gap in its Generalization stage, but it never tests a fourth dot, so the gap is never measured. A small L tells you the line fits these three dots, but it does not tell you how far off the line would be at a new x. A wigglier menu of rules could even pass exactly through all three dots and still be badly wrong at a fourth one. A later lab, How we know a model works, measures the gap by scoring examples the fit never saw. Three families of methods Picture two friends who both want to sort apples into fresh ones and bruised ones, each in their own way. The first writes a list of rules, such as “if there is a soft brown spot bigger than a coin, the apple is bruised”. The second studies hundreds of apples someone has already sorted, measures a few things about each one, and keeps adjusting some numbers until the sorting matches. Those two friends are using two of the three families of methods that What the word hides names when Distinction is set to family: Symbolic methods use rules, search or logic that a person wrote, so the decision is written down rather than fitted from examples. There are no parameters to learn, which makes these methods AI but not machine learning. Statistical ML methods (statistical here means working out numbers from many examples) start with features. Features are the measurable things a person chooses to look at, such as an apple’s color or a house’s floor area. The method then fits its numbers so its answers match examples that already carry the right answer, and linear regression belongs to this family. Deep learning methods fit a whole stack of layers, so they learn which features to look at and how to combine them, both at once. They can start from raw inputs, such as the pixels of a photo, the way the photo-sorting layers did earlier. All three families count as AI, but only the last two are machine learning, because only they fit numbers from examples. Rule-based methods did not disappear when fitting took over, either. A spelling checker or a route planner built from written rules is still AI, with no learned numbers at all. What the word does not claim Setting Distinction to not shows three tiles, called Not consciousness, Not folk understanding and Not a verdict on use. Nothing in the line, the loss or the downhill steps stands for feelings or awareness, so fitting numbers is not the same as being conscious. Folk understanding means the everyday kind of understanding a person has, and matching the answers on some examples does not show that kind of grasp. Finally, a well-fitted model can still be the wrong tool, trained on the wrong answers, or unsafe to use. The other settings come at the same point from different sides, and each one is easier to see with an example. Under scope, a chat assistant looks general because you can ask it about almost anything in words. A spam filter, by contrast, only ever answers one question about emails. The assistant is still a next-token predictor, though, with further training added on top to give it an assistant style. Under job, predicting is kept apart from reasoning. Predicting means giving one quick answer, such as guessing the next word. Reasoning means working through steps, like a chess program that tries several moves ahead and checks where each one leads. A predictor can be one part of that search, for instance by scoring each board position it reaches, but the predictor alone is not the search. The same setting warns that a smooth answer can read like a careful argument without anything having been proved. Sounding sure is not the same as checking the work, the way a confident classmate’s answer still needs checking. A fluent paragraph may only be blending patterns from the text the model learned from. Under memory, fitting the training examples is kept apart from working on new ones, which is the generalization gap from earlier. The answer-key friend fits the practice quiz perfectly, and that says nothing about the next quiz. AGI, artificial general intelligence, is a word for a system that could do any thinking task a person can. People define it in different ways and there is no agreed test for it, so it is a goal rather than something anyone has measured. Nothing in these labs claims it, and fluent text is not evidence of it. Before the neural thread The Era timeline starts before neural nets, with a proposal written in 1955 by four researchers: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon. They asked for a two-month summer study of artificial intelligence at Dartmouth College, and that workshop is the timeline’s first stop, in 1956. Their bet was that any feature of intelligence could be described precisely enough for a machine to copy it. The proposal listed seven open problems and hoped for a big step forward on one or more of them within a single summer. It named problems rather than a method for solving them, which is why the timeline counts it as a stall. Then came two AI winters, which is the name for long stretches when money and interest for AI research dried up. In 1973 Sir James Lighthill, a British scientist, wrote a review of AI for a UK research council. He reported that in no part of the field had discoveries made the big impact that had been promised. Funding fell after his report, and the first AI winter lasted from roughly 1974 to 1980. The timeline’s Why it stalled note for that 1974 stop gives the deeper reason. Methods that worked on small, tidy problems, such as puzzles with a few fixed pieces, did not grow to handle realistic ones. A realistic problem needed so much detailed knowledge that nobody could type it all in by hand. Next came expert systems, which stored a specialist’s knowledge as written rules shaped like “if this is true, then do that”. One of them, XCON, helped the computer maker Digital Equipment Corporation fill orders, and it was first used in 1980. Its knowledge was written rather than fitted, so it was AI without being machine learning. Picture a help desk that answers every question from a binder of written rules, where each new product means new rules. Each new rule can clash with an old one, so keeping the binder correct takes more and more work as it grows. Expert systems ran into that kind of problem, because they cost too much to keep up to date and broke on cases their authors had not foreseen. Lisp machines were special computers built to run AI programs written in a programming language called Lisp. By 1987 cheaper ordinary computers could do the same job, so the market for Lisp machines collapsed. That collapse, along with the cost of keeping rule binders up to date, began a second AI winter. Both winter dates are approximate, so read them as rough landmarks rather than exact start and end points. The neural thread The other seven stops on the timeline follow neural nets, the family of models that grew into the stacked layers of the DL ring. These stops are mixed in by year with the rule-based ones, and each has its own stall. 1958, Perceptron. The perceptron was a single layer of numbers learned from labeled examples, much like your line. It said yes or no by drawing one straight boundary between the two kinds of example. Its stall was XOR, a rule that says yes when exactly one of two switches is on. Draw the four on/off combinations of the two switches as the corners of a square. XOR’s two yes cases then sit in opposite corners, so no single straight line can split them from the two no cases. 1969, Perceptrons critique. A book called Perceptrons, by Minsky and Papert, proved what a single layer cannot work out, with XOR among them. Money and attention then moved away from neural nets to rule lists and search for over a decade. 1986, Backpropagation. Three researchers showed how to train a stack of layers by sending the slopes backward from the loss through each layer. A stack can handle XOR, but there was not yet enough computing power or labeled data for deep nets to win. 1997, LSTM memory. An LSTM, short for long short-term memory, carried information along a text from one word to the next. It read one piece at a time, though, so training could not work on a whole text at once, and very distant words still faded. 2012, AlexNet. A deep network called AlexNet won a big photo-sorting contest by a wide margin. It was trained on about 1.2 million labeled photos, using two graphics chips, the kind of chip built to draw video-game scenes fast. Its stall was that each new task still needed its own big labeled set and its own design. 2017, Transformer. A transformer uses attention, which lets every word in a text look at every other word at the same time. Its cost grows with the square of the text’s length, though, so doubling the length makes that cost about four times as large. 2022, Assistants. Extra training, including feedback from people, turned next-token models into tools that people can talk to. Fluent text is still not a check on whether something is true. Where the right answers come from When a model trains, something has to tell it how it is doing, and whatever supplies the right answers or the score is called the learning signal. With no answers at all, the score can measure how well the model describes the patterns in the data. Four signals cover most of this course, and the What is the learning signal card shows them as four tiles, one for each signal. Supervised: answers from people Picture a workbook where a teacher has already written the correct answer beside every question. In supervised learning, each example comes with its answer, called a label, which a person wrote down or which was kept in a record. The model is then scored against those labels, so it gets better by matching them more closely. The House sale prices scenario is supervised, because every sale record already lists the price the house sold for. Spam emails are supervised too, because people marked each email as spam or not spam. The three dots on the Learning problem card are also supervised, since each y is the label for its x. Because the labels decide what counts as correct, a biased set of labels makes a biased rule. If the people marking emails kept marking one harmless newsletter as spam, for example, the model would learn to do the same. Semi-supervised learning is the same idea when only some of the examples carry labels and the rest do not. Unsupervised: patterns with no answers Picture tipping a jar of mixed buttons onto a table and grouping them by size and color, with no list saying which groups are right. Now think of the data as a table with one row for each example: supervised data has a column holding the answers, and unsupervised data has no such column. In unsupervised learning, then, the model looks for structure in the inputs themselves, such as which records sit close together or which readings are far from the usual pattern. The Customer records scenario groups customers by similar behavior, and the Sensor readings scenario flags readings that look unusual. The k-means method in the Classical machine learning lab works this way, grouping records without ever reading a label. Because there is no answer to check against, a person still has to decide whether the groups mean anything useful. Self-supervised: answers hidden in the data Picture playing fill-in-the-blank with a book: you cover the next word, guess it, then uncover it to check. The book is its own answer key, so nobody has to write any answers for you. In self-supervised learning, part of the data is hidden and the model has to restore it, so the hidden part becomes the label. In the Raw sentences scenario, the next word of each sentence is the label, and it is already sitting in the text. In the Blanked-out photos scenario, the label is the hidden patch of pixels, which were part of the original photo all along. The model still trains against labels, but nobody has to write them, so the practice set can be as big as the raw pile of data. That is how language models can train on far more text than any team of people could ever label by hand. Reinforcement: a reward after acting Picture a friend learning a new video game with no tutorial, where the only feedback is a “You win” or “Game over” screen at the very end. They have to work out for themselves which of their earlier moves actually earned the win. In reinforcement learning, no example ever shows the right move, so the learner acts first and receives a reward or a penalty afterward. It then has to work out which earlier choices earned that reward, much like the friend with the game. In the Charger robot scenario, for instance, the robot gets +1 for reaching its charger and −1 for bumping into a wall. A reward scores how things turned out rather than labeling each step, and it often arrives late and only now and then. That makes this signal harder to train with than labeled pairs, where every example has its own answer. The Reinforcement learning foundations lab runs it later, and the Post-training lab shows how assistants are tuned with rewards based on which answers people preferred. Two kinds of answer What kind of answer a model gives is a separate question from where its right answers came from during training. Classification means the model picks one category from a fixed set, such as spam or not spam. Regression means the model gives a number on a scale, such as a house price, so the line you fit on the Learning problem card is regression too. The answer to one question does not decide the answer to the other, which the two self-supervised scenarios show. Predicting the next token is classification, because the model picks one token from its vocabulary, the fixed list of every token it knows. The card describes this with whole words, which keeps the example simple without changing the idea. Repairing a blanked photo is regression, because the answer is a number for each hidden pixel, so the two share a signal but not a kind of answer. The card’s Output type readout names the kind of answer for each scenario, and it has two more options besides these. It reads “no target” for the unsupervised scenarios, because they predict no answer, and “an action” for the reinforcement ones, because their output is a move.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · What AI actually is
documents.body: This is where the guide starts, and every later lab uses these words as exact mechanisms rather than as labels on a box. Suppose someone tells you that “the AI learned to spot bad reviews”, which sounds clear until you try to check it. To test that claim, you need to know which menu of rules was searched, which loss was shrunk, on which examples, and with which learning signal. If “AI”, “machine learning” and “chatbot” stay interchangeable, there is nothing definite left to check. The line fit sits beside the rings so that “learns from examples” becomes something you can move with your own hands. Two sliders, a score and a button make up the entire learning process on that card, so nothing important is hidden behind the word. The timeline sits beside both so that history reads as a series of stalls rather than a parade of winners. Each era hit a limit that a later idea had to work around, and the stalls make a chain, listed here by year: A goal with no method yet, at Dartmouth in 1956. A single straight boundary that cannot handle XOR, from 1958 to 1969. Results that did not grow from tidy problems to realistic ones, which led to the first winter in 1974. Rule binders too costly to keep up to date, from the 1980 expert systems on, which led to the second winter in 1987. Too little computing power and labeled data for stacked layers, after 1986. Reading one word at a time, which made LSTM training slow from 1997. A new labeled set and a new design for every task, even after AlexNet in 2012. Attention whose cost grows with the square of the text’s length, from 2017. Fluent assistants whose words are still not a check on truth, in 2022. Each link in that chain explains why the next idea mattered. Stacking layers got past XOR. Graphics chips and big labeled sets got past the shortage of computing power and labeled data, and attention got past reading one word at a time. The learning-signal sort is here because the four signals decide where a model’s right answers come from, and the course keeps using their names. The Classical machine learning, Next-token prediction and Post-training labs each lean on a different signal, so knowing which is which now saves confusion later.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · What AI actually is
documents.body: Inspect the rings On Nested methods, use Inspected method, or click a circle or a row of the key, and read what that ring actually learns. Select AI first and then LLM, and watch the note under the rings narrow from a broad goal down to next-token prediction. Then find the small n-gram dot, and say which rings it sits inside and which ones it stays outside. Fit a line by hand Try this: On Learning problem, set Weight w to 0 and Bias b to 0, which lays the line flat along the bottom of the graph. The L MSE readout now shows about 5.54, because the line misses every dot badly. Press Take a downhill step a few times, and watch three things change together: On the left, the three shaded squares shrink as the line swings up toward the dots. On the right, the you-are-here dot walks down across the contour lines toward the green ×, and a dotted path traces its recent steps. The path keeps only about the last 30 steps, so if you press many times, the oldest ones drop off the start of it. Below the plots, ∂L/∂w shrinks toward zero as the ground flattens out near the valley floor. The first press drops L to about 0.086, and the second press brings it down to about 0.027. After that each press helps only a little, because the slopes are now gentle and each step is 0.12 times a small slope. If you keep pressing, something surprising happens. After the third press, ∂L/∂w turns slightly positive. The line is now a bit too steep for how low it sits, because b is still only about 0.62 instead of 0.88. So this slope says to lower w a little, while b keeps rising. From then on the dot creeps slowly along the bottom of a long, narrow valley toward the ×, and reaching it takes dozens of presses. Next, drag one of the sliders yourself and watch the you-are-here dot jump to a new spot on the map. Dragging starts a fresh dotted path, because the path records only presses of the downhill button. The Learning object row above the sliders has five stages: Data, Hypothesis class, Loss, Optimization and Generalization. Click each stage to read a short paragraph about that piece, and notice that clicking changes only the paragraph, not the arithmetic. The formula row lower down, Hypothesis and empirical loss, prints the current line and the three squared misses, so you can check one against the table by hand. “Empirical” means measured on the actual examples in front of you. Cut the word five ways On What the word hides, set Distinction to family and read the three tiles, then switch it to not and compare. The first setting names families of methods, while the second refuses extra claims about minds and understanding. Then try scope, job and memory, and for each one, find the idea from this lesson that its tiles match. Scrub the timeline Move Era from 1956 to 2022 one stop at a time, reading the Idea note and the Why it stalled note before you move on. Stop on 1980, Expert systems, and notice that this stop is AI with nothing fitted at all. Then compare it with 2012, the AlexNet stop, and read what held each of them back. Sort the leftovers On Sort leftover terms, select Hand-written chess rules in the Leftover terms list, and notice that it is marked Unplaced. Set Place in ring to AI and press the Place button, which names the term you selected. Then select Linear regression on house prices, place it in DL, read the correction in the note, and place it again in ML. A guess in an outer ring still counts as wrong here, because the card scores only the tightest ring. The Placed readout counts how many of the five terms you have placed so far, and Tightest-ring matches counts the correct ones. Nesting depth shows how many rings deep the right answer sits. Sort the learning signals Last, open What is the learning signal and select Raw sentences in the Learning scenarios list. Set Learning signal to supervised and press Place to read the correction, then set it to self-supervised and place it again. Now select Blanked-out photos and compare its Output type with the one for Raw sentences, since they share a signal but not a kind of answer. Finish by placing Customer records and the Charger robot, and read what Output type says for each of them.

documents.subtitle: Plain · What AI actually is
documents.body: The same product can sit in several rings at once, because an assistant is an LLM, which is a generative model, which is deep learning. A spelling checker built from written rules can be AI without being machine learning, because nobody fitted it from examples. The table, the shaded squares and L all come from the same three squared misses, so they always agree with each other. The downhill button moves the line using the slopes printed in the readouts, not some separate trick. The first downhill step from the flat line covers most of the distance, and later steps shrink because each is sized by a slope that flattens. Every era has a stall, and even the 2022 stop is still next-token prediction plus later training, not a claim that the field is solved. The n-gram dot sits in ML and outside DL, because it is generative without being deep, so it cannot sit inside the Gen ring. The Expert systems stop is AI with nothing fitted, and both winters followed results that did not scale or methods that cost too much to keep up. Raw sentences and Blanked-out photos are both self-supervised, yet one answer is a category and the other is a number. Customer records and Sensor readings have no answer column, so their Output type reads no target. Placing Raw sentences under supervised draws a correction, because the next word is already in the text and no person had to label it.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · What AI actually is
documents.body: What this lab simplifies or makes up The five rings, their captions and the position of the n-gram dot were written by hand for this lab, so nothing on the card sorts a real product. The eleven eras were written for the timeline card, and their dates, including the approximate winter dates, are landmarks rather than a complete history. The timeline follows only two threads, rule-based AI and neural nets, and no model from any era is actually trained on the card. The five leftovers and the eight learning-signal scenarios were written by hand too, and each one has a single best answer chosen by the card. A wrong placement is corrected by looking up a table, not by a model that judges your answer. The three dots were chosen by hand and the card never tests a fourth one, so the generalization gap is named but never measured. The downhill step is one small update to a two-number line with one fixed step size, and each slider stops its number at the edge of its range. The slopes come from a formula written by hand for this one line, rather than from the automatic method that real training uses for any model. The tiles under Distinction are written explanations, so no system on the card is scored as conscious, general or understanding. Where the real ideas break Product descriptions still blur these words together, and a chatbot demo does not make every method underneath it accurate or safe. Real products also mix methods, so a search tool plus an LLM plus a rule-based filter is still three different rings working side by side. Labels still decide what counts as correct in supervised learning, so biased labels still make a biased rule. A tiny training loss still does not mean the rule works on new cases, because the generalization gap has to be measured separately. Real training uses the same parts you met here: a menu of rules, a loss, a search, and a hope that the result generalizes. The differences are that it uses billions of numbers instead of two, and often a loss that is not squared error. The learning signals blend in real systems, too, so one product is not one box. A chat assistant is first trained self-supervised on raw text and then tuned on answers that people wrote. After that, it is trained further with rewards based on which of its answers people preferred. History is messier than any timeline, because a method can stall for lack of money, data or computing power, or because of a hard mathematical limit. A newer idea also does not erase an older problem, and fluent text is still not a check on truth. AGI still has no agreed test, so no lab here can say that a system has reached it. A common mix-up: people often treat a chat assistant as the definition of AI, or treat a low training loss as a sign of understanding. A large language model is one generative method deep inside the rings, and a low L on the training sample is a fit, not a mind. People also read “unsupervised” as “no human involved”, and “self-supervised” as another word for “unsupervised”, but neither reading is right. Unsupervised learning has no target at all, while self-supervised learning still trains against labels that come free from the data itself. A person is still involved in unsupervised learning, too, because someone has to decide whether the groups it finds mean anything.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · What AI actually is
documents.body: The slopes, written out The slopes on the Learning problem card come from exact formulas rather than from trial and error. The slope ∂L/∂b is the average of 2 × (ŷ − y) over the three dots, and ∂L/∂w is the average of 2 × (ŷ − y) × x. At w = 0 and b = 0, the three misses are −1.4, −2.1 and −3.2, which add up to −6.7. Doubling that gives −13.4, and dividing by 3 gives about −4.467, which matches the ∂L/∂b readout at that spot. Each guess wx + b changes in a straight-line way as you change w or b, and L adds up the squares of those misses. Together, those two facts make this L an exact bowl with one smooth bottom, and every contour line is an oval. Squared error on a deep network does not give such a simple bowl, because its guesses do not change in a straight-line way. The exact bottom is the line w = 0.90 and b ≈ 0.883, and it is called the least-squares line. No other straight line gives a smaller mean squared error on these three dots, which is why the legend labels the green × as the least-squares bottom. Other settings you will meet The step size of 0.12 is the hyperparameter this card names, and later labs add others. Two of them are the batch size, meaning how many examples each step looks at, and the epoch count, meaning how many times training passes through the data. Sources for the early stops The early stops follow the Dartmouth proposal, which was reprinted in AI Magazine in 2006, and the Wikipedia articles on the Lighthill report, on AI winters and on XCON. Where to go next The math you need opens the arithmetic these methods share, which is lists of numbers, slopes and probabilities. Classical machine learning runs k-means with no labels, Next-token prediction trains on answers the text supplies itself, and Reinforcement learning foundations trains from reward. Tokens & embeddings then shows the numbers an LLM actually reads in place of words. Why GPUs explains how graphics chips gave deep nets the computing power they had lacked, around 2012. The architecture zoo explains why attention replaced models that read one step at a time.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · What AI actually is
documents.body: The word AI is applied to a hand-written rule list, a fitted line, and a chat assistant alike. This module gives it structure. Artificial intelligence names a goal. In the vocabulary this course uses, machine learning, deep learning, neural generative models, and large language models (LLMs) are nested methods inside it, drawn as rings in the lab, each with its own mathematical object. The question it answers: when a system is called AI, what was fitted, from which training signal, and what does the label not claim? The module has no prerequisites. It fixes the vocabulary that later labs keep using, starting with parameters θ: the numbers a method fits from examples, as opposed to rules someone writes. Where it shows up A chat assistant sits in several rings at once, and its training blends three learning signals: self-supervised pretraining on raw text, supervised tuning on human-written answers, and reinforcement from rewards based on human preferences. A deployed product can wrap a fitted model in retrieval and written rules, and those parts sit in different rings. Rule-based expert systems of the 1980s, such as XCON, are AI with nothing fitted. Language-model pretraining is self-supervised: the text supplies its own labels. House-price prediction is regression; spam filtering is classification. Why it matters Each distinction blocks a specific error. Without the rings, a rule-based checker gets called machine learning, though no θ was fitted. Without the learning problem, a small training loss gets reported as if it measured error on new inputs. Without a line between what the math does and what the word suggests, fluent output gets read as understanding, reasoning, or AGI (artificial general intelligence), none of which the fitted function or its loss requires. Without the learning signal, nobody asks who defined correct, so a biased label set quietly becomes a biased rule. Without the unsupervised case, a found cluster gets trusted as if it had been scored, though with no target there is nothing to score accuracy against. Without the output-type axis, self-supervised gets confused with classification. What you will be able to explain How machine learning, deep learning, and large language models nest inside AI, and why the terms are not synonyms. The learning problem as a hypothesis class (the set of functions searched), a loss, a search over parameters, and a generalization gap, the difference between training loss and error on new inputs from the same process. How symbolic methods, statistical fitting, and deep stacks differ, and what none of those objects is: consciousness, folk understanding, or AGI. Where a model's training signal comes from (human labels, structure in raw data, labels made from the data itself, or reward), and how classification and regression differ by the kind of output. What the lab shows Six cards, and only one holds live mathematics. Learning problem searches the class of lines ŷ = wx + b to fit three fixed points under mean squared error. Weight w and Bias b set θ; Take a downhill step subtracts 0.12 times the analytic gradient. Learning object pages authored notes on five pieces, from data to generalization, and does not change the arithmetic. L MSE, ∂L/∂w, and ∂L/∂b are exact closed-form readouts of your settings; Minimum L is the fixed least-squares bottom. The points are authored, not measured, and generalization is named, not scored. The other five cards are authored content. Nested methods draws five rings plus a marker for an n-gram, a model that samples from counted word sequences and so is generative without being deep. Inspected method selects one ring and rewrites its caption. What the word hides cuts the word five ways with Distinction. Era timeline’s Era slider steps through eleven stops from 1956 to 2022. Sort leftover terms (pick from the Leftover terms list, then Place in ring and Place) and What is the learning signal (pick from the Learning scenarios list, then Learning signal and Place) check each guess by table lookup; the latter adds an Output type readout. The key experiment: set Weight w and Bias b to 0, where L MSE reads about 5.54, then press Take a downhill step several times. L falls as the dot walks down the contour map toward the least-squares bottom. Then, on What is the learning signal, place Raw sentences under supervised and read the correction.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · What AI actually is
documents.body: Artificial intelligence names a goal: perform a task that used to need judgment. Machine learning is the subset that fits parameters from examples. Deep learning stacks differentiable layers. A generative model draws new samples. A large language model predicts the next token; assistant behavior is added later. The course treats the common modern stack as nested. That is a vocabulary, not a law. A GAN is generative without being an LLM. A linear regressor is machine learning without being deep. An n-gram can be generative without being deep. Nested rings cannot draw a property that crosses a boundary, and generative crosses the deep-learning one. So the Gen ring means neural generative models only, and the diagram marks an n-gram inside ML and outside DL instead of inside Gen. Function approximation Most methods you will meet search for parameters θ so that f_θ(x) is close to a target y, or so that p_θ assigns high probability to observed data. The objects are a hypothesis class, a loss, and an optimizer. They are not a model of a mind. A model is one fixed function f_θ: with θ set, each x maps to one ŷ (or one distribution p_θ(y|x)). Here f_θ is the line wx + b and θ is the pair (w, b). Training searches for θ by lowering the loss on examples. Inference runs the finished f_θ on a new x with θ held still. A setting you choose before the search, like the 0.12 step size, is a hyperparameter. The learning problem On this page the class is every line ŷ = wx + b. Loss is mean squared error on three authored points. A downhill step subtracts 0.12 times ∂L/∂w and ∂L/∂b. Generalization — error on a new x from the same process — is named and not measured. L is exactly quadratic in (w, b), so its level sets are ellipses. The parameter-space map draws them. Its bottom is the least-squares line w = 0.90, b ≈ 0.88, with L ≈ 0.0089. Three families Symbolic AI uses written rules or search and may have no θ. Statistical machine learning chooses features, then fits θ. Deep learning fits a stack of maps, so features and predictor move together. What the word is not Nothing in f_θ or L requires consciousness or folk understanding. Prediction returns ŷ or p_θ(y|x). Reasoning, when it appears later, is search that may call a predictor. Fluency is not a proof. AGI, artificial general intelligence, names a hoped-for or feared system that could do any cognitive task a person can. People define it in different ways and there is no agreed test, so it is a goal, not a measured property. Nothing in these labs claims it, and fluency on text is not evidence of it. The early-AI thread The timeline starts before neural nets. The 1955 proposal for the Dartmouth workshop, by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester, and Shannon and reprinted in AI Magazine in 2006, proposed a two-month summer study of artificial intelligence on the conjecture that any feature of intelligence can be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it. It listed seven open problems and expected a significant advance in one summer. Sir James Lighthill's 1973 report said that in no part of the field had discoveries produced the major impact promised, and funding fell: the first AI winter, roughly 1974 to 1980. Expert systems such as XCON, first used at Digital Equipment Corporation in 1980, held knowledge as written rules, so they are AI with no parameters fitted. Their upkeep cost, and the 1987 collapse of the Lisp-machine market, mark a second winter. The early stops follow the Dartmouth proposal and the Wikipedia articles on the Lighthill report, on AI winters, and on XCON. Winter dates are approximate. Supervised: labels from people The learning signal is where a model's training target comes from, and four signals cover most of this course. A supervised model is fitted on pairs (x, y) where someone supplied y. The labels define what counts as correct, so a biased label set becomes a biased rule. The Learning problem card is supervised: its three y values are the labels. Semi-supervised learning is the same setup when only some rows carry labels and the rest do not. Unsupervised: structure without labels There is no y to match. The model looks for structure in x itself, such as records that cluster together or readings far from the usual pattern. The k-means method in Classical machine learning places centers without reading a label. With no target there is nothing to score accuracy against, so a person still has to judge whether the structure means anything. Self-supervised: labels made from the data Hide part of the data and ask the model to restore it. For text, the label at each position is the next word, which is already in the sentence. For a photo, it is the pixels of a blanked patch. The labels cost nothing, so the training set can be as large as the raw collection. That is why language models can train on far more text than anyone could annotate. Reinforcement: a reward after acting No example gives the right action. The learner acts, receives a reward or penalty afterward, and must work out which earlier choices earned it. The signal is late and sparse, so this is harder to train than labeled pairs. Reinforcement learning foundations runs it later, and Post-training uses human-preference rewards to tune assistants. Classification and regression: the kind of output The output type is a separate question from where the target comes from. Classification returns one category from a fixed set; regression returns a number. A house price is regression, and spam or not spam is classification. A language model's next-word step is classification over a vocabulary, and repairing a blanked photo is regression. So self-supervised and classification answer different questions.

documents.subtitle: Standard · What AI actually is
documents.body: Neighboring labs need those words as mechanisms. If they stay interchangeable, later claims about what was learned, generated, or merely wrapped become untestable. The line-fit sits beside the rings so “learns from examples” is a visible search over two numbers, not a slogan. The timeline sits beside both so each era is a limit: a goal with no method, results that did not scale, rule bases too costly to maintain, XOR, missing compute and data, one-step-at-a-time recurrence, quadratic attention. The learning-signal sort is here because classical methods, next-token prediction, and post-training each lean on a different signal.

documents.body: In this lab the rings, the n-gram marker, the eleven eras, leftovers, distinction tiles, and learning-signal scenarios are authored strings. The timeline shows two threads, symbolic AI and neural nets, and its dates are landmarks. The three points are authored. The optimizer is one fixed step-size with clipped sliders. No classifier runs. documents.body: The math you need is the shared arithmetic of vectors, slopes, and likelihoods. Classical machine learning runs k-means with no labels, Next-token prediction trains on labels the text supplies itself, and Reinforcement learning foundations trains from reward. documents.subtitle: Nested methods · What AI actually is
documents.body: Five rings, one nesting test, and what a ring cannot draw The common modern stack is drawn as nested rings: AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning, which contains neural generative models, which contains large language models. Each ring also names the mathematical object (a goal, a fitted f_θ, a stacked map, a distribution, a next-token model). That is a vocabulary for these labs, not a law. Generative is a property that crosses the deep-learning boundary, which nested rings cannot draw, so an n-gram is marked inside ML and outside DL rather than inside the Gen ring. A kicker that writes the common modern stack in words, a title Five rings, one nesting, and a badge with the selected ring label. Inspected method with five segments: AI, ML, DL, Gen, LLM. Five concentric circles plus a key of five sentences, one per ring, stating the mathematical claim. A small dot labelled n-gram sits in the ML ring below the deep-learning circle. Two notes: what the selected ring learns, and what the drawing cannot show, which is that the Gen ring holds neural generative models only. The rings teach the common modern stack: LLM ⊂ neural generative ⊂ deep learning ⊂ machine learning ⊂ AI. Selecting a ring only stores `ring` in module state. The caption and the key sentence are authored for that ring. No classifier, model, or dataset is evaluated. A method belongs inside another ring only when every example of the inner method is still an example of the outer one. The Gen ring is neural generative models, so it passes that test for deep learning. A generative model that is not neural, such as an n-gram that samples from counted word pairs, fails it, which is why the marker sits outside DL. Inspected method, a click on a circle, or a click on a key row sets the inspected ring. Comparison worth running: select AI, then LLM, and notice the caption narrows from a goal to next-token prediction. Then look for the n-gram dot and say which ring it is in. The same product can sit in several rings at once: an assistant is an LLM, which is a neural generative model, which is deep learning. A rule-based checker can be AI without being machine learning, because nobody fitted it from examples. The n-gram is generative and not deep, so no single ring can hold it and also mean generative. In this lab: the five rings, their captions, and the position of the n-gram marker are authored. Nothing here classifies a shipped system, and the diagram does not draw every generative or non-deep method. In general: product copy still collapses these words. A chatbot demo does not make every method underneath it true or safe, and AGI, the hoped-for system that could do any cognitive task, is not one of the rings.

documents.subtitle: Learning problem · What AI actually is
documents.body: Search θ so f_θ(x) matches y on data Three authored points and the hypothesis class of all lines ŷ = wx + b. Loss is mean squared error on those three points. The sliders choose θ, which is one line in data space and one point in parameter space; Take a downhill step subtracts 0.12 times the closed-form gradient of that same MSE. Generalization is named and not measured. Learning object, a five-stage flow — Data, Hypothesis class, Loss, Optimization, Generalization — with each stage's formula under its name. Clicking a stage rewrites the paragraph below it. Sliders Weight w and Bias b and a Take a downhill step button. Data space: the three points, the current line, a vertical residual at each point, and a shaded square on each residual whose area is proportional to (ŷ − y)². Parameter space: contour ellipses of equal L over w from 0 to 2 and b from 0 to 2.4, each labelled with its L; the current (w, b) as a dot; an arrow to where the next downhill step lands; a dotted path of the steps taken; and a green × at the least-squares bottom. A five-column table of x, y, ŷ, residual, and square, metrics L MSE, ∂L/∂w, ∂L/∂b, and Minimum L (the least-squares bottom), and a formula row that reprints the current line and the three squared residuals. The points are (0.5, 1.4), (1.5, 2.1), (2.5, 3.2). Prediction is ŷ = w x + b. L = mean (ŷ − y)². ∂L/∂w = mean 2(ŷ − y)x and ∂L/∂b = mean 2(ŷ − y). Take a downhill step writes w ← clip(w − 0.12 ∂L/∂w) and b ← clip(b − 0.12 ∂L/∂b). Clips are the slider ranges, not a production optimizer. L is exactly quadratic in (w, b): L = L* + dᵀA d with d = θ − θ* and A = (1/3)[[Σx², Σx], [Σx, 3]]. So every contour is an ellipse, sampled from that formula. The bottom θ* is the least-squares line w = 0.90, b ≈ 0.883, where L* ≈ 0.0089. Learning object only changes which authored paragraph you read. It does not change the arithmetic. Weight w, Bias b, Take a downhill step, and the Learning object stages. Comparison worth running: set w to 0 and b to 0, read L ≈ 5.54, then press Take a downhill step a few times. The squares shrink in data space while the dot walks down the contours toward the green ×. The search is over two numbers. No extra variable stands for understanding or consciousness. A small L on these three points is a fit to the sample. A fourth x is not scored here. In this lab: three authored points, one affine hypothesis class, and an analytic gradient of MSE. There is no held-out point and no automatic differentiation. The path of steps is view state; dragging a slider starts a new one. In general: modern training uses the same objects — H, L, an optimizer, a hope of generalization — in far more dimensions, with a loss that may not be squared error.
