documents.subtitle: What the word hides · What AI actually is
documents.body: Five cuts through the same word Distinction chooses family, scope, job, memory, or not. Each cut is three authored tiles. The card does not classify a product; it names a confusion the rings alone cannot. Distinction, a five-way segmented control whose values are family, scope, job, memory, and not. A title sentence for the cut and a three-tile grid. A note that states the limit of that cut. State stores `distinction` as one of five literals. The tiles are authored strings for that literal. Family separates symbolic rules, statistical fitting, and stacked differentiable maps. Scope separates a single-task map from a wide interface. Job separates p_θ(y|x) from search that may call a predictor. Memory separates training-set interpolation from error on new draws. Not names claims the math does not make. Distinction is the only control. Comparison worth running: family versus not. One names methods; the other refuses extra claims. AGI, artificial general intelligence, names a system that could do any cognitive task a person can. It is a goal that people define differently, not a measured property, so the scope cut treats it as something these labs never claim. Symbolic AI still counts as AI. It fails the machine-learning subset test because no θ was fitted. A fluent continuation can look like reasoning and still be next-token prediction. In this lab: five authored cuts and three tiles each. No system is scored as conscious, general, or understanding; the scope cut defines AGI as a goal with no agreed test and does not claim any system reaches it. In general: a deployed stack can mix a rule filter, a fitted ranker, and a generative model. Each piece still belongs to one of these cuts.
documents.title: Five cuts through the same word

documents.subtitle: Era timeline · What AI actually is
documents.body: Eleven stops, each with a stall Era is a stop on a timeline from the 1956 Dartmouth workshop to 2022 assistants. Each stop names the key idea of that moment and the reason it stopped being enough, so history reads as a sequence of limits rather than a victory lap. The early stops are the symbolic thread: the Dartmouth proposal, expert systems, and the two AI winters. A kicker `YEAR · title` and the heading What changed, and why it stalled. Era, a slider whose output prints the year and the stop's name. Two metrics: Year and Key idea. Two notes: Idea and Why it stalled, both authored for that stop. The slider stores the stop's year, one of 1956, 1958, 1969, 1974, 1980, 1986, 1987, 1997, 2012, 2017, or 2022. They are the Dartmouth workshop, the perceptron, the Perceptrons critique, the first AI winter, expert systems, backpropagation, the second AI winter, LSTM, AlexNet, the transformer, and assistants. Each stop is a pair of sentences written for this card. No archive, paper, or training run is loaded. Early facts follow named sources: the 1955 Dartmouth proposal by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester, and Shannon, reprinted in AI Magazine 27(4), 2006; the Wikipedia articles on the Lighthill report and on AI winters, which cite Lighthill's 1973 report and the 1987 collapse of the Lisp-machine market; and the Wikipedia article on XCON, which cites McDermott's 1980 paper. The winter dates are approximate: about 1974 to 1980 and from about 1987. Move Era one stop at a time and read both notes before you move again. Comparison worth running: 1980 versus 2012. Expert systems fit no parameters and stalled on maintenance; AlexNet fit millions and stalled on needing labeled data for each task. Every stop has a stall. The timeline is not a claim that the last stop solved the field. Expert systems are AI without being machine learning: the knowledge was written, not fitted. 2022 names post-training on a next-token model. Fluency is still not a truth check. In this lab: eleven authored stops. Dates are landmarks, not a complete history, and the card shows two threads, symbolic AI and neural nets, not every approach. Nothing on the card trains a model from that year. In general: a method can stall for funding, data, compute, or a mathematical limit, and the winters were funding downturns as much as technical ones. The next architecture does not erase the earlier failure mode.

documents.body: Where the training target comes from Eight authored scenarios are sorted under the signal that trains the model: human labels (supervised), structure in raw data (unsupervised), labels made from the data itself (self-supervised), or a reward after acting (reinforcement). Each placement is checked at once and corrected with a reason. A separate readout names the output type, classification or regression, because the signal and the output type are different questions. A kicker `N of 8 sorted under the signal that trains them` and a badge unplaced, correct, or corrected for the selected scenario. Four tiles, one per signal, each naming where the answer comes from. The signal names are text, so no meaning rests on colour. Learning scenarios, a listbox of eight buttons. Each row shows a short name, a one-sentence description, and whether it is unplaced, placed, or corrected. Learning signal, four segments, and a Place button that names the selected scenario. State stores `scenario`, `signal`, and `signalPlacements` as strings like `text:self`. Placing a scenario overwrites its earlier guess, and anything malformed is dropped when the state is loaded. Each scenario has one authored best signal and one authored output type. House prices and spam emails are supervised; customer records and sensor readings are unsupervised; raw sentences and blanked-out photos are self-supervised; the win-or-loss game and the charger robot are reinforcement. Output type is read off the answer the model gives: a category is classification, a number is regression, a grouping or score with no predicted answer is no target, and a choice of move is an action. Nothing is trained, and the card does not classify a real system. In general: real projects blend signals. Semi-supervised learning mixes a few labeled examples with many unlabeled ones, and a chat assistant is pretrained self-supervised, tuned on human-written answers, then trained on human-preference rewards.

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: The dominant arithmetic in a dense layer: each output is a dot product of one input row with one weight column, so B rows through a d-by-d layer cost 2·B·d² operations.
documents.title: Matrix multiply

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: One floating-point operation; a multiply-add counts as two. A FLOP count measures arithmetic work and ignores the memory traffic that often decides wall time.
documents.title: FLOP

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: How many operations a chip can finish per second at best, its peak. The lab's illustrative device peaks at 20, 300 and 600 trillion per second for fp32, fp16 and int8.
documents.title: Throughput

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: How many bytes per second can move between the GPU's main memory and its compute units. It caps speed whenever each byte feeds only a few operations.
documents.title: Memory bandwidth

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: Operations performed per byte moved. A batch-1 fp16 matmul does about one FLOP per byte; an fp16 elementwise add does one sixth.
documents.title: Arithmetic intensity

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: A plot of attainable speed against arithmetic intensity, min(peak, bandwidth times intensity). The slanted part is the memory limit and the flat part is the compute limit.
documents.title: Roofline

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: The intensity where the two roofs meet, peak divided by bandwidth. Work below it is memory-bound and work above it is compute-bound.
documents.title: Ridge point

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: Limited by bytes, not arithmetic. Only more bandwidth, fewer bytes, or more reuse per byte shortens the time; extra peak FLOP/s changes nothing.
documents.title: Memory-bound

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: Limited by arithmetic: data arrive faster than the multiply units can use them, so only more peak throughput or fewer operations help.
documents.title: Compute-bound

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: The rows processed together against the same weights, such as examples in a training step or tokens in a prompt. Each weight fetched from memory is reused once per row.
documents.title: Batch

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: Doing many independent pieces of work at once. Every output of a matmul is an independent dot product, the shape a GPU's thousands of lanes need; a long serial dependency is not.
documents.title: Parallelism

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: A GPU program that runs one operation, such as a matmul or an add, over a large grid of threads. Each launch costs a few microseconds, which this lab ignores.
documents.title: Kernel

documents.subtitle: Glossary · Why GPUs
documents.body: The number format and its bytes per value: fp32 is 4, fp16 is 2, int8 is 1. Fewer bytes cut traffic, and matrix units run narrower formats at higher peak rates, at some cost in accuracy.

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Why GPUs · question 1
documents.body: Parallel outputs reads 4,096 dots of 4096 at Batch rows 1. What makes this the kind of work a GPU's thousands of lanes suit? The chip works out which weights matter for the task, so it multiplies only the useful ones and skips the rest The dot products must run one after another, and a GPU runs that single sequence far faster Dot products need almost no data, so thousands of lanes never have to wait on memory Each output is its own dot product that needs no other output's result, so lanes run side by side Each of the B·d outputs of Y = X·W is an independent dot product: regular work with no dependencies, which is the shape thousands of arithmetic lanes need. The chip does not know which weights matter or what the task is; the data and the loss carry the meaning and the GPU multiplies. Parallel work is necessary for speed but not sufficient, because the lanes still need their numbers delivered.
documents.title: Parallel outputs reads 4,096 dots of 4096 at Batch rows 1. What makes this the kind of work a GPU's thousands of lanes suit?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Why GPUs · question 2
documents.body: At Batch rows 1 the lab's fp16 matmul reaches under 1% of peak arithmetic. Which change raises the useful work done per second? A chip with twice the peak FLOP/s and the same memory bandwidth, so the arithmetic finishes in half the time Reusing each fetched weight for more rows, or storing the weights in fewer bytes Nothing: a GPU always runs a matrix multiply at its peak rate, whatever the batch size The operation is memory-bound: each weight byte crosses the bus to feed about one FLOP. More rows per fetch raise intensity (about 2·B / bytes) and fewer bytes cut traffic; both move the dot up the slanted roof. Extra peak only raises the flat roof the dot never reaches.
documents.title: At Batch rows 1 the lab's fp16 matmul reaches under 1% of peak arithmetic. Which change raises the useful work done per second?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Why GPUs · question 3
documents.body: At Batch rows 1024 the fp16 matmul reads compute-bound. You drag Memory bandwidth down to 100 GB/s. What does Bound read now, and why? Still compute: bandwidth only matters at Batch rows 1, where each weight is used once Memory, because the 1024 rows of data no longer fit in the slower memory at this bandwidth Memory: the ridge moves right past the dot, so the work now sits on the slanted bandwidth roof Still compute: the operation's arithmetic is unchanged, so the same limit still applies The ridge is peak divided by bandwidth, so cutting bandwidth pushes it to higher intensity. The matmul's intensity did not change, but it now falls left of the ridge, where bytes rather than arithmetic set the time. Bandwidth is a rate, not a capacity, so the rows do not stop fitting; they simply arrive more slowly than the multipliers could use them.
documents.title: At Batch rows 1024 the fp16 matmul reads compute-bound. You drag Memory bandwidth down to 100 GB/s. What does Bound read now, and why?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Why GPUs · question 4
documents.body: Switch Operation to Elementwise add and raise Batch rows to 4096. Bound stays memory at every batch. Why do extra rows not help here, as they do for the matmul? An add has fewer total operations than a matmul, so it is always too small to reach the ridge Elementwise adds run on a different unit that has no peak arithmetic rate, so no ridge can be measured against it Each value is read, added once, and written, so extra rows bring bytes in proportion and nothing is reused A matmul reads each weight once and uses it for every row, so operations grow with the batch much faster than bytes. An elementwise add does one operation per three memory touches at any batch, so its intensity stays at 1 / (3·bytes), about 0.167 FLOP/B at fp16, far left of the ridge. Real frameworks fuse such operations into the matmul before them to skip the traffic.
documents.title: Switch Operation to Elementwise add and raise Batch rows to 4096. Bound stays memory at every batch. Why do extra rows not help here, as they do for the matmul?

documents.subtitle: Checkpoint · Why GPUs · question 5
documents.body: The Roofline gives the dot's Attainable speed. How should you read that number against a real GPU running a real kernel? As a ceiling: real kernels land at or below it, because the lab assumes perfect overlap of work and traffic As the measured speed of a real kernel, because the lab times it on a real chip and reports the result As a floor: real GPUs can only be faster, because caches and tiling add speed the lab leaves out As exact whenever Bound reads compute, because the memory system stops mattering there Every readout is closed-form arithmetic on shapes: the peaks are round illustrative numbers, arithmetic and traffic overlap perfectly, each operand moves exactly once, and launch costs, caches, and tile shapes are ignored. The roofline is therefore the best any kernel could do on that device. Measured kernels land below it, even compute-bound ones.
documents.title: The Roofline gives the dot's Attainable speed. How should you read that number against a real GPU running a real kernel?

documents.subtitle: Plain · Why GPUs
documents.body: When you ask a chatbot a question, its reply comes out of a huge amount of arithmetic, mostly multiplying pairs of numbers and adding up the results. That arithmetic usually runs on a kind of computer chip called a GPU, short for graphics processing unit. This module asks why that chip suits neural networks so well, and what decides how fast it can go once the work is running on it. The answer has a twist, because a GPU has two separate speeds. One is how fast it can do arithmetic, and the other is how fast numbers can be delivered to it from its memory. A job can only go as fast as the slower of the two allows. That means a chip that calculates very quickly can still spend most of its time waiting for numbers to arrive. Where you have met it Chatbots writing replies: a chatbot writes its answer one small piece at a time, and each piece is a word or part of a word called a token. Writing one token at a time is usually held back by memory rather than by arithmetic. That is why grouping many people’s requests together, or storing the model’s numbers in smaller formats, lets the same chip turn out more tokens each second. Training a model: the network is fed big groups of examples at once, which keeps the arithmetic units busy. So for training, counting the arithmetic steps gives a fair estimate of how long the job will take, an idea the Scaling laws module builds on. Why it matters If you only count the arithmetic a job needs, you can badly misjudge how long it will take. When a job is stuck waiting on memory, a chip with twice the arithmetic power finishes no sooner. The only things that help are faster memory, storing each number in less space, or using each number more times once it has arrived. Knowing which limit you are up against tells you what is worth adding and what is worth saving. What you will be able to explain By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain these three things in your own words: Why a GPU speeds up a neural network, based on the shape of the work, without claiming that the chip understands what the network is doing. Why “how fast the chip can calculate” and “how fast numbers reach it from memory” are two different limits, each with its own clock. How to predict whether a job is held back by memory or by arithmetic, by comparing how much arithmetic it does with how much data it has to move. What the lab shows The lab follows one layer of a neural network on a made-up GPU whose speeds are round numbers of about the right size. Nothing runs on a real chip and nothing is measured. Instead, every number the lab shows, called a readout, is worked out with arithmetic from the size of the layer and the number of rows. So the lab always shows the best possible case, which a real chip can only come close to. The layer is fed rows of numbers. Each row is one input’s list of numbers, such as one token of a chatbot prompt, and you can send many rows through together. The lab is split into three cards, and each one shows a different part of the story: Workload knobs lets you choose the job, the number format, how many rows go through at once, the size of the layer, and the memory speed. Roofline places your job as a dot on a graph and tells you which of the two limits it is hitting. Where the time goes compares the time the arithmetic needs with the time the memory needs, and shows what would change if you doubled either speed. The main experiment is to push more rows of data through the layer at once. You will watch the same job switch from waiting on memory to being limited by arithmetic, and then switch back when you slow the memory down.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Plain · Why GPUs
documents.body: A layer is a huge pile of multiply-and-add In Stacking neurons you met layers of neurons, where each neuron takes a list of input numbers, multiplies each one by its own weight, and adds up the results. Multiplying two lists pair by pair and adding up the answers is called a dot product. The lab sometimes shortens it to “dot”, which is not the same thing as the dot that marks your job on the graph. As a tiny example, with inputs 2, 3 and 1 and weights 4, 0.5 and 10, the dot product is 2×4 + 3×0.5 + 1×10 = 8 + 1.5 + 10 = 19.5. The chip keeps a running total that starts at zero, so each pair costs one multiply and one add. That makes 6 operations for this tiny dot product. The layer in this lab is much bigger, with a starting Layer width of d = 4096. That means each input row holds 4096 numbers and the layer produces 4096 outputs, one for each neuron. In real use, a row can be one training example, or one token of a prompt, which is the text you type into a chatbot. Each neuron has a weight for every input, so you can stand each neuron’s weights up as a column and set all the columns side by side. That gives a square grid with 4096 weights along each side, about 16.8 million in all. A grid of numbers like this is called a matrix, and working out every output of the layer this way is called a matrix multiply. In the lab it is labelled *Matmul X·W*, with matmul short for matrix multiply. X stands for the rows of input numbers, and W stands for the grid of weights. Counting the work Each single multiply or add is one operation, called a FLOP, short for floating-point operation. Floating point is the usual way a computer stores numbers that can have a decimal point, such as 0.5 or 19.5. The Work versus traffic row on the Workload knobs card shows the count as ops = 2·B·d², where ops is short for operations and the raised dot · means times. Here d is the layer width, and B is the number of input rows that go through together using the same weights. A group of rows like this is called a batch, and the Batch rows slider sets its size. Each row needs d dot products, each dot product has d pairs, and each pair costs two operations, which gives 2 × d × d operations for every row. A batch of B rows needs B times as much, which is where the formula comes from. With one row at the starting width, that works out as 2 × 1 × 4096 × 4096 = 33,554,432. That is about 33.6 million operations, which the lab shows as 33.6 MFLOP, with M standing for million. Why a GPU suits this work None of the 4096 dot products for a row needs another one’s answer before it can start, so all of them could be worked on at the same moment. Doing many independent pieces of work at once is called parallelism, and a matrix multiply is full of it. Picture a teacher with a worksheet of 30 separate sums and a class of 30 students. Because no sum depends on another, she can hand one to each student, and the whole sheet gets done in about the time it takes to do one sum. That only works if every student already has their sum in hand, though. Getting the sums to the students is the other half of the story. A GPU is built for exactly that kind of job, with thousands of small arithmetic units, often called lanes, that can all multiply and add at the same time. A layer’s thousands of independent dot products give those lanes plenty to do at once. The chip does not understand any of this, though: it runs the same multiply-and-add whether the numbers came from a sentence or a photo. It never checks what the numbers stand for or which weights matter. The meaning lives in the data and in the goal the network was trained toward, while the GPU does the multiplying. Two speeds, not one Before a lane can multiply a number, that number has to travel from the GPU’s main memory, where the weights are stored, to the lane. So the chip has two separate speeds, and each one is a limit of its own. Throughput is how many operations the chip can finish each second at its very best, called its peak. In its starting number format, called fp16, the lab’s made-up chip peaks at 300 TFLOP/s, which means 300 trillion FLOP every second, since T stands for trillion. Memory bandwidth is how many bytes per second can move from main memory to the lanes, where a byte is the basic unit of computer memory. In this lab, each number takes 1, 2 or 4 bytes depending on its format, with fp16 using 2. The lab starts at 2000 GB/s, where a GB, or gigabyte, is a billion bytes, so that is 2 trillion bytes every second. To picture this, imagine an enormous exam hall where thousands of markers sit at desks ready to mark tests, with one narrow door at the back. Every test and every page of the answer key has to be carried in through that door, and every marked test goes back out the same way. In this picture the markers are the GPU’s lanes, and how quickly things can pass through the door is the memory bandwidth. Each test is one row of input, and the answer key is the grid of weights, which runs to thousands of pages. Once a page of the key is inside the hall, though, it can be used to mark every test in the pile. Now suppose there is only one test, so every page of the key gets carried in to be used once. The markers then spend nearly all their time waiting at the door. With a thousand tests, each page carried in gets used a thousand times, so the marking becomes the slow part, and a wider door would no longer help. The picture stops matching a real GPU in two places. First, the hall has room to keep every page of the key once it is inside. The lab assumes the same, so each number crosses from main memory exactly once. A real GPU has only a small shelf of storage beside its lanes, called a cache. For big grids, some pages have to be carried in more than once, which makes a real chip slower than the lab, never faster. Second, real markers read and judge each answer, while a GPU lane only multiplies and adds numbers, with no idea what any of them mean. Arithmetic intensity: work for each byte Which of the two speeds sets the time depends on how many operations a job does for each byte it moves. That ratio is called arithmetic intensity, and the Intensity readout shows it in FLOP/B, meaning FLOP per byte. To find it you also need the traffic, meaning the number of bytes that have to move. The Work versus traffic row counts them as bytes = (d² + 2·B·d)·2 at fp16, where each number takes 2 bytes. The d² part, d squared, is the weights, which are read once, and the 2·B·d part is the input rows read in plus the output rows written back. The 2·B·d part counts B rows of d numbers coming in and B rows of d results going out. With one row, that is 2 × 1 × 4096 = 8,192 numbers, while the weights are 4096 × 4096 = 16,777,216 numbers. So the traffic is (16,777,216 + 8,192) × 2, or about 33.6 million bytes, which the lab writes as 33.6 MB, where MB means a million bytes. Notice that at one row the weights make up almost all of the traffic. The work and the traffic both come to about 33.6 million, so Intensity starts at 1.000 FLOP/B, which is about one operation for every byte moved. It is really a hair under one, because the rows add a few bytes of their own. The ridge point: where the two limits meet The lab’s chip can do 300 trillion operations each second, but in that same second it can only receive 2 trillion bytes. Dividing one by the other shows that in the time it takes one byte to arrive, the chip could do 150 operations. That break-even value is called the ridge point, which is the chip’s peak divided by its memory bandwidth, and the Ridge readout shows it as 150 FLOP/B. So the ridge moves when you change the memory speed. It also moves when you change the number format, because the chip’s peak is different for each format, as you will see in the lab. It does not move when you change the number of rows. If a job’s intensity is below the ridge, the lanes finish their work before the next bytes arrive and sit waiting, so the job is memory-bound. If a job’s intensity is above the ridge, bytes arrive faster than the lanes can use them and arithmetic sets the pace, so the job is compute-bound. At one row, the job does about one operation per byte, which is far below the ridge, so the Bound readout says memory. The roofline graph The Roofline card draws all of this as one graph, called a roofline because of the shape of its top line. The line along the bottom measures arithmetic intensity, and the line up the side measures the best speed the job can reach. Speed here means useful operations finished each second, not how soon one job ends. Both axes say “log scale”, which here means each grid line is ten times the one before it, so tiny and huge values fit in one picture. The bent line across the graph is the roof, the best speed possible at each intensity. Its slanted left part is the memory limit, where doubling the intensity doubles the speed. Its flat right part is the chip’s peak, which no job can go above. The two parts meet at the ridge, marked with a dashed line, and the area to its left is shaded as the memory-bound zone. The legend gives the roof as min(peak, bandwidth × intensity), where “min” means the smaller of the two. At one row, bandwidth times intensity is 2 trillion bytes per second times about one FLOP per byte, which gives 2 TFLOP/s. That is far below the peak, so the smaller value wins and the Attainable readout shows 2.00 TFLOP/s. That is under 1% of what the chip could do, and the top of the Where the time goes card puts it at 0.67% of peak arithmetic in use.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Plain · Why GPUs
documents.body: A neural network needs an enormous amount of the same simple arithmetic. Pushing 1024 rows through this one layer takes about 34.4 billion operations, which the lab shows as 34.4 GFLOP, with G standing for billion. A real model stacks many layers like this one, so the total grows very quickly. Neural networks became practical at a large scale on GPUs because that arithmetic is regular and parallel. It is the same multiply-and-add, repeated across thousands of outputs that never wait on each other. Not every kind of work has that shape, so picture the worksheet again, but now each sum needs the answer to the one before it. The teacher can only hand out one sum at a time, so the rest of the class sits waiting, however many students there are. A recurrent network, a type of network that works through its input one step at a time, has this chain shape. It must finish each step before starting the next, which leaves a GPU’s thousands of lanes with less to do at once, as The architecture zoo will show. Lots of parallel work is needed for speed, but it is not enough on its own. At one row, the Parallel outputs readout still shows 4,096 dots of 4096, which means 4,096 separate dot products, each 4096 pairs long. That is plenty to share across thousands of lanes, yet only 0.67% of the arithmetic gets used, because each byte carried in from memory feeds only about one operation. So feeding the lanes matters as much as having them, and the roofline is built to show exactly that. The same question comes back in later labs: how many bytes have to move for each piece of useful arithmetic? You will ask it about the notes a chatbot keeps on earlier words, about smaller number formats, and about serving many users at once.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Plain · Why GPUs
documents.body: The lab starts with Operation on *Matmul X·W*, Batch rows at 1 row, Layer width at d = 4096, Precision on fp16, and Memory bandwidth at 2000 GB/s. The four parts below follow the lab’s own four steps, in the same order, starting from those settings. Grow the batch Before you move anything, read the Where the time goes card, whose two bars work like two clocks. Arithmetic at peak shows the arithmetic needs about 111.8 ns, while Memory traffic shows the memory needs 16.8 µs. A nanosecond (ns) is a billionth of a second and a microsecond (µs) is a millionth. So 16.8 µs is 16,800 ns, and the memory takes about 150 times longer than the arithmetic. The lab lets both happen at the same time, so the job ends when the slower clock finishes. That real running time is called the wall-clock, and here memory sets it. The table under the bars, headed Change one thing, re-runs the arithmetic after a single change. The *2× peak arithmetic* row reads no change, while the *2× memory bandwidth* row reads 2.00× faster, because only the slower clock matters. Try this: drag Batch rows up one step at a time, from 1 row to 1024 rows. Each step doubles the rows. Hollow circles mark the same matmul at 1, 4, 16, 64, 256, 1024 and 4096 rows. The dot lands on or between them as it climbs the slanted roof first and then runs along the flat one. Keep an eye on the wall-clock as you go. It barely moves, from 16.8 µs at 1 row to 17.8 µs at 128 rows. The chip does 128 times the work in almost the same time, because it waits for the same weights either way. That is why Attainable climbs, and why grouping rows lets a chip turn out more tokens each second. At 128 rows, Bound still reads memory, and at 256 rows it flips to compute. The Rows to reach ridge readout says about 162, the exact break-even, which the slider jumps past because it moves in doublings. Look at the Change one thing table on either side of the flip. At 128 rows, *2× memory bandwidth* reads only 1.25× faster. At 256 rows, the arithmetic takes 28.6 µs and the memory takes 18.9 µs. Doubling peak arithmetic cuts the arithmetic to 14.3 µs, but then memory is the slower clock at 18.9 µs, so the table shows only 1.52× faster. Near the ridge the two clocks are close, so speeding up one soon hands the job to the other. At 1024 rows, Intensity reads 683 FLOP/B, which is well past the ridge. The wall-clock is now set by the arithmetic, at 115 µs, and the table has flipped. Doubling peak arithmetic now makes the job 2.00× faster, while doubling memory bandwidth makes no change. Rows help so much because every row uses the same weights, so each weight fetched once from memory gets reused for every row. The note under the formula row turns this into a shortcut. When the batch is much smaller than the layer width, almost all the traffic is the weights, about d² numbers. The work is 2·B·d², so dividing work by numbers moved leaves about 2·B operations for each number fetched. Dividing that by the bytes in each number gives the intensity. The note writes this as intensity ≈ 2·B / bytes when B ≪ d. Here “bytes” means bytes per number, ≈ means “about equal to”, and ≪ means “much smaller than”. With 64 rows at 2 bytes per number, that gives 2 × 64 / 2 = 64. The lab shows 62.1 FLOP/B, a little lower, because the rows’ own numbers add some traffic too. Change precision Set Batch rows back to 1, then switch Precision from fp16 to fp32 and then to int8. Precision is the format each number is stored in, and the number in each name is how many bits it uses. The fp stands for floating point, and int stands for integer, which means a whole number. A bit is a single 0 or 1, and 8 bits make one byte. fp32 uses 4 bytes per number, so Intensity drops to 0.500 FLOP/B and Memory traffic grows to 33.6 µs. fp16 uses 2 bytes per number, giving 1.000 FLOP/B and 16.8 µs. int8 uses 1 byte per number and stores whole numbers only, so the lab counts OP instead of FLOP, giving 2.00 OP/B and 8.39 µs. Halving the bytes per number halves the memory time, because the same job now carries half as much through the door. The chip’s peak changes as well, and the note on the card lists it for each format. In fp32 the chip uses its ordinary lanes and peaks at only 20 TFLOP/s. In fp16 and int8 it uses special units built for matrix multiplies, which reach 300 TFLOP/s and 600 TOP/s. Because fp32’s peak is so low, its Ridge drops to only 10 FLOP/B. Smaller formats are not free, though, because they store each number less exactly and can make a model less accurate, a cost this lab does not show. Starve the bandwidth Switch Precision back to fp16, set Batch rows to 1024, then drag Memory bandwidth down to 100 GB/s. The ridge is peak divided by bandwidth, so a slower memory pushes it to the right, from 150 to 3000 FLOP/B. The dot’s intensity stays at 683, so the ridge slides right past it, and Bound flips back to memory. Now Memory traffic takes 503 µs, which is more than four times as long as the arithmetic. The *2× memory bandwidth* row reads 2.00× faster again, while doubling peak arithmetic makes no change. In the exam-hall picture, this is like narrowing the door: the same pages still have to come in, but each one takes longer. Rows to reach ridge now reads never at this d, because every extra row brings its own numbers in and sends its results out. Each extra row adds 2 × 4096 × 4096 operations of work. It also brings in 4096 numbers and sends out 4096 results, which is 16,384 bytes at fp16. That works out to 2048 operations per byte for each new row. So however many rows you add, intensity creeps toward 2048 and never reaches the new ridge of 3000. Try an elementwise op Switch Operation to *Elementwise add* and move Batch rows to 4096. An elementwise add takes two grids of the same size and adds them spot by spot: it reads two numbers, adds them once, and writes one result. That is one operation for three numbers moved, or six bytes at fp16, so Intensity reads 0.167 FLOP/B. Nothing gets reused, so extra rows bring extra bytes in step with the extra work. That keeps Bound on memory at every batch, and Rows to reach ridge reads never. On the graph, a diamond marks the matmul of the same shape for comparison, far to the right of the add. The note at the bottom of the Where the time goes card adds a trick real software uses. It often does an add like this while the matmul’s results are still beside the lanes. That saves writing them out to memory and reading them straight back in, a round trip through the door. You can also try Layer width, which sets d anywhere from 512 to 16384. A narrow layer needs more rows to reach the ridge, about 363 at d = 512, because each row’s own numbers make up a bigger share of the traffic.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Plain · Why GPUs
documents.body: Reuse moves the dot: going from 1 row to 1024 rows multiplies the operations by 1024. The bytes moved grow only 1.5 times, because the weights are fetched once whatever the batch. The table tells you which limit you hit: when Bound reads memory, *2× peak arithmetic* reads no change while *2× memory bandwidth* makes the job faster. Once Bound reads compute, the two rows trade places. Close to the ridge, on either side, the helpful row shows less than a full 2×, such as 1.25× at 128 rows and 1.52× at 256 rows. That is because doubling one speed soon makes the other clock the slower one. Parallel work is not enough: at 1 row, Parallel outputs still shows 4,096 dots of 4096, yet only 0.67% of peak arithmetic is in use. A bigger percentage is not always faster: at 1 row, fp32 shows 5.00% of peak in use, more than fp16 does, yet it takes twice as long. That is because the percentage is measured against fp32’s much lower peak. fp32 reaches its ridge early: fp32 runs on ordinary lanes with a low peak, so its ridge sits at only 10 FLOP/B. That is why Rows to reach ridge reads about 21 in fp32. Slower memory moves the ridge: at 100 GB/s the ridge jumps to 3000 FLOP/B, and the 1024-row matmul turns memory-bound again. The add never catches up: it stays at 0.167 FLOP/B in fp16 at every batch, so it is always memory-bound. The two roofs behave differently: on the slanted roof, doubling the intensity doubles the speed, while on the flat roof it changes nothing.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Plain · Why GPUs
documents.body: What this lab fakes or simplifies Nothing runs on a GPU: every readout is arithmetic worked out from the sizes of the grids, and nothing is measured. A GPU carries out each operation, such as a matmul or an add, by starting a small program called a kernel, and the lab never starts one. The chip is made up: its peaks are round numbers close to those of a real GPU called the A100, but they are not that chip’s exact figures. Arithmetic and traffic overlap perfectly: the lab assumes that carrying numbers and multiplying them happen at the same time without getting in each other’s way. So the time is always the slower of the two clocks, and every dot sits exactly on the roof. Each number moves exactly once: the lab assumes the chip keeps every number it has fetched for as long as it needs it. Real chips get close to this by cutting big grids into smaller tiles that fit in the cache beside the lanes, but they often have to fetch some numbers again. There is also no start-up cost for each kernel, which takes a few microseconds on a real GPU. Both of these make a real chip slower than the lab, never faster. Any shape can reach the peak: in the lab even a small grid can keep every lane busy, but a real small matrix cannot fill a whole GPU. int8 is simplified: the lab treats int8 as 1 byte going in and 1 byte coming out. A real int8 matmul keeps its running totals in a bigger whole-number format called int32, which takes 4 bytes. It needs the bigger format because adding up thousands of products quickly gives totals far too big to fit in 1 byte. When the totals are done, the chip has to scale them back down to a smaller format, extra steps the lab does not count. Accuracy is not shown: smaller formats cost some accuracy, and none of the readouts show it. Where the real mechanism falls short Real programs land below the roof: measured kernels run slower than the ideal line, often far slower for small matrices. Read Attainable as a ceiling, the best any program could do on this chip, rather than as a stopwatch. Real chips have more roofs: the cache beside the lanes has its own speed limit, which adds another roof that this lab does not draw. A real layer also runs several other kinds of step besides the matmul, each with its own kernel and its own start-up cost. Training moves more than weights: it also moves each layer’s in-between results, the corrections worked out for every weight, and the extra records the training method keeps. Large models are also split across many GPUs, which then have to send numbers to each other. Writing one token at a time sits at the far left of the graph: each new token runs every weight grid with only one row per conversation. That is why serving a chatbot is usually memory-bound, and why grouping users together and storing weights in smaller formats both raise the tokens produced each second. A common mix-up: you might expect a GPU with more arithmetic power to run any model faster. Picture two friends comparing chips for running a chatbot, where one chip has twice the peak arithmetic and the other has twice the memory bandwidth. For writing one token at a time, the lab’s arithmetic says the second chip wins, because the job is waiting on memory and extra lanes would only wait too. A memory-bound job gets faster only with more bandwidth, fewer bytes per number, or more reuse of each byte.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Plain · Why GPUs
documents.body: Inference & KV cache looks closely at the one-row corner of this graph. Each new token has to re-read all the weights, plus a growing store of notes about earlier tokens called the KV cache. Quantization stores each weight in fewer bytes, which moves memory-bound work up the slanted roof. Deployment & serving groups many users together, so each weight carried in from memory feeds more rows. Scaling laws measures the cost of training by counting FLOPs, which is fair only because large-batch training sits near the flat roof, where arithmetic sets the time. FlashAttention, a method published in 2022, reorganized a step inside many chatbot models called attention. It sped attention up by moving fewer bytes to and from memory rather than by cutting the arithmetic, which makes it a roofline argument put to work. The architecture zoo comes next, showing other ways to wire a network that differ in how much of this parallel shape they keep. A recurrent network, for example, has to finish each step before it can start the next.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Standard · Why GPUs
documents.body: This module is about why neural networks run on GPUs, and what sets their speed once they do. For one layer operation on a given chip, it asks whether the time is set by arithmetic or by moving bytes from memory. It builds on Stacking neurons: one dense layer, applied to a batch of input rows, is a matrix multiply whose work and memory traffic follow from its shapes. Two rates bound that time. A roofline plots attainable speed against arithmetic intensity, operations per byte moved: a slanted roof set by memory bandwidth, the rate at which bytes reach the arithmetic units, meets a flat roof set by throughput, the chip's peak arithmetic rate. That meeting point, the ridge point, splits memory-bound work, limited by bytes, from compute-bound work, limited by arithmetic. Where it shows up Training. A large training batch reuses each fetched weight across many rows, which puts its big matmuls on the compute-bound side of the ridge. Counting training compute in floating-point operations (FLOPs), as Scaling laws do, is fair for that reason. Serving. Text generation emits one token per step, so each weight matrix sees one row per sequence and serving is usually memory-bound. Batching users together and quantizing weights to fewer bytes raise the tokens served per second. Kernel design. A kernel is a GPU program for one operation. FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) made attention faster without doing fewer FLOPs, by moving fewer bytes to and from the GPU's main memory. Why it matters A FLOP count alone does not predict the time. For memory-bound work, twice the peak arithmetic finishes no sooner; only more bandwidth, fewer bytes moved, or more reuse of each fetched byte helps. Knowing which limit binds says which resource to add or save. Parallel work is necessary but not sufficient. At the lab's defaults, 1 row through a 4096-wide layer at fp16 and 2000 GB/s, the matmul offers 4,096 independent dot products yet uses 0.67% of peak, because each weight byte feeds about one operation. A serial chain, such as a recurrent network in which each step waits for the one before, gives a GPU's thousands of arithmetic lanes less to run at once. What you will be able to explain Why a GPU speeds up a neural net, in terms of the shape of its work, without claiming that the chip understands the task. Arithmetic throughput and memory bandwidth as two separate limits, each setting its own time: operations ÷ peak, and bytes ÷ bandwidth. Whether an operation is memory-bound or compute-bound, predicted from its arithmetic intensity against the ridge point. What the lab shows Nothing in the lab runs a kernel, times one, or trains a weight; every readout is closed-form arithmetic on tensor shapes. Peak rates are fixed round numbers of the same order as an A100-class GPU, and arithmetic and traffic are assumed to overlap perfectly, so every point sits on the roof that measured kernels land below. Workload knobs sets Operation (*Matmul X·W* or *Elementwise add*), Precision, Batch rows, Layer width and Memory bandwidth. Roofline places the operation as a dot and reads Intensity, Ridge, Attainable and Bound. Where the time goes compares the two clocks, arithmetic time (ops ÷ peak) and memory time (bytes ÷ bandwidth), takes the larger as the wall-clock, and re-runs the arithmetic after one change, such as *2× peak arithmetic* or *2× memory bandwidth*. The key experiment keeps the defaults of width 4096 and 2000 GB/s and moves Batch rows from 1 to 1024 on the fp16 matmul. Each fetched weight feeds more rows, so the dot crosses the ridge at about 162 rows and Bound flips from memory to compute. Dropping Memory bandwidth to 100 GB/s, or switching to *Elementwise add*, puts the work back left of the ridge.
documents.title: The big picture

documents.subtitle: Standard · Why GPUs
documents.body: A dense layer is a matrix multiply. Push a batch of B rows through a d-wide layer, Y = X·W, and you do 2·B·d² operations. Each of the B·d outputs is an independent dot product, which is exactly the shape a GPU's thousands of arithmetic lanes are built for. Speed has two separate limits. Throughput is how fast the chip can do arithmetic. Memory bandwidth is how fast bytes reach that arithmetic. Arithmetic intensity, operations per byte moved, says which one binds. The roofline The fastest an operation can run is min(peak, bandwidth × intensity). The ridge point, peak / bandwidth, separates the two regimes. Below it an operation is memory-bound; above it, compute-bound. On the lab's illustrative device at fp16 and 2000 GB/s the ridge is 150 FLOP/B. The device uses round numbers of the same order as an A100-class GPU. Why batch is the lever A matmul reads the d×d weights once, however many rows use them. Its bytes are (d² + 2·B·d)·bytes, so while B is much smaller than d, intensity is about 2·B / bytes. Each extra row reuses weights that were already fetched. An elementwise add has no such reuse. It performs one operation per three memory touches, so its intensity is 1 / (3·bytes) at every batch.
documents.title: What it is

documents.subtitle: Standard · Why GPUs
documents.body: Neural nets became practical at scale on GPUs because their work is regular, parallel arithmetic, not because the chip understands the task. The data and the loss carry the meaning; the GPU multiplies. The same two clocks explain later labs. The KV cache, quantization, and serving are all questions about bytes moved per token, asked against this roofline.
documents.title: Why it’s here

documents.subtitle: Standard · Why GPUs
documents.body: Start with Operation on Matmul X·W, Batch rows at 1, Layer width 4096, fp16, and 2000 GB/s. Intensity reads 1.00 FLOP/B, Bound reads memory, and the kicker shows 0.67% of peak in use. Move Batch rows to 1024. Intensity climbs to 683 FLOP/B, the dot crosses the ridge (Rows to reach ridge reads about 162), and the wall-clock is the 115 µs arithmetic time. Then compare Precision at 1 row, drop Memory bandwidth to 100 GB/s at 1024 rows, and finally switch Operation to Elementwise add.
documents.title: How to play with it

documents.subtitle: Standard · Why GPUs
documents.body: From 1 to 1024 rows, operations grow 1024× while bytes grow only 1.5×. That reuse is what moves the dot. When Bound is memory, the 2× peak arithmetic row reads no change and the 2× memory bandwidth row reads 2.00× faster. At 1 row there are still 4,096 independent dot products. Parallel work is necessary for speed, not sufficient. fp32's ridge is only 10 FLOP/B, because its peak runs on ordinary lanes rather than matrix units. At 100 GB/s the ridge moves to 3000 FLOP/B, so the 1024-row matmul turns memory-bound again. The add stays at 0.167 FLOP/B in fp16 and memory-bound at 4096 rows.
documents.title: What to notice

documents.subtitle: Standard · Why GPUs
documents.body: In this lab. Every readout is closed-form arithmetic on shapes. No kernel runs on a GPU. Peaks are round illustrative numbers, arithmetic and traffic overlap perfectly, each operand moves exactly once, and launch costs, caches, and tile shapes are ignored. int8 is treated as 1 byte in and out, although real int8 matmuls accumulate in int32. In the real mechanism. Measured kernels land below the roof, often far below for small matrices. Training also moves activations, gradients, and optimizer state, and large models add communication between GPUs. Serving differs from training. Generating one token at a time runs every weight matrix at one row per sequence, the far-left corner of this plot. That is why serving is usually memory-bound, and why batching users and quantizing weights raise throughput.
documents.title: Where it breaks

documents.subtitle: Standard · Why GPUs
documents.body: Inference & KV cache is the batch-1 corner of this roofline: every generated token re-reads the weights and the cache. Quantization cuts bytes per weight, which moves memory-bound work up the slanted roof. Deployment & serving batches many users so each weight fetch feeds more rows. Scaling laws count training compute in FLOPs, which is only fair because large-batch training sits near the flat roof. FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) sped up attention by reorganizing it to cut memory traffic, not FLOPs: a roofline argument. The Architecture zoo comes next. Its wirings differ in how much of this parallel shape they keep. A recurrent network, for example, must finish step t before step t + 1.
documents.title: Going deeper

documents.subtitle: Workload knobs · Why GPUs
documents.body: Shape, number format, and memory speed One layer operation is counted from its shapes: how many arithmetic operations it needs and how many bytes must cross the memory bus. Operation, Batch rows and Layer width set the shapes, Precision sets bytes per value and the peak rate, and Memory bandwidth sets how fast bytes arrive. A kicker with the tensor shapes, the precision, and the bandwidth. Operation (Matmul X·W or Elementwise add), Precision (fp32, fp16, int8: 4, 2 and 1 bytes per value), Batch rows from 1 to 4096 in doublings, Layer width d from 512 to 16384 in doublings, and Memory bandwidth from 100 to 5000 GB/s. A formula row with the operation and byte counts at the current values, and a note naming the illustrative device. Matmul Y = X·W with X of B×d and W of d×d: ops = 2·B·d², bytes = (d² + 2·B·d) × bytes per value, which reads W and X once and writes Y once. Elementwise add Y = X + R: ops = B·d, bytes = 3·B·d × bytes per value (two reads, one write). Peaks are round illustrative numbers of the same order as an A100-class GPU: fp32 20 TFLOP/s on ordinary lanes, fp16 300 TFLOP/s and int8 600 TOP/s on matrix units. The A100 datasheet lists 19.5, 312 and 624 (dense). Operation, Precision, Batch rows, Layer width, and Memory bandwidth. Comparison worth running: Batch rows 1 against 1024 at d = 4096 and fp16. Operations grow 1024×, bytes grow only 1.5×. For a matmul the weights dominate the bytes at small batch, so adding rows is nearly free traffic. That reuse is the whole story of intensity. The add has no reuse at all: every value is touched three times for one operation. In this lab: closed-form counts with every operand stored at the chosen precision and moved exactly once. Real int8 matmuls accumulate in int32 and rescale, and real kernels move extra bytes when tiles do not fit on chip. In general: a real layer also has attention, normalization and activation kernels, launch overheads of a few microseconds each, and communication between GPUs. The roofline is a first estimate, not a profiler.
documents.title: Shape, number format, and memory speed

documents.subtitle: Roofline · Why GPUs
documents.body: Attainable speed against arithmetic intensity The roofline says the fastest an operation can run is min(peak, bandwidth × intensity). Left of the ridge point the slanted memory roof is lower; right of it the flat compute roof is lower. The dot is the current operation, placed by its computed intensity. Log–log axes: arithmetic intensity in operations per byte from 0.01 to 10k, and attainable TFLOP/s (TOP/s for int8) from 0.001 to 1000. The roof as one bent line, a dashed ridge line with its value, and a tinted memory-bound zone to its left. A filled dot for the current operation, hollow circles for the same matmul at 1 to 4096 rows (every other one labelled), and a diamond for the other operation at the same shape. Metrics Intensity, Ridge, Attainable, and Bound. Intensity = ops / bytes from the counts on the knobs card. Ridge = peak / bandwidth. Attainable = min(peak, bandwidth × intensity). Bound is memory when bytes / bandwidth exceeds ops / peak. Every point sits on the roof by construction, because the model assumes arithmetic and traffic overlap perfectly. This card has no controls. The knobs above move the dot, the ridge, and both roofs. Comparison worth running: walk Batch rows from 1 to 4096 and watch the dot slide along the hollow circles, then change Precision and see the whole trail shift. On the slanted roof, doubling intensity doubles speed; on the flat roof it does nothing. Lower bandwidth drags the slanted roof down and pushes the ridge right, so work that was compute-bound can become memory-bound. fp32 has a ridge of only 10 FLOP/B here because its peak is low, so even 32 rows are compute-bound in fp32. In this lab: two ideal roofs and nothing else. There is no cache hierarchy, no occupancy or tile-shape effect, and no launch cost, so real kernels land below the roof. In general: measured kernels add more roofs (on-chip cache bandwidth, special-function units) and land below the ideal one, often far below for small or oddly shaped matrices. The roofline tells you which resource to buy or save, not the exact time.
documents.title: Attainable speed against arithmetic intensity

documents.subtitle: Where the time goes · Why GPUs
documents.body: Two clocks, and what would move them Arithmetic time is ops divided by peak; memory time is bytes divided by bandwidth. The roofline wall-clock is the larger of the two. The table re-runs the same arithmetic after one change so you can see which change helps. Two bars, Arithmetic at peak and Memory traffic, with their times and the division that produced them. The one that sets the time is labelled so. A table of wall-clock after doubling peak, doubling bandwidth, or dropping to the next smaller precision, each with its speed-up. Metrics Parallel outputs and Rows to reach ridge, plus a note that changes with the bound. Wall-clock = max(ops / peak, bytes / bandwidth). Utilization in the kicker = (ops / wall-clock) / peak. Rows to reach ridge solves 2·B·d² / ((d² + 2·B·d)·bytes) = ridge for B, which gives B = ridge·bytes·d / (2(d − ridge·bytes)). It reads never when d / bytes is below the ridge. Parallel outputs = B·d, each an independent dot product of length d (or one add). This card has no controls. Use the knobs above. Comparison worth running: at Batch rows 1, compare the 2× peak arithmetic row with the 2× memory bandwidth row. Then repeat at 1024 rows. At Batch rows 1 there are still 4,096 independent dot products, plenty of parallel work, yet utilization is under 1%. Parallelism is necessary but not sufficient. The fp16 → int8 row halves memory time and doubles peak, so it helps in both regimes on this device. In this lab: perfect overlap of arithmetic and traffic, and peak rates that any shape can reach. Small matrices cannot actually fill a GPU, and quantized formats cost accuracy the table does not show. In general: generating text one token at a time runs every weight matrix at a batch of one per sequence, which is why serving is usually memory-bound and why batching many users together and quantizing weights both raise throughput.
documents.title: Two clocks, and what would move them
